title: When Parameter Gradient Flows Close in Representation Space
description:
arXiv:2610.27474v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The represented gradient flow of a parameterized model depends on a mobility that can retain hidden parameter information. We study when one entire represented mobility map works for every autonomous loss from one fixed initialization. For two-factor matrix representations wider than both output dimensions, with individually full-row-rank factors, we classify all admissible joint ranks: closure occurs precisely at effective scalar-balanced minimal joint rank or a two-value signed spectral family at full joint rank. All intermediate ranks are excluded; positive represented flows belong to known square-root families. For general representations with constant ambient representation and gradient-Lie ranks, ordinary closure is equivalent to a local invariant-level metric in the analytic case and specified smooth regimes. An endpoint section forces the initially unrestricted mobility map to admit a locally smooth representative on the represented image. We also separate testing families: linear losses locally admit closure at every submersion, whereas one fixed translated strongly convex quadratic family fails it on a delayed-bracket example. A fixed output readout gives an ordinary squared-loss witness. These supporting results do not characterize quadratic-only closure in general. We retain the unresolved smooth output-rank-two case with Lie rank at least four. A frozen deterministic experiment checks a separate engineered-loss construction; it is distinguished from the squared-loss proof, universal theorems and empirical learning performance.

title: A GitHub Actions Security Gate for Node.js: Block Leaked Keys
description:
A GitHub Actions security gate for Node.js is a single workflow that runs on every pull request. It scans the new commits for leaked API keys, checks new dependencies for known vulnerabilities and confirms the lockfile is honest. If any of those checks finds something real, it blocks the merge. You can build it in an afternoon with free tools, and most of that afternoon goes into tuning, not setup.

You may have found a live Stripe key in a commit from three weeks ago. Or you may have a Dependabot tab full of alerts that nobody has opened since spring. Either way, this walkthrough is for you.

Why do leaked keys and vulnerable packages get past code review?

Code review happens on diffs, and people reviewing a diff read the logic, not the config. A key pasted into a test fixture looks like noise. A risky transitive dependency hardly shows up at all. It sits somewhere in a 2,000-line lockfile change that nobody scrolls through.

AI coding assistants make both problems worse. To get an example working, they hardcode credentials, and they add packages without a second thought. The code runs, the reviewer approves, and the key goes into history.

What does it cost when one slips through?

Deleting a leaked key in a later commit does not remove it. Git history keeps it, and so does every clone and fork. Bots scan public pushes for credential patterns all the time. The only real fix is rotation: you find every service and environment that uses the key, issue a new one and redeploy without breaking production.

A vulnerable dependency costs you differently. You end up doing an emergency upgrade across major versions, under pressure, on code you didn't write.

The hidden cost is a noisy gate. If the check fails on things that don't matter, people stop reading it. They re-run it, or an admin turns on bypass. Then the one real finding goes straight through.

Do you actually need a custom gate?

Maybe not. A solo side project with no paying users and no production credentials may only need what GitHub already gives you: secret scanning with push protection and Dependabot alerts, both free on public repositories. Turn those on and stop there.

You need the gate when several people merge code, when the app holds customer data or payment keys, or when part of the codebase came from an AI builder and nobody has reviewed it line by line.

The workflow

Save this as .github/workflows/security-gate.yml:

name: security-gate
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Scan PR commits for secrets
        uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main # pin a release tag or SHA
        with:
          extra_args: --results=verified,unknown

  dependencies:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/dependency-review-action@v4
        with:
          fail-on-severity: high
          fail-on-scopes: runtime

  lockfile:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - name: Lockfile matches package.json
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - name: Lockfile only pulls from the npm registry over https
        run: npx --yes lockfile-lint --path package-lock.json --type npm --allowed-hosts npm --validate-https

Here is what each job does and why it is set up this way.

Secrets. TruffleHog scans only the commits between the PR base and head, so it stays fast. fetch-depth: 0 gives it that history. --results=verified,unknown means it fails on keys it confirmed are live, plus keys it couldn't check. It ignores ones it proved are dead.

Dependencies. Dependency review looks only at packages this PR adds or changes. That one choice keeps old debt from blocking unrelated work. fail-on-scopes: runtime ignores dev-only tooling. On private repositories this action needs GitHub's paid code security add-on.

Lockfile. npm ci fails when package.json and package-lock.json disagree, which catches the classic "I edited package.json by hand" PR. --ignore-scripts stops install scripts from running inside your gate. lockfile-lint fails if a resolved URL points to an unknown host or plain http, which is a common way to sneak in a tampered package.

If dependency review isn't available to you, swap that job for npx --yes audit-ci@7 --config audit-ci.jsonc with a config like this:

{
  "high": true,
  "skip-dev": true,
  "allowlist": [
    // Only reachable from an internal admin script. Review by 2026-12-01. Owner: backend lead
    "GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx"
  ]
}

How do you tune it so the team doesn't learn to ignore it?

Only fail on findings someone would actually fix today. Everything else goes into a report, not a red X.

  • Start with verified secrets only. Run TruffleHog with --results=verified for the first two weeks, then add unknown. The team's first experience should be a real catch, not ten false alarms.
  • Gate on high and critical in runtime code. Moderate issues in a test runner are real, but they are not merge blockers. Handle them in a scheduled job.
  • Run a nightly full audit separately. A schedule: workflow running npm audit --omit=dev across the whole tree catches newly disclosed issues in old packages. It opens an issue instead of blocking someone's unrelated PR.
  • Every exception needs a reason, an owner and a review date. An allowlist entry with no comment becomes permanent. The allow-ghsas input on dependency review and the audit-ci allowlist both work for this. Read through them once a month.
  • Keep the gate under three minutes. Slow checks get skipped. The three jobs run in parallel for that reason.
  • Make the failure tell people what to do. Add a short note to your PR template: if the secrets job fails, rotate the key first, then remove it from the code. Removing it alone fixes nothing.

How do you make sure nobody can skip it?

In your repository settings, add a branch protection rule (or ruleset) on main and mark secrets, dependencies and lockfile as required status checks. Turn on "Do not allow bypassing" for admins too. A gate that the most senior person can quietly skip only trains everyone else to ask that person.

One honest limit: this gate stops new problems. It doesn't find the key that was committed eight months ago. Run a full history scan once (trufflehog git file://. --results=verified) and rotate whatever it finds before you trust the clean green checks.

If your app started life in Lovable, Bolt, Cursor or a similar tool, the exposure is usually bigger than one pipeline. The vibe coding security guide covers what to check beyond CI. Or send your repo or pipeline to Geminate Solutions for a free review, under NDA, with a reply within 24 hours.

title: How to compare GPU cloud prices without fooling yourself
description:
"H100 from $X an hour" is the least useful number in a GPU price list. Two offers with the same headline can differ by a factor of two in what you pay at the end of the month, and two offers with very different headlines can come out the same.

We publish GPU prices at Runcrate, and other people's comparison sites read them, so I spend a lot of time looking at how a price turns into a bill. This is the checklist I use. It works for any provider, ours included. I'll use our public pricing endpoint for the examples because it's the data I can show you with a script, not because the method depends on it.

1. Get to one unit: dollars per GPU-hour

Some lists quote the machine, some quote the GPU. An 8x H100 node at a per-machine price looks eight times worse than a 1x H100 at a per-GPU price. Divide by the GPU count first, always.

Runcrate's endpoint already reports per GPU-hour and needs no API key:

import requests

data = requests.get("https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing").json()
print("fetched at", data["fetched_at"])

for g in data["gpus"]:
    s = g["specs"]
    per_gpu = s["num_gpus"] or 1
    print(
        f'{g["name"]:12} {g["vram"]:>6}  '
        f'${g["min_price_hr"]:.2f} to ${g["max_price_hr"]:.2f} per GPU-hr  '
        f'{g["available_options"]:>2} configs  GPUs per machine {g["gpu_counts"]}  '
        f'~{s["vcpus"] // per_gpu} vCPU / {s["memory_gb"] // per_gpu} GB RAM per GPU'
    )

Part of what it printed when I ran it (fetched at 2026-10-21T00:51 UTC):

H100 SXM       80GB  $3.38 to $7.79 per GPU-hr   7 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 8]  ~20 vCPU / 128 GB RAM per GPU
A100 80GB      80GB  $1.76 to $4.26 per GPU-hr  12 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 8]  ~28 vCPU / 120 GB RAM per GPU
L40S           48GB  $1.14 to $1.95 per GPU-hr  10 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4, 8]  ~12 vCPU / 72 GB RAM per GPU
A6000          48GB  $0.65 to $2.51 per GPU-hr  18 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4]  ~28 vCPU / 58 GB RAM per GPU

Notice the ranges. One GPU model can have a dozen configurations with a 2x to 4x spread between them. A comparison that keeps only the minimum hides that the minimum might be one 8-GPU node in one region.

2. Compare the same GPU, not the same name

"A100" is two products (40 GB and 80 GB). "H100" is SXM or PCIe, with different memory bandwidth and interconnect. A "4090" with 24 GB will not hold the model your 48 GB card holds. Before comparing prices, match:

  • VRAM (the endpoint has vram per GPU type)
  • form factor and interconnect for multi-GPU work (interconnect, for example NVLink)
  • GPU count per machine, because you can't split an 8-GPU node

If your model needs 80 GB, the price of a 40 GB card is irrelevant, however low it is.

3. Count what comes with the GPU

A GPU-hour also buys CPU cores, RAM and local disk, and those vary a lot. In the output above, an A6000 can come with about 28 vCPUs, an L40S with about 12. For data loading, tokenization or anything CPU-bound in your pipeline, the "slower" card with more cores can finish first.

So note, per GPU: vCPUs, RAM, local disk, and whether persistent storage costs extra. Runcrate's volumes, for example, are billed separately at $0.03 per GB per month. Your other quotes will have their own line for it, or bundle it.

4. Billing granularity matters more than the rate for short work

This is the one most comparisons skip. Take a 7-minute eval on a $1.14/hr GPU:

  • billed per second: 1.14 x 7 / 60 = $0.13
  • billed per started hour: $1.14, nearly 9x more

For long training runs granularity barely matters. For evals, CI jobs, agent experiments and anything bursty, it dominates. Check three things:

  1. The billing increment (second, minute, hour). Runcrate bills most instances by the second and a few GPUs by the minute; the endpoint's min_price_per_minute flag marks the latter.
  2. When the meter starts: at request, at boot, or once the machine is running. Runcrate starts it when the machine is running, so provisioning isn't billed.
  3. When it stops: only when you remember to delete the machine, or also on its own. Idle shutdown and maximum runtimes turn "I forgot it overnight" from a 12-hour bill into a 30-minute one, which is worth more than a few cents on the rate.

5. Listed is not launchable

A price only matters if you can get the machine. Availability moves by the minute: in the same hour I wrote this, a GPU type showed one configuration on the pricing endpoint while a live launch query showed none. When comparing:

  • try an actual launch, or at least a live availability query, in the region you need
  • note the count of configurations and regions, not just the headline price
  • separate on-demand from spot or interruptible capacity, which is cheaper because it can disappear

6. Date every number

GPU prices change weekly, sometimes daily. A comparison without a date is a guess. Put the fetch time next to every price (the endpoint returns fetched_at for that reason), and re-run your script rather than reusing last month's table.

A template you can reuse

For each offer, one row:

Field Why
GPU model, VRAM, form factor same product?
GPUs per machine can you buy just one?
$/GPU-hour the normalized rate
vCPU, RAM, disk per GPU the rest of the machine
Billing increment, meter start cost of short jobs
Auto-stop options cost of mistakes
Storage and egress cost of data
Region, availability checked at can you launch it
Fetched at how old the number is

Then price your actual workload (hours per run, runs per month, data moved) against each row. The offer with the best headline wins less often than you'd think.

Links

  • Live prices: runcrate.ai/pricing
  • The JSON endpoint used above: https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing
  • Billing details: runcrate.ai/docs/billing/pricing

If your comparison method has a step I've missed, I'd like to hear it. Reply here or write to hello@runcrate.ai.

Written with AI assistance. The script and prices above were run against the live endpoint on 2026-10-21.

title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.27450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

title: Progressive Subset Selection and Cascaded Consistency for Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.27515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 2: Entity Lifecycle and the Persistence Context
description:
This is arguably the most important topic in Hibernate. If you understand entity states and what happens inside the Persistence Context, 80% of Hibernate-related bugs cease to be a mystery.

What is the Persistence Context

The Persistence Context is a container of managed entities within a Session/EntityManager. Its key properties are:

  1. It is a first-level cache. All loaded entities live here until the session is closed.
  2. It guarantees identity. Within a single session, calling get(User.class, 1L) twice will return the exact same Java object instance (Identity Map pattern).
  3. It tracks changes. Upon flush, Hibernate compares the current state of entities with their snapshot and generates an UPDATE only for the modified fields (dirty checking).
  4. It implements write-behind. save/persist do not write to the DB immediately — changes are accumulated and synchronized upon flush. 
User u1 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
User u2 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
System.out.println(u1 == u2); // true — the exact same object instance

This is not "optimization for the sake of optimization". It is a semantic guarantee: within a single unit of work, you always work with the same object instance, preventing the scenario of "two objects, both representing User with id=1, one with name='A' and the other with name='B'".

The Four Entity States

1. Transient (New / Unmanaged)

The object is created via new, but Hibernate knows nothing about it.

User user = new User();  // Transient
user.setName("Alice");

This is a regular Java object created with the new operator. It is not associated with the database or the current Hibernate session.

  • Database connection: None. No corresponding record exists in the database.
  • Identifier (ID): Usually null (unless set manually, but Hibernate will ignore it).
  • Tracking: Hibernate does not track changes to its fields. If you modify a field and do nothing else, nothing goes to the DB.
  • Analogy: A document draft written on your desk. It is not yet registered in the archive.

How to transition to another state:

  • To Persistent: call session.save() or session.persist().
  • To Detached: (rarely done directly; usually, the object is saved first, and then the session is closed).

2. Persistent (Managed) 

session.persist(user);   // user is now Persistent
user.setName("Bob");     // changes are tracked
// upon flush, Hibernate will generate an UPDATE

The object is managed by the current session. It has a representation in the database (it is already saved there or will be upon flush).

  • Database connection: Direct. The object corresponds to a row in the table.
  • Identifier (ID): Must have a value (the ID from the DB).
  • Tracking: Hibernate closely monitors the object (via Dirty Checking). If you modify any field of this object, Hibernate will notice and automatically generate and execute an UPDATE SQL query on the next flush().
  • Analogy: A document you pulled from the archive, opened in the system, and are editing. The system sees all your changes and will save them when you click "Save" (flush).

How to get into this state:

  • From Transient: session.save(), session.persist().
  • From Detached: session.update(), session.saveOrUpdate(), session.merge().

How to leave this state:

  • To Detached: close the session (session.close()), clear it (session.clear()), or evict the object from the session cache (session.evict()).
  • To Removed: call session.delete() or session.remove().

3. Detached 

session.close();
// all previously loaded entities are now Detached

The object was in the Persistent state (it has an ID and exists in the DB), but lost its connection to the current session (the session was closed or the object was evicted from it).

  • Database connection: The object exists in the database.
  • Identifier (ID): Must have a value.
  • Tracking: Hibernate does not track it. If you modify a Detached object's field, nothing goes to the DB until you "re-attach" it to a session.
  • Analogy: A document you physically took from the archive to your desk. You can read and even change it, but the archive system knows nothing about it. To apply changes to the archive, the document must be returned (via merge/update).

How to get into this state:

  • From Persistent: close the session (session.close()), clear the cache (session.clear()), or evict the object (session.evict()).

How to transition to another state:

  • To Persistent: call session.update(), session.saveOrUpdate(), or session.merge() (in a newly opened session).

4. Removed 

session.remove(user);  // Removed
// upon flush → DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?

The object is marked for deletion. It is still associated with the session, but "doomed".

  • Database connection: The record still exists in the DB but is marked for deletion.
  • Tracking: On the next flush() or commit(), Hibernate will generate a DELETE SQL query and remove the row from the database.
  • Analogy: A document stamped with a red "DESTROY" mark. It is still in the system, but at the end of the workday (upon commit), it will be sent to the shredder.

How to get into this state:

  • From Persistent: call session.delete() or session.remove().

Key Takeaway

The most common beginner mistake is attempting to modify a Detached object and expecting it to update in the DB automatically.

Remember: changes are automatically pushed to the DB only from the Persistent state. If an object becomes Detached (e.g., you fetched it from the DB in one method, but are trying to update it in another where the session is already closed), you must explicitly "re-attach" it via merge() or update().

persist() vs save()

Feature persist() (JPA) save() (Hibernate)
Returns void Serializable (the generated ID)
INSERT timing Deferred (upon flush) Can be immediate (if the ID is needed)
Outside a transaction Throws an exception Works (but it's a bad practice)
For detached objects Throws an exception May create a new object (or throw an error if ID exists)

Use persist() if you are working via the JPA API. It is the standard.

merge() vs update()

Feature merge() (JPA) update() (Hibernate)
What it does Loads the current state from the DB, copies changes into a new managed object, and returns it "Re-attaches" the passed detached object to the session
Returns A managed copy void
Original object Remains detached Becomes persistent
If the record was deleted Creates a new record Throws an exception

Crucial note: merge() does not make the passed object managed. It returns a different managed copy.

User detached = ...;               // Detached
User managed = session.merge(detached);
// detached — remains Detached
// managed — is now Persistent

get() vs load()

Feature get() load()
DB query Immediate Lazy (returns a proxy)
If not found Returns null Throws EntityNotFoundException upon access
Returns Real object or null Proxy or real object

load() returns a proxy — Hibernate provides a subclass that will fetch the actual data upon the first access to any field (except the ID).

Other Key Methods

  • refresh(): Reloads the object's state from the DB, overwriting it in memory. Useful if data might have been changed externally (another process, native SQL). 
session.refresh(user);  // user is reloaded from the DB
  • evict() / detach(): Removes the object from the Persistence Context. The object becomes Detached. 
session.evict(user);  // user is no longer managed
  • clear(): Completely clears the Persistence Context. All objects become Detached. 
session.clear();  // 1st-level cache is empty
  • flush(): Synchronizes the Persistence Context with the DB. It does not commit the transaction — it only executes INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements. 
session.flush();  // SQL is executed, but the transaction is not committed

When does automatic flush occur?

  • Before a transaction commit.
  • Before executing a query that might affect tables containing "dirty" entities (auto-flush).
  • Upon an explicit flush() call.
  • Upon session.close() (if uncommitted, it triggers a rollback).

Dirty Checking — How Hibernate Detects Changes

When loading an entity, Hibernate saves a snapshot — a copy of all its fields. Upon flush, it compares the current state with the snapshot.

@Transactional
public void rename(Long id, String newName) {
    User u = session.get(User.class, id);  // snapshot is saved
    u.setName(newName);                    // modified in memory
    // flush on commit: snapshot.name != u.name → UPDATE users SET name = ?
}

What this provides:

  • No need to call update() — changes are picked up automatically.
  • Generates an UPDATE only for modified fields (unless disabled).
  • If nothing changed, no UPDATE is executed at all.

Dirty checking triggers on flush, not on set. If you modify a field and roll back the transaction, the change won't reach the DB (which is correct). However, if you modify a field and don't commit, it remains in the object's memory.

Write-behind — Why save Doesn't Write Immediately

persist() does not execute an INSERT immediately. It registers the entity in the Persistence Context, and the SQL is generated upon flush.

Why:

  • Batching: Hibernate can collect several INSERTs and send them as a single batch (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size).
  • Operation ordering: Hibernate automatically sequences INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements to avoid violating foreign key constraints.
  • Efficiency: If the transaction rolls back, the INSERT was never actually executed against the DB.

Exception: If the ID generation strategy is IDENTITY (auto-increment), Hibernate is forced to execute the INSERT immediately to obtain the generated ID. This breaks batching.

Identity Map — The Uniqueness Guarantee

User u1 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
User u2 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
assert u1 == u2;  // true

How it works: The Persistence Context is essentially a Map<EntityKey, Object>, where the key is (entityClass, id). Upon get, Hibernate first checks the map. If the object is there, it returns it. If not, it loads it from the DB and puts it in the map.

Why it's needed:

  • Consistency guarantee: Prevents having two different objects with the same ID in memory.
  • Performance: Repeated get calls do not hit the DB.
  • Accurate dirty checking: Hibernate knows exactly which object instance to track.

The identity map lives only within a session. Across sessions, these are different objects.

// Session 1
User u1 = session1.get(User.class, 1L);
session1.close();

// Session 2
User u2 = session2.get(User.class, 1L);
assert u1 != u2;  // different object instances, both with id=1

Typical Mistakes and Pitfalls

1) LazyInitializationException

@Transactional
public User getUser(Long id) {
    return session.get(User.class, id);  // returns managed
}
// session is closed, user is now Detached

// in the controller:
user.getOrders().size();  // LazyInitializationException!

Solution: Fetch required data within the transaction (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph), or use DTO projections.

2) merge() does not make the original object managed

User detached = ...;
session.merge(detached);
detached.setName("new");  // NOT tracked! detached is still Detached

Solution: Work with the result of merge():

User managed = session.merge(detached);
managed.setName("new");  // NOW tracked

3) Modifying a detached object without merge()

@Transactional
public void update(User user) {  // user came from outside (detached)
    user.setName("new");
    // NOTHING happens — user is not managed
}

Solution: Use session.merge(user) or reload the entity and modify the managed instance.

4) save() vs persist() with an existing ID
If a transient object already has an ID (e.g., assigned manually), save() might assume the object is detached and execute an UPDATE instead of an INSERT. persist() will throw an exception in this situation, which is safer.

5) Long session → Memory Leak
The Persistence Context grows with every loaded entity. If a session is kept open for the entire HTTP request (OpenSessionInView) and loads thousands of objects, memory will leak.

Solution: Do not keep the session open longer than necessary; periodically flush() + clear() during batch processing.

6) flush() does not commit

session.flush();  // SQL is executed, but not committed
// if an exception occurs next — it will roll back

Solution: Remember: flush() is for synchronization, commit() is for finalizing.

7) Auto-flush before queries
Hibernate performs a flush before createQuery() if the query affects tables containing "dirty" entities. This can lead to unexpected UPDATEs in the middle of a method.

Solution: Understand this behavior; if necessary, configure FlushMode.MANUAL or COMMIT.

Example: All States in Action 

@Transactional
public void demo() {
    // 1. Transient
    User user = new User();
    user.setName("Alice");

    // 2. Transient → Persistent
    session.persist(user);
    // upon flush → INSERT

    // 3. Persistent (managed)
    user.setName("Bob");  // dirty checking will pick this up on flush

    // 4. Persistent → Detached
    session.evict(user);
    user.setName("Charlie");  // NOT tracked

    // 5. Detached → Persistent (via merge)
    User managed = session.merge(user);
    // managed is now Persistent, user remains Detached

    // 6. Persistent → Removed
    session.remove(managed);
    // upon flush → DELETE
}

Summary

  1. Persistence Context = 1st-level cache + identity map + dirty checking + write-behind. It is the heart of the Session.
  2. Four states: Transient, Persistent, Detached, Removed. Transitions are managed via session methods.
  3. persist() ≠ save(), merge() ≠ update(). Understand the difference.
  4. merge() returns a copy; the original object remains detached.
  5. Dirty checking triggers on flush, not on set.
  6. flush() does not commit; it only synchronizes.
  7. After session closure, objects are Detached → lazy fields are inaccessible.
  8. The identity map lives only within a session — across sessions, objects are different instances.
  9. Long session = memory leak. Do not keep it open longer than necessary.
  10. LazyInitializationException is a symptom of improper state management, not a "Hibernate bug".

75 Day DSA in Go Challenge

title: API Calls: A Practical Guide
description:
TL;DR

  • An API call is a network transaction governed by standard HTTP specifications where a client exchanges structured messages with a remote server.
  • Robust client implementations require explicit timeout thresholds, idempotent retry policies, and truncated exponential backoff with jitter to survive network instability.
  • Generative AI workloads introduce distinct API call profiles characterized by persistent streaming connections, multi-second latencies, and token-based rate limits.
  • Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway written in Go by Maxim AI, standardizes API calls across multiple foundation model providers while adding automatic failover and sub-millisecond routing.

An API call is a structured network request sent from a client to a server over Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to query, create, modify, or delete a remote resource. Modern software architectures rely on API calls to connect frontend interfaces to backends, decouple distributed microservices, and integrate third-party services such as payment processors and foundation model providers. Managing these network boundaries reliably requires an understanding of transport protocols, HTTP semantics, authentication standards, and error-recovery patterns. Infrastructure tools such as Bifrost help engineering teams orchestrate, govern, and observe high-volume API calls across complex multi-provider environments.

What Happens During an API Call: The Request-Response Lifecycle

An API call executes as a sequence of transport and application-layer operations that establish connectivity, authenticate identity, deliver structured data, and return a parsed response. The entire exchange follows standard client-server semantics defined by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) in RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics.

Before any HTTP payload traverses the wire, the client resolves the domain name into an IP address using the Domain Name System (DNS). Once the IP address is known, the client establishes a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection via a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). If the connection uses Transport Layer Security (TLS), as is standard for HTTPS, client and server negotiate cryptographic parameters, verify server identity certificates, and exchange session keys.

Client                                                  Server
  |                                                       |
  |--- 1. DNS Resolution -------------------------------->|
  |--- 2. TCP Handshake (SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK) --------->|
  |--- 3. TLS Negotiation (Key Exchange, Certificate) --->|
  |--- 4. HTTP Request (Method, Headers, Body) ---------->|
  |                                                       | [Processing]
  |<-- 5. HTTP Response (Status Code, Headers, Body) -----|
  |                                                       |

After the encrypted transport tunnel is open, the client transmits an HTTP request message composed of a method, request target (URI), header fields, and an optional message body. The server processes the request, evaluates permissions, interacts with data stores or downstream services, and sends back an HTTP response message containing a status code, response headers, and response payload.

Anatomy of an HTTP API Request

Every HTTP API call consists of distinct structural components defined by standardized wire formats: the HTTP method, uniform resource identifier (URI), request headers, and request body.

HTTP Methods and Idempotency

HTTP methods indicate the desired action to be performed on the identified resource. RFC 9110 Section 9 categorizes methods by safety and idempotency:

  • Safe Methods: Methods that do not alter server state. GET and HEAD must only retrieve representations without modifying underlying data.
  • Idempotent Methods: Methods where multiple identical requests produce the same server-side outcome as a single request. GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent. If a network timeout occurs during a PUT operation, the client can safely retransmit the request.
  • Non-Idempotent Methods: Methods where repeated requests create additional state transitions. POST and PATCH are typically non-idempotent. Retrying an unacknowledged POST request without an idempotency key can cause duplicate operations, such as double-charging a credit card.
Method Safe Idempotent Request Body Primary Use Case
GET Yes Yes Disallowed/No Semantics Retrieve a resource representation
POST No No Yes Create subordinate resources or run commands
PUT No Yes Yes Replace an entire resource or create if absent
PATCH No No Yes Apply partial modifications to a resource
DELETE No Yes Optional Remove the identified resource
HEAD Yes Yes No Retrieve headers identical to a GET

Headers and Content Negotiation

Headers are key-value pairs that convey operational metadata about the request context, client capabilities, authentication credentials, and body encoding. Key standardized headers include:

  • Host: Identifies the target domain and port number of the server.
  • Content-Type: Declares the MIME type of the accompanying request body (e.g., application/json).
  • Accept: Tells the server which media types the client can process in the response.
  • User-Agent: Identifies the client software originating the request. 
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
  -H "Host: api.example.com" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sec_tok_9942a" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 7b9a5e82-411a-4dc2-b883-93d3b76a0841" \
  -d '{"item_id": "sku-2041", "quantity": 2}'

Authentication and Security Controls

Production API endpoints require verifiable authentication to establish client identity and enforce authorization boundaries. Applications employ three primary authentication mechanisms:

  1. API Keys: Unique alphanumeric strings transmitted via headers (e.g., X-API-Key: value) or query parameters. While simple to implement, static API keys lack granular scoping and cannot expire automatically without client rotation.
  2. Bearer Tokens (OAuth 2.0 and JWT): Short-lived cryptographic tokens transmitted in the Authorization header (Authorization: Bearer <token>). JSON Web Tokens (JWT) contain digitally signed claims that upstream servers can validate statelessly without querying a centralized database for every request.
  3. Mutual TLS (mTLS): A zero-trust security architecture where both client and server present and verify X.509 digital certificates during the initial TLS handshake, establishing bidirectional cryptographic identity verification.

Credentials must never be hardcoded in application repositories. Production codebases inject API secrets at runtime using environment variables, cloud secret managers, or credential injection systems.

Parsing Responses and Interpreting Status Codes

The server answers every API call with an HTTP status code grouped into five functional classes:

  • 1xx (Informational): Request received, continuing process (e.g., 101 Switching Protocols).
  • 2xx (Successful): The request was received, understood, and accepted.
    • 200 OK: Standard response for successful requests.
    • 201 Created: The request succeeded and a new resource was provisioned.
    • 204 No Content: The action succeeded, but no body payload is returned.
  • 3xx (Redirection): Further action needed to complete the request (e.g., 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified).
  • 4xx (Client Error): The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled.
    • 400 Bad Request: Malformed syntax or invalid parameters.
    • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication credentials.
    • 403 Forbidden: Authenticated identity lacks permission for the resource.
    • 404 Not Found: Target resource does not exist.
    • 422 Unprocessable Entity: Syntactically correct payload contains semantic validation errors.
    • 429 Too Many Requests: Client has exceeded rate limit thresholds.
  • 5xx (Server Error): The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.
    • 500 Internal Server Error: Generic unhandled failure on the server.
    • 502 Bad Gateway: Gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream server.
    • 503 Service Unavailable: Server is temporarily overloaded or undergoing maintenance.
    • 504 Gateway Timeout: Gateway or proxy did not receive a timely response from upstream.

Client libraries such as JavaScript's native Fetch API resolve promises even on 4xx and 5xx errors; client applications must explicitly check the response.ok property before parsing JSON bodies:

async function executeApiCall(url, payload) {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Authorization": `Bearer ${process.env.API_SECRET_KEY}`
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload)
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const errorBody = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`HTTP Error ${response.status}: ${errorBody}`);
  }

  return await response.json();
}

Rate Limiting, Retries, and Backoff Strategies

Rate limiting protects servers from resource exhaustion and enforces tiered billing plans. When a client exceeds allowable volume, the server responds with status code 429 Too Many Requests, as specified in RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes.

Parsing Rate Limit Headers

Standards-compliant APIs communicate quota details in response headers:

  • Retry-After: Indicates how many seconds to wait (or provides a UTC date timestamp) before issuing the next attempt.
  • RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset: Standard draft headers detailing quota ceilings, remaining request allowances, and reset epochs.

Truncated Exponential Backoff with Jitter

Retrying failed requests instantly creates a thundering herd problem that overwhelms recovering services. Clients must apply exponential backoff combined with randomized jitter. Exponential backoff multiplies the wait duration exponentially across successive retry cycles, while jitter decorrelates concurrent retries across distributed clients:

$$t_{\text{wait}} = \min(t_{\text{max}}, t_{\text{base}} \times 2^{\text{attempt}}) \times \text{random}(0.5, 1.5)$$

import time
import random
import requests

def call_with_backoff(url, headers, payload, max_retries=5):
    base_delay = 1.0  # seconds
    max_delay = 32.0  # seconds

    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=10)

        if response.status_code == 200:
            return response.json()

        # Retry only on transient errors: 429 or 5xx
        if response.status_code in [429, 500, 502, 503, 504]:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit():
                delay = float(retry_after)
            else:
                calculated = min(max_delay, base_delay * (2 ** attempt))
                delay = calculated * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)

            time.sleep(delay)
            continue

        # Fail fast on non-retryable 4xx errors
        response.raise_for_status()

    raise RuntimeError("Exceeded maximum retry attempts.")

Managing Modern AI and LLM API Calls at Scale

Modern applications increasingly interact with generative AI APIs, such as those provided by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Vertex AI, and AWS Bedrock. While these services expose HTTP interfaces, their operational profiles deviate significantly from standard CRUD REST APIs:

  1. Unpredictable Latencies: Traditional APIs respond within 50 to 200 milliseconds. Large language model (LLM) API calls frequently take 3 to 60 seconds depending on context lengths and reasoning parameters.
  2. Streaming Protocols: Rather than returning a single payload, LLM providers stream output incrementally using Server-Sent Events (SSE) over persistent HTTP connections.
  3. Compound Quotas: Providers throttle both requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM). An application can exhaust its token quota within three large prompt requests despite staying far below RPM thresholds.
  4. Provider-Specific Schemas: Disparate providers require different payload envelopes, authentication schemes, and parameter names. 
Client App ---> AI Gateway (Bifrost) ---> OpenAI (Primary)
                      |
                      +-- [If 429 / 5xx] -> Anthropic (Fallback)
                      |
                      +-- [If Cached] ----> Cache Store (Sub-millisecond)

To eliminate point-to-point coupling, platform teams route AI calls through dedicated infrastructure layers. Bifrost serves as a unified control plane for model traffic. Built in Go, Bifrost functions as a high-performance gateway that adds only 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second, as documented in published benchmarks.

Instead of embedding multi-SDK configurations inside client code, teams use Bifrost as a drop-in replacement for OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Bifrost handles:

  • Automatic Failovers and Model Routing: If an upstream provider returns a 429 or 503 status code, automatic fallbacks seamlessly reroute the API call to an alternate provider or secondary region without throwing an unhandled exception to the calling service.
  • Semantic Caching: Traditional HTTP caching relies on exact URL and header matches under RFC 9111: HTTP Caching. Bifrost implements semantic caching, evaluating embedding vector similarities to return cached completions for semantically identical prompts, cutting token expenditures and latency.
  • Virtual Key Governance: Centralized virtual keys enforce spending ceilings, rate limits, and access controls across internal teams without distributing master provider credentials.

Endpoint AI Governance and Developer Workstations

While backend services route API calls through centralized gateways, an increasing volume of API transactions originates on local employee hardware. Software engineers run terminal coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI), IDE integrations (Cursor), desktop applications, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool servers.

When local workstations send unmonitored API calls directly to external provider endpoints using personal or unmonitored credentials, security teams encounter shadow AI: sensitive source code, customer records, and internal credentials flow outside the perimeter without policy checks or audit logging.

Beyond routing, Bifrost applies governance and security controls (virtual keys, budgets, guardrails, audit logs) centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device.

Operating as an endpoint agent across macOS, Windows, and Linux, Bifrost Edge runs in alpha and deploys silently through standard Mobile Device Management (MDM) platforms such as Jamf and Microsoft Intune via MDM deployment profiles. The agent provides:

  • App Governance: Fleet administrators manage app governance policies, permitting approved developer tools while intercepting unauthorized AI applications before requests leave the local system.
  • MCP Tool Governance: Through MCP governance, the agent discovers local MCP servers configured across tools like Claude Desktop or Cursor, enabling security teams to audit and selectively block dangerous local system integrations.
  • Zero-Config Developer Experience: Developers authenticate once via enterprise Single Sign-On (SSO). The endpoint agent transparently maps local traffic to the organization's Bifrost deployment without requiring manual configuration of proxy URLs or base paths in individual tools.

Production Reliability Checklist for API Calls

To maintain high availability across distributed systems, verify that every client-side API implementation satisfies these operational requirements:

Dimension Risk Mitigated Implementation Standard
Explicit Timeouts Thread pool exhaustion Define separate connect (e.g., 2s) and read (e.g., 10s) timeout limits on all network requests.
Connection Pooling Socket exhaustion / TLS handshake latency Reuse persistent HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 keep-alive connections via pooled HTTP clients.
Idempotency Keys Duplicate writes during retries Send unique UUIDs in the Idempotency-Key header on mutating POST operations.
Circuit Breakers Cascading failure across dependencies Halt outbound calls after a defined failure rate threshold to allow upstream recovery.
Telemetry & Tracing Invisible failures and latency anomalies Propagate W3C Trace Context headers (traceparent) for end-to-end distributed observability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an API call and an HTTP request?

An HTTP request is the network-level message formatted according to HTTP protocol specifications. An API call is the broader architectural transaction where a client uses an HTTP request to invoke a specific programmatic interface, function, or service on a remote system and receive structured data in return.

Why should GET requests never include a request body?

Under RFC 9110 Section 9.3.1, GET requests have no defined semantics for payload bodies. Many caching proxies, gateways, and web servers either drop the body entirely or reject the request outright, making request bodies in GET calls unreliable across internet infrastructure.

What should an application do when receiving a 429 Too Many Requests response?

The application must halt outbound calls to that specific service, inspect the response for a Retry-After header, and wait for the specified period before retrying. If no header is present, the client should apply truncated exponential backoff with randomized jitter before attempting another request.

How does an AI gateway improve API call reliability?

An AI gateway decouples client applications from upstream provider instability. It unifies disparate provider schemas under a single interface, balances loads across multiple API keys, intercepts transient 429/5xx errors, and automatically routes failed requests to functional fallback models without interrupting user sessions.

How do token-based rate limits differ from standard request rate limits?

Standard rate limits measure the absolute count of HTTP requests over a fixed time window (e.g., 100 requests per minute). Token-based rate limits track the cumulative volume of text tokens processed across both prompt inputs and model completions, meaning a single large request can exhaust an organization's entire throughput allocation.

What security risks are associated with shadow AI API calls?

When employees use personal API keys or unmonitored desktop AI tools, proprietary codebases and sensitive enterprise data bypass corporate data loss prevention (DLP) systems, guardrails, and audit logs. This ungoverned traffic exposes organizations to data leakage, compliance violations, and unpredictable third-party data retention policies.

Getting Started

Building robust software requires rigorous handling of API calls across transport boundaries, error states, and rate limits. As software architectures integrate foundation models alongside traditional web services, centralized routing and endpoint governance become essential infrastructure requirements. Teams evaluating AI infrastructure can request a Bifrost demo or inspect the open-source repository to standardize model traffic across production systems and developer endpoints.

Sources

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (IETF Standard)
  • RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes (IETF Standard)
  • RFC 9111: HTTP Caching (IETF Standard)
  • MDN Web Docs: Using the Fetch API

title: Your Website Is Built to Be Contacted, Not Chosen
description:
Originally published on Contento Solutions, where I write about SEO and AI visibility for service businesses.

Most small sites make contacting you easy and choosing you hard. Across the 54 sites we measured, the gap between those two things ran fifteen points. That's a website doing the second half of the job well and the first half barely at all.

Eleven at night, three tabs open

Picture the person you actually want. They have a problem, a budget they haven't said out loud, and three tabs open with three businesses that look roughly the same. They are not going to contact all three. They are going to close two.

Now open your own site and try to be them. What do you learn in ninety seconds that helps you close the other two tabs? For most sites the answer is: what the business does, that it cares, and how to get in touch. All three of those are also true of the competitors.

The fifteen point gap

We scored those 54 sites on two things that sound similar and aren't.

Friction to contact, meaning how hard it is to actually reach you once someone has decided: 75.6 out of 100. Decision served, meaning whether the page gives someone enough to decide at all: 60.5.

Nearly everyone had the contact form working. Far fewer had anything that helps a stranger choose. We have spent about fifteen years as an industry optimising the click, on pages that never earned it.

What a decision actually needs

Here is what people are trying to settle at eleven at night, and what most pages offer instead.

What they need to settle What the page usually says What settles it
Can I afford this "Contact us for a quote" A number, a range, or an honest starting point
Is this for someone like me "We work with businesses of all sizes" Who you're a bad fit for, in your own words
What happens if I say yes "Get in touch to learn more" The first three steps and roughly how long they take
What if it doesn't work Nothing at all What you do about it, stated before they ask

Look at the middle column. Every one of those lines is written to avoid losing anybody. That's the problem. A page that could apply to anyone helps nobody choose, and the person closing tabs is choosing whether they can tell or not.

The price question, honestly

Plenty of businesses can't publish a flat price, and pretending otherwise is bad advice. Scope varies, and a wrong number costs you more than no number.

But "it depends" and silence are not the same thing. You can publish what drives the price up or down. You can publish a floor, the smallest sensible engagement, and say plainly that most work costs more. You can publish what you charged for a real recent project with the client's name removed. All three let someone rule themselves in or out, which is the actual job of the page.

We publish our own numbers for the same reason, and we assume it costs us some enquiries. We can't prove that either way yet, which is the honest version. The bet is that the enquiries a price scares off were heading for a bad fourth call.

The bad fit paragraph

If you only change one thing, write the paragraph that says who shouldn't hire you.

Two or three sentences. Not false modesty, not a humblebrag about being too thorough. The real thing: the budget you can't work under, the timeline you can't meet, the kind of project you turn down. It costs an afternoon, and it's the fastest way to stop being interchangeable with the other two tabs.

It also does something for the machines. An assistant comparing options needs contrast to recommend anyone, and a page that refuses to distinguish itself gives it nothing to work with. That's the same underlying issue as not being confirmable, arriving from a different direction.

Questions we get

Won't publishing prices let competitors undercut me?

They can already call and ask, and most have. The people your silence actually stops are the buyers.

My work genuinely varies. What number do I put?

The floor, plus the two or three things that move it. "From X, and it goes up with Y and Z" is a real answer and rules out the wrong people just as well as a fixed price.

Isn't a bad fit paragraph just turning away business?

It turns away the business you were going to turn away anyway, earlier and for free, instead of after two calls and a proposal.

Where does this go on the site?

On the page that sells the service, not on a separate pricing page nobody reaches. If you have a pricing page, it should repeat rather than replace.

How do I know if my page has this problem?

Give it to someone outside your industry and ask them one question: would you hire this business, and why not. The "why not" is the part worth writing down.

What we can and can't claim

Those two scores come from 54 private therapy practices in ten US metros, measured on one day in September 2026, with our own instrument. We sell to that market. The four sites we couldn't read are named in the published index instead of dropped, and the method is written down so you can run it on your own niche and disagree with us.

What we can't tell you is whether fixing this raises your revenue, because we haven't measured that and nobody has shown us a study that has.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the four questions above, that is a reasonable thing to bring to a call. What the practice does and what gets reported is on the services page, with more detail on the FAQ page. The call is thirty minutes.

If you build sites for clients, does your own site publish a price or a bad fit paragraph? Tell me in the comments what stopped you, or what happened when you did.

title: Caching Makes Web Apps Faster, but Invalidation Makes Them Correct
description:
Caching is one of the first techniques developers consider when an application starts feeling slow.

Instead of repeatedly fetching the same information, the application stores a result and reuses it.

It's a simple idea, and it can be extremely effective.

But I think the more interesting problem begins when the underlying data changes.

Fast data isn't always fresh data

Imagine a dashboard that displays account information.

The application fetches the data once and stores it in a cache. Subsequent visits become much faster because the browser or application doesn't need to request everything again.

Now imagine the user updates their account settings.

If the cache isn't refreshed or invalidated correctly, the interface may continue displaying the old values.

The application is technically faster, but the experience is now misleading.

This is why caching needs a clear freshness strategy.

Different data needs different rules

Not every piece of information should be cached for the same amount of time.

A static configuration file might remain valid for a long period.

A user's profile may need to refresh after an update.

A live dashboard could tolerate a short delay, depending on its purpose.

Financial or transactional information may require more careful handling because stale values can influence decisions.

The right approach depends on how frequently the data changes and how costly it would be to show an outdated result.

Common caching strategies

A few approaches are worth understanding.

Time-based expiration: Keep a result for a defined period, then refresh it.

Event-driven invalidation: Clear or update cached data after a relevant action changes the underlying state.

Stale-while-revalidate: Show previously cached data while requesting an updated version, where displaying stale information is acceptable.

HTTP caching: Use appropriate headers and validators to let clients and intermediaries reuse responses safely.

These strategies can work together, but none removes the need to understand the data's meaning.

What I'd test

I'd test the full lifecycle rather than only checking whether the cache improves load time.

What happens after a user edits a record? Can two components display conflicting versions of the same data? Does the interface recover when a refresh fails? Can sensitive information remain available after a user signs out?

The last question is particularly important when applications share devices or store user-specific data locally.

Caching should improve the experience without weakening privacy or correctness.

Final thoughts

Performance and correctness are connected.

A cache that serves outdated information at the wrong moment can create more problems than it solves. On the other hand, a thoughtful caching strategy can make an application feel faster while keeping its behavior predictable.

For me, the key question isn't simply how much data can be cached. It's which data can safely be reused, for how long, and what should happen when it changes.

What's been more challenging in your projects: choosing the right cache duration or invalidating cached data at the right moment?

title: Claude Haiku 5.5 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Haiku 5.5 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Haiku 5.5 is built for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks such as summarization, context compaction, database queries, and classification. It can also handle coding subtasks alongside larger Claude models. It's the fastest Claude model at standard speed, making it useful for latency-sensitive applications such as live customer support and browser automation.

It's also the first Haiku model with adjustable effort. Choose low, medium, high, xhigh, or max to balance response quality, latency, and token usage. Adaptive thinking is enabled by default. You can disable thinking at low, medium, or high; xhigh and max require it.

title: Input said OK, nothing happened: Xcode 27, Device Hub and a flag that eats your taps
description:
If you drive the iOS simulator from scripts, test tools or AI agents, this one can cost you an afternoon: every tap is acknowledged, every command returns ok, and nothing happens on screen.

I hit it while building a tool that lets an agent and me work on the same running React Native app. Here's what's going on, how to tell you're in it, and how to get out.

All of this is on Xcode 27.0 with iOS 26.3 simulators, on one Mac. If you're on a different setup, your mileage may vary, and I'd love to hear if you see it too.

First, the change: no more Simulator.app

Xcode 27 doesn't ship a separate Simulator.app anymore. You look at simulators through Device Hub inside Xcode.

Two side effects worth knowing:

  • Closing the viewer can shut the device down. If you were relying on "the window is open, so the simulator is running", that's no longer a safe assumption.
  • You don't need a viewer at all. xcrun simctl boot <udid> brings the simulator up without any window, and anything that streams the screen or sends input to it keeps working. For automation this is actually nicer: nothing to keep open, nothing for a human to close by accident.

The bug: input that says yes and does nothing

One day input to one simulator simply stopped working. Not failing: stopped working while reporting success.

I measured it on a local test page that logs every pointer event:

  • 5 taps and one typed word sent to the simulator;
  • every single one acknowledged by the input layer in 52–113 ms, no errors;
  • 0 events reached the page.

Home and App Switcher commands also answered ok. The screen didn't move.

A second simulator on the same machine, same Xcode, same everything, worked fine.

The cause: a flag Device Hub leaves behind

The difference between the two simulators turned out to be one Darwin notification state inside the simulator:

com.apple.coredevice.dtuhidd.active
  • On the broken simulator it was 1, while no Device Hub process was running at all.
  • On the healthy one it was 0.

It's not a defaults key or a plist, it's a notify state held by the simulator's backboardd. As far as I can tell, it means "Device Hub attached to this simulator's input during this boot". While Device Hub is attached, input goes through its channel. When Device Hub goes away, the state stays at 1, and input from any other source is quietly ignored.

Just opening Device Hub and showing the simulator didn't set it in my tests; it stayed 0. Interacting with it from Device Hub seems to be what does. The name isn't documented anywhere I could find (I first saw it in the source of an open-source simulator tool), so treat the mechanism as my best reading of the evidence, not Apple's description.

The state survives closing Device Hub. It survives closing Xcode. It goes away only when the simulator reboots.

After a reboot: flag 0, input reaches the app again.

How to check yours

Two read-only commands. First, the state inside a booted simulator:

xcrun simctl spawn <udid> notifyutil -g com.apple.coredevice.dtuhidd.active

It prints com.apple.coredevice.dtuhidd.active 0 or ... 1.

Then, whether Device Hub is actually running:

pgrep -x DeviceHub >/dev/null && echo "Device Hub running" || echo "no Device Hub process"

How to read the pair:

State Device Hub process Meaning
0 any Free, input from your tools works
1 running Device Hub is attached right now, expected
1 not running Stale: input will be silently dropped

Use notifyutil -g only. -s sets the state, which you don't want to do on a whim. The simulator has to be booted for simctl spawn to work.

The symptom is also easy to recognise once you know it:

  1. Input commands succeed with no errors.
  2. Nothing on screen reacts, including system gestures like Home.
  3. Another simulator on the same machine works.
  4. You (or a teammate, or a tool) used that simulator from Device Hub at some point since it was booted.

If you're in the stale state, reboot the simulator before you debug anything else:

xcrun simctl shutdown <udid>
xcrun simctl boot <udid>

Why this is worse for agents than for people

A person notices within seconds that taps don't do anything. An automated check often doesn't, for two reasons:

  • The acknowledgement is a lie. If your tool treats "input accepted" as "input delivered", every step passes.
  • "The screen changed" can lie too. The simulator's video stream keeps sending frames even when nothing moves, so "a frame arrived after the tap" proves nothing. My own heuristic that looks at frame sizes to decide whether a tap landed said "confirmed" once while in this state, because a page happened to load at the same moment.

So an agent can walk through a whole flow, report success, and never have touched the app.

What I ended up doing in my tool:

  • detect the stale flag (key set, no Device Hub process) and show the human a one-line note under the picture;
  • mark input as unverified instead of confirmed while the simulator is in that state;
  • add a warning to the agent's tool replies: input is likely blocked by a flag Device Hub left on this simulator; ask the user to reboot the simulator.

The last one matters most. The agent can't fix this itself, but it can stop pretending everything worked and ask the human for the one action that does.

Takeaways

  1. On Xcode 27, a simulator doesn't need a window. simctl boot is enough for streaming and input.
  2. Device Hub can leave a state that silently swallows input until the simulator reboots. One notifyutil -g plus one pgrep tells you if you're in it.
  3. "Input accepted" is not "input delivered". If you automate the simulator, verify against what the app actually received.
  4. When the tool can't fix something, it should say so. An honest warning to the agent beats a green check.

Have you run into this, or something like it, on Xcode 27? I'd like to know whether it's my setup or more common than it looks.

title: Companies that sponsored green cards for frontend developers in 2026 (free list from DOL PERM data)
description:
If you're a frontend developer on a work visa, "does this company sponsor green cards?" is one of the hardest questions to answer from a job post. Most listings say nothing, and a recruiter's "we support visas" can mean H-1B only.

There's a better signal: the US Department of Labor publishes every PERM labor certification decision. PERM is the step most employer-sponsored green cards go through, so if a company filed PERM for a frontend role this year, it has actually done the paperwork before.

I went through the latest DOL PERM disclosure file (FY2026 Q3, decisions from Oct 1, 2025 to Jun 30, 2026) and pulled every case with a frontend-style job title (front end, frontend, front-end, UI developer, UI engineer, React developer). That's 151 cases at 103 employers. Here are the top 15.

Free sample: top 15 frontend green card sponsors (FY2026)

Employer PERM cases Certified Median offered wage Top worksite
ByteDance Inc. 17 16 $177,440 San Jose, CA
TikTok Inc. 5 5 $184,662 San Jose, CA
FMR LLC (Fidelity) 4 4 $161,363 Westlake, TX
U.S. Bank National Association 4 4 $142,522 Irving, TX
IBM Corporation 3 3 $153,807 San Jose, CA
Interglobe IT LLC 3 3 $105,997 Irving, TX
Milwaukee Electric Tool Corporation 3 3 $100,500 Brookfield, WI
Snap Finance, LLC. 3 3 $120,000 West Valley City, UT
TruStartIT LLC 3 3 $87,610 Richardson, TX
Advantis Global, LLC 2 2 $164,320 Mill Valley, CA
Apptegy, Inc. 2 2 $62,920 Little Rock, AR
AvidXchange, Inc. 2 2 $144,900 Charlotte, NC
Barclays Services Corp. 2 2 $175,000 Whippany, NJ
LOGIWARE, INC. 2 2 $83,325 Alpharetta, GA
Purchasing Power LLC 2 2 $142,002 Atlanta, GA

Source: DOL OFLC PERM disclosure data, FY2026 Q3. Ties at 2 cases are shown in file order; more employers have 2 cases than fit here.

👉 Get the full list free: Frontend & Software Green Card Sponsors FY2026 (pay what you want, $0 is fine). It has all 103 frontend employers plus a software developer tab with the top 1,150 sponsors, as a Google Sheet and CSV files.

How to read the columns

  • PERM cases: how many PERM applications DOL decided for that employer with a frontend-style title in this window. It counts applications, not people hired.
  • Certified: how many DOL approved (this includes "certified-expired", meaning it was approved but the next step wasn't filed in time). Across all 151 frontend cases, 146 were certified, 3 denied and 2 withdrawn.
  • Median offered wage: the middle of the yearly wages the employer wrote on those applications. It's what they offered for that specific role and location, not a company-wide salary band.
  • Top worksite: where the job actually is. This often differs from headquarters (Fidelity is based in Boston, but most of its cases here are in Westlake, TX).

The full list also has the top job titles per employer and the date of the latest decision, which tells you how recently they filed.

How to use the list in a job search

  1. Start with your location or the places you'd move to. Filter the sheet by worksite. A company with three cases in your city is a better lead than a famous name that only sponsored in another state.
  2. Look at the job titles. Many cases are senior, lead or principal roles. If an employer only filed for "Principal Front End Engineer", that tells you the level they're willing to sponsor.
  3. Check their careers page. Search for frontend, UI or React openings. Past filings don't mean they're hiring now.
  4. Ask early, and ask the right question. "Do you sponsor H-1B?" and "Do you sponsor green cards (PERM)?" are different questions. Ask both in your first recruiter call so neither of you wastes time.
  5. Track who said what. Once you're talking to 20+ companies, it's easy to forget which one said "case by case". I keep mine in a simple sheet (Job Application Tracker), but any spreadsheet works.

If frontend roles are too narrow for you, the software developer tab is much bigger: DOL decided 25,078 PERM cases for software developers and web developers (SOC codes 15-1252 and 15-1254) at 5,188 employers in the same window. The list covers the top 1,150 of them by case count (each with 4 or more cases, 19,254 cases in total). That's not every sponsor: the other 4,038 employers, the smaller filers, aren't in it.

Limits (please read before you rely on this)

  • This is PERM, not H-1B. A company can file lots of H-1Bs and few or no PERM applications, or the other way around.
  • Small numbers. Most frontend employers here (82 of 103) had a single case. A "100% approval rate" on 1–3 cases means very little.
  • Title matching isn't perfect. I matched job titles, not job descriptions. Some titles are senior or managerial, and a few aren't web work at all (Milwaukee Tool's cases are for a "Senior Concept Design Engineer – Front End Innovation", which reads like a product design role). Check the titles in the full list.
  • Staffing and IT consulting firms appear. Some employers place workers at client sites. That's a legitimate route for some people, but it's a different job than working in-house, so look them up.
  • Past filings don't promise future sponsorship. Budgets, policies and headcount change.
  • The data lags. DOL publishes disclosure files quarterly, and this one ends on Jun 30, 2026. Cases decided since then aren't in it yet. The raw files are public on the DOL FLAG site.
  • Not legal advice. For your own case, talk to an immigration attorney.

I left employer tax IDs out of the list on purpose. Everything else comes straight from the public DOL file.

For developers: pull your own fresh list

If you'd rather query the data yourself, by job title, city or salary, I published the tool I used to build this list: PERM Green Card Sponsors on Apify. It reads the DOL disclosure files directly and groups cases by employer. Most job seekers won't need it; the sheet is easier.

Get the full list

The free sample above is 15 of 103 frontend sponsors. Download the full Frontend & Software Green Card Sponsors FY2026 list: pay what you want, including $0.

If you spot an employer that's mislabeled or a mistake in the numbers, tell me in the comments and I'll fix it.
