title: My local AI agent now has coworkers, a wake word, and takes my meeting notes
description:
When I get an idea away from my computer, I tap a button on my Apple Watch's home screen and say it out loud. It lands in my Apple Notes. My agents are watching my notes, and by the time I'm back at my desk, they've already started building it.

That's Flash, an open source AI agent I've been building for the terminal and the browser. It runs on Ollama models you pick, with no API keys and no account, and nothing leaves your computer unless you tell it to. The dev branch is 173 commits ahead of main now. Here's what's in it, starting with the two pieces that make the Watch trick work.

It keeps working after you close the chat

Most agents stop the moment you stop typing. Flash has sparks: small agents you give a name, a standing goal and a schedule, and they just keep going. "Watch the issues on my repo and tell me about new bugs every morning." "Check the price of this every hour." Each run is a shift, and each shift ends with a report you can thumbs up or down. A spark reads every piece of feedback you've ever given it before every shift, so you only have to say "only tell me about the ones labelled bug" once.

Turn on sparks always on and they keep working with Flash closed. The OS starts them at login.

Then it got out of hand, in a good way. Sparks can be on teams now. Teams have leads, an org chart that comes alive while they work, budgets by the hour, day, week or month, and an audit log of every tool call. A lead can propose hiring a new spark, and you approve it like a pull request. Every team has a group chat where you and the sparks talk in one room, with @mentions, replies, emoji reactions and read ticks. A spark can decide to stay quiet when it has nothing to add, which is more than I can say for most group chats.

Connectors (MCP)

Flash speaks the Model Context Protocol now. /mcp add github npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github and GitHub's tools join Flash's own. Same for Notion, Postgres, your filesystem, anything with an MCP server, local or remote. It reads the usual mcpServers config, so you can paste one in from wherever you already have it. Read-only tools run straight away. Anything that changes something asks you first, unless you've put Flash in autonomous mode.

The Watch trick is just this. I added sweetrb/apple-notes-mcp as a connector, which gives my sparks tools to read my Apple Notes, then gave a spark the goal of watching for new ideas there and getting them started. The Watch button is just a fast way to get a note written. Flash does the rest.

"Hey Flash"

Voice mode got a wake word. Say "Hey Flash" with the page open, or flip on the background service and it works with no tab open at all. A slider sets how eager it is, so a YouTube video in the background doesn't set it off.

Everything you hear and say stays on your machine:

  • Listening is Vosk, or Moonshine if you want it to actually get your words right. Moonshine streams, so the words on screen while you talk are already the right ones.
  • Speaking is Piper, or Kokoro, which sounds startlingly human for something running on a laptop CPU.
  • Point your camera at something mid-conversation and ask about it.
  • Say "interrupt" to cut it off mid-sentence. It can also end the conversation itself when you say bye, so you're not stuck talking to a dial tone.

It takes your meeting notes

Hit + then Record a meeting. Flash writes down what's said as it's said, live, on your computer. When you stop, the transcript lands in a new chat and the model writes up the summary, what got decided, who's doing what by when, and what's still open.

There's no bot joining your call, no upload and no "this meeting is being recorded by". It's the same idea as recording your screen to teach Flash a procedure, which you can also do now.

It can pause your music

Off by default. Turn it on and "stop the music", "turn it down" and "open Spotify" just happen. It plays and pauses anything (a YouTube tab, a call, any app) through the media keys. It also opens and quits apps, sets the volume, locks the screen and flips dark mode. It doesn't click around your screen. Yet.

The stuff I use every day

  • Replies aren't just text anymore. Flash answers with charts, calculators, forms and buttons when those say it better.
  • It writes music and plays it in its own player. It builds 3D models and textures them. It drafts designs you can comment on.
  • System One: in autonomous mode, a small fast model looks over every command and edit before it runs, and stops the sketchy ones.
  • Steer it while it works ("actually use the other file"), or queue the next thing without waiting.
  • Edit a message you already sent and keep every version.
  • /btw asks a side question without derailing the task.
  • Email, across as many accounts as you have, plus an Inbox spark that sorts it every 30 minutes and drafts replies you approve.
  • When it needs a package, it shows an Install button and lets you watch the logs.
  • If it misread your typo and titled the chat something dumb, it retypes the title in front of you once it figures out what you meant.

One thing I learned

Models love em dashes. You can ask nicely in the system prompt and they'll keep doing it. So Flash pulls them out in code, a token at a time as the reply streams in, except inside code where a dash means something. This week I found out sparks were sneaking them through one specific tool in the team chat. That's fixed now. If you build on local models, enforce style in code. Prompts are suggestions.

Try it

It's MIT and on GitHub. To get everything above, install from dev:

pipx install "git+https://github.com/Natuworkguy/Flash@dev"
flash --web

You'll need Ollama and a model that can call tools. The repo has a recommended one.

So, what would you have a spark watch? Tell me in the comments. And if you try it, tell me what breaks.

If this looks useful, a star on GitHub helps more people find it.

title: Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Supabase Realtime Connection Reset Under Next.js SSR Load
description:
Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Supabase Realtime Connection Reset Under Next.js SSR Load

The Failure Symptom 

[supabase-js] RealtimeClient connection error: Error: WebSocket closed with code 1006
[Next.js] TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'channel')
[Vercel] Function invocation timeout after 10s

Production dashboard went dark at 1:47 AM. No client errors. Server logs showed Supabase Realtime subscriptions silently dropping after 8-12 seconds under concurrent Server Component render load. The kicker? Local dev was flawless. Staging with 10 concurrent users worked. Production with 200+ simultaneous SSR requests collapsed.

The Red Herring

Every Next.js + Supabase tutorial shows this Server Component pattern:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server'

export default async function Dashboard() {
  const supabase = createClient()
  const channel = supabase
    .channel('public:events')
    .on('postgres_changes', 
      { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'events' },
      (payload) => console.log(payload)
    )
    .subscribe()

  const { data } = await supabase.from('events').select()
  return <EventList events={data} />
}

Under Next.js 15 concurrent RSC streaming, each render creates a new Supabase client instance with a fresh Realtime connection. With 50 users hitting the dashboard simultaneously, we spawned 50+ WebSocket connections to Supabase Realtime within 2 seconds. Supabase's connection pooling throttled us. Connections queued, timed out at 10s, then cascaded into retry storms.

The misleading part? createClient() in Server Components feels stateless and React-idiomatic. But Realtime WebSockets are stateful long-lived TCP connections. React's render concurrency model conflicts with connection pool limits (Supabase Free: 60 concurrent, Pro: 500).

The Root Cause & Runnable Fix

Realtime subscriptions belong in Client Components with singleton connection management, not Server Components. Server Components should handle initial data fetch only.

Fixed Architecture

1. Server Component (RSC) — Initial Data Only

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server'
import { RealtimeEvents } from './realtime-events'

export default async function Dashboard() {
  const supabase = createClient()
  const { data: initialEvents } = await supabase
    .from('events')
    .select()
    .order('created_at', { ascending: false })
    .limit(50)

  return <RealtimeEvents initialEvents={initialEvents} />
}

2. Client Component — Singleton Realtime Connection

// app/dashboard/realtime-events.tsx
'use client'

import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/client'
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
import type { RealtimeChannel } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

let globalChannel: RealtimeChannel | null = null

export function RealtimeEvents({ initialEvents }) {
  const [events, setEvents] = useState(initialEvents)
  const supabase = createClient()

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!globalChannel) {
      globalChannel = supabase
        .channel('events-feed')
        .on('postgres_changes',
          { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'events' },
          (payload) => {
            setEvents((prev) => [payload.new, ...prev].slice(0, 50))
          }
        )
        .subscribe((status) => {
          if (status === 'SUBSCRIBED') {
            console.log('[Realtime] Connected')
          }
        })
    }

    return () => {
      // Keep connection alive across component remounts
      // Only cleanup on actual unmount (e.g., route navigation)
    }
  }, [])

  return (
    <ul>
      {events.map((event) => (
        <li key={event.id}>{event.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

Key Fix: Module-level globalChannel singleton prevents duplicate subscriptions across React StrictMode double-renders and Fast Refresh. Connection count dropped from 50+ to 1 per client browser session.

Monitoring Addition 

// lib/supabase/client.ts
import { createBrowserClient } from '@supabase/ssr'

export function createClient() {
  const client = createBrowserClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!
  )

  client.realtime.onOpen(() => {
    console.log('[Realtime] WS open', new Date().toISOString())
  })

  client.realtime.onClose((event) => {
    console.error('[Realtime] WS closed', event.code, event.reason)
  })

  return client
}

After deployment: zero connection resets, consistent 1-2 second subscription latency even at 500 concurrent users.

Invariant Rule

Realtime subscriptions are stateful I/O—never instantiate them in Server Components or React render loops.

If your Server Component needs live data, fetch the baseline snapshot server-side, then hydrate the Client Component with a singleton Realtime subscription. This pattern applies to any WebSocket/SSE integration (Pusher, Ably, Socket.IO) under Next.js RSC concurrency.

Connection pooling isn't just a backend database concern—it governs client WebSocket fan-out too.

title: You win AI search by influencing the substance of the answer, not just targeting the prompt question.
description:
You win AI search by influencing the substance of the answer, not just targeting the prompt question.

For example: I checked “Which is better, Zoho CRM or HubSpot?” in Ahrefs Brand Radar. A combined volume of around 3,500 per month in searches across ChatGPT & Google.

ChatGPT favoured HubSpot for ease of use and marketing. Zoho for value and customisation. Google AI Mode also flagged Zoho’s steeper learning curve.

If I’m Zoho, that gives me a pretty specific brief for content responses:

  • A timed setup walkthrough content piece: import contacts, build a pipeline, log the first deal etc.
  • A quick cost calculator tool for 5, 20 and 50 users, including feature tiers, add-ons and onboarding.
  • A Blueprint demo video showing how Zoho is easy to use

That’s the substance to work on. Address the reasons behind the recommendation. Don't create a blog on "“Which is better, Zoho CRM or HubSpot?"

title: LoWAgent: A Low-Resource Multilingual Benchmark for Web Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27205v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated on English-language interfaces, leaving their ability to operate across the world's multilingual websites largely unexplored. This gap is especially significant for low-resource languages, where standardized resources for evaluating web agents remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark (LoWAgent), a benchmark for evaluating web agents across different low-resource languages (LRLs) in comparison to the default, English. LoWAgent evaluates web agents across English and four LRLs: Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic. The benchmark comprises of six fully localized websites, instantiated across five languages to yield 3,000 task instances. We evaluate three closed-source and five open-source models across all five languages on all six websites. Our findings show that both closed-source and open-source models experience performance degradation for LRLs compared to English, with substantially greater performance drops observed among the open-source model agents. We further evaluate the robustness of the models on realistic interface disruptions, such as cookie notices and advertisement pop-ups, and find that these further degrade agentic performance. Finally, we show that post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces can significantly improve low-resource language agentic task performance, demonstrating the usefulness of our benchmark.

title: An LLM-Based Agent for Legal Compliance Assessment: Architecture, Memory, and Evaluation in a Canadian and Quebec Context
description:
arXiv:2610.27347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivi\`eres. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.

title: Controllable Multi-Object Insertion for Detection Data Augmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.26922v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controllable object insertion provides a targeted approach to augmenting object detection datasets that require category--count fidelity, annotation alignment, and source-content preservation beyond visual realism. Several approaches have been proposed to address this grand challenge, but most suffer from different constraints in precise category--count requests and visual consistency, limited coordination across categories and instances, and poor localization of multiple objects of specific category and count. We design SceneP2F, a two-stage trainable framework that connects scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation leveraging explicit instance-level layouts. SceneP2F consists of two novel designs. The first is ScenePlan which allocates one class-labeled query per requested instance, jointly predicts scene-compatible object centers, and separately estimates box sizes conditioned on the planned centers and scene context. The second is SceneAlign-Fill which combines geometry- and appearance-aware conditioning, box--class-guided regional attention, and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to render the planned objects while limiting unintended changes to source content. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K show that SceneP2F outperforms representative general-purpose editors and object-insertion methods consistently, demonstrating the value of coordinating instance-level planning and generation for category-targeted detection augmentation.

title: Window Functions, Joins, CTEs and Subqueries in SQL: A Hospital Dataset Walkthrough.
description:
Every hospital runs on data: patients, bills, wards, diagnoses and doctors. Answering real questions from that data, like "Which doctor brings the most revenue?" or "Which patients came back for a second visit?", takes more than just the basic SELECT. In this article I use a small hospital database to explain four SQL topics

  1. Window Functions

  2. Joins

  3. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

  4. Subqueries

The Dataset

The database lives in Postgres and has the following core tables:
doctors (doctor_id, doctor_name, doctor_gender, doctor_specialty, doctor_experience_years, email, city)
patients (patient_id, patient_name, patient_gender, patient_age, county, sub_county)
departments (department_id, department_name, manager_id)
wards (ward_id, ward_name)
diagnosis (diagnosis_id, diagnosis_name, diagnosis_category)
procedures (procedure_id, procedure_name, procedure_category)
fact_visits (visit_id, visit_date, patient_id, doctor_id, department_id, ward_id, diagnosis_id, procedure_id, admission_type, length_of_stay_days, triage_level, insurance_provider, total_bill_kes, payment_method, follow_up_required, patient_satisfaction_score)

fact_visits is the central table. It holds 30 visits from 1 to 15 June 2026, and the other tables describe who, where and why. The total billed across all visits is KES 488,000.

1. Window Functions

A window function performs a calculation across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does. Every window function needs a OVER() clause.

How OVER(), PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and Frames Work

  • OVER() defines the "window" the function operates on.
  • PARTITION BY splits rows into groups, like GROUP BY but each row keeps its identity.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER() defines the order used for ranking or running calculations.
  • A window frame (e.g., ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) limits which rows in the partition the function sees.

Ranking: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), NTILE()

  • ROW_NUMBER() gives a unique number to every row, even when values tie.
  • RANK() gives ties the same rank and then skips numbers (1, 2, 2, 4).
  • DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same rank without skipping (1, 2, 2, 3).
  • NTILE(n) splits rows into n roughly equal groups. 
SELECT
    visit_id,
    total_bill_kes,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS row_num,
    RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS rnk,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS dense_rnk,
    NTILE(4)     OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS bill_quartile
FROM fact_visits;

This ranks every visit from the highest bill to the lowest. Visit 1017 (KES 82,000) comes first. Visits 1008 and 1020 both billed KES 6,500, so they show the difference between the functions: ROW_NUMBER gives them 15 and 16, RANK gives both 15, and the next bill (KES 5,500) gets 17, while DENSE_RANK gives both 15, and the next gets 16. NTILE(4) puts the 8 biggest bills in quartile 1, which helps identify the costliest visits.

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT visit_id, department_id, total_bill_kes,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS rn
    FROM fact_visits
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

Use case: adding PARTITION BY department_id to ROW_NUMBER() and filtering for rn = 1 in a CTE gives the highest billed visit per department. This is a common interview question.

Value Functions: LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE

LAG() reads a value from the previous row and LEAD() from the next row. FIRST_VALUE() and LAST_VALUE() return the first or last value in the frame.

SELECT
    patient_id,
    visit_date,
    LAG(visit_date)  OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS previous_visit,
    LEAD(visit_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS next_visit,
    visit_date - LAG(visit_date)
        OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS days_since_last_visit
FROM fact_visits
ORDER BY patient_id, visit_date;

For each patient, this shows the previous and next visit dates and the gap in days. A patient's first visit has NULL for previous_visit. This is useful for tracking follow-up compliance.

SELECT
    patient_id,
    visit_date,
    total_bill_kes,
    FIRST_VALUE(total_bill_kes) OVER (
        PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date
    ) AS first_bill,
    LAST_VALUE(total_bill_kes) OVER (
        PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    ) AS latest_bill
FROM fact_visits;

This compares each patient's first bill with their latest one. Common mistake: when a window has ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row, so LAST_VALUE() would just return the current row's value. Extending the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING fixes that.

Aggregate Window Functions: SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX()

Used with OVER(), aggregates compute running totals and comparisons while keeping every row.

SELECT
    d.doctor_name,
    f.visit_id,
    f.total_bill_kes,
    SUM(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_total,
    ROUND(AVG(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id), 2) AS doctor_avg,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_visits,
    MIN(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_min,
    MAX(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_max,
    SUM(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (
        PARTITION BY f.doctor_id ORDER BY f.visit_date, f.visit_id
    ) AS running_total
FROM fact_visits f
JOIN doctors d ON d.doctor_id = f.doctor_id;

Every visit row keeps its own details and also shows its doctor's totals. The running_total column grows visit by visit because ORDER BY inside OVER() creates a cumulative window.

Window Frames

A frame decides exactly which rows are included. For example, a moving average of the current and two previous bills:

AVG(total_bill_kes) OVER (ORDER BY visit_date, visit_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

Frame boundaries include UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING and UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

2. SQL Joins

Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column, like fact_visits.doctor_id = doctors.doctor_id.

INNER JOIN

Returns only rows where the match exists in both tables.

SELECT f.visit_id, p.patient_name, d.doctor_name, f.total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits f
INNER JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = f.patient_id
INNER JOIN doctors  d ON d.doctor_id  = f.doctor_id;

This returns 30 rows, one per visit, with the patient and doctor names attached.

LEFT JOIN

Returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right. Unmatched rows get NULL on the right side.

SELECT p.patient_name, COUNT(f.visit_id) AS visits
FROM patients p
LEFT JOIN fact_visits f ON f.patient_id = p.patient_id
GROUP BY p.patient_name
ORDER BY visits DESC;

This returns all 25 patients. Five patients have 2 visits and the rest have 1.

Use case: finding patients who registered but never visited. Adding WHERE f.visit_id IS NULL would check for patients without visits, which in my case returns no rows since every patient has a visit.

RIGHT JOIN

Keeps every row from the right table. It is a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.

SELECT d.doctor_name, f.visit_id
FROM fact_visits f
RIGHT JOIN doctors d ON d.doctor_id = f.doctor_id;

This lists every doctor with their visits, 30 rows here. A doctor with no visits would appear once with NULL in visit_id.

FULL OUTER JOIN

Keeps all rows from both tables, filling NULLs where no match exists; it is useful for data quality checks.

SELECT d.doctor_id, f.visit_id
FROM doctors d
FULL OUTER JOIN fact_visits f ON f.doctor_id = d.doctor_id
WHERE d.doctor_id IS NULL OR f.visit_id IS NULL;

This finds doctors with no visits and visits with no doctor. Here it returns no rows, which confirms the data is consistent.

CROSS JOIN

Produces the Cartesian product: every row from the first table paired with every row from the second. No ON clause.

SELECT d.doctor_name, dep.department_name
FROM doctors d
CROSS JOIN departments dep;

4 doctors x 4 departments = 16 rows. Use case: generating all possible combinations, like a roster of every doctor against every department to plan rotations.

SELF JOIN

A table joined to itself, useful when rows in one table reference other rows in the same table. Here it finds pairs of patients from the same county.

SELECT a.patient_name AS patient_1, b.patient_name AS patient_2, a.county
FROM patients a
JOIN patients b ON a.county = b.county AND a.patient_id < b.patient_id;

The a.patient_id < b.patient_id condition stops a patient from being paired with themselves and avoids duplicate pairs. This results in patients from the same county being listed together.

Quick Comparison

Join Rows kept Best for
INNER Matches in both tables Standard reports
LEFT All left table rows Finding missing matches
RIGHT All right table rows Same as LEFT, flipped
FULL OUTER All rows from both Reconciliation
CROSS All combinations Rosters, testing scenarios
SELF Table joined to itself Hierarchies and comparisons

3. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

A CTE is a named temporary result set defined with WITH, readable only for that query. It makes complex logic clearer than nested subqueries.

Basic CTE 

WITH doctor_revenue AS (
    SELECT doctor_id, SUM(total_bill_kes) AS revenue
    FROM fact_visits
    GROUP BY doctor_id
)
SELECT d.doctor_name, dr.revenue
FROM doctor_revenue dr
JOIN doctors d ON d.doctor_id = dr.doctor_id
ORDER BY dr.revenue DESC;

The CTE totals revenue per doctor first, then the main query joins it to doctor names. This also shows a CTE working with a join and an aggregation.

WITH high_value_visits AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM fact_visits
    WHERE total_bill_kes > 20000
)
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS expensive_visits
FROM high_value_visits
GROUP BY department_id;

The CTE filters bills above KES 20,000 first, then the main query counts them per department. The counts are department 10:3, 20:2, 30:3 and 40:1.

Multiple CTEs

Separate CTEs with commas. Later ones can use earlier ones.

WITH dept_revenue AS (
    SELECT department_id, SUM(total_bill_kes) AS revenue
    FROM fact_visits
    GROUP BY department_id
),
avg_revenue AS (
    SELECT AVG(revenue) AS avg_rev FROM dept_revenue
)
SELECT d.department_name, dr.revenue
FROM dept_revenue dr
JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = dr.department_id
CROSS JOIN avg_revenue a
WHERE dr.revenue > a.avg_rev;

The second CTE consumes the first, showing how CTEs chain. This query lists departments earning above the average departmental revenue. The average is KES 122,000, so only Cardiology is returned.

Recursive CTE

A recursive CTE references itself using UNION ALL to process hierarchical or sequential data. Here in this example it builds a calendar so days with no visits still appear.

WITH RECURSIVE calendar AS (
    SELECT DATE '2026-06-01' AS day
    UNION ALL
    SELECT day + 1 FROM calendar WHERE day < DATE '2026-06-17'
)
SELECT c.day, COUNT(f.visit_id) AS visits
FROM calendar c
LEFT JOIN fact_visits f ON f.visit_date = c.day
GROUP BY c.day
ORDER BY c.day;

Use case: recursive CTEs shine on organization charts (a doctor supervising other doctors but it does not apply on my dataset) or generating date series, like listing all days of June to find dates with zero visits.

CTEs vs Subqueries

  • Readability: CTEs name each step and read top to bottom. Deeply nested subqueries read inside out.

  • Reuse: a CTE defined once can be referenced multiple times in the main query. A subquery must be rewritten each time.

  • Recursion: only CTEs support WITH RECURSIVE.

  • Scope: both exist only for one query. Neither stores data permanently. For reusable storage, use a table or view

WITH avg_bill AS (
    SELECT AVG(total_bill_kes) AS avg_kes FROM fact_visits
)
SELECT f.visit_id, f.total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits f
CROSS JOIN avg_bill a
WHERE f.total_bill_kes > a.avg_kes;

4. SQL Subqueries

A subquery is a query nested inside another query. It can appear in SELECT, FROM or WHERE.

Scalar and Non-Correlated Subqueries

A scalar subquery returns a single value. A non-correlated subquery runs once, independently of the outer query. This one is both:

SELECT visit_id, total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits
WHERE total_bill_kes > (SELECT AVG(total_bill_kes) FROM fact_visits);

The average bill is about KES 16,267, so this returns 10 visits.

Correlated Subquery

A correlated subquery uses a value from the outer row, so it runs once per row. This finds visits where the bill is above that same doctor's average:

SELECT f.visit_id, f.doctor_id, f.total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits f
WHERE f.total_bill_kes > (
    SELECT AVG(f2.total_bill_kes)
    FROM fact_visits f2
    WHERE f2.doctor_id = f.doctor_id
);

It compares each bill with the average for its own doctor, giving a fairer view than one hospital-wide average.

Nested Subqueries

A subquery inside a subquery. This finds patients treated in Cardiology:

SELECT patient_name
FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (
    SELECT patient_id
    FROM fact_visits
    WHERE department_id = (
        SELECT department_id
        FROM departments
        WHERE department_name = 'Cardiology'
    )
);

The innermost query finds the Cardiology ID, the middle one finds its visits, and the outer one returns the patients.

IN and EXISTS

IN checks whether a value is in a list. EXISTS checks whether the subquery returns any row and stops at the first match, so it can be faster on large tables.

-- IN
SELECT patient_name FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (SELECT patient_id FROM fact_visits WHERE admission_type = 'Inpatient');

-- EXISTS
SELECT p.patient_name FROM patients p
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM fact_visits f
    WHERE f.patient_id = p.patient_id AND f.admission_type = 'Inpatient'
);

Both return the same 9 inpatients. Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN when the subquery could contain NULL, because NOT IN then returns no rows at all.

ANY and ALL

> ANY means greater than at least one value in the list. > ALL means greater than every value.

-- Bigger than at least one Mobile Money bill
SELECT visit_id, total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits
WHERE total_bill_kes > ANY (SELECT total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits WHERE payment_method = 'Mobile Money');

-- Bigger than every Mobile Money bill
SELECT visit_id, total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits
WHERE total_bill_kes > ALL (SELECT total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits WHERE payment_method = 'Mobile Money');

Mobile Money bills range from KES 1,900 to 24,000. ANY compares against the smallest, so it returns 28 visits. ALL compares against the largest, so it returns only the 7 visits above KES 24,000.

Subqueries in SELECT, FROM and WHERE 

-- In SELECT: a calculated value per row
SELECT p.patient_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_visits f WHERE f.patient_id = p.patient_id) AS visit_count
FROM patients p;

-- In FROM: a derived table
SELECT department_id, avg_bill
FROM (
    SELECT department_id, AVG(total_bill_kes) AS avg_bill
    FROM fact_visits
    GROUP BY department_id
) dept_avg
WHERE avg_bill > 15000;
--for the WHERE subqueries check the examples above

The first returns 25 rows, one visit count per patient.The second returns departments 10 and 30, with averages af about KES 23,344 and 17,533.

Wrapping Up

  • Window functions add ranking, offsets and running aggregates without collapsing rows.

  • Joins combine tables; pick INNER for matches, LEFT or RIGHT to keep one side, FULL OUTER to keep both, CROSS for combinations and SELF for intra-table relationships.

  • CTEs break complex logic into named, reusable, even recursive steps.

  • Subqueries answer inner questions first; scalar for single values, correlated for row-by-row logic, and IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL for set membership and comparison.

Mastering these four areas turns basic SELECT statements into the analytical queries interviewers and organizations actually need.

title: Your dependencies will break. Your CI will leak. Probably not today.
description:
Your dependencies will break. Your CI will leak. Probably not today.

The day the platform removes the API you depend on, or the tag you
pinned to gets moved, is the day you find out. I wanted to find out
earlier — so I built breakcheck, a zero-dependency Node.js CLI that
scans a project for things that will break or leak before they do.

Why now? Three things happened in the same week:

  • Chrome and Edge are removing XSLT. Python removed imp and distutils in 3.12. Platforms remove things with short notice, and a vendor can halve a shutdown notice and break your migration plan.
  • A workflow pinned to @v4 trusts that the tag still points where it did yesterday. Tags move. Commit SHAs don't.
  • A recent wave hijacked ~1,900 GitHub accounts and reached ~30,000 repos — most of the damage ran through over-privileged automation, not zero-days.

breakcheck doesn't fix any of this for you. It tells you exactly
where it is, with a fix for each finding, so the next breakage is a
planned migration instead of a fire drill.

What it checks

Plain Node.js, no network, no telemetry. It scans locally:

File Rules
package.json Deprecated deps (request, node-sass, tslint, …), moment maintenance-mode warning, floating versions (*, latest, >=), engines.node on an EOL Node
requirements.txt Deprecated Python packages (pycrypto, nose), unpinned requirements
pyproject.toml requires-python allowing EOL Python
.github/workflows/*.yml Actions pinned to a mutable tag instead of a full commit SHA, permissions: write-all, broad contents: write, pull_request_target, hardcoded token-shaped secrets
Dockerfile Base image with no tag, :latest, or a major-only tag
Code (.js/.ts/.py) Removed APIs: browser XSLTProcessor, Python imp, collections.Mapping-style aliases, distutils

Demo

The bundled examples/broken/ project is broken on purpose — one of
almost everything:

$ node bin/breakcheck.js check --path examples/broken
[ERROR] broad-permissions: 'permissions: write-all' grants every permission to the workflow
       fix: Grant only the permissions each job needs, e.g. 'permissions: { contents: read }'
[ERROR] unpinned-action: Action 'actions/checkout@v4' is pinned to mutable ref 'v4'
       fix: Pin the action to a full commit SHA
[ERROR] unpinned-base: Docker base image 'node:latest' uses the mutable ':latest' tag
       fix: Pin the base image, e.g. 'node:22-alpine'
[ERROR] removed-api: XSLT in the browser is being removed from Chrome and Edge
       fix: Move the transform to the server, or pre-render at build time
[ERROR] deprecated-dep: 'request' is deprecated since 2020 and unmaintained
       fix: Replace with node:http / undici, axios, or node-fetch
[ERROR] eol-runtime: engines.node '14' targets Node 14, which is end-of-life
       fix: Move engines.node to '>=18' (20 LTS recommended)
Summary: 10 error(s), 3 warning(s), 7 file(s) scanned.

examples/clean/ passes with Summary: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 6 file(s) scanned.

Use it in CI 

# Scan a project (exit 1 if any error-level finding)
breakcheck check --path ./my-project

# JSON output for CI / scripts
breakcheck check --path ./my-project --format json

# Also fail on warnings (strict mode)
breakcheck check --path ./my-project --fail-on warn

Warnings don't fail the run by default, so you can adopt it without
breaking existing builds. Turn on --fail-on warn once the warnings
are down to zero.

What it deliberately does not do

The deprecation list is small on purpose: every entry is a removal or
deprecation that is public and settled, not a popularity contest. And
the tool never phones home, so it can't check live advisories — pair it
with your package manager's audit for CVEs.

One more deliberate choice: there is no --fix yet, and pinning
:latest to an explicit tag will intentionally never be auto-fixed —
picking the version is a decision, not a chore.

Repo: https://github.com/techdevfun/breakcheck — MIT, zero dependencies,
Node.js 18+.

title: How to Distribute Your Own Tools on Termux: A Guide for Developers
description:
You built a CLI tool. It runs great on Termux. Now you want other Termux users to install it with one command instead of git clone, dependency hunting, and "it doesn't compile on my phone."

Then you open a pull request to the official repository, and it gets closed. Or you try TUR and the review stalls. You're not alone, and it doesn't mean your tool is bad. It usually means the tool doesn't fit that channel.

This guide walks through every realistic way to distribute your own tools on Termux, what each one expects from you, and how to pick the right one.

Disclosure: I maintain Termux App Store, one of the options below. It is an independent community project and is not affiliated with the official Termux project. I'll be upfront about trade-offs for every option, including mine.

TL;DR

Option Best for Review process Users install with
termux-packages (official) Widely used, stable, general-purpose software Strict, maintained by the core team pkg install
TUR (Termux User Repository) Packages that don't fit official but still need a curated home Curated contributor workflow pkg install (after enabling the repo)
Your own APT repository Full control, your own release cadence None (you are the reviewer) pkg install (after users add your repo)
Termux App Store Niche, experimental, or fast-moving community tools Pull request with validation tooling termux-app-store install
GitHub release + install script Quick start, small audience None `curl ... \

If you only read one line: start by asking who your users are and how much control you want over releases, then choose.

Why your package may get rejected

Official and curated repositories exist to protect users and reduce maintenance load. A few common reasons a new tool doesn't fit:

  • Scope. The official repo targets software with broad use. A small or niche tool may not meet that bar.
  • Maintenance burden. Every package needs someone to keep it building across architectures when Termux's toolchain changes.
  • Build reproducibility. Packages must build from source inside the Termux build environment, not just run on your phone.
  • Upstream fit. Projects with bundled binaries, unusual licensing, or heavy patching are harder to accept.

None of this is a judgement on your code. It's a question of which channel matches your project.

Option 1: The official {% raw %}termux-packages repository

The build system and primary set of packages for Termux live in termux/termux-packages. Packages are organized into repository channels such as main, root, and x11, and each package is a directory with a build.sh.

Choose this if your tool is stable, widely useful, and you're willing to maintain it long term.

Do this first: read CONTRIBUTING.md and the Developer's Wiki in that repo. Check whether a similar package already exists, and make sure your project has a clear license and tagged releases.

Option 2: TUR (Termux User Repository)

TUR is described as the Termux equivalent of the Arch User Repository idea: users install pre-compiled packages instead of building on-device. Packages live under tur/<your-package-name>/build.sh (not packages/), and you build with the Termux build scripts:

TERMUX_INSTALL_DEPS=true ./build-package.sh -a <arch> <package-name>

Two things to remember:

  • TUR packages are not official Termux packages. Don't ask the core Termux team for support on them.
  • TUR has a curated contributor workflow, so expect review.

Option 3: Host your own APT repository

If you want full control, you can build .deb packages and host them as an APT repository (for example on GitHub Pages). Users add your repository, then install with pkg or apt.

Pros: your release schedule, your rules.
Cons: you handle signing, hosting, architecture builds (aarch64, arm, x86_64, i686), and user trust. Every user has to add your repo first.

This is the most work, but it's the right call for larger projects with their own ecosystem.

Option 4: Termux App Store (community package layer)

Termux App Store is a community-driven TUI and CLI package manager for Termux. Think of it as an AUR-like layer for tools that are too niche, too experimental, or too fast-moving for the official repository.

Packages are described by a build.sh file. Users can install a pre-built .deb (fast path, SHA256-verified) or force a source build.

Step 1: Get the tooling 

git clone https://github.com/djunekz/termux-app-store
cd termux-app-store

Step 2: Create your build.sh

Every package is just one file: packages/<tool-name>/build.sh. It tells Termux App Store what your tool is, where to download it, and how to install it.

You don't have to write it by hand. Pick whichever of these three ways fits you:

Way Best for Command
A. pkg-scaffold.py (wizard) Beginners. It asks questions and writes the file for you python pkg-scaffold.py
B. termux-build People who want a template or a one-line generator ./termux-build init <github-url>
C. Manual People who already know the format Copy template/build.sh and edit

Way A: the scaffold wizard (easiest)

Run it from inside the cloned repo:

python pkg-scaffold.py

Or give it your GitHub URL up front so it can pre-fill everything:

python pkg-scaffold.py --from https://github.com/yourname/my-awesome-cli

The wizard walks you through a few steps:

  1. Source repository (optional). Paste your GitHub URL and it fetches the description, license, and latest release or tag automatically.
  2. Package info: name (lowercase and hyphens only), description, homepage, license, maintainer, version.
  3. SHA256. It can download your source and compute the checksum for you.
  4. Build method. It scans your repo and detects whether it's a Python script, pip package, shell script, npm, Cargo (Rust), Go, Makefile, CMake, and more.
  5. Entrypoint (for script-type tools) and any extra dependencies.
  6. Review, then confirm, and it writes packages/my-awesome-cli/build.sh.

If you don't give it a GitHub URL, it just asks you to type everything in manually.

Way B: termux-build

Generate a blank template:

./termux-build create my-awesome-cli

Or auto-create from a GitHub repository:

./termux-build init https://github.com/yourname/my-awesome-cli

Both give you packages/my-awesome-cli/build.sh. Note that termux-build is mainly a creation and validation helper. It is not an auto-publish tool, so nothing gets uploaded until you open a pull request yourself.

Step 3: Check the metadata (and fix anything the tools missed)

Whichever way you used, open the generated file and make sure it looks right. A package definition carries metadata like this:

TERMUX_PKG_HOMEPAGE="https://github.com/yourname/my-awesome-cli"
TERMUX_PKG_DESCRIPTION="One-line description of what the tool does"
TERMUX_PKG_LICENSE="MIT"
TERMUX_PKG_MAINTAINER="@yourname"
TERMUX_PKG_VERSION="1.0.0"
TERMUX_PKG_SRCURL="https://github.com/yourname/my-awesome-cli/archive/refs/tags/v${TERMUX_PKG_VERSION}.tar.gz"
TERMUX_PKG_SHA256="<sha256 of the source tarball>"

Get the checksum with:

curl -L <your-source-url> | sha256sum

The exact required fields can evolve, so run ./termux-build guide and ./termux-build template for the current format.

Step 4: Validate before you submit 

./termux-build lint my-awesome-cli       # check the package
./termux-build check-pr my-awesome-cli   # check it's ready for a pull request
./termux-build doctor                    # diagnose your environment

Step 5: Open a pull request

Push your branch and open a PR with your packages/my-awesome-cli/ directory. After it's merged, users can find and install it:

pip install termux-app-store
termux-app-store search my-awesome-cli
termux-app-store install my-awesome-cli

Prefer to compile locally? Users can force a source build with termux-app-store fix-install my-awesome-cli.

The whole flow in 4 commands

git clone https://github.com/djunekz/termux-app-store && cd termux-app-store
python pkg-scaffold.py --from https://github.com/yourname/my-awesome-cli   # 1. generate build.sh
./termux-build lint my-awesome-cli                                         # 2. validate it
./termux-build check-pr my-awesome-cli                                     # 3. check PR readiness
# 4. commit packages/my-awesome-cli/ and open a Pull Request

Trade-off to be aware of: because this is an independent community layer, it is not the official Termux repository and packages aren't installed through plain pkg install. In exchange you get a much lower barrier to entry.

Option 5: GitHub releases plus an install script

The fastest way to ship: publish release binaries or a script on GitHub and document a one-liner.

pkg install git
git clone https://github.com/yourname/my-awesome-cli
cd my-awesome-cli && ./install.sh

It works, but there is no update mechanism, no checksum verification by default, and users have to trust and read your script. Fine for early versions; plan to graduate to one of the options above.

Checklist before you distribute anywhere

  • [x] A clear license file
  • [x] Tagged releases with a stable source URL
  • [x] A SHA256 checksum for every release artifact
  • [x] Tested on at least aarch64, ideally also arm and x86_64
  • [x] Declared dependencies (pkg install ...)
  • [x] No hardcoded /usr/bin. Termux uses $PREFIX (/data/data/com.termux/files/usr)
  • [x] A README with a copy-pasteable install command
  • [x] No telemetry or surprising network calls without disclosure

FAQ

Why was my package rejected from termux-packages?
Usually scope, maintenance burden, or build reproducibility. Read the contributing guide, check for existing packages, and consider TUR or a community layer instead.

What's the difference between termux-packages and TUR?
termux-packages is the official, core-maintained repository. TUR is a separate user repository with its own curated workflow, and its packages are not official Termux packages.

Can I distribute a Termux package without asking anyone's permission?
Yes. Host your own APT repository or release .deb files yourself. You trade review for responsibility.

How do I make a .deb for Termux?
Use the Termux build system (build-package.sh with a build.sh) so paths and prefixes are correct for Termux rather than a standard Linux distro.

Which architectures should I support?
Termux runs on aarch64, arm, x86_64, and i686. aarch64 covers most modern phones.

Wrapping up

There's no single "right" place to publish a Termux tool. Use the official repo for stable, broadly useful software, TUR for curated extras, your own APT repo when you want total control, and a community layer like Termux App Store when your tool is niche or moving fast.

Whichever you choose, ship checksums, document the install command, and test on more than one architecture. Your users will thank you.

If you've got a Termux tool you want more people to use, packaging it is the highest-leverage thing you can do. Questions or war stories about getting packages rejected? Drop them in the comments.

Links

  • Termux App Store: https://github.com/djunekz/termux-app-store
  • Termux packages (official): https://github.com/termux/termux-packages
  • TUR: https://github.com/termux-user-repository/tur

title: Muse Wonder now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Wonder from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. The model is designed for coding, long-running agents, and computer use. It can plan multi-step tasks, delegate work to sub-agents, and recover from errors as work progresses.

Muse Wonder has a 1M-token context window and supports text, image, and PDF input, tool calling, and structured output. Agents can work with code, screenshots, and documents in the same workflow.

You can access the model through AI Gateway with one API key, without creating a separate Meta account.

Set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY in your environment, then use meta/muse-wonder-1.0 as the model name:

For coding agents, run npx vercel ai-gateway setup and select meta/muse-wonder-1.0 in your agent's model settings.

title: Cross-Visibility-Gap Identity Persistence for 4D Scene Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.27505v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding.
  We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity.
  In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.

title: One line removes our app menu, and on macOS that is also the line that removes Cmd+V
description:
Notifio is a one-window desktop app that watches rental searches and tells you when a listing appears. It lives in the tray, it has no documents, no tabs and no zoom, so the first thing it does after ready is throw away the menu Electron gives you for free:

// Remove the default application menu
app.on('ready', () => Menu.setApplicationMenu(null));

I wrote that line for a good reason. Electron's default menu is built for an editor: File, Edit, View with Reload and Toggle Developer Tools in it, Window, Help. On Windows it renders as a visible strip of chrome across the top of a window that is one panel of status rows. Both windows also carry the matching option for the platforms where that strip exists:

mainWindow = new BrowserWindow({
  width: 1000,
  height: 800,
  autoHideMenuBar: true,
  // ...
});

Two settings aimed at two platforms, both in service of the same thing: an app that looks like a utility rather than a word processor.

On macOS that line does something I did not think about, because the Mac does not put the menu in the window. It puts it in the system menu bar, and the menu bar is where the keyboard owns its commands.

What the Edit menu actually is on a Mac

Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All, Undo and Redo on macOS are not keyboard handling in the usual sense. They are menu items with key equivalents. The system matches the keystroke against the menu, and the menu sends the command on. Electron knows this, which is why its menu roles exist at all:

role?: ('undo' | 'redo' | 'cut' | 'copy' | 'paste' | 'pasteAndMatchStyle' | 'delete'
  | 'selectAll' | 'reload' | 'forceReload' | 'toggleDevTools' | ...
  | 'appMenu' | 'fileMenu' | 'editMenu' | 'viewMenu' | ...);

That list is from electron.d.ts in our own node_modules. The whole reason there is a bundled editMenu role, one word that expands into the standard six items, is that an app with no menu has no clipboard shortcuts on macOS and the usual fix is to put exactly that submenu back.

Set the application menu to null and there is nothing to match the keystroke against. On Windows and Linux the same keys are delivered by Chromium inside the web contents, so the shortcuts keep working there. This is a macOS-only hole, which is also why it can sit in a codebase for months without anyone noticing: it works on the machine you tested it on, and it works for the half of your users who are on the other platform.

Six text fields, and one of them says Paste

I went and counted what is actually on screen. The renderer has eight <input> elements across four components. Two are checkboxes. The other six are text fields, and they are not decorative:

// ActivationScreen.tsx, the first screen any new user sees
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" ... />
<input id="token" type="text" placeholder="NTFIO-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX" ... />

The activation token arrives by email as NTFIO- and twelve characters from a deliberately unambiguous alphabet, which is a design I have written about before. The reason that alphabet has no O, 0, I or 1 in it is to make the token safe to read and retype. It should not have to be retyped. It is in an email, two keystrokes away from being in the field.

And then there is this one, in the form where you add a search:

<input
  placeholder="Paste your search results page URL"
  value={newUrl}
  onChange={(e) => setNewUrl(e.target.value)}
/>

The product's own instruction to the user is the word "paste". A search URL from a rental portal with filters on it is sixty to two hundred characters of query string. Nobody is typing that.

There is no second route either

The usual fallback for a missing shortcut is right-click, and Electron does not give you a context menu for free. A text field in a BrowserWindow has no Cut, Copy or Paste item unless the app handles the context-menu event on webContents and builds one. I grepped ours:

$ grep -rn "context-menu\|before-input-event\|globalShortcut" src/

Nothing. No context menu, no before-input-event interception mapping keys onto webContents.paste(), no registered shortcuts. The menu was the only path and the menu is null.

The window where this stings most is not even the main one. Notifio opens a real browser window with no automation in it so you can sign in to a rental site yourself, by hand, in a session the app then reuses. There are no browser extensions in an Electron window, so a password manager cannot fill that form. Paste is how a long generated password gets into it, and that window inherits the same empty application menu as every other window in the app.

The fix is one template, and it is platform-shaped 

app.on('ready', () => {
  // macOS keeps the menu in the system bar, and the Edit submenu is where the
  // clipboard shortcuts come from. Windows and Linux get no menu at all.
  Menu.setApplicationMenu(
    process.platform === 'darwin'
      ? Menu.buildFromTemplate([{ role: 'appMenu' }, { role: 'editMenu' }])
      : null
  );
});

Two roles, no items of my own, and the original goal survives: there is still no File menu, no View menu and no Toggle Developer Tools in a shipped build. The window chrome on Windows stays exactly as bare as it was.

The second half is a context menu, which is worth adding on every platform because right-click on a text field doing nothing is its own small wrongness:

contents.on('context-menu', (_event, props) => {
  if (!props.isEditable) return;
  Menu.buildFromTemplate([
    { role: 'cut' }, { role: 'copy' }, { role: 'paste' }, { type: 'separator' }, { role: 'selectAll' },
  ]).popup();
});

What makes this one uncomfortable is that Menu was already imported and already in use. The tray menu a few lines further down is built with Menu.buildFromTemplate, with a Show Window item and a Quit item, because the window's close button hides rather than quits. The API I needed was on screen while I wrote the line that broke the clipboard.

I found this by reading, not from a support email, and the fix is not shipped yet, so the honest status is: if you are on a Mac, this is the current behaviour. It is also the cheapest thing in the world to check in your own app. Launch it, click into a text field, press Cmd+V. If nothing happens, your menu is the reason, and it is two roles away from being fixed.

The app itself is on the download page as a Mac DMG for each architecture and a Windows installer, the first-run walkthrough is in the help pages, and the search-adding step with that placeholder in it is described per site on the supported sites pages, for example the Kamernet one. It is a one-time licence, which means the activation screen with the two text fields on it is a screen every single customer sees exactly once, on their first launch, and it is the screen this bug lands on hardest.

title: Phương Thức (Method) Trong Java
description:
Phương thức (method) trong Java là một khối mã được định nghĩa trong một lớp, có nhiệm vụ thực hiện một chức năng hoặc một loạt các chức năng cụ thể. Phương thức giúp chia nhỏ chương trình thành các phần nhỏ, dễ quản lý và có thể tái sử dụng. Trong Java, phương thức được chia thành hai loại:

Phương thức không trả về (Void Method)
Phương thức có trả về (Returning Method).

Ảnh mô tả hai phương thức chính trong java.

Khai báo và định nghĩa phương thức

Cấu trúc cơ bản của một phương thức trong Java:


Ví Dụ 
<từ_khóa_truy_câp> <kiểu_dữ_liệu> <tên_phương_thức>(tham_số) {

    // Thân phương thức - chứa các câu lệnh thực thi chức năng

}

Giải thích các thành phần:

↳ <từ_khóa_truy_câp>: Từ khóa truy cập cho phương thức (ví dụ: public, private, static).

↳ <kiểu_dữ_liệu>: Kiểu dữ liệu mà phương thức trả về (có thể là void nếu không trả về giá trị).

↳ <tên_phương_thức>: Tên của phương thức (phải tuân theo quy tắc đặt tên Java).

↳ (tham_số): Danh sách các tham số truyền vào phương thức (mỗi tham số có kiểu dữ liệu và tên).

↳ Thân phương thức: Chứa các câu lệnh thực thi chức năng của phương thức.

Quy ước đặt tên phương thức

↳ Sử dụng tên mô tả, thể hiện rõ ràng chức năng mà phương thức thực hiện.

↳ Tránh đặt tên quá dài hoặc quá ngắn.

↳ Sử dụng chữ thường cho các từ trong tên và viết hoa chữ cái đầu tiên của các từ tiếp theo.

↳ Tránh sử dụng các ký tự đặc biệt, dấu gạch dưới, không được sử dụng dấu cách trong tên.

↳ Sử dụng tên ngắn gọn cho các phương thức đơn giản, tên dài hơn cho các phương thức phức tạp.

↳ Sử dụng tên nhất quán cho các phương thức có chức năng tương tự.

Ⅰ. Phương thức không trả về (Void Method)

Phương thức không trả về là phương thức mà sau khi thực thi, nó không trả về bất kỳ giá trị nào. Kiểu dữ liệu của phương thức này được chỉ định là void. Không cần sử dụng từ khóa return trừ khi bạn muốn kết thúc phương thức sớm. Chức năng chính là thực hiện hành động, thay đổi trạng thái hoặc tương tác với người dùng.


Example.java 
public class Example {

    // Phương thức không trả về giá trị nào (void)

    public void printMessage(String message) {

        System.out.println("Tin Nhắn: " + message);

    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Example example = new Example();


    // Gọi phương thức printMessage
    example.printMessage("Xin Chào, Thế Giới!"); // Output: Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!
}




}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!

Trong ví dụ trên: Phương thức printMessage(String message) không trả về giá trị nào, do đó kiểu trả về của nó là void. Phương thức này chỉ thực hiện nhiệm vụ in ra thông điệp được truyền vào.

Ⅱ. Phương thức trả về (Returning Method)

Phương thức trả về là phương thức thực hiện một chức năng và có trả về giá trị sau khi thực thi.

Đặc điểm phương thức trả về

↳ Được khai báo với kiểu dữ liệu trả về (không phải void) sau tên phương thức.

↳ Sử dụng từ khóa return để trả về giá trị cho chương trình gọi.

↳ Giá trị trả về có thể được sử dụng trong các biểu thức hoặc gán cho biến.


Example.java 
public class Example {

    // Phương thức trả về giá trị kiểu int

    public int add(int a, int b) {

        return a + b;

    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Example example = new Example();


    // Gọi phương thức add và nhận giá trị trả về
    int sum = example.add(5, 3);
    System.out.println("Tổng: " + sum); // Output: Tổng: 8
}




}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Tổng: 8

Trong ví dụ trên: Phương thức add(int a, int b) trả về một giá trị kiểu int. Kết quả của phương thức add(5, 3) là 8, được trả về và lưu trữ trong biến Tổng.

Cách gọi phương thức trả về trong hàm Main

Nếu phương thức không được khai báo là static, bạn cần tạo một đối tượng của lớp chứa phương thức đó để gọi nó. Nếu phương thức được khai báo là static, bạn có thể gọi nó trực tiếp mà không cần tạo đối tượng của lớp. Để gọi một phương thức trong hàm main của Java, bạn cần thực hiện các bước sau:

↳ Khai báo và định nghĩa phương thức trong lớp của bạn.

↳ Tạo một đối tượng của lớp đó (nếu phương thức không phải là phương thức static).

↳ Gọi phương thức thông qua đối tượng (hoặc trực tiếp nếu là phương static).

Cú pháp phương thức trả về

Để gọi một phương thức trong hàm main, bạn sử dụng cú pháp sau:


Cú pháp 
<đối_tượng>.<tên_phương_thức>(<tham_số1_>, <tham_số_2>, ...);

Giải thích từng phần:

↳ <đối_tượng>: Là tham chiếu đến đối tượng của lớp mà phương thức thuộc về.

↳ Dấu chấm: Được sử dụng để phân biệt đối tượng và tên phương thức.

↳ <tên_phương_thức>: Là tên của phương thức cần gọi.

↳ (<tham_số_1>, <tham_số_2>, ...): Là danh sách các tham số truyền vào phương thức (nếu có).


Example.java 
public class Example {

    // Phương thức không tĩnh

    public void printMessage(String message) {

        System.out.println("Tin Nhắn: " + message);

    }

    // Phương thức trả về tổng của hai số nguyên

    public int add(int a, int b) {

        return a + b;

    }

       // Phương thức tĩnh

    public static void printMessage1(String message) {

        System.out.println("Tin Nhắn 1: " + message);

    }

    // Phương thức tĩnh trả về tổng của hai số nguyên

    public static int add1(int a, int b) {

        return a + b;

    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Tạo một đối tượng của lớp Example

        Example example = new Example();


    // Gọi phương thức printMessage thông qua đối tượng example
    example.printMessage("Xin Chào, Thế Giới!"); // Output: Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!
    // Gọi phương thức add thông qua đối tượng example và nhận kết quả
    int sum = example.add(5, 3);
    System.out.println("Tổng: " + sum); // Output: Tổng: 8

    // Gọi phương thức tĩnh printMessage trực tiếp
    printMessage1("Xin Chào, Phương Thức static!"); // Output: Tin Nhắn 1: Xin Chào, phương thức static!
    // Gọi phương thức tĩnh add trực tiếp và nhận kết quả
    int sum1 = add1(5, 3);
    System.out.println("Tổng 1: " + sum1); // Output: Tổng: 8
}




}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!

Tổng: 8

Tin Nhắn 1: Xin Chào, Phương Thức static!

Tổng 1: 8

Lưu ý:

↳ Chỉ có thể gọi các phương thức truy cập công khai (public) từ bên ngoài lớp.

↳ Kiểu dữ liệu và số lượng tham số truyền vào phương thức phải khớp với ↳ kiểu dữ liệu và số lượng tham số được khai báo trong định nghĩa phương thức.

title: Unsupervised Tool Evolution for Coding Agents in Data-Lake Analytics
description:
arXiv:2610.27327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents can answer analytical questions over a data lake by discovering, cleaning, and joining the relevant data. However, they discard this work after each question and redo it from scratch for the next one. Tool evolution, which automatically builds and refines reusable tools across tasks, is a natural fit for this repetition. Since a ground-truth label for a data-lake question requires an expert to solve it first, we consider the unsupervised setting. We propose TEAL (Tool Evolution for Analytics over data Lakes), which evolves a library of tools and usage skills for a given Worker agent without labels. Two agents propose tools from complementary evidence, an Explorer from the data lake itself and a Critic from Worker trajectories. A proposed change is kept only if the Worker adopts the tool on a rerun without extra steps and any changed answer is supported by trajectory evidence. We also introduce TEAL-Q, which generates synthetic questions for tool evolution when real ones are unavailable. We evaluate on KramaBench and LakeQA with four Worker LLMs under step budgets, which cap the number of steps the Worker may take per question. With a tight budget of 10 or 15 steps, TEAL improves every Worker on both benchmarks, lifting Sonnet-5 at 15 steps by 9.3 points on KramaBench and 21.7 points on LakeQA. A tighter budget also yields better feedback for evolution. For example, Sonnet-5's LakeQA library evolved at 20 steps and deployed unchanged at 30 steps scores 68.3, above both the baseline (59.6) and a library evolved directly at 30 steps (64.2). Additionally, a library evolved on synthetic questions performs comparably to one evolved on real questions. These results show that useful tools can be evolved without labels, and hopefully inspire future work on what to evolve and how to obtain feedback in unsupervised agent evolution.

title: ClockMark: Adaptive and Host-Dependent Watermarking for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27079v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) watermarking operates on the next-token distribution that evolves during generation. In streaming generation, each sampled token becomes part of the text and affects subsequent distributions. Embedding therefore proceeds with a changing host, unlike classical watermarking, which adapts embedding to an existing host signal. To accommodate this difference, we formulate a novel embedding framework for LLM watermarking based on two principles. We first argue that embedding should be adaptive, retaining the state of previous sampling decisions to better guide subsequent choices. We further argue that embedding should be host-dependent, using the current LLM distribution to constrain both token selection and state updates. Guided by these principles and the two requirements of distribution preservation and robustness to text editing, we propose ClockMark. It combines adaptive and host-dependent embedding with message spreading, embedding the full payload in each watermarked token. Theoretically, we prove that ClockMark preserves the original LLM sequence distribution, thereby maintaining generation quality. Empirically, extensive experiments against 12 baselines demonstrate improved robustness to text editing, with gains of up to 16.08 percentage points in bit accuracy over the strongest tested baseline.

Correction: API base path limit for Apigee hybrid organizations

The December 16, 2024 release note for enhanced per-environment proxy limits stated that the maximum number of API base paths per Apigee organization is 3000. That number is incorrect. The maximum number of API base paths per organization is 6,000 for both Apigee and Apigee hybrid.

For optimal performance, Apigee recommends using no more than 3,000 API proxy basepaths per environment or environment group. This is a recommendation, not an enforced limit.

For more information, see Limits and Enhanced per-environment proxy limits.

Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta is available in Preview. Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta is a reasoning model trained for agentic workflows and competitive coding. It delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable built-in tool calling with MCP support, and 1M-token long context for multi-step tasks.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.10.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Impact-aware PR delta scanning: Added --diff and --staged flags to cm find to audit modified pull request hunks and 1-hop neighbor files while suppressing pre-existing vulnerabilities.
  • SARIF report export and CI gating: Added SARIF v2.1.0 export (--format sarif, --output) and severity-based CI gating (--fail-on) to cm report to integrate scan results into CI/CD pipelines and code scanning tools.
  • Adaptive hybrid deep scanning: Added --deep and --deep-workers flags to cm find to combine deterministic file pruning, parallel package-batched analysis, and post-triage verification for higher vulnerability recall and precision.
  • Custom workspace directory: Added support for the CM_HOME environment variable to override the default ~/.codemender directory for configuration, local state (state.db), backups, and artifacts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Required build and test validation (build.command) to succeed during cm fix before marking a patch as applied and a finding as fixed.
    • Stabilized vulnerability fingerprints across multiple scans and bound cm verify directly to the target finding ID to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Restored the configured session model automatically when reconnecting to an active session with cm session resume.
    • Updated cm verify to add .exploit to .gitignore before execution so cancelled verification sessions do not leave untracked proof-of-concept scripts.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE ambient networking is now available in Preview through an allowlist.

GKE ambient networking provides a simplified, sidecarless deployment model for a service mesh with Layer 4 capabilities. By moving proxy functionality to node-level components integrated into GKE Dataplane V2, ambient networking reduces resource overhead, eliminates workload restarts for proxy updates, and simplifies mesh lifecycle management.

The Preview release supports single-cluster Layer 4 mesh capabilities using the Gateway API, which includes mutual TLS (mTLS), service discovery, Layer 4 traffic management, and Layer 4 telemetry.

For more information, see Ambient networking overview and Prepare GKE ambient networking.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Knowledge Catalog support for importing dbt metadata is now generally available and includes the following updates:

  • You can import metadata from dbt Cloud job runs using the dbt Cloud interface, the dbt platform CLI, or the dbt Administrative API and webhooks.
  • You can generate and import metadata artifacts from dbt Core 2.x and dbt Fusion in addition to dbt Core 1.x.
  • You can import entry links (--include-entry-links and --skip-bigquery-link) to capture dbt lineage and semantic relationships and link materialized dbt nodes to physical BigQuery tables, and search related BigQuery entries using the lookupEntryLinks method.
  • You can configure dbt metadata import jobs and search or view imported dbt entries using the Google Cloud console, the Google Cloud CLI, or the Dataplex REST API.

For more information, see Import metadata from dbt Core.

Feature

Data products now support configuring a default IAM role in an access group. The default role, once configured, is automatically granted on all packaged and supported assets in the data product. Data product owners can override the default role for individual assets. In addition, the assets table in a data product now shows the permission state of each asset (Applied, Failed, or Unsupported).

For more information, see Create data products and Manage data products.

Announcement

This dialog notifies users that authorizing the connection allows Looker to access data on their behalf, and that privileged Looker users—such as administrators and developers—may have visibility into their data (for example, when an administrator runs queries by using another user's active OAuth token during a sudo session).
