title: Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition with Bidirectional Audio--Text Cross-Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.26868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) are subtle behavioural states that can be expressed through both what a person says and how it is spoken. This paper presents an audio--text framework for video-level A/H recognition. Full-video transcripts and speech waveforms are encoded using pre-trained multilingual BERT and wav2vec~2.0, respectively, and projected into a shared representation space. Two stacked bidirectional cross-attention blocks allow linguistic tokens to attend to acoustic frames and acoustic frames to attend to linguistic context without requiring explicit temporal alignment. The resulting sequences are aggregated through masked mean pooling and combined using concatenation, element-wise products, and absolute differences for binary classification. We evaluate the model on the subject-independent split of the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) dataset. The proposed system achieves 72.19\% accuracy, 75.00\% precision, 81.13\% recall, 77.95\% A/H F1-score, and 70.16\% Macro-F1 on the test set. These results demonstrate the potential of jointly modelling linguistic and acoustic information for automatic A/H recognition.code at:https://github.com/DorriG/ECCV.

title: Blocking Temp-Mail Signups in a React Form with Real-Time Validation
description:
Throwaway addresses from services like Mailinator or 10 Minute Mail pass every basic regex check. They have a valid format, a real domain, and a working inbox, just one that disappears in an hour. If your signup form feeds a trial, a gated download, or a lead list, those signups add noise and sometimes abuse.

Here's a practical way to catch them in a React form: a debounced check while the user types, a small backend proxy so your API key never reaches the browser, and a server-side re-check on submit.

The architecture

Three pieces, and the order matters:

  1. React form that checks the email shortly after the user stops typing
  2. Your own backend route that calls the validation API, so the key stays secret
  3. A final check on submit on the server, because anything running in the browser can be bypassed

Skip piece 2 and you'll end up shipping an API key in your frontend bundle. Skip piece 3 and anyone can post straight to your signup endpoint and avoid the check entirely.

Step 1: A small debounce hook

Without debouncing, you'd fire a request on every keystroke.

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function useDebounce(value, delay) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  }, [value, delay]);

  return debounced;
}

Step 2: The form component 

export default function SignupForm() {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('idle'); // idle | checking | ok | blocked
  const debouncedEmail = useDebounce(email, 600);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Skip empty or obviously malformed input
    if (!debouncedEmail || !/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/.test(debouncedEmail)) {
      setStatus('idle');
      return;
    }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    setStatus('checking');

    fetch('/api/check-email', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ email: debouncedEmail }),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })
      .then((res) => res.json())
      .then((data) => setStatus(data.allowed ? 'ok' : 'blocked'))
      .catch((err) => {
        // Ignore cancelled requests; fail open on real errors
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setStatus('ok');
      });

    // Cancel the in-flight request if the email changes again
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [debouncedEmail]);

  return (
    <form>
      <input
        type="email"
        value={email}
        onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="you@company.com"
      />
      {status === 'checking' && <p>Checking...</p>}
      {status === 'blocked' && (
        <p>Please use a permanent email address, temporary inboxes aren't accepted.</p>
      )}
      <button type="submit" disabled={status === 'blocked' || status === 'checking'}>
        Sign up
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

Two details worth noticing. The AbortController cancels stale requests so a slow response for an old value can't overwrite the result for the current one. And errors fail open: if the validation service has a hiccup, you let the signup through rather than blocking a real user.

Step 3: The backend proxy

A minimal Express route that keeps the key on the server:

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/api/check-email', async (req, res) => {
  const { email } = req.body;
  if (!email) return res.status(400).json({ allowed: false });

  try {
    const url =
      `https://api.gamalogic.com/v1/validate` +
      `?email=${encodeURIComponent(email)}` +
      `&api_key=${process.env.GAMALOGIC_API_KEY}`;

    const response = await fetch(url);
    const result = await response.json();

    res.json({ allowed: isAcceptable(result) });
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Validation error:', err.message);
    res.json({ allowed: true }); // fail open
  }
});

// Placeholder logic: check the API docs for the actual response fields
// and map them here (disposable flag, validity, risk level, etc.)
function isAcceptable(result) {
  if (result.disposable) return false;
  if (result.valid === false) return false;
  return true;
}

app.listen(3000);

I'm calling Gamalogic's real-time validation API here, which runs syntax, domain, SMTP and risk checks in one request. The field names in isAcceptable are placeholders, so check the response schema in the API documentation and adjust the mapping to match.

Step 4: Re-check on submit, server-side

The client-side check is for user experience only. Your actual signup handler should validate again:

app.post('/api/signup', async (req, res) => {
  const { email } = req.body;

  const allowed = await checkEmailServerSide(email); // same logic as above
  if (!allowed) {
    return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Please use a permanent email address.' });
  }

  // ...create the account
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

Without this, a bot or a curious user can skip your React form and post directly to the endpoint.

Things to watch out for

  • False positives. No detection is perfect. Keep the error message polite and let users fix their input, rather than silently rejecting them.
  • Latency. Real-time checks add a delay. The debounce and the "Checking..." state keep the form feeling responsive, and you should test latency against your own traffic and region.
  • Rate limits and cost. Every keystroke pause is a billable call on most services. The debounce helps, and you can add a simple cache for addresses you've already checked.
  • Don't over-block. Some people use privacy aliases from legitimate services (like Apple's hide-my-email) that aren't throwaway inboxes. Decide what your policy is before you ship it.

Why use an API instead of a blocklist

A hand-maintained list of disposable domains goes stale quickly, since new services appear all the time, and it can't confirm whether a mailbox actually exists. A validation API handles the domain matching, the live SMTP check, and the risk scoring together. I work with Gamalogic on this side of things, and its fake and disposable email checker covers this use case. ZeroBounce and Kickbox have comparable APIs if you're already integrated with one of them.

title: I Tested a Map-Based AI 3D Generator on the Bay Bridge: Notes and Limits
description:
I needed a quick 3D blockout of the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge for a lighting and camera test. Hand-modeling 4.5 miles of bridge was out of the question. I wanted something rough enough to answer scale questions in an afternoon, not a survey asset.
So I tried a map-first approach: select the area, generate a model, then fix what the generator cannot know.

TL;DR

  • A selection covering both spans and the island produced a usable massing model in minutes.
  • Scale was close enough for camera blocking, not for measurement.
  • Cables and tunnel portals needed manual work.
  • Good for silhouette and fog tests, bad for structural detail. ## The actual constraint This was previsualization. I wanted cameras at deck level, tower base, and on a hillside, then to see how fog separated the layers. I needed the footprint, deck heights, tower positions, and a rough city backdrop. Not rivets or lane markings. That distinction matters. A model that is wrong about a bolt can still be right about a silhouette. A model that is wrong about deck height cannot. ## Step 1: define the selection I used GenAnywhere, which works by drawing an area on a map and generating a 3D model from that selection. My first selection was too tight, just deck and towers, and the result floated in empty space. The second included the corridor from the San Francisco anchorage to the Oakland touchdown, open water on both sides, Yerba Buena Island, and a thin strip of waterfront. That produced a much better base. The selection is the most important input: too small and the model has no context; too large and you spend an hour deleting buildings you do not need. ## Step 2: generate, then audit scale The first export looked convincing until I put a camera at deck level. The eastern tower read too short relative to the roadway. I checked known dimensions, roughly 160 meters for the tower and 624 meters for the main span, and scaled the tower group. After that, proportions matched well enough for blocking. I also counted the towers. The western span has two; the eastern span has one. A quick count catches more errors than it should. ## Step 3: repair the geometry The generator gave me a massing model, not an engineer's model. Three fixes took most of the time:
  • Cables. The eastern span's fan came in as straight segments. I replaced it with curves and a radial array, then adjusted the anchor points.
  • Suspenders. The western span needed vertical ropes at regular intervals. An array modifier handled it.
  • Tunnel portals. The entrances were merged into the terrain. I cut two openings and added simple concrete surrounds. None of this is hard, but it is not automatic. Budget for it.

Step 4: block the cameras

I set three: bay trail at eye level, under the western span looking up at the truss, and East Bay hills with a long lens. The hillside shot immediately showed a problem: the model's city blocks were too tall and blocked the bridge. I scaled the backdrop down and moved the camera.
That is the point of a blockout. You find composition problems before materials.

Where it earns its place

Fast coverage of a large, complex site. Useful silhouettes for fog and lighting tests. Easy iteration on the selection. Enough context to judge how the bridge sits in the bay.

Where it falls apart

Cable topology is approximate, especially on the self-anchored suspension span. Textures are flat at close range. Railings and road markings are missing. Nothing here is suitable for structural analysis, clearance checks, or construction documents.
I would not hand this to an engineer. I would hand it to a layout artist.

When not to use it

If you need measured accuracy, use survey data, CAD, or photogrammetry. If you need a hero close-up of a cable band, model it by hand. The map-first workflow is for the wide shot, the camera plan, and the early look-development pass.

What I would change next time

Split the selection into two runs: eastern span, then western span plus island. Each half had different geometry problems, and fixing them together was messy. Two smaller models joined in Blender would have been faster.
The blockout took an afternoon. Most of that was cable repair, not generation. Fair trade for a scene I would otherwise have skipped.

title: The Bridge Role: How Operations Liaisons Turn Plant Problems into Reliable Performance
description:
Introduction: the problem nobody owns

Most downtime in a production plant does not come from one dramatic failure. It comes from small, recurring problems that fall between departments. A pump trips every third shift. A recipe change quietly overloads a conveyor. An operator adds a manual workaround that becomes the "standard" without anyone approving it. Each event is handled, logged, and closed, and the underlying pattern survives.

Operations owns the process. Maintenance owns the equipment. Engineering owns the design. The problems that cost the most often live in the gaps between those three groups. This article describes the role that works in those gaps: the operations liaison. It is the person who troubleshoots operational problems, coaches the people running the equipment, gathers improvement ideas, advises project teams, and keeps operations and maintenance working from the same facts.

I will describe the responsibilities in practical terms, show how they fit together, and include a small Java example for one of the most useful tools in this work: a downtime Pareto analysis.

Why the liaison role matters

Reliability programs fail for predictable reasons. Maintenance works from work orders that describe symptoms ("pump 4 tripped") but not context (what the operator was doing, which product was running, what changed in the previous 24 hours). Operations works from production targets that reward keeping the line running, which can encourage workarounds that hide root causes. Engineering designs against assumptions that may not match daily reality.

A liaison does not replace any of these functions. Instead, the liaison makes their information usable across the boundaries. Three things matter most:

  • Shared facts. Everyone is looking at the same downtime data, classified the same way.
  • Short feedback loops. Problems reach the people who can fix them within a shift, not a month later in a review meeting.
  • Clear ownership. Every recurring problem has a named owner and a next action.

When these three conditions exist, plants tend to improve steadily. When they are missing, even well-funded maintenance programs stall.

Responsibility 1: Troubleshoot from the floor up

The first instinct in many organizations is to troubleshoot from the spreadsheet down: pull the data, find the outlier, assign a cause. That approach is useful, but it misses context that only exists on the floor. A structured approach works better:

  1. Describe the event precisely. What stopped, when, for how long, and what the equipment was doing just before. Avoid "it failed" as a description.
  2. Walk the process with the operator who was there. Ask what changed: product, setpoint, crew, raw material lot, ambient temperature. Operators often know about changes that never reached a system.
  3. Separate symptom, mechanism, and root cause. A seal failure is a symptom. Overheating from misalignment is a mechanism. A maintenance procedure that skipped the alignment check is a root cause.
  4. Test the hypothesis with data. Compare the event against the last ten occurrences. If the pattern does not hold, the hypothesis is incomplete.
  5. Record the outcome in a form others can reuse. A short, consistent problem record beats a long narrative nobody reads.

The discipline here is not complicated, but it is easy to skip under production pressure. The value comes from doing it consistently.

Responsibility 2: Coach operators, not just report to them

Operators understand the process in ways that engineers and managers often do not. They hear the equipment change, feel the vibration, and know which valve needs a second turn. Treating them as a source of reports only wastes that knowledge.

Regular operational discussions, such as a fifteen-minute review at the start of each shift, work well when they focus on three questions:

  • What went well in the last shift, and why?
  • What went wrong, and what did we learn?
  • What do we want to try next, and how will we know if it worked?

The goal of coaching is capability, not compliance. An operator who understands why a parameter matters will make better decisions when the situation is not covered by a procedure. That is the difference between a plant that depends on a few senior people and one that can sustain performance when those people are on vacation.

Coaching also means being honest about your own gaps. If a question from an operator reveals that you do not know the answer, say so, and find out together.

Responsibility 3: Turn ideas into project proposals

Improvement ideas are abundant on a plant floor. The challenge is filtering them and developing the good ones into proposals that engineering and management can evaluate. A practical process has four steps:

  1. Solicit ideas broadly. Make it easy to submit a suggestion: a shared form, a board in the break room, or a standing item in shift reviews.
  2. Screen quickly. For each idea, ask three questions: what problem does it solve, how often does that problem occur, and what is the rough cost of the problem? Many ideas can be closed in a few minutes.
  3. Develop the promising ones with the right engineers. Bring the operator who proposed the idea into the design conversation. They know the constraints that a drawing does not show.
  4. Write a proposal with a clear case. State the problem with data, the proposed change, the expected benefit, the cost, the risk, and how success will be measured.

Ideas that come from operators have a high adoption rate once they are implemented, because the people who will run the change helped shape it. That is one of the strongest arguments for building this process deliberately.

Responsibility 4: Advise project teams early

Projects that ignore operational reality tend to create new problems. A new line may be designed without enough space for maintenance access. A control system may be specified without considering how operators will recover from a fault at three in the morning. A commissioning plan may assume ideal raw materials.

The liaison's role is to bring operational experience into the design phase, while there is still time to change it. Useful questions include:

  • How will operators know the system is in a fault state, and what will they do next?
  • What maintenance tasks will be required, how often, and can they be done without shutting down the whole line?
  • What happens during a changeover, and how long will it take?
  • Which parts of this design have we seen fail before, in our plant or elsewhere?

Advice given early is cheap. The same advice given after installation is expensive, and often comes with pressure to accept a workaround.

Responsibility 5: Be the interface between operations and maintenance

This is the responsibility that holds the others together. Operations and maintenance often have different priorities, different vocabularies, and different measures of success. Operations wants the line running. Maintenance wants time to do planned work. Both are right, and both can be wrong about the other's constraints.

A liaison makes the trade-off visible. For example, a recurring stop might be fixed by a thirty-minute planned maintenance task every two weeks. Operations may resist losing thirty minutes, but if the data shows that the recurring stop costs two hours each time, the trade-off becomes concrete. The decision then belongs to the people with the authority to make it, with the facts in front of them.

A practical tool: downtime Pareto analysis in Java

One of the most useful analyses a liaison can run is a Pareto chart of downtime causes. The principle is simple: a small number of causes usually account for most of the lost time. Identifying them focuses effort where it matters.

The following Java example reads downtime events, aggregates minutes by cause, and prints the causes ranked by impact with a cumulative percentage. It uses only the standard library.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class DowntimePareto {

    public record DowntimeEvent(String cause, int minutes) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<DowntimeEvent> events = List.of(
            new DowntimeEvent("Pump seal failure", 95),
            new DowntimeEvent("Conveyor misalignment", 60),
            new DowntimeEvent("Operator changeover delay", 45),
            new DowntimeEvent("Pump seal failure", 120),
            new DowntimeEvent("Sensor fault", 20),
            new DowntimeEvent("Conveyor misalignment", 75),
            new DowntimeEvent("Raw material shortage", 180),
            new DowntimeEvent("Pump seal failure", 80)
        );

        printPareto(events);
    }

    static void printPareto(List<DowntimeEvent> events) {
        Map<String, Integer> minutesByCause = events.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                DowntimeEvent::cause,
                Collectors.summingInt(DowntimeEvent::minutes)));

        int totalMinutes = minutesByCause.values().stream()
            .mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();

        List<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> ranked = minutesByCause.entrySet().stream()
            .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed())
            .toList();

        System.out.printf("%-30s %8s %8s %12s%n", "Cause", "Minutes", "Share", "Cumulative");
        System.out.println("-".repeat(62));

        int running = 0;
        for (var entry : ranked) {
            running += entry.getValue();
            double share = 100.0 * entry.getValue() / totalMinutes;
            double cumulative = 100.0 * running / totalMinutes;
            System.out.printf("%-30s %8d %7.1f%% %11.1f%%%n",
                entry.getKey(), entry.getValue(), share, cumulative);
        }

        System.out.printf("%nTotal downtime: %d minutes%n", totalMinutes);
    }
}

Running this produces a ranked list that makes the priorities obvious. In this sample, the top two causes account for most of the lost time, which tells you where to focus the next root-cause investigation. The value is not in the code itself but in the habit: review this ranking every week, with operators and maintenance in the same room, and agree on one action per top cause.

Two cautions. First, the quality of the analysis depends entirely on consistent cause classification. If "pump seal failure" and "seal leak" are recorded as different causes, the Pareto will understate the problem. Second, a Pareto shows where time was lost, not why. It is the starting point for investigation, not the conclusion.

Best practices

Based on the responsibilities above, these practices consistently improve plant reliability:

  • Classify downtime consistently. Agree on a short list of cause categories and enforce it. Review new categories monthly.
  • Hold short, frequent cross-functional reviews. A weekly thirty-minute meeting with operations, maintenance, and engineering beats a quarterly report.
  • Give every recurring problem an owner and a date. A problem without an owner returns.
  • Involve operators in solutions, not just in reporting problems. Their input improves the design and their buy-in makes adoption faster.
  • Bring operational experience into projects before design freeze. Changes are cheap on paper and expensive on the floor.
  • Measure outcomes, not activity. Track repeat failures, mean time between failures, and time to recover, not just the number of meetings held.

A practical roadmap

If you are taking on this role in a plant that does not have it formalized, a reasonable first ninety days looks like this:

Weeks 1 to 3: Listen and map. Spend time on the floor with operators and maintenance technicians. Map the top five recurring problems and who currently owns each one. Do not change anything yet.

Weeks 4 to 6: Establish the facts. Agree on a downtime classification scheme. Run the first Pareto analysis. Share the results openly, including the parts that are uncomfortable for one group or another.

Weeks 7 to 9: Start the loop. Launch a short weekly cross-functional review. Assign one owner and one action for each of the top three causes. Begin the shift-start coaching conversations.

Weeks 10 to 13: Build capability and pipeline. Open an improvement idea channel, screen the first batch of suggestions, and take the best one or two into a proposal with engineering. Review progress against the metrics you agreed on in week 4.

Expect resistance in the first month. It usually comes from people who feel the analysis is judging them. Address it directly: the purpose is to fix the process, not to find someone to blame.

Conclusion and key takeaways

The operations liaison role is easy to underestimate because its success looks like the absence of problems. But reliable plants are built by people who notice the recurring issue before it becomes a crisis, who respect what operators know, who bring the right engineers into the conversation early, and who make sure operations and maintenance are working from the same facts.

Key takeaways:

  • Most costly downtime is recurring and falls between departments. Someone must own the gaps.
  • Troubleshoot from the floor up, separating symptom, mechanism, and root cause.
  • Coach operators to build capability, not just to collect reports.
  • Turn improvement ideas into proposals by screening quickly and developing the best with the right engineers.
  • Bring operational experience into projects while changes are still cheap.
  • Use simple, consistent data, such as a downtime Pareto, to set priorities and keep operations and maintenance aligned.

If you have built this kind of role in your own plant, I would be glad to hear what worked and what did not. The details differ from site to site, and the shared lessons are worth comparing.

title: Schneider's modular AI design: what the 80% installation-time claim actually measures
description:
Schneider Electric announced RapidScale Modular Data Center Reference Design 115 on October 21, positioning it as a prefabricated blueprint supporting NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure. The announcement also highlights an installation-time study with Compass Datacenters. For project teams, the study's boundaries matter as much as the percentage.

In its October 20 explanation of the work, Schneider reports a reduction from 75.5 to 15 hours per pod, approximately 80%, for the configuration analyzed. The comparison covers onsite activities preparing a pod for IT equipment installation.

The prefabricated durations were observed during a Compass deployment. The traditional comparison combines observed containment-installation durations with schedules developed by mechanical, electrical and plumbing specialists for equivalent additional infrastructure. Offsite manufacturing and activities after installation verification are excluded.

This is a supplier-and-customer study with a defined comparison, rather than an independently reproduced result or a measurement of total campus delivery time.

Operational analysis: put the saved activity on the project schedule

Before using the result in a business case, identify where the comparable work sits in your own programme. Does it delay the start of equipment installation, or can it already happen while another team completes a different dependency?

A shorter task affects the overall completion date when it removes time from the sequence that governs completion. If the project is waiting for another prerequisite, the benefit may instead be lower coordination pressure, additional schedule margin or earlier availability of one work area.

Those can be worthwhile outcomes. They should have their own evidence and cost assumptions.

I would ask the delivery team to show the baseline sequence and the prefabricated sequence side by side, with the same start and finish conditions. Then identify which dependencies changed and which remained. Keep the estimate of onsite installation savings separate from the forecast date for usable compute.

Include the work that moves upstream

Prefabrication creates a different allocation of work between factory and site. A complete procurement comparison should therefore track the manufacturing slot, design freeze, inspection records, transport and site receiving arrangements alongside field installation.

For each major interface, name the party responsible for confirming that the delivered assembly matches the receiving site. Record the approved dimensions, connection locations and configuration version. Changes made after those decisions need a visible route through manufacturing, logistics and site teams.

The purpose is to understand whether work has been removed, performed earlier or transferred to another organization. Each outcome has different implications for risk, staffing and cash flow.

Receiving a larger assembly also deserves a practical plan. Confirm access, staging space, lifting arrangements and the sequence in which work areas become available. These are proposed project checks, not allegations about the deployment studied.

Keep commissioning in the acceptance criteria

Schneider's technical explanation says the complete technology-cooling loop still requires final onsite flushing, pressure testing and commissioning, even where sections receive factory treatment and tests.

For a buyer, that is a useful prompt to define the handover boundary precisely. Request a list of factory checks, field checks and integrated acceptance tests, with an owner and retained record for each. Explain how shipping damage, field connections or a late configuration change affects the test plan.

The acceptance package should show what was verified and under which conditions. An assembly arriving with inspection records can reduce uncertainty, while the connected installation still needs evidence that its interfaces behave as intended.

Ask for a comparable result on your configuration

The reported comparison is a starting point for questions about a specific project. Ask which parts of your proposed configuration match the study and which require additional work. Require the estimate to name exclusions, site assumptions and the experience expected of the installation team.

Then agree how actual durations will be recorded. Distinguish elapsed time from labour effort, and record waiting time separately where it matters. That makes later comparisons more useful and helps the team locate the next constraint.

The new reference design and the study address related questions at different levels. One offers an infrastructure blueprint; the other quantifies a bounded installation comparison. Operators can use both most effectively when they connect them to a complete delivery schedule and explicit acceptance evidence.

title: Why your Node.js API is leaking sensitive files (and how to fix it in 5 minutes)
description:
As developers, we often focus on writing clean code, optimizing database queries, and building robust APIs. But there is one silent killer that takes down hundreds of production environments every day: exposing sensitive files in the public root directory.

I've seen this in Node.js projects, PHP, and static sites deployed to the cloud. You think your .env, your .git folder, or your database dumps are safe... until someone runs a simple curl command and downloads your entire infrastructure.

Let's see how this happens, and how to test your own site in less than 5 minutes.

The Silent Threat: Public Folders

If your web server or CDN is misconfigured, a malicious user can try to access common paths like:

  • https://yourdomain.com/.env
  • https://yourdomain.com/.git/HEAD
  • https://yourdomain.com/backup.zip
  • https://yourdomain.com/db.sql

If the server returns 200 OK instead of 403 Forbidden or 404 Not Found, you have a critical vulnerability. Your database credentials, API keys, and source code are publicly available.

How to check if you are exposed (Right Now)

Open your terminal and run this simple curl command against your own domain:


bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com/.env
Look at the HTTP status code:

If you see HTTP/1.1 200 OK: Panic. Your .env file is exposed. Fix it immediately.

If you see HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden or HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found: You are safe.

How to fix it (Nginx/Apache)
If you are using Nginx, add this block to your server configuration:

nginx
location ~ /\.(env|git|svn|htaccess|htpasswd) {
    deny all;
    return 404;
}

location ~ \.(bak|old|sql|zip|tar\.gz)$ {
    deny all;
    return 404;
}
If you are on Express.js, ensure your static file middleware is not serving hidden files:

javascript
app.use(express.static('public', {
  dotfiles: 'deny',
  index: false
}));
How to automate this check
Checking this manually every time you deploy is a pain. There are tools that can automate this for you and give you a full security report.

I've been building a tool called Sealgrade that runs over 15 external security checks (including this exact file exposure test, SSL, DNS, and missing HTTP headers) and gives you a 0-100 health score. It's free to run an audit, and it gives you concrete remediation snippets like the ones above.

If you are deploying to production, it's worth a 30-second check: Audit your web here.

Stay safe out there, and keep your .env files private!

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.
561666530 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Prometheus library to patch the following vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Issue

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.
  • Container-Optimized OS with containerd (cos_containerd) node pools on GKE versions 1.33 and earlier, 1.34 versions earlier than 1.34.6-gke.1154000, and 1.35 versions earlier than 1.35.3-gke.1389000.

Workaround: For cos_containerd node pools, upgrade the node pool to a version with the required kernel support (for example, 1.34.6-gke.1154000 or later, 1.35.3-gke.1389000 or later, or match the control plane). title: How to design agentic tools for work
description: The Gemini Enterprise team shares their approach to making complex, multi-agent workflows feel simple, intuitive, and trustworthy.

title: cornercase: a terminal multiplexer for running coding agents in parallel
description:
This post is written by the maintainers of cornercase. It's our own project, it's free and open source (MIT or Apache-2.0), and there's nothing paid behind it. We'd like to explain what it does, how it works, and where it still falls short.

The problem

Starting ten coding agents is easy. Keeping up with them is the hard part.

Once you have a few Claude Code or Codex sessions open at the same time, the questions pile up. Which one is waiting for an answer? Which one finished while you were looking at another? What did each one change? Did two of them edit the same file?

We kept answering those questions with tmux, git worktrees and a growing pile of scripts, and we kept re-wiring that setup. cornercase is the tool we built so we could stop.

What cornercase does

cornercase is a terminal multiplexer, in the same family as tmux or Zellij, built around running agents in parallel. It runs inside the terminal you already use.

From an issue to an agent at work. Open an issue from GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Plane, Asana or Shortcut and press start. cornercase creates a worktree on a branch named after the issue, opens a tab in it, and hands the issue to the agent as its first prompt. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Grok, Cursor, Copilot and nine more agents.

One worktree and one tab per agent, with status. Each agent gets its own branch, folder and tab, so two agents never touch the same file. Tabs show who is working (◐), who needs you (!) and who finished while you were away (✓), along with the model and how full its context is. ! and ✓ climb up to the workspace and project rows, and your terminal sends a notification, also over SSH.

The review next to the work. The changes panel shows the workspace's diff as the agent writes it: uncommitted changes, the agent's commits, or everything since a base branch. You can also see what is uncommitted across every project at once. Hover a hunk to open it in your editor, copy it, or hand it back to the agent. Recent releases added staging a file and discarding a file's changes from the same panel.

Close the window. Nothing stops. A background server owns the shells. Quit detaches and running cornercase again reattaches, from any terminal. Several windows can show the same session. cornercase remote <host> keeps the window on your laptop and the shells and agents on another machine, over your own ssh, and reconnects by itself when the connection drops. Below 90 columns the sidebar folds into a menu bar, so it also works from a phone over SSH.

Scripting, so one agent can run the others. Everything in the window is also a command:

pane=$(cornercase start claude --worktree fix-login --prompt 'Fix the login form, then commit')
cornercase wait --pane "$pane" --timeout 1800   # until the agent stops: idle, done, pending or waiting
cornercase read --pane "$pane" --last-message   # what it said, from its own transcript

cornercase --help lists the rest: open projects and worktrees, split panes, type into them, press keys, wait on one agent or several, and follow events as they happen. You can teach the commands to your agents as a skill:

npx skills add usecornercase/cornercase-terminal --skill cornercase -g

An account per pane. If you have separate accounts, for example one for work and one for personal projects, each pane shows its accounts in a row under it. Pick another account there and only that pane changes. Claude Code and Codex restart on the new account in the same conversation; Gemini CLI starts a new one.

One more design choice: everything is a click, and every key goes to the program in the active pane. There are no shortcuts to learn unless you choose a prefix key.

How it works, briefly

cornercase is written in Rust. Two decisions shape most of it.

Status comes from the agent's own files, not from hooks. For Claude Code, cornercase reads the session file Claude Code keeps for each running session in ~/.claude/sessions/. It reads that file and never writes it. We decided against hooks because they mean editing your ~/.claude/settings.json or shipping a plugin, and the Stop hook doesn't fire when you interrupt with Esc. We also decided against screen scraping, because Claude's screen changes too often to match reliably. The session file turns idle right after an interrupt and switches to waiting as soon as a prompt shows.

Panes run on libghostty-vt, Ghostty's terminal core. That is why nvim, fzf, htop and full-screen agents work as expected inside a pane, in your terminal's own colours.

Honest limits

  • It's early. The current release is v0.12.172, and the project changes daily. Expect rough edges, and expect things to move.
  • Linux and macOS only, on x86_64 and arm64. There is no Windows build.
  • It's a TUI. It lives in your terminal. If you want a desktop app with its own window, cornercase isn't that.
  • Building from source needs Zig 0.15.2 on your PATH, exactly that version, because it builds Ghostty's terminal core. The prebuilt binaries don't need it.

Install

With the install script:

curl -fsSL https://usecornercase.dev/install.sh | sh

Or with Homebrew:

brew install usecornercase/tap/cornercase

Then run it:

cornercase

That starts the server and opens the window. From there, + New → open project lets you pick a folder, and Issues → pick one → start gets an agent going. Quit closes the window and leaves everything running.

cornercase checks GitHub for a new release every hour and offers to install it. cornercase update does the same from a shell.

If you'd rather look before installing anything, there's an interactive simulation on usecornercase.dev. The full walkthrough is in First steps.

Feedback

We'd like to hear from people who run several agents at once. What's still painful in your setup? What breaks? What would make you switch from plain tmux?

  • GitHub: usecornercase/cornercase-terminal for issues and pull requests
  • Discord: discord.gg/aYqCa4xC4R for questions and ideas
  • Docs: usecornercase.dev/docs

Thanks for reading.

title: Understanding the Benefits of Scaffolds through Computational Separations
description:
arXiv:2610.27157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference-time harnesses, i.e., external procedures that call a model many times and keep state across calls, can substantially improve model capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the benefits of using such harnesses and the extent to which these benefits can be internalized through training. More precisely, we conceptualize a harness $\mathcal{A}$ as an arbitrary wrapper around a base model $M$ and attempt to distill a student model from the harness's traces. Empirically we find that, even with simple scaffolds and small models, the inference-time harness significantly outperforms a distilled student. We then prove that such a gap is due to a fundamental representational limitation: inference-time harnesses can compute a closure of their per-call primitive that is $\NL$-complete even when the primitive is a trivial $\AC^0$ lookup, and that no fixed-depth forward pass can represent under the widely believed conjecture that $\NL\not\subseteq\TC^0$. Our theory suggests that expanding the representational capacity of the student relative to the task at hand, e.g., by enlarging the model, making the task easier, or lengthening its chain-of-thought, is necessary to close the gap, which we verify empirically. Finally, we scale to an agentic harness on competition math, where the same gap reappears. Overall, our results show that a harness confers on the base model a profound gain in representational power, one that training a same-class student on its traces cannot transfer back into the weights.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: How I keep a living system map of Mầm Văn — every change, before & after
description:
Hi, I'm Vũ Xuân Toàn (Vu Xuan Toan), a software developer and indie maker from Bắc Ninh, Vietnam, and the founder of Vu Xuan Toan Tech. In my intro post I mentioned Mầm Văn — the literature-learning platform I'm building for Vietnamese middle-school students (React, TypeScript, Supabase, Gemini AI). Today I want to share the part of the project I'm most proud of, because it isn't a feature for users — it's how I keep the whole system understandable while it changes every week.

The problem: the system grows faster than memory

Mầm Văn has two big portals (teacher and student), an AI content studio, a question bank, XP and mastery engines, a knowledge tree, grading workflows, notifications, an admin area… After a few months of intense building, "how does this all connect?" stopped being a question I could answer from memory.

So I built a complete map of every flow in the system — 262 nodes covering every screen, every engine, and the relationships between them (for example: publishing a lesson → notifies students, or rejecting a gift request → refunds the student's total XP wallet). Every node also lists the exact code files and functions that implement it, verified automatically against the codebase.

The rule: the map is part of the code

The map only stays true if it can never drift. So I work under one strict rule:

  1. Before changing any flow, I open the map and identify which nodes and relationships the change touches.
  2. After the change, I update the map, regenerate it, and ship it in the same commit as the code.
  3. The map and a full change history are republished automatically to my website in the same round.

You can see both, live:

  • 🗺️ The system map (interactive, click a node to light up its cluster): https://vuxuantoan.me/so-do-mam-van.html
  • 📜 The change history — every work session: what changed, in which files, with lines added/removed: https://vuxuantoan.me/lich-su-mam-van.html

Before & after, for every flow change

The part I like most: whenever a change modifies a flow, the history page automatically gets two buttons — "flow BEFORE this change" and "flow AFTER this change". Every version of the map is archived immutably, so I can reopen exactly how the system looked before any change and compare. When I recently removed an AI status bar from the question bank, the before-map still shows its node in the tree; the after-map doesn't. That makes design review honest: nothing about the system's shape is ever lost or misremembered.

Why bother?

Because an indie maker's scarcest resource isn't code — it's clarity. The map has already caught wrong assumptions before I wrote a line of code, and it lets anyone (a collaborator, a teacher using the platform, future me) understand a fairly complex product in minutes.

If you build long-lived side projects, I'd genuinely recommend stealing this workflow: one living map, updated in the same commit as the code, with archived before/after versions.

—

I'm Vũ Xuân Toàn. My home on the web is vuxuantoan.me, my code lives at github.com/vut08905, and Mầm Văn itself is live at mamvan.vercel.app. Say hi!

title: The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era
description:
title: "The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-29T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [architecture, devops, softwareengineering, cloud]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of software engineering architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Examining Each Factor (Config In Environment: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Stateless Processes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Port Binding: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Software engineering Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Examining each factor (Config in environment, Stateless processes, Port binding, Concurrency, Disposability) through modern containerized application architectures."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Supabase RLS with auth.uid() not working? Causes and fixes
description:
You wrote a tidy Row Level Security policy, something like auth.uid() = user_id, and now one of two annoying things happens: your query returns no rows at all, or it returns everybody's rows. Both are common, both are fixable, and neither means RLS is broken. It means the policy isn't seeing the identity you think it's seeing.

Let's walk the actual causes, in rough order of how often they bite people, with copy-pasteable SQL you can run against your own project.

First, what auth.uid() actually is

auth.uid() reads the sub claim out of the JWT attached to the current request. No JWT, or a JWT without a user, means auth.uid() returns NULL.

That single fact explains most "no rows" bugs. A policy like auth.uid() = user_id becomes NULL = user_id, which evaluates to NULL (not true), so the row is filtered out. Every row. Silently.

So the first debugging question is never "is my policy wrong?" It's "who does the database think I am right now?"

Cause 1: You're on the anon key, so auth.uid() is NULL

Every Supabase project ships two keys, and they are not interchangeable:

  • anon / publishable (role: anon) — public by design. It's meant to sit in your browser bundle. It is not a secret and does not need rotating. RLS is what protects your data when this key is used.
  • service_role (role: service_role) — a server-only secret that bypasses RLS entirely. More on why that's dangerous below.

If you initialize the client with the anon key and the user hasn't logged in, there's no user JWT, so auth.uid() is NULL and auth.uid() = user_id matches nothing.

Confirm which key you're holding by decoding the middle segment of the JWT (base64url-encoded JSON):

echo 'PASTE_KEY_HERE' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool

Read the role field: "anon" or "service_role". The newer key formats make it obvious without decoding: sb_publishable_... is public, sb_secret_... is the secret one.

Then confirm you're actually authenticated. In the browser:

const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser()
console.log(user)   // null here means auth.uid() will be NULL server-side

If user is null, fix sign-in first — no policy change helps until the request carries a user JWT.

Cause 2: RLS isn't actually enabled, so you get everything

The opposite symptom — you see all rows — usually means RLS isn't switched on for the table. Policies are ignored entirely until you enable RLS:

select relname, relrowsecurity
from pg_class
where relname = 'your_table';

If relrowsecurity is false, turn it on:

alter table your_table enable row level security;

One gotcha: the table owner and superusers still bypass RLS. To apply the rules even to the owner, add alter table your_table force row level security;.

Cause 3: You're testing with service_role, so it "works" (misleadingly)

The sneakiest one. Your test passes, data comes back exactly right — because the test client is using the service_role key, which bypasses RLS completely. You're not testing your policies; you're testing with the guard switched off.

service_role belongs only on a trusted server. Never in a browser, never in a public repo, never in a client .env that gets bundled. Anything prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, or EXPO_PUBLIC_ gets inlined into the client bundle at build time — perfect for the anon key and project URL, catastrophic for service_role.

And if service_role has already been committed to a repo: deleting the file is not enough. A committed secret lives in git history forever. Rotate the key in the dashboard and purge history (git filter-repo or BFG). Rotation is the part that actually revokes the leak; history-scrubbing stops the old value from being fetched back out.

Test policies with the anon key plus a real logged-in session, the way your app runs. To check directly in SQL, impersonate a role and a user inside a transaction:

begin;
-- become the anon role
set local role anon;
select * from your_table;   -- honors your anon policies

-- now simulate a logged-in user
set local role authenticated;
select set_config(
  'request.jwt.claims',
  '{"sub":"11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111","role":"authenticated"}',
  true
);
select * from your_table;   -- auth.uid() now returns that sub
rollback;

If it returns rows here but not in your app, the difference is your app's auth state, not the policy.

Cause 4: Missing GRANT

RLS policies do not grant access — they restrict it. A role needs both a matching policy and a table-level privilege. If anon or authenticated was never granted SELECT, no policy will save you; the query errors out regardless of the rows.

select grantee, privilege_type
from information_schema.role_table_grants
where table_name = 'your_table';

Supabase's default setup grants the API roles broad privileges, but if you've been locking things down by hand you may have revoked them:

grant select, insert, update, delete on your_table to authenticated;

Then let RLS decide which rows each user actually touches.

Cause 5: Missing (or wrong) TO clause

A policy with no TO clause applies to every role, including anon. That's a frequent source of "why can logged-out visitors read this?"

Scope policies explicitly:

create policy "Users read own rows"
on your_table
for select
to authenticated                       -- <- this line matters
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Multiple permissive policies are OR'd together, so a broad one you forgot about widens access. List what's really on the table:

select policyname, cmd, roles, qual, with_check
from pg_policies
where tablename = 'your_table';

Read the roles column. If you see {public} where you expected {authenticated}, that's your leak — public means every role, anon included.

Cause 6: Comparing a uuid to a text column

auth.uid() returns a uuid. If your user_id column is text, Postgres resolves uuid = text by casting the text to uuid — which throws invalid input syntax for type uuid the moment any value isn't a well-formed uuid, and adds a per-row cast even when it isn't. Check the type:

select column_name, data_type
from information_schema.columns
where table_name = 'your_table' and column_name = 'user_id';

The clean fix is a real uuid column referencing auth.users:

alter table your_table
  alter column user_id type uuid using user_id::uuid;

If you can't change the schema right now, cast inside the policy so both sides match:

using ( (select auth.uid())::text = user_id )

Prefer fixing the column type — a uuid that references auth.users(id) indexes better and is harder to get wrong later.

The policy pattern to standardize on

Notice I keep writing (select auth.uid()) instead of bare auth.uid(). Wrapping it in a select lets Postgres evaluate the function once per query instead of once per row — a real, measurable win on larger tables, and the pattern Supabase now recommends. A complete per-user set:

alter table documents enable row level security;

create policy "read own documents"
on documents for select
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

create policy "insert own documents"
on documents for insert
to authenticated
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

create policy "update own documents"
on documents for update
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Mental model for the two clauses: USING filters which existing rows a role can see (and which rows an UPDATE/DELETE may touch); WITH CHECK validates the new values being written. INSERT policies have WITH CHECK only. UPDATE usually wants both — USING to pick the row, WITH CHECK so a user can't reassign user_id to someone else.

A 60-second self-audit 

-- tables in public with RLS still disabled
select c.relname
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind = 'r'
  and c.relrowsecurity = false;

-- policies with no role restriction (they apply to anon too)
select tablename, policyname, cmd, roles
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
  and roles = '{public}';

If you want a reproducible sandbox where each failure mode fires on demand — anon-key NULL, missing GRANT, service_role bypass — plus a fuller read-only audit query to paste into the SQL editor, I put a small demo repo together: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. Clone it, run the SQL, and watch the "no rows / all rows" behavior flip as you toggle each cause. It's the fastest way I know to build the intuition.

The takeaway

When auth.uid() "doesn't work," it's almost never that RLS is broken. It's that the request isn't carrying the identity you assume: you're on the anon key with no session, RLS was never enabled, a test used service_role and hid the bug, a GRANT is missing, the TO clause is too wide, or a uuid is being compared to text. Walk the six checks in order and you'll find it.

If you'd rather not hand-audit every time you ship a new table, I maintain a $29 RLS Audit Kit — ready-to-run policy tests and a checklist that flags exactly these six failure modes across your whole schema. Entirely optional; the queries above will get you unstuck today either way.
