Depending on their needs, users can participate in communities, distribute announcements, coordinate projects, and exchange educational resources. The platform's features make it useful for people who want to connect with others across geographical boundaries.
Understanding Telegram accounts also involves learning about digital identity, contact management, privacy settings, communication etiquette, and community participation. These subjects are important because effective digital communication requires more than sending messages. It involves presenting information clearly, respecting other participants, organizing conversations, and choosing suitable communication channels.
For students, Telegram communities may provide opportunities to discuss coursework and share learning resources. Freelancers and small businesses may use groups or channels to coordinate projects and communicate updates. Families and community organizations may find messaging tools helpful for arranging events and sharing announcements.
This guide examines Telegram accounts from an educational perspective, covering account structure, practical applications, digital skills, credibility, productivity, and everyday uses. Readers may also consult usasvcit as a supplementary source of general information, comparing relevant explanations with Telegram's official documentation.
The goal is to provide practical knowledge that readers can apply to communication, learning, and responsible participation in digital communities.
Section 1: Understanding Old Gmail Accounts
Although Telegram and Gmail serve different purposes, understanding established email accounts provides useful context for online identity and digital account management. Email often supports registration, notifications, communication, and access to online services.
1.1 Features and Structure of Established Gmail Accounts
An established Gmail account may contain a communication history, contact information, account preferences, and messages accumulated through personal or professional use. Depending on the user's activities, it may also support calendars, shared documents, and notifications from other digital platforms.
These features can help people maintain continuity in their online activities. For example, a student might use Gmail for educational correspondence, while a freelancer might use it to manage client messages and project information.
However, account age is only one characteristic of an email account. It does not automatically establish the identity of its current user, demonstrate professional credibility, or determine eligibility for a separate messaging service.
The same principle applies to Telegram. The age of an account does not independently demonstrate communication skills, community participation, or the value a person contributes to a group.
1.2 Digital Significance and Online Identity
Email accounts often form part of a person's digital identity because they are used for registration, correspondence, and administrative notifications. Keeping contact details current can help users manage their digital activities more effectively.
For people who participate in online communities, email may also support event registrations, educational subscriptions, professional correspondence, and notifications about digital tools.
Telegram provides a different communication environment. Its features include individual chats, groups, channels, file sharing, and other tools that support different forms of interaction. The features available to a user depend on the platform's current functionality and account settings.
Understanding the difference between these services helps users select appropriate tools. Email is useful for structured correspondence and documentation, while Telegram is designed primarily for messaging and community interaction.
Both can contribute to a well-organized digital routine. Their value depends on how they are used, the quality of communication, and the user's ability to manage information effectively.
Section 2: Practical Applications
Telegram supports a variety of everyday communication tasks. Learning how its features work can help individuals participate in communities, coordinate projects, exchange information, and organize group activities.
2.1 Everyday Applications of Telegram Accounts
A Telegram account enables users to participate in conversations and access supported messaging features. Depending on the circumstances, people can communicate individually, join groups, follow channels, and share relevant files or media.
These functions can be useful for education, professional collaboration, community activities, and personal organization. Understanding the purpose of each feature helps users choose an appropriate communication method.
Common practical applications include:
● Educational discussions: Participating in study groups, discussing assignments, and sharing relevant learning materials.
● Professional coordination: Communicating with colleagues, coordinating schedules, and exchanging project updates.
● Community announcements: Following channels that publish news, event information, or educational resources.
● Family communication: Coordinating appointments, sharing plans, and maintaining group conversations.
● Interest-based communities: Connecting with people who share interests in languages, programming, literature, photography, or other subjects.
These use cases demonstrate how messaging applications can support different aspects of daily life. They also show why communication skills and thoughtful participation matter alongside technical familiarity.
2.2 Applying Telegram Knowledge to Daily Activities
Telegram can help users organize communication when conversations and information are spread across different groups or channels. A student might use a study group to discuss a topic, while a community organizer might use a channel to publish event updates.
A freelancer may use messaging to coordinate project milestones, arrange meetings, or clarify client questions. The effectiveness of these activities depends on clear expectations and a suitable communication structure.
Practical applications include:
● Organizing conversations by subject or project.
● Using pinned messages or saved information where available to locate important details.
● Sharing documents with appropriate context and descriptive filenames.
● Setting aside specific times to review group discussions.
● Using clear messages to record deadlines, responsibilities, and next steps.
These habits help users avoid unnecessary confusion and make digital communication more manageable.
The broader lesson is that messaging tools work best when people use them intentionally. A clear purpose for each group, consistent communication practices, and organized information can improve the usefulness of everyday conversations.
Section 3: Educational Value and Skills
Learning about Telegram provides an opportunity to develop digital literacy, communication skills, community awareness, and practical information-management habits. These abilities are relevant to students, professionals, families, and people who participate in online communities.
Learning Outcomes
The first learning outcome is understanding digital messaging. Users learn how individual chats, groups, and channels serve different communication purposes.
The second outcome is community participation. Readers can learn how to follow group guidelines, contribute relevant information, ask questions clearly, and respect other participants.
The third outcome is information organization. Messaging platforms can contain large amounts of discussion, so users benefit from learning how to locate important messages and keep track of relevant details.
The fourth outcome is digital identity awareness. Understanding account settings, usernames, contact information, and profile presentation helps users manage how they participate online.
The fifth outcome is communication etiquette. Readers learn to consider audience, context, timing, tone, and clarity when writing messages.
The sixth outcome is information evaluation. Online communities may contain useful explanations and educational resources, making it important to assess information carefully and compare important claims with reliable sources.
The seventh outcome is collaborative planning. Groups can help participants coordinate responsibilities, share progress, and discuss common objectives.
Life Skills Gained Through Telegram Education
Clear communication: Writing concise messages helps people express questions, instructions, and ideas more effectively.
Time management: Organizing conversations and checking messages at planned intervals can help maintain focus.
Teamwork: Group discussions provide opportunities to practice cooperation, constructive feedback, and shared decision-making.
Digital organization: Learning to manage messages, files, and community information can improve everyday administration.
Critical thinking: Comparing information and asking follow-up questions encourages thoughtful evaluation rather than automatic acceptance.
Cultural awareness: International communities can expose participants to different perspectives, languages, and experiences.
Planning and coordination: Group messaging can support appointment scheduling, event preparation, and project management.
Independent learning: Educational communities can help learners identify resources, ask questions, and explore new topics.
These skills are useful beyond Telegram. They can support online education, remote work, community participation, customer communication, and many other digital activities.
The main educational benefit comes from learning how to communicate responsibly and organize information, rather than simply increasing the number of conversations or groups a person joins.
Section 4: Building Trust and Credibility
Trust is important in online communication. People are more likely to collaborate effectively when participants communicate clearly, provide accurate information, and behave consistently.
How Established Accounts Relate to Credibility
An established account may contain a longer history of communication and community participation. For example, a person who has participated in an educational group over time may have a record of useful discussions, thoughtful questions, and helpful contributions.
However, account age alone does not prove a person's expertise, identity, or reliability. A newer account can contribute valuable knowledge, while an older account may have little relevant participation.
Credibility in a messaging community is better understood through behavior and contributions. Clear explanations, respectful communication, accurate information, and constructive participation help other members understand what someone contributes.
For educational or professional groups, relevant experience and well-supported explanations are more informative than the age of an account.
Key Factors That Support Credibility
Accurate profile information: Present information that reflects your identity and communication purpose appropriately.
Consistent participation: Contribute when you have something useful to add rather than focusing only on the frequency of activity.
Clear communication: Use understandable language and provide enough context for others to follow your message.
Respect for group guidelines: Follow the rules established by group administrators and community organizers.
Useful contributions: Share relevant explanations, educational materials, and practical insights when appropriate.
Verified information: When discussing factual subjects, check important claims against reliable sources and distinguish confirmed information from personal opinion.
Constructive feedback: Offer suggestions in a respectful way and remain open to corrections.
Professional conduct: Keep discussions relevant, respect other participants' time, and communicate commitments clearly.
These practices help create productive online environments. They also allow participants to build a reputation through meaningful interaction.
The key principle is that credibility develops through conduct over time. An account's age may provide context, but reliable contributions and accurate communication are more meaningful indicators of trustworthiness.
Section 5: Productivity and Workflow
Messaging platforms can improve productivity when they are incorporated into a clear communication routine. Telegram's groups, channels, and message-management features can help users organize conversations and coordinate activities.
How Telegram Can Improve Efficiency
When people manage several projects or communities, important information can become difficult to locate. Conversations may include announcements, questions, files, deadlines, and informal discussion.
A structured approach helps users distinguish important information from general conversation. For example, a study group can keep its purpose clear, share reference materials with descriptive labels, and summarize agreed deadlines in a message that participants can easily find.
A professional group can use concise updates to communicate progress, identify outstanding tasks, and coordinate meetings. A community channel can organize announcements around a consistent subject.
Telegram's available features can support these activities, although the best workflow depends on the group size, communication needs, and current platform functionality.
Productivity also depends on personal habits. Checking every notification immediately can interrupt focused work, while scheduled review periods can help people respond without constantly switching tasks.
Actionable Tips for an Efficient Workflow

  1. Define the purpose of each conversation. Use a clear topic for each group or discussion so participants understand its intended function.
  2. Organize important information. Use available message-management features to make relevant instructions, links, or announcements easier to find.
  3. Write concise messages. State the purpose of a message clearly and include relevant dates, responsibilities, or next steps.
  4. Establish response expectations. For group projects, agree on reasonable response times and identify the preferred channel for urgent coordination.
  5. Schedule message reviews. Set aside time to review discussions rather than allowing every notification to interrupt focused work.
  6. Keep files organized. Use descriptive filenames and explain what shared documents contain.
  7. Summarize decisions. After a substantial discussion, record the agreed outcome and any follow-up tasks.
  8. Review your digital routine. Periodically leave inactive discussions, update notification preferences, and simplify communication habits where appropriate. These practices can reduce confusion and help people manage their time more effectively. A productive messaging workflow does not require constant activity. It requires clear purposes, accessible information, reasonable expectations, and consistent follow-through. Section 6: Case Studies and Examples The following four illustrative scenarios show how Telegram knowledge can support education, work, and everyday coordination. They are hypothetical examples intended to explain practical applications rather than documented accounts of specific individuals. Example 1: A Student Organizing a Study Group A university student is preparing for several examinations and joins a Telegram group with classmates who are studying the same subjects. Initially, conversations include a mixture of questions, informal discussion, and shared learning materials. The group agrees to organize discussions by topic and include descriptive explanations when sharing resources. Students use clear messages to identify questions, discuss difficult concepts, and coordinate revision sessions. One participant summarizes important conclusions after each study session. The summary includes the topics reviewed, unresolved questions, and the next planned meeting. This approach helps group members find relevant information and prepare more effectively. Learning points: ● Give educational discussions a clear purpose. ● Share resources with useful descriptions. ● Summarize important conclusions. ● Use group communication to support independent study. Example 2: A Freelancer Coordinating Client Work A freelance designer collaborates with a client and a small team on a website project. The team needs to exchange design feedback, clarify deadlines, and coordinate revisions. The freelancer helps establish a consistent communication routine. Messages identify the relevant task, describe the requested change, and include any necessary reference material. After important discussions, the team records agreed actions and deadlines in its project-management system. Telegram supports quick coordination, while formal project documents maintain the detailed requirements. This division of responsibilities helps prevent informal messages from becoming the only record of project decisions. Learning points: ● Use concise messages for coordination. ● Record important decisions in an appropriate project document. ● Clarify deadlines and responsibilities. ● Choose communication channels according to the task. Example 3: A Community Organizer Sharing Local Information A volunteer organizer helps coordinate a neighborhood group. Residents need information about meetings, community activities, and changes to event schedules. The organizer establishes a clear channel for announcements and uses group discussions for questions and coordination. Each announcement includes the relevant date, location, purpose, and instructions for participants. When plans change, the organizer posts an updated message and clearly identifies the revised details. This reduces confusion and helps residents find the latest information. The organizer also encourages respectful participation and makes the group's purpose clear to new members. Learning points: ● Use consistent formats for announcements. ● Include practical details in event messages. ● Make changes easy to identify. ● Establish clear community expectations. Example 4: An Adult Learner Exploring a New Subject An adult learner wants to improve knowledge of a foreign language. The learner joins an educational Telegram community where participants share vocabulary exercises, reading suggestions, and language-learning discussions. Rather than joining many groups at once, the learner chooses one community that matches the learning objective. The learner sets aside time each day to review selected discussions and records useful vocabulary in a separate study document. When explanations are unclear, the learner asks specific questions and compares important information with trusted learning materials. Over several weeks, the learner develops a more organized routine and becomes more comfortable participating in online discussions. Learning points: ● Choose communities that support a specific learning goal. ● Review information at planned times. ● Record useful material in an organized format. ● Compare explanations with reliable educational sources. These examples demonstrate how messaging platforms can support practical goals when communication is intentional. Students can improve study coordination, freelancers can organize discussions, community organizers can distribute announcements, and independent learners can use online groups to develop new skills. The common lesson is that useful communication depends on structure, clarity, and participation rather than account age or the number of groups involved. Section 7: Step-by-Step Guide This six-step guide explains how to approach Telegram as a learning tool and incorporate its communication features into everyday activities. Step 1: Define Your Communication Objective Start by identifying what you want to accomplish. Your goal might be coordinating a study group, following educational channels, managing community announcements, or organizing professional conversations. Write down your objective in one sentence. This makes it easier to identify which Telegram features are relevant and which communities are worth your time. For example, a student may want to find subject-specific educational discussions, while a community organizer may need a structured way to distribute event updates. Step 2: Learn About Telegram's Features Consult Telegram's official website and documentation to understand its current features and supported account options. Explore the differences between individual chats, groups, and channels. Learn how users communicate, share files, organize discussions, and manage available settings. Understanding the purpose of each feature helps you choose the appropriate format for your needs. Supplementary resources such as usasvcit may provide general explanations, but platform-specific details should be checked against official Telegram information. Step 3: Set Up Your Own Account If you decide to use Telegram, follow the official setup instructions and provide accurate information as required. Review the available profile, contact, notification, and privacy settings. Choose settings that suit your communication needs and understand how your profile information is presented to other users. Familiarize yourself with the interface before joining several communities. A basic understanding of the application makes it easier to manage conversations as your participation grows. Step 4: Choose Relevant Groups and Channels Identify communities that match your interests, educational objectives, or professional activities. Review each community's description, subject matter, and participation guidelines. Prefer discussions that provide useful information and encourage constructive interaction. Begin with a manageable number of communities so you can evaluate their usefulness. You can adjust your participation as your interests and learning needs develop. Step 5: Organize Your Communication Routine Establish a consistent process for reviewing messages, saving relevant information, and following up on important discussions. Use available organizational features where helpful. Write clear messages, include relevant context, and summarize agreed actions when coordinating group activities. For projects or professional tasks, maintain important decisions and deadlines in an appropriate document, calendar, or task-management system rather than relying entirely on chat history. Step 6: Evaluate and Improve Your Approach After using Telegram for a period of time, consider whether it is helping you achieve your objective. Ask yourself whether you can find important information easily, whether the communities provide useful content, and whether notifications fit your schedule. Adjust your participation, communication habits, and available settings accordingly. Consult official documentation when you need clarification about a feature. Following these steps can help you develop a purposeful approach to Telegram. The emphasis is on selecting suitable communication tools, managing information clearly, and building habits that support learning and everyday productivity. Section 8: Frequently Asked Questions
  9. What is a Telegram account used for? A Telegram account enables users to participate in supported messaging activities, including individual chats, groups, channels, and file sharing. People use these features for personal communication, educational discussions, professional coordination, and community participation.
  10. What is the difference between a Telegram group and a channel? A group is designed for communication among members, subject to its settings and permissions. A channel is primarily used to publish messages to an audience. The best option depends on whether the goal is interactive discussion or distributing announcements and information.
  11. Does an older Telegram account automatically have greater credibility? No. Account age does not independently establish someone's identity, knowledge, or reliability. Clear communication, accurate information, respectful participation, and meaningful contributions provide better context for evaluating credibility.
  12. How can Telegram support education? Telegram can support study groups, educational announcements, resource sharing, language practice, and discussions about specific subjects. Its usefulness depends on the quality of the community and the learner's ability to evaluate information and maintain a consistent study routine.
  13. How can beginners improve their Telegram productivity? Beginners can start by choosing relevant communities, organizing important messages, managing notification settings, and scheduling regular review periods. Summarizing decisions and recording deadlines in a separate planning tool can also make communication easier to manage.
  14. Where can I learn more about Telegram? Telegram's official website and documentation provide information about features, settings, and current functionality. Supplementary sources such as usasvcit may offer general educational guidance, but important platform-specific details should be confirmed through official information. Conclusion Understanding Telegram accounts provides a practical introduction to digital communication, community participation, and everyday information management. Although the phrase “Buy Telegram Accounts” appears in online searches, the educational value of the subject lies in understanding the platform's features and learning how to use messaging tools effectively. Telegram supports individual conversations, group discussions, channels, and file sharing. These functions can help people coordinate activities, exchange educational resources, maintain professional communication, and participate in communities that match their interests. The practical benefits extend beyond one application. Skills such as writing clear messages, organizing information, managing notifications, evaluating online content, and coordinating shared tasks are valuable in education, employment, and personal life. The examples in this guide demonstrate how students, freelancers, community organizers, and independent learners can apply these skills to real-world activities. Each example emphasizes purposeful participation, clear communication, and consistent organization. A structured learning process makes it easier to benefit from messaging platforms. Begin by defining a communication objective, learning the available features, setting up your own account, selecting relevant communities, organizing your routine, and reviewing the results. Readers may also consult supplementary educational resources such as usasvcit while comparing important explanations with official Telegram documentation. This helps keep learning focused on accurate information and practical application. Ultimately, effective digital communication is not determined by the age of an account or the number of conversations a person joins. It depends on how thoughtfully people exchange information, contribute to communities, and manage their time. By applying these principles, readers can improve digital confidence, strengthen communication skills, and make online messaging a more useful part of everyday life. Call to Action Begin improving your digital communication skills by choosing one practical goal, such as organizing a study group, following an educational channel, or coordinating a community activity. Explore Telegram's official documentation, review the features relevant to your needs, and establish a routine for managing messages and important information. Supplementary resources such as usasvcit may provide additional context, but compare platform-specific explanations with official guidance. Focus on skills that remain useful across different communication tools. Clear messages, organized information, thoughtful participation, and consistent follow-up can improve everyday productivity and provide a strong foundation for continued digital learning.

title: Diagnostic Analysis for Large Language Model Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.27245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning structures (e.g., chains and graphs) are increasingly used for probabilistic inference, factuality verification, and uncertainty estimation, but their structural reliability is rarely evaluated directly. We test whether this reliability holds through a proposed two-stage diagnostic evaluation in open-ended multi-hop QA. Stage 1 tests different capabilities required to construct reasoning graphs, showing that graph reliability varies with topology, prompt design, and model family. Stage 2 uses uncertainty estimation as a downstream test case. Generated-edge experiments show that graph-based computation is sensitive to upstream graph errors, with performance dropping relative to the gold-graph setting. Gold-graph experiments further show that graph structure provides little benefit when used only as prompt context, but improves the separation of correct from incorrect answers by confidence score and enables node-level diagnostics.

title: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning for Dual-Use Concepts in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27490v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding).
  In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace.
  We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.

title: MCP Transports Explained: stdio vs Streamable HTTP
description:
MCP Transports Explained: stdio vs Streamable HTTP

An MCP client and server need a path to talk. That path is called a transport. Two common choices are stdio and Streamable HTTP. They carry the same MCP messages, but they fit different jobs.

The short rule is simple. Use stdio when one local app starts one local server. Use Streamable HTTP when many users or services need a server over a network.

## What stdio does

Stdio means standard input and standard output. The client starts the MCP server as a child process. It sends JSON-RPC messages into the process and reads replies from it.

This works well for a desktop tool, command-line app, or local coding helper. Setup is small. There is no web endpoint to run. The process also gives each client a natural session.

The tradeoff is reach. A local process is hard to share with a team. Each user may need the same package, runtime, settings, and secrets. Logs can also sit on many laptops.

Use stdio when:

  • The client and server run on the same machine.
  • One client owns one server process.
  • You want a fast local setup.
  • You do not need a shared network service.

## What Streamable HTTP does

Streamable HTTP puts the MCP server behind an HTTP endpoint. A client sends MCP messages with HTTP POST. The server can also stream messages back when the session needs it.

This fits remote and shared servers. A platform team can run one service for many users. Normal web controls can sit in front of it, such as TLS, access tokens, rate limits, logs, and a load balancer.

HTTP also adds work. Teams must set timeouts, handle retries, protect the endpoint, and watch network errors. If the server keeps session state, the client may receive an Mcp-Session-Id. Later calls send that ID back. A load balancer must then route the session with care, or the state must live in a shared store.

Use Streamable HTTP when:

  • The server is remote or shared.
  • Many clients need the same tools.
  • Central access rules and audit logs matter.
  • The team can run and secure a web service.

The official MCP transport specification gives the wire rules for both choices.

## Side-by-side choice

Question stdio Streamable HTTP
Where does the server run? On the client machine On a remote or shared host
Who starts it? The client starts a process A service platform runs it
Session shape One process is one natural session Stateless or tracked with a session ID
Main strength Small local setup Shared access and central control
Main risk Setup and secrets spread to laptops Auth, retries, scaling, and network failures

## Two setup examples

For stdio, the client config points to a command and its arguments:

{
  "transport": "stdio",
  "command": "python",
  "args": ["server.py"]
}

For Streamable HTTP, the client points to one MCP URL and sends its access token through a safe secret store:

{
  "transport": "streamable-http",
  "url": "https://tools.example.com/mcp"
}

Exact fields differ by SDK. Keep the design choice the same: a local child process or a managed network service.

## Test before you launch

Start with five checks.

  1. Identity: Can the server tell which user or agent made the call?
  2. Secrets: Are tokens outside source files, logs, and client config shared in chat?
  3. Failure: What happens when a process exits or a network call times out?
  4. Session: Can a client reconnect, and does state go to the right place?
  5. Audit: Can the team see which tool ran, when it ran, and whether it failed?

Add cost to the test. A remote service has hosting and network cost. A local setup has support time and repeated setup work. Count retries and human review too. The cheapest request is not always the cheapest safe result.

Where a gateway fits

As the server list grows, teams need one place to find tools, apply access rules, and read audit events. The Axiom Studio platform describes a governed path for model and tool calls. The Axiom documentation covers the wider product set. Teams that also send model requests can use the LLM Gateway guide and its product page to plan routing, credentials, fallbacks, and usage tracking.

A gateway does not remove transport choices. It makes remote access easier to govern. Keep local stdio for small tools. Move shared tools to Streamable HTTP when the team is ready to own the web service and its controls.

A practical decision

Pick stdio for one user, one machine, and one short path. Pick Streamable HTTP for shared tools, remote access, and central rules. Then test identity, failure, sessions, and audit records before more agents depend on the server.

title: 5 Free React UI Libraries to Escape Generic AI Designs
description:
Ever built something with AI that worked perfectly but looked like every other SaaS product?

Same cards. Same gradients. Same boring layouts.

Here are five React UI libraries worth exploring if you want to break the pattern and build something that actually feels different.

  1. Dither UI — Give Your AI Better Building Blocks

AI coding agents can build your UI, but the results often feel repetitive.

Dither UI is a collection of interactive, motion-first React components built with Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui.

Copy the source into your project and give your AI coding agent better building blocks for creating animated cards, interactive buttons, and more distinctive interfaces.

🔗 ditherui.dev

  1. beUI — Make Your Interfaces Feel Alive

Static components are fine, but thoughtful animations can make an interface feel much more polished.

beUI offers free, open-source animated React components built with Motion and Tailwind CSS, from interactive cards to more expressive form controls.

Copy the code, customize the interactions, and make the components fit your product.

🔗 beui.dev

  1. Beautiful UI — Built for AI Interfaces

Building an AI product involves more than putting a chat window on a page.

Beautiful UI focuses on AI-native components, including streaming text, thinking states, tool chips, approval cards, and agent interfaces.

If you're building an AI assistant or an agent-powered product, these patterns can save you from reinventing common AI interactions.

🔗 beautifului.dev

  1. Cult UI — For More Expressive Interfaces

Sometimes, a few well-designed components can completely change how a product feels.

Cult UI offers motion-rich React components for shadcn/ui projects, including animated buttons, creative hero sections, AI prompt inputs, and interactive cards.

Add a component, customize the source, and give your interface a little more personality.

🔗 cult-ui.com

  1. ObsidianUI — Add More Character to Your UI

It's often the little details that make an interface memorable.

ObsidianUI offers animated, interactive React components built with Tailwind CSS and Motion, including draggable marquees, text animations, and interactive visual elements.

Explore the live previews, find something that fits your design, and customize it for your next project.

🔗 obsidianui.dev

Stop Settling for Generic UI

AI has made building products easier than ever. But making your product feel distinct still takes thoughtful design choices.

These libraries are a great starting point. Experiment with different components, customize them to match your vision, and give your AI coding agent better building blocks to work with.

title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: How to Connect AI Agents to Web Apps with Durable Action Receipts & Clean DOM Inspection: An MCP Browser Bridge
description:
How to Connect AI Agents to Web Apps with Durable Action Receipts & Clean DOM Inspection: An MCP Browser Bridge in Python

In 2026, autonomous AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, LangGraph) are routinely tasked with interacting with live web applications: filling checkout forms, retrieving invoices from SaaS portals, triggering CI/CD pipelines, and scraping protected dashboards.

However, developers building agentic workflows quickly run into three severe production bottlenecks:

  1. Context Window Exhaustion: Dumping raw HTML (often 1MB to 5MB with inline SVG, JSON hydration payloads, and telemetry scripts) exhausts the LLM's context window within 2 or 3 turns, driving token costs through the roof.
  2. Lack of Cryptographic Action Receipts: If an agent performs an irreversible transaction—like submitting a payment form or modifying permissions—there is no tamper-evident audit record proving what the DOM state was before and after the action.
  3. Zombie Memory Leaks: Unmanaged headless browser contexts stay resident in RAM when agents drop connections or fail unexpectedly, consuming gigabytes of host memory.

To solve this, we designed and built BrowserBridge: an enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that transforms noisy web pages into compact, token-efficient Accessibility Object Models (AOM) (~95% token reduction), enforces strict session pooling with automated zombie-reaping, and seals every agent action with a cryptographic SHA-256 receipt.

🏗️ The System Architecture

Instead of having your LLM parse raw HTML or blindly dispatch click coordinates, BrowserBridge sits as an auditable MCP sidecar:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |          BrowserBridge Pro MCP Server         |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   |  AOM DOM Filter   |  | Session Pool Mgr  |  |  Durable Receipts |
   |  (-95% token cost)|  | (Anti-Zombie TTL) |  |   (SQLite WAL)    |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      |   Target Web App DOM    |
                      +-------------------------+

1. Slashing Token Bloat: The Accessibility Object Model (AOM)

Raw HTML is packed with tags irrelevant to an AI agent: <style>, <script>, <svg>, tracking pixels, and deep nesting. What an agent actually needs to know is:

  • What buttons exist?
  • What links can be followed?
  • What text fields require input?

Here is the Python implementation that converts messy HTML into structured, interactive @node elements:

import re
from typing import Dict, Any, List

def extract_accessibility_tree(html_content: str, form_state: Dict[str, str]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    aom_nodes = []
    node_counter = 1

    # 1. Extract Buttons
    for m in re.finditer(r"<button([^>]*)>(.*?)</button>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        attrs, content = m.groups()
        text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", content).strip() or "Unnamed Button"
        aom_nodes.append({
            "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
            "role": "button",
            "name": text[:50],
            "selector": f"button:contains('{text[:20]}')"
        })
        node_counter += 1

    # 2. Extract Links
    for m in re.finditer(r"<a\s+([^>]*href=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"'][^>]*)>(.*?)</a>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        _, href, content = m.groups()
        text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", content).strip()
        if text and not href.startswith("javascript:"):
            aom_nodes.append({
                "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
                "role": "link",
                "name": text[:50],
                "target_url": href,
                "selector": f"a[href='{href}']"
            })
            node_counter += 1

    # 3. Extract Text Input Fields
    for m in re.finditer(r"<input\s+([^>]*)/?>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE):
        attrs = m.group(1)
        name_m = re.search(r"name=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"']", attrs, re.IGNORECASE)
        type_m = re.search(r"type=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"']", attrs, re.IGNORECASE)
        name_val = name_m.group(1) if name_m else f"input_{node_counter}"
        type_val = type_m.group(1) if type_m else "text"

        aom_nodes.append({
            "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
            "role": "textbox" if type_val in ("text", "email", "password", "search") else type_val,
            "name": name_val,
            "selector": f"input[name='{name_val}']",
            "current_value": form_state.get(name_val, "")
        })
        node_counter += 1

    return aom_nodes[:50]

By presenting the LLM with @node-1 (role: button, name: "Checkout") instead of 250 lines of tailwind divs, prompt tokens drop by ~95% while dramatically improving selector accuracy.

2. Cryptographic Durability: Action Receipts Engine

When an agent interacts with a web interface, proving what happened and when is critical for compliance and debugging.

BrowserBridge calculates a SHA-256 fingerprint of the DOM before the action (pre_state_hash) and immediately after execution (post_state_hash), persisting the transition to an atomic SQLite WAL ledger:

import uuid
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Dict, Any

class DurableReceiptsEngine:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "receipts.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def _init_db(self):
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
            conn.execute("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS action_receipts (
                    receipt_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    session_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                    action_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                    target TEXT NOT NULL,
                    payload TEXT,
                    pre_state_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    post_state_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    status TEXT DEFAULT 'success',
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
            """)

    def issue_receipt(self, session_id: str, action_type: str, target: str,
                      pre_state_hash: str, post_state_hash: str,
                      payload: str = "") -> Dict[str, Any]:
        receipt_id = f"rcpt_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("""
                INSERT INTO action_receipts (
                    receipt_id, session_id, action_type, target, payload,
                    pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, status, created_at
                ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'success', ?);
            """, (receipt_id, session_id, action_type, target, payload, pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, now))

        return {
            "receipt_id": receipt_id,
            "session_id": session_id,
            "action_type": action_type,
            "target": target,
            "pre_state_hash": pre_state_hash[:16],
            "post_state_hash": post_state_hash[:16],
            "timestamp": now
        }

Auditing State Continuity

Using verify_action_trail(session_id), you can verify that the sequence of actions has not been tampered with or skipped:

def verify_action_trail(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
    receipts = self.list_receipts(session_id)
    for i in range(len(receipts) - 1):
        if receipts[i]["post_state_hash"] != receipts[i + 1]["pre_state_hash"]:
            return False # Chain discontinuity detected!
    return True

3. Preventing Memory Leaks: The Anti-Zombie Session Pool

Headless browser automation easily leaks memory when agents abandon sessions mid-flight. BrowserBridge solves this with an automated session reaper:

from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
from typing import Dict, List

class SessionPoolManager:
    def __init__(self, idle_ttl_seconds: int = 180):
        self.idle_ttl_seconds = idle_ttl_seconds
        self.sessions: Dict[str, BrowserSession] = {}

    def reap_zombies(self) -> List[str]:
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        reaped = []
        for sid, sess in list(self.sessions.items()):
            last_active = datetime.fromisoformat(sess.last_active)
            if now - last_active > timedelta(seconds=self.idle_ttl_seconds):
                del self.sessions[sid]
                reaped.append(sid)
        return reaped

Whenever any session is requested, or on a periodic tick, sessions exceeding the inactivity window are safely terminated and removed from host memory.

4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

BrowserBridge adheres to the standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) JSON-RPC specification. Adding it to Claude Desktop or Cursor is as simple as adding a snippet to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserbridge": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "browserbridge.server"]
    }
  }
}

Now, your AI agent has direct access to:

  • navigate_page(url)
  • extract_clean_text()
  • extract_accessibility_tree()
  • click_element(selector)
  • fill_form_field(selector, value)
  • verify_action_trail(session_id)

🚀 Get Started: Open-Source & Enterprise

The full open-source BrowserBridge Lite is available immediately on GitHub with an MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/browserbridge-mcp

If your team requires the Enterprise Pro Edition—including the persistent SQLite WAL receipts engine, multi-tenant session pool reaper, resilient selector resolver for dynamic SPAs, containerized Docker Compose manifests, and 100% passing Pytest suite:

👉 Get BrowserBridge Pro on Gumroad ($14.99 USD)

title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
description:
arXiv:2610.27400v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.

title: One picker for seven conditions and fourteen allergies, and its hardest rule is that nothing you selected may hide
description:
Munchable asks you two questions before it can answer anything: which digestive conditions you are eating for, and which allergies you need flagged. The seven conditions are listed on munchable.app/conditions, each with its own guide, for example GERD and reflux. The allergies are the fourteen that labels are legally required to declare.

Both questions are the same screen, twice, in onboarding and again in settings. One component renders all of it, and almost every line of it is about one of two problems: a list long enough to be a scroll instead of a choice, and a choice that disappears.

A list is split only when splitting pays 

/**
 * The list is only split once it is long enough that scanning it costs
 * something. Below this every item is simply a row, which is what the seven
 * conditions want; the fourteen allergies get the common set and a search.
 */
const SPLIT_AT = 9;

Seven conditions render as seven rows with no search field at all. Fourteen allergies render the seven with the highest adult prevalence in UK and US surveys, a search, and a "Show 7 more" disclosure.

That threshold is the only configuration either screen passes about layout. Everything else about the shape of the list is derived, so adding an eighth condition one day changes the screen without anybody deciding it should.

Search has to match the word you would actually type

The search runs over three fields: the title, the one-line helper, and a hidden keyword list that is never displayed.

keywords: ['heartburn', 'acid', 'reflux', 'gord', 'oesophageal'],
keywords: ['fodmap', 'irritable bowel', 'bloating'],
keywords: ['bile', 'bile acid', 'diarrhoea', 'diarrhea'],

People do not search for the name of their condition in the form a product team wrote it. They search for the symptom, for the abbreviation they were given at the clinic, and for whichever of two spellings their country uses. Both spellings of diarrhoea are in there for exactly that reason, and so is the British spelling of the reflux acronym, GORD, next to the American GERD.

Matching folds diacritics as well as case, so an accent typed or not typed makes no difference:

/** Lowercase and strip diacritics, so "coeliac" finds "Coeliac" and "é" finds "e". */
function fold(s: string): string {
  return s.normalize('NFD').replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '').toLowerCase();
}

The item arrays are built once at module scope rather than inline in the screens, because three screens render the same list and the search is a useMemo whose dependency is that array. A fresh literal per render means the memo is decorative.

Nothing you chose is allowed to hide

Here is the bug that drove most of this component. Select something from the bottom of the expanded list, collapse the list, and your selection is now behind a disclosure you have to remember to open. The screen says you picked four things and shows three.

So selected rows get pinned into view:

// Hidden items that are selected get pinned into view, so nothing the user
// has chosen is ever behind a disclosure they would have to remember to open.
const [pinned, setPinned] = useState<Set<Id>>(() => new Set(selected));

Then three subtleties, each of which was a real moment of the thing feeling wrong.

Pinning happens when the list closes, not when the item is tapped, because closing is the moment something could go out of sight. While the list is open nothing is pinned at all: every row is already on screen in its own place, and hoisting the row you just tapped up the page moves the thing under your finger.

Selecting from the collapsed list or from a search result pins immediately, because clearing a search is the other way a just-made choice can vanish.

And deselecting does not unpin. The row stays exactly where it is until the next time the screen is opened. Tapping a checkbox should never make the row you are looking at disappear, even when your tap means "not this one".

While a search is running, anything selected that the query does not reach gets named underneath rather than silently dropped:

{missed.length > 0 ? (
  <Text variant="caption" muted>Also selected: {missed.map((i) => i.title).join(', ')}.</Text>
) : null}

The empty state names the edge of the list

A search that matches nothing is the one place a picker can leave somebody stuck, so it does not say "no results":

export const CONDITIONS_NOT_LISTED =
  'Munchable checks seven digestive conditions today. If yours is not here, it cannot be checked yet.';

export const ALLERGIES_NOT_LISTED =
  'Munchable checks the 14 allergens that labels must declare. If yours is not here, it cannot be checked yet.';

Both are deliberately flat. Searching for a condition Munchable does not cover is a real answer and the user has learned something true about the product in one sentence. The alternative, a cheerful "try another search", wastes the only moment where the honest answer is useful.

The clear button sits in the field the whole time, so the way out of an empty result is one tap and is visible before you need it.

The accessibility details are in the labels, not the look

The visible disclosure says "Show 7 more". Its accessibility label says the noun too:

accessibilityLabel={showRest ? `Show fewer ${noun}` : `Show ${hiddenItems.length} more ${noun}`}
accessibilityState={{ expanded: showRest }}

The noun prop exists for that string alone, which is why the component takes "allergies" and "conditions" as text. "Show 7 more" is clear when you can see what it sits under and meaningless read on its own. The clear button announces "Clear allergies search" for the same reason. Rows are role="checkbox" with their selected state attached, rather than a styled pressable that looks chosen.

The only non-visual feedback is one haptic tick per toggle. The app ships no sound files at all, so a selection confirms itself by feel or not at all.

Open the conditions page and you are looking at the same seven items, the same titles and the same one-line helpers the picker shows, just rendered as pages instead of rows. The list is short enough to read in full, which is the whole reason the picker can afford to tell you when your condition is not on it.

description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

Jev passed every other comparison model in its first twelve hours and continued to widen its lead for the rest of the day. By hour 24, nearly 13% of paid teams were using it. That's 2x the GPT-5.6 family and more than 6x Fable 5.1's share.

Jev’s launch shows how quickly a specialized model can find a place in production. Its first-day adoption was unmatched among recent launches; the next test is whether that early adoption lasts.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.

description:
Day 17/90: Lifetimes and lifetime annotations

90 Day Rust Challenge: Zero to Production

Today I wanted lifetimes and lifetime annotations to feel like a real engineering decision, not a syntax demo. The useful shift was making lifetimes and lifetime annotations readable in terms of ownership, borrowing, and lifetime boundaries.

The checks that mattered were which borrowed data must outlive what, how signatures communicate that constraint, and where owned data is simpler than another annotation.

The failure mode I was actively trying to avoid was fighting the borrow checker without first deciding which value should actually own the state. I wanted lifetimes and lifetime annotations to feel like something I could explain at a whiteboard or in a code review, not just something I recognized from docs.

That is the bar I want from this track: code that stays readable when requirements move, not just code that compiles today.

title: ORBIT: Autoregressive Time Series Generation via Next Frequency-Band Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.27000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep generative models provide an effective modern solution to alleviating the problem of data scarcity by synthesizing realistic time series. However, despite the considerable progress achieved by existing deep time series generators, two key challenges remain: (1) learning hierarchical representations for heterogeneous temporal patterns; and (2) coordinating the generation process of heterogeneous temporal dynamics. To address these key bottlenecks, in this work, we propose ORBIT, a unified deep generative framework for time series. Specifically, we develop two key components: the Frequency-Hierarchical VQ-VAE (FH-VQ-VAE) and the Frequency-Band Autoregressive Transformer (FBAR). The former learns hierarchical representations by decomposing latent temporal representations into different frequency bands and applying residual quantization with increasing token budgets. The latter establishes a novel low-to-high frequency autoregressive direction, yielding a time series generation process that first constructs global temporal structures and then incrementally incorporates fine-grained temporal details. These compact designs not only disentangle heterogeneous temporal patterns for more effective representation learning but also mitigate potential interference among different temporal dynamics during generation. Extensive experiments on multiple challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that ORBIT achieves state-of-the-art overall performance while exhibiting superior inference efficiency compared with advanced baselines.
