title: AI Code Invariant Tests: Catch Regressions That Green Test Suites Miss
description:
An AI coding agent can make every visible test pass and still break the one rule your product cannot afford to violate.

That is the uncomfortable failure mode behind many “safe” agent refactors. The diff looks tidy. Unit tests are green. The new code may even have more coverage than before. But a permission check moves after a database lookup, a retry stops being idempotent, or a list endpoint turns into an accidental N+1 query. Nothing in a happy-path test has to notice.

The fix is not a longer prompt asking the agent to be careful. It is to name the behavior that must remain true, then test it as an invariant. This article shows a practical, framework-neutral way to add invariant tests around AI-generated changes—especially where money, access, state, and latency matter.

Why green tests can still hide an AI-generated regression

Most unit tests answer a narrow question: “Does this example produce the expected output?” That is useful, but it leaves room for an implementation that passes known examples while breaking a rule between examples.

Coding agents amplify that gap. They are effective at repairing the assertion directly in front of them. If a refactor changes a test, they may update the test too. The suite turns green, but the original contract has quietly moved.

Recent developer discussions around agentic refactoring repeatedly describe the same pain: tests can remain green while an agent weakens an alert, rewrites an assertion, or creates a slow query loop. Research and benchmark work on coding agents also points toward specification-first and adversarial validation rather than trusting generated code by default.

An invariant is different from a single expected result. It is a property that must hold across many inputs and implementation paths.

Ordinary example test Invariant test
A member can read their own project. A request can never return a project from another organization.
Retrying this request returns 200. Retrying the same operation never creates a second charge.
A search result is sorted in this fixture. Results are always sorted by the promised key, including ties and empty input.
This endpoint completes quickly in a test. Loading 50 records does not issue more than a bounded number of queries.

The aim is not to replace example tests. Keep them. Invariants give them a harder-to-game companion.

Pick invariants before asking an agent to refactor

Do not begin with “clean up this module.” Start with a short, testable list of things that cannot change. This becomes the acceptance contract for the task and a small map for review.

For a typical application, useful categories are:

  • Authorization: one tenant or role never sees another’s data.
  • State: records move only through allowed states.
  • Money and side effects: retries do not duplicate emails, charges, or writes.
  • Data integrity: identifiers, totals, and ownership stay consistent.
  • Reliability: failures leave the system in a recoverable state.
  • Performance: a refactor does not multiply database calls or network work.
  • Compatibility: a public API preserves its documented shape and meaning.

Write each one in plain language first. A good invariant has a subject, a boundary, and an observable result:

For every invoice event with the same idempotency key, at most one payment record exists.

For every authenticated request, every returned document belongs to the requester’s organization.

For a valid workflow, terminal states cannot transition back to pending.

Avoid vague rules such as “keep the code secure” or “do not change behavior.” They are review intentions, not executable claims.

Turn an invariant into a test oracle

An oracle is the thing that says whether behavior is correct. Existing snapshot tests are weak oracles when an agent can update them. For critical changes, use an oracle the change is not allowed to edit without an explicit human decision.

One practical pattern is to put invariant tests in a protected directory and declare them read-only for the task.

repo/
  src/
  tests/
  safety-contracts/
    organization-isolation.spec.ts
    payment-idempotency.spec.ts
    workflow-transitions.spec.ts

Your task brief can then be concrete:

Refactor src/billing/renewal.ts to remove duplication.

Constraints:
- Do not edit safety-contracts/.
- Run npm test and npm run test:contracts after each logical step.
- Preserve one payment per idempotency key.
- Report changed files, commands, and any failing contract.

That instruction alone is not protection. Enforce it in CI: fail a pull request that changes protected contract files unless a designated reviewer approves it. The important part is separation—an agent should not be able to write both the implementation and the only proof it is safe without making that visible.

Example: protect tenant isolation with generated inputs

Imagine a document query that an agent is about to “simplify.” A normal example test might check that one user can fetch a document. An invariant test should try many organizations and document IDs, then assert that every returned record belongs to the caller’s organization.

Here is TypeScript-style pseudocode using a property-testing library:

import fc from "fast-check";

it("never returns another organization's document", async () => {
  await fc.assert(
    fc.asyncProperty(
      fc.uuid(),
      fc.uuid(),
      fc.uuid(),
      async (requesterOrgId, otherOrgId, documentId) => {
        fc.pre(requesterOrgId !== otherOrgId);

        await seedDocument({ id: documentId, organizationId: otherOrgId });
        const result = await listDocuments({ organizationId: requesterOrgId });

        expect(result.every((doc) => doc.organizationId === requesterOrgId)).toBe(true);
      },
    ),
  );
});

The exact library is optional. You can loop over generated cases yourself. The principle matters: test the rule across values the author did not hand-pick.

For a multi-tenant system, add negative cases too:

  • a guessed ID from another organization
  • an empty role list
  • an admin role from the wrong organization
  • soft-deleted records
  • pagination cursors created by another tenant

These are the cases a polished refactor often fails because the happy path still works.

Example: protect idempotency when an agent changes retries

Retries are a classic regression surface. An agent may correctly add timeout handling but accidentally put the side effect before the deduplication check.

The invariant is simple: repeating a request with the same stable key produces one durable effect.

it("creates at most one payment for the same request key", async () => {
  const key = "payment:order-42";

  await Promise.all([
    createPayment({ orderId: "order-42", amount: 2500, idempotencyKey: key }),
    createPayment({ orderId: "order-42", amount: 2500, idempotencyKey: key }),
  ]);

  const payments = await db.payment.findMany({
    where: { idempotencyKey: key },
  });

  expect(payments).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(payments[0].amount).toBe(2500);
});

Run it with sequential and concurrent calls. Then add a failure injection between “reserve key” and “write payment.” If the invariant cannot survive a timeout, it is not really an invariant—it is a best-case assumption.

Test state machines instead of only endpoints

Many business rules are state transitions disguised as API behavior. A support ticket should not reopen after it is permanently closed. An order should not ship before payment. A deleted user should not receive a new session.

Model the allowed transitions in one small table before the refactor:

From Allowed next states
draft submitted, cancelled
submitted approved, rejected, cancelled
approved fulfilled, cancelled
fulfilled none

Then test every pair, not just the common routes:

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  draft: ["submitted", "cancelled"],
  submitted: ["approved", "rejected", "cancelled"],
  approved: ["fulfilled", "cancelled"],
  rejected: [],
  cancelled: [],
  fulfilled: [],
};

for (const from of Object.keys(allowed) as Status[]) {
  for (const to of allStatuses) {
    const canMove = allowed[from].includes(to);
    await expect(changeStatus({ from, to }))
      .resolves[canMove ? "toBeDefined" : "toThrow"]();
  }
}

Use your test framework’s normal assertion style; the point is to enumerate the system’s real state space. If the agent replaces conditionals, extracts services, or switches an ORM call, this test protects the business meaning rather than its old implementation.

Add performance invariants where refactors hide cost

Correct output is not the whole contract. A coding agent can preserve results while turning one query into one query per row.

For known hot paths, count the work. Inject a database query counter in an integration test, execute with a small and a medium fixture, and set a reasonable ceiling.

it("loads project members without an N+1 query", async () => {
  const meter = trackDatabaseQueries(db);
  await seedProjectWithMembers({ memberCount: 50 });

  const page = await getProjectMembers({ projectId: "project-1" });

  expect(page.members).toHaveLength(50);
  expect(meter.count()).toBeLessThanOrEqual(3);
});

Do not turn every test into a brittle microbenchmark. A query ceiling, outbound-call count, or payload-size limit is usually more stable and more useful than an elapsed-millisecond assertion in CI.

A small contract loop for AI-assisted changes

Here is a repeatable workflow that does not require a formal-methods team.

  1. Name the risk. Identify what can be lost, duplicated, leaked, or slowed down.
  2. Write one invariant. Make it observable in code or a controlled integration environment.
  3. Prove the test can fail. Temporarily introduce the forbidden behavior or use a mutation tool. If the test stays green, strengthen it.
  4. Protect the oracle. Keep contract tests out of the agent’s editable scope for the task, or require explicit review for any change.
  5. Give the agent a bounded goal. Specify files, behavior, test commands, and prohibited changes.
  6. Run the contract suite in CI. Store the command output with the pull request.
  7. Review the invariant, not only the diff. Ask whether the rule still means what the product needs.

The third step is the one teams skip. A test that never demonstrates a failure can be theater. For a payment invariant, change the uniqueness guard in a local branch and confirm the test catches two rows. For tenant isolation, deliberately remove the organization predicate and watch the contract fail.

Give coding agents a task contract they can follow

Clear instructions help, especially when they connect a change to a non-negotiable rule. Here is a concise template:

Goal: extract the notification scheduling logic from src/jobs/run.ts.

Behavioral contracts:
1. A job with the same idempotency key sends at most one notification.
2. A cancelled job never sends a notification.
3. A tenant can never schedule a job for another tenant.

Boundaries:
- Do not modify safety-contracts/.
- Do not add dependencies.
- Keep the public handler signature unchanged.

Verification:
- npm run typecheck
- npm test
- npm run test:contracts
- Summarize any command that fails; do not weaken tests to make them pass.

This is stronger than “refactor safely” because it tells the agent what success means. It is also easier for a reviewer to reject a superficially green change: the contract is visible before the code.

Common mistakes when adding invariant tests

Testing implementation details. A contract should survive a refactor. Assert a durable result—number of writes, access boundary, state transition—not which private helper ran.

Using only random input. Generated input expands coverage, but important named cases still matter. Keep regression fixtures for incidents and known edge cases.

Letting the same change rewrite every oracle. If an agent alters production code, snapshots, unit tests, and contract tests in one sweep, reviewers lose their independent evidence. Separate those changes or require a stronger review path.

Making every rule a blocking invariant. Start with the small set whose failure would cause financial loss, data exposure, irreversible writes, or serious reliability damage. A hundred weak contracts will be ignored.

Mistaking test coverage for behavioral coverage. Coverage reports show which lines ran. They do not show whether the line preserved ownership, idempotency, or a state boundary.

Where this fits in an AI-assisted engineering workflow

Invariant tests sit beside, not above, the rest of your quality system:

  • Types and schemas catch malformed values.
  • Unit tests catch local logic mistakes.
  • Integration tests prove boundaries with real infrastructure.
  • Contract tests protect cross-module promises.
  • Invariant tests protect rules across many inputs and paths.
  • Code review checks intent, readability, and operational consequences.

For AI-assisted work, the practical payoff is trustable speed. You can let an agent make a broad mechanical improvement when the most important promises are executable and independently checked. That is safer than restricting agents to trivial tasks—and safer than trusting a green checkmark with no stated contract.

FAQ

What is an invariant test for AI-generated code?

It checks a rule that must stay true across many inputs and execution paths, such as tenant isolation, one payment per idempotency key, or valid state transitions. It complements example-based unit tests.

Are invariant tests the same as property-based tests?

No. Property-based testing is a useful technique for generating many inputs. An invariant is the behavior you want to preserve. You can test an invariant with generated values, fixed fixtures, integration tests, or all three.

Which invariants should a small team add first?

Start with data isolation, authorization, idempotency, money movement, irreversible deletes, and the most expensive performance paths. Choose rules where one regression would create real user or business harm.

Should an AI coding agent be allowed to edit invariant tests?

It can propose a change, but treat that change as a contract decision rather than routine cleanup. Require explicit review and a reason the product rule itself changed; otherwise the agent can make failing evidence disappear.

How do I know an invariant test is strong enough?

Prove it can fail. Temporarily introduce the forbidden behavior, or use mutation testing, and confirm the contract catches it. If it stays green, it is not protecting the rule yet.

Do invariant tests make refactoring slower?

They take time to write, but they reduce the slowest part of refactoring: diagnosing a production regression after a large, plausible-looking change. Start with high-risk paths and keep each contract narrow.

title: Detecting Errors in Large Language Model Responses: The Incremental Predictive Value of Hidden States
description:
arXiv:2610.27455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although large language models support a wide range of tasks, hallucinations remain a major obstacle to user trust. When a model generates an answer, both its internal processing and final output vary with the question. Internal states are often expected to offer richer signals for hallucination detection. However, studies using these states typically report their standalone discrimination performance, while output-side comparisons often use simple baselines with weaker modeling capacity. We integrate output-side information available at inference time into a combined baseline and compare detection performance before and after adding hidden states under identical data splits and evaluation rules. Experiments cover open-ended generation and constrained multiple-choice tasks across different models. Adding hidden states improves AUROC by approximately 0.004 and 0.039 on the two tasks, respectively. Hidden states thus provide additional predictive information, but strong standalone detection performance can still yield only limited additional gains.

title: Tailwind v4 Design Tokens: Colors, Dark Mode and Contrast
description:
TL;DR

Tailwind v4 design tokens are CSS variables: keep the values that change between light and dark in :root and .dark, then map them to utilities with @theme inline, so bg-surface or text-muted-foreground follow the theme with no dark: prefix. A complete set names roles instead of colors: surfaces in the order they stack, text levels, tones split into a solid fill and a readable text color, plus radius, elevation, z-index and motion scales. Check every text and surface pair for 4.5:1 contrast in both themes with a script, because a color that passes on white often fails on a dark popover.

Tailwind CSS v4 moved configuration out of tailwind.config.js and into CSS, and many guides stop at the first step: put a few brand colors in @theme and call them tokens. A component library needs more than a palette. It needs Tailwind v4 design tokens for every decision a component makes: which surface sits in front of which, how muted secondary text can get, what a warning uses as a fill and as text, how round a 32px button is next to a 48px one, how a popover casts a shadow on a black page, and which layer a select opens on inside a dialog. This guide is the token system we use in Wingo UI, a React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4 component library, with the real CSS and the contrast numbers behind each choice. We build Wingo UI, so we are not neutral; outside facts link to their sources and are dated.

What are design tokens in Tailwind v4?

Design tokens in Tailwind v4 are CSS custom properties. Tailwind v4 theme variables, the ones you declare inside an @theme block, do two jobs at once: they are CSS variables you can read with var(), and their namespace decides which utilities Tailwind generates. --color-surface creates bg-surface, text-surface and border-surface; --shadow-raised creates shadow-raised. Tailwind CSS v4.0 shipped this CSS-first configuration on January 22, 2025 (release post), and the theme variables docs list the namespaces. We run Tailwind 4.3.3 as of October 2026.

The namespaces a component library uses most:

Namespace Utilities it creates What we keep there
--color-* bg-*, text-*, border-*, ring-*, fill-* surfaces, text levels, tones, borders, the focus ring
--shadow-* shadow-* three elevation levels
--radius-* rounded-* a legacy scale that new code avoids (see the radius section)
--z-index-* z-* seven stacking layers
--ease-*, --transition-duration-* ease-*, duration-* motion curves and durations
--font-* font-* font families
--spacing p-*, m-*, gap-*, w-*, h-* the 4px grid (0.25rem)

--z-index-* and --transition-duration-* are not in the docs table as of October 2026, but Tailwind 4.3 compiles them: our CSS has .z-modal { z-index: var(--z-modal) }.

How should you layer Tailwind v4 design tokens?

Use three layers. Raw values that change between themes go in :root and .dark. A mapping in @theme inline turns them into utilities. Components then paint through a few runtime variables that a prop sets, so a tone or a custom color never needs its own class.

Here is a trimmed but working excerpt of our app/globals.css, with the real values:

@import "tailwindcss";

@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));

:root {
  --background: oklch(1 0 0);
  --foreground: oklch(0.3211 0 0);
  --surface: #ffffff;
  --popover: oklch(1 0 0);
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.52 0.0234 264.3637);
  --success: #15803d;
  --success-foreground: #ffffff;
  --success-soft: #e7f6ec;
  --success-soft-foreground: #166534;
  --elevation-raised: 0 0 0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.07), 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05), 0 2px 8px -2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.06);
}

.dark {
  --background: oklch(0 0 0);
  --foreground: oklch(0.9219 0 0);
  --surface: #1a1a1a;
  --popover: #262626;
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.7155 0 0);
  --success-soft: #0d2315;
  --success-soft-foreground: #4ade80;
  --elevation-raised: inset 0 1px 0 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.06), 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.08), 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
}

@theme inline {
  --color-background: var(--background);
  --color-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --color-surface: var(--surface);
  --color-popover: var(--popover);
  --color-muted-foreground: var(--muted-foreground);
  --color-success: var(--success);
  --color-success-foreground: var(--success-foreground);
  --color-success-soft: var(--success-soft);
  --color-success-soft-foreground: var(--success-soft-foreground);
  --shadow-raised: var(--elevation-raised);
}

The success fill and its white text are the same in both themes (5.02:1), so this excerpt declares them only in :root and .dark inherits them. Everything that changes is redeclared under .dark, and a component uses the same classes everywhere:

export function InvoiceRow() {
  return (
    <div className="flex items-center justify-between rounded-2xl bg-surface p-4 text-foreground shadow-raised">
      <div>
        <p className="text-[15px] font-medium">Invoice 1042</p>
        <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">Emma Carter, New York</p>
      </div>
      <span className="rounded-full bg-success-soft px-2 py-0.5 text-xs font-medium text-success-soft-foreground">Paid</span>
    </div>
  );
}

The raw names follow shadcn/ui's convention on purpose: --background, --card, --popover and --muted-foreground are shadcn names, and the ones shadcn does not have (--surface, --canvas, the --success-* family) use the same name and name-foreground pattern. A project that already has shadcn tokens can take ours without renaming anything.

When do you need Tailwind v4 @theme inline?

Use @theme inline whenever a theme variable points at another variable, which is every token that changes with the theme. The Tailwind docs say it directly: with inline, "the utility class will use the theme variable value instead of referencing the actual theme variable". Here is what that means in compiled CSS:

/* @theme inline { --color-surface: var(--surface); } */
.bg-surface {
  background-color: var(--surface);
}

/* @theme { --color-surface: var(--surface); } */
:root, :host {
  --color-surface: var(--surface);
}
.bg-surface {
  background-color: var(--color-surface);
}

The difference shows up below the root. A custom property inherits its computed value, and var() is substituted where the property is declared. In the second version --color-surface is resolved once, on :root, and every element inherits that result. A .dark class on <html> still works, because <html> is the root. A dark section inside a light page (<section className="dark">), a dark preview pane or a data-theme attribute on a container does not: the section inherits the light value that :root already resolved. With inline, bg-surface reads var(--surface) on the element itself, so it picks up the nearest override. The Tailwind docs explain the option with the same kind of parent and child example.

One catch remains with inline: if you write var(--color-surface) yourself, in an arbitrary value like bg-[var(--color-surface)] or in plain CSS, Tailwind 4.3 emits --color-surface: var(--surface) on :root to satisfy it, and that reference is resolved on the root again. Inside components, read the raw variable instead: bg-(--surface) or var(--surface).

Two more rules from the docs: theme variables must sit at the top level, never under a selector or a media query, so per-theme values live outside @theme anyway; and Tailwind only emits the theme variables your code uses, unless you write @theme static. The raw variables in :root always ship, which helps when a chart library reads a token with getComputedStyle.

Which semantic color tokens does a component library need?

Name colors by role, never by hue. A component library needs surfaces in the order they stack, text levels with a contrast floor, translucent tints for hover and fills, a border and a focus ring, and status tones. With semantic color tokens, components never contain bg-gray-100 or text-blue-600, so a theme can change every value without touching a component.

Surfaces, back to front

Token Light Dark Use
background #FFFFFF #000000 the page
canvas #F6F7F9 #0E0E10 the page of an app (dashboards, admin), under white panels
card #EBEBEB #121212 flat gray tiles with no shadow
surface #FFFFFF with shadow-raised #1A1A1A raised panels: list groups, stat cards, forms
popover #FFFFFF with shadow-floating #262626 everything that floats: menus, selects, dialogs, sheets, toasts
primary #000000 #FAFAFA the neutral solid fill and tooltips

In dark mode the surfaces get lighter as they come forward: #000, #121212, #1A1A1A, #262626. In light mode most of them are white, so the shadow does the separating. canvas exists because a dashboard on a white page has nothing to set white cards against; a cool gray page makes every bg-surface panel read as a card.

Text levels

Level Class Use Lowest ratio in our token pairs
Primary text-foreground titles, values, labels 10.60:1 (light card)
Secondary text-muted-foreground descriptions, helper text, timestamps 4.62:1 (light card)
Disabled text-foreground/45 disabled labels only none required
Tone text text-success-soft-foreground and its siblings errors, deltas, links 5.28:1 (brand on the light card)

text-muted-foreground is the floor for anything people must read. The disabled level has no contrast target because WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 exempts text in inactive controls, which is why it is never used for anything else.

Tints instead of gray fills

Hover states, field fills, chips, tracks and skeletons use translucent foreground: bg-foreground/5, /7, /10 and /15, plus border-foreground/10 for hairlines. Tailwind 4.3 compiles the opacity modifier to color-mix(), with the plain color as a fallback:

.bg-foreground\/5 {
  background-color: var(--foreground);
  @supports (color: color-mix(in lab, red, red)) {
    background-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--foreground) 5%, transparent);
  }
}

A tint is relative to whatever sits behind it, so it moves one step toward the text color on every surface, in both themes. A fixed fill cannot do that. Our dark --muted is #171717: lighter than the black page and darker than the #1A1A1A surface, so the same field would look raised on one and sunken on the other. The full-strength fallback only shows in browsers without color-mix(), which are all below Tailwind's browser baseline of Chrome 111, Safari 16.4 and Firefox 128.

shadcn/ui's secondary and accent stay in our file so ported components keep working, but our --accent is an orange tint, and new components never use either.

How do status colors work without a class per color?

Give each status tone four tokens: a solid fill, the text on that fill, a soft tinted surface, and tone text that reads on the soft surface and on every neutral surface. Then let components paint through five generic variables that one class sets. That is the whole idea behind the free Tones utility.

The four tokens per tone, for brand, success, warning, destructive and info:

--success: #15803d;                 /* bg-success: buttons, solid badges, progress */
--success-foreground: #ffffff;      /* text on the fill */
--success-soft: #e7f6ec;            /* bg-success-soft: soft badges, alerts, selected rows */
--success-soft-foreground: #166534; /* colored text on the tint and on any neutral surface */

The split between fill and tone text is the easiest rule to skip, and it is where dark mode breaks. Fills are tuned to carry white text, and they make poor text. text-destructive (#DC2626) on our dark popover is 3.13:1; text-destructive-soft-foreground (#FF8A80) on the same surface is 6.63:1. The warning fill is amber (#F5A524) at 2.04:1 against white, so it carries dark text (#2B1700, 8.40:1) and is never used as text on a neutral surface.

Component variables

A component with a tone prop does not map tokens itself. toneClasses[tone] sets five variables, and every variant paints with them:

// lib/tones.ts (excerpt)
success:
  "[--tone:var(--success)] [--tone-foreground:var(--success-foreground)] [--tone-soft:var(--success-soft)] [--tone-soft-foreground:var(--success-soft-foreground)] [--tone-border:color-mix(in_oklab,var(--success)_45%,transparent)]",

The neutral tone maps --tone to --primary (black in light, near-white in dark) and builds its soft surface from color-mix(in oklab, var(--foreground) 7%, transparent), which is why a neutral soft button works on any surface. A badge built this way:

import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { colorVars, toneClasses, type Tone } from "@/lib/tones";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";

type StatusBadgeProps = ComponentProps<"span"> & { tone?: Tone; color?: string };

export function StatusBadge({ tone = "neutral", color, className, style, ...props }: StatusBadgeProps) {
  return (
    <span
      data-slot="status-badge"
      className={cn(
        toneClasses[tone],
        "inline-flex rounded-full bg-(--tone-soft) px-2 py-0.5 text-xs font-medium text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
        className,
      )}
      style={{ ...colorVars(color), ...style }}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}

bg-(--tone-soft) is Tailwind v4's shorthand for bg-[var(--tone-soft)]. The free Badge is the full version of this pattern, with solid, soft and outline variants. colorVars(color) builds the same five variables from any CSS color as an inline style. Its text-on-fill value uses relative color syntax, oklch(from <color> clamp(0, (0.7 - l) * 1000, 1) 0 0): white when the color's OKLCH lightness is below 0.7, black above. As of October 2026, caniuse lists full support for relative color syntax from Chrome 131, Safari 18 and Firefox 133, and partial support before that, so full support arrived later than Tailwind's own baseline. Where a browser cannot compute the value, the declaration is invalid at computed-value time and the text inherits its parent's color. If you support those browsers, force the text color with className="[--tone-foreground:white]".

Live demo: Tones. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Each row paints one tone three ways from the same five variables, and the last row is built by colorVars from one hex value, #0EA5E9. Switch the site theme: the solid fills stay, while the soft tints and the tone text take their dark values). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Tones docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add tones

The free Button is the reference consumer. Its variant map contains no color at all:

const VARIANTS: Record<ButtonVariant, string> = {
  solid: "bg-(--tone) text-(--tone-foreground) shadow-raised",
  soft: "bg-(--tone-soft) text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
  outline: "border border-(--tone-border) text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
  ghost: "text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
  link: "rounded-[4px] text-(--tone-soft-foreground) underline decoration-current/35 decoration-1 underline-offset-4 transition-[color,text-decoration-color] hover:decoration-current",
};

Six tones times five variants, plus any custom color, from five lines. Hover and press are a layer of currentColor at 8% and 12% opacity, so they also work for every tone without extra classes.

How do you design dark mode with tokens?

Treat dark as a second set of values for the same roles, picked by hand, and switch it with a class. Components keep the same classes in both themes, so almost nothing in a component needs a dark: prefix.

The variant: our tokens, like shadcn/ui's, use @custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));. The Tailwind dark mode docs show &:where(.dark, .dark *), which also matches the element that carries the class and adds no specificity. With the class on <html>, both behave the same for normal use. The class itself comes from next-themes, which writes it before the first paint: wrap the app in its ThemeProvider with attribute="class" (the full provider file is in the props section below), and render <html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning> in the root layout, because next-themes changes the class before React hydrates:

// app/layout.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { Providers } from "./providers";
import "./globals.css";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning>
      <body className="bg-background text-foreground">
        <Providers>{children}</Providers>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

What a designed dark theme looks like in practice, from our token file:

  • Surfaces lighten as they come forward. #000 page, #121212 card, #1A1A1A surface, #262626 popover.
  • Fills stay, soft surfaces flip. The brand fill is #D63F00 in both themes, so white text keeps 4.59:1. Its soft surface goes from #FFEFE6 to #2A1509, and its text from #B03400 to #FF8A4C.
  • The neutral fill inverts. primary is black with white text in light mode and #FAFAFA with #171717 in dark, so the neutral solid button keeps 21:1 in light and 17.16:1 in dark.
  • Elevation changes technique. A drop shadow barely shows on black, so dark shadows lean on a lit top edge and a white hairline (see the elevation levels below).
  • The focus ring shifts. --ring is oklch(0.60 0.20 36.93) in light and oklch(0.6617 0.2215 36.93) in dark, deeper on white so a 2px outline keeps 3:1 on white and on the gray card.
  • Some components need an exception. Our soft Card uses bg-card in light but bg-foreground/7 in dark, because the dark --card is the same gray as a dark sidebar or stage and the card would vanish there. An inversion script never makes that call.

How do you check contrast for every token pair?

List the pairs that are meant to be used together, convert both colors to sRGB, compute the WCAG ratio in both themes, and fail the build below 4.5:1. WCAG asks for 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text (1.4.3), and 3:1 for UI components and focus indicators against what is next to them (1.4.11).

Our check covers 54 pairs per theme, 108 in total, and reports 0 below 4.5:1 as of release 1.7.0. The tightest pairs are brand-foreground on brand at 4.59:1 and muted-foreground on the light card at 4.62:1. Here is a self-contained version you can drop into scripts/ and run with npx tsx scripts/check-contrast.ts. It reads hex and oklch() values (decimal or percent lightness), follows var() references and exits with code 1 on a failure. It expects the token names used in this guide; if yours differ, edit SURFACES, TONES and PAIRS:

// scripts/check-contrast.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

type Rgb = [number, number, number];
const css = readFileSync("app/globals.css", "utf8").replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, "");

// every --name: value inside the blocks that start with this selector
function vars(selector: string) {
  const map = new Map<string, string>();
  const block = new RegExp(`(?:^|\\n)${selector.replace(".", "\\.")}\\s*\\{([^}]*)\\}`, "g");
  for (const m of css.matchAll(block))
    for (const d of m[1].matchAll(/(--[\w-]+)\s*:\s*([^;]+);/g)) map.set(d[1], d[2].trim());
  return map;
}

export function oklchToRgb(l: number, c: number, h: number): Rgb {
  const a = c * Math.cos((h * Math.PI) / 180);
  const b = c * Math.sin((h * Math.PI) / 180);
  const l3 = (l + 0.3963377774 * a + 0.2158037573 * b) ** 3;
  const m3 = (l - 0.1055613458 * a - 0.0638541728 * b) ** 3;
  const s3 = (l - 0.0894841775 * a - 1.291485548 * b) ** 3;
  const linear = [
    4.0767416621 * l3 - 3.3077115913 * m3 + 0.2309699292 * s3,
    -1.2684380046 * l3 + 2.6097574011 * m3 - 0.3413193965 * s3,
    -0.0041960863 * l3 - 0.7034186147 * m3 + 1.707614701 * s3,
  ];
  // clamp into srgb, then gamma-encode
  return linear.map((v) => {
    const x = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, v));
    return x <= 0.0031308 ? 12.92 * x : 1.055 * x ** (1 / 2.4) - 0.055;
  }) as Rgb;
}

function parse(value: string, map: Map<string, string>): Rgb {
  const ref = value.match(/^var\((--[\w-]+)\)$/);
  if (ref) return parse(map.get(ref[1]) ?? "", map);
  if (value.startsWith("#")) {
    const hex = value.length === 4 ? [...value.slice(1)].map((ch) => ch + ch).join("") : value.slice(1);
    return [0, 2, 4].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255) as Rgb;
  }
  const ok = value.match(/^oklch\(\s*([\d.]+)(%?)\s+([\d.]+)\s+([\d.]+)\s*\)$/);
  if (ok) return oklchToRgb(ok[2] ? +ok[1] / 100 : +ok[1], +ok[3], +ok[4]);
  throw new Error(`cannot parse "${value}"`);
}

const channel = (c: number) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);
const luminance = ([r, g, b]: Rgb) => 0.2126 * channel(r) + 0.7152 * channel(g) + 0.0722 * channel(b);

export function contrast(fg: Rgb, bg: Rgb) {
  const [hi, lo] = [luminance(fg), luminance(bg)].sort((x, y) => y - x);
  return (hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05);
}

const SURFACES = ["background", "card", "popover", "surface", "canvas"];
const TONES = ["brand", "success", "warning", "info", "destructive"];
const PAIRS = [
  ["foreground", "background"],
  ...SURFACES.map((s) => ["muted-foreground", s]),
  ...TONES.flatMap((t) => [
    [`${t}-foreground`, t],
    [`${t}-soft-foreground`, `${t}-soft`],
    ...SURFACES.map((s) => [`${t}-soft-foreground`, s]),
  ]),
];

const light = vars(":root");
const themes = { light, dark: new Map([...light, ...vars(".dark")]) };
let failures = 0;
for (const [theme, map] of Object.entries(themes)) {
  for (const [fg, bg] of PAIRS) {
    const ratio = contrast(parse(map.get(`--${fg}`) ?? "", map), parse(map.get(`--${bg}`) ?? "", map));
    if (ratio < 4.5) {
      failures++;
      console.log(`FAIL ${theme}: ${fg} on ${bg} is ${ratio.toFixed(2)}:1`);
    }
  }
}
console.log(`${PAIRS.length * 2} pairs checked, ${failures} below 4.5:1`);
process.exitCode = failures ? 1 : 0;

This trimmed version checks 82 pairs. Our full script adds the remaining surface, primary and legacy pairs and composites translucent values over the page first. The pair list is the valuable part: it encodes which text may sit on which surface, so a new token is checked the day it is added. Run it in CI next to the type check.

Should you write Tailwind v4 OKLCH values or hex?

Use whichever format you can reason about; the format does not change contrast. Tailwind's own palette moved "from rgb to oklch, taking advantage of the wider gamut" in v4.0 (release post), and its colors reference lists every Tailwind v4 OKLCH value, such as --color-red-500: oklch(63.7% 0.237 25.331). OKLCH earns its place when you derive colors in code, because lightness is its own channel: you can move it while hue and chroma stay put, and the result still looks like the same color.

In our file, neutrals are oklch() with zero chroma (oklch(0.3211 0 0) is the light foreground), and the tone values are hex, tuned by hand against the contrast check. The theme generator goes the other way: you pick a base color for each tone (brand, success, warning, danger, info), and it derives that tone's fill, soft surface and text in OKLCH. For light mode it puts the soft surface at lightness 0.965 with chroma capped at 0.035, then walks the tone text's lightness down from 0.6 in 0.005 steps until it reaches 4.6:1 on the soft surface and on every neutral surface. Move oklchToRgb and contrast from the contrast script into their own module, scripts/color.ts, so importing them does not run the check, and the same search is a few lines:

import { contrast, oklchToRgb } from "./color";

type Rgb = [number, number, number];

// keep hue and chroma, walk lightness until the color reads on every surface it can sit on
export function findReadable(c: number, h: number, surfaces: Rgb[], from: number, to: number, target = 4.6): Rgb {
  const step = from < to ? 0.005 : -0.005;
  for (let l = from; step > 0 ? l <= to : l >= to; l += step) {
    const rgb = oklchToRgb(l, c, h);
    if (Math.min(...surfaces.map((bg) => contrast(rgb, bg))) >= target) return rgb;
  }
  return oklchToRgb(to, c, h);
}

The target is 4.6 rather than 4.5 so rounding to hex cannot push a color under the line. One caution: a high-chroma OKLCH value can fall outside sRGB, and what a screen then shows depends on the display and the browser. Keep token values inside sRGB, or at least measure the clamped sRGB value, as oklchToRgb does.

How do radius, elevation, z-index and motion become tokens?

They become scales with a fixed set of steps, each with one job, so a component picks a step instead of a number. A Tailwind v4 design system that only tokenizes color still ends up with one-off shadows and a z-[9999] somewhere.

Radius follows size

Tie radius to the control's size. A 32px and a 48px button only read as the same shape when the larger one has the larger radius. Our controls copy this map from the Button:

type Scale = "sm" | "md" | "lg";
type ButtonRadius = "none" | "sm" | "md" | "lg" | "full";

const RADII: Record<ButtonRadius, Record<Scale, string>> = {
  none: { sm: "rounded-none", md: "rounded-none", lg: "rounded-none" },
  sm: { sm: "rounded-[6px]", md: "rounded-[8px]", lg: "rounded-[10px]" },
  md: { sm: "rounded-[8px]", md: "rounded-[10px]", lg: "rounded-[12px]" },
  lg: { sm: "rounded-[10px]", md: "rounded-[14px]", lg: "rounded-[16px]" },
  full: { sm: "rounded-full", md: "rounded-full", lg: "rounded-full" },
};

Surfaces use rounded-2xl (16px) for cards, menus and popovers, rounded-3xl (24px) for dialogs, and rounded-t-[28px] for bottom sheets. Anything inside a padded surface takes the outer radius minus the padding: a rounded-2xl p-1.5 menu has rounded-[10px] items. Sizes follow the same thinking: 32, 40 and 48px, with the 40px size growing to 44px on touch screens, the rule from our mobile-first React components guide.

The trap is a global radius token. Our file still carries shadcn/ui's older scale for ported components: --radius: 0.375rem, --radius-lg: var(--radius) and --radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) - 4px). That remaps Tailwind's rounded-sm, rounded-md, rounded-lg and rounded-xl to 2, 4, 6 and 10px everywhere, including markup pasted from Tailwind's docs (the compiled .rounded-lg is border-radius: var(--radius)), so new components never use those four classes. As of October 2026, shadcn/ui's theming docs derive the scale by multiplication instead (--radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) * 0.6) up to --radius-4xl), which has the same project-wide reach. If you theme radius globally, own every component that uses it.

Three elevation levels

Three levels cover a library: shadow-raised for buttons, cards and thumbs, shadow-floating for popovers, menus and toasts, shadow-modal for dialogs and sheets. Each level carries its own 1px hairline, so an elevated surface needs no border:

:root {
  --elevation-floating: 0 0 0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.06), 0 4px 12px -2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.08), 0 16px 36px -10px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.16);
}
.dark {
  /* on a black page a drop shadow barely shows: a lit top edge and a hairline do the work */
  --elevation-floating: inset 0 1px 0 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.07), 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.09), 0 8px 24px -4px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6), 0 20px 48px -12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.7);
}
@theme inline {
  --shadow-floating: var(--elevation-floating);
}

An interactive Card moves between two of these levels on hover, and the lift runs as a CSS transition on a spring curve (below), so a grid of fifty cards animates without JavaScript.

Live demo: Card. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Hover the card to see it lift from shadow-raised to shadow-floating, then press it to see the dip to 98% (phones get only the press). Switch the site theme to see the dark elevation draw a lit top edge instead). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Card docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add card

Stacking layers

Class Value Use
z-dropdown 1000 in-flow panels that are not portaled
z-sticky 1100 sticky headers, tab bars, CTA bars
z-overlay 1200 the dimmed backdrop
z-modal 1300 dialogs, sheets, drawers
z-popover 1400 portaled menus, selects, popovers
z-toast 1500 toasts
z-tooltip 1600 tooltips, always on top

Popovers sit above modals on purpose: a select inside a dialog has to open over it. No overlay in the library uses a raw number like z-50; small values such as z-10 only order parts inside one component.

Motion

CSS transitions use three durations (duration-fast 150ms, duration-normal 240ms, duration-slow 400ms) and named curves (ease-smooth is cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), ease-sheet is cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)). Our JavaScript springs are also sampled into CSS linear() easings: ease-spring with duration-spring (500ms) matches a spring with stiffness 300 and damping 30.

Can component props work like design tokens?

Yes, for the decisions that are props: the radius of every button, the default size of fields, the variant of every card. CSS variables cannot set a prop, so Wingo UI reads those from a React provider, and UIProvider defaults works as a token layer for props. The free UIProvider merges app-wide defaults under the props each component receives, keyed by its data-slot name:

// app/providers.tsx
"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { ThemeProvider } from "next-themes";
import { UIProvider } from "@/lib/ui-config";

export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <ThemeProvider attribute="class" defaultTheme="system" enableSystem disableTransitionOnChange>
      <UIProvider locale="en-US" defaults={{ button: { radius: "full" }, card: { variant: "outline" } }}>
        {children}
      </UIProvider>
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}

Inside a component, the first line reads the defaults, and the signature defaults stay the last fallback:

export function Button(buttonProps: ButtonProps) {
  const { variant = "solid", tone = "neutral", size = "md", radius = "md", ...rest } = useDefaults("button", buttonProps);
  // ...
}

Explicit props win, then the provider, then the component's own defaults. An undefined prop does not override a provider value, so wrappers can pass props through without erasing the theme. The same signature takes ref as a regular prop, with no forwardRef wrapper; our React 19 forwardRef migration guide moves older components to that pattern, TypeScript types included.

Live demo: UIProvider. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (The first button uses its built-in defaults; the two below get radius full, size lg and tone brand from a UIProvider, and the outline one keeps the variant it passes itself). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the UIProvider docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add ui-config

How do you add these tokens to an existing Next.js project?

Run npx wingo-ui@latest init in a project that has Tailwind CSS v4. It writes wingo-ui.json and lib/utils.ts (the cn helper), installs clsx and tailwind-merge, and merges the tokens into the stylesheet that contains @import "tailwindcss". It only adds missing names and keeps your values; add later brings any tokens a new component needs. The full block, 74 variables in :root plus their dark values and Tailwind mappings, is served at /r/tokens.css, and coding agents get the same CSS from the MCP tool get_theme_tokens (see our component library MCP guide). The theming docs show the main tokens with their light and dark values, and the two dark mode setups the CLI supports: a .dark class, or prefers-color-scheme when your stylesheet already uses it.

To restyle, open the theme generator, pick a brand color, neutrals, radius, font and component defaults, check its contrast report, and apply the export:

npx wingo-ui@latest theme apply ./theme.json

It replaces the values of the tokens the theme sets, in light and dark, adds Tailwind mappings for new ones and prints the UIProvider defaults and locale to paste into your provider.

Coming from shadcn/ui: the shared names line up, but two keep different meanings. Our --card is a flat gray tile where shadcn's is the card background, and our --accent is an orange tint. Because init keeps your existing values, a shadcn project keeps its own --card and --accent, so check the soft Card variant after the merge. Our shadcn alternatives comparison covers the wider differences between the two libraries.

Which mistakes break a Tailwind v4 design system?

The same few mistakes show up in most token files:

  • dark: classes in components. A component that needs dark:bg-zinc-900 is missing a token.
  • Palette names in components. bg-blue-600 cannot follow a theme; use a role or a tone.
  • Fill colors as text. text-destructive on a dark surface fails AA; use the soft foreground.
  • Per-theme values in plain @theme. Keep them in :root and .dark, mapped with inline.
  • A global radius that rewrites Tailwind's scale. Every pasted rounded-lg changes with it.
  • Raw z-index numbers. Two z-50 overlays from two authors will collide.
  • No contrast check. Tokens drift with every tweak; a check in CI catches it the same day.

Where should you start?

Run npx wingo-ui@latest init in your Next.js project, then npx wingo-ui@latest add button, which brings the Tones and UIProvider items with it. Replace one hard-coded color in a real screen with a role token, open it in both themes, and add the contrast script to CI. Two more guides in Next.js and Tailwind CSS cover the component code around the tokens: the React 19 forwardRef migration and an SSR-safe React use mobile hook that hydrates without a mismatch.

Components in this post

  • Button (Free): The button every screen starts with: five variants, six tones, three sizes plus icon sizes, and a loading state that never jumps. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add button
  • Tones (Free): One way to color a component: a tone or any CSS color becomes five CSS variables every variant paints with. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add tones
  • UIProvider (Free): App-wide configuration for Wingo UI: default props for every component, the Intl locale and the reduced-motion policy. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add ui-config
  • Card (Free): The surface listings, stats, settings and plans sit on: media, header, body and footer parts, four variants and a lift-and-press mode. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add card
  • Badge (Free): Status chips, removable filters and animated counts in three variants and six tones, plus an anchor that pins a count or dot to any corner. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add badge

FAQ

Where do design tokens go in Tailwind v4?

In the global CSS file, after @import "tailwindcss". Variables in an @theme block become utilities (--color-surface gives bg-surface), and values that change per theme live in :root and .dark and are mapped with @theme inline. A tailwind.config.js file is no longer required.

What is the difference between @theme and @theme inline in Tailwind v4?

With @theme, the utility references the theme variable, so bg-surface compiles to var(--color-surface), which is resolved once on :root. With @theme inline, the utility gets the referenced value written in, so bg-surface compiles to var(--surface) and resolves on the element that uses it. Use inline whenever a theme variable points at another variable.

Should Tailwind v4 colors be OKLCH or hex?

Either works, because tokens are plain CSS colors and the format does not change contrast. Tailwind's own palette moved to oklch in v4.0. OKLCH helps most when you derive colors in code, since you can keep hue and chroma and move lightness until a contrast target passes.

How do I add dark mode to Tailwind v4 design tokens?

Redefine the same variables in a .dark block and add @custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *)); so dark: utilities follow the class too. next-themes with attribute="class" sets the class before the first paint. Components that use semantic tokens then need no dark: classes.

How do I check color contrast for design tokens?

List every text token with each surface it can sit on, convert the values to sRGB, and compute the WCAG ratio for light and dark. Fail the build below 4.5:1 for body text; focus rings and other UI shapes need 3:1.

Are the Wingo UI design tokens free?

Yes. npx wingo-ui@latest init merges the tokens into your stylesheet without an account, and the Button, Card, Tones and UIProvider items in this guide are free. As of release 1.7.0, 75 of the 326 registry items are free and the rest need Pro.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Tailwind v4 Design Tokens: Colors, Dark Mode and Contrast. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: My Agent Swore It Fixed the UI. The Button Disagreed. 🫠
description:
Hey tech adventurers! 👋

My coding agent told me it fixed the UI. Tests green. Lint green. A very confident little summary with a ✅ at the end.

The button was off-screen. 🫠

So I built Pawprint. Agents now have to bring pics.

Green checks can't see 👀

Here's the thing nobody puts on the slide. Your CI is blind. It knows the function returns true. It has no idea the modal now covers the whole checkout page, or that "dark mode fix" means white text on a white background.

For backend work, tests get you most of the way. For anything a human actually looks at, the only real proof is... looking at it.

And I'm not pulling every branch, running the app, and clicking around to check an agent's homework. That was supposed to be the agent's job. That's the whole deal. 🤝

So the agent shows its work 📸

With Pawprint, the agent publishes evidence for the change and links it in the PR. Each publish has:

  • a description of what changed 📝
  • the list of changes 📋
  • before and after comparisons, side by side 🔀
  • screenshots and video when a still frame isn't enough 🎬

You open the PR, click the pawprint, and know in about ten seconds whether "fixed" means fixed. No checkout. No npm run dev. No vibes.

Your staging app is not public content 🔐

Here's the part I cared about most. Agents screenshot everything, and everything includes your unreleased app.

So the evidence sits behind GitHub sign-in. Share it with your org and the people in it can see it. Leave the org out and only you can. GitHub itself just shows a generic Pawprint card, so the internet sees a dog and nothing else. 🐕

You can make a page public when you actually want to show it off. You can't do it by accident.

"Done" should look like something 🧾

I keep saying it, and I'll keep saying it: agents love the word "done." Done is cheap. Done is a token.

Evidence is expensive in the right way. It's the agent proving it actually opened the thing it changed. And it's the only kind of review that still scales when agents are opening more PRs than you have hours.

Pawprint doesn't replace reviewers. It just means that when someone does look, there's something to look at.

Here's an example evidence page if you want to see what a receipt looks like.

P.S. Yes, everything I build is named after my dog. No, I will not be taking questions. 🐾

title: Vercel Connect now supports TanStack AI
description:
Agents built with TanStack AI can now call OAuth-protected MCP servers through Vercel Connect, with no credentials for you to store or rotate.

The new @vercel/connect/tanstack-ai subpath exports connectMCPTransport, which takes a TanStack transport config and attaches a Connect-backed auth provider. The provider is called before every MCP request, so the token is always fresh.

If the user has not granted access, createMCPClient fails with a consent challenge before the model runs. Catch it with getConsentChallenge and redirect to Connect's consent URL. Otherwise, a consent error raised within a tool call would reach the model as an error string rather than the user as a redirect.

Read the TanStack AI integration docs to get started, or see the full list of supported frameworks and adapters for Vercel Connect.

Read more

title: Sample-efficient learning with Dense Associative Memories
description:
arXiv:2610.27384v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We analytically study the evolution of the energy function of Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) as they train on randomly sampled codewords of random expander low-density parity-check codes (a.k.a. solutions of random XORSAT problems). We identify two distinct regimes and a transition between them, reminiscent of grokking in neural networks. A regime of small training set size is where the model memorizes a few training examples but cannot discover the underlying rules of the entire codeword dictionary generative process. The opposite regime, corresponding to a larger training set size, is where the model has uncovered the sparse constraints that generated the entire data set after seeing only polynomially many patterns. We also design a novel class of DenseAMs with a thresholding learning rule, and show that any amount of thresholding enables the model to perform simplified sparse Hamiltonian learning, which exponentially reduces the number of training examples needed to learn the true underlying data set. In this regime, the model learns how to discover $\exp[\mathrm{O}(n)]$ solutions from only $\mathrm{O}(\log n)$ training samples, which is asymptotically optimal for any learning algorithm. When training on codewords of certain random codes, the model can even learn the underlying code when a small O(1) fraction of bits are latent variables. These latent variables are not shown to the model during learning, but will be discovered by sparsifying observed higher-order correlations. For certain random codes, we show that a simple and conservative algorithm learns a minimal latent representation for the data set. This provides a transparent, physics-motivated, and analytically tractable toy model for how deep latent representations emerge in an associative memory training.

title: useState vs useReducer: Stop Choosing Tools Before Understanding State
description:
Why React state management needs consistent decision criteria, not another library.

When should you use useState instead of useReducer?

The common answer is straightforward:

  • Use useState for simple state.
  • Use useReducer for complex state.

It's not necessarily wrong. But I think it's incomplete.

Because state management complexity isn't just about how many values we store. It's also about who owns the state, how it changes, which rules govern those changes, and how long that state needs to live.

That leads me to a more fundamental question:

Why do we start by choosing a state management tool before defining the criteria that should guide that choice?

1. The Problem with Tool-First Thinking

Imagine we're building a checkout flow in React.

We have a shipping address, payment method, discount code, and several validation rules.

We could use multiple useState hooks. Or we could combine the logic into a useReducer.

But having multiple state variables doesn't automatically justify a reducer.

What matters is how those values relate to each other.

For example, changing the shipping country might invalidate the selected shipping method.

Now we're no longer dealing with independent values. We're dealing with related state transitions governed by business rules.

And that's where the architectural decision becomes interesting.

2. Introducing a State Management Decision Authority

What if we separated the decision-making process from the tools themselves?

I like to think of this as a State Management Decision Authority.

It's not a new React API, an additional library, or an official design pattern.

It's a proposed architectural approach: define a consistent set of criteria that determines which state management strategy fits a particular problem.

Before choosing a tool, evaluate five dimensions.

State ownership

Who needs access to this state?

Is it owned by a single component, a feature, or multiple independent parts of the application?

Update complexity

Does updating the state involve assigning a new value, or applying several related business rules?

State relationships

Are state values independent, or must certain invariants remain true whenever one value changes?

State transitions

Are there explicit transitions between states, such as idle, processing, success, and error?

State lifecycle

Are we managing local UI state, shared client state, or server state that requires fetching, caching, and synchronization?

The answers should determine the tool, rather than the tool shaping how we define the problem.

3. When useState Is the Right Choice

Consider a simple toggle:

const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);

The state is local, the update is straightforward, and there are no complex transition rules.

Introducing actions and a reducer here would add complexity without providing much value.

The same applies to many inputs, visibility flags, and independently updated UI values.

Importantly, the number of state variables alone is not a reliable decision criterion.

A component with five independent state variables might be better served by five useState hooks than by one reducer.

The goal isn't to minimize the number of hooks. It's to minimize unnecessary complexity.

4. When useReducer Becomes More Valuable

Now consider a payment workflow.

We have several possible states, and transitions between them must follow particular rules.

const initialState = {
  status: "idle",
  error: null
};

function paymentReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "PAYMENT_STARTED":
      if (state.status !== "idle") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "processing",
        error: null
      };

    case "PAYMENT_SUCCEEDED":
      if (state.status !== "processing") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "success",
        error: null
      };

    case "PAYMENT_FAILED":
      if (state.status !== "processing") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "error",
        error: action.error
      };

    default:
      return state;
  }
}

Inside the component:

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(
  paymentReducer,
  initialState
);

Instead of allowing different parts of the component to independently decide how the state should change, we dispatch actions describing what happened.

The reducer calculates the next state.

This creates a useful separation:

What happened vs. how the state should respond.

But a reducer doesn't automatically guarantee correctness.

We still need to define valid transitions, protect state invariants, and keep side effects outside the reducer.

In this example, initiating an actual payment request is a side effect, not something the reducer should perform.

5. Decision Authority vs. Transition Authority

There's an important distinction here.

Decision Authority determines which state management approach we should use.

State Transition Authority determines how state changes are evaluated and applied.

A reducer can centralize transition logic within a particular state boundary.

But that doesn't mean every state variable needs a reducer, or that every reducer needs a full state machine.

The architectural objective isn't to centralize everything.

It's to make decisions consistently while preserving the simplest appropriate implementation.

6. Beyond React Hooks: Zustand, Redux Toolkit, and Server State

The same decision criteria can extend beyond useState and useReducer.

When multiple components need the same state, we can first consider lifting state up or using Context.

When multiple features need shared client state, tools such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit may become appropriate.

If the primary challenge involves remote data fetching, caching, invalidation, and synchronization, a dedicated server-state solution such as TanStack Query or RTK Query can be more suitable.

These tools aren't necessarily mutually exclusive.

An application might use:

  • useState for local UI interactions.
  • useReducer for a complex form workflow.
  • Zustand or Redux Toolkit for shared client state.
  • TanStack Query or RTK Query for server-state management.

The decision depends on the responsibility of each state boundary.

7. A Practical Decision Framework

Here's a lightweight framework I would use before making a state management decision.

Question Possible direction
Is the state local with simple, independent updates? Start with useState
Are transitions governed by related rules? Consider useReducer
Is state shared within a component subtree? Consider lifting state or Context
Do independent features require shared client state? Evaluate Zustand or Redux Toolkit
Does the state primarily represent remote server data? Evaluate TanStack Query or RTK Query

This isn't a rigid rules engine.

A shared state doesn't automatically require a global store, and a complex state doesn't automatically require useReducer.

It's a framework for asking better questions before committing to an implementation.

8. The Bigger Architectural Principle

State management discussions often become comparisons between libraries.

Which is faster?

Which has less boilerplate?

Which is easier to learn?

Those questions matter, but they're secondary to understanding the problem.

I believe we should first establish consistent criteria for choosing a state management strategy.

Then evaluate available tools against those criteria.

Unify the decision criteria, not necessarily the tools.

That's the architectural principle I'm exploring here.

The real skill isn't knowing every state management library.

It's understanding why, when, and where each one belongs.

Final Thoughts

useState and useReducer aren't competing solutions where one must win.

They're different approaches to managing state, each valuable in the right context.

And the same reasoning applies when we move toward Context, Zustand, Redux Toolkit, or server-state solutions.

Let the problem define the tool, not the tool define the solution.

I'd love to hear how other developers approach these decisions.

Do you follow explicit state management criteria in your projects, or do team preferences and existing architecture usually drive the choice?

Part 1 of the State Management Decision Authority series.

title: One panic shouldn't kill the scan: isolating rules with catch_unwind
description:
Cloud Cost Analyzer runs 92 rules against your cloud account in a single scan. A rule is a real unit of work: it pulls a resource's config and metrics, evaluates them against a cost model, and maybe emits a finding. They're independent, and every one of them leans on libraries I don't control: cloud SDKs, response parsers, date and math crates.

Any of that can meet an input it didn't anticipate and panic: an unwrap() that couldn't fail until some resource shape I'd never seen, an index out of bounds deep in a dependency, an overflow on a field that's normally small. Usually nobody wrote bad code. A library just hit an edge case nobody dependency-audited for.

The question isn't whether a rule will panic. It's what happens to the other 91 when rule

57 does. A cost report that dies two-thirds of the way through because one rule met one weird EBS volume isn't much use to anyone.

"So handle it with Result"

The obvious objection: this is Rust, so model the failure as a Result and there's nothing to catch. The rules do exactly that for every failure they can see coming. Can't reach the metrics API? Result. Missing a field the check needs? Result. Expected failures travel the normal error path and always have.

A panic is the failure I didn't foresee. You can't write ? for a bug you don't know exists, and you certainly can't for one buried three crates deep in a dependency that panics on input its author never tested. Result handles the errors you anticipated. catch_unwind covers the ones you couldn't, and it only exists in my code because Result can't reach into code I didn't write.

std::panic::catch_unwind runs a closure and hands you back a Result instead of letting the panic tear through your stack. Here's the real dispatch, one rule at a time:

let mut eval = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
    rule.evaluate(resource, metrics, costs)
}))
.unwrap_or_else(|_| {
    tracing::error!(
        rule_id = rule_id,
        resource_id = %resource.resource_id,
        "rule panicked during evaluate; skipping its finding"
    );
    None
})?;

A rule panics, we log which rule and which resource, return None for that one finding, and the loop moves on to the next rule. One panic costs one finding.

What AssertUnwindSafe actually promises

The compiler demands that wrapper, and it's worth understanding why before reaching for it.

catch_unwind only accepts a closure that's UnwindSafe. The idea: if a panic unwinds through the middle of your closure, any state it shared with the outside could be left half-updated, and UnwindSafe is the marker that says there's no such state to observe. My closure captures &rule, &resource, and friends by reference, so the compiler can't prove that on its own and refuses to compile.

AssertUnwindSafe is me telling the compiler I've checked, and that catching this panic won't let anyone observe a broken invariant. That holds here for a concrete reason: on panic I throw the result away. I return None and never read a partially-built finding. There's no torn state to see because I don't look. That's the bar for reaching for AssertUnwindSafe. You should be able to point at why the post-panic state is unobservable.

The setting that silently turns all of this off

catch_unwind only works if panics unwind, which is why it isn't a try/catch. Rust has two panic strategies, and you choose per build:

# Cargo.toml — a size-optimized profile
# Inherits all release settings, adds panic=abort to remove unwind tables
panic = "abort"

Under panic = "abort", a panic doesn't unwind the stack. It calls the abort handler and kills the process immediately, so catch_unwind never gets a chance to run. Every one of those careful per-rule guards becomes a no-op, and rule #57 takes the whole process down with it. That happens in the exact build you ship to production, because panic = "abort" is something you turn on to drop unwind tables and shrink the binary.

So panic isolation is a whole-binary decision rather than a library feature you add. If you want one bad rule to cost one finding, you have to keep the unwinding runtime, and eat the binary size, on purpose. No assert or catch_unwind call can buy that back for you. It's the trade you make once, in the profile, and it's invisible in the code that depends on it.

One more edge: poisoned locks

If a rule panics while holding a Mutex or RwLock, that lock is poisoned and the next rule to touch it inherits the panic. The isolation above holds partly because the shared data these rules read is immutable and lock-free, so there's no lock to poison. If yours mutates shared state under a lock, catching the panic isn't enough. You have to decide what a poisoned lock means.

Where it landed

Rules and the second-stage analyzers both run inside that catch_unwind, under an unwinding profile. When a rule, or a library it leans on, meets an input nobody anticipated, the cost is one missing finding and a log line naming the culprit. The isolation works because the binary is built to allow it, and I can say exactly why the post-panic state is safe to ignore: I never read it.

This is part of a series on building Cloud Cost Analyzer in Rust.

title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.

title: Selling time, not files: hosts, multi-host carts and a 10-minute Join window
description:
A course is a file you can sell a thousand times. An appointment is an hour that can only be sold once. That one difference shapes most of the booking system in VeloxonHub. The 30-second reel shows the flow from the outside. Here's what happens inside.

1. An appointment is a product with booking rules

The host creates an appointment in a 5-step drawer: details, type and host, availability, booking rules and pricing. Under the hood it's a scheduling product with appointment settings: duration, buffers, an advance-booking window, booking, cancellation and reschedule cutoffs, capacity per slot, an approval flag, whether multiple slots can be selected, and the Join window.

2. Free or paid is decided by the price, not a flag

If the appointment has no active price, the booking page shows a plain "Confirm Booking" action and calls the booking endpoint directly. Several slots are booked one by one, and on a partial failure the UI keeps only the slots that still need booking and says exactly which failed. Package appointments use pre-paid credits and go through a batch endpoint instead.

If there is a price, the selection goes into the same cart and checkout as every other product.

3. Slots belong to hosts

Each host has weekly availability rules plus exceptions (extra hours, blocked days, vacations) and site-wide holidays. The booking page loads a month of slots, and every slot carries its host_id. Choosing a host filters the calendar to that host's slots, so the client only sees times that host can actually take. Times are stored in UTC and shown in the visitor's time zone.

4. Multi-host selections are priced per slot

When multiple selection is on, a client can mix hosts: Monday with one host, Thursday with another. Pricing doesn't apply one rate to the whole selection. Each slot is resolved through its own host:

  • if the host has active prices of their own, those win;
  • otherwise the product's default price applies;
  • only active prices count, so an archived host price never sets the total.

The result is a list of lines (time, host, amount) plus a total, and a flag if the selection mixes currencies. The server resolves the final amounts again at checkout, so the browser never decides what anyone pays. There's also a conflict check, so one person can't put two overlapping slots in the cart.

5. Join is a 10-minute window, decided by the backend

After booking, the call shows up in the client's schedule. What the main button does depends on the delivery method (join a room, get directions, check in, wait for a call), and the backend sends that as joining_details.action.

For a virtual call, Join only becomes active join_available_minutes_before the start. The default is 10 minutes (COALESCE(join_available_minutes_before, 10)), and the host can change it. A small ticker on the client re-checks every 15 seconds, so the button turns on without a reload.

What we'd tell someone building the same thing

  • Let "free" fall out of the price data instead of a separate flag.
  • Attach every slot to a host, and price every slot through its host.
  • Never trust a price from the browser, and check for overlapping slots before checkout.
  • Treat "join" as a window with a status check, not a link you hand out at booking time.

Try it with a free trial: https://veloxonhub.com. Happy to go deeper into availability exceptions or multi-host pricing in the comments.
