title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
description:
arXiv:2610.27142v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

title: Correcting Attribution Patching with a Few Exact Measurements
description:
arXiv:2610.27393v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability asks which language model components matter for a behavior, and activation patching answers by changing one component's activation and measuring its effect, at a cost growing with components and prompts. Attribution patching estimates these effects from one gradient pass, but its estimates can be far off, and verifying each one restores the cost. Can the structure of these errors reduce this cost? We propose Guided-AP, which uses a few exact measurements to reveal attribution patching's errors and correct unmeasured estimates. On a single prompt, many components' errors share one sign, so a small exact sample yields one correction for the rest. Over many prompts of one task, components are misestimated similarly, so a few measured prompts show what to verify and how to correct each component's average effect. Our analysis shows that choosing what to verify needs error size, while correction also needs sign. On a single prompt, the correction lowers error by up to 26% across three behaviors at the compute of verifying the largest estimates and also on larger models. Over many prompts, learned corrections cut the error of average effects on factual completion by 75% to 79%, repaying their cost in long analyses.

title: Cap the Fan-Out: Building a UAE Mover-Quote Flow That Does Not Sell Your Phone Number to Ten Companies
description:
TL;DR

  • Most "free moving quotes" products are lead-resale funnels. The customer's number becomes inventory.
  • A useful comparison marketplace needs structured intake, a small matched set of suppliers, and replies people can compare in writing.
  • In Dubai, the quote sits inside a larger dependency chain (building NOC, tenancy registration). Ignoring that produces quotes that cannot be used on the date the customer asked for.
  • We ship a short form, match up to three vetted movers, and keep replies on email or WhatsApp text — no calls required.

Moving flats in Dubai has a familiar failure mode. You fill in a form. Your phone rings. Then it rings again. By evening you have numbers in WhatsApp threads, PDFs, and voice notes. One includes packing. One does not say. One is a single figure with "+ VAT" at the end. Nobody asked which floor you live on.

I am building a small quote-comparison service for movers in the UAE. This post is for people who build two-sided products, not for people looking for a truck. It is about the product decisions that matter before the matching algorithm gets interesting.

The quote is the product — and free text destroys it

A moving price depends on variables customers do not always know they need to share:

  • Home size as a proxy for volume (even "2BR" varies a lot)
  • Floor and lift access, including whether a service lift must be booked
  • Packing scope
  • Distance and route (JVC to Marina is not the same job as Marina to Abu Dhabi)
  • Move date, including weekend and month-end lease turnover
  • Building rules: most towers want a move-in or move-out permit (NOC) with time windows and often a deposit

A free-text "tell us about your move" box captures maybe two of these. The mover then either calls (your phone rings) or quotes high to cover unknowns. Either way, the customer cannot compare like with like.

So the first engineering job is intake design: turn a fuzzy request into a record a mover can price without a call.

What we ask today

We keep the form short. Every field costs completions. The live flow asks for:

  • Name, origin area, destination area
  • Home size from a fixed list (Studio, 1BR, 2BR, 3BR, Villa, Office) — not free text
  • Move date
  • A WhatsApp number and an email
  • Optional notes

The fixed list for home size does more work than it looks like. It turns the biggest pricing variable into an enum, which means routing can prefer movers who actually handle that size of job.

The next product step — and the one I would push anyone in this space to take — is collecting access details as structured fields too: floor, service lift yes/no, NOC already booked yes/no. Each tap removes a reason for a call.

The W3C forms tutorial is still a good reminder that labels, grouping, and clear instructions matter as much as field count.

Lead resale is the default model — and the incentives show

Charging movers instead of customers keeps the service free for the person moving. That part is fine. We do the same: movers pay, customers do not.

The broken part is fan-out. If you earn per lead and the customer does not pay, every extra company that receives the lead is extra revenue. Leads get blasted wide. Customers get ten calls. Movers compete on who dials first, not who quotes best.

Moving is a rare, high-stakes transaction. People move infrequently. The job involves everything they own. There is little repeat purchase to win back if it goes wrong. Volume-first lead models fit poorly.

So we made two decisions that cost short-term revenue:

  1. Each request goes to up to three movers, chosen for fit. Three is enough to compare and few enough that each mover treats the job as winnable.
  2. Replies come by email or WhatsApp text. No calls needed. Written quotes leave a record, sit side by side, and can be forwarded to a partner. Many people moving in the UAE are juggling a job start, a lease, and a school search. A text they can answer at midnight is worth more than a call they missed.

Normalise the output or you are just forwarding messages

Even with good intake, quotes arrive in different shapes. Comparison needs a shared schema. The fields I think belong on a comparable quote:

Field Why it matters
Total price, VAT included or excluded Most common "that's not what you quoted" fight
Packing scope (none / fragile / full) Biggest hidden difference between "similar" quotes
Materials included Often charged separately
Dismantling / reassembly Commonly excluded by default
Crew size and vehicle Proxy for duration
Insurance / liability terms What happens if something breaks
Payment terms Deposit vs balance on completion
Validity date Quotes expire around month-end

You do not need machine learning for this. You need a template movers can fill, plus patience to map free-text replies. Once quotes share a schema, "compare" stops meaning "read three WhatsApp threads."

Honest limitation: you can normalise what is written, not what is left out. If dismantling is not mentioned, the UI should say not stated — not invent "included" or "excluded."

Trust signals customers can check

"Vetted movers" is empty on its own. Trust only works if the customer can verify something, or if the platform states exactly what it checked.

What belongs on a mover profile, in my view:

  • Licensing stated precisely (what was checked, when)
  • Scope of work: residential vs office, local vs inter-emirate, packing in-house vs subcontracted
  • Reviews tied to real jobs where possible, and labelled clearly where not

For search engines, the same honesty applies to structured data. schema.org has a MovingCompany type. Fill only what the page shows. Google's spam policies call out region/city doorway pages that funnel users to one URL. Area pages should exist where there is real coverage and something specific to say — for example, towers in an area known for tight lift booking windows.

The move is not only the truck

In Dubai, the quote sits inside a sequence. The new tenancy often needs registration through Ejari with the Dubai Land Department. Utilities need connecting. The building wants its NOC. If the NOC is not booked, the best quote in the world still cannot happen on the requested date.

A useful quote product nudges these dependencies at the right moment without trying to own every step. A short checklist beside the quote ("Have you booked your building's move permit?") prevents more failed moves than a slightly cheaper price.

Official Ejari fee figures are published by Dubai Land Department on that service page (registration plus knowledge, innovation, and partner fees depending on channel). We do not invent market averages; we point people at the authority and at the operational checklist.

What I'd tell anyone building a lead-gen marketplace

  • Design intake for the supplier's pricing model, not for your CRM's vanity fields.
  • Cap the fan-out. Fewer, better-matched leads produce better quotes and a customer who does not regret giving you a number.
  • Normalise the output. Without a common schema you are a forwarding service.
  • Make trust checkable. Say exactly what you verified.
  • Respect the channel. Let people reply by text.

That is the thinking behind the flow at MoveWise UAE: one short form, up to three matched movers, replies by email or WhatsApp text. There is still more to build on the normalised comparison table. The hard part was never the code. It was deciding what not to do with the customer's phone number.

If you've shipped a marketplace with a "who pays" tension like this, how did you balance supplier revenue against customer experience?

About the author: Waqas Jawed builds MoveWise UAE, which helps people moving in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Ajman compare quotes from vetted movers. Contact: cs@movewiseuae.com.

This post was drafted with AI assistance and edited and fact-checked by the author.

title: The Second Run Is Where the Lies Show Up
description:
Every agent demo I have ever seen works on the first run. Mine did too. The first run has a clean state, a fresh context, and a demo-friendly task that was probably chosen after a few attempts.

The second run is different, and it is the only run I trust.

What changes between run one and run two

  • The state is no longer clean. Files were created, ports were opened, a lock file exists. Half the failures I logged live in this gap.
  • The context is no longer empty. Yesterday's task file may still be around. A note in the notes file may contradict what I am asking today.
  • The task is no longer chosen for the demo. If it works twice on a task I did not specially pick, it probably works.

There is a fourth difference that took me longer to see: on the second run, nobody is watching. On the first run I am looking at the screen, ready to intervene. On the second I am doing something else. That is the real test, and it is also when I find out how good the failure messages are.

The rules I use now

  • A task is not automated until it has run twice, unattended, on a dirty state.
  • I keep the state dirty on purpose for the second run. Cleaning up before testing cleanup tests nothing.
  • If the second run fails, the bug is almost always in what the first run left behind, not in the task.
  • I read the log of the second run, not the first. The first log is a story, the second log is evidence.

Why this matters for how I judge tools

When I look at a tool now, the question is not "does the demo work". It is "what happens when I run it again tomorrow, with the mess from today still on disk". That question filters out a surprising amount, including things I would otherwise have installed.

The same standard applies to my own work, which is the uncomfortable part. Half the things I call automated have never had a second unattended run. I know which ones they are, and I keep not fixing them.

If you test this way, what does your second run look like? I would especially like to hear from anyone whose second run is genuinely clean, because mine never is.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
description:
arXiv:2610.27465v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off.
  Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.

title: AWS Secrets Manager: Rotation, IAM Scoping, and Production Gotchas
description:
Day 17: AWS Secrets Manager

Secrets Manager charges $0.40/secret/month but gives you something Parameter Store does not: automatic credential rotation with pre-built Lambda functions for RDS, Redshift, and DocumentDB.

Retrieving Secrets in Go 

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/config"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/service/secretsmanager"
)

type DBCreds struct {
    Username string `json:"username"`
    Password string `json:"password"`
    Host     string `json:"host"`
}

func getSecret(ctx context.Context, name string) (*DBCreds, error) {
    cfg, _ := config.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx, config.WithRegion("us-east-1"))
    client := secretsmanager.NewFromConfig(cfg)
    result, err := client.GetSecretValue(ctx, &secretsmanager.GetSecretValueInput{
        SecretId: &name,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to retrieve secret: %w", err)
    }
    var creds DBCreds
    json.Unmarshal([]byte(*result.SecretString), &creds)
    return &creds, nil
}

Key Tips

  • Name secrets as env/app/purpose for clean IAM wildcard scoping
  • Always pin the AWS region -- cross-region secret injection is a real attack
  • Rotation Lambda needs VPC + NAT gateway access to reach RDS
  • Cache secrets in-app (1hr TTL default) to reduce costs
  • Cross-account access needs BOTH a resource policy AND a KMS key grant

title: What Stays Intact When the Model Changes? Paper 2 on Externalized Intelligence
description:
I have published the second paper in the Artificial Deterministic Intelligence research series: Externalized Intelligence and Model Substitution.

The question is deliberately narrower than “are smaller models as intelligent as larger models?” They are not assumed to be. The question is whether a bounded operational contract can remain intact when authoritative task state is maintained outside model weights and the inference model changes.

In synthetic first-party studies, a frozen governed package was tested across 8B to 35B, 35B to 8B, and same-model restart controls. All 120 confirmatory handoff trials retained the measured policy contract and task correctness. The study also compares governed scoped context, authorized metadata-filtered lexical retrieval, and an oracle authorized-context ceiling. Each completed 90 of 90 trials under the shared frozen contract; conventional lexical retrieval had the lower measured retrieval-component time.

Those findings do not establish general model equivalence, production readiness, universal continuity, a universal safety guarantee, or retrieval superiority. The companion retains non-acceptances, timeouts, an incomplete scoped study, and a non-confirming cross-environment replication attempt.

Read the Version 2 preprint and evidence companion: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23523687

The public-safe supplementary evidence package provides aggregate outcomes, claim boundaries, hashes, and a verifier without disclosing Cortex, HOPE OS, raw prompts, worker packages, or private implementation.

I welcome technical criticism, alternative experimental designs, and independent work that can challenge these bounded findings.

title: TIL: GBase Database Silent Installation Doesn't Mean the Instance Is Ready
description:
A silent installation of GBase Database(GBase 8s) can finish successfully without leaving you with a database instance that's ready for use.

This is an easy detail to overlook when automating database deployment. The installer may complete the software installation, but instance configuration and initialization depend on the installation method and the steps defined in your deployment workflow.

What Happens After Silent Installation?

Before treating a GBase Database installation as complete, review these areas:

1. Configure environment variables

Set the environment variables required by the target instance. Confirm that the installation directory and instance-specific settings point to the correct locations.

2. Review onconfig

Check the instance configuration file and make sure its settings are appropriate for the target server.

3. Configure sqlhosts

Verify the connection definitions, including the server name, protocol, and configured service or port.

4. Initialize and start the instance if required

If your installation procedure does not already create and initialize the instance, follow the documented initialization process using the designated database operating system account.

For example, oninit -ivy is an initialization command used in applicable GBase Database(GBase 8s) procedures. Do not run it blindly on an existing or already initialized instance; confirm the correct procedure for your installation method first.

Automate the Entire Workflow

The important distinction is between installing database software and delivering a usable database service.

For batch deployment, your automation should account for every required stage:

  • Software installation
  • Environment configuration
  • Instance configuration
  • Instance initialization, where necessary
  • Startup and connectivity checks
  • Error handling and deployment logging

A successful installer exit code alone does not prove that the database can accept client connections.

After deployment, verify the instance status and test connectivity before reporting the server as ready. If any validation step fails, capture the relevant logs and stop the workflow rather than silently marking the deployment successful.

The Takeaway

Silent installation makes GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment more repeatable, but the installer is only one part of the process.

True deployment automation covers the entire workflow, from software installation to a validated, usable database instance.

When automating GBase Database deployment, does your script stop after the installer finishes, or does it also verify instance readiness?

title: How to Design Recoverable Webhook Cleanup — Queue, Cron, Delayed Retries, and Dead Letters
description:
For an edtech platform cleaning up expired enrollment webhooks, the simplest architecture that still recovers cleanly is a durable queue plus a small HTTP worker; use cron to enqueue scans, delayed retries to pace failures, and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for jobs that need a human decision. Keeping retry state in the request handler is the trap. It disappears when the process restarts.

The useful mental model is a conveyor belt: cron puts work on the belt, the queue remembers each package, the worker calls the HTTP endpoint, and the DLQ is the shelf for packages that never made it through. That separation makes an overnight incident a replay exercise instead of a spreadsheet exercise.

A field guide to the decision

Situation Queue Cron Practical choice
A student-status webhook fails and should retry in 30 seconds Durable attempt state and delayed delivery Too coarse unless it runs every minute Queue with a delayed job
Reconcile all records every night Holds individual work items Excellent trigger for a bounded scan Cron enqueues, queue executes
Provider returns 429 for an hour Backoff and visibility timeout Replays the whole batch unless you build more state Queue, with jittered delays
A payload is permanently rejected DLQ preserves payload and reason A cron log is easy to lose Queue plus DLQ

This is a decision table, not a product ranking. A managed queue, a Redis-backed worker, or a database table with leases can all implement the same contract. The contract matters more than the brand: durable state, an attempt counter, a next-run timestamp, and an idempotency key.

Pick cron alone when the job is a bounded report and a missed run can safely be rerun in full. Pick a queue when each webhook has its own retry timing or when one bad student record must not block the rest. Pick a database-backed worker when operating another service is not suitable for your team, and accept that you will own leasing, polling, and cleanup.

What should an HTTP worker record before retrying a webhook?

Record the decision before making the network call. In a Node.js service, a small job document is enough:

type WebhookJob = {
  id: string;
  enrollmentId: string;
  payloadHash: string;
  attempts: number;
  nextRunAt: string;
  status: "ready" | "processing" | "succeeded" | "dead";
  lastStatus?: number;
  lastError?: string;
};

function retryDelay(attempt: number): number {
  const base = Math.min(15 * 60_000, 2 ** attempt * 1_000);
  const jitter = Math.floor(Math.random() * 500);
  return base + jitter;
}

The worker claims one ready job with a lease, increments attempts, and sends the same idempotency key on every delivery. A successful 2xx response marks succeeded. A timeout, 408, 429, or 5xx response schedules nextRunAt; a 400 caused by a schema error goes to dead immediately. Your provider may define different transient codes, so keep that mapping in configuration and test it.

The order is deliberate. If the process dies after the HTTP call but before the success write, the queue will deliver again. The receiver must therefore treat (enrollmentId, payloadHash) as idempotent. HMAC signatures, calculated over the exact body bytes, protect authenticity; RFC 2104 describes the keyed-hash construction. Authentication does not prevent duplicates. Idempotency does.

I once started with a single setTimeout around fetch. It looked wonderfully small. A deploy erased the timer, and three hours of cleanup quietly vanished. That was the moment the retry record became part of the data model, not a detail of the worker process.

The following worker uses generic repository methods so you can back them with Redis, SQL, or another durable store. It keeps the HTTP request short: an API endpoint only inserts a job and returns 202 Accepted.

async function processOne(repo: {
  claimReady: (now: Date, leaseMs: number) => Promise<WebhookJob | null>;
  markSuccess: (id: string) => Promise<void>;
  reschedule: (id: string, at: Date, reason: string, status?: number) => Promise<void>;
  moveToDlq: (id: string, reason: string, status?: number) => Promise<void>;
}, send: (job: WebhookJob) => Promise<Response>): Promise<boolean> {
  const job = await repo.claimReady(new Date(), 60_000);
  if (!job) return false;

  try {
    const response = await send(job);
    if (response.ok) {
      await repo.markSuccess(job.id);
      return true;
    }
    const transient = response.status === 408 || response.status === 429 || response.status >= 500;
    if (!transient || job.attempts >= 8) {
      await repo.moveToDlq(job.id, `HTTP ${response.status}`, response.status);
      return true;
    }
    await repo.reschedule(job.id, new Date(Date.now() + retryDelay(job.attempts)), `HTTP ${response.status}`, response.status);
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    if (job.attempts >= 8) await repo.moveToDlq(job.id, String(error));
    else await repo.reschedule(job.id, new Date(Date.now() + retryDelay(job.attempts)), String(error));
    return true;
  }
}

Run several workers, but cap concurrency per destination. A queue smooths bursts; it does not make a provider's rate limit disappear. Emit counters for claimed, succeeded, retried, dead, and latency_ms. Alert on age of the oldest ready job, DLQ growth, and the ratio of attempts to successes. Logs should include the job ID and attempt number, never the student's personal data.

Cron still has a job. Schedule a reconciliation every 15 minutes, query enrollments whose remote status is stale, and enqueue only missing idempotency keys. The schedule is a trigger, not the delivery mechanism. If the cron process runs twice, the unique key makes the second enqueue harmless.

Testing recovery instead of just the happy path

Test time as data. Freeze the clock, enqueue a job at 10:00:00Z, return a 429, and assert a later nextRunAt. Kill the worker after fetch resolves but before markSuccess; a second run should produce one receiver-side effect. Feed a malformed payload and assert a DLQ record with a human-readable reason.

For an edtech cleanup, the useful fixture is boring: 12 enrollments, two transient 503 responses, one permanent 400, and one duplicate cron tick. Start the fake provider at 10:00:00Z; return 503 for enrollment E-07, then let the second attempt succeed at the calculated nextRunAt. At 10:00:01Z, terminate the worker after fetch resolves but before the repository write, then restart it with the same queue row. The receiver should observe one state change because its idempotency key is stable, while the job record eventually becomes succeeded. The malformed payload for E-11 should skip retries and land in the DLQ with the response code and a redacted reason. The final assertion is 11 eventual successes, one DLQ item, and no duplicate state changes. Your mileage may vary with provider limits, so measure queue age and retry distribution in staging before choosing the eight-attempt ceiling.

Keep the test ugly.

Limits and when to choose differently

The catch is operational ownership. A queue adds a worker deployment, lease recovery, and retention policy. Cron-only is suitable when a complete rerun is cheap and a delay of several minutes is acceptable. A database poller is not suitable when you need sub-second scheduling or very high fan-out; use a queue designed for that load.

Do not retry authorization failures, invalid signatures, or deterministic schema errors. Do not put a student's full webhook body in an alert. Keep DLQ retention long enough to investigate, then delete according to your privacy policy. When the receiver cannot offer idempotency, slow down and add a deduplication table before increasing concurrency.

Three words: persist the decision.

Sources

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/202
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/

References are standards and public documentation; the architecture is vendor-independent.

title: A Decision Brief on CVE-2026-102037 for Security Leadership
description:
A Decision Brief on CVE-2026-102037 for Security Leadership

Executives rarely need the packet-level story. They need to know what could happen, what has to be true for it to happen, and what decision is being asked of them. Here is that brief.

What happened

Juniper published a maintenance release set in October 2026 resolving an XML injection flaw in the Unified Threat Management daemon (utmd) of Junos OS on SRX Series devices. The record in NVD, sourced from sirt@juniper.net, states that an unauthenticated network attacker can commit arbitrary device configuration with root privileges via a malicious response from a configured custom URL-feed server. It is scored 9.2 CRITICAL on CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 HIGH on CVSS v3.1, with CWE-91 as the weakness class.

The business translation

A firewall holds the rules that separate trusted networks from untrusted ones. Configuration authority over it is authority to change those boundaries. If an outside party can influence the configuration, the boundary itself becomes contestable.

That is the risk in plain language. The attacker does not need an account, a session or user cooperation. They need the appliance to accept a feed response they control, and they need the device to be below the fixed build.

What is known and what is not

Known: the defect class, the daemon involved, the outcome described by the vendor, the affected branches and their fixed builds, and the CVSS scores.

Unknown from the public record: whether exploitation has been observed, how many devices in this estate use custom URL feeds, and whether any of them were contacted by an unapproved host. The first item is a vendor and threat-intelligence question. The second and third are questions this organisation can answer this week.

The decision being asked for

Three options, in order of cost. Approve an out-of-cycle upgrade for devices with custom URL feeds and a normal cycle for the rest. Approve a temporary egress restriction on feed traffic as a compensating control while the upgrade is scheduled. Or accept the risk explicitly, with a named owner and a review date.

The third option is defensible only if the feed inventory is complete. Without it, the decision is being made on assumption rather than fact.

Version reference

The fixed builds are 23.4R2-S8.13, 24.2R2-S5.5, 24.4R2-S5, 25.2R2-S2, 25.4R1-S3 and 26.2R1-S2 for branches 23.4, 24.2, 24.4, 25.2, 25.4 and 26.2. Juniper's October 2026 bulletin set, including JSA112186, covers the platform detail.

Exposure context

ZoomEye indexes no assets against this CVE yet. Product queries show the size of the visible estate at 1,500 for product="Junos" and 1,977 for os="Junos". Those are internet-visible systems, not confirmed vulnerable ones, and they do not quantify this organisation's exposure. They are context, not a metric to report upward.

title: Day 17/60: Matrix operations in Rust - Rust DSA
description:
Day 17/60: Matrix operations in Rust

60 Day Rust DSA Challenge

Today I focused on making matrix operations in rust work with Rust slices, strings, and indices without losing correctness. The strongest checkpoints were decide early whether bytes, chars, or slices are the right representation in Rust, keep the transformation or scan state explicit instead of mixing index tricks together, and use iterators and owned buffers deliberately so UTF-8 handling does not become accidental.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was mixing byte indexing and character assumptions in UTF-8 text. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests.

title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
description:
arXiv:2610.27234v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.

title: How Klaviyo shipped 356 internal apps in two weeks on Vercel
description:
Klaviyo on Vercel

  • Built a platform for shipping internal apps

  • 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks

  • Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default

  • Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes

Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. It brings marketing, service, agents, and data together in one platform so brands can deliver customer experiences at scale. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program.

In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali.

Guardrails instead of walls

Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way.

Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. Every builder is managed through Klaviyo's identity provider, which Vercel made possible through Enterprise Managed Users.

Implementing safeguards across the stack

Secure Compute gives Vercel deployments a private network path into Klaviyo's own infrastructure. Apps built in the program read from and write to Klaviyo's databases without any traffic crossing the public internet. That's what made bring-your-own-database work for Klaviyo.

On top of that connection, Vercel Passport and Klaviyo’s identity provider give every app the same access defaults, with nothing for the builder to configure:

  • Apps are private and SSO-gated through Okta

  • Sensitive environment variables are set at the team level, out of builders' hands

  • Klaviyo's hardened GitHub security is inherited by every project

  • Wiz scans every project, and findings feed Klaviyo's SIEM

  • Public deployment is granted case-by-case, so sales can share microsites with prospects, while internal tools stay private

How Klaviyo's app platform turns an idea into an app

Klaviyo wanted anyone with an idea to be able to describe it in plain language, from Slack, Claude, or Cursor, and get back a working app. They designed K:Forge, an in-house pipeline built on the Vercel SDK, to handle everything in between.

K:Forge creates a GitHub repo, deploys the app on Vercel, connects data through Secure Compute, and applies every security default. The output is a live, SSO-gated app, and the builder never touches infrastructure. Changes work the same way: mid-thread in Slack, someone can tell K:Forge what should be different, then it makes the change and redeploys.

Klaviyo built the pipeline and deliberately didn't build the layer under it. CDN behavior, preview environments, analytics, global scale: all of it is R&D Vercel had already done, so builders and engineers at Klaviyo don't have to think about it.

For bigger builds, citizen developers take an app about 80% of the way, and Klaviyo's platform team steps in for the last 20%, for fine-tuning and safety review. The platform team went from being the bottleneck to being the finishing touch. "We don't worry about scale," Mohamed says. "If 100,000 people hit an app, Vercel already solved that."

What people at Klaviyo are building

Employees build everything from microsites that rework a sales process to full-stack apps for problems too niche for any vendor tool. For K:BOS, Klaviyo's flagship event, the team skipped off-the-shelf registration tooling and built its own. Engineering barely touched it.

Klaviyo was one of the first customers of Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents. The platform gave the company a way to let anyone build full-stack apps, with security handled by default.

What's next

Klaviyo sets a high bar for AI fluency. One in five employees has shipped an app so far, and Mohamed intends to get even more people building. The team is also going deeper into Vercel, with MCP and AI Gateway.

About Klaviyo: Klaviyo is an autonomous B2C CRM that powers more valuable customer experiences. We unify a flexible, scalable data platform, intelligence that gets smarter with every interaction, and action across Marketing and Service to help businesses turn real-time customer data into personalization at scale.

title: Crypto Market Data Is Useful Only When You Understand Its Context
description:
Crypto dashboards can show a lot of information in a small space: prices, daily changes, trading pairs, and lists of popular assets.

At first glance, more data seems like a good thing.

But I think the real challenge is helping people understand what the numbers mean without encouraging them to draw conclusions too quickly.

That's a useful way to think about market interfaces, including the one presented by AviorSwap.

A percentage change doesn't tell the whole story

Imagine seeing a token with a positive daily percentage change.

It's tempting to interpret that as a sign of strength. But the number alone doesn't explain the full market situation.

How liquid is the asset? How much trading activity supports the price? Is the movement part of a larger trend or a short-term fluctuation?

A daily percentage change provides a snapshot, not a complete analysis.

The same applies to assets showing negative performance. A single time window doesn't establish what will happen next.

Context makes a dashboard more useful

AviorSwap's public website presents market information alongside its exchange-related features.

I think this combination raises an interesting product-design question: how can a platform help visitors move from exploring market data to understanding a potential transaction?

A useful dashboard should make it easy to identify the asset, understand the time period behind a statistic, and distinguish market information from an executable quote.

That last distinction matters.

A displayed market price may not equal the price a user receives when swapping a particular amount. Liquidity, route selection, fees, and changing market conditions can all affect the result.

Less noise, more meaning

When designing a market dashboard, I'd prioritize three things.

Clear labels. Every percentage should have an understandable time period and reference point.

Relevant details. Users should be able to find liquidity, volume, and other useful context where those metrics are available.

Honest limitations. Market data can be delayed, incomplete, or different across sources. The interface should communicate relevant limitations instead of presenting every figure as universally definitive.

These details can make a dashboard more helpful without filling every available space with numbers.

Information should support decisions, not replace them

I don't think a market interface needs to tell users what to buy.

Its job is to present information in a way that supports independent judgment.

For example, a clear view of market movements can help someone decide what they want to research next. It shouldn't imply that an asset is a good investment simply because its price has risen recently.

That distinction is important in a market where prices can change quickly and losses are possible.

Final thoughts

Market data becomes more valuable when people understand its limitations.

Exploring the relationship between AviorSwap's market presentation and its exchange functionality highlights a broader principle for financial products: showing information is only the first step. Helping users interpret it responsibly is the harder part.

When you open a crypto dashboard, which information helps you most: price changes, trading volume, liquidity, or historical charts?

title: State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.

  • Function and industry findings describe a classified sample rather than the full catalog.

  • Each analysis uses the latest complete data available. Figures may be revised as the underlying data and methodology improve.

title: A lab acceptance is a validity range per rule, not a flag on the vendor
description:
Most systems that store test records model laboratory status as a boolean on a vendor row. is_accredited = true. That column is wrong in a specific way: 16 CFR part 1112 grants acceptance per rule or test method, the scope can be extended later, and it can be suspended for one slice of the scope while the rest stands. A boolean cannot represent any of that.

The correct shape is a range table keyed by rule, with the test date checked against it.

The schema 

CREATE TABLE cab (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  legal_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,
  -- independent | firewalled | government, per 1112.11
  cab_kind      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (cab_kind IN ('independent','firewalled','government'))
);

CREATE TABLE cab_acceptance (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  cab_id        BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cab(id),
  cpsc_rule_id  TEXT NOT NULL,           -- the rule, not a product category
  accepted_from DATE NOT NULL,
  accepted_to   DATE,                    -- NULL means currently open
  status        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active','suspended','withdrawn','discontinued')),
  source_url    TEXT NOT NULL,           -- where the listing said so
  observed_on   DATE NOT NULL            -- the day this row was read, not asserted
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX acceptance_one_open_window_per_rule
  ON cab_acceptance (cab_id, cpsc_rule_id, COALESCE(accepted_to, DATE '9999-12-31'));

The observed_on column is the one people skip. Section 1112.19 has the Commission maintain a listing and update it as scopes change, so every row here is an observation with a date attached, not a fact about the world. A pipeline that overwrites observed_on with now() on every write has thrown away the only field that lets you reconstruct what was known on the test date.

The test record 

CREATE TABLE test_record (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  cpsc_rule_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
  tested_on     DATE NOT NULL,
  prime_cab_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cab(id),
  -- 1112.25: subcontracted work must be identifiable in the prime report
  performed_by  JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',   -- [{cab_id, tests: [...]}]
  report_uri    TEXT NOT NULL
);

The gate query

A test result counts only if the body held acceptance for that rule on that date. That is a join with a range predicate, and it has to run before the certificate row is considered complete.

SELECT t.id
  FROM test_record t
 WHERE NOT EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
           FROM cab_acceptance a
          WHERE a.cab_id = t.prime_cab_id
            AND a.cpsc_rule_id = t.cpsc_rule_id
            AND a.status = 'active'
            AND a.accepted_from <= t.tested_on
            AND (a.accepted_to IS NULL OR a.accepted_to >= t.tested_on)
       );

Zero rows is the pass condition. A non-empty result means the file cites a test whose scope line does not cover the rule, or covers it on a date outside the window. Both look identical in a system that stores is_accredited.

The same predicate is what catches a suspension that lands later. Refresh the acceptance windows on a schedule, rerun the query against existing certificates, and a report that was valid when issued can surface as invalid now. That is not a bug in the file. It is the file being current.

Subcontracting

performed_by exists because 1112.25 requires the prime contractor's report to identify which tests a CPSC-accepted body acting as a subcontractor performed. A single PDF from a trading company that consolidated three laboratories does not satisfy that as data. Model it as an array of (cab_id, tests) and let the same range predicate run over each entry rather than only over the name on the cover page.

type Attribution = { cabId: number; tests: string[] };

function unresolvedParts(t: TestRecord, windows: AcceptanceWindow[]): string[] {
  const covered = new Set<number>();
  for (const w of windows) {
    if (w.status === 'active' && w.acceptedFrom <= t.testedOn &&
        (w.acceptedTo === null || w.acceptedTo >= t.testedOn)) covered.add(w.cabId);
  }
  return t.performedBy
    .flatMap((a: Attribution) => a.tests.map((name) => ({ cabId: a.cabId, name })))
    .filter((row) => !covered.has(row.cabId))
    .map((row) => `${row.name}@${row.cabId}`);
}

unresolvedParts().length === 0 is the assertion worth putting in CI for the ingestion job, because the failure mode is silent. A missing attribution reads as a complete report.

Retention, and what it is not

Section 1112.25 makes the laboratory hold its own test reports and technical records for section 14 tests for at least five years from the date the test was conducted. That is the lab's duty on its own copies. It is not a license to delete your side after five years, and it is not a statement that a report older than five years is unusable. The date that starts the clock is the test date rather than the shipment date, so a slow-moving SKU can carry a report whose retention window closed while the goods were still on the shelf.

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) runs the inbound scan at three China facilities, floor area 13,000 square meters in Suzhou, 8,000 in Dongguan and 3,000 in Shenzhen, where one carton resolves to one product identifier before it resolves to a test file. That is the same join in the other direction. Whatever the storage layer looks like, the question at the dock is identical to the question in the query above. Which body ran this test, against which rule, on which date.

title: Your Flex Child Won't Shrink, and overflow: hidden Isn't the Fix (It's min-width: 0)
description:
You build a dashboard. Sidebar on the left, content on the right, a table or a code block inside. It looks perfect with your sample data.

Then a user pastes a long URL into a field, and the whole page grows a horizontal scrollbar. The sidebar gets squeezed, the layout breaks, and you start adding overflow: hidden to everything until the symptoms go away.

There is a one-line fix, and it is not overflow: hidden.

The Layout That Breaks 

<div class="layout">
  <aside class="sidebar">Menu</aside>
  <main class="content">
    <pre>https://example.com/a-very-long-url-with-no-break-points-in-it-at-all-1234567890</pre>
  </main>
</div>

.layout {
  display: flex;
}
.sidebar {
  width: 240px;
  flex-shrink: 0;
}
.content {
  flex: 1;
}

.content is told to take the remaining space with flex: 1. Nobody told it to stay inside that space, and that is the entire problem.

Why It Happens

Flex items and grid items have a default of min-width: auto. For a flex item, auto means:

Do not shrink narrower than the smallest size your content can be.

For a paragraph of normal words, the smallest size is the longest single word, because the line can wrap between words. For a long URL, a <pre> block, a wide table or an image, there is nowhere to wrap, so the smallest size is the full width of the content.

So the browser is not ignoring your layout. It is obeying a rule you never knew existed: the item refuses to shrink below its content, and the overflow spills into the page.

Why overflow: hidden Looks Like a Fix (Sometimes)

Setting overflow to anything other than visible changes how min-width: auto is calculated. The automatic minimum becomes 0 for that item. That is why overflow: hidden on the right element makes the bug vanish.

It works by accident, and it has a cost: it clips content, can cut off focus outlines and dropdowns, and does nothing useful if you put it on the wrong element. Fixing the cause is cleaner.

Fix 1: min-width: 0 on the Flex Child 

.content {
  flex: 1;
  min-width: 0;
}

You are telling the item that it is allowed to shrink below its content. Now .content stays inside its space, and the long URL can be scrolled, wrapped or cut off by something you control:

.content pre {
  overflow-x: auto;
}

In Tailwind, the utility is min-w-0:

<main class="flex-1 min-w-0">
  <pre class="overflow-x-auto">...</pre>
</main>

Fix 2: Grid's 1fr Has the Same Trap 

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
}

1fr is not "one equal share, and no more". It is shorthand for minmax(auto, 1fr), so the column cannot get narrower than its content. The same long URL stretches the column and the page.

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px minmax(0, 1fr);
}

minmax(0, 1fr) allows the column to shrink to nothing if it has to. A useful side note for Tailwind users: grid-cols-2 and its siblings already compile to repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)), which is why many people never meet this bug in the grid, and then meet it as soon as they write a custom template column.

Fix 3: Truncating Text With an Ellipsis Inside Flex

This one catches almost everybody:

.row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 8px;
}
.title {
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}

It does not truncate, because the flex item sizes itself to the text. Add min-width: 0 to .title and the ellipsis appears. In Tailwind, truncate min-w-0 on the same element does it.

Fix 4: Long Words Need the Right overflow-wrap

For user-generated text such as comments, names and pasted links, allow breaking inside a word:

.comment {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

overflow-wrap: break-word looks equivalent, but it does not change the item's minimum size calculation, so inside a flex or grid item it can still leave the layout stretched. anywhere does take the break points into account, and the item can shrink.

Which One When

Symptom Fix
Flex child pushes the page wider min-width: 0 on that child
Grid column grows past its space minmax(0, 1fr) instead of 1fr
Ellipsis not appearing in a flex row min-width: 0 plus the truncation rules
Long pasted word or URL overflow-wrap: anywhere
Wide table or code block Own scroll container with overflow-x: auto

The Rule

Flex and grid items refuse to shrink below their content by default. If something inside a layout can be wider than the space it is given, tell the container it is allowed to shrink with min-width: 0 or minmax(0, 1fr), and decide where the overflow should scroll or wrap.

Quick audit: open your app and paste a 200-character string with no spaces into every input that is later displayed. Then widen a table to 40 columns. If the page grows a horizontal scrollbar, you have found a missing min-width: 0.

I test every layout in my Next.js and Tailwind templates against this kind of hostile content, because real users do paste long strings, and a dashboard has to survive it.

Get the templates: https://pixelanas.gumroad.com

What is the ugliest layout bug a single piece of user content has caused you? Drop it in the comments.
