title: Giving My One-Off Web Experiments an Actual Brand System
description:
How I stopped every new Plaid Labs experiment from looking like a different AI-generated site, and built a shared brand mark + design system instead.

The problem: every new experiment looked like a different app

I've got a small constellation of side projects living under Plaid Labs — Daily Doodle, a couple of maker tools, and whatever I spin up next on a random night. Each one got built independently, usually in a single sitting, which meant each one also got its own accidental visual identity. Different fonts. Different spacing instincts. Different "vibe."

None of them looked bad exactly. They just didn't look like they belonged to each other.

I posted a link to one thing and someone said, oh did you vibe code that? As if that was a negative I should be ashamed of. I get it not everything Ai is good and it made me think. Am I just ok with how this is or do I want to control the look and branding of this?

Step one: a brand mark that actually travels

The first fix was small and dumb-simple on paper: every Plaid Labs page needed the same little signature in the footer. Not a logo file — I wanted something typographic, something that would render consistently anywhere without shipping an image asset.

What I landed on:

<a class="plaid-mark" href="https://theplaidscientist.github.io/">
  <span class="plaid-mark-row">
    <span class="plaid-mark-lede">a</span>
    <span class="plaid-mark-beaker" aria-hidden="true">🧪</span>
    <span class="plaid-mark-word">Plaid Labs</span>
  </span>
  <span class="plaid-mark-sub">
    <span>e</span><span>x</span><span>p</span><span>e</span><span>r</span><span>i</span><span>m</span><span>e</span><span>n</span><span>t</span>
  </span>
</a>

Two lines: a 🧪 Plaid Labs, then experiment underneath, letter-spaced out to match the width of the line above it. A couple of details I had to fight the browser for, in case they save you the same headache:

The emoji was rendering smaller than the capital letter next to it. Emoji glyphs sit smaller within their own em-box than a capital letter does — a beaker sized at 1em next to bold text at the same font-size visually reads as noticeably smaller than the "P" beside it. Bumping it to 1.4em and nudging the baseline with transform: translateY(0.11em) got it to actually match the cap-height.

Major Mono Display — the font I used for "experiment" — looks completely different in uppercase vs. lowercase. Typed in caps, some of its glyphs render as strange filled-in blocks. Typed in lowercase, it renders as these clean, readable outlined letterforms. So the word is authored in lowercase in the HTML even though it reads like a stylized all-caps treatment — that's the font doing the work, not a text-transform.

Stretching "experiment" to match the width of the line above, at any size: instead of guessing at letter-spacing values, I split the word into ten individual <span> letters and put them in a flex row with justify-content: space-between. Whatever width the row above renders at, the letters spread themselves to fill it exactly. No magic numbers, no breaking at different screen sizes.

Major Mono Display only ships one weight (Regular) — so font-weight: bold does nothing. -webkit-text-stroke fakes it instead:

.plaid-mark-sub {
  font-family: "Major Mono Display", ui-monospace, monospace;
  font-weight: 700;
  -webkit-text-stroke: 0.55px currentColor; /* this is what actually bolds it */
}

Step two: a real design system, not just a shared footer

The footer mark fixed the "who made this" signature, but the pages themselves still had no shared language. So I wrote out an actual spec — colors, three type roles, production CSS — and made it the default for anything new I build:

  • Palette: dark charcoal background (#181818), clinical off-white text (#E1E1E1), one accent — a terminal green (#48C774) — spent deliberately instead of smeared everywhere.
  • Type, three roles:
    • A bold display face reserved only for the page's own title/branding — not every heading, just the one moment that's actually the page introducing itself.
    • A monospace face for tags, badges, status readouts — real structural information, not decoration.
    • A neutral body face for everything else — paragraphs, UI, ordinary section headers.

The point of scoping the display face to just the page title was deliberate. My first pass applied it to every h1/h2/h3, and it immediately stopped feeling special — it just became "the font," which is exactly the generic-template trap I was trying to avoid in the first place.

I really just didn't want all my stuff to look like it was made without a human input.

The part where the font choice backfired

I initially speced the display face as Syne at weight 700/800 — bold, sculptural, "avant-garde lab" energy. It looked great in isolation.

Then I shipped it on a real page — a little "Image Cutout" tool — and it looked stretchy. Wide, flared, almost like the letters had been horizontally scaled. My first assumption was a CSS bug: bad font-stretch, a broken fallback, something synthetic going on.

It wasn't a bug. That's just what Syne looks like at heavy weight — wide counters and flared terminals are the actual design of the typeface. It's a deliberate, characterful choice for the right context. It just wasn't the right context sitting directly above plain body text at a normal reading size.

Rather than argue with myself about it, I built a quick side-by-side comparison page: the exact same heading, in Syne (as shipped), a toned-down Syne, and three alternatives with a similar bold/technical energy but tighter, more normal letter proportions. Landed on Bricolage Grotesque — bold, a little experimental, but nothing about it reads as "stretched."

What I actually shipped

The design system now lives as a spec I reuse on every new experiment by default, with two explicit exceptions: Disco Doodle and the main Plaid Labs landing page both keep their own established look, because they're not "new" — they already have an identity worth protecting.

:root {
  --bg-dark: #181818;
  --text-main: #E1E1E1;
  --accent-green: #48C774;

  --font-display: 'Bricolage Grotesque', sans-serif; /* page title/branding only */
  --font-mono: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace;           /* tags, badges, status */
  --font-body: 'Public Sans', sans-serif;              /* everything else */
}

Made it a skill

I asked Claude to remember all the choices we made and create a repeatable skill that would basically be a branding guide that auto triggers every times we create a new site to publish.

None of this was hard, individually. Emoji sizing, font-weight faking, letter-spacing math — each one's a five-minute CSS fix. The thing that actually mattered was treating "brand consistency across side projects" as a real spec worth writing down once, instead of re-deciding it from scratch every time I open a new repo.

I'm super excited to have each new thing we create feel like its mine. Like it has my signature on it so it doesn't just look the same as something anyone else has created.

title: NEXT_PUBLIC_ and Supabase: Which Env Variables Are Safe to Expose?
description:
If you've ever stared at a .env.local full of Supabase keys and wondered "wait, which of these is safe to ship to the browser?" — you're not alone. It's one of the most common questions I see, and getting it wrong ranges from "totally fine" to "someone just dumped your entire users table." Let's clear it up for good.

The one rule that explains everything

In Next.js, any environment variable prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ gets inlined into the JavaScript bundle at build time. Same story for VITE_ in Vite apps and EXPO_PUBLIC_ in Expo. The prefix is not a suggestion — it's an instruction to the bundler: copy this value into code that runs in the user's browser.

So the question "is this variable safe to expose?" is really "is it safe for this value to sit in plain text inside the client bundle, readable by anyone who opens DevTools?"

For Supabase, the answer depends entirely on which key you're talking about.

Every Supabase project has two keys, and they are not equals

Open your project's API settings and you get two keys. They look similar. They could not be more different.

1. The anon key (newer projects call this the publishable key, formatted sb_publishable_...). Its JWT carries "role": "anon". This key is public by design. It's meant to ship in the browser. It is not a secret, and you do not need to rotate it if it "leaks" — because it was never hidden in the first place. What keeps your data safe when this key is used is Row Level Security (RLS): the anon key can only do what your RLS policies allow.

2. The service_role key (formatted sb_secret_... on newer projects). Its JWT carries "role": "service_role". This key bypasses Row Level Security entirely. Full read, write, and delete on every table, plus Storage. It exists for trusted server environments only. It must never appear in a browser bundle, a public repo, or any client-side config.

Here's a reliable way to tell any Supabase JWT apart — decode the middle segment (it's base64url) and read the role:

# paste your key in place of $KEY
echo "$KEY" | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | grep -o '"role":"[a-z_]*"'
# => "role":"anon"          -> public, safe for the browser
# => "role":"service_role"  -> secret, server-only, never public

(The tr '_-' '/+' converts base64url to standard base64 so base64 -d can read it.) The newer sb_publishable_ / sb_secret_ keys aren't JWTs, but the naming makes the distinction obvious — secret means secret.

So, the safe list

Safe to expose (belongs in NEXT_PUBLIC_):

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://xxxx.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=sb_publishable_xxx   # or the legacy anon JWT

The project URL is public — it's just an HTTPS endpoint. The anon key is public by design. Ship them.

Never public (no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, ever):

SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=sb_secret_xxx
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:password@db.xxxx.supabase.co:5432/postgres

DATABASE_URL contains your database password and gives direct Postgres access. That connection bypasses RLS the same way service_role does — the postgres role is not subject to your policies. Both stay strictly server-side.

Keeping service_role strictly server-side

The safe pattern: the browser talks to Supabase with the anon key (protected by RLS), and anything that genuinely needs to bypass RLS runs on a server you control. Next.js gives you three good homes for that.

Route handlers (app/api/.../route.ts):

// app/api/admin-report/route.ts
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

// No NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix -> stays on the server, never bundled
const admin = createClient(
  process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
  process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY!
)

export async function GET() {
  // runs server-side only; safe to use the service_role client here
  const { data, error } = await admin.from('reports').select('*')
  if (error) return Response.json({ error: error.message }, { status: 500 })
  return Response.json(data)
}

Server Actions work the same way — they only ever execute on the server, so reading process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY there is fine:

'use server'
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

export async function deleteAccount(userId: string) {
  const admin = createClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY!
  )
  await admin.from('profiles').delete().eq('id', userId)
}

Supabase Edge Functions get the service_role key from their own secret store (Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY')), completely outside your frontend build — a great home for privileged jobs.

The mental model: if a file has 'use client' at the top, or gets imported by one, assume everything in it is public. Never read a secret there.

Catch the mistake before it ships

The classic disaster is one character of muscle memory: someone types NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY because every other Supabase var starts that way. Now your RLS-bypassing key is inlined into the client bundle.

Grep for it. Add this to CI or a pre-commit hook:

# Fails if any NEXT_PUBLIC_ / VITE_ / EXPO_PUBLIC_ var references service_role
git grep -nE '(NEXT_PUBLIC_|VITE_|EXPO_PUBLIC_)[A-Z_]*SERVICE_ROLE' && {
  echo "FATAL: service_role key exposed via a public env prefix"; exit 1
} || echo "OK: no service_role key behind a public prefix"

It's also worth scanning the built output itself — a secret can leak through a hardcoded string even without the prefix:

# after `next build`
grep -rE 'sb_secret_|service_role' .next/static && \
  echo "FATAL: secret found in client bundle" || echo "clean"

If a secret already leaked

Two things, in order. First, rotate the key in your Supabase dashboard immediately — a leaked service_role key is a live master key until you do. Second, remember that deleting the file in a new commit is not enough: the value lives in your git history forever, and anyone can git log -p it back. You have to purge history with git filter-repo (or the BFG), then force-push:

git filter-repo --path .env.local --invert-paths

Rotate and purge. One without the other leaves you exposed.

The part people forget: the anon key is only as safe as your RLS

Shipping the anon key is safe only because RLS stands between it and your data. If a table has RLS disabled, or has a policy like USING (true) with no TO clause, then that "public" anon key can read every row — for every user. A SELECT policy of USING (true) is genuinely world-readable. (It's only world-writable if a permissive INSERT/UPDATE/ALL policy exists too — but world-readable is already a breach for most apps.)

Remember the anatomy:

  • USING filters which existing rows a role can see, and which it may update or delete.
  • WITH CHECK validates rows being inserted or updated; INSERT policies have WITH CHECK only.
  • A role needs both a matching policy and the underlying table GRANT. Permissive policies OR together; restrictive ones AND.
  • A policy with no TO clause applies to all roles, anon included.
  • For an anonymous visitor, auth.uid() is NULL — so any policy that quietly assumes a logged-in user needs testing from the anon perspective.

If you want to actually check your own project rather than take my word for it, I put together a free, read-only audit: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. It's a tiny reproducible leak plus a set of SQL queries you can paste into the Supabase SQL editor to list every table with RLS off and every policy that resolves to true for anon. Run it against a staging project and see what falls out — it's usually one or two tables you forgot about.

The takeaway

  • NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY: public by design, ship them.
  • SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and DATABASE_URL: server-only, no public prefix, ever.
  • Decode the JWT role when you're unsure; git grep for the prefix mistake in CI.
  • The anon key's safety is your RLS — so audit your policies, don't assume them.

If you'd rather not hand-roll the whole audit, I also maintain a $29 RLS Audit Kit — the same read-only checks packaged with a policy checklist and a few "here's the fix" templates for the leaks it turns up. Totally optional; the free demo above will already get you most of the way. Either way, go check your policies today — future-you will be glad you did.

title: H2DF: Calibrated Target Bands for Controllable Language-Model Unlearning
description:
arXiv:2610.26864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gradient ascent (GA) is a simple language-model unlearning baseline, but it continues increasing forget loss after useful forgetting has occurred. This unbounded pressure can damage retained utility and make forgotten examples abnormally high-loss. We introduce H2DF, a calibrated target-band objective that applies GA-like pressure below a data-dependent lower target and suppresses, or reverses, that pressure after the target region is reached. The targets are estimated from matched non-member examples before training, so the base objective requires one forget-batch forward/backward pass per optimization step; our reported TOFU variant adds sparse retain replay every tenth step. We instantiate a one-sided objective for TOFU question answering and a two-sided objective for MUSE-News language modeling. Across three TOFU seeds, H2DF obtains a forget NLL of 1.528 with margin 0.049 and retain NLL of 1.165 with margin 0.047, matching GradDiff while using retain replay only every tenth step and showing substantially lower variability than GA. On MUSE-News, H2DF improves retention over GA and NPO and is competitive with SimNPO, but does not dominate it. Ablations show that the upper target reduces overshoot and that validation-based checkpoint selection is important. These results support calibrated target bands as a practical mechanism for controlling forgetting strength, while also exposing sensitivity to random seed and calibration quality.

title: "Design a Calendar System" Looks Easy. Here's Where Candidates Fail in the Interview
description:
"Design Calendar System" sounds simple. Create a meeting, invite people, show a grid of boxes.

It isn't. Underneath sit some of the most interesting problems in system design: a read-heavy workload with a fan-out on every write, notifications that must reach every invitee, reminders that must fire at an exact minute for hundreds of millions of people, and recurring events that never really end.

This walkthrough follows the structure we coach for a 45–60 minute interview: requirements, estimates, APIs, data model, high-level design, then the deep dives where the real signal is, and finally the AI follow-up more interviewers now ask.

1. Requirements

Functional

  • Create, read, update and delete meetings.
  • Invite people by email, including people who don't use the product.
  • Show a user's calendar for a day, week or month.
  • Notify invitees when a meeting is created or changed.
  • Remind participants a few minutes before a meeting (e.g. 15 minutes).

Nice to have: find a free slot across several people (free/busy), recurring meetings, time zones.

Non-functional

  • Highly available: 99.99%. A calendar that's down means missed meetings.
  • Low latency: calendar views in well under 500 ms (p99).
  • Read-heavy: people look at their calendar far more often than they change it.
  • Scalable: hundreds of millions of daily users.
  • Consistency: eventual consistency is fine for invitees, but the organizer must see their own change immediately (read-your-writes).

Interview tip: say why each requirement matters. "Eventually consistent, except read-your-writes for the organizer" shows judgement; "eventually consistent" alone is a buzzword.

2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumptions:

  • 2B users
  • 500M daily active users (DAU)
  • 20% of DAU create 2 meetings a day, and 30% create 1
  • New meetings / day → 0.2 × 500M × 2 + 0.3 × 500M = 350M
  • ~4 participants per meeting → ~1.4B invites per day
  • Calendar views / day → ~10 opens per DAU → 5B

QPS planning:

  • Write QPS → 350M / 86,400 ≈ 3.5K/s average, ~10.5K/s peak
  • Read QPS → 5B / 86,400 ≈ 50K QPS average, ~150K/s peak
  • Read : write ratio ~15 : 1, so read-heavy

Capacity planning:

  • 1 KB meeting + ~100 Bytes per participant ≈ 1 KB + 4 × 100 Bytes = 1.4 KB
  • 1.4 KB × 350M ≈ 0.5 TB/day ≈ ~180 TB/year before replication (no media)

Interview tip: The numbers tell us where to spend effort: optimise reads, make writes reliable, and design the fan-out carefully.

3. APIs 

POST   /meetings                      create (title, start, duration, tz, invitees)
                                      + recurrence?, Idempotency-Key header
GET    /users/{id}/calendar?start&end  meeting summaries for a day/week/month (paginated)
GET    /meetings/{id}                 full details
PATCH  /meetings/{id}                 update only the changed fields (If-Match: version)
DELETE /meetings/{id}                 cancel
POST   /meetings/{id}/invitees        add invitees
DELETE /meetings/{id}/invitees/{uid}  remove an invitee
POST   /meetings/{id}/rsvp            accept / decline / maybe
GET    /free?users&start&end          free blocks only (for slot finding)

Two details interviewers notice:

  • The calendar view returns summaries, not just IDs. Returning IDs and then fetching details is an extra round trip on the hottest path.
  • Updates carry a version (optimistic locking). Even if only the owner can edit, they can edit from two devices at once.

How an update works. The client sends only the fields that changed, never the whole meeting row. Moving a meeting 30 minutes later looks like this:

PATCH /meetings/m_123
If-Match: "7"
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json
{ "start": "2026-10-20T10:30:00Z" }
  • Partial update. Fields that aren't sent stay as they are, and null clears a field. The payload is tiny, and a client can't accidentally overwrite a field it never touched.
  • Version check. If-Match: "7" means "apply this only if the meeting is still at version 7". The Meeting Service runs a conditional write: UPDATE meetings SET start_utc = …, version = 8 WHERE meeting_id = 'm_123' AND version = 7. If another device changed the meeting first, nothing is updated and the API returns 412 Precondition Failed. The client refetches, shows the user the newer meeting, and lets them retry. The response to a successful update returns the whole updated meeting with its new version (ETag: "8").
  • Invitees have their own endpoints. Adding or removing people writes participant rows and sends notifications, so it isn't hidden inside a generic PATCH.

4. Data model

Users

  • user_id (PK) → Shard Key
  • email (unique)
  • metadata

Meetings

  • meeting_id (PK) → Shard Key
  • owner_id
  • title
  • description
  • start_utc
  • duration
  • version
  • metadata
  • list

Participants

  • user_id → Shard Key
  • meeting_id
  • start_utc
  • duration
  • status (invited / accepted / declined)
  • PK(user_id, start_utc, meeting_id)

Why two tables? The two hottest queries want different partitioning:

  • "Show my week" → all of one user's meetings in a time range → partition by user_id, sort by time. One range scan on one shard. Once you get meeting_id, you can easily fetch meeting details based on meeting_id from meetings table.
  • "Change this meeting" → one meeting and all its participants → partition by meeting_id.

The participants table denormalises the start time so the calendar view never has to join. The cost: moving a meeting rewrites one participant row per invitee. Writes are rare and reads are hot, so that's a good trade.

Interview tip: Tables in the same DB can have different shard keys.
To fetch meeting details for a user, don't perform join between participants and meeting table, instead first fetch all the meeting Ids for the user within a day/week and then issue a separate query to DB to fetch meeting details. The Calendar Service does this server-side, so the client still gets summaries in one call.
Optimization → Cache meeting details for the current and next week. Older meetings are rarely read, so caching them wastes memory.

5. High-level design


Async path for notification. Every change in the participants table is captured with change data capture (CDC) into an event queue. Downstream consumers react to it:

  • Event Subscriber Service subscribes to a change and put notifications in a queue.
  • Change notifications (new invite, time changed, cancelled) are sent with immediately delivery to the delay queue. Delay queue with immediate delivery behaves as a FIFO queue.
  • The Reminder Notifications are scheduled with delay delivery.

Using CDC instead of having the Meeting Service publish events directly is deliberate. The database is the single source of truth, so an event can't be lost because a service crashed between "write the DB" and "publish the event".

What if the Participant table can't be updated in the same transaction as meetings table.

Use CDC to update participants table asynchronously.

6. Deep dive: keeping invitees up to date

When a meeting changes, invitees should see it if online. Two options:

Pull (periodic refresh)

  • Simple to build.
  • Wasteful: most refreshes return nothing new, and at 500M DAU that's a lot of empty requests.
  • Changes appear late.

Push

  • Precise and cheap on the network.
  • The server sends a tiny message, "meeting X changed", over Server-Sent Events or WebSocket to open web clients.
  • The client then fetches only what changed.

Use push, and keep a light pull on app open as a safety net (pushes can be missed when a device is offline).

7. Deep dive: reminders 15 minutes before

This is where strong candidates separate themselves. We need to fire hundreds of millions of reminders a day, at the right minute, exactly once, even when meetings move or get cancelled.

8. Where agentic AI fits, and where it doesn't

Interviewers now often add a follow-up: "How would you use AI here?" In agentic AI system design rounds it's sharper: "Which parts of this would you hand to an agent?" The strong answer starts by drawing a line.

Keep the core deterministic. The Calendar DB, CDC, the event queue, fan-out and the delay queue must be exact, fast and cheap. An LLM call takes a second or more, costs real money per request, and can answer the same input differently twice. Nobody wants a reminder that fires "probably around 9:45", or a fan-out that decides which invitees deserve a notification. None of these components should be replaced by an agent.

Put agents at the edges, where the input is human. The good fits are jobs that today need a person to read, judge or negotiate:

  • Finding a time: open everyone's calendar, compare, propose. With Agent → "Find 30 minutes with Priya and Alex next week, mornings, not Friday" → it checks free, ranks slots and drafts the invite
  • Rescheduling after a decline or a new conflict With Agent → Proposes new times to everyone, collects the replies and books the slot that works.
  • Empty meeting descriptions With Agent → Drafts an agenda from the email thread or last meeting's notes.

9. Common mistakes

  • One table for everything, so "show my week" becomes a scatter-gather across shards.
  • Not creating Participants table and read fetch meetings created but not invited. Participants table is required and Invitees, organizer both should be added as participants.
  • Relying on Redis key expiry for reminders.
  • Doing the maths and not using it. Estimates should drive decisions (read-heavy → denormalize data).
  • Putting an LLM in the core path, for example letting an agent decide who gets notified, or giving it direct database access.

Wrapping up

A great answer isn't the biggest diagram. It's a clear story: the numbers say it's read-heavy, so we shape the data for reads; writes fan out asynchronously through CDC; and reminders use a delay queue that survives retries and reschedules. AI belongs at the edges, where people talk to the system, not inside its core. Then you show you know where it breaks.

Preparing for system design interviews, from classic designs like this to agentic AI systems? Crack Tech offers private 1:1 coaching and realistic mock interviews scored the way a hiring committee reads them. Book a free 15-minute call at cracktech.app.

title: BEACON: Bridging Multimodal Semantics and Asynchronous Propagation for Cloud System Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27542v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern large-scale cloud systems continuously generate massive and multimodal observability data, such as time-series metrics, log records, and system dependency graphs, which reflect the health state of the system. To ensure reliable cloud system operation, anomaly detection models identify abnormal states by analyzing these multimodal observations. However, existing approaches rely on simple fusion strategies and graph learning, ignoring the semantic gap among modalities and the asynchronous spatio-temporal dependencies across system instances over time. To this end, we propose BEACON, a framework to Bridge multimodal sEmantics and Asynchronous propagation for Cloud system anOmaly detectioN. Specifically, we introduce a Dynamic Interpretable Multimodal Aggregator (DIMA) that leverages an information-bottleneck mechanism to compress information from the semantics and temporal dynamics of metrics, and aligns them with logs in a shared prototype space. Furthermore, we propose an Asynchronous Spatio-Temporal Propagator (ASTP) that captures temporal dependencies with multi-scale temporal attention and models spatial relations with topology-aware aggregation. This enables asynchronous propagation of anomalies across system instances. Extensive experiments on three real-world cloud system datasets demonstrate that \textbf{BEACON} consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in anomaly detection.

title: Cloudflare says its Rust TypeScript port is 8x faster. I measured 5.3x — and 72% less memory.
description:
Cloudflare says its Rust TypeScript port is 8x faster. I measured 5.3x — and 72% less memory.

Cloudflare announced tsrs today: a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, built with VoidZero and the original tsc-rs author, incubated under Oxc, and developed "in close collaboration with the TypeScript team." The headline numbers are specific, which is an invitation: up to 8x faster and ~70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0, at the same number of type-check workers.

An experimental release is on npm, so the claim is checkable the way all compiler claims should be checked — by installing both and timing them. I did. The short version: the memory claim landed almost exactly, the speed claim is real but "up to" is doing some work, the diagnostics matched perfectly, the emitted JS was byte-identical — and the exit code wasn't.

The setup 

npm install tsrs typescript
tsrs        0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929
            reports: Version 7.1.0-dev.20260930.4 (microsoft/TypeScript@b85298b)
typescript  7.0.2   (the "TypeScript 7.0" baseline from the claim)
machine     2 vCPU Linux VM, Node v24.20.0

One fairness note, because Cloudflare is honest about it in the post and you should be too when quoting me: tsrs tracks TypeScript 7.1 dev, and the post itself says TypeScript 7.1 beta is already up to 2.5x faster than 7.0, partly from optimizations upstreamed from tsrs. So this is not a clean "Rust vs Go, same compiler version" race. It's the race a user actually gets today: the two packages you can npm install right now, run with defaults on the same project. That's the comparison that decides whether you switch.

The corpus is synthetic but not trivial: 400 TypeScript files, 35,199 lines, generated deterministically — a chain of modules, each defining a generic interface, 28 generic functions doing Map construction over typed arrays, and Pick/& type aliases, all under strict: true with skipLibCheck. Both compilers ran tsc --noEmit / tsrs --noEmit, three runs each, timed externally with peak RSS from wait4 rusage (the compiler's own peak, not the npm shim's).

The numbers 

clean project, 400 files / 35,199 lines, --noEmit, defaults
              run 1     run 2     run 3     median    peak RSS
tsc 7.0.2     3.400s    2.508s    1.936s    2.508s    ~392 MB
tsrs 0.18.0   0.581s    0.474s    0.385s    0.474s    ~110 MB

Median-to-median that's 5.3x faster; best-to-best it's 5.0x; first (cold) runs give 5.9x. I couldn't coax out 8x on this box and corpus — but this is a 2-vCPU VM and a mid-size synthetic project, not Cloudflare's benchmark suite, and their wording is "up to." What I can say is that a 5x type-check speedup is not a rounding error or a cherry-picked microbenchmark. It's the difference between a check you run on save and a check you run on commit.

Memory is where it gets almost boring: ~110 MB vs ~392 MB peak is 72% less, against a claim of "~70% less." Reproduced, nearly to the digit. On a laptop that number is trivia; in the environments Cloudflare cares about — Wasm sandboxes, browser-hosted toolchains, Workers — it's the whole argument, and their post makes it explicitly: a Go binary compiled to Wasm carries its garbage collector with it, a Rust one doesn't have one to carry.

Startup overhead, for the small-project case (a one-file project, 5 runs each):

tsc    0.825  0.860  0.552  0.525  0.514   (seconds)
tsrs   0.450  0.354  0.247  0.209  0.217

Even where there's almost nothing to compile, tsrs starts in roughly half the time. Both are dominated by process startup at this size; the ratio is the story, not the absolutes.

Does it agree with tsc?

Speed is worthless if the port quietly checks a slightly different language. I seeded the same project with four errors across two files — two bad assignments, a call to a nonexistent function, and a method call on a number:

tsc:  exit=1, 4 errors
tsrs: exit=2, 4 errors
  src/mod10.ts(89,14):  error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
  src/mod10.ts(90,14):  error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  src/mod10.ts(91,1):   error TS2304: Cannot find name 'nonexistentFunction'.
  src/mod200.ts(89,42): error TS2339: Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'number'.

The four diagnostics are identical in file, line, column, code, and message — in this run even the order matched, though Cloudflare warns diagnostic order is a known current difference, so don't build tooling that depends on it. Then I compiled the clean project to JS with both: 400 output files each, and diff -rq found zero differences — byte-identical emit on this corpus.

The one real divergence I found is small and exactly the kind that breaks a CI script at 2 a.m.: on type errors, tsc exits 1 and tsrs exits 2. Any script doing if [ $? -eq 1 ] instead of -ne 0 will treat a failed tsrs check as success-shaped. It's an experimental release (the version string is a dev build, 0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev), so this is a "file it and move on" difference, not a scandal — but it's the sort of detail the announcement's "compiles like tsc" framing glosses over, and now you know to grep for it.

Verdict

Reproduced, with one qualifier each:

  • "~70% less memory" — yes: 72% less on my corpus.
  • "Up to 8x faster" — I measured 5.3x median on a 2-vCPU VM with a 35k-line synthetic project, against a baseline (7.0.2) that tsrs's own upstream (7.1) is already much faster than. Treat 8x as a ceiling, 5x as plausible, and measure your own repo — the gap will move with project shape and core count.
  • Faithful port — on everything I threw at it: identical diagnostics, identical emit. One exit-code difference to check in your scripts.

The more interesting claim in Cloudflare's post isn't a number at all: it's that frontier models now make ports like this feasible in days, so the maintenance strategy is an agent that reads upstream TypeScript diffs every morning and regenerates a compatibility matrix every night. If that process holds, tsrs stays faithful; if it slips, tsrs becomes a fork with good benchmarks. The 5.3x I measured is real today. Whether it's still the same language in a year is a process question, and for once the vendor said so themselves.

Sources: Cloudflare's announcement (published today, October 20; HN 329 points), the tsrs npm package (0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929). All timings, memory figures, diagnostics, and emit comparisons above were measured locally today; the corpus generator and benchmark script are deterministic (seed 42).

title: Uncertainty Gates the Gradient: Adaptive Updates for Generalized Few-Shot 3D Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.26909v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones. Complementing this, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) to enforce learning from high-confidence dense signals. On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ (1-/5-shot), UGA sets new state of the art with an average +3.08 HM IoU over the strongest prior baseline.

title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
description:
Private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised, allowing attackers to forge certificates for any site. The keys were revealed due to low entropy, not through a known breach. Browsers blocked them using revocation lists, but other software had to remove the emSign ECC G3 root. Unpatched systems remain exposed to forged certificates, including client auth and mTLS.

By Chris Swan

title: Figma launches data residency in Japan
description: Figma strengthens data protection and security for enterprise customers with local data hosting.

title: Article: Distributed Spring Batch Without a Message Broker
description:
Distributed Spring Batch partitioning already needs a shared, persistent job repository. This article makes that database the whole coordination plane and drops the message broker, sizing work to the live node count, a per-job master with no standing coordinator, compare-and-set claiming that prevents double-execution, two-phase heartbeat failover, and where a broker is still the right choice.

By Janardhan Reddy Chejarla

title: WaveCommitments: Private and Verifiable Speech-Agent Marketplaces
description:
arXiv:2610.26867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern speech systems are evolving into ecosystems of autonomous speech agents that speak together, negotiate, and trade assets such as embeddings, spectrograms, or raw data. In such markets, sellers cannot reveal assets for evaluation due to privacy constraints, and buyers cannot price what they cannot test. Thus, we open-source WaveCommitments, an end-to-end design that pairs confidential asset valuation via Data Shapley inside a trusted execution environment with multivariate polynomial commitments. It enables selective openings and tamper-evident provenance to prove that a delivered asset matches the valuation while hiding everything else. Our extensive experiments across three known datasets and various tasks with state-of-the-art encoders, including Whisper, reveal that we speed up the best benchmarks by up to 20x while reducing their proof sizes by up to 39x. We also systematically study how a speaker's value shifts across tasks and encoders, revealing agent-level market prices.

title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
description:
arXiv:2610.27045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

title: What Building an LLM-Offloaded Query Layer Taught Me
description:
Last month, we were working on a feature for one of our projects. The requirement was to build a natural-language interface that would allow users to query a fairly large MySQL dataset without having to know anything about the underlying database structure.

The idea was simple enough. A user asks a question in plain English, the application understands what information they're looking for, and the corresponding records or analytics are returned.

Now, as most crash courses and quick development reels would suggest, we could simply pass the database schema and the user's question to an LLM, ask it to generate SQL, execute the query and return the result.

And for a POC, that would probably be enough to demonstrate the concept.

But there's always been a striking difference between validating an idea through a POC and making sure the same feature continues to behave reliably when it becomes part of an application used by different people.

We were looking at a similar situation. The underlying data was changing regularly, users had different access scopes, and the questions themselves could vary considerably. Some users might only need an aggregate count, while others might want to inspect records across different operational units.

Before moving towards wider usage, we wanted to understand how we could approach this without making every database interaction completely dependent on the LLM.

Understanding what we were trying to solve

Before getting into the implementation, I want to clarify something.

We weren't trying to discover a faster way to retrieve records from MySQL. Database indexing, query planners, pagination, caching and application-level data access are already established approaches. We would need those regardless of whether an LLM was involved.

What interested us was the additional layer introduced by natural language.

Consider a conventional API. The frontend might send a request containing a region identifier, a status filter and a date range. The backend knows what those parameters mean and can construct a corresponding query.

With a natural-language interface, the user might write something like, "How many requests were pending by the end of last month?"

There are no predefined query parameters being supplied by the user. The application now has to understand the requested metric, interpret the time period, determine the appropriate data scope and prepare an execution request.

We can look at the overall application flow like this:

Once we isolated this part of the application, the discussion became less about which LLM to use and more about how much responsibility we should give it.

Looking into NL-to-SQL

We started exploring existing natural-language-to-SQL approaches to understand how similar requirements were being addressed.

The basic idea behind NL-to-SQL is straightforward: translate a question expressed in natural language into a SQL query that can retrieve the requested information.

The interesting part comes when we start thinking about what the model needs in order to generate that query.

An LLM understands language reasonably well, but it doesn't automatically understand our database. It needs context about available tables, columns, relationships and sometimes the business meaning behind those structures.

Take a question such as:

"Show me the requests updated this week that are still pending review."

A model could generate syntactically valid SQL for this. But which table should it use? What does pending review mean in this application? Which timestamp represents the last update? Does the user have access to every operational unit represented in that table?

These questions can't be answered reliably just by asking the model to write better SQL.

One approach would be to provide the entire database schema with every request. But for a large relational database, this introduces its own problems. Most of that schema may be irrelevant to the user's question, and the model still has to identify the appropriate tables and relationships from a much larger context.

This led us towards a more controlled approach using a schema card.

We built a schema-card layer to give the LLM only the database context relevant to the question. Instead of passing the entire schema, we used our baseline schema definition to identify role-permitted tables and rank them based on their relevance to the user's question.

The card included column information, saved query examples, and metadata identifying protected fields and scope-related columns. We also kept live database records out of this step, since the model only needed enough context to propose SQL.

The current selection uses lexical matching, which works with known terminology but can struggle when users describe the same business concept differently. Since the card also depends on a baseline schema, keeping it aligned with database changes is another area we have to account for.

What happens after the LLM generates SQL?

Suppose the model successfully generates a query. What should happen next?

In a simple demonstration, we might execute the generated SQL immediately and display the results.

But for our feature, we had to consider more than whether the statement was syntactically correct.

A SQL statement can be perfectly valid and still reference a restricted table, return sensitive information or perform an operation that the interface was never supposed to allow.

For this reason, we limited the model's responsibility to proposing the query.

The proposal followed a structured output contract. Instead of returning arbitrary text containing SQL somewhere in the response, the model was expected to produce JSON identifying the response type and, where appropriate, containing a SQL statement.

We then parsed that response and evaluated the generated SQL using a SQL parser and classifier.

The classifier inspected the statement's structure, determined its operation category and applied restrictions around permitted database operations. The surrounding policy checks also considered the tables referenced by the query and limits on query complexity.

We used sqlglot for these checks, which allowed us to inspect the SQL structurally rather than relying on string matching.

There is a practical difference between checking whether a string starts with SELECT and parsing the statement to understand what it contains. SQL can include nested expressions, common table expressions, functions and multiple kinds of statements. A parser gives the application a better foundation for enforcing the supported query contract.

Of course, passing those checks doesn't prove that the model selected the correct business records or interpreted every filter correctly. Structural SQL validation and semantic correctness are separate concerns, and the latter still needs evaluation.

Once the proposed query passed the initial checks, we showed it to the user.

The user could review the statement and explicitly choose to run it. The application then reclassified and rechecked the stored SQL before sending it through our existing governed read-execution path.

That path already applied execution controls such as result limits, a statement watchdog, response masking and audit records.

I think the separation between proposing SQL and executing SQL deserves a little attention.

From a frontend perspective, we can still make the interaction feel like a single chat conversation. The user asks a question, sees the proposed query and chooses whether to execute it.

But internally, proposal and execution are separate operations.

That gives the application an opportunity to persist the proposal, retain an audit record and recheck the statement when execution is requested. The model doesn't have to remain active while the user is deciding.

It also doesn't necessarily mean that the model is called twice. The LLM may be involved only in generating the SQL, after which the application handles execution and presents the returned data.

We still need the backend restrictions even with human review. A user approving a query shouldn't become a substitute for proper access control.

Where the grammar layer became useful

While exploring the NL-to-SQL approach, we also had another category of questions to deal with.

Consider:

"How many requests are pending in this region?"

The question is written in natural language, but the requested information is something the application may already understand as a supported metric.

We don't necessarily need the model to construct arbitrary SQL for that.

We built a deterministic grammar layer backed by controlled vocabulary to interpret supported analytics questions and convert them into structured intents containing the required metric, dimensions, scope and time information.

Once an intent was resolved and validated, the analytics service could identify the relevant data partitions and read the corresponding snapshot aggregates.

This is where we began separating natural-language analytics from flexible NL-to-SQL.

For known analytics questions, the system could resolve the request without calling an LLM. If grammar couldn't understand an otherwise permitted request, a configured model provider could be used as a fallback to propose the structured intent.

That proposal still passed through vocabulary, scope and permission validation before execution. A permission refusal wasn't supposed to become an opportunity to try the question again through the model.

The grammar layer naturally has its limitations. It can only interpret questions covered by the supported vocabulary and expressions. Maintaining that vocabulary also becomes part of the application work.

So we weren't attempting to handle every possible question through deterministic rules. We were using them for questions whose meaning and execution contract were already known.

There was also a difference in how results came back.

For analytics, the service returned structured aggregate values from the database rather than passing the result into another model call for narration. It could also include information about the contributing data partitions and errors encountered during retrieval.

This was particularly relevant because the analytics service could retrieve information from more than one backend partition. If one target failed, the response could preserve the available result along with information about the failure rather than silently presenting it as a complete answer.

We also had to consider questions that belonged outside structured database querying. A question about an operational procedure, for example, would be better suited to document retrieval and possibly RAG than SQL generation over operational records. That distinction helped us think about where the natural-language querying feature should have its boundaries.

What we learned from the implementation review

After understanding the query flow, we also looked at what happened further downstream.

One observation was that our natural-language analytics path queried its backend partitions sequentially. The NL-to-SQL execution path already had a concurrent multi-target read mechanism, but the deterministic analytics path hadn't adopted the same approach.

This raised a practical performance question.

Even if grammar resolution avoids an LLM call, the total response time still depends on everything that happens after the intent has been resolved. Multiple database connections, sequential reads and network latency can contribute significantly to the overall request duration.

We already had functional tests covering grammar resolution, generated SQL classification and the successful execution paths. However, we hadn't yet measured how the complete interface would behave under higher concurrency or across a larger number of backend partitions.

Another area worth examining was the absence of a request-wide deadline. Individual database statements had timeout controls, but a request involving multiple operations could still spend considerable time progressing through those individually bounded calls.

These observations gave us a better picture of the work beyond the model interaction itself.

Understanding the performance of this feature would require measurements around grammar resolution rates, model fallback frequency, database execution time and partial failures.

We didn't have a clean benchmark that would let us claim a particular latency or cost improvement from the design, so I'd rather leave those numbers out than estimate them.

Where this leaves me

Looking at the completed query flow, I found it interesting how little of the overall execution actually needed to depend on the LLM. The model still helped us handle flexible questions, but we had enough information within the application to manage known analytics, SQL validation and database execution separately.

There's still more to understand about how this behaves under load, particularly across multiple data partitions. For now, the experience gave me a better appreciation of the engineering decisions that sit between a working NL-to-SQL demo and an application feature.# What Building an LLM-Offloaded Query Layer Taught Me

Last month, we were working on a feature for one of our projects. The requirement was to build a natural-language interface that would allow users to query a fairly large MySQL dataset without having to know anything about the underlying database structure.

The idea was simple enough. A user asks a question in plain English, the application understands what information they're looking for, and the corresponding records or analytics are returned.

Now, as most crash courses and quick development reels would suggest, we could simply pass the database schema and the user's question to an LLM, ask it to generate SQL, execute the query and return the result.

And for a POC, that would probably be enough to demonstrate the concept.

But there's always been a striking difference between validating an idea through a POC and making sure the same feature continues to behave reliably when it becomes part of an application used by different people.

We were looking at a similar situation. The underlying data was changing regularly, users had different access scopes, and the questions themselves could vary considerably. Some users might only need an aggregate count, while others might want to inspect records across different operational units.

Before moving towards wider usage, we wanted to understand how we could approach this without making every database interaction completely dependent on the LLM.

Understanding what we were trying to solve

Before getting into the implementation, I want to clarify something.

We weren't trying to discover a faster way to retrieve records from MySQL. Database indexing, query planners, pagination, caching and application-level data access are already established approaches. We would need those regardless of whether an LLM was involved.

What interested us was the additional layer introduced by natural language.

Consider a conventional API. The frontend might send a request containing a region identifier, a status filter and a date range. The backend knows what those parameters mean and can construct a corresponding query.

With a natural-language interface, the user might write something like, "How many requests were pending by the end of last month?"

There are no predefined query parameters being supplied by the user. The application now has to understand the requested metric, interpret the time period, determine the appropriate data scope and prepare an execution request.

We can look at the overall application flow like this:

[Diagram 1 — End-to-end HLD: Natural-language interface → Application interpretation layer ↔ Optional LLM → Governed execution → Database → Response.]

Once we isolated this part of the application, the discussion became less about which LLM to use and more about how much responsibility we should give it.

Looking into NL-to-SQL

We started exploring existing natural-language-to-SQL approaches to understand how similar requirements were being addressed.

The basic idea behind NL-to-SQL is straightforward: translate a question expressed in natural language into a SQL query that can retrieve the requested information.

The interesting part comes when we start thinking about what the model needs in order to generate that query.

An LLM understands language reasonably well, but it doesn't automatically understand our database. It needs context about available tables, columns, relationships and sometimes the business meaning behind those structures.

Take a question such as:

"Show me the requests updated this week that are still pending review."

A model could generate syntactically valid SQL for this. But which table should it use? What does pending review mean in this application? Which timestamp represents the last update? Does the user have access to every operational unit represented in that table?

These questions can't be answered reliably just by asking the model to write better SQL.

One approach would be to provide the entire database schema with every request. But for a large relational database, this introduces its own problems. Most of that schema may be irrelevant to the user's question, and the model still has to identify the appropriate tables and relationships from a much larger context.

This led us towards a more controlled approach using a schema card.

We built a schema-card layer to give the LLM only the database context relevant to the question. Instead of passing the entire schema, we used our baseline schema definition to identify role-permitted tables and rank them based on their relevance to the user's question.

The card included column information, saved query examples, and metadata identifying protected fields and scope-related columns. We also kept live database records out of this step, since the model only needed enough context to propose SQL.

The current selection uses lexical matching, which works with known terminology but can struggle when users describe the same business concept differently. Since the card also depends on a baseline schema, keeping it aligned with database changes is another area we have to account for.

What happens after the LLM generates SQL?

Suppose the model successfully generates a query. What should happen next?

In a simple demonstration, we might execute the generated SQL immediately and display the results.

But for our feature, we had to consider more than whether the statement was syntactically correct.

A SQL statement can be perfectly valid and still reference a restricted table, return sensitive information or perform an operation that the interface was never supposed to allow.

For this reason, we limited the model's responsibility to proposing the query.

The proposal followed a structured output contract. Instead of returning arbitrary text containing SQL somewhere in the response, the model was expected to produce JSON identifying the response type and, where appropriate, containing a SQL statement.

We then parsed that response and evaluated the generated SQL using a SQL parser and classifier.

The classifier inspected the statement's structure, determined its operation category and applied restrictions around permitted database operations. The surrounding policy checks also considered the tables referenced by the query and limits on query complexity.

We used sqlglot for these checks, which allowed us to inspect the SQL structurally rather than relying on string matching.

There is a practical difference between checking whether a string starts with SELECT and parsing the statement to understand what it contains. SQL can include nested expressions, common table expressions, functions and multiple kinds of statements. A parser gives the application a better foundation for enforcing the supported query contract.

Of course, passing those checks doesn't prove that the model selected the correct business records or interpreted every filter correctly. Structural SQL validation and semantic correctness are separate concerns, and the latter still needs evaluation.

Once the proposed query passed the initial checks, we showed it to the user.

The user could review the statement and explicitly choose to run it. The application then reclassified and rechecked the stored SQL before sending it through our existing governed read-execution path.

That path already applied execution controls such as result limits, a statement watchdog, response masking and audit records.

[Diagram 2 — Zoomed DFD: Grammar-first analytics, optional LLM fallback, governed SQL proposal and execution.]

I think the separation between proposing SQL and executing SQL deserves a little attention.

From a frontend perspective, we can still make the interaction feel like a single chat conversation. The user asks a question, sees the proposed query and chooses whether to execute it.

But internally, proposal and execution are separate operations.

That gives the application an opportunity to persist the proposal, retain an audit record and recheck the statement when execution is requested. The model doesn't have to remain active while the user is deciding.

It also doesn't necessarily mean that the model is called twice. The LLM may be involved only in generating the SQL, after which the application handles execution and presents the returned data.

We still need the backend restrictions even with human review. A user approving a query shouldn't become a substitute for proper access control.

Where the grammar layer became useful

While exploring the NL-to-SQL approach, we also had another category of questions to deal with.

Consider:

"How many requests are pending in this region?"

The question is written in natural language, but the requested information is something the application may already understand as a supported metric.

We don't necessarily need the model to construct arbitrary SQL for that.

We built a deterministic grammar layer backed by controlled vocabulary to interpret supported analytics questions and convert them into structured intents containing the required metric, dimensions, scope and time information.

Once an intent was resolved and validated, the analytics service could identify the relevant data partitions and read the corresponding snapshot aggregates.

This is where we began separating natural-language analytics from flexible NL-to-SQL.

For known analytics questions, the system could resolve the request without calling an LLM. If grammar couldn't understand an otherwise permitted request, a configured model provider could be used as a fallback to propose the structured intent.
