title: Round once, split later: 13 Python tests for LRC timestamps
description:
Disclosure: this is a project-associated, AI-generated developer walkthrough prepared for the AI LRC Generator team. The standalone example and synthetic tests were executed locally; this is not a description of the product's internal implementation or a benchmark of audio recognition.

A timestamp serializer looks like a small formatting task until a rounded value crosses a boundary. An input just below a minute can become exactly a minute at the precision chosen for export. If the code splits the original value into minutes and seconds before rounding, it can produce a seconds field that should have carried into the next minute. The useful design question is therefore not only how many decimal places to print. It is which units the function accepts, when rounding happens, and which invariants should hold after that decision.

This example uses integer centiseconds as its output units and a deliberately narrow contract. One public function accepts nonnegative integer milliseconds. A second accepts unsigned ASCII decimal seconds as text and rounds directly to centiseconds. Both use round-half-up, then split the already rounded total into fields. They do not open recordings, infer words, repair cue order or validate an entire lyric document. Keeping that boundary explicit makes the small module easier to test and prevents its tests from being presented as evidence about problems the code does not attempt to solve.

State the representation before writing the formatter

The chosen output is a bracketed minute, seconds and hundredths representation. Minutes have a minimum width of two digits but are not wrapped at an hour. Seconds and hundredths always stay inside their respective ranges because they are obtained from integer division after rounding. This is an example policy, not a claim that every player accepts an arbitrarily wide minute field. A real export pipeline may need additional limits for its destination. Those limits should be a separate validation decision rather than an accidental side effect of using a clock or date formatting API.

The millisecond interface intentionally rejects floats and booleans. In Python, booleans are integer subclasses, so a broad integer instance check can admit values that were probably not intended as durations. The exact type check here is a policy choice for a small teaching interface. A larger application could accept more numeric types, but it should document their conversion and error behavior. Silent truncation is particularly unhelpful when a caller believes it supplied a fractional duration. Rejecting the unsupported type makes that disagreement visible at the boundary instead of hiding it inside a plausible-looking timestamp.

Round the total, then split the fields

For integer milliseconds, adding five before integer division by ten implements the selected half-up rule for nonnegative values. The result is a total number of centiseconds. Dividing that total by six thousand produces minutes and a remainder; dividing the remainder by one hundred produces seconds and hundredths. A carry across a second or minute is already represented in the rounded total, so the formatting step does not need a collection of special-case repairs. The function is small because the arithmetic order does most of the work.

The decimal-text interface should not round through an intermediate millisecond value. Consider the textual duration 59.9949 seconds. Rounding that first to milliseconds yields 59.995 seconds, which rounds again to 60.00 at centisecond precision. Rounding the original decimal directly to centiseconds yields 59.99. Neither intermediate operation is mysterious; the mismatch comes from composing two quantization steps. If the intended output precision is already known, perform that quantization once. If an upstream system has already delivered integer milliseconds, treat that as its explicit input representation rather than pretending the earlier precision is still available.

"""Strict example LRC serialization; no audio processing or file I/O."""
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP, localcontext
import re

_SECONDS = re.compile(r"[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?", re.ASCII)

def _stamp(cs: int) -> str:
    minutes, remainder = divmod(cs, 6000)
    seconds, hundredths = divmod(remainder, 100)
    return f"[{minutes:02d}:{seconds:02d}.{hundredths:02d}]"

def from_milliseconds(ms: int) -> str:
    """Nonnegative integer milliseconds, round half up to a centisecond."""
    if type(ms) is not int:
        raise TypeError("milliseconds must be an int, not a bool or float")
    if ms < 0:
        raise ValueError("milliseconds must be nonnegative")
    return _stamp((ms + 5) // 10)

def from_seconds_text(text: str) -> str:
    """ASCII decimal seconds; round once, directly to centiseconds."""
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        raise TypeError("seconds must be decimal text")
    if not 1 <= len(text) <= 80 or _SECONDS.fullmatch(text) is None:
        raise ValueError("expected 1-80 characters of unsigned decimal seconds")
    with localcontext() as context:
        context.prec = max(28, len(text) + 4)
        cs = int((Decimal(text) * 100).to_integral_value(rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))
    return _stamp(cs)

Keep decimal parsing separate from permissive conversion

The accepted textual syntax is intentionally smaller than everything Decimal can parse. It permits ordinary unsigned decimal digits with an optional fractional part. It rejects whitespace, signs, exponent notation, missing digits around the decimal point and special values. That policy avoids accepting alternate representations merely because a conversion library happens to understand them. It also gives callers one clear normalization boundary. This is not an argument that other syntaxes are universally unsafe; an application can support them when it has a reason, but that decision should be deliberate and covered by tests.

The eighty-character limit is an example bound for this interface, not an estimate of a reasonable recording duration. The local decimal context has enough precision for the accepted text before multiplication by one hundred. That matters because parsing a long decimal exactly does not guarantee that subsequent arithmetic will ignore the active context's precision. A long-input fixture checks that the intended carry is preserved. For a production service, resource limits, destination limits and how errors reach callers would still need their own review. The small bound and a passing fixture do not constitute a security audit.

Test the boundaries that explain the design

Save the module as lrc_clock.py and the following suite as test_lrc_clock.py in the same directory. Run python3 -m unittest -v from that directory. The suite was actually executed locally with Python's standard library: thirteen test methods passed, including subtests for several invalid inputs. The fixtures cover zero, rounding ties, second and minute carries, an hour boundary without clock wrapping, wide minutes, rejected types, strict decimal syntax and the double-rounding example. They are synthetic examples chosen to exercise this serializer's contract, not a sample of real recordings or a player compatibility study.

import unittest
from lrc_clock import from_milliseconds, from_seconds_text

class ClockTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_zero(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(0), "[00:00.00]")

    def test_integer_rounding_boundary(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(4), "[00:00.00]")
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(5), "[00:00.01]")

    def test_second_carry(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(994), "[00:00.99]")
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(995), "[00:01.00]")

    def test_minute_carry(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(59994), "[00:59.99]")
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(59995), "[01:00.00]")

    def test_no_hour_wrap(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(3599995), "[60:00.00]")

    def test_wide_minutes(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_milliseconds(6000000), "[100:00.00]")

    def test_negative_integer(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            from_milliseconds(-1)

    def test_strict_integer_type(self):
        for value in (True, False, 1.5, "10", None):
            with self.subTest(value=value), self.assertRaises(TypeError):
                from_milliseconds(value)

    def test_decimal_without_double_rounding(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_seconds_text("59.9949"), "[00:59.99]")
        self.assertEqual(from_seconds_text("59.9950"), "[01:00.00]")

    def test_half_up_and_leading_zeroes(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_seconds_text("0.125"), "[00:00.13]")
        self.assertEqual(from_seconds_text("000.0099"), "[00:00.01]")
        self.assertEqual(from_seconds_text("12"), "[00:12.00]")

    def test_invalid_text(self):
        for value in ("", " ", "-1", "+1", "1e2", "NaN", "Infinity",
                      ".5", "1.", "1:02", "١", "1\n", "0" * 81):
            with self.subTest(value=value), self.assertRaises(ValueError):
                from_seconds_text(value)

    def test_text_type(self):
        with self.assertRaises(TypeError):
            from_seconds_text(0.125)

    def test_long_input_keeps_precision(self):
        self.assertEqual(from_seconds_text("1" * 40 + ".995"),
                         from_milliseconds(int("1" * 40) * 1000 + 995))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

The expected strings are intentionally literal in the boundary tests. Computing an expected timestamp by calling the same formatting helper would make the tests less independent and could reproduce the same mistake on both sides of an assertion. The long-input test uses the separately defined integer-millisecond path as a cross-check, while the shorter decimal boundaries still have fixed expected strings. These approaches complement each other. None replaces a careful review of the contract, and a large number of assertions would not make an undocumented rounding rule correct for every consumer.

Connect formatting tests to an honest export workflow

A lyric editor can still need human review even when its serializer is well tested. Someone must check that the words and timing correspond to the exact recording and that the destination understands the chosen format. A browser workspace such as this lrc generator supports editable lyric text, line timestamps, offset adjustments, previews and lyric or subtitle exports. Editing and exports are free; automatic audio processing requires a verified account and credits. Consult its current pricing and storage terms. The module above is a standalone illustration, not a claim about how that service implements exports.

Keep this serializer behind a clear application boundary. Resolve the intended timing representation before calling it, preserve the editable source and make validation errors useful to the caller. Do not infer an offset, delete a repeated line or repair a recording-version mismatch inside a formatting function. Those actions require context the function does not have. An export pipeline can coordinate several small components without making each component responsible for every problem. That separation also makes it easier to state which behavior a local test result does and does not support.

Finally, test the actual exported file in the intended player or editor when that environment is available. Check characters, cue order and the features expected at the destination rather than treating a successful download as proof of compatibility. If destination testing is unavailable, report that limitation. The practical benefit of rounding once and testing boundaries is a more understandable piece of the pipeline, not a promise of perfect synchronized lyrics. Clear units, explicit conversion rules and narrowly stated evidence make the next review more useful than a timestamp that merely looks convincing.

title: 4 Accessibility Mistakes AI Coding Assistants Make, and How to Catch Them
description:
AI coding assistants are good at producing working components quickly. They learned from a huge amount of public code, and public code is full of accessibility mistakes — so the same mistakes come back in generated components, looking clean and passing a quick visual review.

Here are four that show up often, the WCAG criterion each one fails, and how to catch them before they merge.

1. A clickable div with no keyboard support (WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2)

Ask for "a clickable card" or "a custom button" and you'll often get this:

// Works with a mouse. A keyboard user can't reach it or activate it.
<div className="btn" onClick={save}>Save</div>

Adding role="button" alone doesn't fix it: the element still isn't in the tab order and doesn't respond to Enter or Space.

// Fix: use the element that already does all of this.
<button type="button" className="btn" onClick={save}>Save</button>

A <button> is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. Reach for role and tabIndex only when no native element fits.

2. An aria-label that doesn't match the visible text (WCAG 2.5.3)

Assistants like adding aria-label "for accessibility", often with a more descriptive phrase than the button shows:

<!-- Visible text "Buy now"; accessible name "Add product to basket" -->
<button aria-label="Add product to basket">Buy now</button>

The aria-label replaces the visible text as the accessible name. A voice-control user who says "click Buy now" gets nothing, because no control is called "Buy now". WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name) requires the accessible name to contain the visible label.

<!-- Fix: let the visible text be the name -->
<button>Buy now</button>

If you need more context for screen reader users, keep the visible words at the start of the name: aria-label="Buy now: Linen shirt".

3. A placeholder used as the label (WCAG 3.3.2, 1.3.1) 

<input type="email" placeholder="Email address">

The placeholder disappears as soon as someone starts typing, it's usually low contrast, and it isn't a reliable label. Give every input a visible, associated label:

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">

4. Focus outlines removed (WCAG 2.4.7)

Generated CSS often includes a reset like this:

*:focus { outline: none; }

It removes the only sign of where a keyboard user is on the page. If the default ring doesn't fit the design, replace it rather than removing it, and keep it to keyboard focus:

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Catching these in review

Each check below catches a different subset, so use more than one:

  • A linter in the editor. eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y flags click handlers on non-interactive elements and inputs without labels while you type.
  • Prefer native elements in prompts and review. Asking the assistant for "a <button>" or "a native <dialog>" gets better output than "a clickable element".
  • A keyboard pass. Tab through the new component. If you can't reach or operate it, it fails.
  • A check of the rendered page. Mistakes 1, 2 and 4 depend on the rendered page — computed names, focus styles, what's focusable. ADAGuard loads the page in a real browser and checks those, including label-in-name. Scan a page free.

Avoid "fix it at runtime" scripts as the safety net. A script that edits the page in each visitor's browser leaves the source unchanged, so every mistake is still in the code the assistant learned from your repo. See why overlays don't fix accessibility.

AI assistants are useful here too: once a failure is found, they're good at applying a known fix across many files. The part they can't do is notice that a component they just wrote doesn't work with a keyboard. That takes a test.

title: Free SQL practice: why SUM(DISTINCT) doesn't fix inflated payment totals
description:
Free SQL practice, with the full data and solution below. No account, paid course, cloud service, or API key is needed. This is a SQLite exercise using synthetic payment data, with a Python standard-library runner if you do not have the SQLite CLI.

Two distinct capture events are each worth 1000 USD cents. A report should show 2000 cents. After a join, one query reports 4000; adding DISTINCT reports 1000. Both are wrong.

I maintain a free, MIT-licensed fintech data engineering roadmap. This article works through the class of bug explored in its C07 scenario: independent detail tables multiply one another before aggregation.

First, define the report's grain

We want one row for each payment and currency with at least one capture:

  • gross_minor: sum of capture amounts.
  • net_minor: captures minus fees in the same currency.
  • attempt_count: attempts at the payment grain, shared across that payment's currencies.

For this synthetic exercise, a missing fee match means zero fees, and a missing attempt match means zero attempts. That is an explicit fixture contract, not a general rule that unknown monetary data should become zero. Fee-only payments are outside the report's population.

Set up the data

Save this block as setup.sql. Run it once in a fresh database.

CREATE TABLE captures (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payment TEXT, currency TEXT, amount INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE fees (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payment TEXT, currency TEXT, amount INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE attempts (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payment TEXT);

INSERT INTO captures VALUES
  ('c1', 'p1', 'USD', 1000),
  ('c2', 'p1', 'USD', 1000),
  ('c3', 'p1', 'EUR', 500),
  ('c4', 'p2', 'USD', 700);
INSERT INTO fees VALUES
  ('f1', 'p1', 'USD', 50),
  ('f2', 'p1', 'EUR', 20);
INSERT INTO attempts VALUES ('a1', 'p1'), ('a2', 'p1');

c1 and c2 have different event IDs and the same amount. Neither is a duplicate event. p1 has both USD and EUR captures. p2 has a capture but no matching fee or attempt.

Before running anything, calculate p1 / USD by hand: 1000 + 1000 = 2000 gross; subtract the 50-cent fee to get 1950 net; there are two attempts.

The query that looks plausible 

SELECT c.payment, c.currency,
       SUM(c.amount) AS gross_minor,
       SUM(c.amount) - COALESCE(SUM(f.amount), 0) AS net_minor,
       SUM(DISTINCT c.amount) AS distinct_amount_shortcut,
       COUNT(a.id) AS attempt_count
FROM captures AS c
LEFT JOIN fees AS f
  ON c.payment = f.payment AND c.currency = f.currency
LEFT JOIN attempts AS a ON c.payment = a.payment
GROUP BY c.payment, c.currency
ORDER BY c.payment, c.currency;

For p1 / USD, its output is:

Field Wrong output Expected
gross_minor 4000 2000
net_minor 3800 1950
distinct_amount_shortcut 1000 2000
attempt_count 4 2

There are two captures, one USD fee, and two attempts. Their joins create four rows. Each capture appears twice; the same fee appears four times. Summing those joined rows inflates gross and fee totals independently.

SUM(DISTINCT c.amount) removes repeated values. The two valid 1000-cent captures collapse into a single value, so it returns 1000. It does not deduplicate by event ID. This follows SQLite's aggregate DISTINCT behavior.

COUNT(DISTINCT a.id) could repair this particular attempt count, but it would not repair the monetary sums. The report needs a consistent grain for each independent measure.

Aggregate each input before joining

Save this corrected query as report.sql.

WITH capture_totals AS (
  SELECT payment, currency, SUM(amount) AS gross_minor
  FROM captures
  GROUP BY payment, currency
), fee_totals AS (
  SELECT payment, currency, SUM(amount) AS fee_minor
  FROM fees
  GROUP BY payment, currency
), attempt_totals AS (
  SELECT payment, COUNT(*) AS attempt_count
  FROM attempts
  GROUP BY payment
)
SELECT c.payment, c.currency, c.gross_minor,
       c.gross_minor - COALESCE(f.fee_minor, 0) AS net_minor,
       COALESCE(a.attempt_count, 0) AS attempt_count
FROM capture_totals AS c
LEFT JOIN fee_totals AS f
  ON c.payment = f.payment AND c.currency = f.currency
LEFT JOIN attempt_totals AS a ON c.payment = a.payment
ORDER BY c.payment, c.currency;

The independently specified expected output, also checked by executing the query in SQLite, is:

payment currency gross_minor net_minor attempt_count
p1 EUR 500 480 2
p1 USD 2000 1950 2
p2 USD 700 700 0

Each capture and fee CTE has one row per payment/currency. The attempts CTE has one row per payment. The final joins therefore do not multiply these input aggregates.

LEFT JOIN retains p2. Joining fees on both payment and currency prevents an EUR fee from reducing a USD total. SQLite documents the relevant FROM and JOIN processing.

The two attempts appear on both p1 currency rows because the contract measures attempts per payment. Do not sum that column across currencies and report four attempts. Measures with different grains need different aggregation rules.

Run it with Python, without extra packages

If Python includes sqlite3, save the setup and corrected query under the filenames above, then save this as run_report.py in the same directory:

import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as db:
    db.executescript(Path("setup.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    query = Path("report.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for row in db.execute(query):
        print(row)

Run python run_report.py, or py -3 run_report.py on Windows if needed. The in-memory database starts clean each time.

Try breaking your fix

Add a second USD fee with a different ID but the same 50-cent amount. The correct p1 / USD result should become 2000 gross and 1900 net, with two attempts. A DISTINCT-on-fee-amount shortcut would fail that check too.

Then add a third attempt. Gross and net should remain 2000 and 1900; only attempt_count should become three. These changes test that unrelated detail rows cannot change the monetary total.

Pre-aggregation fixes fan-out; it does not establish that the source events are correct or that settlement agrees. Duplicate delivery and conflicting event identities need separate ingestion checks.

Continue with the free practice repository

The C07 task, hints, cases, and reference extend this into a runnable repair exercise. After cloning the repository:

python challenges/run.py init C07
python challenges/run.py grade C07

The starter intentionally contains a defective query. Edit work/challenges/C07.py, then grade it again. The full repository has 100 English lessons, 40 foundation exercises, and 8 scenario labs, freely available on GitHub. Core practice uses Python 3.12+ and SQLite without paid infrastructure.

Disclosure: I maintain the linked repository. Its first edition and this article were prepared with AI assistance using Codex. All data here is synthetic, and these are teaching examples.

title: JUnit 6 Parameterized Tests: The Complete Guide to Data-Driven Testing on the JVM
description:
Writing the same test five times with different inputs is copying, not testing. Parameterized testing breaks that habit by letting you write a single assertion once and run it against as many datasets as the problem demands. JUnit 6 (the Jupiter framework) gives you a rich set of argument sources, clean display names, and enough flexibility to handle everything from a handful of strings to deeply nested domain objects.

For developers building Spring Boot services, getting good at parameterized testing pays compound interest. Service layer logic, validation rules, pricing calculations, and repository queries all share the same structure: given some input, expect some output. Parameterized tests make that pattern explicit and give you a test suite that grows with your domain model.

Most developers run into friction with complex inputs: DTOs, entity objects, configuration records, and the boilerplate required to construct them in Java.

This guide walks through every major parameter source in JUnit 6, shows when and why to reach for each one, covers the specific patterns that surface in Spring Boot test suites across every layer (service, controller, repository, and configuration), and then demonstrates how Kotlin's data classes and named arguments cut test setup code without touching a single line of production Java.

What parameterized tests are

A parameterized test is a test method that JUnit runs multiple times, injecting a different set of arguments on each invocation. You write the assertion logic once, and the framework handles the loop. Each invocation is tracked, named, and reported independently in the test runner, so a failure on input three doesn't mask a pass on input five.

The key annotation is @ParameterizedTest, which replaces @Test. You pair it with a source annotation that tells JUnit where to pull argument values from. JUnit 6 ships with sources for inline values, CSV rows, CSV files, factory methods, and pluggable providers, each suited to a different complexity tier.

Setup for parameterized tests

Required dependencies

If you're starting from a Spring Boot project, spring-boot-starter-test already pulls in the JUnit Jupiter engine. You need to add junit-jupiter-params explicitly if it's not coming in transitively from your BOM.

JUnit 6 raises the minimum Java version to 17 (JUnit 5 only required 8), and if you're writing tests in Kotlin, you'll need Kotlin 2.2 or newer. Spring Boot 4.x already baselines on Java 17 and manages compatible JUnit and Kotlin versions for you, so the simplest path is to build on Spring Boot 4.

Gradle (Kotlin DSL):

plugins {
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
    id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
    kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
}

dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web")
    implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-reflect")
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test")
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter-params")
}

tasks.withType<Test> {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}

For Maven, add junit-jupiter-params with test scope alongside spring-boot-starter-test.

IDE support

IntelliJ IDEA renders each parameterized invocation as a child node in the Run tool window, using whatever display name you configure. It warns you at edit time if you declare @ParameterizedTest without a source, highlights type mismatches between the source and the method signature, and excludes @MethodSource provider methods from "unused declaration" warnings. The gutter run icon lets you execute the entire parameterized suite or rerun only the specific invocations that failed.

Running tests in Maven and Gradle

Both build tools need useJUnitPlatform() (Gradle) or the maven-surefire-plugin configured for JUnit Platform to pick up Jupiter tests. Without this, parameterized tests either skip silently or report as errors rather than test failures.

One JUnit 6 constraint worth knowing up front: Maven Surefire and Failsafe versions older than 3.0.0 are no longer supported. If your pom.xml pins an older plugin version, bump it, or parameterized tests may not execute under the JUnit Platform at all.

Display names

@ParameterizedTest accepts a name attribute. The placeholders {index}, {0}, {1}, and {arguments} let you build readable names from the supplied values:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "[{index}] discount for {0} loyalty years = {1}%")

The test runner displays something like [3] discount for 5 loyalty years = 10%, which makes failures self-explanatory without opening the test body.

Using @ValueSource

@ValueSource supplies a single array of literals (strings, ints, longs, doubles, or class references) and is the right choice when your test needs one argument per invocation and the values are small enough to inline.

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = {"radar", "level", "kayak"})
void isPalindrome(String word) {
    assertTrue(IsPalindromeChecker.check(word));
}

When your data grows beyond three or four values, or when you need more than one argument per invocation, move to @CsvSource or @MethodSource.

Using @NullSource, @EmptySource, and @NullAndEmptySource

These three annotations inject edge-case inputs for null and empty states. They're most useful on service methods and validators that need to handle blank input gracefully.

@ParameterizedTest
@NullAndEmptySource
@ValueSource(strings = {" ", "\t", "\n"})
void rejectsBlankUsername(String username) {
    assertThrows(InvalidInputException.class,
        () -> userService.register(username, "valid@example.com"));
}

Combining @NullAndEmptySource with @ValueSource on the same method covers null, empty string, and whitespace-only inputs in one test method. JUnit 6 supports stacking these annotations.

One interop detail matters if the method under test is written in Kotlin: a Kotlin function with a non-nullable parameter (fun register(username: String, ...)) compiles a null-check at the start of the method body. Feed it a literal null from @NullSource, and you get a bare NullPointerException before your own validation logic ever runs — not the InvalidInputException the test expects. Declare the parameter as nullable (username: String?) and check it with username.isNullOrBlank() if you want @NullAndEmptySource to exercise your validation path rather than Kotlin's own null-check.

Using @CsvSource

@CsvSource supplies multiple arguments per invocation as comma-separated rows defined inline. Use it when you need two or three related values, and you want to keep the data close to the test:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} + {1} = {2}")
@CsvSource({
    "1, 2, 3",
    "5, 5, 10",
    "-1, 1, 0",
    "100, -100, 0"
})
void addsCorrectly(int a, int b, int expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, calculator.add(a, b));
}

JUnit handles type conversion automatically, so the string "3" becomes the int 3 without any adapter code. For values that contain commas, wrap the field in single quotes, as in "'Smith, John', john@example.com, 30".

Under the hood, JUnit 6 replaced the CSV parser (it now uses FastCSV instead of univocity-parsers), and a few edge cases around quoting changed as a result — extra characters after a closing quote now throw instead of being silently ignored, for example. The common case above, including quoted fields containing commas, parses exactly the same as it did under JUnit 5.

@CsvSource starts to strain when you have more than six or seven rows, when values are long, or when you're reusing the same dataset across multiple test classes. At that point, use @CsvFileSource.

Loading test data with @CsvFileSource

@CsvFileSource reads rows from a file on the classpath:

@ParameterizedTest
@CsvFileSource(resources = "/test-data/pricing-scenarios.csv", numLinesToSkip = 1)
void calculatesPriceCorrectly(String tier, int loyaltyYears, boolean isVip, String expectedPrice) {
    // assertions
}

The numLinesToSkip = 1 skips the header row. The file sits under src/test/resources. Reach for this approach when your test dataset is large enough to be maintained separately, when it's shared with non-Java stakeholders (QA, product), or when it's generated by another tool.

Creating dynamic test data with @MethodSource

@MethodSource delegates to a factory method that returns a Stream<Arguments>, a List, or an Iterable. It's the right choice for complex objects, computed values, and any scenario where inline CSV can't express your data structure.

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}")
@MethodSource("pricingScenarios")
void calculatesPriceForAllTiers(PricingScenario scenario) {
    DiscountResult result = pricingService.calculate(scenario.input());
    assertEquals(scenario.expected(), result);
}

static Stream<Arguments> pricingScenarios() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(new PricingScenario(
            "VIP with 5 loyalty years",
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 5, true),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("150.00"), 25)
        )),
        Arguments.of(new PricingScenario(
            "Standard user, no discount",
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0, false),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0)
        ))
    );
}

The factory method must be static by default because JUnit instantiates a new test class per invocation under the default PER_METHOD lifecycle. You can lift that restriction with @TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), which becomes particularly useful in Kotlin (covered in a later section).

Supplying data with a custom ArgumentsProvider

When you want to share a dataset across multiple test classes, or load data from an external source at runtime, implement ArgumentsProvider:

public class DiscountScenariosProvider implements ArgumentsProvider {
    @Override
    public Stream<? extends Arguments> provideArguments(ParameterDeclarations parameters, ExtensionContext context) {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 5, false),
                new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("90.00"), 10)),
            Arguments.of(new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 0, true),
                new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("170.00"), 15))
        );
    }
}

Then reference it with @ArgumentsSource(DiscountScenariosProvider.class). The provider has access to the ExtensionContext, which means it can read annotations on the test class, inspect the test method name, or pull configuration from the JUnit store. That access is useful when you want a single provider to behave differently across different test contexts.

Note the two-argument provideArguments(ParameterDeclarations, ExtensionContext) signature above. The older single-argument provideArguments(ExtensionContext) still compiles and runs under JUnit 6, but it's deprecated — the compiler will flag it, and new providers should use the two-argument form.

Testing complex objects

Passing plain primitives through @CsvSource works until you need to test against DTOs, entity objects, or configuration objects. At that point, use @MethodSource or a custom ArgumentsProvider and construct your objects directly in the factory method.

DTOs. For a Spring Boot user registration endpoint, a validation test might look like this:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}")
@MethodSource("invalidRegistrationRequests")
void rejectsInvalidRequests(String scenario, UserRegistrationRequest request, int expectedViolations) {
    Set<ConstraintViolation<UserRegistrationRequest>> violations = validator.validate(request);
    assertEquals(expectedViolations, violations.size(), scenario);
}

static Stream<Arguments> invalidRegistrationRequests() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of("blank username",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("", "valid@example.com", 25), 1),
        Arguments.of("invalid email",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("alice", "not-an-email", 25), 1),
        Arguments.of("negative age",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("bob", "bob@example.com", -1), 1),
        Arguments.of("blank username and invalid email",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("", "not-an-email", 25), 2)
    );
}

The scenario string argument doubles as a display name fragment and as an assertion message, so a failure tells you exactly which case broke without making you decode an index number.

Entity objects. The same pattern applies directly to JPA entities — construct them in the factory method and assert against their behavior:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0} matches category {1}? {2}")
@MethodSource("productsByCategory")
void filtersProductsByCategory(Product product, String category, boolean expectedMatch) {
    assertEquals(expectedMatch, product.getCategory().equals(category));
}

static Stream<Arguments> productsByCategory() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(new Product("Laptop", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("999.00")), "ELECTRONICS", true),
        Arguments.of(new Product("Laptop", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("999.00")), "BOOKS", false)
    );
}

Configuration objects. Configuration-bound objects can be constructed directly too, which is useful for testing the logic that consumes them without spinning up a Spring context:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: enabled={0}, cap={1} -> bonus={2}")
@MethodSource("pricingConfigurations")
void loyaltyBonusRespectsConfiguration(boolean enabled, int cap, int expectedBonus) {
    PricingProperties properties = new PricingProperties(enabled, cap);
    int bonus = properties.isLoyaltyBonusEnabled() ? properties.getLoyaltyBonusCap() : 0;
    assertEquals(expectedBonus, bonus);
}

static Stream<Arguments> pricingConfigurations() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(true, 10, 10),
        Arguments.of(true, 5, 5),
        Arguments.of(false, 10, 0)
    );
}

This verifies the logic that reads a configuration object in isolation. When you need to verify that Spring actually binds your application.properties values into that object correctly, that's a job for @SpringBootTest or ApplicationContextRunner, covered next.

Parameterized testing in Spring Boot

Combining @ParameterizedTest with Spring test slice annotations gives you data-driven coverage across every layer of a Spring Boot application.

Service layer tests run with plain constructor instantiation or with @SpringBootTest and @Autowired constructor injection:

@SpringBootTest
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class PricingServiceTest {

    @Autowired
    private PricingService pricingService;

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("pricingCases")
    void calculatesPriceCorrectly(DiscountInput input, DiscountResult expected) {
        assertEquals(expected, pricingService.calculate(input));
    }

    Stream<Arguments> pricingCases() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(new DiscountInput(BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 5, false),
                new DiscountResult(BigDecimal.valueOf(90).setScale(2), 10))
        );
    }
}

Validation tests follow the pattern shown earlier, building a jakarta.validation.Validator directly (no Spring context required) and running each invalid payload through it.

Before wiring up controller or repository tests, there's a dependency change worth knowing about: Spring Boot 4 split its test-support autoconfiguration into per-feature modules. spring-boot-starter-test alone no longer pulls in @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest — each needs its own starter:

testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test")
testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test")

The annotations also moved packages. @WebMvcTest is now org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.WebMvcTest, and @DataJpaTest is org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure.DataJpaTest. Spring Boot's own @MockBean was removed in the same release — use Spring Framework's @MockitoBean (org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean) in its place.

Controller tests with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc work naturally with @CsvSource or @MethodSource. You build the request body, fire it through mockMvc.perform(), and assert the response status per invocation:

@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerParameterizedTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockitoBean
    private UserService userService;

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}/{1} -> {2}")
    @CsvSource({
        "alice, valid@example.com, 201",
        "'', valid@example.com, 400",
        "bob, not-an-email, 400"
    })
    void registersUser(String username, String email, int expectedStatus) throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/users")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                    {"username": "%s", "email": "%s", "age": 30}
                    """.formatted(username, email)))
            .andExpect(status().is(expectedStatus));
    }
}

Repository tests with @DataJpaTest can drive @ParameterizedTest to verify query correctness across different filter combinations (entity status enums, date ranges, or tier codes) without repeating setup for each case:

@DataJpaTest
class ProductRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0} has {1} product(s)")
    @MethodSource("categoryExpectations")
    void countsProductsByCategory(String category, long expectedCount) {
        productRepository.save(new Product("Laptop", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("999.00")));
        productRepository.save(new Product("Monitor", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("199.00")));
        productRepository.save(new Product("Novel", "BOOKS", new BigDecimal("15.00")));

        long count = productRepository.findByCategory(category).size();
        assertEquals(expectedCount, count);
    }

    static Stream<Arguments> categoryExpectations() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of("ELECTRONICS", 2L),
            Arguments.of("BOOKS", 1L)
        );
    }
}

Configuration property testing with Spring's ApplicationContextRunner lets you verify that each possible value for a feature flag or config property produces the expected binding, with every scenario named and independently reportable — without the overhead of a full @SpringBootTest:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: enabled={0}, cap={1} -> bonus={2}")
@CsvSource({
    "true, 10, 10",
    "true, 5, 5",
    "false, 10, 0"
})
void loyaltyBonusRespectsConfiguration(boolean enabled, int cap, int expectedBonus) {
    new ApplicationContextRunner()
        .withUserConfiguration(PricingPropertiesConfig.class)
        .withPropertyValues(
            "pricing.loyalty-bonus-enabled=" + enabled,
            "pricing.loyalty-bonus-cap=" + cap)
        .run(context -> {
            PricingProperties properties = context.getBean(PricingProperties.class);
            int bonus = properties.isLoyaltyBonusEnabled() ? properties.getLoyaltyBonusCap() : 0;
            assertEquals(expectedBonus, bonus);
        });
}

This combines Spring's test infrastructure with parameterized execution in both directions: the ApplicationContextRunner builds a minimal context per invocation, and @CsvSource drives the property values through it.

@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) is worth applying to Spring integration tests by default, because it allows @MethodSource factory methods to live as instance methods rather than static methods. This is particularly useful in Kotlin, where a companion object with @JvmStatic is the alternative and instance methods are the cleaner option.

Cleaner parameterized tests with Kotlin

Kotlin's interoperability with the JVM means you can call JUnit 6 from Kotlin without any adapters. The annotations work identically. The gain comes from what Kotlin removes from the picture: builder classes, new, verbose static-factory-method requirements, and the noise that accumulates when you construct several complex objects inline.

How to call JUnit 6 from Kotlin

By default, JUnit's @MethodSource requires a static factory method. Kotlin uses a companion object with @JvmStatic for this purpose. You can avoid that boilerplate entirely by annotating the test class with @TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), which lets the factory method be a regular Kotlin instance function:

@SpringBootTest
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class PricingServiceTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val pricingService: PricingService
) {
    fun pricingCases() = listOf(
        Arguments.of(DiscountInput(BigDecimal("100.00"), 5, false),
            DiscountResult(BigDecimal("90.00"), 10)),
        Arguments.of(DiscountInput(BigDecimal("200.00"), 0, true),
            DiscountResult(BigDecimal("170.00"), 15))
    )

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("pricingCases")
    fun `calculates price correctly`(input: DiscountInput, expected: DiscountResult) {
        assertEquals(expected, pricingService.calculate(input))
    }
}

Data classes for concise test cases

A common pattern in Kotlin test suites is defining a small data class that bundles the inputs and the expected output for a single scenario. Because data class auto-generates a readable toString(), the test runner displays each invocation with a meaningful description rather than an index number.

@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class PricingServiceParameterizedTest {

    private val pricingService = PricingService()

    data class PricingTestCase(
        val description: String,
        val input: DiscountInput,
        val expected: DiscountResult
    )

    private fun pricingScenarios() = listOf(
        PricingTestCase(
            description = "Standard user with no loyalty gets no discount",
            input = DiscountInput(BigDecimal("100.00"), loyaltyYears = 0, isVip = false),
            expected = DiscountResult(BigDecimal("100.00"), 0)
        ),
        PricingTestCase(
            description = "VIP with high loyalty (>=5 yrs) gets 25%",
            input = DiscountInput(BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true),
            expected = DiscountResult(BigDecimal("150.00"), 25)
        )
    )

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{index} => {0}")
    @MethodSource("pricingScenarios")
    fun `should calculate discounted price accurately`(testCase: PricingTestCase) {
        val result = pricingService.calculate(testCase.input)
        assertEquals(testCase.expected, result)
    }
}

(The data class above is declared without private — a public @ParameterizedTest method can't expose a parameter type that's private to the class, so if you factor your test case class out, keep its visibility at least as public as the test method that consumes it.)

Named arguments for improved readability

Kotlin named arguments make each test case self-documenting. Compare the Java version of a complex object construction:

// Java
new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 6, true)

With the Kotlin version:

// Kotlin
DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true)

At a glance, the Kotlin version tells you what each argument means. Scale this across fifteen test cases and the readability difference compounds.

Cleaner object construction than Java builders

When a Java constructor has more than a couple of same-typed parameters sitting next to each other (two ints, two booleans), teams often reach for a builder to make call sites self-describing:

DiscountInput input = new DiscountInputBuilder()
    .basePrice(new BigDecimal("200.00"))
    .loyaltyYears(6)
    .isVip(true)
    .build();

That builder exists purely to work around Java's lack of named arguments — it's an entire extra class (fields, a fluent setter per field, a build() method) whose only job is call-site clarity. Kotlin's named arguments give you the same clarity directly at the call site, with no builder class to write or maintain:

val input = DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true)

For test suites specifically, this matters more than it might in production code: a parameterized test's factory method constructs the same object repeatedly with different values, so every parameter it's missing a name for is a small tax paid on every single test case.

Destructuring declarations and extension functions

Destructuring declarations let you unpack a data class in the test method signature when you prefer to work with its fields directly:

data class ValidationCase(
    val description: String,
    val request: UserRegistrationRequest,
    val expectedViolations: Int
)

private fun validationCases() = listOf(
    ValidationCase("valid payload", UserRegistrationRequest("alice", "alice@example.com", 30), 0),
    ValidationCase("blank username", UserRegistrationRequest("", "alice@example.com", 30), 1)
)

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}")
@MethodSource("validationCases")
fun `validates registration requests`(testCase: ValidationCase) {
    val (_, request, expectedViolations) = testCase
    assertEquals(expectedViolations, validator.validate(request).size)
}

Extension functions on the test class give you reusable assertion helpers scoped to the test context, which is a clean way to extract repeated assertion logic without moving it to a utility class:

private fun DiscountResult.assertMatchesExpected(expected: DiscountResult) {
    assertEquals(expected.discountedPrice, this.discountedPrice)
    assertEquals(expected.discountPercent, this.discountPercent)
}

Java vs Kotlin side by side

The same @MethodSource test in Java and Kotlin illustrates where Kotlin cuts boilerplate:

// Java
static Stream<Arguments> pricingCases() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0, false),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0)
        ),
        Arguments.of(
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 6, true),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("150.00"), 25)
        )
    );
}

// Kotlin
fun pricingCases() = listOf(
    Arguments.of(
        DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("100.00"), loyaltyYears = 0, isVip = false),
        DiscountResult(discountedPrice = BigDecimal("100.00"), discountPercent = 0)
    ),
    Arguments.of(
        DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true),
        DiscountResult(discountedPrice = BigDecimal("150.00"), discountPercent = 25)
    )
)

The Kotlin version is shorter, each argument is named, and there's no static, new, or explicit Stream.of(). The test assertions stay identical because you're calling the same JUnit 6 API against the same JVM bytecode.

For teams with existing Java Spring Boot services, Kotlin test code compiles to the same bytecode and runs on the same JVM, so you can introduce Kotlin in the test source set (src/test/kotlin) without touching a single production class. The two coexist without conflict, which reflects the strategic partnership between JetBrains and the Spring team, a collaboration aimed at improving the experience for backend developers on both sides of the language boundary. For a real-world account of Kotlin running mission-critical backend systems at scale, see this KotlinConf recap of Verifone's work on Kotlin in payments infrastructure.

Best practices for maintainable parameterized tests

  • Keep datasets focused. A factory method that returns forty rows is probably testing more than one logical concept. Split by concern: one method for valid inputs, one for invalid inputs, and one for edge cases.
  • Prefer descriptive argument names. When your test case object has a description or scenario field, surface it in the display name with {0}. A failure that reads [3] VIP with 5 loyalty years gets 25% discount is actionable; [3] is not.
  • Separate data generation from assertions. The factory method should only construct data, and the assertion logic lives in the test method. This separation makes both easier to read and refactor independently.
  • Use reusable providers. When the same dataset validates both a service and a controller, extract an ArgumentsProvider implementation and reference it from both test classes with @ArgumentsSource. Copying and pasting the factory method creates a maintenance problem.
  • Balance flexibility with readability. A generic @MethodSource that builds objects from a dozen intermediate variables is harder to follow than an explicit list of typed data class instances. Optimize for the next developer reading the failure report, not for line count.
  • Organize shared datasets across modules. In multi-module Gradle or Maven builds, a shared test-fixtures source set (Gradle's java-test-fixtures plugin) lets you publish ArgumentsProvider implementations that multiple modules can depend on.
  • Avoid over-parameterization. If every test in a class is parameterized, the class is probably doing too much. Use parameterized tests for cases where variation in data genuinely changes the outcome. A test that always expects the same result with cosmetically varied inputs isn't verifying anything new.
  • Choose the simplest source that fits the problem — whether @ValueSource for a handful of scalars, @CsvSource for related tuples that fit on one line each, @MethodSource for complex objects, or a custom ArgumentsProvider for shared or dynamically loaded datasets. Reaching for the most powerful option by default makes tests harder to scan than necessary.

JUnit 6's parameterized testing API covers how each source annotation works, why you'd choose one over another, and how the patterns map to real Spring Boot test suites across service, validation, controller, repository, and configuration layers.

The Kotlin patterns covered here (data classes, named arguments, @TestInstance(PER_CLASS), extension functions) reduce test setup code without any production-side changes. For teams already on Spring Boot with Java production code, writing Kotlin in the test source set is a low-risk, incremental adoption path. The two languages share the same classpath, the same JUnit 6 runner, and the same Spring test infrastructure. Your production code stays exactly as it is while your test tables get measurably cleaner, which is the right way to evaluate any addition to a working stack: ask whether it solves a real friction point without demanding a wholesale commitment.

title: How we cut CDN metadata lookup latency by 91%
description:
Every request to Vercel passes through our CDN, which executes on average over 80 million routing instructions per second. Part of that work is looking up metadata to determine which paths exist and how to serve them. When that metadata isn’t cached, the CDN has to fetch it before it can serve the response.

We used to fetch and cache metadata one path at a time, retrieving only what each lookup needed. That seemed efficient at the time, but large deployments can contain hundreds of thousands of paths, each with its own cache entry. Every new deployment introduced fresh metadata, making cache misses a recurring cost for large sites that deployed frequently.

Fetching more metadata at once made these lookups faster. By grouping paths together, each fetch could populate the cache for many subsequent lookups. But fetching too much introduced its own costs. Through production experiments, we found a balance that cut P99 metadata lookup latency by 91% and made deployments faster along the way.

How the CDN finds the right route

The path in a request doesn’t always match the path of the content or function that serves it. Framework routing rules connect the two. A request for /blog/hello-world, for example, might resolve to the dynamic route /blog/[slug]. A request for that page’s React Server Component payload might resolve to /blog/[slug].rsc. As the CDN applies these rules, it may need to check several target paths to find the right response.

The framework describes those routes during a build. With framework-defined infrastructure, application code declares which outputs are static, which need Functions, and which responses can be cached or regenerated. Frameworks translate that intent into Build Output API outputs, and Vercel generates the routing metadata the CDN reads.

At request time, the CDN needs to determine which target paths exist and retrieve their metadata. The Bloom filters we added to global routing rule out paths that definitely don’t exist. Remaining paths need an exact metadata lookup.

Originally, we stored that metadata as a separate object per target path. The CDN fetched and cached each object independently. This worked well for smaller projects that deployed infrequently. But every new deployment created a fresh set of cache keys, so the first lookup for each path missed the cache.

Fetching metadata in groups

To reduce cache misses, we grouped metadata for many paths into files called shards. We bounded each shard’s size to control how much data a lookup had to fetch. Fetching a shard brought metadata for all of its paths into the cache, so later lookups for those paths could reuse it.

Each shard also included an index that let the CDN locate an individual path’s metadata without decoding, decompressing, or parsing the other entries. Each fetch warmed many paths, while each lookup still parsed only the record it needed.

Fetching more without parsing more

We built the shards using JSONL layouts already used for other large routing datasets at Vercel. JSONL stores one JSON value per line. We borrowed the sorted, alternating key-value records from Bulk Redirects and the directly addressable Base64 data structures we first built for our Bloom filters.

We kept the data layout separate from the lookup structures over it, so each workload can pick the properties it needs:

  • Inspectable, sorted key-value JSONL records with random access

  • Optional inline indexes for low-overhead binary search

  • Embedded Base64 data with offset-based decoding

  • Bounded shards that control transfer and cache costs

Each shard stores sorted target paths and their metadata as alternating JSONL records. An inline index records where each entry begins, so the routing process can jump directly to it. These positions are stored as fixed-width pointers. Each pointer is a whole number of six-bit Base64 characters, so any single pointer can be decoded in place without first parsing the index line as JSON or decoding the complete Base64 string.

As with Bulk Redirects, the first metadata fetch for a deployment already identifies which shard holds a given path, so selecting the shard adds no extra round trip.

Within that shard, the routing process uses the index pointers to binary-search the encoded paths. Finding a path takes O(log n) pointer reads and string comparisons. Once it finds a match, it parses the metadata value on the next line. The rest of the shard remains unparsed.

Finding the right shard size in production

We initially hoped the path metadata for most deployments would fit in a single shard. Because the index and binary search kept parsing cheap, we started with multi-megabyte shards.

Large shards only made sense if they stayed cached close to the request. Each routing process keeps a small least-recently-used (LRU) cache of recent shards in memory, in front of a larger cache shared by every process in the region. With only a few shards per deployment, we expected LRU hits most of the time, which would offset the cost of transferring larger shards.

In testing, the regional cache hit rate was high but the LRU hit rate was low, because requests were spread across many processes in each region. Transferring the multi-megabyte shards also cost more than we expected.

We settled on shards of about 200 KB, which kept the regional cache hit rate high and made LRU misses cheap to fill.

Production measurements showed lower average and P99 lookup latency:

Metadata lookup metric

Before: per-path metadata

After: indexed shards

Improvement

P99 latency

215.8 ms

19.1 ms

91% lower

Average latency

8.59 ms

1.81 ms

79% lower

Standard deviation

44.9 ms

19.0 ms

58% lower

Shrinking shards further wasn't worth the rollout

Putting fewer entries in each shard lowered transfer cost but raised the shard count. We also evaluated shrinking shards without increasing their number by encoding the same entries more compactly. We tested three approaches:

  • Front-coding the sorted paths so each stores only what differs from the last.

  • Splitting the shard into JSONL documents that deduplicate metadata.

  • Using a more compact custom serialization format.

Offline simulations measured both encoded size and lookup cost.

Each approach produced much smaller shards, but the simulations predicted only modest latency gains. We decided the extra encoding, compatibility, and rollout work wasn't worth it for this migration. When another workload makes more indexing or compression worth the effort, it will go into the shared library.

Changing routing safely

The CDN runs this lookup on requests to every deployment. If the sharded metadata disagreed with the per-path metadata, we would serve a stale route, a wrong status code, or a 404 for a path that exists.

We checked for that disagreement offline first, then in production. Offline, we built test deployments and ran a harness over them that looked up every path both ways and compared the answers.

In production, behind a feature flag, the routing system did both lookups on a random sample of requests while still serving the old result. It compared the new result against the old one in the background, and we watched for mismatches over several weeks without slowing production requests. We called this shadow mode.

Shadow mode found differences, and they were extremely rare. One was a bug in the old encoding, which packed paths into RFC 2047 encoded words to fit non-ASCII text into ASCII-only fields, and only showed up when an emoji was split across two words. The new format stores paths as plain UTF-8, so the bug can't happen there. Catching this edge case increased our confidence in the comparison, so we started letting the shards serve production traffic.

Faster builds

Once the shards were serving production, we went back to the build pipeline and removed the work they had made redundant:

  • Skipping the per-path metadata upload saves about 9.7 seconds.

  • Writing route group metadata into the manifest saves about 4.5 seconds.

  • Not uploading the files those two changes left empty saves about 2.4 seconds.

Together those save roughly 16.6 seconds. Across all deployments, the deploy step is about 10% faster, and for metadata-heavy deployments, where these steps dominate, we estimate closer to 25%.

Faster routing for your next deployment

Faster metadata lookups improved route resolution as a whole. For large sites, P99 route resolution is now roughly twice as fast. On our own marketing and docs sites, P99 metadata lookup latency fell from 203 ms to 31 ms. Median metadata lookup latency stayed around 0.7 ms.

The application’s Build Output API contract stayed the same. Frameworks still describe what the application needs, while Vercel improves how the CDN serves it.

Deployments built after July 17, 2026 already use the new metadata shards. For an older deployment, redeploy your project to pick up the faster lookups.
