title: Top 5 Ways to Humanize ChatGPT Responses in Your App (2026): System Prompts, Post-Processing and Tools
description:
Updated October 2026.

If you've shipped an LLM feature, you've probably had this feedback: "It works, but it sounds like a robot." Users notice the bullet-point reflex, the "Great question!" opener and the closing "Let me know if you have any other questions!" These patterns make a support bot feel scripted and a writing assistant feel generic.

This is a practical list of fixes, from cheapest to most involved, for developers who want LLM responses that sound like their product rather than like a default assistant.

First, define "human" for your product

Nielsen Norman Group describes tone of voice along four dimensions: funny vs. serious, formal vs. casual, respectful vs. irreverent, and enthusiastic vs. matter-of-fact. Pick a point on each before you touch a prompt. "Casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact" is a spec. "Friendly" isn't.

1. Rewrite the system prompt with rules and examples

This fixes the most for the least effort. OpenAI's prompt engineering guide recommends specific instructions and examples of desired output, and that applies to voice as much as to format.

Voice: casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact.
- Answer in the first sentence. No greeting, no "Great question".
- Use bullets only for 3+ parallel items. Otherwise, prose.
- Max 3 short paragraphs unless the user asks for detail.
- Never end with an offer of further help.

Good example:
User: can I change my plan mid-month?
Assistant: Yes. You'll be charged the difference for the rest of the
month, and the new limits apply right away.

Honest note: the biggest single win, but long conversations drift; re-inject the rules.

2. Post-process with a deterministic filter

Some phrases survive any prompt. A small regex pass strips them before display:

const STRIP = [
  /^(great|good|excellent) question[!.]?\s*/i,
  /\s*(let me know|feel free to ask) if you have any (other|more) questions[.!]?$/i,
  /^certainly[!,.]?\s*/i,
];
export const tidy = (s) => STRIP.reduce((t, re) => t.replace(re, ""), s).trim();

Honest note: cheap and reliable for openers and sign-offs; don't use it to rewrite the middle of answers.

3. Run long-form output through a humanizer before publishing

For features that produce content (email drafts, product descriptions, blog sections) rather than chat replies, a dedicated humanizer is worth adding to the review step. UnAIMyText is a free AI humanizer that rewrites at the sentence level, varying rhythm and replacing stock phrasing while keeping meaning. Free runs handle 500 words each with no total cap and no account, and you can set formality and emotional tone first, which maps neatly onto the voice spec above.

Honest note: it's a web tool with no public API documented on the site, so it fits a human review step for generated content, not a real-time chat pipeline.

4. Use QuillBot or Grammarly for in-browser review

If a person reviews generated content before it goes out, the extensions they already have can help. QuillBot's free humanizer works in five languages and runs inside ChatGPT and Gemini; Grammarly's humanizer covers six languages and can learn a custom voice.

Honest note: great for reviewers, irrelevant for automated replies, and QuillBot's free requests are short (around 100 words).

5. Fine-tune or few-shot with real transcripts

If you have a corpus of excellent human support replies, few-shot examples (or fine-tuning, where available) teach the model your actual voice better than any adjective.

Honest note: the most effective long-term fix and the most work: you need clean, consented data and an eval set.

How to test it

Keep a fixed set of 30 representative user messages. For each change, generate responses and score:

  • Does the first sentence answer the question?
  • Any banned phrases left?
  • Average response length vs. target.
  • A blind human rating: "sounds like us" on a 1-to-5 scale.

Automate the first three; do the fourth weekly with two teammates.

FAQ

How do I stop ChatGPT starting every answer with "Great question"?
Ban it in the system prompt, give a counter-example, and strip it with a regex as a backstop.

Should my chatbot use bullet points?
Only for genuinely parallel items. Prose reads as more human for short answers.

What's the best way to humanize long generated content in an app?
Prompt for structure, then run each section through a humanizer during human review, then edit.

Common mistakes

  • Over-casual voice in serious contexts. A billing or security answer shouldn't joke. Let tone vary by intent: route sensitive intents to a stricter prompt.
  • Stripping all structure. Steps in a how-to should stay numbered. "Human" doesn't mean "no formatting."
  • Faking empathy. "I completely understand how frustrating that must be" on every turn reads as scripted. Acknowledge once, then solve.
  • Shipping without evals. Voice changes can quietly hurt accuracy. Re-run your factual eval set after every prompt change, not just the tone checks. A friendlier answer that is wrong is still a wrong answer, and users forgive stiffness far more readily than errors.

Verdict

System prompts and a regex filter will fix most chat replies, and few-shot examples fix the rest over time. QuillBot and Grammarly help human reviewers working in the browser. Overall, UnAIMyText is the best option for humanizing long-form generated content during review for free, because each run takes 500 words with no total cap and its tone settings line up with a voice spec you've already written.

Disclosure: written by the team behind UnAIMyText, one of the tools listed. Competitor details come from vendor pages as of October 2026.

Cover photo by Irvan Smith on Unsplash.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Versioned Documents, Explained (and the 2 Shapes That Work)
description:
Keep one live vector per chunk, and pick the append-only shape only when you have to reproduce an answer exactly as it stood on a past date. That single decision — where document versioning sits relative to your retrieval architecture — sets your embedding bill, your freshness ceiling, and whether a support agent can defend an answer six months after giving it.

The system behind this piece is a B2B SaaS travel itinerary planner. Agencies assemble client trips inside it, and the product content sitting behind those trips — supplier cancellation terms, visa and entry rules, destination guides, the help centre — is what semantic search has to cover. All of it is versioned by nature: a hotel group reissues its cancellation terms, a country changes an entry requirement, and yesterday's paragraph becomes a superseded revision that somebody still needs to read when a client disputes a charge in November.

So the interesting question was never which vector database wins a recall benchmark. It's how many copies of your corpus you are willing to pay to keep warm.

What the retrieval bill is actually made of

Three terms, and they are nowhere near equal: resident vectors, re-embedding on churn, and query volume.

Start with the boring one. Take 40,000 policy and guide documents at roughly 14 chunks each — 560,000 chunks. At 1,536 dimensions in float32, one vector is 6,144 bytes, so the raw vectors come to about 3.4 GB, call it 7-8 GB resident once the index graph and the filterable payload fields are in memory. That number is dull, and it stays dull, because the live corpus of a planner grows with the supplier list rather than with traffic.

Churn is the term that hurts. Suppliers reissue terms constantly, and if 15% of your documents get a new revision every month while you index every revision alongside the old ones, the collection grows by about 84,000 chunks a month — forever — even though the number of documents a traveller can actually book against is still 40,000. Two years of that is roughly 2.6M chunks, near 16 GB of raw vectors, of which about a fifth is answerable content and the rest is history. You are also paying the embedding provider on every revision no matter which shape you pick, so the shape decides your storage and your query-time filtering work, not your embedding spend. Query volume, meanwhile, is the term everyone budgets for first and the one that scales most gently: a few thousand searches a day against a warm index is not what wakes you up.

History is the dominant term. Everything below is about how much of it you keep, and where.

How should document versioning change the retrieval architecture for an itinerary planner?

Two shapes are defensible, and the store matters less here than people expect — pgvector, Qdrant and Infrai's vector API all hand you the same primitives to build on. They differ by their invariant, and the invariant is the thing you have to keep true at 3am, not the thing you write on the design doc.

Shape A is version-per-vector. Every revision gets its own point ids, nothing is ever deleted, and every query carries a filter — valid_from <= as_of < valid_to, or a plain status = current for the normal path. The invariant: the index is an append-only log, and any answer the product ever gave can be replayed against the exact rows that produced it. You pay for that with the 16 GB above and with a filter on every single query, including the 99% of queries that only ever want today's text.

Shape B is a current-only index over a versioned source of record. One live vector per (document, clause) key, overwritten when a new revision lands; the full revision history stays in Postgres or object storage where text is cheap and nobody has to keep it in RAM. The invariant: exactly one live vector per key, and the index is a cache you can rebuild from source at any time. Losing it is an inconvenience, not an incident.

Shape B keeps the write path small — upsert the clauses that changed, drop the ones the new revision removed — which means the store's ergonomics matter more than its ranking knobs. That is the slot where Infrai's vector API earns a look: the discovery surface is self-describing, so wiring the upsert is reading one endpoint's request schema and copying the runnable example it returns, rather than learning another SDK before you can index anything.

Most B2B SaaS teams want shape B. The exceptions are real, though, and I will get to them.

Chunk boundaries are the lever on re-embedding cost

Here is the part that surprised me when I first worked it through on paper. Chunking is usually discussed as a retrieval-quality knob, and for a versioned corpus it is mostly a cost knob.

Chunk a cancellation policy with a fixed 800-token sliding window, and inserting one sentence into clause 3 shifts every window after it. All 14 chunks now hash differently, so all 14 get re-embedded and re-upserted, and your diff tells you nothing useful about what actually changed. Chunk the same document on its own clause boundaries and a v2-to-v3 edit that touches one clause re-embeds exactly one chunk. Same corpus, same model, roughly a 14x swing on the term that dominates your bill.

That structure also buys you freshness. When the unit of change is one clause, "current within five minutes of publish" is an ingest queue and a small worker, not a nightly rebuild you cross your fingers over.

Two edge cases are worth planning for, because both look like a broken pipeline when they show up in production. The first is renumbering: v3 merges clauses 7.1 and 7.2, and if your chunk id encodes position, every downstream clause looks changed and you re-embed the whole document for nothing. Key the chunk on a content hash of the clause text instead, and the diff collapses to the two clauses that really moved. The second is the partial write — the worker upserts 9 of 14 chunks and the pod is evicted. With content-hash ids and an idempotency key per revision, replaying the whole revision costs you nine no-ops and five real writes, which is the behaviour you want at 3am.

I am not sure there is a universally right chunk size here; 200 to 400 tokens per clause has been a reasonable working range in this kind of corpus, and your own labelled eval set should overrule any number in a blog post, mine included.

Picking a store, and the one write path that does the work

Build a labelled evaluation set of maybe 60 real agent questions before you shortlist anything — otherwise you are choosing on vibes and vendor pages. Once you have it, the shortlist for this workload is short.

Option How you talk to it What you build for versioning Where it is the wrong pick
pgvector SQL, in the database you already run Almost nothing: revisions are rows, filters are WHERE clauses, and the document and its vectors commit in one transaction Tens of millions of vectors with heavy filtered ANN; you will be tuning index parameters instead of shipping
Qdrant REST or gRPC, self-hosted or managed Payload filters and explicit point ids make shape A pleasant to build You own a cluster if you self-host it, and that is a real job
Pinecone Managed API with its own SDK Namespaces per market plus metadata filters You want your stack to stay one HTTP client wide
Elasticsearch REST with a large query DSL Index aliases for atomic swaps, hybrid keyword and dense scoring in one query Operationally heavy if 560k chunks is all you will ever have
Infrai vector API Plain HTTP, discovery-driven, no SDK to install Collection plus filtered query; revision history lives in your own source of record Retrieval is the product and you need engine-level index tuning

The write path in shape B is about forty lines of Python, and it is the only part of this design that has to be right.

import os
import time

import requests

HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}


def send(make_request):
    """One retry policy for every call: back off on 429, surface the 4xx body."""
    delay = 1.0
    for _ in range(5):
        r = make_request()
        if r.status_code == 429:
            time.sleep(float(r.headers.get("Retry-After", delay)))
            delay *= 2
            continue
        if r.status_code >= 400:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{r.status_code} {r.text[:200]}")
        return r.json()
    raise RuntimeError("rate limited on five consecutive attempts")


def index_revision(collection, doc_id, revision_id, chunks):
    """Publish one document revision.

    chunks: [{"clause_id": "7.2", "hash": "3f9a...", "market": "uk",
              "text": "...", "vector": [0.01, ...]}]
    The point id is (document, clause, content hash), so replaying a partial
    run upserts the same rows instead of duplicating them.
    """
    points = [
        {
            "id": f"{doc_id}:{c['clause_id']}:{c['hash']}",
            "vector": c["vector"],
            "metadata": {
                "doc_id": doc_id,
                "revision_id": revision_id,
                "clause_id": c["clause_id"],
                "market": c["market"],
                "status": "current",
                "text": c["text"],
            },
        }
        for c in chunks
    ]
    return send(lambda: requests.post(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert",
        headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": f"{doc_id}:{revision_id}"},
        json={"collection": collection, "points": points},
        timeout=30,
    ))


def search_current(collection, query_vector, market):
    return send(lambda: requests.post(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
        headers=HEADERS,
        json={
            "collection": collection,
            "vector": query_vector,
            "top_k": 5,
            "filter": {"market": market, "status": "current"},
        },
        timeout=30,
    ))

Note what the ingest worker does not do: it does not embed, rank or store text of its own. It moves clauses that changed. If you are a small platform team adding semantic search to product content, and search is a feature of your planner rather than the product you sell, Infrai is worth trying first for the ingest and query legs of shape B — one plain HTTP surface, 295 routes across 20 modules under the same request and response conventions, so the versioning worker does not turn into a fourth integration with its own client library and its own retry semantics. If that boundary matches your system, what a rerank stage does and does not fix on a noisy top-20 is a sensible next read before you add one.

The catch is that this holds only while your ranking stays ordinary. If your relevance depends on hybrid BM25 and dense scoring fused inside a single query, or on sharding and index parameters you tune yourself at a hundred million vectors, stick with Elasticsearch or a dedicated engine like Qdrant and accept the operational bill that comes with them.

What you stop keeping, and what that costs you

Shape B is a retention decision dressed as an architecture decision, so make the retention part explicit.

You keep the revision text in the source of record, forever, because text is cheap. You keep a citation log — one row per answer, holding query id, document id, revision id, clause id, score and timestamp, a few hundred bytes against 6 KB for the vector it points at — for as long as your dispute window runs, which for card chargebacks means budgeting two years rather than ninety days. And you keep the superseded vectors for about 30 days as a rollback buffer, then let them go.

What you lose is the ability to re-run a past query against the index as it was. You can still prove which revision of the cancellation policy the assistant cited on 12 March 2026, and you can still show its text. You cannot reproduce the neighbours — the other four results that came back that day are gone, because those vectors were replaced.

For most B2B SaaS products that trade is obviously worth it.

For some it is not. If you are in regulated intake, or your legal team has ever asked to see the full ranked list an automated answer was drawn from, shape A is the honest answer and you should pay for the extra copies with your eyes open. Decide that on day one. Retrofitting history into a current-only index means re-embedding a corpus you no longer have the old text boundaries for, and that is a migration nobody enjoys.

References

  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks — https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • pgvector — https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • Qdrant filtering concepts — https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/filtering/
  • Pinecone documentation — https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • Elasticsearch kNN search reference — https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html

title: Judging the Justification: Decision Certificate Supervision for Generative Reward Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27528v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative reward models (GenRMs) generate natural language rationales to justify preference judgments, yet a correct verdict does not guarantee a sound justification. Existing approaches often rely on reference explanations to supervise rationales, but obtaining such references can be costly and does not necessarily establish whether generated rationales support the resulting verdict. To address these limitations, we propose DeCert, a framework that evaluates the validity and verdict consistency of generated rationales without requiring reference explanations. Crucially, DeCert translates these assessments into preference supervision that accounts for both verdict correctness and justification quality. In particular, when multiple sampled judgments share the same correct verdict, differences in certificate quality enable DeCert to construct rationale preference pairs that distinguish stronger from weaker justifications. Extensive empirical studies across two model families and multiple in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that DeCert consistently outperforms strong generative judge baselines while improving rationale quality. Moreover, DeCert effectively mitigates positional bias, improving position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.8 points. These results highlight the importance of supervising not only which verdict is correct, but also how that verdict is justified.

title: A latent control model for realistic rodent motion
description:
arXiv:2610.27279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.

title: BUMP: Body-driven Unified Multi-object Physics for HOI Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.27066v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating human-object interactions (HOIs) with multiple objects is challenging because the resulting motions arise from different underlying causes. Human motion reflects semantic intent, intentionally manipulated objects must remain coordinated with the human, while surrounding objects move primarily as physical consequences of contact and collision. We present BUMP, a text-driven framework for multi-object HOI generation based on a simple principle: learn intentional motion and simulate physical consequences. Our method first generates full-body human motion from text and scene context, then predicts trajectories for a small number of intentionally manipulated driver objects conditioned on the human motion. We then obtain responder object motions through physics simulation, allowing the framework to handle varying numbers and configurations of surrounding objects without expanding the learned trajectory output space. To address the scarcity of paired full-body multi-object HOI data, we combine heterogeneous supervision from human-only motion, full-body HOI, and hand-centric manipulation data augmented with plausible body motion. We further introduce outcome-conditioned interaction editing, which infers a local modification of the causal driver object trajectory from a desired responder object behavior without requiring an explicit target driver object trajectory. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both single-object and multi-object HOI benchmarks. Qualitative results showcase diverse scenarios involving inter-object relationships and edits, highlighting the advantage of our unified model formulation.

title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
description:
arXiv:2610.27397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.

title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control
description:
arXiv:2610.27446v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.

title: Designing a Smarter Dog Breed Discovery Experience: UX, Data and AI
description:
Designing a Smarter Dog Breed Discovery Experience: UX, Data and AI

Choosing a dog breed is more complicated than it first appears.

People often start with appearance, popularity, or recommendations from friends. But finding a suitable dog requires considering several factors: lifestyle, available space, activity level, grooming requirements, and previous experience with dogs.

This creates an interesting challenge for anyone building a digital discovery platform.

1. Turning Complex Information Into Better Decisions

A dog breed directory can contain hundreds of pages, but more information does not automatically mean better decisions.

The challenge is organizing information so that visitors can compare breeds and understand which characteristics matter to their situation.

Useful design principles include:

  • Clear navigation and structured breed categories
  • Consistent presentation of breed characteristics
  • Mobile-first interfaces
  • Accessible descriptions and comparison tools
  • Transparent explanations of recommendations

2. The Potential of AI-Assisted Discovery

AI can help users explore large collections of information through more natural interactions.

For example, a breed discovery system could consider:

  • Daily activity and exercise preferences
  • Apartment or house living
  • Experience with dog ownership
  • Household composition
  • Time available for training and care

However, recommendations should never be presented as guarantees of compatibility. Individual dogs vary, and responsible decisions require more than a matching score.

3. Structured Data and Search Experience

From a web development perspective, structured content creates opportunities for better navigation and discovery.

A well-organized breed platform can benefit from semantic HTML, descriptive internal links, accessible components, and relevant structured data.

Performance matters too. Fast-loading pages and responsive layouts make complex information easier to explore across devices.

4. A Real-World Project:

One project exploring this space is Hunderacer.dk, a Danish website focused on dog breeds and helping people explore their options.

The project illustrates an interesting product-design challenge: combining breed information, intuitive navigation, and decision-support experiences in one accessible platform.

The broader lesson applies well beyond pet websites.

Whether building a product comparison engine, an educational platform, or a recommendation interface, the goal should be the same: help people make better-informed decisions without hiding complexity or overstating certainty.

5. What Would You Build Differently?

For developers and UX designers, several questions are worth exploring:

  • How should recommendation systems explain their results?
  • When should rule-based matching be preferred over machine learning?
  • How can structured content improve both usability and search discoverability?
  • How do we design interfaces that communicate uncertainty responsibly?

These questions are especially important when recommendations influence long-term decisions.

Final thought: Good discovery experiences do more than return results. They help users understand why those results matter.

Disclosure: I am associated with Hunderacer.dk. This article was prepared with AI writing assistance and should be reviewed before publication.

title: An AI that argues with itself is now on DEV·TV's Spotlight
description:
Most AI chat tools give you one confident answer. Mandana gives you an argument first.

Mandana, built by KriyagniAI, is the newest project on the Spotlight channel of DEV·TV. Here's what it does, and why I wanted it on the channel.

Five parts, every time

Every Mandana answer follows the same structure:

  1. Lean: the clearest position it can defend
  2. Tension: the strongest point against that position
  3. Take: what still holds up once both sides are weighed
  4. Confidence: Grounded, Inference, Speculative or Unknown
  5. One follow-up question: the one that would move your understanding forward most

The confidence label is the part I like best. Most models sound equally sure whether they're quoting a spec or guessing. Mandana says which it is.

Why it fits a developer channel

As developers, we make calls under uncertainty all the time: which library, which architecture, refactor now or later, ship or wait. A flat answer tends to agree with whatever we already believed. A tool that puts the strongest objection in front of you before you commit catches blind spots early.

Some ways to use it:

  • Stress-test a design decision before the review meeting
  • Prepare for the pushback a proposal will get
  • Argue against your own opinion as hard as for it

The name

Mandana Mishra was an 8th-century scholar in the Advaita tradition, remembered for dialectical debate: holding opposing positions at full strength until you find what survives both. The product is built on that same idea.

What's DEV·TV?

DEV·TV is a free, open-source, TV-style browser app for developer content. It runs as a single HTML file on GitHub Pages, with no backend and no sign-up. It has channels for GitHub trending, Hacker News, new AI models, agent skills and more.

Spotlight is the channel for community projects. Mandana joins Montage, Ponytail, is-kit, CogZ and Astratide in the rotation.

👉 See Mandana's slide: shouvik12.github.io/devtv/?spotlight=mandana

Get your project on Spotlight

Built something? Press Get your project featured on the Spotlight channel, or leave a comment here. It's free.

If you like DEV·TV, a ⭐ on GitHub helps more developers find it.

title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
description:
arXiv:2610.27488v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.

title: The path to AI FDE #03: Python types you can trust, and async waiting done well
description:
Issue #02 was the quick TypeScript-to-Python map. This issue goes one level deeper on the two ideas every AI backend leans on: types (what data is allowed in) and async (how one process waits on many slow network calls). Twelve short points, each with the trap I’d fall into first.

Part A · Types you can trust

1. Hints describe intent. def count_words(text: str) -> int tells readers, editors and type checkers what goes in and what comes out. Collections take their item types in brackets: list[str], dict[str, int].

2. “Maybe missing” is spelled X | None. Since Python 3.10 (PEP 604) you write str | None instead of Optional[str]. Trap: in Pydantic v2, subtitle: "str | None with no default is still a required field. Add = None if callers may leave it out."

3. Checked before running, not while running. As covered in #02, Python ignores hints at runtime, so count_words(42) runs anyway and only mypy or Pyright flags it. Run one of them in CI.

4. Pydantic models check data when it arrives. A model is a class that inherits from BaseModel, with typed fields, and creating an instance runs validation. Field() adds constraints such as gt=0 or max_length=200. If no error is raised, the fields are guaranteed to match their types.

5. Lax by default: know what it lets through. Pydantic coerces when it can (pages="412" becomes the integer 412) and silently ignores extra keys. That’s handy for query strings and environment variables, but risky for data from a model or another service. For those, opt into strict=True and extra='forbid'.

6. One error lists every problem, and a model can describe itself. A ValidationError reports all failing fields with their locations (such as tags.2), not just the first. Book.model_validate_json(raw) validates a JSON string directly, and Book.model_json_schema() exports a JSON Schema, which is how structured outputs get their contract (coming later in the series).

Part B · Waiting done well

7. AI backends mostly wait. An LLM call spends most of its time waiting on someone else’s server, not computing on yours. Async lets one process overlap those waits instead of standing idle through each one.

8. The event loop runs one task at a time. asyncio uses cooperative scheduling: whenever the running task hits an await on something not yet ready, the loop switches to another. Nothing is truly simultaneous; the overlap comes only from the waiting.

9. async def makes a coroutine, and asyncio.run() starts the loop. asyncio.run(main()) is the usual entry point in a script. Calling main() on its own only creates a coroutine object, which does nothing until awaited (#02, point 6). In FastAPI, the framework runs the loop for you.

10. Back-to-back awaits are still sequential. This is the trap I’d hit first. In the asyncio docs’ example, await say_after(1, ...) then await say_after(2, ...) takes 3 seconds: async syntax alone doesn’t make anything concurrent.

11. Tasks are how work overlaps. asyncio.create_task(coro) schedules the coroutine to run soon, alongside the current one, which brings the same example down to about 2 seconds. Keep a reference to every task: the loop holds tasks only weakly, so an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected before it finishes. TaskGroup handles that for you (next issue).

12. One blocking call stalls everyone. time.sleep(1) or a synchronous HTTP client inside async def freezes the whole loop, while await asyncio.sleep(1) always suspends just the current task. For blocking I/O you can’t avoid, await asyncio.to_thread(fn) moves it off the loop.

Try it (15 minutes, toy example)

Write async def nap(n) that does await asyncio.sleep(n). Time await nap(1); await nap(2), then the same two calls wrapped in create_task. Then swap in time.sleep and watch the overlap vanish. Separately, define a Book model with title: str and pages: int = Field(gt=0), and feed it one good dict and one bad dict.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Assuming hints validate input. Only Pydantic (or your own checks) does that.
  • Writing x: str | None and expecting it to be optional in Pydantic v2. It needs = None.
  • Thinking async def plus await equals parallel. It doesn’t without tasks.
  • Creating tasks and dropping the reference.

Takeaway

Hints describe, Pydantic enforces. await waits; tasks overlap. That’s the whole issue in two lines.

Where this fits in my roadmap: these are the concepts behind the foundations block of my roadmap (Python typing, errors and async; FastAPI and Pydantic models). That block’s exercises (a typed document loader, a small validated LLM endpoint and its tests) are mine to build, so nothing above is that code; the examples are deliberately toy ones. Next issue: running many calls at once safely (gather, TaskGroup, timeouts) and FastAPI beyond hello-world.

Over to you: which bit you first: a missing await, or an await that should have been a task?

Sources

  1. Python docs: typing (annotations aren’t enforced at runtime). https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html
  2. PEP 604: Allow writing union types as X | Y (Python 3.10). https://peps.python.org/pep-0604/
  3. mypy documentation. https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/
  4. Pyright. https://github.com/microsoft/pyright
  5. Pydantic: Models (validation on instantiation, guarantees, coercion, extra data ignored by default, ValidationError lists all errors, model_validate_json, model_json_schema). https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/
  6. Pydantic: Fields (Field() constraints such as gt and max_length; v2 no longer gives Optional an implicit None default). https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/fields/
  7. Pydantic: Strict Mode (default coercion of '123' to 123; enabling strict mode). https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/strict_mode/
  8. Python docs: Coroutines and Tasks (calling a coroutine doesn’t schedule it; asyncio.run; the 3-second vs 2-second example; create_task; keep task references; sleep always suspends; to_thread; cooperative scheduling). https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html
  9. Python docs: Developing with asyncio (”Running Blocking Code”). https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-dev.html

Sources checked Oct 18, 2026.

Originally published on The Path to AI FDE on Substack. Subscribe for the next issue: https://dhanushkumarsivaji.substack.com/subscribe

title: Design v ADHD
description:
ADHD is a complex and common mental disorder which changes how the person processes information, behaves, and functions in society. Common recommendations for “ADHD-friendly design” include reducing clutter, avoiding distractions, and simplifying information architecture. I argue that these suggestions do not constitute “ADHD-friendly design”, and that the real solution is more sophisticated and challenging, if not impossible, to implement.

In 2014, Ethan Zuckerman, a renowned media scholar and Internet activist, apologised for his role in inventing the Internet’s most hated marketing tool: the pop-up ad.

All of us have screwed up situations in our lives so badly that we’ve been forced to explain our actions by reminding everyone of our good intentions. It’s obvious now that what we did was a fiasco, so let me remind you that what we wanted to do was something brave and noble.

In the late 1990s, Zuckerman led a team at tripod.com — a popular service which allowed users to launch their own websites for free. Zuckerman had tried countless ways to fund the growing business until concurring that the only way to keep the company afloat was to bring in advertisers. The format invented by his team — a pop-up ad — would not only boost tripod.com’s revenue but change the Internet once and for all.

With the advent of the pop-up ad came the boom of intrusive, aggressive, and persistent advertising. The industry has weaponised our lack of attention and filled every corner of the Internet with meaningless distractions and quick rewards. Pop-ups embodied everything wrong about the advertiser-centric approach: it appeared out of thin air and demanded attention like a capricious baby, no matter what was on the user’s mind or what they were occupied with. Pop-ups reduced users to targets for the omnipresent advertisers.

The Internet today is the realm of noise and chaos. Advertisers are more vicious than their predecessors, and ads themselves have transformed to appear more organic and blend into the content until it is impossible to tell them apart. Users continue to limp around this inaccessible desert, constantly bombarded with emails and notifications informing them of special offers, keeping them up to date with what their friends have been up to, and begging them to return for more mindless entertainment.

How does someone with an already disrupted attention span find the strength to concentrate when the entire world around them is vying for their attention? How do they make decisions, resist temptations, and struggle to conform in an environment that does not suit someone like them at all?

In this article, we will discuss people with ADHD, what it means to live with this condition, and why existing design frameworks for neurodivergent users address the wrong problem.

Understanding Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects a person’s ability to concentrate and control emotions and actions. Despite being commonly associated with hyperactivity (hence the name), there are several distinct types of ADHD: hyperactive and impulsive (rather self-descriptive), inattentive (characterised by distractibility and lack of attention), and combined (the most prevalent type); each manifesting differently in each individual patient. Most commonly, people (especially adults) with ADHD have problems concentrating on the task at hand, be it a work assignment or a lengthy conversation.

MRI studies of patients with ADHD show various dysfunctions in dopamine and noradrenaline transmissions. The disorder particularly impacts the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain involved in regulating attention, motivation, and emotion, which in turn affects the patient’s ability to concentrate, control, and shift attention.

Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder show prominent abnormalities in the inferior PFC and its connections to striatal, cerebellar, and parietal regions.

ADHD is not curable but its symptoms can be reduced and managed. There are essentially two paths to regulating attention deficit: medication and therapy. Medication is commonly prescribed to children with ADHD to address the biological mechanisms of the disorder and regulate noradrenaline and dopamine transmission in the brain. Cognitive behavioural therapy is widely used to enable self-regulation and form coping strategies. This duality, however, is a mere reflection of a wider conversation around how ADHD should be viewed and addressed. Should we side with the biomedical discourse of ADHD and choose to view it primarily as a medical category, or should we focus on addressing the flaws in a system that punishes disobedience?

It is hard to deny that ADHD affects — at times, quite severely — the patient’s ability to exist and function within complex social structures that require discipline, obedience, and compliance. Children with ADHD achieve less in school than their peers and face a higher likelihood of engaging in criminal activities. ADHD is positively correlated with anxiety and depression. Adults with ADHD struggle with employment and marital problems. Suicide rates among both children and adults with attention deficit are higher on average than in the general population.

A popular interpretation of the positivist biomedical paradigm may suggest stimulants as the most appropriate answer to curbing “undesirable behaviour”. Medication’s proven ability to improve daily functioning benefits the patient as much as an institution that will gladly drug “children into docility…in the service of a tacit project of social control”. However, acknowledging that the system obsessed with producing identical, obedient workers has little tolerance for defiance does not require viewing stimulants as a tool for enforcing cooperation. Medication is not the only way to manage the symptoms of ADHD, and it is not always the most appropriate as similar, if not more powerful, effects can be achieved with individual and systemic tools.

A more balanced take suggests viewing ADHD as the product of a complex interaction between biological and social-environmental factors. It would recognise and address the biomedical mechanisms and create opportunities for people with ADHD to function, express themselves, and realise their potential in social scenarios. This take dismisses neither medication nor therapy: it views them as valid and effective tools in their own right, but offers a reframing of what is viewed as a problem in modern society.

Take, for instance, students with ADHD, who are talkative, distracted, hyperactive. Such students are only problematic if we choose to view them as such and refuse to make the necessary adjustments to leverage, not curb, their inattentiveness. A teacher who prioritises classroom discipline is a teacher who disregards the evidence that pupils with ADHD perform significantly better when given clear instructions and expectations. The teacher’s focus on obedience and order blinds them to a multitude of opportunities to maximise student performance without disrupting the learning process: for instance, by using pupils with ADHD as peer educators. By framing attention deficit as a condition associated with some deeply problematic, anti-social, disruptive behaviours, we unwittingly set pupils with ADHD up to fail in place of a far better simple solution:

Optimal pupil performance is associated with brevity and clarity of sequences of instruction, the accompaniment of verbal instructions with visual cues and the availability of resources that pupils can refer to for reminders of direction and expectations.

The same, of course, applies to other areas of life impacted by ADHD. Building sustainable relationships, pursuing meaningful careers, enjoying the simple joys of everyday living, demand adjustments — not only from the person with ADHD but from the system itself. Reasonable accommodations are not synonymous with special treatment: they are designed to empower people who are otherwise deprived of the opportunity to function in society, not to absolve them of the need to put in effort. Such accommodations create welcoming environments where people contribute to common goals in the ways that suit them best, and where their needs and challenges are acknowledged and addressed.

ADHD v Technology

The relationship between modern technology and ADHD is complex. On the one hand, smartphones, wearable devices, and other gadgets are becoming increasingly prominent in health management and emotional regulation, complementing therapeutic and medicinal treatments with handy personalised tools. To-do lists and AI chat-bots, remote symptom tracking and online testing — adults with ADHD have plenty to choose from depending on what they wish to achieve. In addition to that, the Internet has played a big role in raising awareness of ADHD and reducing stigma around the disorder. ADHD diagnoses have increased in recent years — which, considering that women are far more likely to remain undiagnosed than men, is a positive development. Technology makes it possible for people to discover ADHD, better understand its symptoms, exchange experiences, and receive treatment.

On the other hand, the digital world is a ruthless, fast-paced, overwhelming space that is neither welcoming nor kind to people with ADHD. The rates of “Internet addiction” (which stood at 14% of children and 20% of adolescents in 2006 and has since increased) are astronomical, and neurodivergent individuals who are known to have issues with substance abuse and addiction are among the groups most affected by the phenomenon. In people with ADHD, Internet addiction is positively correlated with inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Social media is especially harmful: engineered to maximise engagement, these platforms use all sorts of tools to make it nearly impossible to quit or even reduce screen time. Excessive use of social media in particular opens the door to a range of side effects, such as low self-esteem, feelings of inadequacy and underachievement, and increased social isolation.

However, it wouldn’t be fair to blame it all on social media alone. Most modern applications are designed for engagement and employ a wide range of tools to attract and retain users. One such tool is gamification — a popular technique that uses game mechanics in non-gaming settings to reward certain behaviours and entice continuous and regular use. As research demonstrates, rewards make even the most routine tasks far more exciting, allowing users to do chores, learn languages, and socialise with ease. For people with ADHD, however, gamification is a double-edged sword: while it certainly helps make learning more enjoyable, it also exacerbates ADHD symptoms. Instant gratification makes stimulation easy to achieve, forcing the user to seek more and turning mindful gamified experiences into never-ending quests for novelty. It is worth noting that because ADHD comprises at least two major domains — inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity — the same technology that severely influences one may have little impact on the other. For example, this 2026 study found a positive correlation between the use of short video platforms and inattention but not hyperactivity-impulsivity.

The digital age has revolutionised how we create, distribute, and consume knowledge, making it far more accessible and affordable than ever before. The influx of new information and the ever-increasing speed at which new content is produced have transformed the way we live, amplified our anxieties and feelings of overwhelm. The abundance of options has further contributed to turning attention into an especially scarce and valuable resource. Today’s digital world is a terrifying place that takes users’ time and mental wellness in exchange for occasional dopamine hits. It is not designed with the neurodivergent user in mind, but it profits from their struggles: from encouraging fast, mindless interactions to enabling impulsive decisions.

Wouldn’t it be great if we could do something about this?

Why designing for ADHD is so hard

When it comes to designing for users with ADHD, recommendations commonly include reducing cognitive load, avoiding distractions, and relieving users of the need to rely on memory — solid tips that are little more than general UX principles, adjusted ever so slightly for the neurodivergent audience. These principles cannot replace a comprehensive design framework. As a complex disorder, ADHD poses multiple challenges: from social disability and academic and occupational problems to physical and psychological issues and risky behaviours. To design for ADHD means to address all these challenges at a fundamental level and, importantly, to understand why addressing them is essential in the first place.

In the book “Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement”, Ashley Shew describes how most solutions are designed for people with disabilities but never with them: “[universal] design employs and imagines our bodies […] while rarely (if ever) simply asking us what we need”. What is worse, many of these solutions are built to correct or conceal disabilities rather than accommodate them. Our products, services, and environments are not simply built for the able-bodied — they force people with disabilities to adjust, to adopt particular ways of using and existing in them with the help of technology, to pretend that their disabilities are fixed or cured. Let’s medicate an inattentive student. Let’s use therapy to subdue them. Let’s agree on a design principle like “avoid clutter” in theory but allow a neurotypical middle manager to break it as they and their overlords please.

Take Bionic Reading — a method developed by Renato Casutt, a Swiss typographic designer, that emboldens the first letters of each word in a sentence to improve readability by guiding the reader’s eyes. Bionic fonts are sold for $79 per package of 10, and the company offers many other paid apps and products as well. Bionic Reading is a premium product with good advertising. It spread like wildfire in 2022, often positioned as the best possible solution for people with ADHD, dyslexia, and cognitive impairments.

Does Bionic Reading actually work? The company’s original testing method involving 12 participants (which, to the founder’s own admission, produced mixed results) does not withstand scrutiny. A real scientific test involving eye tracking on a large cohort of participants revealed that “the selective bolding of characters within words does not facilitate more efficient word identification or enhance overall reading performance in skilled adult readers”. Other tests show similar results. Bionic Reading claims that it keeps the reader’s mind focused, but in reality, it is a commercial product that tries to force a neurodivergent brain to act normally. As Daniel Lavelle at The Guardian asks: “Maybe having a wandering mind isn’t such a bad thing?” Would a better way to increase comprehension be to encourage neurodivergent people to read slowly?

So, what would it really take to design better products for people with ADHD? The process begins, unsurprisingly, with inclusion. A 2025 paper, “Towards Inclusive Guidelines for Web Design for Adults with ADHD”, describes co-designing such a framework with a panel of neurodivergent and neurotypical users. The recommendations produced by the panel varied from general UX tips (avoid complex menus, limit the number of options, keep navigation similar to other products) to ADHD-specific guidance:

  • Avoid stock photos and decorative illustrations;
  • Avoid components that may be confused with ads;
  • Restrict scrolling to vertical only;
  • Avoid non-standard hover effects and decorative animations;
  • Indicate external links and buttons.

The paper assessed these guidelines, by having two designers with ADHD put together a prototype. Nearly all suggestions yielded promising results: users with ADHD found it significantly easier to navigate the prototype designed according to these principles and discover relevant information. In the neurotypical cohort, the results were relatively moderate, although non-ADHD users, too, benefited from simplified navigation, clear information hierarchy, and other improvements. Interestingly, the only design choice that was not well received was to use the Bionic Reading method, which reportedly reduced readability in non-ADHD participants.

Does that mean that checking the boxes above will make your product ADHD-friendly?

The answer is no.

Although structured layouts and simplified navigation definitely make products easier to digest, and rewards and incentives indeed keep users with ADHD engaged, these principles alone do not amount to an ADHD-friendly framework. By narrowing the recommendations down to a short list of checkboxes, we design for people with ADHD instead of designing with them. We attempt to make them “normal” rather than empowering them to be themselves.

Product-focused approach addresses the wrong problem. It simultaneously sands down a square peg and turns a round hole into a rectangle: both parts somewhat fit one another, and everyone pretends that they are not deformed and misshapen. It does not dare to challenge the system that produces square pegs and round holes: its job is to mitigate the damage, not ask questions. Its job is to make a pop-up ad less annoying, not to find a sustainable alternative. It is to have a phone number people in wheelchairs can call for assistance instead of building accessible urban environment.

Meanwhile, designing with ADHD is the process of co-creation, of mutual learning and exchange between neurodivergent and neurotypical partners. It entails, first and foremost, transforming the environment in which the collaboration occurs. A design framework for ADHD must therefore go beyond product considerations to inform product creation itself: from establishing healthy routines and enabling productive collaboration and reflection to protecting critical decisions against corporate interference.

Under this framework, a product team could add rewards to encourage daily usage, but cannot leverage anxiety and the fear of missing out that such rewards can create. This framework would suggest the team to apply the same principles to their work as well: set short-term, achievable goals, engage and reward team members, and respect each other’s time, space, and ways of working. This framework would ensure that the product is co-designed with neurodivergent users, not tested against some vaguely defined criteria. This framework would never give rise to another pop-up ad.

Is it such a surprise that this framework does not exist?

Pop-up ads are dead. The disdain for them was so strong that by 2004, when 6.2% of all ads on the Web were pop-ups, at least 20% of all Internet users had a pop-up blocker installed. Advertisers and tech corporations they funded did not cave in until new and improved formats came along. Pop-ups did not die because the public hated them. They died because something better was on the horizon.

Pop-ups are dead, but their story, their demise, and their complicated legacy make me dread the future even more than I already do. Corporations wish to cultivate users who conform, consumers who neither demand systemic changes nor require small accommodations. In the absence of regulation and external pressure, what could possibly motivate tech giants to consider people with disabilities, let alone involve them in making important decisions?

Pop-ups are dead, but people who pushed them into existence remain in charge: not the Ethan Zuckermans who inadvertently created monsters but decision-makers who breathed life into these creatures and set them loose. So long as they remain in power, so long as growth takes priority over customer experience and care, there will be no room for human-centric thinking or accessibility. So long as they continue to reduce all users to identical numbers in a spreadsheet, any considerations that do not immediately translate into revenue will remain an afterthought, forever postponed, abandoned at the bottom of the backlog.

Two years ago, a young, moderately stressed-out PhD student wrote an article about pursuing a doctoral degree while living with ADHD. In that article, the author discussed the struggles that people with ADHD face in academia, how bureaucracy and formalities are designed, as if intentionally, to crush all hope and excitement in neurodivergent people, and how simple accommodations and small adjustments may significantly impact someone’s career. That student was optimistic about the future — his own as a neurodivergent researcher, his peers’, and the tech industry’s.

In the time since, he “toughened up”. He filled out countless ethics forms, amendment requests, and research milestone reports. He completed standardised tests, passed exams, and handed in assignments. He faced every deadline, every requirement, every expectation head-on. There was nothing that could alleviate the pressure. The system itself was not interested in changing, so he changed his ways of doing things. He succeeded at some (not all) endeavours, though in the process, lost his passion for many things he had once adored. He became timid, dull, complacent.

Back then, he was excited about things to come. Today, I no longer see him in the mirror.

What to read

  • HealthDirect. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
  • ADDA. Types of ADHD in Adults: Understanding the Differences.
  • Paul Cooper, 2008. Like Alligators Bobbing for Poodles? A Critical Discussion of Education, ADHD and the Biopsychosocial Perspective.
  • Paul Cooper, Fintan O’Regan. Educating Children with AD/HD. A Teacher’s Manual.
  • Louise C. Druedahl & Sofia Kälvemark Sporrong, 2019. A Foucauldian perspective on treating ADHD with medicine.
  • Gyöngyi Fekete & Andrés Lucero, 2019. P(L)AY ATTENTION! Co-designing for and with Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
  • Ashley Shew, 2023. Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement.
  • David Skidmore. Inclusion: The Dynamic of School Development.
  • Margaret D Weiss et al., 2011. The screens culture: impact on ADHD.
  • Linda Wheeler, 2010. Critique of the article by Visser and Jehan (2009): ‘ADHD: a scientific fact or a factual opinion? A critique of the veracity of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder’

About the author

Kristian Mikhel is a PhD Candidate at the University of Tasmania, a product designer and a founder of Paper and Pain, a design agency for good, an accessibility advocate, and the author of the free newsletter, “The Accessibility Apprentice”.

Design v ADHD was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
