title: Workload Identity Federation: Cloud Access Without Keys (2026)
description:
Workload identity replaces stored cloud keys with an identity the platform proves for each workload. The cloud exchanges that proof for short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime, so there is no long-lived key to leak, rotate, or copy.

Workload identity federation extends the same idea across environments: a workload on a Kubernetes cluster, another cloud, an on-premises server, or a CI pipeline presents a signed token from an identity provider the target cloud trusts, and the cloud returns temporary credentials.

TL;DR

  • Static keys are the weak point. Access keys and service account key files leak through source code, CI logs, images, and laptops, and they stay valid until someone disables or rotates them, unless an expiry is enforced by policy.
  • Workload identity and secrets management solve different problems. Secrets managers hold secrets that must exist; workload identity removes the cloud credential from the secret store entirely.
  • Each cloud has a native mechanism: IAM roles and IAM Roles Anywhere on AWS, Workload Identity Federation on Google Cloud, and managed identities and Microsoft Entra Workload ID on Azure.
  • Cross-cloud access works through trust, not keys. Each target cloud trusts a token issuer, and the setup repeats for each provider and often for each cluster.
  • Identity must follow the workload. Credentials tied to one cloud or one cluster can break a failover even when the workload itself starts.

Control Plane gives each workload one identity that works in every cloud and location. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, and the same identity keeps working when a workload fails over to another location.

Why long-lived keys are the problem

A static access key or service account key file is a bearer credential: anyone who holds the string can act as the identity, from anywhere, until the key is disabled. Google Cloud’s best practices for managing service account keys state that “Service account keys can become a security risk if not managed carefully” and tell readers to “choose a more secure alternative for authentication whenever possible.” Keys end up in predictable places:

  • Source code and config files. A key committed once stays in version history.
  • CI logs and environment variables. Pipelines print and pass credentials to many steps.
  • Container images. A key baked into an image travels with every copy.
  • Laptops. A developer downloads a key to debug and never deletes it.

Two public incidents show the downstream cost. Codecov’s Bash Uploader update listed as affected “any credentials, tokens, or keys that our customers were passing through their CI runner that would be accessible when the Bash Uploader script was executed.” CircleCI’s January 2023 incident report urged customers to rotate and revoke secrets. In both cases, customers had to find and replace every credential that might have been exposed.

Rotation rarely happens because it is manual: create a new key, update every consumer, confirm nothing broke, and delete the old key. A missed consumer causes an outage. AWS’s IAM best practices tell readers to “Require workloads to use temporary credentials with IAM roles to access AWS” and treat long-term access keys as the exception.

A shared key breaks least privilege. It must carry the union of everything its services need, so one compromise exposes all of it, and every action appears under the same identity in audit logs. Separate identities per workload grant exactly what each needs and show exactly what each did.

Secrets management vs workload identity

A secrets manager stores a secret that has to exist and controls who can read it. Examples include HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, and Azure Key Vault. Workload identity answers a different question: how a workload proves who it is to a cloud without a stored credential.

Secrets management Workload identity
What it handles Secrets that must exist: third-party API tokens, database passwords, signing keys
Where the credential lives In the secret store, then in the workload’s memory
Rotation Scheduled or automated rotation of stored values
Typical examples Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault
Main risk it reduces A secret leaking from code, config, or logs

Most teams need both: workload identity for cloud services, and a secrets manager for credentials cloud IAM cannot replace, such as a payment processor token. The secrets manager benefits too, since the workload can authenticate to it without a stored credential of its own.

How each cloud does it natively

AWS

  • IAM roles for EC2. Amazon EC2 uses an instance profile as a container for an IAM role, and the application retrieves temporary credentials through the instance metadata service.
  • IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA). On EKS, an OIDC JSON web token is passed to STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, which returns temporary role credentials. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity works with any OpenID Connect-compatible provider.
  • EKS Pod Identity. EKS Pod Identity grants pods access to AWS services; the Pod Identity Agent on each node issues the credentials to the SDKs.
  • IAM Roles Anywhere. IAM Roles Anywhere gives workloads outside AWS temporary credentials using X.509 certificates from your certificate authority, registered as a trust anchor, so you don’t manage long-term AWS credentials for them.

Google Cloud

  • Attached service accounts. Applications using client libraries automatically use the attached service account, with credentials from the metadata server.
  • Workload Identity Federation for GKE. The GKE metadata server uses Security Token Service to exchange the Kubernetes JWT for a short-lived federated access token.
  • Workload Identity Federation for other environments. Workload Identity Federation lets on-premises or multicloud workloads use federated identities instead of a service account key, from X.509 certificates, AWS, Azure, on-premises Active Directory, GitHub, GitLab, or any OIDC or SAML 2.0 provider.
  • Blocking keys. Google lists credential leakage, privilege escalation, information disclosure, non-repudiation, and malicious credential configurations as the main key threats, and the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint disables creation of new external service account keys.

Azure

  • Managed identities. Microsoft’s managed identities overview says: “Manual handling of secrets and certificates are a known source of security issues and outages. Managed identities eliminate the need for developers to manage these credentials.” They come as system-assigned or user-assigned identities.
  • Microsoft Entra Workload ID on AKS. Workload ID on AKS uses federated identity credentials on a managed identity.
  • Workload identity federation for external workloads. Workload identity federation lets a user-assigned managed identity or app registration trust tokens from an external identity provider such as GitHub or Google, for software running in places like on-premises Kubernetes or GitHub Actions.

Cross-cloud and hybrid access

The harder case is a workload in one environment calling another. The pattern is the same in every cloud:

  1. Choose a token issuer: an OIDC issuer or certificate authority on the workload’s platform, such as a Kubernetes cluster, a cloud metadata service, or a CI system.
  2. Configure trust in the target cloud: which issuer to trust and which claims map to which role or identity.
  3. Exchange the token: the workload presents its token at runtime and receives short-lived credentials.
  4. Scope the permissions: the role, service account, or app registration holds only what that workload needs.
Workload runs on Target cloud Native path
GCP or Azure AWS An OIDC identity provider plus STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, or IAM Roles Anywhere with X.509 certificates
AWS or Azure Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation with an AWS or Azure provider
AWS or Kubernetes Azure A federated identity credential on a managed identity or app registration
On premises Any of the three The cloud’s federation feature, backed by an OIDC issuer or X.509 certificates

Every cloud, cluster, and location adds setup. Three clouds and four clusters mean many issuers, trust configurations, and role mappings, each with its own limits and console. Drift between them causes outages that look like authentication errors, and moving a workload means repeating the setup there. That operational load is a main reason teams fall back to static keys.

SPIFFE and SPIRE

SPIFFE, the Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone, is an open standard for workload identity; the project describes SPIFFE and SPIRE as providing “strongly attested, cryptographic identities to workloads across a wide variety of platforms.” SPIFFE defines how an identity is named and carried in an X.509 certificate or JWT, and SPIRE attests workloads and issues those identities. SPIFFE identities can be federated into AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure through the mechanisms above, and teams that run SPIRE take on operating it.

CI federation

CI pipelines are a common source of leaked keys. GitHub’s OpenID Connect documentation says you won’t need to duplicate cloud credentials as long-lived GitHub secrets: configure OIDC trust on your cloud provider and have workflows request a short-lived token. All three clouds support this, and it is often the easiest first migration.

Why cloud credentials break failover

A pod identity bound to one cluster’s issuer stops working when the workload moves to a cluster with a different issuer, unless the cloud also trusts that issuer. The workload starts in the new location, tries to read from S3 or write to BigQuery, and fails with an access error: the failover succeeded and the application is still down.

Teams often find this during an incident, because failover tests check that the workload starts, not that it reaches its dependencies. The fix is identity that follows the workload into every location it runs in, so access depends on who the workload is, not where it runs. That belongs on the checklist for active-active high availability, where every location serves live traffic.

Best practices checklist

  • Inventory every static key across code, pipelines, images, and secret stores.
  • Use short-lived credentials for workloads; automatic expiry removes manual credential rotation and limits the value of a stolen credential.
  • Give each workload its own identity to limit blast radius and keep audit logs readable.
  • Apply least privilege and review permissions on a schedule.
  • Federate CI pipelines instead of storing cloud keys as pipeline secrets.
  • Block new keys by policy. Google Cloud offers the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint. On AWS, a service control policy can deny iam:CreateAccessKey. In Microsoft Entra ID, app management policies can block new client secrets and cap credential lifetimes.
  • Keep a secrets manager for third-party tokens and database passwords.
  • Audit access and alert on unused or unexpected access.
  • Remove old keys after migrating: disable first, watch for failures, then delete.
  • Test credentials during failover: move a workload to another location and confirm it still reaches every cloud service it uses.
  • Document the exceptions with an owner, a reason, and a removal date.

How Control Plane handles workload identity

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, on-premises, and bare-metal location into one Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) and runs workloads active-active in every location of a GVC. Removing long-lived keys matters on a single cloud too, because a static key carries the same leak risk on one cloud or three.

  • What it does. Universal Cloud Identity covers 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services through short-lived, least-privilege credentials issued at runtime.
  • How it works. You attach one identity to a workload. Giving the identity a cloud access rule provisions one principal for it inside your own cloud account: an IAM role on AWS, a service account on GCP, and an app registration on Azure. Per cloud, you either list the permissions for Control Plane to create that principal, or name an existing role or service account to attach to. Control Plane serves the provider’s own instance metadata endpoint inside the workload, so an unmodified cloud SDK finds short-lived credentials exactly where it already looks. Applications that use the cloud SDK’s default credential lookup need no code changes.
  • One identity across clouds. An identity can hold access to one AWS account, one GCP account, and one Azure account at once, so a workload that reads from Amazon S3 and writes to BigQuery uses a single identity.
  • The same identity in every location. Access works the same on compute Control Plane provides, on your own Kubernetes clusters through Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and on Managed Kubernetes locations, including on premises, so a workload fails over between locations or clouds without changing its credentials. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.
  • Proven in an outage. During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.
  • Built-in secrets management. Third-party API tokens and database passwords live in Control Plane secrets. A workload reads one only when a policy grants its identity reveal on that secret, and references it as cpln://secret/NAME, so the value never appears in the workload definition. Teams with an existing secrets manager can keep using it alongside the platform.
  • Traffic and audit. Every workload talks to other workloads over mutual TLS with a certificate unique to that workload, with no certificate management required, and a tamper-proof audit trail records every action.
  • Day-two operations included: autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, automatic TLS certificates, and unified logs, metrics, and traces, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate; see the Kubernetes alternatives guide.
  • Compliance. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant; for regulated data placement, see the data residency guide.

FAQ

What is workload identity?

A way for software, not a person, to prove who it is to a cloud or service. The platform running the workload vouches for it, and the cloud returns short-lived credentials scoped to that workload, so no long-lived key is stored in the application.

What is workload identity federation?

It lets a workload in one environment access another by presenting a token from an identity provider the target trusts; the target validates it and issues temporary credentials. AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure each document a federation path.

How do I stop using long-lived AWS access keys in my applications?

Use IAM roles: an instance profile on EC2, IRSA or EKS Pod Identity on EKS, and IAM Roles Anywhere or an OIDC provider with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity outside AWS. Remove the old keys once nothing uses them.

How do I access AWS from GCP or Azure without storing keys?

Create an IAM OIDC identity provider in AWS that trusts the workload platform’s token issuer, create a role that trusts specific claims from it, and exchange the token through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. IAM Roles Anywhere is the alternative for workloads with X.509 certificates from your own CA.

How do I access GCP or Azure from AWS or Kubernetes without service account keys?

For Google Cloud, configure Workload Identity Federation with an AWS, Azure, or OIDC provider. For Azure, add a federated identity credential to a managed identity or app registration that trusts your cluster’s or provider’s tokens.

What is the difference between secrets management and workload identity?

Secrets management stores and rotates secrets that must exist, such as third-party API tokens; workload identity removes the need to store a cloud credential at all.

Does workload identity keep working during failover?

Only if the identity is not bound to one cluster or cloud. On Control Plane, the identity belongs to the workload’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) and follows it to every location, so a workload that fails over keeps its AWS, GCP, and Azure access.

What are the best practices for secrets management in 2026?

Remove static cloud keys, use short-lived credentials, give each workload its own identity, and apply least privilege. Keep a secrets manager for non-cloud secrets with restricted reads, rotation, and audit, and block new long-lived keys by policy.

How do I manage cloud credentials across multiple clouds?

Federate trust instead of distributing keys, and attach one identity per workload that holds access to each cloud. On Control Plane, a single identity covers one AWS, one GCP, and one Azure account.

What tools help with workload identity and secretless access?

Native options are AWS IAM roles, IRSA, EKS Pod Identity, and IAM Roles Anywhere, Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation, and Azure managed identities with Microsoft Entra Workload ID; SPIFFE and SPIRE are the open standard. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity provides access to AWS, GCP, and Azure services across every location of a GVC, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code.

Next step: start with an inventory of your static keys, then see how one identity can replace them across clouds and locations. Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: Push images to Vercel Container Registry from GitHub Actions
description:
You can now push container images from GitHub Actions to Vercel Container Registry (VCR) without storing long-lived registry credentials.

The new vercel/vcr-action/login action authenticates your workflow using GitHub OIDC. It exchanges the workflow’s OIDC token for a short-lived Vercel access token, then uses that token to log in to vcr.vercel.com. When the job ends, the action logs out and revokes the Vercel token.

To start:

  • Create an OIDC policy on your Vercel team that matches the GitHub repository and workflow, and grants read-write access to VCR.

  • Store your Vercel team ID as a GitHub repo variable, for example VERCEL_TEAM_ID, along with the team slug, project slug, and repo name used in the image tag.

  • Give the workflow or job id-token: write permission.

Then add the login step before you build and push and the image:

The action authenticates Docker by default. Pass engines to use Podman or Buildah instead.

After VCR finishes preparing a linux/amd64 image, you can use it as a custom Vercel Sandbox image. Within the same project, reference it as <repository>:<tag>.

Learn more in the VCR documentation and the GitHub Actions guide.

title: From DevSecOps to Operational Resilience: 26 Engineering Improvements Across Cloud, Kubernetes and ML Infrastructure
description:
*From Security Scanning to Operational Resilience: Engineering Improvements Across DevSecOps, Cloud and ML Infrastructure *

Lessons from integrating security into CI/CD, strengthening observability, automating recovery, modernising API gateways and improving production operations.

Modern platform engineering is not just about deploying applications faster. It is about building secure, reliable, recoverable and maintainable systems while reducing manual operational effort.

In a multi-cloud environment supporting pharmaceutical SaaS applications, API platforms, Kubernetes clusters and machine learning services, operational excellence requires a combination of DevSecOps, observability, automation, capacity management and disciplined change control.

Over time, I have worked on a series of engineering improvements across CI/CD pipelines, on-premises infrastructure, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), API gateways, databases, monitoring platforms and ML workloads.

These improvements share a common objective: shift operational practices from reactive troubleshooting towards proactive controls, repeatable automation and evidence-based engineering decisions.

This article explores the key improvements, the engineering considerations behind them and the operational value they bring.

1. Integrating Gitleaks with CI/CD: Bringing Secret Detection into the Development Workflow

Security vulnerabilities can enter a production environment long before deployment. Hard-coded credentials, API tokens, passwords and private keys committed to source control are examples of risks that should be detected as early as possible.

To address this, I integrated Gitleaks into the CI/CD workflow to identify potential secrets in source code and related repository content.

Why this matters

When credentials are committed to a repository, the risk extends beyond the immediate application. Credentials may be copied into build logs, cached artifacts, cloned repositories or downstream environments. Removing the secret from the latest commit does not necessarily remove it from the repository's history or eliminate the need to rotate it.

Engineering approach

The integration introduces secret scanning into the software delivery process, allowing findings to be identified closer to the point where code changes are introduced.

A mature implementation should include:

  • Scanning code changes and, where appropriate, repository history.
  • Reviewing findings to distinguish genuine secrets from false positives.
  • Assigning ownership for remediation.
  • Rotating exposed credentials rather than relying solely on deleting them from source code.
  • Defining severity-based handling and exception procedures.
  • Retaining scan results and remediation evidence according to policy.

The next level of maturity is to enforce pipeline failure for confirmed policy violations, subject to an agreed exception process. Detection and build-blocking enforcement are separate controls and should be implemented and verified independently.

Operational value: Earlier detection of credential exposure, improved security awareness in development workflows and a foundation for policy-driven DevSecOps.

2. Strengthening Security Visibility with Wazuh Across On-Premises Servers

Security controls are more effective when infrastructure events can be observed centrally.

I worked on installing Wazuh across on-premises servers to improve security monitoring and centralise visibility into relevant host events.

Key considerations

A successful deployment involves more than installing an agent. It requires attention to:

  • Agent connectivity and health.
  • Collection of relevant security events.
  • Alert rules and severity classification.
  • Investigation and escalation procedures.
  • Ownership of findings and remediation.
  • Monitoring of agent coverage and reporting gaps.

The operational objective is to make security events visible to the appropriate teams and provide a consistent basis for investigation.

A useful follow-up measure is coverage: the number of in-scope servers reporting successfully compared with the total number of servers that should be monitored. Additional measures can include alert investigation time and the age of unresolved high-priority findings.

Operational value: Improved security visibility across the on-premises server estate and a stronger basis for operational risk monitoring.

3. Evaluating Root-Access Changes Through a Proof of Concept

Privileged access is one of the most sensitive areas of infrastructure administration. Excessive or poorly controlled root access can increase the impact of accidental changes, compromised credentials and unauthorised activity.

I worked on a proof of concept for changing root-access practices, with broader rollout identified as a subsequent step.

A controlled approach to privileged access should consider:

  • Whether administrative access can be performed through named accounts and approved privilege elevation.
  • Authentication and authorisation requirements.
  • Audit logging for privileged commands and sessions.
  • Emergency access procedures.
  • Service dependencies that may require special treatment.
  • A tested rollback and recovery approach.

A proof of concept should validate compatibility with existing administration procedures before wider deployment. Production rollout should include a staged migration, clear ownership, exception handling and a method to recover access if the new controls fail.

Operational value: A structured path towards stronger privileged-access governance without introducing avoidable operational disruption.

4. Upgrading Trivy to Improve Vulnerability-Scanning Currency

Container and infrastructure security scanning must evolve alongside the tools, libraries and vulnerabilities they are intended to detect.

I upgraded Trivy from version 0.58.1 to 0.64.1 as part of maintaining the security tooling used in the engineering environment.

Tool upgrades are an important operational activity, but the upgrade alone does not establish that vulnerabilities have been eliminated.

A sound upgrade process should include:

  1. Reviewing release notes and compatibility considerations.
  2. Testing the new version against representative images and repositories.
  3. Validating vulnerability database access and scan output.
  4. Comparing findings and investigating material differences.
  5. Confirming that CI/CD integrations continue to operate correctly.
  6. Documenting the deployed version and the upgrade outcome.

The broader objective is to ensure that scanning remains a dependable part of the delivery process and that findings can be prioritised and remediated.

Operational value: Updated vulnerability-scanning tooling and a stronger foundation for maintaining consistent container security checks.

5. Resolving Certificate Trust Issues Between On-Premises Containers and OCI OpenSearch

Secure communication between distributed systems depends on correct certificate trust configuration.

An SSL connectivity issue was encountered when on-premises containers communicated with OCI OpenSearch. The issue was resolved by adding the required CA certificate to the operating system on the OCI server.

This illustrates an important troubleshooting principle: TLS failures are not always caused by application code or network connectivity. They can arise from certificate chains, trust stores, hostname verification, certificate expiry or configuration differences between environments.

A systematic investigation should validate:

  • The certificate presented by the remote endpoint.
  • The certificate chain and relevant CA certificates.
  • The trust store used by the client process.
  • Hostname and certificate validity checks.
  • Certificate expiry and renewal procedures.
  • Connectivity and TLS negotiation using approved diagnostic tools.

The durable fix should also be documented and incorporated into configuration management where appropriate, rather than relying on manual changes that may be lost during rebuilds.

Operational value: Restored secure connectivity and a clearer understanding of certificate trust dependencies between environments.

6. Improving Cloud Hygiene by Removing Unused Route 53 Records

Cloud resources and DNS records can remain after services are migrated, retired or replaced. Unused records create unnecessary configuration complexity and may introduce security, ownership or troubleshooting risks.

I removed unused Route 53 URLs after identifying records that were no longer required.

DNS cleanup should be performed carefully because a record that appears unused may still support a legacy integration, scheduled job, external client or certificate-validation workflow.

A controlled cleanup process should include:

  • Identifying the record owner and associated service.
  • Reviewing traffic and dependency evidence where available.
  • Confirming that the target service has been decommissioned or migrated.
  • Checking certificate, redirect and integration dependencies.
  • Recording the change and retaining a recovery path where appropriate.
  • Validating service behaviour after removal.

Operational value: Reduced DNS clutter and improved configuration maintainability, provided that dependency checks and post-change validation are completed.

7. API Gateway Modernisation: WSO2, Kong, Azure API Management and OCI API Gateway

API gateways are critical infrastructure components because they sit on the path between clients and backend services. Their configuration, availability and migration strategy can directly affect application connectivity.

My API gateway improvement work included WSO2-to-Kong migration activities, Kong failover-related implementation, API migration from Azure API Management to OCI API Gateway and work involving migration of services to Standard API Manager from Basic SKU.

Addressing OCI API Gateway service limits

During the migration to OCI API Gateway, a service configuration constraint involving the limit of 50 APIs per service required attention. The engineering team reduced the number of APIs configured per service to remain below that limit.

This is an example of adapting API architecture to the constraints of the target platform instead of treating migration as a direct copy of the source configuration.

Resolving Jasper API compatibility issues

Jasper APIs that were invoked from Azure did not function as expected after the move to OCI API Gateway. OCI Functions were used to address the integration issue.

The broader engineering lesson is that API migration requires functional validation, not just successful deployment. Differences in request handling, authentication, integration behaviour, routing and platform capabilities can affect API compatibility.

Reliability and failover

Kong failover implementation and related proof-of-concept activities were also part of the improvement work.

A robust failover implementation should verify:

  • Health detection and failure thresholds.
  • Routing to the correct healthy endpoint.
  • Connection and session behaviour.
  • Authentication, rate limiting and TLS configuration.
  • Recovery when the original node becomes healthy again.
  • Logging, alerting and operational ownership.

A failover design should be tested under controlled failure scenarios before it is treated as production-ready.

Operational value: Improved migration readiness, more deliberate gateway architecture and a structured approach to API availability and failover.

8. Automating Kong API Manager Administration

Manual API management can become difficult to maintain as the number of services, configurations and environments grows.

I developed an automated script for managing Kong API Manager activities.

Automation is especially useful for repeatable administrative tasks when it reduces configuration inconsistency and improves execution speed. However, API-management automation must also protect against accidental changes to routes, credentials, upstream services or access policies.

A reliable automation workflow should include:

  • Validated inputs and environment selection.
  • Authentication using appropriately protected credentials.
  • Pre-change checks and configuration validation.
  • Logging of actions and results.
  • Error handling and safe failure behaviour.
  • Change traceability and controlled permissions.
  • Post-change verification.

Operational value: A foundation for more repeatable API administration and reduced reliance on manual configuration steps.

9. Building a More Reliable Backup and Recovery Practice

Backups are only useful when they are available, consistent and recoverable when required.

I implemented automated backup processes across several infrastructure and data platforms, including:

  • Zabbix
  • Kong
  • Grafana
  • Prometheus
  • Weaviate
  • Dgraph
  • Legal-Elastic
  • Redis
  • PostgreSQL
  • MLflow

Additional work included automated PostgreSQL database backups and the use of an NFS server on separate box to receive backups from the five-node Elasticsearch cluster on Master Node.

The objective was to make backup execution more repeatable and reduce dependence on manual intervention.

Backup automation is only the first step

A production-ready backup process should also monitor completion, validate backup integrity, control access, manage retention and verify that the recovery process works.

Key questions include:

  • Did the backup complete?
  • Does the backup contain the expected data?
  • Is it protected from accidental or unauthorised deletion?
  • Can it be restored independently of the production failure?
  • Can the service be recovered within its agreed RTO?
  • Is the amount of data lost within the agreed RPO?

These checks are essential because a successful backup job is not proof of recoverability.

Operational value: More repeatable backup execution across a diverse technology stack and a foundation for better recovery readiness.

10. Restoring Legal-Elastic and Weaviate Data

Backup processes become more meaningful when recovery is demonstrated.

As part of the operational work, I restored Legal-Elastic on Backup Server and restored Weaviate data on Master node.

These activities provided practical experience with data restoration and the operational dependencies involved in bringing data services back into service.

A restoration procedure should validate more than whether a process starts. Depending on the platform, verification may include:

  • Database or index health.
  • Expected collections, indices or records.
  • Data consistency and application connectivity.
  • Authentication and access controls.
  • Application-level queries.
  • Evidence that the restored service is fit for its intended use.

The next maturity step is to formalise recurring restore tests, record the duration and results, and compare them against recovery objectives.

Operational value: Demonstrated restoration capability for the specific systems involved and a basis for improving recovery procedures.

11. Recovering a 2 TB Disk Snapshot for a UAT Environment

A disk recovery activity involved using a 2 TB disk snapshot to create and mount a disk on the UAT virtual machine on Azure. The restored data was checked with Ayan, after which the original 2 TB disk was depleted and decommissioned.

This activity highlights the importance of managing the complete lifecycle of recovered storage—not just creating the disk.

A controlled process should confirm:

  1. The correct snapshot and recovery point were selected.
  2. The restored disk was attached and mounted safely.
  3. The expected data was available and validated by the relevant owner.
  4. The UAT environment could access the required data.
  5. The original disk was no longer required before decommissioning.
  6. The storage change and decommissioning were documented.

The principle is simple: validate the recovery target and data before retiring the original resource.

Operational value: Recovered storage and validated data availability for the UAT environment, followed by the removal of the original disk after confirmation.

12. Expanding Elasticsearch Cluster Capacity

I added Node 4 and Node 5 as Elasticsearch nodes to an existing cluster having 3 nodes.

Adding nodes can increase available capacity and provide more flexibility in distributing data and workload. However, node addition must be accompanied by cluster-health and capacity validation.

Important checks include:

  • Cluster health before and after the change.
  • Node discovery and membership.
  • Shard allocation and rebalancing.
  • Disk utilisation and storage watermarks.
  • Heap utilisation, CPU and query latency.
  • Replication and recovery activity.
  • Any application impact during rebalancing.

Operational value: Expanded the cluster's node footprint, creating additional capacity potential. The actual performance or capacity improvement should be established from before-and-after metrics.

13. Resource Optimisation Through Pod and Docker Profiling

Infrastructure capacity decisions should be based on observed workloads rather than assumptions.

I carried out proof-of-concept work for pod profiling and then profiled pods across Development, QA, Sales and UAT Kubernetes clusters. I also performed Docker profiling for ML services.

Profiling helps identify:

  • CPU and memory utilisation patterns.
  • Workloads with excessive or insufficient resource requests.
  • Potential memory leaks or unexpected growth.
  • Containers that frequently restart or encounter OOM termination.
  • Opportunities for resource right-sizing.
  • Workloads that may benefit from isolation or separate scaling policies.

This is particularly important for ML workloads, where resource demand can vary significantly between model types and execution patterns.

Profiling should cover normal usage as well as peak periods. Reducing resource allocations based only on average usage can introduce instability during traffic spikes or concurrent workloads.

Operational value: Better evidence for capacity planning and resource optimisation across Kubernetes and containerised ML services.

14. ML Service Rationalisation and Ollama Configuration

I worked on ML service deprecation activities, Ollama configuration changes for ML services and Ollama model availability on GPU hosts.

These activities relate to managing an evolving ML infrastructure footprint and aligning deployed services and models with operational requirements.

For service deprecation, a controlled process should verify service ownership, consumer dependencies, traffic usage, replacement availability and rollback requirements before a service is retired.

For model and GPU-host configuration, important operational considerations include:

  • GPU and memory utilisation.
  • Model compatibility and loading behaviour.
  • Concurrent request capacity.
  • Model-serving latency and error rates.
  • Process health and recovery.
  • Version consistency and configuration management.

The objective is to maintain a service footprint that is operationally supportable while ensuring that active workloads continue to meet their functional requirements.

Operational value: Improved management of ML service and model configurations. Quantified resource savings or inference-performance improvements should be reported only after measurement.

15. Automating ML Service Deployment

I completed proof-of-concept work for ML service deployment automation, with broader automation across all ML services identified as a next step.

ML deployment automation can reduce manual configuration, improve repeatability and help maintain consistency across multiple environments.

A mature workflow should cover:

  1. Versioned deployment configuration.
  2. Validation of required secrets and environment variables.
  3. Image and dependency checks.
  4. Resource configuration and health probes.
  5. Deployment execution with appropriate permissions.
  6. Post-deployment smoke tests and service validation.
  7. Failure handling and rollback.
  8. Audit-friendly records of what was deployed and when.

The important distinction is between a working proof of concept and a fully operationalised deployment framework. Broader rollout should include testing, documentation, ownership and support procedures.

Operational value: A foundation for consistent ML deployment and a path towards reducing manual deployment effort.

16. Operational Resilience Through Swap Configuration

Swap configuration was standardised based on available host memory:

  • Hosts with 8 GB RAM: 4 GB swap.
  • Hosts with 16 GB RAM: 8 GB swap.
  • Hosts with 32 GB RAM: 8 GB swap.

Swap can provide a buffer during memory pressure, but it is not a replacement for adequate physical memory. Excessive swapping can also degrade application performance, especially for latency-sensitive services.

A production implementation should monitor swap usage, memory pressure, OOM events and application response times. It should also consider workload characteristics and the performance implications of swapping.

Operational value: More consistent swap configuration across the specified host sizes, with the actual reliability benefit dependent on workload behaviour and monitoring evidence.

17. Safer Service Isolation and Environment Segregation

I worked on separating the vigilance data service by deploying vigilance-qa in the QA cluster and vigilance-prod in the Prod cluster. I also worked on service-ner environment segregation.

Separating services by environment can improve operational isolation, reduce the risk of accidental cross-environment interaction and make deployment ownership clearer.

However, segregation requires more than separate deployment names. It should also consider:

  • Namespace and cluster boundaries.
  • Service accounts and permissions.
  • Network access.
  • Environment-specific secrets and configuration.
  • Database and external-service connectivity.
  • Monitoring, logging and alert routing.
  • Deployment and rollback procedures.

Operational value: Clearer environment separation and a more controlled foundation for managing service configurations across QA and Sales.

18. Improving Kubernetes Deployment Safety with Health Probes and Strategies

I updated deployment.yaml configurations with liveness probes, readiness probes and deployment strategies for backend services across Development, QA and Prod environments.

These controls address different aspects of application availability.

  • Readiness probes help prevent traffic from reaching pods that are not ready to serve requests.
  • Liveness probes help detect applications that need to be restarted.
  • Deployment strategies control how application versions are rolled out and how old and new instances coexist during a change.

Correct configuration is critical. A liveness probe that is too aggressive can cause restart loops, while an inadequate readiness probe can expose users to an application that has started but is not ready.

Deployment validation should cover normal startup, slow startup, dependency failures, rolling updates and rollback scenarios.

Operational value: Stronger deployment-level health controls and a more structured approach to managing backend service updates.

19. Liquibase CI/CD for Database Changes

Database changes require a controlled approach because schema modifications can affect application compatibility, data integrity and recovery.

I worked on Liquibase CI/CD for database delivery.

A well-designed database deployment pipeline should include:

  • Version-controlled migration scripts.
  • Review and approval of changes.
  • Validation against the target database.
  • Controlled execution in the appropriate environment.
  • Compatibility checks between application and schema versions.
  • Verification after migration.
  • A documented recovery or forward-fix strategy.

Database rollback requires special consideration. Not every schema or data transformation can be safely reversed, so the recovery strategy must be designed for the specific change.

Operational value: A foundation for repeatable, traceable database changes and closer integration between application and database delivery processes.

20. Jenkins Upgrade and Deployment Hygiene

I upgraded Jenkins from version 2.479.2 to 2.504.3.

CI/CD infrastructure is itself a critical production dependency. An upgrade should therefore include plugin compatibility checks, configuration and job validation, backup verification, access-control review and post-upgrade testing.

I also updated deployment scripts to automatically delete TAR files from 52 hosts after deployment, and backed up deployment scripts from those hosts to Bitbucket.

These activities address two operational concerns: managing deployment artefacts after use and retaining version-controlled copies of operational scripts.

A strong implementation should verify that:

  • The artefact is no longer needed by the running application or rollback process.
  • Cleanup only targets the intended files and directories.
  • Script failures are logged and surfaced.
  • The deployment outcome is not reported as successful when required cleanup or validation fails.
  • The version-controlled script is accessible to authorised maintainers.

Operational value: More consistent deployment cleanup and improved version-control coverage for deployment scripts.

21. Standardising the Linux Operating-System Baseline

I worked on upgrading Ubuntu from version 20.04 to 22.04.

Operating-system upgrades require a balance between security maintenance, application compatibility and service availability. A safe upgrade process should include dependency assessment, testing, backup validation, change approval, rollback planning and post-upgrade health checks.

For production systems, I would also verify monitoring-agent compatibility, service startup behaviour, network configuration, scheduled jobs and application dependencies.

Operational value: Progress towards a more current operating-system baseline for the systems included in the upgrade.

22. Managing ML Automation with Locking Controls

I worked on a lock script for ML automation.

Concurrent automation can create conflicts when multiple jobs attempt to modify the same resource, deploy the same service or run an operation that should only have one active execution.

Locking controls can help prevent duplicate execution, but they must handle stale locks, abnormal termination, ownership and safe release.

A production-ready implementation should define:

  • What resource is protected.
  • How lock ownership is established.
  • How stale locks are detected and recovered.
  • How concurrent execution attempts are handled.
  • What happens when a job fails midway.
  • How execution is logged and monitored.

Operational value: A mechanism for controlling concurrent ML automation and reducing the risk of conflicting operations, subject to the lock implementation and its failure handling.

23. Infrastructure Connectivity and Network Resilience

Network availability is a fundamental dependency for monitoring, application connectivity and operational support.

I changed the primary ISP from ACT to TATA after the ACT Fair Usage Policy threshold was exceeded and firewall bandwidth dropped to 3 Mbps.

The change addressed an operational connectivity constraint. It also illustrates why network-provider performance should be evaluated against actual business requirements rather than assumed service capacity.

Useful follow-up measurements include:

  • Available bandwidth and utilisation.
  • Packet loss and latency.
  • Connection stability.
  • VPN and remote-access performance.
  • Incident frequency and duration.
  • Failover capability and recovery time.

Where possible, network changes should be validated against representative workloads and documented alongside the associated firewall and routing configuration.

Operational value: A change in primary ISP to address a bandwidth limitation affecting operational connectivity.

24. Observability with OpenTelemetry

I worked on introducing an OpenTelemetry pod in AKS.

OpenTelemetry provides a common approach for collecting telemetry such as traces, metrics and logs through supported instrumentation and collectors. Its value comes from making it easier to correlate application behaviour across distributed components.

For a production rollout, I would validate:

  • Which telemetry signals are collected.
  • Whether the instrumentation covers the required services.
  • Exporter and collector configuration.
  • Access controls and protection of sensitive telemetry.
  • Sampling, retention and data-volume implications.
  • Collector health and telemetry delivery.
  • Integration with the organisation's observability platform.

Operational value: A foundation for more consistent telemetry collection and cross-service troubleshooting, with the actual observability improvement depending on instrumentation coverage and integration.

25. Resolving an Infrastructure Capacity Constraint in the Network Path

The network-provider change from ACT to TATA also illustrates a broader operational principle: infrastructure capacity issues can originate outside the application or server layer.

When firewall throughput falls, application symptoms can resemble a backend problem—slow requests, timeouts, unstable remote sessions or delayed monitoring data.

A layered investigation should therefore examine the full service path, including the local network, firewall, ISP, VPN, routing and remote endpoint.

Operational value: A practical reminder to correlate application symptoms with network performance before making unnecessary changes to application infrastructure.

26. Bringing the Improvements Together

The individual changes become more valuable when managed as part of a coherent operational improvement programme.

I group this work into six engineering themes:

Security and control

  • Gitleaks integration with CI/CD.
  • Wazuh deployment across on-premises servers.
  • Trivy upgrade.
  • Root-access change proof of concept.
  • Certificate trust remediation.
  • DNS hygiene.

Reliability and recovery

  • Automated backups across multiple platforms.
  • Legal-Elastic and Weaviate restoration.
  • Disk snapshot recovery for UAT.
  • Elasticsearch cluster expansion.
  • Kong failover-related implementation.
  • Kubernetes health probes and deployment strategies.

Automation and engineering consistency

  • Kong API Manager automation.
  • Liquibase CI/CD.
  • Jenkins upgrade.
  • ML deployment automation proof of concept.
  • ML automation locking.
  • Deployment-script cleanup and version control.

Cloud and API modernisation

  • WSO2-to-Kong migration work.
  • Azure API Management to OCI API Gateway migration.
  • OCI API configuration-limit remediation.
  • Jasper API integration remediation using OCI Functions.
  • API migration work involving Standard API Manager.

Capacity and platform optimisation

  • Pod and Docker profiling.
  • ML service rationalisation.
  • Ollama configuration and GPU model management.
  • Swap configuration.
  • Elasticsearch node expansion.

Operational hygiene and environment management

  • Linux OS upgrades.
  • Service segregation across environments.
  • Removal of unused DNS records.
  • Network-provider change to address bandwidth constraints.
  • OpenTelemetry deployment work.

27. Measuring Operational Improvement

Engineering changes should ultimately be evaluated using evidence. For this programme, I would track a focused set of measures.

Improvement area Useful measure
Secret scanning Repositories covered, findings triaged and remediation time
Security monitoring Server coverage, agent health and high-priority finding age
Vulnerability scanning Scan coverage, finding severity and remediation status
Backup and recovery Backup success, restore-test success, RPO and RTO
API gateway reliability Availability, request errors, latency and failover test results
Kubernetes operations Pod restarts, OOM events, deployment failures and readiness failures
Capacity optimisation Resource utilisation, headroom and cost per workload
Automation Manual effort avoided, automation failures and repeat-ticket reduction
Database delivery Migration success, rollback or forward-fix events and post-deployment validation
Network performance Latency, packet loss, throughput and connectivity incidents

I would establish a baseline before claiming a percentage improvement. Where measurements are unavailable, the correct approach is to describe the engineering change and its intended benefit without inventing an outcome.

Conclusion: Engineering Operations as a Continuous Improvement Discipline

These improvements demonstrate how DevSecOps, observability, automation, infrastructure management and recovery planning work together.

Security scanning helps identify risks earlier. Monitoring makes operational behaviour visible. Backup and restoration processes support recovery. Kubernetes health controls improve deployment management. API gateway and infrastructure changes address platform constraints. Automation reduces repetitive work, while capacity profiling provides evidence for optimisation.

The next level of maturity is to connect these activities to measurable operational outcomes: fewer recurring incidents, faster and safer recovery, more reliable deployments, stronger security-control coverage and better use of infrastructure resources.

For me, the central principle is straightforward:

Operational excellence is not the absence of incidents. It is the ability to detect problems early, recover safely, learn systematically and engineer the conditions that make the next incident less likely.

That is the direction I continue to pursue across DevSecOps, cloud platforms, API infrastructure and ML operations.

title: Project Scheduling Software Explained: Features, Benefits and Selection
description:
Delivering a project on time requires more than setting deadlines and assigning tasks. Project managers must understand dependencies, estimate activity durations, balance workloads, track progress, and respond to unexpected changes. When several teams work toward the same goal, even a small delay can affect the entire delivery plan.
Managing these activities through spreadsheets and manual updates may work for simple projects. However, as projects become more complex, keeping schedules accurate and communicating changes becomes increasingly difficult.
Project scheduling software helps teams organize activities, visualize timelines, assign resources, and monitor deadlines in one place. It gives project managers a clearer view of what needs to happen, when it should happen, and which activities could delay completion.
This guide explains project scheduling software, its essential features, popular tools, scheduling techniques, and practical ways to build more reliable project plans.
What Is Project Scheduling Software?
Project scheduling software is a digital tool that helps project managers define activities, arrange them in the correct sequence, estimate durations, assign resources, and track progress against planned dates.
It turns a project plan into a structured schedule that teams can update as work progresses.
Depending on the platform, common features include:
Gantt charts and visual timelines.
Task dependencies and milestone tracking.
Critical path analysis.
Resource allocation and capacity planning.
Baseline schedules and progress tracking.
Notifications and automated workflows.
Project dashboards and reports.
Multi-project and portfolio scheduling.
For example, imagine a company preparing to launch a new software product. The schedule may include requirements gathering, design, development, testing, security reviews, user acceptance testing, and deployment.
Some activities can happen simultaneously, while others depend on earlier work. Scheduling software helps teams map these relationships and understand how a delay in one activity could affect the release date.
Why Do Teams Need Project Scheduling Software?
A project schedule is useful only when it reflects the actual work, available resources, and dependencies. Dedicated software helps teams maintain this information as circumstances change.

  1. Create more realistic timelines Manual planning can overlook dependencies, holidays, resource constraints, and approval delays. Scheduling software helps project managers organize activities and calculate dates using the relationships and calendars configured in the system. A realistic schedule gives stakeholders a more reliable basis for planning and making commitments.
  2. Identify delays earlier A task that falls behind schedule may affect several dependent activities. Visual timelines and progress reports help project managers identify these changes before they become larger delivery problems. For example, if a design approval is delayed, the project manager can assess whether development, testing, and deployment dates need to change.
  3. Improve resource utilization Employees often work across several projects. Without a shared view of assignments, managers may allocate the same specialist to multiple tasks during the same period. Resource planning features help identify over-allocation, compare demand with availability, and adjust assignments where necessary.
  4. Strengthen communication A shared project schedule gives team members and stakeholders a common reference point. Instead of relying on separate status spreadsheets and email updates, teams can review task ownership, milestones, deadlines, and current progress in a centralized workspace.
  5. Support better decisions Scheduling software can help managers compare planned and actual progress, identify bottlenecks, and evaluate alternative timelines. These insights support decisions about changing priorities, adding resources, adjusting scope, or revising delivery commitments. Best Project Scheduling Software to Consider Different tools suit different project environments. Some focus on detailed scheduling and critical path analysis, while others emphasize collaboration, flexible workflows, or spreadsheet-style planning. The following options are worth evaluating according to your requirements. Features and pricing can vary by plan, so confirm current capabilities directly with each vendor. Software Best suited for What to evaluate Celoxis Complex projects, resource planning, and portfolio scheduling Dependencies, critical paths, workload management, financial tracking, and portfolio reporting Microsoft Project Detailed schedules and structured project planning Scheduling depth, resource planning, reporting, and integration with your Microsoft environment Smartsheet Teams familiar with spreadsheet-style workflows Timeline views, automation, cross-project reporting, and dependency management Wrike Cross-functional teams coordinating multiple workflows Gantt charts, collaboration, workload visibility, and configurable dashboards monday.com Teams that prefer visual work management Timeline views, workflow customization, automation, and multi-project visibility Zoho Projects Teams looking for general project planning and collaboration Task dependencies, milestones, reporting, integrations, and resource requirements

How to choose the right tool
If your team primarily needs a visual task list and basic deadlines, a lightweight work management platform may be sufficient.
If you manage complex dependencies, multiple projects, shared specialists, or cost-sensitive delivery commitments, prioritize advanced scheduling, critical path analysis, and resource planning.
For organizations with established reporting and business systems, integration capabilities should also be part of the evaluation.
Essential Features of Project Scheduling Software
Not every project requires advanced scheduling functionality. The right feature set depends on project size, delivery approach, team structure, and the consequences of missing deadlines.

  1. Gantt charts and timelines A Gantt chart represents activities as bars across a calendar. It allows users to see when tasks begin and end, how long they take, and where activities overlap. Useful capabilities include: Start and finish dates. Task duration and progress indicators. Milestones and key deadlines. Visual task dependencies. Baseline comparisons. Timeline adjustments. Gantt charts are particularly useful for projects involving multiple phases, approval stages, external vendors, or tightly connected activities.
  2. Task dependencies Dependencies define the relationships between activities. They help the schedule reflect the logical order in which work must happen. The four common dependency types are: Dependency Meaning Example Finish-to-Start (FS) Task B starts after Task A finishes Testing begins after development is completed Start-to-Start (SS) Task B starts after Task A starts Documentation begins once development starts Finish-to-Finish (FF) Task B finishes after Task A finishes Final review cannot finish before the deliverable is complete Start-to-Finish (SF) Task B cannot finish until Task A starts A rare handover arrangement where a new shift begins before the previous shift ends

Most project schedules rely heavily on finish-to-start relationships, but other types may be appropriate for overlapping activities.
Accurate dependencies make it easier to understand the impact of changes and avoid unrealistic deadlines.

  1. Critical path analysis The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities that determines the earliest possible project completion date under the current schedule assumptions. Activities on this path generally have no scheduling flexibility without affecting the final completion date. Critical path analysis helps project managers identify where delays need immediate attention. It can also support schedule compression decisions, such as adding resources to selected activities or performing some work in parallel. However, compressing a schedule may increase cost or introduce additional risk, so changes should be evaluated carefully.
  2. Resource allocation and capacity planning Resource management helps project managers assign work according to availability, skills, workload, and project priorities. Look for features that show: Current and future assignments. Resource availability calendars. Workload by person or role. Over-allocation warnings. Capacity across multiple projects. Options for adjusting assignments. This is especially valuable for organizations where specialist employees support several projects simultaneously.
  3. Milestones and baseline schedules Milestones mark important events, approvals, or deliverables, such as completing a design review or releasing a product. A baseline is the approved version of the project schedule used to compare planned performance with actual progress. Together, milestones and baselines help managers measure schedule variance and explain whether the project is progressing according to the agreed plan.
  4. Progress tracking and reporting Scheduling software should make it easy to update task status, record actual dates, review overdue activities, and understand changes to the expected completion date. Useful reports may include milestone status, delayed tasks, resource utilization, schedule variance, and overall project health. The most valuable reports are those that help people decide what to do next, rather than simply presenting large amounts of information.
  5. Collaboration and notifications Notifications can alert team members when assignments change, deadlines approach, or a dependency is affected. Comments, shared documents, and activity histories can also help teams understand decisions and reduce the need for separate updates. Before enabling automation, define which events deserve notifications. Too many alerts can make important messages easier to overlook. How to Build a Project Schedule Step by Step A reliable schedule begins with a clear understanding of the work. Software can organize a plan, but it cannot compensate for missing activities, unrealistic estimates, or unclear responsibilities. Step 1: Define the project scope Document the project's objectives, deliverables, boundaries, and acceptance criteria. Clarify what must be completed and what falls outside the project's scope. This reduces misunderstandings and makes it easier to identify missing work. For example, a website redesign might include user research, interface design, development, testing, content migration, and launch. Defining the scope helps ensure that these activities are reflected in the schedule. Step 2: Create a work breakdown structure A work breakdown structure (WBS) divides the project deliverables into smaller work packages. These can then be broken into activities that are easier to estimate, assign, and track. For example: Website redesign Research and requirements User experience and design Development Testing and review Launch and handover Each work package should contain enough detail to help the team identify the activities required for completion. Step 3: Identify and sequence activities List the individual tasks needed to complete each work package. Consult the people responsible for performing the work to avoid missing technical steps, reviews, or approvals. Next, determine the logical order of activities. Some tasks must finish before others can start, while some can run in parallel. Record these relationships in the scheduling tool so the plan reflects how the project will actually be delivered. Step 4: Estimate task durations Estimate how long each activity will take using relevant historical information, expert judgment, and the complexity of the work. For uncertain activities, three-point estimating can provide a more balanced forecast by considering optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations. The PERT weighted-average formula is: [ \text{Expected duration}=\frac{O+4M+P}{6} ] Here, (O) is the optimistic estimate, (M) is the most likely estimate, and (P) is the pessimistic estimate. For example, if an activity could take 2 days in the best case, 4 days under normal conditions, and 8 days in the worst case, the expected duration is approximately 4.3 days. This is an estimate, not a guarantee. Add appropriate contingency where uncertainty or project risk warrants it. Step 5: Assign resources Assign a responsible owner to each task and confirm that the required people or equipment will be available. Consider holidays, existing assignments, specialist skills, and competing priorities. Avoid planning as though every team member is available full-time for a single project. If a resource is over-allocated, consider shifting non-critical work, changing priorities, or arranging additional capacity. Step 6: Set milestones and calculate the critical path Identify important review points, approval gates, and delivery dates. Use the scheduling tool to calculate the critical path where supported. Review the activities that have little or no scheduling flexibility and establish how delays will be monitored. This helps the team focus attention on activities that could affect the final deadline. Step 7: Review and approve the baseline Before finalizing the schedule, validate it with the project team and key stakeholders. Confirm that the scope is covered, durations are realistic, dependencies are correct, and resources are available. Once approved, save the baseline. It becomes the reference point for tracking progress and evaluating schedule changes. Step 8: Monitor and update the schedule As work progresses, update task status and actual dates. Review the difference between planned and actual performance and investigate important variances. If a task slips, assess the impact on dependent activities and the final deadline. Document approved changes so the schedule remains a reliable representation of the current plan. Project Scheduling Techniques Every Manager Should Know Software becomes more useful when project managers understand the techniques behind the schedule. Critical Path Method The Critical Path Method (CPM) identifies the sequence of activities that determines the earliest possible completion date. Use it when tasks have clear dependencies and durations can be estimated with reasonable confidence. It is particularly useful for construction, product launches, implementation projects, and other initiatives with several connected stages. Resource leveling Resource leveling adjusts the schedule to address resource conflicts. For example, if the same engineer is assigned to two tasks at the same time, the manager may move one task to a later date. Leveling can extend the overall project duration when resources are limited, so its effect on the deadline must be reviewed. Resource smoothing Resource smoothing aims to reduce workload fluctuations while keeping the project within its existing completion constraints, where possible. It often involves shifting activities that have scheduling flexibility to create a more balanced distribution of work. Fast-tracking Fast-tracking means performing activities in parallel that would normally be completed sequentially. For example, a team might begin preparing training materials while final testing is still underway. This can shorten the schedule, but it may create rework if the earlier activity depends on information that has not yet been finalized. Crashing Crashing shortens selected activities by adding resources or spending more to accelerate the work. Examples include assigning additional specialists or paying for extra shifts. Crashing should focus on activities that affect the critical path. Accelerating a task outside the critical path may not improve the overall completion date. Best Practices for Effective Project Scheduling
  6. Build the schedule with the team Project managers should involve the people who will perform the work when estimating durations and identifying dependencies. Their input can reveal hidden activities, technical constraints, and resource conflicts that might otherwise be overlooked.
  7. Use realistic assumptions Avoid committing to dates simply because they are desirable. Consider the availability of resources, approval times, supplier commitments, and uncertainty in the work. A realistic plan is more useful than an optimistic schedule that must constantly be revised.
  8. Review progress regularly Choose a review frequency that matches the pace and risk of the project. During reviews, focus on overdue activities, upcoming milestones, changes in the critical path, and risks that require decisions. Updating the schedule consistently is essential to keeping forecasts meaningful.
  9. Manage changes through a defined process Changes to scope, priorities, or resources can affect both the schedule and the budget. Before approving a major change, assess its effect on dependent tasks, resource capacity, cost, and delivery commitments. Record the decision and update the plan only when the change has been authorized.
  10. Communicate delays early When a milestone is at risk, communicate the issue along with its likely impact and proposed response. Stakeholders need time to make decisions, adjust expectations, or provide additional resources. Waiting until a deadline has already passed limits their options.
  11. Use dashboards that match stakeholder needs Team members may need detailed task lists, while executives may need milestone status, schedule variance, and forecast completion dates. Create views that provide the right level of detail for each audience. Keep reporting focused on actionable information. How to Choose the Right Project Scheduling Software Before purchasing a platform, evaluate it against your actual working environment. Understand project complexity. Determine whether you manage simple task lists, detailed dependency networks, or multiple interconnected projects. Identify essential capabilities. Decide whether you need critical path analysis, workload balancing, baseline tracking, financial controls, or portfolio-level reporting. Check integration requirements. Confirm that the tool works with your existing collaboration, finance, development, and reporting systems. Evaluate usability. Ask project managers and team members to complete common scheduling tasks during a trial. Review security and deployment. Check permissions, data handling, hosting options, and any organizational security requirements. Compare total cost. Consider licensing, implementation, training, support, and ongoing administration. Test realistic scenarios. Use an actual project plan to verify how the software handles dependency changes, delayed tasks, resource conflicts, and reporting. A structured comparison is more reliable than selecting a tool based on its interface or feature count alone. How Celoxis Supports Project Scheduling Celoxis is a project and portfolio management platform that supports project planning, Gantt charts, task dependencies, critical path analysis, resource management, and project reporting. It may be worth evaluating for organizations that manage complex schedules or need visibility across several concurrent projects. Its scheduling capabilities include interactive Gantt planning, inter-project dependencies, resource assignments, and baseline-based tracking. These functions can help project managers assess how changes in one task or project affect other activities. Celoxis also provides dashboards and reporting capabilities that can help teams monitor project status and review performance. Organizations should evaluate these features using their own project data and reporting requirements. For teams considering a scheduling platform, the best approach is to test a representative project, check resource and dependency behavior, and confirm that the reporting meets stakeholder needs. You can explore the Celoxis project management platform or book a demo to assess whether it fits your scheduling and portfolio management requirements.

Conclusion
Effective project scheduling depends on clear scope, realistic estimates, accurate dependencies, available resources, and consistent progress reviews. Project scheduling software brings these elements together so teams can manage timelines, identify potential delays, and make informed decisions.
The right platform should match the complexity of your projects, support the scheduling techniques you use, and provide useful information without making the process unnecessarily complicated.
Start by understanding your scheduling challenges, define the features that matter most, and test shortlisted tools against a real project. With the right process and software, project schedules can become practical tools for coordinating work and managing delivery, rather than static timelines that quickly fall out of date.

title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.

title: Day 17/75: Binary search in Go - Go DSA
description:
Day 17/75: Binary search in Go

75 Day DSA in Go Challenge

Today I focused on protecting the search interval in binary search in go so every bound update stays justified. The strongest checkpoints were state what the active interval still allows before the first loop iteration, move left and right only when the predicate proves one side is impossible, and test the smallest failing boundary because off-by-one errors hide there first.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was moving left and right without a precise definition of what they still allow. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests. title: Stop random programs from reading your Git and AWS credentials on Windows
description:
The problem

When you use Git or the AWS CLI, your tokens and keys often sit in plain files, or in places any program running as you can read. You would never know if one did.

What I built

Wardkey is a small, experimental tool for Windows. It keeps your Git and AWS credentials in an encrypted vault. When Git or AWS asks for a key, Wardkey checks which program is asking and applies your rules before giving anything out.

Think of it like a doorman. Most tools lock the door but give the key to anyone already inside. Wardkey asks every time: "Which program are you, and do your rules allow you to have this key?"

What it does

  • Stores credentials in an encrypted vault.
  • Works with Git over HTTPS (as a credential helper) and the AWS CLI (through credential_process).
  • Applies rules about which app may get which credential.
  • Can ask you for a Windows Hello check (face, fingerprint or PIN) on each request, when your rule says so.
  • Supports decoy keys. If anything asks for one, the request is denied and logged.
  • Writes every decision to a local log that detects many kinds of edits.

It's written in Go.

Honest limits

This is an early prototype, and I'd rather say so clearly:

  • It cannot stop malware that is already running as you. A program running as you could try to pretend to be Git or AWS. Windows Hello approval on every request is the real protection.
  • No outside expert has reviewed it yet.
  • Builds are unsigned, and it's Windows-only.
  • The activity log can detect many edits, but not someone deleting its last entries.
  • Please test with dummy credentials only.

The full list is in the threat model in the repo.

Try it 

go build -o wardkey.exe .\cmd\wardkey
wardkey help

Setup details are in the README.

Code and docs: https://github.com/Annora998/Wardkey

The code is source-available.

I'd love your feedback

Where do you think the design is weak, especially the caller checks and the approval flow? What would you want it to protect next? Tell me in the comments.
