title: Secure Multi-Tenant SaaS: Node.js, PostgreSQL & Row-Level Security for Scale
description:
Introduction & The Problem

When building Software as a Service (SaaS) products, one of the most significant architectural decisions is how to manage data for multiple customers, or 'tenants'. The goal is simple: each tenant should have a logically isolated view of their data, completely unaware of other tenants' information. The challenge, however, is complex. Common approaches range from entirely separate database instances per tenant (high cost, complex operations) to a single shared database where tenant identification is handled solely at the application layer (high risk of data leaks, complex queries).

Leaving this problem unresolved leads to several severe consequences: spiraling infrastructure costs as your tenant count grows, increased operational overhead for managing numerous database instances, and, most critically, a heightened risk of data breaches where one tenant's data could inadvertently become accessible to another. This not only erodes trust but can incur severe financial and legal penalties, impacting your SaaS's reputation and long-term viability.

This article addresses this fundamental challenge by presenting a robust, production-ready solution: leveraging Node.js with PostgreSQL's powerful Row-Level Security (RLS) feature. This approach offers a secure, scalable, and cost-efficient way to build multi-tenant SaaS applications, ensuring strict data isolation without the overhead of separate database instances.

The Solution Concept & Architecture

Our solution hinges on the 'shared database, shared schema' multi-tenancy model, augmented by PostgreSQL's Row-Level Security. Instead of creating a separate database or schema for each tenant, all tenant data resides within the same tables, but each row is explicitly tagged with a tenant_id. PostgreSQL's RLS policies then enforce that a database session can only see and manipulate rows belonging to its designated tenant_id.

The architectural flow is as follows:

1. Client Request: A client application (web, mobile, or API consumer) initiates a request to the Node.js backend. This request implicitly or explicitly includes the tenant context (e.g., via an API key, JWT token, or a dedicated X-Tenant-Id header).

2. Node.js API Service: The Node.js application, typically an Express.js server, receives the request. It performs authentication and authorization checks. Crucially, it extracts the authenticated tenant's ID.

3. Database Connection with Tenant Context: Before executing any database queries, the Node.js application sets a session-local variable (e.g., app.tenant_id) in PostgreSQL to the extracted tenant ID. This is achieved using SET LOCAL.

4. PostgreSQL RLS Enforcement: With RLS enabled on relevant tables and policies defined, PostgreSQL automatically filters all subsequent queries within that session. Any SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation will only affect rows where the tenant_id matches the session's app.tenant_id.

This architecture elegantly centralizes data isolation logic at the database level, preventing application-level mistakes from compromising tenant data. It reduces the complexity of application code and strengthens your security posture significantly.

Step-by-Step Implementation

Let's walk through building this solution.

Prerequisites:

  • Node.js (LTS version) installed.
  • PostgreSQL database (version 9.5+ for RLS) running.
  • Basic knowledge of SQL and Node.js/Express.

1. Database Setup (PostgreSQL)

First, connect to your PostgreSQL instance and set up the database, a dedicated user, and our tables. Note the tenant_id column in users and products.

-- Connect as a superuser or admin
CREATE DATABASE saas_multitenant;
CREATE USER saas_user WITH PASSWORD 'strong_password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE saas_multitenant TO saas_user;

-- Connect to the new database
\c saas_multitenant

-- Create the Tenants table
CREATE TABLE tenants (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Create the Users table with tenant_id
CREATE TABLE users (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) -- Ensure email is unique per tenant
);

-- Create the Products table with tenant_id
CREATE TABLE products (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Insert some sample data
INSERT INTO tenants (name) VALUES ('Acme Corp'), ('Globex Inc.');

INSERT INTO users (tenant_id, email, password_hash) VALUES
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'), 'john@acme.com', 'hashed_password_acme'),
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Globex Inc.'), 'jane@globex.com', 'hashed_password_globex');

INSERT INTO products (tenant_id, name, description, price) VALUES
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'), 'Acme Product A', 'Description for Acme Product A', 10.50),
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'), 'Acme Product B', 'Description for Acme Product B', 25.00),
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Globex Inc.'), 'Globex Product X', 'Description for Globex Product X', 150.00);

2. Implementing Row-Level Security (RLS)

Now, enable RLS on the tables containing tenant-specific data and define policies. These policies refer to a custom session variable app.tenant_id which we will set from our Node.js application.

-- Enable RLS for users and products tables
ALTER TABLE users ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE products ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- Create a policy for users table
CREATE POLICY user_isolation_policy ON users
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

-- Create a policy for products table
CREATE POLICY product_isolation_policy ON products
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

-- Optionally, create policies to allow tenants to view their own tenant record (if needed)
-- CREATE POLICY tenant_view_policy ON tenants
--     USING (id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

-- Grant specific permissions to our saas_user
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON users TO saas_user;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON products TO saas_user;
GRANT SELECT ON tenants TO saas_user;

3. Node.js Application Setup

Initialize a new Node.js project and install necessary packages.

npm init -y
npm install express pg dotenv

Create a .env file for database credentials:

DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_USER=saas_user
DB_PASSWORD=strong_password
DB_DATABASE=saas_multitenant

Next, create src/db.js to handle database connections. We'll use the pg client directly for more control over session variables.

// src/db.js
const { Pool } = require('pg');
require('dotenv').config();

const pool = new Pool({
    user: process.env.DB_USER,
    host: process.env.DB_HOST,
    database: process.env.DB_DATABASE,
    password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
    port: process.env.DB_PORT,
});

// Middleware to get a client, set tenant_id, and release
async function withTenantDbClient(req, res, next) {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
        const tenantId = req.tenantId; // tenantId set by previous middleware
        if (!tenantId) {
            return res.status(401).json({ message: 'Tenant ID is missing' });
        }

        // Set the session-local app.tenant_id variable
        await client.query("SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = $1", [tenantId]);
        req.dbClient = client; // Attach client to request object
        next();
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error setting tenant_id or getting DB client:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Database error' });
    } finally {
        // The client must be released after the request is complete
        // This will be handled in a final middleware or route handler
    }
}

module.exports = { pool, withTenantDbClient };

Now, create src/index.js for our Express application. We'll implement a simple middleware to extract the tenant ID (from a header for this example, but could be from a JWT) and then use withTenantDbClient.

// src/index.js
const express = require('express');
const { pool, withTenantDbClient } = require('./db');

const app = express();
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.use(express.json());

// Middleware to extract tenant ID (e.g., from X-Tenant-Id header or JWT)
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    // In a real application, this would come from an authenticated JWT token
    // For demonstration, we'll use a custom header.
    // Make sure the tenantId provided corresponds to an actual tenant in your 'tenants' table.
    const tenantId = req.headers['x-tenant-id'];
    if (!tenantId) {
        return res.status(400).json({ message: 'X-Tenant-Id header is required.' });
    }
    req.tenantId = tenantId;
    next();
});

// Apply the tenant database client middleware to routes that require RLS
app.use('/api', withTenantDbClient);

// Release the database client after each request
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    res.on('finish', () => {
        if (req.dbClient) {
            req.dbClient.release();
            // console.log('DB client released.'); // For debugging
        }
    });
    next();
});

// --- API Routes ---

// Get all products for the current tenant
app.get('/api/products', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query('SELECT id, name, description, price FROM products');
        res.json(rows);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching products:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to fetch products' });
    }
});

// Create a new product for the current tenant
app.post('/api/products', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { name, description, price } = req.body;
        if (!name || !price) {
            return res.status(400).json({ message: 'Name and price are required.' });
        }
        // tenant_id is automatically added by RLS policy if not explicitly provided and policy allows
        // However, it's good practice to explicitly include it or rely on the RLS INSERT policy
        // For simplicity, here we let RLS handle it from current_setting('app.tenant_id') for INSERT
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query(
            'INSERT INTO products (tenant_id, name, description, price) VALUES (current_setting(\'app.tenant_id\')::UUID, $1, $2, $3) RETURNING id, name, description, price',
            [name, description, price]
        );
        res.status(201).json(rows[0]);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error creating product:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to create product' });
    }
});

// Get a specific product by ID for the current tenant
app.get('/api/products/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { id } = req.params;
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query(
            'SELECT id, name, description, price FROM products WHERE id = $1',
            [id]
        );
        if (rows.length === 0) {
            return res.status(404).json({ message: 'Product not found or not accessible.' });
        }
        res.json(rows[0]);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching product by ID:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to fetch product' });
    }
});

// Get all users for the current tenant
app.get('/api/users', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query('SELECT id, email FROM users');
        res.json(rows);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching users:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to fetch users' });
    }
});

// Start the server
app.listen(PORT, () => {
    console.log(`Server running on port ${PORT}`);
    console.log('Test with curl, e.g.:');
    console.log('curl -H "X-Tenant-Id: " http://localhost:3000/api/products');
});

process.on('SIGINT', async () => {
    console.log('Shutting down...');
    await pool.end();
    console.log('Database pool closed.');
    process.exit(0);
});

To test, first get the UUIDs for your tenants from the tenants table:

SELECT id, name FROM tenants;

Then, you can use curl:

# For Acme Corp
curl -H "X-Tenant-Id: YOUR_ACME_CORP_UUID" http://localhost:3000/api/products

# For Globex Inc.
curl -H "X-Tenant-Id: YOUR_GLOBEX_INC_UUID" http://localhost:3000/api/products

# Attempt to access without tenant ID (should fail)
curl http://localhost:3000/api/products

You will observe that queries for products or users will only return data belonging to the tenant_id specified in the X-Tenant-Id header, thanks to PostgreSQL's RLS. If you try to create a product, it will automatically be associated with the tenant ID from the session variable.

Optimization & Best Practices

Implementing RLS effectively requires attention to several details:

Performance Considerations

  • Indexing: Ensure that the tenant_id column in all RLS-enabled tables is indexed. This is crucial for query performance, as every query will implicitly filter by tenant_id.
  • RLS Policy Complexity: Keep RLS policies as simple as possible. Complex policies can add overhead. If a table has very specific, varying access rules, consider if a different architectural pattern might be more suitable or if you can simplify the RLS conditions.
  • Query Plan Analysis: Regularly use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your queries to understand how RLS policies affect their execution plans. Identify and optimize any bottlenecks.

Security Best Practices

  • Tenant ID Validation: Always validate the incoming tenant_id against your actual list of active tenants in the tenants table. While RLS prevents cross-tenant data access, ensuring a valid tenant ID prevents unnecessary database lookups or potential attacks where a malicious actor tries to guess valid UUIDs.
  • Authentication & Authorization: The tenant ID should always be derived from a secure, authenticated source (e.g., a signed JWT token after a user logs in). Never trust a raw header from an unauthenticated request.
  • Principle of Least Privilege: Grant your application's database user (saas_user in our example) only the necessary permissions. Avoid giving it superuser or administrative roles. RLS operates regardless of the user's role, but overall security relies on this principle.
  • Secure Coding Practices: Always use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, even when setting session variables like app.tenant_id.

Schema Design

  • Shared vs. Tenant-Specific Data: Not all data needs to be RLS-protected. Global data (e.g., system configurations, public listings) can exist in tables without RLS, while sensitive tenant-specific data requires it. Clearly define which tables fall into which category.
  • Foreign Keys: When establishing foreign key relationships between RLS-protected tables, ensure that the tenant_id is part of the foreign key constraint if it's a composite key, or that the foreign key column itself is also filtered by RLS policies if it references an RLS-protected primary key.

Operational Considerations

  • Tenant Provisioning: Automate the creation of new tenants in the tenants table. This should be part of your SaaS onboarding workflow.
  • Monitoring: Monitor PostgreSQL logs for RLS-related warnings or errors to quickly identify any misconfigurations or potential breaches.

Business Impact & ROI

Implementing multi-tenancy with Node.js and PostgreSQL RLS delivers substantial business value and a strong return on investment (ROI):

  • Significant Cost Reduction: By sharing a single database instance across multiple tenants, you drastically reduce infrastructure costs compared to provisioning a separate database for each customer. This translates directly to higher profit margins or more competitive pricing for your SaaS.
  • Enhanced Security & Compliance: RLS provides a robust, database-enforced layer of data isolation. This significantly mitigates the risk of data leaks and simplifies compliance with regulations like GDPR, HIPAA, or SOC 2, which demand strict separation of customer data. This builds trust with your enterprise clients.
  • Faster Time-to-Market: A standardized and secure multi-tenant architecture allows you to onboard new customers more rapidly. You don't need to spin up new database instances or adjust complex schemas for each client, accelerating your sales cycle and growth.
  • Simplified Operations & Maintenance: Managing a single, well-optimized PostgreSQL instance is far simpler than juggling dozens or hundreds of disparate databases. This reduces the burden on your DevOps team, freeing them to focus on innovation rather than maintenance.
  • Improved Scalability: Your Node.js application can scale horizontally by adding more instances, while PostgreSQL can be scaled vertically or through advanced techniques like read replicas. The RLS approach does not impede database scaling and supports a growing number of tenants efficiently.
  • Reduced Developer Overhead: Developers can write cleaner, more focused queries without needing to manually add WHERE tenant_id = '...' clauses everywhere, reducing the chances of human error and improving code maintainability. The database handles the critical security aspect.

In essence, this architectural pattern not only solves a complex technical challenge but directly contributes to the financial health, security posture, and competitive advantage of your SaaS product.

Conclusion

The journey of building a scalable and secure SaaS application inevitably leads to the critical decision of how to manage multi-tenancy. Relying solely on application-level logic for data isolation is a precarious path fraught with security risks and operational complexity. By harnessing the power of Node.js in conjunction with PostgreSQL's Row-Level Security, we've demonstrated a robust, efficient, and highly secure architectural pattern.

This approach centralizes data isolation directly within the database, providing an impenetrable barrier between tenants' data. It offers significant advantages: substantial cost savings through shared infrastructure, a drastically improved security posture that simplifies compliance efforts, and streamlined operational workflows that allow your team to focus on feature development rather than database management. For any SaaS architect or developer seeking to build a resilient, scalable, and secure platform, adopting PostgreSQL RLS is not just an option, but a strategic imperative that delivers clear, tangible ROI. Embrace this pattern to empower your SaaS to grow securely and efficiently in today's demanding market. Your clients, and your bottom line, will thank you.

title: Long-wave Infrared Polarimetric Remote Sensing Image Fusion for Vehicle Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Blurred vehicle contours and low contrast limit detection performance in infrared remote sensing imagery, while existing fusion methods may introduce polarization noise and fail to integrate complementary information effectively. To address these limitations, we propose a Mamba-based infrared polarimetric remote sensing image fusion model. Infrared polarization information reflects surface material properties and geometry, providing complementary information to infrared intensity. The proposed method first combines long-wave infrared total intensity S0 and the degree of linear polarization (DoLP), using a physics-inspired polarization-response proxy and spatial structural continuity to extract guidance features. It then employs bidirectional state space scanning along horizontal, vertical, and both diagonal orientations to enable cross-modal feature fusion across the entire image. Prior-guided multi-window structural similarity, reconstruction constraints, and a relative lower-bound loss for polarization saliency are jointly introduced to suppress noise while preserving global background structures and target polarization features. In addition, we construct AIR-LWIR-Pol, a dataset of 1,901 accurately registered image pairs acquired using an airborne division-of-aperture long-wave infrared polarimetric imaging system, and evaluate downstream vehicle detection using YOLO11. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the comparison methods on four fusion metrics, including entropy and structural similarity. Vehicle detection mAP50 and mAP50-95 reach 55.0% and 29.4%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining physical priors with state space modeling for long-wave infrared polarization image fusion and support its use for target detection in complex remote sensing scenes.

title: Solving the Ho--Nguyen Conjecture for Gaussian Mixtures: Applications to Mixtures of Experts
description:
arXiv:2610.27265v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Over-fitted Gaussian mixtures can contain many parameter configurations with nearly the same density, making the order of density cancellation central to their parameter-learning rates. Ho and Nguyen encoded these cancellations in a polynomial system and conjectured its exact order as a function of cluster size. The key to resolving the conjecture is a common positive-variance shift that turns the coefficient equations into Gaussian moment matching. For every cluster size $\Mhn\ge2$, we prove that the real, nonzero-weight system has order $2\Mhn$: a sharp sign-change bound forces rigidity at that order, while positive Gauss--Hermite quadrature constructs a non-trivial solution through order $2\Mhn-1$. Population-density calculations at 110-digit working precision recover the predicted leading term for two to six components; finite multistart searches recover the same observed powers for two to five components, with smaller finite-scale constants for three to five components. For parameter learning, the exact order gives an explicit pointwise maximum-likelihood exponent and an exact local minimax order on specified shrinking neighbourhoods of a fixed known mixing measure. The same coefficient viewpoint separates high-order cancellation from exact parameter symmetries in mixtures of experts. Synchronized replication preserves the conditional density while keeping the corresponding parameter losses positive in two broad standard-softmax classes, showing why statistical rate arguments must account for exact parameter symmetries.

title: October 05, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Change

The BigQuery JupyterLab plugin is now enabled independently of the Dataproc plugin: it is enabled by default and can be turned off with the new disable-bigquery instance metadata key, while disable-mixer now controls only the Dataproc plugin.

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Security

Security fixes for the integrated portal and API specs in the Apigee Edge management UIs.

The Apigee Edge UIs for managing integrated portals and API specs were updated to patch vulnerabilities in underlying libraries and serving components. Functionality is unchanged, but some pages might show minor styling differences.

Application Design Center

Feature

Use the recommendeIAMroles API to identify a list of required APIs and Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles that you must configure before you deploy your application.

BigQuery

Feature

Iceberg external tables and Iceberg managed tables now support flexible column names by default. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The gemini-embedding-2 model works well for embedding long strings, including multilingual and unstructured data. It supports a mix of text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. You can use this model in the AI.EMBED, AI.SIMILARITY, and AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING functions. This model is generally available.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

This feature is in Preview.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports Assured Workloads control packages to help you meet regulatory, data residency, and data sovereignty requirements.

Specifically, the Cloud Workstations API (v1, v1beta, and v1alpha) supports the following Assured Workloads control packages:

  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP High
  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP Moderate
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 2 (IL2)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5)
  • US Data Boundary and Support (AW Regional Controls - Premium)
  • EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications

For more information about compliance-supported regions for each control package and API fields that aren't intended for sensitive data, see Regulatory support in Cloud Workstations.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Z3 machine types that have 8 to 44 vCPUs can use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes to synchronously replicate data across two zones.

For more information, see About Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (260900) is available.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Deprecated

Starting on July 1, 2026, Identity Service for GKE is deprecated in GKE version 1.36 and earlier. This feature is also unavailable in organizations that were created on or after July 1, 2025. GKE version 1.37 and later don't support Identity Service for GKE. Before you upgrade clusters to 1.37 and later, disable this feature and migrate to Workforce Identity Federation.

For more information, see Identity Service for GKE deprecation.

Feature

GKE support for using the c4-standard-* machine types (up to 192 vCPUs) as Confidential GKE Nodes with Intel TDX is generally available. For more information, see the following pages:

  • To use this feature with GKE , see Encrypt workload data in-use with Confidential GKE Nodes.
  • To learn more about the feature from Compute Engine, see Confidential VM overview.
  • To see supported configurations, including machine support, see Supported configurations and its "Machine types, CPUs, and zones" section.

Google SecOps

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Terraform and client libraries for multiple features using Chronicle API

Terraform providers and Google Cloud client libraries are now available for several Google SecOps features using Chronicle API including Feeds, Parsers, Rules, Findings Refinements, Retrohunts, Dashboards, Data Tables, Watchlists, Custom Lists, Environments, Environment Groups, Data Export, SOAR Domains, and SOAR Networks. For more information, see Terraform reference.

Terraform providers enable programmatic provisioning and management of Google SecOps resources as code, while Client Libraries enable developers to build custom integrations and automate Google SecOps workflows in their preferred programming languages. For more information, see Client libraries.

Guest Environment

Feature

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following features:

  • The managed workload identity certificate refresher is now a locally bundled extension. For more information, see Managed workload identities overview.
  • The guest telemetry extension is updated to version 1.1 and polls every 15 minutes instead of every 24 hours. However, it will only send data to the API every 24 hours, unless it detects a change in the system since the previous poll. The extension supports the following capabilities:
    • Running a command as the user associated with a discovered process.
    • Configuring regular expressions to match against the version command output.

Fixed

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following fixes:

  • The NetworkManager setup now no longer reloads the primary NIC when it applies changes to the network configuration of secondary NICs, unless necessary.
  • If the core plugin successfully rolls back any configurations, then it force-reloads the configurations to make sure that the instance re-obtains DHCP leases for secondary NICs.
  • The core plugin now respects the address-manager configuration flag and the corresponding metadata attribute.
  • The extensions manager now ignores install and remove requests from ACS for the core plugin and locally bundled extensions.
  • The extensions manager no longer logs that there are no local plugins to install when it's installing local plugins.
  • The metadata script runner now respects the sysprep_specialize configuration flag.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog now support Looker (Google Cloud core) assets. You can package, govern, and share Looker (Google Cloud core) dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, Explores, and LookML projects, models, and views in a data product using Google Group mirroring and IAM access controls. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see About data products and Create data products.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Users may now specify short template names when creating a serverless session.

Network Intelligence Center

Flow Analyzer displays packet drops, allowing you to analyze packet loss in your traffic flows. For more information, see Display flows in packet drop mode.

Virtual Private Cloud

title: A Software Factory on Kubernetes: Gemini Builds, jev Decides (Genkit + senro in Go)
description:
Introduction

The previous article put Genkit flows in Kubernetes pods with senro and let jev, a decision model, route a support ticket. The decisions there were small: which team, how urgent, send or hold.

This one hands jev something bigger to judge: software. A software factory takes a feature request and produces a Go module: a design, a plan, the code, a green build, passing tests and a pull request description. Gemini writes every one of those. jev decides, at every gate, whether the work moves on, goes back, or stops for a human. Each stage runs as a pod, each stage is a Genkit flow, and the whole thing is a few hundred lines of Go.

Everything below ran against the real Gemini API (gemini-3.8-flash) and the real TypeSafe API (jev-latest), on Genkit Go v1.14.0, senro v1.4.5 and a local kind cluster. The code is in genkit-k8s-flows-jev-software-factory.

Why a factory needs a judge, not a second writer

The usual way to review model-written code is to ask another chat model. It works, up to a point. The reviewer writes a paragraph, you parse the paragraph, the paragraph is sometimes wrong in the same way the code is, and a well-written pull request description can talk the reviewer into "looks good to me".

A decision model does not write. It takes a state (the request, the plan, the code, the test log) and answers typed questions with probabilities, in a few hundred milliseconds. There is no prose to parse and nothing to be talked into: BuildGreen is a number, and a red test log drags it down whatever the pull request says.

Chat model as reviewer Decision model as reviewer
Verdict A paragraph you parse Choice[CodeVerdict]: ship, rework or human, with a probability each
Evidence Mentioned, maybe A Noul per question: covers the request, tests are meaningful, build is green
Feedback for the next round Whatever it felt like writing Each question that scored "yes" is one line of feedback
Latency and cost Seconds, thousands of output tokens Milliseconds, tokens for the state only
Can be persuaded by the author Yes No: it never reads instructions, only state

The split that falls out of this is the whole design: Gemini builds, jev decides. And senro is what gives each build step a pod, a workspace, a log, a retry policy and a secret, and each decision a place in the graph.

What we are building

A feature request goes in. A reviewed Go module comes out, or a brief for a human saying why not.

The factory is three senro pipelines and a small state machine over them:

Run Step Where Who What it leaves behind
design clean coordinator none an empty workspace with request.md in it
design design pod Gemini and jev, in a loop design.json, DESIGN.md and one record per review round
design plan pod Gemini plan.json, PLAN.md
implement implement pod Gemini the module's files
implement vet, test pod go vet, go test vet.log, test.log and their exit codes
implement review pod jev review.json: ship, rework or human
rework fix, then vet, test, review pod Gemini, Go, jev the same, after a fix
finish pr then publish pod, coordinator Gemini PR.md and the module under out/<request>/src
finish brief then notify pod, coordinator Gemini BRIEF.md for a human

jev decides three times. Inside the design step, it reviews each design Gemini writes and the loop revises until jev says ready, says reject, or three rounds are up. After test, it reviews the code with the logs in hand and picks ship, rework or human. And the state machine in main turns each verdict into the next senro run, with rework bounded at two.

What you need

  • Go 1.27 or newer, Docker, kind and kubectl
  • GEMINI_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_KEY in your environment
  • the senro CLI if you want the terminal UI (optional) 
go get github.com/firebase/genkit/go@v1.14.0
go get github.com/xavidop/senro@v1.4.5
go get github.com/xavidop/mamori

Step 1: a cluster and an image with a Go toolchain

The cluster setup is the one from the previous article: kind, a namespace, a ServiceAccount with the permissions senro's Kubernetes executor needs (including get on pods/exec), and three environment variables, since senro never reads your kubeconfig. The repo's scripts/cluster-up.sh does it and source scripts/cluster-env.sh exports them.

The one difference is the image. A func step needs only sh and tar in the pod, but this factory also runs go vet and go test as plain command steps, so every step uses the official Go image, pinned to its digest as senro requires:

const stepImage = "docker.io/library/golang:1.27-alpine@sha256:f2c872bcee949b7be9c490efd02b48a8a2fbf947cdf533f1c58525ec9d8170fd"

func pods() senro.ExecutorTarget {
    return k8s.Pod(stepImage,
        k8s.Namespace("factory"),
        k8s.Resources(
            map[string]string{"cpu": "500m", "memory": "512Mi"},
            map[string]string{"cpu": "2", "memory": "2Gi"},
        ))
}

Your pipeline binary is still not in that image. senro cross-compiles it and sends it into each pod, exactly as before.

Step 2: the design loop, with jev inside the flow

The first gate is the one that saves the most money: a bad design produces bad code, a green build and a confident pull request. So the design is reviewed before anything is planned, and the review is a loop inside one Genkit flow.

The questions are a Go type. Every yes/no question is one a revision can act on: a "yes" becomes a line of feedback for the next round.

type DesignVerdict string

func (DesignVerdict) Criteria() map[DesignVerdict]string {
    return map[DesignVerdict]string{
        "ready":  "Complete, unambiguous, scoped to the request, and testable as described",
        "revise": "The right direction, with gaps a revision can close",
        "reject": "The request is too vague or too large to design from; a human has to clarify it first",
    }
}

type Risk int

func (Risk) Levels() []string { return []string{"Low", "Medium", "High"} }

type DesignReview struct {
    Verdict        systemonex.Choice[DesignVerdict] `json:"verdict" jsonschema_description:"Is this design ready to implement?"`
    RequestClear   systemonex.Noul                  `json:"request_clear" jsonschema_description:"Does the request say what to build precisely enough that two engineers would build the same thing?"`
    ScopeCreep     systemonex.Noul                  `json:"scope_creep" jsonschema_description:"Does the design add things the request did not ask for?"`
    Underspecified systemonex.Noul                  `json:"underspecified" jsonschema_description:"Is any component described too loosely to implement without guessing: missing fields, signatures, edge cases or error behaviour?"`
    MissingTests   systemonex.Noul                  `json:"missing_tests" jsonschema_description:"Does the test plan leave any requirement of the request untested?"`
    Risk           systemonex.Score[Risk]           `json:"risk" jsonschema_description:"How risky is implementing this design as written?"`
}

And the loop. Gemini designs; jev reviews; if the verdict is revise, Gemini gets the previous design plus the feedback and tries again:

f.Design = genkit.DefineFlow(g, "designFeature", func(ctx context.Context, request string) (DesignResult, error) {
    var res DesignResult
    feedback := ""
    for round := 1; round <= maxDesignRounds; round++ {
        prompt := "Request:\n" + request
        if round > 1 {
            prompt += "\n\nYour previous design:\n" + asJSON(res.Design) + "\n\nReviewer feedback:\n" + feedback
        }
        d, _, err := genkit.GenerateData[Design](ctx, g,
            ai.WithModelName("googleai/gemini-3.8-flash"),
            ai.WithSystem("You are a senior Go engineer writing a short design for exactly what the request asks. "+
                "Stay inside the request: no extra features. Components are the Go types and functions you will create. "+
                "The test plan names concrete, deterministic test cases. Be brief."),
            ai.WithPrompt("%s", prompt))
        if err != nil {
            return res, err
        }
        res.Design = *d

        out, resp, err := genkit.GenerateData[DesignReview](ctx, g,
            ai.WithModelName("typesafe/jev-latest"),
            ai.WithSystem("The state has a feature request and a design written for it."),
            ai.WithPromptParts(ai.NewDataPart(map[string]any{"request": request, "design": res.Design})))
        if err != nil {
            return res, err
        }

        // jev's verdict, then our rules on top.
        verdict := string(out.Verdict.Choice)
        var notes []string
        if out.RequestClear.Probability < 0.4 {
            verdict = "reject" // nobody should design from a request two engineers would read differently
        }
        if out.ScopeCreep.Probability >= 0.5 {
            notes = append(notes, "remove everything the request did not ask for")
        }
        if out.Underspecified.Probability >= 0.5 {
            notes = append(notes, "specify every component fully: fields, signatures, edge cases and error behaviour")
        }
        if out.MissingTests.Probability >= 0.5 {
            notes = append(notes, "add a test case for every requirement in the request")
        }
        if verdict == "ready" && len(notes) > 0 {
            verdict = "revise"
        }
        res.Rounds = append(res.Rounds, DesignRound{Round: round, Verdict: verdict,
            Ready: out.Verdict.Probabilities["ready"], Feedback: notes /* ... */})
        res.Verdict = verdict
        if verdict != "revise" {
            break
        }
        feedback = fmt.Sprintf("The reviewer rated the design %q (probability of ready %.2f). Do the following:\n- %s",
            verdict, out.Verdict.Probabilities["ready"], strings.Join(notes, "\n- "))
    }
    return res, nil
})

Two things to notice. The verdict is jev's, but the rules around it are yours: a request that two engineers would read differently is rejected whatever the design looks like, and a design with a flagged problem is not ready even if jev leaned that way. And the feedback is built from the questions, not from prose: a decision model never writes a sentence, so the sentences live in your code, one per question, and the next round gets exactly the ones that applied.

The whole loop is one flow, so it is one senro step, one pod, one log, with every round recorded in design.json.

Step 3: plan, implement, and let Go have its say

The plan and the implementation are ordinary Gemini calls with typed outputs: a Plan with files and steps, then a Code with every file in full. The step writes the files into the workspace, refusing anything that would escape it:

type Code struct {
    Files []File `json:"files"`
    Notes string `json:"notes,omitempty"`
}

func writeCode(ctx senro.Ctx, code Code) error {
    root := wsPath(ctx, ".")
    for _, f := range code.Files {
        rel := filepath.Clean(f.Path)
        if rel == "." || strings.HasPrefix(rel, "..") || filepath.IsAbs(rel) || strings.HasPrefix(rel, factoryDir) {
            return fmt.Errorf("refusing to write outside the module: %q", f.Path)
        }
        path := filepath.Join(root, rel)
        if err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(path), 0o755); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(f.Content), 0o644); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(ctx.Stdout(), "wrote %s (%d bytes)\n", rel, len(f.Content))
    }
    return nil
}

Then the compiler and the tests run, as command steps in the same pod image, with no model anywhere near them:

func goStep(w *senro.WorkflowBuilder, id, after, cmd string, ws *senro.WorkspaceRef) *senro.StepBuilder {
    script := "mkdir -p .factory; " + cmd + " > .factory/" + id + ".log 2>&1; echo $? > .factory/" + id + ".exit; " +
        "cat .factory/" + id + ".log; exit $(cat .factory/" + id + ".exit)"
    return w.Step(id, exec.Command("sh", "-c", script)).
        Needs(after).
        Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RW)).
        WorkDir("/repo").
        Env("HOME", "/tmp").
        Env("GOCACHE", "/tmp/gocache").
        Env("GOFLAGS", "-mod=mod").
        Env("GOPROXY", "off").
        Env("GOTOOLCHAIN", "local").
        Env("CGO_ENABLED", "0").
        Timeout(stepTimeout).
        Retry(3, retry.OnInfra()).
        ContinueOnError()
}

goStep(code, "vet", "implement", "go vet ./...", ws)
goStep(code, "test", "vet", "go test -count=1 ./...", ws)

Each one leaves its output and exit code under .factory/ in the workspace, so the reviewer can read them. GOPROXY=off and GOTOOLCHAIN=local keep the pod honest: the request said standard library only, and the pod cannot download anything to pretend otherwise. And ContinueOnError is the important one: a red test is a failed step, but the review still runs. jev gets to see why the build failed, which is exactly the evidence a rework needs.

Step 4: the code review gate

The second gate reads everything a human reviewer would open: the request, the plan, every source file, and what go vet and go test printed.

type CodeVerdict string

func (CodeVerdict) Criteria() map[CodeVerdict]string {
    return map[CodeVerdict]string{
        "ship":   "Builds, tests pass, does what the request asked, no obvious defects",
        "rework": "Fixable problems: failing or missing tests, a missed requirement, sloppy code",
        "human":  "Something a model should not decide: security, data loss, or the request was misunderstood",
    }
}

type Quality int

func (Quality) Levels() []string { return []string{"Poor", "Acceptable", "Good", "Excellent"} }

type CodeReview struct {
    Verdict         systemonex.Choice[CodeVerdict] `json:"verdict" jsonschema_description:"Should this change ship?"`
    Quality         systemonex.Score[Quality]      `json:"quality" jsonschema_description:"How good is the code?"`
    CoversRequest   systemonex.Noul                `json:"covers_request" jsonschema_description:"Does the implementation do everything the request asked for?"`
    TestsMeaningful systemonex.Noul                `json:"tests_meaningful" jsonschema_description:"Do the tests exercise the behaviour the request cares about, rather than just compile?"`
    BuildGreen      systemonex.Noul                `json:"build_green" jsonschema_description:"According to the logs and exit codes, did go vet and go test both pass?"`
}

The flow sends the whole ReviewInput as a data part, reads the answers, and applies the factory's rules on top. A red build never ships, whatever the overall verdict:

f.Review = genkit.DefineFlow(g, "reviewChange", func(ctx context.Context, in ReviewInput) (Review, error) {
    out, resp, err := genkit.GenerateData[CodeReview](ctx, g,
        ai.WithModelName("typesafe/jev-latest"),
        ai.WithSystem("The state has the feature request, the implementation plan, every source file, "+
            "and the output and exit codes of go vet and go test. Exit code 0 means success."),
        ai.WithPromptParts(ai.NewDataPart(in)))
    if err != nil {
        return Review{}, err
    }
    r := Review{
        Verdict:         string(out.Verdict.Choice),
        Confidence:      out.Verdict.Confidence,
        Quality:         out.Quality.Label(),
        CoversRequest:   out.CoversRequest.Probability,
        TestsMeaningful: out.TestsMeaningful.Probability,
        BuildGreen:      out.BuildGreen.Probability,
        Model:           systemonex.ResponseInfo(resp).Model,
    }
    if in.VetExit != 0 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "go vet failed")
    }
    if in.TestExit != 0 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "go test failed")
    }
    if r.CoversRequest < 0.6 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "the implementation does not cover the request")
    }
    if r.TestsMeaningful < 0.5 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "the tests do not exercise the requested behaviour")
    }
    if out.Quality.Level() == 0 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "code quality is poor")
    }
    if r.Verdict == "ship" && len(r.Reasons) > 0 {
        r.Verdict = "rework"
    }
    return r, nil
})

The Reasons are what the fix flow gets, together with the logs. Again: the decision model decides, your code says it in words.

Step 5: three pipelines and a state machine

The module under construction lives in a persistent workspace, so every run of one request works on the same tree. senro insists a persistent workspace is bounded, and refuses one without both bounds:

func repo() *senro.WorkspaceRef {
    return senro.Workspace("factory-repo",
        senro.Scope(senro.ScopePersistent),
        senro.MaxAge(24*time.Hour),
        senro.MaxSize(256<<20))
}

The three pipelines are short. Every AI step gets the same shape through a helper, with only the secrets it needs:

func aiStep(s *senro.StepBuilder, ws *senro.WorkspaceRef, secrets ...string) *senro.StepBuilder {
    s = s.Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RW)).Timeout(stepTimeout).Retry(3, retry.OnInfra())
    for _, name := range secrets {
        s = s.SecretEnv("SENRO_"+name, name)
    }
    return s
}

func buildPipeline(outDir string, rework bool) *senro.Pipeline {
    name, fn := "implement", "factory/implement"
    if rework {
        name, fn = "rework", "factory/fix"
    }
    p := senro.New(name)
    ws := repo()

    code := p.Workflow("code", senro.On(pods()))
    aiStep(code.Step(name, senro.Func(fn, NoParams{})), ws, "Gemini")
    goStep(code, "vet", name, "go vet ./...", ws)
    goStep(code, "test", "vet", "go test -count=1 ./...", ws)
    aiStep(code.Step("review", senro.Func("factory/review", NoParams{})), ws, "TypeSafe").Needs("test")

    handoff := p.Workflow("handoff", senro.Needs("code"), senro.On(senro.Local()))
    handoff.Step("collect", senro.Func("factory/collect", DirParams{Dir: outDir})).
        Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RO))

    return p
}

finish declares both endings and lets a run parameter pick one, the same senro.When pattern as the previous article:

func finishPipeline(outDir, reason string) *senro.Pipeline {
    p := senro.New("finish")
    ws := repo()

    ship := p.Workflow("ship", senro.On(pods()), senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", "ship")))
    aiStep(ship.Step("pr", senro.Func("factory/pr", NoParams{})), ws, "Gemini")

    publish := p.Workflow("publish", senro.Needs("ship"), senro.On(senro.Local()),
        senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", "ship")))
    publish.Step("publish", senro.Func("factory/publish", DirParams{Dir: outDir})).
        Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RO))

    escalate := p.Workflow("escalate", senro.On(pods()), senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", "human")))
    aiStep(escalate.Step("brief", senro.Func("factory/brief", BriefParams{Reason: reason})), ws, "Gemini")
    // ...and a notify workflow on the coordinator that collects BRIEF.md
    return p
}

And main is the state machine. Each run ends with a record jev produced, and the record picks the next run:

state, reason, reworks := "design", "", 0
for {
    switch state {
    case "design":
        if err := run(designPipeline(request, out)); err != nil {
            exit(err)
        }
        var d DesignResult
        read(out, "design.json", &d)
        if d.Verdict == "ready" {
            state = "implement"
        } else {
            state, reason = "human", fmt.Sprintf("the design review ended %q after %d round(s)", d.Verdict, len(d.Rounds))
        }

    case "implement", "rework":
        // A red vet or test is a failed step, so the run is partial; the
        // review still ran (ContinueOnError) and its verdict is what counts.
        if err := run(buildPipeline(out, state == "rework")); err != nil && !partial(err) {
            exit(err)
        }
        var r Review
        read(out, "review.json", &r)
        switch r.Verdict {
        case "ship":
            state = "ship"
        case "rework":
            if reworks >= *maxRework {
                state, reason = "human", fmt.Sprintf("jev asked for rework %d times: %v", reworks+1, r.Reasons)
            } else {
                reworks++
                state = "rework"
            }
        default:
            state, reason = "human", fmt.Sprintf("the code review ended %q: %v", r.Verdict, r.Reasons)
        }

    case "ship", "human":
        if err := run(finishPipeline(out, reason), senro.WithParams(senro.Params{"verdict": state})); err != nil {
            exit(err)
        }
        return
    }
}

Every arrow in the state diagram is one of those cases, and every run is a directory under runs/ with its plan, its events and one log per step.

Step 6: run it

The first request is a token-bucket rate limiter, the kind of package every service ends up with:

# Feature request: a token-bucket rate limiter package

We need a small, dependency-free Go package `ratelimit` (module path
`github.com/acme/ratelimit`) that other services can import.

- `New(rate float64, burst int) *Limiter`: `rate` is tokens added per second,
  `burst` is the bucket capacity.
- `(*Limiter) Allow() bool`: takes one token if available, otherwise returns false
  without blocking.
- `(*Limiter) AllowN(n int) bool` for batches.
- Safe for concurrent use from many goroutines.
- Time must be injectable so tests are deterministic (no sleeping in tests).
- Standard library only. Tests included, run with `go test ./...`.

go run . -request requests/token-bucket.md

The first run is the design. Read back with senro attach --run <id> --ui=plain:

The ready probability moved from 0.44 to 0.57, and the design that came out of it is the one Gemini implemented; this is its component list in DESIGN.md:

## Components

- type Limiter struct { mu sync.Mutex; rate float64; burst float64; tokens float64;
  last time.Time; now func() time.Time } - concurrency-safe state tracking ...
- func New(rate float64, burst int) *Limiter - public constructor delegating to

- func (l *Limiter) AllowN(n int) bool - thread-safe token deduction; edge cases: returns

Gemini wrote the module, go vet and go test ran in the pod against it, and jev read the three files and the logs and said ship, with the build at 0.98 and the tests at 0.95. The module it reviewed:

// AllowN reports whether n tokens can be consumed immediately.
func (l *Limiter) AllowN(n int) bool {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    if n <= 0 {
        return true
    }
    if float64(n) > l.burst {
        return false
    }

    curr := l.now()
    elapsed := curr.Sub(l.last)
    if elapsed > 0 {
        l.tokens += elapsed.Seconds() * l.rate
        if l.tokens > l.burst {
            l.tokens = l.burst
        }
        l.last = curr
    }

    if l.tokens >= float64(n) {
        l.tokens -= float64(n)
        return true
    }
    return false
}

Step 7: when jev says no

The second request is the kind every team gets:

# Request

The app feels slow lately, especially in the afternoon. Can you make it faster?
Nothing specific, just whatever you think is best. Thanks.

go run . -request requests/make-it-faster.md

Gemini did what a chat model does with a vague request: it invented a feature, in this case pprof routes and a latency middleware. jev put the probability that the request is clear at 0.05, and the factory's rule turned that into reject in the first round, before a plan, a line of code or a second model call. The finish run then takes the other ending:

pr skipped_condition
publish skipped_condition
brief stdout | ### What was asked
brief stdout | A user submitted a vague performance complaint stating the app "feels slow lately, especially in the afternoon" and asked to "make it faster" without providing specific endpoints, metrics, or reproduction steps.
brief stdout | ### Why it stopped
brief stdout | The design was rejected on Round 1 (Readiness: 13%, Clarity: 5%). The factory attempted to introduce Go `net/http/pprof` diagnostic routes and custom in-memory latency middleware, triggering a rejection for high scope creep (87%) ...
brief stdout | ### What a human should decide
brief stdout | 1. **Clarify the issue:** Contact the user to identify affected routes, user workflows, and target latency SLOs.
brief stdout | 2. **Authorize observability work:** Determine if the team should prioritize a dedicated ticket for production profiling/metrics ...
brief succeeded

The brief is written by Gemini, from the record jev produced. The two models keep their jobs even in the failure path.

A request jev cannot be talked into

The third request is a glob matcher: *, **, ?, character classes with ranges and negation, backslash escapes, and an error for an unterminated class. It is precise, it is testable, and the factory never got to write it:

clean succeeded
design stdout | round 1: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.39) request_clear=0.68 scope_creep=0.35 underspecified=0.49 missing_tests=0.32 risk=Medium
design stdout | round 2: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.39) request_clear=0.65 scope_creep=0.40 underspecified=0.34 missing_tests=0.22 risk=Medium
design stdout | round 3: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.47) request_clear=0.59 scope_creep=0.66 underspecified=0.33 missing_tests=0.20 risk=Medium
design stdout |   - remove everything the request did not ask for
design succeeded

Gemini's design transpiles the glob into a Go regular expression. jev never called it ready, the ready probability never crossed 0.5 in three rounds, and in two of those rounds none of the specific questions crossed the line either, so the feedback Gemini got was the generic "tighten the approach". The loop cannot converge on a complaint it has no question for, and after three rounds the factory stops and writes the brief:

## What was asked
Implement a standard-library Go package (`github.com/acme/glob`) providing `Compile(pattern string)
(*Glob, error)` and `(*Glob) Match(path string) bool`. ...

## Why it stopped
The design review failed after 3 rounds, ending in a "revise" verdict (`p_ready` plateaued at 0.46).
Automated reviewers flagged persistent specification risks and scope creep regarding the chosen
approach (transpiling globs into Go `regexp`), specifically around complex regex metacharacter
escaping and separator handling in negated character classes.

## What a human should decide
1. **Architecture:** Approve regex transpilation (accepting edge-case escaping risks) or mandate a
   dedicated AST/rune-based glob parser.
2. **Path boundaries:** Explicitly define exact semantics for `**` edge cases and `/` exclusions
   inside negated classes.

That brief is the factory working as designed. A decision model only answers the questions you ask, and when it keeps saying no without any of them firing, the honest move is to stop and ask a person, with the evidence attached. The fix for the next version of the factory is one more field on DesignReview: a question about the approach itself, so that "this should be a parser, not a regex" becomes a sentence Gemini can act on.

What the combination gives you

Concern Who handles it
Design, plan, code, fix, pull request text Gemini, through genkit.GenerateData and GenerateText
Is the design ready, should the code ship jev, through the same GenerateData call with a decision type
Feedback for the next round Your code, one sentence per question jev answered "yes"
Compiling and testing go vet and go test, as command steps in the pod, with no model involved
A red build reaching the reviewer ContinueOnError on the Go steps
The module between runs A bounded persistent workspace
Which ending runs senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", ...))
Credentials mamori resolves, senro delivers a file per pod, per step
Evidence runs/<id>/ per run, plus .factory/ records that travel with the code

Conclusion

A software factory is not one big agent. It is a handful of small, typed calls with a judge between them, and the judge is the part most people leave out. jev makes that part cheap: a design review is one call that answers six typed questions in a few hundred milliseconds, and the questions are Go fields you choose. Put the loop inside a Genkit flow, the flow inside a senro step, the step in a pod, and the verdict in a run parameter, and the factory is a state machine you can read in one screen.
