title: The Interop 2027 CSS shortlist reads like a list of hacks you get to delete
description:
You want hairlines between the cells of a 3×3 grid. Two cells have content. Seven are empty. And an empty grid cell has no element, so there is nothing to put border: 1px solid on.

So you fake it. Paint the grid container red, set gap: 1px, give every child a white background, and pad the markup with seven empty divs so the background only shows through the gaps. It works. It's also seven DOM nodes that exist purely to hide paint.

Josh W. Comeau shows that exact workaround in his new post on Interop 2027, and then shows the property that makes it unnecessary. That's the useful way to read his whole list. Most of the ten features he voted for replace something we currently fake.

How the list gets made

Interop is the yearly project where the browser vendors (Comeau names Google, Apple, Microsoft and Mozilla, along with Igalia and Bocoup) agree on a set of focus areas and work on them together. He writes that a focus area added to Interop often reaches near-100% support across the major browsers within a year.

His example is subgrid. Firefox implemented it in 2019, other browsers barely moved for years, then it went into Interop 2023 and was widely available across modern browsers by the end of that year.

For 2027, the team at Mozilla built a ranking system where developers upvote the features they want, and Comeau writes that they plan to use that ranking data to decide what goes into next year's Interop.

Lines that belong to the grid

Gap decorations add a border-like syntax to the grid itself:

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 1px;
  border: 1px solid red;
  rule: 1px solid red;
}

rule is a shorthand, like border. Width, style, color. Use row-rule or column-rule when you only want lines in one direction.

Comeau lists three problems with the background trick: the empty nodes, the fact that it only works on a solid page background, and the lost flexibility. For example, you can't leave space between the grid's outer border and its inner lines. The mechanism explains all three. The lines come from paint showing through a gap, so the gap is all you get to style. rule makes the line its own thing.

Corners the border box follows

border-radius puts a quarter-circle on each corner. corner-shape swaps that curve for something else: squircle, bevel, notch, scoop.

.box {
  border-radius: 16px;
  corner-shape: bevel;
}

You could already cut shapes like these with clip-path or masks. The difference is where the change happens. According to Comeau, corner-shape changes the shape of the border box itself, so borders, outlines and box-shadows follow the new corner. A clip only hides pixels, so the border and shadow get cut off with everything else instead of tracing the new edge.

border-shape goes a level lower. You draw the border yourself out of straight lines, arcs and Bézier curves, and the same thing holds: the real border box changes, so outlines and shadows trace it. Comeau calls corner-shape a perfect progressive enhancement. Unsupported browsers fall back to the plain rounded corner, which is fine.

auto gets a transition

You can't animate to height: auto. You've hit this. interpolate-size fixes it, alongside the related calc-size() function. Comeau's accordion demo opts in at the root and animates the ::details-content pseudo-element:

html {
  interpolate-size: allow-keywords;
}

@supports (interpolate-size: allow-keywords) {
  details {
    overflow: hidden;

    &::details-content {
      height: 0;
      transition:
        height 300ms,
        content-visibility 300ms;
      transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
    }
    &:open::details-content {
      height: auto;
    }
  }
}

Keep that @supports gate. Comeau warns that without it, unsupported browsers get a brief delay added. He also notes this has been in Chrome since 2024, which is a long time to wait for an accordion.

State you used to read from JavaScript

Several picks are queries for state that CSS couldn't see before.

  • Scroll-state container queries. Put container-type: scroll-state on a sticky header and @container scroll-state(stuck: top) matches once it sticks. The same API answers scrollable: top and scrollable: bottom, which is all you need to fade those scroll-hint gradients in and out.
  • Anchored container queries, from Level 2 of Anchor Positioning. They let you check whether a positioned element is using a fallback position, so a tooltip's pointer can flip when the tooltip does.
  • Scroll-triggered animations. These are a separate proposal from scroll-driven ones: the animation starts when the user scrolls to a point and then runs over a specified duration. Today that means IntersectionObserver.
  • reading-flow and reading-order. Tab order follows the DOM, not the layout, so a grid that rearranges on mobile focuses things in the wrong order. reading-flow: grid-rows on the grid makes focus follow the visual rows.

Functions, and one that exists nowhere

@function lets you define a custom function, such as --gradient-to-transparent(--color, --direction: bottom), and return its value with result. Call it like any other value: background: --gradient-to-transparent(red). Comeau writes that it is already implemented in Chromium browsers.

Then there's inherit(). Comeau says he couldn't find it implemented in any browser. It takes the inherited value and lets you do math on it, which is exactly what nested radii need:

p {
  border-radius: calc(inherit() - 4px);
}

He'd be a bit surprised if it makes the 2027 cut. I'd vote for it anyway.

Where support stands

The support tables in Comeau's post, marked current as of October 2026, list Chrome 155 and Edge 154 as supporting each feature that has a table, and Firefox 157 and Safari 27 as not supporting it. inherit() has no table because it isn't listed on caniuse. That's one engine family carrying every tabled feature today, which is the gap Interop exists to close.

For your next layout, sort by fallback. corner-shape and the gated interpolate-size accordion degrade to something perfectly usable, so ship them now. Gap decorations are harder. The fallback is no lines at all, so the background trick stays until rule ships in more than one engine. Whether that happens in 2027 depends partly on how the Mozilla ranking comes out.

title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
description:
arXiv:2610.27027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

title: Finding striking-distance keywords with the Search Console API and a short Node script
description:
Striking-distance keywords are the queries where your site already shows up, just not quite high enough: average positions somewhere between 8 and 20, with real impressions behind them. They are often the cheapest SEO wins you have, because Google has already decided the page is relevant. The Search Console performance report can show them, but it caps exports at 1,000 rows and makes it awkward to ask the one question that matters: which URL is ranking for each query, and is it the only one?

The Search Console API answers that question in a few dozen lines of Node. Below is a small script for it, and the reasoning behind its thresholds.

Setup: a read-only service account

  1. In Google Cloud, create a project, enable the Google Search Console API and create a service account with a JSON key.
  2. In Search Console, open the property settings and add the service account's email address as a user. Restricted permission is enough for reading performance data.
  3. Install the client library and point it at the key: 
npm install googleapis
export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=./gsc-key.json
export GSC_SITE="sc-domain:example.com"

Use sc-domain:example.com for a domain property or the full URL with trailing slash (https://www.example.com/) for a URL-prefix property. The only scope the script needs is webmasters.readonly. When I built the Search Console connection for Crawl Foundry, the SEO tool I work on in my spare time, it requests exactly that scope and nothing else. A reporting script has no business holding write access to your property.

Pulling query and page rows

The key decision is the dimensions. Requesting query alone gives you one average position per query across all of your URLs. Requesting query and page gives you one row per URL that appeared for that query, which is what you need to see which page Google picked and whether several pages compete.

// striking-distance.mjs
import { google } from "googleapis";

const auth = new google.auth.GoogleAuth({
  scopes: ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/webmasters.readonly"],
});
const gsc = google.searchconsole({ version: "v1", auth });

function daysAgo(n) {
  const d = new Date();
  d.setUTCDate(d.getUTCDate() - n);
  return d.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
}

async function fetchRows(startDate, endDate) {
  const rows = [];
  for (let startRow = 0; ; startRow += 25000) {
    const res = await gsc.searchanalytics.query({
      siteUrl: process.env.GSC_SITE,
      requestBody: {
        startDate,
        endDate,
        type: "web",
        dimensions: ["query", "page"],
        rowLimit: 25000,
        startRow,
      },
    });
    const batch = res.data.rows ?? [];
    rows.push(...batch);
    if (batch.length < 25000) return rows;
  }
}

rowLimit tops out at 25,000 per request, so the loop pages with startRow until a short page comes back. The window ends three days ago because the most recent days are still incomplete, and a four-week window evens out weekday swings.

Filtering for striking distance 

const rows = await fetchRows(daysAgo(31), daysAgo(3));

const byQuery = new Map();
for (const row of rows) {
  const [query, page] = row.keys;
  const pages = byQuery.get(query) ?? [];
  pages.push({ page, impressions: row.impressions, clicks: row.clicks, position: row.position });
  byQuery.set(query, pages);
}

const candidates = [];
for (const [query, pages] of byQuery) {
  pages.sort((a, b) => b.impressions - a.impressions);
  const lead = pages[0];
  const impressions = pages.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.impressions, 0);
  if (impressions < 100) continue;
  if (lead.position < 8 || lead.position > 20) continue;
  candidates.push({
    query,
    page: lead.page.replace(/^https?:\/\/[^/]+/, ""),
    position: lead.position.toFixed(1),
    impressions,
    clicks: pages.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.clicks, 0),
    pages: pages.length,
  });
}

candidates.sort((a, b) => b.impressions - a.impressions);
console.table(candidates.slice(0, 30));

Run it with node striking-distance.mjs and you get a table sorted by impressions, which is a rough proxy for how much traffic page one could bring.

Why the thresholds look like this

The lead page, not the query average. For each query the script takes the URL with the most impressions and uses its position. That is the page you would actually improve.

A minimum of 100 impressions. Average position over a handful of impressions is noise. The number is a starting floor for a four-week window on a small site; raise it for larger sites until the list becomes something you can work through.

The pages column. When it is greater than 1, several of your URLs appeared for the same query. Sometimes that is harmless, a product page and its category page. Sometimes it is keyword cannibalization, and improving either page won't help until you decide which one should own the query.

What the numbers do not tell you

A few caveats before acting on the list:

  • Average position is a blend. It averages the topmost position of your result across all impressions. An 11.4 can mean steady 11s, or 8 on desktop and 15 on mobile. Add device to the dimensions if a candidate looks odd.
  • Rare queries are missing. Search Console leaves out anonymized queries, so query-level rows will not add up to the property totals. That is fine for finding candidates and wrong for estimating total traffic.
  • CTR depends on the result page. Moving from 11 to 7 does not guarantee clicks if the results are full of ads and SERP features. The glossary entry on organic click-through rate covers what drives it.

Turning candidates into work

Each row deserves one of three decisions: improve the lead page for that query, consolidate competing pages, or drop it because the intent does not match what you offer. Write the decision next to the query, for example in a CSV export of the table, so next month's run shows whether it worked.

For that follow-up, Search Console's blended average is a weak instrument. A rank tracker that checks one keyword from a fixed location and device every day shows movement much more clearly. If you would rather not maintain the script yourself, the Search Console integration connects a property read-only to the Site Audit of the same domain. The Google Search Console glossary entry explains the reports this data comes from.

title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
description:
arXiv:2610.27156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Object:
  Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images.
  Materials and Methods:
  Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction.
  Results:
  Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail.
  Discussion:
  Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

title: How to Coordinate Role-Based CLI Seats & Session Handovers for AI Agents: A Governance MCP Server
description:
How to Coordinate Role-Based CLI Seats & Session Handovers for AI Agents: A Governance MCP Server in Python

In 2026, multi-agent software engineering swarms (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, Roo-Code, AutoGen) frequently operate directly on local repositories and shell environments. Teams deploy autonomous agents to build features, fix bugs, run test suites, and execute deployments.

However, operating multiple agent sessions in the same terminal environment quickly exposes three critical concurrency and governance hazards:

  1. Race Conditions & Write Collisions: When two agent sessions attempt to run git commands, build artifacts, or modify configuration files simultaneously, uncoordinated processes overwrite each other, producing corrupt states or broken builds.
  2. Session Handover Amnesia: When an agent session terminates—whether reaching its context window limit, hitting a timeout, or concluding its turn—the successor agent starts blind. Without an auditable session handover ledger, the new agent doesn't know what commands ran, what uncommitted changes exist, or what steps remain pending.
  3. Out-of-Domain Execution: An agent tasked with CLI scaffolding (domain:cli) accidentally runs destructive database or cloud infrastructure commands without boundary enforcement.

To eliminate these hazards, we built CliSeat: an open Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that enforces role-based single-writer seat locks, logs cryptographically hashed session handover briefs to an immutable SQLite WAL ledger, automatically reaps abandoned seats via heartbeats, and redacts sensitive credentials from command I/O.

🏗️ The System Architecture

CliSeat acts as an authoritative governance sidecar between your AI assistants and the host shell:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |            CliSeat Pro MCP Server             |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   | Single-Writer Seat|  | Handover Ledger   |  | Command Governor  |
   | Lock (domain:cli) |  | (SQLite WAL SHA256|  | & Secret Masking  |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      |   Governed Shell I/O    |
                      +-------------------------+

1. Single-Writer Seat Dispatch: Enforcing Mutual Exclusion

Only one agent session should hold mutation rights over a specific architectural domain at any given moment.

CliSeat manages domain seats (domain:cli, domain:db, domain:infra):

class SeatManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seats = {}

    def claim_seat(self, seat_id: str, holder_session_id: str, lease_ttl_sec: int = 180):
        seat = self.get_or_create(seat_id)
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        # Reject if held by an active session
        if seat.status == "occupied" and not seat.is_expired():
            if seat.holder != holder_session_id:
                return {
                    "status": "rejected",
                    "error": f"Seat '{seat_id}' is already held by '{seat.holder}'.",
                    "seat": seat.to_dict()
                }
            # Renew lease if already held
            seat.last_active = now
            return {"status": "renewed", "seat": seat.to_dict()}

        # Grant exclusive lock
        seat.holder = holder_session_id
        seat.status = "occupied"
        seat.claimed_at = now
        seat.last_active = now
        return {"status": "claimed", "seat": seat.to_dict()}

If another session attempts to mutate the repository while domain:cli is occupied, the claim is rejected immediately with the current holder's session ID and remaining lease time.

2. Preventing Context Amnesia: The Handover Ledger

When an agent finishes its task or reaches token budget exhaustion, it must produce a structured sign-off brief.

CliSeat persists every handover to an atomic SQLite WAL database sealed with a SHA-256 state hash:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class HandoverLedger:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "ledger.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def record_handover(self, seat_id: str, event_type: str, session_id: str, brief: str):
        entry_id = f"hnd_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        # Generate tamper-evident cryptographic hash
        hash_payload = f"{entry_id}:{seat_id}:{event_type}:{session_id}:{brief}:{now}"
        state_hash = hashlib.sha256(hash_payload.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("""
                INSERT INTO handover_ledger (entry_id, seat_id, event_type, session_id, brief, state_hash, created_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?);
            """, (entry_id, seat_id, event_type, session_id, brief, state_hash, now))

        return {"entry_id": entry_id, "state_hash": state_hash[:16], "timestamp": now}

When the next agent takes the seat, it simply calls get_handover_history(seat_id="domain:cli") to see:

  • What previous agents completed
  • Unfinished branch names
  • Known issues or test failures
  • Pending pull request links

3. Boundary Enforcement & Secret Masking

To prevent accidents and credential leaks, CliSeat intercepts terminal commands:

  1. Domain Whitelists: An agent on domain:cli is allowed git, npm, pip, pytest, and cargo, but blocked from executing database or infrastructure mutations.
  2. Credential Redactor: Masks GitHub PATs, AWS secret keys, Bearer tokens, and passwords from command arguments and output logs. 
SECRET_PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{15,}", re.IGNORECASE), "Bearer [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?:ghp|gho|ghu|github_pat)_[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}", re.IGNORECASE), "[REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]"),
]

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    for pattern, replacement in SECRET_PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(replacement, text)
    return text

4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

Adding CliSeat to your local AI environment takes seconds. Add the following to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cliseat": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "cliseat.server"]
    }
  }
}

Available MCP tools:

  • claim_seat(seat_id, holder_session_id)
  • heartbeat(seat_id, holder_session_id)
  • release_seat(seat_id, holder_session_id, handover_notes)
  • get_seat_status(seat_id)
  • execute_domain_command(seat_id, holder_session_id, command_line)
  • get_handover_history(seat_id, limit)
  • reap_expired_leases()

🚀 Get Started: Open-Source & Enterprise

The open-source CliSeat Lite is available immediately on GitHub under the MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/cliseat-mcp

For enterprise development teams requiring the persistent SQLite WAL handover ledger, automatic heartbeat reapers for crashed sessions, credential masking, and complete container manifests:

title: Announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a managed ingress solution for your ECS services
description:
AWS announces Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Gateway, a new resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized applications by dynamically provisioning and managing Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and their supporting resources directly in your account.

With ECS Gateway, platform teams define organizational networking standards once on a gateway and associate it with one or more clusters, giving organizations a centralized way to govern how traffic reaches their ECS services. Application teams simply opt in to inherit those standards without requiring networking expertise. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing, allows up to 25 services to share an ALB to optimize infrastructure costs, and gives each service a unique Domain Name System (DNS) hostname. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs when capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. You can inspect these resources and the gateway route to each service to see exactly how requests reach your applications. For traffic and health monitoring, you can use standard ALB metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and target health information from Elastic Load Balancing.

To get started, create an ECS Gateway, associate it with a cluster, and opt in your ECS service by adding the gateway connector parameter using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the awsvpc network mode across all launch types. It is available now in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when your services connect to the gateway. To learn more, refer to the AWS News blog and our documentation page.

title: Meet Harnis: the open-source platform for running AI agents safely across your company
description:
AI agents are finally useful enough to do real work: fix code, answer customers, update tickets, run internal tools. The hard part isn't getting an agent to act. It's letting it act inside a company: across teams and customers, on real systems, with someone accountable for every change and a bill that doesn't surprise anyone.

That's what Harnis is for. It's an open-source, self-hosted platform that gives every agent in your organization the same harness: isolation, approvals, sandboxing, budgets and an audit trail, so teams can ship agents quickly without rebuilding the safety layer every time.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis
  • PyPI: pip install harnis
  • Helm chart: oci://ghcr.io/karawash-projects/charts/harnis
  • License: Apache 2.0

Why a harness?

Every team that builds an agent ends up writing the same plumbing: who is this user, which customer's data can they see, should this action wait for a human, where does model-written code run, how much did that conversation cost, and who approved what. When each team writes it alone, you get ten slightly different answers and no single place to audit.

Harnis turns that plumbing into a platform. Agents plug in; the guarantees come with them.

Three products on one engine

Harnis ships three ready-to-use workloads, all running on the same orchestrator:

1. A coding agent for your developers. Point the CLI at a project and describe the change. The agent works on an isolated copy, shows a diff for every file it wants to write, asks before running any command, runs your tests in a sandbox, and applies the final result to your files only when you confirm.

harnis --workspace ./my-service "add input validation to the signup handler and a test for it"

2. Multi-agent workflows. A router on a small, fast model reads each message and hands it to the right specialist (a support agent, a coding agent, or your own). Agents can hand work to each other or escalate to a person. Add a new specialist with a few lines of plugin code.

3. A multi-tenant agent app. A full API with live streaming over WebSockets and a web console for every role:

  • Users chat with agents and see each proposed change, with diffs inline.
  • Reviewers work an approvals queue and see usage and analytics.
  • Admins manage agents and their prompt versions, API keys and the audit log.
  • Platform admins create and manage tenants.

What every agent gets for free

Customer data stays separated, by the database itself

Every tenant table uses Postgres row-level security, enabled and forced, and the app connects with a role that can't bypass it. The tenant always comes from the verified login or API key, never from the request. Even a query that forgets to filter by tenant can't return another customer's data.

A human approves the exact action

Writing files, running commands and installing packages pause the session until a reviewer approves. The approval is tied to a cryptographic hash of the exact action, so the agent can't get approval for one change and then make a different one. Approvals expire, and separation of duties can stop people approving their own sessions. Paused sessions live in the database, so a decision made hours later resumes the work on any server.

Model-written code runs in a disposable sandbox

Each command gets a fresh Docker container or Kubernetes Pod with no network, a read-only system, no Linux privileges, a non-root user and strict memory, CPU and process limits. gVisor is supported for an extra kernel boundary. Files coming back out are checked, so a model can't sneak a link to a host file into your project.

Need packages? An approved install goes through a proxy that only allows package registries, and it can only change a separate dependency folder, never your code.

Security that checks itself

On Kubernetes, Harnis doesn't just assume the network rules are in place. Before it copies anything into a sandbox Pod, it probes from inside the Pod and only proceeds once the network is confirmed blocked. If the cluster can't isolate the sandbox, the command is refused with a clear error rather than run unprotected.

Costs you can predict

  • Per-turn budgets for steps, tool calls, hand-offs and spend in USD.
  • Per-tenant cost caps.
  • A token and cost ledger per model.
  • A loop breaker: it spots an agent repeating itself, warns it, then hands the session to a person.
  • Confirmed prices: you confirm each model's price at setup, so cost figures and caps are based on real numbers.

Your models, your rules

  • Models: use Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini or Amazon Nova on Bedrock, or self-hosted ones through any OpenAI-compatible API (vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, LiteLLM).
  • Failover: you set the order and Harnis fails over between providers automatically.
  • Data residency: each tenant has its own list of allowed providers, and failover never sends that tenant's data outside it.

Your login, your roles

  • Single sign-on: any OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Google), with group-to-role mapping.
  • Roles: user, reviewer, tenant admin and platform admin.
  • API keys: service keys for CI and automation, with roles, expiry and instant revocation.

Your tools and agents

A plugin SDK lets you add tools, agents and even model providers that register exactly like the built-in ones. Internal APIs, ticketing systems and databases all become tools that inherit approvals, sandboxing and auditing automatically.

Built-in guardrails

  • Prompt injection: incoming messages are checked for injection attempts.
  • Card numbers: they're redacted before the model sees them.
  • Tool output: it's marked as untrusted data, so instructions hidden in a file or web page aren't treated as commands.
  • Semantic cache: repeated questions are answered from the cache, which is fast and costs nothing.

Ready for your auditors and your ops team

  • Audit log: append-only, exportable as JSON or NDJSON.
  • Monitoring: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics and alert webhooks.
  • Data lifecycle: retention jobs, per-user data export and erasure, and backup and restore commands with verification.

Runs where you do

On a laptop, everything starts with Docker Compose on Windows, macOS or Linux. On Kubernetes, the Helm chart deploys:

  • the API, which scales out because sessions resume on any replica;
  • database migrations, run before each install or upgrade;
  • scheduled maintenance;
  • a separate, locked-down namespace for sandbox Pods.

Try it in five minutes, without an API key

The quick start uses a built-in mock model, so you can explore approvals, the sandbox and the loop breaker for free:

git clone https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis.git
cd harnis
python tasks.py install
python tasks.py up              # Postgres, Redis, tracing, demo tenants
python tasks.py sandbox-image
python tasks.py dev             # http://127.0.0.1:8000

Open the console, click Continue as local developer, and type create calc.py. The coding agent proposes two files with diffs, waits for your approvals, then runs the tests in the sandbox. Try repeat: list the files to watch the loop breaker step in, or ignore all previous instructions to see the input guard. When you're ready, python tasks.py check runs a complete feature check against your instance.

Built to be tested

Each release passes:

  • a cross-platform test suite;
  • end-to-end checks against a running API;
  • an evaluation suite and red-team scenarios;
  • sandbox tests under gVisor;
  • a full Helm deployment on a Kubernetes cluster in CI.

The same feature-check script ships with Harnis, so you can verify your own deployment the way the project verifies its releases.

Get involved

Harnis 1.0 is out now, free under Apache 2.0, and provided as is. Star the repo, try it on a real workflow, and tell me what you'd build on it:

https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis

Issues, ideas and pull requests are welcome.

title: Automated Brick Schema Knowledge Graph Completion Across Buildings
description:
arXiv:2610.27339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Brick schema represents building equipment, sensors, spaces, and the relationships between them as typed, multi-relational graphs, providing machine-readable metadata that supports generalizable control applications. Current methods for producing complete Brick models require extensive manual examination of building schematics and point lists. We observe that as Brick models are knowledge graphs, inferring missing relations is naturally posed as a knowledge graph completion problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of knowledge graph completion to Brick model generation. We compare three methods, gradient-boosted trees, Pairwise Brick Relation Ranking, and CompGCN, on the relations feeds, hasPart, and hasPoint, which account for the majority of the schematic-reading work in building a Brick model by hand. Models are evaluated on held-out MORTAR buildings and out-of-distribution Kaggle and Building Time Series data. Although CompGCN is the strongest performer on held-out buildings under metrics resistant to class imbalance, leading macro-F1 and AUPRC, no method generalizes uniformly across datasets or relations.

Sandbox observability memory in the dashboard

The Memory Usage card reports average, P75, and P95 memory across your sandboxes, alongside the existing CPU usage and data transfer metrics on the sandbox overview page and the project and team-level pages.

On the sandbox detail page, charts are designed to show how close a sandbox is running to its memory ceiling by:

  • Adding a dashed reference line at 85% of that limit

Sandbox memory is also available in the Observability query builder as the memoryUsedBytes measure on the sandbox usage event. You can build custom queries against it and create alerts from the chart.

Sandbox memory observability in the CLI

Sandbox observability data is also available through the Vercel CLI via the vercel metrics command under vercel.sandbox.memory_used_bytes. Run the command in a linked project for project-specific data, or append --all to see aggregate data across all projects in your team.

The CLI returns:

  • The metric

  • The reporting period

  • The measurement interval

  • The project the sandbox is associated with

  • A graph of memory usage, with min, max and avg values

Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

title: Day 17/60: Testing HTTP handlers - Go Backend Engineering
description:
Day 17/60: Testing HTTP handlers

60 Day Go Backend Engineering Challenge

Today I focused on making testing http handlers feel like request flow design rather than just handler boilerplate. The strongest checkpoints were name the request boundary, validation step, and response contract before writing handler code, keep routing and middleware explicit enough that ownership of each concern is obvious, and make serialization and status codes follow the service contract rather than handler convenience.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was mixing validation, orchestration, and transport formatting in one handler. The day felt better once the service boundary stayed visible and each component had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next service still feels related to the same design idea. I also want to keep tracing one request path end to end because it exposes weak assumptions faster than a larger demo.

title: My demo build is a config I never commit: the temporary vite setup behind the public preview
description:
My SaaS starter kit has two builds. One ships to customers. One powers the public demo. They come from the same source tree, but the demo gets its own vite config, and that config has a comment at the top that says, in effect: temporary, demo only, do not commit.

Here it is, the whole thing:

// TEMPORARY build config for the /demo/ GitHub Pages deploy ONLY.
// Externalizes vendor deps (loaded via importmap from esm.sh) so the app
// bundle stays small. NOT for the shipped product — do not commit.
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  base: '/laravel-react-saas-starter-kit/demo/',
  build: {
    outDir: 'dist-demo',
    rollupOptions: {
      external: ['react', 'react/jsx-runtime', 'react-dom',
                 'react-dom/client', 'react-router-dom', 'axios'],
    },
  },
});

Twenty lines. Three decisions worth stealing.

Decision one: the demo build externalizes vendor dependencies. The demo runs on GitHub Pages with base set to the /demo/ subpath, and react, react-dom, react-router-dom and axios are declared external so they load from an import map (esm.sh) instead of being bundled. The app bundle stays small, which matters when your demo is the first impression and the visitor is on a phone connection. The shipped product does none of this; its normal vite config bundles everything the usual way.

Decision two: the demo config lives next to the real one, not inside it. I did not add if (demo) branches to the shipped vite.config.js. Demo needs are not product needs. The day a demo special-case lands in the shipped config, every future customer build pays the tax: extra conditionals to read, extra ways for a demo flag to leak into production output. Two configs, one of them labelled disposable, keeps the product's build pipeline honest.

Decision three: the config is honest about being disposable. The comment says do not commit it. In practice that means the demo deploy is a local, manual step: build with this config, push dist-demo to the /demo/ path, and the repo's tracked build config stays the clean one. Nobody inherits a mysterious demo hack six months later and wonders whether it is load-bearing.

How does the app know it is the demo? A build-time flag. The axios client checks it:

const client = isDemoMode() ? createDemoClient() : axios.create({
  baseURL: `${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL || 'http://localhost:8000'}/api`,
  headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
});

VITE_DEMO_MODE=true swaps the real Laravel API for an in-memory mock that mirrors the endpoints and response shapes, so the preview is fully clickable with no backend. The product default is the real API. One seam, one flag, and the demo config never touches a line of application code.

The pattern generalises: anything you build to sell the thing should be physically separated from the thing itself. Demos rot faster than products. When the demo is a labelled, temporary config rather than conditionals woven through your build, deleting it later is a one-line act of hygiene instead of archaeology.

I write about real patterns from client work and the starter kit I sell. If the behind-the-scenes of a $19 boilerplate interests you, the whole thing is here: Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit

title: Build-as-Code, CI Integration, and Build Doctor
description:
• Why treat builds as code: eliminate drift and make builds a pure function
  • CI integration patterns for hermetic builds and remote cache clients
  • Designing and implementing a Build Doctor diagnostics tool
  • Rolling out at scale: onboarding, guardrails, and measuring impact
  • Practical checklists and runbooks for immediate action

Treat every build flag, toolchain pin, and cache policy as versioned code — not a local habit. Doing so converts the build from a mutable ritual into a repeatable, auditable function whose outputs are pure and sharable.

The pain is specific: slow pull requests because CI redoes work, “works on my machine” debugging, cache-poisoning incidents that invalidate hours of developer effort, and onboarding that takes days because local setups differ. Those symptoms trace back to one root cause: build affordances (flags, toolchains, cache policy, and CI integration) live as handwaves instead of code, so behavior diverges between machines and pipelines.

Why treat builds as code: eliminate drift and make builds a pure function

Treating the build as code — build-as-code — means storing every decision that influences outputs in version control: WORKSPACE pins, BUILD rules, toolchain stanzas, .bazelrc snippets, CI bazel flags, and the remote-cache client configuration. That discipline enforces hermeticity: the build result is independent of the host machine and therefore reproducible across developer laptops and CI servers.

What you get when you do this correctly:

  • Bit-identical artifacts for the same inputs, eliminating “it works on my machine” debugging.
  • A cacheable DAG: actions become pure functions of declared inputs, so results can be reused across machines.
  • Safe experimentation via branches: differing toolchain or flag sets are explicit commits, not env leaks.

Practical rails that make this discipline enforceable:

  • Keep a repo-level .bazelrc that defines the canonical flags used in CI and for canonical local runs (build --remote_cache=..., build --host_force_python=...).
  • Pin toolchains and third-party deps in WORKSPACE with exact commits or SHA256 checksums.
  • Treat ci and local modes as two configurations in the build-as-code model; only one (CI) should be allowed to write authoritative cache entries in the early rollout phase.

Important: Hermeticity is an engineering property you can test for; make those tests part of CI so the repository encodes the build’s contract rather than relying on implicit conventions.

CI integration patterns for hermetic builds and remote cache clients

The CI layer is the single most potent lever for accelerating team builds and protecting the cache. There are three practical patterns you will choose from depending on scale and trust.

  • CI-as-single-writer, developers-read-only: CI builds (full, canonical builds) write to the remote cache; developer machines read only. This prevents accidental cache poisoning and keeps the authoritative cache consistent.
  • Combined local + remote cache: Developers use a local disk cache plus a shared remote cache. The local cache improves cold-starts and avoids unnecessary network trips; the remote cache enables cross-machine reuse.
  • Remote execution (RBE) for speed at scale: CI and some dev flows offload heavy actions to RBE workers and take advantage of both remote execution and the shared CAS.

Bazel exposes standard knobs for these patterns; the remote cache stores action metadata and the content-addressable store of outputs, and a build consults the cache before running actions.

Example .bazelrc snippets (repo-level vs CI):

# .bazelrc (repo - canonical flags)
build --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.corp.example:9090
build --remote_download_outputs=minimal
build --host_jvm_args=-Xmx2g
build --show_progress_rate_limit=30

# .bazelrc.ci (CI-only overrides; kept on CI runner)
build --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.corp.example:9090
build --remote_executor=grpcs://rbe.corp.example:8989
build --remote_timeout=180s
build --bes_backend=grpcs://bep.corp.example   # send BEP to analysis UI

CI example (GitHub Actions, illustrating integration with existing cache steps): use the platform cache for language deps and let Bazel use the remote cache for build outputs. The actions/cache action is a common helper for pre-built dependency caches.

name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Restore tool caches
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/bazel
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-bazel-${{ hashFiles('**/WORKSPACE') }}
      - name: Bazel build (CI canonical)
        run: bazel build --bazelrc=.bazelrc.ci //...

Contrast of caching approaches

Mode What it shares Latency impact Infra complexity
Local disk cache per-host artifacts small improvement, not shared low
Shared remote cache (HTTP/gRPC) CAS + action metadata network-limited, large benefit across team medium
Remote execution (RE) executes actions remotely minimizes dev wall-clock time high (workers, auth, scheduling)

Remote execution and remote caching are complementary; RBE focuses on compute scaling while the cache focuses on reuse. The protocol landscape and client/server implementations (e.g., the Bazel Remote Execution APIs) are standardized and supported by several OSS and commercial offerings.

Practical CI guardrails to enforce:

  • Make CI the canonical writer during pilot: developer configs set --remote_upload_local_results=false while CI sets it true.
  • Lock who can clear the cache and implement a cache-poison rollback plan.
  • Send BEP (Build Event Protocol) from CI builds to a centralized invocations UI for later troubleshooting and historical metrics. Tools like BuildBuddy ingest BEP and provide cache-hit breakdowns.

Designing and implementing a Build Doctor diagnostics tool

What a Build Doctor does

  • Acts like a deterministic, fast diagnostics agent that runs locally and in CI to surface misconfigurations and non-hermetic actions.
  • Collects structured evidence (Bazel info, BEP, aquery/cquery, profile traces) and returns actionable findings (missing --remote_cache, genrule calling curl, actions with nondeterministic outputs).
  • Produces machine-readable results (JSON), human-friendly reports, and CI annotations for PRs.

Data sources and commands to use

  • bazel info for environment and output base.
  • bazel aquery --output=jsonproto 'deps(//my:target)' to retrieve action commandlines and inputs programmatically. This output can be scanned for rogue network calls, writes outside the declared outputs, and suspicious commandline flags.
  • bazel build --profile=command.profile.gz //... followed by bazel analyze-profile command.profile.gz to get the critical path and per-action durations; the JSON trace profile can be loaded into tracing UIs for deeper analysis.
  • Build Event Protocol (BEP) / --bes_results_url to stream invocation metadata to a server for long-term analytics. BuildBuddy and similar platforms provide BEP ingestion and a UI for cache-hit debugging.

Minimal Build Doctor architecture (three components)

  1. Collector — shell or agent that runs the Bazel commands and writes structured files:
    • bazel info --show_make_env -> doctor/info.json
    • bazel aquery --output=jsonproto ... -> doctor/aquery.json
    • bazel build --profile=doctor.prof //... -> doctor/command.profile.gz
    • optional: fetch BEP or remote cache server logs
  2. Analyzer — Python/Go service that:
    • Parses aquery for suspicious mnemonics or commands (Genrule, ctx.execute) that contain network tools.
    • Runs bazel analyze-profile doctor.prof and correlates long actions with aquery outputs.
    • Verifies .bazelrc flags and remote cache client presence.
  3. Reporter — emits:
    • a concise human report
    • structured JSON for CI pass/fail gating
    • annotations for PRs (failed hermetic checks, top 5 critical-path actions)

Example: a tiny Build Doctor check in Python (skeleton)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, subprocess, sys, gzip

def run(cmd):
    print("+", " ".join(cmd))
    return subprocess.check_output(cmd).decode()

def check_remote_cache():
    info = run(["bazel", "info", "--show_make_env"])
    if "remote_cache" not in info:
        return {"ok": False, "msg": "No remote_cache configured in bazel info"}
    return {"ok": True}

def parse_aquery_json(path):
    with open(path,'rb') as f:
        return json.load(f)

def main():
    run(["bazel","aquery","--output=jsonproto","deps(//...)", "--include_commandline=false", "--noshow_progress"])
    # analyzer steps would follow...
    print(json.dumps({"checks":[check_remote_cache()]}))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Diagnostic heuristics you should encode (examples)

  • Actions whose command lines contain curl, wget, scp, or ssh indicate network access and likely non-hermetic behavior.
  • Actions that write to $(WORKSPACE) or outside declared outputs indicate source-tree mutation.
  • Targets tagged no-cache or no-remote deserve review; frequent no-cache usage is a smell.
  • bazel build outputs that differ across repeated clean runs reveal nondeterminism (timestamps, randomness in build steps).

A Build Doctor should avoid hard fails on first rollout. Start with informational severities and escalate rules to warnings and hard-gate checks as confidence grows.

Rolling out at scale: onboarding, guardrails, and measuring impact

Rollout phases

  1. Pilot (2–4 teams): CI writes to cache, developers use read-only cache settings. Run Build Doctor in CI and as a local dev hook.
  2. Expand (6–8 weeks): Add more teams, tune heuristics, add tests that detect cache-poisoning patterns.
  3. Org-wide: Make CANONICAL .bazelrc and toolchain pins required, add PR checks, and open the cache for a broader set of write clients.

Key metrics to instrument and track

  • P95 build/test times for common developer flows (changes to a single package, full test runs).
  • Remote cache hit rate: percent of actions served from the remote cache vs executed. Track daily and by repository. Aim high; a >90% hit rate on incremental builds is a realistic, high-leverage target for mature setups.
  • Time to first successful build (new hire): measure from checkout to successful test run.
  • Number of hermeticity regressions: count CI-detected non-hermetic checks per week.

How to collect these metrics

  • Use CI BEP exports to compute cache-hit ratios. Bazel prints per-invocation process summaries that indicate remote cache hits; programmatic BEP ingestion gives more reliable metrics.
  • Push derived metrics to a telemetry system (Prometheus / Datadog) and create dashboards:
    • Histogram of build times (for P50/P95)
    • Time-series of remote cache hit rate
    • Weekly count of Build Doctor violations per team

Guardrails and change control

  • Use a cache-write role: only designated CI runners (and a small set of trusted service accounts) can write to the authoritative cache.
  • Add a cache clear and rollback playbook to respond to cache poisoning: snapshot the cache state and restore from a pre-poisoned snapshot if necessary.
  • Gate merges with Build Doctor findings: start with warnings and move to hard failure for core rules once false positives are low.

Developer onboarding

  • Ship a developer start.sh that sets up the repo-level .bazelrc and installs bazelisk to pin bazel versions.
  • Provide one-page runbook: git clone ... && ./start.sh && bazel build //:all --profile=./first.profile.gz so new hires produce a baseline profile that CI can compare to.
  • Add a lightweight VSCode/IDE recipe that reuses the same repo-level flags so the dev environment mirrors CI.

Practical checklists and runbooks for immediate action

Baseline measurement (week 0)

  1. Run a canonical CI build for the main branch for seven consecutive runs and collect:
    • bazel build --profile=ci.prof //...
    • BEP exports (--bes_results_url or --build_event_json_file)
  2. Compute baseline P95 build times and cache-hit rate from BEP/CI logs.

Setup remote cache and clients (week 1)

  1. Deploy a cache (e.g., bazel-remote, Buildbarn, or managed service).
  2. Put canonical flags into repo .bazelrc and a CI-only .bazelrc.ci.
  3. Configure CI to be the primary writer; developers set --remote_upload_local_results=false in their per-user bazelrc.

Ship the Build Doctor (week 2)

  1. Add collector hooks to CI to capture aquery, profile, and BEP.
  2. Run Analyzer on CI invocations; surface findings as PR comments and nightly reports.
  3. Begin triage for top findings (e.g., genrules with network calls, nonhermetic toolchains).

Pilot & expand (weeks 3–8)

  1. Pilot with three squads and run Build Doctor in PRs as info-only.
  2. Iterate on heuristics and reduce false positives.
  3. Convert high-confidence checks into gating rules.

Runbook snippet: respond to a cache-poison incident

  • Step 1: Identify corrupted outputs via BEP and Build Doctor reports.
  • Step 2: Quarantine suspect cache prefixes and flip CI to write to a fresh cache namespace.
  • Step 3: Roll back to last-known-good cache snapshot and re-run canonical CI builds to repopulate.

Quick rule: make CI the source of truth for cache writes during rollout and keep destructive cache administration actions auditable.

Sources

Hermeticity | Bazel - Definition of hermetic builds, benefits, and guidance on identifying non-hermetic behavior.

Remote Caching - Bazel Documentation - How Bazel stores action metadata and CAS blobs, flags like --remote_cache and --remote_download_outputs, and disk-cache options.

bazelbuild/remote-apis (GitHub) - The Remote Execution API specification and list of clients/servers implementing the protocol.

JSON Trace Profile | Bazel - --profile, bazel analyze-profile, and how to generate and inspect JSON trace profiles for critical-path analysis.

buildbuddy-io/buildbuddy (GitHub) - An example BEP and remote-cache ingestion solution that demonstrates how build event data and cache metrics can be surfaced to teams.

title: Why does a sprite selection border disappear in Windows high contrast?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Make sprite selection and focus survive the user's forced-colors mode. A shadow-only selection ring can disappear when the browser replaces author colors or suppresses shadows. Adapt the controls narrowly instead of disabling the user's display preference for the whole gallery.

Key Takeaways

  • Use structural cues for selection and visible focus.
  • Inspect controls in the actual forced-colors environment.
  • Keep the artwork's presentation separate from control affordances.

A decorative shadow can carry essential state accidentally

The MDN forced-colors reference documents browser adjustments, including shadow handling. An interface that relies entirely on a glow can lose its only visible selection cue.

This does not imply every raster sprite is recolored by the browser. Inspect the actual elements and properties involved. The state indicator surrounding the image may fail while the image itself remains unchanged.

Distinguish selection from focus

Selection tells the reviewer which frame or action will be acted on. Focus identifies the current keyboard location. Both can matter at once. The W3C visible-focus guidance addresses the latter; it does not automatically implement selection.

Use a visible border, outline, text label, or other supported cue that remains perceivable. Avoid relying only on the difference between two custom background colors. Prefer native semantic controls when they fit the task.

Review the meaningful boundary against its actual adjacent colors with non-text contrast guidance. The relevant colors can differ from the normal theme after the user's preference is applied.

Example: the selected attack card

A card uses a teal box shadow when selected. Its plain border is intentionally transparent. In forced colors, the shadow no longer provides the expected cue, so the reviewer cannot tell whether Walk or Attack will be downloaded.

A proposed repair keeps a real border for the selected state and a separate visible focus treatment. A textual Selected label can reinforce the distinction. Test whether moving focus to the download button leaves the selected action understandable.

Do not broadly apply a forced-color opt-out to restore the original design. That can remove display adjustments the user relies on. If the artwork needs a controlled preview surface, isolate that requirement and retain the surrounding controls' support.

Acceptance with user preferences active

Run the review task using the supported operating-system and browser combination. Select a frame, move focus away, switch actions, and activate a control. Verify that both selection and focus are understandable rather than judging a static screenshot alone.

Record the environment and any targeted CSS adjustment. A normal dark theme is not the same test as a real forced-colors mode, and a screenshot with simulated recoloring does not establish equivalent behavior.

This is a proposed browser-interface check. No operating-system setting, CSS change, or keyboard task was executed for this article. It does not claim standards conformance from one visual cue or recommend changing the production sprite's palette to repair a review-control defect.

Related workflow

See game ui animation state screen reader feedback for the adjacent task. Carry the animation handoff checklist with the release, and use the art reference board to retain visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: Provisioning Robust and Efficient LiDAR Perception for Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2610.27617v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LiDAR-based 3D object detection is a core perception service for autonomous driving, but deployment requires robustness to point-cloud corruption while meeting latency and memory requirements. Existing approaches address robustness and resource efficiency separately, resulting in compact detectors that are fragile under corruption or robust detectors that remain costly to deploy. We therefore formulate LiDAR perception provisioning as constructing a detector that remains accurate under point-cloud corruptions while meeting constraints on inference latency and peak GPU memory. To achieve robustness, we first craft corrupted samples that mimic extreme weather conditions. Then we train candidate detectors offline by ordering clean and corrupted samples by perturbation sensitivity, through which detectors learn more from hard corrupted samples. We estimate perturbation sensitivity using an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors by tracking changes in confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections. To improve efficiency, we narrow the network and use offline neighborhood-density measurements to determine how many points and neighbors each sampling stage processes. We evaluate our method using AP (Average Precision) under clean and corrupted conditions, inference latency, and peak allocated GPU memory. On KITTI for Car detection with PointRCNN, our method improves Moderate AP under corruption by 3.32 points over the original detector while reducing mean latency by 19.8% and peak allocated GPU memory by 53.9%. Across two datasets, two detector architectures, and three object classes, our method improves AP under corruption by 4.03 points on average over the corresponding original detectors, while reducing mean inference latency and peak allocated GPU memory by 14.4% and 38.0%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/drunklibai/robust-efficient-lidar-perception.

title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.27047v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

title: Decomposed Relation Extraction from Aviation Accident Narratives: Evaluating Transformer-Based Safety Knowledge Discovery under Relational Sparsity
description:
arXiv:2610.27013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relation extraction from aviation accident narratives is challenging because genuine safety relations are sparse among possible concept pairs. This study evaluates a decomposed framework separating relation classification from concept identification. A benchmark of 300 National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) narratives containing 2,524 unique concept-text nodes was expanded into 21,038 ordered candidate pairs, with only 248 (1.18%) representing RESULTS_IN or CONTRIBUTES_TO relations. A TF-IDF Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) and weighted RoBERTa classifier were developed using an independent graph-annotated resource with hard-negative sampling and frozen before sealed evaluation. Development Macro-F1 scores of 0.4738 (SVM) and 0.4809 (RoBERTa) declined to 0.2741 and 0.2420 under exhaustive evaluation, with Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.0128 and 0.0197. False positives dominated: the SVM recovered 96 reference relations but generated 7,018 false positives, while RoBERTa recovered 125 but generated 9,824. Post-test diagnostics revealed overlapping RoBERTa confidence distributions and false positives even within valid relation-category directions. Complementary end-to-end SmolLM2 evaluation identified missed and unsupported relations alongside malformed outputs. These findings demonstrate that known concept endpoints do not guarantee reliable relation extraction and that sampled-negative development performance may poorly reflect exhaustive evaluation. Controlling false positives and managing candidate-space sparsity remain essential for aviation safety knowledge extraction.

title: Declarative Go CLIs with Commandment
description:
Over the last seven years in IT consulting, I have built more than 50 CLIs for customers and projects. I spent a lot of that time refining workflows around Cobra and Viper, trying to make CLI authoring feel as clean and idiomatic as the rest of the Go around it. I never quite got the workflow I wanted.

There was no single breaking point. The same kinds of friction just kept showing up. I wanted flags and arguments to become ordinary Go values once they reached the application. I got tired of defining the same idea again because help, completion, configuration, or tests needed it. I wanted new capabilities to fit the CLI instead of feeling bolted on. Setup order should only matter when order is actually part of the CLI's meaning.

I also spend a lot of time with Kubernetes and Terraform, so declarative systems were already a natural way for me to think. You declare relationships, validate them, and let the system derive the consequences. After years of trying to improve my CLI workflow, I stopped thinking the remaining friction was another convention I had failed to discover. I thought the underlying authoring model was the constraint.

That line of thinking became Commandment, a declarative CLI framework for Go.

Meet alienctl

I'll use a small fictional CLI called alienctl throughout the article. It has two commands.

$ alienctl scan mars
scanning mars

$ ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH=2 alienctl abduct --beam-strength 4 cow
abducting cow with beam strength 4

BeamStrength has a static default of 1. The host environment can contribute 2 through ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH. The user can contribute 4 through --beam-strength. The accepted value must also be between 1 and 10.

That one value captures the broader problem I kept running into. The flag spelling can live in parser setup, help and completion can need their own description of it, configuration can separately decide whether the flag beats the environment, and tests can encode the same precedence again. Each piece can be reasonable on its own while the same fact ends up with several owners.

Commandment takes a different approach. Application code declares semantic relationships in ordinary Go. Compile validates them and produces an immutable Application, and later operations read from that application instead of rebuilding the CLI's meaning. That's what I mean by declarative here. It does not mean YAML or struct tags, and it does not replace ordinary Go control flow.

Definition -> Compile -> immutable Application

type abductConfig struct {
    Target       string
    BeamStrength int
}

abductCmd := cli.Command[abductConfig]{
    Name: "abduct",
    Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[abductConfig]) {
        cb.Arguments.String(&cb.Config.Target, "target")

        beamStrength := cb.Values.Int(&cb.Config.BeamStrength)
        cb.Values.Default(beamStrength, 1)
        cb.Values.Environment(beamStrength, "ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH")
        cb.Flags.ValueFor(beamStrength).Long("beam-strength")
        cb.Rule.Between(beamStrength, 1, 10)
    },
    Run: func(_ context.Context, cfg *abductConfig) error {
        fmt.Printf(
            "abducting %s with beam strength %d\n",
            cfg.Target,
            cfg.BeamStrength,
        )
        return nil
    },
}

The root also declares a simpler scan command.

type scanConfig struct {
    World string
}

var definition = cli.Definition[struct{}]{
    Name: "alienctl",
    Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[struct{}]) {
        scanCmd := cli.Command[scanConfig]{
            Name: "scan",
            Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[scanConfig]) {
                cb.Arguments.String(&cb.Config.World, "world")
            },
            Run: func(_ context.Context, cfg *scanConfig) error {
                fmt.Printf("scanning %s\n", cfg.World)
                return nil
            },
        }
        cb.Subcommands.Command(scanCmd)
        cb.Subcommands.Command(abductCmd)
    },
}

The separate scanConfig and abductConfig types are deliberate. Each command owns the Go state its handler actually needs instead of contributing fields to one universal root configuration. Commandment's declarations stay ordinary, statically typed Go. The design does not depend on reflection-driven struct or tag decoding.

The process entrypoint is ordinary Go too.

app, err := cli.Compile(definition)
if err != nil {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(1)
}

if err := app.RunFromProcess(context.Background()); err != nil {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(cli.ExitCode(err))
}

For that invocation, the same destination has three candidate values.

static default  -> 1
environment     -> 2
flag            -> 4
resolved value  -> 4

The handler never sees a parser object or a bag of raw strings. It gets an ordinary int. That was one of the things I wanted from the start. The CLI boundary is textual, but application code should work with typed Go values.

int is only the built-in case. An application-defined Go type can use a ValueCodec[T] to define how it crosses the textual CLI boundary. Flags, environment input, defaults, resolution, and inspection can all work with that typed destination instead of inventing separate string representations.

The default, environment variable, flag, and range rule all point at the same typed destination. There is no second BeamStrength definition for configuration or validation.

Help and completion use the compiled application

The compiled application already has enough information to render help.

$ ./alienctl --help
Usage:
  alienctl [flags] <command>

Commands:
  scan
  abduct
  help        Show help.
  completion  Generate shell completion source

Flags:
  --help  Show help.
  -h      Show help.

The abduct command is available through the intrinsic help action as well.

$ ./alienctl help abduct
Usage:
  alienctl abduct [flags] <target>

Arguments:
  <target>

Flags:
  --beam-strength VALUE, --beam-strength=VALUE

I did not define a second command-and-flag model for help. The compiled application already knows the command, positional argument, and flag spelling, so help can present them without another description of the CLI.

Completion uses the same grammar. With incomplete input ab, the application can determine what can legally come next.

completion, err := app.Complete(ctx, cli.CompletionRequest{
    Args: []string{"ab"},
    Cursor: cli.CompletionCursor{
        Argument: 0,
        Byte:     2,
    },
})

For this application, the completion result contains abduct.

abduct

The completion request is not tied to a shell. Shell integration adapts the semantic result for a concrete client without defining another command language.

The compiled application still has the grammar, so execution, help, and completion all use it.

Cobra already does this part well

If you use Cobra, this part should be familiar. Cobra already gives Go applications an executable command model with arguments and flags, generated help, and shell completion.

Viper can sit alongside it as a configuration registry, binding command-line flags and environment variables and resolving multiple configuration sources with an explicit precedence order. In the example above, Cobra + Viper can also resolve the effective value to 4.

Commandment is not a feature-for-feature replacement for Viper. Its boundary is the CLI's semantic model. Broader application configuration can stay in ordinary application code. When external configuration affects CLI semantics, it crosses that boundary as typed input instead of becoming another model of the CLI.

What pushed me toward Commandment was the authoring model. After years of writing CLIs, I was tired of carrying setup knowledge across declarations, follow-up mutations, bindings, lifecycle hooks, and initialization timing. Cobra and Viper can be wrapped and organized carefully. I wanted the relationships themselves to be the source of truth.

Commandment validates those relationships during compilation. Order affects behavior only when order is part of the model. Dependencies between semantic values are declared too, so Commandment can validate scope and cycles and derive evaluation order from the dependency graph instead of callback timing.

A typical Cobra + Viper arrangement separates those responsibilities roughly like this.

Cobra / pflag
    command grammar
    flags
    help
    completion

Viper
    configuration sources
    precedence
    effective configuration

application code
    application-specific policy

             versus

Commandment

BeamStrength destination
    <- default 1
    <- environment ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH
    <- flag --beam-strength
    <- rule Between(1, 10)

             Compile
                |
                v
      immutable Application
                |
       +--------+--------+
       |        |        |
      Run    Inspect   Complete
                |
          semantic tests

Both approaches can produce 4. With Commandment, the application still knows why 4 won.

Inspecting why the flag won 

$ ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH=2 alienctl abduct --beam-strength 4 cow
abducting cow with beam strength 4

A terminal-output test can prove that the program printed 4, but it cannot distinguish normal flag precedence from an ignored environment value, a handler overwrite, or a fallback that happened to produce the same integer.

Because Commandment retained the invocation semantics, Inspect can analyze explicit invocation input without executing the selected handler. The clitest package can assert those observations directly.

func TestBeamStrengthFlagWins(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()

    app := clitest.Compile(t, definition)
    beamStrength := clitest.Command("abduct").Flag("--beam-strength").Value()
    request := cli.InspectionRequest{
        Env: cli.Env{{
            Name:  "ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH",
            Value: "2",
        }},
        Args: []string{"abduct", "--beam-strength", "4", "cow"},
    }
    clitest.Inspect(t.Context(), app, request).Require(t,
        clitest.InspectionReady(),
        beamStrength.Text("4"),
        beamStrength.ContributedBy(cli.ValueProducerKindFlag),
    )
}

That test proves both the effective value and the winning producer.

effective value  = 4
winning producer = flag

The default, environment input, and flag are three producers for one semantic destination. Resolution chooses the effective contribution and retains its provenance.

The test does not recreate Commandment's precedence rules. It asks the compiled application what happened.

Parsing does not erase the reason behind the result. Inspect can explain it later without running the handler or inferring semantics from presentation text.

One semantic authority does not mean one representation

One semantic authority does not require one giant data structure or one implementation path for everything.

Help, completion, inspection, diagnostics, schema, reference data, and runtime value state have different consumers and different lifetimes. They deserve different representations.

A semantic fact should still have one authority. Other operations and artifacts can project that fact for their own purpose, but they should not silently redefine it.

Definition
    |
    | Compile
    v
immutable Application
    |
    +-- Run / RunFromProcess --> execution and intrinsic actions such as help
    +-- Complete -----------> semantic completion
    +-- Inspect ------------> invocation-specific observation
    `-- Schema -------------> detached static artifact

Execution, help, completion, inspection, and schema need different representations, but they should agree on the command and value semantics they share.

That is the design I had been trying to get to. Handlers receive typed Go values, each CLI fact has one owner, and help, completion, inspection, and tests reuse the compiled model. Setup order only matters when the model says it matters.

When would I use this instead of Cobra?

Cobra fits well when the main job is an executable command tree with commands, arguments, flags, dispatch, help, and completion. Pairing it with Viper can also provide configuration through environment variables, defaults, files, and explicit precedence.

Commandment is aimed at CLIs where the command tree is only part of the problem. Typed resolution, provenance, and policy may also need to stay coherent across execution, completion, diagnostics, tooling, and tests.

Cobra can implement the behavior shown in this article. The decision is whether a command tree plus configuration registry is enough semantic authority for the CLI you are building.

For a CLI dominated by routing, flags, help, and completion, Cobra is probably the smaller choice. Commandment starts to earn its extra machinery when you need to ask the compiled CLI why a value resolved the way it did, project the same accepted semantics into tooling, or test those semantics without recreating them.

At that point, I would rather have one source of CLI meaning feeding several views than several reasonable systems that can slowly drift apart.

Commandment RC1

Commandment is now in its RC1 review period and requires Go 1.27.1. I am using this release-candidate period to get the API in front of people building real Go CLIs before I finalize v1.0.0.

The source, examples, and documentation are all in the Commandment repository.

If you try Commandment on an existing Go CLI, I'd especially like to hear what gets simpler, what stays awkward, and anything in the API that you think should change before v1.0.0 is finalized.
