title: REM: What to Store, When to Recall, What to Forget in Experience Memory for Coding Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27377v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. Retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether the agent needs an experience, at which point, or for how long. We introduce REM (Reusable Experience Memory), a framework that manages the memory lifecycle from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions. What to store: each completed trajectory is consolidated into a phase-structured document, two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory. When to recall: the document is injected at the start of the task; the costlier implementation record is withheld until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling. What to forget: the record is evicted after a single exposure. On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM retrieves the related trajectory more accurately than every state-of-the-art memory system (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and improves, in every replicate, end-task resolution (27.6% vs. 24.9%) at 17% lower cost. Injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory, even when oracle-retrieved, does not. Ablating any of the three decisions reduces resolution. Altogether, these results demonstrate that the bottleneck in experience reuse is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, opening a control-theoretic perspective on agent memory.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

title: SuperClip Pyramid for Video Temporal Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.26925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.

title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.

title: PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation
description:
arXiv:2610.27374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural image codecs face a fundamental trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality. Distortion-optimized codecs preserve pixel-wise fidelity but produce blurred reconstructions at low bitrates, whereas generative codecs leverage learned priors to improve perceptual quality but tend to exhibit saturating PSNR at higher bitrates and require separate models for different bitrate targets. We propose PerQ, which reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we define the quantization cell as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols and derive a transport bound showing that reconstructions from this cell remain within a rate-determined radius of the codec output. This motivates performing generative reconstruction within the codec-induced quantization cell, rather than sampling from an unconstrained image prior. PerQ implements this principle by attaching a rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator to a frozen, multi-rate distortion-optimized backbone, enabling perceptual enhancement while preserving the backbone's coding performance. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 show that PerQ achieves perceptual performance comparable to generative codecs such as MS-ILLM in LPIPS and FID, while maintaining competitive PSNR relative to distortion-optimized codecs such as ELIC. A single model checkpoint supports a wide bitrate range with fast decoding, and the compensator provides consistent gains across three different backbones. The implementation is available at https://jasminepp.github.io/PerQ/.

title: AnomalyJev: Towards Evaluating Image Anomaly Explanations via Claim-Level Verification
description:
arXiv:2610.27565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based anomaly detection (AD) methods can generate textual explanations that help interpret their predictions. However, reliably and efficiently evaluating these explanations remains challenging. While LLM judges can assess explanations through structured rubrics, they often require substantial token generation, making evaluation costly and difficult to scale. We instead propose to anchor evaluation in the available ground truth by extracting verifiable claims from each explanation and verifying them against the corresponding annotations. We instantiate this idea as AnomalyJev, a lightweight framework that extracts verifiable claims from contextualised representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer based heads, without token generation. The claims are then verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness. For evaluation, we construct a human-annotated set of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings. Despite its compact design, AnomalyJev achieves stronger agreement with human annotators than most open MLLM judges and approaches that of flagship MLLM judges, at a fraction of their runtime and resources.

title: Running Claude Code with Ollama and Local Models
description:
Claude Code + Ollama: Coding with a Local Model

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads your project, edits files, and runs commands from the terminal. With Ollama, you can run it on a model hosted on your own machine instead of in the cloud.

Why local models?

  • Your code never leaves your machine
  • No API costs
  • Works offline

In this guide, you'll install Claude Code, run it inside IntelliJ IDEA, connect it to Ollama, and test it on a small Java project.

Step 1: Install Claude Code

Install it globally with npm:

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Then open a terminal and run:

claude

If the Claude Code prompt appears, the installation worked.

Step 2: Run It Inside IntelliJ IDEA

You don't need to leave your IDE. Open your project in IntelliJ, open the built-in terminal (View → Tool Windows → Terminal), and run:

claude

Claude Code now has access to your project files and works right next to your code.

Step 3: Connect It to Ollama

Ollama exposes an Anthropic-compatible API, so Claude Code can talk to a local model.

1. Install Ollama
Ollama lets you download and run language models on your own machine. Your code never leaves your computer and there is no per-request cost.

On https://ollama.com you can create a free account. The dashboard shows your free quota for cloud models. For the rest of this tutorial (100% local), it isn't required.

2. Pull a coding model:

ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

3. Point Claude Code at Ollama:

export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
claude --model qwen3.5:9b

On Windows PowerShell, use $env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="ollama" and $env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434" instead of export.

Alternatively, let Ollama handle the setup with one command, using --model

ollama launch claude --model qwen3.5:9b

Step 4: Build a Demo Project

Let's test the setup with a small Java project: a console task manager.

Create an empty Java project in IntelliJ, open the terminal, start Claude Code, and give it this prompt:

Create a simple Java console app: a task manager. Users can add,
list, complete and delete tasks. Save tasks to a text file so they
persist. Keep it to 2-3 classes.

Claude Code will plan the work, create the files, fix the errors, and ask for your permission before making changes. Approve the actions and watch it work.

Then run the app and try it out:

Notice that it doesn't only generate code. It also creates the files, runs the program, and fixes its own errors.

Cloud vs Local: Quick Comparison

Cloud Claude Local model (Ollama)
Privacy Code is sent to the API Stays on your machine
Cost Subscription / API Free
Speed Fast Depends on your hardware
Quality Highest Good for small tasks

Conclusion

Claude Code with Ollama is a practical way to try agentic coding without sending your code anywhere, as long as your machine can handle the model. Start with a small project like this one, then try it on your own code.

Thanks for reading!

title: AWS KMS Key Policies: The Access Model That Trips Up Everyone
description:
Day 13/60 -- AWS KMS key policies.

The single most important thing to understand: KMS key policies override IAM policies. If the key policy does not grant access, IAM cannot grant it. This is different from S3, Lambda, and most other AWS services.

Every customer managed key needs this in the policy:

# Create a KMS key with a policy that separates admin from usage
KEY_ID=$(aws kms create-key \
  --description "app-encryption-key" \
  --query 'KeyMetadata.KeyId' \
  --output text)

# Grant encrypt/decrypt to the app role only
aws kms create-grant \
  --key-id $KEY_ID \
  --grantee-principal arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/app-service \
  --operations Encrypt Decrypt GenerateDataKey

# Add an alias for human-readable reference
aws kms create-alias \
  --alias-name alias/app-encryption \
  --target-key-id $KEY_ID

# Verify key rotation is enabled
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id $KEY_ID
aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id $KEY_ID

Without it, IAM policies in your account have zero effect on that key. Miss it and you call AWS Support.

Practical tip: Use kms:ViaService conditions to restrict which AWS services can use a key:

{
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "kms:ViaService": "rds.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"
    }
  }
}

This ensures your database encryption key can only be used through RDS, not directly by someone with Decrypt permissions.

Audit your existing keys with:

for key in $(aws kms list-keys --query 'Keys[].KeyId' --output text); do
  echo "=== $key ==="
  aws kms get-key-policy --key-id $key --policy-name default
done

Check that every key has the root statement and that admin/user roles are separated. This is Day 13 of the 60 Day Cloud Security Challenge.

title: Persist the practice stop before sending it
description:
Ending a piano practice session sounds like one POST. The tricky case is a lost response: the server may have accepted the stop while the client still sees a timeout. Retrying with a new event ID could turn one user action into two logical events.

In Pianory's account-backed practice flow, we persist the intent before sending it. queuePracticeStop writes both the session snapshot and the pending stop into one IndexedDB readwrite transaction. The pending record contains an ordered list of tick and stop events; each event keeps its ID and seconds. If a tick request had an uncertain response, we keep that same ID for replay.

The replay path sends the events in order. It rejects a failed HTTP response, validates that the stop acknowledgement belongs to the same session and contains a nonnegative integer duration, and only then calls completePracticeStop. That final method updates the session and removes the pending record in another IndexedDB transaction.

The useful invariant is small: an uncertain network result leaves a durable pending record. A later retry refers to the same logical event, rather than inventing a fresh one. The in-memory replay guard also coalesces concurrent sync requests within a client namespace.

A focused test covers replay and retry ordering. The end-to-end check uses a mock endpoint. This does not prove live D1 behavior, exactly-once delivery, or that every elapsed second survives every possible device failure. The contract is limited to account-backed sessions; guest sessions do not queue server practice stops.

This pattern applies beyond music practice: if the user says 'done', save that intent locally before treating the network as reliable.

AI assisted with drafting this article; I checked these claims against the repository and focused tests. I make Pianory, the piano-learning app behind this example.

title: Building a Multi-Role Platform in Spring Boot: What Five User Types Do to Your Design.
description:
Notes from building FarmNomad - an AgriTech platform where farmers, customers, drivers, food banks, and admins all share one system.

The interesting constraint in my dissertation project wasn't any single feature. It was that the platform had five different kinds of user, and each one effectively wanted the system to be a different product.

A farmer wants an inventory tool. A customer wants a shop. A driver wants a task list. A food bank (an "organisation" in the code) wants a feed of claimable surplus. An admin wants oversight of all of it. Five mental models, one backend.

This is a writeup of the design decisions that came out of that, with real code from the project.

The domain, briefly

FarmNomad connects rural UK farmers to buyers, delivery drivers, and food banks. A large share of farm-level surplus in the UK goes to waste not for lack of demand, but for lack of a system that coordinates the parties involved.

So the backend has to handle several flows over the same data:

  • Agricultural e-commerce (farmer lists produce, customer buys).
  • Surplus (products near expiry or overstocked, surfaced for redistribution).
  • Donations (a farmer flags surplus, an organisation claims it, a delivery order is generated).
  • Delivery coordination (a driver moves goods, whether a paid order or a donation).

Same actors, same inventory, different rules. The design job is keeping those rules from tangling.

Decision one: bounded contexts, not one big service package

The default instinct with an MVP is a single Spring Boot app with everything in one service package. The thing that pushed me away from it was noticing how little the flows actually share. A farmer's inventory workflow and an organisation's claim workflow have almost nothing in common except the Product entity - different lifecycles, different permissions, different reasons to change.

So the backend is organised into modules along domain boundaries: authentication, catalogue, orders, donations, surplus, and payments. The practical payoff showed up when I added the surplus-detection logic late in the build, it didn't require touching the ordering or donation code at all. The seams were already in the right places.

Decision two: enforce roles at the method, not the UI

With five roles, it's tempting to hide buttons on the frontend and call that access control. It isn't anyone with a token and curl can hit the endpoints directly. Role enforcement has to live on the server.

I use Spring Security's @PreAuthorize on the controller methods, so the rule sits right on the operation it governs:

@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('CUSTOMER')")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> placeOrder(Principal principal,
                                                @RequestBody OrderRequest req) { ... }

@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('FARMER')")
public ResponseEntity<SurplusResponse> createListing(Principal principal,
                                                     @RequestBody SurplusRequest req) { ... }

@PostMapping("/claim/{productId}")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ORGANISATION')")
public ResponseEntity<Void> claimSurplus(@PathVariable Long productId,
                                         Principal principal) { ... }

@PatchMapping("/{orderId}/status")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('DRIVER') or hasRole('ADMIN')")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> updateStatus(Principal principal,
                                                  @PathVariable Long orderId,
                                                  @RequestParam OrderStatus status) { ... }

A nice consequence is testability: you can assert that a CUSTOMER token gets a 403 on a farmer-only endpoint without standing up the whole application.

Where the rule is more than "which role," I push it into the service. For example, a single order should only be visible to the customer who placed it, the driver assigned to it, or an admin so the controller allows any authenticated user in, and the service decides. Crucially, an unauthorised requester is told the order doesn't exist rather than that they're forbidden, so order IDs can't be probed:

boolean isAdmin    = requester.getRole() == Role.ADMIN;
boolean isCustomer = order.getCustomer() != null
        && order.getCustomer().getId().equals(requesterId);
boolean isDriver   = order.getDriver() != null
        && order.getDriver().getId().equals(requesterId);

if (!isAdmin && !isCustomer && !isDriver) {
    throw new BadRequestException("Order not found");
}

Decision three: make the order lifecycle explicit, and guard the transitions

Orders move through states PENDING → ASSIGNED → IN_TRANSIT → DELIVERED and the transitions that should be impossible matter more than the ones that should be allowed.

The one I care about most: a driver should never be assigned to an order that hasn't been paid. Without that guard, a race between the payment webhook and an admin clicking "assign" could put a driver on the road for an order that never actually paid. So the assignment path checks both the state and the payment status before it does anything:

public OrderResponse assignDriver(Long orderId, Long driverId) {
    Order o = orderRepo.findById(orderId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BadRequestException("Order not found"));

    if (o.getStatus() != OrderStatus.PENDING ||
            o.getPaymentStatus() != PaymentStatus.PAID) {
        throw new BadRequestException("Only paid, pending orders can be assigned");
    }

    User driver = userRepo.findById(driverId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BadRequestException("Driver not found"));
    o.setDriver(driver);
    o.setStatus(OrderStatus.ASSIGNED);
    o.setUpdatedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    return toDto(orderRepo.save(o));
}

Keeping that rule in the service not in a controller, and certainly not only on the frontend means every path that assigns a driver is protected by the same check.

Decision four: two kinds of surplus, deliberately kept distinct

This one is a modelling choice I think is worth calling out. FarmNomad has surplus from two different sources, and they are not the same thing:

  • Auto-detected surplus - products that are near their best-before date or overstocked. This is derived at read time from the product data, not stored as its own rows.
  • A donation - a farmer explicitly flags a quantity of a product as surplus to give away; an organisation claims it; a delivery order is generated.

Early on it's tempting to collapse these into one concept. Keeping them separate turned out to be the right call, because they answer different questions. Auto-detected surplus is "what's at risk of going to waste right now?" A donation is "what has a farmer committed to give, and who's claiming it?" The donation flow even has a claim-and-order endpoint that claims the donation and spins up the delivery order in one step, which only makes sense because a donation is a concrete, stateful thing, where auto-detected surplus is a live view.

Decision five: idempotent payment webhooks

Payments go through Stripe Checkout, and Stripe delivers webhook events at least once so the checkout.session.completed handler has to be safe to run more than once for the same session. I key idempotency on the Stripe session ID: each order records the session that created it, and the handler short-circuits if that session was already processed.

String sessionId = minimalSession.getId();

// Stripe delivers at-least-once; the same event can arrive twice.
if (orderRepo.existsByStripeSessionId(sessionId)) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok("");   // already handled - exit quietly
}

I wrote this one up in more detail as its own post, because webhook idempotency is one of those things that's invisible in development and bites under real traffic.

The stack

Layer Choice
Backend Java, Spring Boot, Spring Security
Frontend React, Next.js, Redux Toolkit Query, TailwindCSS
Database PostgreSQL
Payments Stripe Checkout + Webhooks
Infra Docker, Vercel

As a solo developer building to a deadline, I leaned on modern tooling throughout the architecture, the modelling decisions, and the trade-offs above are mine; the tooling helped me move faster on everything around them.

FarmNomad is live at farmnomad.vercel.app, and it was built as the practical component of my MSc dissertation at the University of Greater Manchester, which was awarded a Distinction.

If you're building multi-role systems in Spring Boot, or working anywhere near AgriTech, I'd like to compare notes - LinkedIn or GitHub.

title: Views vs Materialized Views In PostgreSQL
description:
This one's short compared to some of the earlier topics in this series, but it's also one of those things that's easy to get backwards if you only skim the definitions once. A view and a materialized view sound like variations on the same idea, and syntactically they're not far apart, but they behave in genuinely different ways once you actually use them.

Where the confusion comes from

Say you've got a dashboard summary showing total venues per city, and it's built on a GROUP BY query that's a bit expensive — maybe it's joining against closures too, computing a few aggregates at once. Someone suggests "just make it a view," and that's reasonable advice, except it doesn't actually solve the performance problem people usually mean when they say that. A regular view doesn't cache anything. It just saves you from retyping the query.

The two, side by side 

CREATE VIEW active_venues AS
SELECT * FROM venues WHERE is_closed = FALSE;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW venue_stats AS
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS total FROM venues GROUP BY city;

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW venue_stats;

A regular VIEW is really just a stored query, nothing more. Every time you SELECT * FROM active_venues, Postgres runs the underlying query against venues again, live, right then. It's always current, because it's not storing anything — it's just a name attached to a query definition that gets substituted in and executed fresh each time.

A MATERIALIZED VIEW actually stores the result physically, like a real table. Reading from venue_stats is fast, because it's just reading stored rows, not recomputing anything. The trade-off is that it goes stale the moment the underlying data changes, and it stays stale until you explicitly run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW to recompute and re-store the result.

Picking one

Use a regular VIEW when the underlying query is cheap enough that running it live isn't a real cost, and when the data behind it absolutely needs to be current every time someone reads it. active_venues above is a good fit — filtering on a boolean is trivial for Postgres, there's no real performance reason to cache it, and you'd generally want to know immediately if a venue's status changed.

Use a MATERIALIZED VIEW when the query is genuinely expensive — heavy aggregation, several joins, something that takes real time to compute — and when the consumers of that data can tolerate it being slightly stale in exchange for speed. A dashboard's summary stats are the classic case: nobody's checking venue_stats expecting it to reflect a venue that closed thirty seconds ago, and recomputing that aggregation on every single page load for every user would be wasteful when refreshing it once every few minutes, or on some schedule, is perfectly acceptable.

Where this leaves you

The names sound similar, but the behavior isn't — a VIEW is a saved query that always runs live, a MATERIALIZED VIEW is a saved result that needs an explicit REFRESH to stay current. Picking between them comes down to one question: does this need to be live every time, or is a periodically refreshed snapshot good enough for what it's being used for.

Next up: window functions — a step past GROUP BY that lets you compute things like running totals and per-group rankings without collapsing your rows down to one per group.

title: How to Build a 3-State Uptime Dashboard from Metrics and Logs (Internally)
description:
Short answer: poll recent health metrics and structured logs, reduce them to green, yellow, or red, and keep the raw evidence one click away. For a small healthtech team, the least complex useful version is an internal page backed by two direct queries. It should expose telemetry cost beside operational status, because a dashboard that hides its own cost is unfinished.

Choice Recovery fit Cost attribution Operating burden
Infrai Recent metrics, logs, and error groups behind one API Per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata Polling and aggregation are yours
Datadog Specialist observability suite Dedicated product billing More platform surface to configure
Amazon CloudWatch Natural fit for AWS workloads AWS billing and log-ingestion accounting Strongest inside AWS
Grafana Cloud Flexible cross-source dashboards Separate hosted-service accounting More choices to own
Healthchecks.io Dead-man monitoring for jobs Separate specialist service Narrow complement for silent jobs

My recommendation is narrow: a team already consolidating backend calls should try Infrai for the recent-status query layer, because one key and one bill reduce credential and invoice glue, while per-call metadata gives the dashboard a direct cost-attribution trail. It is not a full incident-management system.

How should Node.js build an uptime dashboard from metrics and logs?

A checkout page needs a decision rule before it needs charts. I use three states because operators can act on them quickly:

  • Green: recent checks are healthy and there is no matching failure evidence.
  • Yellow: checks are degraded, stale, or mixed; an operator should inspect logs.
  • Red: the recent window shows a failed check, with logs available for triage.

This is deliberately modest. A 0/1 status signal says whether the checkout path worked. Structured logs explain which stage failed, such as eligibility, payment authorization, or order persistence. Error groups can connect an outage window to repeated exceptions for the same service. Do not pretend one signal answers all three questions.

For a healthtech checkout, keep sensitive payloads out of the status document. The UI needs a service name, timestamp, state, correlation identifier, and failure stage. It does not need a patient's name, order contents, or free-form clinical text. The available log interface also has no per-user deletion route, which makes it a poor home for data that may later need selective erasure.

The first trap is averaging. Ten successful checks can hide the one failure an operator cares about. Preserve the latest result and failure count separately, then define yellow and red from explicit product policy. Google's four golden signals are a useful check: errors and latency matter, but saturation and traffic can change how the same error rate should be read.

Keep it boring.

Three colors. Two evidence sources. One written policy.

Two criteria beat a feature checklist

The first criterion is recovery speed. Can an operator move from red status to a small set of relevant events without opening four consoles? Infrai puts recent metrics, logs, and error groups under the same key. Its public discovery surface describes 295 routes across 20 modules, including schemas and runnable TypeScript examples. That reduces client glue, but it does not remove the application work: there is no log subscription or batch export surface, so the admin page must poll direct queries and aggregate returned records itself.

The second criterion is cost attribution. Per-call metadata includes cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request identity across the native API conventions. That is more actionable than a month-end total when a team wants to ask which internal screen or recovery loop generated spend. One wallet and one bill also remove invoice reconciliation across backend capabilities routed through the platform. I care about that more than a transient unit price. Prices move. Plumbing lingers.

There is a hard boundary. These limitations matter: retention and cold-storage configuration are limited, so this design is for recent operational visibility, not long-term compliance reporting. It also has no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route. The polling process below updates an internal view; it is not an on-call system. That trade-off is acceptable for an admin panel only when another system owns paging.

Implement the 3-state poller

The query filters for these surfaces are not declared in discovery, so the client must not guess parameters such as service, from, or window. Query the documented routes as exposed, then inspect the returned schema from discovery before adapting record extraction. This TypeScript program makes both authenticated calls, handles rate limiting, surfaces real error bodies, and prints a compact snapshot.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

async function request(url: string, attempt: number): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      Accept: "application/json",
    },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return request(url, attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`${response.status} ${response.statusText}: ${body}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

async function queryMetrics(): Promise<unknown> {
  return request(`${baseUrl}/metrics/query`, 0);
}

async function searchLogs(): Promise<unknown> {
  return request(`${baseUrl}/logs/search`, 0);
}

const [metrics, logs] = await Promise.all([
  queryMetrics(),
  searchLogs(),
]);

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  checkedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  service: "checkout",
  evidence: { metrics, logs },
}, null, 2));

Run it with Node.js 20 or newer so fetch is available.

INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_your_key_here npx tsx checkout-status.ts

This stops before inventing a response shape. Once discovery confirms the current schemas, add a pure reducer that accepts normalized check records and returns one of the three states. Test it with fixed timestamps. Keep network code out of it. That split makes the red/yellow boundary reviewable and prevents a response change from silently rewriting operational policy.

Polling every few seconds by default is config bloat disguised as responsiveness. Choose the interval from the recovery objective and rate-limit budget. Record the last successful refresh separately; a stale green screen is not green. On 429, the example honors Retry-After when numeric and otherwise uses exponential backoff. A production process should add jitter if several replicas can poll together.

Where does each alternative win?

Choose Datadog when the team wants a specialist observability product, especially if managed alerting, tracing, or richer investigation workflows are requirements. Infrai exposes trace and span identifiers in logs but does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree. It also has no source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. Those are decisive gaps for some teams.

Choose Sentry when checkout exceptions, source-mapped stack traces, and application-error investigation dominate the job. Its specialist focus is a better match than this lightweight query layer when developers need crash context rather than a small service-status view.

CloudWatch is the pragmatic runner-up for an AWS-centered checkout. Keeping telemetry beside the workload can simplify ownership, and its published pricing explains log ingestion as a billed dimension. The trade is tighter coupling to the AWS operating model. Compare the bill using your own retention and ingestion pattern; a generic price table will age badly.

Grafana Cloud makes sense when cross-source visualization is the product requirement. Its flexibility is useful when the team already speaks the Grafana ecosystem. For a three-state admin page, that flexibility can mean more configuration than the decision warrants. Benchmark time-to-first-use with your real schema, not a demo dataset.

Add Healthchecks.io when the failure is silence: a reconciliation task, export, or scheduled payment job never ran. Infrai has no synthetic probe or heartbeat monitor, so ordinary logs cannot prove that a task which emitted nothing was supposed to execute. This is a complement, not a duplicate.

The selection rule is blunt. Use direct queries for recent internal visibility and explicit cost attribution. Use a specialist when alert delivery, deep traces, long retention, compliance export, replay, or silent-job detection belongs in the acceptance criteria.

No single winner.

Ship the recovery path, not just the colors

A status page earns its place when red leads somewhere. Put the correlation identifier and a bounded evidence view beside the state. Link repeated failures to an error group after the query response has been normalized. Give operators a timestamp for both the source event and dashboard refresh.

Then test failure handling. Return a 429 from a local stub and verify backoff. Return a non-JSON 403 body and verify the error remains visible. Freeze time and verify a stale success becomes yellow. These cheap tests target the awkward paths dashboard demos skip.

I would benchmark three numbers before choosing a provider: minutes from empty directory to first authenticated response, lines of adapter code after normalization, and credentials the service must rotate. Those are evaluation criteria, not claimed measurements. They expose integration cost without pretending every team values the same features.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the internal uptime page guide and verify the live schemas before writing the reducer.

Further reading

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing
  • Datadog documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Infrai log ingestion discovery

title: MatchCityLoc: Aerial Localization in LoD City Models via Surface Normal Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.27110v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments requires precise pose estimation. Because Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are often unreliable in cities, visual localization serves as a crucial complement. Within this domain, textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a lightweight and privacy-preserving substitute for heavy 3D textured meshes. However, localizing against abstract geometry is challenging. Existing pipelines typically score 2D silhouette overlaps, which can suffer from severe geometric ambiguities. We present MatchCityLoc, a framework that shifts this paradigm to direct feature matching from a noisy 6-DoF pose prior. By extracting surface normals from the query image using a zero-shot foundation model and matching them against rendered LoD normals, we establish explicit 3D-to-2D correspondences. This enables a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) pose solve, which we iteratively refine through a render-and-match loop. Experiments demonstrate strong pose recall and accurate translation and rotation among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods with very few renderings. By bridging the modality gap between aerial imagery and texture-free geometry, MatchCityLoc enables accurate localization using lightweight, privacy-preserving city models.

title: PRIMFLOW: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.27146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher's sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose \method, which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, \method learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that \method achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.

Using the deterministic open datasets published by Sourcey, we audited 105 probed API readiness profiles in agent-readiness.json and 557 vendor records in startup-credits.json anchored to the 2026-10-21 cryptographic release (sha256:95a216ee10b539d5c46c9788448b4962d91d0b92b9f48091deff6a9d46bce5e9).

Every observation in this analysis is reproducible against the live public JSON endpoints:

title: 5 quick checks to make a website load faster
description:
A slow website loses visitors before they read a single word. Here are five checks I run on almost every site, in the order I do them. None need special tools.

1. Measure before you change anything

Open Chrome DevTools, go to the Lighthouse tab and run a mobile report. Note the scores for Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Total Blocking Time. Without a starting number you can't tell whether a change helped.

2. Compress and resize images

Images are usually the heaviest part of a page.

  • Convert photos to WebP or AVIF.
  • Resize them to the size they are actually shown at. A 4000px photo in a 600px box wastes bandwidth.
  • Add loading="lazy" to images below the fold: 
<img src="team.webp" width="600" height="400" alt="Our team" loading="lazy">

Setting width and height also stops the page from jumping around as it loads.

3. Cut unused CSS and JavaScript

Open DevTools → Coverage and reload. It shows how much of each file is never used on that page. Remove unused libraries and load scripts that aren't needed immediately with defer:

<script src="app.js" defer></script>

4. Turn on caching and compression

  • Enable gzip or Brotli on the server.
  • Send Cache-Control headers so returning visitors don't re-download files that haven't changed.

5. Check your fonts

Every font weight is a separate file. Use only the weights you need, and add font-display: swap so text shows straight away instead of staying blank:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
}

Recheck

Run Lighthouse again and compare it with your first result. Most sites improve a lot from just the image and script steps.

What is the biggest speed problem you've run into? Let me know in the comments.

Issue

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the <namespace> segment in these queries.

Queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification. We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases.

Mitigation:

title: How to Build Retrieval Audit Logs for Internal Engineering PDFs in Go (Grounded)
description:
Short answer: build retrieval audit logs as an evidence ledger, not a transcript. For every answer over the PDF folder, pin the corpus revision, preserve the ordered chunk IDs returned by retrieval, record the citations selected by generation, and withhold any answer whose citations cannot be joined to that request's retrieval set.

Suppose the page fires at 02:17. The on-call sees a user report that an internal documentation answer cites release-runbook.pdf, page 18, but the active PDF has only 16 pages. CPU is quiet, latency is inside its objective, and the generator returned fluent prose. None of those signals answers the operational question: which indexed revision and which passages were allowed to support this answer?

The earlier signal should have been a failed evidence join.

Retrieval-augmented generation combines generated output with retrieved non-parametric memory, and the original RAG paper identifies provenance as a benefit of that arrangement. An application still has to turn provenance into an enforceable release rule. For this system, I would make citation validity a separate SLO from request availability — a response can be fast and syntactically valid while being unsuitable for release.

How should retrieval architecture govern audit logs for internal engineering documentation?

Start with governance, before picking an index or writing an event struct. Decide who may inspect a question, who may inspect retrieved PDF passages, how long each class of record survives, and which fields must remain usable after a serving component is replaced. A useful audit event needs enough information to reproduce the evidence boundary without copying every sensitive question, answer, and PDF passage into a second data store. Record a request ID, authenticated actor or calling service, event time, corpus snapshot ID, query digest, retrieval-policy version, ordered chunk IDs and scores, prompt-template version, answer digest, cited chunk IDs, validation result, latency, and final disposition.

Names are display data, not identity. release-runbook.pdf can be replaced while keeping the same filename, so derive a source revision from its content digest. A chunk identifier should also bind the source revision to a page range, chunking-policy version, and ordinal. That gives the evidence ledger stable handles across index rebuilds and makes a corpus snapshot a concrete manifest rather than a timestamp someone hopes is close enough.

Don't log credentials, authorization headers, or unrestricted extracted text. Auditability does not justify widening access to internal engineering documentation. If retention policy prohibits raw questions and answers, their digests plus access-controlled references can still support correlation and replay checks; if investigators must inspect content, keep that content behind the same authorization boundary as the source PDFs.

The retention classes don't have to match. Operational metrics can expire quickly, evidence events can remain for the investigation window, and source content can follow the documentation system's own policy. What matters is preserving the join keys for as long as the organization claims an answer is auditable. Deleting a PDF passage while retaining an event that points to it may satisfy an event-retention rule, but it no longer permits substantive replay; that limitation should be explicit.

Define a portable evidence contract in Go

The key invariant is deliberately narrow: every citation on a released answer must identify a chunk retrieved for that same request under the pinned corpus snapshot. This catches fabricated identifiers, stale cross-request citations, and broken correlation. It does not prove that the prose accurately represents the cited passage. That requires a separate evaluation of support, which is why one green citation_valid field must never be presented as total answer quality.

Keep that contract in application-owned fields rather than opaque component state. The following Go program hashes text that should not be copied into the event, checks citation membership and duplication, and emits one append-oriented JSON record. The sample data is illustrative; the invariant and portable identifiers are the parts to carry into production.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type RetrievedChunk struct {
    ID    string  `json:"id"`
    Score float64 `json:"score"`
}

type GeneratedAnswer struct {
    Text      string   `json:"text"`
    Citations []string `json:"citations"`
}

type AuditEvent struct {
    RequestID        string           `json:"request_id"`
    OccurredAt       time.Time        `json:"occurred_at"`
    CorpusSnapshot   string           `json:"corpus_snapshot"`
    RetrievalPolicy  string           `json:"retrieval_policy"`
    QueryDigest      string           `json:"query_digest"`
    Retrieved        []RetrievedChunk `json:"retrieved"`
    Citations        []string         `json:"citations"`
    AnswerDigest     string           `json:"answer_digest"`
    CitationValid    bool             `json:"citation_valid"`
    FinalDisposition string           `json:"final_disposition"`
}

func digest(value string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func validateCitations(retrieved []RetrievedChunk, citations []string) error {
    if len(citations) == 0 {
        return errors.New("answer has no citations")
    }

    allowed := make(map[string]struct{}, len(retrieved))
    for _, chunk := range retrieved {
        allowed[chunk.ID] = struct{}{}
    }

    seen := make(map[string]struct{}, len(citations))
    for _, citation := range citations {
        if _, ok := allowed[citation]; !ok {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q was not retrieved", citation)
        }
        if _, duplicate := seen[citation]; duplicate {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q is duplicated", citation)
        }
        seen[citation] = struct{}{}
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    retrieved := []RetrievedChunk{
        {ID: "runbook-digest:page-18:chunk-2:v3", Score: 0.84},
        {ID: "policy-digest:page-4:chunk-1:v3", Score: 0.79},
    }
    answer := GeneratedAnswer{
        Text:      "Production changes require the documented approval step.",
        Citations: []string{"runbook-digest:page-18:chunk-2:v3"},
    }

    validationErr := validateCitations(retrieved, answer.Citations)
    disposition := "released"
    if validationErr != nil {
        disposition = "withheld"
    }

    event := AuditEvent{
        RequestID:        "req-7f31",
        OccurredAt:       time.Now().UTC(),
        CorpusSnapshot:   "corpus-a17",
        RetrievalPolicy:  "hybrid-v3",
        QueryDigest:      digest("What approval is required for production changes?"),
        Retrieved:        retrieved,
        Citations:        answer.Citations,
        AnswerDigest:     digest(answer.Text),
        CitationValid:    validationErr == nil,
        FinalDisposition: disposition,
    }

    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(event); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if validationErr != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, validationErr)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Run it with:

go run main.go

Withholding is intentional. If the user interface must always return something, return a non-answer such as “No supported answer was found in the indexed documents” and record that disposition; don't let an uncited fallback bypass the same release rule. The catch is that strict withholding is not suitable when the workflow explicitly values partial discovery over a supported answer, such as exploratory search where users inspect source pages themselves. In that case, label the result as search output, expose the passages, and don't represent generated prose as grounded.

Make migration a replay test

A retrieval migration is acceptable only if old and new paths can be compared through the same evidence contract. Feed both paths the same pinned corpus snapshot and approved question set, then compare candidate membership, citation validity, and disposition. Score values may not be comparable across implementations, so don't declare a migration safe because two arbitrary decimals are close; compare the decisions the scores produce and retain each policy version.

The same replay gives the 02:17 responder a map. Group the affected audit events by corpus snapshot and retrieval-policy version, then compare those groups with the prior healthy window. If an impossible citation ID is absent from its request's ordered retrieval set, investigate request correlation and the release validator. If the expected page is absent from every candidate set, move earlier in the pipeline: PDF extraction, chunk identity, snapshot publication, or retrieval policy. If the page appears in the candidates but the answer does not cite it, move later: prompt assembly and support evaluation. These paths have different owners and rollback decisions. A single “RAG quality” alarm is weak operationally because it asks someone to reconstruct all of them under time pressure.

Build the replay suite from approved question-to-source-page mappings. Measure candidate-set success separately from answer support: did retrieval include an acceptable page, and did each released claim remain inside its cited evidence? A fluent answer can hide poor retrieval, while a good candidate set can be squandered later. Keeping the stages separate makes the alert actionable and keeps component owners from arguing over one blended score.

Migration exposes lock-in in a measurable way. If corpus snapshots, chunk identities, and audit events use an application-owned schema, the serving implementation can change without erasing historical meaning. If those identities exist only inside one index, migration requires preserving two interpretation systems or abandoning replay for older answers. Decide which loss is acceptable before ingestion starts.

One more trap deserves a short rule.

Don't replay against “latest.” Replay against the snapshot that served the request.

Budget retention and ownership before choosing components

Capacity planning follows the evidence path. Estimate ingestion demand from changed PDF bytes and pages per revision, index size from chunks per page and representation size, query demand from peak requests and candidates considered, and ledger retention from events per request times retained fields. Load-test publication separately from query serving. A large documentation update and a query spike consume different resources, and one shared concurrency limit couples two failure domains that the architecture can keep apart.

The build-versus-buy decision then follows the evidence contract rather than preceding it. A managed component can remove index operations from the team's on-call load; a self-hosted component can give the team tighter control over placement, retention, and change timing. Neither choice supplies auditability by itself.

Boundary Build and operate Managed component Decision test
PDF extraction and identity Control digest and chunk rules; own parser drift Reduce parser upkeep; accept the offered identity model Can an unchanged source revision reproduce the same chunk IDs?
Retrieval index Control placement and rollout; own capacity and recovery Transfer more operations; verify event export and version semantics Can a served result be tied to a pinned snapshot?
Evidence ledger Control schema, retention, and access; own durability Reduce storage operations; validate portability and deletion controls Can an investigator replay the join after the serving system changes?
Release validator Keep the invariant in application code Delegate only if behavior is testable and observable Can unsupported output be withheld before it reaches a user?

Stick with managed infrastructure when it exports the identifiers and version context the ledger requires, and the reduction in on-call work matters more than tuning freedom. Build or self-host the boundary when retention, placement, deterministic identity, or replay access cannot be met by the managed contract. A team with no capacity to operate an index should not self-host merely to gain theoretical control; an ownership boundary that routinely misses its SLO is not safer.

Set the page after the policy is testable

Only now is the alert definition defensible. Emit bounded state transitions such as retrieval_started, retrieval_completed, citation_validation_completed, answer_released, and answer_withheld. Outcome and policy version can be metric labels when their value sets are controlled. Request IDs, filenames, and chunk IDs should remain in traces or audit storage rather than metric labels because their value sets grow with requests and the corpus.

The instrumentation change is small: add the evidence-join result and its version context at the release boundary, then carry the same request ID through retrieval, validation, and disposition. The page can now say which invariant failed and which policy state served it. Earlier indicators — rising zero-result rate, a shift in candidate scores after a retrieval-policy change, or a snapshot falling behind its source manifest — belong in a non-paging warning path until replay evidence shows that they predict the release SLO.

I'm not sure any universal numeric threshold for citation-valid answers is defensible. Traffic volume, the base rate of questions the PDFs can answer, and the cost of withholding all change the paging trade-off. What resolves that uncertainty is replaying known questions against real corpus snapshots, observing the failure distribution, and choosing a window that corresponds to an action the on-call can actually take.

Page on sustained user harm: a breach in the objective for releasable, citation-valid answers. A single rejected answer should be withheld and counted, but paging on each rejection imposes a false-positive cost during sparse traffic and trains responders to ignore the signal.

This returns us to the page. A threshold set too tightly wakes the on-call for isolated, correctly withheld requests; one set too loosely lets a sustained grounding regression reach users before anyone acts. The right alert is the narrowest sustained breach that maps to a documented rollback, snapshot repair, or policy rollback — and the audit ledger is what tells the responder which action fits.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: Amazon Connect Customer launches two new layouts for agent workspace
description:
Amazon Connect Customer now offers two different layouts that optimize screen space on the agent workspace. Contact center agents spend hours each day in the agent workspace, which includes all of the contact controls and applications they need to resolve customer issues. Agents who handle different channels and workflows want the workspace arranged differently, so that they can quickly read, respond, and access their tools. Now, administrators can choose the best layout for each team, maximizing agent efficiency and satisfaction.

On the Modern layout, contact controls are at the top of the workspace, maximizing screen space for the applications beneath during voice calls. When agents handle chat, email, and task contacts on the Modern layout, they now have a taller, wider area to read and respond. The Classic layout offers a familiar experience for agents already using the agent workspace, now with contact controls that expand and contract by channel and a resizable agent assist application. Administrators can assign the Modern layout to a team migrating from another agent desktop with controls at the top, while teams already familiar with the agent workspace can use the Classic layout.

You can use the new layouts for the Amazon Connect Customer agent workspace in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more and get started, see the agent workspace in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

title: Codebase X-Ray
description:
I Built Codebase X-Ray: Visualizing Python Codebases and Their Dependencies

Have you ever opened an unfamiliar Python repository and spent more time figuring out how its files connect than actually understanding the code?

That was the problem I wanted to tackle with Codebase X-Ray.

It's a developer tool I'm building to analyze Python repositories and turn their structure and dependencies into an interactive visual graph.

Why I Built It

When working with a multi-file project, understanding the relationships between modules, functions, classes, and imports can be difficult. Jumping between files isn't always the best way to understand the overall architecture.

I wanted a tool that could provide a visual starting point for exploring an unfamiliar codebase.

How It Works

Codebase X-Ray combines static code analysis with an interactive frontend.

1. Python AST Analysis

The backend uses Python's built-in ast module to inspect source files without executing them.

It extracts information such as functions, classes, and imports, which forms the basis of the repository's structural representation.

2. Dependency Extraction

The scanner identifies import relationships between files and builds dependency information that can be visualized.

Dynamic imports and some external dependencies can be difficult to resolve statically, so the results aren't intended to represent every possible runtime relationship.

3. Interactive Graph Visualization

The frontend uses React and React Flow to display relationships between code elements. Dagre helps arrange the graph layout.

Instead of navigating every file individually, developers can explore the structure visually.

4. Technology Stack

  • Python for AST-based analysis
  • FastAPI for the backend API
  • React and Vite for the frontend
  • React Flow for graph visualization
  • Dagre for graph layout

Codebase X-Ray in Action

1. Repository Scanning and System Metrics

The first step is scanning a repository. Codebase X-Ray accepts a GitHub repository URL or a local directory path and analyzes the Python source files.

Once scanning completes, the dashboard displays key metrics, including the number of Python files discovered, import relationships extracted, symbols identified, and parsing errors encountered.

In this example, the scanner processed 23 Python files, identified 15 import relationships, extracted 48 symbols, and reported zero parsing errors.

2. Interactive Dependency Graph

After scanning, the extracted information is presented as an interactive dependency graph. Each node represents a code element or file in the visualization, while the connecting edges represent import relationships.

Files are organized into color-coded project groups, making it easier to distinguish different parts of a repository and understand how they connect.

The graph supports navigation and zooming, allowing developers to explore the structure of a codebase visually instead of relying entirely on manual file-by-file inspection.

3. Inspecting Individual Files

The graph provides an overview of the repository, but sometimes you need to focus on a particular file.

Selecting a file opens the file inspector, which displays its path, project group, and available dependency information. In this example, the inspector shows app.py and its outgoing import to utils.py.

This makes it easier to investigate how a file depends on other modules and navigate the codebase with more context.

What's Next?

I'm continuing to improve Codebase X-Ray, particularly its ability to make larger codebases easier to explore.

I'm also considering optional local AI integration through Ollama to generate code summaries and explain dependency relationships without making AI a requirement for the core scanner.

Check Out the Project

GitHub repository: https://github.com/sreevatsarajesh/Codebase_XRay

I'd Love Your Feedback

  • What would you want to see in a codebase visualization tool?
  • Which parts of understanding an unfamiliar repository take you the most time?
  • Would AI-generated explanations of code relationships be useful, or would you prefer purely static analysis?

Thanks for reading!

title: HierDTA: Hierarchical Structure-Aware Representation Learning for Drug--Target Affinity Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.27001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Drug--target affinity (DTA) prediction plays an important role in computer-aided drug discovery, where reliable computational models can help prioritize compound--protein pairs before experimental validation. A key challenge in DTA prediction is to effectively mine multi-level molecular information from drug structures while accurately modeling the binding-site environment of target proteins. To address these issues, we introduce HierDTA, a hierarchical structure-aware framework for DTA prediction. \textcolor{black}{HierDTA represents each drug as an atom--motif heterogeneous graph and introduces an augmentation module that propagates functional-motif semantics to the corresponding atoms. For proteins, kinase-domain structures are converted into residue interaction graphs. The resulting atom and residue representations are integrated using cross-attention to capture pair-specific relationships, while molecule fingerprints and pretrained ESM-2 embeddings provide complementary global information. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HierDTA achieves superior performance on the Davis dataset across all metrics and attains the highest \(r_m^2\) of 0.791 on KIBA. It also exhibits strong generalization under cold-start settings, particularly on KIBA, where MSE is reduced by 21.7\% in the unseen-protein scenario. Ablation study and interpretability analysis supported the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components.} Case studies further showed that HierDTA provided early enrichment of candidate bioactive compounds. These results indicate that HierDTA is an effective framework for affinity prediction and target-specific virtual screening.

title: 15 of 16 Mac UI tests failed: what SwiftUI on macOS taught us
description:
Our notes app, MindPage, is one SwiftUI codebase for iPad, iPhone and Mac. The iPhone and iPad UI tests were green. Then we ran the Mac suite, which drives the real app with mouse and keyboard through XCUITest. 15 of 16 tests failed. By the end of the day it was 16 of 16, alongside 43 iPhone and 44 iPad tests.

Roughly half the failures were real Mac bugs, and half were the tests. Here is each one, with the cause, because most of them are SwiftUI-on-macOS behaviours that aren't obvious if you build iPad first.

The scoreboard

Run Passing What changed
1 1 / 16 first Mac run
2 6 / 16 sidebar width, a button label, a missing test ID
3 9 / 17 choose() skips disabled items, text queries narrowed, ⌘V fixed (+1 temporary probe test)
4 15 / 16 undo version, pen bar hit area, photo accessibility, Search/Summarize/Word lookups
5 16 / 16 last query narrowed

Real bug 1: toolbar items silently moved to the overflow menu

On macOS, .toolbar items attached to a NavigationSplitView sidebar render in the toolbar above the sidebar. Our sidebar was 148 pt wide. Three buttons plus the system "Hide Sidebar" button didn't fit next to the traffic lights, so macOS moved New folder, sync status and Settings into "more toolbar items". No warning, no layout error.

#if os(macOS)
.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(min: 300, ideal: 300)
#endif

230 pt was not enough; the window controls take about 100 pt.

Real bug 2: a split button announced as "add"

A Menu with a primaryAction becomes a pop-up button on macOS. Its inner button took its accessibility label from the SF Symbol (plus), so VoiceOver said "add". .accessibilityLabel("New notebook") on the menu fixes VoiceOver; in XCUITest you then find it as app.popUpButtons["New notebook"], not app.buttons.

Real bug 3: undo history wiped after every stroke

Our canvas sends each edit to the model as a small value: the page, the strokes before and after, and the version of the page it was drawn on. That version field had a default of 0.

If an edit's version is older than the model's, the page was reloaded by sync in between, so the model redraws from the merged page and bumps its version. The canvas reacts to a version bump by clearing undo history, because older steps may not fit the merged page.

The iPad canvas passed version. The Mac canvas didn't, so every edit had the default 0. Every stroke looked like it came from before a reload, and the history was wiped after each one. ⌘Z never had anything to undo.

The fix stamps the version on edits, and on undo/redo steps as they are replayed. The lesson is about defaults: a field with a harmless-looking default of 0 compiled fine and failed silently.

Real bug 4: .buttonStyle(.plain) only hits the glyph

The pen bar uses .plain so icons keep their own colours. On macOS a plain button's hit area is the drawn content. The accessibility frame of our Undo button was 12×12 pt inside a 30×30 frame, and the centre of arrow.uturn.backward is empty space. XCUITest clicks the centre, so nothing happened. A human hits it some of the time.

Button(action: undo) {
    Image(systemName: "arrow.uturn.backward")
        .frame(width: 30, height: 30)
        .contentShape(.rect)   // the whole square is the target
}
.buttonStyle(.plain)

In the same change we also took the bar's decorative capsule border out of hit testing (.allowsHitTesting(false)), so we can't say which of the two mattered more. Both are cheap; do both.

Real bug 5: ⌘V never reached the notebook

We had a Paste button in an Insert menu with .keyboardShortcut("v"). On macOS the main menu gets key equivalents first, and Edit ▸ Paste found no responder that could paste, so our shortcut never fired. The Mac way is to answer the standard command:

.onPasteCommand(of: [.image, .pdf, .fileURL, .plainText]) { _ in pasteFromClipboard() }

That only works when something in the view has focus, so the canvas also takes focus when the page opens (.focusable(interactions: .edit) plus @FocusState).

Real bug 6: the sign-in sheet had nowhere to appear

Not found by the suite. Google sign-in on Mac showed nothing. ASWebAuthenticationSession asks its context provider for a presentation anchor, and ours returned ASPresentationAnchor(). On iOS that's a fresh UIWindow, which happened to work. On macOS it's a fresh NSWindow that is never on screen. Return the app's key window instead. (The fix is in TestFlight; we're waiting on the first real sign-in to confirm.)

The test bugs

Failure Actual cause
Deleted notebook "still in the library" app.menuItems["Delete"] matched the menu bar's disabled Edit ▸ Delete first. Filter with isEnabled == true.
Can't click "Create" in a dialog The Touch Bar exposes a "Create" button too, and it can't be clicked. Query app.sheets.buttons or app.dialogs.buttons.
"Timed out while evaluating UI query" descendants(matching: .any).matching(predicate) over a page canvas and menu bar. Query typed elements (staticTexts, textViews, buttons) instead.
Word import "didn't open" It did. The page counter's text is in value, not label.
Stroke count unreadable macOS doesn't expose .accessibilityValue on a generic element. We moved the count into the label: "Page, 2 strokes".

What helped most

  1. Screen recordings. XCUITest attached an .mp4 per test to the .xcresult. One frame with ffmpeg -sseof -3 usually showed the answer. Search, Summarize and Word import were all visibly working while their tests failed.
  2. A probe test. A throwaway test that logs app.debugDescription and the state before/after one action found the undo and pen bar bugs in two runs.
  3. A separate bundle id for tests. The Mac suite launches com.mindscend.mindpage.uitest, ad-hoc signed with its own sandbox, so -resetLibrary never touches a real library.

About MindPage

MindPage is a local-first notes app for handwriting and PDFs: sync through your own Google Drive or iCloud Drive, AI on the device. Search runs on our own model, MindPage Search v2, fine-tuned from EmbeddingGemma 2 on what Apple Vision really reads from handwriting (R@1 85.9 vs 80.3 for v1 on 234 Vision-read handwritten pages). iPhone/iPad 1.1 is submitted to App Review, Mac is in TestFlight, and the web app is at mindscend.academy.

More: mindscendinc.com/mindpage
