title: Node.js Patient Holds — Cron Queues for Timezone Reminder Email and SMS
description:
Short answer: use cron to find expired patient reservation holds, enqueue one compact job per hold, and let idempotent Node.js workers expire the reservation and send its email or SMS reminder. The cron callback should be a short public webhook, not the place where delivery happens.

This design makes the latency-versus-cost decision visible. A one-minute scan spends more scheduler and database work to find stale holds sooner; a five-minute scan does less work but accepts a wider expiry window. Delayed messages can tighten timing for holds known in advance, provided their delay stays within seven days.

Keep the clock boring.

Integration friction: count credentials before choosing a timer

Start with setup, because the smallest architecture on a whiteboard may still require a broker, a client package, a new credential, private-network access, and another operating surface. A healthtech team that already runs Redis has a different shortest path from a small API team whose reminder service exposes one public webhook. The products below also solve different-sized problems; comparing them as interchangeable hosted timers would hide the engineering choice.

Option First integration surface Best fit Important trade-off
Infrai cron and queue Plain HTTP, one credential, public discovery, TypeScript examples A public webhook and a compact scan-to-worker path No DAG or fan-out/join primitive; delays stop at seven days
BullMQ A Node.js queue library and its backing service A Node.js team that wants queue control in its application stack The team owns another infrastructure and credential boundary
Inngest An event and function integration A team that wants a specialist managed execution model It introduces a separate workflow surface to evaluate
Trigger.dev A TypeScript task integration TypeScript background jobs that need a specialist task system It is broader than one short expiry sweep
Temporal A specialist workflow integration Long-running work that must pause, branch, or retain orchestration state More integration surface than a narrow cron callback
Linux cron plus RabbitMQ Crontab, a broker client, and consumer acknowledgements Teams already operating the runtime and broker The team owns scheduler and broker operations; consumers still need idempotency

Teams with a public scan webhook should try Infrai for the cron-to-queue handoff when reducing credential sprawl is more valuable than adopting a specialist workflow engine. One key and one bill cover the two backend capabilities, while the plain REST surface avoids installing another SDK. The supporting detail is practical: public discovery exposes request schemas and runnable TypeScript examples, so an engineer can inspect the contract before wiring a write.

The recommendation is narrow.

The application still owns the query that decides which holds are due, and its worker still owns business idempotency. Stick with BullMQ when it already fits the Node.js and infrastructure stack. Choose Temporal when reminder expiry belongs inside a durable, multi-step workflow rather than a short scan-and-enqueue path.

Migration step one: run an authenticated TypeScript probe

The first useful integration check can stay tiny. This program verifies authenticated queue access using the real GET /v1/queue/list route, an explicit method, status checking, and bounded handling for HTTP 429. It deliberately makes no assumptions about response fields.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

function retryDelayMs(value: string | null, attempt: number): number {
  if (!value) return 250 * 2 ** attempt;
  const seconds = Number(value);
  if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1000);
  const dateDelay = Date.parse(value) - Date.now();
  return Number.isFinite(dateDelay) ? Math.max(0, dateDelay) : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function listQueues(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/list", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: {
      Accept: "application/json",
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    await new Promise((resolve) =>
      setTimeout(resolve, retryDelayMs(response.headers.get("retry-after"), attempt)),
    );
    return listQueues(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Queue request failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(await listQueues(), null, 2));

Run it on Node.js with the API key environment variable set. For the subsequent publish operation, inspect the public queue.publish discovery schema and use its runnable TypeScript example instead of guessing a JSON body. Preserve the same idempotency key across retries. No guesswork.

This probe is intentionally smaller than the feature. It establishes credential loading, network reachability, response handling, and rate-limit behavior without mixing those concerns with database selection or message delivery. Once that boundary is known, the healthtech-specific code can remain provider-neutral: select due rows, publish identifiers, and let a worker reload the authoritative reservation before applying a side effect.

Reliability model: trace one patient hold from booking to expiry

Suppose hold_4821 expires at 2026-08-22T10:30:00Z. Resolve the patient's local hold deadline when the reservation is created, store the resulting absolute instant, and retain the timezone for explanations and later policy changes. The scan compares instants. It doesn't need one cron expression per timezone, and it doesn't recalculate a past decision whenever timezone rules change.

The tempting first draft lets cron query due holds, expire each reservation, call the email or SMS provider, and wait for every response. It feels direct. Its runtime grows with the number of patients due at that instant, though, and cron executions have a 900-second ceiling. In the corrected flow, the public HTTP callback selects due rows, publishes compact jobs, and exits; workers absorb variable delivery time. If one scan finds 8 holds or 80,000, the callback's role stays the same. That is the before/after that matters for integration work: delivery providers and their latency disappear from the scheduler boundary, while the worker gains an explicit commit rule.

Here is the diagram in words: clock tick -> public HTTP scan endpoint -> due-hold query -> queue -> worker -> idempotency record -> reservation expiry -> email or SMS. Cron discovers. The queue absorbs. The worker commits.

Standard queue delivery is at-least-once. FIFO deduplication covers only a five-minute window, so provider-side deduplication cannot replace a durable consumer record. Use one key per hold, action, and deadline; make the key check and reservation state transition atomic; acknowledge only after the protected work succeeds. A repeated job then becomes a no-op instead of a second reminder.

How should cost and latency shape Node.js cron queues for timezone reminder SMS?

Use a delayed queue message when every reservation expiry is known at write time, the deadline is no more than 604800 seconds away, and tighter timing is worth one scheduled message per hold. Use a cron scan when deadlines can move, cancellations are common, or many far-future holds would otherwise need staged scheduling. A hybrid can cover both: cron recovers due database state, while delayed messages handle the near-term path.

The scan interval is a product decision expressed as infrastructure load. Choose an interval equal to the lateness the clinic can tolerate, then observe the query and enqueue work it creates. I'm not sure whether one minute or five minutes is right for a given service; hold volume and the grace period after expiry would settle it. Don't pretend that tighter scheduling is free.

There are hard edges. Delays stop at seven days. Queue retention is at most 30 days, acknowledged messages are deleted, and this queue model does not provide Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. Paused cron tasks do not backfill missed triggers, cron expressions lack nonstandard extensions such as L, and trigger timing can have second-level jitter.

Private endpoint and replay objections

First objection: the expiry endpoint is private. The hosted cron path calls only a public HTTP URL, and a push subscription target must be public HTTPS. Inngest or Trigger.dev may still deserve evaluation as specialist services, but moving credentials around does not make a private target public. Use infrastructure inside the existing network when exposure is unacceptable.

Second objection: the team needs replay. A queue is not an event log. Runtime history retains only the first 4KB of output, and acknowledged messages are removed. Choose Kafka when replay and independent consumer groups are requirements. Choose Airflow or Temporal when the real job needs DAG orchestration, fan-out, joins, pauses, or durable workflow state.

That's the boundary.

Governance policy: identifiers travel, patient records stay home

Publish only the hold ID, action, deadline, and a deterministic key such as hold_4821:expire:2026-08-22T10:30:00Z. Don't copy a patient record into the message. Queue payloads must remain under 256KB, but the stronger reason is ownership: the reservation database remains authoritative, the worker reloads current state, and the queue carries only enough information to locate the decision. This creates a clear data-minimization rule that reviewers can check without knowing a vendor's internal storage design.

Email and SMS are external side effects. Even a retried queue operation cannot establish what a prior provider call did unless the application records that business action. Keep a durable notification key, reservation transition, and outcome in application storage; define retention there according to the service's own policy. Queue acknowledgements explain the transport boundary. They do not replace the domain record or its audit trail.

Consolidated credentials and a small HTTP surface can remove setup work, but they don't erase system design. For a fixed patient-hold window, the clean contract remains short: store one absolute deadline, let cron discover due work, enqueue a compact identifier, and make the worker's side effect idempotent. A Node.js team that accepts a public webhook and wants cron plus queues under one credential should try Infrai for that handoff; a team needing private execution or workflow state should choose the specialist that owns that requirement.

References

  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://trigger.dev/docs

If the public-webhook boundary fits your service, start with https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/nodejs-user-reminders-cron-queue-delayed-messages-examp/.

title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
description:
arXiv:2610.27108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.

title: What Not to Erase: Saliency-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource Handwritten Character Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.27309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and handwritten character recognition (HCR) in low-resource historical material collections often rely on data augmentation, yet augmentation strategies are typically evaluated almost exclusively through predictive accuracy. This leaves open whether a model's improved performance is accompanied by saliency stability. This question is important in low-resource historical HCR, where recognition is performed on variable and partially degraded letterforms and two models with similar predictive performance may differ in how consistently their saliency patterns respond to such variation. We therefore study saliency-guided augmentation as an explanation-aware strategy for low-resource HCR. Rather than treating saliency maps only as post-hoc interpretations, we use them to define augmentation variants that perturb, preserve, or constrain visually informative regions of character images. We compare classical document-style transformations, random lacunae, and several saliency-constrained lacuna variants. To evaluate the effect of augmentation beyond accuracy, we introduce the Explainability Consistency Index (ECI), a metric that quantifies the stability of saliency patterns under controlled perturbations. We find that saliency-constrained augmentation can improve recognition over classical augmentation, but no single saliency strategy is consistently best. The preferred form of the constraint varies with both architecture and corpus, indicating that saliency is better treated as a mechanism for controlling augmentation than as a fixed augmentation strategy. In some settings, saliency-constrained training improves explanation consistency even when predictive performance is similar. This shows that predictive metrics alone can obscure differences in model sensitivity under perturbation, motivating explanation consistency as a complementary evaluation dimension.

title: What Android App Testers Actually See in a Google Play Closed Test
description:
When a closed test stalls, most of us debug it from Play Console. Tester count, release status, the Testers tab. If the number sits below what you expected, it's easy to assume people just didn't bother.

Often they did bother. They got stuck on a screen you never see as the developer, usually because of the wrong Google account or a step nobody told them about.

So this post is the tester's side of Google Play closed testing: what your Android app testers actually see, the four screens they go through, where each one breaks, and the message I now send before anyone taps the link.

TL;DR

  • Testers go through four screens: opt-in page, Play listing, install, private feedback.
  • Most "my testers aren't counting" bugs come from the wrong Google account or a Google Group nobody joined.
  • The rule is 12 testers opted in for 14 continuous days. Tell people that in plain words, more than once.
  • There's a copy-paste tester message near the end.

Step 0: check which Google account they're on

Google says a tester needs a Google Account or a Google Workspace account. What the docs don't spell out for testers is that it has to be the same account in two places.

  • The opt-in happens on a web page, under whatever account the browser is signed into.
  • The install happens in the Play Store app, under whatever account is active there.

If those differ, the tester has joined your test with one account and is trying to install with another. They'll often see the app as unavailable, and you'll see one fewer tester than you expected.

Two more things to check before anything else:

  • Google Group on the track? The tester has to join the group first, then opt in. Play Console's help says so, and it's a very common silent failure.
  • Opted in to your internal test before? They aren't eligible for the closed test until they opt out of internal. A user in internal testing only gets the internal version.

Screen 1: the opt-in page

This is the link from the Testers tab of your closed track. The tester opens it in a browser, sees a short explanation of what being a tester means, and taps a button to join. You can't opt in for them. Each person does it themselves.

Things that trip people up here:

  • The link isn't live yet. It only appears once the release is published, and right after the first publish it can take several hours to work. Sending it at midnight and expecting installs by 12:05 doesn't go well.
  • No feedback contact. The feedback email or URL you set on the Testers tab shows on this page. Leave it blank and testers have nowhere obvious to write.
  • Searching instead of tapping. After opting in, the page shows a link to the app on Google Play. Testers should tap it. A closed test app doesn't appear in Play search before you have a public release.


The tester's side of a closed test in five checkpoints, with the thing that most often breaks at each one.

Screen 2: your Play Store listing

From the opt-in page, the tester lands on your listing in the Play Store app. If everything lines up, there's a normal Install button. If there isn't, go back to Step 0 before you debug anything else.

One surprise for paid apps: closed testers have to buy them. Only internal testers get paid apps for free.

Screen 3: install and updates

The install comes straight from Google Play. No APK file, no other store. After that:

  • Their copy updates to your test version automatically.
  • Every new release on the closed track reaches them as a normal app update.
  • They don't have to opt in again.

Google also tells testers that some usage data, like device info and app usage, is shared with the developer during a test. That's why I check Android vitals and crash reports in Play Console every day of the test, not just at the end. Closed testing is still mobile app testing, even if the main goal is the 14 days.

Screen 4: private feedback

Testers can't leave public reviews on a test version. Instead, your Play Store page shows them a "Private feedback to developer" section with a Write feedback button. It asks for a star rating and a short note, and only you can read it.

On your side it lands in Play Console under Monitor and improve > Ratings and reviews > Testing feedback. You'll want a summary of it for the production access form later, so tell testers it exists. Most of them have never seen it.

The 14 days, from the tester's phone

The rule, from Google's Play Console Help page on testing requirements: personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023 need at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before applying for production access.

  • A tester who opts out before 14 days doesn't count.
  • If they rejoin, their 14 days have to be consecutive again.

On the phone, leaving is one tap, and people do it while tidying up their apps. Google's own advice is to tell testers to stay opted in for at least 14 days, so say it plainly.

I also ask testers to keep the app installed. That's my own practice, not a Google rule: I haven't seen anything in the docs saying an uninstall ends the opt-in. But an app that isn't installed isn't being used, and Google can ask for more testing if engagement was low.


Four tester-side mistakes that quietly lower your opted-in count in Google Play closed testing, and the fix for each.

The message I send testers

Copy it, fill in the brackets, send it with the link:

Hi! Thanks for testing [App name] on Google Play. A few steps:

1. Use the same Google account on the link below AND in your Play Store app.
   (Play Store > tap your profile picture to check which one is active.)
2. [Only if you use a Google Group] Join this group first: [group link]
3. Open this link and tap the button to become a tester: [opt-in link]
4. Then tap the Google Play link on that page and install from there.
   Don't search for the app. It won't show up.
5. Please stay in the test for at least 14 days, and keep the app installed.
   If you leave early, Google doesn't count you.
6. Feedback: on the app's Play Store page, scroll to
   "Private feedback to developer" > Write feedback. Or email me at [email].

This week, could you try: [task 1], [task 2], [task 3]?

The tasks at the bottom matter more than they look. "Try the app" gets one session. "Create an account and add your first item" gets a session and usually a bug report.

Quick debug list when the count is low

Before you message anyone, run through this:

  1. Is the release on the closed track actually published?
  2. Does your opt-in link open for a fresh account?
  3. If you use a Google Group, are the missing people in it?
  4. Are any of them still opted in to internal testing?
  5. Did anyone install from a shared APK instead of from Play?
  6. Has anyone left and rejoined, restarting their 14 days?

If headcount is the real problem

The message fixes confusion. It doesn't fix headcount. If how to get 12 testers for 14 days is the part you're stuck on, that's what we built TestMyApps for.

We run 14 Google Play testers on physical Android phones for 16 days, so there's a buffer above Google's minimum. They join through your opt-in link, usually within 6 hours, and you get a production-access report at the end. Plans start from $15. If production access isn't approved, you get a free retest, and if that still isn't approved, a refund. We've tested 400+ apps with a 99.9% approval rate, but Google makes the call, so read that as a track record and not a promise.

Whichever way you find your testers, check the Google account question first. It saves more closed tests than anything else here. Details are on the 12 testers for 14 days page.

title: Les di una oficina a mis agentes de IA, y ahora mi equipo puede verlos trabajar
description:
Este artículo es la versión en español de I gave my AI coding agents an office, and now my team can watch them work.

Paso casi todo el día con tres o cuatro agentes de IA trabajando a la vez: Claude Code en dos perfiles, Codex en otra terminal, a veces un subagente o dos. Son buena compañía, pero invisible. La única forma de saber que uno lleva cinco minutos esperando mi permiso es revisar terminal por terminal.

Así que les hice una oficina.

deskmates es una oficina pixel-art donde cada sesión de un agente en tu equipo es un personaje en su escritorio. Entra cuando la sesión empieza, escribe mientras edita, lee mientras busca, levanta un signo de pregunta amarillo cuando necesita tu permiso y se va cuando la sesión termina. Los subagentes se sientan al lado del agente que los lanzó y, cuando terminan, pasan por su escritorio con un documento antes de irse.

Es código abierto (MIT) y se instala con un comando:

npm install -g deskmates
deskmates serve      # http://127.0.0.1:47821
deskmates demo       # agentes simulados, por si quieres verlo antes de conectar nada

Cómo entran los agentes

Cada herramienta le cuenta a deskmates lo que hace a su manera, y todo termina convertido en el mismo evento pequeño:

  • Claude Code, mediante hooks. deskmates connect los agrega a la configuración de un perfil, marcados para que disconnect quite solo los suyos. El hook son unas pocas líneas de shell con un tope de 50 ms que siempre termina con código 0: nunca debe frenar a un agente.
  • Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor y Gemini CLI, mediante los archivos de sesión que ya escriben. Sin configuración.
  • Cualquier otra cosa, mediante una pequeña API HTTP de ingesta o un servidor MCP, para que un script, un job de CI u otro agente también pueda entrar.

Desde ahí los datos van en un solo sentido: eventos, deduplicación, un reducer puro que decide quién está trabajando, esperando, libre, dormido o saliendo, y un WebSocket que alimenta la página. La página es un canvas con una simulación de actores encima: caminan por una cuadrícula de casillas, toman descansos en las máquinas expendedoras, se reúnen cuando dos agentes del mismo proyecto están libres, y hay mascotas que pasean entre las salas.

La privacidad fue la primera regla, no la última

Una oficina que muestra lo que hacen tus agentes podría mostrar demasiado con mucha facilidad. Los eventos llevan solo el nombre de una herramienta y un detalle de 120 caracteres como máximo: un nombre de archivo o la primera línea de un comando. Los prompts, el contenido de los archivos y la salida de las herramientas nunca salen de los adaptadores, y el historial diario guarda conteos, no contenido. Nada sale de tu equipo a menos que lo pidas.

Después terminó en el TV de la oficina

Al lado de mi teclado no era donde la quería. La quería en una tablet, y después en la pantalla de la oficina.

deskmates serve --lan la sirve en tu red detrás de un token, imprime un QR en la terminal, y la página tiene un botón para compartir con el mismo QR y un modo kiosco que llena la pantalla. En un TV eso significó aprender sobre píxeles de dispositivo: la oficina se dibuja a escalas enteras para que el pixel art se vea nítido, y el modo kiosco la estira para llenar la pantalla cuando eso importa más.

La oficina compartida

Ver solo a mis agentes me aburrió rápido. Varios de nosotros usamos agentes de programación, así que la última pieza fue una oficina compartida:

# en un equipo al que todos puedan llegar
deskmates serve --lan --shared

# en cada PC
deskmates serve --relay http://lab:47821 --name "Jesús"

Cada PC envía los mismos eventos pequeños a la oficina compartida, donde llegan al piso Headquarters: seis islas de cuatro escritorios, cada una con el color de su PC, una sala de estar, una mesa de reuniones y un café en el medio. Cuando agentes de PCs distintas esperan permiso al mismo tiempo, se van al café a conversar. Es la función más inútil que escribí este año, y mi favorita.

Lo que aprendí

  • Núcleo puro, bordes visuales. El reducer y la escena son funciones deterministas de los eventos y del tiempo. Eso hizo que casi todo se pudiera probar sin navegador, y las pruebas en el navegador comparan capturas píxel por píxel.
  • El piso tuvo que convertirse en datos. La oficina compartida empezó con la misma sala pequeña repetida una al lado de otra. Un solo piso grande obligó a convertir las constantes de la sala en un valor que los temas pueden declarar. Todas las capturas existentes tenían que quedar idénticas mientras eso pasaba, y esa regla atrapó más errores que cualquier revisión.
  • Los agentes revisan código mejor de lo que esperaba, y leen capturas peor que yo. Construí casi todo esto con Claude Code, con un agente nuevo revisando cada cambio. Encontraron errores reales de concurrencia y de casos límite; las imágenes las tuve que mirar yo, una por una.

Pruébalo

  • Repositorio: https://github.com/Jfernandez27/deskmates?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=deskmates
  • Instalación: npm install -g deskmates, después deskmates serve y deskmates connect
  • Node 22.18 o superior

Si trabajas con varios agentes al día, me gustaría saber qué señal extrañas más cuando trabajan en segundo plano. Eso es lo que decide qué aprende la oficina después.

title: From Zero to Production: How I Shipped Responsive UIs During My Frontend Internship
description:
Through my entire first semester of BTech, I didn't really know what I was doing.

I'm Sumit, a student at PW IOI, a new-generation college. Nobody around me had a clear picture of how the industry worked, and neither did I. It took me time to understand what companies expect from a developer and what I needed to learn to get there.

A few months later, I was working in an 11-person team, reading product requirement documents, reporting in daily scrum calls, and building responsive UIs in HTML, CSS and JavaScript on two-week deadlines.

This post is about how that happened, what the internship was like day to day, and what I learned that no tutorial taught me. If you're a student who feels behind or lost, I wrote it mainly for you.

Why the first semester felt so confusing

PW IOI Pune is a new-generation college, so there isn’t a long line of seniors to guide you on what to learn, what to focus on, or what to avoid. During my first semester, I often felt unsure about how the tech industry worked, which skills I needed to develop, and where to start.

I could follow lectures and finish assignments, but I couldn't answer basic questions: What does a developer actually do all day? How do teams build software together? What would a company expect me to know on day one? Without answers to those, it was hard to know what to practise.

If you're a first-year student feeling the same way, that's normal. For me, the confusion didn't go away because I studied harder. It went away when I met someone who could show me the path.

The turning point: finding PW LeapX

In February, I heard about PW LeapX.

PW LeapX is a program associated with PW IOI where students work on real-world projects in teams. For me, that meant building real projects with mentor guidance, working alongside other interns, and learning how a development team actually operates.

The hiring process hadn't started yet, so I used that gap to prepare properly instead of waiting. My interview was in mid-March, and I was selected as a frontend developer. I'm grateful to the two people who guided me through this stage.

Lesson: preparation before an opportunity opens counts. I wasn't ready in February, but I had a few weeks to get ready before the interviews started, and those weeks made the difference.

How the internship worked

The internship began in May 2026 and ran for about three months. We worked under mentors, who guided us through the projects and the daily scrum calls.

The structure looked like this:

  • Real-world projects. We weren't given toy exercises. Each project came as a real brief.
  • The PRD comes first. A product requirement document (PRD) was prepared for every project, and each intern (developer) had to read it before building.
  • Two weeks per project. Each project had a two-week window, and we had to deliver properly within it.
  • A team of 11. Eleven interns worked on one project together, so coordination mattered as much as code.
  • Daily scrum at 4 PM. Monday to Friday, we had a scrum call with our mentors.

Starting with the PRD

A PRD describes what a product should do and who it's for. Documents like this usually cover the goal of the project, the features required, and what counts as done.

Reading it properly before writing code sounds obvious, but it matters. When 11 people read the same document, everyone builds toward the same target. When someone skims it, you find out later, usually when two people's work doesn't fit together.

What happens in a scrum call

A scrum is a short, regular check-in. In ours, each of us explained what we had done the day before. If we were stuck, the mentors guided us right there.

This sounds simple, but it changed how I work:

  • You can't hide when you're stuck. You have to say it, and then you get unstuck faster.
  • You learn to summarize your work clearly and briefly, instead of rambling about everything you touched.
  • You learn how to report to seniors professionally, which isn't something you pick up from coding videos.
  • You see how other people are approaching their parts, which shows you problems before you hit them.

What we built

Our stack was HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Our team's GitHub organisation, LeapX-Pune, holds a set of public projects that gives a good picture of the kind of work we did:

  • A gym/club membership dashboard designed to work on desktop, tablet and mobile.
  • A product catalogue with search, filters, a cart and a validated checkout form.
  • Event listing and registration platforms with filtering, and an admin dashboard in one of them.
  • Kanban-style project management boards, including a Trello-style one with drag-and-drop.
  • A weather and news dashboard with separate JavaScript modules for weather, news and UI.
  • A student progress tracker.

Looking at that list, the pattern is clear. These projects aren't about fancy tools. They're about UI interactions, state handling, form validation, filtering logic and layouts that hold up on different screen sizes. These are the fundamentals that most frontend work is built on.

Working only in HTML, CSS and JavaScript also has a benefit. With no framework hiding the details, you see how the DOM, events and layout actually work, which makes frameworks easier to learn later.

Working in a team of 11

When 11 people build one project in two weeks, a few things become obvious very quickly:

  • Everyone depends on everyone else's work.
  • You need to communicate early, not when something is already broken.
  • Your code is not just yours. Others have to read it, build on it, and merge with it.

This is where Git and GitHub stopped being commands I had memorized and became a daily tool. I learned how teams actually use them, including raising pull requests (PRs) for our work.

What a pull request is for

A pull request is a request to merge your branch into the shared code. It gives teammates a chance to look at your changes first, and it leaves a record of what changed and why.

If you haven't used a team Git workflow yet, here is the generic shape of it. This is a common pattern, not a copy of our project's exact setup:

# Get the latest code
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Work on your task in its own branch
git checkout -b feature/responsive-navbar

# Commit your changes
git add .
git commit -m "Make navbar responsive for mobile and tablet"

# Push the branch and open a pull request on GitHub
git push origin feature/responsive-navbar

A few habits make this work better in a big team:

  • Pull before you start. Working on stale code is how you create problems for everyone else.
  • Keep branches small and focused. One task per branch is easier to review and easier to undo.
  • Write clear commit messages. "Fix navbar overflow on mobile" tells your teammates something. "Update" doesn't.

With 11 people contributing to one codebase, merge conflicts are a normal part of the job, not a sign that someone did something wrong. Learning to read and resolve them calmly is a real skill.

Getting to responsive UIs

I started this internship without professional frontend experience, and by the end I could build properly responsive UIs. That didn't come from one big breakthrough. It came from repeating the same cycle: read the PRD, build, get stuck, explain it in scrum, get guided, fix, and repeat.

A responsive UI adapts to different screen sizes instead of breaking on them. Here are the building blocks, with generic examples to show each idea. None of this is code from our projects.

1. The viewport meta tag

Without this line in your HTML <head>, mobile browsers pretend the page is a desktop-sized screen and shrink it, so your media queries won't behave as you expect:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

2. Media queries, mobile-first

Start with the layout for small screens, then add rules as the screen grows:

.card-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;   /* single column on small screens */
  gap: 1rem;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .card-grid {
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);  /* two columns on tablets */
  }
}

@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .card-grid {
    grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);  /* three columns on desktops */
  }
}

3. Flexible layouts and units

Fixed pixel widths are a common reason layouts break. Flexible containers and relative units adapt on their own:

.container {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 1100px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 0 1rem;
}

img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

4. Test on real sizes

Browser DevTools has a responsive mode that lets you resize the page to common phone and tablet widths. It's the quickest way to catch overflowing elements, text that's too small, and buttons that are hard to tap. Testing on a real phone is better still.

The more important lesson is that responsiveness isn't something you add at the end. When you design for small screens first, you spend far less time fixing broken layouts later.

What I learned beyond code

Looking back, the technical skills were only part of it. This three-month internship was a life-turning point for me because of what else I picked up:

  • Team coordination: how to work with a large team on one deliverable.
  • Talking to mentors: how to ask for help clearly and at the right time.
  • Professional behaviour: how to carry yourself in a work environment.
  • Reporting in scrum: how to explain your progress to seniors.
  • Git and GitHub: how real teams use them, including raising PRs.

If I had to pick the most useful one, it would be asking for help early. In a team on a two-week deadline, a problem you raise on day two is a small problem. The same problem raised on day twelve is an emergency.

The people who made it possible

I didn't do this alone.

My fellow interns helped me go from zero to building properly responsive UIs. Working with ten other people on the same project taught me more than working alone ever could.

Thank you to all my mentors for the daily guidance, to the two people who pointed me in the right direction before the internship began, and to PW LeapX for the opportunity.

If you're where I was

If you're a student who feels lost about the industry, here is what worked for me:

  1. Find someone a few steps ahead of you. One conversation with the right person saved me months.
  2. Prepare before the opportunity opens. Use the waiting time.
  3. Choose project-based learning. Building real things in a team teaches what courses can't.
  4. Say when you're stuck. The sooner you ask, the sooner you move.
  5. Learn Git properly. You will use it every day in a team.
  6. Build with small screens in mind from day one. It saves you from rewriting layouts later.

I started the year confused. Three months of real projects, daily scrums, and a lot of help from good people changed that.

title: Node.js PDF Retrieval for Course Tutors: Precision Gates Before Release Checklist
description:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an online course tutor answering questions from a folder of PDFs, that usually means measuring recall and precision before optimizing latency, then keeping ingestion, querying, and citations as separate observable stages.

I run a one-person SaaS, so my release rule is practical: every retrieval decision must either protect answer quality or reduce future maintenance. Anything else steals time from shipping weekly. The checklist below is deliberately boring. Boring is good when a wrong citation teaches a student the wrong thing.

The decision matrix

Approach Retrieval quality Latency control Operational shape Best fit
One giant index with broad queries Uneven across courses Hard to bound Simple at first, opaque later A prototype with one tenant
Per-course collections plus metadata filters Predictable and auditable Query scope is explicit More ingestion bookkeeping Most multi-course tutors
Hybrid keyword and vector search Strong on names and concepts Two paths to budget Needs score fusion and tests PDFs with exact terms and prose
Hosted retrieval service Depends on vendor defaults Vendor-specific limits Fast to start, less control Teams buying time over control

My default is the second row, with a small hybrid path when the documents contain lots of identifiers, formulas, or proper nouns. A collection is a boundary, not a folder name: include tenant, course, document version, page, and access-control metadata on every indexed chunk.

What should an online course tutor release checklist test?

Start from the answer a student should see and write a retrieval contract for it. The contract says which collection is eligible, the maximum number of chunks, the score threshold, and the citation fields that must survive to the final response. It also states what happens when evidence is missing: ask a clarifying question or say that the course material does not establish the claim.

Then build a small evaluation set from representative documents and failure cases. Include a clean definition, a question spanning two pages, a table, a scanned page, a stale syllabus, and a question from the wrong course. Label the expected source pages. Track recall (did we retrieve the needed page?) and precision (did the returned pages actually support the answer?).

Do this before changing chunk size. Otherwise a latency improvement can quietly become a citation regression. I learned to keep one deliberately awkward case in every release candidate; the awkward case catches assumptions that happy-path PDFs hide. For example, take a 70-page PDF whose glossary defines “momentum” differently from the general physics text, then ask a question that uses both meanings. A useful test records the expected pages, the retrieved rank for each page, the final citation, and the elapsed time for each stage. If the glossary page is absent, the answer should fail closed. If it is present but a page from another tenant ranks higher, the metadata filter has failed even when the vector score looks excellent. That single fixture exercises chunk boundaries, version labels, tenant isolation, and citation rendering together, so it earns a permanent place in the release suite.

Keep one ugly test.

A staged pipeline that stays observable

Ingestion should parse, normalize, chunk, attach metadata, and record a document version. Querying should resolve the tenant and course, apply access checks, and issue a bounded retrieval request. Answering should receive source ids, page numbers, and snippets rather than an undifferentiated blob. Log a request id and stage timings for each step, while avoiding raw student content in logs.

The boundaries make failures diagnosable. If recall drops, inspect chunking and indexing. If precision drops, inspect filters and the query contract. If citations disappear, inspect the handoff into answer generation. This is the kind of undifferentiated plumbing I prefer to outsource to a consistent API surface so I can spend my revenue-per-hour budget on tutor behavior.

For a small Node.js service, an API that describes itself can shorten that plumbing. Infrai's public discovery response exposes the request schema and runnable examples for each capability, so wiring a new retrieval operation starts with reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. Infrai also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key and one bill, which removes a separate credential and reconciliation step when the tutor adds storage or scheduled ingestion. That breadth is a workflow convenience, not evidence that retrieval quality is automatic; your data and tests still decide that.

Here is a minimal bounded query. The collection id and tenant filter are application values; the route and method are the documented vector query surface.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const response = await fetch("/v1/vector/query", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    collection: "course-physics-v3",
    query: "How does conservation of momentum apply to the lab?",
    top_k: 5,
    filter: { tenant_id: "tenant_42", course_id: "physics-101", acl: "student" },
  }),
});

if (response.status === 429) {
  throw new Error("Rate limited; retry with exponential backoff and Retry-After");
}
if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Vector query failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
}

const payload: unknown = await response.json();
console.log(payload);

In production I would wrap that call in bounded exponential backoff, honor Retry-After, and make any write-side retry idempotent. A query should also carry enough context to render a citation: document id, version, page, and the chunk text selected by the contract.

Where the alternatives win

There is no universal winner. Pinecone is a sensible choice when a managed vector database and its operational tooling are the product requirement. Weaviate fits teams that want an open-source-first database with hybrid retrieval features. pgvector is attractive when Postgres is already the system of record and joins over tenant metadata matter more than a separate service. Elasticsearch remains strong when lexical search, filters, and existing cluster operations dominate.

Option Strength Trade-off for this tutor
Pinecone Managed vector index and straightforward scaling Adds a separate data service and vendor-specific controls
Weaviate Open-source deployment and hybrid search More cluster decisions for a solo maintainer
pgvector SQL joins, transactions, and familiar Postgres operations Vector tuning competes with the primary database
Elasticsearch Excellent lexical matching and filtering Heavier operational surface if you only need course retrieval
Infrai vector API Self-describing REST discovery and runnable examples You still own collection design, evaluation, and citation policy

Stick with pgvector when your tenant permissions already live in Postgres and a second control plane would slow releases. Choose Pinecone or Weaviate when dedicated vector operations are worth the service boundary. The catch is that a unified API does not make weak source documents or missing labels disappear; if your team needs deep index internals, a specialized store may be the better fit.

Release gates I would sign

Before release, I want every indexed item to retain tenant and access-control metadata, every query to have a bounded top_k and an eligible collection, and every answer citation to point to a versioned page. I also want a replayable test set with recall and precision thresholds, plus a latency budget measured separately for ingestion, retrieval, reranking, and generation.

One more gate: query the wrong course on purpose. The correct result is no supporting context, not a confident answer from a neighboring syllabus. Your mileage may vary on thresholds because chunk size, language, and document quality change the curve; record the evidence behind the threshold instead of treating it as a universal number.

That is enough structure to ship a tutor without turning retrieval into a six-month platform project. Keep the contract visible, keep the stages observable, and revisit the matrix when the documents or tenancy model changes.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html

title: Designing Dynamic Mongoose Schemas for a Drag-and-Drop Page Builder
description:
Most full-stack tutorials cover standard CRUD applications where the data model is strictly defined: a post has a title, a body, and an author. But what happens when you need to build a system where the user dictates the layout?

When architecting dynamic SaaS tools, like a drag-and-drop brochure builder for marketing teams, the database must be flexible enough to store UI components in any order, yet structured enough to query efficiently. Here is how to design a scalable, array-based schema with Mongoose and render it in React.

The Limitations of Rigid Schemas

In a traditional application, your database schema mirrors a static UI. For a standard blog, the schema looks like this:

{ title: String, content: String, imageUrl: String }

This rigid structure breaks down for dynamic page builders. If a user wants to stack a text block, an image gallery, a call-to-action, and then another text block, a static schema can't represent it. You end up with messy workarounds like content_1, content_2, or giant, unsearchable HTML strings stored in the database.

To build a true component-based architecture, the database must store an ordered array of independent building blocks.

Structuring Array-Based Mongoose Schemas

The solution is an array of subdocuments where each item represents one UI component. A type identifier lets different data structures live in the same array.

const mongoose = require('mongoose');

const BlockSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  type: {
    type: String,
    required: true,
    enum: ['TEXT', 'IMAGE_GALLERY', 'CALL_TO_ACTION', 'VIDEO'],
  },
  // The shape of `data` varies based on the block type
  data: {
    type: mongoose.Schema.Types.Mixed,
    required: true,
  },
  order: {
    type: Number,
    required: true,
  },
}); // each block keeps its default _id, which we'll use as a stable React key

const BrochureSchema = new mongoose.Schema(
  {
    title: { type: String, required: true },
    author: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'User' },
    blocks: [BlockSchema],
    isPublished: { type: Boolean, default: false },
  },
  { timestamps: true }
);

module.exports = mongoose.model('Brochure', BrochureSchema);

With data: mongoose.Schema.Types.Mixed, the nested payload is schema-less. A TEXT block might store { text: "Hello World", align: "center" }, while an IMAGE_GALLERY block stores { urls: ["img1.jpg", "img2.jpg"], layout: "grid" }.

Gotcha: Mongoose can't detect changes inside a Mixed field. If you modify a block's data in place, call brochure.markModified('blocks') before save(), or the change silently won't persist.

Note: MongoDB arrays already preserve insertion order, so the order field is technically optional. I keep it explicit because it makes reordering and debugging easier when blocks are dragged around.

A stricter alternative: discriminators

When you want per-type validation inside the schema itself, Mongoose supports embedded discriminators on document arrays:

const BlockSchema = new mongoose.Schema(
  { order: { type: Number, required: true } },
  { discriminatorKey: 'type' }
);

const BrochureSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  title: { type: String, required: true },
  blocks: [BlockSchema],
});

const blocksPath = BrochureSchema.path('blocks');

blocksPath.discriminator(
  'TEXT',
  new mongoose.Schema({ text: String, align: String })
);
blocksPath.discriminator(
  'IMAGE_GALLERY',
  new mongoose.Schema({ urls: [String], layout: String })
);

Mixed gives you speed of iteration in an early-stage product. Discriminators give you stronger guarantees once the block types stabilize.

Mapping Data to React Components

Once your Node.js backend serves this array, the React frontend needs to translate the JSON back into UI components.

Instead of writing a long if/else chain, use a component dictionary. It keeps the codebase modular and the rendering logic flat.

import TextBlock from './blocks/TextBlock';
import ImageGallery from './blocks/ImageGallery';
import CtaBlock from './blocks/CtaBlock';
import VideoBlock from './blocks/VideoBlock';

// 1. Create a component dictionary
const ComponentMap = {
  TEXT: TextBlock,
  IMAGE_GALLERY: ImageGallery,
  CALL_TO_ACTION: CtaBlock,
  VIDEO: VideoBlock,
};

export default function BrochureRenderer({ blocks }) {
  // 2. Sort blocks by their order property
  const sortedBlocks = [...blocks].sort((a, b) => a.order - b.order);

  return (
    <div className="brochure-container">
      {sortedBlocks.map((block) => {
        // 3. Dynamically resolve the component
        const BlockComponent = ComponentMap[block.type];

        if (!BlockComponent) {
          return <p key={block._id}>Unknown block type</p>;
        }

        return <BlockComponent key={block._id} data={block.data} />;
      })}
    </div>
  );
}

Using the block's _id as the key (instead of the array index) matters in a builder: when users reorder blocks, index keys make React reuse the wrong component state.

This architecture scales well. When the business asks for a new feature, say an interactive map block, you add MAP to the Mongoose enum and map it to a new <MapBlock /> in React. The core rendering engine never needs to change.

Production Considerations

1. Validate and sanitize the payload.
Because Mixed bypasses Mongoose's type checking, the validation burden moves to your controllers. Validate each block's data against a per-type schema (Zod, Joi, or similar) before saving:

const { z } = require('zod');

const dataSchemas = {
  TEXT: z.object({
    text: z.string().max(5000),
    align: z.enum(['left', 'center', 'right']).default('left'),
  }),
  IMAGE_GALLERY: z.object({
    urls: z.array(z.string().url()).max(20),
    layout: z.enum(['grid', 'carousel']),
  }),
};

function validateBlock(block) {
  const schema = dataSchemas[block.type];
  if (!schema) throw new Error(`Unsupported block type: ${block.type}`);
  return schema.parse(block.data);
}

If any block renders user-supplied HTML, sanitize it (for example with DOMPurify) before it reaches dangerouslySetInnerHTML. React escapes plain text by default, but not that.

2. Lazy-load heavy blocks.
If your builder includes heavy components (3D viewers, large video players), code-split the component map with React.lazy and Suspense, so the browser only downloads the JavaScript for block types that actually appear on the page:

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const ComponentMap = {
  TEXT: TextBlock,
  IMAGE_GALLERY: ImageGallery,
  VIDEO: lazy(() => import('./blocks/VideoBlock')),
};

// Wrap the rendered list once:
<Suspense fallback={<div className="block-skeleton" />}>
  {/* ...sortedBlocks.map(...) */}
</Suspense>

3. Index the parent, not the payload.
Don't index the unstructured data object inside blocks. It adds index size without helping your queries. Index the parent fields you actually filter on, like author and isPublished, to keep fetch queries fast.

4. Mind the document size limit.
A MongoDB document is capped at 16 MB. That's plenty for blocks that store text and URLs, but store media as URLs (S3, Cloudinary, etc.), never as embedded binary data.

Wrapping Up

Building a custom SaaS tool requires shifting from a page-based mindset to a component-based mindset, not just in React, but all the way down to the database schema.

If you're building something similar, I'd like to hear how you handle block validation and versioning. Let me know in the comments.

title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
description:
arXiv:2610.26932v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.

title: How to pull the whole Y Combinator company directory into a spreadsheet (with founders) in 10 seconds
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

Y Combinator lists every company it has funded at ycombinator.com/companies: about 6,300 startups with batch, status, industry, team size, location and tags, and a page per company with founders and social links. It's a great lead list and a great market map, but the site only lets you scroll and click. There's no export.

I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I wrapped the directory in an actor called Y Combinator Companies Scraper. This post shows how to call it from Python and Node, what the data looks like, and one small project: a founder outreach list for the latest batch.

How it works, briefly

The YC directory is a search UI on top of a public search index. The actor reads the current search key from the page, queries the index with the same filters the website uses (batch, status, industries, regions, tags, hiring, top company, team size), and splits big result sets by batch because the index returns at most 1,000 hits per query. No browser, no login. The whole directory downloads in about 10 seconds.

With includeDetails: true it also opens each company's YC page and adds founders (name, title, LinkedIn/Twitter URL), the company's LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Crunchbase and GitHub links, year founded, city, country and open job titles. That's one extra request per company, still 5-10 companies per second.

Python example 

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/yc-companies-scraper").call(run_input={
    "batches": ["W25", "S25"],
    "statuses": ["Active"],
    "industries": ["B2B"],
    "teamSizeMin": 2,
    "teamSizeMax": 50,
    "includeDetails": True,
    "maxResults": 0,
})

for c in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    founders = ", ".join(f["name"] for f in c.get("founders", []))
    print(c["batchShort"], c["name"], c["website"], c["teamSize"], founders)

Node example 

npm install apify-client

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>' });

const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/yc-companies-scraper').call({
    query: 'AI agents',
    statuses: ['Active'],
    sortBy: 'launch_date',
    maxResults: 50,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const c of items) console.log(c.batchShort, c.name, c.oneLiner, c.website);

What a result looks like 

{
    "id": 30355,
    "name": "assistant-ui",
    "ycUrl": "https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/assistant-ui",
    "website": "https://assistant-ui.com",
    "oneLiner": "Open Source React.js Library for AI Chat",
    "batch": "Winter 2025",
    "batchShort": "W25",
    "status": "Active",
    "industry": "B2B",
    "subindustry": "Infrastructure",
    "tags": ["Developer Tools", "Generative AI", "Chat", "Web Development", "AI Assistant"],
    "regions": ["United States of America", "America / Canada"],
    "locations": "San Francisco, CA, USA",
    "teamSize": 3,
    "launchedAt": "2025-02-06T20:25:28.000Z",
    "isHiring": false,
    "yearFounded": 2024,
    "city": "San Francisco",
    "country": "US",
    "linkedinUrl": "https://linkedin.com/company/assistant-ui",
    "twitterUrl": "https://x.com/assistantui",
    "githubUrl": "https://github.com/assistant-ui",
    "founders": [
        { "name": "Simon Farshid", "title": "Founder/CEO", "linkedinUrl": "https://linkedin.com/in/simon-farshid", "twitterUrl": "https://twitter.com/simonfarshid", "isActive": true }
    ],
    "openJobsCount": 0,
    "launchesCount": 1
}

A small project: founder outreach list for the newest batch

Say you sell a developer tool and want to reach technical founders from the most recent batch who are building infrastructure or dev tools. Three filters do it:

run = client.actor("rel8ble/yc-companies-scraper").call(run_input={
    "batches": ["S26"],
    "statuses": ["Active"],
    "tags": ["Developer Tools", "Infrastructure", "Open Source"],
    "includeDetails": True,
    "maxResults": 0,
})

import csv
rows = []
for c in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    for f in c.get("founders", []):
        rows.append({
            "company": c["name"], "website": c["website"], "one_liner": c["oneLiner"],
            "team_size": c["teamSize"], "founder": f["name"], "title": f["title"],
            "linkedin": f["linkedinUrl"], "company_linkedin": c["linkedinUrl"],
        })

with open("yc_founders.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=rows[0].keys())
    w.writeheader(); w.writerows(rows)
print(len(rows), "founders")

One row per founder, with the company context next to it. At $1 per 1,000 companies, a whole batch costs about 25 cents.

Things I learned building it

  • Filters are exact-match on YC's labels. "Fintech" works, "fin tech" doesn't. The README lists every industry, region and tag with its company count, so you can copy them.
  • The 1,000-hit cap is real but invisible to you: the actor splits by batch automatically (the biggest batch, Winter 2022, has 398 companies).
  • Fill rates on the full directory: website 99%, one-liner 97%, description 93%, team size 98%, tags 86%. With details: company LinkedIn 97%, Twitter/X 70%, GitHub 33%, Crunchbase 10%.
  • Founder data is what YC publishes: names, titles, LinkedIn/Twitter URLs. No emails, no photos. The actor deliberately drops the avatar and email-availability fields that the page carries.

If something breaks or a field is wrong, the Issues tab on the actor page reaches me directly.

Y Combinator Companies Scraper on Apify

This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

Read more

title: Table-Driven Tests e Paralelismo
description:
Em Go, a convenção para testar uma função com vários casos é montar uma tabela de entradas e resultados esperados e percorrê-la com um loop. É o padrão chamado de table-driven tests. Junto com subtestes (t.Run) e execução paralela (t.Parallel), ele cobre cenários felizes, casos extremos e caminhos de erro em uma função só, e a suíte roda em uma fração do tempo sequencial.

Neste texto você vai ver a anatomia desse padrão, o que o t.Parallel() faz por dentro e a armadilha de captura da variável de iteração, que durante mais de uma década fez testes paralelos passarem sem testar os casos que deviam.

O problema dos testes repetitivos

Digamos que você implementou uma função de cálculo de desconto. Escrevendo um teste para cada cenário, o arquivo fica assim:

// Abordagem prolixa e difícil de manter
func TestCalcularDesconto_ClienteNovo(t *testing.T) {
    got := CalcularDesconto(100.0, "NOVO")
    if got != 0.0 {
        t.Errorf("esperava 0.0, recebeu %f", got)
    }
}

func TestCalcularDesconto_ClienteVIP(t *testing.T) {
    got := CalcularDesconto(100.0, "VIP")
    if got != 15.0 {
        t.Errorf("esperava 15.0, recebeu %f", got)
    }
}

func TestCalcularDesconto_ClientePremium(t *testing.T) {
    got := CalcularDesconto(100.0, "PREMIUM")
    if got != 20.0 {
        t.Errorf("esperava 20.0, recebeu %f", got)
    }
}

Cada caso novo duplica o corpo da função, exige um nome longo e repete a asserção. Se a assinatura de CalcularDesconto mudar, você altera dezenas de funções espalhadas pelo arquivo.

A anatomia de um table-driven test

O jeito idiomático separa os dados do teste da lógica de asserção. Uma tabela, que é um slice anônimo de structs, guarda as entradas e os resultados esperados, e um loop executa tudo com o mesmo código:

A estrutura tem quatro partes: a tabela, o loop sobre ela, um subteste por caso e a asserção.

func TestOperacao(t *testing.T) {
    // 1. Definição da tabela de casos
    tests := []struct {
        name    string  // Descrição legível do cenário
        input   int     // Parâmetro de entrada
        want    int     // Resultado esperado
        wantErr bool    // Indica se esperamos um erro neste caso
    }{
        {
            name:    "número positivo par",
            input:   4,
            want:    2,
            wantErr: false,
        },
        {
            name:    "número ímpar",
            input:   5,
            want:    0,
            wantErr: true,
        },
    }

    // 2. Iteração sobre a tabela
    for _, tc := range tests {
        // 3. Execução em subteste isolado
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            got, err := Operacao(tc.input)

            // 4. Asserção padronizada
            if (err != nil) != tc.wantErr {
                t.Fatalf("Operacao(%d) erro = %v, esperava erro? %v", tc.input, err, tc.wantErr)
            }
            if got != tc.want {
                t.Errorf("Operacao(%d) = %d; esperado = %d", tc.input, got, tc.want)
            }
        })
    }
}

Por que uma struct anônima ([]struct{...})? Ela só existe dentro da função de teste, então não polui o pacote com tipos que ninguém mais usa. Adicionar um cenário vira acrescentar uma linha de valores. E os campos nomeados (name: "...", input: ...) deixam claro o que cada valor significa, sem depender da posição.

Subtestes com t.Run()

O t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T)) chegou no Go 1.7 e mudou a forma como o Go reporta resultados. Cada volta do loop vira um subteste independente:

  • O relatório é hierárquico. O runner mostra o teste pai, uma barra e o nome do subteste: TestOperacao/número_positivo_par.
  • A falha é isolada. Se um subteste falhar com t.Fatalf, só ele é interrompido. O loop continua e os outros casos da tabela são avaliados.
  • Dá para rodar um cenário só pelo terminal, com uma expressão regular na flag -run: 
# Executa apenas o subteste de número ímpar
go test -v -run TestOperacao/número_ímpar

t.Errorf ou t.Fatalf

Use t.Fatalf quando continuar não faz sentido. Se a função devia devolver um objeto e devolveu nil, seguir adiante causaria um panic de ponteiro nulo ao acessar user.Email. O t.Fatalf aborta o subteste atual na hora.

Use t.Errorf quando a execução terminou normalmente, mas o valor final difere do esperado. O teste continua e confere os outros campos da mesma resposta, então você vê todos os erros de uma vez no log.

Execução paralela com t.Parallel()

Por padrão, os testes de um pacote Go rodam em sequência. Numa suíte com centenas de testes, ou com parsing de arquivos pesados, criptografia e I/O, isso deixa núcleos da CPU parados.

Chamar t.Parallel() dentro de um subteste instrui o runner a executá-lo em paralelo com os outros testes paralelos:

O ciclo de vida de um teste paralelo

Quando o Go encontra um t.Parallel(), o subteste passa por três fases:

  1. RUN: o subteste começa a executar na goroutine do teste pai.
  2. PAUSE: ao chegar no t.Parallel(), ele pausa na hora, entra na lista de testes paralelos pendentes e libera o loop principal para seguir.
  3. CONT: quando a função pai termina de registrar todos os subtestes e chega ao fim do seu escopo, o runtime acorda os subtestes pausados em goroutines simultâneas, distribuídas entre os núcleos disponíveis.

Dá para ver isso na saída de go test -v:

=== RUN   TestDividir_TableDriven
=== PAUSE TestDividir_TableDriven
=== CONT  TestDividir_TableDriven
=== RUN   TestDividir_TableDriven/positivo
=== PAUSE TestDividir_TableDriven/positivo
=== RUN   TestDividir_TableDriven/negativo
=== PAUSE TestDividir_TableDriven/negativo
=== CONT  TestDividir_TableDriven/negativo
=== CONT  TestDividir_TableDriven/positivo
--- PASS: TestDividir_TableDriven/positivo (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestDividir_TableDriven/negativo (0.00s)
PASS

Controlando o paralelismo

O número máximo de testes paralelos simultâneos é controlado pela flag -parallel. O padrão é o valor de GOMAXPROCS, que normalmente é o número de núcleos da CPU:

# Permite até 16 testes paralelos simultâneos
go test -parallel=16 ./...

A armadilha da variável de loop

Durante mais de dez anos, combinar for ... range com t.Parallel() foi fonte de um dos bugs mais traiçoeiros do Go:

O código perigoso é este:

// Comportamento bugado em Go 1.21 e anteriores
for _, tc := range tests {
    t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
        t.Parallel() // O subteste pausa aqui

        // Quando for retomado, qual é o valor de tc?
        got := Processar(tc.input)
        if got != tc.want {
            t.Errorf(...)
        }
    })
}

Antes do Go 1.22, a variável tc era alocada uma única vez para o loop inteiro. A cada iteração o Go só sobrescrevia o mesmo endereço de memória com o próximo item.

O t.Parallel() pausa a goroutine do subteste, e o loop principal continua correndo até o fim da tabela. Quando os subtestes acordam, todos enxergam o valor da última iteração. O teste reporta sucesso em todos os casos, mas na prática rodou o último caso várias vezes e ignorou os primeiros.

As duas soluções

Em Go 1.21 e anteriores, a saída é redeclarar a variável dentro do loop, o que cria uma cópia nova a cada volta:

for _, tc := range tests {
    tc := tc // Cria uma cópia local isolada na stack
    t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
        t.Parallel()
        // Agora tc aponta para a cópia segura
        got := Processar(tc.input)
        ...
    })
}

No Go 1.22 e superiores, a semântica da linguagem mudou: cada iteração do for cria uma nova instância da variável por padrão. A linha tc := tc deixou de ser necessária, e essa classe de falha desapareceu.

Dica: se você mantém uma biblioteca de código aberto que ainda dá suporte ao Go 1.20 ou 1.21, deixe a linha tc := tc explícita. Assim a suíte continua correta em qualquer versão do compilador.

Um exemplo completo

Vamos montar uma suíte para um validador de transações financeiras, com erros sentinela e t.Cleanup().

O código de negócio, em transacao.go:

package financeiro

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

var (
    ErrValorInvalido       = errors.New("o valor da transação deve ser positivo")
    ErrContaInvalida       = errors.New("número de conta de origem ou destino inválido")
    ErrLimiteUltrapassado  = errors.New("valor excede o limite diário da conta")
)

type Transacao struct {
    ContaOrigem  string
    ContaDestino string
    Valor        float64
}

// ValidarTransacao aplica as regras de conformidade bancária.
func ValidarTransacao(t Transacao, limiteDiario float64) error {
    if t.Valor <= 0 {
        return ErrValorInvalido
    }
    if len(t.ContaOrigem) < 5 || len(t.ContaDestino) < 5 {
        return ErrContaInvalida
    }
    if t.ContaOrigem == t.ContaDestino {
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: conta de origem idêntica ao destino", ErrContaInvalida)
    }
    if t.Valor > limiteDiario {
        return ErrLimiteUltrapassado
    }
    return nil
}

A suíte, em transacao_test.go. O loop abaixo assume Go 1.22 ou superior; em versões anteriores, acrescente tc := tc no início do corpo do for.

package financeiro_test

import (
    "errors"
    "testing"

    "meu-modulo/financeiro"
)

func TestValidarTransacao(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel() // A suíte pai roda em paralelo com outras do pacote

    // Tabela abrangente de cenários de teste
    tests := []struct {
        name         string
        transacao    financeiro.Transacao
        limiteDiario float64
        wantErr      bool
        expectedErr  error
    }{
        {
            name: "transação regular aprovada",
            transacao: financeiro.Transacao{
                ContaOrigem:  "12345-6",
                ContaDestino: "98765-4",
                Valor:        150.00,
            },
            limiteDiario: 1000.00,
            wantErr:      false,
            expectedErr:  nil,
        },
        {
            name: "transação com valor zero",
            transacao: financeiro.Transacao{
                ContaOrigem:  "12345-6",
                ContaDestino: "98765-4",
                Valor:        0.00,
            },
            limiteDiario: 1000.00,
            wantErr:      true,
            expectedErr:  financeiro.ErrValorInvalido,
        },
        {
            name: "transação com valor negativo",
            transacao: financeiro.Transacao{
                ContaOrigem:  "12345-6",
                ContaDestino: "98765-4",
                Valor:        -50.00,
            },
            limiteDiario: 1000.00,
            wantErr:      true,
            expectedErr:  financeiro.ErrValorInvalido,
        },
        {
            name: "conta de origem com menos de 5 dígitos",
            transacao: financeiro.Transacao{
                ContaOrigem:  "123",
                ContaDestino: "98765-4",
                Valor:        100.00,
            },
            limiteDiario: 1000.00,
            wantErr:      true,
            expectedErr:  financeiro.ErrContaInvalida,
        },
        {
            name: "transferência para a mesma conta",
            transacao: financeiro.Transacao{
                ContaOrigem:  "12345-6",
                ContaDestino: "12345-6",
                Valor:        100.00,
            },
            limiteDiario: 1000.00,
            wantErr:      true,
            expectedErr:  financeiro.ErrContaInvalida,
        },
        {
            name: "valor excede o limite diário",
            transacao: financeiro.Transacao{
                ContaOrigem:  "12345-6",
                ContaDestino: "98765-4",
                Valor:        1500.00,
            },
            limiteDiario: 1000.00,
            wantErr:      true,
            expectedErr:  financeiro.ErrLimiteUltrapassado,
        },
    }

    for _, tc := range tests {
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            t.Parallel() // Cada subteste executa em paralelo

            // t.Cleanup executa garantidamente no final deste subteste
            t.Cleanup(func() {
                // Ideal para fechar arquivos, resetar variáveis ou limpar caches locais
            })

            err := financeiro.ValidarTransacao(tc.transacao, tc.limiteDiario)

            // 1. Verificação da ocorrência de erro
            if (err != nil) != tc.wantErr {
                t.Fatalf("ValidarTransacao() erro = %v, esperava erro? %v", err, tc.wantErr)
            }

            // 2. Verificação precisa do tipo/causa do erro com errors.Is
            if tc.expectedErr != nil && !errors.Is(err, tc.expectedErr) {
                t.Errorf("ValidarTransacao() erro retornado = %v, esperava conter = %v", err, tc.expectedErr)
            }
        })
    }
}

Checklist antes de dar a suíte por concluída

  1. Compare erros com errors.Is, nunca por texto. Um if err.Error() == "texto" quebra na primeira vez que alguém reescrever a mensagem. Valide contra o erro sentinela com errors.Is(err, ErrAlvo).
  2. Rode com o detector de corridas na integração contínua: 
   go test -race ./...

Se os subtestes paralelos acessarem uma variável global ou outro recurso compartilhado sem proteção, o detector aponta as linhas em conflito.

  1. Dê nomes descritivos aos subtestes. O campo name deve dizer o que o cenário cobre e por quê, por exemplo "idade negativa deve retornar erro de validação".
  2. Não compartilhe estado entre testes paralelos. Um teste com t.Parallel() não deve alterar variáveis globais, tabelas de banco sem transação isolada ou o diretório de trabalho.
  3. Chame t.Helper() na primeira linha de qualquer função auxiliar de asserção. Assim o Go reporta a linha do teste que falhou, e não a linha dentro do utilitário.

Beba Água <3
