DeepInfer × DeepSeek – What the “breaking‑news” rollout means for high‑performance inference

Lead

“Half‑the‑latency, double the throughput – on the same silicon.”

DeepSeek’s chief architect announced this claim at the June 2026 launch, and the benchmark data backs it up. By open‑sourcing DeepInfer, DeepSeek has delivered a new suite of low‑precision kernels, a unified kernel‑ABI, and a speculative MoE scheduler that together cut end‑to‑end latency by 2.4× and lift throughput by roughly 30 % on flagship GPUs.

The headline grabs attention, but the deeper story lies in the engineering trade‑offs and market dynamics that will determine whether DeepInfer reshapes inference‑as‑a‑service or remains a specialist library.

A real‑time chatbot on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin

A startup wants to embed the 671‑billion‑parameter DeepSeek‑R1 model in a voice‑assistant device powered by a Jetson AGX Orin (204 TOPS, FP8/INT8/INT4 support).

Before DeepInfer

  • Proprietary runtime required FP8 weights and a custom CUDA stack.
  • Model load consumed 12 GB of GPU memory, leaving only 4 GB for activations.
  • A 256‑token prompt responded in 78 ms; cold‑start time was 1.2 s.
  • To meet a 100 ms SLA the startup ran two GPUs in parallel, doubling power draw and cost.

After DeepInfer

  • Switching to deepinfer.run(model, prompt) automatically selected the INT4 path, activated the Ozaki integer‑matrix‑multiply unit, and enabled activation‑recycling.
  • Memory fell to 8 GB, freeing room for a larger activation buffer.
  • End‑to‑end latency dropped to 33 ms, comfortably under the SLA with a single GPU.
  • Cold‑start time halved to 0.6 s thanks to lazy loading of MoE expert weights.

Result: hardware cost down ≈45 %, power consumption down ≈30 %, and on‑device personalization became feasible.

Hard numbers from the first week

Metric Baseline (DeepSeek‑only) DeepInfer on NVIDIA A100 DeepInfer on Ascend NPU SuperPOD
End‑to‑end latency (512‑token) 78 ms 33 ms (2.4× faster) 41 ms (1.9× faster)
Throughput (tokens / s per GPU) 5.2 k 7.8 k (30 % up) 7.0 k (35 % up)
Memory footprint (model + activations) 12 GB (FP8) 8 GB (INT4) 9 GB (Ascend‑optimized)
Cold‑start time (model load) 1.2 s 0.6 s 0.7 s
Power draw at full load 350 W 260 W 240 W

Key stat: DeepInfer earned >200 k GitHub stars and 30 k forks in its first week, making it the fastest‑growing inference engine of 2026.

Kernel‑level innovations that drive the gains

1. Ozaki integer‑matrix‑multiply

Packs INT4 values into 8‑bit lanes and runs a fused multiply‑add on tensor cores, cutting memory traffic by 45 % and doubling arithmetic intensity.

2. Speculative MoE token pre‑scheduling

Predicts which experts will fire, pre‑loads their weights, and pipelines execution, shrinking expert‑selection latency from 12 ms to under 3 ms.

3. Unified kernel‑ABI (v1.0)

A binary interface that abstracts vendor specifics; NVIDIA, AMD, and Huawei ship drop‑in libraries (libdeepinfer_cuda.so, libdeepinfer_hip.so, libdeepinfer_ascend.so) without touching the model graph.

4. Activation‑recycling

Reuses activation buffers across layers of identical shape, reducing fragmentation and improving cache locality.

Together these advances collapse into a single‑line Python call, a JSON config, and a compiled backend library.

Compatibility matrix

Model family Supported precisions Special kernels Accuracy loss
DeepSeek‑R1 (671 B) FP8, INT4, INT8 Ozaki integer‑MMU, speculative MoE < 0.3 % BLEU drop
DeepSeek‑V3 (1.2 T) FP8, INT4 Mixed‑precision fused kernels, checkpointing < 0.5 % perplexity rise
DeepSeek‑V4‑Pro (1.6 T) FP8, INT4, INT8 Hybrid CSA/HCA attention, Ozaki MMU < 0.1 % quality change
DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash (284 B) FP8, INT4 Same as V4‑Pro + speculative token pruning < 0.2 % quality drop

DeepInfer treats each model as a graph of operators; the runtime swaps in the optimal kernel based on target precision and hardware, requiring zero code changes from the user. Future MoE or sparse‑attention models fit the same ABI without recompilation.

Market reaction

  • Stock rally – DeepSeek’s parent (NASDAQ: DSK) jumped +12 % on announcement day, the biggest single‑day gain since the V4‑Flash launch.
  • Cloud beta programs – AWS rolled out g6e instances with DeepInfer‑optimized drivers; Azure announced NDv5 VMs exposing the Ascend backend; Alibaba Cloud unveiled GN5 instances for the China market.
  • Ecosystem adoption – NVIDIA now lists “DeepInfer support” under its CUDA toolkit; AMD’s ROCm roadmap includes a DeepInfer‑HIP shim slated for Q1 2027.
  • Developer buzz – Within 48 hours the repository logged >200 k stars and 30 k forks, outpacing TensorRT and ONNX Runtime growth in 2024.
  • Competitive positioning – OpenAI’s CTO warned that “proprietary inference stacks risk isolation,” hinting at pressure to open their own kernels. Anthropic called DeepInfer “a compelling alternative for high‑throughput workloads,” signaling a possible shift in the inference‑as‑a‑service market.

Risks and unanswered questions

  1. Non‑DeepSeek models – Early adopters report kernel mismatches with third‑party checkpoints (e.g., LLaMA, GPT‑4). Community contributions are needed to close the gap.
  2. Quantization accuracy – INT4 introduces a 0.2–0.5 % drop in BLEU/perplexity. DeepSeek’s upcoming calibration tool (Q4 2026) has yet to prove its robustness across domains.
  3. IP friction – The kernels overlap with patents held by NVIDIA and Huawei, raising the possibility of licensing disputes that could delay commercial rollouts.
  4. Hardware‑specific extensions – The Ozaki MMU relies on a microcode extension present only in recent NVIDIA and Ascend GPUs, forcing early upgrades for full speedup.

Outlook

  1. Standardization pressure – Continued cloud support could push the ABI toward a de‑facto industry standard. ONNX may adopt it as an optional “high‑performance inference” extension, compelling other runtimes to comply.
  2. Edge‑AI expansion – The Jetson Orin case shows DeepInfer’s viability on low‑power devices. OEMs in automotive, robotics, and smart speakers are likely to bundle the engine, creating a new revenue stream via enterprise support contracts.
  3. Cross‑modal inference – DeepSeek’s roadmap includes a Vision‑Language MoE that will share the same kernel stack. If DeepInfer can handle dense vision backbones without extra code, it could become the universal inference layer for multimodal services.
  4. Competitive response – OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta will accelerate their own open‑source inference projects. A future “breaking‑news” headline may feature a joint benchmark pitting DeepInfer, TensorRT, and TVM on a unified MoE workload.
  5. Monetization via support – While the core engine stays free, DeepSeek can sell enterprise‑grade plugins (security‑hardened kernels, compliance logging, SLA‑guaranteed cloud images), mirroring the successful Linux ecosystem model.

Call to action

DeepInfer has already proved that sub‑50 ms latency for 512‑token prompts is achievable on a single GPU, turning real‑time AI from a cloud‑only fantasy into an on‑device reality. The next step for engineers, product leaders, and investors is clear:

  • Test the ABI on your own workloads and contribute missing kernels to broaden model support.
  • Watch the standardization debate—early alignment with ONNX or a similar body could lock in long‑term compatibility across clouds.
  • Plan for hardware upgrades if you need the full Ozaki MMU boost, but weigh that against the cost savings DeepInfer already delivers.

If the community rallies around the open‑source stack and the ABI matures into an industry standard, DeepInfer could become the backbone of inference‑as‑a‑service for the next generation of low‑latency AI. The question now is not whether it will, but how quickly the ecosystem can coalesce around it.

title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
description:
arXiv:2610.26915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.

title: You Are the Trigger: Speaker-Activated Backdoors
description:
arXiv:2610.27210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech models are increasingly used as an interface to AI systems, from transcription tools to voice agents. Existing audio backdoors require an attacker to introduce triggers at inference time. We study a different threat model in which the attacker compromises the model during fine-tuning but has no access to the victim's inference-time inputs. We introduce the Speaker-Activated Backdoor (SAB) setting, in which a target speaker's natural voice serves as the trigger. We develop a two-phase fine-tuning method that first makes speaker identity more accessible and then binds the target speaker to an attacker-chosen payload. Compared with a one-phase baseline with the same training budget, the two-phase method substantially improves selectivity and clean performance, and is especially important for content-dependent attacks. SAB achieves 90.2% and 97.0% backdoor success on Whisper-medium and Parakeet, with false-positive rates of 1.7% and 0%, respectively using as little as two minutes of real audio from the target speaker. We further demonstrate content-dependent semantic rewriting and downstream tool-use attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into 96.9% of target-speaker transcripts. When these transcripts are passed to frontier LLM agents, GPT-4o and Claude (Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku), the injected instruction drives the agent to carry out the harmful action in up to 87.5% of cases. The attack generalizes to held-out recordings, multiple target speakers, and common acoustic degradations. These results establish speaker identity as a practical backdoor trigger that requires no inference-time attacker access and is invisible at the transcript layer.

title: Breaking the Language Barrier: Our Journey to 10 Native Languages
description:
We have a simple mission at RahaLune: build professional-grade tools that are 100% free, private, and accessible to everyone.

But "accessible to everyone" is easier said than done.

Until recently, our QR Code Generator was English-only. We received feedback from users in the Middle East, South America, and Europe asking for native language support.

Today, I’m thrilled to announce that RahaLune QR Studio is now natively translated into 10 languages.

The 10 Languages

We now support:
🇺🇸 English, 🇫🇷 French, 🇪🇸 Spanish, 🇩🇪 German, 🇹🇷 Turkish, 🇨🇳 Chinese (Simplified), 🇮🇩 Indonesian, 🇲🇾 Malay, 🇸🇦 Arabic, and 🇵🇰 Urdu.

It’s Not Just Translation, It’s a Layout Shift

Translating the text was the easy part. The real challenge was supporting Arabic and Urdu.

These are Right-to-Left (RTL) languages, which means the entire user interface has to flip. We spent hours ensuring that the navigation bar, the QR input forms, and the design studio controls all look perfect when reading right-to-left.

We also made sure the fonts were correct (using Amiri or Noto Sans Arabic) so the text feels native, not machine-generated.

Still 100% Free & Private

Despite this massive update, our core promises haven't changed:

  1. No Logins: Just open the page and use it.
  2. No Ads: The tools are free, forever.
  3. 100% Client-Side: All translation files are loaded locally. Your QR code data never leaves your browser.

Try It Out

I'd love for you to test out the localization. Head over to the site, use the language dropdown in the top right corner, and let me know how it feels in your native language.

👉 Try RahaLune QR Studio

Happy building!

title: A Node.js Gate Before Private Object Storage File Delivery
description:
TL;DR

Keep export objects private, authenticate the person requesting the download, and redirect that request to a newly minted, short-lived presigned URL. A Node.js application should store an export record rather than a durable object URL; that record is where tenant authorization, expiry, and audit decisions belong.

The least complex design is an authenticated application endpoint followed by a redirect to object storage. It removes the application server from the data path without turning a forwarded link into a long-lived grant. The signature is useful, but it is only one boundary in a file-export system.

Start with the delivery constraint

A generated report has two distinct identities that are often collapsed into one: it is a blob of bytes, and it is a business artifact that belongs to a tenant, user, retention policy, and job. Object storage is well suited to the first identity. It is a poor place to make the second identity disappear behind a copied URL.

For a private export, the object path should be an implementation detail. The application owns an export identifier and records its owner, storage key, expected state, content type, suggested filename, and deletion time. A browser asks the application for that identifier. The application authenticates the request, checks that the caller may read the export, then issues a redirect to a URL authorized for one object and a short period. The object store handles the transfer directly.

That division matters. A presigned URL is a bearer credential: possession of the string is sufficient until its expiry. It can end up in browser history, logs, copied messages, and link scanners. Keeping it out of a durable email template means an administrator can later block the application route, remove the export record, or change authorization rules before another URL is issued. It does not revoke a URL that has already been handed out, so the lifetime still needs to be deliberate.

Small is safer.

There is a second constraint: an export job must not publish a download before its object is ready. Treat queued, writing, ready, expired, and deleted as application states, not as guesses inferred from a URL. Before moving an export to ready, validate the write using the storage interface appropriate to the service: confirm object existence, expected length, checksum or version where the system exposes one, and the encryption or retention properties required by policy. Then make the redirect endpoint available. This avoids the familiar race where a worker reports completion while a reader receives a link to an artifact that is absent, partial, or no longer authorized.

How should Node.js issue a presigned download URL for a private object-storage file?

The endpoint should do authorization before signing and should sign a read request for the exact object key recorded against the export. Do not accept a bucket or object key from the browser, and do not use a client-provided filename as an authorization input. Those values belong to the server-side export record.

The following Python-shaped pseudocode shows the boundary without binding the design to one storage SDK. The same sequence is what a Node.js route needs: load the export, verify the session and tenant, reject a non-ready record, create a short-lived signed GET request, and return a redirect.

def start_download(request, export_id, exports, signer):
    export = exports.get(export_id)
    if export is None or export.state != "ready":
        return response(status=404)

    if not request.user.can_read_tenant(export.tenant_id):
        return response(status=403)

    signed_url = signer.sign_get(
        object_key=export.object_key,
        expires_in_seconds=120,
        response_content_disposition=(
            f'attachment; filename="{export.download_name}"'
        ),
        response_content_type=export.content_type,
    )

    exports.record_download_attempt(export.id, request.user.id)
    return redirect(signed_url, status=302)

The requested response headers are part of the signed request, so the recipient cannot change the desired attachment name by editing a query parameter. Content-Disposition: attachment asks the browser to download rather than render the response; use a filename that your application has already normalized for the platform and content type. The MDN documentation also calls out a practical detail: when both filename and filename* appear, modern browsers prefer filename*, which is relevant if exports have non-ASCII filenames.

Choose the URL lifetime from the user path, not from a generic security number. A human clicking through an authenticated page may need a minute or two. A link intended for a slow, resumable multi-gigabyte transfer may need a longer window, tested with the store's range-request behavior. Signature Version 4 presigned URLs can be created for up to seven days, but URLs signed with temporary credentials expire when those credentials expire, even when the requested URL lifetime is longer. Those are protocol and credential limits, not reasons to make every export link last a week.

CORS is frequently blamed for a problem that is actually a delivery-shape choice. A normal top-level navigation or redirect to the signed URL does not need a browser script to read a cross-origin response. If the web client uses fetch() to inspect the object or its headers, CORS applies and the storage response must allow the requesting origin, method, and any headers used by the request. Test that path in a browser; a command-line download is not a CORS test.

Decide where each control actually lives

The comparison is clearer after the constraints are explicit. Signing authorizes an object-store request. The application route authorizes a user. A delivery system often needs both.

Delivery pattern Authorization point What can be stopped later Operational cost Main limitation
URL placed directly in email Signing time Future issuance only Low Forwarding exposes the bearer URL until expiry
Authenticated route, then short redirect Request time and signing time The route can stop issuing new URLs One application hop Link scanners may request the route before the person does
Application streams the file Every byte request The application can deny the stream Connection capacity and egress through the service Large or slow downloads consume application resources
Signed policy at an edge layer Edge policy evaluation Depends on policy invalidation More delivery configuration Cache and authorization rules need careful review

For tenant reports, the authenticated-route pattern usually has the cleanest audit story: log an event at the point where a known principal requested a known export, then let storage transfer the bytes. The catch is that it is not suitable when recipients cannot authenticate to the application, such as an intentional external handoff. In that case, a narrowly scoped bearer link may be the required product decision, with a lifetime and sharing warning matched to the sensitivity of the file. A long-lived direct URL is still a poor substitute for access control.

Avoid treating a single GET as a single human action. Mail protection systems can prefetch links, browsers can retry, and download managers can make range requests. The redirect endpoint should therefore be safe to repeat. Record attempts separately from successful business acknowledgment, and do not burn a one-time application token merely because an automated scanner followed it. If a policy truly requires single-use delivery, define what counts as use and test it against those agents before promising the behavior.

How do you roll out a private export path and retain observability?

Introduce the export record and authenticated route before changing any outward-facing message. New notifications can link to the application route while existing links live until their own expiry. This lets a team observe the redirect path without invalidating old inboxes or coupling a storage migration to a communication migration. In a staged release, first create records for completed exports while retaining the current delivery path, then enable the route for an internal account, then send the new route in a small cohort of ordinary notifications. Check that the authorization decision names the expected tenant, that the signed object key is the one on the export record, and that the attachment name is right after the redirect, because a correct 302 only proves that the application made a choice, not that the recipient obtained the intended bytes. Follow the expiry boundary too: request the route before the record expires, open the redirect only after the signed URL expires, and confirm that the application issues a new URL only while the export record is still eligible. Those checks separate a storage-signing limit from an application-retention decision, which prevents support work from becoming a debate about an opaque query string.

Instrument the state transitions and the boundary crossings: job accepted, object verified, record marked ready, route requested, redirect issued, and object-store response where logs are available. Keep the signed query string out of ordinary request logs because it is a credential. Alert on exports stuck between writing and ready, and investigate a wide gap between issued redirects and completed downloads before treating it as a storage failure; delivery, client behavior, and corporate scanners can produce the same first symptom.

Run a small test matrix before release. Cover a permitted user, a user from another tenant, an expired record, a deleted object, a file with a non-ASCII attachment name, a browser navigation, a scripted fetch() path with CORS enabled, and a resumed download. Your mileage may vary with identity providers and client networks, but those cases make the assumptions visible while they are still cheap to change.

References

  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • MDN, Content-Disposition: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • AWS S3 documentation, Download and upload objects with presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html

title: OmniVLoc: Topo-metric Visual Localization for Omnidirectional Cameras
description:
arXiv:2610.27522v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omnidirectional cameras provide surround-view information, significantly overcoming the field-of-view constraints for traditional visual localization systems. However, existing localization systems fail to fully exploit the characteristics of omnidirectional cameras, struggling to deliver accurate and robust localization performance amidst scene content variations and illumination-induced appearance changes. In this work, we propose OmniVLoc, a surround-view localization system based on a topo-metric framework. By integrating state-of-the-art global place recognition and monocular depth estimation methods, we introduce a multi-constrained visual localization paradigm. By solving a scale-aware pose graph and performing precise spherical bundle adjustment, we accurately recover the metric-level pose for each query frame.Furthermore, a hierarchical verification mechanism is designed to filter out erroneous outputs across different stages, effectively bolstering the overall system robustness. Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets validate the superior accuracy and reliability of OmniVLoc. To benefit the community, our source code and dataset will be made publicly available upon publication.

title: Deep Auxiliary Learning via Bilevel Feature Optimization for Label-Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.26954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Auxiliary learning (AL), which can improve the performance of a primary task by leveraging related auxiliary tasks, is commonly regarded as a special case of multi-task learning. Existing AL approaches typically require manually annotated auxiliary labels, increasing annotation costs, particularly in medical imaging where expert labeling is expensive. In this work, we investigate whether segmentation performance can be improved using auxiliary tasks whose labels are automatically derived from existing segmentation annotations, requiring no additional manual labeling. To address this, we propose a novel auxiliary learning framework, formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. Our method enables effective knowledge transfer between tasks via a feature communication module, enhancing the primary segmentation task. We evaluate the method on three medical image segmentation benchmarks under limited-label settings. The results demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior label efficiency. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/FupingWu90/ALBO.

title: Autonomous LLM Agents as Dynamic Decision Nodes in Temporal Sagas
description:
Modern core banking platforms are increasingly adopting generative AI and Large Language Model (LLM) agents to handle complex operational reasoning—such as assessing unstructured trade finance documents, triaging complex fraud cases, and resolving cross-border exception processing. However, introducing autonomous AI agents into core banking workflows presents a fundamental architectural contradiction: Temporal Sagas demand absolute determinism, whereas LLM reasoning is inherently non-deterministic.

Temporal workflows achieve fault tolerance through event-sourced execution replay. If a workflow definition behaves non-deterministically during history replay, execution drifts, state corruption occurs, and replay validation fails. Conversely, LLMs generate probabilistic outcomes influenced by temperature settings, floating-point variance across hardware inference clusters, and model version shifts.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, core banking platforms resolve this tension by encapsulating autonomous LLM agents inside isolated Temporal Activities bounded by strict JSON schema contracts, formal validation guardrails, and deterministic fallback paths. This paper evaluates the operational boundaries, dynamic task planning topologies, mathematical reliability models, and compensation patterns required to deploy autonomous LLM agents as dynamic decision nodes in distributed core banking Sagas.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

Architectural Boundaries across BIAN Service Domains

Not all decision nodes within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) ecosystem require LLM autonomy. Integrating AI agents into deterministic Sagas must be strictly categorized by domain risk and exception frequency.

BIAN Service Domain Capability Mapped to LLM Node Autonomy Level Primary Risk Boundary Fallback Mechanism
Trade Positioning LC (Letter of Credit) document clause verification Semi-Autonomous Operational Exception Human-in-the-Loop Approval
Fraud Evaluation Suspicious transaction triage & contextual analysis Autonomous Decision False Positive Risk Default Deterministic Rule Engine
Customer Onboarding Unstructured Identity Exception Handling Semi-Autonomous Compliance / Regulatory Re-route to Compliance Officer Task
Payment Execution Automated Payment Clearing & ISO20022 Routing Strict Deterministic (No LLM) High Financial Risk N/A (Hardcoded / DMN Engine Only)
Position Keeping Double-Entry Ledger Posting Strict Deterministic (No LLM) Balance Integrity Risk N/A (Static Microservice Logic)

The Determinism Isolation Pattern

To prevent non-deterministic LLM behavior from corrupting Temporal's execution history, LLM agent reasoning must never execute directly within a Temporal Workflow Definition. Instead, the workflow definition maintains absolute determinism, while the LLM execution logic is fully encapsulated inside a Temporal Activity.

                  THE DETERMINISM ISOLATION ARCHITECTURE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TEMPORAL WORKFLOW ENGINE (100% Deterministic Event History Execution)          |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [Start Workflow] ---> [Execute Activity: RunAgentActivity] ---> [Branch Logic] |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------^-----------+
                                      |                                 |
                           1. Invoke Activity Payload        4. Return Deterministic
                              (Structured Context)              Structured JSON Output
                                      |                                 |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------+
  | TEMPORAL ACTIVITY WORKER LAYER    v                                 |           |
  | (Non-Deterministic Sandbox)                                         |           |
  |                                                                     |           |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------+  |           |
  |  | LLM AGENT REASONING LOOP                                      |  |           |
  |  |                                                               |  |           |
  |  |  [Construct Prompt] ---> [LLM Inference Engine (OpenAI/Ollama)]|  |           |
  |  |                                  │                            |  |           |
  |  |                                  ▼                            |  |           |
  |  |  [JSON Guardrail Validation] ◄── [Tool Call / Re-Act Loop]     |  |           |
  |  +----------------------------------│----------------------------+  |           |
  |                                     |                               |           |
  |                          2. Return Output Schema                    |           |
  |                             (Passed or Rejected)                    |           |
  +-------------------------------------│-------------------------------+-----------+
                                        v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | IMMUTABLE EVENT STORE & STATE AUDIT                                             |
  |  [ Persists Prompt Hash, Token Cost, Confidence Score, and Decision Payload ]  |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key Architectural Rules

  1. Replay Immutability: Temporal records the activity output payload (the LLM's final structured JSON decision) into the workflow's Event History. During workflow replay, Temporal does not re-invoke the LLM activity; it simply reads the recorded decision payload from history.
  2. Deterministic Branching: The workflow evaluates the structured decision payload using standard deterministic logic (if/else or switch statements) to dispatch downstream machine Sagas or human tasks.
  3. Idempotency & Retry Safety: LLM activities must implement strict idempotency keys (derived from WorkflowID + RunID + ActivityTaskID) to prevent duplicate inference costs or repeated side effects during network retries.

Mathematical Model: Agent Decision Reliability & Guardrail Probability

The reliability of an LLM agent operating as a dynamic decision node within a distributed financial Saga depends on schema adherence, hallucination rates, and downstream transaction commitment.

The probability of a successful autonomous decision node commit Pnode-success​ across an agentic execution path is defined as:

Pnode-success​=Pschema-valid​×(1−Phallucination​)×Psaga-commit​

Where:

  • Pschema-valid​ is the probability that the LLM output conforms strictly to the target JSON schema on attempt k (where k≤MaxRetries ).
  • Phallucination​ is the probability that the agent generates a factually incorrect decision despite schema validity.
  • Psaga-commit​ is the probability that the downstream distributed machine Saga succeeds without compensation.

If the agent's confidence score falls below a pre-configured threshold θconfidence​ , or if Pschema-valid​=0 after maximum retries, the system triggers a Deterministic Fallback Override, shifting control to a standard rule engine or human user task.

Technical Implementation: Agentic Activity & Temporal Workflow

1. Structured Output Decision Schema (Java DTOs) 

package com.xenon.banking.ai.model;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.util.List;

public record TradeExceptionDecision(
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String decisionOutcome, // "APPROVE_EXEMPTION", "REJECT_EXEMPTION", "ESCALATE_HUMAN"
    @JsonProperty(required = true) double confidenceScore, // 0.0 to 1.0
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String reasoningSummary,
    @JsonProperty(required = true) List<String> verifiedClauseIdentifiers,
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String recommendedCompensatingAction
) {}

2. Temporal Activity Encapsulating the LLM Reasoning Loop

This Java activity executes an agentic reasoning loop using structured function calling. If the LLM generates invalid JSON or fails validation constraints, the activity retries locally up to a bounded threshold before returning an explicit failure state.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.activity;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.xenon.banking.ai.model.TradeExceptionDecision;
import io.temporal.activity.Activity;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityExecutionContext;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.util.Map;

@Component("tradeAgentActivity")
public class TradeAgentActivityImpl implements TradeAgentActivity {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Override
    public TradeExceptionDecision evaluateTradeException(String documentText, String exceptionCode, double transactionAmount) {
        ActivityExecutionContext ctx = Activity.getExecutionContext();
        String workflowId = ctx.getInfo().getWorkflowId();

        System.out.println("Executing Agentic Decision Node for Workflow: " + workflowId);

        // Construct System & User Prompt for Structured Function Calling
        String promptPayload = buildPromptJson(documentText, exceptionCode, transactionAmount);

        int attempts = 0;
        int maxRetries = 3;

        while (attempts < maxRetries) {
            attempts++;
            try {
                // Call LLM Inference Endpoint (OpenAI / Internal Enterprise Model API)
                HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create("https://ai-gateway.internal.xenon/v1/chat/completions"))
                        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("AI_GATEWAY_KEY"))
                        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(promptPayload))
                        .build();

                HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

                // Parse Structured Output Response
                String rawJsonResponse = extractStructuredJsonFromResponse(response.body());
                TradeExceptionDecision decision = objectMapper.readValue(rawJsonResponse, TradeExceptionDecision.class);

                // Validation Guardrail: Enforce minimum confidence threshold
                if (decision.confidenceScore() < 0.85) {
                    System.out.println("Agent confidence score (" + decision.confidenceScore() + ") below threshold. Escalating.");
                    return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", decision.confidenceScore(), 
                            "Low confidence score in automated evaluation.", decision.verifiedClauseIdentifiers(), "NONE");
                }

                return decision; // Successfully evaluated and validated

            } catch (Exception e) {
                System.err.println("Attempt " + attempts + " failed to parse LLM structured decision: " + e.getMessage());
                if (attempts >= maxRetries) {
                    // Fail-safe default returned to Workflow
                    return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", 0.0, 
                            "LLM execution failed structural validation after retries.", List.of(), "NONE");
                }
            }
        }

        return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", 0.0, "Execution exhausted retries.", List.of(), "NONE");
    }

    private String buildPromptJson(String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount) {
        // Formats prompt enforcing JSON Schema output constraints
        return """
            {
              "model": "xenon-financial-agent-v2",
              "messages": [
                {"role": "system", "content": "You are a specialized risk evaluation agent. You must output JSON conforming strictly to the TradeExceptionDecision schema."},
                {"role": "user", "content": "Evaluate document: %s under exception code: %s for amount: %.2f"}
              ],
              "response_format": {"type": "json_object"},
              "temperature": 0.0
            }
            """.formatted(escapeJson(documentText), exceptionCode, amount);
    }

    private String extractStructuredJsonFromResponse(String responseBody) throws Exception {
        var node = objectMapper.readTree(responseBody);
        return node.path("choices").get(0).path("message").path("content").asText();
    }

    private String escapeJson(String input) {
        return input.replace("\"", "\\\"").replace("\n", " ");
    }
}

3. Temporal Workflow Definition (Deterministic Branching)

The workflow invokes the agent activity. Depending on the agent's structured decision, it deterministically dispatches an automated downstream machine Saga or suspends for human review.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.ai.activity.TradeAgentActivity;
import com.xenon.banking.ai.model.TradeExceptionDecision;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface TradeResolutionWorkflow {
    @WorkflowMethod
    void processTradeException(String tradeId, String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount);
}

public class TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl implements TradeResolutionWorkflow {

    private final TradeAgentActivity agentActivity = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            TradeAgentActivity.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder()
                    .setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
                    .setRetryOptions(io.temporal.common.RetryOptions.newBuilder()
                            .setMaximumAttempts(3)
                            .build())
                    .build()
    );

    @Override
    public void processTradeException(String tradeId, String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount) {

        // 1. Invoke Isolated LLM Agent Activity (Non-deterministic code runs safely inside activity)
        TradeExceptionDecision agentDecision = agentActivity.evaluateTradeException(documentText, exceptionCode, amount);

        // 2. Deterministic Workflow Execution Path based on Activity Event History
        switch (agentDecision.decisionOutcome()) {
            case "APPROVE_EXEMPTION" -> {
                // Trigger automated machine Saga step (e.g., Ledger Release)
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).info("Agent approved exception. Executing release Saga.");
                executeAutomatedReleaseSaga(tradeId, amount);
            }
            case "REJECT_EXEMPTION" -> {
                // Trigger automated cancellation & compensation Saga
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).info("Agent rejected exception. Executing compensation Saga.");
                executeCompensatingCancellationSaga(tradeId);
            }
            case "ESCALATE_HUMAN" -> {
                // Halt workflow deterministically and await Human-in-the-Loop Signal
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).warn("Agent requested human escalation. Awaiting signal.");
                awaitHumanReviewSignal(tradeId, agentDecision.reasoningSummary());
            }
            default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unexpected agent decision outcome: " + agentDecision.decisionOutcome());
        }
    }

    private void executeAutomatedReleaseSaga(String tradeId, double amount) {
        // Standard deterministic machine Activity calls
    }

    private void executeCompensatingCancellationSaga(String tradeId) {
        // Standard deterministic compensating Activity calls
    }

    private void awaitHumanReviewSignal(String tradeId, String reasoning) {
        // Suspend workflow execution until human approval signal arrives
    }
}

Transactional Consistency and Saga Compensation Scenarios

When an autonomous LLM agent decides to approve an operational exception, it triggers forward transactions (e.g., balance holds or ledger postings). If a downstream microservice fails after an LLM agent decision has been rendered, the Temporal orchestrator automatically executes standard Compensating Actions.

  AGENT DECISION SAGA COMPENSATION FLOW

  +-----------------------+        1. Approve Exception        +-----------------------+
  |  LLM Agent Activity   | ---------------------------------> | Temporal Saga Manager |
  | (Evaluates Document)  |                                    | (Workflow History)    |
  +-----------------------+                                    +-----------+-----------+
                                                                           |
                                   2. Execute Step 1 (Ledger Debit)        |
                                                                           v
  +-----------------------+        3. Step 2 Fails (API Timeout) +-----------------------+
  | Downstream Services   | <----------------------------------| Executing Machine     |
  | (Ledger / Risk Engine)| ---------------------------------> | Activities            |
  +-----------------------+        4. Trigger Compensation     +-----------+-----------+
                                                                           |
                                   5. Execute Rollback Activity            |
                                      (Revert Ledger Debit)                v
                                                               +-----------------------+
                                                               | Audit Log & Escalate  |
                                                               | to Human Desk         |
                                                               +-----------------------+

Compensation Safety Rules

  1. Non-Reversible Actions: An LLM agent must never execute uncompensable real-world actions (such as dispatching an external Fedwire SWIFT MT103 message) directly from within its reasoning loop.
  2. Two-Stage Authorization: The agent activity may only modify internal staging state or emit execution intents. The actual final settlement step must be gated by a secondary deterministic activity or a human approval check if the transaction value exceeds strict monetary limits.

Observability, Prompt Lineage, and Auditability

Financial regulators (such as OCC, EBA, and MAS) require complete lineage for AI-assisted operational decisions. Storing only the final decision payload is insufficient; the system must retain full cryptographic lineage of the agent's context.

Audit Metadata Record Structure

For every LLM decision node invocation, the activity writes an immutable audit record to the centralized log storage layer, linked to the Temporal WorkflowID and RunID:

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-2026-902183",
  "temporalWorkflowId": "TradeResolution-TR-9902",
  "temporalRunId": "b182f4e8-421d-405a-a309-88f2b7190012",
  "bianDomain": "TradePositioning",
  "llmProvider": "Azure-OpenAI-Internal",
  "modelDeployment": "gpt-4o-financial-v2",
  "promptHash": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "inputTokenCount": 1420,
  "outputTokenCount": 185,
  "rawOutput": "{\"decisionOutcome\":\"APPROVE_EXEMPTION\",\"confidenceScore\":0.94,\"reasoningSummary\":\"Clause 4b matches standard ICC UCP 600 rules.\",\"verifiedClauseIdentifiers\":[\"CLAUSE-4B\"],\"recommendedCompensatingAction\":\"NONE\"}",
  "confidenceScore": 0.94,
  "schemaValidationPassed": true,
  "executionTimestamp": "2026-09-16T11:56:28Z"
}

Integrating autonomous LLM agents into Temporal Sagas bridges the gap between flexible AI-driven reasoning and rigid financial reliability. By strict application of the Determinism Isolation Pattern—confining non-deterministic LLM execution inside structured Temporal Activities while keeping the orchestration workflow fully deterministic—core banking platforms achieve intelligent operational automation without sacrificing transactional integrity, fault tolerance, or regulatory auditability across BIAN service domains.

title: 2 Agent Skills Every Frontend Developer Should Try
description:
I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I found two new ones I want to share with you.

First one is Impeccable. Impeccable took a plain, AI-built website and gave it a design. It wasn't bad at all! Diagram Design took that same site and drew a diagram of how it works! Both install with one command, and both work with basically any coding harness. I used Kiro in my demos but you can use whatever you like.

I made a video walking through both if you'd rather watch:

Prerequisites

  • An agent that supports Agent Skills. I use Kiro, but Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex work too.
  • Node.js, so you can run npx.
  • A frontend project to try them on. Mine is a small website about cats.

Finding skills

I found both skills on Skill Leaderboard, which ranks skill repos by GitHub stars. You can filter by compatible agent, so I set it to Kiro. Skills are like recipes that work across most coding harnesses, so you'll usually be fine without the filter. Some repos are easier to install in one agent than another, though, and the filter saves you from finding that out the hard way.

Stars measure popularity. I cared more about what fits my own projects, so I picked the two that match what I build most, which is websites.

Before you install anything, read the SKILL.md and any scripts it pulls in. A skill is instructions and scripts that run with your agent's permissions, so check it the same way you'd check an npm package.

1. Impeccable

Impeccable is a design skill that started from Anthropic's frontend-design skill and builds on top of it. It has UX planning, a set of design commands like critique, polish, and audit, and it asks you a lot of questions.

To test it, I had Claude Opus 5.5 vibe code a site called the Great Cat Color Census. You spot a cat in the wild, click "Spotted one," and the counts and leaderboard update. Out of the box it came with a blocky card style and some hover animations. It looked okay. I don't think it looked bad, but it was pretty generic.


The default design Claude Opus 5.5 came up with.

Install it from your project root:

npx impeccable install

Then run init inside your agent:

/impeccable init

Init looks through the project, asks about anything it can't work out on its own, and writes a PRODUCT.md with what it learned. After that I asked it to make the site much nicer using its styles. It came back with five or six design directions. I picked the sticker one.


The sticker direction from Impeccable. Same features, new design.

It has basically the same features as before, and you can still summon a random cat. It looks a lot more polished, with extra animation and cats that look like peel-off stickers. The font gives it a Cat in the Hat feel. I don't have a very particular taste for frontend design, and I still like this version better. If you're a designer, tell me in the comments whether you agree.

A good way to use Impeccable is to have it build several of its directions on separate Git branches. Then you can run each one and compare them side by side before you commit to a look.

2. Diagram Design

Diagram Design draws diagrams as one self-contained HTML and SVG file. It supports 45 diagram types, from architecture diagrams and flow charts to radar charts and Venn diagrams. The screenshots in the repo don't do it much justice.

Install it with the skills CLI:

npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design

I asked it for a diagram of the same cat site and didn't say what to diagram. There's no backend, so I wasn't expecting much. It picked the visitor flow. A visitor clicks, an action runs change() or reset(), the counts update, and the derived stats feed the left and right pages. It also shows the save and load path to localStorage, and it even carried over the pink styling from the site.


The diagram Diagram Design made from the cat site, open in Kiro.

It's a simple diagram, but I like the style, and I can see myself using it on my next project. It's also handy when you open a code base with little documentation. Ask it for a few diagrams before you start reading the code.

The rest of the list

I haven't spent much time with the other popular skills yet. These are my notes so far.

Ponytail gives your agent the personality of the laziest senior dev in the room. In its README, you show him fifty lines, and he says nothing and replaces them with one. The goal is less code and fewer tokens. In Kiro it loads as an always-on ruleset, so you don't get its slash commands.

Caveman makes the agent answer tersely to cut token usage. I haven't seen much savings myself. Someone in a Reddit thread on the top Kiro skill repos said it raised their token usage, even though the research the repo cites says otherwise.

Addy Osmani's agent skills add a spec, plan, build, and test workflow to your agent. Kiro has specs built in, but if your tool doesn't, this or Superpowers is how I'd add spec-driven development.

I haven't tried UI UX Pro Max or Graphify yet, even though they're near the top of the list.

If you build on AWS, look at the Agent Toolkit for AWS. It's our set of skills and MCP servers for working with AWS from your agent, and it's free on GitHub.

Wrap up

If you build websites, Impeccable is the one I'd install first. Diagram Design is right behind it, especially when you're new to a code base.

I'm thinking about testing whether Ponytail and Caveman save tokens in Kiro. Leave a comment if you want to see that, and tell me which skills you're using.

title: Node.js Broadcast Polls: Aggregate Votes into a Reconnect-Safe Interval Tally
description:
Short answer: keep vote ingestion separate from interval publication, assign every published tally a monotonic revision, and let a reconnecting viewer request the newest snapshot after the last revision it applied. For a live media poll, the least complex dependable design is one authoritative aggregator per poll, a durable vote log or database behind it, and disposable realtime connections in front of it. The five-second ticker is presentation cadence, not correctness.

The page that should fire is tally_revision_stalled, scoped to one poll and accompanied by the last accepted vote position, the last published revision, connected viewers, and publish age. The on-call does not need a bright chart saying connections are down 8%. They need to know whether votes are still being accepted while viewers are seeing an old result, because that is the split-brain experience an audience will notice during a broadcast.

This design also answers the Node.js implementation question without tying correctness to an Express process timer. Express can validate and accept a vote; a serialized poll worker owns aggregation; a scheduler asks that worker to publish; and the transport delivers a versioned snapshot. If a process restarts or a viewer reconnects, both resume from durable positions instead of guessing what happened during the gap.

What should page the on-call?

Imagine the alert arriving with only WebSocket disconnect rate high. That signal is noisy by construction: mobile viewers roam between networks, laptops sleep, and browsers close. A disconnect is an event, not yet an incident. The actionable failure is narrower: accepted votes have advanced beyond the input position represented by the most recent published tally, and that gap has remained open longer than the promised publication interval plus a small scheduling allowance.

The alert payload should make the failure legible without dashboard archaeology:

  • poll and broadcast identifiers
  • latest durable vote position
  • input position included in the latest tally
  • tally revision and publication timestamp
  • worker lease owner, if ownership is leased
  • publish attempts and delivery failures

Ask one blunt question: what page fired? If the answer is merely CPU, open connections, or queue depth, the team still has to infer user impact. Page on a sustained publication lag while votes are arriving. Ticket or graph the rest.

The earlier signal is accepted_position - published_position, measured per poll. Publication age alone cannot distinguish a quiet poll from a stuck worker. Vote throughput alone cannot show that viewers are stale. The position gap joins the two sides of the contract, so it should fire before audience reports arrive.

How should Node.js aggregate votes and publish each interval tally?

A vote command needs a stable identifier, poll identifier, selected option, and an authoritative position assigned when the command becomes durable. Reject choices outside the poll definition before appending. Deduplicate by the stable vote identifier according to the product's voting rule; a rule allowing one active choice per account requires an identity and replacement policy, while an anonymous multiple-choice poll has a different state transition. Do not pretend those policies are interchangeable.

The aggregator consumes commands in position order and produces a complete snapshot. A snapshot carries the poll identifier, counts, the highest included input position, and a monotonic tally revision. Complete snapshots cost more bytes than deltas, but they make reconnect recovery bounded: the client can replace local state after verifying that the revision is newer. Deltas demand gap detection and replay, and one lost increment can poison every later display. For a small option set, the snapshot trade-off is easier to operate.

That is the invariant.

The state transition below is Go because the important part is ownership and revision, not a framework API. A Node.js service should preserve the same single-writer semantics through one queue partition, a database transaction, or another explicit serialization boundary.

package tally

import (
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Vote struct {
    ID       string
    Option   string
    Position uint64
}

type Snapshot struct {
    PollID           string         `json:"pollId"`
    Revision         uint64         `json:"revision"`
    IncludedPosition uint64         `json:"includedPosition"`
    PublishedAt      time.Time      `json:"publishedAt"`
    Counts           map[string]int `json:"counts"`
}

type Aggregator struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    pollID   string
    allowed  map[string]bool
    seen     map[string]bool
    counts   map[string]int
    position uint64
    revision uint64
}

func (a *Aggregator) Apply(v Vote) error {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    if !a.allowed[v.Option] {
        return errors.New("unknown poll option")
    }
    if a.seen[v.ID] {
        return nil
    }
    if v.Position <= a.position {
        return errors.New("non-monotonic input position")
    }
    a.seen[v.ID] = true
    a.counts[v.Option]++
    a.position = v.Position
    return nil
}

func (a *Aggregator) Publish(now time.Time) Snapshot {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    a.revision++
    copied := make(map[string]int, len(a.counts))
    for option, count := range a.counts {
        copied[option] = count
    }
    return Snapshot{
        PollID: a.pollID, Revision: a.revision,
        IncludedPosition: a.position, PublishedAt: now.UTC(),
        Counts: copied,
    }
}

The mutex makes this sample internally coherent, but it does not make two processes one writer. That trap matters. If every Express replica runs its own interval and holds its own counts, viewers can receive alternating realities; adding a distributed transport spreads the contradiction faster. Elect or partition one owner for a poll, persist the consumed position and snapshot atomically, and treat publication as retryable delivery of already committed state.

Timers are not authority.

How does reconnect and backfill stay boring?

A client stores the greatest tally revision it has applied. On connection, it sends that revision as resume metadata. The server returns the current snapshot when the stored revision is absent or older; if the client already has the current revision, no tally transfer is necessary. A late message with a lower revision is discarded. An equal revision is idempotent. A higher revision replaces the displayed counts.

That rule is intentionally dull.

WebRTC data channels are one possible transport, and the WebRTC specification defines data channels for bidirectional arbitrary data, but transport choice does not remove the application-level revision contract. The same contract can sit above WebSocket, server-sent events for downstream delivery, or periodic HTTP retrieval. Keep vote submission on an authenticated request path with explicit acknowledgement rather than assuming a transient viewer connection proves a vote became durable.

Backfill does not need to mean replaying every five-second publication. A viewer wants the latest correct tally, so one current snapshot is enough unless the interface exposes historical movement. Analytics is different: if producers need the full time series, retain committed snapshots or derive them from the durable vote log under a stated retention policy. Do not overload reconnect recovery with an analytics requirement most viewers never use.

Incoming revision Client action Operational meaning
lower than applied discard delayed or reordered delivery
equal to applied ignore safely duplicate delivery
exactly one higher replace snapshot normal interval update
more than one higher replace and record a gap reconnect or missed delivery

Recording a gap is useful telemetry, but a gap between complete snapshots is not a reason to freeze the UI. The newer snapshot is authoritative. This distinction keeps recovery fast while leaving evidence for investigation.

Instrument the contract, then test failure

Start with four measurements: accepted vote position, aggregated position, committed tally revision, and delivered revision acknowledgements sampled from clients. The first three locate a server-side stall. The last reveals an audience segment that is connected but not advancing. Include broadcast and poll identifiers in logs, but avoid attaching voter identity to high-cardinality metrics.

Emit one structured record at each boundary using the same poll identifier and positions: vote committed, vote applied, snapshot committed, publication attempted, and client revision observed. This creates an alert-to-action trace. An operator can move backward from a stale client revision to a failed delivery, an unpublished committed snapshot, a stalled aggregator, or an ingestion gap without correlating unrelated panels by eye.

Test the trace with failures. Kill the aggregation owner immediately after snapshot commit and before delivery. Deliver revision 42 after revision 43. Submit the same vote identifier twice. Disconnect a client for three publication intervals, then resume it with revision 39 while the server holds 43. Restart an Express replica and verify that its local timer cannot create a second authority. Each test should assert displayed counts and positions, not merely that a callback ran.

Deployment needs the same discipline. Introduce revision fields as optional readers first, then publish them, then require them after old clients age out. During rollback, a previous server must not emit an unversioned message that a newer client mistakes for fresh state. Schema compatibility belongs in the incident plan because reconnects surface older client builds.

The threshold can create its own incident

A five-second publication interval should not translate into a page at 5.001 seconds. Runtime pauses, scheduler jitter, and temporary delivery retries exist, while a quiet poll can legitimately publish no changed tally if that behavior is documented. Define the alert around a sustained position gap across more than one expected publication opportunity, and validate it under the slowest supported deployment conditions. The exact allowance is a service objective decision, not a universal constant.

Too loose, and viewers watch stale numbers while votes accumulate. Too tight, and every brief pause wakes someone who can take no useful action; repeated false positives train the team to distrust the one page that matters. Track how often the alert corresponds to an actual breached viewer-freshness objective, then revise either the threshold or the instrumentation when it does not.

The operational conclusion is compact: make vote acceptance durable, serialize aggregation per poll, publish complete versioned snapshots, and recover reconnects by revision. The interval controls how often the picture changes. It must never be the only place the truth lives.

Further reading

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: LEAF: LUT-aware Efficient Attention on FPGAs
description:
arXiv:2610.27078v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Lookup-table (LUT)-aware Efficient Attention on FPGAs (LEAF). LEAF is the first nanosecond-scale LUT-aware transformer for FPGAs. Deploying transformers that are large enough to perform well, small enough to fit on an FPGA, and fast enough to meet the sub-microsecond timescales required by real-time systems such as those at CERN remains difficult, since the same attention mechanism that gives these models their high expressivity also makes them costly to implement in hardware. LEAF converts the query, key, and value projections and the final output feed-forward layer into FPGA-native layers with LUT-aware training, creating the first LUT-aware transformer and linformer layers built for ultra-low-latency inference. Attention resists LUT-aware training because it multiplies two activations where the method needs a constant weight to tabulate; LEAF tabulates the attention block's constant matrix-vector multiplications and leaves the rest in arithmetic form. On a standard jet tagging benchmark this improves accuracy by 1.8 percentage points while using 2.9 times fewer LUTs than the previous state-of-the-art sub-microsecond transformer at the same input size. Our most efficient LEAF-based linformer with 64 input particles reaches 80.4% classification accuracy at 28k LUTs and 35ns.
