title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4
description:
arXiv:2610.26942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.

title: Aprendiendo a soltar: volví a programar después de dos años y todo había cambiado
description:
Permítanme presentarme primero, de tal manera que puedan entender lo que siento.

Me gradué como ingeniero informático en agosto de 2025, pero en realidad tengo desde diciembre de 2024 de no escribir una sola línea de código, cuando terminé mi trabajo final de graduación.

En la Universidad fueron muy enfáticos en dos cosas:

  1. Aprender los lenguajes vanilla.

No me enseñaron ningún framework. C++, Java, C#, HTML, CSS, JS… Todo vanilla, sin frameworks. Llegué incluso a hacer exámenes de C++ y Java a lápiz y papel.

“Lo importante es que aprendas el fundamento, porque los frameworks cambian a cada rato y se aprenden en un par de semanas con un curso, aprendan el lenguaje vanilla y así los frameworks serán muy fáciles de comprender”.

Por supuesto que entiendo las razones detrás de esa decisión, no la critico. De hecho, agradezco haber hecho esos exámenes a lápiz y papel, la cantidad de horas que me quemé las pestañas aprendiendo los fundamentos no las cambio por nada.

¿Pero qué pasó? Que, al llegar al mercado, éste pedía un stack de habilidades y herramientas completamente diferente al que me enseñaron en la Universidad. Casi se sentía como que para poder ejercer mi profesión tenía que llevar dos carreras: la ingeniería + lo que pedía el mercado.

Por un lado, sentía que había perdido mi tiempo, porque no sabía nada de lo que pedía el mercado. Pero por otro, viendo hacia atrás, comprendí que tampoco podía prescindir de lo que aprendí en la universidad, porque esos fundamentos son importantísimos.

En una frase: siento que salí a medio cocinar.

  1. No IA

Entre mis graduaciones de diplomado y de bachillerato se dio el boom de las IAs generativas, el pánico en la academia era palpable. Usarla para redactar un proyecto escrito estaba prohibido (imagino que lo sigue siendo), pero eso no era lo grave, sino que también la prohibieron para programar. Al igual que con el punto anterior, insistieron muchísimo en que programar a mano era lo mejor.

De nuevo, no critico esa decisión, porque entiendo el razonamiento que hay detrás. Pero volviendo a lo mismo, al llegar al mercado lo que me encontré fue otra cosa: todo el mundo usa IA. Todos son súper veloces. Nadie programa ya a mano.

Lo que la academia me dijo que era lo correcto chocó directamente con lo que me encontré en el mercado, que me decía exactamente lo opuesto.

Terminé mi trabajo de graduación en diciembre de 2024, me gradué en agosto de 2025.

No he vuelto a programar desde entonces. Mis manos no han escrito una sola línea de código.

Razones (o excusas) hay muchas:

  • Tengo casi 5 años trabajando en puestos B2B y administrativos en Amazon que no requieren programación. Sí he de decir que en esos puestos he aprendido un montón de habilidades que también considero muy importantes como la documentación y mejora continua de procesos, coordinación entre equipos multidisciplinarios y mentorear personas… Habilidades blandas, más que técnicas.
  • Quedé exhausto luego de mi trabajo final de graduación, que requirió un año entero de desarrollo, desde la etapa de planeación y de ingeniería de software y de requerimientos, hasta el deployment final. Quería descansar un poco la cabeza.
  • Acontecimientos importantes en el ámbito personal que he disfrutado muchísimo y me han hecho sentirme pleno y feliz, pero no me han permitido dedicarle mucho tiempo a seguir estudiando y actualizándome profesionalmente.

Sea cual haya sido el motivo (o los motivos), la verdad es que dar el salto para ejercer mi profesión como ingeniero informático cada vez me da más miedo.

El síndrome del impostor, la falta de experiencia laboral, la falta dominio de stacks que el mercado pide sí o sí, el irme haciendo mayor y haber sido junior a estas alturas…

Son cosas mentales, algunas arreglables con cursos, otras solo con experiencia, otras requieren adoptar una nueva forma de ver las cosas.

Me propuse empezar a buscar trabajo como programador a partir de enero del próximo año. Los dos meses y un poquito que le quedan a éste los estoy dedicando a prepararme, porque (por supuesto) no puedo pretender salir a buscar trabajo solo con el título, me van a hacer pruebas técnicas, me van a pedir un portafolio…

Quería atacar ambos con un solo movimiento: programar mi propio portafolio en un proyecto MVC en ASP .Net Core.

No quería usar IA, para desoxidarme y recordar cosas, y para practicar para una eventual prueba técnica.

Lo que me enseñaron en la universidad (aprender lenguajes vanilla, no usar IA) sigue muy pegado en mi mente. Quería hacerlo a mano.

Quería, pero la tentación de usar IA me ganó. Era tan conveniente, tan rápida, tan eficiente, tan correcta. Sabe mucho más que yo, conoce más métodos, funciones y librerías que yo. Probablemente lo hace mejor que yo.

Entonces cedí a la tentación, y la usé para montar mi portafolio.
Un proyecto perfecto, prolijo, sin errores, a mi gusto y funcionando desde la primera vez. En un par de horas tenía lo que a mí solo me habría tomado días o semanas.

El conflicto moral que me causó ver el proyecto terminado me golpeó muy duro.

"¿Puedo llamar a esto “mío”? ¿Lo hice yo? ¿Soy capaz de me meterme al código y explicar todo lo que pasa, siendo que no lo programé yo?"

La IA que usé tiene un log donde explica todo lo que hace, mentiría si digo que entiendo algo de lo que me suelta.

“Aprender a soltar”

Las dos cosas que me enseñó la universidad (aprender lenguajes vanilla, no usar IA) siento que son como los ruedines que le ponen a las bicicletas para que los niños se acostumbren y aprendan a manejarla. Una vez el niño está listo, se le quitan para que maneje sin ellos.

Siento que me llegó el momento de soltar esas dos cosas. El proceso de entrenamiento que tuve en la universidad ya pasó, es momento de que haga el cambio de mentalidad, donde lo conveniente no es malo, sino lo preferible porque ahorra tiempo y esfuerzo.

Quería un portafolio en MVC en ASP .Net Core. Ya lo tengo. Ya puedo moverme a otra cosa.

¿Puedo detenerme a explicar cierto método dentro de un CRUD concreto? Tal vez no, pero sí puedo explicar por qué se lo pedí a la IA así: decisiones de diseño, de arquitectura, de requerimientos e historias de usuario. Para mí eso es valioso, no sé si lo será para los recruiters.

Pero confío en mí y en los fundamentos que tengo, en mi capacidad de aprender y adaptarme, de no estancarme en el pasado y avanzar hacia el futuro.

title: Transactional Email API: The Complete Cresca Guide
description:
Cresca's transactional email API is a REST API at https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1 that sends one-to-one email, such as password resets, receipts and verification codes, from your own verified domain. You authenticate with an API key in an Authorization: Bearer header, POST JSON to /emails, and get back an id you can use to check delivery. This guide covers every v1 endpoint, with a full worked example and code you can copy.

In this guide

  • Every endpoint at a glance
  • Authentication: API keys and the Bearer header
  • Worked example: your first email, end to end
  • Emails API: send, batch, list, reschedule, cancel
  • Templates API: create, publish and send by alias
  • Contacts API
  • Idempotency, lifecycle, suppression, limits and errors
  • Frequently asked questions

All requests go to https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1 over HTTPS, and requests and responses are JSON. There is no SDK package to install: any HTTP client works, so the examples below use cURL, Node.js 18+ (built-in fetch) and Python (requests). Field names follow the conventions of popular email APIs, so an existing integration is mostly a change of base URL and key.

The API is for transactional email: messages a person expects because of something they did. Newsletters and promotions belong in Cresca campaigns. If the line is unclear, read transactional vs marketing email.

Every endpoint at a glance

Paths are relative to the base URL. "Sending" means a sending-access key works; "Full" needs a full-access key.

Method Path Purpose Key Docs
POST /emails Send one email (up to 50 recipients) Sending Send email
POST /emails/batch Send up to 100 emails in one request Sending Send batch
GET /emails/:id Retrieve one email and its last_event Full Retrieve email
GET /emails List emails, newest first Full List emails
PATCH /emails/:id Reschedule a scheduled email Full Update email
POST /emails/:id/cancel Cancel a scheduled or queued email Full Cancel email
POST /templates Create a template draft Full Create template
GET /templates/:id Retrieve a template by id or alias Full Retrieve template
GET /templates List templates Full List templates
PATCH /templates/:id Update the draft Full Update template
POST /templates/:id/publish Publish the draft as the next version Full Publish template
DELETE /templates/:id Delete a template Full Delete template
POST /contacts Add up to 1,000 contacts to a list Full Add contacts

Authentication: API keys and the Bearer header

Create keys on the API keys page of the Cresca app. Keys start with cr_live_ and are shown once; Cresca stores only a hash. Send the key as a bearer token:

Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx

The X-API-Key header also works. Keep keys on your server, never in browser code, URLs or public repositories.

Permission Can do Use it for
Sending access Send emails and batches. Can be limited to one verified domain. Production servers
Full access Everything: send, read and cancel emails, manage templates, add contacts Scripts and internal tools

Authentication errors: 401 missing_api_key (no key), 403 invalid_api_key (unknown or revoked key, or suspended account) and 401 restricted_api_key (a sending-access key called a full-access endpoint). Details are on the Authentication docs page.

Worked example: send your first transactional email

This is the whole path from a fresh account to a delivered email. It mirrors the quickstart.

Step 1: Verify a sending domain

In the app, open Sending Domains, add your domain and publish the DNS records Cresca shows you: DKIM, a custom MAIL FROM domain and an ownership record. If your DNS is on Cloudflare, Cresca can publish them for you. The domain becomes active once the records verify. A subdomain such as mail.acme.com keeps the reputation of app email separate from campaigns. See sending domains and SPF, DKIM and DMARC done right.

Step 2: Add a sender

On the same page, create a sender such as hello@acme.com with a display name and an optional Reply-To. Every API from address must be an active sender on a verified domain.

Step 3: Create an API key

Create a Sending access key for your server and store it as CRESCA_API_KEY. Create a separate full-access key for the status check in step 5.

Step 4: Send the email

The Idempotency-Key header makes the request safe to retry.

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: password-reset/reset-request-9f2c' \
  -d '{
    "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
    "to": "user@example.com",
    "subject": "Reset your password",
    "html": "<p>Click <a href=\"https://acme.com/reset?token=abc\">here</a> to reset your password.</p>"
  }'

// Node.js 18+, run as an ES module for top-level await
const response = await fetch('https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Idempotency-Key': 'password-reset/reset-request-9f2c',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: 'Acme <hello@acme.com>',
    to: 'user@example.com',
    subject: 'Reset your password',
    html: '<p>Click <a href="https://acme.com/reset?token=abc">here</a> to reset your password.</p>',
  }),
});

const data = await response.json();
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${data.name}: ${data.message}`);
console.log(data.id);

import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}",
        "Idempotency-Key": "password-reset/reset-request-9f2c",
    },
    json={
        "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
        "to": "user@example.com",
        "subject": "Reset your password",
        "html": '<p>Click <a href="https://acme.com/reset?token=abc">here</a> to reset your password.</p>',
    },
    timeout=30,
)
response.raise_for_status()
print(response.json()["id"])

A 200 response returns the id as soon as the email is accepted; sending happens in the background within seconds.

{ "id": "4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c" }

Step 5: Check the status

Retrieve the email with your full-access key, or open Transactional in the app for the full timeline.

curl 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

{
  "object": "email",
  "id": "4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c",
  "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  "to": ["user@example.com"],
  "cc": null,
  "bcc": null,
  "reply_to": null,
  "subject": "Reset your password",
  "html": "<p>Click <a href=\"https://acme.com/reset?token=abc\">here</a> to reset your password.</p>",
  "text": "Click here (https://acme.com/reset?token=abc) to reset your password.",
  "created_at": "2026-10-19T09:14:03.120Z",
  "scheduled_at": null,
  "last_event": "delivered",
  "tags": []
}

last_event moves from queued through sending and sent to delivered (or bounced). Emails are kept for 30 days; another account's id returns 404 not_found.

Emails API

The email sending API has six endpoints. POST /emails takes these fields; the deep dive is in the send email API guide.

Field Type Required Notes
from string Yes* hello@acme.com or Acme <hello@acme.com>; an active sender
to string or string[] Yes Up to 50 recipients across to, cc and bcc
subject string Yes* Single line, up to 998 characters
html / text string One of html, text, template Text is generated from HTML if omitted; "" leaves it out
cc, bcc, reply_to string or string[] No reply_to defaults to the sender's Reply-To
template object No { "id", "variables" }; cannot be combined with html or text
scheduled_at string No ISO 8601, up to 30 days ahead; a past time sends now
tags object[] No Up to 10 { "name", "value" } pairs
headers object No Up to 50 custom headers; Cresca-controlled ones are refused
attachments object[] No Up to 20, 7 MB total, base64 content and filename

*Optional when a template supplies a default. Unknown fields are ignored. Attaching by URL (path) is not supported.

The shorter Node.js examples below use this helper:

const cresca = (method, path, body) =>
  fetch(`https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    },
    body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
  }).then((res) => res.json());

Send a batch

POST /emails/batch takes a JSON array of up to 100 emails with the same fields, except attachments and scheduled_at. A batch is all or nothing: if one email is invalid, nothing is sent and the message names it, for example Email 3: ... (zero-based).

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/batch' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: weekly-digest/2026-10-19' \
  -d '[
    { "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>", "to": "ana@example.com",
      "subject": "Your weekly summary", "html": "<p>Hi Ana, here is your summary.</p>" },
    { "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>", "to": "ben@example.com",
      "subject": "Your weekly summary", "html": "<p>Hi Ben, here is your summary.</p>" }
  ]'

const { data } = await cresca('POST', '/emails/batch', emails); // array of up to 100 emails

{
  "data": [
    { "id": "b6d1f2a0-5e2f-4c8e-9a51-0c8b5f1d2e33" },
    { "id": "0f7e3c11-9b2a-4f6d-8e44-7a1c2d3e4f55" }
  ]
}

List emails

GET /emails accepts limit (1 to 100, default 20) and either after or before (an email id). Items leave out html and text.

import os
import requests

response = requests.get(
    "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}"},
    params={"limit": 1},
    timeout=30,
)
print(response.json())

{
  "object": "list",
  "has_more": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "object": "email",
      "id": "4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c",
      "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
      "to": ["user@example.com"],
      "cc": null,
      "bcc": null,
      "reply_to": null,
      "subject": "Reset your password",
      "created_at": "2026-10-19T09:14:03.120Z",
      "scheduled_at": null,
      "last_event": "delivered",
      "tags": []
    }
  ]
}

For the next page, pass the last item's id as after while has_more is true.

Reschedule and cancel

PATCH /emails/:id takes one required field, scheduled_at, and only works while the status is scheduled. POST /emails/:id/cancel works while the email is scheduled or queued; a canceled email does not count toward your allowance.

curl -X PATCH 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "scheduled_at": "2026-10-21T09:00:00Z" }'

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c/cancel' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

await cresca('PATCH', `/emails/${id}`, { scheduled_at: '2026-10-21T09:00:00Z' });
await cresca('POST', `/emails/${id}/cancel`);

Both return { "object": "email", "id": "4ef9a417-..." }. Rescheduling an email that is not scheduled, or canceling one that is already sending, returns 422 validation_error.

Common Emails API errors: 403 invalid_from_address (not an active sender, or the key is limited to another domain), 422 missing_required_field (no to, from or subject), 422 validation_error (bad address, more than 50 recipients, template combined with html), 422 invalid_attachment, 429 monthly_quota_exceeded and 404 not_found.

Templates API

Templates let you design an email once, publish it, and send it by alias with variables written as {{{NAME}}}. Edits change the draft; sends always use the published version. All six endpoints need a full-access key, and :id accepts the id or the alias. More depth: the email templates API guide and Templates and variables.

Field Required Notes
name Yes Up to 120 characters, unique in your account
html Yes Body with {{{VARIABLE}}} placeholders
alias No Lowercase letters, numbers, dashes, underscores; up to 64
subject, text, from, reply_to, preview_text No Defaults used at send time
variables No Up to 50 { "key", "type", "fallback_value" }; type is string or number

Create and publish 

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "Password reset",
    "alias": "password-reset",
    "subject": "Reset your password",
    "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
    "html": "<p>Hi {{{NAME}}},</p><p><a href=\"{{{RESET_LINK}}}\">Reset your password</a>.</p>",
    "variables": [
      { "key": "NAME", "type": "string", "fallback_value": "there" },
      { "key": "RESET_LINK", "type": "string" }
    ]
  }'

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset/publish' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

const { id } = await cresca('POST', '/templates', { name: 'Welcome', alias: 'welcome', html: '<p>Hi {{{NAME}}}</p>' });
await cresca('POST', `/templates/${id}/publish`);

Create returns 201 with { "object": "template", "id": "6713b1f4c2a94e0012ab34cd" }. Publish returns the new version number:

{ "object": "template", "id": "6713b1f4c2a94e0012ab34cd", "version": 1 }

Send by alias with variables 

const response = await fetch('https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    to: 'user@example.com',
    template: {
      id: 'password-reset',
      variables: { NAME: 'Ana', RESET_LINK: 'https://acme.com/reset?token=abc' },
    },
  }),
});
console.log(await response.json()); // { id: '...' }

Subject and sender come from the template unless your request sets them. Values are HTML-escaped in the HTML body. A variable with no value and no fallback stops the send with 422 validation_error naming it; an unpublished template also returns 422.

Retrieve, list, update and delete 

curl 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset' -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'
curl 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates?limit=10' -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'
curl -X PATCH 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "subject": "Reset your Acme password" }'
curl -X DELETE 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset' -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

await cresca('GET', '/templates/password-reset');
await cresca('GET', '/templates?limit=10');
await cresca('PATCH', '/templates/password-reset', { subject: 'Reset your Acme password' });
await cresca('DELETE', '/templates/password-reset');

Retrieve returns the template object (list wraps the same objects in { "object": "list", "has_more", "data" }):

{
  "object": "template",
  "id": "6713b1f4c2a94e0012ab34cd",
  "name": "Password reset",
  "alias": "password-reset",
  "subject": "Reset your password",
  "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  "reply_to": null,
  "preview_text": null,
  "html": "<p>Hi {{{NAME}}},</p><p><a href=\"{{{RESET_LINK}}}\">Reset your password</a>.</p>",
  "text": null,
  "variables": [
    { "key": "NAME", "type": "string", "fallback_value": "there" },
    { "key": "RESET_LINK", "type": "string", "fallback_value": null }
  ],
  "status": "published",
  "version": 1,
  "published_at": "2026-10-19T08:30:00.000Z",
  "created_at": "2026-10-18T16:02:11.000Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-19T08:30:00.000Z"
}

Update returns { "object": "template", "id" } and changes only the draft; send null for alias to remove it. Delete returns "deleted": true, and later sends that reference the template fail with 404 not_found. Typical errors: 422 missing_required_field (no name or html) and 422 validation_error (duplicate name or alias, bad variable).

Contacts API

POST /contacts adds up to 1,000 contacts per request to a list for your marketing campaigns, creating the list if needed. It needs a full-access key and is limited to 120 requests per 15 minutes. Full walkthrough: the contacts API guide.

Field Type Required Notes
list_name string Yes Created if it does not exist
contacts (string \ object)[] Yes 
import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/contacts",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}"},
    json={
        "list_name": "Newsletter signups",
        "contacts": [{"email": "ana@example.com", "first_name": "Ana"}, "ben@example.com"],
    },
    timeout=30,
)
print(response.json())

{
  "object": "contact_import",
  "list": { "id": "6713b2a8c2a94e0012ab3511", "name": "Newsletter signups", "created": false },
  "summary": {
    "received": 2, "created": 1, "updated": 0, "already_present": 1,
    "rejected": 0, "added_to_list": 1, "limit_reached": false
  },
  "errors": []
}

Invalid, disposable, role, suppressed and duplicate addresses are listed in errors with their index; the rest are still added. An inactive plan returns 403 plan_inactive; a missing list_name returns 422 missing_required_field.

Idempotency, lifecycle, suppression, limits and errors

Idempotency

Send an Idempotency-Key (1 to 256 characters) on POST /emails or /emails/batch. The same key and body within 24 hours return the original response with idempotent-replayed: true and nothing is sent again. The same key with a different body returns 409 invalid_idempotent_request; a key still in flight returns 409 concurrent_idempotent_requests. A failed request releases its key. Derive keys from the event, such as invoice/inv-2026-0042. See Idempotency.

Email lifecycle: statuses and events

last_event Meaning
queued / scheduled Accepted, waiting to send (or to its scheduled_at)
sending / sent Being handed to, then accepted by, the mail infrastructure
delivered The recipient's server accepted it
delivery_delayed Delivery is being retried
bounced / complained Rejected, or marked as spam
failed / suppressed / canceled Not sent, every recipient suppressed, or canceled

Status only moves forward, while last_event is the latest event. delivered means the receiving server accepted it, not that it reached the inbox. Full table: Email lifecycle.

Suppression

Hard bounces, repeated soft bounces (3 in 30 days), spam complaints and manual suppressions block API email; suppressed recipients are skipped and the others still receive it. A marketing unsubscribe does not block a password reset. If every recipient is suppressed you still get 200, and the status is suppressed. See Suppression.

Rate limits and quotas

Plan Requests per second Emails per second with batches
Free 2 up to 200
Professional 10 up to 1,000
Premium 20 up to 2,000
Ultra 50 up to 5,000
Enterprise 100 up to 10,000

The limit is per account, shared by all keys, and an inactive plan gets the Free limit. Authenticated responses carry ratelimit-limit, ratelimit-remaining and ratelimit-reset; a 429 rate_limit_exceeded adds retry-after. API email shares your plan's monthly email allowance with campaigns, one unit per recipient; when it runs out you get 429 monthly_quota_exceeded. Request bodies are capped at 10 MB. See Rate limits and quotas and pricing.

Errors

Every error has the same shape. Branch on name, not message:

{
  "statusCode": 422,
  "name": "validation_error",
  "message": "Invalid `to` field. The email address needs to follow the `email@example.com` or `Name <email@example.com>` format."
}

Retry 429 rate_limit_exceeded, 409 concurrent_idempotent_requests, 500 application_error, 503 service_unavailable, timeouts and network errors with exponential backoff and jitter, using an Idempotency-Key. Do not retry other 4xx responses; fix the request. The full list is on Errors.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an official SDK for the Cresca email API?

No. Cresca does not publish an SDK package; the API is plain HTTPS and JSON, so cURL, Node.js fetch, Python requests or any HTTP client works. Field names and responses follow the conventions of popular email APIs, so moving an existing integration is mostly a change of base URL and API key. The docs show every request in cURL, Node.js and Python.

Can I send marketing email through the transactional email API?

No. The API is for messages a person expects because of something they did, such as receipts, password resets and alerts. Newsletters and promotions belong in Cresca campaigns, which add the unsubscribe link and sender address marketing email legally requires. Keeping them apart also protects deliverability, as explained in transactional vs marketing email.

How do I know an email was delivered?

Call GET /emails/:id with a full-access key and read last_event, or open Transactional in the Cresca app for the per-recipient timeline of sent, delivered, bounced and complained events. delivered means the receiving server accepted the email. Webhooks are on the roadmap; today you read status from the API or the dashboard.

Does API email count toward my plan?

Yes. API email uses the same monthly email allowance as your campaigns, and each recipient in to, cc and bcc counts as one email. Suppressed recipients, canceled emails and emails that fail before sending are given back. When the allowance is used up, sends return 429 monthly_quota_exceeded until the next billing period or an upgrade. See pricing.

What happens if my server retries after a timeout?

If the request carried an Idempotency-Key, the retry returns the original response with the header idempotent-replayed: true, and no second email is sent. Without a key, a retry can send a duplicate. Derive the key from the event that caused the email, such as welcome/user-123, so every retry produces the same key.

Do I need SPF, DKIM and DMARC to send transactional email?

Your from address must be on a domain verified in Cresca, which means publishing the DKIM, custom MAIL FROM and ownership records Cresca shows you. Gmail and Yahoo also expect a DMARC record from bulk senders. The Gmail and Yahoo sender requirements post lists every rule.

Start sending

A transactional email service should take minutes to set up: verify a domain, create a key, send one request. Try Cresca free for 30 days, then follow the quickstart to send your first email.

title: The Definitive Guide to the Service Integration Bus
description:
TL;DR

  • A Service Integration Bus (SIB or SIBus) is a managed messaging infrastructure that provides asynchronous transport, publish/subscribe routing, and mediation across distributed application servers.
  • Bus members host messaging engines that manage persistent storage through database-backed data stores or filesystem-backed file stores.
  • Enterprise applications interact with the bus through Java Message Service (JMS) resources and Java EE Connector Architecture (JCA) activation specifications.
  • High availability relies on cluster coordination and active/standby failover governed by database-level lock tables such as SIBOWNER.
  • As architectures shift toward event streaming and AI workloads, modern infrastructure pairs asynchronous messaging foundations with centralized gateways for governance and protocol translation.

A Service Integration Bus (often abbreviated as SIB or SIBus) is an interconnected messaging infrastructure that provides asynchronous communication, message routing, and service mediation across distributed application servers. Originally popularized within enterprise Java platforms such as IBM WebSphere Application Server, the architecture decouples message producers from consumers by hosting intermediate message destinations inside a managed environment.

Production systems rely on asynchronous messaging to prevent cascading failures when downstream services experience latency spikes or transient outages. Modern enterprises frequently operate heterogeneous environments that blend traditional service integration topologies with modern API and AI gateways. Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway written in Go, reflects similar decoupling principles at the intelligence layer by unifying downstream model routing, load balancing, and failover across disparate providers. Understanding the fundamentals of the Service Integration Bus provides platform engineers and system architects with the conceptual foundation required to manage reliable, transactionally sound message topologies.

Core Architecture and Components of a Service Integration Bus

At its foundation, a Service Integration Bus consists of cooperating nodes inside a common management cell. Rather than requiring applications to establish point-to-point network connections with every remote consumer, the bus serves as a logical virtualization layer.

The architecture comprises four primary building blocks:

  1. Bus Members: An application server, server cluster, or external IBM MQ queue manager that has been explicitly added to the bus definition. Adding a member grants it the ability to host messaging components and store messages.
  2. Messaging Engines (MEs): The core runtime execution units hosted inside bus members. A messaging engine receives incoming payloads, serializes them, routes them across bus boundaries, and delivers them to attached subscribers or consumers. In a clustered bus member, messaging engines can run in active/standby configurations or operate concurrently across multiple servers.
  3. Destinations: The logical addresses to which applications transmit messages. Destinations are decoupled from physical addresses and include:
    • Queue Destinations: Point-to-point endpoints where a message is delivered to exactly one consumer.
    • Topic Spaces: Publish/subscribe endpoints supporting multiple subscribers with optional durable subscriptions.
    • Mediation Destinations: Intermediary destinations that route messages through transformation logic before forwarding them to their final destination.
    • Alias Destinations: Logical pointers that map an abstract destination name to another concrete bus destination.
  4. Message Stores: The persistence subsystem utilized by a messaging engine to maintain transactional state and ensure delivery guarantees.

The following table summarizes the structural distinctions between these core components:

Component Scope Primary Responsibility Failure Recovery Mode
Bus Member Server or Cluster Provides the compute environment and network identity for the bus. Handled by application server node management.
Messaging Engine Subsystem within Bus Member Processes message delivery, client connections, and transactions. Managed by High Availability Manager (HAManager) failover policies.
Queue Destination Logical Bus Resource Holds messages intended for a single receiver using FIFO or prioritized order. Stored on disk or database until acknowledged.
Topic Space Logical Bus Resource Dispatches copies of published events to all matching active or durable subscribers. Durable subscriptions persist across engine restarts.
Message Store Storage Subsystem Stores unconsumed persistent messages, transaction state, and lock metadata. Relies on relational ACID guarantees or journal file replay.

Message Persistence: Data Store vs. File Store

A messaging engine requires persistent storage to support guaranteed message delivery across restarts. The two standard implementations are:

  • Data Store (Relational Database): The messaging engine connects via a JDBC data source to a relational database (such as DB2, Oracle, PostgreSQL, or Microsoft SQL Server). The database maintains a dedicated schema containing seven internal tables:
    • SIBOWNER: Establishes exclusive engine ownership of the database schema via row-level locks.
    • SIBOWNERO: Used in auxiliary locking routines.
    • SIBCLASSMAP: Maps Java class types for serialized message payloads.
    • SIBLISTING: Catalogs the dynamic storage tables allocated for queues.
    • SIBXACTS: Tracks active two-phase commit (XA) transactions.
    • SIBKEYS: Allocates monotonically increasing identifiers for message tracking.
    • SIBnnn (such as SIB000, SIB001): The actual storage tables holding persistent and non-persistent message bodies.
  • File Store (Operating System Filesystem): The messaging engine writes directly to three binary files on a local or networked filesystem: a log file, a data file, and a metadata file. File stores provide lower latency and higher sequential throughput by eliminating relational database overhead, but they require shared storage mechanisms (such as NFSv4 or SAN) when configuring high-availability failover across distinct physical hosts.

Message Exchange Patterns and Transport Semantics

The Service Integration Bus supports multiple communication patterns designed to accommodate varying reliability and latency requirements.

+------------------+         +----------------------------+         +------------------+
| Message Producer | ------> |  Service Integration Bus   | ------> | Message Consumer |
|  (JMS Client)    |         |                            |         |      (MDB)       |
+------------------+         | +------------------------+ |         +------------------+
                             | | Messaging Engine (ME)  | |
                             | |                        | |
                             | |   [ Queue Point ]      | |
                             | |          |             | |
                             | |   [ Message Store ]    | |
                             | +------------------------+ |
                             +----------------------------+

Point-to-Point Messaging

In a point-to-point exchange, an application sends a message to a queue destination. The message is deposited on a specific queue point located on a messaging engine. The bus ensures that even if multiple consumers are listening concurrently on the same queue, only one consumer receives and acknowledges each message. This pattern provides horizontal scaling for background worker pools processing compute-heavy jobs.

Publish/Subscribe Messaging

Publish/subscribe messaging distributes events to multiple independent subscribers through a topic space. When a producer publishes to a topic hierarchy (such as orders/na/processed), the bus evaluates subscription filters and delivers identical copies to every matched subscriber. Subscriptions can be configured as non-durable (messages are delivered only while the consumer is connected) or durable (the messaging engine retains messages on behalf of disconnected clients until they reconnect).

Reliability Qualities of Service

The SIBus specification defines distinct reliability levels that dictate how messages survive system crashes:

  1. Best Effort Non-Persistent: Messages are held exclusively in volatile memory. If the hosting messaging engine terminates abnormally, messages are permanently lost. This level offers minimal latency for telemetry or heartbeat metrics.
  2. Express Non-Persistent: Messages are held in memory and discarded upon server shutdown, but the engine employs internal buffer optimizations to prevent memory starvation under high load.
  3. Reliable Non-Persistent: The bus guarantees delivery unless a failure occurs while the message is in flight.
  4. Reliable Persistent: Messages are written to persistent storage (data store or file store). The message survives server restarts and engine crashes, ensuring at-least-once delivery semantics.
  5. Assured Persistent: Messages are committed to persistent storage under strict transaction boundaries. This mode provides exact-once semantics when paired with XA two-phase commit transactions.

Integrating Enterprise Applications via JMS and JCA

Enterprise applications interact with the Service Integration Bus using standard Java specifications: the Java Message Service (JMS) API and the Java EE Connector Architecture (JCA). In modern deployments running on Open Liberty or WebSphere Liberty, this extends to Jakarta Messaging 3.0.

Rather than exposing engine connection sockets directly to code, application servers use administered objects configured in JNDI:

  • Queue Connection Factory (QCF): Configures connection pooling, authentication credentials, and transport properties for establishing sessions with the bus.
  • JMS Destination Object: Maps an application-level JNDI lookup name (such as jms/OrderQueue) to the physical bus destination identifier.
  • JCA Activation Specification: Bridges asynchronous Message-Driven Beans (MDBs) to bus destinations. The activation specification defines concurrency limits, maximum batch sizes, and acknowledgment modes.

Configuration Code Example

The following standard Enterprise JavaBeans snippet demonstrates a Message-Driven Bean consuming incoming JSON order payloads from a Service Integration Bus queue using an activation specification:

package com.example.messaging;

import jakarta.ejb.ActivationConfigProperty;
import jakarta.ejb.MessageDriven;
import jakarta.jms.JMSException;
import jakarta.jms.Message;
import jakarta.jms.MessageListener;
import jakarta.jms.TextMessage;
import java.util.logging.Level;
import java.util.logging.Logger;

@MessageDriven(
    name = "OrderProcessingMDB",
    activationConfig = {
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "destinationType", 
            propertyValue = "jakarta.jms.Queue"
        ),
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "destinationLookup", 
            propertyValue = "jms/OrderQueue"
        ),
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "maxEndpoints", 
            propertyValue = "10"
        ),
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "acknowledgeMode", 
            propertyValue = "Auto-acknowledge"
        )
    }
)
public class OrderProcessingMDB implements MessageListener {

    private static final Logger LOGGER = Logger.getLogger(OrderProcessingMDB.class.getName());

    @Override
    public void onMessage(Message message) {
        try {
            if (message instanceof TextMessage) {
                String payload = ((TextMessage) message).getText();
                LOGGER.info("Processing order payload: " + payload);
                // Execute business logic, database transactions, or service calls
            } else {
                LOGGER.warning("Unrecognized message format received: " + message.getJMSMessageID());
            }
        } catch (JMSException e) {
            LOGGER.log(Level.SEVERE, "Failed to parse message from SIBus", e);
            // Throwing RuntimeException triggers container rollback for persistent messages
            throw new IllegalStateException("Message processing failure", e);
        }
    }
}

High Availability, Clustering, and Failover Mechanics

When high availability is required, adding an application server cluster as a bus member allows messaging engines to fail over between cluster nodes.

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |               High Availability Cluster       |
           |                                               |
           |  +--------------------+  Heartbeat   +-----+  |
           |  | Node 1 (Active ME) | <----------> | Node|  |
           |  +--------------------+ (HAManager)  | 2   |  |
           |            |                         +-----+  |
           +------------|----------------------------|-----+
                        | Exclusive Lock             | Standby
                        v                            v
               +----------------------------------------+
               |          Shared Message Store          |
               | (Database SIBOWNER Table / Shared Disk)|
               +----------------------------------------+

The Role of the High Availability Manager (HAManager)

The application server cluster uses an internal cluster coordinator known as the High Availability Manager (HAManager). HAManager forms logical core groups that exchange heartbeats to detect JVM hangs, network partitions, or hardware failures.

When an active messaging engine terminates unexpectedly, HAManager initiates a failover sequence:

  1. HAManager marks the local engine instance as offline and isolates its network channels.
  2. A standby cluster member is selected according to core group policies.
  3. The standby node starts its messaging engine instance, which immediately attempts to acquire an exclusive lock on the underlying message store.
  4. Once the lock is verified, the standby engine reads the persistent log, re-instantiates active transactions, and opens the queue points for inbound consumer traffic.

Resolving the SIBOWNER Lock Contention Problem

A persistent challenge in clustered deployments involves orphaned locks on the SIBOWNER table. During startup, an active messaging engine writes a unique instance identifier into SIBOWNER and maintains an open database transaction or continuous row-level lock.

If a server crashes abruptly or loses its network connection to the database without executing a clean shutdown, the database engine may continue holding the TCP socket and associated row lock until a database timeout expires. When HAManager attempts to start the standby messaging engine on another server, the new engine outputs warnings such as:

CWSIS1538I: The messaging engine, ME_UUID=..., INC_UUID=..., is attempting to obtain an exclusive lock on the data store.
CWSIS1593I: The messaging engine has failed to gain an initial lock on the data store.

By default, the engine retries for up to 15 minutes before the HAManager disables the component. To eliminate prolonged failover intervals, modern versions introduce the Restrict Long Running Locks capability. Under this setting, the messaging engine does not hold an open database lock indefinitely. Instead, it uses short-duration locks combined with a periodic ownership revalidation timestamp, ensuring rapid release and handoff during ungraceful terminations.

Automating SIBus Provisioning via Jython Scripting

Configuring complex buses, queue destinations, and bus members through administrative graphical consoles is error-prone. Enterprise administrators automate these operations using wsadmin scripting in Jython.

The following script automates the creation of a bus, registers a cluster member with a JDBC data store, and defines a queue destination:

# SIBus Provisioning Automation via wsadmin / Jython
import sys

def configure_sibus():
    bus_name = "EnterpriseOrderBus"
    cluster_name = "MessagingCluster"
    data_source_jndi = "jdbc/SIBusDataSource"
    queue_name = "OrderQueue"

    print "Initializing Service Integration Bus creation: " + bus_name

    # 1. Create the Service Integration Bus
    existing_buses = AdminTask.listSIBuses().splitlines()
    if bus_name not in existing_buses:
        AdminTask.createSIBus(['-bus', bus_name, '-description', 'Primary transactional order bus'])
        print "Bus created successfully."
    else:
        print "Bus already exists. Skipping creation."

    # 2. Add Cluster Member with Data Store configuration
    print "Adding cluster member: " + cluster_name
    AdminTask.addSIBusMember([
        '-bus', bus_name,
        '-cluster', cluster_name,
        '-datasourceJndiName', data_source_jndi,
        '-createDataStore', 'true',
        '-authAlias', 'SIBusDBAlias'
    ])

    # 3. Create a Queue Destination on the Bus
    print "Configuring Queue Destination: " + queue_name
    AdminTask.createSIBJMSQueue([
        '-bus', bus_name,
        '-name', queue_name,
        '-queueName', queue_name,
        '-cluster', cluster_name,
        '-reliability', 'ReliablePersistent'
    ])

    # 4. Commit configuration changes
    print "Saving configuration changes to master repository..."
    AdminConfig.save()
    print "SIBus automation complete."

if __name__ == "__main__":
    configure_sibus()

Architectural Evolution: From SIBus to Event Streams and Modern Gateways

The Service Integration Bus model resolved core coupling issues for monolithic and service-oriented architectures (SOA) built in the 2000s and 2010s. However, changing operational requirements have shifted how organizations design integration backbones:

  • Log-Based Streaming vs. Stateful Queues: Technologies such as Apache Kafka and Apache Pulsar replaced message deletion semantics with immutable, append-only commit logs. While an SIBus deletes a message as soon as a consumer acknowledges it, stream platforms retain events, allowing disparate services to replay historical records at independent rates.
  • Microservices and Protocol Decentralization: Contemporary microservices favor lightweight protocols (gRPC, HTTP/REST) over enterprise Java Connector specifications. Rather than consolidating all inter-service traffic onto a heavyweight application bus, teams deploy lightweight message brokers alongside API gateways that govern request routing, rate limiting, and observability.
  • AI and Intelligence Integration: Modern systems increasingly integrate non-deterministic LLM endpoints alongside standard business logic. Unlike predictable database or queue transactions, AI model requests involve variable latencies, rate limits, and external vendor dependencies.

Modern infrastructure relies on unified edge and gateway components to govern traffic across distributed systems. Beyond internal routing, modern enterprise architectures require end-to-end policy management: Bifrost applies governance and security controls centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device. This pairing reflects the historical lesson of the Service Integration Bus: integration logic must be decoupled from application code to preserve organizational security, observability, and operational control.

Common Production Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

Operating an enterprise Service Integration Bus requires continuous monitoring of queue depths, database storage consumption, and engine availability. Production engineers regularly encounter three primary categories of operational failures:

1. Poison Messages and Exception Destinations

When a message contains corrupted data, an unparseable schema, or values that trigger application exceptions, a Message-Driven Bean may consistently fail and roll back the transaction. By default, the messaging engine re-delivers the message up to a configured threshold (typically five attempts).

Once exhausted, the message is routed to an Exception Destination (often formatted as _SYSTEM.Exception.Destination.ME_NAME) to prevent queue stalls. Monitoring teams must configure automated alerting on these exception queues to detect application-level contract breaks before upstream backpressure develops.

2. Message Engine Split-Brain and JVM Termination

When core group heartbeats fail across an unstable network, HAManager may conclude that an active node has failed while the node is still executing requests.

To preserve data integrity and prevent multiple engines from writing to the same data store simultaneously, the local member initiates a panic shutdown. In the server logs, this manifests as:

HMGR0130I: The local member of group WSAF_SIB_BUS=...,type=WSAF_SIB has indicated that it is not alive. The JVM will be terminated.
SystemOut O Panic:component requested panic from isAlive.

Mitigating these failures requires tuning HAManager heartbeat intervals, isolating cluster replication networks onto dedicated network interfaces, and guaranteeing low latency between the application server cluster and the backing database.

3. File Store and Database Storage Exhaustion

If consumer processing halts while producers continue publishing, messaging engines retain persistent payloads in storage. In a data store configuration, this leads to rapid table space expansion across the SIBnnn tables.

If table limits are reached, the messaging engine pauses all inbound producers by blocking socket connections. Operational teams must monitor database filesystem headroom and set maximum message depth quotas on queue destinations to shed load gracefully when consumers fall behind.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the primary difference between a Service Integration Bus and IBM MQ?

A Service Integration Bus is an application server component embedded directly within WebSphere Application Server, whereas IBM MQ is a standalone enterprise messaging middleware platform. IBM MQ offers broader multi-platform support across mainframes and external systems, while SIBus provides native integration for Java EE applications inside the application server runtime.

When should a data store be selected over a file store?

A data store should be chosen when an organization already maintains robust database replication, backup, and high-availability infrastructure. A file store is preferable when minimizing I/O latency is critical or when database licensing constraints prevent the provisioning of dedicated SIBus database schemas.

How does an activation specification differ from a listener port?

Listener ports rely on WebSphere-specific background threads to poll destinations and dispatch work to message beans. Activation specifications implement the standardized JCA 1.5/1.6 inbound resource adapter contract, offering superior thread pooling, standardized lifecycle management, and native workload distribution.

Can a Service Integration Bus communicate with external message brokers?

Yes. A Service Integration Bus can link to external systems through MQ Link connections, foreign bus definitions, or JMS bridges. This allows applications attached to an SIBus to route messages transparently to queues managed by external messaging platforms.

What occurs when an active messaging engine loses its database connection?

If the messaging engine loses connectivity to its data store, it cannot guarantee transactional consistency. The engine terminates its client connections and signals HAManager to halt the local instance, allowing an alternate standby node in the cluster to re-acquire the lock and resume message processing.

Sources

  • IBM Support: WebSphere Service Integration Bus 101 Architecture Guide
  • IBM Support: Troubleshooting SIBus Messaging Engine Failover Problems
  • Open Liberty Documentation: JMS Activation Specification Configuration

title: On the LLM Verification for Argument Graph Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.27361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems can formalize natural-language argumentation end-to-end, turning plain text into structured graphs by classifying components, connecting them with relations, and enriching the resulting graphs into formal models. Quality assurance for those graphs is almost always another LLMs: a reviewer, judge, or critic agent. On the other side, in adjacent neuro-symbolic fields, such generated output is often verified symbolically by external checks and solvers. In this work, we argue that in argument graph verification, the allocation should be similar, and based on what each instrument can guarantee. We propose layered verification: starting from deterministic checks, moving to solver-based and LLM reviews, and utilizing debate only under uncertainty, leaving human judgment for what no other instrument can decide. We ground our principle with a study on human-annotated graphs with injected structural defects. An LLM reviewer detects them at near-ceiling recall, including cycles in the support relation, but it objects to almost one in a ten correct graphs, even though it should not, happens to be inconsistent in verdict on identical inputs and is significantly slower than the equivalent exact check. It shows that while LLM reviewer does not lack the ability to detect structural defects, it is worth having a deterministic verification gates.

title: Three owners of one token: how my AuthContext, my axios client, and localStorage split auth state
description:
In my starter kit, the Sanctum token has exactly one name and exactly two modules that touch it. That was a deliberate decision, and it is the reason I can change my auth storage strategy in an afternoon instead of a week.

The name is saas_token. It lives in localStorage. Here is everyone who is allowed to know that.

Owner one: the axios client. Every request passes through a request interceptor that reads the key and attaches the header:

client.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('saas_token');
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

And a response interceptor owns the "token died" path. On a 401, it clears the key and sends the user to login, unless they are already on the login or register page (redirecting someone off the login page because their non-existent token is invalid would be a special kind of bug):

client.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,
  (error) => {
    const status = error?.response?.status;
    const path = window.location.pathname;
    if (status === 401 && path !== '/login' && path !== '/register') {
      localStorage.removeItem('saas_token');
      window.location.href = '/login';
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

Note this happens at the network layer, outside React. No component, no context, no state update involved. An expired token redirects you before React has an opinion about it. And the interceptor still rejects the promise, so a form that triggered the 401 can still show its error state if it wants to.

Owner two: the AuthContext. It holds the token in React state, initialised from the same key, and it is the only place that writes it:

const [token, setToken] = useState(() => localStorage.getItem('saas_token'));

const login = useCallback(async (email, password) => {
  const res = await client.post('/auth/login', { email, password });
  localStorage.setItem('saas_token', res.data.token);
  setToken(res.data.token);
  setUser(res.data.user);
  return res.data;
}, []);

const logout = useCallback(async () => {
  // Best-effort: the session is cleared locally no matter what.
  try {
    await client.post('/auth/logout');
  } catch {
    // Ignore — token is being discarded either way.
  }
  localStorage.removeItem('saas_token');
  setToken(null);
  setUser(null);
}, []);

Login and register write both localStorage and state in the same breath. Logout tries the server first (revoking the token server-side is polite) but clears locally regardless. The session dies on the client even if the server call fails, because a logout that depends on a healthy network is a logout that fails exactly when the user needs it most.

On mount, the context restores the session: read the key, call GET /auth/me, and if that fails, remove the key and settle into logged-out. One code path for "returning visitor" and "dead token".

Owner three: nobody. That is the point. No component reads localStorage directly. No page checks the token itself. Every component goes through useAuth(), which exposes exactly six things: user, token, loading, login, register, logout. And useAuth throws if you call it outside the provider, so forgetting the wrapper fails loudly in development instead of silently shipping undefined auth everywhere:

export function useAuth() {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useAuth must be used within an AuthProvider');
  return ctx;
}

The payoff: if I ever move from localStorage to httpOnly cookies, the change surface is two files, client.js and AuthContext.jsx. Every consumer keeps working because they never knew where the token lived. Ownership is a contract: one name, two modules, and a public API of six values. Everything else just asks.

This is the auth layer of the starter kit I maintain and sell. The full thing, with the Sanctum backend and this exact frontend, is here: Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit
