title: AI doesn’t care about your job title
description:
Exposure to artificial intelligence runs through the tasks you do each week, not the role on your badge. Here’s how to measure yours and lower the risk.

My mom doesn’t understand my job, and it isn’t her fault. The closest I’ve ever come to explaining it is “I design how it works,” which is true and tells her almost nothing about my day.

It also works best when I’m wearing a black turtleneck and holding an iPhone, channeling my inner Steve Jobs.

That’s the curse of knowledge, and I’ve never directly defined my role in many of the places I’ve worked. Over decades I’ve managed design, product management, and engineering, and more than once I started without a job description. It wasn’t about my job title, it was about judgement applied through my experience building software.

Artificial intelligence doesn’t care about your job title or mine. It’s probabilistically predicting an outcome without looking at your LinkedIn.

In GPTs are GPTs, published in 2023, researchers from OpenAI and the University of Pennsylvania scored occupations task by task. They estimated that 80% of U.S. workers could see at least a tenth of their tasks affected, and about 19% could see at least half.

Those averages hide what matters for one person. Your exposure depends on how much of your week can be specified briefly and checked quickly, and seniority protects you only when it changes that mix.

For her work, she’s not exposed even though she’s in the models. From Claude:

The main trace of Jean Neeman in the art world is a single, well-documented piece: a teapot titled “Tea on the Go,” made in 1994 by Jean Neeman (American, b. 1948) from silver, copper, brass, and cocobolo wood, measuring about 8.4 x 7.75 x 4.5 inches. That puts her work alongside some serious company.

She doesn’t have to measure her risk because she’s an artist. I measure mine all the time so I can add value that AI can’t add, and that’s judgement.

The five steps below show how to measure yours, each with a prompt to run in Claude.

List Your Actual Tasks

Start with a week, not a job description.

List everything you spent more than half an hour on: the usability readout, the stakeholder review, the status update nobody read. Note the hours, how often each task repeats, and who reviews the result.

Also leave room for the white space between tasks.

Unblocking a teammate, the quick answer that saves someone a day, the thinking before a hard review: none of it shows up in a job description or on a calendar. It also goes unseen when people judge what you do, whether that’s a manager at review time or a researcher scoring tasks for exposure.

It’s often where you absorb complexity that, as Tesler’s Law puts it, can be moved but never removed.

Write it down anyway.

For a checklist, O*NET OnLine, the Labor Department’s occupational database, lists 31 tasks for Web and Digital Interface Designers. In Putting Tasks to the Test: Human Capital, Job Tasks and Wages, a 2009 paper, economists David Autor and Michael Handel found that tasks vary substantially within occupations, enough to predict wage gaps among people who hold the same job.

In Toil and Technology, written for the International Monetary Fund in 2015, economist James Bessen showed how automated teller machines took over dispensing cash and taking deposits. The tellers needed to run an average urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so the jobs held.

The title stayed the same while the job underneath it was rebuilt.

My own title changed in March, from director to senior principal designer. Neither title would tell you which of my tasks a model can do, but my calendar would.

Try It in Claude

Run these prompts in one Claude conversation. The first one drafts your week from your role, so you correct a list instead of writing one, and you can check its tasks against O*NET OnLine.

To map my exposure to artificial intelligence, don’t read my calendar or connected accounts, or ask me to describe my week. If you don’t know my title, ask once. Name the O*NET occupation you matched, and say if you’re recalling its tasks from memory. Draft 15 to 20 tasks from it, plus the undocumented work between them, for a normal week. Give hours, frequency, and reviewer for each, marked as guesses. Then have me correct it, including whether I manage anyone.

Score Each Task’s Exposure

Difficulty is a poor guide to exposure. In a 2023 experiment for Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, a team led by Fabrizio Dell’Acqua gave 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants realistic work.

With the model, they did far better on 18 tasks inside its abilities but were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer on one task outside them. Coauthor Ethan Mollick calls this the jagged frontier in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier: tasks that look equally hard can sit on opposite sides of an invisible wall.

Score each task with two questions instead. I call it the spec-and-check test.

  • Specify the result. Ask whether you could describe a finished version in two sentences that someone else could follow.
  • Check the output. Ask whether someone could confirm it’s right in less time than it took to make.
A task that’s quick to specify and quick to check is exposed, whatever your title says.

Twenty variations of an empty state pass both questions. Deciding which of three problems to fund this quarter fails both, and for now that decision stays yours.

Then weight the list by hours, because the Pareto Principle usually holds and a few tasks fill most of the week. A task that passes both and fills two days a week is where your risk sits.

When leadership reviews a pie chart of where a team’s hours go, you don’t want to be on the wrong side of it.

Passing the test means a model could do the task, not that one already does. In Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence, from its own March 2026 usage data, Anthropic found Claude covering about 33% of computer and math tasks, against 94% rated feasible in GPTs are GPTs.

So the prompt below has Claude try one.

Try It in Claude

Paste this after the task table. It ends with Claude attempting your most exposed task, so you judge real output instead of a forecast.

Score each task in my table: could a finished version be described in two sentences, and checked faster than it took to make? Answer yes, partly, or no for each. Then say honestly if you could do each task today, fully, partly, or not yet, and why. Mark tasks with two yeses as exposed, sort by hours, and tell me what share of my week is exposed. Offer to try my top exposed task so I can judge it.

Check Your Career Stage

In the August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found no economy-wide job displacement in payroll data. Employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, though, sits 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mostly because companies are hiring fewer young people.

Experienced workers show no comparable gap, and the authors call these early indicators, not proof of cause.

Entry-level work is often the most specified on a team, handed down with clear instructions and reviewed by someone senior, which is where a model does best. Experience protects through judgment and context that rarely fit in a two-sentence spec.

A senior title over a week of status decks is junior exposure with a bigger paycheck.

If you’re early in your career, ask to own one small decision from start to finish. If you’re senior, hand your juniors judgment calls along with tasks.

Management will also change because there will be smaller teams.

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organizations build systems that copy their communication structures, which I cover in Conway’s Law. My extension is that much of management exists to carry that communication, so a smaller team needs less of it. Four people share six possible pairs, while 10 people share 45.

The flattening predates these tools. For The Manager Mass Exodus: How SMBs Are Flattening the Org Chart, Gusto studied payroll at about 8,500 small and midsize businesses. The share of their workers who manage anyone fell from just under 25% in 2019 to about 15% by late 2024. If you manage, move your hours from relaying information toward the decisions and coaching a smaller team still needs.

Try It in Claude

This prompt compares your task list against your experience. Correct it if it gets your background wrong.

Based on my title and experience, split my tasks into entry-level work (well specified and reviewed by others) and judgment work only I can do. If you don’t know my years of experience, ask once. Give the share of hours in each and, if I manage, how much goes to relaying information. Name the knowledge I bring that you could supply without my judgment. Tell me plainly if my week looks junior for my title, and suggest one decision I could own this quarter.

Deepen Your Domain Expertise

Knowing your field pays off more than knowing your tools. For Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, published in June 2026, Anthropic studied about 400,000 Claude Code sessions.

People made about 70% of the planning decisions — that’s human agency — and the agent made about 80% of the execution decisions.

The researchers rated expertise task by task and said it differs from job title: a senior engineer asking a first question about the Rust language counts as a beginner at Rust. Expert sessions succeeded about twice as often as novice ones, and a working grasp of the domain captured most of that gain, the same early-steep curve as the Power Law of Practice.

The person who understands the problem and not the model gets more out than the person who understands the model and not the problem.

Knowledge on its own doesn’t protect you anymore: If what you know can be pulled from a large language model without judgment to apply it, you’re at risk.

Companies don’t need you to tell them something they already know, they need the person who knows which answer fits this customer and this quarter, and the person who acts as connective tissue between people, building trust and getting decisions made rather than relaying status.

If you’re neither, your expertise is a search ot an AI Assistant result.

For designers, the domain is the user’s world and the business around it. Get closer to your users’ domain than your product manager is: read the regulations your customers follow, sit with support for a day, and learn how the money moves.

Try It in Claude

Answer the way you would with a new manager, without polishing. Short, unsure answers show the gaps fastest.

If you don’t know what my company sells, ask once. Tell me in one sentence who my product serves, and let me correct it. Ask me eight to 10 questions, one at a time, about their regulations, money, metrics, and workflow; “not sure” is a fine answer. Rank my knowledge gaps by how much they’d change my design decisions, suggest one way to close the top gap in 30 days, and revise the decision you suggested earlier.

Rebuild Your Portfolio

Employers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum’s The Future of Jobs Report 2025. A portfolio of polished final screens puts the fastest-changing part of your job up front and hides the part that holds its value.

Rebuild it around decisions: the problem you chose and the ones you turned down, the tradeoff and why, and what happened after launch. Show one case where you directed a model, caught its mistake, and shipped the fix.

Show the work a model couldn’t have done without you.

Look sideways too.

O*NET lists 10 related occupations for the same designer category, from software developers to graphic designers, and jobs overlap where their tasks do. As I wrote in We’ve Seen This Movie Before: Desktop Publishing Already Showed Us How AI Prototyping Plays Out, typesetting effectively ended as a profession while graphic design grew into web, motion, and product design. They all adjusted, and we’re seeing this move now too.

Whole economies have also made this move before.

The agricultural revolution let fewer people grow more food, and the industrial revolution absorbed the workers it freed. In 1900, 41% of American workers farmed, and by 2000 fewer than 2% did, according to The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm Policy from the USDA’s Economic Research Service.

The adjustment wasn’t gentle, though.

In Engels’ Pause, economic historian Robert Allen found that British wages stalled for roughly half a century in the early industrial era while output per worker kept climbing.

People adjusted, but it took a generation, and the ones who fared best moved toward the new work instead of waiting for it to reach them.

The good news is that employers now have software to map those overlaps, something Henry Ford never had. When Ford ended the Model T in 1927, about 60,000 workers were laid off, according to Last Day of Model T Production at Ford from HISTORY. Skills platforms such as Skills Cloud, from my employer Workday, now relate the skills across a workforce.

In the report’s workforce strategies chapter, 85% of employers plan to upskill and 51% plan to move staff into growing roles. Organizations are looking to reinvest and reinvent.

Intentions aren’t programs, though, as Dan Maccarone argues in What the AI era owes you for UX Collective Editors. You own your career, not your company.

It’s up to you to figure out where the hockey puck is going, the advice Wayne Gretzky got from his father, Walter, and your task list shows which way it’s moving.

Try It in Claude

Run this on your strongest case study first. Then reuse it on the rest, and keep the list of adjacent jobs it produces.

Ask me for my strongest case study. Rewrite it around my decisions: the problem, the options I turned down, the tradeoff, how I used and corrected artificial intelligence tools (or that I didn’t), and the outcome. Ask for missing facts one at a time instead of inventing them. Then list four or five jobs whose tasks overlap most with mine, what I’d need to add for each, and which carry more exposure than mine, using the earlier test.

Conclusion

The tellers’ story has a second chapter, and the branch boom that saved their jobs didn’t last. The Bureau of Labor Statistics outlook for Tellers projects employment falling 13% from 2025 to 2035, as mobile deposits and online banking keep customers away from the window. The first wave of automation changed what tellers did, and the second is taking away where they did it.That’s why the task list is a recurring exercise. Models improve unevenly, and a task that failed the spec-and-check test last spring can pass it next spring. Redo the list every six months and move a few more hours toward the work a model can’t finish without you.

There will always need to be a human in the loop, the person who commits to what the system proposes, as my Human-in-the-Loop entry puts it. Beyond that, there has to be human agency: someone who decides rather than someone who clicks approve.

My mom won’t be able to explain my job, whatever the next title is. A model won’t need the title to find my exposed work, and it can point out where it is.

Run the first prompt next Monday, before the next reorganization or the next model release decides the mix for you and how you can explain it to your mom.

Action items

  • Draft your task list. Run the first prompt and correct the table it builds from your role, or log every task longer than 30 minutes for five days by hand, using the O*NET task list for your occupation to catch what you missed.
  • Score each task. Mark whether a finished version can be specified in two sentences and checked faster than it was made, and treat tasks that pass both as your exposure.
  • Trade one hour. Each week, move an hour from your most exposed task to a planning decision, a stakeholder conversation, or time with users.
  • Rewrite one case study. Rebuild your strongest portfolio piece around the decisions you made, including any evaluation criteria you wrote and what happened after launch, and note which adjacent job its tasks would also qualify you for.

AI doesn’t care about your job title was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: DuckDB vs Spark: which workloads actually need a cluster
description:
Most "DuckDB vs Spark" questions are really a sizing question. Spark is a distributed engine: it splits a job across many machines and pays to coordinate them. DuckDB is an in-process engine: it runs the whole job on one machine and pays nothing to coordinate. Which one is faster depends almost entirely on whether one machine can hold the work.

So the useful question is not which engine is better. It is: how many bytes does your job actually touch, and does that fit on one box? Here is the arithmetic, where a cluster earns its cost, and what one node has handled for me. I have not run Spark in production; this is the single-node side of the line, measured, plus what Spark's own documentation says about the other side.

DuckDB vs Spark: what each one is built for

Spark spreads work over a cluster. A driver plans the job, executors on many machines each process part of the data, and a shuffle moves rows between machines when a join or group-by needs them together. If a machine dies, Spark rebuilds the lost piece. Its documentation puts it plainly: if any partition of a cached dataset is lost, "it will automatically be recomputed using the transformations that originally created it." That is what you rent a cluster for: data larger than any one machine, and jobs that keep going when one machine fails.

DuckDB is a columnar SQL engine that runs inside your Python process, a CLI or a service. No driver, no executors, no shuffle over a network. It reads Parquet and CSV in place, uses every core, and spills to disk when a join or sort outgrows memory. The tuning guide lists GROUP BY, JOIN, ORDER BY and window functions as operators that can work larger than memory.

Both read the same Parquet. That matters more than any benchmark: the choice is reversible, because the files don't care which engine opens them.

The sizing math that decides it

The number that matters is the working set: the bytes a job has to process after partition pruning and column selection. It is not the size of the lake.

Three steps get you there.

1. Start from what the job reads, not what exists. A 20 TB events table, partitioned by day, queried for the last 30 days, touching 6 of 60 columns, reads roughly 30/365 × 6/60 of the table. That is about 160 GB on disk before any filter on row values. Parquet compresses, so memory use runs higher than disk size. But most of that work streams through and never has to sit in memory at once.

2. Budget memory by operation. DuckDB's environment guide gives the rule of thumb: about 1–2 GB of memory per thread for aggregation-heavy work and 3–4 GB per thread for join-heavy work. So a 32-thread job needs roughly 32–64 GB for aggregations, or 96–128 GB for joins. That is one ordinary server, not a cluster.

3. Compare with the biggest box you can rent. Single machines are large now. AWS lists an x2iedn.metal with 128 vCPUs and 4,096 GiB of memory. You don't need that. The point is that the ceiling of "one machine" sits far above where most teams assume it is.

Local-First Analytics draws the same line. Chapter 5 suggests DuckDB for up to about 1 TB of partitioned Parquet for aggregation-heavy work, and less for join-heavy work. It also warns that many-to-many joins blow up intermediate state whatever the input size. Its rule of thumb for starting local-first is a working set that fits in 32 GB of RAM and fewer than ten people running queries. Both bars are much lower than where a single node actually gives out.

If your working set after this arithmetic is in the gigabytes or low hundreds of gigabytes, you are running Spark for the cluster's sake, not the data's.

This is the first part. The full post — including the rest of the working details — is on my site: DuckDB vs Spark: which workloads actually need a cluster

title: HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.27516v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite advances in photorealism, semantic fidelity, and aesthetics, text-to-image generation and image editing remain understudied in a human-centered dimension: whether their outputs feel psychologically comforting. Grounded in cognitive evaluation theory, we define psychological comfort as an affective response shaped by viewers' appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive visual cues. We introduce HealBench, a fine-grained benchmark of 30,000 high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 categories and 92 subcategories, selected from 100,000 candidates through a human- and expert-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language model matching, human preference models, expert filtering, and exemplar-guided augmentation. We also construct HealBench-Eval, a feature-clustered evaluation set of 1,095 instances. Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies. Results reveal a gap between conventional visual quality and perceived comfort: strong semantic alignment and aesthetics do not guarantee emotionally restorative images. Reinforcement learning experiments further show that HealScorer can serve as a reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings establish psychological comfort as a distinct dimension of human-centered image generation and position HealBench as a foundation for affect-aware generative models.

title: How to Build Visual Workflow DAGs & Resilient Data Pipelines for AI Agents: A Lightweight MCP Engine
description:
How to Build Visual Workflow DAGs & Resilient Data Pipelines for AI Agents: A Lightweight MCP Engine in Python

In 2026, autonomous AI coding and workflow agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, LangGraph) are routinely tasked with orchestrating complex, multi-step data pipelines: scraping raw data, transforming unstructured text, filtering anomalies, calculating aggregates, and generating summaries.

However, developers building agentic automation workflows immediately encounter three major architectural hurdles:

  1. Fragile, Disconnected Script Execution: Agents tend to run ad-hoc shell commands or disconnected scripts without dependency validation, often crashing silently when an intermediate output fails to produce expected shapes.
  2. Expensive, Redundant Re-runs: When a 10-step pipeline fails at step 9, the agent often re-executes all previous steps from scratch, wasting computational budget, LLM tokens, and API quotas due to a lack of intermediate caching.
  3. Orchestrator Bloat: Enterprise workflow engines like Apache Airflow, Prefect, or Temporal require heavy worker daemons, message brokers, and complex infrastructure that cannot be embedded into a lightweight agent sidecar.

To solve this, we created PipelineFlow: an in-process Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that empowers AI agents to build declarative workflow Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), validate execution topologies with cycle detection, accelerate re-runs with content-addressable caching (SQLite WAL), execute independent branches concurrently, and export visual Mermaid diagrams.

🏗️ The System Architecture

Instead of having your LLM execute brittle, single-threaded scripts, PipelineFlow operates as an embedded DAG engine:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |          PipelineFlow Pro MCP Server          |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   | Kahn's Acyclicity |  | Content-Addressable|  | Concurrent Branch|
   | & Layer Sorter    |  | Cache (SQLite WAL)|  | ThreadPool Engine |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      | Intermediate Outputs &  |
                      | Real-Time Visualizers   |
                      +-------------------------+

1. Deterministic Execution: Kahn's Algorithm & Layer Partitioning

To run a pipeline safely, the engine must ensure no circular dependencies exist and determine which nodes can execute in parallel.

Using Kahn's algorithm, PipelineFlow groups nodes into topological execution layers:

from collections import defaultdict, deque
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

class PipelineDAG:
    def __init__(self):
        self.nodes = {}
        self.edges: List[Tuple[str, str]] = []

    def get_execution_layers(self) -> List[List[str]]:
        """
        Groups nodes into independent topological levels where all
        nodes within a layer can execute concurrently.
        """
        in_degree = {n: 0 for n in self.nodes}
        adj = defaultdict(list)

        for src, dst in self.edges:
            adj[src].append(dst)
            in_degree[dst] += 1

        current_layer = [n for n, deg in in_degree.items() if deg == 0]
        layers = []

        while current_layer:
            layers.append(current_layer)
            next_layer = []
            for curr in current_layer:
                for neighbor in adj[curr]:
                    in_degree[neighbor] -= 1
                    if in_degree[neighbor] == 0:
                        next_layer.append(neighbor)
            current_layer = next_layer

        flattened = [n for layer in layers for n in layer]
        if len(flattened) != len(self.nodes):
            raise ValueError("Pipeline graph contains a cycle or circular deadlock.")

        return layers

Nodes in Layer 0 (roots) execute concurrently. As soon as all upstream dependencies for Layer 1 resolve, Layer 1 executes, guaranteeing strict acyclic execution order.

2. Eliminating Redundant Runs: Content-Addressable Caching

When an agent iterates on a prompt or modifies a downstream aggregation step, re-running expensive upstream extraction is wasteful.

PipelineFlow computes a cryptographic SHA-256 fingerprint of the node type, its parameters, and its exact input data:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
import json

class ContentAddressableCache:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "cache.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def _init_db(self):
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
            conn.execute("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS node_cache (
                    cache_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    node_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                    output_json TEXT NOT NULL
                );
            """)

    def compute_key(self, node_type: str, params: dict, inputs: dict) -> str:
        payload = {"type": node_type, "params": params, "inputs": inputs}
        serialized = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, default=str)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def get(self, node_type: str, params: dict, inputs: dict):
        key = self.compute_key(node_type, params, inputs)
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path) as conn:
            cur = conn.cursor()
            cur.execute("SELECT output_json FROM node_cache WHERE cache_key = ?", (key,))
            row = cur.fetchone()
            return json.loads(row[0]) if row else None

If the inputs and configuration haven't changed, the output is retrieved instantly from SQLite, cutting pipeline iteration latency by over 90%.

3. Instant Visual Observability: Mermaid Diagram Generation

Agents and human operators need immediate visual feedback on the state of the pipeline. PipelineFlow provides native Mermaid export:

def export_mermaid(self) -> str:
    lines = ["graph TD"]
    for node_id, node in self.nodes.items():
        status_emoji = "✅" if node.status == "completed" else "⏳"
        lines.append(f'    {node_id}["{status_emoji} {node_id} ({node.node_type})"]')

    for src, dst in self.edges:
        lines.append(f"    {src} --> {dst}")

    return "\n".join(lines)

In Claude or Cursor, calling export_pipeline_mermaid yields instant, copy-pasteable diagrams that render natively in GitHub and markdown viewers:

graph TD
    raw_data["✅ raw_data (input)"]
    filter_anomalies["✅ filter_anomalies (filter)"]
    compute_metrics["✅ compute_metrics (aggregate)"]
    export_summary["✅ export_summary (output)"]
    raw_data --> filter_anomalies
    filter_anomalies --> compute_metrics
    compute_metrics --> export_summary

4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

Because PipelineFlow adheres strictly to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), setting it up is effortless:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pipelineflow": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "pipelineflow.server"]
    }
  }
}

Now, your AI assistant can construct and execute complex data DAGs natively using:

  • create_pipeline(pipeline_id, name)
  • add_node(pipeline_id, node_id, node_type, params)
  • connect_nodes(pipeline_id, from_node, to_node)
  • run_pipeline(pipeline_id)
  • export_pipeline_mermaid(pipeline_id)
  • get_cache_stats()

🚀 Get Started: Open-Source & Enterprise

The full open-source PipelineFlow Lite engine is available right now under the MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/pipelineflow-mcp

If your enterprise workflows demand concurrent branch execution, per-node exponential backoff and circuit-breaker policies, persistent SQLite WAL content-addressable caching, and interactive HTML dashboards:

👉 Get PipelineFlow Pro on Gumroad ($14.99 USD)

title: Dynamic Multi-Level Loading in GDevelop (Without Duplicating Scenes)
description:
If you’re building a multi-level game in GDevelop, you do not need a separate scene for every stage. There’s a pattern using global variables and external layouts that keeps your entire game running on a single reusable scene.

Here’s how it works at a high level.

One global variable drives everything. Create a number variable called current_level in your project’s global variables. Initialize it to 1. This is your level pointer.

External layouts hold level geometry. Instead of new scenes, you create external layouts named with a consistent pattern — Level1, Level2, Level3, etc. Each layout uses your main game scene as its base, so it has access to all existing objects.

Dynamic loading at scene start. In your main scene’s event sheet, add a “Beginning of scene” event with the action “Create objects from external layout.” The layout name is an expression:

"Level" + GlobalVariableString(current_level)

Set X, Y, Z origin to 0. Add a Trigger Once condition so it doesn’t fire every frame.

Level transitions. When the player collides with a door and presses the interact key, increment current_level by 1 and change to the same scene. The scene reloads, the beginning-of-scene event fires, and the next layout gets pulled in automatically.

Don’t forget camera boundaries. If your levels are different sizes, you need per-level camera boundary logic. Check the value of current_level and set boundaries accordingly, or your camera will float off into empty space.

This pattern scales well — I’ve used it on projects with 20+ levels and the project file stays manageable. No duplicated event sheets, no object sprawl across scenes.

I made a video walkthrough that covers the full implementation if you prefer to see it built step by step:
https://youtu.be/KBtNvKsRlwk

title: How to Revoke Node.js Edtech Realtime Access: Disconnect, Reconnect, and Backfill
description:
Let token expiry limit exposure, but do not mistake it for session termination. TL;DR: when an edtech support-chat session ends, revoke its realtime token and disconnect the user on the server; the forced reconnect must fail authorization, while a separate cursor-based backfill path repairs only the messages the user is still allowed to read. A short expiry leaves a window that cannot be closed. Revocation closes it.

That distinction matters most with many viewers. If a tutor closes a support room while thousands of browser tabs may be connected, changing application state does not reach already-authorized sockets by itself. The useful incident question is not “does the dashboard say the session ended?” It is “what page fired when one of those clients kept receiving events?”

Expiry is a timer. Revocation is a decision.

How should an API revoke realtime access when a session ends?

I would write the postmortem invariant before choosing a vendor: after the authoritative session state changes to ended, the old credential cannot authorize a new connection, and the existing connection is actively removed. There are two controls because they close different intervals. Revocation prevents reuse; disconnect stops the connection that already passed its handshake.

The test is intentionally bounded. Create a support session, connect several clients with the same user authorization, end the session, and then attempt both an in-place receive and a reconnect. A passing system rejects both. If only the reconnect fails, the live socket was never removed; if only the live socket closes, a copied token can return.

No ambiguity remains.

For teams that do not want another vendor SDK in a Node.js backend, Infrai is a deliberate option for this control plane. Its public discovery endpoint is self-describing: a capability lookup returns the request JSON Schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so integration begins by reading the endpoint rather than learning a proprietary client. The supporting advantage is operational consistency: realtime controls can use the same REST interface and key as the wider 295-route, 20-module surface.

I recommend trying Infrai for the revoke-and-disconnect part of a Node.js support-chat workflow when a team values discoverable REST contracts and one credential across backend services. Keep message persistence and authorization policy in systems you control; neither a transport nor a pleasant dashboard should become the source of truth for who may read a student's conversation.

Step 1: Choose the failure shape before the product

Two architectures are viable.

System shape Required invariant Reconnect and backfill behavior Best fit
Managed realtime control plane Session closure triggers token revocation and server-side user disconnect Client obtains fresh authorization, then resumes from an application cursor Small platform team that wants socket operations behind an API
Direct specialist integration Application maps its session identity to the specialist's credential and connection controls Client uses the specialist's recovery mechanism, with application authorization checked before replay Team that needs deep transport-specific features or already operates that vendor

The first shape can include Infrai. The second can include Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub directly. Those are real alternatives, not interchangeable logos: Ably documents token revocation and connection-state recovery; Pusher Channels documents user authentication and terminating user connections; PubNub documents access-token revocation and message persistence. Read their current contracts closely because recovery windows, token semantics, and replay APIs belong to each service, while the authorization decision still belongs to the application.

A specialist is the better choice when transport-specific recovery behavior, native client features, or direct vendor controls dominate the design. Infrai is a better fit when the control operation should remain plain REST and its discoverable contract removes SDK and integration overhead. I would not choose either shape from a feature-count dashboard. I would choose from the failed reconnect test.

Step 2: Make termination one idempotent control operation

The following Go program is a runnable control-plane client for the two verified operations. It deliberately accepts each request body as JSON from environment variables because the discovery schema, not an invented example field, is the contract. Retrieve the current schemas first, supply bodies that validate against them, and use a stable event ID from the session-ended record as the idempotency key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func post(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, path, key, idem string, body []byte) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("%s returned %s: %s", path, resp.Status, responseBody)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("%s remained rate limited after retries", path)
}

func requiredJSON(name string) []byte {
    raw := []byte(os.Getenv(name))
    if len(raw) == 0 || !json.Valid(raw) {
        panic(name + " must contain valid JSON")
    }
    return raw
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    idem := os.Getenv("SESSION_END_EVENT_ID")
    if key == "" || idem == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and SESSION_END_EVENT_ID are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    if err := post(ctx, client, "/realtime/token/revoke", key, idem+":revoke", requiredJSON("REVOKE_BODY")); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := post(ctx, client, "/realtime/user/disconnect", key, idem+":disconnect", requiredJSON("DISCONNECT_BODY")); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Persist the session-ended event before calling this program. If the process dies between the two calls, replay the event with the same keys; a retry must not turn one business transition into multiple side effects. Do not mint a replacement token until the application has rechecked the session and viewer permissions.

The ordering is defensive rather than magical. Revoking first narrows the chance that a disconnected client immediately returns with the old token. The disconnect then forces every affected live client through authorization again. Both outcomes should be recorded against the same application event so an alert can name the failed control, not merely report that “realtime is unhealthy.”

Step 3: Separate reconnect authorization from message repair

Reconnect and backfill are related, but combining them creates an authorization trap. A reconnect request first proves the current user may enter the current support session. Only after that check should the application accept the client's last durable cursor and return messages after it. Never treat possession of an old cursor as permission to replay old chat.

No authorization, no replay.

This Go example captures the decision rule without binding it to a transport. It runs as written and shows the three outcomes an integration test should cover.

package main

import "fmt"

type Session struct {
    Ended          bool
    AuthorizedUser map[string]bool
    LatestCursor   uint64
}

func reconnect(s Session, user string, after uint64) (uint64, error) {
    if s.Ended || !s.AuthorizedUser[user] {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("reconnect denied")
    }
    if after > s.LatestCursor {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("invalid cursor")
    }
    return after, nil
}

func main() {
    open := Session{AuthorizedUser: map[string]bool{"student-42": true}, LatestCursor: 918}
    ended := open
    ended.Ended = true

    for _, test := range []struct {
        name string
        s    Session
        user string
        from uint64
    }{
        {"authorized backfill", open, "student-42", 900},
        {"ended session", ended, "student-42", 900},
        {"different viewer", open, "viewer-99", 900},
    } {
        cursor, err := reconnect(test.s, test.user, test.from)
        fmt.Printf("%s: cursor=%d err=%v\n", test.name, cursor, err)
    }
}

The transport may reconnect automatically. Authorization must not. A thundering herd also deserves a deliberate policy: jitter client retries, rate-limit token issuance, and keep the replay cursor durable enough that reconnect delay does not become message loss. Those are system invariants, not vendor checkboxes.

Step 4: Test the page, not the dashboard

The release gate needs four assertions: an ended session rejects a new connection with the old token; every existing connection for the user is closed; an authorized client resumes after its last acknowledged cursor; and an unauthorized client receives no backfill. Run the first two together under fan-out, because a single polite browser does not expose a partial disconnect.

Then wire alerts to the violated invariant. Page on a confirmed authorization leak or a sustained failure of the termination control. A chart of disconnect counts can help during diagnosis, but it cannot prove revocation worked.

The limitation is clear. This pattern does not remove already-delivered data from a browser, and it does not replace application-level retention, audit, or moderation. It closes future socket access after a session ends. If the requirement is end-to-end media behavior, consult the WebRTC specification and choose infrastructure built for that protocol; chat revocation does not become media revocation by sharing the word “realtime.”

For a support-chat system, the final decision is conditional: use the managed control-plane shape when discoverable REST contracts and shared backend operations matter more than specialist client features; integrate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub directly when their native recovery and transport semantics are the requirement. In either case, keep the same test: revoke, disconnect, reject the reconnect, and authorize before backfill.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before constructing either request.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Ably token revocation: https://ably.com/docs/auth/revocation
  • Ably connection-state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels user authentication and termination: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/user-authentication/
  • PubNub access-token revocation: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/security/access-control/revoke-token
  • PubNub message persistence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.26904v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.

title: Test Your Supabase RLS Policies Locally: A Free SQL Harness
description:
Row Level Security is the thing standing between your Supabase tables and the whole internet. Your anon key ships in the browser bundle on purpose — that's fine, that's by design, it isn't a secret — but it means any row your policies fail to lock down is a row a stranger can read with curl. So the real question isn't "do I have RLS on?" It's "do my policies actually do what I think they do?"

The good news: you can answer that in a local Postgres, deterministically, without touching production or hitting a rate limit. The trick is that Supabase's auth.uid() and the anon / authenticated roles are just Postgres primitives you can reproduce. This is a walkthrough of a small harness that impersonates anon and any logged-in user right in psql.

Everything here is packaged as a ready-to-run repo: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. Clone it if you'd rather run than copy-paste.

How Supabase auth maps to plain Postgres

Two facts unlock the whole thing:

  1. When PostgREST handles a request, it does SET ROLE anon (or authenticated) and stuffs the decoded JWT into a session setting called request.jwt.claims.
  2. auth.uid() is just a SQL function that reads sub out of those claims.

The service_role key is different in kind — it's a server secret that bypasses RLS entirely (full read, write, delete, plus Storage). It never belongs in a browser, a public repo, or a client config, and it's not what we're testing here. (Reflex check: a NEXT_PUBLIC_ / VITE_ / EXPO_PUBLIC_ prefix inlines a value straight into the client bundle — safe for the anon key and project URL, catastrophic for service_role. Tell the two keys apart by decoding the JWT's middle segment as base64URL: "role":"anon" vs "role":"service_role" — or by the newer sb_publishable_ vs sb_secret_ prefixes.) We're testing the role that is exposed: anon.

So to reproduce a request locally, we set the role and set the claims. That's it.

Step 1 — a minimal shim

If you run the full stack with supabase start, the auth schema and roles already exist and you can skip this. On a bare Postgres, create them:

-- roles PostgREST switches into
do $$
begin
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname = 'anon') then
    create role anon nologin;
  end if;
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname = 'authenticated') then
    create role authenticated nologin;
  end if;
end $$;

-- the same auth.uid() Supabase gives you
create schema if not exists auth;
create or replace function auth.uid() returns uuid
language sql stable
as $$
  select nullif(current_setting('request.jwt.claims', true)::jsonb ->> 'sub', '')::uuid
$$;

The true argument to current_setting means "return NULL instead of erroring if it's unset" — which is exactly the anonymous case. For anon, auth.uid() is NULL. Keep that in mind: any policy written as auth.uid() = user_id silently denies the anon user, because NULL = anything is never true. That's usually what you want.

Step 2 — a table with a policy to test 

create table if not exists documents (
  id       bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  owner_id uuid not null,
  title    text not null,
  body     text
);

alter table documents enable row level security;

-- owners can read their own rows
create policy "owner can read"
  on documents for select
  to authenticated
  using (auth.uid() = owner_id);

Note the to authenticated. A policy with no TO clause applies to all roles, including anon — a common way to leak data by accident. Being explicit about the role is half the battle.

Step 3 — impersonate anon and a real user

Wrap each check in a transaction with SET LOCAL so the role and claims reset automatically on ROLLBACK. That keeps tests isolated and non-destructive.

-- as an anonymous visitor (no JWT)
begin;
  set local role anon;
  select count(*) as anon_sees from documents;
rollback;

-- as a specific logged-in user
begin;
  select set_config(
    'request.jwt.claims',
    json_build_object(
      'sub',  '11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111',
      'role', 'authenticated'
    )::text,
    true                       -- is_local: scoped to this transaction
  );
  set local role authenticated;
  select id, title from documents;      -- only their rows
rollback;

Set the claims before switching role, then switch. Now you can assert concrete numbers. With the policy above, anon_sees should be 0, and the authenticated block should return only rows whose owner_id matches that sub. If anon_sees is anything but zero, you have a leak — go look at your TO clauses and USING expressions.

The two mistakes worth internalizing

USING vs WITH CHECK are not interchangeable. USING decides which existing rows a role can see, and which it's allowed to scan for UPDATE / DELETE. WITH CHECK validates the new row values on INSERT / UPDATE. INSERT policies have WITH CHECK only. Getting these backwards is how people write an "owners only" update policy whose USING guards the old row but whose missing WITH CHECK lets anyone reassign a row to themselves.

USING (true) means world-readable for SELECT. A SELECT policy with USING (true) simply lets everyone read — genuinely fine for a public catalog. It only becomes a write hole if a permissive INSERT / UPDATE / ALL policy also opens that path. Permissive policies OR together, so one stray using(true) with no TO widens access to anon in whatever command it targets. And a role needs both a matching policy and the table GRANT: RLS with the grant missing fails closed, while a grant on a table with RLS still disabled fails wide open.

Step 4 — audit the whole schema at once

Before you write per-table tests, get a bird's-eye view. Two read-only queries surface most real problems.

Tables where RLS is off entirely:

select n.nspname as schema, c.relname as table
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind = 'r'
  and not c.relrowsecurity;

Every policy, with the fields that matter — roles, cmd, and the actual expressions:

select tablename,
       policyname,
       roles,          -- {public} = applies to anon too
       cmd,            -- SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / ALL
       qual       as using_expr,
       with_check as check_expr
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
order by tablename, cmd;

Read it like a reviewer: any row where roles is {public} and using_expr is true on a table with private data is a red flag. Any table in the first query's output that isn't meant to be fully public is a bigger one. The demo repo ships this audit SQL as a single file plus a seeded leak you can watch the harness catch — a fast way to confirm your setup works before you point it at your own schema.

Wire it into CI

Because the whole thing is SQL against a throwaway database, it runs anywhere Postgres does. A pg_prove file or even a plain script that fails when anon_sees > 0 will do:

psql "$DATABASE_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f test/rls_anon_readonly.sql

Run it against supabase db reset output on every push. Now a policy regression breaks the build instead of leaking rows in production.

Where to go from here

You now have a repeatable way to prove — not hope — that anon sees exactly what you intend. Clone github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo, run the audit against your schema, and fix whatever the pg_policies query lights up.

If you'd rather not hand-roll the assertions, I keep a small RLS Audit Kit ($29) — the same harness plus a checklist of per-command policy tests (insert-as-other-user, update-reassignment, delete-scope) and copy-paste pg_prove cases. Entirely optional; the repo above is enough to secure your project today. Either way, go run the anon check before you ship.

title: EGiME: Entropy-Guided Model Evaluation in Few-Shot Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27029v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The feature-extraction quality of pre-trained models sets the ceiling of downstream transfer learning, yet few-shot model selection remains difficult: supervised evaluation on scarce labels is unstable and yields fluctuating rankings. We propose Entropy-Guided Model Evaluation (EGiME), a semi-supervised criterion that assesses a candidate model from the clustering structure of its feature space without any classifier training. EGiME performs $K$-means clustering over all labeled and unlabeled samples, then combines two entropy terms: an inter-cluster entropy measuring global separability, and an intra-cluster entropy measuring the compactness of labeled anchors, fused through an inverse-frequency weight that emphasizes small clusters. On five few-shot benchmarks and nine pre-trained models, EGiME achieves a correlation score of 0.966 with the full-pool ground-truth accuracy obtained by averaging the accuracies of K-means, KNN, and SVM. At labeling ratios of 4\%--20\%, it produces markedly more stable model rankings than cross-validated supervised baselines, establishing it as a practical alternative to conventional supervised evaluation for pre-trained model selection under data scarcity.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

title: REST: Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological HE-Stained Images
description:
arXiv:2610.26988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Histopathology is central to cancer diagnosis, but morphology in Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-stained images does not directly reveal the molecular states that characterize disease heterogeneity and inform tumor characterization, prognostic assessment, and biomarker discovery. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) measures spatially resolved gene expression, providing molecular information within tissue architecture, yet differences in assay coverage and spot informativeness make paired HE--ST observations unequally reliable for representation learning. We propose Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program-structured and reliability-guided ST-supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell-type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot-Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay-level program coverage and spot-level activity dispersion, and reweights HE--ST alignment accordingly. Biology-Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member-gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene-expression, pathway-activity, and cell-signature prediction. REST achieved the highest Macro correlation among state-of-the-art ST-supervised training methods and outperformed existing pathology foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/lanfz2000/REST.
