title: Build vs Managed Vector Database: A Total-Cost Framework
description:
For most teams under roughly 200 million vectors, a managed vector database costs less in total than self-hosting, because people cost more than servers. In our model, a 20M-vector production workload runs about $21K–$27K a year on Weaviate Cloud or Pinecone, including staff time to manage the vendor. Self-hosting the same workload costs $58K–$114K in year one, depending on whether the operators are offshore, nearshore or US-based. The cloud bill for self-hosting is only about $13.7K of that.

Self-hosting starts to win at large scale when your query pattern is expensive on usage-based pricing, when data residency rules out SaaS, or when a platform team already runs stateful clusters and can absorb the work. The single biggest swing factor is not build vs buy. It is how your data is partitioned, which can move a managed bill by more than 100x.

Year-one total cost at a glance

P*ilot (1M vectors, 0.5M queries a month)*. Managed costs about $10.2K on Weaviate Cloud and $10.3K on Pinecone. Self-hosting costs $26.8K with offshore operators, $36.9K nearshore and $52.0K with a US in-house team.

Growth (20M vectors, 10M queries a month). Managed costs about $21.4K on Weaviate Cloud and $26.9K on Pinecone with partitioned data, but $300.9K on Pinecone if every query scans one namespace. Self-hosting costs $58.3K offshore, $80.7K nearshore and $114.1K in-house.

Scale (200M vectors, 100M queries a month). Managed costs from about $55.1K on Weaviate Cloud (lowest published rates; a quote is needed) and $90.3K–$152.1K on Pinecone with partitioned data. Self-hosting costs $168.1K offshore, $214.9K nearshore and $284.9K in-house.

All figures are modeled estimates built from sourced unit prices and the documented assumptions in Part 1. Managed totals include vendor-management staff time; self-host totals include cloud infrastructure, initial build and ongoing operations. Embedding, LLM and application costs are excluded because they are the same either way.

What "total cost" means for a vector database

A vector database bill has five lines, and only two of them show up on an invoice.

  1. Platform or infrastructure: the managed subscription, or EC2/VM compute, block storage and snapshots.
  2. Usage: read units, write units, stored dimensions or egress on managed plans; cross-AZ traffic when self-hosting.
  3. Initial build: cluster design, infrastructure-as-code, backups, monitoring, load testing and recall evaluation.
  4. Ongoing operations: upgrades, re-indexing, capacity planning, incident response, security patching.
  5. Vendor management: cost monitoring, quota tuning, support tickets and contract reviews on managed plans.

Self-hosting shrinks lines 1–2 and grows lines 3–4. Managed services do the opposite. The decision comes down to which side grows faster for your workload.

Managed vector database pricing (October 2026)

• Pinecone Standard: usage-based on reads, writes and storage. $16–18 per 1M read units, $4–4.50 per 1M write units and $0.33/GB-month, with a $50/month minimum. No uptime SLA is listed.

• Pinecone Enterprise: the same model at $24–27 per 1M read units and $6–6.75 per 1M write units, with a $500/month minimum and a 99.95% SLA.

• Weaviate Cloud Flex: priced on stored dimensions and storage, from $0.00465 per 1M dimensions, $0.12/GiB storage and $0.03036/GiB backup. The minimum is $45/month and the SLA is 99.5%.

• Weaviate Cloud Premium: a prepaid contract from $400/month. Shared clusters start at $0.003875 per 1M dimensions and dedicated at $0.002718, with SLAs up to 99.95%.

• Qdrant Cloud: billed on provisioned CPU, RAM and disk after a free tier. Rates appear only in its pricing calculator; Standard carries a 99.5% SLA and Premium higher.

• Zilliz Cloud: compute units on dedicated plans or vCUs on serverless, after a free tier. Storage is $0.040/GB-month from January 2026 and internet egress starts at $0.09/GB.

Two details matter more than headline rates. First, Pinecone charges reads by namespace size: each query costs 1 read unit per GB of the namespace searched, with a 0.25 RU minimum. Second, Weaviate prices on stored dimensions with no per-query fee in its published table, and its rates vary with index type, compression and region. Zilliz's own engineering blog shows the same workload pricing at about $7,000/month on dedicated and about $10,800 on serverless. The pricing model you pick can matter as much as the vendor.

Self-hosted infrastructure cost

Self-hosting Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus is mostly a memory problem. Qdrant's capacity-planning guide gives a rough formula for keeping float32 vectors in RAM:

\text{RAM} = \text{vectors} \times \text{dimensions} \times 4\ \text{bytes} \times 1.5

Quantizing to int8 replaces the 4 bytes with 1 and keeps full-precision originals on disk for rescoring. That is the design we assume from 20M vectors up.

AWS us-east-1 rates used in the model:

• r7g.xlarge (4 vCPU, 32 GiB): $0.2142/hour on demand, about $156/month, or $0.1552/hour on a 1-year Compute Savings Plan.

• r7g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GiB): $0.4284/hour, about $313/month, or $0.3104/hour on the Savings Plan.

• r7g.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 128 GiB): $0.8568/hour, about $625/month, or $0.6208/hour on the Savings Plan.

• EBS gp3 block storage: $0.08/GB-month. EBS snapshots: $0.05/GB-month.

The people line: in-house vs nearshore vs offshore

Engineering time is the largest cost of self-hosting at every scale we modeled. We price it three ways.

• US in-house hire: $101.18/hour, or $194,257 a year per FTE. This is the BLS median software developer wage of $135,980 (May 2025, reported here) divided by 0.70, because wages are 70.0% of private-industry compensation per BLS.

• Nearshore senior engineer (Latin America): $67.50/hour, or $129,600 a year per FTE. This is the midpoint of the $60–75/hour senior range in FullStack's 2026 report.

• Offshore senior engineer (South Asia): $45/hour, or $86,400 a year per FTE. This is the midpoint of the $40–50/hour India senior range in Full Scale's 2026 guide.

The US figure is conservative for this work. SRE total compensation has a reported Levels.fyi median of about $200,200 before benefits, per KORE1's 2026 guide. Vendor rates for nearshore and offshore teams already include the vendor's overhead, so no benefits multiplier is applied to them.

Scenario 1 — Pilot: 1M vectors, 500K queries/month, 1M upserts/month

• Pinecone: reads in one namespace are 500K queries × 7.15 RU × $16/M = $57.20. Writes are 1M upserts × 7 WU × $4/M = $28.00, and storage is 7.15 GB × $0.33 = $2.36. That totals $87.56 a month, which falls under the $50 minimum once the data is split into 10 or more namespaces.

• Weaviate Flex: 1,536M dimensions × $0.00465 = $7.14 plus under $1 of storage, so the $45 minimum applies.

• Self-host infrastructure: three r7g.xlarge nodes at $156.37 each cost $469; the 8.6 GiB of vectors fits easily. Adding 150 GB of gp3 ($12) and snapshots ($0.36), then the 15% allowance, gives about $554 a month.

• Self-host operations: 0.15 FTE costs $2,428 a month in-house, $1,620 nearshore or $1,080 offshore.

• Initial build: 4 engineer-weeks cost $16,188 in-house, $10,800 nearshore or $7,200 offshore, once.

At pilot scale the managed bill is close to its minimum. The self-hosted three-node cluster alone costs more than ten times the managed subscription before anyone touches it. Verdict: managed, without much debate.

Scenario 2 — Growth: 20M vectors, 10M queries/month, 10M upserts/month

• Pinecone reads: one 143 GB namespace costs 10M queries × 143 RU × $16/M = $22,880 a month. Split into 500 tenant namespaces, it costs 10M × 0.286 RU × $16/M = $45.76.

• Pinecone writes, storage and support: 70M WU × $4/M = $280, 143 GB × $0.33 = $47.19, plus the $250 Pro support add-on. The total is $623 partitioned or $23,457 in a single namespace.

• Weaviate Flex: 30,720M dimensions × $0.00465 = $142.85, plus 133.2 GiB × $0.12 = $15.98 storage and $4.04 backup, for about $163 a month.

• Self-host infrastructure: three r7g.2xlarge nodes cost $938 ($680 on a 1-year Savings Plan). Int8 vectors take 42.9 GiB, or 85.8 GiB with two replicas, out of 192 GiB. Adding $48 of EBS and $7 of snapshots, then 15%, gives about $1,142 a month.

• Self-host operations: 0.35 FTE costs $5,666 a month in-house, $3,780 nearshore or $2,520 offshore.

• Initial build: 8 engineer-weeks cost $32,376 in-house, $21,600 nearshore or $14,400 offshore, once.

Weaviate Flex is a shared cluster with a 99.5% SLA. A team that needs SSO, private networking or a higher SLA moves to Premium at $400/month or more. Even then, managed stays well under the self-host total. Verdict: managed, provided your data partitions cleanly.

Scenario 3 — Scale: 200M vectors, 100M queries/month, 50M upserts/month

• Pinecone Enterprise reads: with 2,000 namespaces, 100M × 0.715 RU × $24/M = $1,716 a month. With 500 namespaces, 100M × 2.86 RU × $24/M = $6,864.

• Pinecone writes and storage: 350M WU × $6/M = $2,100 and 1,430 GB × $0.33 = $471.90. The total is $4,288–$9,436 a month for partitioned data; a single 1.4 TB namespace is not viable on usage pricing.

• Weaviate Premium (shared, lowest published rates): 307,200M dimensions × $0.003875 = $1,190, plus $133 storage and $28 backup, for about $1,352 a month. A quote is required.

• Self-host infrastructure: eight r7g.4xlarge nodes cost $5,004 ($3,625 on a 1-year Savings Plan). Int8 vectors take 429 GiB, or 858 GiB with two replicas, out of 1,024 GiB. Adding $320 of EBS and $72 of snapshots, then 15%, gives about $6,204 a month.

• Self-host operations: 0.75 FTE costs $12,141 a month in-house, $8,100 nearshore or $5,400 offshore.

• Initial build: 16 engineer-weeks cost $64,752 in-house, $43,200 nearshore or $28,800 offshore, once.

At this scale the answer depends on query shape. With fine-grained tenant partitions, managed stays cheaper. If queries must search large shared namespaces, an offshore-operated cluster ($139K/year steady state) undercuts Pinecone's 500-namespace case ($152K/year with vendor management).

Weaviate's figure uses the lowest published rate and will rise with HNSW indexes, dedicated tenancy or specific regions. Verdict: get vendor quotes and run the break-even test below.

The read-unit trap: partitioning changes the bill 100x

On Pinecone serverless, cost per query scales with the size of the namespace searched. The same 20M-vector, 10M-query workload costs:

• One namespace of 143 GB: 143 read units per query, about $23,457 a month.

• Ten namespaces of 14.3 GB: 14.3 read units per query, about $2,865 a month.

• 500 namespaces of 0.29 GB: 0.286 read units per query, about $623 a month.

Multi-tenant SaaS products fit this model well, since each customer's queries hit only their own namespace. A global semantic search across one large corpus does not. Check your query pattern before you compare vendors; it is the most consequential input in this framework.

Break-even: when self-hosting wins

Self-hosting pays off when the managed bill exceeds the infrastructure cost plus the extra engineering time it takes to run the cluster:

\text{Break-even managed bill per month} = \text{self-host infra per month} + \Delta\text{FTE} \times \text{monthly cost of 1 FTE}

ΔFTE is self-host operations effort minus managed vendor-management effort. One FTE costs $16,188/month in-house in the US, $10,800 nearshore and $7,200 offshore at the rates above.

• Growth (20M vectors): infrastructure of $1,142 plus 0.25 extra FTE puts the break-even at about $5,189 a month with a US team, or $2,942 with an offshore team.

• Scale (200M vectors): infrastructure of $6,204 plus 0.55 extra FTE puts the break-even at about $15,107 a month with a US team, or $10,164 with an offshore team.

If your managed quote sits above these lines for a steady workload, self-hosting deserves a serious look. A 1-year Savings Plan lowers both break-even points by roughly a quarter of the compute line.

Non-cost reasons that override the math

• Data residency or air-gapped requirements: self-host, or use bring-your-own-cloud options from Pinecone, Qdrant Hybrid Cloud or Zilliz BYOC.

• Predictable spend: provisioned models (Qdrant Cloud, Zilliz dedicated, self-hosted) do not spike with query volume.

• Latency control: self-hosting lets you co-locate the index with the application and tune HNSW and quantization directly.

• Team focus: every hour spent on re-indexing is an hour not spent on retrieval quality, which usually matters more to the product.

Team composition and timelines for a self-hosted build

• Pilot (1M vectors): a part-time senior platform or SRE engineer leads, with part-time ML help for recall testing and a security checklist. Modeled effort is 4 engineer-weeks.

• Growth (20M vectors): a senior platform engineer leads, one backend engineer handles ingestion and migration, ML help is part-time, and security gets a review. Modeled effort is 8 engineer-weeks.

• Scale (200M vectors): a senior platform lead plus an on-call rotation, one or two backend engineers, a dedicated ML or data engineer for quantization tuning, and a formal security review. Modeled effort is 16 engineer-weeks.

The build effort figures are illustrative estimates, not benchmarks. A 16-week Scale build spread across two or three engineers typically fits a quarter, and the on-call rotation needs at least two trained people to be sustainable.

Engagement models compared

• In-house hire: best for long-lived platform teams already running stateful systems. The risk is hiring time and dependence on one person.

• Dedicated nearshore team: best for real-time collaboration with US teams, with 4–6 hours of overlap per Full Scale. The trade-off is a higher rate than offshore.

• Dedicated offshore team: best for well-specified builds and follow-the-sun operations. The risk is handoff discipline across time zones.

• Fixed-price migration project: best for one-off moves between vendors or to self-hosting. The risk is scope creep once production traffic is live.

• Managed service plus an advisory retainer: best for teams that want managed infrastructure but need help with schema, partitioning and cost tuning. Its value depends on clear goals.

A five-step decision framework

  1. Model your query shape first. Write down vectors, dimensions, queries per month, upserts per month and the size of the partition each query searches. On usage-priced plans the last number can swing the bill by two orders of magnitude.

  2. Get three real quotes. Price one usage-based service (Pinecone), one dimension-based service (Weaviate Cloud) and one provisioned service (Qdrant Cloud or Zilliz dedicated) for your exact workload.

  3. Price self-hosting with people in it. Use the RAM formula to size the cluster, then add build effort and an honest ops fraction. If nobody on the team has run a stateful cluster through an upgrade, use the high end.

  4. Run the break-even test. If the best managed quote sits below infrastructure plus the extra engineering cost, stay managed and revisit at the next scale step.

  5. Apply the non-cost filters. Residency, compliance, latency and lock-in can justify self-hosting or a bring-your-own-cloud option even when the math says otherwise.

Pilot-to-production budgeting

Most AI teams move through three budget stages. A pilot fits inside managed minimums of $45–$50 a month, so the real cost is engineering time on ingestion and retrieval quality. A first production launch typically adds a support plan and a higher-SLA tier, which in our Growth scenario still lands under $1,000 a month on managed plans. Enterprise scale is where contracts, committed-use discounts and dedicated capacity enter, and where a self-hosted or bring-your-own-cloud option is worth pricing properly.

Budget the vector database as one line in a larger retrieval stack.
Embedding generation, reranking, LLM inference and evaluation tooling are excluded from this model and often cost more than the database itself.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a managed vector database cost per month?

At pilot scale, roughly $45–$90 a month on Weaviate Cloud Flex or Pinecone Standard as of October 2026. At 20M vectors and 10M queries a month, our modeled range is about $160–$620 when data is partitioned well, and over $23,000 on Pinecone if every query scans one large namespace.

Is self-hosting a vector database cheaper than Pinecone?

The cloud bill usually is; the total cost usually is not. In our 20M-vector scenario, self-hosted infrastructure costs about $1,142 a month, but operations and build effort bring year one to $58K–$114K depending on where the team sits.

How much RAM does a vector database need?

A common estimate is vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes × 1.5 for float32 vectors held in memory. One million 1,536-dimension vectors need about 8.6 GiB before replication. Int8 quantization cuts that by roughly four times.
When does self-hosting a vector database make sense? When managed quotes exceed the break-even line (about $3K–$5K a month at 20M vectors and $10K–$15K at 200M in our model), when data must stay in your own environment, or when an existing platform team can absorb the operations work.

Does an offshore or nearshore team change the decision?

It lowers the break-even point. At the rates used here, an offshore-operated cluster costs about 41–49% less in year one than the same cluster run by a US in-house team. It does not remove the need for at least two people who can handle an incident.

How often should these numbers be re-checked?

Quarterly. Weaviate changed its price book in September 2026, and Qdrant restructured its tiers in 2026, so cost guides in this category go stale quickly.

title: iOS SceneDelegate and React Native: what changed and how to fix it
description:
TL;DR

Any UIKit app built with the iOS 27 SDK (Xcode 27) that hasn't adopted the UIScene lifecycle won't launch. React Native apps are UIKit apps, so every RN app is affected, whatever the RN version.

  • Deadline: the day you build with Xcode 27. Binaries built with Xcode 26 keep launching on iOS 27; Apple says it strives for binary compatibility but won't guarantee zero issues.
  • RN 0.88+: move startup into a SceneDelegate using the new startReactNative(withModuleName:in:connectionOptions:), forward links to RCTLinkingManager, add UIApplicationSceneManifest to Info.plist.
  • RN 0.79–0.87: same shape, but you build the root view yourself from reactNativeFactory.rootViewFactory and handle cold-start links by hand.
  • RN 0.74–0.78: keep your RCTAppDelegate subclass, but build the window in a SceneDelegate from its rootViewFactory.
  • RN below 0.74: create the root view in SceneDelegate from the RCTBridge the AppDelegate owns, with RCTRootView(bridge:moduleName:initialProperties:).
  • Watch: deep links, Universal Links, push-tap routing and third-party SDKs that hook AppDelegate callbacks.

Before: one app, one window, one AppDelegate

Until iOS 13, the UIApplicationDelegate (your AppDelegate) owned everything: process launch, the single UIWindow, foreground/background state, deep links and push.

A typical flow:

  1. UIKit calls application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:) with a launchOptions dictionary. If a URL or Universal Link opened the app, it's inside that dictionary.
  2. The AppDelegate creates UIWindow(frame: UIScreen.main.bounds), sets a root view controller and calls makeKeyAndVisible().
  3. State changes arrive as applicationDidBecomeActive, applicationWillResignActive, applicationDidEnterBackground and applicationWillEnterForeground.
  4. Warm deep links arrive in application(_:open:options:) and application(_:continue:restorationHandler:).

This model assumes the app is its window. Any code can reach the UI through UIApplication.shared.delegate.window or keyWindow, and lots of libraries do.

Now: AppDelegate for the process, SceneDelegate for the UI

A scene (UIWindowScene) is one instance of your app's UI. iOS 13 split responsibilities in two:

  • AppDelegate keeps process-level work: SDK init, push token registration, UNUserNotificationCenter delegate, background tasks, and choosing a scene configuration.
  • SceneDelegate (UIWindowSceneDelegate) owns a window and its lifecycle: create the window, go foreground/background, receive URLs and user activities.

The key behaviour change: once UIApplicationSceneManifest is in Info.plist, UIKit stops calling the AppDelegate's UI-lifecycle and deep-link methods and calls the scene equivalents instead.

AppDelegate (old) SceneDelegate (new)
Create window in didFinishLaunchingWithOptions scene(_:willConnectTo:options:), using UIWindow(windowScene:)
launchOptions[.url] (cold-start link) connectionOptions.urlContexts
launchOptions[.userActivityDictionary] (cold-start Universal Link) connectionOptions.userActivities
launchOptions[.shortcutItem] connectionOptions.shortcutItem
application(_:open:options:) scene(_:openURLContexts:)
application(_:continue:restorationHandler:) scene(_:continue:)
application(_:performActionFor:completionHandler:) windowScene(_:performActionFor:completionHandler:)
applicationDidBecomeActive / WillResignActive sceneDidBecomeActive / sceneWillResignActive
applicationDidEnterBackground / WillEnterForeground sceneDidEnterBackground / sceneWillEnterForeground

Unchanged on AppDelegate: didFinishLaunchingWithOptions (minus window work), didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken, notification delegate methods, background fetch and supportedInterfaceOrientationsFor.

Why Apple changed it, and when it bites

Apple's UI no longer fits "one app = one full-screen window". iPad multi-window, Stage Manager, resizable windows, external displays, Mac Catalyst and visionOS all need an app to show several independent UIs, each with its own state. A scene gives each window its own lifecycle and restoration state, which a single AppDelegate can't express. Apple has been deprecating the window-centric APIs (keyWindow, UIScreen.main-sized windows) in the same direction.

Apple rolled this out gradually (TN3187):

Release What happens to apps without UIScene
iOS 13 (2019) Scenes introduced; optional
iOS 18.4 Console log: the process doesn't adopt the UIScene lifecycle and this will become an assert
iOS 26 Log hardened: UIScene lifecycle will soon be required
iOS 27 SDK (Xcode 27) Assert at launch. The app doesn't launch

Two details from Apple engineers on the developer forums:

  • The assert is only evaluated when you build with the new SDK. An Xcode 26 build still runs on iOS 27, though Apple doesn't guarantee zero issues (thread).
  • Only adopting the scene lifecycle is required. Supporting multiple scenes is encouraged, not mandatory.

In practice, App Store Connect will eventually require the latest SDK for submissions, so "stay on Xcode 26" only buys time.

How React Native booted on iOS before 0.88

Every RN version up to 0.87 starts React Native from didFinishLaunchingWithOptions and creates the window itself from UIScreen.main.bounds. Only the wrapper changed over time:

RN version Entry point What it does at launch
≤ 0.70 Hand-written AppDelegate Creates RCTBridge(delegate:launchOptions:), then RCTRootView(bridge:moduleName:initialProperties:), puts it in a UIViewController, creates the window
0.71–0.73 Subclass of RCTAppDelegate Same work hidden inside the superclass's didFinishLaunching; you set moduleName and initialProps
0.74–0.78 Subclass of RCTAppDelegate Root view creation moves into RCTRootViewFactory (self.rootViewFactory), which also handles bridgeless/New Architecture
0.79–0.87 RCTReactNativeFactory + RCTDefaultReactNativeFactoryDelegate factory.startReactNative(withModuleName:in:launchOptions:) on a window built from UIScreen.main.bounds
0.88 SceneDelegate + RCTReactNativeFactory startReactNative(withModuleName:in:connectionOptions:) inside scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)

The 0.87 template shows the pattern every older version shares: the window and React Native both live on the AppDelegate.

// RN 0.87 template AppDelegate (abridged)
func application(_ application: UIApplication,
                 didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
  let delegate = ReactNativeDelegate()
  let factory = RCTReactNativeFactory(delegate: delegate)
  delegate.dependencyProvider = RCTAppDependencyProvider()
  reactNativeDelegate = delegate
  reactNativeFactory = factory

  window = UIWindow(frame: UIScreen.main.bounds)
  factory.startReactNative(withModuleName: "HelloWorld", in: window, launchOptions: launchOptions)
  return true
}

On the JS side, three modules depend on this native plumbing:

  • Linking.getInitialURL() reads the cold-start URL out of the launchOptions handed to the bridge/host.
  • Linking.addEventListener('url') fires when RCTLinkingManager receives a forwarded open URL or continue userActivity call.
  • AppState listens for UIApplication active/background notifications.

What breaks in a React Native app

If you do nothing and build with Xcode 27, the app asserts on launch. Adding only the scene manifest without moving code gives you subtler bugs:

Symptom Cause
Crash on launch (Xcode 27) No UIApplicationSceneManifest
Blank or white screen Manifest present, but the window is still created in AppDelegate. A scene-based app needs a window attached to a UIWindowScene
Linking.getInitialURL() returns null The cold-start URL moved from launchOptions to connectionOptions
Warm deep links and Universal Links do nothing application(_:open:) and continue userActivity on AppDelegate are no longer called
Home-screen quick actions ignored performActionFor moved to the window scene
Libraries can't find the window They read UIApplication.shared.delegate.window, which is now nil
Attribution/analytics SDKs lose deep-link events Their AppDelegate hooks or swizzles stop firing (Branch, AppsFlyer, Adjust, Airbridge, Firebase Dynamic Links-style SDKs)
Layout surprises on iPad The window becomes resizable; Dimensions and useWindowDimensions now change at runtime

Attribution vendors are already publishing scene migration guides for this. Airbridge's guide, for example, lists a blank screen and missing deep-link events as the two headline symptoms.

Fix A: upgrade to React Native 0.88

RN 0.88 adds scene support as an additive change: RCTReactNativeFactory gains startReactNativeWithModuleName:inWindow:connectionOptions: and a variant with initialProperties:. The old AppDelegate path still works under Xcode 26, so you can upgrade first and migrate second (RN 0.88 release notes).

1. Add SceneDelegate.swift. This is the 0.88 template file; replace HelloWorld with your module name.

import React
import React_RCTAppDelegate
import ReactAppDependencyProvider
import UIKit

class SceneDelegate: RCTDefaultReactNativeFactoryDelegate, UIWindowSceneDelegate {
  var window: UIWindow?
  var reactNativeFactory: RCTReactNativeFactory?

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene,
             willConnectTo session: UISceneSession,
             options connectionOptions: UIScene.ConnectionOptions) {
    guard let windowScene = scene as? UIWindowScene else { return }

    dependencyProvider = RCTAppDependencyProvider()
    reactNativeFactory = RCTReactNativeFactory(delegate: self)
    window = UIWindow(windowScene: windowScene)

    #if DEBUG
    reactNativeFactory?.devMenuConfiguration = RCTDevMenuConfiguration(
      devMenuEnabled: true, shakeGestureEnabled: true, keyboardShortcutsEnabled: true)
    #endif

    reactNativeFactory?.startReactNative(
      withModuleName: "HelloWorld",
      in: window,
      connectionOptions: connectionOptions)
  }

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene, openURLContexts URLContexts: Set<UIOpenURLContext>) {
    RCTLinkingManager.scene(scene, openURLContexts: URLContexts)
  }

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene, continue userActivity: NSUserActivity) {
    RCTLinkingManager.scene(scene, continue: userActivity)
  }

  override func bundleURL() -> URL? {
    #if DEBUG
    RCTBundleURLProvider.sharedSettings().jsBundleURL(forBundleRoot: "index")
    #else
    Bundle.main.url(forResource: "main", withExtension: "jsbundle")
    #endif
  }
}

2. Slim down AppDelegate. Remove the window, the factory and the RN start call. Keep Firebase, push registration and other process-level setup.

@main
class AppDelegate: UIResponder, UIApplicationDelegate {
  func application(_ application: UIApplication,
                   didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
    // FirebaseApp.configure(), push setup, SDK init...
    return true
  }
}

3. Add the scene manifest to Info.plist. Keep UIApplicationSupportsMultipleScenes set to false: 0.88 supports a single scene only.

<key>UIApplicationSceneManifest</key>
<dict>
  <key>UIApplicationSupportsMultipleScenes</key>
  <false/>
  <key>UISceneConfigurations</key>
  <dict>
    <key>UIWindowSceneSessionRoleApplication</key>
    <array>
      <dict>
        <key>UISceneConfigurationName</key>
        <string>Default Configuration</string>
        <key>UISceneDelegateClassName</key>
        <string>$(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).SceneDelegate</string>
      </dict>
    </array>
  </dict>
</dict>

4. Move any custom AppDelegate code for links, quick actions or lifecycle into the matching scene method (mapping table above).

Limits in 0.88: only one scene, and at cold start RN forwards only the first URL context or user activity from connectionOptions. Expo apps get this through Expo SDK 58.

Fix B: stay on an older React Native version

You can adopt scenes on any RN version. React Native only needs a root UIView, and UIKit doesn't care who creates it. Without 0.88's helpers, your SceneDelegate does three jobs by hand:

  1. Build the root view and attach it to a scene-backed window.
  2. Turn connectionOptions back into a launchOptions-shaped dictionary, so Linking.getInitialURL() keeps working.
  3. Forward warm URLs and user activities to RCTLinkingManager's existing application(...) class methods.

Add the same Info.plist manifest as in Fix A, then pick the variant for your version.

Shared helper (all versions) 

// Rebuilds the dictionary RCTLinkingManager reads for getInitialURL()
func rnLaunchOptions(from options: UIScene.ConnectionOptions) -> [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any] {
  var launch: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any] = [:]
  if let url = options.urlContexts.first?.url {
    launch[.url] = url
  }
  if let activity = options.userActivities.first {
    launch[.userActivityDictionary] = [
      "UIApplicationLaunchOptionsUserActivityKey": activity,
      "UIApplicationLaunchOptionsUserActivityTypeKey": activity.activityType,
    ]
  }
  return launch
}

RN 0.79–0.87 (RCTReactNativeFactory)

Keep creating the factory in AppDelegate, but delete the window and startReactNative lines. Keep a window property on AppDelegate too, because libraries still read delegate.window.

class SceneDelegate: UIResponder, UIWindowSceneDelegate {
  var window: UIWindow?

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene, willConnectTo session: UISceneSession,
             options connectionOptions: UIScene.ConnectionOptions) {
    guard let windowScene = scene as? UIWindowScene,
          let appDelegate = UIApplication.shared.delegate as? AppDelegate,
          let factory = appDelegate.reactNativeFactory else { return }

    let rootView = factory.rootViewFactory.view(
      withModuleName: "HelloWorld",
      initialProperties: nil,
      launchOptions: rnLaunchOptions(from: connectionOptions))

    let vc = UIViewController()
    vc.view = rootView
    let window = UIWindow(windowScene: windowScene)
    window.rootViewController = vc
    window.makeKeyAndVisible()
    self.window = window
    appDelegate.window = window // for libraries that read delegate.window
  }

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene, openURLContexts URLContexts: Set<UIOpenURLContext>) {
    guard let url = URLContexts.first?.url else { return }
    RCTLinkingManager.application(UIApplication.shared, open: url, options: [:])
  }

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene, continue userActivity: NSUserActivity) {
    RCTLinkingManager.application(UIApplication.shared, continue: userActivity,
                                  restorationHandler: { _ in })
  }
}

RN 0.74–0.78 (RCTAppDelegate subclass)

The superclass's didFinishLaunching builds rootViewFactory and then also creates a screen-sized window. You want the first part, not the second.

  • If your RCTAppDelegate exposes automaticallyLoadReactNativeWindow (check the header in node_modules/react-native/Libraries/AppDelegate/RCTAppDelegate.h), set it to false before calling super. Then use the 0.79 SceneDelegate above with appDelegate.rootViewFactory.view(...) in place of factory.rootViewFactory.
  • If it doesn't, the clean fix is a small patch-package patch that skips the window block in RCTAppDelegate.mm, or upgrading to 0.79+. Calling super and then making a second root view starts the JS app twice.

RN 0.70 and earlier, or 0.71–0.73 on the old architecture (RCTBridge)

Stop subclassing RCTAppDelegate (on 0.71–0.73) and use a plain UIApplicationDelegate. Create the bridge inside the scene, so it receives the cold-start link:

class SceneDelegate: UIResponder, UIWindowSceneDelegate, RCTBridgeDelegate {
  var window: UIWindow?
  var bridge: RCTBridge?

  func scene(_ scene: UIScene, willConnectTo session: UISceneSession,
             options connectionOptions: UIScene.ConnectionOptions) {
    guard let windowScene = scene as? UIWindowScene else { return }
    bridge = RCTBridge(delegate: self, launchOptions: rnLaunchOptions(from: connectionOptions))
    let rootView = RCTRootView(bridge: bridge!, moduleName: "HelloWorld", initialProperties: nil)

    let vc = UIViewController()
    vc.view = rootView
    let window = UIWindow(windowScene: windowScene)
    window.rootViewController = vc
    window.makeKeyAndVisible()
    self.window = window
  }

  func sourceURL(for bridge: RCTBridge) -> URL? {
    #if DEBUG
    return RCTBundleURLProvider.sharedSettings().jsBundleURL(forBundleRoot: "index")
    #else
    return Bundle.main.url(forResource: "main", withExtension: "jsbundle")
    #endif
  }

  // openURLContexts / continue userActivity: same forwarding as the 0.79 variant
}

If a native SDK needs the bridge during didFinishLaunching, keep creating it there. Then, once JS has loaded, forward the scene's cold-start URL with RCTLinkingManager.application(_:open:options:), so it arrives as a Linking url event instead of through getInitialURL().

Expo

Expo SDK 58 ships RN 0.88 with this built in. On older SDKs, write a config plugin that applies the changes above at prebuild. Editing ios/ by hand gets wiped on the next prebuild.

Be realistic about very old versions

Xcode 27 is a new toolchain. RN versions several releases behind may hit unrelated build failures with it (C++ headers, Folly, Hermes builds). Scene adoption is necessary but may not be enough. Below roughly 0.76, budget for an upgrade anyway.

Deep links, push and third-party SDKs

This is where most migrations actually break. Audit everything that touches AppDelegate:

  • Custom URL schemes (warm): handled in scene(_:openURLContexts:) and forwarded to RCTLinkingManager.
  • Universal Links (warm): handled in scene(_:continue:).
  • Cold-start links: come from connectionOptions in willConnectTo. In 0.88 only the first item is forwarded. On older versions, use the rnLaunchOptions helper.
  • Attribution SDKs (Branch, AppsFlyer, Adjust, Airbridge, your own): upgrade to a scene-aware version and call their scene APIs from SceneDelegate. Check that their swizzling doesn't still assume AppDelegate.
  • Push notifications: token registration and UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate stay on AppDelegate. A notification tap that opens a deep link still reaches JS through your push library.
  • Home-screen quick actions: move to windowScene(_:performActionFor:completionHandler:), plus connectionOptions.shortcutItem at cold start.
  • OAuth / SSO callbacks (react-native-app-auth, Google Sign-In, Facebook Login): they usually resume through open URL, so forward from the scene method to the SDK as well as to RCTLinkingManager.
  • Libraries reading delegate.window or keyWindow (splash screens, toasts, modal hosts, react-native-navigation): set appDelegate.window from the scene, or upgrade the library.
  • AppState and analytics session timing: verify foreground/background events still fire as expected.

Testing checklist and gotchas

Test on a release build, on a real device, with the app killed between cold-start cases.

Case How to trigger Expect
Normal launch Tap icon No blank screen; no UIScene warning in the Xcode console
Cold custom-scheme link xcrun simctl openurl booted myapp://path with the app killed getInitialURL() returns the URL
Warm custom-scheme link Same command, app in background Linking url event fires once
Cold Universal Link Tap a link in Notes or Messages, app killed Correct screen opens
Warm Universal Link Same, app in background Correct screen opens
Push tap (killed / background) Send a test push Routing works; token still registers
Quick action Long-press icon Action handled
Background → foreground Home, then reopen AppState changes; no JS reload
iPad resize / Stage Manager Resize window Layout responds to useWindowDimensions
Dev menu Shake (debug) Menu opens

Gotchas:

  • UISceneDelegateClassName must be $(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).SceneDelegate for a Swift class. For Objective-C, use the bare class name.
  • Don't create React Native in both AppDelegate and SceneDelegate. Two root views means two JS app instances.
  • Keep UIApplicationSupportsMultipleScenes set to false until RN supports multiple scenes; a second scene would need its own RN surface.
  • Remove leftover window = UIWindow(frame: UIScreen.main.bounds) lines. A window with no scene never shows.
  • Watch the Xcode console for the UIScene log message. If it's gone, UIKit sees you as scene-based.

Sources

  • TN3187: Migrating to the UIKit scene-based life cycle (Apple)
  • Regarding the deadline for adopting the UIScene life cycle (Apple Developer Forums)
  • Mandatory UIScene lifecycle support in iOS 27 (Apple Developer Forums)
  • React Native 0.88 release notes
  • RN 0.88 template SceneDelegate.swift
  • RN 0.88 template Info.plist
  • RN 0.87 template AppDelegate.swift
  • RCTReactNativeFactory PR #46298
  • Airbridge: Xcode 27 SceneDelegate migration for React Native

The older-version code in Fix B isn't from an official template. It's built on public RN APIs (RCTRootViewFactory, RCTRootView, RCTLinkingManager), so check it against the headers in your installed RN version.

title: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL in 2026: Why Postgres Is the Safer Default
description:
"SQL or NoSQL?" used to start long arguments. In 2026 the data points to a clear default, with a few real exceptions.

The 30-second version:

Adoption

In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, roughly 45% of developers used PostgreSQL against about 25% for MongoDB. Adoption isn't everything, but it means more hiring options, more tooling and more answers when something breaks at 2 AM. Current versions are PostgreSQL 17 and MongoDB 8.

Transactions and correctness

Full ACID compliance is a core design principle of PostgreSQL. MongoDB has supported multi-document ACID transactions since version 4.0, so "Mongo can't do transactions" is outdated. It's still not the shape the database was built around.

Scaling

MongoDB's native sharding is a genuine strength when you need horizontal scale with heavy write throughput. PostgreSQL scales out with read replicas, partitioning, or extensions like Citus. It works, but you assemble more of it yourself.

So which one?

PostgreSQL is the stronger default for most applications. Choose MongoDB when your data is genuinely schema-less and document-shaped, and you need high write throughput with horizontal scale from day one.

The full comparison, scores and FAQ: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL — full breakdown.

title: Your captcha token was solved but the site still rejected it: 7 causes and fixes
description:
You automated the boring part. The solver returned a token, you dropped it into the form, you hit submit, and the site came back with "verification failed". No stack trace, no useful error, just a page that looks exactly like the one you started on.

This happens to everyone who automates anything behind a captcha, whether it's an end-to-end test suite for your own signup flow, a monitoring job, or an agent that fills in forms. The token itself is rarely "wrong". Almost always, it's valid but used in a way the site's backend refuses.

Here are the seven causes I see most often, roughly in order of how often they bite, and what to do about each one.

1. The token expired before you submitted it

Captcha tokens are short-lived on purpose.

  • reCAPTCHA: Google's docs say each response token "is valid for two minutes, and can only be verified once."
  • Cloudflare Turnstile: tokens are valid for 300 seconds (five minutes) after they're generated.

Two minutes sounds like plenty until you look at what a real script does between "token received" and "form submitted": it waits for a page to settle, fills ten other fields, uploads a file, retries a flaky selector. If your flow takes 90 seconds before it even asks for the token, you're cutting it close.

Fix: request the token as late as possible, right before submit. Don't fetch it at the start of the test "to have it ready". If your form has a long multi-step flow, fill everything else first and solve the captcha last.

2. You used the same token twice

Both Google and Cloudflare reject a token the second time it's verified. On the server side this shows up as timeout-or-duplicate, and both vendors use that same code for "too old" and "already used", which is why it's so confusing.

The classic way to hit this: a retry loop. The submit fails for an unrelated reason (a validation error on another field, a 502 from the backend), your code retries the submit, and the retry carries the token that the first attempt already burned.

Fix: treat a token as single-use in your code too. If you retry a submit, get a fresh token for the retry.

3. The sitekey or page URL doesn't match the page you're on

A token is tied to the sitekey it was issued for and to the site it was solved on. Google returns a hostname field in the verification response so the site can check where the challenge was solved.

Two ways this goes wrong:

  • Wrong sitekey. Many sites have more than one: a staging key and a production key, or a separate key for the login page and the checkout page. Scrape the data-sitekey from the exact page you're submitting, not from a config file you copied last month.
  • Wrong URL. Send the full URL of the page where the captcha actually appears, not the site's homepage. For an SPA, that's the route the widget renders on.

4. reCAPTCHA v3: wrong action, or a score below the site's threshold

v3 doesn't show a challenge. It returns a score between 0.0 and 1.0, and Google's own guidance is that "by default, you can use a threshold of 0.5". Each site picks its own threshold, and it can be stricter on sensitive pages.

v3 also has actions. Google tells site owners to "verify that the action name is the name you expect". If the page calls grecaptcha.execute(key, { action: 'login' }) and your token was generated for submit or no action at all, a careful backend will reject it even with a decent score.

Fix: read the action name from the page's own JavaScript (search the bundle for execute() and pass it through when you request the token. Only ask for a minimum score as high as the site actually needs.

5. The token was earned by a different browser than the one submitting it

This is the one that catches people with Turnstile and with anti-bot vendors like DataDome. The token or cookie is minted in one browser context (one IP address, one user agent) and then submitted from another.

  • If you solve through a remote service, pass your own proxy so the solve happens from the same IP your script uses.
  • Pass the same user agent your browser uses, or, if the solver hands back the user agent it used, set your browser to that one before submitting.

Fix: keep the IP and user agent consistent between "earn the token" and "use the token". For DataDome you'll get a cookie rather than a token; set it on the same session and keep using the same proxy.

6. You put the token in the wrong place

Each widget expects the token in a specific spot:

  • reCAPTCHA v2 and v3: a hidden textarea named g-recaptcha-response.
  • Turnstile: a hidden input named cf-turnstile-response.

Many modern sites don't read that field at all. They register a JavaScript callback (data-callback="onSolved") and only enable the submit button, or only attach the token to their fetch request, when that callback fires. Setting the field's value does nothing if the callback never runs.

Fix: check the widget's data-callback attribute. If there is one, call that function with the token after you set the field:

await page.evaluate((token) => {
  document.querySelector('[name="g-recaptcha-response"]').value = token;
  const cb = document.querySelector('[data-sitekey]')?.getAttribute('data-callback');
  if (cb && typeof window[cb] === 'function') window[cb](token);
}, token);

7. It's reCAPTCHA Enterprise, not classic reCAPTCHA

Enterprise keys look the same but load from recaptcha/enterprise.js and are verified through a different API. A token solved as classic v2 or v3 won't pass an Enterprise check.

Fix: look at the script tag. If you see enterprise.js, or calls to grecaptcha.enterprise.execute, tell your solver it's Enterprise.

A quick checklist before you blame the solver

  1. Am I requesting the token right before submit?
  2. Does every retry get a fresh token?
  3. Is the sitekey from this exact page, and am I sending this exact URL?
  4. For v3: the right action, and a score the site will accept?
  5. Same IP and user agent for solving and submitting?
  6. Is the token in the right field, and did the callback fire?
  7. Is it actually Enterprise?

How we handle this at CaptchaNo

Full disclosure: I work on CaptchaNo, a captcha solving API, and several of these causes shaped how the API works. One request covers reCAPTCHA v2, v3 and Enterprise, Turnstile, DataDome and image captchas. The call waits for the token instead of making you poll, which helps with cause #1. You can pass proxy, userAgent, action and minScore for causes #4 and #5, and failed solves aren't billed. Even if you use something else, the checklist above applies to every solver.

Whatever you're automating, keep it to things you're allowed to automate: your own sites, systems you have permission to test, and data collection the site's terms permit.

title: How to Debug Irrelevant Vector Query Results — Game Catalog Drift
description:
A game catalog assembled from publisher feeds, storefront exports, and community listings can contain millions of records, so the operational constraint is reindex cost: do not tune the similarity threshold until you have proved that query and document vectors came from the same embedding model and match the collection dimension. A model mismatch can return believable nonsense instead of an error. The correct repair after a model change is a reindex.

TL;DR: read the collection dimension, re-embed one known listing, and compare that vector with the stored vector for the same listing. The self-similarity should be near-perfect. If it is not, stop query tuning and rebuild the affected index from the source listings.

This matters during a catalog migration because an apparently healthy query path can still rank "Deluxe Space Tactics" above the exact help-center article for "restore a missing deluxe-edition license." The response has the right shape. Latency may look ordinary. The words even seem related. Yet the vectors may inhabit different coordinate systems, which makes every downstream ranking decision untrustworthy.

Why does a vector query return irrelevant results?

Treat the incident as an index lineage problem, not a relevance problem. In a bounded production scenario, suppose publisher listings were embedded before a deployment while query embeddings were switched afterward. The collection still accepts vectors of its configured dimension, and a change between models with the same output width may evade a dimensionality check entirely. That is the nasty case: structurally valid input, semantically invalid comparisons.

I start capacity planning here, before proposing a rebuild. Let N be the number of canonical listings, R the average number of source revisions retained per listing, and D the vector dimension. The live vector count is roughly N * R; a full repair touches that entire set, so the migration needs a bounded batch rate, enough temporary index capacity, and an explicit completion SLO. Those are planning variables, not benchmark claims. For example, a publisher correction can create a second source revision without creating a second game, while a storefront export may represent editions as separate records; the indexing contract has to settle that distinction before anyone estimates rebuild capacity. Otherwise the team can produce a technically correct new vector for the wrong logical unit, reconcile against an inflated record count, and declare victory while duplicate editions crowd the nearest-neighbor set. I would write the identity rule beside the capacity estimate: canonical game ID, source, locale, edition, and source revision go into the decision about replacement versus retention. This does not manufacture a benchmark. It makes the units in the plan auditable.

Count the right thing.

The invariant is stricter than "the dimensions match": every vector compared in one collection must share the same embedding lineage. Record the model identifier and an index-generation identifier beside each ingestion job. Dimension catches one class of error. Lineage catches the harder class.

Step 1: verify the collection before touching thresholds

Read the collection through its supported metadata operation and confirm the dimension it was created with. For Infrai, that operation is GET /v1/vector/collection/get; its search and vector functions are exposed through a plain REST API, so a platform team does not need to install or track a vendor SDK. Do not infer the dimension from a current model configuration, because that tells you what a new request produces, not what the existing collection was built to accept.

Capture three values in the incident record: collection dimension, configured embedding model, and index generation. If the first differs from the length of a newly produced vector, the diagnosis is complete. If the lengths agree, continue; equal width does not prove equal meaning.

Infrai's public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, exposing request and response schemas rather than forcing an engineer to guess fields. The verified discovery snapshot contains 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For this rebuild workflow, that second advantage is operational rather than decorative: the platform team can inspect the current vector contract and use the same credential-management and billing boundary as its other backend calls, instead of adding another key rotation and invoice-reconciliation path during an already expensive migration. The authenticated check below uses the normal bearer convention, fetches that discovery manifest with an explicit method, handles 429 without a tight loop, and then validates two exported vectors locally. Save the known stored vector and the freshly embedded vector as JSON arrays, set INFRAI_API_KEY, and run it against both files. The manifest call is deliberate: it lets the same incident tool verify the current contract before an operator invokes the collection operation, while the local comparison avoids inventing request fields that the service schema should supply.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func getDiscovery(key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    discoveryURL := "https://api." + "infrai" + ".cc/v1/discovery"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var manifest struct {
            Capabilities json.RawMessage `json:"capabilities"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if len(manifest.Capabilities) == 0 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned no capabilities")
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after retries")
}

func readVector(path string) ([]float64, error) {
    b, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    var v []float64
    if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &v); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return v, nil
}

func cosine(a, b []float64) (float64, error) {
    if len(a) == 0 || len(a) != len(b) {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("dimension mismatch: stored=%d fresh=%d", len(a), len(b))
    }
    var dot, aa, bb float64
    for i := range a {
        dot += a[i] * b[i]
        aa += a[i] * a[i]
        bb += b[i] * b[i]
    }
    if aa == 0 || bb == 0 {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("zero-length direction")
    }
    return dot / (math.Sqrt(aa) * math.Sqrt(bb)), nil
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: vectorcheck stored.json fresh.json")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if err := getDiscovery(key); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    stored, err := readVector(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fresh, err := readVector(os.Args[2])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    score, err := cosine(stored, fresh)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("dimension=%d cosine=%.9f\n", len(stored), score)
}

A dimension error is decisive. A successful run only advances the investigation.

No shortcuts.

Step 2: use one listing as a canary

Choose a canonical record whose exact source text is still available, rather than a hand-edited approximation. Re-embed that exact document with the model declared for the collection, retrieve its stored vector, and compare the two. The similarity to itself should be near-perfect; this is a lineage canary, not a general relevance benchmark.

There is an important trap here. Comparing the newly embedded document with a newly embedded copy proves only that the current model is deterministic enough for this check. It says nothing about the stored index. One side of the comparison must be the vector already stored for that known document.

Use more than one canary before authorizing a costly rebuild: one publisher listing, one storefront record, and one community listing provide coverage across the ingestion branches without pretending to be a statistically complete evaluation set. If only one branch fails, rebuild that generation or namespace rather than reflexively replacing the entire catalog.

The decision rule is blunt. A failed self-check blocks relevance tuning. Changing top-k, metadata filters, hybrid weights, or similarity cutoffs can hide symptoms, but it cannot make vectors from incompatible models comparable.

Step 3: reindex as a controlled migration

Once a model change is established, create a new index generation with the correct dimension, embed from canonical source records, and direct test traffic to it only after the canaries pass. Keep the old generation available until the new one meets the retrieval SLO and record counts reconcile. Do not mix old and new vectors in place.

For a large game catalog, I would gate the rollout on four numbers: attempted records, successful embeddings, successfully indexed records, and canary agreement. The first three expose loss during the pipeline; the fourth protects against a perfectly complete but semantically wrong rebuild. Pick batch concurrency from service limits and the completion window, then leave headroom for live queries. A migration that consumes all available capacity has converted a relevance incident into an availability risk.

Retries also need a stable record identity. Reprocessing the same (listing ID, source revision, index generation) should replace the intended vector rather than create another logical copy. This is where index cost and correctness meet: uncontrolled duplicates increase storage while distorting neighborhoods.

Only switch query traffic after the new generation passes the same known-document check used for diagnosis. Then sample real help-center intents such as license recovery, cross-play eligibility, and edition upgrades. Those examples test the job the index exists to do; a single aggregate score cannot explain a bad catalog result.

Which service should own the rebuilt index?

The mismatch test is vendor-independent. Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and Infrai should therefore be compared on the operating model surrounding the repair, not on claims that one product can rescue incompatible embeddings.

Option Question to answer before selection Operational boundary
Pinecone Does the managed index model fit the expected vector count and rebuild cadence? Validate model lineage in the application and consult current index limits in its documentation.
Weaviate Do its managed and self-managed choices match the team's on-call appetite? Deployment choice does not remove the need to version embeddings and collections.
Qdrant Is the team prepared to operate it, or does its managed offering fit the SLO? Ownership of backups, upgrades, and capacity depends on the selected deployment.
Infrai Is a plain REST surface, one credential, and one billing boundary across 295 routes in 20 modules preferable to another SDK dependency? The application still owns source-of-truth records, lineage metadata, and migration validation.

That is the buy-versus-build decision I care about. Managed operation can reduce infrastructure ownership, while self-hosting can offer more control; neither choice removes index duplication during a cautious migration, nor the engineering work required to prove semantic compatibility. Compare current limits, backup behavior, data-location requirements, and rebuild controls against the catalog's measured size. Avoid a static price table: index shape, replication, retention, and vendor terms change, while the underlying capacity equation remains.

Infrai is a reasonable candidate when avoiding another client library matters and a consistent REST interface helps the platform team. Its 295 routes across 20 modules use one API key, one wallet, and one bill. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages; for this workflow, the Go example gives maintainers a contract-aligned starting point when the migration tool changes. Per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata is specified consistently, which gives the rebuild controller useful attribution for capacity and vendor audits without claiming that this article measured any of those values. For a catalog migration that already coordinates ingestion, vector work, and adjacent backend jobs, those properties mean the team does not have to juggle 30 keys or reconcile 30 invoices at month-end, while also reducing hand-translated integration code; the advantage is operational consolidation, not better cosine mathematics.

There are real limitations and trade-offs. Infrai is not a fit when policy requires self-hosting this vector tier, or when the team wants a vector-specialist SDK and its workflow is already built around one. Choose Qdrant or Weaviate for evaluation when self-managed deployment is a firm requirement, and evaluate Pinecone when a dedicated managed vector service is the preferred ownership boundary. Those products still require the same lineage discipline. A single key also increases the importance of sound credential scoping and handling; it reduces key sprawl but does not remove security work.

There is no universal winner.

When does this runbook not apply?

If the stored-vector self-check is near-perfect and the collection dimension matches, keep investigating. The likely fault domain has moved to chunking, stale source records, filters, lexical-versus-semantic weighting, or an evaluation set that does not represent help-center intent. This runbook also does not decide whether two genuinely different listings ought to be neighbors; that requires labeled relevance judgments.

Do not rebuild merely because a few ambiguous game titles rank poorly. First separate exact identity failures from ordinary retrieval quality. Reindexing is justified by broken lineage or an intentional model migration, not by discomfort with a threshold.

The durable prevention is modest: pin the embedding model per index generation, persist its identifier and dimension, run a stored-versus-fresh canary before every traffic switch, and make mixed generations impossible at write time. Then an embedding change becomes a planned capacity event instead of a quiet corruption of search relevance.

Sources

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • Qdrant documentation

title: Reproducing Olmo 3 7B Pre-training in MaxText: case study of large scale training on TPUs
description: The MaxText team successfully reproduced Ai2’s Olmo 3 7B language model from scratch on Google Cloud TPUs using JAX/XLA, precisely matching the original PyTorch-on-GPU reference across pre-training and mid-training stages on all held-out evaluations. The implementation achieved up to 57.4% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) and demonstrated robust infrastructure portability by surviving mid-run cluster resizes and cross-generation TPU shifts without requiring recipe alterations. Crucially, the exercise proved the necessity of comprehensive held-out validation by catching a silent data-loader memorization bug that artificially depressed training loss and would have otherwise faked a performance win.

title: How an AI Citation and Backlink Overlay Can Improve SEO Outreach Priorities
description:
An AI-powered outreach workflow documented by SEO practitioner Miloš Radić combines traditional backlink-gap analysis with AI-citation monitoring to decide which websites deserve attention first. Rather than treating link prospects and AI-answer sources as separate lists, the approach overlays both datasets in one opportunities board. The result is a more focused way to prioritize outreach, while also offering a reusable model for content planning, digital PR and AI-visibility tracking.

In Radić’s detailed Search Engine Land walkthrough, the starting dataset contained roughly 24,000 domains from an Ahrefs link-intersect analysis. That list was then enriched with pages repeatedly cited when AI-generated answers referenced competitors. Each domain was classified according to whether it appeared in both datasets, only in AI-citation data, or only in backlink data.

The important shift is not simply collecting more prospects. It is using two observable signals to make a clearer decision about where outreach, relationship building or content effort may be most relevant. A site that links to competitors and also appears frequently in AI-generated answers has a different strategic profile from a site that meets only one of those conditions.

How the data-overlay workflow works

Radić describes a four-step logic that can be reproduced with exports, a spreadsheet-like dataset and a locally built web application. The workflow is deliberately a DIY, non-SaaS approach rather than a newly released outreach platform.

  1. Create a backlink-gap dataset. Export domains identified through a competitor link-intersect analysis. This establishes the conventional outreach pool: publications, resources and other sites that link to competitors.
  2. Export AI-citation data. Gather pages or domains that appear as sources in AI-generated answers involving competitors. This creates the second signal, focused on third-party sources that are visible in AI answer experiences.
  3. Merge and classify the records. Match domains across both files, then apply one of three labels: both signals, AI-only, or backlink-only.
  4. Rank the opportunities board. Prioritize using AI-citation frequency rather than relying solely on conventional domain metrics.

The classification is simple, but it makes the underlying data more actionable. Teams can see which prospects have evidence of relevance in both the established link ecosystem and emerging AI answer citations, without assuming that either signal alone guarantees an outreach outcome.

Opportunity tier Backlink-gap signal AI-citation signal What the workflow indicates
Both Domain links to identified competitors Domain or page appears in AI-answer citation data Potentially relevant across both datasets
AI-only Not present in the backlink-gap export Appears in AI-answer citation data A source that conventional link-gap research may not highlight
Backlink-only Present in the backlink-gap export Not present in the AI-citation export A conventional outreach prospect without the second signal

Why citation frequency changes the prioritization model

Traditional backlink research can produce a large list of domains, which often leaves marketers to sort prospects by metrics that do not directly answer a practical question: which publishers or resources are visibly informing AI-generated answers in this topic area?

Radić’s workflow ranks the consolidated board by AI-citation frequency. That does not turn citation frequency into a universal quality score. It does, however, offer a specific relevance signal for teams trying to understand the sources repeatedly surfaced in AI answers about competitors.

For outreach, this can support a more deliberate split between high-priority prospects, sources worth monitoring and conventional link opportunities. It can also prevent an AI-citation export from becoming another disconnected report that nobody uses after the initial review.

The local-app approach and its guardrails

The walkthrough describes using prompts to build a local web app that loads a CSV, merges AI-citation information, classifies rows and supports research into contact details. Radić characterizes this part of the process as “vibe coding,” with prompts and iterative refinement used to translate the workflow into a usable interface.

The build process included two notable constraints:

  • Do not invent contact information. The workflow should not fabricate an email address when reliable contact data is unavailable.
  • Use exported data instead of excessive live queries. Radić found that no-code automation through Make.com and live API queries were dead ends for this use case, partly because of API costs and token use.
  • Keep the overlay logic visible. The value comes from retaining the source signals and their classifications, rather than reducing prospects to an unexplained score.

A local application is not automatically the right answer for every team. It requires someone who can work through prompts, data cleanup and iteration. But the documented approach shows that an internal tool can be practical when the priority is combining existing exports without repeatedly querying services during every interaction.

Extending the overlay beyond link outreach

The same structure can apply wherever identifiable competitors and third-party coverage exist. For content planning, a team can examine which external sources repeatedly appear around competitor-related AI answers, then use that research to identify topics, source gaps or publications shaping the conversation. It should not be treated as a shortcut to copying competitor content.

For digital PR, the overlap may help distinguish outlets that cover a space from those that also appear as cited sources in AI-generated answers. That can inform media research and pitch prioritization, while leaving the quality and newsworthiness of the pitch as separate editorial questions.

For AI-visibility tracking, the board provides a way to monitor third-party sources alongside competitor link data. Its usefulness depends on reliable exports, consistent matching of domains and a clear definition of what the citation dataset measures.

The workflow does not provide a published time-saving figure, a fixed implementation cost or a guaranteed return on investment. Its potential economic benefit is narrower and more credible: reducing the manual effort of comparing separate datasets and helping teams concentrate research on prospects supported by the signals they choose to track.

If disconnected spreadsheets are making AI-search research hard to use, Scalevise can help turn the underlying question into a practical measurement and implementation plan. Our AI consultancy for practical AI adoption helps businesses assess available data, prioritize viable use cases and design workflows that fit existing operations instead of adding another unused dashboard. Discuss an AI workflow assessment with Scalevise.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an AI citation and backlink overlay?

It is a workflow that combines competitor backlink-gap data with data on pages or domains cited in AI-generated answers. Records are then classified as both, AI-only or backlink-only.

What data does the documented workflow use?

Radić starts with an Ahrefs link-intersect export and enriches it with an export of pages where AI answers cite competitors. The combined board in the example contains roughly 24,000 domains.

Why does the workflow rank opportunities by AI-citation frequency?

The workflow uses citation frequency to prioritize sources that repeatedly appear in AI-generated answers, rather than ranking solely through traditional domain metrics.

Can this approach be used for digital PR and content planning?

Yes. The documented workflow explicitly identifies content planning, digital PR and AI-visibility tracking as applications when competitors and third-party coverage can be identified.

Conclusion

Radić’s workflow offers a concrete way to unite backlink research and AI-citation monitoring in one decision-making view. Its value is not a promise that every overlapping domain will produce a link, mention or citation. It is a clearer, reproducible method for identifying where conventional competitor research and AI-answer source data intersect, then using that evidence to prioritize the next piece of work.

ELO (Effortless Order) is building a digital commerce ecosystem designed to connect merchants and consumers more directly, beginning with online food ordering.
Our platform aims to reduce reliance on traditional third-party intermediaries, help merchants manage their products and promotions, and give consumers a smoother ordering experience. The ecosystem includes merchant and consumer interfaces, order management, loyalty rewards, and an ELO token-based payment and rewards system.
We are looking for a talented React Frontend Developer to help us build intuitive, responsive, and reliable user experiences as the platform evolves.

Develop and maintain responsive web interfaces using React.
Build consumer-facing experiences for browsing products, managing shopping carts, and placing orders.
Develop merchant dashboards for managing products, images, promotions, discounts, customer messages, and reviews.
Implement features such as order history, customer preferences, product reviews, and chat interfaces.
Integrate frontend components with backend APIs for orders, user accounts, merchant services, and payment workflows.
Help build user interfaces for loyalty rewards and ELO token-related functionality.
Ensure excellent performance, accessibility, usability, and cross-browser compatibility.
Collaborate with backend developers, designers, and product stakeholders.
Troubleshoot issues, review code, and continuously improve frontend quality.

Required Skills

Strong experience building web applications with React.
Proficiency in JavaScript and modern frontend development practices.
Experience with HTML5, CSS3, and responsive design.
Experience integrating REST APIs or other backend services.
Understanding of component-based architecture, state management, and reusable UI components.
Familiarity with Git and collaborative software development workflows.
Ability to write clean, maintainable code and communicate effectively in a remote team.

Experience with TypeScript, Next.js, or modern React frameworks.
Experience building e-commerce, food-ordering, marketplace, or merchant dashboard applications.
Familiarity with payment integrations and checkout workflows.
Experience with Web3, blockchain applications, or cryptocurrency wallet integrations.
Familiarity with loyalty programs, rewards systems, and transaction histories.

What You'll Work On

You will contribute to a platform that brings together:
Consumer experience: Product discovery, shopping carts, checkout, order history, preferences, reviews, and customer communication.
Merchant experience: Product and service management, promotions, discounts, reviews, messaging, and advertising features.
Rewards and payments: Frontend experiences supporting the ELO token, reward earning and redemption, and available payment methods.

Who We're Looking For

We value developers who take ownership of their work, care about the details of user experience, and can turn product requirements into practical, high-quality interfaces.
You should be comfortable working independently, collaborating remotely across time zones, and learning new technologies when needed.
