  4. Your expected salary or hourly rate.

title: The Agent Bumped a Major Version and CI Stayed Green
description:
The PR looked like housekeeping. The agent bumped one dependency across a major version, updated the lockfile, described it as "chore: upgrade queue-client to v4," ran the suite, and merged. CI was green.

Three days later, the nightly sync job started returning only the first page of records. The queue library kept responding, the job kept logging success, and nobody had touched pagination logic. The bump had.

Why a green suite missed the break

Unit tests rarely call the real dependency. They build a fake that matches the surface the wrapper remembers from the previous version. That fake still answers when the code calls the old method with the old arguments, so the test passes whether or not the installed package still behaves that way.

A major version exists because something on the outside changed. The suite proves your wrapper compiles against your mock. It does not prove the installed package still returns what the wrapper expects. Agents usually resolve "upgrade" to "latest" and never open the upstream removed list; the context window fills with the diff it generated, not the document that explains what changed.

The three breaks tests cannot see

A renamed response field. The client used to return { "records": [...] }. v4 renamed the key to { "items": [...] }. The wrapper reads records, gets undefined, iterates an empty list, and logs a clean run. The hand-written fixture in the test still builds records, so the test never meets v4's real shape.

A dropped config option, silently ignored. v4 removed the maxPerPage setting and capped page size at the SDK default. Old code passes the key; the new client ignores it. No exception, no deprecation warning, just shorter pages.

A changed callback contract. A hook that used to receive a second argument (the raw page token) drops it in v4. The handler reads the argument, gets undefined, computes "no more pages," and stops after the first response.

Each of these fails quietly: the program keeps running, the log line looks normal, the test stays green. The failure lives in the gap between the mock and the real backend, which CI never bridges.

The habit that costs one extra pass

Keep one direct dependency per PR. Never let the agent fold a major bump into a feature diff. A reviewer reading both cannot tell which change altered runtime behavior, and the agent cannot reason about the upgrade when the feature context dominates the prompt.

Read the breaking-changelog section for the target range, not the marketing "what's new" line. The breaking list for a major bump is usually short — renamed exports, removed options, response-field changes. The "new features" section tells you what you gained; the removed list tells you what you lost.

Run the built app against a sandbox, not just the suite. Execute the real job path against a test backend and compare the record count, page length, and response shape before merge. A mocked suite cannot reveal a renamed field; one real call does.

Review the lockfile diff by hand. Major bumps ride transitive dependencies along for free. Pin those separately so the reviewer sees what moved and can skip the ride-along upgrades on the first pass.

When the dependency wraps your own backend

If the upgraded package is an API client generated for your own service, the cheapest check is to replay recorded request/response pairs against the local OpenAPI spec and a live sandbox endpoint before merge. A renamed response field or a dropped option shows up as a red diff against the contract instead of as a partial nightly job three days later. That is the local-first loop we built into Powerduck: the spec stays the source of truth, and drift appears in front of the reviewer rather than in the logs.

What I check now

Before approving an agent-authored major bump, I ask three things:

  1. Is this PR a single direct dependency, or did the upgrade ride along with feature work?
  2. Did anyone open the breaking-changelog section for the target range, or only the release-notes headline?
  3. Did the agent run the real path against a sandbox, or did it stop at the mocked suite?

A green CI on a major bump means your mocks still compile. It does not mean the new version behaves.

title: ReconD: pull-based deployments for one server, without a platform
description:
The simple use case is this:

  • You have a machine
  • And a containerized app running on that machine.
  • Your CI pipeline already builds and publishes images.
  • You do not want a full container orchestrator for this workload, but you also do not want to SSH into the box and manually run deploy scripts every time a new image is ready.

That is the space reconD is designed for. reconD is a single-host deployment reconciliation agent. To put it simply, it watches your deployment metadata and deploys the latest version of your app.

A typical workflow for a sample app called my-app

Your CI publishes:

  • a container image to GHCR
  • a GitHub Release
  • a deployment-metadata.json file that specifies the image, its immutable manifest digest, and the git SHA.

On your virtual machine, reconD periodically asks: "What is the latest desired deployment for dev-my-app or staging-my-app?"

Then it checks: "Is this server already running that digest?" If not, it runs the command you configured:

sh make redeploy-app

That command can be a shell script, a Make target, a Docker command, or something that wraps Docker Compose.

reconD does not try to understand your whole app topology. It does not manage networking, volumes, secrets, scaling, scheduling, ingress, or clusters. That narrowness is intentional. It only owns the reconciliation loop:

  1. Fetch desired deployment metadata.
  2. Compare desired digest with local state.
  3. Inspect the runtime container.
  4. Apply an optional strategy, such as updating an env file with the new image tag.
  5. Run your deploy command.
  6. Wait for health.
  7. Commit deployment state.
  8. Roll back if the deployment fails.
  9. Notify you of deployment status

reconD just keeps asking: "Is this host running the latest version of your app yet?" And if the answer is no, it runs the one command you already trust. It is not Kubernetes. It is not trying to become Kubernetes. It is a small reconciliation loop for single-host deployments, built for the cases where that is exactly enough.
That's the whole model. The server pulls; nothing pushes into it. No inbound SSH from CI, no deploy keys in your pipeline, no open webhook port.

What reconD deliberately doesn't do

reconD doesn't know what Compose is. It runs your command. That command can be docker compose up -d, docker run ..., make redeploy, or a script that runs migrations first. All the knowledge about how to deploy on this particular machine stays in that command, where you can read and test it.

That keeps reconD small. It doesn't manage networks, volumes, secrets, ingress, scaling, or clusters. If a problem needs to understand your app's topology, it belongs in your deploy command, not in the agent.

Failure handling

The interesting part of deployment automation isn't the happy path. It's what happens with a bad release.

Bounded retries. Forward deployments and rollbacks retry with exponential backoff and jitter, up to limits you set:

deployment_retry:
  max_retry_forward_deployment: 3
  max_retry_rollback: 2

It remembers failures. Without this, a bad image gives you an endless loop: deploy, fail the health check, roll back, next poll, deploy the same bad image again. reconD records the failed digest in its state file and doesn't try it again automatically. If the rollback succeeds, your service is back up, but the failed version stays blocked. Pushing a newer release unblocks deployment.

It survives restarts. The current deployment, the previous one (the rollback target), and any terminal failure live in one JSON state file on disk. Restart the agent, or the host, and it picks up where it left off.

You can also point reconD at a Slack webhook to hear when a deployment starts, succeeds, or fails.

Try it

If you run apps on a single server and want deployments that are pulled, health-checked, and can roll back, without adopting a platform, give it a try:

github.com/ercross/reconD

Issues, ideas, and "this broke on my distro" reports are all welcome.

title: How Rogo ships agent-written code to production in 5 minutes on Vercel
description:
Rogo on Vercel

  • 73,000+ deployments in a single month

  • Agent-written code shipped to production in 5 minutes

  • 6 production AI agents automating work from churn analysis to deal desk

title: What If We Built a Stock Market That Had to Wait for You to Grow Up?
description:
Imagine opening an investment app on your eighteenth birthday.

Instead of confetti, it shows you a receipt.

Not just a balance. A record of every fee charged, every investment decision made on your behalf, every organization that benefited, and every risk someone accepted with money that belonged to you.

At the bottom, there is a button:

Ask why.

That is the product I want to explore.

Not a trading app with cartoon rockets. Not a leaderboard for wealthy children. Not a casino wearing a financial-literacy costume.

A financial system whose operators must eventually explain themselves to the person who was too young to question them.

Call it the Childhood Exchange.

This is a design proposal, not an existing product or legal blueprint. And its most interesting feature might be that it should barely resemble an exchange at all.

Giving a child a share is easy to imagine. Designing the relationship is harder.

Start with a simple thought experiment: every child receives a share in a company.

The immediate questions are financial:

What is it worth? Who holds it? Can it be sold? What happens if its value falls?

But a developer should see another set of questions:

Who controls the account? What does the interface encourage? What data gets collected? Whose interests does the recommendation engine serve? What happens when the child disagrees?

A share is an asset.

The software around it is a system of permissions, incentives, and power.

We can make the asset belong to the child while designing everything else around someone else’s objectives.

That is the problem worth building against.

Please do not build a brokerage app with smaller buttons

There is an obvious version of this product:

  • Colorful charts.
  • A friendly mascot.
  • Daily streaks.
  • Trading challenges.
  • Notifications announcing “opportunities.”
  • A leaderboard comparing returns.

It would be easy to pitch. It might even look educational.

But learning about markets and being encouraged to trade are not the same product.

The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority tested digital engagement features in an experiment involving more than 9,000 consumers. It found that features such as notifications and prize draws could increase trading frequency and risk-taking. That study was not about children, so it does not establish the effects on them. It does give designers a reason not to treat engagement mechanics as harmless decoration. fca.org

Here is the alternative design principle:

Make understanding easy. Make consequential financial action deliberate.

A child should be able to explore a concept without entering a transaction funnel.

Curiosity does not need a buy button.

The product needs two worlds—and a wall between them

I would separate the system into two environments.

The learning world

This is a simulation.

Users can investigate businesses, test assumptions, watch hypothetical portfolios change, and discover that a plausible story is not a guaranteed return.

They should be able to lose imaginary money without losing real money—or dignity.

No public wealth rankings. No rewards for being the most aggressive trader. No implication that winning a simulation proves investment skill.

The ownership world

This contains real assets.

It needs legally appropriate custody, clear authority boundaries, understandable disclosures, and a transition process that follows the rules of the relevant jurisdiction.

Adult-managed investment accounts for children already exist; US UGMA/UTMA custodial accounts are one example. Their existence means “children can own investments” is not, by itself, the innovation. fidelity

The innovation would have to be the quality of accountability around that ownership.

And there should be no automatic bridge from “excellent simulator score” to “permission to trade real assets.”

Learning achievement != financial authorization

That is not a minor UX detail.

It is a boundary the architecture should enforce.

The most important dashboard belongs to a future user

The child using the product today is not its only audience.

There is also the future adult who will inherit the consequences.

So I propose a requirement:

Every consequential action must be explainable to the account holder when they gain control.

Call it the Eighteen-Year Test—a memorable name, not a claim that control transfers at eighteen in every jurisdiction.

For each action, the system should help answer:

  • Who authorized this?
  • What authority did they have?
  • What information was available?
  • What did it cost?
  • Who received the payment?
  • What alternatives were considered?
  • What uncertainty remained?

Notice the difference between this and a performance chart.

A chart says what happened to the balance.

An accountability record helps explain what people did.

Those are different questions.

Build the receipt before the recommendation engine

Here is a conceptual event record:

type AccountDecision = {
  id: string;
  occurredAt: string;

  actor: {
    id: string;
    role: "guardian" | "authorized_manager" | "account_holder";
  };

  authorityReference: string;
  action: string;

  rationale: {
    plainLanguage: string;
    policyVersion: string;
    alternativesConsidered?: string[];
  };

  costs: Array<{
    amount: string;
    currency: string;
    recipient: string;
    reason: string;
  }>;

  disclosedConflicts: string[];
  evidenceReferences: string[];
};

This is not a production-ready financial schema.

It illustrates a product priority: the explanation is part of the transaction record, not a paragraph generated years later to make the decision sound reasonable.

Recording a rationale does not prove the decision was good.

But a system that cannot preserve who acted, under what authority, and at what cost cannot meaningfully promise accountability.

An audit trail also needs privacy boundaries. “Preserve evidence” must not become an excuse to retain every childhood interaction forever.

Keep what is necessary to explain the management of the assets. Do not turn the account into a permanent behavioral biography.

What would success look like if we refused to optimize for trading?

For this proposal, I would not make daily active use or transaction count the primary success metrics.

I would test measures such as:

  • Can users explain what they own?
  • Can they distinguish a simulated result from a real financial outcome?
  • Can they find the fees without assistance?
  • Can they identify who has authority over the account?
  • Can they challenge an error?
  • Does the eventual transfer of control work?
  • Can they leave without being manipulated into staying?

These metrics are less exciting than a growth chart.

They also tell us more about whether the product serves its stated purpose.

A teenager opening the app less often could be perfectly compatible with success.

The goal is not to make a child think about markets every day.

The goal is to help preserve options for the adult they will become.

Children should own assets. They should not become assets.

There is a boundary this idea must never cross.

We are discussing investments held for children.

We are not discussing shares in children.

No markets in their future earnings. No tradable claims on their potential. No public “talent valuations.” No investment thesis built around pressuring a child to become a particular kind of adult.

The distinction needs to survive the business model.

If the product becomes more profitable when children disclose more, compete more, or make more financial moves, we should examine that incentive before polishing the interface.

Good intentions are not an access-control policy.

They are not a revenue model, either.

A child must be allowed to reject the future we funded

Suppose a child receives an investment connected to a particular vision of progress.

They grow up.

Then they decide they want something else.

They do not want to work in that industry. They disagree with the company. They care more about a local river than a distant technological frontier.

Does the product still consider them a success?

It should.

An investment made for a child should expand their choices, not quietly assign them a mission.

The eventual account holder must be free to ask difficult questions, change direction, and—subject to the applicable rules—exit.

Gratitude should not be a condition of ownership.

The uncomfortable question: do we need an exchange at all?

Perhaps not.

An actual exchange would introduce questions this essay does not solve: who trades, how prices form, what liquidity exists, which assets qualify, and how the market is supervised.

Those are not implementation details to postpone until after launch.

If the objective is long-term ownership, education, and accountability, the better first product might be a protective layer around existing financial infrastructure.

That would make “Childhood Exchange” a provocative name for a design exercise—not necessarily the right company structure.

Before handling real assets, I would prototype three things:

  1. A clearly labeled simulator.
  2. An explanation interface using synthetic account histories.
  3. A transfer-of-control walkthrough.

Then test whether people understand them.

Not whether they click more.

Whether they understand.

The feature that matters most

Picture that eighteenth-birthday screen again.

The balance might be larger than expected. It might be smaller. No responsible interface should rewrite uncertainty as a promise.

But underneath the number is something the system can deliberately provide:

An intelligible record.

Here is what belonged to you.

Here is who managed it.

Here is what they charged.

Here is why they acted.

Here is how to challenge an error.

Here is what you control now.

That would not solve inequality. It would not make investing risk-free. It would not substitute for education, public institutions, or a livable world.

It would establish a narrower, demanding principle:

When we build systems for people who cannot yet fully question us, we should prepare to answer them later.

The best financial app for a child might not be the one that teaches them to behave like a trader.

It might be the one that forces the adults to behave like trustees.

title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.26951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks- MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K-1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

title: The Twenty Minute Review That Keeps My Agent Honest
description:
I do a short review every Friday. Twenty minutes, sometimes less. It is the only maintenance ritual I have kept for more than two months, and it is the reason the setup has not quietly rotted.

What I look at

Five things, in this order:

  1. The refusals. Every task the agent declined or escalated. Not to fix them, just to check whether the reason still holds. Half of them were right last week and wrong now.
  2. Tasks that took more than twice my estimate. Either the estimate was wrong or the task is not automatable yet. Both are worth knowing.
  3. The retries. Any task run more than once this week. The reason for the retry is the bug, not the retry.
  4. One log, read end to end. Not skimmed. One, chosen at random. Skimming ten tells you less than reading one.
  5. Things I approved without reading. If the list is long, my approval gate has become a rubber stamp, and the gate is now decoration.

What I do with the output

Usually two or three lines of change. A pre-flight check gets added, a task file gets a better finish condition, a note gets written to the notes file so the same thing does not happen next month.

Most weeks there is nothing dramatic. That is the point - the review is not for finding incidents, it is for catching drift before it becomes one.

Why twenty minutes and not an hour

An hour-long review becomes a project, and projects get postponed. Twenty minutes fits between other things on a Friday, so it actually happens. The value is in the repetition, not the depth.

The failure mode of an agent setup is not a dramatic break. It is a slow accumulation of exceptions that everyone remembers exists but nobody wrote down, until one day the automation is a fragile museum piece that only its author can operate.

I have run that setup before, in other forms. The review is cheap insurance against building it again.

If you do something similar, I would like to know what you look at that I do not. Mine has stayed the same for two months, which probably means it is missing something.

title: A Hybrid TFT-NBEATS Framework for Robust Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.27155v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate multi-horizon photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for grid stability, energy scheduling, and the efficient operation of PVbatterygrid systems. However, existing models often fail to jointly capture short-term variability and long-term temporal patterns, while lacking unified multi-horizon capability and interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel hybrid deep learning framework that integrates a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and N-BEATS within an attention-based fusion architecture. The proposed model leverages TFT to learn short-term temporal dependencies and dynamic feature importance, while N-BEATS captures long-term trend and seasonal components through interpretable basis decomposition. An adaptive attention mechanism dynamically fuses both branches, enabling balanced multi-scale learning. The framework simultaneously generates forecasts for 30-minute, 2-hour, 6-hour, 12-hour, and 24-hour horizons within a single unified pipeline. The model is evaluated using multi-year real-world datasets from the Desert Knowledge Australia Solar Centre (DKASC). Experimental results demonstrate superior performance over statistical, machine learning, and deep learning baselines. The proposed model achieves RMSE values of 42.35, 46.27, 52.29, and 48.11 across the 20162017, 2023, 2024, and 20252026 datasets, respectively, corresponding to a 3540% reduction compared to the best baseline (TFT). Additionally, MAPE remains below 5% across all datasets, indicating high predictive accuracy and stability. The model also provides interpretability through attention visualization and trendseasonality decomposition, and is deployed on a cloud-based platform for real-time forecasting. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework is robust, interpretable, and suitable for practical renewable energy applications.

title: Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training for Long-Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.26910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.

title: Stop Storing Tracking Numbers as Numbers: a float64 Bug Hiding in Your CSV Pipeline
description:
If any part of your stack reads a shipping CSV, this one is probably already in your data and nobody has noticed. A tracking number is a label, but almost every tool in the chain is happy to treat a long run of digits as a quantity - and quantities get rounded.

The failure, in two shapes 

9214490424550000386431   ->  9.2144904245500004E+21
9400150206217912         ->  9400150206217910

The first is loud. The second is the one that costs you a week: same length, no exponent, no warning - the final digit is now a zero. Every downstream lookup returns "not found" for parcels that are completely fine, and the first instinct is to blame the carrier's API.

Why

IEEE-754 double precision carries about 15-17 significant decimal digits. Look at what common formats need:

Format Length All digits? Survives a float?
USPS IMpb 22 yes no
FedEx Ground 15 yes borderline
DPD parcel number 14 yes yes, but still reformatted
UPS 1Z + 16 18 chars no safe
S10 postal (AA999999999CC) 13 chars no safe

The pattern that matters: the formats that survive are the ones containing letters, because a letter forces the value to stay a string. The all-digit formats are the exposed ones - and that includes the single most common barcode in the world, the 22-digit USPS IMpb.

This is also why the bug feels intermittent. A column of 1Z... numbers round-trips perfectly, someone concludes the pipeline is fine, and then the first USPS batch of the month is silently mangled.

In code

Pandas will do this to you by default:

# wrong - pandas infers int64/float64 and your 22-digit numbers are gone
df = pd.read_csv("shipments.csv")

# right - say it explicitly
df = pd.read_csv("shipments.csv", dtype={"tracking_number": "string"})

# or, when you do not want to name every column
df = pd.read_csv("shipments.csv", dtype=str)

The same rule in the other languages:

  • JS/TS: never Number(tn) or parseInt(tn). A 22-digit value is already past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991, 16 digits), so the damage happens before you can validate it. If you need a numeric type, use BigInt - but you almost never do, because you never do arithmetic on a tracking number.
  • SQL: VARCHAR, not BIGINT. Leading zeros are real and significant in several postal formats, and a numeric column eats them without comment.
  • JSON: quote it. An unquoted 22-digit literal is a double in most parsers.
  • Excel/Sheets exports: format the column as Text before the first paste. Formatting a column that already holds broken values does not recover the digits - that information is gone, not hidden.

Validating a column you inherited

Cheapest checks first:

s = df["tracking_number"].astype("string")

s.str.contains("E+", regex=False).sum()   # loud corruption
s.str.len().value_counts()                # a USPS column should be all 22s
s.str[-1].value_counts(normalize=True)    # an implausible pile of "0" = rounding

That last one is the useful one. If a column has the right lengths but an unreasonable share of values ending in 0, you are looking at rounding, not coincidence.

The validation rule that actually helps

Do not validate tracking numbers with a numeric range or a length-only check. Check the shape: a letter-anchored prefix plus a fixed length is both cheap and specific. ^1Z[0-9A-Z]{16}$ identifies UPS exactly. ^[A-Z]{2}\d{9}[A-Z]{2}$ is the S10 international postal form, and the last two letters are the issuing country - not the destination, which is a different and equally common mix-up.

And if the number survives shape validation but returns nothing, check whether the label was merely created before you conclude anything is lost - "we have the order details but not the parcel" is a legitimate state, not an error.

Written by the team behind 24hTrack, a free package tracker for 3,200+ carriers - paste any tracking number and the carrier is detected automatically, no sign-up. Shape and format notes come from the carrier formats we maintain at package-tracking-guide (CC BY 4.0).

title: ER Diagram vs Database Schema: What’s the Difference?
description:
An ER diagram and a database schema can look like the same thing at first. They are related, but they are used at different moments: first, you plan how the data should connect; then you create the real tables, columns, keys, and rules in the database.

Think of a clinic named HyperClinic. This clinic needs to store patients, doctors, specializations, and appointments.

A quick way to do this is to store everything in one table, called appointments:
appointment_id patient_name patient_phone doctor_name specialization appointment_time
16 Marit Solheim 555-0147 Owen Wilson Cardiology 2026-10-20 10:00

This approach works for one row, but it causes problems when you add another appointment for Marit, change Dr. Wilson's specialization, or have two patients with the same name.

The patient information is repeated. The doctor information is repeated. A typo can lead to inconsistency. And nothing prevents creating an appointment for a doctor who does not exist.

To avoid these problems, the team needs to plan the database before creating tables.

ER Diagram vs Database Schema

The key point of differentiation is not the shape of the boxes and arrows. It is the stage of development.
Stage Key question Objects defined What the diagram shows
Conceptual ER diagram What does the company need to store? Entities and relationships Boxes and lines, no fields
Logical data model How should the data be structured? Attributes, keys, normalized relationships Fields with key icons and relationship lines, no data types
Physical database schema How will PostgreSQL implement it? Tables, columns, data types, constraints, indexes, and DDL statements Fields with data types

A *schema diagram* is a graphic representation of the database schema. Such diagrams are also referred to as physical ER diagrams.

A *database schema* is the actual structure stored in PostgreSQL and comprises objects such as tables, columns, primary and foreign keys, constraints, and indexes.

Thus, this is not a binary choice. A database design is typically developed from an ER diagram through the logical data model to the database schema.

In this article, we will build HyperClinic in the same order: Step 1 is the conceptual ER diagram, Steps 2 to 4 build the logical model, and Step 5 creates the physical PostgreSQL schema.

Start with the Requirements

Nobody will start writing CREATE TABLE before the team figures out the task.

In our case, HyperClinic must be able to:

  • save patient information
  • save doctors and their specializations
  • create appointments
  • show which patient sees which doctor
  • ensure appointments refer to existing patients and doctors

The job names depend on the company. Requirements may be gathered by a business analyst and designed by a database architect, data modeler, backend developer, or DBA. In a small company, one person may do several of these jobs.

What is important is the workflow, not the name.

The team should ask itself such questions as:

  • Is it possible for one patient to have several appointments?
  • Is it possible for one doctor to have many patients?
  • Do all doctors have only one specialization?
  • Is it possible to create an appointment without a doctor?
  • Is it possible to create two appointments with the same doctor for the same time?

These are the business rules that PostgreSQL won't be able to guess.

Step 1: Create the Conceptual ER Diagram

Before deciding on columns, data types, or SQL, first identify what HyperClinic needs to store:

  • Patient
  • Doctor
  • Appointment
  • Specialization

An *entity* is simply something the system needs to store.

This is a *conceptual ER diagram*. It helps the team see the big picture without getting into implementation details. The boxes show the entities. The lines show their relationships. There are no columns, primary keys, foreign keys, or PostgreSQL data types yet.

The relationships are:

  • A patient has many appointments.
  • A doctor has many appointments.
  • An appointment is made by one patient and one doctor.
  • A specialization has many doctors.
  • Each doctor has one specialization.

Step 2: Add Attributes and Primary Keys

This is the point where the model becomes *logical*.

The conceptual diagram tells us that HyperClinic has patients, doctors, appointments, and specializations. The logical model answers the next question: *what information belongs to each one?*

You now add attributes, choose identifiers, and organize the data so the same fact is not stored in several places. You are still designing the structure. You are not choosing PostgreSQL types such as VARCHAR(100) or TIMESTAMP yet.

Think of it like planning a house:

  • the conceptual diagram says the house needs a kitchen, bedrooms, and a bathroom;
  • the logical model decides what belongs in each room;
  • the physical schema gives the builder the exact materials and measurements.

The logical model takes three steps: attributes and primary keys (this step), normalization (Step 3), and foreign keys (Step 4).

Start with the attributes. For each entity, write down what the system needs to know about it:
Entity Attributes
Patient first name, last name, date of birth, phone
Doctor first name, last name, specialization
Specialization name
Appointment patient, doctor, date and time, reason, status

Then give every entity a *primary key*. A primary key is a column, or a set of columns, that uniquely identifies a row.

For instance, patient_id = 1 must identify only one patient. A name cannot be used as a primary key, as patients can have the same name and names change over time.

The same holds for doctors, specializations, and appointments: doctor_id, specialization_id, and appointment_id.

Step 3: Normalize the Logical Model

Normalization means organizing data so each fact is stored in the right place, instead of being repeated in several places.

You do not finish the ER diagram and normalize it later as a separate task. Usually, you draw the entities, test the structure, notice repeated data, and improve the model.

The examples below start from a flat table. The services are only for illustration: the final HyperClinic model does not include them.

First Normal Form: One Value per Field

First normal form, or *1NF*, means that one field should contain one value, not a list.

× Not in 1NF:
appointment_id patient_name doctor_name services appointment_at
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson Consultation, ECG 2026-10-20 10:00

The services field contains two values. This makes the data harder to filter, validate, or update.

✓ In 1NF:
appointment_id patient_name doctor_name service appointment_at
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson Consultation 2026-10-20 10:00
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson ECG 2026-10-20 10:00

Each row now contains one service. However, the appointment, patient, and doctor information is repeated. The next step fixes that.

Second Normal Form: Each Field Depends on the Whole Key

Second normal form, or 2NF, applies when a table uses a combined key.

Here, one appointment can have more than one service. The combination of appointment_id and service identifies one row.

× Not in 2NF:
appointment_id service patient_name doctor_name appointment_at
16 Consultation Marit Solheim Owen Wilson 2026-10-20 10:00
16 ECG Marit Solheim Owen Wilson 2026-10-20 10:00

The patient_name, doctor_name, and appointment_at values depend only on appointment_id. They do not depend on the full combination of appointment_id and service, so they are repeated.

✓ In 2NF:

appointments
appointment_id patient_name doctor_name appointment_at
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson 2026-10-20 10:00

appointment_services
appointment_id service
16 Consultation
16 ECG

Now the appointment information is stored once. The appointment_services table only stores the services linked to that appointment. The patient and doctor names are still text here. Step 4 replaces them with IDs.

Third Normal Form: Do Not Repeat Details That Belong Elsewhere

Third normal form, or 3NF, removes indirect repetition.

× Not in 3NF:
doctor_id first_name last_name specialization_id specialization_name
1 Owen Wilson 1 Cardiology
6 Odile Marchetti 1 Cardiology

The specialization name depends on specialization_id, not on the doctor. Storing it in doctors means it will be repeated for every cardiologist.

✓ In 3NF:

doctors
doctor_id first_name last_name specialization_id
1 Owen Wilson 1
6 Odile Marchetti 1

specializations
specialization_id specialization_name
1 Cardiology

Now Cardiology is stored once. If the clinic changes its name, the team updates one row in specializations, not every doctor.

After normalization, each table holds only its own facts:
Table Example Columns
patients patient_id, first_name, last_name, date_of_birth, phone
doctors doctor_id, first_name, last_name
specializations specialization_id, specialization_name
appointments appointment_id, appointment_at, reason, status

The lines show which tables are related, but the link columns, such as specialization_id in doctors, are not here yet. They come in the next step.

Step 4: Link Related Tables with Foreign Keys

To connect two tables, you add a column to one of them. That column is a foreign key: it stores the ID of a row in the other table. This is how a relationship is made.

An appointment should not store redundant information like a patient's name, phone, and date of birth.

Instead, it stores the ID of the linked patient:

appointment_id: 16
patient_id: 1
doctor_id: 1

The field appointments.patient_id is a foreign key that references patients.patient_id.

The field appointments.doctor_id links to doctors.doctor_id.

The field doctors.specialization_id links to specializations.specialization_id.

A foreign key performs two functions:

  1. It describes the relationship between tables.
  2. It prevents invalid references.

Without a foreign key, you can insert an appointment with patient_id = 9999, even if patient 9999 does not exist.

If there is a foreign key, PostgreSQL rejects this record.

A column named patient_id alone does not create a foreign key. The REFERENCES constraint creates it.

The diagram now shows the foreign key columns, marked with a link icon, and an arrow for each relationship. There are still no data types. Types depend on the database engine, so they come in the physical stage.

Step 5: Define the Physical PostgreSQL Model

The physical model describes the PostgreSQL tables, columns, data types, and rules that you want to create.

In this example, INT is used for IDs (the diagram shows it as INTEGER, which is the same type), VARCHAR for text, DATE for a date, and TIMESTAMP for a date and time.

Create the Database Schema

The physical model is ready. Now you need to create it on the PostgreSQL server.

You can do this in either of two ways:

  1. Run the CREATE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE statements in the SQL Editor.

The following statements are DDL, short for Data Definition Language. DDL is the SQL used to create the database structure.

CREATE SCHEMA clinic;

CREATE TABLE clinic.specializations (
  specialization_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  specialization_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE clinic.doctors (
  doctor_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  specialization_id INT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES clinic.specializations(specialization_id),
  first_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE clinic.patients (
  patient_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  date_of_birth DATE NOT NULL,
  phone VARCHAR(30)
);

CREATE TABLE clinic.appointments (
  appointment_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  patient_id INT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES clinic.patients(patient_id),
  doctor_id INT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES clinic.doctors(doctor_id),
  appointment_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  reason VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  status VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'scheduled',
  CONSTRAINT appointments_status_check
    CHECK (status IN ('scheduled', 'completed', 'cancelled'))
);

This is how you can create it in VisuaLeaf's SQL Editor:

  1. You can also use Materialize instead of running the SQL yourself. Starting with an empty database, VisuaLeaf creates the clinic schema and its tables directly from the physical model.

Materialize can also apply later changes. In this example, the four original clinic tables already exist, so they are marked as up to date while the new lab_results table is created.

Use one method to create the original schema. If you run the same CREATE TABLE statements after the tables already exist, PostgreSQL returns an “already exists” error.

Step 6: View the Created Database Schema

After either option succeeds, open Schema Manager and select the clinic schema.

You can now see the patients, appointments, doctors, and specializations tables on the PostgreSQL server. This is the implemented database schema: it is no longer only a model or a plan.

This schema contains several constraints:

  • NOT NULL requires a value.
  • PRIMARY KEY makes each ID unique.
  • REFERENCES creates foreign-key relationships.
  • UNIQUE prevents duplicate specialization names.
  • DEFAULT 'scheduled' gives new appointments an initial status.
  • CHECK prevents unsupported status values.

For example, PostgreSQL will reject this appointment if patient 9999 does not exist:

INSERT INTO clinic.appointments (
  patient_id,
  doctor_id,
  appointment_at,
  reason
)
VALUES (
  9999,
  3,
  '2026-11-20 10:00',
  'Annual check-up'
);

PostgreSQL returns an error like this:

ERROR:  insert or update on table "appointments" violates foreign key constraint "appointments_patient_id_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (patient_id)=(9999) is not present in table "patients".

This is the difference between drawing a relationship in a diagram and enforcing it in the database.

ER Diagram vs Database Schema: The Difference

The conceptual, logical, and physical models are the steps between the first idea and the finished database.

ER diagram Database schema
Main job Plans what data the system needs and how it connects Stores the real database structure
Includes Entities, attributes, and relationships Tables, columns, data types, keys, constraints, and indexes
In this example The HyperClinic models before the schema is created The clinic schema after the SQL is run or the model is materialized
Where you see it In the diagram designer In PostgreSQL and Schema Manager

An ER diagram helps the team decide what to build. The database schema is the structure PostgreSQL creates from that plan.

The tool used for this demonstration is VisuaLeaf. You can download it for free and follow the same steps: design the model, create the schema, and view the tables and relationships in one place.

title: How Delphi ships 100 times a day with its Python backend on Vercel
description:
Delphi on Vercel

  • 10 engineers with no dedicated infrastructure role

  • Everyone ships code, including product and design

  • 100+ production deploys a day behind feature flags

Delphi builds digital minds. They capture what someone has written, recorded, and taught, so anyone can tap that expertise on demand. Delphi is “a destination where you can find and interact with interesting minds,” says founding engineer Spencer Schoeben.

Nobody has built a digital mind network before, so Delphi figures out what to build by shipping features and watching how people use them. That only works if the product is fast to change. "If we are going to win, we need to have an excellent developer and agentic experience," Spencer says. "Otherwise, we could not adapt to how fast our user’s demands change."

Delphi's frontend had run on Vercel since day one. "The frontend has always been easy," Spencer says, "but the backend was a nightmare." Six months ago, the team rebuilt its Python backend on Vercel as well. Today the whole team ships to production 100+ times a day.

Building a Python backend that's easy to work on

The backend slowed every change

Delphi's backend previously ran on AWS, with ECS, Docker Desktop, and local databases. In the earliest days, the setup worked because the team was small and much of the context lived in people’s heads. As Delphi grew, that made onboarding slower than the team wanted: getting a new engineer to their first deploy took a full day of environment setup. 

Delphi could have fixed that without leaving AWS. But fixing it properly would have meant designing and owning the infrastructure themselves, and the team didn't want to own infrastructure at all. "That is not our current goal as a company," Spencer says. After moving the backend to Vercel, new engineers could get to production much faster, with the same deploy workflow the rest of the team used every day.

Workflows and Queues made the move possible

When Delphi was founded, Vercel Workflows and Vercel Queues didn't exist. Without them, Spencer says, the move would have been much harder, if possible at all.

Delphi's backend depends on long-running work and queued background jobs. Digital minds need durable agents that generate content ahead of time, plus ingestion that turns a person's books and talks into a knowledge graph.

Workflows handles the long-running work and Queues handle the background jobs. Neither requires setup. A developer writes the workflow or the queue handler as a function in the codebase, and Vercel provisions what's needed to run it on deploy.

100+ deploys a day, straight to production

Moving the backend to Vercel let Delphi stop treating backend changes as heavyweight releases and ship them as everyday product work. The team used to deploy to staging, then production. Now it skips the middle step, shipping 100+ times a day behind feature flags and running A/B tests instead of batching changes into a release.

Vercel Agent's anomaly detection watches production at that pace, flagging when something is misbehaving and why. Before, Spencer says, they often would not have known.

Moving fast has helped clear a backlog of small experiments that never used to make the priority list. Many of those experiments test how to turn a visitor into an owner, someone who arrives to talk to a mind and leaves having started their own.

Shipping isn't limited to engineers, either. Delphi's CPO and its growth teams build and deploy dashboards, prototypes, and experiments themselves, which Spencer says wouldn't have happened on the old setup.

Infrastructure built for agents and engineers

Preview deployments are how agents check their work

Delphi's engineers hand problems to cloud agents, with very little development happening locally. The preview deployment is where they first see what the agent built. Vercel preview deployments give every push its own live URL, so anyone can check the result from a phone or a Slack thread without pulling the branch.

When an agent fails, it's usually because it couldn't get at the information it needed. Vercel exposes the data and controls agents need through the SDK, MCP, and CLI, so an agent can read logs, inspect a deployment, or change an environment variable through whichever it's using. For Delphi, agents are now the main users of those tools, so the platform has to be as easy for them as it is for people.

An internal agent on Sandbox for customer success

Delphi's own agents run on Vercel as well. One of them, an internal agent on Vercel Sandbox, simplifies working with the company's codebase. The customer success team uses Slack to ask it about reported issues, find the problem, and hand an engineer a root cause and a proposed fix.

Edge cases used to fall through the cracks. "Before, we either couldn't get to everything, or we had to spend way more time than we had available," Spencer says. "Now we have an agent they can just ask in Slack."

Vercel Sandbox gives the agent an isolated environment with a file system, where it can check out the codebase, run it, and pull in whatever data a question needs. The agent itself is built with eve, Vercel's agent framework. Delphi's first version ran on a hosted agent platform and could only use the integrations that platform offered. In eve, tools are code Delphi writes, so when a question needs one that doesn't exist, the team adds it.

AI Gateway picks the model for each mind

Delphi's chat traffic runs through AI Gateway. Every digital mind is different, and some come out better on one model than another, so Delphi picks the model for each customer and adjusts as its own evals change. When a new model ships, open-source or otherwise, Delphi can route to it the same day.

Gateway also handles failover. Before, Delphi worked directly with a model provider to line up fallback capacity on other clouds, and it was hard. "With AI Gateway, we always know that we're going to get the fallbacks if they exist," Spencer says.

What's next

Delphi's first chapter was training digital minds and letting people chat with them. Now it is building the interface beyond chat. Spencer describes a search page where you bring a question, get perspectives from several minds at once, and have the page adapt to who you are.

That work runs as long-running agents on Workflows, with AI Gateway supplying whichever model each experiment calls for.

About Delphi: Delphi is a platform that turns a person's knowledge, thinking, and voice into a digital mind others can talk to. Anyone can create their own Delphi to make their expertise discoverable and accessible, part of a network of minds people can seek out, learn from, and converse with.

title: Concurrency Programming (11): Shared Memory and Message Passing — How They Work Together
description:
Table of Contents

  • 0. Picking Up Where We Left Off
  • 1. How Are the Two Models Related?
  • 2. How Can They Work Together?
  • 3. Closing Thoughts

0. Picking Up Where We Left Off

The preceding articles examined two concurrency models: Shared Memory and Message Passing.

We can now look at how they relate, and how to choose and combine them for a given concurrency problem.

1. How Are the Two Models Related?

With shared memory, execution units cooperate by accessing the same state. With message passing, they cooperate by sending and receiving messages. These are different ways of organizing work, not mutually exclusive approaches.

As we saw in the previous article, producers and consumers can exchange messages through a queue or channel even though the communication component itself relies on shared state.

Consider Java's ArrayBlockingQueue:

Producer
    |
    v
ArrayBlockingQueue
    |
    +-- Array: stores messages
    |
    +-- ReentrantLock: protects queue state
    |
    +-- Condition: waits when empty or full
    |
    v
Consumer

Multiple producers and consumers may enqueue or dequeue concurrently. ArrayBlockingQueue therefore protects queue operations with a lock and uses conditions to coordinate waiting and wakeups when the queue is empty or full.

Go channels use the runtime's hchan structure to manage buffers and waiting senders and receivers, coordinating access with locks, atomic operations, and goroutine scheduling. CPython's queue.Queue uses a mutex and condition variables to protect its queue state.

Message passing does not eliminate shared state inside the implementation. Instead, channels and queues encapsulate the synchronization required for message handoffs. That is why our investigation of message passing led back to mutexes, atomics, conditions, and memory ordering: they help implement the atomicity, visibility, and ordering guarantees of message handoffs.

2. How Can They Work Together?

Real programs often use both models.

Suppose a task-processing system has multiple producers submitting work, multiple workers processing tasks in parallel, and shared counters tracking successes and failures:

Producer A ──┐
             ├──> Task Queue ──> Worker 1 ──┐
Producer B ──┘                └─> Worker 2 ──┤
                                            |
                                            v
                                     Shared Statistics
                                     (Mutex / Atomic)

Here, message passing handles task handoffs: producers enqueue tasks and workers dequeue and execute them. Shared memory handles statistics: workers update the same counters, using a mutex or atomic operations to synchronize access.

Alternatively, workers can send their results to a dedicated owner:

Producer --> Task Queue --> Workers
                               |
                               v
                          Result Queue
                               |
                               v
                          Stats Owner
                               |
                               v
                           Statistics

Now only the Stats Owner modifies the statistics; workers no longer access that state directly.

Both designs can ensure correctness, but their costs differ. For this example, updating shared state directly is simpler. Having a single owner process updates makes it easier to manage multiple fields and their constraints together, but adds message handoffs and owner lifecycle management, and may create a serial bottleneck.

3. Closing Thoughts

This article examined how shared memory and message passing relate at the implementation level and how they can be combined in practice.

The next article is the final installment. We will look back over the entire concurrency programming series and bring it to a close with a summary of the key ideas.

This article was first published on ThinkerQAQ's personal blog and syndicated here by the author. The original article may be revised over time; please refer to the personal blog for the latest version.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

Read more

title: Node.js Push API Pull Model for 3 Small SaaS Custom Metrics Dashboards
description:
A small SaaS comparing a Prometheus alternative for custom metrics needs more than a Node.js dashboard that says revenue dipped; it must show which pricing rule was active. The operational constraint changes the design: preserve enough context to reconstruct a rollout before optimizing the collection mechanism.

TL;DR: record three decisions for every pricing evaluation: the rule version, the flag variant, and the outcome. Use pull collection when a long-running Node.js service can expose current counters reliably. Use a push API when short-lived jobs or network boundaries make scraping impractical, but treat delivery, retries, and event time as application concerns. The dashboard is the last step. The evidence model comes first.

This is deliberately a small system. It supports shipping a pricing change weekly without turning observability into a second product.

Evidence first.

What must survive the incident?

Imagine a new e-commerce rule behind a flag: customers in one market receive volume pricing when a cart crosses a threshold. Two hours after rollout, completed orders fall. A graph of checkout_total cannot answer the useful questions. Was the new variant evaluated? Which rule revision produced the quote? Did the quote become an order?

Those are separate decisions, and collapsing them into one success counter destroys the join points needed later. I would keep the telemetry vocabulary small:

Signal Required dimensions Reconstruction question
Pricing evaluations rule_version, flag_variant, result Which logic produced the displayed price?
Checkout outcomes flag_variant, outcome Did exposed sessions complete or fail?
Rule errors rule_version, error_class Did evaluation fail before checkout?

Do not attach customer IDs, cart IDs, or raw URLs to metric labels. Metrics aggregate repeated measurements; an unbounded identifier creates an unbounded set of time series. Keep a correlation ID in logs or traces instead, where one event can be inspected without turning every customer into a dashboard dimension.

This separation also prevents a subtle mistake: treating absence as zero. No samples might mean no traffic, a dead process, a failed push, or a broken scrape. The collection path needs its own health signal, and an incident review must distinguish those cases.

The smallest Node.js implementation

The application code should not know whether a collector pulls or an adapter pushes. A tiny interface keeps the pricing path stable while the transport changes. It also makes the behavior testable without starting a monitoring stack.

type Labels = Record<string, string>;

interface CounterSink {
  add(name: string, value: number, labels: Labels): void;
}

type PricingDecision = {
  ruleVersion: string;
  flagVariant: "control" | "volume_v2";
  result: "standard" | "discounted" | "error";
};

export function recordPricingDecision(
  sink: CounterSink,
  decision: PricingDecision,
): void {
  sink.add("pricing_evaluations_total", 1, {
    rule_version: decision.ruleVersion,
    flag_variant: decision.flagVariant,
    result: decision.result,
  });
}

That is enough instrumentation for the business decision. It is intentionally boring. The metric name describes a cumulative count, while labels carry a bounded set of states that can be grouped during an incident.

For a pull model, the in-process adapter accumulates these values and exposes a snapshot on an HTTP endpoint. The collector owns the schedule and records when a target could not be reached. A long-running Node.js web process fits this shape well because its current state is available between scrapes.

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const counts = new Map<string, number>();

const sink: CounterSink = {
  add(name, value, labels) {
    const ordered = Object.entries(labels).sort(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b));
    const key = JSON.stringify([name, ordered]);
    counts.set(key, (counts.get(key) ?? 0) + value);
  },
};

function snapshot(): string {
  return [...counts.entries()]
    .map(([key, value]) => `${key}\t${value}`)
    .join("\n");
}

createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.url !== "/metrics") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }

  response.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" });
  response.end(snapshot());
}).listen(9464);

The serializer above demonstrates the boundary; it is not a claim of compatibility with a particular exposition format. In production, use a maintained metrics library or an OpenTelemetry SDK exporter rather than owning serialization. Outsource the undifferentiated parts. Spend engineering time on the pricing rule and the evidence it needs.

For push, the same sink can buffer points and hand batches to a transport adapter. That adapter must define event timestamps, a timeout, a bounded queue, and retry behavior. Never block checkout indefinitely to report checkout telemetry. If the queue fills, increment a local dropped-measurement counter and surface adapter health through a separate path.

Should a small SaaS push custom metrics or use a pull model?

The choice is less about dashboard taste than failure ownership.

With pull, the collector initiates collection. A failed scrape is visible from outside the application, and the scrape time supplies a consistent observation clock. Process-local counters disappear on restart unless the collector captured them first, so resets must be handled in queries. Brief jobs may start and finish between collection intervals. That limitation rules out a pure pull design for work that routinely begins and ends unseen.

With push, the application or an agent initiates delivery. That works across inbound network restrictions and for jobs whose lifetime is shorter than a scrape interval. It also moves work into the sending path: buffering, backoff, duplicate handling, authentication, and timestamp semantics now need explicit answers. A successful HTTP response only proves that one receiver accepted a request; it does not prove the future dashboard will preserve the point. The trade-off is more application-owned delivery state, so push is not a fit when the team cannot operate a queue or verify duplicates.

For the pricing rollout, I would use pull for the long-running checkout service and push only for a short-lived backfill that recalculates catalog prices. Mixing collection modes is acceptable when the metric schema stays consistent. Forcing every workload through one transport is tidy on a diagram and expensive during an incident.

The practical test is direct. On the Node.js 22 runtime used for the service, kill the collector, restart the process, and run the backfill twice. Then ask whether the resulting timeline lets you distinguish missed collection, a counter reset, duplicated delivery, and a genuine drop in evaluations. Repeat the exercise with one delayed batch and one rejected batch, because a clean happy-path replay hides the exact ambiguity an incident creates: the same empty interval can represent zero pricing evaluations, an unreachable target, discarded buffered points, or a query that filtered the new rule version. Record which layer exposes each failure and how an operator proves recovery. If the answer depends on remembering an undocumented retry interval, the design is not ready.

More panels will not help.

Build the dashboard backward from three queries

Start with the incident questions, not chart types. One view compares pricing evaluations by flag_variant and result. A second compares checkout outcomes by variant. A third shows rule errors by rule_version beside collection health.

Avoid calculating causality from those charts. They support correlation and triage. A variant can coincide with fewer purchases because traffic composition changed, inventory ran out, or payment processing degraded. The metrics narrow the search; logs and traces carry the per-request detail required to inspect a specific path.

OpenTelemetry describes a metrics data model with instruments and aggregations, and it can provide a stable instrumentation boundary even when storage changes. Prometheus uses a pull-oriented model for scraping HTTP metric endpoints. Grafana can visualize data from multiple sources. Hosted systems such as Datadog, New Relic, and Honeycomb differ in ingestion APIs, query models, retention controls, and how metrics relate to traces and logs. Those boundaries matter, but none repairs missing rule context at emission time.

Evaluate any backend with a replay exercise. Feed a fixed set of decisions, include one process restart, and delay one batch. Check whether the three incident questions produce understandable answers. Also inspect export, retention, cardinality controls, and delivery visibility before committing. A polished default dashboard ranks below recoverable evidence.

What I would change at scale

At higher traffic, I would move schema definitions into a shared package, enforce an allowlist for label values, and add automated tests that reject customer-derived dimensions. I would also sample detailed traces while retaining low-cardinality counters for the full rollout window. Metrics answer “how much”; traces and logs explain individual paths.

Multiple service instances introduce another trap. A process-local counter belongs to one process lifetime. Aggregate rates across instances with reset-aware queries rather than pretending each counter is a durable global total. For pushed points, include a stable producer identity only if the backend needs it for deduplication, and keep that identity bounded.

There is a revenue-per-hour line here. Building custom storage, query execution, alert delivery, and access control rarely advances an e-commerce pricing feature. A solo operator should own the event semantics and tests, then choose interchangeable collection and storage components that meet the reconstruction exercise. Ship weekly. Revisit the transport when workload lifetime, network topology, or operational burden actually changes.

The final decision rule is short: choose pull when external collection can observe a persistent service and scrape failures are valuable evidence; choose push when the producer cannot be scraped, after budgeting for delivery state. In both cases, preserve rule version, variant, outcome, and collection health. That is what turns a graph into an incident timeline.

Sources

  • https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/overview/
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/exposition_formats/
  • https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/datasources/
  • https://logback.qos.ch/manual/appenders.html

title: EviDial: When Correct Depression Predictions Lack Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.27541v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Depression dialogue benchmarks commonly assess models by comparing predicted symptom labels with clinical scale scores. However, a prediction may agree with a benchmark label even when the dialogue lacks enough evidence to justify it. We introduce EviDial, a benchmark that distinguishes label agreement from evidence-grounded assessment. EviDial comprises 382 depression dialogues from three sources and 2,744 participant-symptom cells, each classified as having absent, partial, conflicting, or sufficient evidence. Because evidence sufficiency lacks a directly observable gold standard, we derive calibrated evidence references from multiple judgments using generalizability theory, many-facet Rasch measurement, and random-effects latent class analysis. Our audit reveals that 82.8% of participant-symptom cells lack sufficient textual evidence for the corresponding symptom assessment, with substantial variation across sources. Across model families and prompting strategies, 69.2%-96.9% of predictions judged correct by benchmark labels are nonetheless unsupported by sufficient dialogue evidence. Further analyses show that strong agreement among LLM evaluators need not reflect independent evidence judgments, underscoring the need to calibrate automated reference panels. These findings demonstrate that label-based evaluation can overestimate evidence-grounded performance by conflating agreement with clinical labels and support in the observed dialogue. EviDial provides a measurement layer for separating these constructs and auditing LLM-based depression assessment more faithfully.
