title: The Culture Within: Towards Mechanistic Understanding of Cultural Reasoning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.27202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate across culturally diverse settings, yet existing evaluations largely measure cultural behavior at the output level. We introduce CultureLens, a reference-grounded benchmark and mechanistic study of how LLMs use cultural information. CultureLens contains 9,261 scenarios across 75 countries and systematically varies country, value, true-norm, and contradictory-norm evidence. Across Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B, and Qwen-3.5-27B, stating a contradictory norm lowers aligned answers by 32-47 percentage points, even when the model answers correctly from the country alone. Mechanistically, models default to Anglophone norms when no country is given. The failure under a contradictory norm is not one of missing knowledge, as blocking the norm inside the model restores the correct answer in most cases. Models accept a stated norm according to how it is presented and not whether it is true, which leaves them most exposed to errors in retrieved content. Supervised fine-tuning with contradictory-norm examples raises aligned answers under a contradictory norm to 85-93%, including on unseen countries, at a small cost under a true norm.

title: Day 13/90: Traits and default implementations
description:
Day 13/90: Traits and default implementations

90 Day Rust Challenge: Zero to Production

Today I wanted traits and default implementations to feel like a real engineering decision, not a syntax demo. The useful shift was using traits and default implementations to express shared behavior without making the type story fuzzy.

The checks that mattered were behavior shared through traits, type constraints that explain intent, and generic helpers that stay readable at the call site.

The failure mode I was actively trying to avoid was adding generic or trait machinery before the shared behavior is clear. I wanted traits and default implementations to feel like something I could explain at a whiteboard or in a code review, not just something I recognized from docs.

That is the bar I want from this track: code that stays readable when requirements move, not just code that compiles today.

title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
description:
arXiv:2610.27140v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.

title: FocusOVD: Geometric and Contextual Feature Refinement for Open-Vocabulary Small-Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27479v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to detect both seen and unseen categories by leveraging the semantic knowledge of vision-language models. However, existing methods often struggle with small objects due to insufficient preservation of high-resolution details, ineffective information aggregation across feature levels, and limited region-level discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose FocusOVD, an open-vocabulary object detector that enhances small-object representations without modifying the frozen VLM backbone. FocusOVD introduces three complementary components: a Reweighted Cross-scale Feature Fusion module, which learns normalized level-wise weights to adaptively balance shallow appearance details and deep semantic cues during feature pyramid aggregation; a Residual Pinwheel-shaped Gated Convolution module, which strengthens local geometric responses in high-resolution features; and a Residual Convolutional Gated Linear Unit module, which suppresses background-dominated activations and enhances RoI discriminability before prediction. Extensive experiments on COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD demonstrate the effectiveness of FocusOVD. On COCO-OVD, FocusOVD achieves a novel-category AP of 36.3%, outperforming CORA, UniDetector, and SAMP by 1.3%, 1.1%, and 1.5%, respectively; on LVIS-OVD, it achieves an overall AP of 33.7%, surpassing the strongest competing method by 0.6%. These results demonstrate the strong generalization ability of FocusOVD for open-vocabulary small-object detection.

title: Robustness of Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When given an image and a text prompt, vision-language models (VLMs) can produce seemingly sophisticated text responses. However, they are also prone to hallucinate objects in their output, which can have detrimental consequences in safety-critical applications. To detect these hallucinations, certain methods interestingly leverage internal signals from the VLM as it generates the text response; potentially, these methods use the same signals that led to a hallucination to detect it. We conduct an in-depth analysis to understand the robustness of these detection methods. First, we show that a naive baseline of a generated word's token position in the VLM text response achieves competitive performance. Further, we reveal how some detection methods rely on token position and use this heuristic as a shortcut. Second, we explore detection methods' sensitivity to language and vision modalities. Our experiments suggest that strong detection performance is often driven by detecting language-based hallucinations, and when methods rely on token position, they tend to be less visually grounded and exhibit reduced robustness when hallucinations occur earlier in a text response. Lastly, we demonstrate that different detection methods can carry complementary signals; when ensembling methods together, adding weaker methods to an ensemble of higher performing ones still offers performance improvements. Altogether, while there may be useful internal VLM signals to detect hallucinations, our investigation reveals important limitations of the current methods that try to leverage them.

title: Give your coding assistant a design brief, not just a screenshot
description:
A screenshot can show a coding assistant the shape of a design. A short brief with actual colors, typography and spacing gives it values it can work with. You can collect those values with browser DevTools; a CSS inspection extension can reduce some of the clicking.

Disclosure: I'm working on Stylegrab, the extension used in the accompanying demo. The workflow below also works manually.

Editorial disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance. The examples and product demo use our own sample page; the extension does not call an AI model.

Choose the part of the reference that matters

Start with a page you own or have permission to reuse. Pick one component and a small set of visual rules: a page background, text and accent colors, body and heading type, common spacing and corner radii. Keep your own product's content and identity.

Read rendered values as well as source rules

The declaration with the highest selector specificity doesn't always win. Cascade layers, importance and other parts of the cascade come first. In DevTools, use the Computed panel to check the final value before copying it. For a tool, this is a useful regression test:

@layer base, overrides;
@layer base { #example { color: red; } }
@layer overrides { .example { color: blue; } }

For <div id="example" class="example">, the normal declaration in the later layer wins: blue. A copier that sorts only by selector specificity will give you the wrong starting point.

Write a compact brief 

Use these reference values for our settings panel:
Background #0E1016; surface #171B24.
Text #E7E9EE; secondary text #A6ACBA; accent #7C6CFF.
Body: system sans-serif, 16px, line-height 1.5.
Heading: 28px, weight 700.
Spacing: 8px / 16px / 24px. Cards: 12px radius.
Keep our own copy and product identity.
Verify contrast and keyboard focus.
Check the result at 390px and 1280px widths.

These are illustrative values. Replace them with the values you actually need, and compare them with your project's existing design tokens.

Export a component as a starting point

A static HTML/CSS export can help with a button or card. It doesn't bring along the application's state, JavaScript interactions or all responsive rules. Check asymmetric borders and radii too: four different corners cannot be represented by one uniform rounded class.

Verify in the destination page

Check the narrow layout, focus and hover states, text contrast, and the influence of your own theme. With Tailwind, make sure the generated classes are included in your build and that your theme hasn't changed the meaning of a named utility.

The Stylegrab guide includes the workflow and demo. Its free inspection tools and Pro trials are being prepared for the Chrome Web Store release; the page shows the current installation and payment availability.

title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability
description:
arXiv:2610.26964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with classical planning, but benchmarks rarely distinguish structural difficulty from the difficulty of interpreting symbolic vocabulary. We examine seven STRIPS domains with BFS-optimal plan lengths. For predicting structural difficulty without solving an instance, the zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic $h_{\mathrm{add}}$ outperforms learned alternatives on held-out domains (mean Spearman $|\rho|=0.931$), including ridge regression ($0.707$), object count ($0.657$), and the episodic retrieval architecture ARC ($0.400$). ARC also fails to outperform a linear model using the same features. To isolate semantic effects, we progressively rename predicates while preserving states, transitions, and optimal plans. Valid LLM planning success drops from $67.5\%$ to $40.0\%$ between $0\%$ and $100\%$ renaming, while refusals remain at $0\%$. An LLM supplied with ARC's conditioning information predicts difficulty in context better than trained ARC (mean $|\rho|=0.826$). Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner depends more on calibration to the target LLM's outcomes than on the structural score selected. Thus, established symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty well; improving hybrid planning requires modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than developing more structural predictors.

title: Compline: The Radical Laziness of Sleep — Building an Offline Gothic Sanctuary with Gemma 2, a Real-Time 3D Astrolabe, and Vinyl Crackle
description:
This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: Slow and Steady. 🦥

I'm Arnav, from Bengaluru. For Week 1's "Touch Grass" challenge, I built WildTrail to get people outdoors. For Week 2's "Side Hustle", I built GhostLedger for sovereign freelancer tax intelligence.

For Week 3, the prompt honors International Sloth Day:

"Build something with open-weight models or open-source AI that rewards laziness: a tool for relaxation, an automation for a task you dread, or anything that makes life easier."

One of the challenge's suggested sparks caught my eye immediately:

"A wind-down companion that generates a calming bedtime story or ambient soundscape, running entirely offline."

So I decided to lean fully into radical laziness and built Compline: a candlelit gothic wind-down companion that transforms your nightstand into an ancient, tranquil monastic scriptorium.

  • 🌌 Live Web App: https://complineapp.vercel.app
  • 💻 Open-Source Repository (MIT): https://github.com/XiaoArnav/complineapp

🦥 The Lazy Payoff

Falling asleep in the modern world is an exhausting, high-friction chore:

  1. Decision fatigue: You scroll endless Netflix menus, podcast libraries, or algorithmic YouTube feeds just trying to pick something relaxing.
  2. Blue light bombardment: Bright modern interfaces, push notifications, and recommendation carousels stimulate your brain when you should be slowing down.
  3. SaaS extortion: Sleep apps want $14.99/month, demand account signups, gate basic rainfall audio behind paywalls, and send your bedroom telemetry to cloud servers.

Sloths have it figured out: move at your own pace, conserve your energy, and let the universe come to you.

With Compline, going to sleep requires zero cognitive effort:

  • You open the app in pitch darkness. Tap once. A match strikes, a candle flame flickers to life, and warm amber light floods the sanctuary.
  • The Abbey Phonograph drops its physical needle onto a spinning vinyl platter, filling your room with authentic analog crackle and choral vespers.
  • Google's open-weight Gemma 2 running locally (or our built-in offline hypnagogic generator) streams an unhurried medieval tale word-by-word with illuminated drop-caps and drying golden ink.
  • A 3D celestial astrolabe queries your device's geolocation to orient the 89 classical constellations and 7 wandering planets to match the exact night sky directly above your roof.
  • You don't search. You don't swipe. You don't configure. You just close your eyes.

🏛️ What I Built: The Gothic Nightstand Experience 

flowchart TD
    subgraph Client ["Gothic Nightstand Sanctuary (Zero Dependencies)"]
        Candle["🕯️ Cinematic Candle Ritual (Match-Strike / Blackout)"]
        Astrolabe["🧭 3D Celestial Astrolabe (Real Sky LST Alignment)"]
        Phono["📻 Abbey Phonograph (The Needle & The Groove)"]
        Scribe["📜 Scriptorium Tome (Illuminated Ink Stream)"]
        Tarot["⚙️ Wheel of Fate & Gothic Slumber Tarot"]
        Grimoire["📖 Scriptorium Grimoire (Local Bookmark Storage)"]
    end

    subgraph AudioEngine ["Web Audio Procedural Engine"]
        Needle["📍 Needle Drop & Arm Physics"]
        Crackle["🪵 Vintage Surface Crackle (Pink Noise + Lowpass)"]
        Tracks["💿 Opus I: Nocturne / Opus II: Vespers"]
    end

    subgraph AI ["Open-Source AI & Hypnagogic Core"]
        Gemma["🧠 Google Gemma 2 (Local Ollama gemma2:2b / 9b)"]
        Offline["🕯️ Offline Hypnagogic Decrescendo Generator"]
    end

    Candle --> Astrolabe
    Phono --> AudioEngine
    Scribe --> AI

1. 🌌 3D Celestial Astrolabe & "Tonight's Real Sky" Alignment

The nightstand sky isn't a generic looping starry wallpaper. It is an interactive 3D celestial sphere rendering 89 classical constellations (Ursa Major, Cygnus, Orion, Cassiopeia, Lyra, Taurus...), armillary coordinate rings, and the 7 classical wandering planets.

Tapping the dedicated [🌌 Tonight's Real Sky] header button queries your browser's Geolocation API, calculates the exact Greenwich Sidereal Time (GST) and Local Sidereal Time (LST) for your longitude, and rotates the entire celestial sphere so that the stars above your bed match what is overhead in reality.

2. 📻 The Abbey Phonograph (The Needle & The Groove)

A tactile analog player built entirely on the native Web Audio API:

  • Physical Needle Drops: Interactive tone-arm mechanics with authentic physical needle-drop thuds and lift-off crackles.
  • Vintage Surface Noise: A procedural audio synthesis pipeline (pink noise passed through highpass and biquad filters) that recreates warm vinyl record crackle.
  • The Sacred Repertoire: Integrated with atmospheric nocturnal arrangements:
    • Opus I: Abbey Nocturne — Solitary nocturnal piano & cello.
    • Opus II: Gothic Vespers — Sanctuary bells & ethereal Gregorian choral harmonies.

3. 📜 Scriptorium Story Generator & Hypnagogic Decrescendo

Bedtime stories should never have cliffhangers, sudden shocks, or escalating conflict. Compline connects to local Gemma 2 (via Ollama at http://localhost:11434) using structured relaxation prompts designed around hypnagogic decrescendo:

  • Focuses entirely on rich, sensory descriptions (moss-covered stone arches, distant rainfall, flickering beeswax, cedar incense).
  • Streams word-by-word with animated glowing quill cursors, illuminated rubricated drop-caps, and a simulated wet ink drying effect.
  • If Ollama is offline or you're in airplane mode, a procedural Markovian offline scriptorium generates endless non-repeating bedtime tales without needing any internet connection.

4. ⚙️ Wheel of Fate & Gothic Slumber Tarot

An ornate brass-and-stained-glass mechanical wheel with procedural ratchet audio. Giving it a gentle spin draws from an 8-card Gothic Slumber Tarot deck (The Hermit of the Bell Tower, The Alchemist's Crucible, The Scribe of Midnight...) to seed the night's meditation.

5. 📖 Scriptorium Grimoire

Sleepers can bookmark chapters directly to their personal Grimoire, stored privately in the browser's local storage with zero cloud accounts.

🧠 Why Open Innovation & Gemma 2 Matter Here

In the DEV community discussion on running local LLMs, developer Kennedy Raju noted that side projects rarely need an external API key when open-weight models have gotten this good. And as highlighted in recent local AI benchmarks, running smaller models locally achieves real-time streaming speeds with zero network overhead.

Compline only works as a true sleep companion because of open-weight models:

  1. Sacred Bedroom Privacy: Bedtime thoughts, sleep schedules, and relaxation habits are deeply intimate. With Gemma 2 running locally, no prompts, reading history, or timestamps ever leave your room.
  2. Airplane Mode Safe: You can put your laptop or phone in full Airplane Mode to avoid late-night notifications, and Compline continues to write new stories, play vinyl audio, and chart the cosmos.
  3. Zero Marginal Cost: Cloud AI APIs charge per token. A bedtime app running streaming models all night on proprietary cloud APIs would bleed developer money or force obnoxious $15/month subscriptions onto tired users. Gemma 2 is 100% free to run.

🛠️ What Went Wrong (The Engineering Hurdles)

Just like my previous challenge submissions, I made a commitment to test every detail and inspect real network and runtime behavior. That uncovered three tricky technical challenges:

1. The Vercel Edge Node Cache Ghost Trap

After deploying a critical UI fix, I visited the live Vercel URL and noticed the changes weren't appearing. Opening terminal and inspecting HTTP response headers with curl -sI https://complineapp.vercel.app/ revealed the culprit:

HTTP/2 200 
age: 558
cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
x-vercel-cache: HIT

Even with max-age=0, Vercel edge nodes (like bom1 in India) cache static assets at the CDN layer unless explicitly told otherwise. The fix was updating vercel.json to enforce edge invalidation across all routes:

{
  \"headers\": [
    {\n      \"source\": \"/(.*)\",\n      \"headers\": [\n        {\n          \"key\": \"Cache-Control\",\n          \"value\": \"no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, max-age=0, s-maxage=0\"\n        }\n      ]\n    }\n  ]\n}

Setting s-maxage=0 forced edge cache misses (age: 0, x-vercel-cache: MISS) and instant propagation on every new commit!

2. The Celestial Sidereal Time Math

Translating GPS coordinates into an accurate 3D celestial sphere required real celestial mechanics. Standard clock time doesn't match star time because the Earth rotates once relative to the stars in 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds (one sidereal day).

To compute the celestial rotation angle, I implemented Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time (GMST) and Local Sidereal Time (LST):

// Calculate Julian Date from UTC
const jd = 2440587.5 + (date.getTime() / 86400000);
const d = jd - 2451545.0; // Days from J2000.0

// Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time in degrees
let gmst = (280.46061837 + 360.98564736629 * d) % 360;
if (gmst < 0) gmst += 360;

// Local Sidereal Time
let lst = (gmst + longitude) % 360;
if (lst < 0) lst += 360;

// Rotate the celestial sphere canvas
const lstHours = lst / 15;
stellarSky.rotationAngle = -(lstHours / 24) * Math.PI * 2;

Now, when you look at Cygnus or Ursa Major in Compline, they are in the exact same orientation as the real night sky outside your window.

3. Killing the Over-Engineered Feature (The Rose Window Prism)

During development, I got excited and spent hours building a volumetric stained-glass god-ray lighting engine (\"Rose Window Prism\"). It rendered animated caustic light shafts and chromatic dust motes across the screen.

When I actually tested it at bedtime, it felt completely wrong:

  • It was visually busy and distracted from the calm scriptorium text.
  • It caused unnecessary GPU strain on mobile devices.
  • It violated the fundamental sloth principle of the challenge: simplicity, calm, and conservation of energy.

So I ruthlessly deleted all 400+ lines of it. Recognizing when to delete code is just as important as knowing what to write. Stripping away the excess left the sanctuary feeling peaceful, quiet, and effortless.

🔍 Behind the Scenes: The Full Agent Session

To give the Hacktoberfest judges a transparent look into how Compline was planned, built, tested, and polished, here is the complete recorded agent session:

Compline: Building an Offline Gothic Sleep Sanctuary with Gemma 2 & 3D Astrolabe
You

Let us build Compline: a classical gothic wind-down sanctuary for Hacktoberfest Week 3. It needs to reward radical laziness with offline sleep induction, local Gemma 2 storytelling, ambient phonograph acoustics, and an interactive 3D astrolabe.

Agent

Architecture designed and implemented:
- Candle Awakening Ritual with match strike illumination and tap to blackout mode
- Abbey Phonograph with physical needle drops, vintage vinyl crackle, and Gregorian choral vespers
- Scriptorium Story Generator powered by local Gemma 2 via Ollama or built in offline hypnagogic generator
- 3D Celestial Astrolabe with 89 classical constellations and 7 wandering planets
- Wheel of Fate with 8 card Gothic Slumber Tarot deck
- Local Grimoire with private bookmarking

You

Can we align the 3D astrolabe to tonight real sky overhead using geolocation?

Agent

Implemented Tonight Real Sky celestial alignment:
- Obtains observer latitude and longitude via browser Geolocation API
- Computes Julian Date from UTC timestamp
- Calculates Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time and Local Sidereal Time
- Rotates the 3D celestial sphere coordinate system to match the exact stars visible overhead

You

Make the astrolabe simple to use and aesthetic.

Agent

Redesigned the astrolabe into a compact Gothic Reliquary:
- Dedicated Tonights Real Sky alignment header button
- Compact 2x2 layer toggle grid for Constellations, Planets, Coordinate Rings, and Deep Sky figures
- Zodiac tokens for quick navigation
- Constellation search selector

You

Investigate why the deployed Vercel site is serving cached HTML and fix it.

Agent

Diagnosed Vercel edge CDN caching behavior. Configured s-maxage=0, max-age=0, must-revalidate in vercel.json across all routes to guarantee instant edge cache invalidation on new commits.

You

Remove the rose window prism feature, it distracts from the calm experience.

Agent

Removed the volumetric lighting shader, deleted prism scripts and canvas elements, and restored the clean tranquil monastic scriptorium. Committed and verified deployment.

You

Update the README and remove unnecessary clutter.

Agent

Streamlined README from 109 lines to 55 lines, added direct live demo badge, and focused on core sleep sanctuary features and offline privacy.

You

Write the post for DEV Week 3 challenge and show me the post.

Agent

Authored and staged the official DEV submission post for Week 3 Slow and Steady, claiming the Featured Best Use of Gemma category, and staged as an unpublished draft on DEV.

14 of 14 messages
  • 🔗 Interactive Session on DEV: Compline: Building an Offline Gothic Sleep Sanctuary with Gemma 2 & 3D Astrolabe

🏆 Prize Categories Entered

  • Overall Winner: A complete, beautifully crafted wind-down sanctuary engineered specifically for radical laziness, low cognitive load, and effortless sleep.
  • Featured Category: Best Use of Gemma ($200): Leverages Google's Gemma 2 open-weight model via Ollama for private, low-tension bedtime storytelling with zero cloud telemetry.

🚀 Try Compline

  • 🌌 Live Web Application: https://complineapp.vercel.app
  • 💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/XiaoArnav/complineapp

To run it locally with zero external dependencies (pure Python 3 standard library):

git clone https://github.com/XiaoArnav/complineapp.git
cd complineapp
python3 app/server.py

Then visit http://localhost:7777.

Connect local Gemma 2 anytime with ollama run gemma2:2b.

May your nights be restful and peaceful. Channel your inner sloth. 🦥✨

title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

title: What Magento hosting on AWS costs a month
description:
Running a small Magento shop on AWS in Frankfurt costs from about USD 204 to about USD 804 a month, according to AWS price lists as of 12 October 2026. Where you land depends on how many services you hand to AWS and whether you pay for a standby in a second zone. On shared hosting, Magento 2.4 usually won't even install, because it needs a search engine that cheap plans don't include.

I assumed a shop with up to about 10,000 products and about 30 people browsing at once, with most pages served from the Varnish cache, so 4 vCPU and 16 GB of RAM in total are enough.

Magento 2.4 needs a separate search engine

Since Magento 2.4, Adobe requires Elasticsearch or OpenSearch in every installation. For the latest release, 2.4.9, the system requirements table lists only OpenSearch 3.

Hostinger's help centre says Elasticsearch isn't available on its web and cloud plans, so Magento 2 needs a VPS. A Hostinger VPS for Magento with 4 vCPU and 16 GB of RAM costs about USD 29 a month after the promotional period, according to its price list on 14 October 2026.

On a VPS you administer the system, the database and OpenSearch yourself, and keep a backup off the server. My post on Hetzner or AWS for a small company covers how much work that is.

Three versions of the same shop on AWS

I priced all three at on-demand rates before VAT, in Frankfurt, with 200 GB of data transfer out to the internet a month.

  • A single EC2 server with 4 vCPU and 16 GB of RAM runs the whole shop, database and search engine included, for about USD 204. In practice it is a VPS inside AWS, so when that machine goes down, the shop stops.
  • For about USD 428, the application gets a smaller server, and the database, cache and search engine move to managed AWS services. All of it runs in one Availability Zone, one of three separate groups of data centres in the Frankfurt region, so there is still nothing to fail over to.
  • The version with standby has two application servers behind a load balancer, a database with a standby copy in a second zone, two cache nodes, and images in S3 served through a CDN. It costs about USD 804. Only search stays on one node in one zone, so if it fails, category pages and search stop.

The chart for this part is in the original post.
The calculator shows a similar setup under the “Web application, shop or CMS” profile, next to Hetzner and OVH prices.

A second zone nearly doubles the bill

The database adds the most. RDS Multi-AZ keeps a standby instance in another zone and fails the database over to it when the primary stops working. AWS charges twice the single-zone rate for both the instance and its storage.

The Magento shop I moved to AWS runs on similar services: RDS MySQL, OpenSearch, Redis, Varnish and a CDN. Its hosting bill is higher than before the move, because the shop had to hold up through campaign traffic peaks and recover quickly from a failure.

What it means for a small shop

If the shop sells evenly all year and can live with a few hours of downtime after a server failure, a VPS or a Magento hosting plan with OpenSearch is enough.

For a shop that makes its money in campaigns and can't go down while they run, I recommend the third version. In the second version you pay for managed services, yet when its only application server or database fails, the shop goes offline.

Before you choose the third version, open the sales report in the Magento admin and work out the revenue per hour on the best day of your last campaign. Multiply it by the hours a server failure would keep the shop down. Compare that with what the third version would cost you extra over a year: the gap between about USD 804 and your current monthly hosting bill, times twelve. If one outage costs you more, the standby pays for itself even with one failure a year.

Originally published on codelevel.pl. Prices are net, for businesses. AWS, Hetzner and OVH are trademarks of their owners; CODELEVEL is not a partner, reseller or representative of any of them.

title: Make your v0 or Cursor app stop looking AI-built in 10 minutes
description:
If you've built a landing page with v0, Cursor, Lovable or Bolt, you've probably had this moment: you put it next to someone else's and it's the same page. Purple-to-blue gradient, centred headline, one font, three feature cards with an icon in a circle, a pricing table, and a "Get started" button that does nothing you can see.

Nothing on that page is broken. It's the average of every landing page the model has seen, and that's what you get when you don't ask for anything specific. Visitors recognise it within seconds, though, and some of them decide the product behind it got the same amount of thought.

Here are the five tells I look for and a fix for each. Every fix is a couple of minutes in a Next.js App Router project with Tailwind CSS v4. I put the result in a free starter (MIT) so you can copy single pieces or start from the whole thing:

  • Repo: https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter
  • Live demo: https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-next-starter/

The five tells

  1. A gradient where a brand colour should be.
  2. One font at one weight for everything.
  3. Everything centred.
  4. An illustration where the product should be.
  5. Buttons that don't respond.

0. Get a page to work on (1 minute)

To try the fixes on a clean page:

npx create-next-app@latest my-app -e https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter
cd my-app
npm run dev

Or open your own project. The steps assume Next.js 15 (App Router) and Tailwind v4, the setup where globals.css starts with @import "tailwindcss".

1. Swap the gradient for three colours (2 minutes)

Delete the bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-500 to-blue-500 (or whatever your hero has). In Tailwind v4 the palette lives in CSS, and every variable in @theme becomes a utility class:

/* app/globals.css */
@theme {
  --color-ink: #0a0a0d;
  --color-paper: #f3f1ea;
  --color-volt: #c6ff3d;
}

Now bg-ink, text-paper and bg-volt exist. Ink is the page, paper is the text (swap them for a light theme), and the accent goes on one or two things per screen: the main button, a status dot. Once the accent is on every element it does the gradient's job again.

2. Two fonts with some character (1 minute)

Pick a display face for headings and UI and a mono for numbers and small labels. The starter uses Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono. The font @import has to be the first line of the file:

@import url("https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=JetBrains+Mono:wght@400;500;600;700&family=Space+Grotesk:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap");
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --font-sans: "Space Grotesk", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-mono: "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, monospace;
}

One trap I hit while testing this: a project set up with shadcn init (v0 projects use shadcn) already has an @theme inline block with --font-sans: var(--font-sans). That block wins, the variable points at itself, and the page falls back to Times New Roman. Edit the --font-sans and --font-mono lines inside that existing block instead of adding new ones. Also delete any font-family: Arial left on body by the default template, and put font-sans on <body>.

Then use contrast in size and weight: a bold 7xl headline with tracking-tight leading-[1.02], body text at text-lg and 60% opacity, mono at text-xs for the small stuff.

3. Move the hero off centre (1 minute)

Centred layouts are the default because they never look broken. A left-aligned hero with a width limit on the headline looks like someone placed it:

<section className="mx-auto max-w-6xl px-5 pt-28 pb-16">
  <h1 className="max-w-3xl text-5xl leading-[1.02] font-bold tracking-tight sm:text-7xl">
    Know your servers are down before your users do.
  </h1>
  <p className="mt-6 max-w-xl text-lg text-white/60">
    Uptime, latency and deploys on one screen. Set up in two minutes, no agent to install.
  </p>
</section>

Write the headline as one sentence about the visitor's problem. "Supercharge your workflow" is the copy version of the purple gradient.

4. Show the product (2 minutes)

Generated heroes get a blob or a 3D shape because the model has never seen your app. You have. Screenshot your best screen at 2x and put it in a plain browser frame:

import Image from 'next/image';
import shot from '@/assets/dashboard.webp';

<div className="mt-16 overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-white/10 bg-ink">
  <div className="flex items-center gap-1.5 border-b border-white/10 px-4 py-3">
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
  </div>
  <Image src={shot} alt="The dashboard" priority sizes="(max-width: 1200px) 100vw, 1152px" />
</div>

The static import gives next/image the width and height, so nothing shifts when it loads, and it keeps working if you deploy under a sub-path. priority is there because it's the biggest thing above the fold.

No app to screenshot yet? The starter has a /dashboard route you can use as a placeholder. Swap in your real screen before you launch.

5. Make every button respond (3 minutes)

People feel this one without being able to name it. Click "Start free" on most generated pages and nothing visible happens. A loading state that turns into a confirmation tells the visitor their click did something.

I use the free Toast Stack component for this. It installs from a registry URL with the shadcn CLI, so the source lands in your project and you can edit it:

npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/toast-stack.json

Mount the toaster once in app/layout.tsx:

import { Toaster } from '@/components/toast-stack/ToastStack';

// inside <body>
{children}
<Toaster />

Then wrap your signup call:

'use client';
import { toast } from '@/components/toast-stack/ToastStack';

const start = () => {
  toast.promise(createWorkspace(), {
    loading: { title: 'Creating your workspace…' },
    success: (name) => ({ title: 'Workspace ready', description: `${name} is live. The first check runs in 30 s.` }),
    error: () => ({ title: 'That didn’t work', description: 'Try again in a minute.' }),
  });
};

The spinner stays up for at least 600 ms so a fast request doesn't flash, then turns into a check. Hover the stack and the toasts fan out.

Pricing gets the same treatment. The Pricing Switch component replaces a static three-column table with a monthly/yearly switch whose prices roll like an odometer:

npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/pricing-switch.json

<PricingSwitch
  plans={plans}
  header={<h2>Pay for monitors, not seats.</h2>}
  onSelect={(plan, yearly) => startCheckout(plan.id, yearly ? 'year' : 'month')}
/>

Its digits use Saira Condensed, so add &family=Saira+Condensed:wght@700;800 to the font import from step 2.

Bonus: motion that respects people (30 seconds)

If you add scroll-in animations, put them behind prefers-reduced-motion. In the starter the sections fade up with a CSS scroll timeline and no JavaScript:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .reveal {
    animation: reveal-up linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 28%;
  }
}
@keyframes reveal-up {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(28px); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}

Add className="reveal" to a section. The components in the starter check the same setting on their own.

If you'd rather hand it to Cursor

This prompt covers steps 1 to 4. I haven't compared how each tool handles it, so read the diff before you accept it:

Restyle the landing page in this Next.js App Router + Tailwind v4 project.
1. Remove every gradient background. In globals.css add --color-ink #0a0a0d, --color-paper #f3f1ea and --color-volt #c6ff3d to @theme. Use volt only on the primary button and one status dot.
2. Fonts: Space Grotesk for headings and UI, JetBrains Mono for numbers and small labels. Add a Google Fonts @import as the first line of globals.css. If an @theme inline block already defines --font-sans or --font-mono, change those lines instead of adding new ones. Put font-sans on <body>.
3. Left-align the hero: one-sentence headline (max-w-3xl, text-5xl sm:text-7xl, tracking-tight), one supporting line (max-w-xl).
4. Replace the hero illustration with next/image of src/assets/screenshot.webp (static import) inside a simple browser frame.
Don't change any other copy. Don't add dependencies.

What's in the starter

  • /: hero with a product shot, a log upload section with progress and retry (Upload Dropzone), pricing (Pricing Switch), toasts on every action (Toast Stack), and a light/dark switch (Day/Night Toggle).
  • /dashboard: Orbit, an observability dashboard with simulated live data.
  • Next.js 15.5, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion 11. next build passes and every page is static, so it deploys anywhere. The README has a one-click Vercel button.

About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign, so the components in this post are mine. Everything here is free and MIT: the starter and the free components and dashboards in qodesign-free. The paid components are $3 each or $29 for all of them, each with a React + Tailwind version and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools, at qodesign.dev.

If you run the five fixes on your own app, I'd like to see the before and after.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code is copied from the starter repo, and every command above was run in a fresh Next.js 15 app (one plain, one set up with shadcn init) with next build passing before publishing.

title: Same SQL, Fast for One Value, Slow for Another
description:
The order-history screen is fast for every customer except one. Or it's fast all morning and crawls all afternoon. Or it was fine for months and became slow the night after a restart, with nobody deploying anything. You pull the statement and run it yourself with the problem value, and it comes back instantly. The SQL is identical. The data hasn't changed. The plan in the execution history is the same plan it always uses.

That last sentence is the clue. The statement uses a bind variable, which is the right thing to do, and the cursor for it holds one plan. That plan was chosen for whichever value happened to arrive first. On a column where values are wildly unevenly distributed, that's a plan built for one kind of caller and handed to every other. This post is how that happens, why Oracle's safety net for it, adaptive cursor sharing, doesn't always catch it, how to see it in the cursor cache, and how to fix it, with a lab that reproduces it on demand.

Bind peeking: the first caller picks the plan

When a statement with a bind variable is hard-parsed, the optimizer peeks at the actual bind value and costs the plan as if that value were a literal. That's usually good: a plan built for a real value beats a plan built for an average. The catch is what happens next. The finished cursor goes into the shared pool and every later execution reuses it, whatever value it binds. The plan is decided once, by the first caller.

On a column with evenly spread values, that doesn't matter: one value costs about the same as another. It matters on a skewed column, where a few values are rare and one is everywhere: a status code where 99.9% of rows are CLOSED, a country column dominated by one country, a flag that's almost always N. If the column has a histogram, the optimizer knows about the skew and builds very different plans for the rare value and the common one. Peeking means it builds one of them, and everyone gets that one.

The classic shape is a join. For a rare value, a few hundred driving rows, the best plan is nested loops: for each order, look up its customer by primary key. For the common value, hundreds of thousands of rows, the best plan is a hash join: read both tables once and match them in memory. Nested loops for the common value means one index probe per row, hundreds of thousands of times.

A bind-variable statement is optimized once, for the first value it sees, and the cursor is reused for every value after. On a skewed column with a histogram, a rare first value produces a nested-loops plan that is right for a few rows; the common value then inherits it and pays for one index probe per row. Adaptive cursor sharing can split the cursor into one plan per kind of value, but only once it has seen executions that differ enough; until then every caller gets the first caller's plan.

Adaptive cursor sharing: the safety net, with holes

Oracle has known about this since 11g, and adaptive cursor sharing (ACS) is its answer. A cursor that peeked a bind on a column with a histogram is marked bind-sensitive. Oracle then watches its executions, sorting each one into a small number of buckets by how much work it did. If executions with different bind values land in clearly different buckets, the cursor becomes bind-aware: from then on, each new value is checked against the existing child cursors, and a value that needs a different plan gets its own child cursor with its own plan.

That works well when the difference is visible. The hole is in "clearly different". If the rare value's first execution and the common value's executions land in the same bucket, ACS sees nothing to react to, and the cursor stays exactly as it was. And whether you're protected can depend on the order in which values arrive after each restart, shared pool flush, or statistics refresh, which nobody controls.

Prove it

The lab builds ORDERS with 200,000 rows and a skewed STATUS, 200 OPEN and 199,800 CLOSED, with a frequency histogram on the column, and joins it to a 1,000,000-row CUSTOMERS table. It flushes the shared pool, runs the statement once with 'OPEN', then five times with 'CLOSED', each in a fresh session, measuring session logical reads from V$MYSTAT and the child cursor each execution ran:

>> Fresh shared pool. The SAME statement, bound:  ... where o.status = :s
   OPEN    rows=200     logical reads=2624     child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603391   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS

The optimizer peeked 'OPEN', estimated 199 rows from the histogram, and chose nested loops, which is right for 200 rows. Every 'CLOSED' run then reused child cursor 0 and its nested loops: 603,354 logical reads, five times in a row. Adaptive cursor sharing never marked the cursor bind-aware. The first 'OPEN' execution, including its hard parse, and every 'CLOSED' execution fell into the same middle bucket, so the safety net never saw a difference. (The plan was even an adaptive plan, with a statistics collector that can switch join methods, but an adaptive plan settles on its first execution and the settled plan is what gets reused.)

Give 'CLOSED' its own plan and the cost collapses:

>> The fix for a skewed, low-cardinality column: the predicate as a literal -> one cursor + plan per value
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=34716    child cursor=0  plan=HASH JOIN
   OPEN    rows=200     logical reads=806      child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS

34,716 logical reads instead of 603,354: the same rows, 17 times less work, because the plan was built for the value it runs. And 'OPEN' keeps its cheap nested loops at 806.

Don't take my word for it — run it. The bind-peeking lab builds the skewed tables on Oracle Database Free, peeks the rare value, and asserts that every common-value run inherits nested loops on the same cursor at 10 times or more the work of a hash join, without adaptive cursor sharing splitting it. Then it gives each value its own plan and asserts the common value drops to 10% or less of that work. If the trap stops reproducing or the fix stops working, the run fails. Proven on every CI push.

See it in your own system

Start from the statement, not the plan. A query whose cost swings by value shows up as high variance in buffer gets per execution for one SQL_ID. Then look at its cursors:

-- one row per child cursor: which ones are bind-sensitive / bind-aware, and what each costs
SELECT child_number, plan_hash_value, is_bind_sensitive, is_bind_aware,
       executions, ROUND(buffer_gets / NULLIF(executions, 0)) AS gets_per_exec
FROM   v$sql
WHERE  sql_id = '&sql_id'
ORDER  BY child_number;
  • Bind-sensitive Y, bind-aware N, one child, huge gets per execution: the lab's situation. The cursor knows the bind matters, but it never split.
  • Several children with different plan hash values, bind-aware Y: ACS is doing its job.
  • V$SQL_CS_HISTOGRAM shows how its executions were bucketed; all executions in one bucket means ACS has nothing to react to.

To see which value the plan was built for, ask for the peeked binds:

SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR('&sql_id', 0, 'TYPICAL +PEEKED_BINDS'));

In the lab that prints :S ... 'OPEN' above a nested-loops plan, the whole diagnosis in one screen. In AWR, the same statement appearing with more than one plan hash value over time, with very different elapsed times, is the historical fingerprint: the plan changes whenever the cursor is rebuilt with a different first value.

The fix

Pick by how the column behaves. In order of preference:

  • For a skewed, low-cardinality column, use a literal for that predicate. A status code with five values makes five cursors, each with the right plan. That's no hard-parse storm: the storm comes from literal values with high cardinality, like IDs. Keep binds for everything else in the statement. This is the exception to "bind everything" that the bind variables post ends on, and the lab's fix.
  • Split the query in the application when it already knows which kind of value it has: a separate statement for the "open orders" screen and the "history" screen. Two statements, two plans, no guessing.
  • A SQL plan baseline with more than one accepted plan. Baselines cooperate with adaptive cursor sharing: accept the nested-loops plan and the hash-join plan, and each value can use the one that fits. See SQL plan management.
  • Remove the histogram, if one plan is genuinely acceptable for every value. Without it the optimizer stops distinguishing values and picks one middle-of-the-road plan. It's a legitimate choice when no value is catastrophic, but a bad one when, as here, the wrong plan costs 17 times the work.

What not to do: don't "fix" it by flushing the shared pool or purging the cursor when it goes bad. That just rolls the dice again on which value arrives first, and the problem returns on its own schedule.

What teams get wrong

  • Blaming the data or the database for "random" slowness. It isn't random: it's the plan built for whichever value arrived first, and it changes when the cursor is rebuilt.
  • Testing by hand. Paste the statement into a SQL tool with the slow value typed in and it's different SQL text, so it gets its own hard parse and the right plan, and it's fast. The problem only shows on the shared, bind-variable cursor the application uses.
  • Trusting adaptive cursor sharing to handle it. It helps when executions differ enough to land in different buckets, and quietly does nothing when they don't, as the lab shows five times in a row.
  • Flushing the shared pool as the fix. It resets the lottery; it doesn't change the odds.
  • Disabling bind peeking database-wide. It's a hidden parameter, and switching it off trades one wrong plan for a plan built for no real value at all, for every statement in the database.
  • Turning a whole application to literals to escape it. That's the hard-parse storm all over again. Use literals only for the skewed, low-cardinality predicate.

Frequently asked questions

What is bind peeking in Oracle?

Bind peeking is the optimizer's behavior of looking at the actual value of a bind variable when it hard-parses a statement, and optimizing the plan as if that value were a literal. It produces a plan suited to a real value rather than to an average. The resulting cursor is then stored in the shared pool and reused by every later execution of the same statement, regardless of the value those executions bind. So the plan is effectively chosen by whichever value happened to arrive first when the cursor was built. On columns with evenly distributed values this rarely matters; on skewed columns with histograms it can make the same SQL fast for one value and very slow for another.

Why is the same Oracle query fast for one value and slow for another?

Usually because the statement uses a bind variable on a skewed column and the cursor's single plan was built for a different kind of value. If the first execution peeked a rare value, the optimizer may have chosen nested loops or an index-driven plan that is ideal for a few rows; every later execution reuses that plan, and a common value matching hundreds of thousands of rows then pays for one index probe per row. In the companion lab the same join costs 2,624 logical reads for a rare value and 603,354 for the common value on the inherited plan, versus 34,716 with its own hash-join plan. Running the query by hand with the slow value often looks fast, because a manual run with different text gets its own hard parse and the right plan.

What is adaptive cursor sharing?

Adaptive cursor sharing, introduced in Oracle 11g, lets a statement with bind variables have more than one plan. A cursor that peeked a bind on a column with a histogram is marked bind-sensitive, and Oracle monitors how much work its executions do, sorting them into buckets. If executions with different bind values land in clearly different buckets, the cursor is marked bind-aware, and new bind values are then checked against the existing child cursors; a value that needs a different plan gets a new child cursor with its own plan. You can see it in V$SQL (IS_BIND_SENSITIVE, IS_BIND_AWARE and multiple child cursors) and in V$SQL_CS_HISTOGRAM.

Why didn't adaptive cursor sharing fix my plan?

Because adaptive cursor sharing only reacts when it sees executions that differ enough to fall into different workload buckets. If the rare value's first execution and the common value's executions land in the same bucket, the cursor stays bind-sensitive but never becomes bind-aware, and every execution keeps using the original plan. In the companion lab the first execution with the rare value, including its hard parse, and all five executions with the common value fell into the same bucket, so the cursor never split even though the common value did 17 times the necessary work each time. Whether a given workload is protected can also depend on the order in which values arrive after a restart, a shared pool flush, or a statistics refresh.

How do I find which bind value a plan was built for?

Use DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR with the PEEKED_BINDS format option, for example SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR('sql_id', child_number, 'TYPICAL +PEEKED_BINDS')). The output includes a Peeked Binds section showing the value the optimizer saw when it built that child cursor's plan. Combine it with V$SQL for the same SQL_ID: one row per child cursor, its plan hash value, whether it is bind-sensitive and bind-aware, and buffer gets per execution. A single child with huge gets per execution and a peeked value from the rare end of a skewed column is the bind-peeking signature.

Should I use literals instead of bind variables to avoid bind peeking problems?

Only for the specific predicate on a skewed, low-cardinality column, such as a status code or a flag with a handful of values. Each distinct literal gets its own cursor and its own plan, and with only a few distinct values that means only a few cursors, which is no burden on the shared pool. Keep bind variables for high-cardinality values like IDs, names, and dates: using literals there causes a hard-parse storm, with thousands of nearly identical cursors, shared pool pressure, and latch contention. The rule is bind by default, literal by exception, and the exception is low-cardinality skew.

Does flushing the shared pool fix a bad bind-peeked plan?

Only by accident, and only temporarily. Flushing the shared pool, or purging the one cursor with DBMS_SHARED_POOL.PURGE, forces a new hard parse, and the new plan will be built for whichever bind value arrives first afterwards. If that is the common value, things look fixed until the next time the cursor is rebuilt with the rare value first; if it is the rare value, nothing changes. It resets the lottery without changing the odds. Fix the cause instead: give the skewed predicate a literal, split the statement in the application, or use a SQL plan baseline with more than one accepted plan.

Should I disable bind peeking?

No. Disabling bind peeking requires a hidden parameter, which should only be changed under Oracle Support's guidance, and it applies to every statement in the database. Without peeking, the optimizer builds plans using average selectivity rather than any real value, so instead of a plan that is right for some values you get a plan that is right for none of the skewed ones. Address the specific statements that suffer: literals for low-cardinality skewed predicates, separate statements per case, SQL plan baselines, or removing a histogram that does more harm than good.

Bind peeking sits right at the meeting point of two other posts in this series. Bind variables are why the cursor is shared in the first place, and that's the right default; indexes are why the same predicate deserves an index for one value and a full scan for another. The plan itself is something you can read in the execution plan, the histogram that sets the trap comes from optimizer statistics, and SQL plan management is one way to pin more than one good plan. When one statement is fast for some values and slow for others, look at the peeked bind before anything else, and prove it the way that ends the argument — with the bind-peeking lab, where the same query costs 2,624 reads for one value and 603,354 for another until each value gets its own plan.

Originally published at uptimearchitect.com.

title: Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now in public beta
description:
Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now available in public beta on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. It isn’t tied to a single sandbox, so you can reuse the same Drive across runs and different sandbox instances.

Use Drives to preserve an agent's workspace or on-disk memory, or to reuse datasets, models, and dependency trees.

Create and mount a Drive

Create or retrieve a Drive and mount it at a path when starting a sandbox. Read and write files through the sandbox filesystem at that path.

Anything stored under /data remains on the Drive after the sandbox stops.

Share Drive data across sandboxes

A Drive supports one read-write mount at a time. After the Drive has been written to, multiple sandboxes can read from it concurrently by mounting point-in-time, read-only snapshots.

Each snapshot reflects the Drive at the moment it's mounted. Later writes aren’t included; mount a new snapshot to access them.

Limits and pricing

Each sandbox can mount up to four Drives at separate paths. Drives default to a maximum size of 1 TiB (1 GiB on Hobby) and can be configured up to 16 TiB, with higher limits available by request.

Drives are available in every Sandbox region. Each Drive stays in the region where it was created. Sandboxes that mount it must run in that region and can’t use failover regions.

Drive pricing is based on storage, reads, and writes, with rates varying by region. In iad1, storage costs $0.05 per GB-month, reads $0.0015 per GB, and writes $0.004 per GB. Hobby includes 15 GB of Drive storage and 30 GB each of reads and writes per month. See Sandbox pricing for regional rates and plan details.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: How to Reconcile Healthtech Payments in Node.js — Queueing Delayed Webhook Retry Callbacks
description:
For a failed payment webhook, the safest retry queue pattern lets delayed callbacks arrive more than once but never applies the payment twice.

Short answer: use a queue with delayed retries and a dead-letter queue (DLQ), keep the durable payment record in your application database, and deduplicate every delivery by the provider's event or delivery ID.

That is the beginner-friendly pattern. It separates transport from truth. The queue controls when work becomes eligible; the database decides whether that work has already changed a payment. For a healthtech system, that separation also makes the trust boundary visible: the queue should carry references, not a growing history of payment or patient data.

How should a Node.js queue retry failed webhook callbacks and delayed jobs?

Start with a diagram in words: payment provider -> public webhook receiver -> queue -> reconciliation worker -> application database. A nightly scheduler enters through the same queue, so the webhook path and the reconciliation path share one idempotent worker. On a transient failure, the worker records the attempt and next retry time, then schedules another delivery. Once the retry budget is exhausted, the task moves to the DLQ for inspection and controlled redrive.

Before this pattern, the receiver tries to reconcile synchronously. A slow provider call holds the request open, and retry state gets scattered between HTTP handlers and logs. After it, the receiver has one small job: validate the callback, persist its identity, and publish a compact task. The worker owns retries. The database owns the result.

Keep the message deliberately dull:

  • eventId, the stable deduplication key
  • paymentId, the lookup reference
  • attempt, the delivery count
  • notBefore, the next eligible processing time

Do not put the full webhook history in each message. This queue limits messages to 256KB, delayed delivery to 7 days, and retention to at most 30 days. An acknowledged message is deleted. Those limits point toward the same design even on another queue: durable business state belongs in the database, while the queue carries enough information to find it.

Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery, so duplicate processing isn't an edge case. It is part of the contract. Use a unique constraint on eventId or the provider delivery ID and commit the deduplication marker in the same database transaction as the payment update. Checking a cache first is not equivalent; two workers can both pass that check before either writes.

Duplicates happen.

One more boundary matters. Region, retention, deletion, and subprocessors are deployment and contract decisions, not properties a retry loop can manufacture. For Infrai, inspect the public discovery record's regions field before choosing a deployment. I'm not sure which region meets your organization's policy without that policy and the current discovery response; security and legal owners must resolve that against the payment provider, queue provider, and database processor agreements.

Build the delivery state machine before choosing a provider

The cleanest state machine has four outcomes: processed, duplicate, retry, and dead-letter. Here is a runnable TypeScript model. It uses an in-memory queue so the delivery behavior is visible without inventing a vendor request schema; replace MemoryQueue and MemoryLedger with adapters for your chosen queue and transactional database.

type ReconcileTask = {
  eventId: string;
  paymentId: string;
  attempt: number;
  notBefore: number;
};

type DeadLetter = ReconcileTask & { reason: string };

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const queueName = process.env.QUEUE_NAME ?? "nightly-payment-reconciliation";

async function publishWithRetry(task: ReconcileTask): Promise<void> {
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let retry = 0; retry < 5; retry += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": task.eventId,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        queue: queueName,
        message: task,
        delay_seconds: Math.max(0, Math.floor((task.notBefore - Date.now()) / 1_000)),
      }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    const reason = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || retry === 4) {
      throw new Error(`Queue publish failed (${response.status}): ${reason}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : Math.min(500 * 2 ** retry, 8_000);
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
}

class MemoryQueue {
  ready: ReconcileTask[] = [];
  dead: DeadLetter[] = [];

  publish(task: ReconcileTask): void {
    this.ready.push(task);
  }

  next(now: number): ReconcileTask | undefined {
    const index = this.ready.findIndex((task) => task.notBefore <= now);
    if (index === -1) return undefined;
    return this.ready.splice(index, 1)[0];
  }
}

class MemoryLedger {
  private readonly processed = new Set<string>();

  applyOnce(task: ReconcileTask): "processed" | "duplicate" {
    if (this.processed.has(task.eventId)) return "duplicate";

    // A real adapter inserts eventId and updates the payment in one transaction.
    this.processed.add(task.eventId);
    return "processed";
  }
}

const queue = new MemoryQueue();
const ledger = new MemoryLedger();
const maxAttempts = 4;

function backoffSeconds(attempt: number): number {
  return Math.min(60 * 2 ** attempt, 3_600);
}

function handle(task: ReconcileTask, providerAvailable: boolean, now: number): void {
  if (!providerAvailable) {
    const nextAttempt = task.attempt + 1;
    if (nextAttempt >= maxAttempts) {
      queue.dead.push({ ...task, attempt: nextAttempt, reason: "retry budget exhausted" });
      return;
    }

    queue.publish({
      ...task,
      attempt: nextAttempt,
      notBefore: now + backoffSeconds(nextAttempt) * 1_000,
    });
    return;
  }

  console.log(task.eventId, ledger.applyOnce(task));
}

const now = Date.now();
const task: ReconcileTask = {
  eventId: "evt_20260909_0042",
  paymentId: "pay_1048",
  attempt: 0,
  notBefore: now,
};

queue.publish(task);
handle(queue.next(now)!, true, now);

// Simulate at-least-once redelivery of the same provider event.
queue.publish(task);
handle(queue.next(now)!, true, now);

await publishWithRetry(task);

Run it with npx tsx reconcile.ts. The output contains processed and then duplicate. That tiny before/after is the core guarantee. The production database adapter must make applyOnce atomic; the in-memory implementation only makes the rule easy to see.

The example uses four attempts and caps backoff at 3,600 seconds as an application policy, not as a vendor promise. Tune both values to the payment provider's recovery pattern and your reconciliation deadline. Keep the next retry below the queue's delay ceiling. If recovery can take longer than 7 days, write a durable due date to the database and let a scheduler publish a fresh task later rather than pretending one delayed message is long-term storage. The publish call uses a stable idempotency key, reads the bearer token from the environment, sets the HTTP method explicitly, honors Retry-After on a 429, and surfaces every other non-success response. In production, the consumer needs equivalent status handling and must acknowledge only after the database transaction commits.

Fetch the current request and response schema from public discovery before binding the rest of the adapter. Successful processing must acknowledge only after persistence, while permanent failure belongs in the DLQ.

Put observability around decisions, not queue motion

A useful log answers, “What did the worker decide?” Record eventId, paymentId, attempt, outcome, and next retry time. Do not log full webhook bodies or authorization material. A useful metric counts outcomes by processed, duplicate, retry, and dead-letter; another measures the age of the oldest eligible task. Alert on a sustained DLQ increase or on task age crossing the nightly reconciliation deadline.

This is where delivery guarantees become operational. A queue depth of 400 could be normal just after the nightly run. One task that has missed the settlement deadline may be the real incident. Tie alerts to age and business deadlines, then give operators a redrive procedure that reuses the same event ID. Redrive must not create a new identity, or the database cannot recognize the old work.

Deletion needs equal care. An ack removes a queue message, but it does not delete the corresponding payment row, provider record, application log, backup, or DLQ export. Write a deletion map that names each processor and store. The map should say who can delete data, which identifier links the copies, and how completion is verified. Queue retention is one line in that map, not the whole policy.

Keep sensitive fields out of labels and metric dimensions too. IDs can still be sensitive, and high-cardinality event IDs make poor metric labels anyway. Put correlation identifiers in access-controlled structured logs; keep metrics aggregated by outcome and queue.

Compare the queue pattern against workflow and replay requirements

Provider choice comes after the state machine because the hard promise lives in your idempotent transaction. The products below solve different shapes of work.

Option Best fit in this design The catch
Infrai Compact delayed webhook tasks and a DLQ behind one REST API Standard delivery is at-least-once; delay is capped at 7 days, retention at 30 days, and push targets require public HTTPS
BullMQ A Node.js team that wants a Redis-backed job queue The team owns the Redis and worker operating boundary
Inngest Event-driven functions and durable execution Compare its processor and region boundary with the payment-data policy
Trigger.dev TypeScript background jobs Validate delivery and retention behavior against the same state machine
Temporal Multi-step workflow orchestration where the process itself must be modeled A queue-plus-DLQ design is simpler when the job is only retry, reconcile, and record
Apache Airflow DAG-oriented scheduled data work It is a different operating model from a small callback worker
Apache Kafka Replay and multiple consumer-group requirements An ack-delete queue cannot substitute for Kafka-style replay
GitHub Actions Repository automation on a schedule Keep it for repository workflows, not as the source of truth for payment delivery state

Infrai is worth trying for a team that wants the delayed queue portion of this healthtech reconciliation flow behind the same key and bill as its other backend services. The supporting benefit is concrete: its plain REST interface avoids adding a queue-specific SDK to the Node.js worker. Public discovery describes the current capability schemas, and the broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules.

The catch is equally concrete. It is not suitable when the process needs a DAG, fan-out/fan-in joins, Kafka-style replay, multiple consumer groups, native debounce, or native topic fan-out. Stick with Temporal or Airflow for workflow orchestration, and evaluate Kafka when retained event replay is the requirement. If the worker is private-only, push delivery is also the wrong boundary because push subscriptions require a public HTTPS target; polling from the worker may fit, subject to your network and processor review.

There is no magic “exactly once” checkbox here.

FIFO deduplication on this platform has a 5-minute window, while a reconciliation retry can outlive it. The application database still needs the durable event-ID constraint. Likewise, a cron trigger has a 900-second execution ceiling and does not backfill triggers missed while paused, so a long nightly reconciliation should use cron only to enqueue work and let workers consume it. Expect second-level scheduling jitter rather than treating the trigger timestamp as a financial clock.

What should the production readiness review prove?

First, prove duplicate safety. Deliver the same eventId concurrently to two workers and verify that one payment transition commits. Then force retries past the configured budget, inspect the DLQ record, and redrive it without changing the event identity. Test a delayed task near your chosen operational horizon, but stay within the 604,800-second platform limit.

Second, prove the trust boundary. Review the currently advertised regions, retention settings, deletion procedure, logs, backups, and every processor that can see a payment reference. Confirm that public HTTPS exposure is acceptable if push delivery is selected. Do not infer contractual residency from an API region field alone — the contract and processor list have to agree with the technical configuration.

Finally, prove that the on-call signal survives the happy path. A successful nightly run should leave an auditable count of processed, duplicate, retried, and dead-lettered tasks without preserving full payload history in the queue. A failed callback should be visible before its business deadline. And an operator should be able to redrive it safely, with the database stopping a second application if the original result committed but its acknowledgment was lost.

That is the decision rule: choose the smallest queue that meets the region and processor boundary, then build correctness in the database. Move to a workflow engine when the job becomes a workflow. Move to an event log when replay becomes the product requirement.

If this boundary fits your system, use the Infrai Node.js webhook worker guide as a low-pressure next step and verify its live discovery schema before integrating.

title: Securing Agentic Commerce Through Behavior-Aware Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity for Trusted AI-Agent Payment Authorization
description:
arXiv:2610.27483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing use of autonomous artificial intelligence agents in digital commerce creates new security concerns involving agent impersonation, unauthorized payments, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. This research introduces the Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System (ACAGS), a cybersecurity framework combining supervised machine learning, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and explainable AI. The framework was evaluated using synthetic financial transaction data augmented with simulated agent characteristics and five adversarial scenarios. XGBoost was selected following comparisons with alternative classifiers. Across ten experimental runs, behavioral features improved mean F1-score from 52.12% to 67.49%, with agent-specific features increasing performance to 69.46%. The framework achieved detection rates of 99.77% for abnormal agent behavior, 99.73% for impersonation, and 100% for malicious delegation and authorization-scope violations. Compromised-agent detection reached 72.27%. ACAGS also supported APPROVE, REVIEW, and REJECT authorization outcomes, with SHAP explanations providing model interpretability. The results demonstrate the potential of combining behavioral intelligence and delegated authorization controls to strengthen simulated agentic-commerce payment security, while highlighting the need for validation using real-world transactions.

title: 주소모음 서비스를 만들면서 사이트 탐색 UX를 단순화한 방법
description:
주소모음 서비스를 만들면서 사이트 탐색 UX를 단순화한 방법

웹사이트를 만들 때 처음에는 콘텐츠가 많을수록 사용자에게 도움이 될 거라고 생각했습니다.

그래서 다양한 사이트를 한 화면에 최대한 많이 보여주려고 했습니다.

그런데 실제로 운영하면서 반대 문제가 생겼습니다.

사이트가 많아질수록 사용자는 선택하기 어려워졌고, 원하는 사이트를 찾으려면 화면을 계속 내려보거나 여러 페이지를 돌아다녀야 했습니다.

결국 문제는 사이트 개수보다 탐색 구조에 있었습니다.

사이트를 먼저 보여주는 대신 카테고리를 먼저 보여줬습니다

제가 운영하고 있는 프로젝트는 레이더(Radar)입니다.

radarjuso.com은 여러 분야의 웹사이트를 카테고리별로 정리해서 보여주는 주소모음 서비스입니다.

초기에는 사이트 목록 자체를 강조했지만, 운영하면서 사용자가 먼저 원하는 분야를 선택할 수 있도록 구조를 바꿨습니다.

현재 가장 중요하게 보고 있는 탐색 흐름은 단순합니다.

카테고리 선택 → 관련 사이트 탐색 → 여러 선택지 비교 → 필요한 사이트 확인

예를 들어 사용자가 AI 관련 사이트를 찾고 있다면 전체 사이트 목록을 훑는 대신 AI 카테고리부터 들어갈 수 있도록 하는 방식입니다.

카테고리마다 역할을 나눴습니다

카테고리가 늘어나면서 또 다른 문제가 생겼습니다.

서로 다른 페이지들이 비슷한 설명과 키워드를 사용하기 시작했습니다.

그래서 각 페이지의 목적을 다시 정리했습니다.

  • 홈은 서비스 전체를 설명
  • 카테고리는 특정 분야의 사이트를 탐색
  • 상세 페이지는 개별 사이트의 기본 정보를 확인

이렇게 역할을 구분하니 UX뿐 아니라 콘텐츠를 작성할 때도 훨씬 명확해졌습니다.

검색과 탐색을 같은 기능으로 보지 않았습니다

처음에는 검색창만 잘 만들면 사용자가 원하는 사이트를 쉽게 찾을 거라고 생각했습니다.

하지만 검색은 이미 사이트 이름을 알고 있는 사람에게 더 유용했습니다.

반대로 어떤 사이트를 써야 할지 아직 모르는 사람에게는 탐색 기능이 더 중요했습니다.

그래서 Radar에서는 검색뿐 아니라 카테고리를 둘러보면서 새로운 사이트를 발견할 수 있는 구조도 같이 중요하게 보고 있습니다.

사용 목적이 다른 두 사용자를 모두 고려하는 셈입니다.

알고 있는 사이트 찾기 → 검색

새로운 사이트 찾기 → 카테고리 탐색

내부 링크도 사용자 흐름에 맞췄습니다

페이지가 늘어나면서 처음에는 관련 페이지를 최대한 많이 연결했습니다.

하지만 내부 링크가 많아질수록 사용자가 어디로 이동해야 하는지 오히려 모호해졌습니다.

지금은 현재 페이지와 실제로 관련 있는 이동 경로만 남기는 방향으로 조정하고 있습니다.

기본 구조는 다음과 같습니다.

홈 → 카테고리 → 사이트 정보 → 관련 카테고리

SEO를 위해 링크를 추가하는 것보다 실제 사용자가 다음에 어떤 페이지를 필요로 할지를 먼저 생각하게 됐습니다.

주소모음 서비스도 결국 정보 구조 문제였습니다

Radar를 만들면서 가장 크게 바뀐 생각은 이것입니다.

주소모음 사이트라고 해서 링크만 많이 모으면 되는 게 아니었습니다.

사이트가 늘어날수록 더 중요한 것은 분류, 탐색, 비교, 재발견이었습니다.

사용자가 원하는 사이트를 빨리 찾는 것도 중요하지만, 몰랐던 사이트를 발견할 수 있게 만드는 것 역시 디렉터리 서비스의 중요한 역할이라고 생각합니다.

현재 이런 구조를 실제로 적용하면서 계속 테스트하고 있는 프로젝트가 radarjuso.com입니다.

카테고리형 서비스나 디렉터리를 만들고 있다면 사이트 수를 늘리기 전에, 사용자가 어디에서 시작하고 어떤 순서로 원하는 정보까지 이동하는지부터 확인해보는 것이 꽤 도움이 될 수 있습니다.

title: LazyList AI: Let Local AI Organize Your Day 🦥
description:
LazyList AI: Let Local AI Organize Your Day 🦥

This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What I Built

I built LazyList AI, a simple AI productivity assistant that transforms a messy to-do list into a prioritized, low-stress action plan.

Users enter their tasks, choose their energy level, and receive suggestions for what to focus on first. The goal is to spend less time organizing tasks and more time completing them.

Demo

I tested the application locally and captured a screenshot of LazyList AI generating an action plan.

Demo screenshot: Attached to this post.

This is an early prototype that currently runs on my machine.

Code

GitHub repository: https://github.com/DhanushRajUrs/lazylist-ai

How I Built It

  • Python for the application logic
  • Streamlit for the user interface
  • Ollama to run the model locally
  • Gemma 3:1B as the open-weight language model

The application sends the user's task list and selected energy level to Gemma running locally through Ollama. The model generates a prioritized plan with explanations and manageable first steps.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Running an open-weight model locally gives users more control over their data and lets developers experiment without relying on a paid hosted AI API.

After the software and model have been installed, inference can run without an internet connection. Developers can also explore compatible models and adapt their applications to different needs.

The Lazy Payoff 🦥

LazyList AI helps reduce the mental effort of deciding where to start when a person has many tasks. It is an early prototype, and future improvements could include task tracking, deadlines, and saving plans.

Building it helped me practise Python, Streamlit, Git, GitHub, and local AI integration while exploring how open AI tools can make everyday work easier.

Thanks for checking out my project!
