title: HiQGS: Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Querying for Feed-Forward Gaussian Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.27604v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction from sparse posed monocular frames requires reasoning over observations that vary jointly in viewpoint and time. Existing methods either predict Gaussian primitives from observation-aligned features or aggregate multi-frame information through compact latent queries. However, the former tightly couples Gaussian allocation to individual frames, while the latter does not explicitly structure observed evidence according to its temporal relation to the requested timestamp. Consequently, evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps can be difficult to align and integrate. We present \textbf{HiQGS}, a query-based hierarchical framework for feed-forward Gaussian scene reconstruction from sparse monocular frames. HiQGS introduces a \textbf{Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder} that organizes multi-resolution geometry-appearance visual features according to image location, observation time, and camera pose, thereby preserving complementary appearance and structural cues. Our \textbf{Time-Adaptive Decoder} use target timestamp queries the resulting hierarchical representation to retrieve relevant spatiotemporal evidence and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state. Experiments on static and dynamic scene reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy, validating the effectiveness of hierarchical visual encoding and target-time-aware Gaussian querying.

title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences
description:
arXiv:2610.27256v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.

title: Building Query Conditions In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import static net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqFields.*;

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

Using JooqTemplate

Method 1: conditions() — Field-Value Pair Varargs (Recommended)

conditions(Object... fieldValuePairs) takes arguments in pairs of "field name, value"; the operator is written directly after the field name string, and when no operator is written the default is ==. It returns a List<Condition>, and conditions whose values are null are automatically ignored:

// name = 'Smartphone' and price > 1000 and status = 'on_sale'
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions(
        "name", "Smartphone",
        "price>", 1000,        // the > operator follows the field name
        "stock<=", 50,         // the <= operator
        "status", "on_sale");  // default operator ==

// You can also separate the field and operator with a colon: "price:>"
List<Condition> conds2 = jt.conditions("price:>", 1000);

When a parameter value is null, that condition is ignored — ideal for dynamic queries: if the frontend doesn't send a value, no filter is applied:

// When nameParam is null, no name condition is generated
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions("name", nameParam, "category", categoryParam);

You can also mix native jOOQ Condition objects directly into the varargs:

Condition other = DSL.field("price").ge(1000);
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions("category", "Electronics", other);

Method 2: and() / or() — Directly Returning a Single Combined Condition

and(...) and or(...) take arguments exactly like conditions(); the difference is the return value: multiple conditions are merged with AND / OR into a single Condition, and null is returned when there are no conditions at all:

// AND: name = 'John' and age > 30 and status = 'active'
Condition cond = jt.and("name", "John", "age>", 30, "status", "active");

// OR: name like 'Soph%' or name like 'Fra%'
Condition cond2 = jt.or("name:%l", "Soph", "name:%l", "Fra");

// Empty arguments return null
Condition empty = jt.and();   // null

Find two users with OR (corresponding to the user_table example in JooqTemplateOrTest):

// name = 'John' or name = 'Lee'
Condition cond = jt.or("name", "John", "name", "Lee");
List<LowerCaseRecord> records = jt.queryLowerCaseRecord("user_table", cond);

Method 3: condition() — Single-Condition Method

condition(Name fieldName, String operator, Object[] values) accepts a jOOQ Name, an operator string, and a value array, and generates a single Condition. The number of values must match what the operator requires, otherwise an IllegalArgumentException is thrown:

import org.jooq.Condition;
import org.jooq.Name;
import org.jooq.impl.DSL;

// Equality: == requires 1 value
Condition c1 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{"Smartphone"});

// Comparison: > requires 1 value
Condition c2 = jt.condition(DSL.name("price"), ">", new Object[]{1000});

// in: requires 1 value, and the value must be a Collection or Object[]
Condition c3 = jt.condition(DSL.name("category"), "in",
        new Object[]{Arrays.asList("Electronics", "Appliances", "Apparel")});

// between: requires 2 values
Condition c4 = jt.condition(DSL.name("created_at"), "between",
        new Object[]{beginDate, endDate});

// isnull: requires 0 values
Condition c5 = jt.condition(DSL.name("remark"), "isnull", new Object[]{});

This method also follows the null rules: a null value returns null (ignored); wrapping with ND(null) generates is null; a null field name or operator returns null; an invalid operator throws IllegalArgumentException:

// Value is null → returns null, condition ignored
Condition c = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{null});   // null

// ND wrapping null → generates name is null
Condition c2 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{ND(null)});

// Value count mismatch → throws IllegalArgumentException("Operator require value count is 1")
Condition c3 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{});

not() — Negating a Condition

not(Condition) negates an existing condition and returns null when the input is null:

Condition original = jt.and("status", "disabled");
Condition notDisabled = jt.not(original);   // not (status = 'disabled')

orOne() — Multiple Fields Matching the Same Value

orOne(Object... sameOneValues) starts with several "fields" (single-value operators), and the last argument is the shared value, generating field1 op value or field2 op value .... A typical "global keyword search" scenario:

// name = 'Apple' or nick_name = 'Apple' or remark = 'Apple'
Condition cond = jt.orOne("name", "nick_name", "remark", "Apple");

Null Fallback for between

between / notbetween take 2 values; when either end is null, it automatically falls back to a one-sided comparison, and when both ends are null the whole condition is ignored:

// Both begin and end are non-null: price between 100 and 500
jt.conditions("price:between", 100, 500);

// begin=100, end=null: price >= 100
jt.conditions("price:between", 100, null);

// notbetween fallback: begin=null, end=500 → price > 500
jt.conditions("price:notbetween", null, 500);

Operator Reference

Condition operators (written after the field name or passed to condition(); all are case-insensitive):

Operator Value Count Meaning
== (default) 1 Equal to
<> 1 Not equal to
> >= < <= 1 Comparison
% / like 1 Contains %value%
%l / llike 1 Prefix match value%
%r / rlike 1 Suffix match %value
in / notin 1 Value is a Collection or Object[]
between / notbetween 2 Range; a null end falls back automatically
isnull / isnotnull 0 Null check

Sort operators (only used in the order part of a query or in orders()): asc, ascnf (nulls first), ascnl (nulls last), desc, descnf, descnl.

Null handling rules:

  • In queries (conditions() / and() / or() / condition()), a null value → the condition is ignored.
  • A value wrapped with ND(null) → generates field is null.
  • In UPDATE / DELETE, a null value → generates field is null.

title: Our proposal screen arrives already written, and every part of it has a Change button instead of an empty field
description:
Nakodo emails creators and businesses on a brand's behalf, which means somewhere in the product the brand has to say what it wants and what it gives in return. A fee, a product, a trial, a commission, a free month. That screen started life as the usual thing: a card with two textareas labelled "What you'd like" and "What they get", a save button, and a blank page.

That version is easy to build and hard to finish, because it asks somebody to write marketing copy from a standing start, in a product they signed up to five minutes ago, before they have seen a single creator. The standing rule in this codebase is now the opposite:

Anything readable off the brand's own site is found automatically and shown as found, with a Change button. Never an empty box.

This post is the 941 lines that rule turned into, and the five pieces of state that carry it.

Nothing is asked for that can be read

The editor is one client component, opened from two places: the campaign setup flow and the outreach tab of a running campaign. Its props are the whole world it needs, including what we already know about the brand:

export type ProposalEditorProps = {
  campaignId: string;
  kind: CampaignKind;
  domain: string;
  platforms: Platform[];
  range: { min: number; max: number }; // the brief's follower range
  currency: Currency;
  saved: Proposal | null; // the brand's own, once there is one
  suggestion: ProposalSuggestion | null;
  pricing: string; // the brand's prices as found on its site, for what a customer is worth
  suggest: boolean; // ask for a suggestion when there's neither
  fits: Audience[]; // the campaign's good fits so far
  approval: "review" | "auto";
  mode: "setup" | "outreach";
};

saved and suggestion are the two sources, in that order of authority, and startingDraft is the whole merge:

function startingDraft(p: ProposalEditorProps): Draft {
  const creators = p.kind === "creators";
  const s = p.saved ?? p.suggestion;
  if (!s) return { idea: "", ask: "", offer: "", terms: creators ? plainTerms(p.range, p.currency) : null };
  return {
    idea: s.idea ?? "",
    ask: creators ? "" : s.ask ?? "",
    offer: creators ? "" : s.offer ?? "",
    terms: creators ? (s.terms ?? plainTerms(p.range, p.currency, s.ask, s.offer)) : null,
  };
}

The interesting line is the last one. Creator campaigns used to have one ask and one offer for everybody; now they have a set of terms per size of creator. Rather than migrating a jsonb column, the old shape is upgraded on read: plainTerms(range, currency, s.ask, s.offer) builds a tier per size and seeds every one of them with the single ask and offer that were saved before tiers existed. A brand that saved a proposal in September opens this screen and sees their own words, repeated across the sizes, ready to differ where they want them to.

A migration in a component is not a thing to be proud of in general. It is right here because the old shape is still a legal shape for a business campaign, so the code has to understand both anyway, and the alternative is a database rewrite plus a component that understands both.

The first open writes the whole thing while you wait

With nothing saved and nothing suggested, the screen does not render a form. It asks for a suggestion immediately, once:

const [writing, setWriting] = useState(!saved && !props.suggestion && props.suggest);
const asked = useRef(false);

// No proposal and no suggestion: ask for one straight away, once.
useEffect(() => {
  if (!writing || asked.current) return;
  asked.current = true;
  askForSuggestion();
}, []);

The ref rather than the empty dependency array is what makes that safe. An effect with no dependencies still runs twice in React's development mode, and this one spends real money, so the guard has to be a value that survives a second run.

While it works, the screen is an honest wait rather than a spinner:

<EmptyState illustration={<Notebook size="m" className="illo-loop" />} title="Writing your proposal.">
  Nakodo is working out what to ask {w.many} for and what to offer them, from what it read on {domain}. This usually takes 10 to 20 seconds.
  <Asides lines={creators ? WRITING_ASIDES : BUSINESS_ASIDES} className="mt-1" />
</EmptyState>

Three things in there are deliberate. The domain is named, because "from what it read on acme.com" tells the reader where the answer is coming from and sets up the Change buttons they are about to use. The estimate is a range with a unit, because "10 to 20 seconds" is a promise the code can keep and "please wait" is not. And Asides rotates a few lines of genuinely useful context, which is the only honest thing to put in a wait that long:

const WRITING_ASIDES = [
  "Smaller creators often say yes to the product and commission. Bigger ones expect a fee.",
  "Fees come from each creator's typical views at market rates, not from their follower count.",
  "A business buyer is usually worth a little more per viewer than a shopper.",
];

Failure has its own branch, with two ways out rather than one: try again, or write my own. A screen whose only recovery is a retry button is a screen that can trap somebody behind a provider outage.

A suggestion that is only on screen is not saved 

// Nothing saved yet counts as unsaved: a suggestion only takes effect once saved.
const [dirty, setDirty] = useState(!saved);

This is the most important line in the file. The suggestion arrives, fills the screen, and reads exactly like a finished document, so it would be entirely reasonable for the reader to assume it is already in effect. It is not: nothing is written to the campaign until Save. Initialising dirty from !saved means the bar at the bottom says "You have unsaved changes" from the first paint, and the browser asks before the tab closes:

// Leaving with unsaved edits asks first.
useEffect(() => {
  if (!dirty || writing) return;
  const warn = (e: BeforeUnloadEvent) => e.preventDefault();
  window.addEventListener("beforeunload", warn);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("beforeunload", warn);
}, [dirty, writing]);

!writing in the guard because a half-written proposal that does not exist yet is not something worth warning about, and the warning would land while the reader is watching a progress state they did not cause.

Facts, with Change on them

Each part of the proposal is a card. Closed, it is a description list. Open, it is fields with a Done button. The state is one union:

// What's open for changing: the idea, a business's ask and offer, or a size.
type Open = "idea" | "business" | CreatorSize | null;

One union rather than a boolean per section, so only one thing is ever open and the rest of the page stays readable while you type. The closed view:

<dl className="space-y-3">
  <Fact label="Ask">{draft.ask.trim() ? cap(draft.ask.trim()) : <Unset />}</Fact>
  <Fact label="They get">{draft.offer.trim() ? cap(draft.offer.trim()) : <Unset />}</Fact>
</dl>

Unset is 1 line and exists to be rare:

export const Unset = () => <span className="text-muted-foreground">Not set yet</span>;

It is what "never an empty box" looks like when the box genuinely is empty: still a sentence, in the muted colour, in the same layout as a filled fact, rather than an input waiting for you.

The Change button carries the distinction the reader cares about:

<Button variant="ghost" size="sm" onClick={onClick} aria-label={`${empty ? "Add" : "Change"} ${label}`}>
  <PencilIcon />
  {empty ? "Add" : "Change"}
</Button>

aria-label spells out which thing is being changed, because fifteen buttons on one page all named "Change" are useless in a list of landmarks, and the visible label stays short because the card's title is right next to it.

Section, ChangeButton, Editing, Fact, Unset and Segmented live in one 122-line file, imported by four screens: the proposal, the campaign details, the reply settings and the setup flow. That is the whole reason those three screens feel like one screen.

Segmented controls in there are real radios with no JavaScript:

<label className="cursor-pointer rounded-md px-3 py-1.5 text-sm text-muted-foreground has-checked:bg-card has-checked:font-medium has-checked:text-foreground has-focus-visible:outline-2">
  <input type="radio" name={name} value={o.value} checked={value === o.value} onChange={() => onChange(o.value)} className="sr-only" />
  {o.label}
</label>

The input is visually hidden rather than replaced, inside a fieldset with a legend, so arrow keys, the focus ring and the accessible name all come from the platform. has-checked: and has-focus-visible: do the styling that a custom toggle would otherwise need state for.

Typing something by hand changes the rules for that field

This is the detail that took three tries to get right. Each creator size has a content format (a mention, a dedicated video, a Reel) and an ask written in words. Choosing a different format should update the words, because the words describe the format. But if you wrote your own ask, a format change must not throw your sentence away:

// Sizes whose ask was typed by hand: a new format no longer replaces it.
const [typedAsks, setTypedAsks] = useState<Set<CreatorSize>>(() => new Set(saved ? draft.terms?.tiers.map((t) => t.size) : []));

const chooseFormat = (tier: Tier, format: AskFormat) => {
  const suggested = suggestion?.terms?.tiers.find((t) => t.size === tier.size);
  editTier(tier.size, {
    format,
    ...(!typedAsks.has(tier.size) && { ask: suggested?.format === format ? suggested.ask : DEFAULT_ASKS[format] }),
  });
};

Two rules in four lines. A size the reader has typed into is left alone for ever. A size they have not gets new words, and if the format they just picked is the one that was originally suggested, the words that come back are the suggested ones rather than the generic default, so clicking away and clicking back is not destructive.

The initial value of that set is the other half of it: when a proposal was loaded from the database, every tier counts as typed by hand, because we have no idea which parts of it the brand wrote and have to assume all of it.

Reasons expire when the draft stops resembling the suggestion

The preview panel beside the editor shows the suggestion's reasoning: why this ask, why this offer. Those sentences are about the suggestion, so they stop being true once the proposal has been rewritten:

// Whether the draft still mostly says what Nakodo suggested, so its reasons
// still apply.
function followsSuggestion(d: Draft, s: ProposalSuggestion): boolean {
  if (d.idea === s.idea) return true;
  if (!d.terms) return d.ask === s.ask || d.offer === s.offer;
  return d.terms.tiers.some((t) => s.terms?.tiers.find((x) => x.size === t.size)?.ask === t.ask);
}

reasons={suggestion && followsSuggestion(draft, suggestion) ? suggestion.reasons : []}

It is a deliberately loose test: any one part still matching counts. A strict equality check would drop the explanation the moment somebody fixed a typo, and the explanation is most useful precisely while they are editing. The honest failure mode of loose is an explanation that outlives one of the three things it explains, which is better than an explanation that vanishes when you touch anything.

One level of undo, in one piece of state

There is a "Suggest again" button, which throws the current proposal away and asks for a new one. That needs an undo, and undo in a form usually turns into a history stack nobody asked for:

const [undo, setUndo] = useState<Draft | null>(null);

// in askForSuggestion:
setUndo(replacing ? draft : null);

One slot. It holds the draft as it was immediately before the replacement, and the button only exists while it is full:

{undo && (
  <Button variant="ghost" onClick={() => { setDraft(undo); setUndo(null); }}>
    <Undo2Icon /> Undo
  </Button>
)}

The draft is a plain object of strings and small arrays, so storing a copy of it costs nothing and restoring it is one setState. The first suggestion sets undo to null, because there is nothing to go back to and a disabled Undo button is a worse answer than no Undo button.

Saving, and the question that only exists on one of the two routes 

const [saving, runSave] = useAction();

const next = mode === "setup" ? `/campaigns/new/${campaignId}` : `/campaigns/${campaignId}/outreach`;

const save = () =>
  runSave(
    () => saveProposalAction(campaignId, asInput(draft)),
    (r) => {
      setDirty(false);
      setOpen(null);
      if (mode === "outreach" && r.redraft) setRedraft(r.redraft);
      else router.push(next);
    },
  );

useAction is an 18-line file over useTransition that runs a server action, turns its result into a toast, and calls onOk only on success. Every mutating button in the app goes through it, which is why the whole codebase has one idea of what "saving" looks like.

mode decides where Cancel and a successful save go, so the same component is a step in a wizard on one route and a settings screen on another, without either route knowing about the other.

And then the case that only exists in the running-campaign route. Changing the proposal while emails are already drafted and waiting means those drafts were written from details that are now out of date, so instead of navigating away, the save opens a dialog:

Rewrite the 7 emails waiting to go out?

They were written from your old details. Rewritten emails wait for your approval again. It takes about a minute.

with a checkbox that only appears if some of those drafts were edited by hand:

{edited > 0 && (
  <Label htmlFor={id}>
    {edited === total ? `Replace your own edits too (you edited all ${edited})` : ...}
  </Label>
)}

Default off. The thing a person typed is the thing a bulk action must not quietly destroy, which is the same rule as typedAsks, two screens apart.

What the shape is worth

Five pieces of state carry all of it: draft, open, dirty, typedAsks and undo. No form library, no reducer, no field-level validation layer. The reason that stays manageable is that the screen is not really a form. It is a document that arrives written, with the parts you can change marked, and a single save at the bottom.

If you want the public version of the thinking behind the numbers in it, the sponsorship cost calculator is the same arithmetic with nothing hidden, and the pricing page describes what Nakodo does with a proposal once it is saved. The suggestion's own instructions and the fee tables stay in the app, where they belong.

title: Turn your REST APIs into MCP tools with Google Cloud API Gateway

title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
description:
arXiv:2610.27192v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.

title: Unified Sharp Bounds on Probabilities of Causation
description:
arXiv:2610.27398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) have developed steadily, from the binary measures first introduced by Pearl to the non-binary setting recently studied by Shu et al. As the theory has matured, PoCs have found applications in a growing range of areas, including personalized medicine, marketing and legal attribution. Shu et al. proposed closed-form bounds for multi-valued treatments and outcomes and proved them valid, but left their sharpness in high dimensions open. We close this gap with a mathematical proof. We further show that $\PNS$, $\PSub$, $\PRep$ and $\PN$ are all special cases of a single, more general formula. Combined with their equivalence classes, this settles the question of sharp bounds for discrete PoCs from experimental and observational data: in every dimension, they are given in closed form by a single theorem.

title: How I run my content pipeline with two AI bots, Cloudflare R2 and Postiz
description:
I'm a dev trying to grow on X, LinkedIn and dev.to without spending my whole day posting. so I set up a small pipeline where AI bots do the repetitive part and I only show up twice a day, around 8h and 19h (Brazil time), to do the stuff that needs a human, like replying to people.

this is a build log of how it works today. it's not finished and some parts broke along the way, so I'll show those too.

the setup in one paragraph

there are two bots. a creative bot makes the images (carousels) and the Instagram posts in Portuguese. a manager bot owns everything else: it uploads the files to a public Cloudflare R2 bucket, plans the day, writes the English posts for X, LinkedIn and dev.to, and schedules them through Postiz. I only talk to the manager. the manager talks to the creative bot.

why two bots and not one

at first each bot did a bit of everything. the creative bot was also uploading to storage, also scheduling stuff, and I had no idea who did what. when something broke I didn't know where to look.

so I split it by responsibility:

  • creative bot: makes the art, drops it in a handoff folder, tells the manager it's ready, and schedules Instagram once it gets the public URLs back
  • manager bot: storage, calendar, scheduling for every English channel, and my daily checklists

the creative bot doesn't have write access to the bucket anymore. one writer, one source of truth.

R2 as the archive

I didn't want my disk (or the bots' disk) filling up with PNGs. so the rule is: if it's published, it lives in R2, and the local copy gets deleted.

the layout is boring on purpose:


<insta|x>/YYYY/MM/<YYYY-MM-DD>_<HHhMM>_<slug>/

    <slug>_01.png

    <slug>_02.png

    notes.txt

    caption.txt

so a carousel scheduled for 12h today about a company called Conductor ends up in x/2026/10/2026-10-21_12h00_conductor/. there's also an x/latest.txt that just contains the prefix of the day's X carousel, so any routine can find today's files without listing the bucket.

notes.txt is the important one. it has the numbers for the case, where they came from, when they were checked, and which X handles were verified. the post writer is only allowed to use numbers that are in that file. that rule alone killed most of the "AI made up a stat" problems.

uploading with TypeScript

R2 speaks the S3 API, so the upload is just @aws-sdk/client-s3 pointed at the R2 endpoint:


// upload.ts

import { readdir, readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

import { join } from "node:path";

import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";



const s3 = new S3Client({

  region: "auto",

  endpoint: process.env.R2_ENDPOINT!,

  credentials: {

    accessKeyId: process.env.R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID!,

    secretAccessKey: process.env.R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY!,

  },

});



const BUCKET = process.env.R2_BUCKET!;

const PUBLIC_BASE = process.env.R2_PUBLIC_BASE!; // your r2.dev or custom domain



const contentType = (name: string) =>

  name.endsWith(".png") ? "image/png" : "text/plain; charset=utf-8";



export async function uploadFolder(localDir: string, prefix: string) {

  const names = (await readdir(localDir)).sort();

  const urls: string[] = [];



  for (const name of names) {

    const Body = await readFile(join(localDir, name));

    await s3.send(

      new PutObjectCommand({

        Bucket: BUCKET,

        Key: `${prefix}${name}`,

        Body,

        ContentType: contentType(name),

      }),

    );

    urls.push(`${PUBLIC_BASE}/${prefix}${name}`);

  }

  return urls;

}



export async function setLatest(prefix: string) {

  await s3.send(

    new PutObjectCommand({

      Bucket: BUCKET,

      Key: "x/latest.txt",

      Body: prefix,

      ContentType: "text/plain; charset=utf-8",

    }),

  );

}

keys come from env vars, never from the code. and set the ContentType, or the public URL may download the PNG instead of showing it, which breaks things downstream.

checking before deleting anything

after upload the manager checks every public URL returns 200 before it deletes the local copy. Node 18+ has fetch built in, so no extra deps:


// verify.ts

import { rm } from "node:fs/promises";

import { uploadFolder, setLatest } from "./upload";



async function allOk(urls: string[]) {

  const res = await Promise.all(urls.map((u) => fetch(u, { method: "HEAD" })));

  const bad = urls.filter((_, i) => res[i].status !== 200);

  if (bad.length) console.error("not public yet:", bad);

  return bad.length === 0;

}



const local = "handoff/x/2026-10-21_12h00_conductor";

const prefix = "x/2026/10/2026-10-21_12h00_conductor/";



const urls = await uploadFolder(local, prefix);

if (await allOk(urls)) {

  await setLatest(prefix);

  await rm(local, { recursive: true });

}

if any URL fails, nothing gets deleted and latest.txt doesn't move. boring, but it means I never lose a file.

a tiny Go check

I also wanted a dumb health check I can run from anywhere, so here's one in Go. it reads latest.txt over plain HTTP and checks that the first slide is actually there:


package main



import (

    "fmt"

    "io"

    "net/http"

    "os"

    "path"

    "strings"

)



func main() {

    base := os.Getenv("R2_PUBLIC_BASE")



    res, err := http.Get(base + "/x/latest.txt")

    if err != nil || res.StatusCode != 200 {

        fmt.Println("latest.txt not reachable")

        os.Exit(1)

    }

    defer res.Body.Close()



    b, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)

    prefix := strings.TrimSpace(string(b))

    slug := strings.SplitN(path.Base(prefix), "_", 3)[2]



    slide := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s%s_01.png", base, prefix, slug)

    head, err := http.Head(slide)

    if err != nil || head.StatusCode != 200 {

        fmt.Println("missing:", slide)

        os.Exit(1)

    }

    fmt.Println("ok:", prefix)

}

no SDK, no credentials. if the public side works, the bots can work.

Postiz for scheduling

Postiz is the piece that actually posts. it has an MCP server, so the manager bot can call it like a tool: upload media from a URL, get the schema for each platform, schedule a post with comments, list what's queued.

the nice part is that one call shape works for all channels. a post is a list where the first item is the post and the next items are comments. that's how sources end up in the first comment.

for media, I don't upload files from disk. the bot passes the public R2 URL to Postiz's upload-from-URL tool, gets back a hosted path, and attaches that. that's also why R2 has to be public.

the daily routines

everything runs on a schedule (Sao Paulo time):

  • 7h30: the morning plan. schedules the original X posts for the day, then sends me a checklist with replies to write and one quote tweet. I copy, paste, done
  • 10h: carousel day. reads x/latest.txt, reads notes.txt, uploads the PNGs to Postiz, writes the English text and schedules it on X for 12h
  • 18h30: the evening check. confirms the day's posts actually went out and sends me fresh replies plus a reminder to answer people who commented
  • Sunday 18h: drafts next week's posts so I can veto anything I don't like

the routines never ask me stuff during the day. if a step needs me, it goes into the 8h or 19h checklist. that was the only way this was going to survive my real life.

stuff that broke (lessons)

Postiz strips links on X. my first test post went out without the source link. now the source goes in the first comment as text, naming the creator and where to find it. no URL needed, and the person gets tagged, which is better anyway.

blank lines disappear. content goes in as HTML paragraphs, and two paragraphs in a row get glued together on X. to keep a visible blank line I need an empty

between them.

280 characters is real. I'm not on premium, so the writer counts characters before scheduling, and long ideas become a short post plus comments.

Postiz can't reply to other people. it can post and comment on my own posts, but not reply to someone else's tweet, and it can't delete something that already went live. so replies stay manual, which is why my checklists exist.

it wrote like a robot. the first posts were too clean. I had the bot read my real tweets and match them: lowercase, short blocks, no hashtags, no emojis.

no generic opinions. every original post needs a real number and a real source, usually a bigger account or founder.

what's next

LinkedIn and dev.to just joined the pipeline. LinkedIn gets the day's case rewritten in first person with the carousel images, dev.to gets one technical post a week like this one, in TypeScript or Go. all in English, only Instagram stays in Portuguese.

if you're running something similar, I'm curious what you automated and what you kept manual. drop it in the comments.

I post indie app breakdowns daily on X @felipe_rohde (https://x.com/felipe_rohde) and Instagram @feliperohde.dev (https://instagram.com/feliperohde.dev)

title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.

title: Preference-Aware Pareto Steering for Multi-Task Speech LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.27200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) perform multiple tasks, including automatic speech recognition (ASR), timestamp prediction (TS), and speech translation (ST). Joint training of speech LLMs creates task trade-offs, yet standard training with fixed loss weights does not generally control the resulting trade-off according to deployment preferences. To address this, we propose Endpoint-Anchored Preference-Aware Sampling Uniformly along the Pareto Front (EA-SURF), an a priori method that adapts scalarization weights so that the resulting task trade-off reflects the desired preference. EA-SURF retains the standard weighted-loss training pipeline, tracking the current model's performance relative to each task-specific reference and adapting the scalarization weights as training proceeds. We theoretically show that EA-SURF can match a desired preference, with the update becoming stationary at the target under checkable regularity conditions. Across six three-objective speech LLM requests, EA-SURF empirically converges toward the requested targets and increases endpoint-inclusive normalized hypervolume by 17.8% over fixed loss weighting.

title: Gemini 4 Argon now available on AI Gateway
description:
Gemini 4 Argon from Google is now available on AI Gateway.

Gemini 4 Argon is built for coding, agentic work, and complex reasoning. It has a 1M token context window, accepts text, image, PDF, and video input, and supports tool calling.

On coding tasks, Gemini 4 Argon builds features, fixes bugs, and researches unfamiliar codebases, carrying longer tasks through multiple steps. The model also reads dense diagrams, spreadsheets, layout-heavy documents, and video, which suits tasks like a financial analysis spread across several spreadsheet tabs. Beyond code, it handles work in finance, health, and law, and hard problems in math and science. Gemini 4 Argon uses thinking levels (low, medium, and high) instead of thinking budgets.

title: VitronEdit: Universal Visual Editing across Images, Videos, and 3D Scenes
description:
arXiv:2610.27049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data-scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry-aware post-training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera-pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi-view consistency. The project page: https://vitron-llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.

title: Spring Boot Integration Tests Are Slow and Messy: Here's How to Fix Them
description:
Integration test suites can get slow without anyone deciding they should. Another @SpringBootTest here, some in-memory H2 wiring there, a flaky test "fixed" with a stray @DirtiesContext – and eventually the suite is the thing everyone quietly dreads before merging a PR, flaky on every other CI run, with nobody able to point to the one change that caused it.

Spring Boot integration tests do real work, validating behavior across controllers, services, repositories, databases, and messaging systems. That breadth is what makes them valuable, and it's also what makes them expensive. When you wire together a real application context, connect to databases, and exercise multiple layers in a single test run, costs add up fast. The question is whether those costs are unavoidable or whether your test suite pays for things it doesn't need.

This article walks through the specific mechanisms that make Spring Boot integration suites slow and brittle, and the practical strategies that address them. You'll also see how Kotlin's extension functions, DSLs, data classes, named arguments, and scope functions reduce the boilerplate that accumulates in integration test code over time, making the resulting suite easier to maintain regardless of the language you're already using.

Why Spring Boot integration tests slow down over time

Most suites start with a single @SpringBootTest class and a handful of tests. That first test class is harmless. The problems compound when a second developer adds another @SpringBootTest with a slightly different configuration, a third adds @ActiveProfiles("integration") to one class and @ActiveProfiles("test") to another, and a fourth drops a @DirtiesContext on a test that was flaky. Six months later, the suite boots five or six separate application contexts across a single run, and nobody realizes it.

Before you optimize anything, profile the actual bottleneck. Spring Boot's context initialization is usually the dominant cost, but database container startup and heavyweight test setup can be significant too. Run your tests with -Dspring.test.context.cache.maxSize=10 alongside JUnit's --report-dir output to see how many contexts are being created. If you see more than two or three distinct contexts in a moderate-sized suite, context proliferation is your problem.

Nearly every fix in this article reduces to a single idea: repeated initialization is the thing you're paying for, not the tests themselves. Whether that initialization is a Spring application context, a database container, or heavyweight test data, the fastest fix is almost always to do it once and reuse it rather than make each instance cheaper.

Keep the number of Spring application contexts small

@SpringBootTest loads your full application context, all beans, all configuration, all auto-configuration. For a non-trivial Spring Boot application, that initialization can take several seconds. The Spring TestContext Framework caches loaded contexts and reuses them across compatible tests, so the first test in a group pays the startup cost and subsequent tests don't.

The cache key is a composite of everything that affects the context, including configuration classes, active profiles, property sources, and context customizers. Change any of these between two test classes and Spring boots a second context. Common cache-busting patterns include using different @ActiveProfiles values across test classes, importing different @TestConfiguration classes with incompatible beans, and overusing @DirtiesContext.

@DirtiesContext signals that a test has modified the application context and that Spring should discard it. Using it broadly because a single test is flaky trades a flakiness problem for a performance problem. The test that genuinely modifies shared mutable state may warrant it, but the test that just needs a clean database table doesn't.

The practical target is a single shared context for your full integration tests, achieved by keeping configuration consistent. A shared base class or a single shared @TestConfiguration import applied consistently across test classes is the most reliable way to ensure the cache key matches. In Kotlin, the recommended approach combines constructor injection with @TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL), which avoids lateinit vars and keeps test fields immutable:

@SpringBootTest
@TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL)
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest(
    private val orderService: OrderService,
    private val orderRepository: OrderRepository
) {

    @Test
    fun `placing an order persists it to the database`() {
        val order = orderService.place(OrderRequest(productId = "p-42", quantity = 3))
        val saved = orderRepository.findById(order.id)
        assert(saved.isPresent)
    }
}

The Kotlin plugin.spring compiler plugin automatically opens Spring-annotated classes, resolving the friction Kotlin's default final classes would otherwise cause with Spring's proxying, so no additional configuration is needed for this to work correctly.

None of this means avoiding @SpringBootTest. A full application context is the right tool whenever a test genuinely needs to exercise behavior that spans multiple layers, for example, an HTTP request that flows through a controller, a service, and a repository. The goal isn't eliminating full-context tests; it's making sure you're not accidentally paying the full-context startup cost two, three, or five times over in a single suite when one shared context would do.

Test slices selectively, not as a default performance fix

Spring Boot's test slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JdbcTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest) load only the portion of your application relevant to a specific concern. A @DataJpaTest context contains JPA repositories and the JPA layer, nothing else. A @WebMvcTest context contains MVC infrastructure without starting a full servlet container.

Slices are useful when a test genuinely exercises only one layer. A repository test that validates a complex JPQL query doesn't need your HTTP layer. A controller test that validates request validation logic doesn't need your database. For those cases, a slice gives you a faster, more focused test.

The trap is treating slices as a general performance fix. Each distinct slice configuration that differs from another creates its own application context. A suite with ten @DataJpaTest classes using the same configuration shares one context. A suite with five different slice types, each loaded with different imports, creates five separate contexts, and the cumulative startup cost can exceed that of a single, well-shared full context.

Use a slice when it provides a meaningful testing boundary for the layer under test. For tests that validate behavior spanning multiple layers, prioritize reusing a small number of shared full contexts over reaching for a narrower slice.

Use Testcontainers without repeatedly starting containers

H2 is a convenient in-memory database for local testing, but it doesn't behave like PostgreSQL or MySQL in ways that affect production correctness. PostgreSQL enforces stricter type checking, so implicit casts that H2 accepts silently will fail at runtime against Postgres. Indexing semantics differ, and constraint enforcement, particularly around deferred constraints and transaction isolation, behaves differently. A green test suite against H2 can mask bugs that surface only under the production database engine.

Testcontainers solves this by running your actual database engine in a Docker container during tests. The startup cost is real (a PostgreSQL container cold-start typically takes a few seconds), but you pay it once per suite, not once per test class.

With Spring Boot 3.1+, the @ServiceConnection annotation eliminates the boilerplate of manually wiring container ports into Spring's datasource configuration, and it's unchanged under Spring Boot 4. Declare the container in a shared @TestConfiguration class and import it wherever needed:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    fun postgresContainer(): PostgreSQLContainer<*> =
        PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine")
}

For @DataJpaTest slices, Spring attempts to replace your datasource with an embedded database by default. Suppress that behavior with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE) and import your shared container configuration:

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class BookmarkRepositoryTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val bookmarkRepository: BookmarkRepository
) {

    @Test
    fun `should find bookmark by id`() {
        val bookmark = bookmarkRepository.save(
            Bookmark(title = "Kotlin Docs", url = "https://kotlinlang.org")
        )
        val found = bookmarkRepository.findById(bookmark.id!!)
        assertThat(found).isPresent
        assertThat(found.get().title).isEqualTo("Kotlin Docs")
    }
}

Two dependency details are worth getting right here if you're on Spring Boot 4. First, @DataJpaTest itself now lives in spring-boot-data-jpa-test, pulled in via the spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test starter, not the plain spring-boot-starter-test. Second, @AutoConfigureTestDatabase moved too: it's now org.springframework.boot.jdbc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureTestDatabase, shipped in a separate spring-boot-starter-jdbc-test starter that spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test doesn't pull in automatically, so you need to add it explicitly:

testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test")
testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc-test")
testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-testcontainers")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:junit-jupiter")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:postgresql")

@ServiceConnection itself, by contrast, didn't move; it's still org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection on Spring Boot 4. Not everything in the test-support space was reshuffled, just the test-slice annotations and the autoconfiguration classes that back them.

If you prefer declaring the container directly in the test class, Kotlin's companion objects with @JvmStatic ensure the container lifecycle spans all methods in the class rather than restarting for each test:

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    companion object {
        @Container
        @ServiceConnection
        @JvmStatic
        val postgres = PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine").apply {
            withDatabaseName("testdb")
        }
    }

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var orderRepository: OrderRepository

    @Test
    fun `should save and retrieve an order`() {
        // test body
    }
}

The goal is to combine a reused container with a reused Spring context. When your test configuration is consistent, Spring's cache keeps the same context alive across all test classes that share the same container configuration, and the database container itself stays running for the duration of the build.

For database state, build only what each test actually needs. A test that validates order retrieval doesn't need a populated product catalog. Lightweight, targeted setup with @BeforeEach and @AfterEach cleanup (or transaction rollback via @Transactional) keeps tests isolated without requiring full database resets between every run.

A practical strategy for a fast integration test suite

The context sharing model below keeps a suite fast by mapping each test type to its context and container lifecycle:

The diagram below is the editable Mermaid source — useful if you want to adjust colors or labels. A rendered image follows it.

flowchart TD
    A[Full Integration Tests<br/>@SpringBootTest + Testcontainers] --> B[Single shared<br/>Spring context]
    C[Slice Tests<br/>@DataJpaTest etc.] --> D[Shared slice<br/>context per type]
    E[Unit Tests] --> F[No Spring context]
    B --> G[Postgres container<br/>started once]
    D --> G

The strategy has seven parts:

  1. Keep one @TestConfiguration class that declares your Testcontainers beans with @ServiceConnection and import it consistently across all tests that need it.
  2. Align profiles. If some test classes use @ActiveProfiles("test") and others don't declare a profile at all, Spring treats them as different configurations and creates separate contexts.
  3. Reserve @DirtiesContext for tests that genuinely modify application-level state, not for tests with database state issues. Database state cleanup belongs in @AfterEach or via transactional rollback.
  4. Reach for a test slice only when the test's meaningful scope is genuinely limited to that layer. A repository test for a complex query is a good slice candidate. A test that exercises an HTTP endpoint through to the database is not.
  5. Start containers once and reuse them. Use withReuse(true) on your container definition to persist containers across JVM runs during local development, where it cuts iteration time substantially.
  6. Build only the database state each test actually needs. Seeding a full product catalog for a test that only checks order retrieval adds setup cost without adding coverage.
  7. Measure before and after changes. Run the test suite twice and enable DEBUG-level logging on org.springframework.test.context.cache (or equivalent context cache reporting) to confirm that context creation counts dropped and wall-clock time improved.

Make integration tests readable with Kotlin

Kotlin reduces the boilerplate that accumulates around integration tests, meaning less noise when a test fails and less maintenance when fixtures change. The techniques below don't make a suite faster on their own; they make an already-fast suite easier to read and maintain, which is what keeps it fast six months from now instead of sliding back into the state this article opened with.

Data classes eliminate the Java builder pattern for test fixtures. A Bookmark data class with sensible defaults can be constructed with a single named argument for the one field a specific test cares about:

data class BookmarkFixture(
    val title: String = "Default Title",
    val url: String = "https://kotlinlang.org",
    val isActive: Boolean = true
)

Named arguments make test data construction self-documenting. BookmarkFixture(title = "Archived Post", isActive = false) is readable without a builder chain.

Extension functions let you add setup utilities or assertion helpers directly to Spring test classes without inheritance hierarchies. A setup helper for building a JSON POST request:

fun MockMvc.postJson(url: String, payload: Any, objectMapper: ObjectMapper): ResultActionsDsl =
    post(url) {
        contentType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
        content = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(payload)
        accept = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
    }

If you're on Spring Boot 4, the ObjectMapper import above is worth double-checking. Spring Boot 4 defaults to Jackson 3, pulled in through a new spring-boot-starter-jackson module, and Jackson 3's base package moved from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson, so the type you inject here is tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, not the Jackson 2 class of the same simple name. If you're posting a Kotlin data class as the request body, also add tools.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin (the Jackson 3 equivalent of the familiar jackson-module-kotlin) as a dependency. Without it, Jackson can't resolve the data class's primary-constructor parameters, and the request fails with a 400 instead of a compile error, making it easy to lose an afternoon to.

And an assertion helper, scoped to the type it asserts on rather than to a test class:

fun Bookmark.assertIsActiveWithTitle(expectedTitle: String) {
    assertTrue(isActive)
    assertEquals(expectedTitle, title)
}

Kotlin DSLs built on extension functions and lambdas-with-receivers are what make the postJson helper above readable in the first place: post(url) { contentType = ...; content = ... } reads as configuration, not as a chain of setter calls. Spring's own MockMvc Kotlin DSL (post, get, .andExpect { status { isCreated() } }) follows the same pattern, and it's worth reaching for directly rather than only through a wrapping extension function when a test doesn't need one.

Scope functions (apply, also, run) clean up construction and setup code at the declaration site without extracting helper methods. apply is the one you'll reach for most, configuring an object and returning it, as in the companion-object container declaration from the Testcontainers section:

@JvmStatic
val postgres = PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine").apply {
    withDatabaseName("testdb")
    withUsername("test")
    withPassword("test")
}

also is useful when you want to do something with a value, like logging it, without changing what gets returned, and run is useful for computing a value inline from a short block instead of a separate val statement:

val fixture = BookmarkFixture(title = "Kotlin Docs").also {
    println("creating bookmark fixture: ${it.title}")
}
val request = run {
    BookmarkRequest(title = fixture.title, url = fixture.url, isActive = fixture.isActive)
}

Put together, a small integration test combining a fixture, the postJson extension function, and a scope function reads as a short, flat sequence of steps rather than a wall of setup:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.MOCK)
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
@TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL)
class BookmarkControllerIntegrationTest(
    private val mockMvc: MockMvc,
    private val objectMapper: ObjectMapper
) {

    @Test
    fun `creating a bookmark returns it in the response`() {
        val fixture = BookmarkFixture(title = "Kotlin Docs").also {
            println("creating bookmark fixture: ${it.title}")
        }
        val request = run { BookmarkRequest(title = fixture.title, url = fixture.url, isActive = fixture.isActive) }

        mockMvc.postJson("/api/bookmarks", request, objectMapper)
            .andExpect { status { isCreated() } }
    }
}

Note that @AutoConfigureMockMvc moved packages in Spring Boot 4 too, same as @WebMvcTest: it's org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureMockMvc now, shipped in spring-boot-webmvc-test via the spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test starter.

These are incremental improvements, not architectural changes. You can introduce Kotlin test code into an existing Java Spring project without touching production code, which makes it a low-risk starting point for teams evaluating what Kotlin brings to their codebase.

Organize integration tests for long-term maintainability

A suite that's fast today becomes slow again if there's no shared understanding of its structure. Keep three distinct categories separate: unit tests (no Spring context, run fast), slice tests (partial context, targeted), and full integration tests (full context, shared container). Mixing these in the same test source set makes it difficult to see at a glance why a build is slow. Consistent naming helps here too; a suffix convention like *Test for units and slices versus *IntegrationTest for full-context tests, or separate source directories, lets you tell at a glance (and in CI timing reports) which category is growing.

Integration tests should assert on business behavior, not implementation details. A test that verifies the correct HTTP status code and response body when a user places an order is durable. A test that verifies the exact SQL statement executed against the database is brittle and couples the test to an implementation that can change without breaking the business requirement.

Avoid duplicating setup logic across test classes just because it's easier than sharing it. A second @TestConfiguration import that's nearly identical to an existing one is exactly the kind of inconsistency that busts the context cache described earlier, so the maintainability concern and the performance concern point to the same fix.

Shared base classes are worth using when they genuinely simplify the suite, typically for consistent annotation setup and shared infrastructure, and worth avoiding when they become a dumping ground for setup logic that only some tests need. A shared annotations file (using Kotlin's @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) composed annotations) is often cleaner:

@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS)
@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
@TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL)
annotation class IntegrationTest

Any @SpringBootTest class that uses @IntegrationTest instead gets a consistent cache key by definition, because the annotation composition is identical.

Treat test suite performance as an ongoing metric. Add context creation count and total suite duration to your CI output so regressions are visible before they compound. A suite that takes four minutes today will take twenty-two again in six months if nobody is watching the cost.

The fixes that move the needle on Spring Boot integration test performance share a common thread: reducing repeated initialization. Keep your Spring application contexts few and consistent so the cache does its job. Start Testcontainers infrastructure once and keep it alive across the test run. Use test slices when they define a genuine testing boundary, and avoid them when the goal is just a smaller context. Measure before and after so you know which bottleneck you actually solved.

Kotlin's language features sit naturally on top of this foundation. Data classes, extension functions, DSLs, named arguments, and scope functions cut boilerplate without changing how Spring tests work, making them a practical addition to a Java Spring project even before you change any production code. The formal partnership between JetBrains and Spring reflects this kind of incremental integration, with Kotlin as a natural evolution of the JVM development experience that complements your existing ecosystem. For a sense of what that looks like at scale, Verifone's architect discussed running Kotlin in mission-critical payment systems at KotlinConf, where reliability requirements are just as unforgiving as anything a slow test suite is standing in for.

title: WaveSpec: Multi-Spectral Iris Presentation Attack Detection via Wavelength-Conditioned Spectral Coherence Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.27608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multispectral iris presentation attack detection benefits from observing the same iris across multiple near-infrared wavelengths, but existing methods often use wavelength information mainly for conditioning or fusion. This can limit their ability to explicitly model whether the spectral response of a sample is coherent across bands. In this paper, we propose \textbf{WaveSpec}, a multispectral iris PAD framework that performs feature-level spectral coherence adaptation. Each NIR band is first encoded with a DINOv2 backbone. The proposed Set Conditioned Spectral Coherence Adapter then updates each band feature using the consensus of the available spectral set, the band-specific deviation from that consensus, and wavelength identity. The adapted features are projected into structural, spectral, and anomaly representations, adaptively pooled, and classified as bona fide or attack. We evaluate WaveSpec on the MSIrPAD benchmark under a strict cross-artefact protocol, where the model is trained with one presentation attack instrument and tested on unseen attacks. WaveSpec reduces the average D-EER from 8.45\% for SpectraIrisPAD to 3.33\%, and reduces average BPCER@APCER=1\% from 43.16\% to 12.07\%. Ablation results show that the SCSA adapter and spectral residual are central to the improvement, while a band-subset analysis shows that WaveSpec remains effective under partial spectral observations and performs best when all five bands are available. The method adds only modest computational overhead, with 11.15 ms end-to-end latency per five-band sample on an NVIDIA L40S-48Q GPU.
