title: REA: Giving My Coding Agent Real Reverse-Engineering Tools (and What I Had to Verify First)
description:
Ask an AI coding agent how a program works and it will usually tell you. Fluently, in detail, and mostly from memory: what programs like that tend to do, reconstructed from training data. The actual file on your disk never gets opened.

REA changes that. This post covers what it is, what it's useful for, how I set it up, what I had to verify before I trusted it, and two tests that show it working.

What REA is

REA ("Reverse Engineer Anything") is a free, open-source, MIT-licensed tool that connects AI coding agents to real reverse-engineering software. It's published as the npm package rea-agents from the GitHub repo morluto/rea.

It works as an MCP server. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the plug standard coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI use to call outside tools. REA doesn't do the decompiling itself. It's a routing layer that picks the right engine for the target:

  • Native programs (Linux/Windows/macOS executables): Ghidra, the NSA's open-source reverse-engineering suite, or IDA/Hopper if you have them.
  • Android apps (APKs): JADX, the standard open-source Android decompiler.
  • JavaScript/Electron apps, .NET assemblies, websites, saved network captures: built-in static analysis, no extra engine needed.

What comes back isn't a chat answer. It's structured evidence: decompiled code, strings, addresses, cross-references, an ID for each finding, and a list of limitations, meaning what this analysis can't tell you. Everything runs locally.

The project moves fast and has attracted copycats, so its README says to install only from morluto/rea, rea.tools, or the rea-agents npm package. There's also an older @morluto/rea package on npm from the same author, stuck at version 0.2.1. The current one is rea-agents.

What it's useful for

  • Learning how software actually works: pick a feature and read the real code behind it.
  • Security practice: crackmes, CTF binaries, malware-analysis exercises.
  • Checking what an app really does: why does this app want location access? What does it send, and where?
  • Debugging your own builds: what actually ended up in the shipped bundle or binary.

One rule I hold to: only analyse software you own, open-source projects, or things you're explicitly allowed to examine. REA's own docs scope it to lawful research, education, interoperability and authorised analysis.

How I set it up

My goal was simple: type rea, land in an agent session with every tool ready, and keep all of it away from my everyday agent setup, which touches production scripts.

1. A local install, pinned

Rather than a global install, I installed it into its own folder at an exact version, with dependency install scripts disabled:

mkdir -p ~/rea-sandbox && cd ~/rea-sandbox
npm init -y
npm install --ignore-scripts --save-exact rea-agents@6.7.0

It needs Node 22.19+ (or 24.11+, or 26+).

2. A separate agent profile

REA's installer registers itself with whichever agents you choose. Claude Code reads its configuration from a directory you can override with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and REA's setup respects that. So everything went into a second profile:

CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-rea ./node_modules/.bin/rea setup --client claude_code --dry-run

--dry-run prints exactly which files it will write. It wanted two paths, both inside ~/.claude-rea: the tool registration and a workflow "skill". It also detected four other agents on my machine and left them alone, because only claude_code was selected. After reading the plan, I ran it again with --yes instead of --dry-run.

3. Ghidra, for native programs

Ghidra needs a Java 21 runtime. I took the release straight from the NSA's GitHub and checked the SHA-256 published in the release notes:

sudo apt install openjdk-21-jdk-headless
gh release download Ghidra_12.1.4_build -R NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra -p 'ghidra_*.zip'
sha256sum ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_20260921.zip   # compare with the release notes
unzip ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_20260921.zip

Then I re-ran setup with GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR pointing at the unpacked folder. REA checks the installation and saves the path into the agent registration. 12.1.4 is the version REA lists as supported.

4. JADX, for Android apps

This was the part that needed the most care, so it gets its own section below. The short version: REA talks to JADX through a small third-party wrapper called jadx-headless-mcp, pinned to version 0.7.1. I built it from source, confirmed my build matched the published release byte for byte, and pointed REA at it with REA_JADX_MCP_JAR.

5. One command: rea

A short script in ~/.local/bin/rea ties it together:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# rea          → open the agent in the REA profile, all tools wired
# rea <args>   → run the REA CLI itself (rea doctor, rea analyze FILE, ...)
SANDBOX="$HOME/rea-sandbox"
export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="$HOME/.claude-rea"
export GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR="$SANDBOX/ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC"
export JAVA_HOME="/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64"
export REA_JADX_MCP_JAR="$SANDBOX/jadx/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar"

if [ $# -gt 0 ]; then
  exec "$SANDBOX/node_modules/.bin/rea" "$@"
fi
cd "$SANDBOX/targets" && exec claude

The two-mode design matters. rea is also the name of REA's own CLI, and the agent inside the session calls it. If bare rea only launched the agent, the agent calling rea doctor would try to launch another agent inside itself.

Finally, a settings.json in the new profile pre-approves REA's tools ("allow": ["mcp__rea"]), so analysis doesn't stop for a permission prompt on every call. That approval exists in this profile only.

Health check:

rea doctor --client claude_code --skill --json   # healthy: true, ghidra + jadx available

What I had to verify first

The install was an afternoon. Most of that afternoon went on one question I didn't expect to be the hard part: what does each check actually prove?

The profile isn't a sandbox

A separate profile felt like isolation. REA's own docs are blunt about what it is:

Both routes control which sessions discover REA's MCP server and skill. They leave shell commands, filesystem access and network access available.

The profile controls which tools the agent is offered, not what it can reach. It still runs as my user and can still read my files and use the network. A real boundary needs a separate OS account or a container. For learning and inspecting software I'm allowed to inspect, that's fine. But it's a menu, not a wall, and I wrote it down in those words.

The commit that "didn't exist"

REA's third-party notices pin the JADX wrapper to commit 5844800a, the source its authors say they audited. The wrapper's v0.7.1 release tag points to a different commit, 7dc6b5e3, and GitHub said the two have no common ancestor.

That reads like a supply-chain incident. It wasn't, and the way to check is worth knowing. Every git commit points to a tree, the hash of the complete file contents:

git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.7.1 https://github.com/1013503897/jadx-headless-mcp.git
cd jadx-headless-mcp && git rev-parse 'HEAD^{tree}'
# 0f280ac59d851c4a126f9f5efbe26366d2fd033c — same tree as REA's pinned commit

Same tree, same date, same message. The only difference was the author name. Someone had rewritten the repo's history to change how their name appears, which gives every commit a new hash while leaving every file identical.

Commit hashes identify history. Tree hashes identify content.

The checksum proved the download, not the source

The release offers a prebuilt JAR and a .sha256 file. The hash matched. But both came from the same release page, published by the same account. A matching checksum proves the file wasn't corrupted on the way to my disk. It doesn't prove the JAR was built from the audited source. A tampered release would ship a tampered hash, and it would still match.

A checksum from the same source as the file proves integrity, not origin.

The Ghidra hash had the same shape: it sits on the same page as the download. I trust it because of who publishes it, which is a judgement about the publisher, not something the hash proves.

Build it yourself and compare bytes

The only real test was to build from source. First I read the build script: two well-known Gradle plugins and standard libraries from Maven Central and Google, with no custom download steps and no shell commands. Then I checked the bundled Gradle wrapper. That's the small JAR that fetches the build tool, and a classic place to hide something. Its hash matched the one Gradle publishes on its own site, a different publisher, so that check actually means something:

sha256sum gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar
curl -sL https://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-9.7.1-wrapper.jar.sha256

The build needs a JDK 17 toolchain:

sudo apt install openjdk-17-jdk-headless
JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64 ./gradlew --no-daemon \
  -Dorg.gradle.java.installations.paths=/usr/lib/jvm/java-17-openjdk-amd64 \
  shadowJar -x test
sha256sum build/libs/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar

My agent refused to run that build itself. Its safety layer treats executing a freshly cloned repo's build scripts as running outside code, and it held that line even after I approved it. I ran it by hand, which is the right division of labour.

The build is configured to be reproducible: timestamps stripped and file order sorted, so the same source gives the same bytes. Mine came out as:

6e5eacf500b64292bfb73c49797c1958f6ee44646e43e868039ae7feb573ff75

The release JAR's hash is exactly the same: 6e5eacf500b64292bfb73c49797c1958f6ee44646e43e868039ae7feb573ff75.

Byte-identical. Now the prebuilt JAR is proven. That's not because its own hash file says so. It's because an independent build from audited source produced exactly the same file.

A reproducible build turns a checksum from a claim into a test.

Two real tests

A Linux program, with Ghidra

The danger with an AI explaining code is a fluent answer from memory. So the first test used a program every model already "knows": the base64 utility, copied from my own system. I asked how it decides between encoding and decoding, and to show the code behind the -d flag.

What came back was specific to the file, not to base64 in general:

  • The binary is stripped (no function names left), so it identified functions by address.
  • It found the string decode at file offset 0x71ff, referenced from the long-options table that's passed to getopt_long.
  • It showed the option loop comparing against 100 (the character code for d) and setting a one-byte flag. A single later branch reads that flag to choose between the encode and decode paths.
  • It decompiled the four-character decode routine and its 256-entry lookup table.

I checked what I could without trusting it. strings -t x base64 puts decode at 71ff and invalid input at 71f1, and the character codes are right.

What earned more trust was what it flagged. It said its function names were guesses, because they're inferred from behaviour and there are no symbols. It said its description of the decode loop was a cleaned-up reading of tangled decompiler output, not literal code. And every finding came with an evidence ID.

An Android app, with JADX

For the second test I used Binary Eye, an open-source barcode scanner from F-Droid. I compared the APK's hash with the one in F-Droid's repository index; I didn't verify the index's own signature, so by this post's standards that's a same-publisher check. Then I asked REA to inspect it. JADX loaded it in about seven seconds:

  • 2,800 classes and 930 resources. Only 20 classes still had readable names. The build's code shrinker had renamed the rest to things like bo and uu0, which is normal for release Android builds.
  • 11 permissions, including camera (obvious), plus Wi-Fi, internet, location and Bluetooth.

So the question was: why does a barcode scanner want all that?

  • Wi-Fi: explained. One of the readable classes manages Wi-Fi network suggestions. That's what runs when you scan a Wi-Fi QR code and tap "connect."
  • Internet: probably explained. A settings class stores a URL, which fits a "send scans to a server" option. The code that actually sends sits in the renamed classes and wasn't traced.
  • Location and Bluetooth: not explained in this pass.

That last line is the honest result of a seven-second look, and I'd much rather have "not explained yet" than a plausible story.

Honest limits

  • It isn't a sandbox. The separate profile hides the tools from your other sessions; it doesn't contain them. Use a separate user or a container if you need a real boundary.
  • The engines are bring-your-own. Native analysis needs Ghidra, IDA or Hopper, and Android needs the JADX wrapper. Several other targets need their own tools too.
  • It moves fast. REA's docs say to keep it updated, but I pinned an exact version on purpose. Updating is a deliberate step, with a --dry-run first.
  • Evidence still needs checking. REA is far better than an agent reciting from memory, but decompiler output is a reading, not the source. Spot-check the parts you can.

What each check was actually worth

Check What it looked like What it proved
Separate agent profile Isolation Which tools the agent is offered
Hash from the same release page Authenticity The download wasn't corrupted
Hash from a different publisher Authenticity The file matches what that publisher vouches for
Matching tree hash — Two commits contain identical files
Byte-identical rebuild — The binary came from that source
Agent's explanation Analysis Only as much as you can check against the file

None of these checks was wasted. Each one just had a narrower job than its name suggested. The setup became trustworthy at the point where I stopped asking "did it pass?" and started asking "what would have to be true for this to pass while being wrong?"

title: Getting Started with AWS S3: Creating a Bucket, Uploading an Object, and Understanding Why the Object URL Says Access Denied
description:
Introduction

I'm starting a new series on AWS, and this first article covers Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), one of the most widely used services on AWS. I did this lab in my own personal AWS free-tier account, and I'll explain every term as it comes up.

By the end, you'll know how to:

  • Create an S3 bucket with a consistent naming convention
  • Read the bucket's ARN and properties
  • Upload a file to the bucket
  • Find an object's URL, and understand why opening the image works while opening the Object URL doesn't

What is Amazon S3?

Amazon S3 is an object storage service. Instead of organizing data in a traditional disk with a file system, S3 stores data as objects inside buckets. You can store and retrieve any amount of data from anywhere, and you pay only for what you use.

Three terms to know first:

  • Bucket: a container for your data. Every object in S3 lives inside a bucket.
  • Object: the thing you store. It's the file itself plus its metadata (size, type, last modified date and so on).
  • Key: the object's unique name inside the bucket. For my file, the key is datacenter.png.

Step 1: Open the S3 service

In the AWS Management Console, I typed S3 into the search bar and selected S3 (Scalable Storage in the Cloud) from the results.

This opens the Amazon S3 landing page, where Create bucket is the first thing you see.

Step 2: Create a bucket

I clicked Create bucket, and the only thing I had to provide was the bucket name. The region was already set for me (more on that below), and I left everything else at the defaults to keep things simple.

Region

I didn't pick the region on this page. The Create bucket page shows it as plain text, not a dropdown: Europe (Stockholm) eu-north-1. That's because S3 creates a bucket in whichever region your console is currently set to, and mine was already set to Stockholm. If you want a different region, switch it with the region selector in the top bar of the console before you click Create bucket.

A region is a physical geographic location where AWS runs data centers. Your bucket's data stays in the region it was created in, and the region affects latency (how close the data is to your users) and pricing.

Bucket type

I kept General purpose, which AWS recommends for most use cases. The other option, Directory, is for low-latency workloads that use a single Availability Zone.

Bucket namespace

I kept Global namespace. A namespace is the set of names in which yours has to be unique. In the global namespace, a bucket name must be unique across all AWS accounts, in every region. If someone else already has my-bucket, you can't use it. The console also offers an Account Regional namespace (labelled "recommended"). Buckets created there are unique only within your own account, so no other AWS account can ever claim the same name. I stayed with the global namespace for this lab.

Bucket name and the prefix naming convention

I named my bucket aws-lab1-rahimah.

The aws-lab1- part is a prefix I chose as a naming convention. A consistent prefix gives you three things:

  • It keeps names unique, since adding your own name or project helps avoid clashes in the global namespace.
  • It groups related resources together (aws-lab1-..., aws-lab2-...).
  • It makes resources easy to find and to clean up later.

S3 bucket names must be 3 to 63 characters long, can contain only lowercase letters, numbers, periods and hyphens, and must begin and end with a letter or number.

Default encryption

Further down the page, Default encryption was already set to Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). This means S3 automatically encrypts every new object at rest, using keys that AWS manages for you. You don't have to do anything. I left it as it was and clicked Create bucket.

S3 confirmed with a green banner: Successfully created bucket "aws-lab1-rahimah". The Objects tab shows Objects (0) because the bucket is empty.

Step 3: Look at the bucket's properties and ARN

I opened the Properties tab. The Bucket overview shows three things:

  • AWS Region: Europe (Stockholm) eu-north-1
  • Creation date: October 20, 2026
  • Amazon Resource Name (ARN): arn:aws:s3:::aws-lab1-rahimah

What is an ARN?

An Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is the unique identifier AWS gives every resource. It's how you point at a specific resource in IAM policies, logs and other services. The general shape is:

arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource

For S3 buckets, the region and account sections are empty, which is why you see three colons in a row (:::). The bucket name is the final part.

The Properties tab also shows two settings that were off by default:

  • Bucket Versioning: Disabled. Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object, so you can recover from accidental overwrites or deletions. With it disabled, uploading a file with the same key replaces the old one.
  • Multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete: Disabled. This extra layer of security requires MFA before you can permanently delete object versions.

Step 4: Upload a file to the bucket

Back on the Objects tab, I clicked Upload.

On the Upload page, I clicked Add files and picked an image called datacenter.png from my Downloads folder. You can also drag and drop files, or use Add folder to upload a whole folder.

The page then listed the file as 1 total, 2.4 MB, type image/png, with the destination shown as s3://aws-lab1-rahimah.

Scrolling down, you'll see two collapsed sections:

  • Permissions: where you can grant public access and access to other AWS accounts.
  • Properties: where you can set the storage class, encryption settings and tags.

I left both alone and clicked Upload.

The next page showed Upload succeeded, with a summary of 1 file, 2.4 MB, 100% succeeded and 0 failed.

Back in the bucket, Objects (1) now lists datacenter.png, size 2.4 MB, and storage class Standard.

Storage class controls how your data is stored and what it costs. Standard is the default and is meant for frequently accessed data. Other classes, such as Glacier, are cheaper for data you rarely need to retrieve.

Step 5: Explore the object's details

I clicked datacenter.png to open its details. The Object overview shows:

  • Owner: the canonical ID of the AWS account that owns the object
  • AWS Region: eu-north-1
  • Last modified, Size and Type
  • Key: datacenter.png
  • S3 URI: s3://aws-lab1-rahimah/datacenter.png
  • ARN: arn:aws:s3:::aws-lab1-rahimah/datacenter.png
  • Entity tag (ETag): an identifier for this specific version of the object's content
  • Object URL: https://aws-lab1-rahimah.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/datacenter.png

Two of these are easy to confuse:

  • The S3 URI (s3://bucket/key) is what AWS tools like the AWS CLI and SDKs use to refer to an object.
  • The Object URL is the HTTPS address of the object on the internet, in the form https://bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com/key.

The ARN here is the bucket's ARN with the object key added on the end.

Step 6: Open the image vs. use the Object URL

This is the part that surprised me, and it taught me the most. There are two ways to view the uploaded image, and they behave differently.

Option 1: Click "Open"

Clicking the Open button displays the image in a new browser tab. The address bar shows a very long URL that carries extra parameters such as X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256.

That is a presigned URL. When you click Open, the console uses your own credentials to generate a temporary, signed link that grants access to the object for a short time. S3 sees the signature, confirms that a permitted user created it, and serves the file.

Option 2: Paste the Object URL

When I copied the plain Object URL into the browser, I got this:

<Error>
  <Code>AccessDenied</Code>
  <Message>Access Denied</Message>
  ...
</Error>

Why the difference?

The Object URL is an unauthenticated request. When you paste it into a browser, there's no signature and nothing that tells S3 who you are, so S3 treats you as an anonymous visitor. S3 buckets and objects are private by default, and only the owner can access them unless permissions are explicitly granted. So the anonymous request is refused with AccessDenied.

The error is not a bug. It shows S3's security model working as designed: nothing is public until you deliberately make it so.

Making objects public

If you need public access, for example to host images on a website, you'd have to change two things: turn off the relevant Block Public Access settings on the bucket, and then grant read access through a bucket policy or object permissions. Only do this for data that's genuinely meant to be public. For private files, presigned URLs are a safer way to share something temporarily.

Key Takeaways

  • A bucket is a container and an object is a file inside it, identified by its key.
  • Bucket names must be globally unique, so a naming prefix like aws-lab1- helps keep names unique and organized.
  • The region determines where your data physically lives.
  • An ARN uniquely identifies any AWS resource, and an object's ARN is its bucket's ARN plus the key.
  • The S3 URI is for AWS tools, while the Object URL is the HTTPS address.
  • S3 is private by default. Opening an object from the console works because it uses a presigned URL, while the plain Object URL returns AccessDenied.

Clean up

To avoid unexpected charges, delete what you created. You must empty a bucket before you can delete it:

  1. Select datacenter.png and click Delete. Make sure you tick it, so that the Delete button is not greyed out.


Then confirm deletion.

  1. Go back to the bucket list, select aws-lab1-rahimah and click Delete.

Conclusion

In this first lab, I created an S3 bucket, uploaded an object, and learned why access to it is blocked by default. Next in the series, I'll build on this with more S3 features and other AWS services.

If you're learning AWS, let me know in the comments which service I should cover next.

title: Retries Are a Distributed Systems Bug Waiting to Happen: Designing Idempotent APIs
description:
Every network call can fail in three ways: it fails, it succeeds, or it succeeds and you never find out. The third case is where most production incidents live.

Junior instinct: "Request timed out, retry it."
Senior question: "What if the first one actually went through?"

The core problem 

Client                 Server                  DB
  | --- POST /charge --> |                      |
  |                      | --- INSERT charge -> |
  |                      | <------- OK -------- |
  |   X (response lost)  |                      |
  | --- POST /charge --> |   (retry)            |
  |                      | --- INSERT charge -> |   <- duplicate

The client can't tell "never arrived" from "arrived, reply lost." Retrying blindly means double charges, duplicate orders, double emails.

Fix 1: Idempotency keys

The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it on every attempt. The server stores the result and replays it.

Client                       Server
  | POST /charge                |
  | Idempotency-Key: abc-123 -> | not seen: process, store result
  |  X (response lost)          |
  | POST /charge                |
  | Idempotency-Key: abc-123 -> | seen: return stored result, no new charge

app.post("/charge", async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.get("Idempotency-Key");
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Idempotency-Key required" });

  // Atomic claim: unique constraint on key
  const claimed = await db.idempotency.insertIfAbsent({
    key, status: "in_progress", requestHash: hash(req.body),
  });

  if (!claimed) {
    const existing = await db.idempotency.get(key);
    if (existing.requestHash !== hash(req.body))
      return res.status(422).json({ error: "Key reused with different payload" });
    if (existing.status === "in_progress")
      return res.status(409).json({ error: "Request in progress" });
    return res.status(existing.code).json(existing.response); // replay
  }

  const result = await chargeCard(req.body);
  await db.idempotency.complete(key, 200, result);
  res.json(result);
});

Details that matter:

  • Make the claim atomic (unique constraint, not check-then-insert).
  • Hash the payload. Same key with a different body is a client bug, so reject it.
  • Handle the in-progress state so concurrent retries don't race.
  • Set a TTL (24-72h is common).

Fix 2: Retry correctly

Retries without backoff turn a blip into an outage (the retry storm).

Attempt:  1    2      3         4              5
Wait:     0 -> 1s -> 2s ------> 4s -----------> 8s   (exponential)
               +-jitter: random within each window

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function retry(fn, { retries = 5, base = 200, cap = 10_000 } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (err) {
      if (i >= retries || !isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      const backoff = Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** i);
      await sleep(Math.random() * backoff); // full jitter
    }
  }
}
  • Jitter is not optional. Without it, every client retries in lockstep.
  • Only retry transient errors (timeouts, 429, 503), never 400/401/404.
  • Respect Retry-After. Put a retry budget at the service level.

Fix 3: The dual-write problem 

await db.save(order);        // succeeds
await queue.publish(event);  // crashes here -> DB and queue disagree

You can't make two systems commit atomically. Use the transactional outbox:

+---------- one DB transaction ----------+
|  INSERT order       INSERT outbox_event |
+-----------------------------------------+
              |
     relay polls outbox -> publishes to queue -> marks sent

This gives at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent too (dedupe by event ID).

What I'd standardize on

Layer Rule
Write endpoints Require Idempotency-Key
Clients Exponential backoff + full jitter + cap
Messaging Outbox + idempotent consumers
Semantics Assume at-least-once, design for it

Takeaway

"Exactly-once" is mostly a myth. What you actually build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which behaves like exactly-once from the outside.

Design every write as if it will be sent twice, because eventually it will be.

How does your team handle idempotency? Keys, natural dedupe, or hope? Let me know in the comments. 👇

title: Using Set Learning to Improve Set-Valued Classifiers on Long-tailed Data
description:
arXiv:2610.27443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Set-valued classification (SVC) offers a practical approach to communicating uncertainty while maintaining accuracy by predicting variable-sized sets per input rather than fixed-sized sets (e.g. top-1 or top-5). However, set-valued classifiers (SVCs) exhibit significantly degraded performance on long-tailed and imbalanced datasets, a setting for which they are ostensibly well-suited. This becomes apparent under macro-average evaluation, which weighs all classes equally. SVCs are typically formed during a post-hoc calibration stage, so little is known about how training dynamics affect their behaviour. In this work, we investigate how different neural network training strategies and loss functions impact downstream SVC performance on highly imbalanced data. In addition to methods such as label smoothing and class-balancing, we investigate whether loss functions that operate over sets of examples in a batch, rather than treating all examples as independent, lead to better downstream SVCs. We adapt the recently proposed odd-K-out (OKO) loss function, which learns from sets of training samples, improving its sample efficiency whilst introducing algorithmic modifications that reduce its computational overhead from 3.2x to just 1.36x that of standard cross-entropy training. Experiments on highly long-tailed datasets demonstrate our modified OKO approach significantly improves macro-accuracy across multiple SVC methods - including top-k, average-k, and conformal prediction - while maintaining competitive micro-accuracy. This improved performance on minority classes occurs without substantially increasing prediction set sizes, suggesting that carefully constructed set-based training can produce networks better suited to imbalanced data.

title: Verify CBE and Telebirr payments in your app with a free API
description:
If you sell anything online in Ethiopia, you know the flow: the customer pays by bank transfer or Telebirr, then sends a screenshot. Someone on your team looks at it and decides whether to ship. Screenshots are easy to edit and easy to reuse, so that decision is a guess.

I maintain cheki.et, a free, MIT-licensed receipt checker, and this post is the developer version: how to confirm a payment against the bank's own record from your backend, in a few lines of Node or Python.

One thing first, because it's the most common confusion I see. Searching "telebirr api" or "cbe api" mostly turns up payment collection: merchant APIs where you start a payment and get a callback. Those need a merchant agreement with the bank. What I'm describing is the other half. The customer has already paid, the normal way, and you want to check the receipt they sent you. That needs no contract with anyone, because Ethiopian banks and wallets publish every receipt at a public URL.

How it works

Each bank has its own receipt page: transactioninfo.ethiotelecom.et/receipt/{number} for Telebirr, mbreciept.cbe.com.et/{receiptId} for CBE, a JSON endpoint for Bank of Abyssinia, a PDF for CBE Birr, and so on. cheki fetches the right one, parses it, runs a few sanity checks (positive amount, the reference you asked for, no failed or pending status), and returns the same JSON for every bank. There are 10 banks and wallets live: CBE, Telebirr, BOA, M-Pesa, Dashen, Awash, CBE Birr, Siinqee, eBirr and ZamZam. Three of those (M-Pesa, ZamZam, CBE Birr) are marked beta because they've been checked against few or no real receipts.

One request 

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"}'

No signup and no API key. The body takes bank plus whatever that bank needs:

Field When
reference Almost always: a receipt link, Receipt ID, transaction number or FT Ref
accountNumber BOA (last 5 digits) and older CBE FT receipts (last 8 digits)
phoneNumber CBE Birr (the payer's phone)
qrData A scanned QR payload (BOA, CBE Birr, Telebirr)

That reference is made up, so you'll get a 422 back. A confirmed receipt looks like this (names and numbers are fake):

{
  "success": true,
  "verified": true,
  "bank": "Commercial Bank of Ethiopia",
  "bankCode": "cbe",
  "reference": "FT26SAMPLE01",
  "senderName": "ABEBE KEBEDE",
  "receiverName": "TIGIST ALEMU",
  "receiverAccount": "1****6171",
  "amount": 1250.5,
  "currency": "ETB",
  "date": "2026-10-01",
  "sourceUrl": "https://apps.cbe.com.et:100/?id=FT26SAMPLE0100006171",
  "cached": false
}

The rule that matters: only verified: true means the bank confirmed it. success: true only means the request was handled. A BOA QR that BOA couldn't confirm comes back with success: true, verified: false, decodedOnly: true, and a QR can be copied. Don't ship on that.

The error codes are what you'd expect: 400 bad input, 404 unknown bank, 413 body too large, 422 the bank has no such receipt, 429 rate limited (with Retry-After), 502 the bank couldn't be reached. A 502 for a geo-blocked bank includes a fallbackUrl, which is the bank's own receipt page.

Node: cheki-verify 

npm install cheki-verify   # 1.6.0, no dependencies, Node 20+

Here's the check I'd run before marking an order paid. Confirm it with the bank, then make sure it's actually this order's payment:

import { Cheki, isVerified, ChekiAPIError } from "cheki-verify";

const cheki = new Cheki();
const seen = new Set(); // use a UNIQUE column in your database instead

async function checkPayment(order, bank, reference) {
  let r;
  try {
    r = await cheki.verify(bank, reference);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof ChekiAPIError) {
      // 422: the bank has no such receipt. 502 + fallbackUrl: bank not reachable from the server.
      return { ok: false, why: e.serverMessage ?? e.message, openAtBank: e.fallbackUrl };
    }
    throw e; // network error or timeout: try again later, don't accept
  }
  if (!isVerified(r)) return { ok: false, why: "not confirmed by the bank" };
  if (r.amount !== order.amount) return { ok: false, why: `amount is ${r.amount}` };
  if (!r.receiverAccount?.endsWith(order.accountLast4)) return { ok: false, why: "paid to another account" };
  const key = `${r.bankCode}:${r.reference}`;
  if (seen.has(key)) return { ok: false, why: "receipt already used" };
  seen.add(key);
  return { ok: true, payer: r.senderName, date: r.date };
}

console.log(await checkPayment({ amount: 1250.5, accountLast4: "6171" }, "dashen", "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"));

The last two checks are the ones people skip. A real receipt for a transfer to someone else's account passes isVerified. So does a real receipt the same customer already used last week. The bank can't know about your orders, so those checks have to live in your code.

In the TypeScript SDK, any non-2xx response throws a ChekiAPIError (with statusCode, fallbackUrl and checkedUrl), and a 429 throws ChekiRateLimitError. It retries at most once, and only where that's safe.

Python: cheki 

pip install cheki   # 1.6.0, needs only requests, Python 3.10+

The Python client returns a result for API errors instead of raising, so it reads as one if:

from cheki import ChekiClient

with ChekiClient() as cheki:
    r = cheki.verify("cbe", "https://mbreciept.cbe.com.et/fHCxExampleRcpt01")

    if r.is_verified:
        print(r.sender_name, "paid", r.amount, r.currency, "to", r.receiver_account, "on", r.date)
    elif r.fallback_url:
        print("Bank not reachable from the server. Open:", r.fallback_url)
    else:
        print(f"Not verified ({r.http_status}): {r.error}")

It also installs a small CLI, which is handy in a terminal: cheki-verify telebirr DET0SAMPLE --json. It exits 0 only when the bank confirmed the receipt.

End-of-day reconciliation

POST /api/verify/batch takes up to 20 receipts:

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify/batch \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"receipts": [
        {"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"},
        {"bank": "boa", "reference": "FT26SAMPLE07", "accountNumber": "12345"}
      ]}'

You get back total, verified, failed, cached and one result per receipt. Both SDKs wrap it as verifyBatch / verify_batch.

Limits and what's kept

  • Server side only. The API sends no CORS headers, so call it from your backend, not the browser.
  • Rate limits per IP: 30 checks a minute (each batch item counts), and 5 batch requests a minute. The SDKs export RECOMMENDED_BATCH_CHUNK (15) for long lists.
  • Storage: no accounts and no database. A receipt the bank confirmed stays in the server's memory for up to six hours, so a repeat check returns cached: true without asking the bank again. Failed checks are never kept.

The full reference is in the API docs, and the developer page has the Go, PHP and Dart SDKs as well.

Telebirr and M-Pesa: self-host it

Telebirr's and M-Pesa's receipt pages only answer requests from Ethiopian networks. The hosted cheki.et API runs in Frankfurt, so for those two it returns a 502 with fallbackUrl. That's fine for a person at a counter, who can open the link on their phone, but not for an automated checkout.

The fix is to run your own copy on a server in Ethiopia:

git clone https://github.com/1RB/cheki.git
cd cheki
docker compose up -d   # serves on http://localhost:3000

Then point the SDK at it:

const cheki = new Cheki({ baseUrl: "http://your-server:3000" });

cheki = ChekiClient(base_url="http://your-server:3000")

Every option is an environment variable, and all are optional. For example, CHEKI_CACHE=off turns off the in-memory cache if you'd rather keep nothing. There's a longer walkthrough in the self-hosting guide.

Other options

cheki isn't the only way to do this. check.et, verify.et and qbirr offer hosted APIs with keys and dashboards, and there are open-source libraries if you'd rather parse receipts inside your own app, such as tx-verify for Python and telebirr-receipt for Node. They all read the same public receipt pages. Pick based on which banks you need, whether you want an account and a dashboard, and whether you can run something on an Ethiopian network.

Help wanted

The weakest spots are the beta banks. If you have a real M-Pesa, ZamZam or CBE Birr receipt that cheki gets wrong, an issue on GitHub with the names and accounts redacted helps a lot. The repo has npm run probe -- <receipt-url> --redact for exactly that.

cheki.et is MIT licensed and isn't affiliated with any bank or Ethio Telecom.

title: October 07, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Deprecated

Negative backend deadlines are deprecated

A negative backend deadline in an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule uses the default deadline, the same as 0. Negative values there are deprecated and will be rejected in a future release; until then, creating an API config with one returns a warning in the operation metadata. OpenAPI 3.x backends already reject a negative deadline. To use the default, omit the field or set it to 0.

For more information, see OpenAPI 2.0 extensions and OpenAPI 3.x extensions.

title: From Localhost to Production: Deploying Your Spring AI Agent
description:
Running an AI agent on your laptop is one thing. Putting it in front of real users is another. The agent itself doesn't change — but everything around it does.

API keys need to stay out of your code. Token costs add up fast if you're not watching. A slow model call that was fine during testing becomes a timeout in production. And when something goes wrong, you need logs that actually tell you what happened.

This article covers the practical side of shipping a Spring AI agent: secrets management, cost awareness, rate limiting, timeouts, and what to monitor once you're live.

The API key problem

During development, it's tempting to put your API key directly in application.properties:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=sk-proj-abc123...

Don't do this. That file gets committed to version control. The key leaks. You get a bill.

The right pattern: read the key from an environment variable.

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}

Now start the application with the key set in the environment:

export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-abc123...
java -jar your-app.jar

On a cloud platform (Railway, Render, Fly.io, AWS), set this as a secret environment variable in the deployment settings — never in a config file that gets pushed.

What about local development? Use a .env file that is listed in .gitignore, and load it with a tool like direnv or just set the variable in your shell profile. Never commit .env.

Separating configuration by environment

Your app needs different settings in development vs production:

  • Dev: verbose logging, low timeouts, a small token limit so you don't burn through a quota while testing
  • Prod: tighter timeouts, higher token limits, structured logging

Spring Boot's profile system handles this cleanly.

src/main/resources/application.properties — shared defaults:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}
app.agent.timeout-seconds=30
app.agent.max-tokens=2000

src/main/resources/application-dev.properties — development overrides:

logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
app.agent.timeout-seconds=60
app.agent.max-tokens=500

src/main/resources/application-prod.properties — production overrides:

logging.level.com.example=INFO
app.agent.timeout-seconds=20
app.agent.max-tokens=4000

Activate a profile at startup:

java -jar your-app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

Your agent code reads these values without knowing which profile is active:

@Value("${app.agent.timeout-seconds}")
private int timeoutSeconds;

@Value("${app.agent.max-tokens}")
private int maxTokens;

Timeouts — set them everywhere

In development, a slow model call is annoying. In production, it blocks a thread, holds a connection, and can cascade into a full outage.

Set a timeout at every layer.

On the ChatClient call:

String response = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> chatClient.prompt()
        .user(request.message())
        .tools(travelTools)
        .call()
        .content())
    .get(timeoutSeconds, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

On the HTTP client Spring AI uses internally, you can configure it via properties:

spring.ai.openai.chat.options.timeout=20000

On your REST endpoint with Spring MVC:

@PostMapping("/chat")
@ResponseTimeout(20000)
public ResponseEntity<String> chat(@RequestBody ChatRequest request) {
    // ...
}

Pick one consistent timeout value and apply it everywhere. Thirty seconds is a reasonable ceiling for most agent calls. If your agent needs longer, it's probably doing too much in a single request — consider breaking it into smaller steps.

Token costs — what you're actually paying for

Every call to the model costs money based on tokens — roughly three-quarters of a word each. The bill comes from two places:

  • Input tokens: your system prompt + conversation history + the user's message + tool definitions
  • Output tokens: the model's response

Output tokens cost more than input tokens. A verbose system prompt that runs 500 tokens fires on every single request. Multiply by 10,000 users and it becomes significant.

Where token costs hide:

Source What it contains What to watch
System prompt Your instructions Keep it concise — every word fires on every call
Tool definitions @tool descriptions Long descriptions add up across many tools
Conversation history All prior messages Window size directly controls cost
Tool results What tools return Verbose JSON returns cost more than plain strings

How to track usage in Spring AI:

Every ChatResponse contains usage metadata:

ChatResponse chatResponse = chatClient.prompt()
    .user(request.message())
    .call()
    .chatResponse();

Usage usage = chatResponse.getMetadata().getUsage();
log.info("tokens — input: {}, output: {}, total: {}",
    usage.getPromptTokens(),
    usage.getGenerationTokens(),
    usage.getTotalTokens());

Log this on every production request. After a few days you'll see exactly where cost is coming from and whether it's growing as expected.

Rate limiting — protect yourself and the API

The model provider's API has rate limits — requests per minute and tokens per minute. Hit them and your app gets 429 errors.

Two problems to solve:

1. Protect against a single user hammering the API:

Use a simple in-memory rate limiter per user (or per IP if you don't have user identity):

@Component
public class RateLimiter {

    private final Map<String, AtomicInteger> callCount = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Long> windowStart = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private static final int MAX_CALLS_PER_MINUTE = 10;

    public boolean allow(String userId) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long start = windowStart.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> now);

        if (now - start > 60_000) {
            callCount.put(userId, new AtomicInteger(0));
            windowStart.put(userId, now);
        }

        return callCount.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> new AtomicInteger(0))
                        .incrementAndGet() <= MAX_CALLS_PER_MINUTE;
    }
}

Check it in your controller:

if (!rateLimiter.allow(request.userId())) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(429)
        .body("Too many requests. Please wait a moment.");
}

2. Handle 429s from the provider gracefully:

try {
    return chatClient.prompt().user(message).call().content();
} catch (OpenAiHttpException e) {
    if (e.statusCode() == 429) {
        return "The service is busy right now. Please try again in a moment.";
    }
    throw e;
}

Never let a raw 429 surface to the user as a 500 error.

Retry with backoff — for transient failures

Model APIs have transient failures — brief network blips, occasional 500s. A single retry with a short wait handles most of them.

Spring Retry makes this straightforward:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.retry</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-retry</artifactId>
</dependency>

Enable it in your main class:

@EnableRetry
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application { ... }

Add retry to your agent call:

@Retryable(
    retryFor = { OpenAiHttpException.class },
    maxAttempts = 3,
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2)
)
public String callAgent(String message) {
    return chatClient.prompt().user(message).call().content();
}

This retries up to 3 times, waiting 1s then 2s between attempts. It only retries OpenAiHttpException — not your own application errors.

Do not retry on 429 errors with short delays — you'll just accelerate into the rate limit. Retry on 500s and network errors only.

What to log in production

Good production logs answer: "What did the agent do, for whom, and how did it go?"

Minimum log fields on every agent request:

@PostMapping("/chat")
public ResponseEntity<String> chat(@RequestBody ChatRequest request) {
    String requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

    log.info("[req:{}] agent call — userId={} conversationId={}",
        requestId, request.userId(), request.conversationId());

    try {
        String response = callAgent(request.message(), request.conversationId());
        long durationMs = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;

        log.info("[req:{}] agent complete — durationMs={} responseLength={}",
            requestId, durationMs, response.length());

        return ResponseEntity.ok(response);
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        log.warn("[req:{}] agent timeout after {}ms", requestId, timeoutSeconds * 1000);
        return ResponseEntity.status(504).body("Request timed out.");
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("[req:{}] agent error — {}", requestId, e.getMessage(), e);
        return ResponseEntity.status(500).body("Something went wrong.");
    }
}

The requestId ties every log line for a single request together. The durationMs tells you if calls are getting slower over time. The error path always logs the full stack trace.

Health checks and readiness

Before a request reaches your agent, you want to know the application is healthy. Spring Boot Actuator gives you this for free:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized

GET /actuator/health returns {"status":"UP"} when the app is running. Your deployment platform (Render, Railway, Kubernetes) pings this endpoint — if it returns anything other than UP, traffic stops going to that instance.

Add a custom health check that verifies your model API is reachable:

@Component
public class ModelApiHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final ChatModel chatModel;

    public ModelApiHealthIndicator(ChatModel chatModel) {
        this.chatModel = chatModel;
    }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            chatModel.call(new Prompt("ping"));
            return Health.up().build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down()
                .withDetail("reason", e.getMessage())
                .build();
        }
    }
}

If the model API is down, your health check returns DOWN and the platform can route around the broken instance or alert you.

A deployment checklist

Before you ship:

Secrets

  • [ ] API key is in an environment variable, not in any committed file
  • [ ] .env is in .gitignore
  • [ ] No secrets appear in log output

Reliability

  • [ ] Every agent call has a timeout
  • [ ] 429 errors are caught and returned as readable messages
  • [ ] Transient errors have retry with backoff

Cost

  • [ ] Token usage is logged on every request
  • [ ] System prompt is as concise as possible
  • [ ] Conversation history window is bounded (chatHistoryWindowSize)

Observability

  • [ ] Every request gets a unique request ID
  • [ ] Duration is logged on every request
  • [ ] Errors log the full stack trace

Operations

  • [ ] Health check endpoint is configured
  • [ ] Logs go somewhere you can actually read them (not just stdout on a server you can't SSH into)

What's next

The agent is deployed and handling real traffic. The next question is scale — what happens when many users hit the agent at the same time, when conversation histories grow large, and when you need to update the model or tools without downtime.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: Transformers Learn Two Competing Sorting Algorithms, and Only One Length-Generalizes
description:
arXiv:2610.26974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that two-layer transformers trained to near-zero loss on a sorting task converge to one of two mechanistically distinct solution classes depending on their initialization. One solution class consists of solutions that do not use the second attention layer to sort, but also fail to length-generalize. The other, which uses both attention layers, length-generalizes perfectly, despite only being trained to sort sequences of a fixed length. By carefully choosing the weight initialization, we demonstrate that we can steer the model toward learning one solution or the other. We identify input types that are rare at the training length but increasingly common at longer sequence lengths as a source of this disparity in length-generalization, and find that layer-wise specialization of the second class of solutions allows them to handle these rare sequences more accurately. In the second class, we discover a mechanism by which the second layer attention can use the contextual information gathered by the first layer attention to reduce its search space. On the related task of finding the minimum of a sequence, we find a similar two solution-type phenomenon, but with the opposite generalization pattern, where a different form of layer-wise specialization causes the two-layer solution to length-generalize worse than the single-attention solution.

title: Deadline-Driven Object Storage: Large ZIP Export Multipart Upload and Signed Download Link
description:
Short answer: for an edtech system exporting signed documents, stream the archive into bounded multipart parts, publish it only after completion, and issue a short-lived signed download link only while the retention record permits access.

The deadline is the design constraint. A signed link is a temporary capability, not evidence that the bytes have been deleted. Keep the deletion deadline in the job or compliance database, keep the object private, and make the download endpoint check the export state before asking object storage to sign the exact key.

Large-file throughput is a separate constraint. A worker that creates a multi-gigabyte ZIP and sends it in one request has one large failure boundary: a process eviction, network reset, or exhausted disk can force the archive to be rebuilt. Multipart upload gives the worker smaller retry units, but it does not make an unfinished session a finished object, and it does not decide when deletion is allowed.

Start with the deadline, then budget the archive

Model an export as a state machine rather than a file path. A useful record contains an export ID, a unique object key, the retention deadline, an upload session identifier, completed part numbers and tags, an explicit status, and a completion timestamp. The worker writes state transitions; the download endpoint reads the completed state before issuing a capability.

The key should include the job identity, such as exports/{export_id}/documents.zip. That prevents two retries from treating a shared name as a lock. It also makes cleanup auditable: a lifecycle process can target completed objects by prefix, while an application job can remove one object when its deadline arrives. Do not put a signed URL in the authoritative record. It will expire; the key and deadline should not.

Throughput needs its own budget. Let P be the part size, W the number of concurrent uploads, and R the retry reserve. A worker needs room for the ZIP writer, W * P in-flight buffers, and enough local scratch space for its archive strategy. Bigger parts usually reduce request overhead, but they also increase the work lost when one part fails. Your mileage may vary; the right value comes from measurements of compression, memory pressure, link capacity, concurrent exports, and the cost of rebuilding a part.

That is the uncomfortable part.

A deadline that is precise in the database but vague in cleanup is not precise in production. For example, if a district administrator requests a signed-document ZIP at 09:00 and its deletion deadline is 18:00, a link expiring at 09:15 limits the capability window; it does not authorize the cleanup job to wait until tomorrow.

Keep it private.

How should a Node.js worker handle a large ZIP export with multipart upload and a signed download link?

Keep the browser out of the archive-writing path. The worker can stream source documents into a ZIP, buffer one bounded part, upload that part, and persist the returned part metadata before moving on. After every required part is acknowledged, complete the multipart session. Only then should the application create a signed download link for the object key and an expiry that matches the user's download window.

The following Python sketch shows the control flow without pretending that every object-storage system has the same SDK or request vocabulary. The adapter is the boundary to test against a real implementation; the job logic is where retention and publication rules belong.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterable
import zipfile


@dataclass
class ExportRecord:
    export_id: str
    object_key: str
    delete_after: datetime
    upload_id: str | None = None
    completed_parts: list[dict] | None = None


class StorageAdapter:
    def create_multipart(self, object_key: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def upload_part(self, upload_id: str, part_number: int, data: bytes) -> dict:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def complete_multipart(self, upload_id: str, parts: list[dict]) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def abort_multipart(self, upload_id: str) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def signed_download(self, object_key: str, expires_in_seconds: int) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError


def build_zip(paths: Iterable[Path], output: Path) -> None:
    with zipfile.ZipFile(output, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as archive:
        for path in paths:
            archive.write(path, path.name)


def publish_export(storage, record, source_paths, scratch_dir, part_size):
    record.completed_parts = record.completed_parts or []
    archive = scratch_dir / f"{record.export_id}.zip"
    build_zip(source_paths, archive)
    record.upload_id = record.upload_id or storage.create_multipart(record.object_key)

    try:
        with archive.open("rb") as stream:
            part_number = 1
            while chunk := stream.read(part_size):
                part = storage.upload_part(record.upload_id, part_number, chunk)
                record.completed_parts.append(part)
                part_number += 1

        storage.complete_multipart(record.upload_id, record.completed_parts)
        return storage.signed_download(record.object_key, expires_in_seconds=900)
    except Exception:
        storage.abort_multipart(record.upload_id)
        raise

In a real worker, persist the record after each successful part and make the retry path reconcile that record with the storage session before uploading more data. The sketch intentionally leaves the adapter abstract: request methods, part-size limits, checksum fields, and signed-link options vary, and inventing a universal endpoint would create false confidence. The completion call is the publication barrier. A link created before it can point at an object that is not ready.

There is a second failure boundary worth testing: the worker may finish uploading the final part and die before completion. On retry, the job should first load the export record, inspect the stored upload identifier and completed part metadata, and determine whether the completion transition was already recorded; if it was, the retry can verify the ready state and issue a link, while if it was not, the retry can reconcile the session and submit completion with the durable part list. Only after that state is clear should it consider a new archive. Otherwise a queue retry can rebuild a multi-gigabyte ZIP, leave an abandoned session behind, and create two possible objects for one export identity, which makes both cleanup and access review harder. Idempotency belongs in the job record and queue design, not in hope.

No premature link.

Failure modes to test before measuring throughput

A large-file design should name its failures before it names its provider. These are the cases I would put in a review:

Failure mode Required behavior Evidence to retain
Worker stops during ZIP creation Retry from source data or a durable intermediate, with bounded disk use Job status and worker attempt ID
Part upload is interrupted Retry only the affected part when its prior result is not durable Part number, checksum or storage tag, attempt timestamp
Final part arrives before completion Keep the object unpublished until explicit completion succeeds Upload ID and completion state
Link is requested after the deadline Refuse issuance, even if the object still exists briefly Decision timestamp and retention deadline
Cleanup job is delayed Alert and retry deletion; do not extend access silently Deletion attempt and final deletion state
Duplicate job is enqueued Use a stable export identity and unique object key Queue ID, export ID, object key

The deletion path deserves the same attention as the upload path. A scheduled lifecycle rule can help, but an application deadline still needs monitoring because cleanup timing, rule granularity, and retention configuration are separate from signed-link expiry. Never treat URL expiry as proof that the bytes were deleted.

For student records, log the decision to issue a link without logging the link itself. A URL containing a signature is a bearer capability. Apply least privilege to the worker credential, keep the object private, and make the download service check job ownership before asking storage to sign anything.

Which object-storage trade-offs belong in the design review?

Multipart support is only one row in the decision. Record the exact behavior for incomplete sessions, lifecycle deletion, checksums, conditional writes, versioning, object immutability, regional placement, egress, and signed-request expiry. An S3-compatible interface does not prove identical retention or authorization semantics across systems.

Decision axis Why it matters for this export Question to answer
Part retry and completion Determines rebuild cost after a worker failure Can the job resume from durable part metadata?
Lifecycle deletion Determines how closely storage cleanup follows the deadline What is the documented minimum or granularity?
Immutability and versioning Determines whether an overwrite can be recovered Are accidental replacement and legal retention separate controls?
Signed retrieval Determines who can read a completed archive and for how long Can the service sign one private object without making the bucket public?
Operational surface Determines what the team must monitor and rotate Are credentials, regions, quotas, and audit events visible to operators?

The catch is that this pattern is not suitable when the requirement is a permanent public asset, anonymous browser access, immutable legal hold, or built-in cross-region replication. Use a separately managed public delivery layer, an immutability-capable repository, or a replication design when those guarantees are mandatory. Stick with a simpler single upload when the archive is small enough that a retry is cheaper than multipart state, but record that choice as a measured constraint rather than a default.

I’m not sure a single numeric threshold can serve every school or district. Compression ratio, source locality, concurrent exports, and the user's download window change the answer. Run a representative archive through the worker, kill it at each state transition, and use the resulting memory, retry, and completion data to set the policy.

A compact rollout for signed-document exports

Ship the smallest state machine first: queued, building, uploading, completing, ready, expired, and deleted. Add metrics for bytes produced, part retries, active sessions, completion latency, link-issuance decisions, and deletion lag. Alert on sessions that remain incomplete beyond the job timeout and on objects past their deadline.

Then test the contract, not just the happy path. A worker should survive termination during ZIP creation, a failed part, and the gap after the final part. A download request after expiry should receive no signed capability. A cleanup retry should be visible and idempotent. A duplicate queue message should not publish two records for one export identity.

That rollout gives the team a decision rule: choose multipart when large-file throughput and restart cost dominate, choose a simpler path when archive rebuilds are cheap, and choose stronger retention controls when deletion deadlines are not the only obligation. The signed link is the last step in that chain, never the chain itself.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/signed-urls

title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System
description:
arXiv:2610.26948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. However, extending these methods to many product domains faces a dilemma: deploying a separately adapted VLM per domain scales cost linearly with the number of domains and requires routing each dialogue to the right model, while naively merging all domains into a single VLM degrades accuracy because product characteristics vary widely across categories. We propose LightCRS, a lightweight, query-conditioned framework for unified multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations once offline with frozen encoders. Online, a compact 5.3M-parameter module fuses this evidence for each dialogue via query-conditioned cross-attention, whose parameters are shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing natural Reddit recommendation-seeking conversations with Amazon product listings. LightCRS achieves state-of-the-art average HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, improving HR@1 by 35.4\% over the strongest baseline while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. Joint multi-domain training itself improves HR@1 by 15.2\% over separately trained single-domain models.
