title: A Multi-granularity Interaction Network for Relational Triple Extraction
description:
arXiv:2610.26952v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relational triple extraction identifies entity relations from raw sentences without depending on entity type information. The performance of traditional methods is seriously degenerated by ``unseen'' entities, because these methods can't build contextual dependencies relevant ``unseen'' entities. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a multi-granularity interaction network that leverages word-word, entity-relation, and head-tail interactions to capture deep semantic dependencies. By incorporating multiple iterations, the multi-granularity interaction network is effective to refine the representations corresponding to head and tail entities. It enhances the global semantic features associated with relational triples, aiding in the remediation of triples that may have been overlooked or omitted in earlier steps. Strong and consistent performance is achieved by our method on two rearranged datasets, with a significant improvement in identifying relational triples, including those involving ``unseen'' named entities. For example, our model improves F1-score by 3.1%/20.5% over previous approaches on the NYT-R/WebNLG-R datasets in the Unseen metric. Code: https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/Interaction-Network.

title: Cloud Cost Optimization in 2026: 10 Levers That Cut Your Compute Bill
description:
Most cloud compute waste comes from paying for capacity your workloads do not use: over-provisioned requests, idle nodes, standby capacity, and per-service add-ons. The biggest savings come from changing how capacity is reserved and packed, not only from discounts or dashboards.

TL;DR

If you already hold reserved instances or savings plans and run a FinOps dashboard, your unit rate is likely fine and your unit count is the problem. Pull these levers in this order:

  1. Right-size CPU and memory from observed usage.
  2. Pack workloads densely onto fewer, fuller nodes.
  3. Autoscale on real signals and scale idle workloads down.
  4. Stop paying for idle standby; in active-active, failover capacity also serves live users.
  5. Commit after you shrink, against the smaller baseline.
  6. Use spot capacity for fault-tolerant work only.
  7. Control egress between zones, regions, and the internet.
  8. Count the add-ons: load balancers, NAT gateways, observability.
  9. Count the platform team that operates Kubernetes.
  10. Use capacity across providers and neoclouds where price or availability is better.

Control Plane applies right-sizing, autoscaling, active-active without idle standby, and built-in day-two operations at the platform layer, on one cloud or several, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

Sources of avoidable compute spend

Source of spend Why it happens Lever
Over-provisioned CPU and memory requests Teams set requests high to avoid incidents and never lower them 1
Low node utilization and idle nodes Pods do not fit together well, or autoscalers leave spare nodes running 2, 3
Standby and duplicate environments Disaster recovery, staging, and preview environments run all the time 4
Data transfer and egress Traffic crosses zones, regions, clouds, or the internet 7
Managed add-ons billed separately Load balancers, NAT gateways, observability, certificates, and secrets each bill per unit 8
People cost of operating Kubernetes Clusters, upgrades, and add-ons need engineers and on-call time 9

Why Kubernetes bills run high

Kubernetes schedules pods by their requests, not by what they use. The Kubernetes resource management docs explain that the scheduler places a pod on a node only if the sum of resource requests, including the new pod’s, stays within the node’s capacity, even when actual usage is low. A pod that requests 2 vCPU and uses 0.3 still blocks 2 vCPU, and across hundreds of pods the cluster needs far more nodes than the real load requires.

The CNCF’s 2023 Cloud Native and Kubernetes FinOps microsurvey found that “Kubernetes has driven cloud spend up for nearly half (49%) of those surveyed…” and that “Over-provisioning came first by a long way at 70%” among causes of overspending. It drew just over 100 responses, so treat it as directional.

The 10 levers

1. Right-size CPU and memory

What it is. Compare each workload’s requests to its actual usage over a full business cycle, then set requests to match with headroom. The Kubernetes project documents the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, an add-on you install separately, for this purpose.

Effort. Low to measure, medium to change across teams, and recurring, because usage drifts as code and traffic change.

What it can save. Often the largest single lever: over-provisioning was the top cause of overspending in the CNCF survey, and every unit you stop requesting lowers the number of nodes needed to hold it.

Reliability risk. Medium if done by hand. Memory limits below peak usage cause out-of-memory kills, and memory requests below real usage make pods eviction candidates when a node runs short. Use a high percentile of usage over several weeks and change a few services at a time.

On Control Plane, Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory between a minimum and maximum you set, based on historical usage, on both Control Plane-provided and customer-provided compute.

2. Pack workloads densely

What it is. Bin-packing places pods so nodes run close to full. Utilization can be measured as requested (the share of a node’s allocatable CPU and memory that pods request) or actual (the share pods use); low numbers on either mean you pay for instances that do little.

Effort. Medium. Right-size first, since packing inflated requests only packs the waste more tightly, then tune node sizes and consolidation.

What it can save. Fewer nodes for the same workload, compounding with right-sizing.

Reliability risk. Medium. Dense nodes raise the blast radius of a node failure. Spread critical replicas across nodes and zones, and set pod disruption budgets to limit how many replicas voluntary evictions, such as consolidation, can remove at once.

On Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory reserved for each workload, by the millicore and the megabyte, rather than for whole nodes, so node packing is not your cost to manage.

3. Autoscale on real signals

What it is. Horizontal autoscaling adds and removes replicas as load changes. Requests per second, latency percentiles, and queue depth track demand better than CPU for many services, and KEDA extends Kubernetes autoscaling to event and custom metrics, including scaling to zero.

Effort. Medium: pick a signal, set minimum and maximum replicas, and load test.

What it can save. Capacity follows demand instead of peak, and workloads that scale down when idle stop billing for unused replicas.

Reliability risk. Medium. Scaling too slowly under a spike hurts latency, so keep a sensible minimum for user-facing services.

On Control Plane, workloads scale on requests per second, a latency percentile, or custom metrics through KEDA. Serverless workloads scale to zero natively, and standard and stateful workloads do so through KEDA.

4. Stop paying for idle standby

What it is. Active-passive disaster recovery keeps a second copy of your stack running, or ready to start, in another region or cloud. That copy bills for compute, databases, load balancers, and NAT gateways whether or not it serves a request, and staging, QA, and preview environments add to the pattern.

Effort. High if you redesign it yourself: active-active needs workloads that run in several places at once, routing to a healthy location, and a data strategy, covered in how to build active-active high availability.

What it can save. In active-active, every location serves live traffic, so failover capacity is also production capacity. Each location still needs headroom to absorb a failed location’s traffic (1/(N-1) of its normal load: 100% with two locations, 50% with three), and autoscaling can add that capacity when needed instead of holding it idle, as long as quotas are confirmed in advance.

Reliability risk. Lower than standby when done correctly, because failover is continuous and tested by real traffic, while a standby environment that has never carried production load often fails during the failover itself.

On Control Plane, a workload deployed to a Global Virtual Cloud runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so you get active-active failover without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

5. Commit after you shrink

What it is. Commitments trade flexibility for a lower rate over one or three years. AWS Savings Plans and Standard Reserved Instances save up to 72% compared with On-Demand. Google Cloud committed use discounts discount a committed level of resources or spend, with overage charged at the on-demand rate. Azure reservations save up to 72% on virtual machines and the Azure savings plan for compute up to 65% on select services, compared with pay-as-you-go.

Effort. Low to buy, high to manage well, since commitment utilization must stay high.

What it can save. A lower rate on steady usage; these are provider maximums, and your result depends on term, payment option, and how much of your usage is steady.

Reliability risk. None to uptime. Commitments bought before right-sizing can go unused, with limited exchange or resale options depending on provider and type, so commit to a conservative share of the reduced baseline.

6. Use spot capacity for fault-tolerant work

What it is. Providers sell spare capacity at a discount and reclaim it on short notice: AWS Spot Instances (up to 90% off On-Demand, two-minute notice), Google Cloud Spot VMs (about 30 seconds to shut down), and Azure Spot Virtual Machines (about 30 seconds’ notice).

Effort. Medium. Workloads must handle shutdown signals and checkpoint their work.

What it can save. A much lower rate on interruptible capacity.

Reliability risk. High for stateful or latency-sensitive services, low for batch jobs, CI runners, and stateless workers with retries.

7. Control egress

What it is. Providers charge per gigabyte for traffic that leaves a region or goes to the internet, and AWS and Google Cloud also charge for traffic between zones in the same region. Inbound traffic is free, and each provider includes a small monthly free tier for internet egress. Check AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure rates.

Effort. Medium: find the top flows by volume, keep chatty services together where reliability allows, cache at the edge, and compress.

What it can save. For data-heavy services, egress can rival the compute bill.

Reliability risk. Low to medium. Pinning traffic to one zone saves money but reduces zone redundancy.

8. Count the add-ons

What it is. Many managed services bill separately from the compute they support. NAT gateways on AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure charge for the gateway and for data processed. AWS Elastic Load Balancing bills per load-balancer hour plus capacity units, Google Cloud Load Balancing for forwarding rules and data processed, and Azure Load Balancer per rule-hour plus data processed. Observability usually bills by volume, and secret stores per secret or request.

Effort. Low to medium: share load balancers where safe, move NAT traffic to private endpoints, and set log retention and sampling.

What it can save. Small per item, large across dozens of services.

Reliability risk. Low, if you keep redundancy where it matters.

On Control Plane, load balancing through a global endpoint, automatic TLS certificates, secrets management, and unified logs, metrics, and traces are part of the platform for no additional cost.

9. Count the platform team

What it is. Running Kubernetes means operating clusters, planning upgrades, keeping versions compatible, and maintaining ingress, certificate, secrets, logging, and autoscaling add-ons. To estimate the cost, list every engineer who spends time on cluster operations, multiply their time share by loaded cost, and add it to the compute and add-on bill.

Effort. Low to measure, high to reduce: keep operating clusters, use a managed offering, or move to a platform with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. The Kubernetes alternatives guide compares the options, and how to cut cloud compute costs without rewriting your apps covers the move itself.

What it can save. Engineer hours spent on upgrades, add-on maintenance, and cluster on-call, which for many teams cost more than the infrastructure they maintain.

Reliability risk. Depends on the option; moving off clusters is a migration, so plan it service by service.

10. Use capacity across providers and neoclouds

What it is. Prices and capacity differ by provider, region, and hardware. Neoclouds and bare-metal providers can offer lower prices or capacity a hyperscaler region lacks, and several providers reduce dependence on one vendor, as covered in how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

Effort. High if each provider needs its own stack, low on a platform that treats each provider as a location; see how to add a neocloud without running a second stack.

What it can save. A lower rate on part of your capacity, plus capacity you cannot get elsewhere.

Reliability risk. Medium, since each provider adds failure modes; a global endpoint that routes to the nearest healthy location reduces that risk.

On Control Plane, Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) and Managed Kubernetes let existing clusters or your own servers join a Global Virtual Cloud as locations, so you can use capacity you already own or buy it from a neocloud.

Where FinOps tools fit

Cost visibility and allocation tools show where money goes and who owns it, and some recommend or automate changes. Listed in no specific order:

Tool What its own pages say it does
AWS Cost Explorer AWS’s cost analysis tool, including Savings Plans recommendations
Google Cloud Billing reports Reports for viewing and analyzing Google Cloud costs
Microsoft Cost Management Cost analysis and management for Azure (formerly Azure Cost Management)
IBM Kubecost Kubernetes cost allocation by cluster, team, namespace, and workload, with automated actions such as request sizing and namespace turndown
Vantage Cost reporting across providers, autopilot purchasing of AWS Savings Plans, Kubernetes rightsizing, anomaly detection, and budgets
CloudZero Cost allocation across cloud, Kubernetes, and AI spend, with unit costs such as cost per customer
Cast AI Kubernetes optimization that sets requests from observed usage, bin-packs pods, and moves eligible workloads to spot; you can start read-only and turn on automation later

Native tools give a first pass at no extra tooling cost, allocation tools add showback by team or customer, and automation tools apply recommendations. Standby copies, per-service load balancers, and cluster operations stay on the bill until the platform underneath changes.

A 30-day plan

Week Focus Actions Done when
1 Measure Tag spend by team and service, pull requested versus used CPU and memory, list idle and duplicate environments, and list the top network flows and add-on charges You can rank the top ten sources of waste
2 Right-size Lower requests on the most over-provisioned services a few at a time, keep memory headroom, and shut down idle environments Requested capacity is close to used capacity on the top services
3 Pack and autoscale Consolidate nodes, add pod disruption budgets, scale on request rate, latency, or queue depth, and scale dev and batch workloads down when idle Node count follows load
4 Commit and decide Buy commitments against the smaller baseline, fix the top egress and add-on charges, and decide whether to keep operating clusters or move to a platform with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate Commitments cover a conservative share of steady usage and the platform decision is written down

Change one tier of services at a time and watch error rate and latency after each change.

How Control Plane cuts compute costs

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one Global Virtual Cloud and cuts over-provisioning, idle standby, and per-service add-ons at the platform layer. The savings do not depend on running several clouds: one provider is enough.

  • Right-sizing: Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory between a minimum and maximum you set, based on historical usage.
  • Billing: on Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory reserved for each workload, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums, and Capacity AI sets that reservation. See Control Plane pricing.
  • No idle standby: every location of a Global Virtual Cloud serves live traffic, and the 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.
  • Day-two operations included: autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, load balancing through a global endpoint, automatic TLS certificates, secrets management, unified logs, metrics, and traces, mutual TLS, and a tamper-proof audit trail, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate.
  • Keep your managed services: Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code.
  • Cost visibility: a Cost and Usage view shows spend per org and per resource, with a projected total.

Result: Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

FAQ

How do I reduce my AWS costs?

Measure requested versus used CPU and memory first, since paying for capacity workloads do not use is the main source of waste. Then right-size, pack workloads onto fewer nodes, autoscale on real signals, and shut down idle environments before buying Savings Plans or Reserved Instances. Control Plane applies right-sizing, autoscaling, and active-active without idle standby at the platform layer, and customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

What is the right order for cloud cost optimization?

Reduce the capacity you pay for before you reduce the rate: right-size, pack, autoscale, and remove idle standby, then apply commitments and spot capacity to what remains.

How do I lower my Kubernetes bill?

Kubernetes schedules by requests, so inflated requests force extra nodes. Right-size requests, consolidate nodes, and scale idle workloads down. On Control Plane there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, and Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory automatically.

Base requests on measured usage over several weeks, keep headroom for memory, and automate the review so it does not drift. Control Plane’s Capacity AI does this between a minimum and maximum you set, using historical usage.

Are reserved instances and savings plans worth it?

Yes, for steady usage you have already right-sized. Bought before right-sizing, they lock in waste for the term, with limited exchange or resale options.

How much does running Kubernetes cost, including the platform team?

Add compute, add-ons, and the loaded cost of the engineers who operate clusters, handle upgrades, and maintain add-ons; the people cost never appears on a cloud invoice. A platform with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, such as Control Plane, removes most of that people cost.

What are hidden cloud costs?

Charges that scale with traffic or service count instead of compute: egress, NAT gateway processing, per-service load balancers, observability volume, and idle capacity, which is often the largest because it looks like ordinary instance spend. Control Plane includes load balancing, automatic TLS, secrets management, and unified observability in the platform.

For visibility on hyperscaler bills, use AWS Cost Explorer, Google Cloud Billing reports, and Microsoft Cost Management, and add Kubecost, Vantage, CloudZero, or Cast AI for allocation, recommendations, or automation.

When should I use spot instances?

For fault-tolerant work that handles shutdown signals: batch jobs, CI runners, and stateless workers with retries. Keep stateful and latency-sensitive services on on-demand or committed capacity, since AWS gives two minutes’ notice and Google Cloud and Azure about 30 seconds.

title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
description:
arXiv:2610.27438v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce \textbf{MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing)}, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$--$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$--$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.

title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
description:
arXiv:2610.27227v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present \textbf{GRSE}, \textbf{G}roup-\textbf{R}elative \textbf{S}kill \textbf{E}volution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent--skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions ($+6.7$ and $+3.2$ F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library ($+6.3$ points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

title: Think Before You Transcribe: Context-Steered Reasoning for Hotword-Aware Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.26986v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contextual automatic speech recognition (ASR) improves rare-entity recognition by supplying candidate hotwords, but retrieved candidates may be incomplete or incorrect. A reliable system must therefore exploit a relevant candidate without allowing unsupported alternatives to override the acoustic evidence. We propose a context-steered reasoning framework that generates a short, audio-grounded caption before transcription. This task-specific representation lets the model assess candidate relevance before making a lexical decision. Supervised fine-tuning establishes the structured caption-to-transcription behavior, while targeted trajectory injection strengthens group relative policy optimization when difficult utterances yield only unsuccessful rollouts. Experiments across diverse context conditions show that the proposed method consistently improves both transcription quality and hotword recognition while remaining robust to irrelevant candidates.

title: Your Go Code Works. But Is It Efficient?
description:
At GopherCon Africa 2026, one of the things that caught my attention during the Go workshop was profiling.

It got me thinking about something: we spend so much time making sure our code works, but how often do we stop to ask whether it's working efficiently?

So, I did a little more reading, and here's what I learned.

So, what is profiling?

Simply put, profiling helps you understand what's happening inside your application while it's running.

Is your code using too much CPU? Is it consuming more memory than necessary? Is something slowing it down?

Instead of guessing, profiling helps you investigate what's actually happening.

And apparently, Go has a tool for this called pprof.

Why should we care?

Imagine building an application that works perfectly during development. Then more users start using it, and suddenly, things get slower.

Your first instinct might be to start changing things until performance improves. But what if you're fixing the wrong thing?

That's where profiling comes in. It helps you identify potential bottlenecks so you can focus on the parts of your code that actually need attention.

And here's the part I found particularly interesting: small improvements can have a bigger impact than we think.

If an application is wasting resources, fixing the problem could improve performance and potentially reduce infrastructure costs, especially at scale.

It's a reminder that software development isn't just about getting things to work. It's also about understanding how they work.

Where does pprof come in?

Go's pprof tooling helps developers investigate different aspects of an application's performance.

For example:

  • CPU profiling helps identify where processing time is being spent.
  • Memory profiling helps you understand how your application uses memory.
  • Goroutine profiling helps you investigate what your goroutines are doing.

You don't necessarily need to know everything about profiling to appreciate why it matters. Even understanding what these tools can help you investigate is a good starting point.

Of course, profiling doesn't automatically fix your code. You still need to understand what the results mean, make changes, and check whether those changes actually helped.

My biggest takeaway?

Sometimes, improving software isn't about adding more features or rewriting everything.

Sometimes, it's about looking at what you already have and asking, "Could this be working better?"

I'm still learning Go, and profiling is one of those concepts that reminded me how much there is to explore beyond simply writing code that works.

One thing's for sure: I'll be paying more attention to what happens behind the scenes from now on.

If you've worked with Go before, have you used pprof? I'd love to hear about your experience!

Further reading

  • Profiling Go programs
  • Go diagnostics

title: Building a Backend for My Old Furniture Store
description:
A few years ago, I started a side project: a storefront that lists furniture for prospective customers. It was my first time understanding how a CMS works under the hood, so I decided to learn Sanity with it. I remember trying to understand GROQ queries and how all of it worked. I got there, and I built the storefront.

Then years went by.

Recently I decided to understand how the backend part of applications works. This was another friction moment. As a frontend engineer, I was used to consuming backend APIs, but I didn't really understand how they worked. So I went back to the furniture store and built a backend for it with NestJS and Postgres. Lo and behold, I found my way around.

This post walks through what I built, flow by flow: auth, cart, orders, and payments.

The mental model that helped

One mental model made everything click: build the logic from services up to controllers.

  • Services hold the core logic: creating a user, adding to a cart, placing an order.
  • Controllers set up the routes for those services. These are what I always saw as endpoints from the frontend side.

So when my frontend calls POST /auth/register, a controller receives the request and hands it to a service, which does the actual work. For years I only saw the endpoint. Now I know what sits behind it.

The new terms

Around services and controllers, NestJS has a few more pieces I had to learn.

  • Modules group everything for one feature: the auth module holds auth's controller, service, and guards.
  • Imports bring in other modules a module depends on. My auth module imports the users module and the JWT config module, because auth needs both.
  • Exports make parts of a module available to other modules. I export the auth guards so other modules, like cart and orders, can protect their routes.
  • Providers are the classes NestJS creates and manages for you, like services.
  • Constructors are where a class asks for the providers it needs. NestJS sees what a service asks for in its constructor and passes it in. This is called dependency injection.
  • Guards run before a request reaches the controller and decide whether it's allowed through. My auth guard blocks any request without a valid token.

Auth: creating an account and logging in

The core logic lives in the auth folder.

Registration. I collect basic information about the user. The password is never stored as the user typed it. It's hashed, which is one-way: there's no key that turns a hash back into the password. Even if someone got access to the database, they couldn't read the passwords.

The way it clicked for me: hashing is like a blender. You can't un-blend the result, but the same ingredients always produce the same mush.

Login. Nothing gets decrypted. The backend hashes the password the user just typed, the same way it was hashed at registration, and compares the result to the stored hash. If they match, the password is correct.

Tokens. After login, the user gets an access token. It contains the user's ID and is signed with the server's secret key, so the backend can tell that it issued the token and nobody changed it. Access tokens are short-lived, so I also use refresh tokens. These are long-lived and let users stay logged in without signing in again every time the access token expires.

Cart

The cart module is where a user goes through the store listing and saves items. Users can add available items to their cart, edit a cart item, and delete it.

There's no product table in my database. Products still live in Sanity, so the backend fetches them from Sanity before building a cart. Postgres holds the cart, orders, and inventory; Sanity holds the catalog.

When adding to the cart: if the item is already there, update it. If it isn't, create it.

Prices also come from Sanity on the backend. Before an order is created, the backend computes the cart items and their total. The frontend never sends a price, so nobody can change it before paying.

Orders and reservations

The goal here: no two customers can pay for the same item, even under high traffic.

When a customer places an order, the backend reserves the items in the database. The reservation is kept for 15 minutes. If the user doesn't complete payment in that time, the order expires, a background job releases the reservation, and the items become available again.

The tricky part is the reservation itself. If I checked stock first and reserved it after, there'd be a gap where two users both see "1 left" and both reserve it. So I do both in one statement:

const reservedRows = await tx.$executeRaw`
  UPDATE "Inventory"
  SET reserved = reserved + ${item.quantity}
  WHERE "productId" = ${item.productId}
  AND quantity - reserved - sold >= ${item.quantity}
`;

if (reservedRows === 0) {
  throw new BadRequestException(`${item.productName} is out of stock`);
}

The UPDATE only succeeds if enough stock remains. When two requests hit the same row at the same moment, Postgres makes the second one wait. It then re-checks the condition against the updated row. If the first request took the last item, zero rows are updated and the second user gets "out of stock."

Available stock is quantity - reserved - sold. Reserving doesn't reduce quantity; it increases reserved.

All of this runs inside a database transaction, along with creating the order and its order items. Either everything succeeds or nothing does. If a cart has three items and the third is out of stock, the reservations for the first two are rolled back too.

The order also stores its total and each item's price at the moment it's created. If a price changes in Sanity later, it doesn't affect an order that's already being paid.

Payments with Paystack

Once an order is created, the user pays through Paystack's widget. Paystack is in test mode for this project.

Starting a payment. The request first goes through my auth guard. The backend then calls Paystack with my Paystack secret key as a Bearer token in the authorization header. That key only ever lives on the backend. One gotcha: Paystack takes amounts in kobo, not naira, so the total has to be multiplied by 100.

The webhook. This was the flip for me as a frontend engineer. Normally I call the API. With a webhook, Paystack calls my backend to tell me the payment's status.

The webhook doesn't use my auth guard, because Paystack can't log in as a user. Instead, Paystack signs each webhook with my secret key and sends the signature in the x-paystack-signature header. My backend recomputes the signature and compares. If it doesn't match, the request is rejected, so nobody can fake a successful payment.

Paystack sends back the transaction reference, which is the order ID I sent when initializing the payment. What happens next depends on the order's status:

  • Pending: process the payment.
  • Already paid, processing, shipped, or delivered: treat it as a duplicate webhook and ignore it. Paystack can send the same webhook more than once, and this makes sure an order is never processed twice. This is called idempotency.
  • Cancelled, expired, failed, or refunded, or the amount doesn't match the order total: log the payment, but don't touch the inventory, because the customer hasn't received value for this transaction.

If a customer actually paid for an expired order, their money was taken, so the payment is flagged for a refund. For now, refunds are done manually.

Updating the order. For a valid payment, all the updates run in one database transaction, so either everything succeeds or nothing does. The order status changes to paid, the reservation is released, the sold count goes up, the cart items are deleted, and a successful payment row is created.

Where it stands

The backend runs locally, with Paystack in test mode. Next, I'm connecting the furniture storefront to these APIs, then deploying it. After that, I want to add AI features to the store.

title: Accelerating Spatio-Temporal Attention for Video Diffusion on TPUs
description: To address the quadratic latency bottleneck of self-attention in high-resolution video diffusion models, developers implemented Sparse VideoGen (SVG) to dynamically route attention heads to highly structured spatial or temporal sparse masks. Translating this algorithmic sparsity into physical hardware speedups on TPUs required optimizing the Splash Attention kernel by bypassing empty memory tiles, restricting exact coordinate masking strictly to boundary tiles, and permuting token memory layouts into temporal-major order for contiguous access. By aligning these sparse masks with actual hardware tile execution, the combined optimizations significantly reduced wasted matrix operations and achieved up to a 1.69x end-to-end inference speedup for 1440p video generation.

title: TIL: GBase Database Silent Installation Requires License Acceptance
description:
Today, I ran a silent installation of GBase Database(GBase 8s), only to have it fail on the first attempt. The cause? The license acceptance parameter was missing.

It is a small configuration detail, but it can stop an unattended installation before deployment gets anywhere.

Why Does License Acceptance Matter?

Unlike an interactive installation, silent installation has no graphical prompt where an operator can review and accept the license during execution. The required acceptance must be provided explicitly through the supported installation parameters.

For a GBase Database(GBase 8s) silent installation, the response file may contain:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Alternatively, you can pass the parameter directly in the installation command:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Confirm the exact parameter name and syntax against the documentation for your installation package, and make sure the applicable license terms have actually been reviewed and accepted before setting the value to TRUE.

Make It Part of Your Deployment Standard

When deploying GBase Database across multiple servers, a missing parameter can cause repeated failures and unnecessary troubleshooting.

To avoid this:

  • Include the required license-acceptance setting in your response file template.
  • Validate the response file before running a batch deployment.
  • Test the complete installation procedure on one machine first.
  • Check the installer logs and exit status rather than assuming the installation succeeded.

The broader lesson goes beyond licensing: every confirmation required by an interactive installation must be handled explicitly in an unattended workflow.

For reliable GBase Database deployment automation, small prerequisites deserve the same attention as installation paths, component selection, and post-installation configuration.

Have you ever lost time debugging a silent installation because of one missing parameter?

title: Causal Spatiotemporal State Evolution for Monocular 4D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.27594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While feed-forward models excel in static 3D geometry estimation, extending them to dynamic 4D scenes requires modeling visual geometry as a causally evolving state. Current methods typically rely on unordered temporal aggregation, which lacks the directional structure of physical time. Furthermore, existing supervision often treats geometry and motion as disjoint objectives, failing to exploit their inherent physical coupling. Consequently, they lack a unified constraint to effectively supervise temporal state transitions, leading to inconsistent 4D scene representations. To address this, we propose a feed-forward framework for causal 4D visual geometry learning from monocular videos. At its core, Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba augments temporal aggregation with directional state propagation. Through complementary Temporal-Spatial and Spatial-Temporal Scans, CSM continuously propagates geometry-aware states across frames to model spatiotemporal evolution. To align this causal state evolution with observable dynamics, we introduce Unified Motion Supervision. Rather than treating motion as an independent objective, UMS leverages geometry-aware predictions from the camera and depth heads to construct a unified forward motion field that is consistent with the underlying 3D structure. This geometry-grounded supervision explicitly constrains inter-frame state transitions, enabling stable states propagation across frames. Extensive evaluations on dynamic benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across video depth, camera pose, and optical flow estimation. These results validate that the synergy between the directional state propagation of Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba and Unified Motion Supervision effectively captures continuous scene evolution, significantly reducing temporal drift and reinforcing spatial-temporal consistency in 4D representation learning.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

title: SciFigBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Method Figure Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.27087v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper's methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse-grained tasks, such as context-based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine-grained content and inter-module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real-world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question-answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training-free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow-induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method-figure reasoning. Experiments across open-source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.

title: Two Parallel Agents Edited the Same File; the Merge Dropped One Quietly
description:
Two tickets landed the same morning, so I split them across two worktrees and let each agent run on its own branch. Both came back green: their own tests passed, their own review approved, their own CI ran clean. Both merged. A week later, the feature flag from ticket A was missing in production, even though ticket A's PR had shipped.

What actually merged

Each agent reached for the same shared file, the feature-flag registry: ticket A added a new flag, ticket B added a different flag and switched a default next to it. The code paths were separate, and so were the tests. When B merged on top of A's older base, Git kept B's hunks in that file and A's flag hunk was gone. It was not a conflict Git flagged loudly; B's version was authored against a stale copy, the rebase took B's region in the registry, and the suite never asserted the registry's full contents.

Each test only proved its own flag existed. Nobody asked whether the shared file still carried everyone's knobs.

Why green on every side hides it

Tests prove your own path, not the shared manifest. A unit test for ticket A asserts that A's flag behaves as expected in isolation. It does not read the registry after B merged and confirm A's entry is still present. The dropped change lives in the gap between two isolated suites.

Agents work in isolation and cannot see sibling branches. Each prompt described one ticket on one worktree; neither agent knew another branch touched the same registry, so neither claimed ownership, rebased against the current file, or flagged the overlap.

A clean merge means line numbers reconciled, not intent preserved. Git reports no conflict when hunks sit in different lines, even on the same file. A rebase onto a stale base can quietly take one branch's region wholesale. Git does not warn that this file already changed upstream.

The dropped surface has no integration assertion. Flags, router tables, shared type registries, and script blocks usually lack a test that enumerates the whole file, so a missing entry fails nowhere — it just vanishes after deploy.

The cheap habits that prevent the clobber

Own the file before editing it. When an agent reaches for a cross-cutting shared file — a flag registry, router table, shared types, package.json scripts, env schema, or the OpenAPI spec — check open sibling PRs that touch it. Claim the file for this branch or defer to the other branch instead of both editing blind.

Push per-feature config out of the shared manifest. A feature-owned config file loaded by a registry shrinks the collision surface to almost zero; each branch edits its own directory, and the shared file stays a loader, not a data dump.

Require a fresh rebase when a shared file moved upstream. A cheap CI check lists open PRs modifying the same file and flags a merge that overlaps a sibling hunk, rather than trusting a clean line-level merge.

Assert the shared file in one integration smoke test. Enumerate the expected entries in the registry and fail if one is missing; a dropped knob then fails at merge, not a week after deploy.

When the shared file is the contract

If the shared file is the OpenAPI spec or the generated shared types, two branches changing it independently produce clients that silently diverge. A dropped operation survives a green suite exactly the same way: each branch tests its own slice, and nobody reads the contract after merge. The cheap guard is to replay recorded request/response pairs against the local spec and a live sandbox before merge, so the missing operation shows as a red diff in front of the reviewer rather than as a gap in production traffic. That is the local-first loop we built into Powerduck: the spec stays the source of truth, and drift appears on screen instead of in a post-deploy check.

What I check now

  1. Did this PR edit a shared manifest, and is an open sibling PR touching the same file?
  2. Did the branch rebase onto a current base that already includes the sibling merge?
  3. Does any test assert the shared file's full contents, or only my own slice?

A clean merge means Git reconciled line numbers. It does not mean both branches' intent survived.

title: Runtime Control for AI Agents: Closing the Evaluation--Execution Gap in Operational Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.27480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly participate in operational workflows where approvals, binds, and payments create commitments. An approval valid when issued may no longer authorize execution after relevant facts, evidence, policy, or authority change. We call this the evaluation--execution gap. We specify a state-bound runtime assurance layer that separates probabilistic measurement from deterministic adjudication, binds an execution allowance to the decision-relevant basis of an approval, invalidates that allowance after relevant logged changes, and rechecks admissibility at dispatch. This distinguishes the continued validity of a prior approval from a current-state policy check. We describe eight failure modes, an assurance model, a reference architecture, and prospective interventions with retrospective remediation. In a scripted 42-case replay, the state-bound configuration identifies 15 later-invalidated approvals that a deliberately non-re-evaluating point-in-time comparator does not revisit; it holds 14 affected actions before dispatch and compensates one landed effect. These results illustrate behavior under the stipulated policies and event orders, not superiority over dispatch-time enforcement designs or production effectiveness. Under explicit interception, ingestion, dependency, and serialization assumptions, the model establishes dispatch-time validity within the registered execution surface.

title: A Practical Python Checklist for Automating Repetitive Work
description:
Python automation works best when it removes a repeatable step without making the process harder to trust. Before writing a script, define the input, output, rules, and what should happen when something is missing.

Start with a one-sentence specification

Write down the job in this form: “Given this input, produce this output, using these rules, and stop or report when this condition occurs.” If those details are still changing, clarify the process before automating it.

For example, a monthly contact export might need consistent names and email addresses. That is a good candidate for a small Python script if the file format and rules are stable. A workflow that includes judgment, approvals, or exceptions may need a human review step instead of full automation.

Separate reading, validation, and writing

A reliable workflow has a few visible stages:

  1. Read the source without changing it.
  2. Check that required fields and assumptions are present.
  3. Transform the data in memory.
  4. Write a new output only after validation succeeds.
  5. Report what happened so the result can be checked.

Here is a small standard-library example for cleaning a CSV. Test it on a copy of the input first. It refuses to overwrite an existing output file, so a previous report is not silently replaced.

import csv
from pathlib import Path

source = Path("inbox/contacts.csv")
destination = Path("reports/contacts_clean.csv")
required_columns = {"name", "email"}

with source.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    missing = required_columns - set(reader.fieldnames or [])
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Missing columns: {', '.join(sorted(missing))}")

    cleaned_rows = []
    for line_number, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):
        name = (row.get("name") or "").strip()
        email = (row.get("email") or "").strip().lower()
        if not email:
            raise ValueError(f"Missing email on row {line_number}")
        cleaned_rows.append({"name": name, "email": email})

destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with destination.open("x", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["name", "email"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(cleaned_rows)

print(f"Wrote {len(cleaned_rows)} rows to {destination}")

The example makes the rules explicit: trim whitespace, normalize email casing, and stop if a required value is missing. It does not send messages, delete source data, or make decisions about whether a contact is valid. Those boundaries are part of a safe automation design.

Make reruns predictable

A script should be safe to run again. Prefer a clearly named output, avoid accidental appends, and decide what to do if that output already exists. For tasks that update an external system, add a way to identify work already completed so a retry does not create duplicates.

Also plan for failure. A useful run should make it clear which input was processed, how many records succeeded, and where an error occurred. For sensitive or business-critical tasks, add logging, alerts, access controls, and a human review before the automation performs an irreversible action.

Start manually, schedule later

Run the script by hand on representative sample files. Compare its output with a known-good result and test missing columns, blank values, empty files, and existing output paths. Only after those checks should you consider a scheduler such as cron or Windows Task Scheduler.

Where AI fits

Python automation is a strong fit when rules are known and repeatable. AI or machine learning may help when the input is unstructured or patterns are difficult to express as fixed rules, but it adds uncertainty. Keep a measurable baseline, test representative examples, and route uncertain or high-impact decisions to a person.

A short checklist

  • Is the task repeated often enough to justify automation?
  • Are the inputs, rules, and expected outputs clearly defined?
  • Can the script validate data before changing anything?
  • Is rerunning safe, and are failures visible?
  • Has the result been tested on copies before scheduling?

A small, well-scoped Python tool can be more valuable than a large system. Start with one stable task, make its behavior observable, and expand only when the first version is dependable.

I'm Kyle Keon, a Python developer in Pembroke, Ontario, focused on practical work across Python, workflow automation, AI, machine learning, and web development. Portfolio and contact.

title: Top DevOps Service Providers for Cloud Infrastructure Management
description:
Moving to the cloud is the easy decision. Running it well month after month is where teams lose weekends: drifting environments, untagged resources, clusters nobody dares to upgrade. If you are shortlisting DevOps development services for your cloud, or comparing DevOps service providers for cloud infrastructure management more broadly, the eight companies below cover everything from hands-on engineering to full managed operations.

A good provider treats infrastructure as software. That idea sits behind infrastructure as code, the practice of defining and managing resources through machine-readable files instead of manual setup. It also underlies the broader model of managed services, where a third party keeps your IT environment running on a proactive, subscription basis instead of break/fix support. And for container-based systems, Kubernetes is the open source platform most providers on this list build around.

The providers

N-iX

N-iX was founded in 2002 and reports 2,400+ engineers, with a DevOps group of 70+ experts and 270+ certified cloud specialists. It holds AWS Premier Tier, Microsoft Solutions Partner and Google Cloud partner status, plus ISO 27001. Its DevOps page covers infrastructure as code (Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation), cost optimization, CI/CD, container orchestration and monitoring, and cites a UK energy supplier whose operational costs fell 70% after cloud modernization. Natural fit for large, multi-cloud estates.

AppRecode

AppRecode, working since 2019 from Delaware and Lviv, lists cloud infrastructure management, managed AWS and Azure cloud, FinOps and Kubernetes among its services, backed by team certifications such as AWS Solutions Architect, Certified Kubernetes Administrator, HashiCorp Terraform Associate and FinOps Certified Engineer. The most relevant case for this topic is a migration for a US provider of AI-powered contact center software. The team moved services from EC2 to Amazon EKS with Terraform covering the infrastructure, a Direct Connect link to the on-premises environment, GitOps with ArgoCD and GitHub Actions pipelines, and monitoring in Datadog and Logz.io. The case is described in qualitative terms (dynamic scaling, fewer manual interventions, faster deployments) with no percentages.

A longer engagement is the Media Intelligence Platform: a New York AdTech company with about 150 employees. Over roughly three years, three dedicated AppRecode engineers codified AWS environments in Terraform, built Jenkins and GitLab pipelines, ran workloads on Kubernetes and ECS, connected accounts and regions through Transit Gateway peering, and set up CloudWatch and New Relic alerting. Reported results include 70% less deployment time, 99.995% uptime and a mean time to recovery under one day.

Sigma Software

Sigma Software divides its offer into cloud DevOps consulting, DevOps transformation and cloud managed services, the last including infrastructure management and monitoring under an SLA and cloud disaster recovery. It is an AWS Advanced Tier Services Partner and cites 100+ projects in migration, DevOps and infrastructure automation. One cited case is a platform migrated from on-premises to Azure for a client called Mikz, described as delivering the same performance at 10% of the earlier infrastructure cost.

Ciklum

Ciklum advertises 3,000+ engineers certified across AWS, Azure and GCP. Its DevOps page mentions IaC, FinOps, serverless, DevSecOps with automated GDPR, HIPAA and SOC 2 checks, and 24/7 RunOps with observability. Cases include Doxy.me, where it automated CI/CD and HIPAA-compliant cloud operations for a telemedicine product.

Mirantis

Mirantis is closer to a platform vendor than a services shop. Based in Campbell, California, it builds the k0rdent and k0s Kubernetes projects, offers cloud platform operations and workload migration services, and says it serves thousands of customers in 90 countries with 200+ staff on managed and professional services. Useful when your main challenge is running Kubernetes across several data centers or clouds.

ELEKS

ELEKS lists CI/CD, IaC, containerization, continuous monitoring and cloud management, holds SOC 2 and ISO 9001 badges and partner status with AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft. Its DPD case describes a six-year cloud migration and re-engineering program, and Pace gets L2 support for a cloud product with 99.99% effective uptime.

Binbash

An AWS specialist with Advanced Tier status, the AWS DevOps Services Competency and Amazon EKS delivery designation, plus a Well-Architected Review offer and a reusable infrastructure library. A good choice if you want AWS depth rather than breadth.

Opsfleet

Opsfleet embeds 90+ engineers into client teams and is an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner. Its list includes Kubernetes adoption, a shift to Graviton instances, DevSecOps and disaster recovery plan implementation.

How to compare them

Look at who owns the code afterwards, how cost reporting works, and whether the provider can show an environment that was rebuilt from scratch. Ask for the upgrade plan for Kubernetes and for the last disaster recovery test. Providers that answer with dates rather than adjectives are usually the ones that run infrastructure for a living.

title: My Laptop Is Too Slow to Chat With an AI, So I Gave It the Night Shift
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

My Downloads folder is where files go to be forgotten. invoice (3).pdf. Screenshot 2026-10-12 141502.png. Document1.docx, which could be anything. Every few months I promise myself I'll clean it up, and every few months I don't.

So I built sloth, about 200 lines of Python that do it while I sleep. Every night it goes through my Downloads folder with Gemma 4 running on my laptop. It reads each document, looks at each image, gives the file a name a human would pick, and moves it into a folder. In the morning, a report is waiting:

invoice (3).pdf                  -> Finance/2026-10-01_acme_cloud_services_invoice.pdf
Document1.docx                   -> Work/2026-10-01_sprint_meeting_notes_prakhar_meera_jonas.docx
Screenshot 2026-10-12 141502.png -> Screenshots/2026-10-01_error_message_screenshot_python_app.png
export (1).csv                   -> Finance/2026-10-01_salary_and_transaction_report.csv
VSCodeUserSetup-x64-1.105.1.exe  -> Installers/VSCodeUserSetup-x64-1.105.1.exe
scan0001.pdf                     -> left alone (Gemma wasn't sure)

If I don't like what it did, python sloth.py undo ~/Downloads puts everything back.

Anyone with a Downloads folder gets to be a little lazier, which is everyone. It's especially for people whose laptop, like mine, has no business running AI.

Here's a real run on my test folder. Read the timings, because they're the point:

$ python sloth.py tidy ~/sloth-test
[1/13] 2409.11873v2.pdf -> Reading/2026-10-01_quantization_aware_training_paper.pdf (14s)
[2/13] data.bin -> left alone, unknown type
[3/13] Document1.docx -> Work/2026-10-01_sprint_meeting_notes_prakhar_meera_jonas.docx (13s)
[4/13] e-ticket.pdf -> Personal/2026-10-01_train_ticket_booking_confirmation.pdf (11s)
[5/13] export (1).csv -> Finance/2026-10-01_salary_and_transaction_report.csv (15s)
[6/13] image (2).png -> Images/2026-10-01_quarterly_revenue_by_region_report.png (21s)
[7/13] invoice (3).pdf -> Finance/2026-10-01_acme_cloud_services_invoice.pdf (11s)
[8/13] notes.txt -> Personal/2026-10-01_banana_bread_recipe_personal.txt (11s)
[9/13] photos_backup.zip -> Archives/photos_backup.zip (0s)
[10/13] resume_final2.docx -> Personal/2026-10-01_resume_final_dok_prakhar_a.docx (11s)
[11/13] scan0001.pdf -> left alone, not sure (9s)
[12/13] Screenshot 2026-10-12 141502.png -> Screenshots/2026-10-01_error_message_screenshot_python_app.png (19s)
[13/13] VSCodeUserSetup-x64-1.105.1.exe -> Installers/VSCodeUserSetup-x64-1.105.1.exe (0s)

The folder actually held 15 files. The other two are skipped on purpose: a boarding pass I'd downloaded that day (I might still need it) and a half-finished Ubuntu download.

Code

Prakhar0013 / sloth

sloth

Tidies your Downloads folder overnight with a local Gemma model, so you don't have to.

While you sleep, sloth reads each file (or looks at it, for images), gives it a real name, and files it into a folder. In the morning there's a SLOTH_REPORT.md waiting for you, and one command puts everything back if you don't like it.

invoice (3).pdf                   -> Finance/2026-10-01_acme_cloud_services_invoice.pdf
Screenshot 2026-10-12 141502.png  -> Screenshots/2026-10-01_error_message_screenshot_python_app.png
notes.txt                         -> Personal/2026-10-01_banana_bread_recipe_personal.txt
VSCodeUserSetup-x64-1.105.1.exe   -> Installers/VSCodeUserSetup-x64-1.105.1.exe
scan0001.pdf                      -> left alone (Gemma wasn't sure)

Everything runs on your machine through Ollama. No file, filename, or snippet ever leaves it.

Setup

You need Ollama and Python 3.9+.

ollama pull gemma4:e2b-it-qat
pip install -r requirements.txt

Use

python sloth.py tidy ~/Downloads --dry-run   # show the plan, move nothing
python sloth.py tidy ~/Downloads             # do it
python sloth.py undo ~/Downloads             # put the last run back

Run it every night

Windows (PowerShell)…


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The constraint. My laptop has an Intel Core i3-1215U, 8 GB of RAM and no graphics card. While I was testing, Windows had about 1 GB of memory free. Chatting with a model on this machine would be miserable: you type a question and go make tea.

But tidying files isn't a chat. Nobody is waiting for an answer at 2 a.m. That's the whole project: slow inference is fine when nobody's waiting for it.

The model. Gemma 4 E2B (gemma4:e2b-it-qat), served by Ollama. It's the smallest Gemma 4, a 4.3 GB download. The QAT build was trained to keep its quality after being squeezed down to 4 bits, which is what lets it fit in 8 GB. It can also see, so a screenshot gets named after what's in it, not after when I took it.

The pipeline, in the order the script runs it:

  1. Skip what I might still need. Anything modified in the last 24 hours stays put, and so does any .crdownload or .part file.
  2. Don't think unless you have to. Installers, archives, audio and video are sorted by extension and keep their names. The model is never called for them. A sloth saves its energy.
  3. Read a little. The first two pages of a PDF (via pypdf), the text inside a .docx (which is just a zip of XML), the first 1,500 characters of a text file, or the whole image.
  4. Hand Gemma a form, not a blank page. Ollama can force the reply to match a JSON schema, and the category field is an enum of eight folders. A 4.6B-parameter model can't invent a "Misc Stuff 2" folder, because the schema won't let it.
  5. Never trust a model with a date. The 2026-10-01_ prefix comes from the file's timestamp. Gemma only supplies the words.
  6. Write down every move as it happens. If the laptop dies at 3 a.m., undo still knows what went where.

The heart of it is a single HTTP request to Ollama:

body = {
    "model": "gemma4:e2b-it-qat",
    "messages": [message],  # prompt, plus the image as base64 if it's a picture
    "format": SCHEMA,       # category must be one of 8 folders
    "think": False,
    "stream": False,
    "options": {"temperature": 0, "num_ctx": 4096},
}

It uses no framework and no SDK, just the Python standard library plus pypdf.

The one line that made it 7 to 30 times faster. When I ran ollama show on the model, it told me something I didn't expect: Gemma 4 has a thinking mode, and it's on by default. I timed the same three files both ways:

File Thinking off Thinking on Tokens generated (off / on)
invoice (3).pdf 8.7 s 59.8 s 31 / 533
export (1).csv 4.3 s 60.4 s 32 / 535
Screenshot of a Python error 2.7 s 91.7 s 23 / 667

It picked the same folder every time, and the same name for two of the three. On a CPU, 500 tokens of deliberating over whether an invoice is an invoice costs a full minute per file. So "think": False it is. Even a sloth has limits. (These timings come from a separate test. In full runs, with Windows fighting for memory, it takes 8 to 26 seconds per document and more than a minute for a large photo.)

The bug was in my test, not my code. My first prompt gave Gemma two example names: acme_cloud_invoice and python_import_error. The first run looked perfect. Then I noticed that my test folder contained an Acme Cloud invoice and a screenshot of a Python import error. I'd been grading the model on how well it could copy my examples. I swapped them for examples that match nothing in the folder (dentist_appointment_reminder, github_actions_failed_build). It still put every file in a sensible folder, so it really was reading them. Lesson learned: if your examples look like your test data, your test isn't testing anything.

What it still gets wrong. Some names are clumsy. banana_bread_recipe_personal repeats its own folder, and my résumé came out as resume_final_dok_prakhar_a (I have no idea what "dok" means). A scanned PDF with no text layer gets left alone, because all Gemma can see is the filename. That's the right call, but a smarter version would turn the page into an image and let Gemma look at it.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Look at what's in a Downloads folder. My little test folder alone had a bank export showing a salary, a résumé, a train ticket with a booking number, and an invoice. My real one is worse.

A version of this tool built on a closed API would only work by uploading all of that, every night, to a server I don't control. I wasn't going to make that trade to save ten minutes of dragging files around. With Gemma running in Ollama, no file, filename or snippet ever leaves the laptop. I can turn the Wi-Fi off and it still works.

Then there's cost. It runs every night, on as many files as I've downloaded, for nothing. There's no API key, no rate limit, and no surprise bill if a bug makes it loop.

And there's control, three kinds of it:

  • I picked a model that fits my machine. I chose the size (E2B) and the quantization (4-bit QAT) specifically so it would fit in 8 GB of RAM.
  • I can swap it. The model is one constant at the top of the file. When a better small model comes out, upgrading is a one-line change.
  • I can share it. ollama show lists Gemma 4's license as Apache 2.0, so anyone can run sloth without signing up for anything.

Where open beat closed. A hosted frontier model would be faster per file, and it would probably come up with better names. But speed is the one thing this job doesn't need. At 2 a.m., one second per file and fifteen seconds per file both mean "done before I wake up." Once speed stopped mattering, everything that was left (privacy, cost, working offline, no account) pointed to the model on my own laptop.

My Agent Session

TODO: save the session with DevRelay and embed it here, or delete this section.

The Lazy Payoff

Test folders are polite. So I pointed sloth at my real Downloads folder, with --dry-run so it planned everything and moved nothing.

  • 72 files were old enough to touch, going back to February.
  • 36 would have been filed. Gemma read 31 of them and gave each a name, and 5 were sorted by extension alone.
  • 3 were left alone because Gemma wasn't sure what they were. That's exactly what I want it to do when it can't tell.
  • 33 were left alone because sloth can't read them yet: 25 Excel files, 6 PowerPoints, an old .doc and an .mpeg. Spreadsheets turned out to be the biggest kind of clutter in my real folder, and my test folder had none. That's the most useful thing the run taught me, and reading .xlsx and .pptx is next on the list. (Two of those "Excel files" were really Office lock files, ~$…. Sloth skips those now, and .mpeg now goes to Media.)

The whole folder took 11.5 minutes on the i3, with no GPU. Documents took 8 to 26 seconds each. The two images took 70 and 106 seconds, because big pictures are slow on a CPU. It's a lot of minutes, and I was asleep for all of them.

The best result was an ebook whose filename was a website prefix followed by six ISBNs. It came out as the_art_of_thinking_clearly_ebook. It also found two receipts and sent both to Finance, and it spotted two editions of the same book, filed under filenames that looked nothing alike, and gave them both the same clean title.

It made mistakes too. Two versions of the same report got identical names, so the only way to tell _v2 apart is the date prefix. El Niño became el_ni_o, because my filename cleaner threw away accented letters (my bug, not Gemma's, and it's fixed now). A WhatsApp photo got a name that just repeated its old filename. And it would have filed my coding agent's instruction file, CLAUDE.md, under Reading. To be fair, that's technically correct.

Opening 34 documents one at a time to work out what they are is exactly the chore I'd been putting off since February. Sloth did it in 11 minutes while I did nothing at all.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B runs locally through Ollama and does all of the reading. It reads documents, looks at screenshots, and decides each file's name and folder. Vision is what turns Screenshot 2026-10-12 141502.png into error_message_screenshot_python_app.png.

Hiring A Web Design Agency

In the digital age, a website is more than just an online presence; it's the digital face of your business. Hiring a web design agency can significantly enhance your brand's visibility and user engagement. This article explores why off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fall short and provides three key takeaways to guide your decision.

Why Off-the-Shelf Templates and Generic Forms Fail

  1. Lack of Customization: Templates are designed for mass appeal, which means they rarely align with a specific brand's identity. This generic approach can lead to a lackluster online presence that fails to resonate with your target audience.

  2. Scalability Issues: As your business grows, so do its digital needs. Generic templates often lack the flexibility to adapt, which can hinder scalability and limit future growth opportunities.

  3. SEO and Performance Problems: Generic sites may not be optimized for search engines or user experience. Poor performance can lead to higher bounce rates and lower search rankings, negatively impacting your online visibility.
