title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.27379v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. This can produce inconsistent drafts and reduce acceptance length. Iterative refinement mitigates this limitation by conditioning later predictions on previously committed tokens, though additional passes increase drafting cost. To address this trade-off between draft fidelity and inference latency, we introduce DStill, a two-stage framework that distills a target-conditioned drafter's own multi-step refinement into one-step drafting. We first train the drafter to complete partially revealed blocks, then use its refinement trajectories to train a student to predict the final completion in one pass. Using a curriculum that gradually transitions from partial to fully masked inputs, we successfully transfer the multi-step refinement capabilities into one step. Across reasoning, math, code benchmarks on three model families DStill improves acceptance length by up to 28% and speedup by up to 25% over one-step DFlash, achieving up to 6.45x speedup over auto-regressive decoding.

title: Joint Constraint Aggregation for Qualifier-Sensitive Retrieval-Augmented QA
description:
arXiv:2610.27114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented QA can fail even when the correct answer is in the retrieved evidence. This can happen when a competing answer satisfies some, but not all, of the question's requirements and is mentioned frequently in the retrieved documents, which can make it appear to be the best-supported answer. To test whether this retrieval skew actually affects the decision, we manipulate it directly: increasing the prevalence of passages that favor the competing answer makes the model more likely to select it. This points to a decision problem that candidate-level support alone cannot resolve. We therefore introduce Joint Constraint Aggregation (JCA), which compares candidates against the same question-derived requirements using the retrieved evidence. Across three evaluation settings and three instruction-tuned backbones, JCA improves overall accuracy, and its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer. Together, these results suggest that when partial matches and retrieval prominence pull models toward a competing answer, comparing candidates against the question's full requirements can make selection more reliable.

title: is-kit Reached 100 Stars ⭐🎉 Here’s What Changed Since 50
description:
Hoi hoi!

YAY! is-kit just reached 100 GitHub stars⭐ 🎉🎉🎉

When it reached 50 stars, I wrote about how we use it in a production TypeScript application serving more than 100,000 users. 👇

is-kit Reached 50 Stars ⭐ Here’s How We Use It in Production

Real-world scale for type safety
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
Follow
Aug 12

is-kit Reached 50 Stars ⭐ Here’s How We Use It in Production

#typescript #opensource #webdev #frontend
97 reactions
21 comments
7 min read

I could write the same story again. But that would be boring. 😹

A lot has happened since then.

The library gained new APIs, some existing APIs became stricter, I started using it in more of my own OSS projects, and one real-world use case even exposed a type inference edge case in Effect.

So this time, instead of explaining the production adoption again, I want to look at:

  • What changed between 50 and 100 stars
  • Some of the most important APIs added since then
  • How I am actually using is-kit outside the original production application
  • A real bug report involving Effect.catchIf
  • What 100 stars means to me now

Let's dive in! 🔧

⭐ First, What Did 50 Stars Mean?

At 50 stars, the biggest thing I wanted to show was that is-kit was not only a toy project.

It was already being used in a real production application. 🚀

The application had repeated runtime checks like

typeof value === "string";
typeof value === "number";
value === null || value === undefined;

and several larger user-defined type guards for things like HTTP errors, literal unions, arrays, API values, and plain objects.

The interesting part was not that is-kit made those checks shorter.
The interesting part was that it gave them one reusable shape.

Small guards could be composed.

Application-owned helpers could sit between the library and feature code. And the result could still participate in normal TypeScript control flow.

That part has not changed.

But since 50 stars, the library itself has moved quite a bit. 👀

🔑 Property Refinement Became a First-Class Use Case

One thing I kept running into was this.

I already have a good type guard.
I just want to apply it to one property.

For example

declare const input: unknown;

Maybe I already know how to validate a string

import { isString } from "is-kit";

But now I want to express

"This object has a name property, and that property is a string."

That sounds simple, but there are actually a few different cases.

A required property is not the same as an optional property.
An array index is not the same as an object property.

And an optional property that becomes known to be defined should narrow differently from one that is still optional.

So is-kit added three property refinement helpers:

  • refineKey
  • refineDefinedKey
  • refineIndex

The idea is simple

Take a type guard you already trust and lift it onto a property or array element.

For example

import { isString, refineKey } from "is-kit";

const hasStringName = refineKey("name", isString);

Now the string guard is reusable at a deeper level instead of being rewritten inside another custom predicate.

This is a small API, but I like it because it follows the same design goal as the rest of is-kit.

Do not build one giant validator.

Build small checks that can be reused in normal TypeScript code.

🔍 Then discriminatedUnion Got Much More Serious

The biggest addition since the 50-star article is probably the exhaustive discriminated union API introduced in v1.15.0.

Consider a common TypeScript type

type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };

At runtime, validating this is not difficult.

You can check ok, then validate the corresponding fields.

But there is another question

Can TypeScript verify that the validator itself covers the whole union?

That is where discriminatedUnion comes in.

import { discriminatedUnion, isString, oneOfValues, typedStruct } from "is-kit";

type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };

const resultUnion = discriminatedUnion<Result>();

export const isResult = resultUnion("ok", [true, false], {
  true: typedStruct<Extract<Result, { ok: true }>>()({
    ok: oneOfValues(true),
    value: isString,
  }),
  false: typedStruct<Extract<Result, { ok: false }>>()({
    ok: oneOfValues(false),
    error: isString,
  }),
});

The runtime behavior is useful.

But the more interesting part is the compile-time contract.

The builder checks things like:

  • Missing discriminant branches
  • Extra branches
  • Incompatible branch guards
  • Incomplete discriminant tuples

So if the union changes, the guard cannot silently stay incomplete.

That matters because one of the easiest ways for a hand-written type guard to become dangerous is drift.

The TypeScript type evolves.
The runtime guard does not.
And the compiler cannot normally tell you that the two are no longer aligned.

discriminatedUnion is one attempt to make that class of mistake harder.

💪 The Library Also Became Stricter

Not every improvement between 50 and 100 stars was a new feature.

A lot of work was about making existing behavior more precise.

For example, recent releases included fixes around:

  • recordOf literal-key narrowing
  • native Error brand checks
  • array guards with overridden iterators
  • exact struct validation
  • symbol-keyed struct schemas
  • cross-realm struct schemas

There was also more package-level testing.

is-kit now checks published-package behavior from both ESM and CommonJS TypeScript consumers, and also has Deno / JSR smoke coverage.

This part is less exciting to show in a code snippet.

But for a small library, I think it is important.

Making sure they behave correctly in weird JavaScript and TypeScript environments is where things become real.

🤖 I Started Using is-kit in Other OSS Too

Since reaching 50 stars, I've also started using is-kit more naturally in other OSS projects I maintain.

For example, in my changelog tooling of changelog-bot, I use define to keep small predicates reusable and composable instead of turning every runtime check into an isolated helper.

A simplified example looks like this 👇

import { define, oneOfValues } from "is-kit";

const CHANGELOG_SECTIONS = ["Added", "Changed", "Fixed", "Removed"] as const;

const isChangelogSection = define<(typeof CHANGELOG_SECTIONS)[number]>(
  oneOfValues(CHANGELOG_SECTIONS),
);

The exact code is not the important part.

What changed for me is that I no longer think

"I should use my library here."

I just reach for the guard I need.

A library starts becoming useful to its maintainer when it stops feeling like a demo of itself.

🚀 Then an is-kit Guard Ran Into an Effect Type Bug

This was one of the most interesting things that happened recently.

An is-kit user was using a type guard with Effect's catchIf.

Conceptually, the refinement looked like this 👇

(error: unknown): error is SomeError => ...

That is completely normal for is-kit.

In fact, unknown is exactly where the library is designed to start.

But with Effect.catchIf, that refinement could affect generic inference in an unexpected way.

The error channel could become widened to unknown.

The reported case resulted in this Effect PR 👏 And merged 🚀

fix(effect): Made catchIf NoInfer Refinement's first arg with generic Err param #9252

nikelborm posted on Oct 15, 2026

Type

  • [ ] Refactor
  • [ ] Feature
  • [x] Bug Fix
  • [ ] Optimization
  • [ ] Documentation Update

Description

When passing (arg: unknown) => arg is SomeError to some catchIfs, it turned the error channel into unknown. This PR makes only self's Error slot influence the types, regardless of the type taken by refinement.

Validation: the Channel, Effect, and Stream type-test files pass on TypeScript 5.9.3 and 6.0.3, and pnpm check passes. Temporarily reverting the implementation reproduces unknown error-channel widening in Channel data-last usage and in unrelated-refinement cases across all three APIs. The matching data-first refinement cases also pass without the fix. No tests were changed during maintainer validation.

Closes EFF-2233

View on GitHub

The relevant type originally looked roughly like this

refinement: Predicate.Refinement<E, EB>;

and the fix changed it to

refinement: Predicate.Refinement<NoInfer<E>, EB>;

The important idea is that the refinement's input type should not be allowed to redefine the error type already established by the Effect.

The PR also adds type tests for cases like

const result = Effect.catchIf(
  mixedEffect,
  (e: unknown): e is AiError => e instanceof AiError,
  () => Effect.succeed("ok"),
);

Without the fix, the refinement input could participate in inference and widen the error channel.

With NoInfer, the original error type remains the source of truth.

The same pattern was fixed for Channel and Stream too.

There was also a Bluesky post about the issue

Not like the lib itself caught it, but when I created a reusable operator: export const isNotFoundError = and( isObject, refineDefinedKey('reason', equalsKey('_tag', 'NotFound')), ) I noticed my streams having unknown in the error channel github.com/Effect-TS/ef...

— Evangeline Rome 🌵🦎🌱🐢🐍🐸 🥦 (@evadeva.bsky.social) 2026-10-15T16:38:16.787Z

I really liked this bug because it came from an interaction I would probably never have discovered by testing is-kit alone.

is-kit did not "break Effect". And Effect was not doing something absurd either.

It was a subtle TypeScript inference interaction between a generic API and a refinement whose input was intentionally broad.

That is exactly the kind of edge case that appears when libraries start meeting each other in real code.

👍 This Is the Kind of Feedback I Wanted

When is-kit reached 50 stars, I wrote

"Someone found this idea useful."

That was already enough to make me happy.

100 stars still does not mean the library is huge.

A star is still not a benchmark.
It is still not proof of correctness.
And it definitely does not mean every TypeScript project should install is-kit.

But something has changed.

People are not only starring the repository anymore.

They are

  • Using the library
  • Asking questions
  • Finding edge cases
  • Reporting bugs
  • Comparing it with other validation approaches
  • Using its guards with other TypeScript libraries
  • Making me reconsider APIs I thought were already finished

That is much more valuable than the number itself. 💖

💬 The Project Is Also Becoming Easier to Explain

Another thing changed between 50 and 100 stars.

I became much clearer about what is-kit is not.

It is not trying to replace every schema library.
It is not trying to turn every runtime value into a schema-first workflow.
And it is not trying to hide normal TypeScript control flow.

The core question is still very small

"Can this unknown value safely enter this branch?"

Sometimes a schema library is the right answer.

For example, if I need:

  • Rich validation errors
  • Transformations
  • Form validation
  • A contract shared across systems

I may want Zod, Valibot, ArkType, or something else.

But sometimes I already have normal TypeScript code and I only need a reusable narrowing function.

That is where I want is-kit to be useful.

if (isUser(value)) {
  value.id;
}

if (isHttpClientError(error)) {
  // Handle HTTP client errors
}

items.filter(isString);

result.catch(isHttpClientError);

const isMaybeNumber = nullish(isNumber);

Small runtime decisions.
Normal functions.
Normal TypeScript.

🐱 What 100 Stars Means to Me

100 stars is still small compared with the largest TypeScript OSS projects.

No problem.

What matters to me is that the project is becoming more real in ways that have nothing to do with the star counter.

Since the 50-star milestone:

  • New APIs were added
  • Existing APIs became stricter
  • Runtime edge cases were fixed
  • Package compatibility testing improved
  • I started using is-kit naturally in other OSS
  • External usage produced feedback I could not generate alone
  • An unknown-based refinement even helped expose an inference edge case in Effect

That last part is probably my favorite.

Because the goal was never to build a library that only looks nice in its own README!!!

The goal is to make reusable runtime narrowing work naturally inside real TypeScript code.

And now I am starting to see that happen outside my own repository too.

Thank you to everyone who starred the project, tried it, reported something, asked a question, opened an issue, or simply read the code. 🙏

There is still a lot I want to improve.

But 100 feels pretty nice. 😸⭐

If small composable type guards fit your TypeScript style, give it a try!

nyaomaru / is-kit

Build small guards. Compose them. A lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards that compose, refine, and preserve natural narrowing. Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨.

is-kit

Build small guards. Compose them.

is-kit is a lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards.

is-kit is not just a collection of isX helpers. Its main focus is composing small runtime checks into reusable guards while preserving useful TypeScript narrowing.

It helps you write small isFoo functions, compose them into richer runtime checks, refine properties on values you already know about, and keep TypeScript narrowing natural inside regular control flow. Use it at runtime boundaries when needed, without requiring a schema-first workflow.

Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨ without asking you to adopt a heavy schema workflow.

  • Build and reuse typed guards
  • Compose guards with and, or, not, oneOf
  • Use refineKey to narrow a child property while preserving its parent type
  • Validate object shapes and collections when that is useful
  • Parse or assert unknown values without a large schema framework

title: Node.js Background Worker HTTPS Push Subscriptions — Receiving Queued Logistics Jobs
description:
Short answer: a Node.js background worker can receive queued jobs through a public HTTPS push subscription, but it should authenticate every request and acknowledge only after an idempotent reservation transition.n that expires after a fixed hold window, use an authenticated HTTPS push endpoint, acknowledge only after an idempotent state transition, and make retries boring.

Keep the edge boring. It is not glamorous, but it is where auth belongs.\n\nThe useful mental model is a conveyor belt. A scheduler puts an expiry job on the belt; a public worker endpoint receives it; a database decides whether the reservation can still move to expired. Delivery is at-least-once in most practical queue systems, so duplicate messages are normal input, not an exceptional path.

What should a Node.js worker check before accepting queued jobs securely?

Start with the message contract, not the framework. The payload needs a stable jobId, reservationId, holdUntil, and an event type such as reservation.expire. The producer should include an expiry timestamp, while the worker uses the database clock for the final decision. Client-supplied time is useful context, not authority.

Delivery choice Pick this when Main cost
HTTPS push to a worker Jobs are irregular and you want low idle overhead Public ingress, signature verification, and replay controls
Long polling Your network cannot accept inbound HTTPS Open connections and slower scale-out behavior
Pulling from a broker You need consumer-controlled rate and ordering More worker state and operational plumbing
A cron sweep The job is naturally periodic and lateness is acceptable Coarse timing and repeated scans

For a reservation hold, push is a good fit when the queue can retry delivery and the worker can answer quickly. A cron sweep remains reasonable for a small system that can tolerate a few minutes of delay. The choice is about failure handling, not fashion.

A retry-safe expiration path in Express or Fastify

Treat the HTTPS handler as an adapter. Authentication, schema validation, and a short transaction belong at the edge; business work belongs behind a function that both Express and Fastify can call.

type ExpiryJob = {
  jobId: string;
  reservationId: string;
  holdUntil: string;
  event: "reservation.expire";
};

type ReservationStore = {
  expireIfHeld: (reservationId: string, now: Date) => Promise<"expired" | "already_done" | "not_due">;
};

export function makeExpiryHandler(store: ReservationStore, verify: (raw: string, signature: string) => boolean) {
  return async (request: { body: string; headers: Record<string, string | undefined> }, reply: { code: (n: number) => { send: (v: unknown) => void }; send: (v: unknown) => void }) => {
    const signature = request.headers["x-queue-signature"];
    if (!signature || !verify(request.body, signature)) return reply.code(401).send({ error: "unauthorized" });

    let job: ExpiryJob;
    try {
      job = JSON.parse(request.body) as ExpiryJob;
    } catch {
      return reply.code(400).send({ error: "invalid_json" });
    }
    if (job.event !== "reservation.expire" || !job.jobId || !job.reservationId) {
      return reply.code(400).send({ error: "invalid_job" });
    }

    const result = await store.expireIfHeld(job.reservationId, new Date());
    // A duplicate delivery gets the same successful acknowledgement.
    return reply.send({ accepted: true, outcome: result });
  };
}

The transaction should look like UPDATE reservations SET status = 'expired' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'held' AND hold_until <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Check the affected-row count. One row means this delivery won the transition; zero rows means another attempt already handled it or the hold is not due. Put a unique constraint on jobId if you retain a delivery ledger, but do not use that ledger as a substitute for the conditional state change.

I once started with a boolean processed flag in a design review. It sounded tidy until two workers read false before either wrote true. The repair was to make the reservation transition itself the idempotency key. That small change also made metrics honest: duplicates are counted, while inventory is changed once.

Return a 2xx only after the durable decision is complete. Return a retryable status for a transient dependency timeout, and make the queue's backoff bounded with jitter. A five-second first retry and a maximum delivery age are easier to reason about than an infinite storm.

Making public HTTPS delivery observable

Log one structured record per delivery: jobId, reservationId, attempt number, outcome, and latency. Never log the signature or full customer payload. Emit counters for accepted, duplicate, rejected, and expired-too-early jobs; alert on a rising rejected rate and on age of the oldest queued job.

A trace should connect enqueue, delivery, database transition, and acknowledgement. The useful dashboard is a before/after: queue age and held reservations before the worker change, then the same two measures after. Your mileage may vary when traffic is bursty; use a 95th-percentile age window rather than a single average.

Test the ugly cases deliberately. Send the same jobId twice in parallel, deliver a job before holdUntil, replay a valid signed body after its maximum age, and kill the process after the database commit but before the response. The expected result is one expiry, a successful duplicate acknowledgement, and a retry that cannot create a second side effect.

A useful failure drill follows one reservation from enqueue to reconciliation. Imagine reservation R-1842 with a 15-minute hold. The scheduler emits one job at minute 15, the queue delivers it twice because the first acknowledgement is delayed, and a deploy restarts the worker between the SQL commit and the HTTP response. The first transaction matches status = held and hold_until <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, changing exactly one row. The duplicate sees zero affected rows and returns a normal success response. After the restart, the redelivery sees the same zero-row result. Metrics show two deliveries, one state transition, and no inventory double-release. Now move the clock to minute 14: the conditional update changes nothing, and the handler returns not_due; the queue should treat that as a completed delivery only if the job policy allows early delivery to be discarded. Otherwise, schedule a delayed retry based on the remaining hold window. This is why a single processed flag is weak: it records a message, while the reservation row records the business truth. The same test works against an in-memory store in unit tests and a real transactional database in an integration test. Keep both.

Limits and a practical decision rule

The trade-off is clear: this limitation matters. Public HTTPS push is not suitable when policy forbids inbound traffic or when work routinely exceeds the queue's acknowledgement deadline. Choose a pull-based consumer in that environment. Long polling is also a better boundary when signatures cannot be verified at the edge.

This pattern does not provide ordering across different reservations, and it cannot make a non-transactional downstream API idempotent by itself. Use an outbox or a downstream idempotency key when expiry triggers a carrier call. Keep a cron sweep as a reconciliation path, but make it issue the same conditional update instead of inventing a second expiration rule.

The rule is simple: select the delivery mode your team can observe, authenticate, retry, and replay safely. For fixed-window logistics holds, that usually means a small HTTPS adapter wrapped around one database transition.

References

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://nodejs.org/api/http.html

title: Why does a Bevy sprite preview image stay blank when used as a camera target?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

A Bevy image used as a camera target must support render attachment usage. If the same image is later displayed by a Sprite, it also needs texture binding usage. A preview can remain blank even though its handle exists and its PNG sources loaded. The Bevy 0.17.2 pixel-grid example shows the producer camera and displayed canvas.

Key Takeaways

  • World-retention flags and GPU texture usages are separate settings.
  • Render the preview before the camera that displays its image.
  • Keep the preview camera from drawing its own output sprite.

Create an image for the target role

An ordinary imported sprite image is not automatically the right render destination. Start with a purpose-built target of known dimensions and an explicit format supported by your rendering path.

Bevy 0.17.2 provides a helper for that role:

// Configuration fragment, not executed here.
let canvas = Image::new_target_texture(
    256,
    256,
    TextureFormat::Bgra8UnormSrgb,
);
let canvas_handle = images.add(canvas);

The Bevy Image helper implementation sets texture binding, copy destination and render attachment usages. If you construct the descriptor manually, preserve the capabilities required by your use instead of copying only its size and format.

Do not confuse those flags with RenderAssetUsages. The latter controls main-world/render-world retention, as defined in the asset usage source. Retaining a CPU image does not give a GPU texture permission to act as a render attachment.

Separate producer and consumer

The preview camera produces the image. A second view displays a Sprite using that handle. Give the producer an earlier render order than the consumer and assign appropriate layers to both views.

Inspect the pinned example's Camera.order and RenderTarget::Image configuration rather than assuming startup system order determines rendering order. A source sprite may exist before both cameras while the cameras still need an explicit rendering relationship.

Keep the canvas Sprite outside the preview camera's selected layers. Otherwise the preview may sample the image it is currently producing or form an unintended recursive display. The intended result is the isolated character, not an image of its own monitor.

Diagnose with a solid clear color

Use a conspicuous preview clear color and one simple source Sprite. If the displayed image shows only the clear color, the target may be working while the source sprite is excluded or outside the camera view. If it stays unchanged after the clear color changes, inspect the target handle, consumer Sprite and camera execution.

Result Next boundary
Target creation reports a validation error Texture descriptor and format capabilities
Clear color visible, character absent Layers, framing, image readiness and visibility
Previous preview persists Producer execution or target/handle replacement
Scene appears inside its own preview Producer/consumer layer separation

The Bevy loading guide covers source readiness. The mobile texture-budget guide helps bound target dimensions; a larger preview is not a free fix.

Acceptance after resize and replacement

Open and close the preview repeatedly, replace the character, and resize the target deliberately. Confirm both camera target and displayed Sprite use the intended handle after a replacement. Keep export/readback as a separate requirement.

Record the target size, camera order and layer policy in the handoff checklist. This is a source-grounded Bevy 0.17.2 recipe. No GPU validation or rendering run was performed here.

Keep a replacement target coherent

If resizing creates a new image handle, treat the camera target and the displayed canvas as one small replacement set. Updating only one makes the producer write into an image the consumer no longer displays. Keep the old valid pair until the new pair is ready, then publish both references through the same transition owner. Include any export or thumbnail consumer in that inventory. This recommendation concerns handle coordination; it does not assert that creating an image synchronously means every downstream GPU operation has already completed.

Sources and editorial ownership

Primary references checked on October 20, 2026:

  • Official camera-to-image and canvas example
  • Target image capabilities
  • World-retention flags

Editorial owner: FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial and verification policy. Report a documentation correction.

title: Half-written files and fs.watch on Windows: what I measured, and why rename fixes it
description:
A lot of small desktop tools talk to other programs through a drop folder: the writer puts a JSON file in a directory, and the app watches the directory with fs.watch. It is simple and needs no ports or sockets. It also has a trap: the watcher can see the file before the writer has finished writing it.

I wanted to know how real that trap is on Windows, so I measured it instead of guessing. Everything below was run on Windows 11 with Node 24. I did not benchmark speed, only which events arrive and what a reader can see.

What fs.watch reports for a plain write

In a single process I wrote a 200 KB JSON file with fs.writeFileSync straight into the watched folder:

rename  a.json
change  a.json

So one write gives two events: rename (the file appeared) and change (the content was modified). Windows reports a file creation as rename, which surprises people who expect create. If the handler assumes one event per file, it runs twice.

Now the same payload written to b.json.tmp and then moved with fs.renameSync to b.json:

rename  b.json.tmp
change  b.json.tmp
rename  b.json.tmp
rename  b.json

The temp name produces its own events (it appears, is modified, then disappears), and the final name gets exactly one rename. When the consumer later deletes b.json, that arrives as one more rename, now with the file gone. Two lessons: filter by the final extension so .tmp events are ignored, and when you get a rename, check whether the file still exists. A rename event does not tell you whether the file was created or removed.

The torn read

A same-process test can't show a half-written file, because writeFileSync has finished before the watcher callback runs. The realistic case is two processes. I made a child process write a 2 MB JSON file in 50 KB chunks with a few milliseconds between them, and read the file from the watcher callback in the parent. Real event files are tiny, so this exaggerates the window. The point is only to show that the failure exists.

Plain write, straight to e.json:

rename e.json  bytes=50021    parses=false
change e.json  bytes=50021    parses=false
change e.json  bytes=2000023  parses=true

The first event fired after the first chunk, and the reader got 50 KB of invalid JSON. Write to e.json.tmp and rename when finished:

rename e.json  bytes=2000023  parses=true

One event, complete file. On the same volume, rename into place is the step that makes the file appear whole, which is why the pattern works. (I am describing what I observed on NTFS here; cross-volume moves are a copy and lose this property.)

Why a delay is not a fix

A common patch is "wait 150 ms, then read". In the plain-write run above, a reader that waits a fixed time is right whenever the writer finishes inside that time and wrong otherwise. The tiny files a hook writes usually finish in well under a millisecond, so it works nearly always, and "nearly always" is the dangerous kind of working. The bigger problem is what happens next. If the reader treats an unparsable file as garbage and deletes it, the event is lost for good: the writer later finishes the file, but it was already removed, and the follow-up change finds nothing.

The pattern I use now

Writer:

const tmp = path.join(dir, `${id}.json.tmp`);
fs.writeFileSync(tmp, JSON.stringify(event));
fs.renameSync(tmp, path.join(dir, `${id}.json`));

Reader:

fs.watch(dir, (_e, file) => {
  if (!file || !file.endsWith('.json')) return;      // ignores *.tmp
  const full = path.join(dir, file);
  let text;
  try { text = fs.readFileSync(full, 'utf8'); }
  catch (e) { if (e.code === 'ENOENT') return; throw e; } // delete event or already handled
  let event;
  try { event = JSON.parse(text); }
  catch { return; }                                  // leave it; do not delete
  fs.unlinkSync(full);
  handle(event);
});

Three details matter. First, ignore names that don't end in .json. Second, treat ENOENT as normal, because the rename event for your own unlink comes back through the same callback. Third, don't delete a file you could not parse. Quarantine it by renaming it to .bad, or leave it, so a bug in a writer leaves evidence.

Also scan the folder once at startup. Events that arrived while the app was closed produce no watcher events at all.

What this does not cover

Rename makes the file appear whole, but it does not make the event unique. Two writers choosing the same name will overwrite each other, so put a timestamp and a random suffix in the name. It also does nothing about a writer that crashes before the rename: you will be left with stale .tmp files, which are worth cleaning up on startup.

My measurements come from one machine, one Node version and one filesystem. A network drive, antivirus filters or a different Windows build may behave differently, so run your own test before relying on any of this.

If you are building a small Windows tool that listens to hooks from other programs, the one rule that held up for me: write elsewhere, rename into place, and never delete what you cannot read.

Context: I hit this in a tray app I sell, CatCode. I'm the author. The details above apply to any Node watcher, with or without that app.

title: How Tailscale built a customer-facing model router on AI Gateway
description:
Tailscale on Vercel

  • Hundreds of AI models shipped to customers in-product

  • Model access granted and revoked by tailnet network identity

  • Went from model routing prototype to paying customers in months

Tailscale connects a company's laptops, servers, cloud instances, and personal devices into one private network called a tailnet. Remy Guercio, who leads product for Aperture by Tailscale, describes it simply: "It's basically like a VPC that can span any cloud, on-prem, your house, and your phone."

Aperture takes that same idea and applies it to AI. Instead of giving every employee, agent, or tool a separate provider API key, Aperture lets companies control model access through the tailnet itself. Add someone to the network, and they can immediately use approved models. Remove them, and access disappears.

Under the hood, Aperture is built on Vercel AI Gateway and Vercel Sandbox. AI Gateway gives Tailscale one API for hundreds of models. Sandbox gives agents a safe place to run. Together, they let Tailscale offer model access and agent execution inside a customer's private network, without their team building every piece of AI infrastructure from scratch.

Model routing is harder than it looks

Tailscale is an infrastructure company, so building the routing and execution layers in-house was the obvious first option. But once they took a deeper look into the engineering effort required, they chose not to.

The provider layer looked deceptively simple from the outside. "You would think all of the endpoints are the same," Remy says. "They are not."

David Carney, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, has the receipts, because Tailscale still maintains that plumbing for a few customers who haven't migrated to Aperture yet. "There are a lot of things the big providers don't do that blow my mind that the gateway does, like simply putting the cost in the response," he says. "We initially built those systems for customers ourselves, and the complexity is insane."

Agents raised the stakes further. An agent that can read private data, act on the text it reads, and reach the public internet is a security problem now called the "lethal trifecta." The right mitigation is an isolated sandbox with identity and access controls baked in. "I think we wouldn't have been able to deliver the product if we were also trying to build a sandbox ourselves," David says. "But we were able to go from prototype to paying customers in months on Vercel."

Building a custom model router on AI Gateway

Tailscale shopped the routing layer first. "We did talk to a lot of other folks, including providers themselves, and Vercel just made it very easy," Remy says. AI Gateway gives Aperture one API across hundreds of models, and returns cost and usage on every request, so Aperture can surface spend to customers without Tailscale maintaining price tables for each provider.

Tailscale's customers care about protecting their data, and Zero data retention (ZDR) was table stakes for Aperture. Tailscale chose AI Gateway because:

  • The AI Gateway itself retains no data.

  • They can set ZDR globally or use the per-request zeroDataRetention flag, which automatically restricts routing to ZDR-compliant providers.

"All this ZDR stuff is a moving target, like, which models have zero data retention versus not," David says, "but we don't have to write any of that logic, because it's all handled for us."

Zero cost markup for Tailscale and their customers

AI Gateway doesn't mark up token costs on any provider or model, including when Tailscale's customers bring their own keys. Aperture's customers pay the same rate they would going direct, across every model in the catalog.

Time to first token, from signup

Ask David what Vercel is worth to Aperture, and his answer is simple: time to first token. But that means something different to David than it does to Remy, and both are right.

"[David] Carney likes to overload the term time to first token," Remy says. "In the AI infrastructure world it has a very specific meaning, which is how long it takes to load the cache, generate the response, and deliver it back to the user." Remy explains David's definition: "It's the time from user signup to their first model call, which is the real value Aperture provides to our customers."

And Aperture's success is measured by that time-to-value. "I constantly push the team to remove the most barriers possible to get someone to that wow moment as fast as we can," David says. "After months of testing different products, Vercel was the answer to the infrastructure side, because AI Gateway has such low latency."

Running agents on the tailnet in Vercel Sandbox

Once Aperture had model access in place, the team focused on making it safe to run agents inside a tailnet. This is the workflow:

  • A sandbox spins up and connects to Aperture.

  • Aperture connects to AI Gateway.

  • Tailscale validates the identity.

  • The agent does its work.

  • The sandbox shuts down.

No key is ever issued to the agent.

Tailscale shopped the sandbox layer too, and even had a working implementation on a different provider before deciding to switch. "We wanted to focus on network identity, not sandbox security boundaries, and Vercel's sandboxes are bulletproof," says Remy.

Migrating Tailscale's internal AI layer to AI Gateway

Tailscale's own AI usage had grown the way most companies' has: a mix of direct provider accounts and cloud endpoints, accumulated one team at a time. Internally, those requests went through Aperture, but behind the proxy, it was still calling separate providers directly. After implementing AI Gateway for their customers, they knew they wanted to make the migration themselves.

Tailscale's engineering team built a switch in Aperture that pointed requests to AI Gateway instead of the individual provider APIs, so now they have one integration rather than separate ones for each provider. Nothing changed for employees. Aperture was still the endpoint they called, and every model they were already using was in the AI Gateway catalog, so the cutover happened with zero interruption. Tailscale now uses their own migration as the playbook for enterprise customers juggling dozens of provider accounts and keys.

What's next

Aperture started as a raw gateway for engineers to point a coding agent at. It now has a chat UI, MCP connectors, and sandboxes launchable as ephemeral nodes, all running on tailnet identity.

Aperture's new goal is time to first app. David wants users to sign up, run a prompt, build an app, and share it, all in ten minutes or less.

"We don't exactly know what that's going to look like, but we know we're going to have to iterate quickly," Remy says. "Having partners you can work with hand in hand on that is incredibly important."

David's advice to other companies is to focus on the product they deliver to customers, not the infrastructure required to run it. "A lot of people want to build their own router. And look at us, we tried to do it too," he says. "But you don't need to build another router."

About Tailscale: Tailscale is a secure connectivity platform that connects a company’s users, devices, servers, cloud infrastructure, and services through an identity-based private network. Their model router, Aperture by Tailscale, extends that network to AI models and agents.

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
description:
arXiv:2610.27099v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
description:
arXiv:2610.27030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27406v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.

title: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback
description:
arXiv:2610.26914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.

title: When Does Hate Transfer? A Large-Scale Study of Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27285v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective detection of hate content is essential for maintaining healthy online communities, yet performance can vary substantially across languages. This work investigates a core practical question: Can training data from one language support hate-speech detection in another language with comparable performance? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale study across 14 languages. \change{We observe consistent patterns in which certain language pairs transfer more effectively than others. Among the factors we measure, linguistic similarity is the strongest predictor of these patterns, with temporal overlap and dataset-size difference playing smaller roles. These measurable factors do not fully explain the observed patterns; a complementary qualitative analysis suggests that shared cultural cues and communicative norms may be associated with some of the remaining cases, particularly within several clusters. We present this cultural interpretation as a hypothesis from qualitative inspection rather than a measured cause.}{} Our analysis includes low-resource languages, offering practical insights into when cross-lingual transfer can support them and where its limitations emerge. These findings inform the design of more reliable multilingual hate-detection systems.

title: Sharp Degree Bounds for Putinar Certificates in Terms of the Positivity Margin via Analytic Sums of Squares
description:
arXiv:2610.26976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We establish sharp degree bounds for Putinar sum-of-squares (SOS) certificates in terms of the positivity margin $\delta$. For any fixed Archimedean quadratic module with prescribed generators and any fixed bound on the degree of the objective, we prove a uniform certificate-degree upper bound of $O(\delta^{-1/2}\log^2(2/\delta))$ for normalized polynomial objectives. We show that this bound is sharp by constructing a matching lower-bound example in three variables, thereby establishing that the dependence on $\delta$ is optimal. These matching bounds also yield sharp worst-case convergence rates for the Lasserre hierarchy.

title: The Clipped Dropdown in a Collapsed Sidebar — the Hidden Meaning of overflow-y: auto
description:
The QA report

"When the sidebar is collapsed, the '+ Create' menu gets cut off."

The screenshot showed exactly that: with the sidebar collapsed to 60px, the dropdown menu was sliced clean off at the sidebar's right border. Only the first character of "New folder" was visible.

The strange part: with the sidebar expanded (244px), the same menu rendered fine. Same code, same 190px menu width. It only broke when collapsed.

Where I got stuck

My first suspect was z-index — maybe the menu was hiding under something. But DevTools showed the menu was in the DOM with a plenty-high z-index. It wasn't hidden; it was being physically clipped at the sidebar's boundary.

Next suspect: overflow. But all the sidebar had was this:

.sidebar {
  width: 60px; /* collapsed; 244px when expanded */
  overflow-y: auto; /* vertical scroll for long item lists */
}

No overflow-x anywhere. "The horizontal axis is still visible, so anything sticking out should show" — or so I thought.

The cause: one non-visible axis drags the other along

The CSS spec has this rule:

When one of overflow-x / overflow-y is set to something other than visible, a visible value on the other axis computes to auto.

So the moment you write overflow-y: auto, the unspecified overflow-x silently becomes auto. Sure enough, the Computed tab in DevTools showed overflow-x: auto.

Now everything added up:

  • The menu was floated inside the sidebar with position: absolute
  • The sidebar was effectively an overflow: auto auto scroll container
  • A 190px menu inside a 60px container → the horizontal overflow gets clipped (or scrolled)

It had survived in the expanded state only because 244px happened to fit most of the menu, so the clipping wasn't noticeable. Structurally, it was doomed to clip from day one.

The fix: position: fixed only while collapsed

I couldn't drop overflow-y: auto — the scroll is needed. So instead, while collapsed, the menu escapes the scroll container's coordinate system. position: fixed positions against the viewport, so ancestor overflow can't clip it (caveat: an ancestor with transform etc. changes the containing block).

The position comes from the button's getBoundingClientRect(). In React, I store the coordinates in state on click and feed them into style:

const [menuPos, setMenuPos] = useState<{ top: number; left: number } | null>(null);

const handleOpen = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => {
  if (collapsed) {
    const rect = e.currentTarget.getBoundingClientRect();
    // float it just to the right of the button
    setMenuPos({ top: rect.top, left: rect.right + 8 });
  }
  setOpen(true);
};

<ul
  className={collapsed ? "menu menu--fixed" : "menu menu--absolute"}
  style={collapsed && menuPos ? { top: menuPos.top, left: menuPos.left } : undefined}
>

.menu--absolute {
  position: absolute; /* expanded: as before */
  top: 100%;
  left: 0;
}
.menu--fixed {
  position: fixed; /* collapsed: escape the sidebar */
}

I kept the expanded state on the old absolute path. Moving everything to fixed was tempting, but the expanded state has existing scroll-following behavior tangled in, so I limited the blast radius to the collapsed state.

To verify, I opened the menu in the collapsed state on a local build and compared rectangles in the console:

const menu = document.querySelector(".menu--fixed").getBoundingClientRect();
const sidebar = document.querySelector(".sidebar").getBoundingClientRect();
console.log(menu.left >= sidebar.right); // true → the menu is outside the sidebar
console.log(menu.right, document.documentElement.clientWidth); // still within the viewport?

menu.left sat to the right of the sidebar's edge and the whole menu fit in the viewport. Done.

Takeaways

Two lessons from this one.

1. A popover inside a scroll container will eventually get clipped.
The instant you write overflow-y: auto, that element becomes a container that clips horizontally too. Any dropdown or tooltip floated inside it with absolute gets cut the moment it outgrows the container. "It looks fine now" just means it happens to fit today. Put popovers on fixed or in a Portal — outside the scroll container — from the start.

2. Auxiliary states like "collapsed" deserve one pass per feature.
That same day we got three bug reports tied to the collapsed state: a drawer opening as a 60px sliver, the hamburger icon showing at desktop width, and this clipped menu. All of them worked perfectly when expanded and broke the moment you collapsed. We had only ever tested the default state. Of all the state combinations (expanded × collapsed, light × dark, desktop × mobile), the side you don't personally use is exactly the one worth a full lap.

Hope this saves someone the same detour.

title: Is my Supabase anon key exposed? What's actually safe (and what isn't)
description:
You pushed your app, opened DevTools, and there it is in plain sight: your Supabase key, sitting in the JavaScript bundle for the whole world to read. Your stomach drops. Did you just leak the keys to your database?

Take a breath. In the overwhelming majority of cases, the answer is: no, that key is public by design and you did nothing wrong. But there's a real version of this panic that is an emergency, and the difference between the two is worth understanding precisely. Let's sort it out calmly.

Every Supabase project has two keys

When you spin up a project, Supabase hands you two API keys, and they could not be more different:

  • anon / publishable key (role: anon) — the public one. It is meant to ship in your browser bundle, your mobile app, your public repo. It is not a secret. It does not need rotating just because someone saw it.
  • service_role key (role: service_role) — a server-only secret. It bypasses Row Level Security entirely — full read, write, and delete on every table, plus Storage. This one must never touch a browser, a public repo, or client config.

Newer projects use the sb_publishable_... and sb_secret_... formats, where the prefix alone tells you which is which. Older projects use JWTs that both start with eyJ... and look nearly identical at a glance — which is exactly why people panic.

So the first question isn't "is my key exposed?" It's "which key is exposed?"

Decode the key to find out which one you have

Both legacy keys are JWTs: three base64url segments separated by dots. The middle segment is the payload, and it names the role. You never need a library — just decode the middle part.

In the browser console:

const key = "eyJhbGciOi..."; // paste your key
JSON.parse(atob(key.split(".")[1]));
// { "role": "anon", "iss": "supabase", ... }  -> public, safe to ship
// { "role": "service_role", ... }             -> secret, get it out now

Or from a terminal:

echo "eyJhbGciOi..." | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null

If you see "role":"anon" — relax. That key in your bundle is doing exactly what it's supposed to.

If you see "role":"service_role" — this is the real emergency. Skip to the last section.

Why is the anon key safe to make public?

Because the anon key isn't what protects your data. Row Level Security (RLS) is.

Think of the anon key as a library card that only says "this person is an anonymous visitor." It gets you through the front door of the API. What you can actually read or touch once inside is decided by RLS policies on each table. With RLS enabled and no policy granting access, the anon role sees nothing.

This is the mental-model shift that dissolves the panic: exposing the anon key is only a problem if your tables aren't protected by RLS. The key was never the wall. It's the doorbell.

The actual thing to check: is RLS on and scoped?

Here's where the genuine risk lives, and it has nothing to do with the key being visible. Run this in the Supabase SQL editor to find every table in public with RLS switched off:

select relname as table_name, relrowsecurity as rls_enabled
from pg_class
where relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
  and relkind = 'r'
order by relrowsecurity, relname;

Any row where rls_enabled is false is readable and writable by anyone holding your anon key — which, again, is everyone. That's the leak that matters.

Enabling RLS is one line per table:

alter table public.profiles enable row level security;

But RLS with no policies means nobody except service_role can read anything — so you then add policies that scope access. A quick model of how policies work, because the details trip people up:

  • USING filters which existing rows a role may see, and which it may UPDATE/DELETE.
  • WITH CHECK validates rows being inserted or updated. INSERT policies have WITH CHECK only.
  • A role needs both a matching policy and the table GRANT. Permissive policies OR together; restrictive ones AND.
  • A policy with no TO clause applies to every role, including anon. Classic footgun.
  • For the anon role, auth.uid() is NULL — so auth.uid() = user_id naturally matches nothing for anonymous callers.

A typical "users only see their own rows" policy:

create policy "own rows are visible"
on public.profiles
for select
to authenticated
using ( auth.uid() = user_id );

Now audit what you actually have. This lists every policy and its expressions so you can eyeball the dangerous ones:

select tablename, policyname, cmd, roles, qual as using_expr, with_check
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
order by tablename, cmd;

Two patterns to hunt for:

  • using (true) on a SELECT policy that reaches anon = world-readable table. Sometimes intentional (a public blog); often not.
  • using (true) on an INSERT, UPDATE, or ALL policy = world-writable. That's how strangers end up inserting rows into your database.

If reading raw pg_policies output makes your eyes cross, I put together a small public repo that reproduces the exact leaky-vs-safe setup on a throwaway project, with the read-only audit SQL ready to paste: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. Clone it, run the queries against your own project, and you'll see immediately which tables are exposed.

The NEXT_PUBLIC_ question

Frameworks inline any env var prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ (Next.js), VITE_ (Vite), or EXPO_PUBLIC_ (Expo) directly into the client bundle. That's correct for the anon key and project URL — they're meant to be public:

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://xxxx.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJhbGci...   # fine, this is public

The catastrophe is putting the service_role key behind a public prefix. NEXT_PUBLIC_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY ships an RLS-bypassing master key to every visitor. Service_role belongs only in server code — API routes, Edge Functions, backend jobs — under an unprefixed name.

If you exposed the service_role key

This is the one case that's a genuine incident. Do this now:

  1. Rotate it. Supabase Dashboard -> Project Settings -> API Keys -> roll the service_role key. Every copy of the old one stops working immediately.
  2. Purge it from git history. Deleting the file isn't enough — a committed secret lives in history forever. Use git filter-repo or BFG: 
   git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .env
   # or: bfg --delete-files .env && git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now
  1. Force-push, then rotate anything else that shared that file.

The takeaway

  • Anon key in your bundle? Expected. Safe. Don't rotate it.
  • The real question is whether RLS is on and correctly scoped on every table.
  • Service_role key anywhere public? Rotate and purge history immediately.

Decode your key, run the two audit queries above, and you'll know exactly where you stand in about five minutes.

If you'd rather not hand-audit every policy — especially on a project with dozens of tables where one stray using (true) is easy to miss — I've packaged the full policy checklist, annotated audit queries, and a scoring rubric into a $29 RLS Audit Kit. Totally optional; the free demo repo above gets most people what they need. Either way, don't let a screenshot of your anon key ruin your afternoon. Check RLS instead.

title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.26903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of Environment-Aware Out-of-Distribution Detection for Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27211v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual vision-language models (VLMs) encounter a stream of environments and must also reject inputs that do not belong to the environment at hand.
  Class information from earlier environments can aid out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, yet existing detectors score each environment in isolation, and when previous environments help or hurt is theoretically unclear. We develop a theory of environment-aware OOD detection built on contribution scores, pairwise cosine expectations measuring how the image and text features of one environment align with those of another. We propose a cross-environment maximum-concept-matching (MCM) score with two terms: a primary term matching the test image against the current class texts, and a secondary term matching it against the class texts of a previous environment, weighted by the intra-modal alignment between the two environments. We prove that, under a positive environment transition and a bounded class-matching margin for OOD inputs, this score attains a false-positive rate no larger than that of the standard MCM detector at an adjusted threshold. We then show that the score gap of an MCM detector between two environments equals the self-contribution of the in-distribution environment minus its cross-modal contribution into the OOD environment, which separates soft OOD environments, with explicit AUROC, true-positive, and false-positive guarantees, from hard ones, which no threshold that retains the in-distribution data can reliably reject. For cascaded detection, in which the text prototypes of all seen environments are pooled, the false-positive rate on every past environment is non-decreasing in time, and we characterize when detection provably fails. A contribution balance factor applied to the gradients of the classification loss and of a smoothed false-positive rate completes the framework.

title: Learning-Theoretic Foundation for General Coded Computing: The Adversarial Setting
description:
arXiv:2610.27440v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial workers pose a severe challenge in distributed computing systems by returning corrupted outputs that can substantially distort the recovered computations. Coded computing addresses this threat by introducing redundancy across worker assignments. Existing exact and approximate coded-computing methods typically handle adversarial outputs by explicitly locating and correcting or removing erroneous evaluations, which adds significant computational overhead at the master node. Moreover, existing analyses do not characterize how the recovery error scales with the number of workers and the adversarial budget.
  In this paper, we develop an adversarially robust extension of general coded computing (GCC), a learning-theoretic approximate coded-computing framework that designs the encoder and decoder by minimizing an upper bound on the end-to-end recovery error. Rather than identifying corrupted workers, the proposed method uses smoothness regularization to limit the influence of their outputs. The resulting encoder and decoder can be implemented using smoothing splines with linear master-side complexity. We derive a non-asymptotic bound on the worst-case end-to-end approximation error by decomposing it into three components: (1) the encoder approximation error, (2) the decoder reconstruction error under fully honest results, and (3) the adversarial perturbation error. For maximum of $q\geq 1$ adversarial workers among $N$ workers results in a worst-case error of order $\mathcal{O}((q/N)^{6/5})$ with appropriate selection of smoothness parameter, demonstrating that the approximation error vanishes asymptotically whenever the number of adversaries grows sublinearly with the network size. Experiments on scalar computation and neural-network inference are consistent with the predicted convergence behavior.

title: SynCalib: Breaking Dataset Shortcuts in LiDAR-Camera Calibration via Extrinsic-Controllable Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.27547v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online LiDAR-camera calibration remains a fundamental yet challenging task in the field of robotics. Recently, deep learning-based data-driven approaches have emerged, offering high-precision, targetless calibration capabilities. However, existing methods often suffer from a critical dataset shortcut phenomenon due to the lack of extrinsic diversity in their training data. Networks tend to overfit to fixed nominal extrinsic configurations, leading to severe performance degradation and poor generalization in real-world deployments. To address this limitation, we propose a highly generalizable data generation framework tailored for training LiDAR-camera calibration networks. Our framework leverages existing omnidirectional image datasets annotated with depth ground truth to synthesize multi-modal calibration data under rigorous extrinsic constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the data generated by our pipeline significantly enhances the generalization and robustness of typical learning-based calibration networks. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive real-world evaluations across various camera-LiDAR configurations, validating the zero-shot transfer capability of models trained exclusively on our synthetic data. To facilitate future research and community use, the code for data generation, the pre-trained models, and online benchmark datasets will be made publicly available.
