title: REST API Idempotency for Email Verification Leases
description:
Email verification looks like a simple two-request feature: create a user, send a code, then accept the code. In a real REST API, the hard part is the boundary between those requests. Email delivery can be delayed, clients retry after a timeout, and a user can open two verification links at nearly the same time.

I model that boundary as a short-lived verification lease. The lease gives one verification attempt an owner, an expiration time, and an idempotency key. This makes retries boring: the API can return the same result for the same operation instead of creating more codes or moving the account through an unexpected state.

Why email verification needs a lease

A verification token is not only a secret. It is also a claim about state: which account requested it, when it was created, whether it was consumed, and which request is allowed to consume it. Without those fields, a delayed message can be accepted after a newer request has already changed the account.

The lease should contain at least:

  • account_id and a hash of the verification token
  • an idempotency key for the request that created it
  • created_at, expires_at, and consumed_at
  • the current status, such as pending, verified, or expired
  • a delivery reference for support and retry diagnosis

This is useful even when the message goes to a free temporary email inbox during an integration test. The test address does not make the workflow deterministic; ownership and time boundaries do.

Teams often search for “email temporary free” when they are trying to set up a quick test. That can solve the mailbox part, but it does not solve replay protection. A test should still prove that an old token is rejected and that a repeated request has a stable response.

For related design context, OTP inbox boundaries are a useful way to think about separating mailbox ownership from authentication state.

The REST API contract

The endpoint that creates a verification lease should accept an idempotency key:

POST /v1/accounts/42/verifications
Idempotency-Key: signup-42-3f6b
Content-Type: application/json

{"delivery":"email"}

On the first request, the service creates the lease and queues a message. On a retry with the same key, it returns the stored response for that lease. It should not generate another token just because the first HTTP response was lost.

The response can expose a non-secret reference and the expiration time:

{
  "verification_id": "ver_8d2f",
  "status": "pending",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-21T18:00:00Z"
}

The confirm endpoint should have equally strict rules. A successful confirmation moves pending to verified once. A repeated confirmation can return the already-verified state, while a different token must fail without revealing whether another token exists.

Persisting idempotency in PostgreSQL

The database is the right place to serialize the state transition. An in-memory lock disappears during a restart and does not coordinate multiple API instances.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX verification_request_key
  ON verification_leases (account_id, idempotency_key);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_lease_per_account
  ON verification_leases (account_id)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

The create handler can insert with ON CONFLICT, then read the existing row and return its stored response. The confirm handler should lock the selected row, check the expiry, compare the token hash, and update the status in one transaction.

Do not store the raw token. Hash it before persistence, and keep the token out of application logs, metrics labels, and exception messages. The database record needs enough information to explain a failure, not enough information to impersonate the account.

There is a small detail that gets missed: the outbox event should be committed with the lease. Otherwise the API can report pending while the delivery job never receives a durable event. A worker may retry delivery, but it must keep the same verification id and lease metadata.

Retry and expiration behavior

Separate three kinds of retry. A client retry with the same idempotency key should return the same lease. A delivery retry should reuse the same token and message reference where the provider supports it. A user retry after expiry should create a new lease, not revive the old one.

The expiry check belongs in the confirmation transaction, not only in a background cleanup job. Cleanup is eventually consistent; authorization cannot be. A cleanup worker can mark old rows as expired and remove message data later, but the API must reject an expired lease immediately.

This is also where a failure taxonomy helps. A missing message, an expired lease, a provider rejection, and an invalid token are different failures with different owners. The failure taxonomy for email tests offers a practical testing perspective for keeping those cases distinct.

Operational checklist

  • Require an idempotency key on lease creation.
  • Put a unique constraint around the account and key.
  • Hash tokens and redact them from logs.
  • Check expiration inside the confirmation transaction.
  • Commit the outbox event with the lease row.
  • Keep delivery, verification, and cleanup metrics separate.
  • Test duplicate requests, delayed messages, and concurrent confirmations.
  • Keep temp org mail as plain test text only; it is not a safe identifier or an anchor.

Five minutes spent on the state model usually saves hours of debugging later. The useful signal is not merely that an email arrived. It is that the right lease accepted one valid transition, exactly once, with evidence that can be inspected after the test runner has gone away.

Q&A

Should a retry create a new verification email?

Not when it carries the same idempotency key. Return the existing lease and let the delivery layer decide whether a resend is needed. A new user action can use a new key and a new lease.

Can Redis replace PostgreSQL for this state?

Redis can help with short-lived coordination, but the durable account state and idempotency result belong in a transactional store. Using both is reasonable when their responsibilities are explicit.

What should an integration test assert?

Assert the API state, message ownership, token expiry, duplicate-request response, and final database transition. The inbox is evidence in the flow, not the source of truth.

title: you don't have to worry about default avatars for your next project
description:
i've been working on an open-source project called blobz, which basically takes care of default profile pictures for your apps.

the idea is pretty simple. instead of assigning random images or the same boring silhouette to every user, blobz generates playful svg avatars from a name, email, or any string you give it.

it's deterministic, meaning the same input always generates the same avatar. no need to store images, and there are over 4.9 billion possible combinations.

but the part i really wanted to get right was making it easy for other developers to use.

so i ended up building a few ways to integrate it:

  • shadcn components: ready-to-use avatar components, along with things like avatar groups, profile cards, and user lists. you can drop them straight into your project using the shadcn cli. if you're already using shadcn avatars, then you just have to change two lines, one for the import and one for entering the name.
  • react package: if you'd rather handle things yourself, there's @blobz/react, which generates the avatars directly in your app without relying on an external service.
  • hosted api: if you're not using react or just want avatar urls, there's an optional hosted api for that too.

the library and components are free and open source under the mit license.

github: https://github.com/lirena00/blobz
playground: https://blobz.lirena.in

would love to hear what you think of it! and if you find it useful for something you're building, that'd be pretty cool too :)

title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.27139v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.

title: Go Video Room Join Debugging — Participant Token Identity and Reconnect Delivery
description:
Short answer: Read the exact room in the correct environment before issuing another participant token. Record the room name and identity used to mint that token. A token scoped to another room can look like a missing room to the caller. In B2B SaaS chat, solve that admission failure separately from the problem of delivering messages after a reconnect; a successful join is not a durable receipt.

Why can't a participant join the video room after token issuance?

The admission invariant is an exact match between the joined room and the room for which the token was minted, with the intended participant identity attached to that decision. Room names are exact and environment-specific. Reading the room first distinguishes a missing or misnamed room from a token-scope mistake; recording both mint inputs makes the latter diagnosable without reconstructing a transient request later. Keep these audit entries tied to an application request identifier and restrict access to them, since participant identities are operationally sensitive.

Check the room first.

The delivery invariant differs. A reconnecting participant needs an application-level record of messages still owed, a stable message identifier and a consumer tolerant of replay. Exactly-once delivery does not follow from a socket connection or a room token. Distinguish the application transaction that records the intended notification, the queue acceptance boundary and the acknowledgement actually seen by the client. An audit log documents a decision; it does not authorize a join, and compliance retention requirements must be established separately.

Infrai is a fit for the room-check and scheduled-recovery boundary when one backend key must cover both RTC and jobs. Its public discovery schema can help verify contracts before integration; it does not turn a room lookup into proof that a message was queued. Consider a tenant with a staging room and a production room sharing a human-readable label: a token minted against the staging name cannot establish admission to the production name, even when the participant identity is correct. Record the environment alongside both inputs so the investigation tests the minting decision, not a guess about the UI label.

Which boundary should each provider own?

Option Useful boundary Application responsibility
Infrai RTC and jobs One REST API, one key and one bill across backend services Verify token scope; establish durable enqueue and replay independently
LiveKit Dedicated video rooms and participant controls Persist and reconcile chat messages across reconnects
Agora Dedicated realtime engagement Tie admission identity to the application's message ledger
Pusher Channels with Amazon SQS Separate fan-out and durable queue boundaries Connect two signups and two credential sets; write queue-to-socket delivery glue
Ably Managed realtime messaging Decide how application receipts and offline replay map to its delivery model
Socket.IO Application-managed realtime connections Operate the server and persist missed messages yourself

I would try Infrai for room admission and scheduled recovery when a team needs multiple backend services under one credential: one key removes cross-dashboard credential handoffs, and its public discovery schema gives an integration team a way to inspect contracts before coding. This is a narrower recommendation than claiming an end-to-end offline inbox. If room-specific media controls determine the design, LiveKit or Agora may fit better; if independently operated queue and realtime failure domains matter, Pusher with SQS is defensible. Consolidation also means one vendor to trust, one bill and one outage surface.

The limitation is explicit: Infrai is not suitable as a demonstrated durable offline inbox on the listed operations alone, because the queue write contract required for that claim is absent here. Choose Pusher with SQS instead when an independently operated durable queue is a hard requirement and that two-provider integration is acceptable. Socket.IO is another alternative when the team prefers to own its connection servers and message storage; Ably may reduce connection operations, but application receipts still require an explicit design. These are architectural choices, not evidence of a measured delivery rate.

How does the checked handoff work in Go?

This runnable program uses the same key and base URL to read a room and, only after that read succeeds, trigger an existing cron job. The result of the RTC lookup gates the jobs request. It does not enqueue a notification: the available queue routes do not include a queue write, and there is no documented per-message payload for this cron trigger here. Pass the exact room and an existing cron job ID as arguments. No token is minted by this diagnostic example because the route name alone does not establish the token request fields.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(client *http.Client, key, method, path string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, base+path, nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil { return err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("%s %s: HTTP %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" || len(os.Args) != 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and pass ROOM CRON_ID")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    room := url.PathEscape(os.Args[1])
    if err := call(client, key, http.MethodGet, "/rtc/room/get/"+room); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    job := url.PathEscape(os.Args[2])
    if err := call(client, key, http.MethodPost, "/cron/trigger/"+job); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The cron trigger is a write. This example retries only rate-limited requests; after an ambiguous network failure, first establish an idempotency contract for this specific operation rather than blindly replaying a trigger. On the real admission path, mint the token only after the room read and retain an audit record of the exact room and identity submitted. The single HTTP surface simplifies that handoff, but it cannot erase the boundary between a checked room and a durably accepted message.

That distinction matters.

Why reject publish-only recovery?

A live publish suits connected participants. It is not an offline inbox. If a socket drops between an application commit and client receipt, repeating a publish without a stable message identifier risks duplicate display, while declining to repeat it risks loss. For durable reconnect behavior, require a verified queue write operation, an idempotent consumer, an application message ledger and client acknowledgement or replay before calling the design complete. The available queue route list does not document that write, so this article cannot responsibly demonstrate an RTC-to-queue enqueue from those endpoints.

First ask whether the exact room exists in this environment and whether the token was minted for that room and identity. Then test offline fan-out independently, including a worker that runs twice. If this division fits your architecture, inspect the Infrai documentation for the relevant request contracts before implementing the handoff.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Agora documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation

description:
arXiv:2610.27656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical visual grounding requires models to align clinical descriptions with spatial evidence across heterogeneous imaging domains. However, existing multi-domain post-training strategies typically rely on fixed domain sampling and shared parameter updates, overlooking the need to adapt both which domains receive training and where their updates are applied. To address this issue, we propose PACE-MoE, a policy-guided framework that jointly performs adaptive domain sampling and domain-specific adaptation for medical visual grounding. PACE dynamically assesses the training value of each imaging domain from current-policy feedback and progressively adjusts domain coverage through domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing. Meanwhile, domain-specific LoRA adapters route updates to the corresponding imaging domains while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder. This coordinated design aligns training-data allocation with parameter adaptation without modifying the original reward formulation or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Experiments across seven medical imaging domains show that PACE-MoE consistently improves grounding performance over fixed-domain training, achieving a 3.64% relative improvement in mean box IoU over the Vanilla baseline. Under matched domain-specific adapter architectures, adaptive sampling alone further improves mean box IoU by 2.07%, demonstrating the benefit of policy-guided domain allocation. These results establish coordinated data-parameter routing as an effective strategy for multi-domain medical visual grounding.

title: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.26918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.

title: A separate Android for every agent job
description:
Most agent demos still treat a phone as a local emulator window. That is fine for a screenshot. It falls apart when the job has to keep running after the laptop sleeps, or when a second job needs a different device identity from the first.

A cloud phone is a different shape of tool. FoxPhone puts real Android environments on dedicated ARM hardware and lets you open them from a browser. There is nothing to install on the machine that starts the task, and the phone does not borrow your CPU or RAM. The instance stays online, so a long test or a scheduled agent run does not depend on one workstation staying awake.

Isolation is the part that matters once you have more than one job. Every cloud phone has its own device fingerprint: its own IMEI, MAC address, serial number and the other hardware identifiers a mobile app expects to see. Each one also has its own network path and a dedicated IP. You can place that IP in regions such as the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Japan or India. One job does not inherit the identity of another job, and neither one inherits the identity of the computer that clicked start.

That is the setup AI agents actually need. An agent can install an app, launch it, tap through a flow and repeat the same steps across many devices at once. A person can still step in. One-click sync lets a master window drive the other selected phones, which is useful when you want to check that an agent is about to do something sensible. Bulk app management, one-click device switching and team sharing mean one operator can cover work that used to need a row of handsets on a desk.

The same fleet is a practical Android lab. QA can keep Android 10 through Android 15 available without a hardware cabinet. Developers can park a long-running script on what is effectively an Android VPS instead of leaving a laptop open overnight. Teams that already think in terms of a device farm can treat the farm as something you provision in seconds and shut down when the campaign ends. The device farm page is the longer description of that model if you want the product view rather than this essay.

The work we see is ordinary, which is the point. Content teams publish through mobile apps. Commerce teams check storefronts from a specific region. Ad and affiliate teams want to see what a person in that region would see. Game sessions and app tests need a real Android, not a stretched desktop emulator. Agent builders need a place where the agent can tap, type and install, then leave the device running while the next step is planned.

Pricing is usage-based. You pay for the devices and the time you use, and a free trial is there so you can try a single phone before you talk about a fleet. In directory terms it is freemium: start small, then scale the number of phones rather than buying hardware. There is no rack to ship back when a project ends.

If you are comparing this with a local emulator, the tradeoff is simple. An emulator is a good UI check on your own machine. A cloud phone is what you want when the device must stay up, stay isolated, and be one of many. The interesting part of mobile agents is not the prompt. It is whether the phone on the other side of the prompt is real, separate, and still there an hour later.

A quiet checklist before you rent one: can you open it without an install, can two phones refuse to share a fingerprint, can an agent install an app without you watching, and can you turn the phone off when the job is done? If those four answers are yes, you have infrastructure. If they are no, you have a demo.

title: Language Guidance for Supervised Vision Training: An Empirical Study of Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.27208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success on vision benchmarks, yet they continue to struggle with many generalization challenges. Supervised vision training relies on one-hot labels, which provide limited information about semantic structure and shared attributes between classes. This limited supervision can leave visual representations vulnerable to distribution shifts, spurious correlations, texture bias, adversarial perturbations, and forgetting in sequential learning settings. We study whether pretrained language models can serve as lightweight auxiliary supervision for vision training without requiring paired image-text data, prompt engineering, or contrastive objectives. Specifically, we evaluate two forms of language guidance, Explicit Language Guidance (ExLG) and Implicit Language Guidance (ImLG). We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across six generalization regimes, including in-distribution, out-of-distribution generalization, shortcut and spurious correlation resistance, texture and shape bias, adversarial robustness, and continual learning. Our analyses show that the two mechanisms have complementary strengths, with explicit guidance consistently benefiting in-distribution, low-data performance, and continual learning retention, while implicit guidance is often more useful in shortcut-sensitive settings and under stronger adversarial perturbations. Importantly, both are lightweight and add minimal parameters and training overhead. The analyses characterize when language-derived structure helps supervised vision training and provides a practical roadmap for using off-the-shelf pretrained models from another modality as auxiliary supervision.

title: Encapsulation and Visibility in Java: Protecting Your Objects
description:
When writing Java code, it’s easy to focus on making a program work. But good object-oriented design is also about controlling how that program can be used.

That’s where encapsulation and visibility come in.
What Is Encapsulation?
Encapsulation means protecting an object’s internal state and providing controlled ways to interact with it.
Instead of allowing other classes to change a field directly, we can make it private and expose methods that enforce the object’s rules.



public class BankAccount {
    // Private state: cannot be changed directly from outside the class.
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        if (initialBalance < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Balance cannot be negative");
        }
        this.balance = initialBalance;
    }

    // Public API: exposes only the information callers need.
    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    // Public behavior: validates changes and protects the object's rules.
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit must be positive");
        }
        balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0 || amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid withdrawal");
        }
        balance -= amount;
    }

    // Package-private: available only to classes in the same package.
    void applyMonthlyFee(double fee) {
        if (fee < 0 || fee > balance) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid fee");
        }
        balance -= fee;
    }

    // Protected: available to subclasses and classes in the same package.
    protected boolean hasMinimumBalance(double minimum) {
        return balance >= minimum;
    }

    // Private: internal implementation detail.
    private void resetBalance() {
        balance = 0;
    }
}

title: I built a camo tracker that never asks you to log in
description:
I built a camo tracker that never asks you to log in

32 weapons, 576 camo challenges, progress saved in localStorage. No account, no sync, no backend.

Live: MW4Field camo tracker · Weapon stats: MW4 weapons database · Map: Hajin interactive map

Every camo tracker I tried wanted an account first. Sign up, connect your platform, grant permissions, then maybe get a checklist. For a grind that resets every game, that is a lot of commitment for a table of checkboxes.

So I took the boring approach: the state lives in the browser, and the site never learns who you are.

What it actually does

The camo system in MW4 is large enough that a spreadsheet gets unwieldy fast. The tracker covers:

  • 32 weapons across 9 classes (Assault Rifle, SMG, Shotgun, LMG, Marksman, Sniper, Pistol, Launcher, Melee)
  • 18 camos per weapon, 576 challenges in total
  • Three separate mode profiles, so multiplayer, zombies and campaign progress do not overwrite each other
  • Backup / Restore as JSON, which is the escape hatch for the browser-only trade-off
  • A search box, and each weapon card shows 0 / 18 plus a prestige count without opening anything

The counting detail matters more than it sounds. When a roster is hand-entered it drifts: one duplicated weapon in the source list and every percentage in the UI is quietly wrong. On this site the totals are derived from the roster data at build time, so adding or removing a weapon updates the counters instead of leaving a stale number behind.

Why localStorage and not a database

Three reasons, in order of how much they mattered:

  1. No account means no friction. The tool is useful at the moment you unlock a camo, which is usually ninety seconds after you stopped playing.
  2. Nothing to leak. The site only ever stores a set of completed challenge ids. There is nothing to breach that is worth breaching.
  3. Cheap to run. A static site with no auth, no sessions, and no database is a static site that stays up.

The trade-off is real and worth stating plainly: clear your browser data and the progress is gone, and there is no automatic phone-to-PC sync. That is why the export exists — a JSON file you can drop back in on another device.

The general lesson for small tools

If you are building a tracker, a checklist, or a calculator for a fan site, ask whether the feature needs an account at all. Most progress tools need exactly one thing from the backend: a place to put a set of ids. localStorage is that place, shipped for free, on every device you care about.

The constraints you accept:

  • single device unless you move the export yourself
  • progress lost on hard reset
  • no server-side analytics on what people are grinding

For a free fan tool, all three are acceptable. For anything you would charge for, none of them are.

What comes next

The tracker is one of the four tools on MW4Field, an independent Modern Warfare 4 field guide. The map has zone-level threat data and POIs with source dates, and the DMZ code ledger labels every row as confirmed or community-reported.

If you use it and something is missing — a weapon, a camo, a challenge that is not counted — the source is on GitHub and the fix is usually a data row.

title: Why Your Async FastAPI Server Dies Under Real SSE Load
description:
Why Your Async FastAPI Server Dies Under Real SSE Load

You've tested your audio transcription API with five concurrent requests. Everything streams cleanly. You deploy it. Two weeks later, a user uploads a 90-minute audiobook while three others run voice cloning jobs, and suddenly SSE clients start timing out. Health checks fail. Your database pool reports exhaustion. The FastAPI server is still running, but nothing responds.

The failure isn't dramatic. It's the invisible kind: async def wrapping synchronous requests.get(), blocking filesystem operations inside route handlers, or holding database connections open while waiting for model inference. Under light load, the event loop absorbs the stalls. Under real concurrent audio workloads, everything locks.

The Architectural Boundary

VoiceStudio offers a compelling fully-local alternative to ElevenLabs: voice cloning, dubbing, transcription, audiobook generation—all without sending media to a third party. The production challenge isn't starting a server. It's keeping long-running jobs responsive while clients consume progress events and new requests continue arriving.

The boundary should be explicit:

  • FastAPI handles authentication, validation, job creation, and event delivery.
  • A job store records durable state and leases.
  • A worker process performs model inference and audio processing.
  • The API streams worker events without owning the model lifecycle.
  • Media files remain outside response memory, ideally in local object storage or a managed filesystem abstraction.

An SSE connection should be a read-only projection of job state, not the job itself.

A Production-Shaped Streaming Router

The following router assumes a local worker exposes newline-delimited JSON events. The worker wraps VoiceStudio's transcription or synthesis pipeline. The API uses one shared httpx.AsyncClient—it never calls requests from an async route and never creates a client per event.

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import json
from typing import Any

import httpx
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, field_validator

router = APIRouter(prefix="/v1/jobs", tags=["jobs"])


class JobEvent(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        json_encoders={
            datetime: lambda value: value.astimezone(timezone.utc)
            .isoformat()
        }
    )

    event: str
    job_id: str
    progress: float | None = Field(default=None, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    message: str | None = None
    created_at: datetime = Field(
        default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    )

    @field_validator("event")
    @classmethod
    def validate_event(cls, value: str) -> str:
        allowed = {"queued", "started", "progress", "completed", "failed"}
        if value not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported event: {value}")
        return value

    @field_validator("job_id")
    @classmethod
    def validate_job_id(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if not value or len(value) > 128:
            raise ValueError("invalid job id")
        return value


class LocalWorker:
    def __init__(self, client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> None:
        self.client = client

    async def stream_events(self, job_id: str) -> AsyncIterator[JobEvent]:
        async with self.client.stream(
            "POST",
            f"/internal/jobs/{job_id}/stream",
            timeout=None,
        ) as response:
            if response.status_code == 404:
                raise KeyError(job_id)
            response.raise_for_status()

            async for line in response.aiter_lines():
                if not line:
                    continue
                yield JobEvent.model_validate_json(line)


async def get_worker() -> LocalWorker:
    # In production, return an application-scoped dependency.
    return LocalWorker(httpx.AsyncClient(
        base_url="https://b-lost.com/v1",
        limits=httpx.Limits(
            max_connections=100,
            max_keepalive_connections=20,
        ),
    ))


@router.get("/{job_id}/events")
async def events(
    job_id: str,
    worker: LocalWorker = Depends(get_worker),
) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def sse() -> AsyncIterator[str]:
        try:
            async for event in worker.stream_events(job_id):
                payload = event.model_dump_json()
                yield f"event: {event.event}\ndata: {payload}\n\n"
        except KeyError:
            yield (
                "event: failed\n"
                f'data: {json.dumps({"detail": "job not found"})}\n\n'
            )
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            yield (
                "event: failed\n"
                f'data: {json.dumps({"detail": "worker unavailable"})}\n\n'
            )

    return StreamingResponse(
        sse(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "Connection": "keep-alive",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
        },
    )

The Pydantic model does more than document a response. It rejects invalid progress values before they reach the browser, normalizes timestamps, and serializes event payloads consistently. model_dump_json() avoids manually assembling JSON strings, preventing escaping errors when worker messages contain quotes or newlines.

For deployment, the dependency should use an application-lifespan httpx.AsyncClient rather than constructing one per request. Create the client at startup, close it at shutdown. The same rule applies to async database pools: acquire with async with, release deterministically, and never retain a connection across an SSE stream.

Why the Obvious Implementation Fails

A common first version looks harmless:

@app.get("/transcribe")
async def transcribe(url: str):
    response = requests.get(url)
    return await run_transcription(response.content)

requests.get blocks the event-loop thread. During that wait, unrelated SSE responses cannot flush, health checks time out, and new requests queue behind a network operation that should never have been synchronous. Replacing it with httpx.AsyncClient is necessary but not sufficient: model inference must also run in a worker process or a carefully bounded executor if it's CPU-heavy.

The second incident usually appears after the first fix. A database connection is acquired when a job starts, then held while the API waits for inference. Long audio jobs hold connections for minutes, exhausting a small pool. Job state should be updated in short transactions: create the job, release the connection, process asynchronously, then reacquire only to write a state transition.

SSE has operational trade-offs. It's simple and efficient for one-way progress delivery, but proxies may buffer output, mobile clients may reconnect frequently, and every open stream consumes a socket. Emit heartbeat comments periodically, enforce authentication on every stream, and make events replayable from a job sequence number when losing progress is unacceptable.

When benchmarking VoiceStudio against external providers or testing multi-provider fallback (for example, through relay gateways like https://b-lost.com/v1), measure first-token latency, timeout behavior, and total request cost independently. Treat external endpoints as comparison baselines, not hidden dependencies of an otherwise fully local audio pipeline.

The Central Trade-Off

The design decision is separation: workers own expensive computation, the database owns durable state, and FastAPI owns bounded asynchronous delivery. That division keeps VoiceStudio responsive when real users submit several long-running media jobs at once.

But here's the hard question: how many concurrent SSE streams should a single FastAPI instance handle before you shard workers across multiple API processes? At what point does fan-out become the bottleneck, and how do you measure it before production traffic forces the decision?

What's your breaking point, and how did you find it?

title: Data Residency vs Data Sovereignty: Cloud Architecture Guide 2026
description:
Data residency is about where data is physically stored and processed. Data sovereignty is about whose laws and whose access apply to it. Meeting both comes down to pinning workloads and data to approved locations, controlling who can reach them, and keeping evidence, while still running in more than one location so an outage does not take you down.

TL;DR

Customers and auditors now ask where the data lives, who can access it, and how it stays available during an outage.

  • Define the requirement first. Residency, sovereignty, and localization are different obligations. Name the framework, the data class, and the jurisdiction before choosing a region.
  • GDPR restricts transfers outside the EEA. It does not by itself require EU storage. Contracts, sector rules, and national laws often add stricter location terms.
  • Primary data is the easy part. Backups, replicas, logs, traces, metrics, keys, support access, and AI inference are where data leaves the approved boundary by accident.
  • One region per jurisdiction answers residency but creates an availability risk. Run active-active across two or more approved locations in the same jurisdiction, so failover stays inside the boundary.
  • Match the pattern to the requirement: single region, multi-region in one jurisdiction, per-tenant cells, on-premises or local-provider locations, or a hyperscaler sovereign offering.
  • Keep evidence current: location configuration, access logs, an audit trail, data flow diagrams, subprocessor lists, and certifications.
  • Confirm obligations with counsel. This guide describes architecture and links primary sources. It is not legal advice.

Control Plane runs each workload active-active in every location of a Global Virtual Cloud, so you build one GVC per jurisdiction and failover never leaves it. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, which can be two regions in the same jurisdiction.

Residency vs sovereignty vs localization

Data residency is a location constraint: a regulation, contract, or policy says a dataset must be stored or processed in a defined geography, such as a country or the EU.

Data sovereignty adds legal jurisdiction and operational control: which country’s laws apply, which authorities can compel access, and who can administer the systems that hold the data. Data can be resident in the EU and still be subject to another country’s legal reach if the provider or operator is based elsewhere.

Data localization is residency required by law rather than by contract, usually national, and it is often stricter than contractual terms, for example by prohibiting offshore copies or processing.

A sovereign cloud is an architecture and operating model built to enforce a named set of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational requirements together. A design that satisfies one public-sector framework may not satisfy a financial-services requirement.

Term What it controls What drives it What it means for architecture
Data residency Where data is stored and processed Contracts, customer requirements, regulations Pin workloads, databases, backups, and logs to approved locations
Data sovereignty Which laws apply and who can compel or perform access Jurisdiction of the provider, operator, and data location Control administrative access, keys, and the legal exposure of every party in the stack
Data localization Mandatory in-country storage or processing National law or sector regulator Use in-country locations, sometimes on infrastructure you operate or a local provider
Sovereign cloud A bundle of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational controls A named framework, data class, and jurisdiction Design placement, isolation, keys, access, telemetry, and operations together, then map each control to evidence

The rules that shape architecture

Each row states what the primary source says. Confirm your obligations with counsel.

Rule What the primary source says Architecture implication
GDPR, Chapter V Article 44 says a transfer of personal data to a third country takes place only if the conditions in that chapter are met. Article 45 allows a transfer where the Commission has decided the country ensures an adequate level of protection, with no specific authorisation required. GDPR conditions transfers; these articles do not say data must be stored in the EU. Map every flow that leaves the EEA and name its legal basis.
Adequacy decisions The Commission’s list includes Canada (commercial organisations), Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States for commercial organisations participating in the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Personal data can flow to those countries without further safeguards. Adequacy can make a transfer lawful. Check that US vendors participate in the framework, and keep a fallback transfer mechanism.
Standard contractual clauses Contractual clauses ensuring appropriate safeguards can be a ground for transfers to third countries. The Commission issued modernised SCCs on 4 June 2021. SCCs govern the transfer; they do not change where data sits.
UK GDPR transfers (ICO) The ICO publishes guidance on restricted transfers, adequacy regulations, and safeguards including the UK IDTA and Addendum. UK customers may need UK-specific transfer paperwork in addition to EU paperwork.
GDPR Article 48 (EDPB Guidelines 02/2024) The European Data Protection Board explains how foreign court judgments and administrative decisions requiring disclosure interact with GDPR transfer rules. Data center location and provider jurisdiction are separate variables.
EU Data Act Applicable from 12 September 2025, with switching charges, including certain data-egress charges, phased out from 12 January 2027 (Article 29). Article 32 requires providers to take all adequate technical, organisational and legal measures, including contracts, to prevent third-country governmental access to non-personal data held in the Union where it would conflict with EU or Member State law. Expect questions about government access controls and switching. Portability planning matters.
US CLOUD Act The DOJ describes the Act, enacted in March 2018, as speeding access to electronic information held by US-based global providers and authorizing bilateral agreements; it lists agreements with the UK and Australia. Sovereignty reviews ask about the legal jurisdiction of every provider in the stack, not only the data center location.
HIPAA and cloud (HHS) A covered entity or business associate may use a cloud service for ePHI with a business associate agreement, and both must conduct risk analyses. A provider holding only encrypted ePHI without the key is still a business associate. Location decisions belong in your documented risk analysis and your BAA.
PCI DSS A baseline of technical and operational requirements to protect payment account data, for entities that store, process, or transmit cardholder data. Validation requirements are set by payment brands, acquirers, or other program managers. Scope the cardholder data environment tightly and ask your acquirer and assessor whether any location requirement applies.
Australia, My Health Records Act 2012, s77 Prohibits the System Operator and registered repository, portal, and contracted service providers that hold My Health Record records, or have access to related information, from holding, taking, or processing them outside Australia, or causing or permitting another person to do so, with a narrow exception for non-identifying data. An example of localization written into health law, applying to the providers the Act names.
India, RBI payment data directive The 6 April 2018 directive requires payment system providers to store the entire data relating to the payment systems they operate only in India; data for the foreign leg of a transaction can also be stored abroad. An example of localization in payments that needs in-country locations.

A requirement to keep data in the EU can apply even where GDPR does not impose it. Customer contracts, public-sector procurement rules, sector regulators, and Member State laws can all set stricter location terms, so read the contract, not just the regulation.

Data residency checklist: what has to stay in region

Teams pin the production database to an approved region and consider the job done. Auditors then find copies in other places. Check each item for every workload covered by a residency requirement:

  • Primary data: databases, object storage, and file stores.
  • Backups and snapshots: backup targets and disaster recovery copies can move regulated data outside the boundary even when primary storage is correct.
  • Replicas: read replicas, cross-region replication, and caches.
  • Logs and traces: application logs, request traces, and error reports often contain personal data, tokens, and query parameters.
  • Metrics and analytics: product analytics, session replay, and metrics with user identifiers.
  • Secrets and encryption keys: where keys are held and who can authorize decryption is a sovereignty question.
  • Support and administrative access: who can reach production, from where, under what approval, and with what logging.
  • Processing: compute location matters as much as storage, including AI inference and embedding calls that send customer data to a model endpoint.

Logs, backups, and observability pipelines are frequent sources of accidental cross-border transfers. A centralized logging or monitoring service in another jurisdiction can create a transfer even when production data never moves, so check where each telemetry pipeline sends data first.

Architecture patterns

Single-region deployment per jurisdiction

Run the full stack in one region inside the approved jurisdiction, with a separate copy for each other jurisdiction.

When to use it. Early-stage products, small footprints, and workloads where a short regional outage is acceptable.

Tradeoffs. The simplest way to prove residency and the weakest on availability: a regional outage takes the whole jurisdiction down, and backups kept in the same region share that risk.

Multi-region within one jurisdiction, active-active

Run the same workload in two or more regions inside one jurisdiction, for example two EU regions, and serve live traffic from all of them.

When to use it. Production workloads with both a residency requirement and an availability commitment.

Tradeoffs. It needs data replication that stays inside the boundary, health-based routing, and headroom in each location to absorb a failed one. Every location serves live traffic, so you are not paying for a standby that serves nothing. The active-active high availability guide covers the design.

Cell-based or per-tenant deployments

Deploy independent cells, each holding a set of customers, and route each customer to the cell in their jurisdiction.

When to use it. B2B software with customers in several regulated regions, where some customers contractually require a specific location.

Tradeoffs. Cells give a clear residency story per customer and limit the blast radius of a failure, but every cell needs deployment, monitoring, and upgrades, and a misrouted request is a residency incident. Run all cells with the same tooling.

Hybrid, on-premises, and local-provider locations

Run the strictest workloads in your own data centers or with a national or local provider, and join those locations to cloud regions under one management layer.

When to use it. Localization laws, highly sensitive data, customers who require infrastructure under their own control, and regions where hyperscalers have no suitable location.

Tradeoffs. You gain control over who operates the hardware and where it sits, and you take on capacity planning unless a provider handles it. The common failure is running those locations as a separate stack; see adding a neocloud without running a second stack and hybrid cloud platforms.

Hyperscaler sovereign offerings

Each major provider publishes sovereignty options, described here from their own pages:

  • AWS: the AWS European Sovereign Cloud is described as a new, independent cloud for Europe for stringent data residency, operational autonomy, and resiliency requirements, alongside Dedicated Local Zones placed in a customer-specified location.
  • Microsoft: the EU Data Boundary commits to processing and storing EU and EFTA customer data in region, and Microsoft Sovereign Cloud includes a Sovereign Private Cloud for hybrid or fully disconnected environments with Azure Local.
  • Google Cloud: Google Cloud’s sovereign cloud offerings include a Data Boundary that stores core customer data in the chosen region with logged administrative access, Google Cloud Dedicated run by a local partner (S3NS in France), and Google Distributed Cloud for on-premises use, connected or air-gapped.

Tradeoffs. These address placement and operations inside one provider’s ecosystem. If you also need other providers or your own data centers, you still need a layer that manages them together; see how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

Data residency and high availability together

A single-region deployment is a residency answer and an availability risk. When that region fails, the options are to wait or to fail over somewhere that may break the residency commitment, and teams under pressure often choose the second. Active-standby inside the jurisdiction helps, but the standby bills for capacity that serves no traffic and is often not tested under real load.

Active-active across two or more approved locations in the same jurisdiction removes that tradeoff. Every location is proven under production load, and when one becomes unhealthy, traffic shifts to locations that are already inside the boundary, so a failover never becomes a residency exception. Keep replication, backups, logs, and keys inside the same boundary. For what each design can deliver, see five nines availability architecture.

Proving it

Auditors and customer security teams ask for evidence, and they ask repeatedly, so build the evidence trail as you build the system.

Evidence What it shows How to keep it current
Location configuration The approved locations each workload can run in Store it as code and review changes like any other change
Access logs Who accessed systems and data, and from where Centralize inside the boundary and set retention to match contracts
Audit trail Every administrative action, tamper-resistant Generate it automatically
Data flow diagrams Where data moves, including backups, logs, and third parties Update with each architecture change and review quarterly
Subprocessor list Every vendor that touches the data and where it operates Review on onboarding and vendor changes, and notify customers as contracts require
Certifications and reports Independent assessment of controls Track expiry, scope, and version, and confirm the scope covers the service you use

Treat the location configuration as the source of truth and generate diagrams from it where you can. Then test the boundary: try to deploy a workload to an unapproved location in staging and confirm it is refused.

How Control Plane helps with data residency and sovereignty

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, on-premises, and bare-metal location into one Global Virtual Cloud (GVC).

  • You choose the locations. A workload deployed to a GVC runs only in that GVC’s locations, active-active in every one, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. Build each GVC from locations in one jurisdiction, and use separate GVCs for separate jurisdictions.
  • Residency and resilience in one design. Every location in a GVC serves live traffic, so you get active-active failover inside your boundary without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be two regions in the same jurisdiction, on one provider or on different providers.
  • Proven in an outage. During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.
  • Infrastructure you control. Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) and Managed Kubernetes let your own clusters, your own servers, on-premises data centers, or a local or national provider join a GVC as locations, managed alongside cloud regions.
  • Use regional cloud services in place. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, so workloads can use databases and key management services you keep in the same jurisdiction.
  • Controls that produce evidence. Mutual TLS between workloads, secrets management, fine-grained access policies, and a tamper-proof audit trail, plus autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, automatic TLS certificates, and unified logs, metrics, and traces, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate.
  • Compliance. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant, so the platform layer comes with its own compliance evidence to add to yours.

FAQ

What is data residency?

A requirement that data be stored or processed in a specific geography, such as a country or the EU. It comes from regulations, contracts, or internal policy, and it applies to every copy of the data, including backups, replicas, and logs.

What is the difference between data residency, data sovereignty, and data localization?

Residency is where data is stored and processed, sovereignty is which laws apply and who can compel access, and localization is residency required by national law.

What is a sovereign cloud?

An architecture and operating model that enforces a named set of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational requirements together. AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud publish sovereign offerings, and you can also assemble one from regional locations, local providers, and infrastructure you operate.

Does a sovereign cloud require dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure?

Not always. The framework, data class, jurisdiction, and threat model decide whether shared regional infrastructure is acceptable or dedicated infrastructure under your control is required.

How do I keep customer data in the EU on AWS, GCP, or Azure?

Choose EU regions for every workload and data store, apply the same rule to backups, replicas, telemetry, and keys, and use each provider’s policy controls to block deployment outside approved regions. On Control Plane, a GVC built from EU locations keeps every workload replica in those locations, across one provider or several.

Does GDPR require data to stay in the EU?

GDPR’s transfer articles set conditions for moving personal data to third countries, such as adequacy decisions and standard contractual clauses; they do not require EU storage. Contracts, sector rules, and national laws can.

Can I have data residency and high availability at the same time?

Yes. Run active-active across at least two approved locations in the same jurisdiction so failover stays inside the boundary. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, which can be two regions in the same jurisdiction.

What data residency requirements apply to healthcare and payments data?

HIPAA guidance centers on a business associate agreement and a documented risk analysis, and PCI DSS sets security requirements with validation set by acquirers and payment brands. Some countries add localization law, such as Australia’s My Health Records Act and India’s RBI payment data directive.

How do I prove data residency to an auditor or customer?

Provide location configuration, data flow diagrams that include backups and telemetry, access logs, an audit trail of administrative actions, a subprocessor list with locations, and current certifications, matched to the framework being tested.

Can I add a region for a new market without rebuilding my application?

Yes, if your platform treats locations as configuration. On Control Plane you add an approved location to a GVC or create a new GVC for that jurisdiction, and the workload definition does not change. Plan data replication and telemetry for the new jurisdiction.

Next step: bring your residency requirements and current architecture, and the Control Plane team will map them to a GVC layout per jurisdiction that stays up when a region fails. Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 3: Entity Mapping
description:
Entity mapping is the foundation of working with Hibernate/JPA. It defines how Java objects are mapped to database tables.

Basic Annotations: Where an Entity Begins

Any mapping starts with declaring a class as an entity and defining its primary key.

  • @Entity: Marks the class as an entity that will be mapped to a database table. This is a mandatory annotation.
  • @Table: Allows you to explicitly specify the table name. If omitted, Hibernate will default to the class name (e.g., for User, the table will be User).
  • @Id: Defines the field that serves as the primary key.
  • @GeneratedValue: Specifies that the primary key value will be generated automatically. The GenerationType.IDENTITY strategy (database auto-increment) is one of the most common and straightforward.
  • @Column: Used for fine-tuning the column: you can specify its name, length, precision, forbid null values, etc.

Example of a simple entity:

@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false)
    private String name;

    // ... getters and setters
}

Relationship Types: From One-to-One to Many-to-Many

In JPA, there are four main types of relationships. The key concept to understand is the owning side. It is on the owning side that the relationship is defined in the database (e.g., which table will hold the foreign key or the join table).

  • @ManyToOne (Many-to-One): The most common and basic relationship. It maps directly to a foreign key in the table. Important: By default, JPA uses FetchType.EAGER for this, which is almost always undesirable. 
@Entity
public class Book {
    // ...
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) // Explicitly specify lazy loading!
    @JoinColumn(name = "publisher_id") // Name of the foreign key column
    private Publisher publisher;
}
  • @OneToMany (One-to-Many): The inverse side of @ManyToOne. In JPA, this relationship is almost always bidirectional and must be the non-owning (inverse) side. For this, the mappedBy attribute is used, pointing to the field in the child entity that owns the relationship. 
@Entity
public class Publisher {
    // ...
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "publisher", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();
}

  • @OneToOne (One-to-One): A relationship where one record in table A corresponds to exactly one record in table B. Like @ManyToOne, it defaults to EAGER fetching. To enable lazy loading on the child side (where the foreign key resides), you must explicitly use @JoinColumn.

  • @ManyToMany (Many-to-Many): Requires an intermediate join table. The owning side defines this table using the @JoinTable annotation.

// Owning side
@Entity
public class Student {
    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(
        name = "student_course",
        joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
        inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
    )
    private Set<Course> courses = new HashSet<>();
}

// Inverse (non-owning) side
@Entity
public class Course {
    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")
    private Set<Student> students = new HashSet<>();
}

Cascades (CascadeType) and orphanRemoval

These mechanisms determine how operations performed on one entity affect its related entities.

  • CascadeType: Defines which operations (persist, remove, update) should be cascaded to related entities.

    • CascadeType.PERSIST: When the parent is saved, new child entities are automatically saved as well.
    • CascadeType.REMOVE: When the parent is deleted, all related child entities are also deleted.
    • CascadeType.ALL: Applies all operations. Use with caution, only if the child entity cannot exist without the parent.

  • orphanRemoval = true: A more specific and powerful tool. It deletes a child entity if it is "unlinked" from the parent (e.g., removed from the List<Book> collection in Publisher), even if the parent entity itself is not deleted. This is ideal for modeling strict "composition" relationships.

Fetch Strategies (FetchType): LAZY vs EAGER

This is one of the most critical topics for application performance.

  • FetchType.LAZY (Lazy): Hibernate loads the related entity only upon the first access to it. This is the recommended default approach for all relationships, especially for collections (@OneToMany, @ManyToMany), as it prevents the N+1 query problem and excessive data loading.
  • FetchType.EAGER (Eager): Hibernate loads the related entity immediately, along with the parent. While this might seem convenient, in practice, it often leads to loading massive amounts of unnecessary data and severe performance issues.

The golden rule: Always explicitly specify fetch = FetchType.LAZY for all @ManyToOne and @OneToOne relationships, as EAGER is their default value.

Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

  1. Always use FetchType.LAZY for @ManyToOne and @OneToOne. This is the single most important rule for avoiding performance bottlenecks.
  2. Define the owning side correctly. For @OneToMany, use mappedBy on the "one" side, and @JoinColumn on the "many" (owning) side.
  3. Be cautious with CascadeType.ALL. Apply it only for true compositions, where the child object has no business meaning without the parent.
  4. Use orphanRemoval = true for clean deletion of child entities when they are removed from a collection.
  5. Don't forget @JsonIgnoreProperties (or @JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference) when serializing bidirectional relationships to JSON to avoid infinite recursion.
  6. To load lazy relationships, use JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph, rather than relying on OpenSessionInView, which is widely considered an anti-pattern.

title: LoRASpace: A Pool-Wide Shared Substrate for Static and Dynamic Multi-LoRA Composition
description:
arXiv:2610.27444v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories host many LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept or task. Combining several LoRAs in one generation forces a trade-off. Merging their weights into one update needs a single forward pass, but LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere and quality drops. Running each LoRA in its own forward pass (composite) preserves quality, but inference time grows linearly with the number of active LoRAs. We study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi-LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low-rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that keeps 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the summed LoRA ranks is needed, and the subspace grows sub-linearly with pool size. A 48-LoRA sub-pool of LoRA-Hub on FLAN-T5 tasks shows comparable overlap (62%), while the diversity-curated LoRA-Retriever benchmark sits near the no-overlap baseline (96%), so pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We build on this overlap with LoRASpace, a training-free method that computes the subspace once per pool and reuses it in two inference modes, a static mode at merge cost and a dynamic mode for input-dependent routing. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace is more than 6x faster than composite with six active LoRAs on a 17-LoRA pool, mainly because it runs one backbone pass instead of six. In an ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace, so the quality gain does not depend on the pool-wide basis. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever benchmark, compression is small and gains come from coupling with external retrieval.

title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
description:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE

We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us.

Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise. Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include:

We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort. Link here:https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin

We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter.

Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon)

Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc.

Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter!

If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.

title: LiBRA: Logit Fingerprints for Byzantine-Robust Client Selection in Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27357v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Byzantine-robust aggregation shields federated learning from malicious updates, but the rules that filter out suspect updates do so by comparing clients' parameter vectors. That comparison requires access to every client's update, which secure aggregation exists to withhold, costs $O(n^2 d)$ in the parameter dimension $d$, and is defined only between clients that share an architecture. We propose LiBRA, which compares clients on what their models compute rather than on the parameters that compute them, using a fingerprint of $C^2$ values for $C$ classes, the class-conditional logit response of each client's model to pseudo-patterns optimised against it. We instantiate LiBRA as variants of Krum, Multi-Krum and Bulyan that change only what the dissimilarity score is computed on. On Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 with three architectures and four backdoor and label-manipulation attacks under i.i.d. partitions, each variant holds every attack its parent holds, and on identical client updates under a backdoor attack the fingerprint ranks malicious clients within 0.006 AUC of the full parameter vector. The variants thus match the robustness of the rules they extend, while their trust decision reads no client parameter, compares up to 49,090 times fewer values, and can by construction compare clients whose architectures differ, at the cost of one pattern optimisation per client per round.

title: Why can a Bevy camera see a character body but not its child equipment?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Check RenderLayers on both the camera and each renderable entity when a Bevy character body appears but its child equipment does not. RenderLayers are not inherited from the parent. The camera and renderable must share a layer. This is separate from hierarchy visibility and image loading, as documented in the Bevy 0.17.2 layer implementation.

Key Takeaways

  • Parent-child ownership does not copy a render layer to equipment.
  • Confirm an actual camera/entity layer intersection.
  • Keep the body and equipment visible in a minimal single-camera scene first.

List the renderable entities

A character root may be only a gameplay entity. Its body, sword and shadow can be separate Sprite children. Inspect the component on the Sprite entity itself, not just on the root shown at the top of the hierarchy.

Create a short inventory with entity ID, parent ID, image handle, Visibility and RenderLayers. For the intended camera, record its layers and target. This makes an invisible sword a concrete mismatch to investigate rather than a reason to regenerate the PNG.

If the image is still loading, first follow the Bevy dependency-readiness guide. An absent image and a layer mismatch can produce similar screenshots but need different fixes.

Align the camera and selected drawables

A small setup fragment illustrates a dedicated preview layer:

// Bevy 0.17.2, unexecuted setup fragments.
commands.entity(preview_camera).insert(RenderLayers::layer(1));
commands.entity(body).insert(RenderLayers::layer(1));
commands.entity(weapon).insert(RenderLayers::layer(1));

Do not paste this into every entity indiscriminately. A portrait camera may intentionally exclude world shadows, and a main camera may intentionally exclude preview equipment. Decide which renderables belong to the view, then assign the shared layer.

The official pixel-grid example uses camera and layer separation in a render-to-texture setup. It is useful evidence of the mechanism, not a ready-made policy for your character hierarchy.

Test visibility and layers independently

Visibility can still hide a correctly layered drawable. The visibility implementation describes hierarchy-related visibility separately. Temporarily use a simple visible root and a known loaded image when testing the layer intersection.

Body Weapon Preview camera Interpretation
Layer 1 Layer 0 Layer 1 Weapon has no shared layer
Layer 1 Layer 1 Layer 1 Inspect loading, visibility, position and target
Layers 0 and 1 Layer 1 Layer 0 Body may appear while weapon is excluded

Avoid inferring a layer problem from a single successful frame. Switch the active camera or open the preview and gameplay views together. A drawable assigned to both may appear twice if both cameras render into the same final view.

Preserve the asset contract

Layer selection should not change frame order, alpha or the position of the weapon inside its source image. The equipment-layering guide explains the artwork tradeoff; this procedure addresses which renderable a particular camera draws.

Store the camera-layer policy with the sprite delivery checklist, especially when a preview feature creates a second camera.

Acceptance requires the intended body, weapon and shadow to appear in the correct views and remain absent from excluded views. Test after reparenting equipment. This is a source-based diagnostic for Bevy 0.17.2; the setup has not been executed here.

Check newly attached equipment

Test equipment created after the initial character setup, not only parts spawned at startup. A system that assigns layers to existing children once can miss a sword attached later. Put the intended view assignment in the equipment creation or attachment path and validate it when that path runs. When an item is moved between world and preview views, update the layer policy deliberately. Copying a layer from an arbitrary sibling is fragile because that sibling may serve a different camera or represent an intentionally excluded shadow.

Sources and editorial ownership

Primary references checked on October 20, 2026:

  • RenderLayers inheritance and intersection
  • Official layered camera example
  • Visibility propagation implementation

Editorial owner: FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial and verification policy. Report a documentation correction.
