title: Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Logs Said 1970-01-21 (and the Seconds vs Milliseconds Fix)
description:
Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Logs Said 1970-01-21 (and the Seconds vs Milliseconds Fix)

I spent a solid forty minutes last Tuesday staring at a billing page that claimed every subscription in our system had expired on 1970-01-21.

Not 1970-01-01, the date everyone learns to recognize instantly. 1970-01-21, a much more specific flavour of wrong. That particular wrongness has exactly one cause: a millisecond timestamp got handed to code that expected seconds.

The API was fine. My frontend was not.

If you have ever debugged a date that landed in 1970, or a "today" that showed up eight hours early, this is the checklist I wish I had taped to my monitor. Three ways to convert a Unix timestamp, then three traps I keep stepping in.

Method 1: Python 3.11.1

Server side, datetime.fromtimestamp() is the whole job. The one argument that matters is the second one.

# Python 3.11.1
import datetime

ts = 1761000000

utc = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, datetime.timezone.utc)
print(utc.isoformat())
# 2025-10-20T22:40:00+00:00

print(datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts).isoformat())
# 2025-10-21T06:40:00   <- same instant, my laptop is UTC+8

Skip the timezone argument and you get a naive datetime silently rendered in local time. That is where off-by-eight-hours bugs are born.

Going the other direction, build an aware datetime and read .timestamp():

# Python 3.11.1
import datetime

d = datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
print(int(d.timestamp()))
# 1792540800

print(datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat())
# 2026-10-21T01:47:19.575814+00:00

I always store UTC and format at the edge. The Python datetime docs spell out the naive-vs-aware rules better than I can, and they are worth reading once.

Method 2: Node.js 22.13.1

JavaScript's Date constructor takes milliseconds. Full stop. It does not guess, and it does not warn.

// Node.js 22.13.1
const seconds = 1761000000;

console.log(new Date(seconds).toISOString());
// 1970-01-21T09:10:00.000Z   <- wrong, this is my bug from Tuesday

console.log(new Date(seconds * 1000).toISOString());
// 2025-10-20T22:40:00.000Z   <- correct

Backwards is Date.now() (milliseconds) or Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) when the backend wants seconds:

// Node.js 22.13.1
console.log(Date.now());
// 1792547248983

console.log(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000));
// 1792547248

MDN's Date page is the reference I keep open, especially the section on date-string parsing, which never behaves the way people assume.

When I am already in a terminal, GNU date is faster than opening an editor:

TZ=UTC date -d @1761000000 '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z'
# 2025-10-20 22:40:00 UTC

TZ=UTC date -d "2026-10-21 01:47:19" +%s
# 1792547239

Method 3: paste it into a browser

Sometimes I am reading a stranger's log line and do not want to boot anything. A free online Unix timestamp converter handles both directions in one input box, and shows UTC and local time side by side, which is the part I actually care about when the number came from a server in another region.

I keep this browser-based timestamp converter bookmarked for exactly that. Nothing is uploaded, the arithmetic happens in the page, and I can hand the link to a support engineer who has never opened a REPL.

Three traps worth memorizing

1. Seconds versus milliseconds. Symptoms: a date in January 1970, or a year around 57000. In Node, new Date(1761000000) returns 1970-01-21T09:10:00.000Z. In Python, passing the millisecond value straight in does not degrade gracefully, it throws:

>>> datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(1761000000000)
ValueError: year 57773 is out of range

That traceback is a gift. It means milliseconds, and the fix is to divide by 1000.

2. Timezone drift on round trips. A date-only string is parsed as UTC, but a date-time string without an offset is parsed as local. On Node 22.13.1 with TZ unset on a UTC+8 box:

new Date('2026-10-21').toISOString()
// 2026-10-21T00:00:00.000Z
new Date('2026-10-21T00:00:00').toISOString()
// 2026-10-20T16:00:00.000Z

Python mirrors the trap in reverse. datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0).timestamp() returned 1792512000.0 on my machine, while the same value marked UTC returned 1792540800.0. Eight hours apart, because a naive datetime is interpreted in local time. Set TZ explicitly in CI, or your tests pass locally and fail in the container.

3. The 2038 ceiling and 32-bit storage. 2147483647 is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. Store timestamps in a 64-bit column or as bigint, because a signed 32-bit int wraps one second later. Postgres integer and legacy MySQL INT columns are the usual offenders, and they will not complain until they do.

I also stopped trusting shell date syntax across machines. GNU wants date -d @1761000000; macOS and BSD want date -r 1761000000. Run the GNU form on a BSD box and you get:

date: 1761000000: No such file or directory

Same command, same number, completely different parsing. Any script that might run on a laptop needs the branch.

Task Python 3.11.1 Node.js 22.13.1 Shell
Epoch to UTC datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, timezone.utc) new Date(ts * 1000) TZ=UTC date -d @$ts
Date to epoch int(aware_dt.timestamp()) Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) TZ=UTC date -d "$str" +%s
Unit seconds, float milliseconds seconds
Main trap naive datetime reads local seconds treated as ms BSD date -r vs GNU date -d

Two habits fixed this class of bug for me: I name every timestamp field with its unit (expires_at_s, created_ms), and I never let a naive datetime cross a function boundary. When I do need to eyeball a number fast, the timestamp converter at utilvy shows both directions at once, which is usually enough to confirm whether I am off by a factor of 1000.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com

title: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.27120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final performance. Thus, we propose Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering (EDMA), which uses logical entropy to formalise multimodal QA as an iterative process of entropy reduction and to quantify the contribution of each modality in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidate answers. This enables the construction of quantifiable answering trajectories, where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction. EDMA introduces (i) modality-conditioned partitioning to estimate unimodal entropy reduction, (ii) entropy-driven multimodal fusion to capture complementary information across modalities, and (iii) entropy-based selection of the answering trajectory that minimises the most logical entropy. Evaluated across standard MMQA benchmarks, EDMA outperforms competitive prompting baselines, with average gains of 12.8 F1 and 4.6 LLM-J points over Planning Prompting and 18.6 F1 and 8.3 LLM-J points over Chain-of-Thought. Moreover, EDMA outperforms self-consistency baselines and is competitive with the multi-agent system baseline. Moreover, we show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and, through controlled trajectory selection, demonstrate that logical entropy serves as an effective, monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths, validating entropy level as a reliable proxy for performance.

title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.27043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. Task 1 (cheque extraction) and Task 2 (Mintaka QA with pinned evidence across nine languages and nine model-effort configurations) test whether accuracy and effort settings transfer; Task 3 (FinanceBench pilot, 50 items over SEC 10-K filings in four languages) validates whether these patterns generalise to financial content. Accuracy reusability is broadly confirmed: Gemini 3.5 Flash achieves 95.2-97.6% extraction accuracy across prompt languages, and FinanceBench per-language means span 5.8pp (77.1-82.9%), though the language-difficulty ranking reverses between domains (Hindi is worst on Mintaka, best on FinanceBench at 82.9%). Effort reusability is domain-dependent: higher reasoning effort yields marginal gains on general-knowledge QA but up to 8pp on financial content, and effort configurations that help in English help proportionally in other languages. Behavioural reusability holds: citation-set overlap with English averages 77-79% Jaccard, with no single language consistently worse. Together, these results support qualified reuse of English-built pipelines, but per-domain, per-language validation remains necessary--neither semantic similarity nor self-reported confidence reliably predicts cross-lingual accuracy.

title: How to Deliver SaaS File Export Downloads with Signed URLs (Without App-Server Storage)
description:
Short answer: for most healthtech SaaS exports, write each completed report to private object storage and return a short-lived signed GET URL; keep authorization, retention, and deletion decisions in your application database. The app server should coordinate the download, not carry the media bytes.

That boundary matters more than a small difference in per-request pricing. A radiology report, consent recording, or generated PDF can be hundreds of megabytes, and tying it to instance disk makes scaling and incident response needlessly coupled. The design below keeps access control in the system that knows the patient and tenant, while storage handles delivery. Infrai is a candidate at this boundary when a team wants storage alongside other backend capabilities under one REST contract; it is not a reason to weaken tenant authorization.

The second advantage is a self-describing discovery surface: the public schema and runnable examples make the storage contract inspectable before credentials reach a developer laptop. That matters when a healthtech team adds notification, scheduling, or observability around the same export workflow, because the platform has 295 routes across 20 modules behind one consistent set of conventions rather than a new SDK shape for every capability.

Start with the trust boundary, not the bucket

An export has two identities: the business record (tenant_id, report_id) and the object key. Generate the key in application code, for example exports/tenant-42/report-0187.pdf, and store it with an authorization record. A download request first checks that record, then asks storage for a signed URL. The client receives a URL with a short expiry and downloads directly from storage. The REST surface is plain HTTP, so a Node.js service, a Python worker, or a small Go utility can use the same contract without installing a storage SDK; the public discovery document also exposes schemas and runnable examples before a key is issued.

This is simpler than streaming through a Node.js process. The process handles a small control request instead of buffering or piping the entire file, so a slow browser cannot consume an application worker. It also avoids assuming that a particular app instance will still have the file on its local disk after a deploy.

There is a sharp edge: private signed delivery is not the same as a permanent public link. The storage capability has no public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. That is a good fit for protected reports, but it is the wrong tool for a public image host or static website. Use a provider with public hosting semantics for those cases.

How should cheapest, simplest file export delivery use signed URLs and object storage?

Treat the export as a state machine: generating, stored, available, and expired. A worker claims one (tenant_id, report_id) in a database transaction, writes a unique object key, and marks the row stored only after the write succeeds. The API issues a presigned GET only from the available state, after checking the caller's tenant and role.

Consider a real retry sequence. A report worker receives a queue message, reserves tenant-42/report-0187, and starts uploading a 640 MB PDF while the user's browser is still waiting on a job page. The worker loses its network connection after the storage service has accepted the final bytes but before the response reaches the process. A second delivery of the queue message must not create report-0187-copy.pdf, and it must not overwrite latest.pdf either. The worker asks the database whether the deterministic claim is already stored; if it is, it records a reconciliation event and returns the existing key. Only an available row can mint a signed URL, and only an authorization check tied to tenant-42 can request that mint. When the URL expires, the bytes remain governed by the retention row, not by a browser cache. This is the boring machinery that prevents a transient network ambiguity from becoming a cross-tenant disclosure or an unexplained duplicate in a clinical export ledger.

Do not replace exports/tenant-42/latest.pdf. There is no object versioning or object lock here, so an overwrite is not recoverable from this storage layer. Unique filenames make retries and audits legible. There is also no If-Match conditional write; if two workers can produce the same report, coordinate the claim in your database or queue before either worker writes bytes.

Here is a small Python adapter. It uses only the documented object write and presign routes, reads the key from an environment variable, sets methods explicitly, and retries a 429 without a tight loop. The database remains responsible for the idempotency record; the object key is the deterministic identity for this example.

import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def request(method, path, body=b"", content_type="application/octet-stream"):
    for attempt in range(4):
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            BASE + path,
            data=body,
            method=method,
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
                "Content-Type": content_type,
                # The application derives this from tenant_id + report_id.
                "Idempotency-Key": "tenant-42:report-0187",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                return response.status, response.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)


def put_export(bucket, tenant_id, report_id, pdf_bytes):
    key = f"exports/{tenant_id}/{report_id}.pdf"
    status, _ = request("PUT", f"/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", pdf_bytes)
    if status < 200 or status >= 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"object write returned HTTP {status}")
    return key


def presign_export(bucket, key):
    presign_url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    status, payload = request(
        "POST", presign_url.removeprefix(BASE), b"{}", "application/json"
    )
    if status < 200 or status >= 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign returned HTTP {status}: {payload.decode(errors='replace')}")
    return payload

The application should persist the returned key and state transition before exposing the presigned response. If a retry occurs after a timeout, the same key and idempotency identity let the worker reconcile the result instead of inventing a second report. Your mileage may vary on expiry defaults, so set the URL lifetime in the request according to the live discovery schema and your policy; never make a clinical download effectively permanent.

Compare the real delivery options

Object storage is a family of trade-offs, not a single product. AWS S3 is the broadest specialist choice for lifecycle controls, replication, and compliance integrations. Google Cloud Storage is a natural fit when the rest of the system and residency controls already live in Google Cloud. Cloudflare R2 can be attractive when egress economics and Cloudflare delivery are central. Infrai covers storage backends including S3-compatible, R2, OSS, and COS through one REST surface, but it does not cover GCS in this capability set.

Option Access and delivery Data-handling strengths Where it is a weaker fit
AWS S3 Mature private objects and presigned URLs Lifecycle, object lock, and multi-region patterns More provider-specific IAM and account surface
Google Cloud Storage Signed URLs with Google IAM Strong GCP residency and governance integration A poor match if the rest of the stack is outside GCP
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible private delivery Cloudflare edge integration and egress-focused design Compliance and replication choices need careful review
Infrai storage One REST contract for put and presign Broad backend capability behind one key and consistent discovery examples No public ACL, versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or GCS coverage

Infrai is worth trying when the team wants breadth behind a simple surface: adding storage to an existing backend integration is another documented endpoint rather than another SDK and credential set. The supporting benefit is operational consistency; discovery exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which reduces the integration-specific glue around a small export adapter. I would recommend it for private export delivery when those boundaries are acceptable, not as a substitute for a specialist's compliance controls.

In concrete terms, Infrai exposes a plain REST API with no SDK required, so any language can serve the export writer, its notification hook, and the audit job with the same Bearer authentication and HTTP conventions. That keeps a Node.js SaaS from growing a second client library just because a worker was written in Python.

Retention, deletion, and processor boundaries

A signed URL controls who can fetch an object for a period; it does not decide how long the processor retains the object or where the bytes are replicated. Put region and retention commitments in your contract with the storage provider, and record deletion intent in your own audit log. Lifecycle rules can remove old exports, but the shortest lifecycle granularity here is one day, not an hour. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup policy.

Deletion should be a two-step job: mark the export expired in the database, then call the object deletion operation and record the result. A failed deletion is a reconciliation item, not permission to issue another URL. Metadata is not server-side searchable beyond prefix listing, so keep patient, tenant, and report attributes in your database rather than trying to query them from object metadata.

The catch is regulatory immutability. If a financial or clinical retention rule requires WORM storage, version history, or automatic cross-region replication, choose S3, GCS, or another specialist system that provides those guarantees and keep the application adapter narrow. If browser-direct uploads need configurable CORS, this surface does not expose an independent CORS route for self-service policy changes; route uploads through a service with that control instead.

Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes, so production-like export storage needs a billable account. That is a deployment prerequisite, not a reason to put files back on app disks.

A rollout that can be audited

Start with one report type and a private bucket. Add a database uniqueness constraint for (tenant_id, report_id), emit an audit event for each state transition, and make the signed URL lifetime shorter than the user session. Measure object bytes, download bytes, expired rows, and deletion lag separately; those numbers tell you whether the storage boundary is working.

Keep the storage adapter behind one interface so a specialist provider can replace it without changing authorization code. Run a migration that copies existing files to unique keys, verifies checksums, and flips reads only after the new object is confirmed. Then remove the app-server copy according to your retention policy.

If your system needs public links, WORM guarantees, browser-configurable CORS, GCS, or cross-region replication, stick with a specialist provider. If it needs private SaaS exports and a consistent REST contract across backend capabilities, Infrai is a reasonable storage boundary to test first.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability index and verify the live request schema before wiring the adapter.

title: Modern CSS: :has(), :is(), nesting
description:
CSS Just Got a Whole Lot Smarter: Embracing the Power of :has(), :is(), and Nesting!

Hey there, fellow web tinkerers and design aficionados! Ever feel like CSS is still a bit of a wild west, where you're wrestling with convoluted selectors and a growing mountain of utility classes? Well, dust off your keyboards, because the game is changing, and it's getting seriously exciting. Today, we're diving deep into the world of Modern CSS, specifically focusing on three game-changers: :has(), :is(), and nesting.

These aren't just fancy new toys; they're tools that promise to make our CSS more readable, more maintainable, and frankly, a lot more powerful. So, grab a coffee, settle in, and let's explore how these bad boys are about to revolutionize the way we style the web.

The "Why Now?" Moment: A Brief Intro to Modern CSS

For years, CSS has been evolving, but sometimes it felt like we were inching forward with incremental improvements. Then, bam! Suddenly, we're seeing massive leaps in functionality. :has(), :is(), and nesting are part of this new wave, bringing us closer to a more intuitive and expressive styling language. Think of it as CSS finally catching up to the demands of modern web development. We're moving away from brute-force selector matching and towards more intelligent, context-aware styling.

Prerequisites: What You Need to Know (Don't Worry, It's Not Rocket Science!)

Before we get our hands dirty with these shiny new features, a quick refresher on the basics will serve you well:

  • Solid HTML Fundamentals: You'll need to understand how HTML elements are structured, their relationships (parent, child, sibling), and how to create semantic markup. The better your HTML, the more effective your CSS will be.
  • Basic CSS Selectors: Familiarity with class selectors, ID selectors, attribute selectors, and descendant selectors is crucial. These new features build upon these foundational concepts.
  • Browser Support Awareness: While these features are gaining widespread adoption, it's always good practice to be aware of browser compatibility. Tools like Can I Use (caniuse.com) are your best friends here. For the most part, modern browsers are now quite good with these.

Meet the MVPs: A Deep Dive into Each Feature

Let's introduce our star players, one by one.

1. The Parent Selector: :has() - It Knows Its Children!

What is it?
Imagine you want to style a div only if it contains an <h2> element. Traditionally, you'd have to do some JavaScript gymnastics or resort to more complex, potentially brittle CSS. Enter :has(). This pseudo-class allows you to select an element based on the presence (or absence) of its descendants. It's essentially a "parent selector" in disguise!

The Magic in Action:

Let's say you have a card component and you want to add a special border to a card that contains an image.

HTML Example:

<div class="card">
  <h2>Card Title</h2>
  <p>Some content here.</p>
</div>

<div class="card featured">
  <img src="awesome-image.jpg" alt="An awesome image">
  <h2>Featured Card Title</h2>
  <p>This card has an image and should look special!</p>
</div>

CSS (Before :has() - a bit clunky):

.card {
  border: 1px solid #ccc;
  padding: 20px;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

/* This would require JS or a specific class like '.card.has-image' */
.card.has-image {
  border-left: 5px solid blue;
}

CSS (With :has() - clean and declarative!):

.card {
  border: 1px solid #ccc;
  padding: 20px;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  transition: border-color 0.3s ease; /* Added for visual flair */
}

/* Style the card if it CONTAINS an <img> element */
.card:has(img) {
  border-left: 5px solid rebeccapurple;
  background-color: #f0e6ff; /* Subtle visual cue */
}

/* You can even be more specific! */
.card:has(h2:first-child) {
  box-shadow: 0 2px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.1); /* Add a shadow if the h2 is the first child */
}

Why is this a game-changer?

  • Reduces JavaScript Dependency: No more relying on JavaScript to add or remove classes based on DOM structure for styling. This leads to cleaner, faster applications.
  • Improved Readability: The CSS now clearly states the condition for styling, making it much easier to understand the intent.
  • More Dynamic UI: Enables truly dynamic styling based on content. For instance, you could change the layout of a form if it has a required field, or style a navigation menu differently if it has many items.
  • Component-Based Styling: Perfect for styling components based on their internal structure, leading to more robust and reusable components.

A Word of Caution: While :has() is incredibly powerful, try not to go overboard with deeply nested :has() selectors, as this can still impact performance. Focus on clear, purposeful selections.

2. The Selector Simplifier: :is() - One Rule to Rule Them All!

What is it?
Ever found yourself writing the same styles for multiple selectors? For example:

h1, h2, h3 {
  font-family: 'Montserrat', sans-serif;
  color: #333;
}

.button-primary, .button-secondary, .button-danger {
  padding: 10px 20px;
  border-radius: 5px;
}

It's repetitive, right? :is() comes to the rescue! It takes a list of selectors as its argument and applies the declared styles to any element that matches any of the selectors in the list. It's like a universal selector, but with specific targets.

The Magic in Action:

Let's refactor the above examples using :is():

CSS (With :is() - concise and elegant!):

/* Apply styles to any h1, h2, or h3 */
h1:is(h1, h2, h3) { /* Note: You don't even need to repeat the outer selector here, but it's good for clarity */
  font-family: 'Montserrat', sans-serif;
  color: #333;
}

/* Or even simpler when the outer selector is the same as the first in the list */
:is(h1, h2, h3) {
  font-family: 'Montserrat', sans-serif;
  color: #333;
}

/* Apply styles to various button types */
.button:is(.button-primary, .button-secondary, .button-danger) {
  padding: 10px 20px;
  border-radius: 5px;
}

Why is this a game-changer?

  • Drastic Reduction in Code: Say goodbye to repetitive selectors and code duplication. This makes your stylesheets significantly shorter.
  • Improved Maintainability: When you need to update styles for a group of elements, you only need to change one rule. Less searching, less editing, fewer mistakes.
  • Enhanced Readability: The intent of applying a set of styles to multiple elements becomes immediately clear.
  • Flexibility: You can combine :is() with other selectors for more complex scenarios. For example, :is(h2, h3).section-title would target h2 or h3 elements that also have the class section-title.

A Note on Specificity: :is() inherits the specificity of its most specific argument. This is important to understand when dealing with complex selector scenarios.

3. The Nested Structure: CSS Nesting - Bringing Order to Chaos!

What is it?
This is perhaps the most visually intuitive of the bunch. CSS nesting allows you to write CSS rules inside other rules, mirroring the HTML structure. This brings a much-needed sense of organization and hierarchy to your stylesheets, making them feel more like a structured document.

The Magic in Action:

Let's style a common component like a card with an internal button.

HTML Example:

<div class="card">
  <div class="card-content">
    <h2>Card Title</h2>
    <p>This is some descriptive text for the card.</p>
  </div>
  <button class="card-button">Learn More</button>
</div>

CSS (Before Nesting - scattered and potentially repetitive):

.card {
  border: 1px solid #eee;
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 20px;
  box-shadow: 0 4px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);
}

.card-content h2 {
  margin-top: 0;
  color: #222;
}

.card-content p {
  color: #666;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

.card-button {
  background-color: #007bff;
  color: white;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  border: none;
  border-radius: 4px;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: background-color 0.3s ease;
}

.card-button:hover {
  background-color: #0056b3;
}

CSS (With Nesting - organized and logical!):

.card {
  border: 1px solid #eee;
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 20px;
  box-shadow: 0 4px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);

  /* Nesting the content styles */
  .card-content {
    h2 { /* Styles for the h2 within card-content */
      margin-top: 0;
      color: #222;
    }

    p { /* Styles for the p within card-content */
      color: #666;
      line-height: 1.6;
    }
  }

  /* Nesting the button styles */
  .card-button {
    background-color: #007bff;
    color: white;
    padding: 10px 15px;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 4px;
    cursor: pointer;
    transition: background-color 0.3s ease;

    /* Nesting the hover state */
    &:hover { /* The '&' refers to the parent selector (.card-button) */
      background-color: #0056b3;
    }
  }
}

Why is this a game-changer?

  • Improved Readability and Organization: Your CSS now visually reflects the structure of your HTML, making it incredibly easy to understand which styles apply to which elements.
  • Reduced Repetition: No need to repeat parent selectors over and over again. The nesting handles it automatically.
  • Better Maintainability: When working on a component, all its related styles are grouped together, making it easier to find and modify them.
  • Logical Flow: It promotes a more logical way of thinking about your styles, leading to more coherent and maintainable codebases.
  • The & Parent Selector: The & symbol is crucial here. It represents the parent selector, allowing you to style pseudo-classes like :hover, :focus, and :active or combine selectors within the nested scope.

Nesting Nuances:

  • Avoid Deep Nesting: Just like with :has(), excessive nesting can lead to overly specific selectors and potential performance issues. Aim for a reasonable level of nesting (typically 2-4 levels).
  • Pseudo-classes and Elements: Use the & symbol to correctly target pseudo-classes and elements within nested rules.

Advantages of Embracing Modern CSS

The benefits of adopting :has(), :is(), and nesting are numerous and impactful:

  • Enhanced Readability and Understandability: Code becomes more intuitive, making it easier for you and your team to grasp the styling logic.
  • Reduced Code Bloat and Duplication: Shorter, more concise stylesheets lead to faster loading times and easier maintenance.
  • Improved Maintainability and Debugging: Finding and fixing issues becomes a breeze when your CSS is well-organized and logical.
  • Increased Developer Productivity: Less time spent wrestling with selectors and repetitive code means more time for creativity and building features.
  • Reduced Reliance on JavaScript for Styling: This leads to leaner, more performant web applications.
  • Better Component-Based Development: These features are perfectly suited for creating self-contained and reusable UI components.
  • More Expressive and Powerful Styling: You can achieve complex styling scenarios with greater ease and clarity.

Potential Disadvantages and Considerations

While the advantages are compelling, it's important to be aware of potential downsides:

  • Browser Support: While improving rapidly, older browsers might not fully support these features. You might need fallbacks or polyfills for wider compatibility.
  • Learning Curve (Slight): While the concepts are straightforward, mastering their effective application and understanding their intricacies (like specificity with :is() or the & in nesting) takes a little practice.
  • Over-Nesting/Over-Complexity: As mentioned, excessive nesting or overly complex :has() selectors can lead to performance issues and make code harder to debug. Discipline is key.
  • Tooling and Build Processes: Your build tools (like Sass, Less, or PostCSS plugins) might need to be configured to properly handle these newer CSS features if they don't natively support them. (Though this is becoming less of an issue as native browser support grows).

Practical Applications and Real-World Scenarios

Let's paint a picture of how these features can be used in your everyday development:

  • Form Styling: Style input fields based on their state (:valid, :invalid, :focus) or whether they have a parent with a specific class (.form-group:has(input[required])).
  • Navigation Menus: Conditionally style navigation items based on their content or whether they are active.
  • Card Components: Dynamically change the appearance of a card based on the type of content it holds (e.g., :has(video) vs. :has(img)).
  • Layout Adjustments: Create responsive layouts by targeting parent containers based on the number or type of child elements they contain.
  • Theming: Apply different styles to elements based on a global theme class applied to the body or a parent element, using :is() for a concise selector.
  • Accessibility Improvements: Enhance focus states and visual feedback for interactive elements more elegantly.

The Future is Now: Embracing the Evolution

:has(), :is(), and nesting are not just trendy additions to CSS; they represent a fundamental shift towards a more intelligent, readable, and maintainable styling language. By embracing these features, you're not just staying up-to-date; you're actively investing in the future of your projects and your own development workflow.

Start experimenting with them in your next project, even if it's just a small component. You'll quickly discover how much easier and more enjoyable styling can become. The days of CSS spaghetti are numbered, and the era of elegant, context-aware styling is here.

So, go forth, experiment, and let these modern CSS superpowers transform your web development experience. Happy styling!

title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
description:
arXiv:2610.27605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg

title: Rate as a Feature, Not a Nuisance: Curriculum FiLM Training for Event-Based Graph Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.26933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An event camera emits events at a rate given by the scene motion, object texture, illumination, its own contrast thresholds, and other settings. Across the N-Caltech101 dataset, recorded by a single event camera, the event rate varies by roughly 26x. Standard event-based Graph Neural Network GNN pipelines do not make use of the variable event rate. They either normalize each event's timestamp into a fixed window or train the network to be invariant to the event rate. We argue that both choices lose information that could instead be used to improve the performance of a pipeline. Per-recording normalization is non-invertible, incurring about 6pp (percentage points) of natural-rate accuracy loss in our setting. And invariance training trades accuracy for robustness to shifts in the event rate. We instead take a different path and condition on the event rate directly. We add a per-recording log-rate scalar that modulates every stage of a PointNet++ backbone through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), initialized to identity, so that training begins at the unmodified baseline. A two-stage curriculum (natural event rates first, then rate-augmented fine-tuning) reaches 67.2% on N-Caltech101 (+6.3pp) and 82.5% on DVS128 Gesture (+14.0pp) with an additional ~0.2M parameters. A matched-capacity control experiment shows that the gain is not from the increase in model capacity but from the rate conditioning. We will make the implementation publicly available upon acceptance of this work.

title: Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.27571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.

title: Four small problems from shipping a local-first task app
description:
OpenTodo is a self-hosted, local-first task manager: a Go server with SQLite, a React app embedded in the binary, and sync built on a field-level operation log. Every device applies changes locally first and converges with the others later. Version 0.9.0 came out today. The user-facing story is on the project blog. This post is about four problems from building it that turned out more interesting than they looked.

1. A title parser that only reads what you just typed

Quick add has always understood Call Anna tomorrow 3pm p1 #home. The obvious next step was to do the same when you edit an existing title: add tomorrow p1 at the end and the task gets a date and a priority.

The trap is the rest of the title. Parse the whole string again and "Review may report" suddenly gains a May date. That was there all along, but nobody asked for it.

The fix is to read only the edit. When editing starts, the current title becomes the base. On commit, the parser finds the common prefix and the common suffix of the base and the draft, treats those spans as if they were quoted, and reads only the text in between. Whatever it recognises becomes one patch: scalar fields overwrite, labels are added to the task's labels, and reminders become new records. The function is pure, with no reads and no writes, so it is easy to test with a table of before/after pairs. The whole change is undone by one Undo.

The parser has a Go twin (the CLI and the importers use it), and both are pinned to the same JSON test vectors, so #Home/Docs resolves to the same project in the browser and in ot add --natural.

2. One running timer, even when two devices started one offline

Time tracking has one rule that users care about: one timer runs at a time. On a single server that is a uniqueness check. In a local-first app it isn't. Your laptop and your phone can each start a timer while offline, and both writes are valid when they are made.

Refusing one of them at sync time would lose work. Instead, the rule is a deterministic repair that every device can compute on its own:

  • Among a user's running entries, the one to keep is the one with the greatest started_at, with ties broken by the greatest id.
  • Every other running entry is ended at the kept entry's started_at.

Because every device sees the same entries and applies the same ordering, every device writes the same ended_at values. The repairs converge like any other edit, and nobody's tracked time disappears; it just stops where the newer timer began. The rule lives in a small Go package with no dependencies besides ciphertext detection, and the TypeScript side is its twin, pinned by shared fixtures.

3. Importing issues without ever writing back

0.9.0 can turn the GitHub or GitLab issues assigned to you into tasks. The design decision that shaped everything else was that nothing is ever written back. The task follows the issue (completed when it closes, renamed when it's renamed), and that is all.

"Follows" needed a precise meaning, because the user can also edit the task. The rule: your own edits stand until the issue changes the same thing again. If you rename the task and the issue keeps its title, your name stays. If the issue is renamed later, the issue wins for that field.

Two more constraints come from running on someone else's server:

  • The server owner opts in. The feature is off by default, and the personal access tokens are kept outside the database and its backups.
  • Requests go only to the host you typed. Every request goes through one outbound policy: http(s) only, no private-network targets unless the owner allows them, the connection pinned to the address that was checked, and no redirects followed. The same policy covers webhooks and calendar subscriptions, so a typed URL can't be turned into a probe of the server's own network.

4. Encrypting a field as one value

Tasks now remember where they came from: a captured page, an email's Message-ID, an issue link. The field is a small object, {kind, provider?, id?, url?, title?}.

For accounts with end-to-end encryption, the server never sees task content. The question was which parts of the origin count as content. kind alone looks harmless, but url, title and id name the page, the mail or the issue, and even the combination leaks something. So the origin is encrypted as one whole value: the object is serialised, then encrypted into one ciphertext string. The server accepts that string wherever it would accept the object, stores it and serves it back unchanged. Another unlocked device decrypts it and shows the chip as usual.

It also fits the sync model. The origin is one last-writer-wins register, like the due date, so two concurrent origins never mix fields from both.

How it was built

Every change above started as a written spec, using the OpenSpec workflow: proposal, design, spec deltas, tasks, then code. That sounds heavy for a one-person project, but it is what made it possible to do most of this release in a few days with AI coding agents doing the typing. The specs are the contract the agents work against and that I review, and they are all in the repository.

OpenTodo is AGPL-3.0. You can try it without installing anything on the demo, read the 0.9.0 release notes, or run it with one container: ghcr.io/pixari/opentodo:stable.

title: SITO: Sifting a Commercial Text-Safety API for Missed Harm and False Flags in English, Ukrainian and Surzhyk
description:
arXiv:2610.27178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Platforms that host young users screen messages with commercial text-safety APIs, but independent evidence on how often such systems miss harm or flag harmless text is scarce, especially outside English, and the documentation of the one studied here leaves its false-positive rate unquantified. We evaluated one such API, Tuteliq Detect as deployed under the release identifier tuteliq-detect-v5.20261011 (not the separately published v6 model), on six harm categories: authorised push-payment fraud, money-mule recruitment, social engineering, romance scams, gambling harm and bullying. We built SITO (Synthetic Independent Text-safety benchmark with Overflagging tests; sito is Ukrainian for 'sieve'), 2,332 synthetic cases in English, Ukrainian and mixed Ukrainian, with each harmful case matched by hard harmless ones: same-topic messages, minimal-edit contrasts, warnings and retrospective accounts. On English text the system flagged 84.9-94.1% of harmful cases and 0-4.3% of harmless ones per category. It missed third-party reports of ongoing harm far more often than perpetrators' messages (63.6% against 95.1% recall, all languages), when sent without the settings the API offers for reports of harm. Ukrainian and mixed-language input was detected at least as often as English, recall was lower on text from a held-out generator family, so headline recall may be optimistic, and 3.2% of cases received a different decision in repeated runs. A platform should measure false positives on its own traffic and check how bystander reports are handled. The datasets, generation prompts and code are released.

title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
description:
Private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised, allowing attackers to forge certificates for any site. The keys were revealed due to low entropy, not through a known breach. Browsers blocked them using revocation lists, but other software had to remove the emSign ECC G3 root. Unpatched systems remain exposed to forged certificates, including client auth and mTLS.

By Chris Swan

title: Tailwind CSS Alternatives: Which One Fits the Problem You Actually Have
description:
"Tailwind alternatives" is one of those searches where the results are almost always useless, because every list gives you the same twelve tools ranked by GitHub stars and none of them ask why you're looking.

So let's start there. In my experience there are four reasons people go looking, and they lead to completely different answers. Three of them don't require leaving Tailwind at all.

First, work out what you're actually escaping

"My markup is unreadable." You open a component and there's a class attribute with forty utilities in it. This is by far the most common complaint, and it's the one where switching frameworks helps least. The problem isn't Tailwind, it's that nothing is giving names to your repeated patterns.

"I don't want a build step." You're working on a Django template, a Rails view, a static page, or something embedded, and running a watcher feels absurd for what you're doing.

"The engine is slow or awkward in my setup." Usually a large codebase, an unusual bundler, or a monorepo where the content scanning is painful.

"I don't want utility CSS at all." Fair enough. It's a style of working and it doesn't suit everyone.

Work out which one is yours before reading any further, because the right answer differs completely.

If your markup is unreadable: you don't need an alternative

This is worth saying plainly, because a lot of people switch frameworks to solve this and find the new one has the same problem.

Class soup happens when every button in your project spells out its own appearance. The fix is to name the pattern once. You can do that three ways, and only one of them involves leaving Tailwind.

Use @apply sparingly. It works, and it's built in. It's also widely discouraged because you end up with a second stylesheet that drifts from your markup, and the Tailwind maintainers themselves suggest reaching for components instead.

Extract components in your framework. A <Button> in React or a {% include %} in Django keeps the utilities in one file. This is the official answer and it's a good one, if you're in a framework that has components.

Use a component class library. Something that ships btn and card as real classes, built on top of Tailwind rather than instead of it. Frutjam is one, DaisyUI is the best known, and there are others. Your markup becomes <button class="btn btn-primary"> and the utilities are still there when you need to override something.

None of these are alternatives to Tailwind. They're ways to keep it and stop fighting it.

If you don't want a build step

Two real options here.

Tailwind's own browser build. A single script tag and you're writing utilities with no tooling. It's explicitly not for production, but for a prototype, an email template preview, or a page you edit by hand, it's exactly right.

A stylesheet you just link. Plenty of CSS frameworks are a single file, and so are the component libraries built on Tailwind if they publish a compiled bundle. Frutjam does, which means you can drop in a <link> tag and get every component without Node existing anywhere in the project:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/frutjam@2/dist/frutjam.components.css">

That ships everything rather than only what you use, so it's the wrong choice for an app and the right one for a prototype.

If you want a different utility engine

These are genuine Tailwind alternatives in the sense that they replace the engine while keeping the idea.

UnoCSS is the one most people land on. It's an atomic CSS engine with pluggable presets, and presetWind4 gives you Tailwind-compatible class names, so migration is mostly mechanical. It also does things Tailwind doesn't, like attribute mode, where <button btn="primary lg"> is valid input. It's fast and it's Vite-native.

Panda CSS takes a different angle: you write styles in TypeScript, it generates static CSS at build time, and you get type safety and design tokens as first-class things. Good fit if you're already deep in a typed React codebase. Heavier conceptually than Tailwind.

StyleX is Meta's take, also compile-time, also typed, built for very large codebases where style collisions are a real operational problem. Narrower audience.

Vanilla Extract is CSS-in-TypeScript with zero runtime, closer to CSS Modules than to Tailwind. Worth a look if the thing you miss is writing actual CSS.

A note on Windi CSS, which still appears on every list: it's no longer maintained, and its author went on to build UnoCSS. Don't start a project on it.

If you don't want utility CSS at all

Open Props is a set of CSS custom properties: colours, spacing, typography, easings, animations. No classes, no build, no opinions about your markup. You write normal CSS and use the variables. It's the gentlest step away from a framework.

Pico CSS is classless. You write semantic HTML and it looks good immediately. Brilliant for documentation, internal tools and prototypes; limiting the moment you need a specific design.

Bulma is a traditional CSS framework with component classes and no JavaScript. Mature, calm, nothing clever.

Bootstrap still exists and is still fine. You get components and a utility layer, and some interactive pieces want its JavaScript. If your team already knows it, that knowledge has real value.

Plain modern CSS deserves to be on this list. Nesting, custom properties, color-mix(), container queries, :has(), cascade layers. A lot of what frameworks were invented to paper over is now in the platform.

Quick comparison

Tool Replaces Tailwind? Build step Best for
Component class library No, sits on top Same as Tailwind Unreadable markup
Tailwind browser build No None Prototypes
UnoCSS Yes Yes Speed, attribute mode, Vite
Panda CSS Yes Yes Typed design tokens, React
StyleX Yes Yes Very large codebases
Vanilla Extract Yes Yes Writing real CSS with types
Open Props Yes None Tokens without opinions
Pico CSS Yes None Docs, internal tools
Bulma Yes None Classic components, no JS
Bootstrap Yes Optional Teams who already know it
Plain CSS Yes None Small projects, full control

Where Frutjam fits

Frutjam is a CSS-only component library. It gives you btn, card, modal, alert and sixty-odd others as real class names, so your markup reads like markup. Every colour pair is contrast-tested to WCAG AA, and interactive components use what the browser already has, so modals are <dialog> with the popover attribute, accordions are <details>, and tabs are radio inputs. There's no JavaScript bundle.

As of 2.3.0 it runs three ways, which is why it's in a post about alternatives at all:

With Tailwind, as a plugin. One line, and Tailwind ships only the components your markup uses.

@import "tailwindcss";
@plugin "frutjam";

With UnoCSS, as a preset generated from the same source files as the Tailwind plugin, so the two can't drift.

import { presetFrutjam } from 'frutjam/unocss';

export default defineConfig({ presets: [presetWind4(), presetFrutjam()] });

With neither. Import the stylesheet and you're done. No utility engine, no plugin, nothing to configure.

import 'frutjam/css';

So if what you want is to stop writing class soup, Frutjam solves that without you leaving Tailwind. And if you've decided to leave anyway, it follows you to UnoCSS or to plain CSS without changing a single class name in your templates.

Frequently asked questions

Is Tailwind actually a problem?

No. It's a good tool and the ecosystem around it is the best in the category. Most "Tailwind alternatives" searches are really "how do I stop my markup looking like this" searches, and that has a better answer than switching.

What's the closest drop-in replacement?

UnoCSS with presetWind4. Class names are largely compatible, so you're mostly changing config rather than templates.

Which alternative needs no build step at all?

Open Props, Pico, Bulma, Bootstrap and plain CSS. Frutjam also works this way through a single <link> tag or import 'frutjam/css'.

Can I use a component library and still write utilities?

Yes, and that's the normal way to use one. Components cover the repeated patterns, utilities handle the one-off spacing and layout. Frutjam emits its components into a cascade layer that sorts below utilities, so a utility always wins when you need to override something.

Is it worth migrating an existing Tailwind project?

Usually not for its own sake. Migrate when you have a concrete problem the new tool solves, not because something else is newer.

The bottom line

Pick by the problem, not the popularity.

Markup you can't read is a naming problem, and a component library fixes it without a migration. No build step points at a stylesheet or a CDN tag. A slow or awkward engine points at UnoCSS. Not wanting utilities at all points at Open Props, Pico, or writing the CSS yourself, which is more viable in 2026 than it has been in a decade.

If you want the component-library route, browse the Frutjam components or read the installation guide, which covers all three setups in about a page.

title: I Built a Whole Desktop App Because I Couldn't Pick a Gacha Banner
description:
It was 1:47 AM.

I had 42 pulls, a credit card that was dangerously within reach, and two banners staring back at me. On the left, the character everyone said was meta. On the right, the one I actually liked. Both were limited. Both would disappear in a few days.

I did what any reasonable person does in that situation: I opened a coin flip website.

Then I closed it, because a cookie banner asked me to accept 847 partners.

Then I opened another one. It wanted an account.

Then I opened a random number generator that looked like it had been designed in 2003 and had a 3-second ad before showing me a number.

And somewhere between the third pop-up and the fourth "accept all", I thought:

Why is the simplest decision in the world the hardest thing to do on a computer?

That night, I didn't pull. I opened my code editor instead.

The tiny problem behind the big project

The gacha dilemma is silly. I know that. But it's also the perfect example of a much more common problem.

We hesitate constantly:

  • Which of these two apartments should I take?
  • Which candidate do we hire?
  • Which feature do we build next?
  • Which restaurant do we pick when nobody wants to decide?

And for all of these, we either overthink for 40 minutes, or we ask a friend who cares way less than we do.

I didn't want to build "a random generator". I wanted to build the thing I wished existed at 1:47 AM: something that opens instantly, does one job perfectly, and gets out of the way.

No account. No ads. No cookie banner. No loading spinner. No internet.

Just a decision.

So I built Capricio

Capricio is a small desktop app for Windows, made with Tauri 2, Angular 22 and Rust.

It does four things, and it tries very hard to do them well:

  • Coin flip: with custom labels, so you can flip between "Banner A" and "Banner B" instead of Heads and Tails.
  • Random number: min/max, optional no-repeat, instant result.
  • List draw: paste a list, pick one or several winners, with or without replacement.
  • Weighted pros & cons: list your arguments, give them a weight, and get a verdict with a score and a percentage gap.

The whole thing is designed around one rule: a decision should take less than three clicks.

There's a short animation, a "Play again" button, full keyboard navigation, four languages (English, French, German, Spanish), light/dark/system themes, and a local history so you can look back at what you decided, and whether you actually followed through.

And here's the part I'm most proud of: it's 100% offline.

No account. No telemetry. No tracking. No ads. Your arguments, your lists, your history, they never leave your machine. Not because of a privacy policy, but because there is no server to send them to.

What building it taught me

I thought this would be a weekend project. It wasn't.

1. Rust makes "fast" feel effortless

All the sensitive logic lives in Rust: the random draws, the weighted scoring, the bias detection when only one side of a pros/cons list is filled. Angular only renders. That separation is not just architectural purity, it's what makes the app feel instant.

Cold start is under 1.5 seconds. The installer is under 15 MB (without the system WebView). Idle memory stays under 50 MB.

When you're half-asleep trying to make a decision, those numbers are not specs. They're the difference between using the app and closing it.

2. The hardest part of a decision tool is trust

If I'm going to let an app decide something for me, even something small, I need to trust it. So I unit-tested the scoring and random modules heavily. Not because it's a checklist, but because a decision helper that is subtly wrong is worse than no decision helper at all.

3. Constraints are a feature

I removed things. A lot of things. No cloud sync in V1. No export. No social features. No "AI-powered decision engine".

Every feature I added was a reason for someone to hesitate before making a decision, which is exactly the opposite of the goal.

4. The pause is the product

This is the one that surprised me most.

People don't actually want an app to decide for them. They want permission to stop circling. The coin flip doesn't choose for you, it shows you how you feel about the result.

Capricio is not an oracle. It's a pause button with a clean interface.

The moment it became real

A few days after publishing it, a friend texted me a screenshot.

He had used the pros & cons screen to decide whether to accept a job offer. He told me he already knew the answer, he just needed to see it written down, weighted, and laid out in front of him.

That's when it stopped being "the app I built because of a gacha banner" and became something I actually want to maintain.

Try it

Capricio is free, open source, and available now.

  • Microsoft Store: Download Capricio
  • GitHub: Martzcode/Capricio

It's built for Windows 10/11 today, with a cross-platform architecture underneath (macOS and Linux builds are possible).

If you try it, two small favors

  1. Star the repo on GitHub. It takes two seconds, and for a solo open-source project, it genuinely helps more than you'd think, it's often how other developers discover the project.
  2. Leave a rating on the Microsoft Store if the app is useful to you. Ratings are the main signal that tells new users "this is legit, and it's maintained." If something's missing or broken, tell me in the review or open an issue, I read everything.

And if you have a better idea for the next feature, open an issue. I built this because I couldn't decide between two banners. I'd love to hear what you can't decide between.

Final thought

We spend so much energy trying to optimize decisions, and so little energy noticing that most of them don't need optimizing. They need a nudge.

So here's my nudge to you: next time you're stuck between two options, don't open fifteen tabs. Flip a coin. Notice your reaction to the result.

You'll probably have your answer before the animation even ends.

That's how Capricio was born. Not from a product strategy, but from a very tired developer, a gacha banner, and a refusal to accept one more cookie pop-up.
