title: CoASFL: Coupled Consistency Optimization for Asynchronous Split Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.26992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training large-scale deep models on resource-constrained edge devices. Although asynchronous SFL alleviates the straggler bottleneck caused by system heterogeneity, it inevitably introduces two coupled dimensions of inconsistency: horizontal inconsistency across clients and vertical inconsistency between clients and the server. These inconsistencies, further exacerbated by statistical heterogeneity, result in biased activation representations, model divergence, and severe client drift. To address these challenges, we propose CoASFL, an inconsistency-aware asynchronous SFL framework that incorporates a dynamic activation merging mechanism and a consistency-aware model aggregation mechanism. Specifically, CoASFL constructs more consistent activation sequences from heterogeneous clients to alleviate horizontal inconsistency, and dynamically adjusts aggregation weights according to client participation frequencies and progress gaps to mitigate vertical inconsistency. By jointly coordinating activation-level and model-level consistency, CoASFL effectively suppresses inconsistency propagation during asynchronous training. Extensive experiments on an 80-device heterogeneous edge testbed demonstrate that CoASFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SFL approaches, accelerating training by 1.61$\times$ to 3.74$\times$ and improving final model accuracy by up to 3.26\% under heterogeneous scenarios.

title: Why Do Some Minimal Websites Feel Distinctive While Others Look Like the Same Template?
description:
Open a few online stores and you will see white backgrounds, large images, fine rules, and short headlines. They all look clean. Yet after you close them, some leave you with a distinct sense of character. Others leave little beyond “that looked nice.”

This is a familiar problem when a brand builds a website: the references are good and the pages contain very few elements, so why does the result still lack an identity of its own?

Our view is that minimalism makes a brand’s choices more visible. With less decoration, it becomes easier to see whether typography, imagery, content, and proportion share a common rationale. A few beautiful references can shape the appearance of a page. They do not necessarily establish how the brand should keep expressing itself over time.

Original WESWOO editorial concept: minimal design with character. AI-generated, not a built architectural project. Chinese subtitle.

A Clean Appearance and a Clear Brand Expression Are Different Things

Imagine two homeware brands that both use off-white backgrounds and black text. One wants to convey durable materials and an architectural sensibility. The other focuses on the easy, approachable relationships of everyday life. Both can be visually restrained, but they should not have exactly the same photographic distance, tone of voice, or spatial rhythm.

The first might use fuller spatial relationships, defined edges, and substantial headlines to draw attention to structure. The second might retain signs of daily use, with closer viewpoints and natural descriptions that suggest someone actually lives with these objects. These are hypothetical design directions, not rules that a product category must follow.

The question is whether one choice supports the next. If the images describe a relaxed way of living but the copy reads like a technical tender, the signals pull apart. If the homepage emphasizes craftsmanship but the product page switches to glossy, futuristic materials, each page may work on its own while the overall brand impression remains unclear.

Before designing, try writing one sentence that can guide actual decisions. For example: “We want people to see the traces that materials acquire through real life.” That is more useful than “premium, international, and refined,” because it can inform photography, cropping, and copy. Each subsequent visual decision can be discussed in relation to that sentence.

A Real Example: Making the Work the Focus of the Visual System

The website project for architecture studio Telha Clarke offers a useful starting point. In the design team’s Awwwards case study, the work itself is the narrative focus. Layout and motion support the presentation of the content, rather than forcing the work into a predetermined framework of visual tricks. The design team’s case study

Actual Telha Clarke website screenshot, October21,2026. Static browser capture only, not evidence of complete animation playback, conversion results or a Shopify implementation. Site and artwork belong to their respective owners.

When we opened the studio’s website, the first screen combined a large brand wordmark, very restrained navigation, and an architectural image surrounded by space. Even this single frame gives us three things to discuss: the wordmark establishes identity, the empty space establishes an order of attention, and the image shows what the practice actually does. They are not all competing to be the loudest element.

For an online store, the useful lesson is to give visual assets different jobs. The brand name answers “Who is this?” Product or spatial imagery shows “What is distinctive here?” The detailed content explains “Why should I keep looking?” If every section uses a giant headline and a huge photograph, the page may look consistent while losing its points of emphasis.

We are drawing on the design method here. This is an architecture studio’s website, not a Shopify store or a WESWOO client project. Neither the case study nor the screenshot provides sales conversion data, so they cannot establish that a particular layout necessarily earns more money.

Typography, Imagery, and Space Should Express the Same Character

When a client says “the type feels wrong,” the problem is not always that the font is unattractive. The character of the typography may simply be at odds with what the brand wants to express.

Typography does more than supply letterforms. Headline length, line length, the contrast between headings and body text, and the arrangement of product codes and prices all change the viewing rhythm. A brand that wants to feel precise cannot rely on one font to carry that impression if model numbers change size from page to page and numbers and units follow unrelated styles.

When examining the design in more detail, distinguish at least these three areas:

  • Typography. Define the roles of headlines, body copy, supporting information, and numbers. Check whether Chinese, English, and product names still work together. Headlines can carry personality; purchase conditions must remain clear and readable.
  • Art direction. Establish a rationale for lighting, materials, settings, people, and cropping. A brand can have several photographic themes, but the team should be able to explain how they belong to the same world.
  • Composition. Decide which pieces of content belong close together, where readers need a pause, and how much visual weight a product should carry. Space should help people understand relationships, rather than leaving the same large gap in every section.

These decisions need to be reviewed together. Choosing a font from a specimen, adding photographs from a library, and then asking a developer to “make the layout feel premium” usually divides a shared design judgment into several disconnected decisions.

Two fictional brand studies of the same chair compare typography, imagery and spatial composition. AI-generated concept, not real client work or a ranking. Chinese subtitle.

Product photography is especially easy to underestimate. Following current trends in packaging, lighting, and backgrounds can produce a polished individual image. But if the brand emphasizes real materials and daily use, an excessively flawless image can also weaken that meaning. A beautiful photograph and an accurate expression of the brand are two things that deserve separate discussion.

A Distinctive Design Should Be Able to Grow

A designer can spend a long time refining the first screen. The more practical question is whether the brand still comes through when a new product is added, a long product name appears, or an image arrives in a different format.

A useful design system therefore needs room for variation. Portraits and close-up details can use different compositions. Short and long headlines can have different arrangements. What connects them is a comparable approach to contrast, tone, and information priorities. Consistency does not require every image to look the same.

Test the design with three pieces of content: a featured product, a product with complex information, and a real explanation that is difficult to arrange attractively. See whether the same rules can accommodate all three. If the system only works with carefully chosen short words and landscape images, it is closer to a poster exercise than a dependable way for the website to communicate.

In a Shopify project, these principles also have to reach the actual content structure. Do editors have clear guidance on image proportions? Do longer headlines wrap naturally? Can campaign pages and regular product pages share the same typographic and photographic principles? What is possible depends on the theme and the actual development scope. The approach has to work beyond the design file.

How to Tell Whether You Have Built a Brand, Rather Than Just a Style

When reviewing a proposal, set aside “Is it minimal enough?” for a moment. Ask instead: which choices make particular sense for this brand?

Temporarily covering the logo and looking at whether the typography, images, and narrative still express a shared character can help the discussion. It is not a substitute for brand recognition research with real users. It can, however, reveal whether the team has placed the entire burden of identity on the mark in the top-left corner.

A more practical exercise is to put the homepage, a product page, and one campaign asset side by side. Ask someone who was not involved in the design what each one feels like, then ask which specific details gave them that impression. Listen to their own words first. Do not build an answer into the question by asking, for example, whether it “feels premium.”

If the response goes no further than “lots of white” and “big pictures,” investigate whether the brand expression has reached the content itself. If the person mentions a material, a way of living, or an attitude toward the work, the team can begin to examine whether that is the impression it intended to build.

At WESWOO, we carry these judgments through the design and implementation of a brand’s website: first clarify how the brand wants to be understood, then translate that into typographic, photographic, and compositional principles that can be sustained. Minimalism can be an outcome, but it cannot replace that thinking. What is worth preserving is a distinctive way of expressing the brand that survives content updates and a growing product range.

title: I broke an Elementor site on purpose, then built a tool to find the bugs
description:
The night I broke my own site

I'm 53, I work in a factory, and in the evenings I build things in vanilla JavaScript.

Lately I've been looking at freelance WordPress jobs. Almost every one of them says the same thing: "Elementor site, layout is broken, fix it."

So I did something a bit crazy. I took an empty test site, installed Elementor, and asked an AI to break it for me — 5 hidden CSS bugs, packed into an encoded script so I couldn't just read the answer.

Then I tried to find them.

It was humbling. The page looked wrong, but the console said nothing. Of course: CSS doesn't throw errors. A bad rule is still a valid rule, so the browser applies it silently. That's exactly why clients say "everything moved and I don't know why."

I found the first bug the slow way — DevTools, Styles panel, unchecking rules one by one until I saw it:

.elementor-section, .e-con { margin-right: -60px !important; }

Twenty minutes for one line. I thought: there must be a faster way.

So I built one: CSS hunt

🐞 BeeLadybug is my zero-dependency debugging overlay. You paste one line in the console and it attaches to any page — WordPress dashboards, Elementor pages, mobile viewports. It already showed element size, classes, display type, FPS and memory.

Version 0.5 adds a new mode: CSS hunt (press F6).

When you hover an element, it tells you what's wrong with it:

  • !important rules that match the element, and where they come from (<style> inline or the stylesheet URL)
  • Overflow causes: which element actually leaves the viewport, plus negative margins
  • Invisible text: color: transparent, opacity: 0, or text the same color as its background
  • Click blockers: what sits on top of the element's center, including fixed ::before / ::after on html / body
  • Stretched images: natural ratio vs rendered ratio, when object-fit is fill

Press S to scan the whole page. Click a line and the element gets a red outline.

The hard part: telling the truth without noise

My first version was technically right and practically useless.

One card overflowing the screen produced ten red lines: the card, its article, its p, its h2… All "overflowing", because they inherited it. A fixed overlay blocking clicks? One warning per element underneath it.

A real developer doesn't want ten alarms. They want the culprit.

So the scan now:

  1. Reports the cause, not the containers. An ancestor is skipped if a descendant overflows by the same amount (±2px).
  2. Groups by cause. Instead of 12 lines you get: 
▾ body::after blocks clicks on 12 elements
    div.elementor-element-629ef32
    img#1301
    summary.elementor-element-3925463
    …
  1. Separates bugs from info. Red = bug. Grey = info, like unreadable sheet: fonts.googleapis.com (cross-origin stylesheets can't be read — that's a browser rule, not a problem on the page).
  2. Keeps the log calm. Hover and DOM-mutation lines are hidden unless you turn on verbose mode (F3). Each issue is logged once per element every 5 seconds. Press P to pin the panel on an element and read it in peace.

The real test

The demo page bugs are easy — I wrote them. The real test was the broken Elementor page, with Elementor V4 "atomic" widgets, Google Fonts, Altervista ad scripts and all the usual mess.

Result: CSS hunt found the click blocker, the negative margin overflow, the invisible button text and the stretched image on a live page I didn't build the bugs for.

Try it

Open any page, press F12, paste this in the console:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.5.3/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Then press F6, hover, and press S.

No build step, no framework, no dependencies. Just vanilla JavaScript.

What I learned

  • CSS bugs are silent. The console won't help you. You need to look at computed styles and geometry.
  • The right answer is not enough. A debugging tool must point to the cause, or it's just another wall of text.
  • Breaking things on purpose is the best teacher. I recommend it to anyone who wants to do WordPress fixes for clients.

I'm still learning. If you try CSS hunt on a broken page and it misses something, tell me in the comments — that's how the next version gets better.

🐞 npm: bee-ladybug

title: Do Not Choose an AI Platform Until It Passes a Portability Drill
description:
Do Not Choose an AI Platform Until It Passes a Portability Drill

An enterprise AI platform is not a model leaderboard with an admin console attached. It is an operating dependency: prompts, retrieval, tools, safety rules, identities, telemetry, evaluations, and business decisions gradually conform to its abstractions. A platform can look cheapest and most capable during procurement while becoming the most expensive option two years later because the organization cannot reproduce its behavior anywhere else.

The practical response is not to demand perfect portability. That is usually unrealistic. It is to define which assets must remain portable, measure the cost of moving a representative workload, and deliberately price the dependencies that you choose to keep.

This article adapts AI-Due's comparison of enterprise AI platforms into a vendor-neutral decision system. The source correctly separates foundation models, enterprise suites, and specialist platforms. The missing procurement question is: if a provider changes price, removes a model, degrades a region, or no longer fits the risk boundary, can the organization move an important workflow without rebuilding its business logic from memory?

The answer should come from a drill, not a promise.

The decision in one sentence

Choose the platform that produces the best accepted business outcomes inside your risk and operating constraints, while keeping the cost and time of a tested exit below an explicit ceiling.

That sentence has four parts:

  1. Accepted outcomes, not benchmark scores or attractive demonstrations.
  2. Risk constraints, including data location, identity, authorization, audit, and human control.
  3. Operating constraints, including latency tails, quotas, support, skills, and incident recovery.
  4. A tested exit ceiling, expressed in time, money, lost functionality, and quality change.

If procurement measures only the first invoice and a generic accuracy score, it has not compared platforms. It has compared sales offers.

Why feature matrices fail

A conventional matrix gives every vendor a row and every advertised capability a column. The cells quickly turn green: chat, embeddings, agents, retrieval, fine-tuning, guardrails, regional hosting, connectors, monitoring. Yet identical labels can hide materially different semantics.

“Structured output” may mean a valid JSON response, schema-constrained decoding, or best-effort formatting. “Private data” may refer to training exclusion while leaving retention, abuse monitoring, subprocessors, and regional processing unanswered. “Agent tools” may use different retry, timeout, idempotency, and approval rules. “Evaluation” may measure model quality but not authorization failures or downstream rework.

Feature presence therefore has weak decision value. What matters is whether the complete workload behaves acceptably under your inputs, identities, load, failures, and evidence requirements.

The AI-Due platform comparison is useful as a market map: foundation-model providers, enterprise suites, and specialized platforms solve different layers of the problem. Treat that map as the beginning of discovery. Do not turn its product descriptions, indicative prices, or model claims into a purchase decision without current contractual and workload evidence.

Define the workload before comparing platforms

“We need an AI platform” is not a testable requirement. Define a workload packet instead. One packet describes one business outcome and contains everything needed to evaluate it consistently.

A useful packet includes:

  • the decision or artifact the system must produce;
  • representative inputs, including rare and adversarial cases;
  • the data classes involved and prohibited destinations;
  • permitted tools and maximum authority;
  • required citations, evidence, or provenance;
  • quality acceptance rules and abstention conditions;
  • latency and availability objectives;
  • expected volume and concurrency distribution;
  • human review and escalation steps;
  • retention, deletion, and audit requirements;
  • a known-good baseline from the current process.

Use several packets rather than one synthetic prompt. A customer-support summarizer, a coding assistant, a multilingual document extractor, and a tool-using finance agent create different rankings. A platform that wins one may lose another.

Separate hard gates from scored preferences

Hard gates are binary. A platform is inadmissible if it cannot meet them. Examples include an approved processing region, single sign-on, tenant isolation, auditable tool approval, a required deletion path, or a contractual prohibition on training with customer data.

Preferences are scored after gates pass: response quality, integration effort, latency, cost, support, or developer experience. Never allow an excellent model score to compensate for a failed legal or security gate. A weighted spreadsheet that lets strengths offset prohibitions is mathematically tidy and operationally wrong.

Dimension Example gate Example scored measure Evidence
Data Approved processing and retention Transfer overhead Contract plus technical test
Identity SSO and least privilege Admin effort Configuration export and access test
Quality Critical error rate below ceiling Accepted outcome rate Frozen evaluation set
Operations Required region and support path P95/P99 latency Load and incident test
Tools Explicit approval for high-impact actions Completion rate Sandbox traces
Exit Required assets exportable Migration hours and quality delta Portability drill

Build a platform-independent control plane

Portability begins with ownership boundaries. The enterprise should own the workload definition, evaluation set, policy, business rules, outcome history, and route decision. Providers can supply excellent models, hosting, connectors, and managed controls without becoming the only place where the organization understands how its work is performed.

flowchart LR
    U[User or business event] --> I[Enterprise identity and policy]
    I --> R[Workload router]
    R --> A[Platform A adapter]
    R --> B[Platform B adapter]
    R --> L[Local or private endpoint]
    A --> V[Output validator]
    B --> V
    L --> V
    V --> H{Human approval required?}
    H -->|yes| Q[Review queue]
    H -->|no| X[Bounded action]
    Q --> X
    X --> O[Outcome and evidence ledger]
    O --> E[Evaluation and routing updates]

This diagram does not imply that every request must be dynamically multi-cloud. It shows where durable enterprise assets should sit. A single provider can remain the default. The boundary simply prevents prompts, permissions, evaluations, and outcome semantics from being trapped inside a proprietary studio with no reproducible representation.

What belongs outside the provider-specific layer

Keep the following assets under enterprise version control when feasible:

  • workload schemas and task instructions;
  • evaluation cases and acceptance thresholds;
  • retrieval source identifiers and authorization mappings;
  • tool contracts, idempotency keys, and approval rules;
  • output schemas and validators;
  • routing rules and fallback prohibitions;
  • redaction and retention policies;
  • outcome labels, reviewer decisions, and incident records;
  • dependency and configuration manifests.

Provider adapters translate those assets into each platform's API or managed features. Some functionality will remain proprietary. Record it explicitly as a dependency with an owner, benefit, replacement option, and exit estimate.

Run an evaluation that measures completed work

Public benchmarks are useful context, not acceptance tests. MLCommons explains that MLPerf Inference uses defined datasets, quality targets, load scenarios, and rules to compare system performance in a reproducible way. Its datacenter suite measures latency and throughput under specified conditions, which is far stronger than an undocumented vendor chart (MLCommons). But even a strong infrastructure benchmark does not know your policies, documents, tool errors, review costs, or customer consequences.

Create a frozen enterprise evaluation set. Preserve the same inputs, expected evidence, tool fixtures, policies, and scoring logic across candidates. Include ordinary cases, long-tail cases, malicious instructions, missing information, ambiguous requests, unavailable tools, rate limits, and permission denials.

Measure at least:

  • accepted outcome rate;
  • critical error rate;
  • correct abstention rate;
  • evidence or citation validity;
  • tool-selection and argument accuracy;
  • unauthorized-action attempts;
  • human review minutes;
  • downstream rework;
  • P50, P95, and P99 end-to-end latency;
  • successful recovery after timeout or partial failure;
  • total variable and fixed cost per accepted outcome.

Do not mix all cases into one average. Segment by risk, language, input length, tool count, and complexity. A 92% average can hide a 40% success rate on the regulated cases that justified the purchase.

Use paired comparisons

Send the same case to each candidate under controlled settings. Blind reviewers to the provider when practical. Store raw outputs securely, but score normalized outcomes with the same rubric. Where outputs are subjective, use multiple reviewers and record disagreement rather than manufacturing precision.

Repeat a subset across days and load levels. Generative systems can vary, and managed platforms change. The goal is not to declare an eternal winner. It is to establish an evidence snapshot with enough variance information to support a bounded decision.

Why one score is not enough

The research record supports multi-dimensional comparison. The HELM project evaluated language models across scenarios and, where feasible, seven dimensions: accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency. Its authors also found that prominent models had often been tested on only a small fraction of the same core scenarios before standardization improved coverage (HELM paper). The procurement lesson is not to copy HELM's exact suite. It is to resist collapsing incompatible concerns into one leaderboard number.

Maintain a scorecard with separate floors. A platform that is fast but violates an authorization rule fails. A platform that is accurate on routine English requests but unreliable for the languages your customers use needs a segmented decision. A platform that wins quality by consuming far more review labor should expose that cost rather than hiding it inside an aggregate score.

Also preserve test limitations. Evaluation cases are samples, graders can disagree, and production distributions move. Record coverage, excluded populations, confidence intervals where defensible, and the date of every result. Revalidation should be triggered by meaningful model, policy, retrieval, tool, or workload changes—not merely by a calendar reminder.

Calculate cost at the accepted-outcome boundary

Token price is only one term. The relevant unit is the cost of a business result that passes acceptance.

Use:

cost_per_accepted_outcome =
  (platform_fees
   + model_usage
   + retrieval_and_storage
   + integration_labor
   + operations_and_security
   + human_review
   + rework
   + expected_failure_cost)
  / accepted_outcomes

A cheaper model that produces more rework can cost more. A managed suite with a higher license may be economical if it removes identity, observability, and support work that the organization would otherwise perform. Conversely, bundled credits can disguise high switching and administration costs after usage grows.

Model price changes, caching, batch discounts, reserved capacity, region premiums, and tool-call expansion with realistic traffic distributions. Include unsuccessful calls and retries. Estimate the cost of incident response and temporary manual fallback. State every assumption and rerun the model when the provider or workload changes.

Measure lock-in instead of arguing about it

Lock-in is neither automatically bad nor fully avoidable. Organizations accept dependencies because integrated services accelerate delivery. The right question is whether the dependency is understood, priced, monitored, and reversible enough for the workload.

BCG reports that 62% of 500 surveyed IT decision makers were concerned about digital-platform lock-in, while 79% said the value justified the cost. That tension is important: dependency can coexist with value (BCG). The aim is not purity. It is informed exposure.

Create a dependency ledger with these categories:

  1. Data dependency: prompts, files, embeddings, indexes, fine-tuning data, feedback, and logs.
  2. Behavior dependency: system instructions, hidden orchestration, safety behavior, and model-specific prompt conventions.
  3. Tool dependency: proprietary connectors, action semantics, retries, approvals, and state.
  4. Identity dependency: users, groups, service principals, permissions, and audit roles.
  5. Operational dependency: quotas, regional capacity, dashboards, alerts, incident processes, and support.
  6. Commercial dependency: commitments, discounts, egress, minimum spend, termination terms, and price-change rights.
  7. Skill dependency: expertise that exists only in a vendor studio or configuration language.
  8. Cognitive dependency: business logic that teams can no longer explain without the platform.

For each dependency, record the benefit, replacement path, export format, estimated migration effort, evidence freshness, and maximum tolerated outage.

The portability drill

A questionnaire asks whether switching is possible. A drill discovers what switching means.

Select one representative, production-shaped workload. It should be valuable enough to expose real complexity but bounded enough to migrate safely in a test environment. Freeze its current version and baseline results. Then move it to a second platform or a local compatible endpoint.

Step 1: inventory the complete workload

Export prompts, schemas, retrieval documents, chunking settings, embeddings assumptions, tool definitions, policy rules, identities, secrets references, evaluation cases, telemetry fields, and approval flows. Do not export live secrets or personal data into an uncontrolled test environment.

Mark anything that cannot be exported. “We can recreate it” is not equivalent to an export until someone reproduces it and verifies the result.

Step 2: implement the smallest adapter

Translate model calls, structured outputs, streaming events, and tool invocation into a neutral internal contract. Avoid normalizing away meaningful differences. If Platform B lacks a feature, implement a visible substitute or record the gap.

const workload = {
  id: "support-resolution-v3",
  input: { ticketId: "T-1042", locale: "en-GB" },
  policy: { maxRisk: "low", requireEvidence: true },
  outputSchema: {
    type: "object",
    required: ["decision", "evidence", "confidence"],
  },
};

async function runWith(provider, packet) {
  const start = performance.now();
  const raw = await provider.execute(packet);
  const validation = validateOutput(raw, packet.outputSchema);
  return {
    provider: provider.name,
    accepted: validation.ok && policyAllows(raw, packet.policy),
    latencyMs: Math.round(performance.now() - start),
    reasons: validation.reasons,
    output: raw,
  };
}

const result = await runWith(selectedAdapter, workload);
console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2));

In production, add authenticated identities, timeouts, idempotency, redaction, durable evidence, and bounded retries. The important pattern is that the business packet and validator do not belong to the provider adapter.

Step 3: replay the frozen evaluation

Run both implementations on identical cases. Compare accepted outcomes, critical failures, abstentions, latency distribution, review time, and cost. Investigate semantic differences. A syntactically compatible API can still produce different tool timing, refusal behavior, context handling, or evidence quality.

Step 4: test operational failure

Simulate quota exhaustion, regional unavailability, malformed tool output, slow retrieval, expired credentials, and partial streaming. Confirm that fallback behavior respects data and risk policy. A sensitive workload must not silently route to an unapproved provider merely because the default is unavailable.

Step 5: account for the move

Track engineering hours, security review, data movement, contract work, retraining, parallel running, reviewer time, degraded features, and remaining cleanup. Measure elapsed calendar time as well as labor. A five-day implementation that waits six weeks for contractual or regional approval is a six-week exit.

Step 6: produce an exit receipt

The receipt records:

  • workload and versions tested;
  • source and destination platforms;
  • assets successfully exported and reconstructed;
  • features lost, substituted, or redesigned;
  • quality, latency, and cost deltas;
  • labor and elapsed time;
  • unresolved dependencies;
  • rollback result;
  • next drill date.

Set thresholds before the test. For example: no critical-policy regression, less than five percentage points loss in accepted outcomes, recovery within one business day, and migration below 15 person-days. Your thresholds will differ, but retrospective rationalization is not a control.

Portability law helps, but it does not migrate your application

The EU Data Act has applied since 12 September 2025. Its Chapter VI addresses switching between data-processing services and requires measures intended to remove switching obstacles. The European Commission explains that relevant customer input, output, and metadata are part of the switching scope, that SaaS and PaaS providers must make open interfaces available and export data in a commonly used machine-readable format, and that switching and egress charges are due to be removed from 12 January 2027 (European Commission).

This is meaningful leverage, not a substitute for engineering. Exportable data does not automatically reproduce prompts, retrieval ranking, model behavior, tool semantics, identities, approvals, observability, or accepted outcomes. Legal scope may also vary by service and asset; protected intellectual property and trade secrets affect what is included. Obtain legal advice for your contract and jurisdiction rather than treating this article as legal guidance.

Use regulation to strengthen contract questions, then prove technical and operational portability with the drill.

Contract for evidence, not adjectives

Procurement language should be concrete enough to verify. Ask for:

  • processing locations and subprocessors by service and feature;
  • retention, deletion, backup, and abuse-monitoring behavior;
  • exportable asset list, formats, interfaces, time limits, and assistance;
  • change notice for models, APIs, regions, safety behavior, and prices;
  • version pinning or migration windows where available;
  • service objectives and remedies by region;
  • incident notification and evidence access;
  • audit-log fields, retention, and export;
  • termination assistance and credential revocation;
  • ownership and permitted use of inputs, outputs, tuning data, and feedback;
  • a tested path for bulk export without production interruption.

Avoid relying on “enterprise-grade,” “secure,” “open,” “portable,” or “responsible” unless the contract, configuration, and test evidence define the claim.

Contradictions and trade-offs

More abstraction can improve portability and reduce useful capability

A lowest-common-denominator gateway makes providers easier to swap, but it may hide valuable features such as constrained decoding, prompt caching, regional capacity controls, or native tool governance. Preserve a neutral core, then allow declared extensions. Test whether each extension earns its dependency.

Multi-platform architecture can improve resilience and increase failure surface

Two providers introduce two identities, policies, billing systems, incident paths, and behavior profiles. Multi-platform is not automatically safer or cheaper. Use it where the recovery or specialization benefit exceeds the operating burden.

Open weights can reduce provider dependence and create new dependence

Self-hosting changes the dependency from an API vendor to model artifacts, serving infrastructure, accelerators, security updates, and scarce operational skills. It can be the right choice, but it is not dependency-free.

The best model today may be the wrong platform decision

Model rankings move quickly. Enterprise integration and governance move slowly. Prefer a platform and control plane that can absorb model change without repeatedly rebuilding policy and evidence. At the same time, do not sacrifice a critical outcome merely for theoretical interchangeability.

A successful export does not prove equivalent behavior

Files and metadata can move while functionality degrades. The Commission's description of “functional equivalence” for shared infrastructure features does not mean generative models will return identical judgments. Portability acceptance must include outcome evaluation.

Failure modes and controls

Failure mode: demo winner

The team selects the most impressive hand-picked demonstration.

Control: use frozen representative packets, blind scoring, risk segments, and repeated tests.

Failure mode: token-price procurement

The business ignores integration, review, rework, operations, and failure cost.

Control: compare total cost per accepted outcome under realistic traffic.

Failure mode: weighted-gate bypass

A high capability score offsets a failed security or legal requirement.

Control: apply hard admissibility gates before weighted scoring.

Failure mode: proprietary-policy trap

Business rules exist only in a vendor console and cannot be reproduced.

Control: version neutral policy definitions and record platform translations.

Failure mode: silent fallback

A failed primary route sends sensitive data to an unapproved endpoint.

Control: bind fallback to data and action policy; fail closed when no approved route exists.

Failure mode: benchmark theater

The team quotes public performance results that do not match its workload.

Control: use public benchmarks for context and internal packets for acceptance.

Failure mode: paper portability

The contract promises export, but no one has restored a working workload.

Control: run a timed migration and retain an exit receipt.

Failure mode: abandoned source platform

After a test migration, data, credentials, indexes, or logs remain in the old environment.

Control: include verified revocation, deletion, retention expiry, and billing closure in the exit plan.

Failure mode: evaluator capture

The same vendor feature generates, judges, and explains outputs.

Control: keep business acceptance logic independent and use human or cross-system checks for critical cases.

A 90-day selection sequence

Days 1–15: frame

Choose three to five workload packets. Establish hard gates, baselines, outcome metrics, risk owners, and an initial dependency ledger. Remove candidates that cannot meet gates.

Days 16–35: evaluate

Implement thin adapters and replay the frozen cases. Test quality, evidence, tools, latency, load, denial, and failure recovery. Model total cost per accepted outcome.

Days 36–50: drill exit

Move one workload between the two leading candidates. Time the work, test reconstruction, compare outcomes, and produce the exit receipt.

Days 51–65: contract

Use the evidence to negotiate regions, changes, export, support, termination, and pricing. Resolve gaps or formally accept them with an owner and exposure limit.

Days 66–90: controlled production

Launch a bounded population with human review and explicit rollback. Monitor accepted outcomes, critical errors, tail latency, review effort, cost, and dependency changes. Do not expand until the production evidence meets the predeclared gates.

Validation checklist

Before approving an enterprise AI platform, verify:

  • [ ] Workload packets describe outcomes, inputs, risks, tools, and baselines.
  • [ ] Hard gates are separated from weighted preferences.
  • [ ] Every candidate received the same frozen evaluation cases.
  • [ ] Results are segmented by risk, language, complexity, and load.
  • [ ] Accepted outcomes, critical errors, abstentions, and rework are measured.
  • [ ] P50, P95, and P99 end-to-end latency are measured under realistic concurrency.
  • [ ] Cost includes integration, operations, review, rework, and failure.
  • [ ] Business rules, policies, validators, and evaluation cases remain enterprise-owned.
  • [ ] Retrieval authorization is preserved outside provider-specific shortcuts.
  • [ ] Tool calls use typed contracts, least privilege, approval, and idempotency.
  • [ ] Platform-specific extensions have explicit benefits and exit estimates.
  • [ ] Data, behavior, tools, identity, operations, commercial, skill, and cognitive dependencies are logged.
  • [ ] Export formats and interfaces have been exercised, not merely documented.
  • [ ] One representative workload has been migrated and replayed.
  • [ ] Quality and policy deltas after migration remain within declared ceilings.
  • [ ] Fallback routes cannot bypass data or action restrictions.
  • [ ] Regional outage, quota, credential, and partial-failure scenarios have been tested.
  • [ ] Contract terms cover location, retention, changes, export, incidents, and termination.
  • [ ] Cleanup covers credentials, data, indexes, logs, commitments, and billing.
  • [ ] The exit receipt has an owner and a future drill date.

The final decision rule

Do not buy the platform with the longest feature list, the most famous model, or the cheapest million tokens. Buy the operating arrangement that passes your hard gates, delivers the strongest accepted outcomes for the full cost, and keeps chosen dependencies within a tested exit budget.

The goal is not to switch providers constantly. The goal is to retain the ability to make a real choice when conditions change. A portability drill converts that ability from procurement language into evidence.

title: Reconstruction-Optimized Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse expert activation, but deployment still requires storing a large number of expert parameters. We study post-training expert pruning using task-domain calibration data as a subset-selection problem: given a pretrained MoE layer, select a fixed number of experts that best reconstruct its original output. Exact subset search is combinatorial and becomes intractable for modern MoE models with many experts per layer. We develop OptEP, a scalable continuous relaxation that directly optimizes differentiable expert-selection variables, followed by a lightweight reconstruction-based update of the retained expert weights. Across multiple MoE architectures and tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approach improves over the strongest existing expert-pruning baselines, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 15.05% on Qwen3-30B-A3B, 14.55% on Qwen3-235B-A22B, 11.06% on GLM-4.5-Air, and 16.20% on Mixtral-8x7B. The improvements are particularly pronounced under aggressive pruning, demonstrating that reconstruction-driven expert selection and weight adaptation can preserve substantially more of the original model's performance while reducing the number of retained experts.

title: DuckDB 2.0 LTS adds server mode, triggers and VARIANT
description:
DuckDB released version 2.0.0 on October 21, 2026, as a long-term support (LTS) release that the project will support until at least October 2027. It adds a built-in server mode, SQL triggers and a new parser. It also makes a one-way change: database files written by 2.0 cannot be opened by any earlier version, so upgrades need a plan.

DuckDB is an open-source SQL database for analytics. Like SQLite, it runs inside your program rather than as a separate server. Unlike SQLite, it is built for big analytical queries over large tables and files such as Parquet and CSV.

What DuckDB 2.0 adds

The DuckDB announcement calls 2.0 the team's largest feature release so far, built from close to 20,000 commits since version 1.5. "DuckDB 2.0 is above all a feature release," the DuckDB team writes. The release is codenamed "Cinnamon Teal," after the duck species Spatula cyanoptera. The GitHub release uses the name "Cyanoptera."

Feature What it does
Quack server mode Runs DuckDB as a server that other clients connect to
Triggers CREATE TRIGGER runs SQL automatically, before or after a change to a table
VARIANT type Stores semi-structured data, such as JSON, and splits out its common structure for better compression and speed
Async I/O Reads Parquet and CSV files while queries run, with several requests in flight, mainly to speed up cloud storage like Amazon S3
New SQL parser A PEG-based parser is now the default; extensions can add their own SQL syntax, and errors show where the problem is
Native time zones Time zones, calendars and collations no longer need the ICU library

A trigger is a rule stored in the database: when a row changes, run this SQL too. DuckDB 2.0 supports BEFORE and AFTER triggers, at row or statement level. Some combinations are not supported yet, such as a BEFORE ... FOR EACH ROW trigger on UPDATE.

Quack turns DuckDB into a server

Until now, DuckDB served one program at a time. With Quack, CALL quack_serve(...) starts a server, and a client connects with ATTACH 'quack:...'. A new CONNECT statement switches a whole session to a remote database. The command-line tool gains matching -serve and -connect flags.

The server listens only on the local machine by default. For remote access, the DuckDB team recommends putting it behind a reverse proxy that handles TLS encryption. InfoWorld reported in August that Quack also makes it easier to query PostgreSQL and MySQL databases remotely.

Breaking changes to check before upgrading

According to the release post and the GitHub release notes, these changes can break existing code or builds:

  • Files are one-way. DuckDB 2.0 reads and writes existing database files. "DuckDB versions before 2.0 cannot read database files created by DuckDB 2.0," the team warns.
  • New parser by default. SET enable_legacy_parser = true; brings back the old one.
  • Single-arrow lambdas are off. Syntax like x -> x + 1 is disabled. SET lambda_syntax = 'enable_single_arrow'; turns it back on until version 2.1 removes it.
  • Integer division by zero now raises an error instead of returning NULL.
  • Builds need C++17, up from C++11, and release builds now use the Clang compiler. Amalgamation builds are deprecated.
  • Intel Macs are being phased out. Community extensions are no longer built for macOS on x86_64, and DuckDB 2.1 drops support.

The sources disagree on one detail. InfoWorld's preview described a stable C API for extensions. The release post says the revamped C API v2 is "not yet marked as stable," because the team wants to test it in the field first.

Support windows

Version Supported until
DuckDB 2.0 (LTS) At least October 2027
DuckDB 1.5 March 2027 (extended)
DuckDB 1.4 Late November 2026

What this means for developers

Treat this as a planned migration, not a routine bump.

  • Copy your database files before the first open. Once DuckDB 2.0 writes to a file, an older tool or teammate on 1.5 can no longer read it. Upgrade every reader of a shared file together.
  • Test on a copy of production. The DuckDB team recommends a shadow system first. For mission-critical work, it suggests waiting for the first patch release, due in November.
  • Check your client. The command-line tool and Python client are ready now. Go, R and Java clients, and some extensions, "may take a few days," the team says.
  • Search your SQL for two patterns. Look for single-arrow lambdas and any integer division that could hit zero. Both behave differently now.
  • Do not expose a Quack server directly. Keep it on localhost, or put a TLS reverse proxy in front, as the team advises.
  • Teams on 1.4 should move first. Its support ends in late November 2026, so upgrade to 2.0, or to 1.5 for a smaller step.

This article was first published on Tech AI Wire.

Also available in

Deutsch · 日本語 · Français · Español · Português

Sources

  • Announcing DuckDB 2.0.0 - DuckDB
  • DuckDB v2.0.0 release notes - GitHub
  • DuckDB 2.0 coming this fall with client-server mode - InfoWorld

title: How to get the best and fairest performance out of your ASR system using activation steering
description:
arXiv:2610.26994v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering for ASR systems is an underexplored technique in improving both ASR performance and demographic fairness. We investigate two forms of activation steering: paired activation subtraction, and supervised optimization. We find the former to be ineffective at ameliorating ASR performance whatsoever, while the latter is quite effective at deriving steering vectors (SVs) that improve at once overall ASR performance and demographic fairness along such diverse axes as gender, age, and dialect. We also explore what types of data---from the most to the least personal---are necessary for calculating or training SVs. First, we show significant performance in performance from training SVs using an eclectic group of speakers from the same dataset. Furthermore, we find that vectors trained using acoustically similar speakers leads to ASR performances that are competitive or superior to vectors trained on the same speaker, or speakers from the same labeled demographic group. This finding shows that we can harness activation steering for few-shot adaptation given access to a speaker's demography, or zero-shot adaptation to unseen speakers without the need for any labels at all.

title: The Multi-Cloud Drawdown
description:
The exclusive frontier partnership died the moment enterprise procurement stepped in.

OpenAI announced that its frontier models and Codex workflows are coming to Google Cloud's Model Garden, letting corporate customers draw down their existing Google Cloud spend commitments to run GPT workloads. Six months ago, the exclusive intellectual property license with Microsoft quietly ended, followed twenty-four hours later by an agreement with Amazon Web Services. OpenAI's models now sit natively inside all three hyperscalers.

Industry coverage frames this as a distribution race, but the underlying accounting tells a more constrained story. Enterprise buyers rarely pay for AI API calls out of fresh discretionary cash. They pay out of multi-year, nine-figure minimum spend commitments negotiated with their primary cloud infrastructure provider. If a Fortune 500 bank or insurer has committed three hundred million dollars over five years to Google Cloud or AWS, every dollar routed to Azure to query an OpenAI endpoint counts as an unbudgeted cash leak. The CFO asks why the lab cannot simply burn down the committed balance sheet credits sitting on GCP.

For two years, Microsoft used exclusivity to force those buyers onto Azure, treating OpenAI's frontier weights as the sole anchor tenant capable of moving legacy workloads. That works when frontier models hold a wide, unquestioned performance lead. It breaks down once Anthropic and open-weights models close the capability gap, while enterprise CIOs refuse to take on multi-cloud egress penalties or duplicate security audits just to run inference. The cost of friction began to exceed the value of the exclusivity payout.

On the lab side, OpenAI is raising capital at a 1.4 trillion dollar valuation while managing staggering compute bills and an impending public offering. At that scale, you cannot leave two-thirds of the addressable enterprise balance sheet untouched. Frontier labs have transitioned from proprietary research institutions into software wholesalers. They need every sovereign balance sheet and corporate committed-spend bucket open for depletion.

The hyperscalers accept the arrangement because they have already won the base layer. Hosting competing frontier models keeps enterprise data pipelines, vector indexes, and compute instances inside their own data centers. When model margins inevitably compress under cross-cloud price matching, the underlying kilowatt-hours and networking egress remain high-margin annuities for the landlord.

title: Declared value is an allowlist sum, not a total you defend
description:
A valuation service that adds up invoice lines is implementing the wrong shape. 19 CFR 152.103 builds dutiable value from a base plus a fixed set of additions, and the regulation says the additions cover those items and no others, counted only to the extent they are not already inside the base. That is an allowlist with a de-duplication rule, which is a very different data structure from a sum.

The model 

type ChargeKind =
  | 'goods'
  | 'packingBuyer'          // 152.103(b)(1)(i)
  | 'sellingCommissionBuyer' // (ii)
  | 'assist'                 // (iii)
  | 'royaltyConditionOfSale' // (iv)
  | 'resaleProceedsToSeller' // (v)
  | 'foreignInlandFreight'   // excluded only under 152.102(a)(5) conditions
  | 'internationalFreight'
  | 'merchantDiscount'
  | 'unclassified';

type Charge = {
  kind: ChargeKind;
  amount: number;
  currency: 'USD';
  separatelyStated: boolean;
  incurredBy: 'buyer' | 'seller';
  evidence?: 'throughBillOfLading' | 'other';
};

The unclassified member is the honest one. Any charge the ingestion step cannot name lands there, and the pipeline must fail rather than silently include or exclude it. A model with no unknown bucket is a model that guesses.

The additions are a closed set 

const ADDITIVE: ReadonlySet<ChargeKind> = new Set([
  'packingBuyer', 'sellingCommissionBuyer', 'assist',
  'royaltyConditionOfSale', 'resaleProceedsToSeller',
]);

function dutiableValue(charges: Charge[]): number {
  const base = charges.filter((c) => c.kind === 'goods').reduce((n, c) => n + c.amount, 0);
  let value = base;
  for (const c of charges) {
    if (c.kind === 'unclassified') throw new Error('UNCLASSIFIED_CHARGE: cannot value');
    if (!ADDITIVE.has(c.kind)) continue;
    if (c.incurredBy !== 'buyer' && c.kind !== 'resaleProceedsToSeller') continue;
    value += c.amount;
  }
  return value;
}

Two details in that loop come straight from the text rather than from taste. The buyer-incurred test is there because the packing and selling commission items are worded as costs incurred by the buyer, while the royalty item is worded as a fee the buyer is required to pay as a condition of the sale for export. And the base already contains whatever the parties priced in, so an addition that is inside the invoice total should not be added twice. If the ingestion step cannot tell which case it has, the charge belongs in unclassified.

Freight is a documentation predicate

A foreign inland freight line does not become excludable just because someone typed it on its own row. Under 152.102(a)(5) the exclusion needs two facts at once. The charge has to appear as a separate item, and it has to arise after the goods were sold for export to the United States and handed to a carrier for through shipment. Proof of that second fact runs through a through bill of lading, with other paperwork available only where using one clearly would have been impossible.

function freightExcludable(c: Charge, seq: { soldForExportAt: Date; handedToCarrierAt: Date }): boolean {
  if (!c.separatelyStated) return false;
  if (seq.handedToCarrierAt < seq.soldForExportAt) return false;
  if (c.evidence === 'throughBillOfLading') return true;
  return false;   // 'other' needs the impossibility record, which is a human call
}

The last branch returns false on purpose rather than trusting a string. The impossibility route exists, but it is a documented exception rather than a document type, and a service that treats other as equivalent to a through bill of lading has quietly deleted the condition.

Note the direction of the correction as well. The same section points the other way too. If checking reveals that a foreign inland freight figure, or an equivalent international shipment charge, was padded, the appraiser can still add the difference back into dutiable value. Overstating a deductible line is not conservative. It is a different error with the same endpoint.

The order of methods is a resolver chain

152.101(b) fixes the sequence: transaction value, then identical merchandise, then similar, then deductive, then computed, then a residual method consistent with the subpart's principles. A resolver that lets an operator pick a method has modeled a preference rather than a rule.

const METHOD_ORDER = ['transactionValue', 'identical', 'similar', 'deductive', 'computed', 'residual'] as const;

function resolve(charges: Charge[]): { method: typeof METHOD_ORDER[number]; value: number } {
  try { return { method: 'transactionValue', value: dutiableValue(charges) }; }
  catch { /* fall through to the next method only because this one could not be determined */ }
  throw new Error('MANUAL_METHOD_SELECTION_REQUIRED');
}

The fallbacks each have their own inputs, and none of them is "the number we would like". 152.108 removes the convenient bases outright, including the US selling price of domestically produced goods, any system that appraises at the higher of two alternative values, and the price in the exporter's domestic market. A shop-floor shortcut like "use the Amazon price minus a margin" is the first of those with extra steps.

What the warehouse layer contributes

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) records weights, counts and packing configuration per SKU at receipt across three sites, the largest being Suzhou at 13,000 square meters, then Dongguan at 8,000 and Shenzhen at 3,000. That record is evidence rather than a valuation. It lets a packing cost be identified separately and dated, which is the condition the exclusion turns on. The declared number stays the seller's, and the log is what makes it defensible rather than merely stated.

title: I built a 30 MB API client with Tauri and Rust (Postman is 214 MB)
description:
use an API client every single day. And for a long time, every single day it was the heaviest app on my machine.

So I built my own. It's called Elisa, it's free, and its Windows installer is 30 MB.

Client Windows installer
Elisa 30 MB
Bruno 122 MB
Postman 214 MB
Insomnia 525 MB

Official installers of each stable version as of October 19, 2026.

This post is about how it gets there, and what I learned building it.

Why not Electron?

Almost every API client is built on Electron. That's not a bad choice: it's mature and it lets you ship one codebase everywhere. But every Electron app ships its own full copy of Chromium, plus Node.js. That's where most of those megabytes go, and it's why five Electron apps open at once feel like five browsers.

Tauri takes the opposite approach: it uses the web engine your OS already has (WebView2 on Windows), and the backend is Rust instead of Node.

For Elisa that means:

  • A much smaller download.
  • It opens faster and uses less memory, so it can sit next to your editor, your browser and Docker without your laptop complaining.
  • A real native backend for the heavy lifting.

The frontend is plain React 19, built with Rsbuild. The same frontend also runs as a web app, so you can try it in the browser with nothing to install.

What Rust does under the hood

The fun part of Tauri is that the Rust side isn't just a wrapper. In Elisa it does real work:

Requests go out from Rust. On desktop, requests are sent with reqwest, not from the browser. That means no CORS, real cookie handling, multipart uploads, timeouts and custom certificates. If you've ever had to tell someone "it works in curl but not in the browser", you know why this matters for an API client.

Scripts run in a sandbox. Pre-request and test scripts run in QuickJS through rquickjs, with a pm.*-style API. Postman collections with scripts can come along when you import them.

Load tests stream live. The load tester runs in Rust with Tokio and streams progress to the UI through a Tauri Channel, so the chart updates while the test runs instead of waiting for the end.

A mock server, for real. You can serve any collection as a local API. It's a small hyper server that answers with your saved examples. A browser can't open a port on your machine, so this one is desktop only.

A real terminal. The built-in terminal uses portable-pty (ConPTY on Windows), the same idea VS Code uses.

Local-first, not cloud-first

The other thing I cared about: your collections are yours.

Everything is stored on your machine first, in IndexedDB. Elisa works with no account and no internet. If you want to work with your team, you can sign in and sync to the cloud in real time, but that's optional, not the price of opening the app.

When you're offline, changes go into a queue and sync on their own when the connection comes back.

What else it does

Lightweight doesn't have to mean basic:

  • REST, GraphQL and MCP. You can test MCP servers with auto-generated forms, or turn on "Elisa for agents" so Claude Code or Cursor can read your collections (every change asks for your permission).
  • Flows: drag requests onto a canvas and chain them. Capture the login token once and the rest of the flow uses it.
  • Code and types from any response: TypeScript, Zod, Go, Rust, Python, C#, Java, Kotlin, Swift and Dart.
  • Import from Postman, Insomnia, OpenAPI, HAR or a cURL command.
  • Git: save a collection to a folder and commit, branch and push from the app.

What I learned

  • Tauri is not "free" size. You give up a bundled browser, so you have to respect the system web engine. Testing on the real WebView matters.
  • Moving work to Rust pays off twice: it's faster, and it removes whole classes of bugs, like CORS, that a pure web app can't fix.
  • Local-first changes how you design everything. Every feature has to answer "what happens offline?" before it ships.

Try it

Elisa is free, with no account needed:

👉 elisa.develoops.dev

You can import your Postman collection in seconds and see the difference on your own machine.

I'm building it on my own, end to end: the app, the Rust engine and even the little mascot. So feedback means a lot. What's the one thing that annoys you most about your current API client? Let me know in the comments 🙂

title: How can an artist inspect a large sprite contact sheet without a mouse?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Choose an explicit keyboard model for the contact sheet instead of making every frame a mouse-only target. A simple list of frame buttons and an interactive grid are different interfaces. Use the simpler model unless two-dimensional navigation materially helps the review task.

Key Takeaways

  • Keep frame identity stable while sorting or filtering.
  • Make selection and keyboard focus distinct.
  • Implement the complete chosen interaction model.

A visual grid is not automatically an accessible grid

The WAI-ARIA grid pattern describes a composite interaction model with keyboard responsibilities. Adding a grid role to a group of thumbnails does not implement those behaviors.

For a small contact sheet, ordinary labeled buttons in a meaningful document order may be easier to maintain. For a large sheet, a grid can support efficient directional movement if navigation, focus management, and semantics are implemented together.

Define what each command does

Write down how a reviewer enters the sheet, moves between frames, selects a frame, opens details, and returns to the surrounding controls. Decide what arrow keys do at row boundaries and after filtering.

The keyboard criterion concerns operating functionality without requiring a pointing device. A reviewer should be able to inspect a frame and reach approval controls through the supported keyboard path.

Keep the focused frame identifiable using visible-focus guidance. A selected frame may remain selected while focus moves to a download button. Showing only one of those states makes navigation confusing.

Example: sorting by an error score

A contact sheet initially displays frames in playback order. The reviewer focuses frame 17, then sorts by an alignment score to inspect outliers. If focus remains at the same array position, it can now refer to a different frame.

Track focus by stable frame identity, not by the previous visual index. If the focused frame remains present, restore focus to its new location. If filtering removes it, move to an appropriate remaining control and make that change understandable.

Keep playback order available even when visual review uses another order. Sorting thumbnails must not silently change the exported sequence.

Test the real review path

A proposed task sequence is to enter the sheet, reach a named frame, inspect its metadata, filter results, restore the original view, and leave the sheet. Test with keyboard alone and then with the assistive technologies the tool claims to support.

Check focus after asynchronous thumbnail loading and after removal of a frame. A browser's default focus handling may not preserve the user's place when the focused element is replaced.

Acceptance should record the chosen interaction model and demonstrate that every review action remains reachable. Avoid describing a grid as accessible solely because it has ARIA attributes or a visible border.

This is a proposed browser-review workflow, not an executed keyboard or screen-reader test. It extends the content of a contact sheet into its interaction contract; it does not alter the underlying sprite frames.

Related workflow

See sprite team review contact sheet not preview for the adjacent task. Carry the animation handoff checklist with the release, and use the art reference board to retain visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: Building a Zero-Dependency Interactive T-Shirt Size Calculator (S-5XL) in Vanilla JavaScript
description:
One of the highest-friction moments in online apparel e-commerce is the size selector. Most stores still rely on a static table of numbers that leaves shoppers guessing whether they should measure their body or an existing shirt — and whether a unisex Medium will still fit after its first trip through the dryer.

While building the sizing tooling for Tshirts I Want (Wear what you're really into. — an online store for original graphic apparel printed on demand in the USA), we wanted a fast, zero-dependency, client-side tool that solves both individual fit questions and bulk group orders (family reunions, charity 5Ks, school drama casts, and company teams).

You can try the live tool here:
Live Demo: Interactive T-Shirt Size Calculator (S-5XL)

1. The Domain Problem: Garment Width vs. Body Chest Circumference

When shoppers read a size chart, two completely different measurements often get confused:

  1. Flat-Lay Half-Chest Width (Armpit-to-Armpit): Measured across a shirt lying flat on a table, 1 inch below the armholes.
  2. Full Body Chest Circumference: Measured around the fullest part of the wearer's chest with a flexible tape.

A classic adult unisex crewneck (sizes S through 5XL) needs 2 to 4 inches of ease over body chest circumference for a standard everyday fit, less ease for a tailored silhouette, and more ease for a relaxed streetwear drape.

To document the underlying garment specifications clearly, we paired the calculator with four reference guides:

  • Unisex T-Shirt Size Chart: Chest, Length & Fit Guide (S-5XL)
  • How Should a T-Shirt Fit? Shoulder Seam, Chest, Sleeve & Length Checkpoints
  • Men's vs. Women's vs. Unisex T-Shirt Sizing Compared
  • Does Cotton Shrink? Ringspun Cotton vs. Heavy Cotton vs. Cotton-Poly Blends

2. Modeling the S-5XL Garment Measurement Matrix in Vanilla JS

Rather than loading a heavy third-party sizing widget that blocks main-thread rendering or requires external API calls, we modeled the S-5XL size chart as a deterministic lookup table in vanilla JavaScript:

const UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX = [
  { size: "S",   flatWidthIn: 18.0, lengthIn: 28.0, chestMinIn: 34, chestMaxIn: 37 },
  { size: "M",   flatWidthIn: 20.0, lengthIn: 29.0, chestMinIn: 38, chestMaxIn: 41 },
  { size: "L",   flatWidthIn: 22.0, lengthIn: 30.0, chestMinIn: 42, chestMaxIn: 45 },
  { size: "XL",  flatWidthIn: 24.0, lengthIn: 31.0, chestMinIn: 46, chestMaxIn: 49 },
  { size: "2XL", flatWidthIn: 26.0, lengthIn: 32.0, chestMinIn: 50, chestMaxIn: 53 },
  { size: "3XL", flatWidthIn: 28.0, lengthIn: 33.0, chestMinIn: 54, chestMaxIn: 57 },
  { size: "4XL", flatWidthIn: 30.0, lengthIn: 34.0, chestMinIn: 58, chestMaxIn: 61 },
  { size: "5XL", flatWidthIn: 32.0, lengthIn: 35.0, chestMinIn: 62, chestMaxIn: 65 }
];

function recommendByFlatShirt(flatWidthInches, lengthInches, fitOffset = 0) {
  const targetWidth = flatWidthInches + fitOffset;
  for (const row of UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX) {
    if (row.flatWidthIn >= targetWidth - 0.5 && row.lengthIn >= lengthInches - 1.0) {
      return row;
    }
  }
  return UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX[UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX.length - 1];
}

Handling Fit Preference & Cotton Shrinkage Buffers

As detailed in our Does Cotton Shrink? laundering study, 100% ringspun and heavy cotton tees typically shrink 3% to 5% when tumble-dried on medium-to-high heat. When a shopper lands on the boundary between two sizes (for example, a 41-inch chest sitting right between M and L) and plans to machine-dry their shirts, the calculator surfaces a boundary recommendation so they can size up confidently.

3. Zero-Latency UX & Accessibility Details

  • Instant Unit Conversion (in to cm): Every input and table cell converts dynamically using 1 in = 2.54 cm without page reloads.
  • Dual Input Modes: Users can switch between Compare My Favorite Shirt (Flat-Lay) and Body Chest + Height + Fit Preference depending on whether they have a measuring tape or an existing tee handy.
  • Shareable URL for Group Orders: Event organizers collecting shirt sizes for a reunion, club, or race can link directly to https://tshirtsiwant.com/tools/size-calculator/ inside Google Forms or registration pages.

Check out the live calculator at tshirtsiwant.com/tools/size-calculator/ and explore our full graphic apparel collection at tshirtsiwant.com.

title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
description:
arXiv:2610.27307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (**T**ool **U**se **R**elated **T**asks with **L**ong-Horizon **E**volution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $\tau$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165\% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.

title: Crafting a Professional Services Website RFP: A Comprehensive Guide
description:
Crafting a Professional Services Website RFP: A Comprehensive Guide

In the digital age, a well-crafted Request for Proposal (RFP) is essential for professional services firms seeking to build a website that truly reflects their expertise and meets their unique needs. However, many firms fall short by relying on generic templates, which often fail to address the specific challenges and requirements of their industry. This guide outlines why standard RFPs are inadequate and provides actionable insights to ensure your RFP stands out.

Why Off-the-Shelf Templates Fall Short

1. Lack of Customization

Generic RFPs are one-size-fits-all solutions that rarely align with the specific needs of professional services firms. These templates often overlook critical aspects such as showcasing expertise, managing client confidentiality, and presenting complex service offerings.

2. Insufficient Technical Depth

Professional services websites often require advanced functionalities like secure client portals, project management tools, and custom reporting. Off-the-shelf RFPs lack the technical depth needed to address these requirements, potentially leading to underwhelming results.

3. Poor User Experience Focus

The user experience (UX) is crucial for professional services websites, as they aim to inspire trust and professionalism. Generic templates often fail to emphasize the importance of a seamless, intuitive UX, which can hinder user engagement and retention.

Engineering Takeaways for a Tailored RFP

1. Start with User Personas

Begin by defining detailed user personas for your website. This includes potential clients, existing clients, and internal stakeholders. Understanding their needs, pain points, and behaviors will help you craft an RFP that addresses their specific requirements.

2. Prioritize Technical Architecture

Ensure your RFP includes a detailed technical architecture section. This should outline the necessary backend systems, integration points, and security measures. By doing so, you can attract vendors who can deliver a robust, scalable solution.

3. Include Detailed UX Requirements

A professional services website must offer a seamless and intuitive user experience. Specify UX requirements such as navigation structure, content hierarchy, and mobile responsiveness. Consider including wireframes or mockups to provide a clear vision.
