title: CrashLoopBackOff: how to find the real cause (and why deleting the pod won't help)
description:
A config change goes out. A couple of minutes later every request to the app fails, and kubectl get pods shows the status nobody wants to see:

NAME                      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4 (15s ago)   115s

I broke a small Go service on purpose to walk through this one properly, from the first symptom to a fix you can prove. The commands work on any cluster. The specific bug is just one example, and I'll come back at the end to the other things that cause the same status.

What CrashLoopBackOff actually tells you

It is easy to read CrashLoopBackOff as an error. It isn't one. It is Kubernetes describing what it is doing about an error.

The container starts and then exits. The kubelet on the node restarts it, because the pod's restartPolicy says so. If it exits again, the kubelet waits before the next try, and the wait grows each time: 10 seconds, 20, 40, and so on, capped at five minutes (Kubernetes docs: container restarts). While it is waiting, the pod shows CrashLoopBackOff.

So the status answers "what is happening?" (the container keeps dying) and says nothing about why. That second question is the whole job, and the pod has already written the answer down somewhere. You just have to know where to read it.

First, check whether anyone is still being served

Before digging into the crash, it's worth thirty seconds to find out how bad things are. A crash loop during a rollout is often harmless: with a rolling update and a readiness probe, the old pods keep serving until a new one becomes Ready. If the new pod never gets there, the rollout just stalls.

A Deployment keeps one ReplicaSet per version of its pod template, so listing them tells you whether an older version is still up:

$ kubectl get rs -n go-api
NAME                DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
go-api-5d8497557b   0         0         0       5m46s
go-api-7b45497dfd   1         1         0       2m9s

Not good. The old ReplicaSet is at zero, and the new one wants a pod and has none ready. Nothing is serving. In my drill I set it up that way on purpose, but you get the same picture in real life with a Recreate strategy, or when the crash only starts after the pod has already passed its readiness check. Either way, this isn't a stuck rollout any more. It's an outage.

The browser agreed:

That message comes from the ingress. It had a route for the app and no ready pod to send the request to.

A detour worth taking: the dashboard that says everything is fine

This was the part of the drill that surprised me most. Here is the Grafana dashboard during the outage. On the left is the app's own error rate (HTTP 5xx). On the right is the failure rate seen by k6, the load generator sending traffic from outside.

The app reports zero errors. The client sees 100% of requests fail. Both are telling the truth: a process that never finishes starting can't count the requests it never received, so its own metrics go quiet rather than red. If your alerting only looks at what the service says about itself, a total outage can look like a calm afternoon. Watch at least one signal from the client side too, whether that's an ingress or load balancer metric, a synthetic check, or a probe from outside the cluster.

Read the crash's last words: kubectl logs --previous

Plain kubectl logs shows the current container. In a crash loop the current container has often just started, or hasn't started yet, so you get nothing useful. The container that just died is still on the node, and --previous (or -p) asks for its logs:

$ kubectl logs -n go-api go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2 --previous
{"level":"INFO","msg":"server starting","port":"80800","service":"go-api"}
{"level":"ERROR","msg":"server error","error":"listen tcp: address 80800: invalid port"}

(I trimmed the timestamps.) Two lines, and the second one is the answer. The server tried to listen on port 80800. Port numbers stop at 65535, so the bind fails and the process exits.

Most of the time the logs get you this far. When they don't, the next command usually does.

Confirm it from Kubernetes' side: kubectl describe pod

describe is long, so I pipe it into less and search for Last State:

$ kubectl describe pod -n go-api go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2 | less
...
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       Error
      Exit Code:    1
    Ready:          False
    Restart Count:  4
    ...
    Environment:
      PORT:                 80800
      READINESS_FAILURE:    false
      SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT:     10s

Three things to take from this block.

The exit code. 1 means the app chose to exit with an error. Nothing killed it. If you see 137 instead, the process got a SIGKILL (128 + 9), and a Reason of OOMKilled tells you it ran out of memory. Those two numbers send you down completely different paths, so it's worth reading this line before anything else.

The environment. The same 80800 again, now in the spec. So the bad value isn't something the app made up at runtime. Kubernetes handed it over.

The events at the bottom. In this case they only confirm the loop: Back-off restarting failed container. For other causes they carry the real clue, such as Liveness probe failed, a missing ConfigMap or Secret, or an image that can't be pulled.

The fix everyone tries first

With the pod clearly broken, deleting it is tempting. I tried:

$ kubectl delete pod -n go-api go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2
pod "go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2" deleted

$ kubectl get pods -n go-api
NAME                      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
go-api-7b45497dfd-4c995   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   1 (21s ago)   22s

A new name, the same crash, within seconds. The pod was never the problem. A pod owned by a Deployment is a copy of the Deployment's pod template, and the ReplicaSet will keep making fresh copies of the same mistake for as long as you delete them. The only thing deleting achieved was resetting the restart counter, which made the situation look less serious than it was.

Fix it where it lives: the pod template

So the question becomes where the template gets PORT=80800 from. describe deploy shows the template:

$ kubectl describe deploy go-api -n go-api | less
...
  Containers:
   go-api:
    Image:      go-api:v1.2.0
    Port:       8080/TCP (http)
    Liveness:   http-get http://:http/health delay=15s timeout=5s period=10s
    Readiness:  http-get http://:http/ready delay=10s timeout=3s period=5s
    Environment:
      PORT:                 80800

The container declares port 8080, both probes use that named port, and the environment variable says 80800. One zero too many. The fix goes on the Deployment:

$ kubectl -n go-api set env deploy/go-api PORT=8080
deployment.apps/go-api env updated

Changing the template starts a new rollout. In a real team you'd make the same change in whatever produced the manifest (the Helm values, the Kustomize overlay, the GitOps repo) or the next sync will put the typo straight back. kubectl set env is fine for stopping the bleeding, as long as the real fix follows it.

kubectl rollout undo deploy/go-api -n go-api would have worked too. It returns the template to the previous revision, environment included. When you're paged and you know the last change caused it, rolling back first and investigating second is often the right call.

Prove the fix instead of assuming it

Don't eyeball get pods a few seconds after the change. rollout status waits until the new pods are actually Ready:

$ kubectl -n go-api rollout status deploy/go-api
Waiting for deployment "go-api" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "go-api" successfully rolled out

$ kubectl get pods -n go-api
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
go-api-5d8497557b-r47rn   1/1     Running   0          26s

$ kubectl get rs -n go-api
NAME                DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
go-api-5d8497557b   1         1         1       9m8s
go-api-7b45497dfd   0         0         0       5m31s

Look at the ReplicaSet names. Kubernetes didn't create a third one. The fixed template is identical to the one from before the bad change, so the Deployment scaled the old ReplicaSet back up. It's a small detail, but it's a nice confirmation that the template now matches the last version that worked.

Then check from outside, the way users see it. The health URL answered again, and the request rate on the dashboard came back.

Try it on your own cluster

You don't need anything special to reproduce this. On a test cluster, take any Deployment whose app reads its port from an environment variable and give it an impossible one:

kubectl set env deploy/<your-test-app> PORT=80800
kubectl get pods -w

With the default rolling update you'll likely see the stalled-rollout version: the old pod stays Running while the new one crash-loops. That's a useful thing to see for yourself, because it's exactly why the ReplicaSet check at the start matters. Put it back with:

kubectl rollout undo deploy/<your-test-app>

If you'd rather practise the full outage version, with traffic, dashboards, alerts and a check that tells you when you've actually fixed it, this drill is one of the incidents in SnowOps Labs, a free, open-source Kubernetes lab that runs on a laptop. Disclosure: I build it. Every screenshot above is from it, and the code is on GitHub.

Other causes of the same status

The port typo is one cause among many. The Kubernetes docs group the usual suspects into application errors, configuration errors, resource limits, and failing health checks. In practice that looks like:

  • A bug or a missing dependency in the app. Logs with --previous usually say so, often as a stack trace or a "connection refused" to a database that isn't there.
  • Missing or wrong configuration. A typo like this one, a variable renamed in one place and not the other, a config file mounted at the wrong path, or a value that's fine in staging and wrong in production.
  • Not enough memory. Exit code 137 with Reason: OOMKilled in describe. Raise the limit or fix the leak, but find out which one first.
  • A liveness probe that kills a healthy app. The app starts, the probe fails (too strict, wrong path, too short a delay for a slow start), and the kubelet restarts the container. The events say Liveness probe failed.
  • The container never really starts. A wrong command or args, an image built for another CPU architecture, a missing binary. Here the logs are often empty, because nothing ran long enough to write any. describe and its events carry the message instead.

One extra tip from the docs on finding why a pod failed: set terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError on your containers. When a container fails without writing a termination message, Kubernetes then copies the last lines of its log into the pod status, so describe shows the error even after the logs are gone.

The short version

When a pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, this order gets you to the cause quickly, whatever the cause turns out to be:

  1. kubectl get pods shows the symptom and the restart count.
  2. kubectl get rs tells you whether anything is still serving, which decides how urgent this is.
  3. kubectl logs <pod> --previous gives you the dead container's last words.
  4. kubectl describe pod <pod> gives the exit code, the reason and the events.

Then fix the thing the pod was copied from, not the pod, and let rollout status tell you when it's really done.

title: Graceful Shutdown in Production Web Servers: Draining In-Flight Requests and Closing Connections
description:
title: "Graceful Shutdown in Production Web Servers: Draining In-Flight Requests and Closing Connections"
published: true
published_at: "2027-02-03T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Graceful Shutdown in Production Web Servers: Draining In-Flight Requests and Closing Connections. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [backend, nodejs, devops, docker]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Graceful Shutdown in Production Web Servers: Draining In-Flight Requests and Closing Connections is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Graceful Shutdown in Production Web Servers: Draining In-Flight Requests and Closing Connections matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of backend development architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Handling Sigterm And Sigint Os Signals: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Stopping New Connections While Allowing Active Http Requests To Complete Within Timeout: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Closing Db Pools: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Docker Stop Timeout: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Graceful Shutdown in Production Web Servers: Draining In-Flight Requests and Closing Connections functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Backend development Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Handling SIGTERM and SIGINT OS signals, stopping new connections while allowing active HTTP requests to complete within timeout, closing DB pools, and Docker stop timeout."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: How to Give Claude & Cursor Safe Database Access Without Crashing Production (Zero-Trust MCP Guard in Python)
description:
How to Give Claude & Cursor Safe Database Access Without Crashing Production (Zero-Trust MCP Guard in Python)

Giving an AI assistant or autonomous agent access to a live database is one of the most powerful workflows for modern software teams: Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Windsurf can write complex analytics queries, optimize slow joins, and inspect schemas in seconds.

However, granting raw database credentials to an LLM is dangerous:

  • Accidental Disasters: One misaligned prompt or prompt injection can lead the agent to execute DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, or unconstrained UPDATE / DELETE queries.
  • Production Freezes: A query missing a WHERE clause or missing an index on a million-row table can trigger a full sequential table scan, consuming 100% CPU and locking transactions.
  • PII Exposure: Raw customer records (plaintext emails, password hashes, credit cards) get pulled into prompt contexts and third-party LLM server logs.

The modern, standardized solution is to place a Zero-Trust Model Context Protocol (MCP) guard between your agent and the database engine.

In this guide, we will walk through how PgSafe MCP was engineered in Python to provide secure, read-only database exploration, forced LIMIT injection, real-time PII redaction, and dry-run mutation simulation.

The Zero-Trust MCP Architecture

Rather than connecting Claude directly to Postgres or SQLite with an unrestricted superuser connection, the MCP server acts as an intelligent firewall:

[ AI Agent: Claude / Cursor / Antigravity ]
                      │  JSON-RPC 2.0 (stdio)
                      ▼
             [ PgSafe MCP Server ]
                      │
           [ ReadOnlyGuard (AST Analysis) ]
           ├─ Blocks DROP, TRUNCATE, DELETE, ALTER
           └─ Blocks Semicolon Chaining
                      │
           [ CostAnalyzer (LIMIT Guard) ]
           ├─ Forces max 1,000 row limits
           └─ Warns on missing WHERE clauses
                      │
            [ Database Connection ]
            (PostgreSQL / SQLite / MySQL)
                      │
             [ Real-Time PII Masker ]
           ├─ Redacts emails (u***@domain.com)
           ├─ Masks credit cards (****-****-****-1234)
           └─ Redacts password hashes
                      │
                      ▼
[ Clean, Safe JSON-RPC Output to Agent ]

1. Enforcing Read-Only SQL Lexical Validation

A secure read-only guard must inspect every statement before it ever reaches the database cursor, stripping comments and blocking destructive keywords:

import re

BLOCKED_KEYWORDS = [
    r"\bDROP\b", r"\bTRUNCATE\b", r"\bDELETE\b",
    r"\bUPDATE\b", r"\bINSERT\b", r"\bALTER\b",
    r"\bCREATE\b", r"\bGRANT\b", r"\bREVOKE\b"
]

class ReadOnlyGuard:
    @staticmethod
    def validate(sql: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
        # Disallow multi-statement injection (semicolon chaining)
        statements = [s.strip() for s in sql.split(";") if s.strip()]
        if len(statements) > 1:
            return False, "Semicolon chaining disallowed."

        # Verify query begins with read-only keyword
        first_word = statements[0].split()[0].upper()
        if first_word not in {"SELECT", "EXPLAIN", "WITH", "PRAGMA", "SHOW"}:
            return False, f"Statement '{first_word}' is forbidden."

        for pattern in BLOCKED_KEYWORDS:
            if re.search(pattern, sql, re.IGNORECASE):
                return False, "Destructive SQL operation detected."

        return True, "Query verified safe."

2. Dynamic LIMIT Injection

Runaway SELECT * FROM audit_logs queries can crash your client's memory. PgSafe intercepts every query and caps row limits:

import re

def enforce_limit(sql: str, default_limit: int = 100, max_limit: int = 1000) -> str:
    cleaned = sql.strip().rstrip(";")
    match = re.search(r"\bLIMIT\s+(\d+)\b", cleaned, re.IGNORECASE)
    if match:
        limit_val = int(match.group(1))
        if limit_val > max_limit:
            return re.sub(r"\bLIMIT\s+\d+\b", f"LIMIT {max_limit}", cleaned, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
        return cleaned
    return f"{cleaned} LIMIT {default_limit}"

3. Real-Time PII Redaction Before Agent Ingestion

When the query returns data, sensitive columns (password_hash, ssn, token) and customer PII are redacted on the fly:

import re

EMAIL_REGEX = re.compile(r"\b([A-Za-z0-9._%+-])[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]*@([A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,})\b")
CARD_REGEX = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{4}[-\s]?){3}(\d{4})\b")

def redact_pii(text: str) -> str:
    text = CARD_REGEX.sub(r"****-****-****-\1", text)
    text = EMAIL_REGEX.sub(r"\1***@\2", text)
    return text

4. Configuring Claude Desktop & Cursor

Add the server to your claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pgsafe": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "pgsafe.server"],
      "cwd": "/path/to/pgsafe-mcp",
      "env": {
        "DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/my_db"
      }
    }
  }
}

Now you can prompt Claude:

"Inspect the orders table, find the top 5 customers with pending invoices, and suggest indexes to speed up this query."

Enterprise Edition: Dry-Run Mutation Simulation Harness

When agents need to draft data mutations or migrations, the Enterprise Pro edition includes an isolated simulation harness:

  • Executes INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE queries within an isolated transaction.
  • Returns row diffs, affected count, and execution time.
  • Guarantees auto-ROLLBACK: changes are never committed to your database.
  • Includes automatic index recommendation advisors and Docker Compose setups.

  • Lite Version (Open Source): Read-only guard and SQLite/Postgres schema inspection.
  • Enterprise Pro Edition ($14.99): PII masking, dry-run mutation simulation, index advisor, Docker Compose, and automated test suite.

  • Digital product marketplace: DpMarket.

title: The Supabase Security Checklist to Run Before You Launch
description:
If you built something on Supabase with a lot of AI help and you're about to ship it, this checklist is for you. Supabase is secure by default in the sense that the tools are all there — but "vibe coding" tends to skip the boring parts, and the boring parts are exactly where data leaks live. Every item below is a one-line check plus the fix. Run them in order. It's maybe 30 minutes, and it's the difference between a launch and an incident.

1. RLS is enabled on every table in the public schema

The single most common Supabase mistake: a table exists, the anon key can reach it over PostgREST, and Row Level Security was never turned on. With RLS off, the table's GRANTs are the only gate — and because Supabase exposes the public schema to the anon role by default, that means anyone holding your (public) anon key can read it.

Check — run this in the SQL editor to list every public table with RLS off:

select tablename
from pg_tables
where schemaname = 'public'
  and rowsecurity = false;

Any rows returned are exposed. Fix each one:

alter table public.your_table enable row level security;

Enabling RLS with no policies is deny-all — a safe default. Now add the policy you actually want.

2. Every table has owner-scoped policies (not using (true))

Enabling RLS isn't enough if your policy waves everyone through. The classic leak is using (true) with no to clause. A SELECT policy like that is world-readable, anon included. Two facts to keep straight: a policy with no TO clause applies to all roles, and for anon, auth.uid() is NULL — so any check that compares against it silently fails open or closed depending on how you wrote it.

Check — list every policy and read it:

select tablename, policyname, cmd, roles, qual, with_check
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public';

qual is the USING expression; with_check is the WITH CHECK expression. A bare true in qual on a SELECT policy is world-readable. (It's only world-writable if a permissive INSERT/UPDATE/ALL policy also allows it — reads and writes are separate policies.) Fix with owner scoping:

-- users can only read their own rows
create policy "own rows are selectable"
on public.todos for select
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

-- and only insert rows they own
create policy "insert own rows"
on public.todos for insert
to authenticated
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Two things people get wrong here:

  • USING vs WITH CHECK. USING filters which existing rows a role can see, and which it may update or delete. WITH CHECK validates rows being written. An INSERT policy has WITH CHECK only — there are no existing rows to filter. UPDATE uses both. If you protect reads but forget WITH CHECK on writes, users can insert or update rows they shouldn't own.
  • A policy and a grant. A role needs a matching policy and the table GRANT. Multiple permissive policies OR together; restrictive policies AND. If access feels "too open," look for a second permissive policy widening things.

3. You're using the right key in the right place

Every Supabase project has two keys, and confusing them is catastrophic.

  • anon / publishable (role: anon, new format sb_publishable_...) is public by design. It's meant to ship in your browser bundle. It is not a secret, and it does not need rotating. RLS is what protects your data when this key is used.
  • service_role (role: service_role, new format sb_secret_...) is a server-only secret that bypasses RLS entirely — full read/write/delete across every table, plus Storage. It must never appear in a browser, a public repo, or a client config file.

Not sure which is which? Decode the JWT payload — the middle segment, base64URL — and read the role:

# paste your key; this prints the payload
echo 'PASTE_KEY' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null; echo

"role":"anon" is the browser key. "role":"service_role" must never leave your server.

The trap in frontend frameworks: any env var prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, or EXPO_PUBLIC_ is inlined into the client bundle at build time. That's correct and safe for the anon key and project URL. Putting the service_role key behind one of those prefixes ships your master key to every visitor. Check your env files:

grep -rE 'NEXT_PUBLIC_|VITE_|EXPO_PUBLIC_' .env* | grep -i 'service\|secret'

Anything returned is a bug. The service_role key belongs only in server-side env — API routes, edge functions, backend — never behind a public prefix.

4. No secrets in the repo — or in git history

Deleting a secret file doesn't help if you already committed it once. A committed secret lives in git history forever. AI tooling makes this worse by scattering config files people don't think to check.

Check the working tree, including the easy-to-miss ones:

grep -rnE 'service_role|sb_secret_|eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}' \
  . --include='*.json' --include='*.env*' --include='*.ts' 2>/dev/null

# the ones vibe-coders forget:
git ls-files | grep -E '\.env|\.claude/settings\.local\.json|\.cursor/mcp\.json'

.claude/settings.local.json, .cursor/mcp.json, and .env.local love to hold live keys and DB connection strings. Then check history:

git log --all --full-history -p -- '.env*' '**/mcp.json' '.claude/settings.local.json'

Fix, in this order:

  1. Rotate first. If a service_role key (or DB password) was ever committed, treat it as compromised. Regenerate it in the dashboard under Project Settings → API. Deleting the file does not un-leak it.
  2. Purge history with git filter-repo (or BFG), then force-push: 
git filter-repo --path .env.local --invert-paths
  1. Add the patterns to .gitignore so it can't recur: 
.env*
.claude/settings.local.json
.cursor/mcp.json

Order matters: rotate before you spend time rewriting history, because the old key is public the moment the repo is.

5. Storage buckets have real policies

Storage is Postgres too — access lives in storage.objects and obeys RLS. A public bucket means the files are readable by URL to anyone. A private bucket with no policy means no one can read it, which is usually not what you shipped either.

Check your buckets and their object policies:

select id, name, public from storage.buckets;

select policyname, cmd, roles, qual
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'storage' and tablename = 'objects';

Decide per bucket: are these files meant to be world-readable (avatars, marketing images) or private (invoices, uploads)? For an owner-scoped private bucket, a common pattern keys access to a per-user folder:

create policy "users read own folder"
on storage.objects for select
to authenticated
using (
  bucket_id = 'user-uploads'
  and (select auth.uid())::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]
);

6. Do a real self-audit before you trust the checklist

Reading policies by hand is exactly where over-confidence creeps in — a policy can look scoped and still leak because of a second permissive policy or a missing TO. So verify empirically.

I keep a small free repo for this: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. It's a minimal reproduction of the classic RLS leak plus read-only audit SQL you can paste into your own SQL editor to list tables without RLS, policies with no TO clause, and using (true) permissive policies in one shot. It changes nothing in your database — it just tells you where you stand.

The most honest test, though, is to hit your project the way an attacker would: with nothing but the public anon key.

curl "https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/rest/v1/your_table?select=*" \
  -H "apikey: <ANON_KEY>"

If that returns rows you expected to be private, RLS is not doing what you think. Fix it before launch, not after.

Run all six and you've closed the failure modes behind almost every "Supabase leaked my data" post-mortem: RLS off, using (true), the wrong key in the bundle, and a secret buried in git history.

If you'd rather not assemble this by hand, I packaged the whole thing — the audit queries, owner-scoped policy templates for the common table shapes, the Storage patterns, and a printable pre-launch checklist — into a $29 RLS Audit Kit. The free demo repo above is genuinely enough to secure your project; the kit just saves you the afternoon of writing the SQL yourself. Either way, ship it locked down.

title: Evaluating Tibetan Speech Recognition Across Dialects and Adaptation Regimes: A Multi-Granularity Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.27002v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tibetan speech recognition is usually evaluated with character or syllable error rates because the writing system does not mark word boundaries. These metrics can rank systems differently and respond differently to adaptation failures. We combine character error rate, syllable error rate, and segmented word error rate in one evaluation framework. We use dictionary-based, neural, and language-model-based segmentation and compare their boundaries with expert annotations. We evaluate five ASR architectures on Lhasa Tibetan, then test zero-shot transfer and target-corpus adaptation on five additional corpus subsets. We also vary LoRA rank and training-data size to examine adaptation failure. The results show that a lower character error does not always lead to a lower syllable or segmented-word error. These ranking differences persist across corpora. Metric correlations also weaken in some unsuccessful adaptation settings. Higher LoRA ranks improve syllable and segmented-word scores but remain worse than full fine-tuning in the tested range. A standardized phonological representation provides another view of spelling errors. These findings support evaluation at several linguistic levels and motivate better segmentation and adaptation methods for low-resource ASR.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

Stay tuned for more in next month's report.

Also in August’s data

  • Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image spend for the first time, at 50% to GPT Image's 44%, even as GPT Image took back the lead in images generated, 46% to 39%.

  • Google's Veo rose to second in video spend, at 20%, up from 15% in July. Seedance remained in first on both videos generated and video spend.

  • The share of videos generated by xAI’s Grok Imagine has more than halved since June, from 42% to 31% to 19%.

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through August 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input, and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated using labs’ published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Statements about where volume moved compare changes among the same teams. They do not trace individual tokens between models.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, which is broader than the definition used in earlier reports.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.

Application Integration

Security

An Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the AuthConfig validation and integration execution runtime in Application Integration versions prior to August 27, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve capacity by using future reservation requests, you can specify that Compute Engine delivers your reserved capacity as specifically targeted reservations. Specifically targeted reservations help you track and control which Compute Engine instances consume your reserved capacity. For more information, see About future reservation requests.

Feature

Generally available: You can increase the size of a Google Cloud Hyperdisk volume that's in multi-writer mode while the volume is attached to multiple instances. Previously, you had to detach the volume from all instances before you could resize it.

For more information, see Share disks between instances and Change the size or provisioned performance of a Hyperdisk volume.

Dataform

Feature

You can automatically preserve BigQuery data policies and data governance tags (Preview) applied to tables across Dataform executions by enabling the preserveGovernanceControls option in your table or workflow configuration. For more information, see Preserve access controls metadata. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in the United Kingdom

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in the United Kingdom.

  • Location availability: Supported in the UK (europe-west2) in-country region with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).
  • App availability: Turned on by default in the web app for the UK region. Administrators can manage access with the Gemini 3.8 Flash toggle under Model availability.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in Workflow Builder

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for Workflow Builder. Gemini 4 Argon is also available in Workflow Builder workflow agents. Updates take up to a day to appear in workflow agents.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.

For more information, see Workflow Builder.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Priority PayGo support for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1

Priority Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) is available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1) on the global endpoint.

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Enhanced SARIF 2.1.0 reporting: Updated cm report SARIF output with standardized rule descriptors, severity properties, and repository-relative artifact locations for improved GitHub Code Scanning compatibility.
  • Model invocation metrics: Added model invocation tracking to cm stats --json, providing total, per-session, and per-turn invocation counts.
  • Bug fixes:

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is available in Public Preview

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from DeepSeek is available as a fully managed model (MaaS) in Model Garden. The model accepts text and image input, targets agentic and coding tasks, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens.

For more information, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Microsoft Teams
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Microsoft Teams. Creating one gives your organization a Teams bot that your apps and agents run. People can @mention it in channels or message it directly, and your code receives the message and replies as the bot.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel registers the Entra app and Azure Bot resource in your tenant, so there's no client secret to store. A tenant administrator with an Azure subscription completes setup once. Incoming Teams activities are verified and forwarded to your project as Connect trigger.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Once the connector is set up, your code requests a token only when it needs one. Use it with the @vercel/connect SDK, eve channel or Chat SDK adapter:

Each token is scoped to what you request and refreshed automatically, so there's nothing to rotate by hand. Connectors only work in the environments you attach them to, and you can revoke access at any time with vc connect revoke-tokens.

Read the Vercel Connect documentation, view details about the Teams connector in the Vercel Connect catalog, or create a Teams connector to get started.

title: Botnets, AI, and the Next Frontier of Cybersecurity
description:
What happens when the attackers start adapting faster than the defenders can respond?

It's a question I've been thinking about while building BotSentinel, a machine-learning prototype designed to identify botnet traffic.

Botnets are a reminder that cyber threats aren't always isolated devices or individual attackers. They're networks of compromised machines that can be coordinated to carry out malicious activities at scale.

And as AI continues to evolve, I can't help wondering what happens when the people behind these threats gain access to increasingly intelligent, automated systems.

The uncomfortable truth? Our defences need to evolve just as quickly.

From detecting threats to defending autonomously

Traditional security tools remain essential, but I believe the next frontier lies in more autonomous defence systems.

Imagine security agents that continuously monitor network activity, detect suspicious behaviour, investigate anomalies, coordinate responses, and adapt as new attack patterns emerge.

Not systems that simply raise an alert and leave a human staring at a dashboard at 2 a.m. (We've suffered enough.)

I'm talking about systems that can do more than detect a threat. They can help contain it, learn from it, and improve future responses.

Of course, autonomy doesn't mean removing humans from the equation. Human oversight, accountability, and the ability to intervene will remain critical, especially when automated decisions can disrupt legitimate systems.

The goal isn't to replace security professionals. It's to give them systems that can operate at machine speed while keeping consequential decisions under appropriate human control.

**

The real challenge: keeping up

**

Here's where things get interesting.

Building an intelligent defence agent is one thing. Keeping it relevant as threats evolve is another.

What happens when an agent is trained on yesterday's attack patterns, but tomorrow's attacker has already changed tactics?

We need systems that can incorporate fresh threat intelligence, recognise unfamiliar behaviour, adapt to changing conditions, and be reassessed when their assumptions no longer hold.

That also means testing updates, monitoring performance, and ensuring that an agent's ability to adapt doesn't become a new security vulnerability.

Because imagine taking days to deploy a defence against an attack technique that appeared hours ago.

The attackers pull up with precision-guided missiles. We're still checking whether the pistol has ammunition. 😭

**

Where does BotSentinel fit into this?

**

For me, BotSentinel is a step towards understanding that bigger picture.

It's currently a machine-learning prototype for classifying network traffic as botnet or non-botnet traffic. But building a detector has made me think beyond classification accuracy.

Detection is important. What happens next matters just as much.

How do we turn a detection into a timely response? How do we keep the system updated? How do we make it resilient to new attack patterns without blindly trusting its predictions?

These are questions I want to keep exploring as I develop my understanding of AI and cybersecurity.

I don't think the future belongs to AI alone, or to humans trying to do everything manually.

I think it belongs to intelligent systems that can adapt, work autonomously within defined boundaries, and collaborate with humans who remain accountable for the outcomes.

The next frontier isn't simply building smarter attackers or smarter defenders.

It's building defences that can evolve at the pace of the threats they face.

And we're going to need them.

What do you think: will autonomous security agents become the backbone of cyber defence, or will the complexity of keeping them trustworthy limit how much we can delegate to them?

title: After one React edit, what can your build skip?
description:
Compare an unchanged run with a run after a small source edit—and check the output before interpreting the timer.

An unchanged build and a build after an edit answer different questions. For this walkthrough, use a small React label change that you can actually see in the built app. Keep the command and project setup the same. That gives you a more useful comparison than a single “fast build” number: what happened with no edit, and what happened after the source changed?

Why should a frontend developer care?

You want to know whether the build loop improves when you are actually editing, not only when nothing changed. A visible mutation gives the comparison an output check that a timer cannot provide.

1. Keep one direct pilot command

Use one existing supported app. Keep the team’s existing scripts, linting and tests. Add a distinct script if you need one:

{
  "scripts": {
    "build:ionify": "ionify build"
  }
}

Merge this entry into the existing scripts object; do not replace other scripts. Record the installed package version and lockfile. From the app directory run:

pnpm run build:ionify

Let the process exit and run the same command again unchanged, retaining local state and output. Use fresh processes, the same configuration and the same command for the edited run too.

2. Change an imported React component

Replace the original rendered button with the edited version:

// Before
<button id="save-button">Save</button>
// After
<button id="save-button">Save draft</button>

These JSX fragments are illustrative, not observations. Build again. Serve the generated output with the app’s normal preview setup. For a root-page app using the default dist output, one local static preview is:

python3 -m http.server 4173 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory dist

Open http://127.0.0.1:4173/ and inspect #save-button. Expected after the edit: Save draft. Record what you actually see. Adapt the directory if you intentionally selected another output path; Python’s simple server does not supply SPA route fallback.

3. Name the state you compared

Case What it tells you Output check
Whole task restored, if applicable The task runner reused its recorded result; the engine may not have run Inspect the restored app
Task executed with retained engine state The command ran; unchanged and edited runs remain separate observations Inspect the exact label after each run
Fresh-state control in a separate disposable copy A different starting state, with the original fixture preserved Inspect that copy’s built app

The first row is conceptual. This walkthrough does not establish a named task-runner integration or provide invented runner commands. If your repository already has one, use its documentation to declare inputs and outputs, then verify restored versus executed status from its actual logs. If the label changed but the task remains a hit unexpectedly, preserve the evidence and investigate input declarations.

Running pnpm run build:ionify directly bypasses that orchestration. Do not compare its elapsed boundary with a whole-task restore as if they were identical work.

4. Separate output evidence from interpretation 

Installed version / checkout / exact command:
Mutation and retained local state:
Task outcome: restored / executed / unknown
Engine outcome: not invoked / completed / failed / unknown
Expected and observed label:
Served directory / URL / cache observations:
Elapsed boundary and observations, if measured:

A prior label experiment initially displayed an old label through same-origin HTTP 304 reuse; a fresh origin serving the retained-state output displayed the new one. Check the served directory, URL and browser reuse before concluding that generated output or engine reuse is correct or incorrect. Generated-string presence alone is not browser verification.

No timing, log or internal skip count is fabricated here. Use diagnostics supported by your installed release if you need to explain the work, and report an unexpected result as carefully as a favorable one. Which edit would you use as your smallest useful check?

title: I rewrote VS Code's Live Server in Rust: one 3 MB binary, no Node.js
description:
I like VS Code's Live Server: click Go Live, the page opens, save a file and it reloads. What I didn't like was everything behind it: a Node.js process, a node_modules tree, and about 230 MB of memory to serve a few HTML files.

So I rewrote it in Rust. live-serve is a single binary of about 3 MB that serves a folder, reloads the page when a file changes, and swaps stylesheets in place without reloading.

Try it 

brew install nguyentruong354/tap/live-serve   # macOS, Linux
scoop install live-serve                      # Windows (after: scoop bucket add nguyentruong354 https://github.com/NguyenTruong354/scoop-bucket)
cargo install live-serve                      # anywhere with Rust

live-serve --open

In VS Code, install the extension live-serve-rs (also on Open VSX for VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf). It bundles the binary, so nothing else needs installing; click Go Live in the status bar.

What it does

  • Live reload over a WebSocket; saving a stylesheet swaps only the sheets from your own origin
  • --https with a self-signed certificate made on the fly, or --cert/--key for one from mkcert
  • --proxy /api=http://localhost:3000 so a static frontend can call a local backend without CORS
  • --spa for single-page apps, --host 0.0.0.0 to open it on your phone
  • Refuses requests from other websites (DNS rebinding, cross-origin reads) and hides .env and .git
  • live-serve init vscode / init zed adds an editor task to the project

Numbers

Against live-server, the package VS Code's Live Server runs, on the same machine and folder (median of six rounds; method):

live-serve live-server
Folder listing, 1,200 entries 2.0 ms ~48 ms
HTML page with the reload script 0.50 ms 0.7–1.5 ms
First response after start 44 ms ~1.4 s
Memory 11 MB ~230 MB

Static files cost about the same for both: reading the file and the loopback connection dominate. The difference is everything around the files.

Things that were harder than they looked

The watch dies with the folder. Build tools love rm -rf dist && build. A file watcher on dist stops when dist is deleted, so after the first rebuild nothing reloads anymore. live-serve also watches the parent folder and re-arms the watch when the folder comes back. macOS made this fun: FSEvents can report the folder's creation late, after the removal, so "created" alone can't mean "it's back".

Two programs on one port. On Windows and macOS, one program can listen on 0.0.0.0:5500 while another binds 127.0.0.1:5500, and both succeed. live-serve used to "take" localhost away from a server that was already running. It now checks the other kind of address before binding and moves to the next port.

HTTPS without setup. --https makes an ECDSA certificate with rcgen for localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 and, with --host 0.0.0.0, your network address, keeps it in a cache folder and renews it before it expires. TLS is rustls with ring, which added about 1.2 MB to the binary. A plain http:// request to the HTTPS port gets a redirect instead of a confusing error.

CSS swaps and editors. Many editors save by writing a temporary file and renaming it. The reload script has to recognise that the stylesheet changed (not that some random .tmp appeared) and swap only the sheets from the page's own origin, so a stylesheet from a CDN or Google Fonts isn't fetched again on every save.

It's built on axum, tokio and notify.

How it was built

I wrote the core myself and used Claude (an AI assistant) for parts of the HTTPS, proxy and file-watching work, the tests and the release pipeline. I reviewed every change before merging.

Feedback welcome

The code is MIT-licensed on GitHub: https://github.com/NguyenTruong354/live-serve

I'd especially like to hear how the file watching behaves with your build tool, and whether the HTTPS setup works on your machine. Issues and PRs are welcome.

title: September 23, 2026
description:
Apigee API hub

Feature

Preview launch of AWS API Gateway and Azure API Management plugins

API hub now includes two new built-in plugins for ingesting API metadata from third-party gateways: AWS API Gateway and Azure API Management. Both plugins are in Public Preview, extending API hub's multi-cloud governance to give you a single pane of glass across your Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure APIs.

What's new

  • Automated discovery and onboarding: Connect your AWS account or Azure API Management (APIM) service and API hub automatically discovers your existing deployed APIs and related metadata.
  • Scheduled pull sync: A full metadata sync runs every 6 hours by default, with reconciliation (upserts and orphan deletes) to keep your catalog in sync with the source gateway.
  • Optional near-real-time push sync: Deploy a customer-managed AWS Lambda function (for AWS API Gateway) or Azure Function (for Azure API Management) to relay control-plane change events to API hub in near real time. For sample deployment code, see the apigee-samples repository.

For more information, see About plugins, Manage third-party plugins, and Create a plugin instance.

Feature

Spec-to-deployment linkage and gateway revision tracking in API hub (GA)

API hub now provides a first-class, bidirectional link between API specifications, operations, and the deployments that serve them, together with native tracking of the underlying gateway revision.

What's new

  • Direct visibility between specs and deployments: See exactly which API specification and operations are served by a specific deployment, and navigate from a spec to the deployments that serve it.
  • Native gateway revision tracking: Deployments now capture and display their underlying gateway revision (for example, an Apigee proxy revision) via the new source_revision field on the Deployment resource.
  • More accurate operation resolution: When multiple revisions expose overlapping operations (same method and path), API hub associates each operation with its specific specification instead of dropping duplicates.
  • Multiple spec revisions per API: API hub can store multiple revisions of the same spec for an API deployed across different environments.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Asset
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/CostAssessmentJob

Cloud Key Management Service

Feature

Preview: Cloud EKM supports external key migration. For keys with the EXTERNAL or EXTERNAL_VPC protection levels, you can create new key versions with either of these protection levels. You can also change the protection level of existing external key versions to change how you access your existing key material with zero downtime and without reconfiguring your applications.

For more information about migrating external keys, see Migrate external keys.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Regional endpoints (workstations.REGION.rep.googleapis.com) are generally available (GA) for Cloud Workstations. Regional endpoints help you meet data residency requirements by routing and terminating HTTPS connections to the Cloud Workstations API within a specific region, keeping data in transit within your chosen regional boundary.

Regional endpoints for Cloud Workstations are available in the following regions:

  • asia-south1 (Mumbai, India, APAC)
  • europe-west6 (Zurich, Switzerland, Europe)
  • us-central1 (Council Bluffs, Iowa, North America)
  • us-east1 (Moncks Corner, South Carolina, North America)
  • us-east4 (Ashburn, Virginia, North America)
  • us-east5 (Columbus, Ohio, North America)
  • us-west1 (The Dalles, Oregon, North America)
  • us-west4 (Las Vegas, Nevada, North America)

You can also use the Google Cloud CLI gcloud workstations command group to configure regional endpoints. For more information, see Regional service endpoints and the Cloud Workstations REST API reference.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue that led to increased startup latency and errors for mobile and web chat sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly demoted to an Unresponsive status and removed from the routing pool despite successfully receiving call offers.

  • Fixed an issue where dialed numbers on Twilio BYOC SIP inbound calls were incorrectly formatted with extra digits from the SIP host and port.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented chat transcripts from being generated and delivered for sessions containing structured message content.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter incorrectly showed a call as on hold after a carrier failed to process the hold request, leaving the audio channel open between the agent and the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed media download caused the service to restart unexpectedly.

  • Fixed an issue that caused queue-specific wrap-up and disposition settings to reset to global defaults after changing unrelated fields on the Queue Settings page.

  • Fixed an issue where machine translation didn't activate for chats that were transferred into a non-English language queue if the session originated with a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where generative knowledge assist answers that contain long URLs were cut off at the edge of the panel.

  • Fixed an issue where queued calls were neither routed to available agents nor offered a callback.

  • Fixed an issue where voicemails were automatically dismissed and marked as read if a playback error occurred.

  • Fixed an issue where agent call recordings were missing or attached to the wrong call record after a virtual agent deflection.

  • Fixed an issue where unanswered DCR calls that were routed using Nexmo disconnected the caller instead of requeuing the call.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented virtual agents from transferring calls to a human-agent queue.

  • Fixed an issue where calls lacking a carrier hangup reason were incorrectly categorized as "customer abandoned", even when the call center didn't answer the call.

  • Fixed an issue where the call event API payload for DCR calls contained incorrect virtual agent parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where custom data from chat interactions wasn't recorded in Salesforce records.

  • Fixed an issue where Mexico time zones were incorrectly applying daylight saving time adjustments.

  • Fixed an issue where agents and end-users were joined to separate conferences, preventing audio communication between them.

  • Fixed an issue where call recording deletion tasks entered an endless loop if the provider didn't return a successful response.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR voice calls didn't send custom wrap-up events to Dialogflow CX under certain configurations.

  • Fixed an issue where a trailing slash in the host URL caused the web SDK to unexpectedly re-enable features that had been previously disabled for specific deployments.

Announcement

Fixed

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed a reconciliation loop issue in metrics-server by checking the ConfigMap on the target cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue in split-datacenter environments where cluster validation and diagnostics incorrectly reported missing datastores for PersistentVolumes residing in the user datacenter.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.500-gke.142:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where node drain in maintenance mode did not wait for attached storage volumes to detach.
  • Fixed BareMetalMachine conditions during maintenance mode transitions.

  • Fixed an issue where the status for Ingress resources didn't update when using bundled ingress.

  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster stalled indefinitely because node pool controllers recreated machine resources during deletion.

title: CorteXforge: Scenario-Based RF Dataset Generation on Real Testbeds
description:
arXiv:2610.26999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep learning for radio frequency (RF) signal analysis relies on large annotated datasets, yet synthetic datasets trade physical realism for controllability, while uncontrolled over-theair measurements offer realism but limited reproducibility. We present CorteXforge, a scenario-based framework for generating realistic and reproducible RF datasets on programmable software defined radio (SDR) testbeds. High-level RF scenarios are automatically translated into synchronized experiments executed on the SLICES-RI/CorteXlab platform, producing fully annotated Signal Metadata Format (SIGMF) datasets that capture hardware impairments and propagation effects. We validate CorteXforge through automatic modulation classification using ModForge, an over-the-air (OTA) dataset generated with the framework. Cross-domain experiments reveal a synthetic-to-real performance gap and show that synthetic pretraining remains beneficial for adaptation to OTA data. CorteXforge provides a practical foundation for reproducible RF dataset generation and future research on domain generalization.

title: Ways to Generate IDs in JavaScript
description:
ID generation in JavaScript is the process of creating identifiers, usually strings or numbers, that distinguish one record, element, or session from another in a JavaScript program. Common approaches include random numbers, timestamps, universally unique identifiers (UUIDs), and third-party libraries such as nanoid. The right method depends on whether the ID must be secure, short, sortable, or unique across systems.

Overview

Applications need identifiers for database rows, DOM elements, uploaded files, orders, and sessions. A good identifier is unique, hard to guess when exposed publicly, and suited to how it will be stored or displayed. JavaScript has no single built-in "ID" function, so developers choose between language features, the Web Crypto API, and external packages.

Methods

Math.random()

Math.random() returns a pseudo-random number that can be converted into a string.

const id = Math.random().toString(36).slice(2);

It requires no dependencies, but it is not cryptographically secure and collisions are possible. It is suitable only for temporary or non-sensitive keys.

Date.now()

Date.now() returns the current time in milliseconds.

const id = Date.now();

The result is sortable by creation time. Two IDs created in the same millisecond can be identical, and the values are easy to guess.

crypto.randomUUID()

crypto.randomUUID() returns a version 4 UUID generated from a cryptographically secure random source.

const id = crypto.randomUUID();

It is available in modern browsers (secure contexts only, meaning HTTPS or localhost) and in Node.js 14.17 and later. It is widely regarded as the default choice.

nanoid

nanoid is a small third-party library that produces compact, URL-safe string IDs. The default length is 21 characters.

import { nanoid } from 'nanoid';

const id = nanoid();

It is commonly used for share links and short codes.

UUID version 7

UUID version 7 embeds a timestamp in the leading bits, so identifiers are roughly ordered by creation time. It is available through the uuid package.

import { v7 } from 'uuid';

const id = v7();
