title: Why 12% of Agents Fail Without FlowState – The Secret to 83% Success
description:
FlowState — Turning Execution State into Memory for Long‑Horizon LLM Agents

The Lead

“Only 32 % of autonomous agents finish a 20‑step planning task without hitting the token limit,” reported a benchmark from the Stanford LLM Lab in March 2026. The headline reads like a warning: as LLM‑driven agents stretch toward multi‑day projects, the very mechanism that lets them remember—prompt history—runs out of space.

Enter FlowState, a framework that treats an agent’s execution state as a first‑class memory artifact. By persisting variables, tool outputs, and control‑flow flags in a versioned graph, FlowState lets the same LLM replay exact snapshots instead of reconstructing a fuzzy summary. The result: fewer tokens, higher success rates, and a clean audit trail for safety‑critical deployments.

The Case Study: A Multi‑Day Travel Planner

Imagine a consumer‑facing chatbot that builds a two‑week European itinerary, books flights, reserves hotels, and coordinates local tours. The user supplies preferences over several days, and the agent must:

  1. Query flight APIs and store confirmation numbers.
  2. Retrieve hotel availability and keep track of cancellation policies.
  3. Adjust earlier bookings when a new travel‑restriction emerges.

A naïve ReAct‑style agent would dump every API response into the prompt. After eight steps, the token budget swells beyond 8 k, forcing the system to truncate or summarise. Summaries lose ordering information—crucial when a later step must reference the exact hotel ID returned in step 3.

FlowState solves the problem by checkpointing after each tool call that crosses a relevance threshold. The graph below shows a simplified execution trace:

S0 (init) → S1 (flight query) → S2 (flight booked) → S3 (hotel query) → 
S4 (hotel booked) → S5 (policy change) → S6 (rewind to S4) → S7 (hotel re‑book)

When the policy change arrives at S5, the agent calls flow.rewind(S4). The LLM receives the exact state snapshot from S4—including the original hotel ID—without re‑sending the full history. The next inference step re‑books a compliant hotel, and the system logs the transition as an immutable node.

In a controlled experiment published on arXiv (2609.34565v2), the authors ran this exact workflow on a 30‑step benchmark that mixes booking, rescheduling, and compliance checks. The FlowState‑enabled agent consumed 68 % fewer tokens than the full‑history baseline and lifted task success from 71 % to 83 %.

Key stat: 12 percentage‑point jump in success rate on the Multi‑Day Code‑Synthesis benchmark.

The case study illustrates why execution‑state memory matters: it preserves causality, reduces prompt bloat, and offers a deterministic rollback mechanism—features that pure semantic summarisation cannot guarantee.

The Meat: Technical Deep‑Dive and Hard Numbers

1. State‑Graph Abstraction

FlowState models every inference call as a node in a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node stores:

Field Description
state_id UUID v4, immutable.
variables JSON map of scalar and tensor values.
tool_output Raw response (e.g., JSON payload from a REST API).
policy_flags Boolean markers (e.g., needs_rewind, high_risk).
parent_id Link to the previous node.
hash SHA‑256 over the serialized node for tamper‑evidence.

Edges encode the causal order of actions. Traversing the graph from any node yields a minimal, ordered history that the LLM can query with flow.get(state_id). Because the graph stores deltas rather than full prompts, storage grows linearly with the number of meaningful changes, not with raw token count.

2. Selective Checkpointing

Persisting every step would defeat the purpose. FlowState introduces a relevance‑change threshold (RCT). The system computes a cosine similarity between the current variables vector and the last checkpoint’s vector. If similarity falls below τ = 0.85, a new node is created; otherwise, the delta is merged into the existing node.

Empirical results on the Long‑Horizon Code‑Synthesis suite show that RCT reduces checkpoint count from 30 to 9 on average, while preserving 99.3 % of the decision‑impact information (measured by downstream task accuracy).

3. Unified API

Developers interact with FlowState through three primitives:

state = flow.get(state_id)                # fetch snapshot
flow.update(state_id, delta)              # append delta, auto‑checkpoint if needed
flow.rewind(target_state_id)              # set current context to an earlier node

The API plugs directly into LangChain’s BaseMemory abstract class. The open‑source repo (github.com/flowstate-ai/flowstate) ships a FlowStateMemory class that implements load_memory_variables and save_context using the above calls. The same class works with LlamaIndex, Auto‑GPT, and the upcoming OpenAI Functions plugin.

4. Safety Hooks

Each node’s hash enables non‑malleable memory. In a companion paper (2606.24322), the authors demonstrate that an adversary who tampers with a stored node can be detected with > 99.9 % probability because the downstream LLM refuses to load a node whose hash mismatches the signed manifest. This property satisfies emerging regulatory demands for immutable audit trails in finance and healthcare.

5. Benchmarks

Benchmark Baseline (full‑history) FlowState Token Reduction Latency Overhead
30‑step planning (travel) 71 % success 83 % 68 % +12 ms
Multi‑Day Code‑Synthesis (12 steps) 71 % 83 % 62 % +15 ms
Long‑Form Reasoning (50 steps) 58 % 70 % 71 % +9 ms

All latency numbers assume a Redis‑JSON backend with sub‑millisecond I/O. The dominant cost stems from serialising JSON deltas; the authors report that a pure‑in‑memory KV store can shave another 5 ms per checkpoint.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

1. Storage Explosion in Highly Parallel Agents

FlowState’s graph grows with the number of meaningful state changes. In multi‑agent simulations where dozens of bots interact simultaneously, checkpoint proliferation can strain even fast KV stores. Mitigation strategies—such as periodic state compaction (merging leaf nodes whose variables converge) and sharding by agent ID—remain research‑grade.

2. Consistency Across Distributed Deployments

When agents run on edge devices (e.g., autonomous drones) and sync to a cloud store, network partitions may produce divergent state graphs. The current implementation resolves conflicts by last‑write‑wins based on timestamped hashes, a heuristic that could violate causal ordering. Future work must integrate CRDT‑style merges or consensus protocols.

3. Privacy of Stored Execution Artifacts

Because FlowState persists raw API responses, it may inadvertently capture PII (e.g., user emails in a booking confirmation). The framework supplies encryption‑at‑rest hooks, but developers must still audit the schema of tool_output. A mis‑configured policy could expose sensitive data to downstream LLM calls.

4. Dependency on Deterministic Tool Calls

FlowState assumes that re‑executing a node yields the same result. Non‑deterministic APIs (e.g., recommendation engines with stochastic outputs) break this guarantee. The authors recommend tagging such calls with a non_deterministic flag and avoiding checkpointing, but that reduces the benefits for certain domains.

The Outlook: Where Execution‑State Memory Could Lead

  1. Enterprise Automation – Accenture’s $2 M joint grant aims to embed FlowState in compliance bots that must prove every decision to regulators. Immutable state graphs satisfy audit requirements without manual logging.

  2. Robotics – Boston Dynamics’ pilot integrates sensor tensors (LiDAR point clouds, joint torques) into FlowState nodes. Early results show that a manipulation agent can recall the exact grasp pose from a day‑old node, improving repeatability by 23 %.

  3. OpenAI Ecosystem – The partnership announced on 1 Nov 2026 makes FlowState an optional plugin for ChatGPT‑Plugins. Users can now request “show me the exact API payload that led to the last purchase” and receive a cryptographically signed snapshot.

  4. Standardisation – The NeurIPS 2026 workshop on “Memory‑Centric Agents” earmarked FlowState as a reference implementation for a future LLM‑Agent Memory Interoperability specification. If the community adopts a common graph schema, tool vendors could exchange state graphs across platforms, unlocking plug‑and‑play long‑horizon agents.

  5. Research Frontiers – Combining FlowState with retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) may yield hybrid memory systems: the graph stores deterministic execution artifacts, while a vector store caches semantic embeddings for fuzzy lookup. Early prototypes suggest a 9 % boost on open‑ended QA tasks that require both precise facts and contextual reasoning.

Closing Thoughts

FlowState flips the conventional wisdom that an LLM’s prompt is the only memory it can access. By externalising execution state into a versioned, queryable graph, it sidesteps token limits, preserves causal order, and offers tamper‑evidence—features that matter to anyone building agents that must operate across days, weeks, or even months.

The framework’s open‑source release, sizable Series A funding, and partnerships with OpenAI, AWS, and Boston Dynamics signal strong market momentum. Yet the path forward carries non‑trivial engineering challenges: storage management for massive parallelism, consistency under network partitions, and privacy safeguards for stored artifacts.

If the community tackles these hurdles, execution‑state memory could become the default substrate for long‑horizon LLM agents, turning today’s token‑budget nightmare into a manageable, auditable data structure. In that scenario, FlowState will not just be a clever add‑on—it will be the backbone that lets autonomous AI finally think beyond the next few hundred tokens.

title: CityPaint: A Free Lunch from 2D Diffusion for City-Scale 3D Texturing
description:
arXiv:2610.27564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating high-fidelity, city-scale 3D environments plays a crucial role in applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and urban digital twins. However, the scarcity of real-world city-scale 3D training data forces existing methods to either stitch independently generated assets or learn from synthetic urban corpora, often sacrificing realism and global consistency. In contrast, 2D image data and their corresponding generative models are abundant and encode rich visual priors. To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a novel framework that leverages 2D diffusion models to generate globally consistent city-scale 3D textures without relying on city-scale 3D training data. Specifically, CityPaint integrates geometric priors with the generative power of 2D diffusion models, introducing a robust top-$K$ camera baking strategy for iterative texture projection. To address the artifacts of 2D-to-3D projection, we further propose a decoupled refinement mechanism that separately optimizes terrain and building textures. Extensive experiments show that CityPaint produces globally coherent textures with fine local details and achieves favorable results against strong baselines in both visual quality and cross-view consistency.

title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
description:
arXiv:2610.27439v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.

title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

title: CSS Logical Properties: How Browsers Translate Them to Physical Styles
description:
You’ve probably hit this subtle bug before: you write some CSS using logical properties like margin-inline-start, expecting your layout to just work regardless of text direction. But then you flip your app to RTL or switch writing modes, and suddenly things don’t line up as you expected. Margins that should shift to the left stay put, or worse, shift in the wrong direction.

I ran into this during a recent localization sprint. Our UI had mixed LTR and RTL content, and rather than duplicating styles or using awkward hacks, I leaned on CSS logical properties. They’re supposed to abstract away physical directions like left/right and top/bottom. But debugging why my margins weren’t behaving as I imagined forced me to dig under the hood , how exactly do browsers turn these logical properties into physical ones?

Logical vs Physical CSS Properties: The Basic Idea

Traditional CSS uses physical directions:

margin-left: 10px;
padding-top: 5px;

These are fixed to the box’s edges, regardless of the document’s writing mode (LTR or RTL) or layout direction (horizontal or vertical).

Logical properties, introduced in CSS Logical Properties and Values Module, let you specify styles based on the writing mode and flow:

  • margin-inline-start applies margin at the start of the inline flow
  • padding-block-end applies padding at the end of the block flow

So in a left-to-right language, margin-inline-start equals margin-left. In right-to-left, it maps to margin-right. This makes your CSS more adaptable without duplication.

But here’s the kicker: browsers do this mapping internally, translating your logical properties to physical ones at layout time. Understanding that translation explains many layout quirks.

How Browsers Translate Logical Properties

When the browser’s CSS engine parses a rule like:

.my-box {
  margin-inline-start: 16px;
}

it doesn’t leave it as margin-inline-start. Instead, it figures out the physical edge corresponding to "inline start" for the element’s writing mode and direction.

For example, suppose your document is LTR horizontal:

  • inline direction goes left to right
  • inline start is left

The browser will apply the margin as margin-left: 16px internally. But if the same element is in RTL horizontal:

  • inline direction is right to left
  • inline start is right

Now the browser applies margin-right: 16px.

This mapping happens during style computation, after resolving the element’s writing-mode and direction but before layout.

What about vertical writing modes?

When the writing mode is vertical (like Japanese or Mongolian vertical text), "inline" and "block" directions swap:

  • Inline flows top to bottom or bottom to top
  • Block flows left to right or right to left

So margin-inline-start could map to margin-top or margin-bottom depending on writing-mode and direction. This can be surprisingly confusing if you only think in LTR horizontal terms.

Behind the Scenes: The Browser’s Style Computation Pipeline

In the browser’s rendering engine (think Blink, Gecko, or WebKit), style computation is a multi-step process:

  1. Parsing CSS , The engine parses your CSS, creating a style tree where each node has declarations like margin-inline-start.

  2. Resolving Computed Styles , The engine resolves computed values for each property. For logical properties, it uses the element’s computed writing-mode and direction to map logical properties to physical ones.

  3. Applying Physical Styles , The engine applies these physical styles to layout boxes, which then participate in the box model and flow layout calculations.

This means that from the layout engine’s perspective, it never really sees margin-inline-start; it only sees margin-left or margin-top, etc., depending on context.

Why This Matters for Debugging Layout Issues

  1. Unexpected Margins on RTL or Vertical Text

If your app flips to RTL but some margins don’t move as expected, check if you’re mixing logical and physical properties. Physical properties like margin-left don’t adapt, so your layout breaks.

  1. Overriding Logical Properties with Physical Ones

Sometimes, authors override logical properties with physical ones elsewhere in CSS. Because physical properties have the same specificity and cascade rules, the last one wins. This can cause logical properties to be silently ignored.

  1. DevTools Show Physical Properties

Inspecting elements in browser DevTools often shows the physical properties after translation, not the logical ones you wrote. This can confuse you into thinking your CSS isn’t applied.

Practical Tips When Using Logical Properties

  • Always use logical properties consistently in your CSS for layout margins, paddings, borders, and positioning.

  • Be mindful of writing mode. If your app supports vertical writing modes, test your layouts carefully. Logical properties behave differently there.

  • Check DevTools carefully. Don’t expect to see margin-inline-start in computed styles. Look for the mapped physical properties.

  • Use computed styles and layout debugging tools. Some browsers let you visualize box model edges and directions, which can help understand how logical properties translate.

  • Avoid mixing physical and logical properties for the same edge. This reduces cascade confusion.

A Real Debugging Example

I had a sidebar that used:

.sidebar {
  padding-inline-start: 20px;
  border-inline-end: 1px solid #ccc;
}

It looked perfect in LTR, but in RTL, the padding stayed on the left, and the border appeared on the left instead of the right. Turns out, somewhere else in the stylesheet, there was a physical property:

.sidebar {
  padding-left: 10px;
}

Because padding-left came after in the cascade, it silently overrode the logical padding on the physical left edge.

Removing the physical property and relying solely on logical properties fixed the problem.

Wrap-up

CSS logical properties are a powerful way to write adaptable, locale-friendly styles. But they’re not magic. Browsers internally translate them to physical properties based on the element’s writing mode and direction, and understanding that helps you debug those sticky layout issues in multilingual or vertical writing layouts.

Next time your margin-inline-start feels stubborn, remember: it’s actually a margin-left or margin-right in disguise, chosen based on your document’s flow.

Happy styling!

title: We're fed up with Rust's borrow checker. It's time to break free.
description:
I like Rust. I also dread the moment the borrow checker says no and the compiler refuses to
explain what it assumed.

That is not a complaint about competence. Rust's borrow checker is one of the most valuable
things to happen to systems programming. It is a complaint about posture: the compiler stands
outside your program, announces a verdict, and the burden of proof lands on you. When the verdict
is wrong, there is often no receipt to inspect.

We built Loment around a different posture. It keeps the
checks; it moves the burden. This post is about what that means precisely, because "we removed the
borrow checker" would be a lie, and the interesting part is not the removal.

What Loment keeps

Loment is a systems language with a Rust-flavoured surface. It still checks the ownership
mistakes that matter most:

  • use after move (E006),
  • a mutable borrow alongside another borrow (E007),
  • a dangling reference (E012).

It also adds capability domains (capability disk[0..4] plus guard), compiles to a native
ELF/PE artifact with no runtime by default, and has two implementations — a Python reference and
a self-hosted one — that must emit byte-identical IR.

What it does not do is pretend to be Rust's borrow checker. The boundary is written down in
the repository: it proves three things and explicitly does not prove four others (no lifetimes, no
cross-function reasoning, no field-level moves, no branch-sensitive move sets). Keep that in mind
for the rest of this post.

From verdict to receipt

The change is a seventh choose dimension called LSPE — Loment Safety Police Espace. It does
not change any verdict. It changes what a verdict leaves behind.

With lspe_open_admin (the default), every allowance is recorded in the artifact's Potato v16
ledger: the site, the obligation, the evidence, and what is still unproved. With
lspe_close_admin, the recording is turned off; the LMS, runtime and capability decisions are
unchanged. The audit is not a second checker bolted on top — it is a ledger of the compiler's own
decisions, answerable offline.

The design document puts it more bluntly than I can:

Rust's borrow checker is a god. LSPE is a shop assistant.

A god stands outside the transaction and says "no". An assistant stands inside it, has to name the
price, and gives you a receipt. Concretely, LSPE has three outcomes instead of two:

  • PROVED — here is the evidence;
  • UNDECIDED — here is the site where my proof has a hole;
  • REFUTED — here is a counterexample, so this is a hard no.

"Undecided" is a first-class result. In strict mode it becomes E034; the ledger's own consistency
failures are E035–E037. The point is not that the compiler is always right. The point is that when
it is wrong, you can point at the site and the obligation instead of arguing with a verdict.

"Gentle" is a measurable claim

It is easy to say a checker is friendlier. We tried to make it falsifiable:

  1. Same verdicts. Compile the same corpus with the audit open and closed: the set of decisions is identical. The audit changes the ledger, not the language.
  2. No silent permit. Every allow has a source, or an explicitly recorded assumption. An allow with neither is an error in the ledger.
  3. No overclaiming. LSPE does not claim to prove more than Rust. What it adds is accountability, not completeness. The remaining cases are UNDECIDED and labeled.

That is the sense in which it is "gentler with nearly the same safety": not that it catches
everything Rust catches, but that the same checks no longer arrive as an unaccountable verdict.

Loment also has a memory-safety ladder, lms, with seven levels and four tiers
(lms_full, lms_forensic_admin, lms_daily_admin, lms_manage_only_admin). The default is
full; writing a lower tier is a downgrade and carries _admin. The literal-out-of-range check is
E028; use-after-free is E029.

What it looks like

The defaults, written out:

module demo
choose runtime
choose lms_full
choose lspe_open_admin

capability disk_slots : disk[0..4] revocable

fn write_slot(slot: u32) -> u32 {
    guard disk_slots(slot);
    return slot;
}

fn _start() {
    let xs: [u32; 3] = [1, 2, 3];
    let i: u32 = 5;
    if i < 3 {
        xs[i] = 7;          // a runtime index: you guard it, the language does not guess
    }
    syscall4(60, 0, 0, 0);
}

Two details matter here. guard bounds the index, not the subject — it is not authorization.
And the array write is still your responsibility: Loment refuses a literal out-of-range index
at compile time (E028), but a runtime index is not silently checked.

What this does not mean

I would rather say this before the comments do:

  • Loment is early. 0.1.5 is the release where LSPE lands; the packaged front end is still being finished. Do not rewrite your service in it this weekend.
  • It is not Rust. The borrow checking is a subset. No lifetimes, no cross-function reasoning, no field-level moves, no branch-sensitive move sets.
  • "No receipt" is not the same as "no bug". LSPE records the compiler's decisions; it does not make the compiler omniscient.
  • Defaults are not free. lms_full is the default and it changes the emitted artifact (inline bounds checks on alloc(<const>)-derived accesses). That exception is documented, not hidden.
  • The benchmark is a pilot. We measured an LLM agent writing Loment from the guide alone: three tasks, one attempt each, Rust and Python as controls. It is a direction, not a confidence interval.

The reason I care about the receipt is not abstract. Rust's own tracker has a soundness bug
(#164250) where an obligation was not rechecked after substitution, and it stayed invisible for
years — not because Rust's team is careless, but because a verdict-only compiler leaves nothing
to audit when the verdict is wrong. LSPE's answer to that shape is a record with a site id
(Q004 stale_wf), readable offline. That is the part I want other language designers to steal,
whether or not they like Loment.

Try it, then tell us where the receipt is wrong

  • Source: https://github.com/Loment-Lang/Loment

We are not asking you to believe the slogan. We are asking you to compile something, read the
ledger, and tell us which line is wrong. That is the whole point of moving the burden.

Disclosure: I'm one of Loment's authors. This draft was prepared with an AI assistant and
reviewed before publishing.

title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
description:
arXiv:2610.26979v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 4: Querying
description:
The chapter on querying languages is where Hibernate stops being just "magic" and becomes a manageable tool. Here, it is crucial to understand three approaches and their boundaries: HQL/JPQL (declarative, object-oriented), Criteria API (programmatic, type-safe), and Native SQL (direct database access). In Spring projects, there is an additional layer on top of this: Spring Data JPA, which changes how you write 90% of your queries.

HQL and JPQL: Object-Oriented SQL

HQL is Hibernate's proprietary language, while JPQL is the JPA standard inspired by early HQL. It is important to know the relationship: HQL is a superset of JPQL. Any valid JPQL query is a valid HQL query, but not vice versa: HQL supports more features (e.g., insert ... select, which is absent in JPQL).

The main difference from SQL is that you operate on entities and their fields, not tables and columns. In HQL, Book is a Java class, and book.title is its field. Direct referencing of database table and column names is prohibited. Because of this, HQL is more compact than SQL and portable across different databases.

Mapping Example:

-- SQL
SELECT book.title, pub.name
FROM Book AS book
JOIN Publisher AS pub ON book.publisherId = pub.id
WHERE book.title LIKE 'Hibernate%'
ORDER BY book.title

// HQL / JPQL
SELECT book.title, pub.name
FROM Book AS book
JOIN book.publisher AS pub
WHERE book.title LIKE 'Hibernate%'
ORDER BY book.title

Note: the join is performed on the association (book.publisher), not on the foreign key column. Hibernate knows how to resolve it automatically.

Key HQL features you need to know:

  • Parameters: Named (:name) and positional (?1). Named parameters are preferred for readability, while positional ones are often used in native queries.
  • JOIN FETCH: The primary tool for combating the N+1 query problem. It loads the association immediately in a single query.
  • DTO projections: You can return a DTO directly instead of an entity, e.g., new com.example.dto.BookDto(book.title, pub.name). This saves memory and avoids creating managed objects.
  • update / delete: Bulk operations executed as a single SQL statement that bypass the Persistence Context (in-memory entities will not be updated — this is a pitfall).

HQL Pitfalls:

  • Bulk update/delete does not synchronize with the first-level cache. If you loaded a Book into the session and then executed update Book set title = ..., the in-memory object will retain the old title. You need session.clear() or refresh().
  • JOIN FETCH on two collections simultaneously results in a MultipleBagFetchException or a Cartesian product. The solution is to use @BatchSize / SUBSELECT, or split it into two separate queries.
  • JOIN FETCH + pagination (setMaxResults) can yield incorrect results: Hibernate applies the limit in memory, not in the SQL query. This is a known limitation.

Criteria API: Queries as Code

The Criteria API is a programmatic way to build queries. Instead of a string, you construct the query from objects: CriteriaBuilder, CriteriaQuery, Root, and Predicate. This provides type safety (the compiler checks field names if you use the metamodel) and flexibility for dynamic conditions.

When the Criteria API is indispensable:

  • Search screens with a variable set of filters. For example, a user might specify a price, category, brand — or nothing at all. Concatenating an HQL string with if statements is a source of bugs; the Criteria API handles this cleanly.
  • Dynamic sorting and pagination with type checking.
  • Building queries in libraries and frameworks where you do not know the entity structure in advance.

Example (simplified):

CriteriaBuilder cb = session.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Book> cq = cb.createQuery(Book.class);
Root<Book> book = cq.from(Book.class);

List<Predicate> predicates = new ArrayList<>();
if (title != null) predicates.add(cb.like(book.get("title"), "%" + title + "%"));
if (minPrice != null) predicates.add(cb.ge(book.get("price"), minPrice));

cq.where(predicates.toArray(new Predicate[0]));
cq.orderBy(cb.asc(book.get("title")));

List<Book> result = session.createQuery(cq).getResultList();

Drawbacks of the Criteria API:

  • Verbosity. A simple query turns into 10–15 lines of code.
  • Poorer readability compared to HQL, especially for complex joins.
  • Not for "one-off" queries. If a query is static, HQL is shorter and clearer.

Practical rule: static queries → HQL/JPQL; dynamic queries (search, filters) → Criteria API.

Native SQL: When ORM is Powerless

Sometimes you need to drop down to the database level. Native SQL is justified when:

  • You need a database-specific feature (window functions, LATERAL JOIN, hints, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, specific syntax).
  • The query is too complex for HQL and easier to write in SQL than to assemble via Criteria.
  • You need maximum performance in a bottleneck where HQL generates suboptimal SQL.
  • You are working with stored procedures.

Example:

Book book = session.createNativeQuery(
    "SELECT * FROM books WHERE isbn = ?1", Book.class)
    .setParameter(1, isbn)
    .getSingleResult();

Native Query Pitfalls:

  1. Flush behavior: Hibernate does not flush by default before executing native queries, because it does not know which tables the query will affect. If there are unsaved changes in the Persistence Context, the native query might return stale data. The solution is an explicit session.flush() before the query or configuring the FlushMode.
  2. Result mapping: For simple cases (SELECT * matching an entity), Hibernate infers the mapping automatically. For complex queries (aliases, aggregates, joins), you need @SqlResultSetMapping or manual parsing of Object[], which is cumbersome and fragile.
  3. Portability: Native SQL ties you to a specific database dialect. If you plan to switch databases, use it sparingly.

Spring Data JPA: How It Looks

In Spring Boot, you rarely write session.createQuery() directly. Instead, you use Spring Data JPA repositories, which offer three levels of abstraction:

  • Derived queries (from method names): findByEmailAddressAndLastname(String email, String lastname) is automatically translated into JPQL: SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.emailAddress = ?1 AND u.lastname = ?2. This works for simple queries, but method names become cumbersome with 3+ conditions.
  • @Query with JPQL/HQL: An explicit query on a repository method. This is the standard for medium-complexity queries: 
   @Query("SELECT b FROM Book b JOIN FETCH b.author WHERE b.title LIKE %:title%")
   List<Book> findWithAuthorByTitle(@Param("title") String title);
  • @Query(nativeQuery = true): Native SQL when JPQL is insufficient. The nativeQuery flag explicitly tells Spring Data that this is not JPQL.

Important: Spring Data JPA does not generate JPQL for UPDATE and DELETE from method names — only for SELECT. For modifications, you need @Query + @Modifying.

What to Use When

Approach When to choose Pros Cons
HQL/JPQL Static queries, 80% of cases Compact, portable, readable Not for dynamic queries; strings are not checked by the compiler
Criteria API Dynamic filters, search, libraries Type-safe, flexible Verbose, harder to read
Native SQL DB specifics, complex queries, performance Full control over SQL Not portable, requires manual mapping, flush nuances
Spring Data (derived) Simple CRUD and selections Minimal code Cumbersome names, SELECT only
Spring Data @Query Medium-complexity queries Explicit, readable, located in the repository Strings are not checked by the compiler

What to Remember

  1. HQL is a superset of JPQL. Write in JPQL for portability; use HQL features consciously.
  2. HQL operates on entities, not tables. This is its strength (compactness, portability) and its limitation (cannot use DB-specific features).
  3. Criteria API is for dynamic queries, HQL is for static ones. Do not try to build a simple query using Criteria — it is overkill.
  4. Native SQL is a targeted tool. Always remember about flush and result mapping.
  5. JOIN FETCH is your best friend against N+1, but it has limitations (pagination, two collections).
  6. Bulk update/delete in HQL does not synchronize with the first-level cache. You need clear() after them.
  7. In Spring Data, 90% of queries are @Query with JPQL. Derived queries are for simple cases, native queries are for exceptions.

title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27119v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

title: I built a browser for AI agents, then benchmarked it against Playwright MCP and browser-use
description:
Every agent I tried on the web had the same problem: it was reading too much. A browser tool hands the model a page snapshot, the model clicks, and then gets a fresh snapshot of the whole page again. Most of the tokens go on re-reading things that didn't change.

So I built AgentGo, a Chromium browser for Windows (Rust, on CEF) made to be driven by an agent over MCP. Then I measured it against the two tools most people use today.

The result

Same model (gpt-6-luna, medium reasoning), same 24 BrowserGym MiniWoB++ tasks, a fresh agent session for every task, only that browser's MCP tools, and the page's own reward decides.

Setup Solved Median time Input tokens Agent turns
AgentGo 0.1.5 22/24 32 s 94.7k 7.7
browser-use 0.13.11 19/24 92 s 209.9k 13.2
Playwright MCP 0.0.83 18/24 42 s 178.4k 13.0

About half the tokens, roughly half the turns, and the fastest median per task.

Why it uses fewer tokens

Three design choices do most of the work:

  1. A compact outline instead of a snapshot. browser_open returns headings plus the things you can act on, one per line, as [ref] role "name". The refs stay stable while the page changes.
  2. Only what changed. After browser_act, the reply is the diff: + for new elements, - for removed ones, ~ for changed values. The model doesn't re-read the page to find out whether its click worked.
  3. The browser waits, not the model. Each action waits for the page to settle before answering, so the agent doesn't spend turns calling "wait" and reading again.

It's also a real browser rather than a test harness: its own pointer and keyboard (so date pickers, sliders and key-listening widgets behave), the agent can have its own signed-in accounts, and payments or final submissions pause until the person approves them in the browser window.

What it got wrong

Two tasks beat every setup, AgentGo included:

  • form-sequence-2: the instruction never says to press Submit, and no agent did.
  • click-pie: every agent opened the pie menu and clicked the item, and the page didn't count the click.

And the limits of the test itself: one machine, one run per task and setup, one model. MiniWoB++ pages are small; a different model or another run will move single tasks. The full method, every task's result, and a separate check on 20 real websites are in the benchmark write-up.

GoMini

AgentGo also ships GoMini, a small model (322M parameters) that runs on your own GPU and takes routine steps, like filling the values you supplied, so the big model doesn't have to read every page. On 13 held-out task types it went from 15 to 39 of 65 subgoals between versions. It's still in development: with it on, AgentGo solved the same 22/24, at slightly more tokens.

Try it

  • AgentGo (Windows 11, free): https://github.com/Moha2005269/agentgo
  • Claude Code: /plugin install agentgo --marketplace Moha2005269/agentgo-mcp
  • Other MCP clients: the installer connects Claude Code, Codex or Droid, or run agentgo mcp. It's also on the official MCP Registry as io.github.Moha2005269/agentgo.

I built this solo. I'd love to hear what breaks, and which sites you want me to try next.

title: Implementing DDD and Hexagonal Architecture in NestJS: A Complete Practical Guide
description:
1. When a service starts doing everything

A NestJS application often begins with a controller, a service, and a few Prisma calls. That structure is easy to understand when the business operation is “save these fields.” Then the requirements change.

An order needs a technician before work can be registered. Required tasks must be completed before finalization. A visit must fit the technician's schedule. Closing an order must record a business event together with the updated state.

When all those decisions live in services that also handle HTTP responses and database records, changing one rule means navigating several technical concerns. Testing the rule can require constructing much more of the application than the rule itself needs.

In this guide, we will follow a service-management API built with TypeScript, NestJS, Prisma, and PostgreSQL. We will use Domain-Driven Design (DDD) to express business behavior and Hexagonal Architecture to control dependencies around it.

You should be comfortable with TypeScript classes, interfaces, async functions, and basic NestJS controllers. You do not need previous DDD experience. The goal is to understand where each responsibility belongs and how the pieces fit together.

The complete example is available in nest-ddd-hexagonal on GitHub. The snippets below are selected from that project; excerpts omit unrelated code and imports where indicated. This is an educational implementation with concrete limits, which we will discuss alongside its benefits.

2. Start with the business and its language

Imagine a company that sends technicians to customer sites. A service order captures the work commitment: customer, contract, address, service level, required tasks, performed activities, and materials used. A visit captures a scheduled appointment with a technician.

The project organizes those concerns into two modules:

Module Main concepts Responsibilities
service-orders ServiceOrder, activities, materials, required tasks Record work, enforce the order lifecycle, finalize and close orders
visits Technician, Visit, TimeSlot, TechnicianAvailability Register technicians, schedule visits, check availability, cancel appointments

These modules are candidate context boundaries within a modular monolith. They run in the same process and share PostgreSQL, while maintaining separate models and application contracts. A directory alone does not establish a bounded context; the useful boundary comes from ownership of language, rules, and integration.

Several requirements make this example useful beyond basic CRUD:

  • Service level determines order priority.
  • A technician must be assigned before activities or materials can be registered.
  • Finalization requires at least one activity and no pending required tasks.
  • Closing requires prior finalization and records a domain event.
  • Visits last between 30 minutes and four hours and cannot start in the past.
  • Scheduling checks technician activity, overlapping visits, order status, and assignment.

DDD helps us turn these sentences into named operations. order.finalize() communicates a business decision more directly than assigning a status field in an HTTP handler. Those names also give tests a useful vocabulary.

3. Dependencies point toward the core

In Alistair Cockburn's original Hexagonal Architecture article, the application can be driven and tested independently of its external interfaces. Ports describe interactions with the application; adapters connect those interactions to particular technologies.

This repository implements that idea through three layers:

Layer Owns Depends on
Domain Business concepts, invariants, behavior, domain errors Its own model and standard runtime APIs
Application Use cases and contracts for external capabilities Domain and application ports
Infrastructure HTTP, DTO validation, persistence, integration adapters Application, domain, and technical libraries

The core consists of domain and application. In this project, neither imports NestJS or Prisma. It does use standard Node.js APIs such as randomUUID, so framework independence does not imply independence from every runtime.

The following arrows represent source-code dependencies:

HTTP controller ----------> Use case ----------> Domain model
                               |
                               v
                        Application port
                               ^
                               |
Prisma adapter ----------------+
       |
       v
Prisma client / PostgreSQL

Nest module: selects adapters and constructs use cases

At runtime, the use case calls an adapter through the port. The dependency direction remains inward because the use case imports the interface, while the adapter implements that interface.

The repository places outgoing ports in application/ports, where the use cases consume them. Putting ports in the domain can also be reasonable when that layer owns the contract. Hexagonal Architecture does not require one universal folder location.

Incoming operations are exposed through use-case methods. Controllers call them directly; there is no additional interface for every incoming port. The important question is whether the core can execute independently of HTTP and persistence.

4. Organize by capability, then by layer

Here is a shortened view of the project:

src/
├── main.ts
├── app.module.ts
├── shared/
│   ├── domain/
│   └── infrastructure/
└── modules/
    ├── service-orders/
    │   ├── domain/
    │   │   ├── model/
    │   │   ├── events/
    │   │   └── errors/
    │   ├── application/
    │   │   ├── ports/
    │   │   └── use-cases/
    │   ├── infrastructure/
    │   │   ├── http/
    │   │   └── persistence/
    │   └── service-orders.module.ts
    └── visits/
        ├── domain/
        ├── application/
        ├── infrastructure/
        │   ├── http/
        │   ├── persistence/
        │   └── integration/
        └── visits.module.ts

prisma/    # Schema and SQL migrations
test/      # Domain, application, HTTP, and adapter tests

Grouping by business capability keeps related work close together. Within each module, the three layers explain responsibilities. This follows the feature-first organization often associated with vertical slicing, although the repository also retains explicit layers within each module.

The result is easier to navigate than global folders containing every controller, every service, and every entity. It does not make modules automatically independent: visits integrates with service-orders, so extracting one would still require addressing that integration and the shared database.

The shared directory contains small mechanisms such as DomainError, DomainEvent, and AggregateRoot, plus infrastructure support. Business models remain in their owning modules. A shared generic repository would add little value when each module has different persistence needs.

5. Model rules inside the domain

5.1 An aggregate protects a consistency boundary

ServiceOrder is the aggregate root for the order and its child collections. Code changes the order through operations such as assignTechnician, addActivity, completeRequiredTask, finalize, and close.

An aggregate defines a boundary within which related state and rules are managed together. In this implementation, the repository persists the root, activities, materials, and required tasks as one transactional snapshot.

The main lifecycle is:

CREATED -> ASSIGNED -> IN_PROGRESS -> FINALIZED -> CLOSED
             ^              |
             |              +-- activities or materials start work
             +-- technician assignment can be changed before work starts

Finalization additionally requires:
  assigned technician + at least one activity + all required tasks completed

The aggregate implementation has a private constructor and separate factories for creation and rehydration. Creation derives priority from service level and starts the order in CREATED. Rehydration reconstructs an existing order and validates snapshot consistency without replaying business operations.

Here is the actual finalize method, shown without the surrounding class:

finalize(now = new Date()): void {
  this.ensureOperationallyMutable();
  this.ensureTechnicianAssigned();

  if (this.activitiesValue.length === 0) throw new ActivityRequiredError();

  const pending = this.requiredTasksValue
    .filter((task) => !task.completedAt)
    .map((task) => task.id);

  if (pending.length > 0) throw new PendingRequiredTasksError(pending);

  if (this.statusValue !== ServiceOrderStatus.IN_PROGRESS) {
    throw new ServiceOrderInvalidStateError(
      `Only an in-progress service order can be finalized; current state is ${this.statusValue}`,
    );
  }

  const latestWork = Math.max(
    this.createdAtValue.getTime(),
    ...this.activitiesValue.map((activity) => activity.performedAt.getTime()),
    ...this.requiredTasksValue.map((task) => task.completedAt?.getTime() ?? 0),
  );

  const finalizedAt = validDate(now, 'finalizedAt', new Date(latestWork));
  this.statusValue = ServiceOrderStatus.FINALIZED;
  this.finalizedAtValue = finalizedAt;
}

The operation validates its prerequisites before changing status. Registering material alone moves an assigned order into progress, but still does not satisfy the activity requirement for finalization. The timestamp must also be consistent with the recorded work.

These rules apply whether a controller, a test, or a future batch adapter invokes the model. They remain meaningful without any knowledge of status codes or database columns.

5.2 Encapsulation requires protecting references

The aggregate is mutable through its methods. Its getters return frozen child snapshots and copied dates, preventing callers from modifying internal collections indirectly.

That detail matters in JavaScript: readonly is a compile-time restriction, and a Date can change even when its containing property cannot be reassigned. Copying dates on input and output protects the aggregate from those reference mutations.

The implementation also validates rehydrated metadata, child identifiers, lifecycle dates, and state consistency. This is a deliberate safety choice with extra validation cost. Persisted data still crosses a boundary and must be converted into a valid model.

5.3 A value object gives time intervals a meaning

Technician and Visit are entities: their identity persists as their state changes. TimeSlot is a value object: it describes an interval through its values, without a separate identifier or lifecycle. Its role is to represent a valid interval and answer questions about it. The complete source includes date-validation and duration helpers; this excerpt contains its main behavior:

export class TimeSlot {
  private constructor(
    private readonly startsAtValue: Date,
    private readonly endsAtValue: Date,
  ) {}

  static create(startsAt: Date, endsAt: Date): TimeSlot {
    if (!isValidDate(startsAt) || !isValidDate(endsAt)) {
      throw new InvalidTimeSlotError('Start and end dates must be valid dates');
    }

    const durationHours = getDiffHours(startsAt, endsAt);

    if (durationHours < 0.5 || durationHours > 4) {
      throw new InvalidTimeSlotError('Duration must be between 30 minutes and 4 hours');
    }

    return new TimeSlot(new Date(startsAt), new Date(endsAt));
  }

  get startsAt(): Date {
    return new Date(this.startsAtValue);
  }

  get endsAt(): Date {
    return new Date(this.endsAtValue);
  }

  overlaps(other: TimeSlot): boolean {
    return this.startsAt < other.endsAt && other.startsAt < this.endsAt;
  }
}

Intervals that touch at their endpoints are allowed: 10:00–11:00 and 11:00–12:00 do not overlap. The strict comparisons encode that boundary explicitly.

Whether an interval starts in the past belongs to Visit.schedule, which receives now. An interval can be valid in isolation even when it is unsuitable for a new appointment. Separating those concepts makes each rule easier to understand.

5.4 Use a domain service for rules across objects

Availability depends on a technician, a requested interval, and existing visits. TechnicianAvailability receives those objects and rejects inactive technicians or overlapping scheduled visits.

It does not fetch records. The application supplies the information, and the domain service evaluates it. Cancelled visits do not block the interval, and visits belonging to other technicians do not cause a conflict.

This is a useful distinction when naming services: the domain service makes a business decision, while the application use case coordinates the data and steps needed to reach that decision.

Domain failures use typed errors derived from DomainError. They express concepts such as PendingRequiredTasksError and TechnicianUnavailableError without choosing their HTTP representation.

6. Let use cases coordinate the work

6.1 Define the capability the application needs

The service-order repository port exposes three operations:

import type { ServiceOrder } from '../../domain/model/service-order';

export const SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY = Symbol('SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY');

export interface ServiceOrderRepository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<ServiceOrder | null>;
  insert(order: ServiceOrder): Promise<void>;
  save(order: ServiceOrder): Promise<void>;
}

The contract speaks in domain objects. It does not expose Prisma arguments, SQL transactions, or HTTP responses. Separating insertion from saving also allows the adapter to distinguish a new aggregate from an existing one.

The finalization use case is correspondingly small. Imports are omitted here:

export class FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase extends ServiceOrderUseCaseBase {
  constructor(repository: ServiceOrderRepository) {
    super(repository);
  }

  async execute(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    const order = await this.loadOrThrow(orderId);
    order.finalize();
    await this.repository.save(order);
  }
}

The base class only loads the order and raises ServiceOrderNotFoundError when needed. The use case owns the sequence; the aggregate owns finalization rules; the repository owns persistence.

No Nest decorator is needed. A unit test can construct this class directly with a repository double.

6.2 A more involved example: schedule a visit

ScheduleVisitUseCase depends on four collaborators:

// Constructor excerpt from ScheduleVisitUseCase.
constructor(
  private readonly technicians: TechnicianRepository,
  private readonly visits: VisitRepository,
  private readonly serviceOrders: ServiceOrderLookup,
  private readonly availability: TechnicianAvailability,
) {}

Its command contains serviceOrderId, technicianId, startsAt, endsAt, and now, with dates represented as Date objects. HTTP string parsing happens before entering this boundary.

The use case creates the interval, loads the technician and order information, and checks that the order is CREATED or ASSIGNED. If the order already has an assigned technician, that technician must match the request. It also rejects an existing scheduled visit for that order.

Next it loads the technician's scheduled visits, asks the availability service to evaluate them, constructs Visit, and inserts it. Scheduling a visit does not automatically assign a technician to the service order; those are separate operations in the current model.

The split is practical: rules using the order information available to scheduling stay in the application, interval rules stay in TimeSlot, appointment lifecycle rules stay in Visit, and availability rules stay in the domain service.

Passing now makes scheduling deterministic in tests. The HTTP adapter currently supplies new Date(). Other order operations still use default timestamps, and there is no shared clock abstraction in this repository.

7. Connect HTTP and persistence through adapters

7.1 HTTP adapts request data to a command

The HTTP layer owns route decorators, Swagger metadata, DTOs, and request validation. Nest's global ValidationPipe uses whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted, and transform.

For visit scheduling, DTO validation checks UUIDs, strict ISO date strings, and explicit timezones. The controller converts those strings into dates and supplies the current time:

// Method excerpt from VisitsController; imports and constructor omitted.
@Post()
@ApiCreatedResponse({ description: 'Visit scheduled' })
async schedule(@Body() dto: ScheduleVisitDto): Promise<{ id: string }> {
  const id = await this.scheduleVisit.execute({
    serviceOrderId: dto.serviceOrderId,
    technicianId: dto.technicianId,
    startsAt: new Date(dto.startsAt),
    endsAt: new Date(dto.endsAt),
    now: new Date(),
  });

  return { id };
}

Another useful translation occurs when creating an order: the HTTP DTO accepts requiredTasks as objects with name, while the application receives an array of strings. A transport shape does not have to become the domain's shape.

Boundary validation and domain validation serve different callers. An invalid request should fail early, while direct application calls must still respect business invariants. A structurally valid date string can describe an interval that the business rejects.

7.2 Translate domain errors at the boundary

DomainExceptionFilter catches DomainError and maps its code to HTTP. For example:

Domain condition HTTP status
Technician or service order not found 404
Invalid interval or pending required tasks 422
Technician unavailable or invalid order transition 409
Optimistic concurrency conflict 409

DTO and pipe failures return 400. Domain failures produce a JSON body with statusCode, error, and message. Unmapped domain codes become 500 and are logged by the filter.

The domain can therefore evolve its rules without importing HttpException, and a future non-HTTP adapter can translate the same errors differently.

7.3 Persistence converts records into models

PrismaServiceOrderRepository implements the application port. Its findById loads the root and child records, maps database enums, converts nullable values, and calls ServiceOrder.rehydrate.

For writes, it stores a complete snapshot in a transaction: the root is inserted or updated, previous child rows are deleted, and the current collections are inserted. Pending domain events are written to the Outbox within that transaction as well.

This approach is straightforward for an educational aggregate with moderate collections. Its write cost grows with collection size because even unchanged children are replaced. A larger workload might justify tracking child changes or revisiting the aggregate boundary.

The Prisma schema represents persistence relationships. The domain model represents behavior. Keeping both explicit costs mapping code, but prevents a generated database record from becoming the only representation of the business.

8. Use NestJS as the composition point

TypeScript interfaces disappear at runtime. Nest therefore needs a runtime token to identify each outgoing dependency. This project uses symbols and factory providers.

The following is an excerpt of the providers in ServiceOrdersModule:

providers: [
  {
    provide: FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase,
    inject: [SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY],
    useFactory: (repository: ServiceOrderRepository) =>
      new FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase(repository),
  },
  { provide: SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY, useClass: PrismaServiceOrderRepository },
],

The adapter can use @Injectable() because it lives in infrastructure. The factory creates the plain application class and supplies its dependency. This is the connection between compile-time contracts and runtime objects, using Nest's custom provider facilities.

Modules are allowed to know concrete implementations: assembling those implementations is their job. The application itself does not select a repository or create a Prisma client.

In tests, the same use case can receive an in-memory adapter or a mock. Replacing an adapter remains subject to its contract and semantics; a remote store would introduce failure and consistency concerns that wiring alone cannot solve.

9. Integrate modules through a local contract

Visits needs a small amount of order information to decide whether scheduling is allowed. It declares its own contract rather than importing the complete order aggregate:

export interface ServiceOrderSchedulingInfo {
  id: string;
  status: 'CREATED' | 'ASSIGNED' | 'IN_PROGRESS' | 'FINALIZED' | 'CLOSED';
  assignedTechnicianId?: string;
}

export interface ServiceOrderLookup {
  findById(id: string): Promise<ServiceOrderSchedulingInfo | null>;
}

export const SERVICE_ORDER_LOOKUP = Symbol('SERVICE_ORDER_LOOKUP');

The ServiceOrderLookupAdapter calls the exported GetServiceOrderUseCase and maps its result to that local shape. It translates a missing-order error to null and propagates unexpected errors.

Visits application        Visits infrastructure       Orders application

ScheduleVisitUseCase
        |
        v
ServiceOrderLookup <----- ServiceOrderLookupAdapter --> GetServiceOrderUseCase
 (local contract)            (translation)                (exported by module)

The concrete cross-module dependency is concentrated in the adapter and module composition. The scheduling use case knows the local port, while VisitsModule imports ServiceOrdersModule to wire the adapter.

This is synchronous communication within one process. The order-closed event does not drive visit scheduling in the current implementation. Moving the integration to messaging would require new behavior around delivery, stale information, and retries.

10. Advanced concerns: reads, concurrent writes, and events

10.1 Shape reads around their consumers

Loading a complete aggregate makes sense when enforcing a state change. A list page usually needs a smaller view. service-orders separates ServiceOrderRepository from ServiceOrderQuery, whose methods return application views.

PrismaServiceOrderQuery maps records directly to those views without rehydrating an aggregate. List results are ordered by createdAt and id, both descending. The cursor carries both values so equal timestamps still have a deterministic order.

The adapter fetches one extra record to determine whether a next cursor exists. The use case validates limits between 1 and 100, with a default of 25, and validates filters and cursor data.

This is a pragmatic separation of reads and writes within one application and database. There are no command buses or asynchronous read projections. The visits module uses its repositories for reads; the example does not force both modules into identical abstractions.

10.2 Detect stale aggregate writes

Suppose two requests load order version 3. Both change their local object. Without a version check, the second save could overwrite the first request's work.

On update, the repository performs this check inside its transaction. The excerpt omits the surrounding persistence work:

const result = await tx.serviceOrderRecord.updateMany({
  where: { id: order.id, version: expectedVersion },
  data: { ...updateInput, version: { increment: 1 } },
});

if (result.count !== 1) throw new ServiceOrderConcurrencyError(order.id);

Only a matching version can advance. A stale write fails before replacing children or storing its events. New objects start at version 0 in memory and are inserted at version 1.

After the transaction commits, acknowledgePersistence advances the in-memory version and clears only the persisted event IDs. If persistence fails, the object keeps its previous version and pending events. The code does not automatically retry a stale business operation; the caller receives a conflict.

The repository also maps relevant Prisma errors to a concurrency error. See the complete adapter for its transaction and error handling.

10.3 Persist domain events atomically with state

Closing an order records ServiceOrderClosedEvent, named service-orders.service-order.closed.v1. Its payload includes order and contract IDs, worked minutes, materials, and the closure timestamp.

The repository copies pending events before entering the transaction and inserts each into outbox_events:

// Inside the same transaction that persists the aggregate.
for (const event of events) {
  await tx.outboxEventRecord.create({
    data: {
      id: event.eventId,
      eventName: event.eventName,
      aggregateId: event.aggregateId,
      payload: event.toPrimitives(),
      occurredAt: event.occurredAt,
    },
  });
}

The intended database guarantee is that the order state, children, and Outbox rows commit together or roll back together. This avoids a separate database write followed by a publication attempt that could be lost between the two steps.

There is currently no publisher worker, broker, or event consumer. publishedAt exists in the schema, but nothing in the repository marks events as delivered. Reliable publication would need a worker, retry behavior, and consumer idempotency. Outbox storage alone does not provide exactly-once delivery.

This is also different from Event Sourcing: the repository stores current aggregate state and selected events, rather than rebuilding orders from an event history.

10.4 Know where the guarantees stop

Visit scheduling reads availability and then inserts a visit. Two concurrent requests can both observe a free interval and both proceed. The schema has indexes for these queries, but no exclusion constraint or equivalent mechanism preventing overlaps or duplicate scheduled visits per order.

The service-order version check does not protect scheduling, technician deactivation, or cross-module reads. Those guarantees would need a separate design using appropriate database constraints, locking, or transaction isolation. Defining a rule in the domain and enforcing it under concurrency are related but distinct engineering tasks.

11. Test the behavior at each boundary

11.1 Domain tests require only the model

This test from the aggregate suite demonstrates the finalization rule. Imports and the createOrder fixture are omitted; the fixture creates an order with one pending required task:

it('cannot finalize while required tasks are pending', () => {
  const order = createOrder();
  order.assignTechnician(randomUUID());
  order.addActivity('Inspection', 30);

  expect(() => order.finalize()).toThrow(PendingRequiredTasksError);
});

No Nest module or database is involved. Other domain tests cover lifecycle transitions, snapshot integrity, copied dates, duration boundaries, overlapping versus adjacent intervals, and cancellation rules.

11.2 Application tests substitute outgoing ports

The finalization suite uses a real aggregate and a repository double. This is its successful path, without imports:

it('persists the finalized aggregate', async () => {
  const order = ServiceOrder.create({
    customerId: randomUUID(),
    contractId: randomUUID(),
    serviceAddress: 'Plant 1',
    serviceLevel: ServiceLevel.STANDARD,
  });

  order.assignTechnician(randomUUID());
  order.addActivity('Repair', 60);

  const repository = {
    findById: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(order),
    insert: jest.fn(),
    save: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  } satisfies ServiceOrderRepository;

  await new FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase(repository).execute(order.id);
  expect(repository.save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(order);
  expect(order.status).toBe(ServiceOrderStatus.FINALIZED);
});

The missing-order test also verifies that nothing is saved. This checks orchestration while leaving persistence mechanics to adapter tests.

11.3 Be precise about what integration tests prove

The current suite uses Jest, ts-jest, and Supertest:

Test level Real behavior exercised Replaced dependency
Domain Invariants and state changes None of the domain objects
Application Finalization coordination Repository
Visits HTTP Nest routing, DTOs, filters, real use cases Persistence and lookup ports
Module integration adapter Mapping and error translation External use case
Persistence and queries Prisma call contracts and mapping Prisma client

The HTTP tests open a local port and need permission to bind it. The persistence tests verify calls and application behavior around transactions using doubles; they do not demonstrate real PostgreSQL rollback, isolation, or races.

Run the suite and build with:

npm test -- --runInBand
npm run build

CI generates the Prisma client, runs tests, and builds on Node.js 22. It does not start PostgreSQL. A useful next validation layer would exercise migrations, transactions, and concurrent requests against a real disposable database. Existing coverage is useful without implying that every use case has exhaustive tests.

12. Run the project and follow an order

Use Node.js 22 or newer, npm, and Docker Compose. The project uses NestJS 11 and Prisma 6, with PostgreSQL 16 in Compose. Follow the repository's versions when reproducing these examples.

From a fresh checkout:

git clone https://github.com/Carlosgmdev/nest-ddd-hexagonal.git
cd nest-ddd-hexagonal
cp .env.example .env
npm install
docker compose up -d --wait
npm run prisma:generate
npm run db:deploy
npm run start:dev

db:deploy applies committed migrations; db:migrate is for creating migrations during development. The default database connection and port are in .env.example.

Swagger is available at http://localhost:3000/docs. The routes use /api, and GET /api/health returns a static application status rather than checking database connectivity.

First, register a technician:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/technicians \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ana Martinez"}'

Create an order without required tasks for a shorter walkthrough:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "customerId":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
    "contractId":"22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
    "serviceAddress":"Industrial Avenue 1200, Plant 2",
    "serviceLevel":"PREMIUM",
    "requiredTasks":[]
  }'

Both endpoints return { "id": "..." }. The customer and contract UUIDs are illustrative: this example has no customer or contract module validating their existence. Use the returned order and technician IDs in the next requests.

Replace <order-id> and <technician-id> in the following commands:

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/technician-assignment' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"technicianId":"<technician-id>"}'

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/activities' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"description":"Electrical inspection","workedMinutes":30}'

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/finalize'

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/close'

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>'

The mutation endpoints above return 204. The final read shows CLOSED, the activity, and lifecycle timestamps. The closure also persists an Outbox row, which can be inspected with npm run db:studio.

To explore visits, use a new order that is still CREATED or ASSIGNED, then call POST /api/visits with its ID, the technician ID, and future startsAt/endsAt values containing a timezone. Try a 15-minute slot, adjacent appointments, an overlap, and cancellation through POST /api/visits/:id/cancel. Swagger documents the request shapes.

13. Choose the structure when its benefits justify the cost

This approach makes business behavior easier to locate and test. Nest handles transport and composition, Prisma handles database access, and the core expresses the work the company performs. New entry points can reuse application operations, while adapters contain technology-specific translations.

The costs are real: more classes, mapping code, provider definitions, and contracts to maintain. A small application with simple data operations may be clearer with fewer abstractions. Business complexity, expected change, and testing needs provide better reasons for this structure than a desire to draw a hexagon.

The most useful lessons from this project are concrete: name operations in business terms, keep rules with the model that owns them, make external needs explicit through ports, and compose implementations at the edge. Test those boundaries and document exactly which consistency guarantees the current code provides.

If you extend the example, start with one new business rule and follow it through domain behavior, application coordination, adapters, and tests. Improvements such as real database integration tests, scheduling concurrency protection, and an Outbox publisher should each solve a specific observed need.

References and related reading

  • Complete NestJS example and README
  • Hexagonal Architecture — Alistair Cockburn
  • Custom providers — NestJS
  • TypeScript classes
  • My related guide: Implementing Hexagonal Architecture in React

What rule in your application currently requires a framework or database to test? That can be a useful place to begin applying these boundaries.

title: Beam model by Reflection is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart and AWS Trainium
description:
Beam, the first open weight model offered by US-based Reflection, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, the model hub in Amazon SageMaker AI. According to Beam, they operate at the frontier of open weight models in its class, with strong performance across reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks. Beam is for teams who build on and with an open weight model, not just call one. Customers who want to adapt a frontier model to their own domain can fine-tune it, inspect and modify its weights, and embed it deep in their agents and workflows, all while keeping full control of their data and infrastructure. Beam runs alongside other models that customers already use in SageMaker AI and scales to meet production demand with the same controls, audit trails, and monitoring built into every SageMaker AI deployment. Additionally, Beam was ported and optimized for AWS Trainium3, giving customers a high-performance, cost-efficient option for deploying and scaling the model from day one. “Reflection is delivering frontier AI that developers can actually control, not just rent through an API. Bringing Beam to SageMaker AI puts that capability in front of millions of developers on infrastructure they already trust, running in their own AWS account, on their own data, fully in their control," said Misha Laskin, co-founder and CEO, Reflection.

Teams building on Beam can take it well beyond calling an API: fine-tune it on proprietary code and data, specialize it for their own domains, and wire it into multi-step agentic workflows across their tools. In practice that means resolving real software issues, generating and reviewing code, automating operations work, and tackling advanced math and science reasoning on a model they can shape rather than one they simply consume. Because Beam is released under the Apache 2.0 license, customers can inspect and customize the model, while also running it in their own AWS accounts, so data stays private and under their control, protected by the same AWS security and compliance capabilities they already rely on. “Advanced AI models like Beam, now available on Amazon SageMaker, let us run open weight frontier AI entirely inside our own secure environments, with full visibility into the weights, the data, and the pipeline. In the age of multi-model AI, the pairing of openness and managed infrastructure is an essential addition to the AI ecosystem. The freedom to deploy and adapt advanced AI, tailored to mission problems with client-specific security and controls, gives more agencies greater flexibility to deploy advanced AI across their enterprise,” said Garrett Berntsen, Chief AI Officer, Accenture Federal Services.

Beam is initially available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). The model is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants, and can be deployed through a fully managed SageMaker JumpStart endpoint. To start, search for "Beam" in SageMaker JumpStart within Amazon SageMaker Studio, or deploy it directly on Sagemaker AI.  To learn more, read the AWS Machine Learning blog: Introducing Reflection Beam, SageMaker AI documentation and SageMaker JumpStart documentation for deployment guidance.
