title: We pointed AI testing agents at our own apps. 36/100, 79 issues. Here is what they found and what we fixed.
description:
Disclosure first: I'm on the team behind Preetest, an AI website-testing platform built by Yamama Software (Saudi Arabia). This post is about running that platform on Yamama Software's own apps. These are our own apps scanned with our own platform, not an independent audit. Every number below comes from a real report; the report links are public (they open behind a cookie-consent prompt you can decline, so I have also put a screenshot of each report's summary page below). This write-up was drafted by the AI assistant that runs our testing and fixes, from those reports, at the founder's direction.

What Preetest is, in one paragraph

Preetest is a platform, not a company. You give it a URL (and a login if the app needs one). It runs AI testing agents, each with a specialty (accessibility, performance, security headers, mobile layout, SEO, forms, caching and so on; the platform lists 17 specialties, and each of the standard runs below used 9 agents covering 8 of 14 aspects), and writes one report: a score out of 100, every issue with severity and the element it was found on, and a fix prompt per issue that you can paste into Cursor, Claude Code or whatever you build with.

Run 1: our internal office suite

A 10-page signed-in scan of the staff suite we use ourselves (documents, mail, calendar, chat).

Score: 36/100. 79 issues: 0 critical, 3 high, 31 medium, 45 low, 0 info. Known-screen coverage 44 %.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/z1LctGGKyBvPlZIcTkeh4w

The findings that mattered:

  • Every static file was served with Cache-Control: max-age=0. Every visit re-downloaded every script. High severity, and correct.
  • The cross-app sign-in put the user's email and name in a GET ?t= parameter. Medium. Also correct; that lands in server logs and browser history.
  • The "export all my data" action was a plain GET link with no confirmation. Medium.
  • Bottom navigation at 390 px wide cut off the "Mail" label. Low, but it is the first thing a phone user sees.

Run 2: the same app, after two small fixes. The score went down.

We fixed the export confirmation and one accessible-name issue, re-ran with the same settings, and got 29/100. 101 issues: 0 critical, 8 high, 35 medium, 57 low, 1 info (the report's issue card shows 100, because it does not count the info item). Known-screen coverage 51 %.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/AIykp03BiPhDdXf2jn-Lww

Why worse? The second run reached more screens (the calendar, the staff guide, the privacy and download pages), so it found more. Coverage is budget-based: each run stops when its token reservation runs out, and the two runs stopped at different pages. So this is not a clean before/after, and I am not going to present it as one. What the second run added was the most useful finding of the day:

  • The calendar had 49 column-header cells with no role="row" parent, and 42 day buttons using aria-pressed, which their role does not support. Plus text at 4.12:1 contrast where 4.5:1 is required.
  • LCP of 4.7 s on the documents page. The assistant greeting waited on about 1.5 MB of scripts.

Run 3: a small Expo web app

Score: 53/100. 27 issues: 0 critical, 5 high, 11 medium, 10 low, 1 info (the issue card shows 26 for the same reason). 100 % known-screen coverage, 143 tokens used.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/BTlW0oUUg-ybJZQxCpPyKA

  • Unknown URLs returned 200 instead of 404 (soft 404). High.
  • No header / main / footer / nav landmarks. High.
  • The onboarding "Next" control was not exposed as a button to screen readers. High.
  • sitemap.xml served as HTML; a JSON data file served with no caching.

What we changed, and how much of it is proven

Plainly: none of the fixes below has been confirmed by a Preetest re-run yet. The only full rescan we did after fixing anything is run 2 above, and it scored lower because it covered more screens. There is no improvement to show, implied or otherwise. What follows is what we changed and how we checked each change ourselves.

Changed, and verified by us (not by the platform):

  • Calendar ARIA: headers and weeks now sit inside role="row", day cells use aria-selected, arrow keys move between days. Verified with axe-core on that page: 92 ARIA violations plus 33 contrast failures before, 0 after.
  • Contrast: the faint purple went from #7c6fd6 (4.12:1) to #5a4cc0 (6.5:1). Verified by computing the ratio.
  • Mobile bar: five apps plus a "More" button. Verified with our own screenshots at 360, 390 and 412 px; nothing cut off.
  • Caching: versioned JS/CSS now sent with a one-year cache header. Verified by reading the response headers; a repeat visit to the documents page renders in under a second in our timing.
  • Expo app: unknown URLs now return a real 404 status, the page has landmarks, "Next" has a real button role, sitemap.xml is served as XML, versioned files get a long cache. Verified with HTTP requests and a DOM check, not with a rescan.
  • A bug the 404 fix exposed: 19 icon font files had been missing from the deploy the whole time. The old catch-all returned an HTML page with status 200 for them, so nothing ever errored. Restored and checksum-checked. Soft 404s hide real breakage; that one finding paid for the run.

Not fixed, or not proven:

  • The documents page first load is still about 4 s. Only repeat visits got faster.
  • We moved the sign-in token out of the URL, but have not yet tested a real signed-in hop between apps with a staff account, so I am not calling it fixed.
  • No Preetest rescan since the bigger fixes, so there is no "after" score. When there is one, I will add it here, whichever way it goes.

Where the agents were wrong

  • It flagged /api/config on the Expo app as "returns private data with no auth". It returns public settings (app name, support links, public client ids). False positive.
  • It flagged a missing aria-current on the docs sidebar. The source already renders it on the active button.
  • It flagged noindex on the internal editor as high. That is intended; it is a staff tool.

So: a sharp junior QA that works at 3 a.m., not an oracle. Read the report, do not paste every fix prompt blindly.

Pricing, honestly

The free plan is 50 tokens. Our smallest real run above used 143, so the free tokens get you a project set up and a look at the flow, not a full inspection. A standard inspection is roughly 1,000 tokens, which is the $29/month plan. The platform also refuses to scan its own domain, so you cannot run it on preetest.com.

If you try it on your own app, I would genuinely like to hear where it was wrong. That list above is the one we work from.

Honest reviews wanted (from the Preetest team)

We are collecting reviews from people who actually used Preetest, good or bad.

Try it on your own site, then write a review on Trustpilot: https://www.trustpilot.com/evaluate/preetest.com. We give one month of the Starter plan ($29) free for a published review. The month is for writing a review, not for a rating: a 1-star review with real reasons gets it exactly like a 5-star one. Please say in the review that you received free access.

To have enough tokens for a full scan, sign up through https://app.preetest.com/register?ref=KJZDCYB4 (adds 300 bonus tokens to the 50 free ones once you confirm your email).

Email preetest.team@mail.tab.bot with the address you signed up with and the link to your review.

title: Run Terminal-Bench and other Harbor evals on Vercel Sandbox

You can now run Harbor evals on Vercel Sandbox.

Harbor is the open-source harness behind Terminal-Bench, whose registry includes many other benchmarks such as SWE-bench, tau3-bench and OSWorld. Pass --env vercel to harbor run and each trial executes in its own isolated Firecracker microVM, so you can parallelize far beyond what your local machine is capable of.

A task's network policy is enforced at the sandbox firewall, outside the VM. Optional credential injection attaches secrets to matching outbound requests at that firewall, so they never enter the sandbox.

Paired with AI Gateway, one AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY reaches hundreds of models from multiple providers, and benchmarking another model is the same command with a different --model:

title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
description:
arXiv:2610.27230v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

title: Batch Deploying GBase Database with a Response File
description:
Deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s) across multiple servers can become repetitive if every installation requires manual interaction. A response file provides a more consistent approach by defining installation parameters once and reusing them across deployment targets.

Combined with shell scripts and remote execution tools such as SSH, silent installation can become part of a repeatable database deployment workflow.

The goal is not simply to install software faster. It is to make the deployment process easier to validate, maintain, and reproduce.

1. Prepare the Response File

Start by preparing a bundle.properties response file using the template supplied with your GBase Database installation media or by recording a supported interactive installation.

Review the installation directory, selected components, license-acceptance settings, and any other required parameters.

Before deploying to multiple machines, test the response file on one representative server. Confirm that the installation succeeds and that the resulting database instance can be configured and started correctly.

Keep environment-specific settings separate where necessary. Different servers may require different paths, resource configurations, or connection definitions.

2. Create a Reusable Installation Script

The following Bash example checks for the response file and installer before starting silent installation.

#!/bin/bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

RESP="/opt/bundle.properties"
INSTALLER="/opt/ids_install"

# Verify required files
[[ -f "$RESP" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing response file: $RESP" >&2
    exit 1
}

[[ -x "$INSTALLER" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Installer is missing or not executable: $INSTALLER" >&2
    exit 1
}

# Run silent installation
"$INSTALLER" -i silent \
    -f "$RESP" \
    -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

echo "Silent installation command completed."

Save the script as install_gbase.sh and make it executable:

chmod +x install_gbase.sh

The script uses set -Eeuo pipefail to help detect command failures and prevent certain errors from being silently ignored.

The installer command shown here is an example. Confirm its supported options and license-acceptance requirements against the documentation for your specific installation package.

Also note that a successful installer exit does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for application connections. Post-installation configuration and validation remain necessary.

3. Execute the Installation on Multiple Servers

For a small environment, SSH and SCP can distribute the response file and execute the installation script remotely.

For example:

#!/bin/bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

RESP="/opt/bundle.properties"
SCRIPT="/opt/install_gbase.sh"
HOSTS=(node1 node2 node3)

[[ -f "$RESP" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing response file" >&2
    exit 1
}

[[ -f "$SCRIPT" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing installation script" >&2
    exit 1
}

for host in "${HOSTS[@]}"; do
    echo "Deploying to $host..."

    scp "$RESP" "$SCRIPT" "root@$host:/opt/"

    ssh "root@$host" \
        "bash /opt/install_gbase.sh"

    echo "Installation command completed on $host."
done

This example processes the hosts sequentially, which makes execution easier to follow and failures easier to isolate.

Before using it, ensure that SSH authentication, host-key verification, remote permissions, and installation prerequisites are configured correctly.

The example also assumes that the installer is already available at /opt/ids_install on every target server. If it is not, include distribution and verification of the installation media in the deployment workflow.

Important: Running the installer as root should follow the supported installation procedure. Instance initialization may require switching to the designated database account, such as gbasedbt. Do not assume installation and initialization use the same account.

4. Add Post-Installation Configuration and Validation

Batch installation should not stop when the installer exits.

A complete GBase Database deployment workflow should also address:

  • Environment variables: Configure the required instance-specific environment.
  • Configuration files: Review onconfig and sqlhosts for the target server.
  • Instance initialization: Run the documented initialization procedure using the appropriate operating system account.
  • Service validation: Confirm that the instance starts and client connections succeed.
  • Logging: Record the host, installation result, and relevant diagnostic output.

These steps should be implemented according to the selected installation method and the requirements of your environment.

Avoid reporting a server as successfully deployed until the required validation checks have passed.

5. Make Batch Deployment Reproducible

For larger deployments, consider a few additional safeguards.

Version-control the response file and scripts. Review changes before they are used in production.

Protect sensitive configuration. Do not store passwords, private keys, or other secrets in ordinary response files or source repositories.

Control deployment concurrency. Start with sequential execution. Introduce parallel deployment only after validating resource requirements and failure handling.

Make reruns safe. Check whether a target already has an installation or running instance before executing the installer again. A failed deployment should not automatically trigger an unsafe reinstall.

Maintain a recovery procedure. Record installation logs and define how failed or partially completed deployments will be investigated and corrected.

For larger fleets, configuration-management tools can provide better inventory management, controlled concurrency, and centralized execution reporting than a collection of ad hoc shell commands.

Conclusion

Batch deployment of GBase Database(GBase 8s) starts with a validated response file and a reliable installation script. SSH and SCP can extend that workflow across multiple machines, while configuration management and automated checks help maintain consistency as the environment grows.

The essential principle is simple: standardize the installation inputs, validate the results, and make failures visible.

How does your team manage database deployments across multiple servers: shell scripts, SSH automation, or a configuration-management platform?

title: Python Automation, Machine Learning, or AI? A Practical Guide
description:
Python gives you several ways to solve a problem: a deterministic script, a machine-learning model, or an AI feature that works with unstructured input. The right choice is usually the least complex approach that meets the requirement and can be checked.

Start with the shape of the problem

Ask what the software must do, what information it can use, and what happens when it is wrong. A stable rule and a fuzzy prediction are different engineering problems, even if both can be described as “using AI.”

Need A sensible starting point Why
Move, rename, validate, or transform known data Python automation The rules are explicit and results are repeatable.
Apply a stable business rule Ordinary Python logic A test can describe the expected result directly.
Predict a category or value from examples Machine learning A model may help when patterns are difficult to encode as fixed rules.
Summarize or extract meaning from varied text A language model with review The input is unstructured, and outputs need evaluation and guardrails.

The table is a starting point, not a substitute for requirements. A Python application can combine these approaches: validate inputs with ordinary code, call a model for one uncertain step, and keep a person in the loop when the result matters.

When rules are enough

Use a regular Python function when the rule is known and should behave the same way every time. Rules are easier to test, explain, and maintain. They are often the right answer for file processing, format checks, calculations, integrations, and workflow automation.

If the rule list keeps growing because inputs vary in subtle ways, that is a signal to review the problem. More exceptions do not automatically mean machine learning is needed; the process or data may simply need clarification.

When machine learning may help

Machine learning is worth evaluating when there are representative examples, a pattern to learn, and a measurable definition of success. Before training or selecting a model, check that the examples reflect real use, labels are consistent, and the evaluation data is kept separate from training data.

Choose a metric that matches the cost of mistakes. In a screening workflow, for example, a false negative may matter more than a false positive. Accuracy alone can hide that difference. Review errors by category and test on new examples before relying on predictions.

When generative AI fits

A language model can be useful for varied text tasks such as drafting, summarizing, or extracting candidate fields. Its output is probabilistic: the same prompt can produce different wording, and a confident answer can still be wrong.

Treat generated output as a suggestion unless the task is low risk and quality has been carefully tested. Validate structure, protect sensitive data, set clear limits, and provide a review path for uncertain or consequential results. A model should not quietly make a decision that the process owner expects a person to make.

A practical evaluation sequence

  1. Define the outcome and what counts as an acceptable result.
  2. Build the smallest deterministic baseline you can measure.
  3. Collect representative examples and identify likely failure cases.
  4. Compare alternatives using the same evaluation set and cost assumptions.
  5. Decide how to handle low-confidence, invalid, or high-impact cases.
  6. Monitor behavior after release; input patterns and model performance can change.

Python is useful across this process: it can prepare data, run checks, connect services, expose a web API, and automate repeatable work. The model is only one component. Good system design also accounts for privacy, latency, cost, maintenance, and a way to recover when something fails.

The short version

Choose Python rules when the rules are known. Evaluate machine learning when examples reveal a pattern that is difficult to express directly. Consider generative AI for genuinely unstructured tasks, with testing and human oversight appropriate to the risk. If a simple baseline solves the problem, keep the solution simple.

I'm Kyle Keon, a Python developer in Pembroke, Ontario, focused on practical work across AI, workflow automation, machine learning, and web development. Portfolio and contact.

title: Do We Need the Largest LLMs for Every Clinical Decision?
description:
arXiv:2610.26937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large clinical language models often require multi-GPU infrastructure, limiting local deployment. We introduce CERTA, a decision-level statistical certificate that determines when a quantized model may substitute for its native BF16 reference and escalates decisions that cannot be certified to it. Across eleven instruction-tuned models, both general-purpose and domain-adapted, from three families (7-72B), we evaluated 2,500 clinical-verification decisions from de-identified patient contexts (2,484 patients), with patient-disjoint calibration and testing. In the higher-power operational analysis, round-to-nearest 8-bit quantization at BF16 storage served 99.8-100% of held-out decisions across all eleven models; formal finite-sample guarantees were assessed separately using the exact split-sample procedure. In the same operational analysis, the class-conditional 4-bit frontier reduced the amortized, BF16-equivalent deployment cost to 25.8% and 27.3% of the BF16 reference for Qwen2.5-72B and HuatuoGPT-o1-72B, respectively, with measured peak memory of 43.0 and 42.7 GB, below the nominal capacity of a single 48 GB accelerator. Deployment on that specific hardware was not directly tested. Under the exact split-sample certificate, which also accounts for configuration selection, these costs were 26.7% and 27.9%. On external disease named-entity benchmarks against human annotations, the frontier-selected NF4 configurations had a mean absolute F1 change of 0.045 on both datasets, with substantial model-specific variation. CERTA converts compression from a fixed precision choice into a risk-controlled deployment policy for this verification task.

title: v0 now reads npm credentials from shared environment variables
description:
v0 now installs private packages from npm and custom registries using credentials stored as shared environment variables on Vercel.

This makes it easier for teams to build with their existing design systems, component libraries, and internal packages directly in v0.

To get started, add one of the following as a shared environment variable on Vercel, scoped to Development and/or Preview:

  • Use NPM_TOKEN for private packages hosted on registry.npmjs.org.

  • Use NPM_RC to configure custom or multiple registries.

NPM_RC supports scoped registries and references to other environment variables. For example, configure an organization scope such as @acme for GitHub Packages, or direct package requests through a private JFrog Artifactory registry.

Credentials can be marked sensitive, and v0 never exposes them to the model or writes them to the sandbox filesystem.

You can view the integration status from Settings → Integrations in v0.

Learn more in the private dependencies docs.

title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
description:
arXiv:2610.27159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.

title: Dark Mode Design Best Practices: What Google, Apple, and the Research Say
description:
Dark mode is a table-stakes feature now, and most teams still build it the laziest way possible: take the light theme, flip the colors, ship it. The result is an app that looks like a photographic negative — gray text on black soup, brand colors that scream, cards you can barely tell apart from the background. Google and Apple both wrote detailed specs explaining why that approach is wrong. And the battery story that justifies half of it? For most users it's 3–9%, not the headline numbers.

The battery myth: 47% is real, and it almost never applies to you

The strongest battery claim comes from good science. Purdue researchers Pranab Dash and Y. Charlie Hu built a per-pixel OLED power profiler and tested four phones (Pixel 2, Moto Z3, Pixel 4, Pixel 5) across six Google apps. Switching from light to dark mode saved 39–47% of display power — at 100% brightness. That's the number everyone quotes.

Here's the part that doesn't fit in a headline: at 30–50% brightness, the saving was 3–9%. Most people use auto-brightness, which sits around 30–40% indoors. The researchers' verdict was blunt: the saving is so small at normal indoor brightness that most users wouldn't notice. On LCD screens — budget phones, most laptops, older iPads — it's essentially zero, because the backlight stays on regardless of pixel color.

Dark mode is a real battery feature outdoors at max brightness, where the 39–47% shows up. Everywhere else it's a comfort and aesthetics feature. Stop selling it as battery management and start designing it as what it is.

Don't invert — rebuild: what Google's spec actually says

Google's Material Design dark theme guidance reads like a direct answer to the invert-and-ship crowd. The baseline surface is #121212, not pure black. Text comes in two tiers: white at 87% opacity for high-emphasis text, 60% for medium. The big idea is elevation: since dark shadows are invisible on a dark background, depth is communicated by making higher surfaces brighter — thin white overlays on top of the base surface, getting stronger with elevation. In Google's codelab, a bottom app bar gets the base #121212 plus a 12% white overlay. Cards, dialogs, and sheets all follow the same logic.

Color gets a rule most teams skip: desaturate. Saturated brand colors vibrate against dark backgrounds, so Material tells you to pull them back and use them sparingly — "limited color accents," preferring the surface color over the primary color in most chrome. Even your error red needs a dark-mode version: the same fire-engine red that reads fine on white vibrates on black, so the guidance is a dustier, dimmer red. If your red is still shouting at the same volume in dark mode, nobody adjusted it.

Apple took a different path — and both agree on one rule

Apple's approach is semantic instead of numeric. iOS (since 2019's iOS 13) and macOS define colors as roles — label, secondaryLabel, systemBackground — that automatically adapt to the trait environment. Use UIColor.label and dark mode mostly handles itself; hardcode a hex for your text and you've broken dark mode before you tested it. Apple's actual values show the same discipline as Material's: label text is white at 85% opacity, elevated cards step up through dark grays (#1C1C1E, #2C2C2E) to signal depth, and community measurements put dark-mode systemBlue slightly brighter than its light-mode counterpart to hold its contrast.

One disagreement worth noting: Apple's base system background is pure black (#000000), where Material explicitly avoids it. The honest reading: Apple's black maximizes OLED savings and contrast for content; Material's dark gray is friendlier for long sessions and makes elevation layering visible. Both are defensible. What neither defends is a theme nobody designed.

Contrast doesn't retire when you go dark

A common assumption is that dark mode is automatically more accessible. The opposite can be true: light text on black at full strength causes halation — text that seems to bleed into the background — which is why the platforms cap text opacity at 85–87% instead of pure white. WCAG's 4.5:1 ratio for body text still applies; it just gets harder to eyeball on a dark canvas, especially for saturated accents.

Practical checks that catch the most failures: view the whole UI in grayscale to expose contrast problems instantly; re-check every accent color against its dark background (your light theme's accessible blue is often a failing blue in the dark); and never trust the simulator — test on a real OLED screen outdoors, where dark interfaces lose legibility fastest. For contrast science beyond the old 4.5:1 rule, the perceptual color work in my OKLCH and APCA guide applies here too.

Type, images, and the ten small things

The details that separate a designed dark theme from a flipped one: bump font weights slightly — thin type that was elegant in black-on-white turns spindly in white-on-black; small text may need a size bump too, since the readability gap between modes grows as type gets smaller. Images and logos need dark-mode variants or at least transparent backgrounds, or you'll ship white boxes around every logo. QR codes are a real gotcha: an inverted QR code won't scan. Interactive states (hover, pressed, disabled) must stay distinct without relying on brightness alone. And animate the theme switch with a subtle transition — a hard flash at midnight is the kind of detail users feel even if they never name it.

Respect the user: give them the switch, then listen to the data

Ship both modes, default to the system preference via prefers-color-scheme, and always offer a manual toggle that persists. A Nielsen Norman Group survey of 115 mobile users found opinion split exactly three ways: a third want dark, a third want light, a third switch. There is no default everyone loves.

And here's the finding every designer should sit with: in NNGroup's summary of the German readability research (Piepenbrock and colleagues, Institut für Experimentelle Psychologie Düsseldorf), light mode won on every measured dimension — visual acuity and proofreading, for young and old adults — and produced no difference in fatigue. Yet participants reported no difference in readability. As NNGroup puts it: don't listen to users. Measure the reading task.

The takeaway isn't "ship light mode only." It's that the mode that looks good in a screenshot and the mode that performs in a reading test are different problems, and a designed dark theme accounts for both.

What to do this week

Audit your dark theme with five checks: is your base surface dark gray rather than pure black (or pure black with a deliberate reason)? Does elevation make cards brighter instead of relying on shadows? Is your loudest accent color desaturated relative to light mode? Does body text clear 4.5:1 on the actual dark background? And can a user override the system default? If any answer is no, you don't have a dark theme yet — you have an inverted light one.

References

  • Nielsen Norman Group — "Dark Mode vs. Light Mode: Which Is Better?" — summary of Piepenbrock et al. readability studies; 115-user preference survey (1/3 dark, 1/3 light, 1/3 mixed)
  • ScienceDaily — "Dark mode may not save your phone's battery life as much as you think" — Purdue Dash Hu OLED profiler study (MobiSys '21): 3–9% savings at 30–50% brightness, 39–47% at 100%
  • Google Codelabs — "Design a dark theme with Material and Figma" — #121212 surface, 87%/60% text opacity, elevation overlays, limited color accents
  • Android Developers — Material Design 2 in Compose — elevation overlay behavior, primarySurface limited-accent guidance
  • Median.co — "Apple's Human Interface Guidelines: Dark Mode do's and don'ts" — semantic colors, vibrancy, base/elevated backgrounds
  • AppCherish — "Dark Mode Isn't Optional Anymore" — iOS semantic-color checklist, hardcoded-color pitfalls since iOS 13

title: The 13% Penalty: Why Synchronous APIs Still Scale Better Than You Think"
description:
When I built a lightweight framework to act as a data marshal for my decoupled single page apps, I didn’t intend to write an architectural thesis, but along the way, the data forced me to confront three pervasive myths in modern web development. First, PHP is inherently slow, second that synchronous APIs can’t scale to modern demand, and finally that you must trade developer experience for raw performance. I confronted these assumptions the only way that matters, by building. I created a framework called mouse-php, created CLI tooling that eliminated micro-framework friction, and stress tested said framework to failure. What the benchmarking revealed was illuminating. The industry consensus around these three ideas aren’t built on hard engineering limits but misattribution, vendor marketing, cargo-culting, and outdated assumptions. Here’s the story of that build, the benchmark data behind it, and why low-level simplicity routinely beats over-engineered complexity.

When I set out to build mouse-php, my goal was to create a lightweight API that acted strictly as a data marshal for decoupled single page applications. Some choices were obvious, like stripping out framework bloat and keeping execution linear. However, I quickly realized that most lightweight solutions sacrifice developer velocity in the name of absolute performance. This exposes a false dichotomy in modern web development: the belief that developer conveniences must always come at the expense of runtime performance. Because I built mouse-php to solve my own production friction, I focused on creating low overhead pipelines that preserve developer ergonomics, this led to three distinct architectural choices.

1. The Inverse-MVC Pattern & Thin PDO Data Marshals

Traditional MVC frameworks push heavy ORMs and deep object graphs into giant models. In mouse-php, I inverted this relationship and completely ditched the ORM in favor of a clean, structured PDO wrapper. My primary motivation for dropping the ORM wasn’t raw performance, it was Developer Experience. The idea that ORMs deliver a superior DX is a shallow illusion. ORMs make trivial queries like User::find(1) look convenient, but simple requests were never difficult to manage in the first place. The moment an API requires real world database operations requiring complex JOINs, aggregations, or precise index targeting the ORM becomes a hindrance rather than helpful. Developers end up having to fight method chains, specific esoteric syntax, and performance killing abstractions just to perform queries that could have been written in three lines of SQL. By replacing ORM with an easy to parse PDO wrapper, mouse-php models act as bare metal data marshals executing raw, prepared SQL statements while still being easy to maintain.

  • Better DX: Developers write clear, explicit SQL without fighting dynamic query builders or dynamic relation tracking.
  • Zero Hydration Tax: Bypasses object instantiation and reflection entirely, fetching database results directly into native arrays at C-speed.
  • High Reusability: Because models are reduced to simple data pipes rather than stateful domain objects, a single query model can be applied across multiple controllers or background jobs without instantiating heavy object trees.

The performance boost of keeping database overhead under 1ms is simply the natural byproduct of choosing a cleaner developer interface.

2. Associative Array First Routing

Industry standard routers rely heavily on complex regex engines to parse dynamic URIs on every incoming request. In mouse-php, the routing engine uses associative array hash lookup first. Because decoupled SPAs communicate most efficiently via explicit RPC-style endpoints, direct match routes can be resolved instantly at C-speed using PHP’s native array key lookups. While dynamic URIs are still supported for standard REST compatibility, they are treated as secondary paths. Bypassing regex route parsing for the majority of API traffic eliminates a massive chunk of per-request CPU tax.

3. One Way Middleware (Abandoning the Onion Model)

Most modern frameworks use an “onion model” where middleware wraps both the incoming request and outgoing response in nested closure. I always hated dealing with onion middleware in heavy frameworks, debugging nested execution stacks across response boundaries was a constant source of friction as well as trying to just figure out how to use it in some cases. I moved mouse-php to a strict one way pipeline simply to make middleware easier to write, manage, and debug. But just as with the PDO wrapper, simplifying the DX revealed a blueprint built for high-throughput performance. In this linear model, middleware has only two jobs: guarding the application and injecting context.

  • Fast Escapes: If an authentication check fails, the pipeline immediately triggers an escape hatch and terminates the request early, preventing the request from controller instantiation entirely.
  • Direct Context Injection: For example if an auth check queries user details, it injects that data directly into the request payload. The downstream controller receives pre-hydrated context without making a second query.

Middleware never touches outgoing responses. Any final response formatting happens predictably in the controller layer via lightweight utilities. By replacing wrapped stack frames with a simple, unidirectional pipeline, we gain total debugging clarity and linear execution speed.

Once mouse-php was running, I needed empirical data to verify its throughput limits. Benchmarking modern HTTP APIs accurately is surprisingly nuanced; preliminary tests with closed loop tools like autocannon produced inconsistent, warped latency figures, likely due to Coordinated Omission. To get accurate, un-skewed latency profiles, I migrated the test bench to wrk2, an open loop benchmarking tool that maintains a fixed, constant throughput rate.

The Test Environment

All benchmarks were executed locally on bare-metal hardware to isolate the stack’s raw execution capability:

  • Hardware: Lenovo IdeaPad 5 2-in-1 (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, 16GB LPDDR5)
  • Operating System: Arch Linux (Kernel 7.2.8, KDE Plasma, non-essential background processes terminated)
  • CGI & Web Server: Apache httpd paired with PHP 8.5 PHP-FPM
  • PHP Runtime Tuning: OPcache enabled with aggressive timestamp checking disabled, JIT compiler active.

Test Parameters & Sweeps

  • Load Profile: wrk2 was configured with 4 threads, 100 concurrent connections, and a 60-second duration per run.
  • Rate Sweeps: Tests began at a 100 Req/s baseline and scaled up in increments to locate the framework's saturation knee.
  • Averaging & Outliers: Each target request rate was executed in three 60 second rounds and averaged together. If an anomalous system hiccup occurred, a 4th validation run was conducted to eliminate system jitter.
  • Thermal Mitigation: Because mobile SoCs aggressively thermal-throttle under sustained multi-core loads, a mandatory 5 minute system idle break was enforced between every run above 10,000 Req/s to prevent thermal soak from skewing tail-latency measurements.
  • Middleware Context Disclosures: Test endpoints were assigned to the native global_bypass middleware group. This bypassed client facing rate limiters and payload formatting guards that would otherwise reject standard synthetic wrk2 traffic, while mirroring how high throughput public endpoints are configured in production.

Using these test parameters, our control run targeted a route that returned a static JSON payload, isolating mouse-php’s routing request handling, and output pipeline from external I/O bound dependencies.

Static Endpoint Results

Req/S Average Latency(ms) P99 Latency(ms) Max Latency(ms)
100 1.6 3.75 4.69
500 1.58 3.58 4.64
1000 1.43 2.49 3.29
2000 1.41 2.12 2.75
5000 1.7 2.82 14.74
10,000 3.08 4.59 45.18
12,000 1.66 3.13 37.12
14,000 1.78 4.81 51.7
15,000 1.79 4.53 52.73
15,500 2 11.88 74.94
16,000 1.93 13.61 68.73
17,000 1.99 12.4 57.15
17,500 2.27 19.4 72.04
18,000 3550 6843.33 7446.67

Analyzing this dataset reveals clear systems level behaviors regarding where the stack excels and precisely where hardware limits force it to break:

  1. The 2000 Req/s Efficiency Sweet Spot:

    Across the entire test suite, 2000 Req/s represents the optimal operational state. At this rate, latency hits its absolute minimum across all metrics : 1.41ms Average, 2.12ms P99, and a tight 2.75ms Max Latency. This is where request frequency perfectly aligns with CPU governor frequency scaling, worker process scheduling, and L1/L2 cache retention without triggering thread contention or queue accumulation.

  2. The 15,000 Req/s P99 stability Zone:

    While Max Latency tail drift begins decoupling after 2000 Req/s as individual process scheduling delays occur, the Average and P99 latency curves remain tightly locked together all the way to 15,000 Req/s. P99 latency does not break 5ms across a 15x increase in load. This proves that under normal operating conditions, 99% of requests pass through the framework’s array routing and one-way pipeline nearly instantaneously.

  3. The Warning Sign (15,500 Req/s):

    At 15,500 Req/s, P99 jumps from 4.53ms to 11.88ms. This decoupling between Average Latency(~2.0ms) and P99 marks the inflection point where OS socket backlogs and FastCGI worker queues begin running near capacity.

  4. The 17,500 Req/s Saturation Knee:

    The system maintains stability up to 17,500 Req/s with a 2.27ms average response time. Pushing the load to 18,000 Req/s causes the latency to explode immediately to 3.55 seconds.

This vertical wall isn’t an application level framework crash, it is classic FastCGI socket backlog exhaustion. When incoming connection rates exceed available PHP-FPM process slots, the OS TCP backlog fills up, incoming requests queue in kernel space, and the system hits its absolute physical CGI throughput ceiling on this hardware.

With the static baseline established, the next phase of stress-testing targeted an API endpoint that executes a live database query on every request, simulating a realistic application workload.

Database Endpoint Results

Req/S Average Latency(ms) P99 Latency(ms) Max Latency(ms)
100 2.2 4.94 5.59
500 1.66 3.8 5.04
1000 1.52 2.64 3.46
2000 1.63 2.63 4.03
5000 1.96 3.2 15.48
10,000 3.43 5.83 55.38
12,000 1.69 3.29 37.42
13,000 1.93 6.02 56.91
14,000 1.98 11.38 59.11
15,000 2.26 13.71 60.84
15,250 2.27 16.4 58.37
16,000 3380 6755 7280

Comparing this dataset directly against our static control run reveals a great deal about mouse-php's execution efficiency under real-world I/O pressure:

  1. The Remarkable 13% Delta:

    The standout takeaway from these benchmarks is how little performance degrades when introducing a database query. Moving from a static JSON response to a live MariaDB lookup shifts our maximum stable throughput ceiling from 17,500 Req/s down to 15,250 Req/s is a mere 13% reduction. In typical web frameworks, the ORM and object hydration layer create a massive performance cliff. Here, because mouse-php uses a thin PDO wrapper that bypasses hydration overhead entirely, the database roundtrip adds less than 1ms of average latency across the board.

  2. The Persistent 2,000 Req/s Sweet Spot:

    Just like the static control run, 2,000 Req/s remains the absolute peak efficiency zone. Even with database reads executing on every single request, the system hits its tightest latency alignment (1.63ms Average, 2.63ms P99) right at this threshold. This confirms that CPU cache locality and process scheduling dynamics dominate the profile long before database I/O becomes the bottleneck.

  3. Predictable P99 Coupling & Early Decoupling:

    The P99 latency behavior mirrors the static control curve, though it begins its upward drift slightly earlier (~13,000 to 14,000 Req/s). This minor variance makes complete sense: as concurrent requests climb, the local MariaDB connection pool and socket buffers absorb additional load, causing occasional tail-latency stretching just before the saturation threshold.

  4. The 15,250 Req/s Saturation Wall:

    At 15,250 Req/s, the system holds the line with a sub-3ms average latency (2.27ms). Pushing past this edge to 16,000 Req/s triggers an immediate system blowout, with average latency jumping to 3.38 seconds. Just like the static run, this wall represents the physical concurrency limit of our local FastCGI and database socket queues on mobile hardware, rather than an application-layer failure.

The parallel behavior of these two charts tells a definitive story. mouse-php is bounded primarily by operating system socket limits, CGI throughput, and local hardware constraints, not by the application code or data-fetching pipeline. When your database backed endpoints can sustain over 15,000 requests per second with sub 2.5ms latency on a laptop, the argument that "synchronous PHP can't scale" completely falls apart.

Now with the data we have from our benchmarks we can more closely examine and determine the validity of pervasive myths and popular beliefs that dictate many of the design choices in web development. The numbers show us that the limitations that are often attributed to entire programming languages or execution models are almost always the result of something more specific that became an artificial dependency.

Myth 1: “PHP is Inherently Slow”

For over a decade, “PHP is slow” has permeated the zeitgeist of web developers through the industry. This is usually cited as a reason to justify migrating simple applications to heavier enterprise run times or microservices. However, this myth is the product of two sources that this data shows are both incorrect now or assigning the blame to the wrong source. The first source of this was likely from bad experiences from old versions of PHP, and the other misattribution: blaming the language runtime for the sins of the framework.

PHP a decade ago when this argument started was a much different beat then what we have now, and part of the problem is these critics of PHP have not been paying attention to that fact. As shown with these benchmarks PHP 8.2+, PHP-FPM, and optimizations like OPcache can make even synchronous PHP extremely fast and reliable while still letting you have the advantages of synchronous operations. There are also operations in PHP that are just faster than anything else with the same accessibility as PHP, like database operations and encryption. One of the things I learned building mouse-php and mRPC/colby-jack was how to implement HMAC for both PHP and Javascript, and not only was PHP’s implementation more performant but far easier which means more secure as there are less chances for me as a developer to make an error.

The other source of this becomes obvious because mouse-php makes engineering choices that removes many of the sources of bloat that come from typical frameworks. As a result the performance uplift over a typical batteries included framework is obvious. I wasn’t the first to notice this naturally, microframeworks like slim exist to address this same bloat but this remains a source of this myth because typically people bench marking PHP reach for Laravel or Symfony as that’s what most people outside the PHP ecosystem think of for PHP backends. What our benchmarks show just like the outdated idea of PHP that the framework tax and the abstraction baggage that comes with the massive frameworks is the true performance killer and not the language runtime.

Myth 2: "Synchronous APIs Can’t Scale to Modern Demand”

The modern cloud-native ecosystem is built on the premise that synchronous execution models hit a hard wall under real world load, necessitating complex asynchronous event loops, reactive streams, or Kubernetes-orchestrated microservices.

Our MariaDB benchmark challenges this assumption. By pushing a database backed endpoint to 15,250 requests per second with sub 2.5ms baseline latencies we showed that a simple synchronous request response model can absorb massive production traffic. To put this number in perspective 15,250 requests per second equates to 1.3 billion requests a day running on a laptop not built for web hosting. For 99% of web applications, microservice splits and async complexity solves problems they will simply never have and just introduces operation overhead, or latency taxes that definitely don’t need.

This does reveal the source of this myth however, cargo-culting and vendor marketing, the idea that these complex solutions are the best practice primarily comes from people seeing FAANG companies use these solutions in their own stacks. The problem with this is the colossal delta in traffic and developers between even a decently high traffic application and Google. The scale that a FAANG corporation’s infrastructure is working at means that the economics and what makes something efficient change drastically meaning that trying to copy their infrastructure leads to unnecessary complexity or even worse performance in certain areas then the simpler solution.

Myth 3: “Performance vs. DX is a Zero-Sum Game”

Perhaps the most damaging myth in web development and one I began to be frustrated with the trade off narrative: the belief that if you want high performance, you must write low level, tedious boilerplate; and if you want great Developer Experience(DX), you must accept a heavy runtime tax.

Building mouse-php showed me that not only was this not true, but many features touted as making things easier for developers are shallow making the performance trade offs bad deals for the convenience, actually make things more difficult when you actually try building something, are just a development tool and don’t need to affect the performance of the production runtime. The interesting part of the performance uplift shown in this post was that it wasn’t the direct target of the choices made, removing ORMs and simplifying middleware management and flow was all done to just make it easier to understand and work with. These benchmarks are particularly interesting because this API was created from a blank directory. From that blank directory I created and configured the endpoints in around ten minutes, which was a great demonstration that performance doesn’t need to be hard.

Good developer experience isn’t about hiding complexity behind magic abstraction, it's about making the complexity easier to understand or removing redundant work. True DX is about clarity, predictability, and getting out of an engineer’s way. When tools are simple to reason about, high performance isn’t something you have to explicitly aim for; good engineering choices become obvious as a natural byproduct of clean design.
When we strip away industry dogma, cargo-culted microservices, and multilayered abstraction taxes, web architecture becomes remarkably clear. The benchmarks suggest to us: simplicity scales, hardware is rarely the real bottleneck, and high performance is simply the natural byproduct of clean design.
For 99% of web applications, the push toward "cloud complex" architecture solves a scaling problem they will never face, while saddling them with operational overhead they definitely don't need. You don't need a thousand dollar auto scaling cluster to build something fast.
What all of this has shown me is that respecting developer velocity and application performance are not mutually exclusive. When you look past industry assumptions and focus on building well reasoned solutions to immediate problems, you can create outcomes that defy expectations.
This approach gave me a tool that not only delivered sub 3ms latencies on database backed requests, but did so with a backend that took ten minutes to build from an empty directory, all without the added complexity of managing asynchronous loops, explicit state lifecycles, or heavy framework abstractions.
Sometimes, all it takes is stepping back, cutting out the bloat, and letting the metal do what it was built to do.

title: Flexbox or Grid? A simple rule for choosing
description:
"Should I use Flexbox or Grid?" is one of the most common CSS questions. Here is the rule I use.

Flexbox is for one direction. Grid is for two.

Use Flexbox for a row or column of items

Navigation bars, button groups, centering one thing:

.nav {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

The items decide how much space they take, and the container lines them up.

Use Grid for rows and columns together

Card layouts, page layouts, galleries:

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

This one rule gives you a responsive layout with no media queries. The number of columns changes as the screen gets narrower.

Combine them

A common pattern is Grid for the page and Flexbox inside each piece:

.card {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

That keeps the buttons at the bottom of every card, even when the text lengths differ.

Quick check

  • Laying things out along one line? Flexbox.
  • Need to control rows and columns? Grid.
  • Not sure? Start with Grid, and use Flexbox for the small parts.

Which one do you reach for first? Tell me in the comments.

title: Explore More, Validate Less: Efficient Reflective Prompt Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.27367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reflective prompt optimization improves instructions using task feedback, but coupling candidate generation with full-validation-based selection can make search costly and sequential. We propose a two-stage framework that decouples reflective candidate-pool construction from validation allocation. During construction, we sample multiple parents and reuse each parent's training responses across parallel reflection branches. Each revision is screened against its parent on a small training minibatch, allowing locally improved candidates to support further revisions without full validation. After construction, an exploration policy selects candidates from the frozen pool under a fixed full-validation budget, and the prompt with the highest measured validation score is returned. This separation allows candidate-pool size and validation budget to be set independently. We evaluate random selection and learned score prediction with similarity-based exploration on five benchmarks using Qwen3.5-9B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. With 100 retained candidates and 20 full validations, our framework improves over the initial solver by up to 11.22 percentage points. Learned selection improves over the initial solver in all ten comparisons, although neither selection policy consistently outperforms the other. These results support separating reflective search from budgeted validation while leaving room for stronger candidate-selection policies.

title: 5 timing bugs I hit building timed blocks with Screen Time's DeviceActivity (iOS)
description:
I build minulo, an iPhone app that hides Reels and Shorts. One feature is a timed block: lock the official Instagram app with Screen Time for, say, 30 minutes, and have it unlock on its own even if minulo isn't running. That part runs on DeviceActivity (DeviceActivityCenter.startMonitoring + a DeviceActivitySchedule, with the unlock happening in a DeviceActivityMonitor extension's intervalDidEnd).

It took five rounds of bugs to get the timing right. All five are about how the schedule's start and end are interpreted, so they apply whether you write Swift directly or go through a wrapper like react-native-device-activity (which I use, with my own additions).

1. Windows shorter than 15 minutes are rejected

Pass a 5-minute window to startMonitoring and you get an error. In my testing on device, anything under 15 minutes was refused.

My first workaround was "now + 15 minutes", which meant a 5-minute break stayed unlocked for 15. The fix was to keep the end fixed and move the start back instead:

// keep the end; pull the start back so the window is 15 minutes
export function shortWindow(untilMs: number) {
  const now = new Date();
  const e = new Date(Math.ceil(Math.max(untilMs, now.getTime() + 60000) / 60000) * 60000);
  if (e.getTime() - now.getTime() >= 15 * 60000) return { s: now, e, dated: false };
  const s = new Date(e.getTime() - 15 * 60000);
  // if the start falls on the previous day, include the date (see #3)
  return { s, e, dated: s.getDate() !== now.getDate() };
}

A start in the past is fine; intervalDidEnd still fires at the end.

2. Same hour and minute for start and end is rejected

With hour/minute-only DateComponents, a 24-hour block (13:05 today to 13:05 tomorrow) reads as start == end and is refused. I shift the start one minute later, giving a 23h59m window. Shifting it earlier would make a 1-minute window, which runs into #1.

if (s.getHours() === e.getHours() && s.getMinutes() === e.getMinutes()) {
  s = new Date(s.getTime() + 60000);
}

3. Just after midnight, hour/minute isn't enough

Because of #1, a break ending at 00:05 starts at 23:50. Sent as hour and minute only, that was read as 23:50 today, and the window broke: a 5-minute break after midnight stayed open for 15. When the start falls on the previous day, I now include year, month and day:

export function winEdge(d: Date, dated: boolean) {
  return dated
    ? { year: d.getFullYear(), month: d.getMonth() + 1, day: d.getDate(), hour: d.getHours(), minute: d.getMinutes(), second: 0 }
    : { hour: d.getHours(), minute: d.getMinutes(), second: 0 };
}

4. The number of monitored activities is limited

Registering one activity per weekday for each schedule (bedtime, class hours…) adds up fast, and the number of monitored activities is reportedly capped at around 20. Past that, startMonitoring fails, and the block simply never unlocks. Two changes:

  • daily schedules are a single activity without a weekday
  • failures are stored instead of swallowed, so the app can show that something is wrong 
DA.startMonitoring(FOCUS_ACTIVITY, { intervalStart, intervalEnd, repeats: false }, [])
  .catch((x) => set('focus:nativeErr', String(x?.message ?? x).slice(0, 120)));

5. "Unblock everything" also unblocks things that should stay blocked

Clearing all shields in intervalDidEnd also removed other blocks that should still be active at that moment, like a bedtime schedule or an app whose daily limit was used up. A manual block ending in the middle of the night took the bedtime block down with it until morning.

Now the end action re-applies whatever should still be active at that time, computed when the block starts:

DA.configureActions({ activityName: FOCUS_ACTIVITY, callbackName: 'intervalDidEnd', actions: [
  { type: 'resetBlocks' },
  // re-apply schedules that are still in their window at the end time
  ...during.map((id) => ({ type: 'blockSelection', familyActivitySelectionId: id })),
] });

The extension also drops re-applies that belong to schedules already finished, so a repeating registration doesn't carry them into the next day.

Summary

  • Windows under 15 minutes (on device) are refused: fix the end, move the start back.
  • Identical start and end hour:minute are refused: move the start one minute later.
  • After midnight the start lands on the previous day: include the date only then.
  • Monitored activities are capped: merge daily schedules and record failures.
  • Clearing everything clears too much: re-apply what should stay, at the end time.

Related: opening your own app from a Screen Time block screen (ShieldAction can't open URLs, so I go through a notification).

title: Real-Estate Listing Discovery: Ranking Signals for Fresh, Cited Retrieval
description:
Short answer: choose a retrieval path by the answer contract first. Use live web search when listing freshness is the ranking signal; use a vector collection when you need stable semantic matches and citations; combine both when a property answer needs durable policy context plus current inventory.

That decision sounds obvious until the first stale listing is cited as available. In a real-estate discovery service, ranking is not one score. It is a contract between the user question, the retrieval unit, metadata filters, freshness rules, and the citation you can show beside each result. I write those invariants down before comparing products.

Infrai is an early option to test when one backend needs both live and vector retrieval because its plain REST API needs no SDK install. Infrai also uses one key across those capabilities, avoiding separate retrieval credentials while the ranking contract is still moving. It won't choose the contract for you.

What should a retrieval contract contain for listing discovery?

Start with the unit. A whole brochure, a listing record, and a paragraph about an HOA rule produce very different rankings. Store the listing identifier, source URL, update timestamp, price, geography, and status as metadata. The text can carry amenities; filters should enforce facts such as city or active status. A citation then points to the exact record that survived those filters.

Freshness is a separate invariant. Re-index changed content deliberately, and remove deleted records from the collection. A nightly batch is fine for neighborhood descriptions; it is a poor promise for a listing that can disappear between two clicks. Treating a delete event as an ordinary update leaves a withdrawn unit eligible for retrieval, and the result still looks plausible. That failure mode is easy to miss because nothing crashes: the citation resolves, the prose reads cleanly, and only the listing status is wrong.

Stale evidence is a ranking failure.

Keep a small labeled evaluation set before rollout: queries, expected listings, and the evidence span that justifies the answer. Measure retrieval quality on that set before tuning weights in production. Your mileage will vary with market and catalog churn; the labels are what make that uncertainty visible.

How do web search and vector retrieval rank real-estate results?

Web retrieval and vector retrieval optimize different signals. A web search path can see newly published pages and changing availability. A vector path gives you control over chunking, metadata filters, and repeatable semantic similarity. Neither signal alone proves that a listing is still valid.

Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so a team can inspect the capability schema before wiring a payload; that shortens the first useful experiment while the contract is still changing.

For a live intent such as “two-bedroom rental near the station listed this week,” I would query the web path, capture source URLs, and apply an application-level freshness check. For “which buildings allow subletting,” I would retrieve indexed policy text and cite the chunk plus its document timestamp. A hybrid flow runs both, then deduplicates by listing identifier before a reranker considers distance, price fit, freshness, and evidence quality.

The integration surface matters too. Elasticsearch gives deep control and a large operational surface. Algolia is fast to adopt for hosted keyword and faceting workflows. Pinecone focuses on managed vector search. Infrai exposes a plain REST API, so a Python service can call it without installing an SDK; its discovery surface documents capabilities and runnable examples, which keeps the first integration small. One key covers the platform's 295 routes across 20 modules, so a prototype does not need a separate credential for each backend capability. That is a developer-experience advantage, not a claim that it wins every ranking benchmark.

Option Strong fit Trade-off for this workflow
Elasticsearch Fine-grained lexical ranking, filters, and custom scoring More cluster and schema decisions to operate
Algolia Quick hosted text search with facets Less natural for a citation-first semantic archive
Pinecone Managed vector similarity at scale You still assemble web freshness and citation plumbing
Infrai One HTTP surface for web and vector retrieval Application code still owns the contract, deduplication, and evaluation

The practical rule is simple: let the source of truth decide the first hop, then use the other path to fill the evidence gap.

A minimal critical path with explicit retry behavior

The example below keeps the request body in payload, because the discovery schema for the capability is the authority for fields and filters. It also makes retry behavior visible. A query is read-only, so a retry does not create a second record; write paths need an idempotency key.

import os
import time
import requests


def post_search(path, payload, attempts=4):
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" + path
    headers = {
        "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    }
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=10)
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("retrieval rate limit did not clear after retries")


def retrieve_listing_evidence(payload, use_live_web):
    path = "/v1/web/search" if use_live_web else "/v1/vector/query"
    return post_search(path, payload)

In production, payload should encode the retrieval unit, metadata filters, and freshness requirement you defined earlier. Keep the returned source identifier attached to every chunk passed to generation. If a citation cannot be mapped back to a listing or source URL, drop that candidate instead of inventing support. Put this check in the retrieval layer, not in a prompt, because a prompt cannot repair a missing source identifier.

Where the unified HTTP surface helps, and where it does not

I would recommend Infrai to a team that wants to test both live search and semantic retrieval from one backend service, especially when the team has multiple languages or already has an HTTP client convention. One key and one REST interface reduce credential and SDK coordination while the team iterates on ranking signals. The supporting benefit is breadth with a consistent discovery surface: the same platform covers the two retrieval modes without making the article’s architecture depend on a vendor-specific client library.

The catch is ownership. Infrai does not decide whether a listing is legally active, whether a source is trustworthy, or which ranking weights satisfy your market. A specialist search stack is a better choice when you need mature, domain-specific ranking controls, an existing Elasticsearch operations team, or a vector-only deployment with no web hop. Stick with Algolia for a facet-heavy consumer search experience that already fits its hosted model; choose Pinecone when managed vector infrastructure is the only boundary you want to outsource. A mixed design is valid when freshness and durable citations are both non-negotiable.

Do not use price as the architecture decision. Measure recall and citation correctness on the labeled set, then watch delete propagation and freshness in the same dashboard as click metrics. Small experiments beat a confident vendor verdict.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the vector retrieval guide.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html
  • https://www.algolia.com/doc/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/

title: Rust vs C++: Who Checks the Lifetime, and When
description:
Short version for the impatient: the real difference between Rust and C++ is not speed. Both compile to native code and both can hit the same hardware limits. The difference is who checks your lifetimes, and when. C++ lets you check them yourself, with discipline and tooling. Rust makes the compiler check them before the program exists.

I want to show that with a small program rather than a slogan, because I've read a lot of "Rust vs C++" posts that are just two benchmark charts and a fan club. I write mostly PHP, Go and TypeScript for clients, so I'm not a systems programmer, and I won't pretend to have shipped a game engine in either language. What I can do is take a mistake that every C++ beginner makes, run it on a real machine, and compare it to what Rust does with the same idea.

The bug that compiles

Here is a C++ program that moves a string out of a smart pointer and then reads from the pointer anyway.

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

int main() {
    auto name = std::make_unique<std::string>("report.pdf");
    auto other = std::move(name);
    std::cout << *name << "\n";
}

I built this with g++ -Wall -Wextra on a Linux box. No warnings. No errors. It ran and died with a segmentation fault (exit code 139). The move constructor did exactly what it promises: name is now an empty pointer, and dereferencing an empty pointer is undefined behaviour. The compiler knew that std::move had just been called on name. It let me carry on anyway, because the language says a moved-from object is valid but unspecified, and the language leaves it to me to remember.

That's not a knock on C++. A segfault in a toy program is the good outcome. The bad outcome is the same mistake inside a request handler where the pointer isn't null but points at memory something else now owns. Nothing crashes. Something gets quietly overwritten.

Now the same idea in Rust:

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("report.pdf");
    let other = name;
    println!("{name} {other}");
}

This does not build. The compiler stops with error E0382, "borrow of moved value", and points at the line where name was moved and the line where I used it afterwards. There is no runtime to crash, because there is no executable. The Rust Book chapter on ownership states the rules in three lines: each value has an owner, there is one owner at a time, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. The move bug above is simply the second rule being enforced.

Ownership is a rule, not a convention

C++ has all the same ideas. Smart pointers, RAII and move semantics are the C++ answer to manual memory management, and modern C++ written with them is far safer than the C-with-classes code that gave the language its reputation. The C++ Core Guidelines are full of advice in exactly this direction: prefer unique_ptr, avoid raw owning pointers, don't hold references past the lifetime of the thing they point at.

So if both languages have the idea, what's the difference? Enforcement. In C++ the guidelines are guidelines. A tool such as clang-tidy or a static analyser can flag many violations, and a code reviewer can catch more, but the language itself accepts the program. In Rust the same rules are part of the type system, and a program that breaks them is not a valid Rust program.

I find it useful to think of it as the difference between a speed limit sign and a speed bump. Most drivers slow down for both. Only one of them works at 3am when you're tired.

There's a cost, and I'll get to it. First, the second kind of bug, because it is the one that actually worries me.

Dangling references and the lifetime annotation

Returning a reference to something that no longer exists is the classic. In C++ it looks harmless:

const std::string& longer(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) {
    return a.size() >= b.size() ? a : b;
}

int main() {
    const std::string& r = longer("a long literal", std::string("hi"));
    std::cout << r << "\n";
}

The temporary std::string("hi") is destroyed at the end of the full expression. If it happened to be the longer one, r would now refer to a dead object. Here the literal wins, so this particular run probably prints correctly, which is the whole problem: it works until the inputs change. I'm describing that behaviour from the language rules, I didn't run this one to see what my compiler does with it.

Rust forces you to say how long each reference lives:

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    let result;
    {
        let short = String::from("hi");
        result = longest("longer text", &short);
    }
    println!("{result}");
}

The 'a says that the result lives no longer than the shorter of the two inputs. Because short is dropped at the closing brace and result is used after it, the compiler rejects the program with E0597, "short does not live long enough". The function is correct. The caller is wrong, and Rust tells the caller.

Those annotations are the most disliked part of the language, and I get why. They look like noise until you've been bitten by the thing they prevent. The Rustonomicon is blunt about where the boundary sits: in safe Rust the compiler guarantees the absence of this class of bug, and in unsafe blocks the guarantee becomes your job again. That is a much smaller area to audit than "the whole codebase".

What Rust costs you

I'd be doing the thing I complained about at the top if I stopped here. Rust costs real time.

The borrow checker will reject programs that are fine. Graph structures, doubly linked lists and anything with cyclic references fight the ownership model, and the usual escape hatches (Rc<RefCell<T>>, indices into a Vec, unsafe) each give up something. When I read Rust written by people who are new to it, the pattern I see most is .clone() sprinkled on until the errors go away. That works, and it quietly spends the performance you chose Rust to keep.

Compile times are slower than I'd like. The ecosystem is younger, so a library you take for granted in C++ for audio, CAD or an old hardware vendor's SDK may not exist, or may be a thin wrapper over the C++ one anyway. And if you have a decade of C++ in production, rewriting it is a business decision, not a technical one. I covered a smaller version of that trade in my post on Rust 1.99 and the box leak habit I had to drop, where even a language that polices ownership still lets you leak memory on purpose if you ask.

C++ has costs too, and they're mostly invisible until they aren't. The language is huge, with decades of overlapping ways to do one thing. Two engineers on the same team can write "modern C++" that looks like two different languages. Undefined behaviour doesn't announce itself.

How I'd choose

I'd pick C++ when the code has to live next to an existing C++ codebase, when a library only exists there, or when the team already has people who know where the bodies are buried. Rewriting a working system to get memory safety is rarely worth it by itself, and incremental approaches that put new code in Rust next to the old code are usually kinder to the schedule.

I'd pick Rust for new code that handles untrusted input, runs for a long time, or gets maintained by people who weren't in the room when it was written. Parsers, network services, command-line tools and anything that sits between the internet and a database are good fits. The ownership rules double as documentation. When a function takes String instead of &str, that signature tells the next developer who is responsible for the memory.

For the kind of work I do for clients, neither is the default. A Laravel app or a Go service covers most of what people hire me for, and I reach for a systems language only when a hot path justifies it. You can see what that mix looks like on my portfolio.

Try it yourself this week

Don't take my word, or any benchmark's word, for any of this. Spend an hour on it:

  1. Write the unique_ptr move bug above in C++ and compile it with -Wall -Wextra. Then compile the same file with -fsanitize=address,undefined and run it. See what each tool tells you.
  2. Install Rust with rustup and write the longest function with the nested block. Read the full E0597 message, not just the first line. Then delete the 'a annotations and read the different error you get.
  3. Pick one small function from your own C++ code that returns a reference or a pointer. Write down, in a comment, who owns the thing it points at. If you can't answer in one sentence, you've found the kind of bug Rust is built to catch.

If step three turns up a real question, that is a better reason to learn Rust than anything I've written here.

Originally published at abrarqasim.com. I write there about React, PHP, Rust, Go and the AI tooling around them.
