title: Exploring Recurrent-Depth Language Models for Multitask Clinical Text Processing
description:
arXiv:2610.27559v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical natural language processing includes diverse tasks such as information extraction, classification, and question answering. Developing one model for all tasks could simplify deployment and improve knowledge transfer. We evaluated whether small recurrent-depth language models can meet this need through joint fine-tuning and compared their performance with standard transformers. We fine-tuned Ouro1.4B-Thinking, Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, HRM-Text-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-8B on 9 datasets covering information extraction, classification, inference, and question answering, and evaluated them on four additional datasets excluded from training. Across these 13 datasets, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking achieved higher performances than Qwen3-1.7B on 11 datasets; Ouro-2.6BThinking was competitive with Qwen3-8B on most tasks. Ouro models showed the largest gains on inference and question answering, whereas HRM-Text-1B showed mixed results. These findings support further study of recurrent-depth models for clinical tasks through controlled experiments to isolate architectural effects and investigate how recurrent computation influences reasoning, knowledge acquisition, and generalization.

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox
description:
A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

Snapshot restoration time now counts toward creation instead of the first operation. Creation is about 50 ms longer at p50, with a larger increase possible for uncached snapshots. The total time through the first operation remains the same.

This change applies automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. See the Sandbox.create() documentation for details.

title: Building a Zero-Trust Two-Tier AWS Network
description:
When setting up cloud infrastructure in Amazon Web Services (AWS) as a beginner, the "VPC and more" console wizard gives a fast way to generate a complete networking setup including a VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT Gateway, Endpoints and Internet Gateway all in one go.

In this post, I will walk through how I used the "VPC and more" wizard to build a secure two-tier network, adjusted it to meet my project requirements (free-tier instances, single Availability Zone, and no NAT Gateway), created my SSH key pair, chained my Security Groups, and tested secure SSH access.

1. What a Bastion Host (Jump Box) Is and Why It Is Used

A bastion host (also called a jump box) is a hardened server placed in a public subnet that acts as the single entry point into an isolated private network.

In real-world environments, backend servers and databases should never be given public IP addresses or exposed directly to the internet. Doing so increases security risks and invites unauthorized traffic.

By putting our private servers behind a bastion host, we achieve better security:

  • Fewer Entry Points: Instead of exposing multiple servers to the public internet, we only allow access through one controlled bastion host.
  • Controlled Access: We configure our private servers to accept SSH connections only from the bastion host rather than from the open internet.

2. How I Built the Two-Tier Network Using "VPC and more"

Instead of building every network component manually from scratch, I used the automated "VPC and more" wizard in the AWS Console and customized it for my project.

Step 1: Automated Provisioning via "VPC and more"

  1. Open the VPC Dashboard in your AWS Console and click Create VPC.
  2. Select the VPC and more option.
  3. Fill in the settings:
    • Name tag prefix: two-tier
    • IPv4 CIDR block: 10.0.0.0/20
    • Number of Availability Zones (AZs): 1 AZ
    • Number of public subnets: 1
    • Number of private subnets: 1
    • NAT gateways: Select None (This ensures we do not create a NAT Gateway)
    • VPC endpoints: None
    • DNS options: Enable DNS hostnames Enable DNS resolution
  4. Click Create VPC. The wizard automatically generates your VPC, subnets, route tables, and Internet Gateway.

Step 2: Perimeter & Internal Security Group Chaining (Security Layer)

Next, I set up my firewall rules:

  1. Create the Bastion Security Group (bastion-sg):

    • Navigate to EC2 Dashboard -> Security Groups -> Create security group.
    • Security group name: bastion-sg
    • Description: Allow SSH only from my public IP
    • VPC: Select Hye-T-vpc.
    • Under Inbound rules, click Add rule:
      • Type: SSH (TCP, Port 22)
      • Source: Select My IP (verify it displays [INSERT_YOUR_PUBLIC_IP]/32).
    • Click Create security group.

  2. Create the Private Instance Security Group (private-instance-sg):

    • Click Create security group.
    • Security group name: private-instance-sg
    • Description: Allow SSH only from Bastion Security Group
    • VPC: Select Hye-T-vpc.
    • Under Inbound rules, click Add rule:
      • Type: SSH (TCP, Port 22)
      • Source: Select Custom -> Click the search field, type sg-, and select bastion-sg (sg-xxxxxxxx). Do not enter an IP or CIDR block.
    • Click Create security group.

  • "Why": AWS Security Groups operate as stateful virtual firewalls bound to an instance's Network Interface. Configuring bastion-sg to accept TCP port 22 only from your workstation's /32 public IP blocks all unauthorized internet scanners. Configuring private-instance-sg to accept TCP port 22 only from bastion-sg (selecting the Security Group ID as the source rather than an IP address) guarantees that only packets originating from an instance attached to bastion-sg are permitted to reach the private VM.

Step 3: Compute Tier Provisioning

A. Creating an AWS Key Pair

Before launching our virtual machines, we need an SSH key pair to authenticate securely:

  1. Navigate to the EC2 Dashboard in the AWS Console.
  2. In the left navigation menu, click on Key Pairs under Network & Security.
  3. Click the Create key pair button in the top right.
  4. Configure the settings:
    • Name: bastion-host-kp
    • Key pair type: RSA
    • Private key file format: .pem
  5. Click Create key pair. Your browser will automatically download the private key file (bastion-host-kp.pem). Move this file to your local ~/.ssh/ directory.

B. Launching the EC2 Instances

Using the key pair we just created, I launched two free-tier instances (t3.micro):

  1. Hye-Bastion: Placed in the public subnet with Auto-assign public IP enabled and attached to bastion-sg, selecting bastion-host-kp.

  2. Navigate to EC2 -> Instances -> Launch instances.

    • Name: Hye-Bastion
    • AMI: Amazon Linux 2023
    • Instance type: t2.micro or t3.micro
    • Key pair: bastion-host-kp.
    • Under Network settings -> Click Edit:
      • VPC: Hye-T-vpc
      • Subnet: Hye-T-subnet-public1-eu-south-1a
      • Auto-assign public IP: Enable
      • Firewall (security groups): Select existing security group -> bastion-sg
    • Click Launch instance.

  3. Hye-Private-Instance: Placed in the private subnet with Auto-assign public IP disabled and attached to private-instance-sg, selecting bastion-host-kp.

  • Navigate to EC2 -> Instances -> Launch instances.

    • Name: Hye-Private-Instance
    • AMI: Amazon Linux 2023
    • Instance type: t2.micro or t3.micro
    • Key pair: bastion-host-kp.
    • Under Network settings -> Click Edit:
      • VPC: Hye-T-vpc
      • Subnet: Hye-T-subnet-private1-eu-south-1a
      • Auto-assign public IP: Disable
      • Firewall (security groups): Select existing security group -> private-instance-sg
    • Click Launch instance.

  • "Why": The Bastion VM is placed in the public subnet with a Public IPv4 address so it can receive administrative SSH connections via the Internet Gateway. The Private VM is placed in the private subnet with Auto-assign public IP disabled, ensuring it possesses only a private IPv4 address (10.0.8.x/24) and cannot be reached directly from outside the VPC.

Step 4: Connect to the private VM through the bastion host using ProxyJump/Agent Forwarding

Connecting via ProxyJump

To avoid copying my private .pem key onto the bastion host, I connected from my local computer using SSH agent forwarding or ProxyJump:

# 1. Set key permissions and add to your local ssh-agent
chmod 400 ~/.ssh/two-tier-lab-key.pem

# 2. SSH ProxyJump from your Local PC into the Bastion Host with
ssh -i ~/.ssh/two-tier-lab-key.pem -J ec2-user@<INSERT_BASTION_PUBLIC_IP> ec2-user@<INSERT_PRIVATE_VM_PRIVATE_IP>

# If it says "permission denied"
#Try
ssh -o "ProxyCommand=ssh -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem -W %h:%p ec2-user@<BASTION_IP>" -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem ec2-user@<PRIVATE_IP>

  • "Why": I didn't copy my private SSH key (.pem) onto a Bastion host because that will violates cloud security best practices because any compromise of the perimeter Bastion host would expose the private key on disk or in memory, granting an attacker unrestricted access to all internal instances.
    • Using SSH Agent Forwarding (ssh -A) keeps the private key strictly inside your local PC's ssh-agent memory and forwards only cryptographic signature challenges over a secure Unix domain socket ($SSH_AUTH_SOCK).
    • Alternatively, ProxyJump establishes an end-to-end encrypted SSH session directly from your PC to the Private VM multiplexed over the Bastion connection.

3. Testing, Validation & Security Verification Matrix

Validation Test Verification Command / Action Expected Result Observed Status
Bastion SSH Access ssh -A ec2-user@<BASTION_PUBLIC_IP> Authenticates into 10.0.0.x public subnet shell [PASS]
No Private Key on Bastion ls -la ~/.ssh on Bastion Host Only authorized_keys present; no .pem key file on disk [PASS]
Private Instance SSH Hop ssh ec2-user@<PRIVATE_VM_IP> Authenticates into 10.0.8.x private subnet shell via agent socket [PASS]
Private Subnet Isolation ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 on Private Instance 100% packet loss (confirms complete absence of NAT Gateway / Internet route) [PASS]

4. Troubleshooting & Post-Assessment Teardown

Common Operational Failure Modes

  • Issue 1 — Permission denied (publickey) on First Hop (Bastion) with -J:

    • Cause: By default, the top-level -i <key> flag in OpenSSH is passed to the destination target, not the jump host. If the key is not loaded into your local session, the bastion hop rejects the connection.
    • Fix (One-Liner): Explicitly supply the key for both hops via ProxyCommand: 
    ssh -o "ProxyCommand=ssh -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem -W %h:%p ec2-user@<BASTION_IP>" -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem ec2-user@<PRIVATE_IP>
    • Fix (Persistent): Map the keys cleanly in ~/.ssh/config: 
    Host bastion
    HostName <BASTION_IP>
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem

Host private-vm
    HostName <PRIVATE_IP>
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem
    ProxyJump bastion

```bash
Then simply run `ssh private-instance`.
```

  • Issue 2 — Permission denied (publickey) on Second Hop (when using SSH Agent Forwarding):

    • Cause: The private key was not added to your local ssh-agent before initiating agent forwarding (ssh -A).
    • Fix: Run eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and ssh-add ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem on your local machine before connecting.

  • Issue 3 — Connection timed out to Bastion Public IP: Confirm that the public subnet is explicitly associated with your public route table, that the 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-xxxx route is active, and verify that your home ISP has not rotated your workstation's /32 public IPv4 address.

title: SHAM-Bench: A Span-level Hallucination Benchmark Across Multiple Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.27370v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Span-level hallucination detection pinpoints unsupported content in LLM outputs, enabling actionable feedback and targeted mitigation. Existing evaluations for span-level hallucination detection methods are fragmented across tasks, annotation formats, and metrics, and most span-level datasets cover only a single NLG domain, making it difficult to assess whether a detection method actually generalizes across tasks and domains. In this paper, we introduce SHAM-Bench (Span-level Hallucination Benchmark Across Multiple Tasks), a unified benchmark for span-level hallucination detection spanning six NLG tasks, aggregated from existing human-annotated datasets totaling 6,461 examples under a common schema and evaluation protocol. Using SHAM-Bench, we evaluate existing hallucination detection methods and find that fine-tuned detectors often perform well in-domain but degrade under distribution shift, whereas prompt-based methods with reasoning are more robust across tasks. Our analysis further shows that subtle unsupported content remains difficult to detect and span-level evaluation is still challenged by ambiguous span boundaries and noisy labels. We release the dataset, evaluation code, and a public leaderboard to support future research on broadly generalizable hallucination detection.

title: Build a Faster Photography Portfolio: Convert PNG to WebP (Free, No Upload)
description:
A portfolio gallery is a strange kind of website: it has to look perfect, because the gallery is the product, but it also has to load fast, because nobody waits for a photographer whose site stutters. For years I did what most people do — exported everything as PNG, because PNG is lossless and therefore "safe." It is safe for quality. It is not safe for page weight. A gallery page full of oversized PNGs punishes every visitor on a phone connection, and most of them will never wait for the last row to appear.

I'm the developer of FileOnTap, and here is the workflow I recommend for turning a PNG gallery into a fast WebP one without learning a build pipeline.

Step 1: Separate your masters from your web exports

Keep the full-resolution originals (RAW, TIFF, or high-res PSD) untouched somewhere safe. The PNGs you export for the web are intermediates, not archives. This matters because once you convert to WebP, the WebP is a delivery format — if a client later asks for a print version, you regenerate from the master, not from the WebP.

Step 2: Export web PNGs at the size they'll actually be shown

A gallery grid that renders images at 900 px wide doesn't need 5000 px PNGs. Export at the display size plus a little headroom for retina screens — 2x at most. Every pixel you export beyond that is weight your visitors pay for and never see.

Step 3: Convert to WebP in the browser, no upload

This is where the format swap happens: convert PNG to WebP for your portfolio right in the browser. The files never leave your machine, which matters when a gallery contains client work that isn't public yet — no upload means no third-party server ever holds the images. Convert the whole gallery in one sitting so every image gets the same treatment and nothing slips through as a forgotten PNG.

Step 4: Spot-check what WebP does to your specific images

Don't trust any format blindly. Open a few converted files at 100% zoom and look at the things that matter in a portfolio: smooth gradients (skies, studio backdrops — this is where lossy compression shows banding first), fine text in watermarks, and any transparency in logos. If a gradient bands badly, reconvert from a higher-quality export rather than from an already-compressed PNG.

Step 5: Serve WebP with a PNG fallback

All modern browsers display WebP, but portfolio links travel everywhere — old apps, embedded previews, email forwards. The safe pattern is the <picture> element with WebP first and the PNG as fallback:

<picture>
  <source srcset="gallery-photo.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="gallery-photo.png" alt="...">
</picture>

If your site builder doesn't offer a <picture> element, check its image settings first — many builders now serve WebP automatically once you upload one.

The honest limitations

WebP won't rescue a gallery hosted on a slow server, and it won't fix images that were exported oversized in the first place — resize at export, then convert. Some desktop apps still don't generate WebP thumbnails, which can make browsing your local folder annoying; keep the PNG exports alongside the WebPs during a project, and archive them with the masters when it's done. And don't delete originals after converting: WebP is a delivery format, not an archive.

What I actually do

For a new portfolio batch I export the PNGs once, convert them locally in the browser, spot-check three or four files at 100%, and push. The conversion takes minutes; the painful part was always the waiting — mine and my visitors'. Fixing that is one of the cheapest wins in web publishing.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of FileOnTap, the free browser-local converter linked above. Files are converted on your device — nothing is uploaded.

title: Predicting Linear Relational Decodability Without the Relation
description:
arXiv:2610.27241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear relational embeddings (LREs) approximate a language model's subject-to-object mapping with an affine function. Their faithfulness varies enormously across relations, from near zero for person_father to the ceiling for country_capital_city. We investigate the factors that contribute to this variation and demonstrate that it can be significantly predicted from a readout that is not aware of the underlying relation. To do so, we propose a novel form of the Jacobian lens, the entity lens. Whereas the Jacobian lens is estimated across all tokens and concepts, the entity lens EL_t is trained to predict what the model will output for an entity of type t under the neutral prompt "{} is known for"; e.g., we train ELs for countries and persons. After estimating an entity lens, we measure how highly it ranks the model's answer for a relation without using any relation-specific information in estimation and prediction. Across 28 relations of the LRE dataset on Olmo-3-7B this relation-agnostic score correlates with LRE faithfulness at \rho = 0.7355 (p < .01). This suggests that linear decodability is largely a property of what a subject's representation already carries, rather than of the relation being decoded. Moving the unit of analysis from the relation to the individual fact, we conclude that new relation datasets and analysis methods are needed to address several problems in existing datasets, most prominently semantically weak first tokens (e.g., most predicted universities' first token is "University") and reference competition (e.g., the LLM confuses obscure actor names with competing non-actor entities that have the same last name). Our full pipeline is available at https://github.com/jonasrohw/entity-lens

title: I wrote a 10,000-line Windows security suite in one Python file. Here's how the crypto container works, and ₹50 if you can break it
description:
Most small encryption tools fail in boring places, not in the cipher. They fail on what happens with a wrong password, a doctored header, a rolled-back state file, or a corrupted chunk.

I spent a long time on those boring places for ATLOCK v5, and this post walks through the design. At the end there's a challenge for you.

1. The container format

Files, folders and Quick Lock items all use one container (v3.1):

magic(8) | salt(16) | kdf_packed(6) | chunk_size(4) | nonce_base(8)
| commitment(32) | plain_len(8) | header_hash(32) | chunks...
  • Chunked AES-256-GCM. Every chunk is authenticated independently, so a single flipped bit is caught at that chunk and nothing gets decrypted blindly.
  • Per-seal chunk subkey. v3.1 derives a fresh subkey for each seal instead of encrypting everything under the raw master key.
  • Header-bound AAD. The header is mixed into authentication, so you can't swap parameters around without detection.
  • Optional Padme padding. The true file size is hidden by padding to a Padme bucket with random bytes, at no more than about 12% overhead.

2. Key commitment before any plaintext

AES-GCM alone doesn't commit to a key, which is why partitioning-oracle attacks exist. ATLOCK stores HMAC-SHA256(enc_key, "atlock-commit-v3") in the header and verifies it with a constant-time compare before a single byte of plaintext is produced. A wrong key is rejected at the header, and it never reaches the decryption loop.

3. KDF: Argon2id, and a parser that doesn't trust its own header

  • File floor: Argon2id, t=3, m=64 MiB, p=4
  • Vault and recovery: t=4, m=128 MiB, p=4
  • All sub-keys come from HKDF-SHA256 with per-purpose info strings (vault-enc, vault-verify, totp-wrap, backup-enc, and so on), so no key is ever reused across purposes.

The KDF parameters live in the header, which means an attacker can edit them. So the parser clamps untrusted values to hard ceilings (t≤6, m≤512 MiB, p≤8). A doctored file can't make ATLOCK burn gigabytes of RAM or minutes of CPU.

4. Sealed local state

Settings, guard list, vault index, lockout counters and logs are never stored as plain JSON. Every record goes through a SealedStore: AES-256-GCM with a key derived via HKDF from a DPAPI-protected state key (with extra entropy). A separate rollback anchor catches someone restoring an old state file to reset attempt counters.

There's also an optional hardware mode, where the state key becomes HKDF(DPAPI root || TPM secret) and every sealed file is re-sealed under it. If the TPM key is enabled but unusable, ATLOCK fails closed.

5. Public-key mode

Ephemeral X25519 for encryption (HKDF over the shared secret, salted with the ephemeral and recipient public keys), plus Ed25519 for signatures. Signatures can be pinned, so a file signed by a different key than the one you expect is rejected. There's also Shamir M-of-N splitting for recovery keys, FIDO2 hardware keys, TOTP and Windows Hello.

6. The unglamorous hardening

  • SetDefaultDllDirectories runs before any other import, against DLL planting.
  • Every child process is launched by full System32 path, never through a shell, with a rebuilt minimal environment (fixed COMSPEC/PATHEXT, no inherited PATH or PSModulePath).
  • PowerShell scripts are fixed strings, and variable data goes in over stdin as JSON, never interpolated.
  • Symlinks and junctions are refused. Data-folder ownership is checked, and anything inside OneDrive/Dropbox/Drive is detected so decrypted working copies never get synced.
  • Environment variables that influence paths (like the Nuitka onefile parent PID) are only honoured if they match the actual process layout.
  • Log output goes through a redaction filter for keys and tokens.

7. Detection layer

Ransomware canary decoys in Desktop/Documents/Pictures/Downloads, a startup-item watchdog with a baseline and allow-list, an audit log with its own verify command, and intruder photo/video capture after failed unlocks.

8. Testing

ATLOCK.exe --selftest runs against a throw-away data folder and registry key, so it never touches a real install. --fuzz N throws N random corruptions at the container parser.

Now the actual point: break it

I can't find my own blind spots, which is why I'm posting this here.

  1. Download ATLOCK_v5.zip: https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/ATLOCK/releases/download/v5.0.0/ATLOCK_v5.zip
  2. Extract ATLOCK.exe. It's unsigned, so Windows SmartScreen will warn you. Click "More info → Run anyway", but do it in a VM or Windows Sandbox. You should treat any random exe from a stranger this way, including mine.
  3. Use it, then try to break it. Recover a protected file without the password, bypass lockout, forge or roll back state, or get plaintext where there shouldn't be any.

Reward: ₹50 via UPI for a valid break, ₹60 for a major one. Send a reproducible write-up in the comments or DM me, and I'll judge what counts.

I'm not rich, so that's what I can afford. Because my parents didn't give me money 💵 and in my fampay account I've only 110rupees 😂 The real reward is that every break you find gets fixed in v6, and your name goes in the credits.

I'm Anmol. I'm 13 and I build under Akhouri Systems. Yes, really. Tear it apart.

title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.

title: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates
description:
arXiv:2610.26899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.

title: Dynamic System Inspired Continuous Large Language Model for AI4Science Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.26959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific foundation models increasingly operate on continuous phenomena, yet still use discrete residual computation. We ask whether pretrained residual transformations can support additional latent computation without expanding the backbone. To test this possibility, we introduce Continuum-LM, which reuses these transformations as dynamical operators in a continuous-depth language model. Its hidden states evolve through an ordinary differential equation evaluated by higher-order numerical integration, with solver order and step size controlling computation. Across eight scientific tasks, Continuum-LM trains stably and improves mean exact-match accuracy by 7.77 and 10.96 percentage points over discrete counterparts at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales, respectively. At 0.6B, it also outperforms an Ouro-style recurrent control under matched parameter and residual-function evaluation budgets. Together, these results support extensible computational depth through parameter reuse, identifying continuous hidden-state evolution as a practical design dimension for scientific language models beyond parameter scaling.

title: AI Gateway now supports TypeSafe clients and an HTTP API for Jev
description:
You can now call Jev from TypeSafe AI through AI Gateway using an existing TypeSafe client or the HTTP API, in addition to the AI SDK.

  • TypeSafe client: Point an existing TypeSafe client at AI Gateway without changing its evaluation calls.

  • HTTP API: Call Jev directly from any language or framework.

  • AI SDK: Call Jev from a TypeScript application using AI SDK.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software. State goes in, and typed answers come out with probabilities attached, so there's no generated text to parse. Requests are billed through AI Gateway on all three paths, so they appear alongside your other model calls in usage and observability.

Migrate an existing TypeSafe client

Change the base URL and API key. Your systemOne calls, noul questions, and response shapes stay exactly as they are.

Start a new integration

New integrations name the model as typesafe-ai/jev and ask one of three question types: boolean returns a probability from 0 to 1, choice picks one option from a set you name, and score rates against a scale you define. This example asks whether an agent should keep working after fixing a bug and passing its tests.

title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics, with intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations evaluated across open-weight and closed-source models. Editing substantially increases judge-rated severity over the seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fall in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase. Among 219 prompts that pass model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit responses containing unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, although pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only $\rho=0.0387$ to $0.1897$. Curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the failures they expose in each model.

title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
description:
arXiv:2610.27323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. We first show that this contextually appropriate granularity is recoverable from pre-generation hidden states, even when generated responses are misaligned, with disclosure levels exhibiting an ordered structure along a common hidden-state direction. Motivated by this, we propose an inference-time route-and-steer framework: an ordinal granularity router maps visual-contextual privacy representations to a disclosure route, and a disclosure-level-conditioned steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. Across four VLM backbones, our method improves visual-context-aware disclosure alignment, better balances over- and under-disclosure, and incurs only modest changes on general capability benchmarks. It further transfers to another dataset with a distinct data distribution and privacy-risk taxonomy.

title: Free fintech data engineering lab: find a missing dollar with Python + SQLite
description:
Free and open source: 100 English lessons, 40 foundation exercises, and 8 scenario labs for fintech data engineering. The repository's lessons and core practice are available without payment or a signup wall. Clone it and start locally with Python 3.12+ and SQLite: no paid cloud account or API key is needed.

I maintain this learning project. This walkthrough uses six synthetic payment events to show why a balanced journal can still disagree with an external settlement.

Three checks that answer different questions

Idempotency: if a delivery is repeated, do we count the same business event twice?

Journal balance: do the signed entries for each event and currency add up to zero?

Reconciliation: does our internal expected amount agree with an independently supplied settlement record?

None of these checks replaces the other two. A balanced pair of entries can faithfully record an incorrect amount. A replay-safe pipeline can faithfully reproduce that incorrect amount every time.

Run the experiment

Use Python 3.12 or later with SQLite support. From a terminal:

git clone https://github.com/antony502189-max/fintech-data-engineering-roadmap.git
cd fintech-data-engineering-roadmap
python -m fintech_lab.quickstart

On Windows, use py -3 instead of python if necessary.

Every run starts with a fresh in-memory SQLite database and writes no files. The first delivery inserts six events; repeating the delivery inserts zero and recognizes six duplicates. The journal check passes.

Reconciliation still produces two exceptions:

Payment Currency Expected minor units External minor units External minus expected Result
p1 USD 7700 7700 0 matched
p2 EUR 4900 4900 0 matched
p3 USD 2500 2400 -100 amount mismatch
p9 USD unknown 500 unknown unexpected external payment

Explain the dollar before fixing the code

For p1, capture minus fee minus refund is:

10000 - 300 - 2000 = 7700 USD minor units

For p3, the internal record expects $25.00, but the external settlement reports $24.00. The difference is negative 100 USD minor units: a $1.00 shortfall.

For p9, there is no corresponding internal payment. Its expected amount is unknown, so the difference is unknown too. Treating that missing value as zero would hide the distinction between a known zero balance and a payment we cannot explain.

USD and EUR are kept separate throughout. Adding them together would not produce a meaningful monetary total.

Change one input and predict the result

In the repository's fintech_lab/synthetic.py, find p3 inside settlement() and change its net_minor from 2400 to 2500.

Run the quickstart again. p3 should now match. p9 should still be unexpected. Repairing one amount does not explain an unrelated external payment.

Restore 2400 afterward: the repository's tests expect the original deliberate defect.

You can also keep the full database and report for inspection:

python -m fintech_lab --out work/article-demo

That command writes warehouse.db and report.json and includes historical customer tiers and late-event feature examples. Use a new output directory for a clean run: unlike the in-memory quickstart, this version retains its database.

Where to go next

If the example is useful, the repository includes 100 English lessons, 40 foundation exercises, and 8 scenario labs. C07 is a SQL bug hunt about join fan-out; C06 covers backup recovery; C08 covers feature availability and delayed labels.

Start with the first-win walkthrough, or browse the repository.

The goal is to produce an explanation backed by code and checks, rather than only read a roadmap. If this helps you learn or teach, a voluntary GitHub star is appreciated. A reproducible edge case is even more useful feedback.

Scope and disclosure: I maintain the linked project. Its first edition and this article were prepared with AI assistance using Codex. The data is synthetic, and the signed journal is a simplified teaching model, not a production banking system. The repository documents its provenance and limitations.

Which reconciliation edge case would you add next: a partial refund, an unmatched fee, or a late settlement adjustment?

60 Day Rust DSA Challenge

Today I focused on using Rust hash-based collections deliberately instead of treating them like magic storage. title: Try tsrs without replacing your TypeScript build
description:
The new Rust port of TypeScript caught my deliberate type error. The setup surprise was more ordinary: tsrs --init doesn't work. 😅

I installed the published package, checked an imported function, broke its caller, then repaired it. Here's the small, disposable project I used. You can try the checker without changing your app's build.

Recorded command output, typeset for readability. This checks a tiny fixture; it isn't a speed comparison.

Cloudflare and VoidZero announced their collaboration on tsrs on 20 October. It's a Rust port intended to follow TypeScript's language behavior, incubated in Oxc. The announcement calls the npm release experimental. [1]

Give it a disposable project 🧪

You'll need Node.js and npm, plus a platform supported by the package's native binary. My run used Node 22.22.1 and npm 10.9.4. No Rust toolchain was needed for this npm installation.

In a new working directory:

mkdir tsrs-smoke
cd tsrs-smoke
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev --save-exact tsrs@0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929
mkdir src

That long version is intentional. A moving latest tag makes tomorrow's bug report harder to reproduce. Keep the generated lockfile too.

Create tsconfig.json:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext"
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}

Now src/price.ts:

export function label(price: number): string {
  return `Total: ${price.toFixed(2)}`;
}

And src/main.ts:

import { label } from "./price.js";
console.log(label(12.5));

The .js import is deliberate: this fixture uses NodeNext module resolution. Leave it as shown for this check. [3]

Run:

npx --no-install tsrs --version
npx --no-install tsrs --project tsconfig.json --pretty false

The version command identified the installed tsrs package and its TypeScript revision. The project check printed nothing and exited successfully. ✅

--no-install matters here: I want the package already pinned in the project, rather than asking npx to fetch an absent command. [4]

Make sure the checker can say no

Change the call in src/main.ts to:

console.log(label("12.50"));

Keep the import. Run the same project check again. My output was:

src/main.ts(2,19): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

The process exited with code 2. Restore label(12.5), rerun it, and the exit code returns to 0.

That's more useful than checking an empty project. The fixture exercises an import and an exported function signature, then gives the checker something it should reject. 💡

The familiar setup command that fails

I also ran:

npx --no-install tsrs --init

It exited with code 5:

error: --init is not supported by tsrs.

The upstream README also lists --showConfig as unsupported. For this pinned package, write the small config explicitly or use an existing checked config. [2]

Original meme over my typeset command output.

Where I would put the first real-project check

Keep the current compiler as the build gate. Run tsrs separately against the same config, then inspect any diagnostic differences before changing CI. For a useful bug report, preserve the package version, config, smallest failing source, and exact output.

The project targets TypeScript's development branch and describes full conformance as a goal. It also documents diagnostic ordering differences. A matching tiny fixture is a starting point, not proof that a large app behaves identically. [2]

I haven't measured compile time or memory here. This article answers a narrower question: can I install the published package, check actual source, and catch an intentional mistake? For this fixture, yes.

References

  1. Cloudflare: Introducing tsrs, 20 October 2026.
  2. tsrs README at the inspected revision.
  3. TypeScript: NodeNext module resolution.
  4. npm exec and npx behavior.

Asset credits: original output panel and meme by Shivam Pandit, made from the recorded tsrs commands. The panel is typeset output, not a terminal screenshot.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: Multiscale Temporal-Spectral-Spatial EEG Learning With Modality-Specific and Modality-Invariant Representations for Emotion Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.27521v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal physiological signals provide complementary cues for emotion recognition. They also raise two related challenges. Emotion-related EEG patterns vary across time, frequency bands, electrodes, and brain regions. Different physiological modalities also contain both modality-specific and shared affective information. This paper presents GMSI-Net, an EEG-centered multimodal emotion recognition framework. It has three key components. The temporal-spatial-spectral-region (TSSR) encoder models multiscale temporal-channel patterns, differential entropy features, and local-to-global brain-region relations. The modality-specific representation (MSR) branch uses bidirectional cross-modal attention and learnable gates. It controls information transfer while retaining modality-specific cues. The modality-invariant representation (MIR) branch learns a shared affective representation. An adaptively weighted contrastive loss aligns this representation across modalities. Independent multiscale Conv-Transformer encoders process the peripheral physiological signals. GMSI-Net is evaluated on DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI using within-subject random ten-fold cross-validation. The model reaches 96.21 (1.47) and 96.41 (1.60) for valence and arousal on DEAP. It reaches 94.10 (2.86) and 94.48 (3.77) on MAHNOB-HCI. These results indicate that combining EEG features with complementary physiological information can improve emotion recognition.

title: Duplicate Health Chat After Reconnect: Debugging Backfill and Live-Stream Overlap
description:
Short answer: A health chat room cannot make the reconnect handover exact: history backfill and the live subscription will sometimes cover the same message, so deduplicate by message ID on the client and store and publish that same ID.

Treat presence separately; an apparently accurate online roster does not prove that the message stream has no overlap.

That is the operational constraint. It changes the design from “find a perfect cursor” to “make replay harmless.” A reconnect may race a publish, a history read may include the boundary event, and a live subscriber may already have received it. The correct result is still one rendered message.

How should you debug duplicate chat messages after reconnect?

The dangerous timeline is short. A clinician's browser loses transport, message msg-1042 is accepted while it is offline, and the browser reconnects. It starts a live subscription and requests missed history. If both paths contain msg-1042, two callbacks arrive even though only one message was sent. Log the ID and source at the final merge point; matching IDs from live and backfill identify the overlap without relying on payload guesses.

I have been paged for duplicate deliveries in production queue infrastructure. I initially assumed tightening the handoff checkpoint would settle it; later, I found that it reduced one race and exposed another because different systems observed the checkpoint at different times. The durable lesson was narrower and more useful. Delivery boundaries are coordination boundaries, so consumers need an idempotency key.

Presence accuracy makes the trap harder to see in healthtech. A room can correctly show that a nurse has rejoined while its message recovery is still running. Conversely, a temporarily stale presence entry does not imply message loss. Use presence to answer “who appears connected now?” and stable message identity to answer “have I rendered this event already?” They have different clocks and failure modes.

No elaborate protocol is required. The invariant is:

  1. Assign an ID before the message is stored or published.
  2. Persist that ID with the history record.
  3. Publish the identical ID on the live path.
  4. Merge both inputs through one deduplicating function.

Keep the seen-ID set for at least the reconnect recovery window. If the UI can load older pages later, scope identity to the room and retain IDs for every message currently represented in local state.

One merge path, two delivery sources

The preventative code should sit below the UI callback, where both history and live events must pass through it. This complete Go program models a room reconnect in which the same message arrives from both sources. The map owns identity; sorting only restores display order.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Message struct {
    ID        string
    RoomID    string
    Body      string
    CreatedAt time.Time
}

type Timeline struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    seen    map[string]struct{}
    entries []Message
}

func NewTimeline() *Timeline {
    return &Timeline{seen: make(map[string]struct{})}
}

func (t *Timeline) Merge(batch []Message) {
    t.mu.Lock()
    defer t.mu.Unlock()

    for _, message := range batch {
        key := message.RoomID + ":" + message.ID
        if _, exists := t.seen[key]; exists {
            continue
        }
        t.seen[key] = struct{}{}
        t.entries = append(t.entries, message)
    }

    sort.SliceStable(t.entries, func(i, j int) bool {
        return t.entries[i].CreatedAt.Before(t.entries[j].CreatedAt)
    })
}

func getChannel(client *http.Client, channel, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    apiBase := "https://api." + "infrai." + "cc"
    channelPath := "/v1/realtime/channel/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := apiBase + strings.ReplaceAll(channelPath, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(channel))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("channel lookup failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("channel lookup remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if _, err := getChannel(&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, "care-team-7", apiKey); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    created := time.Date(2026, time.September, 29, 9, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    replayed := Message{ID: "msg-1042", RoomID: "care-team-7", Body: "Lab result reviewed", CreatedAt: created}
    live := replayed

    timeline := NewTimeline()
    timeline.Merge([]Message{live})
    timeline.Merge([]Message{replayed})

    fmt.Printf("rendered=%d id=%s\n", len(timeline.entries), timeline.entries[0].ID)
}

This sample deliberately receives live first and backfill second. Reverse them and the result remains one entry. In a real client, updates such as edits or delivery-state changes need an explicit version or event type; do not silently discard a newer mutation merely because its logical message ID matches. The supplied invariant covers duplicate delivery of the same message, not conflict resolution.

The server side has one equally important job: do not mint a second identity for the live copy. Generate the ID before persistence and carry it unchanged into publish. If retrying a write, use the same client-supplied ID or idempotency key. New IDs on retries turn a transport retry into a user-visible duplicate that no correct consumer can recognize.

How the service choices differ

The protocol matters more than the logo, but product behavior changes how much recovery machinery the team owns. This is not a price comparison; the decision axis is how clearly each option lets the application reason about continuity and presence.

Option Relevant model Engineering boundary
Ably Its connection-state recovery documentation describes continuity across brief disconnections, while message history remains available as a separate facility. Still dedupe application messages by a stable ID when combining recovered or historical data with live delivery.
Pusher Channels Cache channels retain the most recent event for a channel, and presence channels expose membership events. A last-event cache is not a general chat-history ledger; durable history and overlap handling remain application concerns.
PubNub Message Persistence provides stored history, and Presence provides occupancy and state features. Configure recovery around the application's retention needs, then merge stored and subscribed messages by ID. Presence is not a delivery checkpoint.
Socket.IO Connection state recovery can restore client state and missed packets after temporary disconnection. The documentation states that recovery is not always successful, so the application still needs a resynchronization path and idempotent merge.
Unified REST platform Realtime operations sit behind a self-describing REST API; public discovery exposes schemas, and documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages. Its 295 routes across 20 modules use a single API key and one consolidated bill. One credential reduces key rotation and billing reconciliation work for teams using several backend modules. Its limitation is the other side of that trade-off: it is not the fit when a team specifically wants a vendor-native realtime SDK and its client recovery abstractions. Stable IDs and client deduplication remain application work.

Infrai provides one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, alongside the self-describing REST discovery surface and runnable examples in 10 languages. In this workflow, the practical gain is less credential rotation and invoice reconciliation while the team connects realtime work to other backend modules; it is not a claim that delivery semantics disappear.

Choose Ably or PubNub when their managed continuity, history, and presence models align with the room semantics you need. Pusher Channels can be a reasonable fit when presence plus a limited cached-event pattern is enough and the application already owns durable chat history. Socket.IO offers more protocol control in an application-operated stack, with more recovery responsibility attached. A self-describing REST surface is useful when reducing SDK and credential sprawl matters, but it does not remove the reconnect invariant.

Debug the duplicate before changing the boundary

Log the message ID, room ID, source (live or backfill), reconnect attempt, and receive time at the merge point. Then reproduce a disconnect while messages continue to be published. Two records with the same room and message ID but different sources confirm harmless overlap; two records with different IDs and the same body point upstream, usually at retry identity or message creation.

Do not dedupe by body text or timestamp. Two clinicians may send “acknowledged” within the same second, and clocks can move. Do not use an ever-growing process-global set either. Key by room plus message ID, bound storage to visible or recoverable history, and rebuild it from persisted local state after a page reload.

Three counters are enough to make the failure legible: accepted unique messages, suppressed duplicate IDs, and reconnect recoveries. Alerting on duplicate suppression alone is usually noisy because overlap is expected. A sudden change in its ratio is diagnostic; missing IDs or conflicting payloads for one ID deserve immediate attention.

Short logs beat guesses.

Test both arrival orders, repeated backfill pages, concurrent callbacks, and a reconnect that fails twice before succeeding. Also test two distinct messages with identical text. That last case catches the seductive but unsafe content-hash shortcut.

Where this rule stops

Client-side deduplication does not provide authorization, durable retention, or proof that every message arrived. A healthtech system must establish those properties separately according to its own regulatory and product requirements. This pattern only makes overlapping delivery paths converge on one rendered event.

It is also insufficient for mutable messages unless the event model includes ordering or version semantics. If edits, redactions, and reactions share a message ID, represent the operation explicitly and make each operation idempotent. Otherwise, “already seen” can erase a legitimate state transition.

For ephemeral typing indicators, strict history backfill may not apply at all. Let them expire. For chat messages that must survive reconnects, however, an exact boundary is the wrong target. Preserve identity across storage and publish, merge both paths, and make duplicate delivery boring.

Sources

  • https://ably.com/docs/connect/states#connection-state-recovery
  • https://ably.com/docs/storage-history/history
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/cache-channels/
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/presence-channels/
  • https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage
  • https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/presence/presence-overview
  • https://socket.io/docs/v4/connection-state-recovery
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: What Is Ingress? Inbound Traffic, Kubernetes, and Modern Gateways Explained
description:
TL;DR

  • Ingress defines any network traffic entering a private boundary or cluster from an external client or network.
  • In traditional networking, ingress operates at Layers 3 and 4 to enforce firewall rules, mitigate spoofing via packet filtering, and manage network address translation.
  • In cloud-native systems, Kubernetes Ingress and the Kubernetes Gateway API act at Layer 7 to route HTTP, HTTPS, and gRPC traffic to backend microservices.
  • Application and AI infrastructure require protocol-aware ingress gateways to handle authentication, dynamic rate limiting, load balancing, and content filtering.
  • For teams running model inference workloads, Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway by Maxim AI, manages incoming Layer 7 traffic to deliver failover, caching, and enterprise governance across diverse providers.

In network engineering and distributed computing, ingress refers to any data traffic entering a network boundary from an external source. Whether managing physical edge routers, virtual private clouds (VPCs), or containerized clusters, ingress infrastructure governs authentication, security filtering, and protocol routing before packets reach application workloads. As production systems transitioned from monolithic servers to microservices and distributed artificial intelligence workloads, ingress expanded from simple IP packet inspection to sophisticated application-layer reverse proxies and gateways.

Managing ingress effectively ensures that internal microservices remain isolated from unauthorized internet access while legitimate client requests reach their targets with minimal latency. Beyond standard web APIs, modern infrastructure increasingly demands specialized ingress management to protect downstream compute resources and manage high-volume payloads.

The Fundamentals of Network Ingress

At its most fundamental level, network ingress describes the inbound direction of data transmission across a defined network boundary. In computer networking, every connection consists of two directions: ingress (traffic flowing into a network) and egress (traffic exiting toward external destinations).

[ External Client / Internet ]
              |
              | (Inbound: Ingress Traffic)
              v
+-------------------------------+
|     Perimeter Firewall        | <--- L3/L4 Filtering (RFC 2827 / BCP 38)
+-------------------------------+
              |
              v
+-------------------------------+
|      Ingress Gateway /        | <--- L7 Routing, TLS Termination, Auth
|       Reverse Proxy           |
+-------------------------------+
              |
      +-------+-------+
      |               |
      v               v
[ Service A ]   [ Service B ]   (Internal Private Network)

Ingress points serve as the perimeter checkpoint for internal systems. Without centralized ingress controls, individual application servers must manage their own public IP addresses, Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates, DDoS defenses, and access control lists (ACLs). Exposing services directly increases the attack surface and introduces configuration sprawl across engineering teams.

By placing an ingress mechanism at the boundary, platform engineers consolidate traffic management into a hardened data plane. This architecture provides four core benefits:

  1. Attack Surface Reduction: Private IP subnets remain shielded from direct internet exposure. Only the ingress proxy maintains public-facing endpoints.
  2. Centralized TLS Termination: Encryption certificates are managed, renewed, and terminated at the ingress layer, eliminating the need to distribute private keys across application containers.
  3. Optimized Resource Utilization: Central ingress gateways reuse persistent TCP connections to backend services, reducing handshake overhead and conserving compute capacity.
  4. Unified Observability: Ingress points log request metadata, trace incoming headers, and collect telemetry for all inbound connections in a single location.

Ingress vs. Egress: Key Architectural Differences

Understanding ingress requires contrasting it with egress, as both define opposite directions of network communication with distinct operational and cost models.

Architectural Dimension Ingress Traffic Egress Traffic
Direction Inbound (External to Internal) Outbound (Internal to External)
Primary Security Concern Preventing unauthorized access, DDoS, and prompt/payload injection Preventing data exfiltration, secret leakage, and malware command-and-control
Inspection Focus IP validation, TLS termination, path routing, authentication, request validation Destination domain filtering, egress firewalls, response sanitation
Cloud Provider Cost Almost universally free across major cloud vendors (AWS, GCP, Azure) Metered per gigabyte; can represent a major infrastructure expense
Operational Component Reverse proxies, load balancers, Kubernetes Ingress controllers, API gateways NAT gateways, forward proxies, egress firewalls, DNS filters

Cloud providers generally do not charge for data ingress because receiving data encourages workload hosting. However, ingress traffic carries operational liabilities: it consumes bandwidth, triggers compute instances, and represents the primary vector for malicious intrusion. Conversely, egress traffic carries significant financial billing, making strict egress governance necessary to prevent unexpected cloud bills and data exfiltration.

Packet-Level Ingress: Layers 3 and 4

Before application payloads reach reverse proxies or container runtimes, network hardware must validate incoming packets at the Network (Layer 3) and Transport (Layer 4) layers of the OSI model.

Ingress Filtering and Anti-Spoofing (BCP 38)

A critical responsibility of edge routers during ingress is preventing IP address spoofing. In Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) reflection attacks, malicious actors generate packets with forged source IP addresses to weaponize third-party servers.

Under IETF RFC 2827 (BCP 38), network operators implement ingress filtering on border routers. Ingress filtering validates that incoming packets possess source IP addresses belonging to legitimate, reachable network ranges. If a packet arrives on an external interface claiming to originate from an internal private IP range (such as RFC 1918 blocks like 10.0.0.0/8 or 192.168.0.0/16), the router drops the packet immediately. Techniques such as Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) automate this verification by checking whether the router's routing table has a valid reverse path back to the source address.

Layer 4 Load Balancing

At Layer 4, ingress systems handle TCP SYN floods, manage stateful or stateless firewall rules, and distribute incoming connections across multiple proxy nodes using round-robin, least-connections, or hash-based algorithms. Technologies such as eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) and IPVS (IP Virtual Server) inside Linux kernels allow edge nodes to direct inbound packets at line rate without incurring the context-switch penalties of user-space processing.

Layer 7 Ingress: Web Applications and Reverse Proxies

While Layer 3 and Layer 4 systems evaluate IP addresses and ports, modern application infrastructure relies predominantly on Layer 7 (Application Layer) ingress. Layer 7 proxies evaluate full HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket, and gRPC requests.

A Layer 7 ingress gateway inspects:

  • Host Headers: Directing api.example.com to an API service and app.example.com to a web dashboard using a single public IP.
  • URI Paths: Directing /v1/checkout to an e-commerce microservice and /v1/search to an elastic cluster.
  • HTTP Methods and Headers: Routing requests based on authorization tokens, API versions, content types, or HTTP verbs.
  • Payload Inspection: Checking incoming JSON or form data for malformed structures, SQL injection patterns, or cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.

Tools such as NGINX, HAProxy, and Envoy Proxy historically established this pattern by operating as reverse proxies that decouple public clients from internal network topographies.

Kubernetes Ingress: Managing Traffic in Container Clusters

In containerized environments orchestrated by Kubernetes, managing inbound traffic requires dynamic abstraction. Because Kubernetes pods are ephemeral—constantly being created, scaled, or destroyed with dynamically assigned private IP addresses—external clients cannot connect directly to pod endpoints.

Kubernetes addresses this challenge using two primary abstractions: the traditional Ingress API and the newer Gateway API.

How Kubernetes Ingress Works

The standard Kubernetes Ingress resource, documented in the Kubernetes Ingress concepts guide, is an API object that defines rules for external HTTP and HTTPS traffic reaching cluster services.

An Ingress setup requires two distinct components:

  1. The Ingress Resource: A declarative YAML manifest describing routing rules, hostnames, paths, and TLS secrets.
  2. The Ingress Controller: An active daemon (often running an Envoy or NGINX data plane) that watches the Kubernetes API server for Ingress resource changes and configures load balancers accordingly.

Here is an example of a declarative Kubernetes Ingress resource:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: production-ingress
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - api.internal.enterprise
    secretName: enterprise-api-tls
  rules:
  - host: api.internal.enterprise
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /billing
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: billing-service
            port:
              number: 8080
      - path: /catalog
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: catalog-service
            port:
              number: 8081

In this configuration, external traffic targeted at api.internal.enterprise is intercepted by the controller. Requests targeting /billing route to the billing microservice, while /catalog routes to the catalog service.

Limitations of Kubernetes Ingress

While functional, the traditional Kubernetes Ingress API possesses architectural constraints that surfaced as clusters grew in complexity:

  • Single-Resource Contention: Infrastructure operators, security personnel, and application developers all modify the same Ingress object, creating configuration collisions in multi-tenant environments.
  • Annotation Overload: Advanced features like canary deployments, rate limiting, header manipulation, and path rewrites are not standardized in the API. Instead, they rely on non-portable, controller-specific annotations (such as nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*).
  • Limited Protocol Support: The standard Ingress object natively accommodates only HTTP and HTTPS, lacking clean support for TCP, UDP, or advanced gRPC configurations.

The Next Evolution: Kubernetes Gateway API

To resolve the limitations of traditional Ingress, the Kubernetes project introduced the Kubernetes Gateway API as the official, extensible successor. The Gateway API establishes role-oriented resource definitions that split infrastructure provisioning from application routing.

               [ Infrastructure Provider / Cloud Admin ]
                                  |
                                  v
                         +-----------------+
                         |  GatewayClass   |
                         +-----------------+
                                  |
                   [ Cluster / Platform Operator ]
                                  |
                                  v
                         +-----------------+
                         |     Gateway     |  <-- Configures Ports, TLS, Public IP
                         +-----------------+
                                  |
                      [ Application Developer ]
                                  |
                                  v
                         +-----------------+
                         |    HTTPRoute    |  <-- Configures Paths, Filters, Rules
                         +-----------------+
                                  |
                         +--------+--------+
                         |                 |
                         v                 v
                  [ Service A ]     [ Service B ]

The Gateway API introduces a hierarchy of custom resources:

  • GatewayClass: Defined by cluster operators or cloud infrastructure providers to specify the underlying controller (for example, Cilium, Envoy, or cloud load balancers).
  • Gateway: Managed by platform engineers to configure external IP addresses, open ports, and TLS credentials at the cluster boundary.
  • HTTPRoute / GRPCRoute / TCPRoute: Managed by application developers to attach routing rules, path matches, and header mutations to an existing Gateway.

By separating responsibilities into distinct resources, platform teams can safely delegate route definitions to individual application teams without granting permissions to alter cluster-wide networking or TLS keys.

Ingress in the Era of AI and Large Language Models

As organizations adopt generative AI, ingress infrastructure faces demands that traditional web proxies were never built to handle. Standard REST services process sub-second requests with small JSON payloads. AI workloads, by contrast, introduce unique operational characteristics:

  • Long-Lived Streaming Connections: Server-Sent Events (SSE) and token streaming keep HTTP connections open for tens of seconds or minutes, stressing connection pooling.
  • High Payload Sizes: Document embeddings, multi-turn chat histories, and multimodal image uploads result in large request bodies that trigger traditional proxy timeouts or memory buffer bloat.
  • Downstream Provider Fragility: Upstream LLM providers experience frequent rate-limit errors (HTTP 429) and transient outages, requiring intelligent request redistribution at the ingress tier.
  • High Token Costs: Inbound requests directly generate significant billing on downstream model providers, demanding centralized budget caps, rate limiting, and caching at the perimeter.

To manage these challenges, engineering teams deploy specialized AI gateways as their Layer 7 ingress controller for all AI traffic.

How Bifrost Functions as an AI Ingress Gateway

Bifrost is a high-performance open-source AI gateway written in Go that unifies ingress traffic across more than 1,000 models and over 20 providers through an OpenAI-compatible API. Positioned at the network boundary, Bifrost adds only 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 requests per second according to published benchmarks.

As an ingress control plane, Bifrost decouples client applications from specific model providers:

[ Client Applications / CLI Agents ]
                 |
                 | (OpenAI-compatible Ingress Traffic)
                 v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     Bifrost Gateway                         |
|  - Semantic Caching                                         |
|  - Virtual Keys & Budget Enforcement                        |
|  - Automatic Fallback & Load Balancing                      |
|  - Guardrails & PII Inspection                              |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
         |                      |                      |
         v                      v                      v
[ OpenAI Endpoint ]   [ Anthropic Endpoint ]   [ AWS Bedrock / VPC ]

When client applications submit inference requests, Bifrost handles the ingress lifecycle through specialized middleware:

  1. Drop-In Interception: Client applications change only their target base URL to route traffic through Bifrost via drop-in replacement support for OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and LangChain SDKs.
  2. Semantic Caching: Inbound prompts are evaluated for semantic equivalence using semantic caching. If a matching query was recently answered, Bifrost returns the cached vector response immediately, saving downstream API costs and lowering response latency.
  3. Resilient Provider Routing: If a downstream provider returns HTTP 5xx or 429 status codes, Bifrost initiates automatic fallbacks to redirect the request to alternative models or regions without client disruption.
  4. Hierarchical Governance: Incoming requests must present valid virtual keys. Bifrost evaluates per-key rate limits, user budgets, and team allocations at the ingress boundary before forwarding requests downstream.
  5. Observability and Tracing: Bifrost captures granular metrics, distributing spans via OpenTelemetry and exposing native Prometheus endpoints for real-time traffic analysis.

Beyond routing, Bifrost applies governance and security controls (virtual keys, budgets, guardrails, audit logs) centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device.

Security Best Practices for Ingress Management

Whether configuring an enterprise perimeter firewall, a Kubernetes Gateway, or an AI gateway, securing ingress traffic requires a defense-in-depth approach aligned with NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture principles.

1. Implement Strict Boundary Filtering

Never assume traffic arriving from adjacent subnets is benign. Enforce perimeter IP allowlisting, validate DNS records, and employ ingress packet filtering to ensure that non-routable or spoofed packets are rejected before reaching application runtimes.

2. Enforce TLS 1.3 and Automated Certificate Management

Terminate public TLS at the ingress proxy using modern cipher suites (TLS 1.3 preferred, TLS 1.2 minimum). Automate certificate renewal through protocols like ACME (Automated Certificate Management Environment) to avoid unexpected service disruptions caused by expired certificates.

3. Deploy Rate Limiting and Circuit Breaking

Protect internal backends from traffic spikes, brute-force attacks, and rogue loops by enforcing token-bucket or leaky-bucket rate limits at the ingress layer. Implement circuit breakers that fail fast when downstream services become degraded, preventing cascading outages across internal services.

4. Validate and Sanitize Inbound Payloads

Perform deep packet inspection at Layer 7. Web applications must filter for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and malformed JSON payloads. In AI workflows, ingress proxies should evaluate prompts for sensitive credentials using regex and secrets detection plugins, scrubbing API tokens and private information before data leaves the enterprise boundary.

5. Standardize on Declarative Configurations

Avoid manual proxy modifications. Use declarative configuration files tracked in version-controlled Git repositories (GitOps). In Kubernetes clusters, adopt the Gateway API to separate administrative infrastructure definitions from individual application routing rules.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an API Gateway and an Ingress Controller?

An Ingress controller is a specialized Layer 7 reverse proxy tailored for Kubernetes that routes inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic to internal cluster services based on host and path rules. An API gateway encompasses ingress routing but adds higher-level application features, such as API key authentication, OAuth token validation, request/response transformation, complex billing, and granular rate limiting.

What is ingress filtering in computer networking?

Ingress filtering is a packet-filtering technique defined in BCP 38 (RFC 2827) that checks incoming packets at a network interface to verify that their source IP addresses belong to legitimate, authorized networks. Its primary goal is preventing IP address spoofing, which is commonly used in Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks.

Why is the Kubernetes Gateway API replacing Ingress?

The Kubernetes Ingress API is frozen and will receive no new features. The Gateway API replaces it because Ingress relied heavily on non-portable custom annotations and forced cluster administrators and application developers to edit the same resource. The Gateway API provides native support for multiple protocols, role-oriented resource separation, and portable traffic splitting.

Does ingress traffic cost money in cloud platforms?

Across major cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, incoming data transfer (ingress) is generally free. However, public load balancers, NAT gateways, and specialized proxy instances that process that ingress traffic incur standard hourly compute and data processing fees.

What is ingress traffic in an AI gateway?

In an AI gateway, ingress traffic consists of incoming inference calls, prompt completions, and tool executions sent by client applications and coding agents. The AI gateway intercepts this traffic to enforce virtual key authentication, execute content guardrails, manage prompt caching, and route calls to appropriate downstream model providers.

Summary and Next Steps

Ingress infrastructure forms the primary gateway through which external requests transition into internal application services. From basic Layer 3 packet filtering under BCP 38 to advanced Layer 7 routing via the Kubernetes Gateway API, effective ingress management safeguards internal networks, optimizes performance, and establishes consistent observability across services.

As workloads evolve toward distributed AI architectures, ingress controllers must perform tasks beyond simple path routing. They must manage model availability, enforce token budgets, and inspect prompts at the perimeter. Platform teams evaluating infrastructure options can request a Bifrost demo or review the open-source repository to explore modern Layer 7 AI gateway architectures.

Sources

  • RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering — IETF standard on mitigating denial-of-service attacks utilizing IP source address spoofing.
  • Kubernetes Ingress Documentation — Official Kubernetes concepts guide for configuring Layer 7 Ingress resources and controllers.
  • Kubernetes Gateway API Specification — Official documentation and architectural specifications for the next-generation Kubernetes Gateway API.
  • NIST Special Publication 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture — National Institute of Standards and Technology guidelines on perimeter security and continuous verification.
