title: Node.js EU Storage Decision: Cheap Multipart Browser Uploads for Large Files
description:
Short answer: for a European startup doing large browser uploads directly to object storage, use S3-style multipart upload with presigned parts when low cost and a small control surface matter more than a polished resumable protocol. Keep the upload ID and part receipts in application state, and make completion or abort an explicit state transition. Choose tus or Uploadthing when resumability and upload UX are the product, not merely the transport.

The Node.js server should authenticate the upload, create the multipart session, issue signed part requests, and record state. It should not proxy the file bytes. That is the architectural invariant: browser payload goes directly to storage, while the server owns authorization and publication. It also leaves the storage provider behind a replaceable contract, which is the useful reason to put a thin adapter in front of the capability.

The hard part is not splitting a file. It is deciding who is responsible for an upload that stops after part 11.

What should a Node.js startup verify before choosing browser multipart upload?

I start with four invariants.

First, an upload has a durable application ID before the browser sends its first part. The storage upload ID belongs beside that record. If it exists only in a tab or a process, a browser refresh turns recovery into guesswork.

Second, every part is independently retryable. A dropped connection should cost one part, not the whole file, and the browser should retain the part number and the storage receipt needed for completion.

Third, completion is a deliberate publication boundary. Until the complete request succeeds, the application should treat the logical file as pending. A list of uploaded fragments is not a published object.

Fourth, abandoned sessions have an owner. This capability does not provide an automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum. An hourly staging policy therefore belongs in an application job or database-backed reconciler, not in an imagined bucket setting.

Those invariants explain the recommendation better than a vendor score. Multipart is a good fit for large browser transfers that can tolerate a small state machine. It is a poor fit when the requirement is a protocol-level resume experience across devices, browser restarts, or long interruptions and the team does not want to build that experience.

The options are similar on the happy path and different after failure

Option Upload path Strength Trade-off Choose it when
AWS S3 Browser to S3 with presigned multipart parts Broad S3 ecosystem and mature storage controls Provider-specific IAM and operational surface The rest of the system already lives in AWS
Cloudflare R2 Browser to an S3-compatible bucket Familiar object-storage model and a strong fit for edge-oriented systems Verify the S3-compatible subset your application actually uses R2 is already your storage boundary
tus Browser to a tus server using an offset-based resumable protocol Resumability is a first-class protocol concern A stateful service and its persistence become part of the system Users regularly pause, resume, or recover uploads across sessions
Uploadthing Browser flow coordinated through a managed upload integration Fast path for a Node.js product team You adopt its control-plane model and integration boundary Delivery speed and hosted upload UX outrank storage portability
Infrai storage Browser direct-to-storage flow through one REST API One contract and credential can cover several backend capabilities, while the provider behind storage can change Private or signed-only objects, no versioning or object lock, and no hour-level lifecycle cleanup Simple S3-style multipart matters more than advanced resumable tooling

The comparison is intentionally not a price table. Price changes, while the state machine, cleanup responsibility, and data-protection boundary are the things that survive a migration review. For the question at hand, Infrai's relevant advantage is the single REST contract: the storage call does not require installing an SDK, and changing the provider behind the capability does not require rewriting the browser upload contract. That is useful for a small team with several backend capabilities. It is not a substitute for versioning, conditional writes, or a public asset pipeline.

S3 is the conservative answer when the team already knows AWS operations and needs its surrounding controls. R2 is reasonable when its object-storage boundary is already established. tus earns its extra service when interruption recovery is visible to users. Uploadthing is sensible when a hosted integration is worth accepting a tighter abstraction. There is no honest universal winner.

The critical path is four storage operations, plus state you own

The sample below shows the route shape supplied for this capability. It keeps the bearer key on the server and makes the HTTP method explicit. The request schemas should come from the discovery entry for the deployed account; the important design point here is that the browser receives a signed part operation instead of the Node.js server receiving the bytes.

import os
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
BUCKET = os.environ["STORAGE_BUCKET"]
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def api_request(method, path, payload=None):
    response = requests.request(
        method,
        urljoin(BASE_URL + "/", path.lstrip("/")),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        json=payload,
        timeout=60,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("rate limited: retry with backoff and Retry-After")
    if response.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path}: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()


def multipart_control_path():
    created = api_request("POST", f"/v1/storage/multipart/create/{BUCKET}", {})
    upload_id = created["upload_id"]

    # Persist upload_id before returning it to the browser.
    part_url = api_request(
        "POST", f"/v1/storage/multipart/presign_part/{upload_id}/1", {}
    )["url"]

    return {"upload_id": upload_id, "first_part_url": part_url}

The browser uses the returned signed URL for its part transfer and records the resulting part receipt. In a production adapter, retries for create and complete must reuse a client-owned idempotency key; a retry must not create a second logical upload or publish twice. On a 429, back off and honor Retry-After. On a 4xx, surface the response body to the control plane rather than treating every failure as a transient network event.

The exact example is deliberately narrow. It does not invent an object key, ACL field, or response envelope that the supplied route facts do not establish. Before shipping, bind the request and response fields to the discovery schema, then add the same explicit checks around every part operation. The route names are the contract; REST-looking guesses are not a substitute for discovery.

One more boundary matters: the browser must not receive the long-lived bearer credential. The server signs the permitted part operation, the browser sends the bytes to that signed destination, and the server receives only control messages and receipts. That separation is what makes direct upload meaningful for a Node.js application.

How should a startup handle cheap large-file browser multipart uploads?

An incomplete upload is not merely a bad user experience. Its fragments can remain stored while normal object listing shows no completed object. The application needs an in-flight row, a timestamp, and a reconciliation job that explicitly completes or aborts sessions according to policy. Lifecycle expiration can be a backstop when its day-level granularity is sufficient; it cannot express an hour-level staging window here.

Overwrite coordination is another boundary. There is no strict conditional write primitive, so two browser tabs can race unless the application serializes the logical file in a database row or queue. Do not use the object key as if it were a lock. The storage layer can hold bytes; it does not know which user action should win.

The same caution applies to durability policy. This capability has no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite is therefore not recoverable through a storage-history feature, and a financial or compliance archive that needs WORM behavior requires an external design or another provider. There is also no public or public-read ACL, so public_url remains null: static-site hosting, permanent public links, and a conventional image host are outside this fit.

Browser direct upload has a practical prerequisite too. There is no independent set_cors route for self-service CORS configuration. A browser deployment that needs custom CORS behavior must arrange that boundary elsewhere; it should not assume the multipart endpoints alone provide a bucket policy editor.

These are capability limits, not defects. They're selection criteria.

When should a startup reject this design?

Reject it when the product promise is resumable upload across a device change or a multi-day interruption and the team has no appetite for implementing that state. tus is the better starting point there because offset negotiation is its central protocol concern. Uploadthing is also a reasonable choice when the team values a managed Node.js integration over a provider-neutral storage adapter.

Reject it for permanent public media, immutable regulated records, or a topology that requires automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration. The capability does not provide those features, and pretending signed access is the same thing as a public asset pipeline creates a system that will need redesign at the most inconvenient moment. Its provider coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS or B2, so a startup already standardized on the latter should compare direct integration costs before adding an abstraction.

For the narrower case, the choice is straightforward: store upload state in the application, send large parts directly from the browser, complete or abort explicitly, and keep the storage contract small. Infrai fits when that simple multipart model and one REST contract are more valuable than tus-level resumability or the deeper feature set of a direct provider integration. Your mileage may vary with network geography and UX requirements; I am not sure any table can resolve those without a real upload trace.

It won't be the right answer for every upload.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • https://tus.io/protocols/resumable-upload
  • https://uploadthing.com/

title: Automating Repetitive Clicks for Everyday Testing
description:
You do not need to be a programmer to automate a bit of testing. If you check a website or an app by clicking through the same steps after every change, a macro recorder can do those clicks for you. It is not a full test framework, but for small teams, shop owners and anyone checking their own site, it is a quick win.

What kind of testing this fits

  • Checking a form still works. Fill in the same fields, press submit, look at the result.
  • Clicking through a checkout. Add an item, go to the cart, start checkout, stop before paying.
  • Repeating a bug. If a problem only shows up after twenty clicks, let the tool do the twenty.
  • Smoke tests after an update. Open the main pages in order and make sure nothing is broken.

Recording the steps

I use the macro recorder in autoclickr. It captures mouse clicks, mouse movement and keyboard input. Microsoft has a getting started guide for Power Automate in Windows 11 if your tests grow more complex.

  1. Open the page or app in the same window size you will always use.
  2. Press F3 to start recording.
  3. Go through the steps slowly and carefully.
  4. Press F3 to stop.
  5. Press F4 to play it back and watch.

You can play it once, a set number of times, or in a loop, and change the playback speed. Recordings can be saved and loaded again later.

Building steps instead

For steps that need exact text, like typing a test email address, a built macro is tidier. You add steps one by one, such as click, type, wait, press Enter, then save it by name and run it with F8. If a button moves, you only change one step. I compared the two approaches in macro vs auto clicker.

Tips that save frustration

  • Add waits. Pages load at different speeds. A recording that moves too fast will click before things appear.
  • Use the same window size and position. Clicks are tied to screen position.
  • Start from a known state. Log out, clear the form, or open a fresh tab before each run.
  • Watch the first few runs. A replay that goes wrong can submit the same form many times.
  • Use test data. Never point a looped recording at a real payment or a live customer record.

Where this stops being enough

If you need checks that pass or fail on their own, or tests that run on every update without anyone watching, you will want a proper test tool. For quick, repeatable checks that a person can glance at, a recorder is often all you need.

title: What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams, measured
description:
Kafka Streams scales by dividing the work. Each partition of the input becomes a task. The tasks are spread over the stream threads of all the instances that share an application.id. Add an instance, or raise num.stream.threads, and the group hands the new threads some of the tasks.

The threads share no state, so they need no coordination among themselves. The consumer group coordinates them instead. It distinguishes a working thread from a stuck one by the poll: a thread has to call poll() at least every max.poll.interval.ms. If it does not, the group rebalances. It takes the thread's tasks away and hands them to the others.

A rebalance has a cost. Whatever a thread had done since its last commit is done again by the next owner of its tasks. A stateful task that moves to another instance cannot resume until its state stores are restored from their changelog topics. Kafka's docs name that restoration as the main cost of moving a task (Fault Tolerance). A standby replica shortens it. Another instance keeps a copy of the state up to date, and the task moves there. Standbys are off by default.

When you add an instance, the rebalance that follows is worth its cost. When a slow thread causes one, it is best avoided. This post is about the second kind.

Polling in time is easy while each record takes microseconds or milliseconds. A remote call changes that. Each record takes as long as the service takes to answer, or until a timeout cuts the call off. The thread waits either way. This is not yet the common case for Kafka Streams, and the standard advice is not to block a stream thread at all. On the other hand, we expect such calls to become more common. More teams now call external services on events as they arrive: an AI model's API above all, but also a scoring service, or anything else that answers in seconds.

A service's answer time also changes over the day. It answers quickly when it is quiet and slowly when it is busy. It is often busiest just when your stream has the most to send it. A slow service is a known hazard. A service that becomes slow is a different one. It hurts the threads that had been keeping up, not the ones that were already behind. We come to why later in the post.

The usual reading is that max.poll.interval.ms bounds one call. Keep each call under it, and the thread keeps its tasks. It bounds something larger. On Kafka Streams 4.2.0, we saw threads evicted from the group even though every call took well under the poll interval. Here is what we found, with the section that shows each:

  • The poll interval bounds more than one call. A thread with several tasks makes a call for each of them between two polls (the round).
  • A thread that had been fast was evicted again and again once its service slowed, at the default settings (a fast thread's service slows down).

Two things depend on the group, not the thread. A rebalance opened by another member can evict a thread whose settings are safe. And under Kafka's newer streams protocol, what an eviction costs depends on who else is in the group. Both are measured in a coming post.

We measured each case in a run, and predicted each run before it ran. Every run used a single machine with one broker and a stub HTTP service whose latency we set. Every run used the classic group protocol, Kafka Streams' default group.protocol. A mapValues called it and blocked until it answered. The use case is illustrative: a stream that sends each new security advisory, a CVE, to a service that scores it. The records were real, newly published CVEs, replayed from one captured window. The numbers describe the shape of the problem, not your cluster. The method, and the predictions that were wrong, are in How the numbers were made.

The stream thread's loop

Matthias J. Sax explains the stream thread's loop in his talk The Nuts and Bolts of Kafka Streams. From about nine minutes in, he covers the buffers, the bursts of records per task and why their size is adjusted. We build on his picture and follow one case: what that adjustment does to a thread whose every record waits on a slow call.

Between two polls, the thread has work that comes due. A commit is due once the commit interval has passed, and a poll before the poll interval runs out. A punctuation is due when it is scheduled. Checking for due work after every record would cost time. Checking too rarely would make that work late. So the thread works in passes of up to N records per task and checks after each pass. While nothing is due, it adds one to N, and the passes grow. When something comes due, it halves N, so the next check comes sooner. It is the rule TCP uses for its congestion window: grow slowly, back off fast. The rule assumes a record is cheap, microseconds or milliseconds. A remote call breaks that assumption. The rest of this post follows what happens then, and which settings keep a thread in its group.

A poll hands its records to queues, one for each task and input partition. When a queue holds more than buffered.records.per.partition records, 1,000 by default, its partition is paused (StreamTask). The thread stops fetching from it until the queue is back within the limit. It still has to poll in time. In a pass, the tasks take turns. Each runs up to N records from its queue, one after another, before the next task starts (TaskExecutor). With three tasks, A, B and C, and N at 2, a pass runs two records from each in turn: A, A, B, B, C, C. After each pass, the thread decides what comes next (StreamThread, lines 1298 to 1320).

The loop: what a stream thread does after each pass, in Kafka Streams 4.2.0.

after each pass:
  run any punctuation that is due
  commit, if commit.interval.ms has passed on the commit clock
  if the pass processed nothing:
      go back and poll
  else if the time since the last poll is past half of max.poll.interval.ms:
      halve N, and go back and poll
  else if the pass committed or punctuated:
      halve N, and run another pass
  else:
      add one to N, and run another pass

The figure below follows the loop for three tasks at the default settings. Each call takes 40 seconds, longer than most, so that every pass is wide enough to see. Every pass takes longer than the 30-second commit interval, so every pass ends in a commit. Each commit halves N, and N never drops below 1, so each pass runs one record per task. The first pass ends at 120 seconds, short of the half-way mark, and the thread runs another. The second ends at 240 seconds, past the mark, and the thread polls with 60 seconds to spare.

Almog Gavra's Kafka Streams 101 on configs names the half-interval check. Two facts the rest of this post leans on are less known. N starts at 1 when the thread starts (line 877) and is never reset. It is carried from one poll to the next and, as we will see, across a rebalance. And a pass processes nothing only when none of its tasks has a record it can process. With a slow call and a backlog there always is one, so only the half-interval check sends the thread back to poll.

This is the default loop of 4.2.0. A second one, with processing threads, sits behind an internal flag that defaults to false. The code itself describes it as incomplete, and nothing here applies to it.

The unit is the round

A thread polls only after a whole pass, so what has to fit inside max.poll.interval.ms is not one call. It is at least one record of each of the thread's tasks, one after another. We call that a round: with T tasks on a thread and a call of L seconds, about T x L. A. Sophie Blee-Goldman put it in one sentence in Kafka Streams 101: Optimizing your apps: a thread makes progress as long as it processes one record per task within the poll interval.

The round grows with the tasks on a thread, as the figure below shows. An input topic of 32 partitions gave a single thread 32 tasks, and a round of 32 calls. With 32 threads, each had one task, and a round of one call.

In the figure above, every round fits the poll interval with room to spare, so a slow call costs only throughput. A round longer than the poll interval costs more. To show it, we set up a case on purpose: three tasks on one thread, a 12-second call, and a 30-second poll interval, so a round takes 36 seconds. The figure below draws its first pass. Every call fits well inside the poll interval, even inside half of it. The round does not, and at 30 seconds the client leaves the group.

We stopped the run after 210 seconds. In that time the thread was evicted four times and never committed. Each CVE should give one output record, but the thread had written 17 records for only 7 CVEs, the first few of each partition, again and again. Left running, it would have written more records for the same 7, and never reached the rest of the backlog.

The 30-second poll interval is the default of 300 scaled down tenfold, only to keep the run short. Later sections call these runs the scaled runs. At the default, the same case is thirty tasks and a 12-second call. Thirty tasks is what the default of one thread gets from a topic with thirty partitions, and an AI model writing a long answer can take 12 seconds. Or it is three tasks and a 120-second call. A call can take that long when the service is overloaded, or when the client retries with backoff. Several later runs use a 120-second call on a single task. What counts is the round, and ten tasks at 12 seconds make the same 120-second round. One task is simply easier to follow.

The commit interval is the other clock

With slow calls, leave commit.interval.ms at its default. Raising it saves little, and it opens a way to be evicted. The mechanism still matters, because a pass without a commit is also how a later case ends in an eviction: a thread whose service slows.

The round is not the whole story. How many rounds a thread runs before it polls depends on commits, as the loop shows. A commit is due when commit.interval.ms has passed on the thread's commit clock, which starts at the last commit (maybeCommit). A pass that commits halves N, the number of records each task runs in a pass. A pass without a commit grows it.

The defaults are a 30-second commit interval against a 300-second poll interval. Every pass longer than 30 seconds then commits, so N stays at 1, and a thread whose round fits the poll interval polls in time. That holds for a latency that has been steady since the thread started, and in a group with no rebalance under way. The first condition comes back below, and the second in a coming post. We checked it without scaling: one task, a 120-second call, 15 minutes. The thread committed after every record and never rebalanced, and the output held 7 records of 7 CVEs.

Each commit costs work: the thread flushes its state stores and writes its offsets, and processes nothing meanwhile. Raising commit.interval.ms saves some of that, which can buy throughput. With calls that take seconds, the saving is small, and the cost is what follows.

Raise commit.interval.ms above the length of a round, and a pass can end with no commit due. We ran the same one-task, 120-second call with both intervals at 300 seconds. The first pass after the poll ended at 120 seconds. That was not past the half-way mark of 150, and no commit was due. So N went to 2, and the next pass took two records, another 240 seconds. The thread could poll again only at 360 seconds, past the poll interval. A rebalance followed at 363.8 seconds, and the output held 7 records for 4 CVEs.

We call the range this round falls in the band: longer than a third of the poll interval, shorter than half. A round in the band ends its first pass before the half-way mark, so the thread does not poll. With no commit due, N goes to 2, and the second pass takes two rounds. The thread can poll only after three rounds, and three rounds run past the interval. A round under a third survives, because three rounds still fit. A round over half survives too, because its first pass crosses the half-way mark and the thread polls.

It is the client that leaves. When the poll timer expires, its own heartbeat thread sends the leave, and the processing thread learns of it at its next commit.

Runs on both sides of the band agree. In the scaled runs, the commit interval was left at 30 seconds against a 30-second poll interval, so commits were rare by accident. A round of 12 seconds (0.4 of the poll interval) was evicted and wrote 96 duplicates in 256 records. Rounds of 9 seconds (0.3) and 17 seconds (0.57) were not. One case needs care even at the defaults. A round just under half polls only after two rounds, seconds before the poll interval runs out. We measured the band with the commit interval equal to the poll interval. Other settings above the round follow from the loop, not from a run.

The same clock explains a smaller oddity. Commits land later than the commit interval says: about 35 seconds apart with a 300 ms call, and 35 to 40 with a 3-second one in a scaled run. A commit waits for the pass in progress, and between commits the passes grow by a round each. Apurva Mehta and A. Sophie Blee-Goldman's exactly-once guide calls the commit interval a lower bound, and this is why.

After an eviction

Go back to the band run of the last section: one task, a 120-second call, and both intervals at 300 seconds. It was evicted, and rebalanced at 363.8 seconds. Our first reading of the loop said it would then be evicted every time it rejoined, since it would start the same way again. It was not. After rejoining, it kept its place, because a rebalance is not a fresh start. One thing survives it that a restart would reset, and one thing restarts.

N survives. The failed commit that reveals the eviction throws from the commit check, before N is adjusted, and N is reset only when the thread starts. So the first pass after rejoining took two records, 240 seconds, crossed the half-way mark and polled in time.

The commit clock restarts. The clock counts the time since the last commit. Once it passes the commit interval, the next commit check commits, and restarts the clock even when there is nothing to commit (line 1881). After the rejoin, the task needs a moment to start, and the thread runs a few passes that process nothing. The first of them finds a commit overdue, commits nothing and restarts the clock. So the next real commit falls due 300 seconds after the rejoin. The log does not show those empty passes. We inferred them because nothing else fits the timings, and we predicted the next eviction from them.

We ran the same settings again for 1,500 seconds, and they did what that predicted. The thread rebalanced at 363.4 and 1,203.9 seconds, committed once between them at about 725, and wrote 12 records for 7 CVEs. A thread in the band is evicted again, but not every time it rejoins. When depends on where N and the commit clock stand. Each eviction costs the calls made since the last commit, made and written again.

When a fast thread's service slows down

That N survives a rebalance has a consequence that matters more than the band, and it needs no setting raised. N has no upper limit in the code. It grows by one after every pass that neither committed nor punctuated, however few records the pass held. A stream that keeps up therefore carries a large N. Ours, at 25 records a second with the service answering at once, reached 221 in two minutes. A pass runs at most N records per task, but only the records waiting in the queues. So a large N means a pass takes everything waiting.

A commit halves N only when the check falls on a pass that held records. On an idle pass it leaves N alone, and most passes of a stream that keeps up are idle. In another run of the same two minutes, one check did land on a pass with records, and N ended at 124. Kafka logs N at DEBUG in every pass, as "iterations", which is where these numbers come from (line 1283).

Then we slowed the service to 10 seconds a call, a thirtieth of the poll interval, with 40 records waiting and every setting at its default. The thread took the 40 as one pass of 400 seconds, with no look at the clock inside it. The poll timer expired at 300. The pass's commit, the first attempt in 415 seconds, failed. N was 222 after the rebalance as before it, so the next pass was the same records again. It was evicted every time it rejoined: 401, 811 and 1,222 seconds after the slow-down, and a fourth was under way when the run ended. In all, 155 records were written for 41 CVEs, 154 of them from calls of 10 seconds, and not one was committed.

The same 40 records at the same 10 seconds were no trouble for a thread that starts on them. N went 1, 2, 1, 2, with a commit after every second pass. There was no rebalance, and all 40 were done in about 400 seconds. The two threads differ only in their history. No setting states it, and nothing about the slow call shows it.

Ten seconds after an instant answer is an extreme slow-down. We chose it so that one run would be short and leave no doubt. The arithmetic of the loop puts the line much lower. With N at 222 and that many records waiting, a pass is 222 calls back to back. It has to end within the 300-second poll interval, so each call can take at most 300 ÷ 222, about 1.35 seconds. Any slower, and one pass outlasts the poll interval. The 222 is measured. The 1.35 seconds is only that division: we did not run a slow-down to it.

One more condition belongs here. We placed the backlog whole: the thread was held in one call while the 40 arrived, so that its next poll returned all of them. A backlog that builds by itself reaches the thread one poll at a time. Each pass then takes what arrived during the one before. When records arrive faster than the service answers, each pass is longer than the last. Arriving more slowly is not enough on its own: a backlog already waiting is taken in one pass, up to max.poll.records of it, and that pass still has to fit the poll interval. This follows from the loop, and we did not run it either.

The thread does not get out by itself. Each time it rejoins, N is still 222, the pass is the same 40 records, and the commit that would halve N is the one that fails. Only a new thread starts N at 1 again. Restarting the instance gives one, and so does replacing the thread at runtime with removeStreamThread() and addStreamThread(). The thread that started on the backlog shows what follows. A restart redoes the uncommitted records once. It is a cure, not a prevention: once the service is fast again, N grows back, and the next slow-down sets the same trap. To stay out, cap max.poll.records, so that a poll's worth of slow calls fits inside the poll interval. It saved this thread with nothing else changed, as the levers below show.

The levers, and what each costs

max.poll.interval.ms. Raising it lets a longer round fit, so a thread that was being evicted keeps its place and its calls are not made again. It adds no throughput: a stream that was being evicted falls behind quietly instead. And it has two costs.

The first: a thread that is alive but stuck, on a call with no timeout, keeps its partitions until the poll interval runs out. A process that dies is still noticed sooner, by the session timeout, because heartbeats come from a thread of their own.

The second: with the classic protocol, the default, a rebalance waits for every member to rejoin, up to the poll interval, as Blee-Goldman's guide to rebalancing describes. A busy thread rejoins only after the pass that takes it past half the poll interval. So with a 30-minute poll interval, a new instance can wait 15 minutes for its tasks, and longer by however long that pass takes. That follows from the loop, and we did not measure it. Until Kafka 2.3, Streams set this interval to effectively infinite. KIP-442 returned it to the consumer's default.

commit.interval.ms. Lowering it means more commits, and each one is a flush and an offset write during which the thread processes nothing. Raising it above the length of a round opens the band from a third to a half of the poll interval. Keep a round under a third then.

max.poll.records. Streams sets it to 1,000, and every run but one left it there. It caps what one poll hands the thread. For a thread whose N is larger than that, it caps the pass. We ran the fast stream that slows once more, with nothing changed but this setting, at 20. The poll returned 20 of the 40 waiting records, and the pass was 200 seconds. Its commit went through with 100 seconds to spare and halved N, and the other 20 went the same way. There was no eviction, and each record was done once, where at the default it had been evicted every time it rejoined.

KAFKA-14382 names lowering it as a workaround that shortens the processing loop. This is that, measured for one value. By the loop, the rule is that a poll's worth of calls has to fit the poll interval: max.poll.records times the call. What it costs a stream while it is fast, more polls for the same records, we did not measure.

More instances. They add threads, and threads add throughput when a round fits. They do not rescue a round in the band. A coming post shows that a second instance made the repeated work worse.

For a long call, then, these settings keep a thread in its group. Start with a timeout on every call, retries included. The other settings rest on it: without a timeout, no record has an upper limit, and no setting is safe. Keep commit.interval.ms at its default, below a round, so every pass commits and N stays at 1. Give each thread few enough tasks that a round fits well inside the poll interval. Cap max.poll.records so that a poll's worth of calls at the timeout fits too. That cap is what kept the thread whose service slowed. Raise max.poll.interval.ms last, for the costs above.

What we did not measure

A single machine with one broker, and a stub whose latency has no tail. A round just under half the poll interval has no margin for one.

A latency that changes, beyond one case. Every run but two held the call's latency steady from the start. The fast stream that slows was run twice, at 10 seconds, on one task, with its backlog placed whole: once at the default max.poll.records, and once at 20. A slow-down that comes gradually, a backlog that builds by itself, a service that recovers while a pass is under way, and other latencies are readings of the loop.

Exactly-once. Every run was at-least-once. A transactional commit takes another path through the broker, and the commit interval's default is different.

Kafka Streams 4.2.0 only. In that version, restoration runs on a separate state-updater thread by default, which is one way the loop can differ from older versions. We make no claim about any version whose source we have not read. Nor do we claim anything about the loop with processing threads, which 4.2.0 keeps switched off.

And one thing we saw and have not explained. In the run of The unit is the round, three tasks at 12 seconds against a 30-second poll interval, the rebalances came 36 seconds apart. Once, the gap was 72. If you know why, or have seen the same on your own cluster, tell us in Discussions. We will add what we learn to this post.

How the numbers were made

Every run was written down as a prediction before it ran. Its result was added after, without editing the prediction. The early runs were predicted from a model of the loop, the later ones from its source.

Several predictions were wrong, two of them about the mechanism. The first model, one round per poll, predicted that one task per thread would make a 12-second call safe against a 30-second poll interval. It was evicted. Reading StreamThread is how we found the adaptive pass. Sax's talk, which we found afterwards, explains it too. The prediction for the 120-second call with rare commits rested on a false detail, that the first pass would commit, so its eviction came earlier than predicted. Two more missed a number: commits predicted 30 seconds apart came 35 apart, and one end count was an arithmetic slip.

A note on names, for readers who open the source. The field that holds N is called numIterations. Kafka's thread metrics count an iteration as one poll and all the processing after it, which can hold several passes. We say pass to keep the two apart.

The stub, the replay script and the application are not published. If you want to run them against your own numbers, write to info@alginte.com and we will send them.

This post is one of a few on calling a service from Kafka Streams. A coming one starts from the timeout on every call: how to make sure a call is really cut off, and the arithmetic that then says which settings are safe. To get it, follow the blog's RSS feed or @alginte_sw on X, where we post each one.

Related reading

  • Matthias J. Sax, The Nuts and Bolts of Kafka Streams (Current 2023): the architecture this post rests on, from the threading model to restoration.
  • A. Sophie Blee-Goldman, Kafka Streams 101: Optimizing your apps (2025): the round, in one sentence.
  • KAFKA-14382: stream threads that process too long miss rebalances, and what shortens it.

title: Why do sprite review labels and approval controls disappear at browser zoom?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Let review labels and controls reflow around a sprite that may need its own pan or zoom surface. A large two-dimensional image does not justify clipping the approval button, metadata, or correction link when the browser is zoomed. Separate the artwork viewport from the surrounding document layout.

Key Takeaways

  • Preserve all review actions when text grows or the viewport narrows.
  • Keep image navigation distinct from page navigation.
  • Check reflow and text resizing as related but different tasks.

The canvas can hide a layout failure

W3C reflow guidance includes scope and exceptions for content requiring two-dimensional layout. Apply those carefully. A sprite contact sheet may have a spatial purpose, while its labels and controls often can reflow normally.

Do not place the entire review interface in one fixed-width bitmap or clipped container. That couples readable text, interaction, and image inspection to the same scaling decision. An artist may need a large image without wanting tiny labels.

Separate the review regions

Use a bounded artwork viewport for panning or zooming the source. Place action names, revision, metadata, and approval controls in normal responsive document layout. Keep the relationship between the selected image and its details explicit.

The text-resize guidance concerns preserving content and functionality when text is enlarged. Browser zoom, text resizing, and an in-image zoom slider are not interchangeable tests.

Make scroll behavior predictable. A user should understand whether a wheel, arrow key, or drag moves the image or the page. Avoid trapping them inside the artwork area when they want to reach the next field.

Example: an approval button below a clipped panel

A review page uses a fixed-height side panel aligned with a large sprite canvas. At normal scale, the panel shows action metadata and Approve. When text grows, longer labels occupy more lines and push Approve below the panel's clipped edge.

Making the source image smaller does not repair the control layout. Allow the detail panel to grow or scroll appropriately, and preserve a clear route to its actions. On a narrow viewport, move details below the image rather than overlaying essential text across it.

Check that the selected frame remains identified after layout changes. Reflow should not reset selection or associate metadata with a different thumbnail.

Verify the full task

Use keyboard guidance to review access without a pointer. At the intended zoom and text sizes, select a frame, read its revision, enter a correction, reach approval, and leave the image viewport.

Record the browser, viewport, zoom, and text settings. Check long action names and translated labels as well as short defaults. A single narrow screenshot can reveal clipping but does not prove the whole interaction works.

This is a proposed browser-review test, not an executed responsive-layout or standards-conformance result. It does not require shrinking the sprite's production resolution; the repair concerns presentation and access to the review controls.

Related workflow

See sprite team review contact sheet not preview for the adjacent task. Carry the animation handoff checklist with the release, and use the art reference board to retain visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: Projected Distillation: On Learning to Solve Hard Problems from Close, Correct Targets
description:
arXiv:2610.27467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy learning is central to post-training: training on a model's own generations limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On hard problems, however, on-policy RL provides no reward-based learning signal when all attempts fail. On-policy distillation provides next-token supervision from a teacher, but on hard problems, if a rollout goes wrong early, subsequent supervision is conditioned on prefixes that already contain the mistake. Correct behavior can instead come from a gold or teacher solution, but such off-policy targets can differ substantially from the model's generations and, as we show, may erode existing capabilities. We therefore treat on-policyness as a continuum and propose projected distillation, which minimally edits the student's failed attempts into correct targets. The method uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. Theoretically, we prove that the student's learning regret grows with the edit size: it scales linearly with the horizon under minimal correction, as in DAgger, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. Empirically, across two students (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) and five domains spanning math, code, science, and tool use, projected distillation gives the highest area under the specialization-retention frontier (best on 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA). Our ablations highlight the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness: moving targets farther off-policy steadily worsens the specialization-retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions.

title: Partner commissions on serverless Node and Postgres, with no server to run
description:
I run a small software company in Malaysia. We sell through referral partners and agents, and we pay them a share of what customers pay, not once, but for as long as the customer keeps paying.

That sounds simple until you try to do it. A customer pays on the 3rd. You promise the partner 25%, but only after a 30-day hold, in case the customer asks for a refund. In month 13 the rate drops to 20%. A refund arrives for half of one payment. The partner quits, and now you owe their unpaid commission to the house. Every one of those is a place where money can be wrong.

Of course, there are many existing tools in the market that does this out of the box, some even self-hosted. However, most tools that do this want their own server. A hosted CRM, or a self-hosted one with a Docker container, a background worker and a queue. We run on a serverless stack: Next.js functions on Vercel and one Postgres database. There is no machine of ours that stays switched on, and we felt like the cost vs benefit doesn't justify maintaining one just to pay partners.

Since we could not find a tool that did this and ran as a library inside our stack, we built one. It is called Tandem CRM, it is open source (MIT), and this post is about how it works and what I learned.

The idea: a CRM that is just a library and a schema

Tandem is an npm package plus a set of SQL migrations. You point it at a Postgres database you already have, and it adds a tandem schema with leads, agents, partners, commissions and payouts. There is no separate server and no container to run.

That is the part that matters for serverless. Each call is just a function that opens a database connection, does its work inside one transaction, and returns. Nothing holds state in memory between requests, so it does not care how many function instances you have or how often they start and stop. The state lives in Postgres, and Postgres is what keeps two requests from stepping on each other: the code locks the lead's row before it writes, so two payment webhooks arriving at the same moment cannot both win. Hold periods and releases are plain SQL, so a scheduled job (a cron route on Vercel works, and is how we do it) calls one function, release_due_commissions(), and that is the only background work there is.

npm install tandem-crm
npx tandem-crm init --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" --sample-data

init applies the migrations, runs a health check, and can seed a small demo workspace so you have something to look at.

Every payment gets its own commission line

Here is a lead being created and a payment being recorded. Everything goes through one shared writer, so the rules apply the same way whether the call comes from your app, a webhook or the admin screen.

import { defineTandemConfig } from "tandem-crm";
import { createTandemPool, withTandemSession, createLead, recordPayment } from "tandem-crm/db";

const pool = createTandemPool(process.env.DATABASE_URL);

const config = defineTandemConfig({
  commission: {
    holdDays: 30,
    rateSchedule: [
      { fromMonth: 0, basisPoints: 2500 },   // 25% for the first year
      { fromMonth: 12, basisPoints: 2000 },  // 20% after that
    ],
  },
});

const { leadId } = await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  createLead(client, {
    workspaceId,
    companyName: "Aman Logistics",
    contactPhone: "+60 12-345 6789",
    qualificationMetric: 8,
    productTag: "starter",
    partnerId: "rajesh",
    config,
    source: "signup",
    sourceEventId: "signup-1042",
  })
);

await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  recordPayment(client, {
    workspaceId,
    leadId,
    config,
    source: "stripe",
    payment: {
      paymentId: "inv_001",
      amountMinor: 30000,          // RM300.00, always whole sen
      currency: "MYR",
      confirmedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
    partnerStatus: async (id) => ({ id, active: true }),
  })
);

Each payment produces one commission line with its own rate and its own 30-day hold. A scheduled job releases lines once they are due. If a refund comes in, the matching line is reduced or clawed back. If a partner is deactivated, their unpaid lines move to a house account. That policy is something you configure, not something we decide for you. We just decided to set ours up this way.

Why events

Tandem stores what happened, not just the current state. A lead is a stream of events: created, qualified, converted, paid, refunded. The current status is calculated by replaying them.

The practical benefit is that every decision is saved in the event it was made in. The rate that applied, the qualification result, who the beneficiary was. If you change your commission settings next year, old payments do not quietly change. And when a partner asks "why did I get this amount?", you can answer with the actual history.

Row-level security, so one tenant cannot read another

Tandem uses Postgres row-level security. Every query runs as a role called authenticated, and every row belongs to a workspace. Agents can only append three kinds of event (lead.lost, lead.stage_changed, conversion.confirmed). Anything that moves money needs an owner or admin, and the database enforces it, not just the application code.

The one setup step people trip on: the role you connect with must be able to grant authenticated. init explains this clearly if it cannot.

What two audits found

I am not a programmer by training, and I built this with quite a bit of help from AI and learning each step of the way (I make sure I understand at least fundamentally what the code is supposed to do). That is exactly why I did not want to trust it on my own. I had two independent audits run over the money code, and I wrote tests against a real Postgres instead of mocks.

The audits found real problems. A scheduled release job that could crash part way through. A case where a payment could silently produce no commission at all. Writes that were not safe if two requests arrived at the same moment. All of them are fixed, and each fix has a test that fails without it.

The rules we now follow for anything that touches money:

  • Money is integer minor units. No floating point anywhere.
  • Every write to a lead locks the lead row first, replays the history plus the new events, and only then inserts.
  • Retrying a request with the same source id returns the existing result and never creates a duplicate.
  • A fix needs a test that fails without it.

Where it is tested

The test suites run against real Postgres 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 in CI, on Node 20 and 22, and also as a limited, non-superuser admin account, which is what most managed hosts give you. I have also run it by hand on Neon, Supabase, Layerbase and Aiven. Aiven needs its own certificate file, and the docs say how.

What it is not (yet)

It is early and pre-1.0, and it has not been proven at scale. It has run the partner commission ledger for our own product, Utuh, since 20 October 2026, and I checked it end to end on the live Stripe account, with a real card payment from an outside account and a real refund. No outside developers use the package yet, and we still pay partners by hand, by bank transfer. It is one Postgres and an append-only events table, which should be fine for small and medium use, but I have not load tested it.

Try it, and tell me what breaks

  • Repo: https://github.com/angkutdigital/tandem-crm
  • Docs: https://tandemcrm.dev

The most useful thing you can do is run it against your own Postgres host and open a "Postgres host report" issue, whether it worked or not. If a guide confused you, that is a bug in the guide, and I would like to know.

title: CEFR-oriented Russian Text Simplification Using Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27237v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a study on controlled automatic simplification of Russian texts using preference-based optimization algorithms with a focus on adapting texts to the A1, A2 and B1 proficiency levels. We fine-tune YandexGPT using Rejection Sampling and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) methods to improve control over the complexity of the generated text. We compare several training configurations that differ in dataset composition, text type and the strategy used to construct preference pairs for DPO. For automatic evaluation we train a regression model based on ruRoBERTa-large to predict continuous complexity scores corresponding to CEFR levels. We also consider semantic similarity, lexical coverage and quantitative readability metrics. Human evaluation assesses simplicity, fluency and adequacy. Our best model achieves 87.15\% target level accuracy, an MAE of 0.35 CEFR levels and a target interval MAE of 0.11. Manual assessment shows that 75% of the evaluated simplifications match the target morphological and syntactic level, and fluency and adequacy scores are especially high for A2 and B1. Although A1 remains the most challenging level, the model significantly reduces the proportion of vocabulary and grammatical constructions beyond the target level while generally preserving meaning. Our model is freely available on $\href{https://huggingface.co/kmustakova/RuSimplifier_DPO}{HuggingFace}$.

title: Why do SDL3 nine-grid UI corners look wrong after resizing a panel?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

SDL3 SDL_RenderTexture9Grid takes source-pixel border sizes and a separate corner scale. The destination rectangle controls the panel's overall size; it does not redefine which pixels belong to its corners. Measure the source cuts before tuning the destination. The official nine-grid reference defines each argument.

Key Takeaways

  • Border widths refer to the selected source region.
  • Corner scale and panel dimensions are separate choices.
  • Stretching and tiling the panel center produce different results.

Mark the actual source rectangle

If a panel is packed into an atlas, first verify its source rectangle with an ordinary textured draw. A nine-grid operation cannot repair a source region that already includes the neighboring icon.

Use temporary marks at the four border cuts. For an illustrative 64 by 64 source panel with eight-pixel decoration, the inner area begins after those source cuts. Do not express them as percentages of a changing destination width.

The sheet preparation guide covers atlas dimensions and source organization. Keep those packing choices independent from the display-size decision.

Supply explicit corners and destination

An example configuration is:

/* SDL 3.2+ fragment; not compiled or run here. */
SDL_FRect source = {0, 0, 64, 64};
SDL_FRect destination = {20, 20, 240, 96};
if (!SDL_RenderTexture9Grid(
        renderer, panel_texture, &source,
        8, 8, 8, 8, 1.0f, &destination)) {
    SDL_Log("Nine-grid draw failed: %s", SDL_GetError());
}

These are constructed dimensions for a symmetrical panel. Measure asymmetric ornamentation separately. A left border of eight pixels is inappropriate if a flourish extends farther into the source.

The documented scale parameter controls how source corners are transformed into destination corners. Do not increase it merely to make the center pattern larger. That changes the decorative frame as well.

Decide whether the center may stretch

A flat fill often tolerates stretching. A grid, fabric weave or repeated rivet pattern may need repetition instead. SDL provides SDL_RenderTexture9GridTiled for the related tiled operation starting in SDL 3.4.0. A build targeting only SDL 3.2 cannot assume this additional function is available.

For a baseline comparison, SDL_RenderTexture draws the source as a single scaled image. Showing that beside the nine-grid result makes it easier to see which corner distortion the split actually addresses.

Panel content Inspection priority
Flat center, ornate corners Border placement and corner scale
Repeated center pattern Pattern size under resize
Illustration crossing every cut Separate illustration from scalable frame
Small destination Room for borders and readable content

The UI button-state checklist covers appearance across interaction states. Nine-grid drawing does not generate those states or define their clickable regions.

Acceptance at minimum size

Draw narrow, wide and tall destinations and inspect all four corners. Test the smallest supported panel, not only the attractive large version. Keep text and icons outside border decorations through explicit layout rules.

Repeat with an atlas-packed source to ensure the cuts remain relative to that region. Record source rectangle, border pixels, corner scale and minimum destination in the delivery checklist.

No SDL rendering run was performed here. The main operation is documented since SDL 3.2.0; related newer operations must be checked against the actual linked runtime.

Measure a content-safe inset separately

Define the panel's content-safe area independently of the source border cuts. Decorative corners may extend inward beyond the simple cut line, leaving less usable room for text or a portrait. Check the longest supported label and the smallest intended panel before approving the asset. If content cannot fit, provide a larger minimum size or a simpler compact frame. Do not shrink every corner until the label fits without reviewing whether the visual design remains readable. Nine-grid sampling and interface layout solve different parts of the task.

Sources and editorial ownership

Primary references checked on October 20, 2026:

  • Nine-grid source borders and corner scale
  • Related tiled nine-grid operation
  • Ordinary scaled source comparison

Editorial owner: FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial and verification policy. Report a documentation correction.

title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
description:
arXiv:2610.26866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.

title: Look Before You Reason: Implicit Visual Thinking for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.27341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.

title: Cohort Feature Flag API — Malformed JSON and Invalid Payload Diagnosis
description:
Rollback safety changes the answer: validate a small, provider-neutral feature flag API command before it crosses the network, and preserve the last accepted command so reversal does not depend on reconstructing malformed JSON during an incident. For an e-commerce experiment split across tenant cohorts, a 400 or 422 invalid payload is first a contract failure, not evidence that the service is down.

TL;DR: Reject a missing key, an unknown operation, or a rollout percentage outside 0 through 100 locally. Keep cohort assignment out of vendor-specific request structs. Send only the validated command through a narrow adapter, and record enough information to replay its inverse. This prevents malformed JSON and invalid payloads from turning a routine rollback into guesswork.

How should a feature flag API reject malformed JSON or invalid payloads?

The invariant is plain: an operator must be able to stop the experiment without inventing a new payload under pressure. A successful rollout request and its rollback command belong to the same change record. If the original change moved checkout_recommendations to 20 percent for the high_volume tenant cohort, the record should retain that intent and the prior accepted state. Do not infer it from whichever dashboard happens to be open.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries in cron and queue infrastructure. The recurring lesson was uncomfortable: retries do not repair an ambiguous command. They repeat it. The same reflex applies here. A malformed body should fail before transport; a syntactically valid but semantically impossible percentage should fail before transport too.

For this experiment, keep assignment, flag intent, and provider translation separate. Assignment decides which tenant belongs to a cohort. The command expresses set, toggle, or rollout intent. The adapter translates that command into one external contract. That separation makes a provider reversible. A generic interface alone is not proof of portability. The application must own the key grammar, percentage range, cohort vocabulary, and rollback record, while each adapter owns its wire shape. Infrai can fit at this adapter boundary when a team wants flags alongside other backend modules: its public discovery needs no key and returns the full request JSON Schema, so the adapter can be checked against a current contract before rollout.

Validate before the provider sees JSON

This Go program accepts a backend command, validates the fields this application permits, and then fetches the live flags.set contract. It does not pretend every provider shares one payload schema. The actual write adapter should marshal only fields verified against that contract; guessing a write body would defeat the safeguard.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "regexp"
)

type Operation string

const (
    Set Operation = "set"
    Toggle Operation = "toggle"
    Rollout Operation = "rollout"
)

type FlagCommand struct {
    Key string `json:"key"`
    Operation Operation `json:"operation"`
    Enabled *bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
    Percentage *int `json:"percentage,omitempty"`
    Cohort string `json:"cohort"`
}

var keyPattern = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,63}$`)

func (c FlagCommand) Validate() error {
    if !keyPattern.MatchString(c.Key) {
        return errors.New("key must be 3-64 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores")
    }
    if c.Cohort != "high_volume" && c.Cohort != "standard" {
        return fmt.Errorf("unknown tenant cohort %q", c.Cohort)
    }
    switch c.Operation {
    case Set:
        if c.Enabled == nil || c.Percentage != nil {
            return errors.New("set requires enabled and forbids percentage")
        }
    case Toggle:
        if c.Enabled != nil || c.Percentage != nil {
            return errors.New("toggle accepts neither enabled nor percentage")
        }
    case Rollout:
        if c.Percentage == nil || *c.Percentage < 0 || *c.Percentage > 100 {
            return errors.New("rollout requires percentage from 0 through 100")
        }
        if c.Enabled != nil {
            return errors.New("rollout forbids enabled")
        }
    default:
        return fmt.Errorf("unsupported operation %q", c.Operation)
    }
    return nil
}

func Encode(c FlagCommand) ([]byte, error) {
    if err := c.Validate(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return json.Marshal(c)
}

func FetchSchema() ([]byte, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/flags.set", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }
    response, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer response.Body.Close()
    body, err := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
    }
    return body, nil
}

func main() {
    percentage := 20
    command := FlagCommand{
        Key: "checkout_recommendations", Operation: Rollout,
        Percentage: &percentage, Cohort: "high_volume",
    }
    body, err := Encode(command)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
    schema, err := FetchSchema()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(schema))
}

The 3-to-64-character key rule and two cohort names are application policy here, not claims about a vendor API. That distinction matters. A team can tighten its contract without misrepresenting an upstream one. Provider-specific required fields should come from current schemas or documentation.

Test rejection as seriously as success. Valid JSON can still describe no valid operation: set without enabled, toggle with a stray field, or rollout at 101 percent. Those three fixtures belong in table-driven tests alongside the accepted 20-percent command.

Short tests, sharp boundary.

Read 400 and 422 as clues

HTTP status alone cannot identify the bad field. Providers differ in error mapping. Start with evidence you control: operation, normalized key, cohort, content type, serialized byte length, response status, response request ID if present, and a redacted response body. Never log authorization credentials or the complete tenant payload.

A 400 can direct attention toward parsing or the request contract, while a 422 can suggest that the server parsed the body but rejected its meaning. That is a heuristic, not a portable guarantee. Read the response and current schema. Fixing a field name and blindly replaying every failure is how cleanup becomes a second incident.

Retry only when the operation is safe to repeat under the provider's documented contract. The platform specifies Idempotency-Key, a deterministic server-derived fallback, and a 24-hour default deduplication window for capabilities marked idempotent. Confirm capability metadata before relying on it. Validation failures are not transient, so backoff cannot repair them.

Deletion needs a separate guard. These flags have no recycle bin. Keep deletion outside automatic rollback, require confirmation, and restore a known prior state instead.

Compare the boundary, not the logo

The choice depends on how much of the flag lifecycle the team wants to own. Run the same reversal drill against each candidate; do not assume their request shapes match.

Option Better fit when Boundary or limitation to test
LaunchDarkly A specialist feature-management product is the priority Map the application's neutral command and cohorts to its documented model
Unleash A dedicated flag system and its available deployment approaches fit the operating model Include the chosen operating model in the rollback drill
ConfigCat A focused managed flag product fits the evaluation workflow Keep product-specific evaluation details behind the adapter
Infrai Several backend modules should sit behind one key and one REST contract No flag audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, recycle bin, or client push
Sentry Error grouping is needed to explain failures around the rollout It complements rather than replaces flag state management
Datadog Logs and metrics already drive the team's operational investigation Keep telemetry correlation separate from the rollback command
Grafana Existing dashboards are the main experiment view A dashboard does not provide a reversible flag write contract

This is not a feature-count contest. LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat are natural candidates when specialist flag behavior is the main requirement. Sentry, Datadog, and Grafana answer the adjacent observability question: they can help investigate what happened around a bad release, but they do not replace the flag command boundary. The broad platform's relevant advantage differs: Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key. That lets a migration check the adapter against a current request JSON Schema before credentials or writes enter the test. Discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. Calls use plain HTTP through one REST API, with no SDK required, so the Go adapter does not introduce a provider library into application code. Another backend capability can remain another endpoint under the same contract rather than another integration.

Teams centralizing several backend services should try Infrai for the flag command adapter when discovery-driven schemas reduce migration work; the supporting benefit is that later modules can use the same key and REST contract without another SDK integration.

Keep the limit beside the recommendation. An experiment requiring flag change history, evaluation analytics, complex parent-child trees, or pushed client updates should use a specialist product. There is also no alert or notification route, so detecting a silent scheduled transition requires polling and a separate monitor such as Healthchecks. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but the service does not provide distributed-trace queries or a span tree.

Rehearse the reversal first

A rollout is ready after a rehearsal proves four things: the validator rejects bad fixtures; the adapter sends the accepted fixture in the provider's documented shape; the inverse command restores the recorded prior state; and monitoring notices a scheduled transition that never happened. Run the drill against a non-production tenant cohort. Record a provider request ID where available.

Compare experiment results outside the flag service. Cohort assignment must remain stable, and analysis must distinguish exposure from eligibility. The service does not provide flag evaluation statistics, so a team choosing it needs a defensible backend measurement path. Never substitute a configured rollout percentage for observed exposure.

This advice has boundaries. A temporary internal switch with no cohorting and a completely local rollback may not justify a provider abstraction. At the other extreme, a regulated release needing immutable history should begin with governance and audit requirements; local validation is necessary but insufficient.

The stopping rule is simple. If the team cannot reverse the cohort experiment using only the stored change record and adapter, it is not ready to roll out.

If this boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's malformed flag payload guide and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the adapter.
