  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • W3C Trace Context

title: The path to AI FDE #02: Python for AI backends: a TypeScript engineer's refresher
description:
Most AI engineering tutorials assume Python. I’ve written TypeScript for years and have working, not deep, Python. My roadmap starts with a short Python + FastAPI refresher rather than a full course, and this post is the map I’m following through it: eight concepts AI backends lean on, each mapped to TypeScript I already know, plus the spot where my TS instincts are most likely to mislead me.

Each concept gets its own figure first, then the short version in words.

Setup and types: concepts 1–3

1. Isolated dependencies: node_modules ↔ virtual environments. A virtual environment is a self-contained directory with its own interpreter and packages, so two projects can pin different versions of the same library. Create it with python -m venv .venv, then activate it: activation changes your shell so python points into that environment. The TS instinct that misleads: there’s no automatic per-folder install. Forget to activate, and pip targets whichever Python comes first on your PATH. On Pythons marked “externally managed” (PEP 668), as some OS-provided ones are, pip refuses to install outside a virtual environment and exits with an error.

2. Type hints are for tools, just like TS types. The TypeScript handbook shows types being erased when tsc compiles to JavaScript. Python’s typing docs say the runtime does not enforce annotations; they exist for type checkers, IDEs and linters. So def f(x: float) -> str happily accepts a string at runtime. Run mypy or Pyright in CI, the way you’d run tsc --noEmit.

3. Runtime validation: Zod ↔ Pydantic. Since annotations aren’t enforced, untrusted data needs a validator. Zod describes itself as TypeScript-first schema validation with static type inference. Pydantic plays the same role in Python: validation is driven by type annotations, and once data passes, the fields are guaranteed to match the declared types. For LLM work, FastAPI uses it to validate requests and responses, and OpenAI’s Python SDK accepts a Pydantic class directly (client.responses.parse(..., text_format=MyModel)): it converts the class to a JSON Schema, sends it and parses the reply back into the model. Only the subset of JSON Schema that structured outputs supports will work.

Errors and cleanup: concepts 4–5

4. Errors: throw/catch ↔ raise/except. The shape maps closely, plus one extra: else, which runs only if the try block raised nothing. Idiomatic Python catches specific exception classes. In FastAPI, raise HTTPException(...) returns an HTTP error and ends the request, even from deep inside a helper. But FastAPI’s docs call HTTPException a normal Python exception, so a broad except Exception: between the raise and FastAPI swallows it. One more reason to catch narrowly.

5. Guaranteed cleanup: using ↔ with. TypeScript 5.2 added using declarations (explicit resource management). Python has had the with statement for a long time: the cleanup step runs whether the block finishes normally or raises, and async with is the asynchronous version. In AI backends, that’s the home for HTTP clients, open files and database sessions.

Async: concepts 6–8

6. Starting async work: the subtle one. The syntax looks the same; what happens at call time doesn’t. MDN: an async function runs synchronously up to its first await, so calling fetchDoc() starts the work immediately. Python’s asyncio docs: simply calling a coroutine will not schedule it. Nothing runs until you await it or wrap it in a task, so a forgotten await means the work never happens. asyncio emits a RuntimeWarning (”coroutine ... was never awaited”); treat it as a bug.

7. Blocking the event loop: same trap, both runtimes. Node’s docs warn against blocking the event loop. Python’s asyncio docs say a CPU-intensive calculation that takes 1 second delays every concurrent task by 1 second, and blocking I/O (time.sleep(), a synchronous HTTP client inside async def) does the same. The fix depends on the work: for blocking I/O, an awaitable client or asyncio.to_thread(), which the docs say is mainly for I/O-bound work because the GIL usually stops threads speeding up CPU-bound Python; for CPU-bound work, a process pool via loop.run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), fn); in FastAPI, a plain def endpoint runs in a threadpool instead of on the loop.

8. Fan-out: Promise.all ↔ asyncio.gather / TaskGroup. You’ll want this for parallel calls, like embedding several chunks or querying two retrievers. Promise.all rejects with the first rejection but doesn’t stop the other operations: MDN notes promises have no built-in cancellation (you’d reach for AbortController). asyncio.gather behaves the same by default, and with return_exceptions=True it collects every result and error, much like Promise.allSettled. asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) is the real difference: when one task fails, the rest of the group is cancelled, and the failures are raised together as an ExceptionGroup. That’s usually what you want when partial results are useless.

Takeaway

Coming from TypeScript, the biggest shift isn’t syntax. It’s where the guarantees live. In both languages, types vanish at runtime. Real safety comes from validating at the edges (Pydantic, the way Zod does on the front end), closing resources deterministically (with) and respecting the event loop. Points 6 and 8 are the two I expect to trip over most, so they go on my checklist.

Where this fits in my roadmap: the foundations block (Python typing, errors, environments and async, plus the FastAPI tutorial’s request/response models, errors, dependencies and testing), building toward a small typed LLM API. Next post: structured outputs, from “please return JSON” to contracts.

Over to you: if you moved from TypeScript to Python, which habit took longest to unlearn?

  2. PEP 668: Marking Python base environments as “externally managed”. https://peps.python.org/pep-0668/
  3. TypeScript Handbook: The Basics, “Erased Types”. https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/basic-types.html
  4. Python docs: typing (”The Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations”). https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html
  5. mypy documentation (”a static type checker for Python”). https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/
  6. Pyright (”a full-featured, standards-based static type checker for Python”). https://github.com/microsoft/pyright
  7. Zod documentation (TypeScript-first schema validation).

https://zod.dev/

  11. Python docs: Developing with asyncio (”Running Blocking Code”; “Detect never-awaited coroutines”). https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-dev.html
  12. Python docs: Event loop, run_in_executor with ProcessPoolExecutor. https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-eventloop.html
  13. Node.js: Don’t Block the Event Loop (or the Worker Pool). https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop
  14. FastAPI: Concurrency and async / await (plain def path operations run in a threadpool). https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/

  16. MDN: Promise (no first-class cancellation; use AbortController). https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise

title: KPHarness: Co-Evolving Knowledge and Probing for Long-Horizon Gaming Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.27417v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,

title: Ubuntu 26.10 Finishes the Rust Coreutils Switch. What Should Developers Test?
description:
A deployment script can carry years of undocumented assumptions: a particular cp option, an error string parsed by a build step, or a crypto library loaded through an old interface. Most of the time, those assumptions stay invisible.

Ubuntu 26.10 Stonking Stingray, released on October 15, 2026, gives developers a reason to look for them. Its default cp, mv, and rm now come from Rust-based uutils. It also ships OpenSSL 4, a refreshed language and compiler stack, ROCm 10, and a Linux 7.3-based kernel.

There is a catch: 26.10 is an interim release, supported only through July 2027. That makes the decision different for a CI image, a personal workstation, and a production server.

TL;DR: Ubuntu 26.10 is worth testing, not blindly adopting. Check GNU-versus-uutils behavior, OpenSSL 4 dependencies, and your actual build pipeline. Containers cover userspace regressions; kernel and driver changes need a VM or host. For long-lived production systems, 26.04 LTS remains the sensible default.

Here is the checklist I would use before changing a real workload. The commands are reproducible suggestions, not results from a benchmark I ran.

First, understand what changed in cp, mv, and rm

Ubuntu had already moved many command-line utilities to uutils in earlier releases. The three remaining GNU holdouts — cp, mv, and rm — stayed on GNU in 26.04 LTS because of unresolved compatibility concerns. Canonical says the migration is complete in 26.10.

The language behind a command is usually irrelevant to a shell script. Its observable behavior is not. Consider the things scripts routinely depend on:

  • accepted flags and option combinations;
  • exit statuses, especially under set -e;
  • the precise output of --version and error messages;
  • symbolic links, permissions, ownership, and cross-filesystem moves;
  • behavior on unusual filenames or non-UTF-8 input.

The uutils project aims to be GNU-compatible. It does not claim every GNU edge case is already identical. An upstream compatibility tracker still lists options such as cp --keep-directory-symlink and mv --no-copy as missing in its September comparison. That is a reason to inspect the packaged version you actually run, not evidence that every installation of 26.10 currently fails those cases.

An independent DevOps Daily comparison tested 162 command cases in an Ubuntu 26.10 beta environment and reported 150 byte-identical captured results and 12 differences. The differences included version identification, Unicode handling, exit codes, partial decoding, and diagnostic wording.

Those are their measurements, not mine; 162 selected cases do not measure the entire compatibility surface.

A ten-minute smoke test that stays inside a temp directory

Start with identity. This is safe to run on the system you intend to test:

cat /etc/os-release | grep -E '^(NAME|VERSION|VERSION_ID)='

for tool in cp mv rm; do
  printf '%s: ' "$tool"
  "$tool" --version | head -n 1
done

If Ubuntu's prefixed GNU tools are available, the following probe checks option visibility without replacing system binaries. The script prints observations, not predetermined pass/fail claims:

for pair in 'cp --keep-directory-symlink' 'mv --no-copy'; do
  read -r tool option <<< "$pair"

  for bin in "$tool" "gnu$tool"; do
    if ! command -v "$bin" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      printf '%s: not installed\n' "$bin"
    elif "$bin" --help 2>&1 | grep -Fq -- "$option"; then
      printf '%s: %s listed\n' "$bin" "$option"
    else
      printf '%s: %s NOT listed\n' "$bin" "$option"
    fi
  done
done

--help is only an initial check. It cannot establish that an option has correct semantics. Follow it with fixtures from your actual build and deployment workflows.

For a small, non-destructive filesystem comparison, run this in a disposable Ubuntu 26.10 VM or container where gnucp and gnumv are available:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

for bin in cp mv gnucp gnumv; do
  command -v "$bin" >/dev/null || {
    echo "Missing $bin; cannot compare implementations" >&2
    exit 2
  }
done

work="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf -- "$work"' EXIT

mkdir -p "$work/input/sub"
printf 'alpha\n' > "$work/input/a.txt"
printf 'beta\n' > "$work/input/sub/b.txt"

for implementation in uutils gnu; do
  prefix=''
  [[ "$implementation" == gnu ]] && prefix='gnu'

  mkdir -p "$work/$implementation"

  "${prefix}cp" -R \
    "$work/input" \
    "$work/$implementation/copied"

  "${prefix}mv" \
    "$work/$implementation/copied/a.txt" \
    "$work/$implementation/moved.txt"

  (
    cd "$work/$implementation"

    find . -type f -exec sha256sum {} + |
      LC_ALL=C sort
  ) > "$work/$implementation.manifest"
done

diff -u \
  "$work/uutils.manifest" \
  "$work/gnu.manifest"

A zero exit code means this tiny fixture produced matching file paths and content hashes.

It says nothing about ACLs, extended attributes, sparse files, symlink semantics, timestamps, ownership, or error handling. Add those deliberately when your application requires them. You can also capture stdout, stderr, exit codes, and the resulting tree for each case.

One more practical point: a --version check that searches for the string GNU can silently select the wrong branch in a legacy script. Search your repositories for these probes before an upgrade.

Figure 1. A testing map compiled from Canonical's release notes; it does not represent benchmark results.

OpenSSL 4 may be the harder migration

The Rust switch attracts attention because everyone recognizes cp. OpenSSL 4 deserves at least as much attention if you maintain native software, hardware-security-module integrations, or older TLS infrastructure.

OpenSSL 4 removed the ENGINE API. Ubuntu's 26.10 notes specifically explain that PKCS#11-engine configurations must move to the PKCS#11 provider model.

OpenSSL 4 also removes older interfaces and legacy protocol behavior. These changes are relevant even if your own application never calls the openssl executable directly.

Useful read-only inspection commands are:

openssl version -a
openssl list -providers

Then inspect the OpenSSL configuration used by your application for references to engine_id, dynamic_path, and pkcs11.

Redact secrets before sharing logs. Rebuild native dependencies against the target headers, and test a real TLS handshake or HSM operation. openssl version alone cannot prove application compatibility.

For older systems, this is a more specific question than “Does it support OpenSSL 4?”:

Is a provider available for the key material and algorithms the application actually uses?

Newer toolchains: choose tests that match the dependency

Canonical lists the following in its Ubuntu 26.10 release notes:

Component Listed version A useful regression check
Python 3.14.7 Build a fresh environment, install native wheels, and run the suite
Go 1.27 go test ./..., go vet ./..., code generation, cross-builds
LLVM 22.1.8 Rebuild LLVM plugins, generated IR, sanitizers, native extensions
.NET 10.0.112 Check dotnet --info, restore, build, test, publish, native dependencies
ROCm 10.0 Check supported GPUs, rebuild AMD SMI users, run actual GPU workloads
Kernel 7.3-based Test drivers, DKMS, eBPF, virtualization and filesystem behavior

The version numbers are those listed in the release notes, not a claim about the latest patch currently installed on every updated machine.

ROCm has a particularly concrete breaking boundary: Canonical documents an AMD SMI SONAME change to libamd_smi.so.27, removed deprecated AMD SMI APIs, and removal of rocsparse_indextype_u16.

Software that links to the changed library needs rebuilding. For GPU work, verify the exact device against the supported hardware list before planning a migration.

The Ubuntu release image also uses a 7.3.0-9.9 kernel built from upstream 7.3-rc6. The upstream 7.3 final release arrived after Ubuntu 26.10's release date.

To troubleshoot a driver issue, record uname -r and the installed Ubuntu package rather than just writing “Linux 7.3”.

A container is not a kernel test

You can use a 26.10 container to detect userspace regressions, for example:

docker run --rm ubuntu:26.10 bash -lc \
  'cat /etc/os-release | grep VERSION=; cp --version | head -1'

Verify image availability and pin a digest for repeatable CI.

But the container shares its host kernel. uname -r inside that container reports the host kernel, not a separately installed Ubuntu 26.10 kernel.

Kernel modules, DKMS, real device drivers, and most GPU integration problems need a VM or physical test host.

That distinction matters when someone says an upgrade passed “in Docker.” It may have passed only the userspace portion.

There are desktop and operational changes too

Ubuntu 26.10 uses GNOME 51.

It also offers Myna, an optional, not-preinstalled local speech-to-text technology preview: transcription runs on the device rather than sending audio to a network service.

These may matter to workstation users, but neither answers whether a production build is ready to move. Canonical documents both.

On servers, inspect SSH authentication before touching a remote box.

In 26.10, GSSAPI/Kerberos-capable OpenSSH packages are split into the openssh-gssapi family; the ordinary client/server packages do not provide that feature. If access depends on it, stage and test that exact access path first.

Canonical also says upgrades from 26.04 LTS with TPM-backed full-disk encryption were not supported at the initial 26.10 release.

Consult the current known-issues section before any encrypted-system upgrade, because restrictions may be updated during the release lifecycle.

My upgrade decision would depend on the workload

Figure 2. A recommended rollout sequence, not an Ubuntu policy or a guarantee of compatibility.

For a developer laptop, 26.10 is attractive if your hardware and dependencies need the new stack and you are comfortable with a nine-month support window. Save a recovery path first.

For CI, add 26.10 in parallel with the existing image.

Compare builds, packages, automated tests, and shell scripts. Use a container job for userspace; use a VM or host runner when kernel behavior is part of the test.

Do not assume ubuntu-26.10 is a valid GitHub-hosted Actions runner label just because an Ubuntu version exists.

For a production server, my default would remain 26.04 LTS unless there is a specific capability worth the maintenance and migration cost.

Check crypto configuration, SSH/Kerberos, drivers, and a tested rollback path before rollout. An interim release is a poor substitute for a support-lifecycle decision.

The checklist I'd save before upgrading

  • Shell compatibility: Inventory the exact command implementations and GNU-only options your scripts use.
  • Behavioral testing: Run real shell fixtures under GNU and uutils. Compare side effects, not just output.
  • Automation: Find scripts that parse version strings, diagnostic messages, or exit codes.
  • OpenSSL 4: Rebuild native integrations and migrate ENGINE-based PKCS#11 configurations.
  • Toolchains: Install Python dependencies from scratch. Build and test .NET, Go, and LLVM projects where applicable.
  • GPU workloads: Validate ROCm against supported hardware and rebuild affected AMD SMI consumers.
  • Kernel compatibility: Test drivers, DKMS, and other kernel-dependent features outside containers.
  • System access: Verify Kerberos/GSSAPI authentication and TPM-backed encryption upgrade constraints.
  • Rollback readiness: Confirm the nine-month support window and rehearse a recovery procedure.

My practical takeaway is to add Ubuntu 26.10 to the compatibility matrix before making it a default.

Even if you plan to stay on LTS, this release is a useful early warning for assumptions buried in tooling and deployment scripts.

Have you seen a real GNU-versus-uutils incompatibility in a build or deployment?

A small reproducible case — exact command, package version, expected and observed behavior — would make a far more useful comment than a generic upgrade verdict.

References

  • Canonical — Ubuntu 26.10 release announcement
  • Ubuntu 26.10 release notes (features, breaking changes, known issues)
  • uutils coreutils project
  • uutils GNU-compatibility issue tracker
  • DevOps Daily's independent 162-case test on 26.10 beta
  • OpenSSL 4.0 removed APIs
  • OpenSSL migration guide

Technical scope: release documentation and community test evidence reviewed October 21, 2026. The shell examples are provided for readers to execute and verify on their own systems; no first-party Ubuntu 26.10 benchmark is claimed in this article.

title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
description:
arXiv:2610.27304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.

title: Keep Dynamic Icon Groups from Breaking Your List Layout
description:
A list looks tidy when every row starts with one icon. Then one item gets three icons, another gets five, and the labels stop lining up.

The tempting fix is to adjust the gap. That works for one row and breaks another. The gap was consistent already; the space before it was changing.

Give every row the same leading slot, then put a limit on what can occupy it. In this React example, that means a shared CSS Grid column, a bounded icon stack, and an explicit rule for overflow.

Why the labels drift

Suppose a row contains an icon group followed by its label:

<li className="source-row">
  <IconGroup members={item.members} />
  <div className="row-content">{item.label}</div>
</li>

With a content-sized group in a flex row, the label follows the group's width. One badge takes less space than three overlapping badges. Even with identical icon sizes and gaps, the labels start at different positions.

That is reasonable flex behavior. It becomes a problem when the design expects a common label column across independent rows.

A concrete instance appears in Magpie issue #2498: model rows have a single provider icon, while routing groups have stacked icons. The issue describes reserving a common leading width. This tutorial uses that reported problem as a starting point, with an independent teaching implementation.

Define the stack policy before choosing the width

A fixed column alone does not stop its children from overflowing. Decide how many positions the component can display first.

For this example:

Number of sources Visible content
0 Empty slot, with the label still aligned
1–3 All source icons
4 or more First two icons and a counter for the remaining sources

Five sources therefore render as two icons and +3. The counter occupies the third position; it is not appended as a fourth item.

Use 28px badges, with each overlapping badge starting 16px after the previous one. Three positions occupy:

28 + (3 - 1) × 16 = 60px

A 64px slot leaves 4px of spare space. With a 16px root font size, those dimensions are 1.75rem, 1rem, and 4rem.

Choose a width from the actual badge geometry and overflow policy. A 3rem slot, for example, would be too small for this particular stack.

Build the React component

The example uses three Tabler SVGs retrieved through the SVGicons catalogue:

  • Folder
  • Bell
  • File Settings

They are by Paweł Kuna and distributed under the MIT licence. Keep the copyright and licence notice with redistributed assets.

Save them in your application's public directory so they are available at /icons/folder.svg, /icons/bell.svg, and /icons/file-settings.svg.

The layout does not require a particular icon library. Using local image files keeps SVG markup out of the component's layout logic.

function IconGroup({ members }) {
  const visible = members.length > 3 ? members.slice(0, 2) : members;
  const hidden = members.length - visible.length;

  return (
    <span className="icon-slot" aria-hidden="true">
      <span className="icon-stack">
        {visible.map((member, index) => (
          <span
            className="badge"
            key={member.id}
            style={{ '--index': index }}
          >
            <img src={member.src} alt="" width="18" height="18" />
          </span>
        ))}

        {hidden > 0 && (
          <span className="badge count" style={{ '--index': 2 }}>
            {hidden > 99 ? '99+' : `+${hidden}`}
          </span>
        )}
      </span>
    </span>
  );
}

function SourceList({ items }) {
  return (
    <ul className="source-list">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li className="source-row" key={item.id}>
          <IconGroup members={item.members} />

          <div className="row-content">
            <span className="row-label">{item.label}</span>
            <span className="sr-only">
              {item.members.length
                ? `. Sources: ${item.members.map((m) => m.name).join(', ')}`
                : '. No connected sources'}
            </span>
          </div>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Each member needs a stable, unique id, a readable name, and a trusted local src. For example:

const files = {
  id: 'files',
  name: 'Files',
  src: '/icons/folder.svg',
};

const alerts = {
  id: 'alerts',
  name: 'Alerts',
  src: '/icons/bell.svg',
};

const config = {
  id: 'config',
  name: 'Configuration',
  src: '/icons/file-settings.svg',
};

const archive = {
  id: 'archive',
  name: 'Archive',
  src: '/icons/folder.svg',
};

const monitoring = {
  id: 'monitoring',
  name: 'Monitoring',
  src: '/icons/bell.svg',
};

const items = [
  {
    id: 'documents',
    label: 'Documents',
    members: [files],
  },
  {
    id: 'activity',
    label: 'Project activity',
    members: [files, alerts],
  },
  {
    id: 'overview',
    label: 'Workspace overview',
    members: [files, alerts, config],
  },
  {
    id: 'operations',
    label: 'Operations across all connected workspaces',
    members: [files, alerts, config, archive, monitoring],
  },
  {
    id: 'empty',
    label: 'No connected sources yet',
    members: [],
  },
];

export default function App() {
  return <SourceList items={items} />;
}

The source names are exposed once as text. The overlapping images and counter are hidden from assistive technology, avoiding a second announcement of the same source information.

This approach suits a static list. If users need to inspect or select individual sources, provide a visible details view with equivalent keyboard access. A tiny overlapped badge should not be the only way to reach an action.

Localize the source sentence and counter formatting for your product.

Reserve the column and contain the stack

Apply these styles:

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

.source-list {
  --badge-size: 1.75rem;
  --stack-step: 1rem;
  --icon-slot: 4rem;

  list-style: none;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
}

.source-row {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: var(--icon-slot) minmax(0, 1fr);
  column-gap: .75rem;
  align-items: start;

  padding-block: 1rem;
  border-block-start: 1px solid #e3e8f1;
}

.icon-slot {
  min-inline-size: 0;
  inline-size: var(--icon-slot);
}

.icon-stack {
  display: block;
  position: relative;
  block-size: var(--badge-size);
}

.badge {
  position: absolute;
  inset-inline-start: calc(var(--index) * var(--stack-step));
  inset-block-start: 0;

  inline-size: var(--badge-size);
  block-size: var(--badge-size);

  display: grid;
  place-items: center;

  background: #dce8ff;
  border: 2px solid white;
  border-radius: 50%;
}

.badge:nth-child(2) {
  background: #dcf5ec;
}

.badge:nth-child(3) {
  background: #efe3ff;
}

.badge img {
  display: block;
  inline-size: 1.125rem;
  block-size: 1.125rem;
}

.count {
  font-size: .625rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  color: #17233b;
}

.row-content {
  min-inline-size: 0;
}

.row-label {
  display: block;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

.sr-only {
  position: absolute;
  inline-size: 1px;
  block-size: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;
}

There are two separate constraints here:

  • The shared --icon-slot keeps the label position consistent across rows.
  • The component's three-position limit keeps the stack within that slot.

An empty group keeps its wrapper, so zero icons does not become another alignment exception.

The absolutely positioned badges need an explicit stack height because they do not contribute to their parent's normal flow height. Later badges paint over earlier ones in this simple stack.

The label track uses minmax(0, 1fr) so its minimum track size does not default to a content-based minimum. min-inline-size: 0 lets the content wrapper shrink, while overflow-wrap: anywhere allows long unbroken identifiers to wrap.

These choices address different parts of overflow handling. Replacing the icon column alone will not fix every long-text case. See MDN's references for grid track sizing and minimum widths.

If labels must stay on one line, use a deliberate truncation design instead. Make the full text available through an accessible details interaction; do not rely only on a mouse tooltip.

Keep the same rule on narrow screens and in RTL

As the container narrows, the fixed slot stays put and the text wraps in the remaining track. Top alignment keeps a multi-line label beside the top of its icon stack.

If a compact design needs a smaller slot, change its geometry for the entire list. For example, 24px badges with a 12px step occupy 48px across three positions:

.source-list.compact {
  --badge-size: 1.5rem;
  --stack-step: .75rem;
  --icon-slot: 3rem;
}

Never make this choice independently for each row, or the common column disappears again. Check that the counter remains readable in the smaller badges.

For right-to-left layout, place dir="rtl" on the list or an ancestor. Grid's inline direction places the leading column on the right. inset-inline-start moves the badge stack from that same side.

<div dir="rtl">
  <SourceList items={items} />
</div>

Use real translated labels when reviewing the result. Changing direction on English text checks the layout rule, but does not verify Arabic or Hebrew typography, punctuation, or mixed-direction identifiers.

Test the relationship that matters

A screenshot can catch an obvious regression. A geometry assertion can also express the actual requirement: every label container has the same leading edge.

Here is a Playwright test for a page containing one .source-list. Serve the component on the / route and configure Playwright's baseURL to point to your development server.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

for (const width of [420, 1100]) {
  for (const direction of ['ltr', 'rtl']) {
    test(`label alignment: ${width}px ${direction}`, async ({ page }) => {
      await page.setViewportSize({
        width,
        height: 1000,
      });

      await page.goto('/');

      await page.locator('.source-list').evaluate((list, dir) => {
        list.dir = dir;
      }, direction);

      const edges = await page.locator('.row-content').evaluateAll(
        (nodes, dir) => nodes.map((node) => {
          const rect = node.getBoundingClientRect();
          return dir === 'rtl' ? rect.right : rect.left;
        }),
        direction
      );

      expect(edges.length).toBeGreaterThan(1);

      expect(
        Math.max(...edges) - Math.min(...edges)
      ).toBeLessThan(1);
    });
  }
}

Also check that every badge stays within its slot, images have loaded, and the document has no horizontal overflow. A component can keep its labels aligned while its icons still collide with them.

Use fixtures with:

  • Zero, one, two, three and five sources.
  • A very large source count.
  • A multi-line label.
  • A long unbroken identifier.
  • Larger text.
  • Both LTR and RTL directions.

Check keyboard navigation if the rows contain links or buttons. Keep screenshot baselines only after reviewing the initial renders, and rerun the checks in your supported browser engines.

The useful invariant is simple: source count may change the content of the icon slot, but it must not change where the label begins. Once that rule is explicit, new data has much less room to rearrange the list.

title: Day 17/75: Binary search in Java - Java DSA
description:
Day 17/75: Binary search in Java

75 Day DSA in Java Challenge

Today I focused on protecting the search interval in binary search in java so every bound update stays justified. The strongest checkpoints were state what the active interval still allows before the first loop iteration, move left and right only when the predicate proves one side is impossible, and test the smallest failing boundary because off-by-one errors hide there first.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was moving left and right without a precise definition of what they still allow. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests. title: Trail-Weighted Influence Scores for Approximate Outcome Prediction in Bayesian Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.27366v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction. A traversal enumerates the active trails from each evidence node to the outcome, scores each trail by the product of its edge strengths, and drops evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, we show that the trail score equals the exact correlation between a trail's endpoints, that a chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, and that the pruned posterior is within a computable sum of per-trail terms of the exact posterior when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node. We prove this bound, check it exhaustively on all small trees, and show that it fails when dropped trails share a branch. In simulations on random trees, thresholding trail scores gives 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. We also apply the score, as an unproven heuristic, to seven bnlearn networks with colliders and loops. Keeping the top half of the active evidence by trail score gives lower error than random pruning on all seven, but it is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven, so we show no speedup. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on networks they never saw do not beat the trail score or mutual information, but trail features carry most of what they use and clearly outperform generic graph features. A bound for general networks is left to future work.

title: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.26926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and task-reward optimization. Comprehensive experiments show that AtomSD consistently outperforms strong reward-based and distillation methods, exceeding the state-of-the-art baseline by up to 9.31 points in average performance. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed Procedural Atoms provide effective guidance, highlighting the value of atom-level procedural knowledge for policy learning.

title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.27233v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

title: Mistral Large 4 Benchmark for Coding vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
description:
Mistral Large 4 scored 0.5462 on our Gauntlet benchmark, 28th of 44. About a third of what it lost came from a check of ours that read its table the wrong way round. All 12 amounts it put on screen were correct. I went in expecting to write about a slow, expensive model, and on our Forge benchmark that part holds up.

If you pay for a coding agent, this model is pitched at your budget. Mistral released Large 4 on 6 October as a Public Preview, 1.05 trillion parameters with 52 billion active and a 1M-token context, at half its list price for the first two weeks. Their launch post puts it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro on their own Coding Agent Index (49.8%), which is the kind of claim that moves a budget, so we ran it through both of our agentic coding benchmarks. The Gauntlet has an agent build a payments console with two services and a 3D view inside 150 model calls, then scores it on 99 checks. Forge 2.0 asks for a v2 upgrade of a working Jira Forge app inside 300 calls and scores it on 105 checks against three seeded Jira sites.

Getting a Gauntlet score took four attempts. The first, on 9 October, ended after 49 calls on OpenRouter's "Upstream idle timeout exceeded". On 18 October the second was ended by Mistral's servers. Early on 19 October the third was ended by a bug in goose, the open-source coding agent we run (our own fork), and the fourth finished that afternoon. Its Forge 2.0 pair scored 0.1086 and 0.3304 for at least $10.95. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 did better on the same Forge task. It's the 17 October snapshot I wrote about in my DeepSeek piece, and it scored 0.2422 and 0.6618 for at least $0.62 in about a quarter of the time.

On the Gauntlet the low score is mostly our scorer's fault. On Forge the code losses were Mistral's own. Our harness also gave it a smaller context window than DeepSeek. The build trees show where each loss came from. This is one scored Gauntlet run and one Forge pair, in our setup, on a model whose vendor says it can change silently while it's in preview.

Mistral Large 4 benchmark results: Gauntlet 0.5462, Forge 2.0 median 0.2195

Mistral Large 4 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
Gauntlet 7.2 0.5462, 144 min, $4.93 0.6957, 23 min, $0.21
Forge 2.0 build 1 0.1086, 118 min, at least $5.40 0.2422, 28 min, $0.30
Forge 2.0 build 2 0.3304, 106 min, $5.55 0.6618, 30 min, at least $0.32
Unscored Gauntlet attempts 9 Oct: idle timeout after 49 calls, at least $1.43. 18 Oct: Mistral 503 after 30 calls, at least $1.18. 19 Oct: our 400 after 97 calls, $3.04 none

I checked these on the live boards on 21 October; if a run page says something else now, trust the run page. All six Mistral runs together cost at least $21.53, with three of the bills only lower bounds.

Six things we found in the Mistral Large 4 builds

  1. The x0.6 "wrong money" critical on the Gauntlet is our bug. Our money check compares the amounts on screen with the oldest 50 payments, and Mistral's table opens on the newest.
  2. Mistral's money formatter works on integer digits with a per-currency decimals table, the same approach as DeepSeek's.
  3. Forge build 1, by my reading, lost most of its gap to build 2 to a throttle it wrote itself: it booked 25 to 34 times the real cost of a list call and paused its own scheduled work each hour, before its v1 migration could run.
  4. Neither Forge build ever displayed its admin page, and neither ran a browser self-test.
  5. The 18 October attempt opened with one 37,853-word thought that ran 18 minutes, hit a 65,536-token output limit and was thrown away.
  6. Mistral's API refused a message order that three other providers' endpoints had answered, through OpenRouter, in our runs two weeks earlier.

Mistral Large 4 on our Gauntlet: 0.5462, about 0.70 without a check of ours that misread its table

Most Gauntlet checks just add to a weighted average, but a handful are critical, and when one of those fails it multiplies the whole score down, by as much as x0.6. Wrong money in a payments console is one of those. The money check is called b_money_rendered. A browser probe reads the amount cell of the first 12 rows of the payments table. Then the scorer checks that the digits match a stored amount and that the decimals match the currency, because amounts are stored as integers in the currency's smallest unit (cents, or fils for the Kuwaiti dinar). A correct cell shows two decimals for EUR and USD, none for yen and three for dinars. Mistral's run scored 0.00 on it, with the detail line "0.00 of 12 cells exponent-correct; JPY/KWD traps 0.00", and the multiplier took the whole run from 0.9104 down to 0.5462.

What Mistral rendered

These are the 12 cells the probe read, verbatim: KWD 111.000, ¥594, ¥199, $4.47, ¥809, €224.00, KWD 82.400, €33.10, KWD 2.420, ¥1,060, $1,840.00, KWD 72.400. Our probe also records each row's id, and joined to the fixture, pay_12287 is stored as KWD 111000, so 111.000 dinars is right, and pay_12286 is JPY 594, which needs no decimals. All 12 are right. So are the probe's 12 extra rows.

Its formatter in web/app.js (lines 7 to 25, with the source's \u escapes shown as characters) never touches a float:

const CUR = {
  EUR: { sym: '€', exp: 2 },
  USD: { sym: '$', exp: 2 },
  JPY: { sym: '¥', exp: 0 },
  KWD: { sym: 'KWD ', exp: 3 },
};
...
const s = String(a).padStart(exp + 1, '0');
const int = s.slice(0, s.length - exp) || '0';
const frac = exp > 0 ? s.slice(s.length - exp) : '';

It planned this before writing it. At 10:58 our time (EEST), 27 minutes in, it checked the contract's example and two real payments in its thinking: "129900 EUR → €1,299.00 ✓; JPY 8564 → ¥8,564 ✓; KWD 8263000 → KWD 8,263.000 ✓". Our scorer's own screenshot of the inspector shows that dinar payment as KWD 8,263.000, and the inspector check (q_payment_context) passed.

Why the check said zero

Here is the scorer, score_sb7.py around line 973:

first_page = c.pack.payments[:50]
by_cur: Dict[str, set] = {}
for row in first_page:
    by_cur.setdefault(row["currency"], set()).add(row["amount_minor"])

payments is stored in date order, so payments[:50] is pay_00000 to pay_00049, the oldest fifty. A rendered cell only passes if its digits equal one of those fifty amounts, so the check assumes, without saying it, that the table opens oldest first. Mistral's opens newest first (sort: '-created_at', web/app.js:49). None of its 12 cells could ever match. Our probe even collects the row ids "so the scorer can join against fixtures", in its own comment. No scorer file reads them.

I re-graded the run with the scorer's own _money_ok function, copied unchanged. It gives 0.0 as written, 1.0 against the 50 rows actually on screen, and 24 of 24 when each cell is joined to its payment by row id.

Was opening newest first a mistake by Mistral? Its contract fixes the API's default order ("created_at (default, ascending by INSTANT)") and says the Date header toggles, but it never says which way the table starts. Mistral saw the gap and decided, at 11:48 our time: "The grader might check the first page shows specific rows? Unlikely to assume an order. I'll default to '-created_at' (newest first) — most console-like." It bet that the grader would not assume an order, and the grader did. You can argue the UI should inherit the API's default. I'd listen. Even then it's a sort-order quibble. The check charged it as wrong money.

Who did better at money

All five models I compared passed with 1.0: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol (the model behind Jev Router's top Forge score), GPT-6.1 Sol Pro and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. All of them open their table with sort: 'created_at', and so does our own reference app, which is why our release validation never met a descending default. Grade those five tables against the newest 50 payments and four score 0.0, Sol 0.05.

DeepSeek's formatter is close to a copy of Mistral's:

let digits = String(Math.abs(minor));
if (exponent > 0) digits = digits.padStart(exponent + 1, '0');
const whole = exponent > 0 ? digits.slice(0, digits.length - exponent) : digits;

Same idea, same output. It got 1.0 and Mistral got 0.0. Sol and Sol Pro call Intl.NumberFormat and divide the integer by 10**exp first, and Sonnet does the same with Math.pow, which is fine for amounts this size. So on money code it's a tie between Mistral and DeepSeek. The sort order made the difference.

Mistral did leave one real money bug, in its own test. Its browser self-test checks the first amount against /^[€$¥]\d[\d,]*\.\d{2}$|^KWD [\d,]+\.\d{3}$/, which would reject a correct ¥594 because it demands two decimals after a yen sign. It printed "PASS money formatted" four times, and my guess is that its own first row was never a yen payment. I can't see which row it was.

Without our false critical: about 0.70 and 11th of 44

The score path for this run goes like this. Its checks earned 0.9104. Our false critical multiplied that by 0.6, to 0.5462. Separately, a run that fails some of the 3D checks gets a ceiling on its score, and Mistral's partial failures on picking, the coasting camera and the overview's legibility set it at 0.709. The ceiling formula keeps a score just under the cap, so without the false critical the run would come out at about 0.7048. That's my arithmetic, not a re-score. The board still says 0.5462. It would sit 11th of 44, two places above DeepSeek 1017's 0.6957. The 3D failures, which are Mistral's own, cost it about 0.2 on top.

My audit of that check turned up a second flaw. The yen and dinar "traps" score 0 when no yen or no dinar row happens to be among the cells the probe reads (up to 12). A run whose visible amounts are all right can still pay x0.92. Four ranked runs paid it that way: Elorian Glimpse, Step 5 Preview, Qwen3.8 Omni Flash and GLM-5.3. Across every Gauntlet 7.2 build I could reach, Mistral is the only one the sort assumption hit.

Is Mistral Large 4 good for coding? Forge 2.0 builds of 0.1086 and 0.3304

Forge 2.0 tests the same habits harder: the agent reads a long spec, upgrades a working Forge app under a Jira rate model, and has to prove it all in a local sandbox (our Forge emulator kit) before the calls run out. My piece on the September DeepSeek V4.1 Flash covered this same task, with medians of 0.33 for it and 0.67 for Opus 5.5 in an earlier comparison group. Both Mistral builds and DeepSeek 1017's pair are in the same comparison group on our board. That means the same task, seeds, scorer and engine build. All four asked for the same effort setting.

A Forge 2.0 score is the earned score times a critical multiplier times a reliability factor, where reliability starts at 1 and loses up to 10% for each group of checks whose worst check failed, with a floor of 0.25. Build 1 sat on that floor (its unfloored product was 0.2194) and build 2 came out at 0.4718. Neither triggered a critical. My reading is that most of the 0.22 gap comes from build 1's throttle and the order it ran its migration in.

Build 1 throttled itself and never migrated

The task gives each Jira site a rate budget of 2,400 points an hour, and background work may use 70% of it, so 1,680. Build 1 wrote a gate for that in src/dose.js (lines 76 to 88):

if (dose.bg + estimatedCost > limit) {
  const untilMs = hourStartOf(now) + 3600000;
  await kvs.set(PAUSE_KEY, { untilMs });
  throw new QuotaPaused(untilMs);

The gate is fine. The estimates feeding it were not. With no points header from the site, it charged its own counter from guesses. It booked 51 points for a board or sprint list page (src/config.js:43, cost: 1 + 50), 105 for a search and 260 for a changelog bulk fetch. On the scoring site its first scheduled run had counted 1,567 points after 21 seconds. The next estimated call would have taken it past 1,680. So it paused for the rest of the hour. Yet the site's own ledger for that run says it had spent 715 points over 27 requests, with list pages costing 1.5 to 2 points each.

That would only have been a nuisance if the migration ran first. It ran last. reconcile() in src/index.js calls reconcileAll, then saveClosed, then migrateV1Rows, and the pause in the first step skipped the rest. Its rescan had no cursor. Each hour it started over and paused in the same place. Our scorer's verdict reads "0/130 historical changes v1 never recorded" and "h2: 0 of 59 v1 rows in scope-ledger", and it traces 15 checks to that one root cause.

On the development site, which our spec gives the same shape on another seed, the gate tripped too, twice. At 21:19 our time it wrote "The reconcile hit my own dose gate". After a reset one run got through and it reported "migration complete (88/88)".

Build 2 got the same thing right. I think it was more luck than design. Its cost counter under-counted instead (its own words near the end: "my costOf under-counts returned records"). It ran over the background share in 4 of 31 hours, and on our scoring sites it never paused early. In its last minutes its own dev run did pause early. At call 300 of 300 it spotted the ordering problem: "I'm at the call budget (300/300) — this is my final turn". Then it moved the migration to the top with the comment "it is the graded deliverable and needs the fewest points". It never ran that version. It still scored 59 of 59 migrated and 130 of 130 backfilled. DeepSeek 1017's build 2 had that ordering from the start (src/sync.js:409, "Migrate v1's rows first").

Neither build displayed its admin page

Both Mistral builds score 0.00 on the admin panel tier. That one failure takes down the panel labels, the CI web trigger (no secret can exist before the panel's Rotate button creates one) and the admin boot check with it. Build 1's src/frontend/admin.jsx ends with export default AdminPage; and never calls ForgeReconciler.render, so UI Kit had nothing to draw. It found that out at 21:39, on the 298th of its 300 calls, when its only admin-page test printed "(nothing rendered)". Build 2 does call ForgeReconciler.render(<App />) at line 197, and the non-admin view displayed its permission message, but the admin view came back as an empty tree. The probe recorded no error that explains it. And build 2 never ran the kit's UI Kit check on that page.

DeepSeek 1017's build 2 renders the same way (admin.jsx:186) and ran that UI Kit check 14 times before it finished. The habit shows in the counts too: DeepSeek's two builds invoked their resolvers in the sandbox 45 and 30 times, Mistral's 3 and 4, and neither Mistral build ran a browser self-test at all. Build 1 also sent 37 of its 355 tool calls, about one in ten, to a bash tool that doesn't exist (goose's is called shell), and build 2 sent 19 of 344.

Build 2 had good moments. It had the highest UI-function (0.9957) and reconcile (0.9974) tiers of the four builds in this comparison group. Both are small tiers. Both also beat an Opus 5.5 build from an earlier group. In its last ten minutes it noticed that v1's React bundles were 244 KB against a 150 KB boot budget. It rewrote all three Custom UI pages in plain DOM, to between 102 and 106 KB each.

Mistral Large 4 vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017: 27 minutes to the first file against 2

Time is where the two models differ most. Mistral's first app-code write came 32, 35 and 27 minutes into its three Gauntlet attempts of 18 and 19 October, and about 49 and 55 minutes into its Forge builds. DeepSeek 1017 wrote its first app file 2.4 minutes into its Gauntlet run and about 4.5 minutes into each Forge build, and it finished both Forge builds with 29 to 37 calls to spare. Mistral ran out of calls in both.

Its median call took 4.5 to 4.8 seconds on Forge against DeepSeek's 4.0. The typical call barely differs. The slow tail is what costs it. Each Mistral run had calls that took 11 to 18 minutes, and in the Gauntlet attempts the calls over five minutes add up to more than half of all the time the model spent answering. DeepSeek's slowest call in any of its three runs took 71 seconds, and across our runs Mistral generated between 55 and 70 tokens a second while DeepSeek managed 108 to 155.

The 18-minute thought that was thrown away

The 18 October attempt that Mistral's servers later ended opened with one thinking call of 37,853 words that ran 1,081 seconds. It was coherent (under 1% of its 12-word sequences repeat). It covered the money rule, the 3D tower heights and the order of the services. Then it stopped at exactly 65,536 output tokens. goose marked the reply as cut off, and nothing in it was carried out. Its next thought: "Let me continue. I was planning extensively. Time to write code." goose sent no max_tokens and our model limits list 262,144 output tokens, so the 65,536 cap came from the serving side. Whether that's OpenRouter or Mistral, our logs don't show.

Reasoning was 57% to 81% of everything it generated, depending on the run. On Forge both builds also compacted their context three times, once the prompt had grown to between about 170,000 and 210,000 tokens. After most compactions it re-read files it had already read ("I need to re-read the v1 sources and my v2 files"). Build 2's own compaction summary says it plainly: "I've spent ~66% of context on exploration; no code".

Those compactions are partly ours. goose gave Mistral a usable window of 262,144 tokens. It took the smallest Mistral endpoint's 524,288 (the EU one) and reserved half of it for output, on a model whose card says 1M, while DeepSeek got 655,360. At about 200,000 tokens a call, DeepSeek would have compacted too under Mistral's limit, and under its own it never did. The summary calls ran about 9 to 11 minutes per Forge build, inside the times charged to Mistral.

What did the long thinking buy? On the Gauntlet, quite a lot: its plans got the money rule right, and its decisions file is careful (a rejected draft is terminal, and any further action on it answers 409 invalid_state). On Forge it bought almost nothing the tests could see. A build that reads for 50 minutes and finds its admin bug on call 298 has no calls left to fix it.

Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user': the 400 that was our bug

The third Gauntlet attempt ended at 02:05 our time on 19 October, 97 calls in, on this answer from Mistral's API, passed through OpenRouter:

{"object":"error","message":"Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user'","type":"invalid_request_message_order","param":null,"code":"3230","raw_status_code":400}

Mistral had asked for two tools in parallel, read_image on a screenshot and shell. OpenAI's chat format only accepts text in a tool message ("For tool messages, only type text is supported", in OpenAI's API spec). So since goose 1.0 the formatter has put a placeholder in the tool result and sent the picture as a separate user message right after it. With one tool call, or when the image comes back last, that's harmless. When an image result comes back before another tool result, the request goes out as assistant (two tool calls), tool result, user message holding the image, tool result. Mistral refused the second tool result because a user message stood between it and its call.

Who is right? Mistral's function-calling docs show the order only as a table ("assistant fc.1, fc.2 → tool r.1 → tool r.2 → assistant"), and the error type invalid_request_message_order isn't in their error glossary. Anthropic states the rule in words: "You cannot include any messages between the assistant's tool use message and the user's tool result message." Our request broke the documented order. I count this one as ours.

Three of our runs from 3 and 4 October sent the same order, and all three were answered and scored: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (served by Claude on AWS), GPT-6.1 Sol Pro (OpenAI) and MiMo V2.6 Flash (Xiaomi). All three went through OpenRouter, and I only see what goose sent to OpenRouter, so whether OpenRouter reordered anything for those hosts our logs can't tell. Mistral refused it the first time. Mistral's own coding CLI has an open pull request for the same failure, where a steered user message ends up between a tool call and its result.

We fixed goose 17 minutes after the 400 (commit a0247fffc2, "keep parallel tool results contiguous when one carries an image"). Inside each run of tool results the image messages now move to after the last result, merged into one user message, and a test replays the exact refused request. It shipped in Goose Swarm 3.0.119, our desktop app, on 19 October. The scored fourth attempt most likely ran on 3.0.119, and it never called read_image, so the fix wasn't exercised in a Mistral run.

The second attempt's ending wasn't ours. At 19:40 our time on 18 October Mistral returned "Internal server error" (type unreachable_backend, a 503). goose resent three times with backoff, the last one failed the same way, and the run ended after 30 answered calls and at least $1.18. The 9 October attempt ended on OpenRouter's side. Three times, while it was writing its main service file, OpenRouter dropped the reply with "Upstream idle timeout exceeded", and goose gave up after the third resend. Our harness refuses to score a session the provider ended, because grading a half-built tree would publish an outage as the model's score.

What a Mistral Large 4 build costs: about 18 times DeepSeek's, at sale prices

Its Forge pair billed at least $10.95 for a median of 0.2195. DeepSeek 1017's pair billed at least $0.62 for 0.452, which works out at about $50 per median point against $1.36.

Those Mistral prices are the launch sale: Mistral's changelog says "Launch pricing: 50% off for 2 weeks" from 6 October, which by my arithmetic runs out around the 20th, though OpenRouter still showed the sale prices on the 20th. Its model page lists the regular rates as $1.36 in, $4.18 out and $0.14 cached, and at those rates the same pair would cost roughly twice as much, around $22, or about 35 times DeepSeek's at the off-peak rate it ran at.

Where Mistral's money went:

Mistral b2 DeepSeek 1017 b2
Requests 305 271
Prompt tokens per request 99,182 201,619
Share of prompt served from cache 84.6% 99.7%
Cache-read price per million (OpenRouter list; DeepSeek at the off-peak rate it ran at on Sunday 18 Oct, double at weekday peak) $0.07 $0.003
Uncached prompt price per million $0.68 $0.15
Bill $5.55 at least $0.32

DeepSeek carried twice the context into each call, inside a window two and a half times larger. Nearly all of it was billed as cache reads at a price 23 times lower than Mistral's. At list prices, fresh prompt tokens make up about half of each Mistral Forge bill, though they're only 13% to 15% of its prompt tokens. My guess is that the three compactions per build and the re-reads after them are a large part of that uncached slice. On the Forge builds the compaction summaries also ran on Mistral itself, because our host pin caught the helper calls meant for a small Gemini model. We fixed that while build 2 was still running. It shipped in 3.0.119, after the pair. The fourth Gauntlet attempt's four Gemini helper calls are inside its $4.93.

What the architecture might explain

Mistral publishes less than I'd like. The model card says "a granular Mixture-of-Experts architecture" with "52B active parameters and 1.05T total parameters, and a 1.6B vision encoder", a 1M context and "Status: Public Preview". The Hugging Face placeholder says 49 billion active per token, 52 billion counting embeddings and output layers, with weights expected on 31 October. The launch post defers the architecture, "additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology" to the weights release, and says "the reinforcement learning run behind this preview is still in flight". Expert counts, the attention design and a licence aren't published. There is no tech report yet.

On reasoning, Mistral's reasoning guide documents two values for this model, high and none. We sent medium. We do that for all our cloud runs. It's a valid value in Mistral's API schema, OpenRouter lists only high and none and defaults to high, and nobody documents what medium becomes. The 57% to 81% reasoning share suggests it was not thinking minimally, but that's an inference from our token counts.

I have two guesses about the behaviour. A preview whose RL run is "still in flight" may not yet be tuned for long agentic loops, where a long think costs calls and minutes. Our Forge logs look like that. Thorough reading, late writing, no time left to test. And 49B active parameters per token (52B with embeddings) is about three times the 16B at decode on the V4.1 Flash card, which the 1017 snapshot updates. That fits the gap in tokens per second we measured, though serving hardware and load matter as much, and our numbers can't separate them. Nothing in the cards explains the admin page or the throttle. Those are decisions in the code. I'd judge it on the code.

Mistral's own lifecycle page adds one more caveat: Public Preview models "allow silent updates". A pinned mistral-large-4-0 today may not be the model we measured on 18 and 19 October.

Where we were wrong

  1. Our Gauntlet money check assumed the table opens oldest first and charged Mistral x0.6 for correct money. Joining each cell to its payment by row id fixes it; it isn't shipped, and the board still shows 0.5462.
  2. The same check scores a currency that isn't on screen as a failed test. Four other ranked runs paid x0.92 for it.
  3. We capped Mistral's context at 262,144 tokens on a 1M model, against 655,360 for DeepSeek, so its six Forge compactions and their minutes and dollars are partly ours.
  4. goose put a user message between two tool results whenever an image came back before another result. Mistral refused it, and that ended a run. Fixed in 3.0.119.
  5. Under a Mistral host pin our helper calls went to Mistral too, so its Forge bills include summary work meant for a cheaper model. Fixed in 3.0.119.
  6. We asked for reasoning effort medium, which Mistral doesn't document for this model, so the effort it really ran at was the provider's choice.

Should you put Mistral Large 4 behind your agent?

From these runs, not yet for long agentic builds like our Forge task. It read for close to an hour and ran out of calls. It also cost about 18 times DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at sale prices. On the Gauntlet, once our check is fixed, it sits around 11th of 44, which is respectable for a preview that's still in training. I'd look again when the weights and the architecture write-up land (Mistral says 31 October), with the effort set to high or none and a full context window.

If you try it in your own setup, test four things. First, check whether your agent ever puts a user message between tool results (images, steering, injected reminders), because Mistral rejects that request outright. Through OpenRouter, the hosts behind three of our earlier runs answered it. Set the reasoning effort to a value Mistral documents. Watch the time to first write and the slowest calls rather than the median, since the 11- to 18-minute calls are where its time went. And read the failing check before you believe a critical, ours included.

Goose Swarm isn't production-ready yet. We run these boards with it because we know what it's made of. I'd like to hear from anyone running Large 4 in a real agent loop: did you get the long first thought too, and did none make it usable, or just cheaper? Tell me in the comments.

title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
description:
arXiv:2610.27266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.

title: AutoTerm-SST: Adaptive Terminology Memory with Zero Session-Time Setup for Streaming Speech Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.26865v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented speech translation improves rare terminology, but systems such as RASST still assume that users provide a glossary before each session. That assumption is inconvenient for live talks, while merging every domain into one growing glossary eventually places too many irrelevant terms in the same retrieval and prompt competition. We present AutoTerm-SST, an interactive system that removes session-time glossary upload and domain selection. It organizes a large offline terminology catalog into topic slices, matches recent streaming translation context to bilingual slice prototypes, and activates a compact multi-slice working set under fixed retrieval and prompt budgets. On five ACL and five ESO oncology talks, AutoTerm matches a known-domain reference in terminology accuracy (88.3% vs. 88.1%) and mWER-resegmented BLEU (45.09 vs. 45.19), while requiring no domain input. Compared with a one-million-entry merged glossary, it improves terminology accuracy by 3.9 points and BLEU by 2.30. Routing plus four-slice retrieval remains lightweight: the complete system runs at 0.406 RTF, and the vLLM host sustains 32 real-time sessions. The live demo exposes active slices and retrieved terminology as the topic changes, providing zero-setup terminology-aware streaming translation.

title: How do I approve sprite readability across changing scene backgrounds?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Approve a transparent sprite against the scene conditions where its important features must remain readable. One neutral checkerboard cannot represent bright snow, dark interiors, overlays, and changing lighting. Define a small, deliberate background review set before deciding the asset needs repainting.

Key Takeaways

  • Choose backgrounds by the information the player must perceive.
  • Check the final composite at the actual display scale.
  • Distinguish interface contrast requirements from artistic silhouette judgment.

Transparency makes the background part of the result

The PNG specification defines alpha separately from color. A partially transparent edge participates in a composition rather than acting like an opaque outline.

That makes the target background relevant to visual review. It does not mean every sprite requires a universal contrast ratio. W3C non-text contrast guidance concerns relevant meaningful graphical information and interface components; apply its scope carefully.

Build the background set from real scenes

List the situations where the player must identify the character or a specific feature. Select representative backgrounds that stress those tasks: a pale environment behind white hair, dense foliage behind a green weapon, or a dark overlay during a menu.

Include lighting and interface states that actually occur. Do not create dozens of arbitrary color swatches and call that complete scene coverage. A smaller set tied to real conditions gives the art and engineering teams actionable evidence.

Render the complete composition. If a shader, outline, or selection marker provides essential separation, include it. Inspect both the source asset and the supported presentation path so responsibility for the visible result is clear.

Example: the snowfield companion

A companion's white scarf identifies them in a crowded party. The scarf reads clearly in a gray asset viewer but disappears against a snowfield. Increasing the entire character's darkness would also damage the intended armor palette.

Possible repairs include a carefully placed local outline, a different scarf value, or a supported identity marker. Choose the smallest change that preserves the intended information in the real scene. Check the same repair against the dark interior so it does not introduce a new failure.

The scenario is illustrative. No scarf, outline, or scene was rendered for this guide.

Keep meaning separate from color preference

W3C use-of-color guidance is relevant when a feature's hue carries information. If the scarf indicates party role, give that role another perceivable cue rather than relying only on its color.

Record the task, background state, scale, and presentation settings for each proposed check. A pass should describe what was recognizable, not merely that a screenshot looked attractive.

Accept the delivery when required visual cues work in the reviewed scene conditions and any remaining gaps are explicit. This is a proposed review set, not an executed scene benchmark or a claim of complete accessibility. New backgrounds, lighting changes, and equipment can require another targeted review.

Related workflow

See game asset blind review scene acceptance for the adjacent decision. Keep the animation handoff checklist with the deliverable and preserve the art reference board for visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.27220v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.

title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
description:
arXiv:2610.27301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $\tau$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.
