External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

Backup and DR

Support for backing up and restoring workloads managed via the legacy appliance management console is deprecated.

Key milestones for this deprecation include the following:

  • End of Support for New Backups: After September 30, 2027, you will no longer be able to run new backups using the legacy stack.
  • End of Standard Restores: Support for standard restores, exports, and migrations using the legacy appliance management console continues till March 31, 2028.

For more information, see Deprecations.

BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Security center is now available in the Google Cloud console. You can use the Security center to analyze your data security profile, create and manage row- and column-level security policies, and configure and manage data governance and policy tags. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

BigQuery jobs explorer layout and filtering improvements, including status counts in the filter bar, resource grouping, and timeline metric charts, are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use the OBJ.LIST function to perform spontaneous discovery and analysis of unstructured data. The OBJ.LIST function returns a table of metadata and ObjectRef values for files stored in Cloud Storage, and does not require you to create a persistent object table.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now view the UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, and EXPORT execution steps in your query plans.

Capacity Planner

Feature

Preview: You can use Capacity Assist, which provides AI-powered assistance through Gemini in Capacity Planner, to help you understand and manage your resource usage and plan capacity (Preview). You can use natural-language prompts in Capacity Assist to do the following:

  • Analyze historical usage patterns across regions and resources.
  • Forecast capacity needs and identify quota risks early.
  • Simulate growth events to plan future capacity.
  • Get answers to your Capacity Planner questions.

For more information, see Plan capacity with Capacity Assist.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

A new quota system governing the configuration size of Application Load Balancers is now generally available. This update increases the individual URL map size limit from 64 KB and 128 KB to 1 MB. For more information, see URL map size and quota units.

Key aspects of this feature include:

  • Complexity-based quota: Quota units reflect URL map complexity (number of rules, hostnames, and path matchers).
  • Scoped measurement: Quota is measured and enforced on a per-project, per-region, or per-VPC depending on Application Load Balancer type.
  • Active consumption: Only URL maps currently referenced by forwarding rules contribute to quota usage.
  • New URL map size limit: The new quota has a new URL map size limit increased to 1 MB for global and regional external and internal Application Load Balancers. Classic Application Load Balancers remain restricted to 64 KB.

For more information on increasing your limit, please contact Google Cloud Support.

Cloud Monitoring

Announcement

The application topology graph is now generally available (GA). This graph helps you to understand relationships between applications, services, and workloads, and shows you traffic flow and incidents in the context of your applications.

Cloud Storage

Feature

Cloud Storage client libraries now provide automated, end-to-end checksumming by default for object read and write operations to help maintain data integrity from client to storage. For more information, see data validation.

Cloud Tasks

Feature

Cloud Tasks support for the following is generally available (GA):

  • Set retry parameters when creating a task and override the queue-level retry configuration for the task.
  • Create a batch of tasks and add the batch to an existing queue.
  • Delete a batch of tasks from a queue.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can specify a 120-second preemption notice duration while creating Spot VMs. Use this feature for workloads on Spot VMs where you want up to an additional 120 seconds for handling preemption. If you want to migrate existing Spot VMs workloads, make sure you update your workload to handle preemption outside of a shutdown script and test preemption. For more information, see Spot VMs and Create and use Spot VMs.

Datastream

Feature

Datastream now supports partial backfill for SQL Server, Spanner, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and MySQL sources. Partial backfill lets you load a specific subset of data from the source into the destination by providing a SQL WHERE clause as a custom filter.

For more information, see Initiate partial backfill.

Dialogflow

Fixed

Dialogflow CX: An issue in Dialogflow CX was identified where sensitive authentication tokens stored in conversational session parameters could be returned in cleartext via DetectIntent API responses. A server-side fix has been applied to redact and sanitize authentication credentials from conversational API outputs. No customer configuration changes or updates are required.

Deprecated

All generative features: gemini-2.5-flash and gemini-2.5-flash-lite models will be deprecated by Dec 23, 2026. Upgrade to newer Gemini models such as gemini-3.1-flash-lite before the deprecation date.

BidiStreamingAnalyzeContent API has become generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Cloud Trace integration with Agent Gateway (Preview)

Agent Gateway integrates with Cloud Trace in Preview to provide end-to-end request observability for agent workloads. Enabling Cloud Trace gives you visibility into how requests travel from your agents through the gateway and across Google Cloud services, tools, agents, and MCP servers.

For more information, see Use Cloud Trace.

xAI's Grok 4.7

Grok 4.7 is available in Preview in Model Garden.

CodeMender updates (v0.11.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Tiered location configuration: Added support for configuring the service location using the CM_LOCATION environment variable or location in config.yaml (defaulting to global), replacing the --location command-line flag.
  • CI gate severity validation: Updated cm find to validate --fail-on severity values (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, or NONE) up front instead of silently ignoring misspelled severities.
  • Sandboxed VCS branching and hardening: Enabled vcs_branch creation and candidate branch cleanup inside the default sandboxed worker for --architecture sessions, and hardened VCS template expansion against shell metacharacters and command injection.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Normalized vulnerability type casing and relative file paths during cm find and consensus runs to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Extended HTTP 429 retry backoff (Retry-After support and up to 60-second quota refill windows) and automatic stream reconnection to improve scan resilience under rate limiting.
    • Preserved standalone cm find, cm verify, and cm fix sessions on interrupt (SIGINT/SIGTERM) so interrupted runs can be resumed with cm session resume, while still canceling parallel consensus worker operations.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

The App Topology API that provides agent topologies in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is now generally available

This launch introduces the following changes:

  • A new query builder for customizing suggested quick queries or creating your own query on the Topologies page. Custom queries let you explore more data related to your agents, such as identity, alerts, vulnerabilities, and underlying infrastructure. For details, see View topologies for a project.
  • A streamlined experience for the single-agent topology in Agent Registry. A topology with single-hop traffic to and from the agent automatically loads on the page.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Headless mobile SDK

The headless mobile SDK, for Android and iOS, is now available. With this SDK, you can embed the capabilities of Google Cloud CCaaS into your mobile app while retaining full control over the UI. The headless mobile SDK supports calls (including scheduled calls), chats, and email.

The following is a comparison of the headless mobile SDK and the mobile SDK v2.

Headless mobile SDK:

  • Google Cloud CCaaS provides the core SDK engine: sessions, routing, channel logic, and more.

  • You build the UI using your own design and components.

  • Best for organizations that need brand consistency and full control over the look and feel of their mobile app.

Mobile SDK v2:

  • Google Cloud CCaaS provides a pre-built UI with customization options.

  • Best for organizations that want faster product deployment with less design and engineering effort.

For more information, see the following:

  • Headless Mobile SDK v3 for iOS: Get started

  • Headless Mobile SDK v3 for Android: Get started

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE now automatically applies protection tier labels to TPU node pools created from Compute Engine reservations. Depending on your configuration, GKE adds:

  • Node pool resource label: goog-gke-node-pool-protection-tier (standard or capacity_optimized)
  • Kubernetes node label: cloud.google.com/protection-tier (STANDARD or CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED)

To learn more, see Automatically applied labels.

Expanded read-only permissions for Chronicle API Restricted Data Access Viewer

Google SecOps has updated the predefined Chronicle API Restricted Data Access Viewer (roles/chronicle.restrictedDataAccessViewer) IAM role to include all read-only permissions available in the Chronicle API Viewer (roles/chronicle.viewer) role, excluding global data access (chronicle.globalDataAccessScopes.permit).

With this update, users assigned to roles/chronicle.restrictedDataAccessViewer IAM role will have read-only access across Google SecOps features—including SOAR cases and playbooks, investigations, threat collections, findings, security validation, and ingestion resources within their assigned data access scopes.

For more information, see Configure data RBAC for users.

Enhanced observability metrics, including user engagement and estimated token usage data on the Token usage tab of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard, are now generally available (GA) for Looker (original) instances that are on Looker 26.16 or later. This launch also adds a Daily Token Utilization visualization and supports token usage observability for Conversational Analytics data agents that are published to Gemini Enterprise.

title: Voyage Rerank 3 and Rerank 3 Lite are now available on AI Gateway
description:

The models reorder search results by relevance before passing documents to a language model. The series improves retrieval quality across domains, with the largest gains on long documents and code.

Rerank 3 focuses on accuracy, while Rerank 3 Lite is optimized for latency and cost. Both handle up to 32K tokens per query-document pair and follow instructions in the query to guide ranking.

To use Rerank 3, set the model to voyage/rerank-3:

For Rerank 3 Lite, change the model to voyage/rerank-3-lite.

Try Voyage Rerank 3 in the AI Gateway model playground, or explore the model catalog.

title: September 26, 2026
description:
Backup and DR

Security

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

Security Bulletin – Appliance:

  • Addressed multiple input sanitization vulnerabilities, including SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS), across appliance platform server utilities.
  • Remediated an authorization and validation vulnerability in user management workflows.

Security Bulletin – Host Agent:

  • Strengthened local RPC interface access controls and improved credential isolation between concurrent backup jobs on the Host Agent.
  • Hardened database layer against command injection, path traversal, and unauthorized directory permission modifications.
  • Remediated local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Oracle and SAP HANA host agent environment and profile handling.
  • Improved temporary file creation and link handling across Windows and Linux Host Agents to mitigate symlink race conditions.
  • Addressed buffer overflow vulnerabilities in Linux Host Agent components.

Libraries Bugs (Appliance):

  • Upgraded third-party runtime and application libraries (including Go and Java packages such as Netty and Jackson Databind) on the appliance management server.
  • Updated the Linux kernel and base operating system packages across Backup and DR appliance virtual machine images to mitigate reported vulnerabilities.

Fixed

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

These issues have been resolved for the Host Agent:

  • Resolved an issue where Oracle ASM backups failed with the error "Failed to create ASM staging disk group".
  • Resolved an issue causing Oracle RAC database restores to fail with error 6407 due to invalid node names in the nodelist.
  • Fixed a PostgreSQL backup failure during snapshot preparation where the database user lacked execute permissions on pg_backup_start.
  • Corrected an issue where the Oracle mount process was unable to locate the undo catalog configuration file.
  • Improved Oracle backup metadata processing to support databases containing a large volume of datafiles.
  • Resolved an issue where discovery of SAP Sybase instances failed when multiple instances were configured under different user accounts.
  • Fixed an issue causing PostgreSQL database discovery to fail during host agent discovery workflows.
  • Resolved an issue that prevented successful discovery of MySQL database applications.

Change

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

Non-Breaking Changes (Host Agent):

  • Modernized host agent database integration scripts for IBM Db2, MySQL, MariaDB, SAP Sybase IQ, and MaxDB to standard Bash execution for improved stability and security hardening.

Feature

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

These features are now available for the Host Agent:

title: Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS now support On-Demand Capacity Reservation
description:
Starting today, you can reserve compute capacity for your Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS DB instances in one or more Availability Zones for as long as you need it. Reserving capacity helps ensure that DB instance create, restore, scale-compute, and start operations don't fail because of insufficient capacity.

On-Demand Capacity Reservation is designed for workloads that need assurance that specific DB instance capacity will be available when they need it for business-critical events, such as migrations, product launches, seasonal peaks, high-availability deployments, or disaster recovery. You choose the DB instance class, engine, Availability Zones, and reserved capacity per Availability Zone, and RDS holds that capacity for you. Capacity can be reserved in two or more Availability Zones to support Multi-AZ deployments. To use the reserved capacity, reference the reservation when you create, restore, modify, or start a DB instance.

You can reserve capacity for immediate use with no commitment and cancel at any time, or schedule a reservation to begin 5 to 120 days in the future with a minimum commitment. Reserved capacity is billed at On-Demand rates while the reservation is active, whether or not DB instances within the reservation are running. title: AI-Generated Frontend Tests: Fake Green vs Real Coverage
description:
I asked an agent to “add tests for this React form.” Ten minutes later CI was green, coverage jumped 12 points, and I felt productive. Then I broke the submit handler on purpose. Every test still passed.

That’s fake green: the suite looks healthy, the badge is bright, and the product is still unprotected.

AI is great at producing tests. It’s mediocre at choosing what those tests should prove. If you don’t constrain it, you get a wall of renders, snapshots, and happy-path clicks that never touch the bug you actually ship.

What fake green usually looks like

I keep seeing the same patterns from agent-written suites:

  • Render-only tests — screen.getByText("Save") after mount. Proves the string exists, not that save works.
  • Implementation spies — assert useState was called, or that an internal helper ran. Refactors break the test; bugs don’t.
  • Snapshot soup — one giant DOM dump per story. Any class rename fails CI; none of it catches a wrong API payload.
  • Mocked everything — fetch, router, analytics, even the button’s onClick. The only thing left under test is the mock setup.
  • Coverage theater — lines execute because the test imports the module and calls every export with empty props. Branch that handles null user? Never hit.

Coverage went up. Confidence went down. That’s the trap.

What I ask for instead

I stopped saying “add tests.” I paste a short contract into the prompt:

Write tests that fail if these user-visible behaviors break. Do not assert on implementation details. Prefer one integration-ish test per critical path over five shallow renders.

Then I list the behaviors explicitly:

  1. Submit with empty email shows the inline error and does not call the API
  2. Valid submit posts { email, plan } to /api/signup and lands on /welcome
  3. Server 409 shows the “already registered” message without clearing the form
  4. Keyboard: Tab order reaches email → plan → submit; Enter submits when focused on email

If the agent can’t fail a test by breaking one of those lines, the test is decoration.

A quick litmus test before I merge

I run three checks on every AI-authored PR that “improves coverage”:

  1. Mutate and watch — flip a condition, rename a field in the payload, remove an await. At least one test must go red. If none do, delete or rewrite.
  2. Read the asserts — if every expect is toBeInTheDocument() or toMatchSnapshot(), send it back.
  3. Count the mocks — more mocks than asserts is a smell. Prefer a small MSW handler over stubbing fifteen internals.

I also glance at the coverage report for branches, not lines. Fake green loves line coverage. Real confidence lives in the if you almost never take.

How I split work with the agent

Agents are fine at scaffolding: test file layout, MSW handlers, Testing Library queries once I name the roles. Humans still own:

  • Which paths matter (checkout, auth, billing — not every Tooltip)
  • What “done” means (the four behaviors above, not “80% coverage”)
  • What not to mock (the component under test, the form library’s real validation if that’s the point)

My default prompt ending:

Do not add tests for private helpers. Do not increase coverage by importing unused modules. Every new test must map to one bullet in the behavior list.

That sentence alone cut a lot of snapshot noise.

Coverage as a signal, not a goal

I still look at coverage — as a map of untested branches, not a score to maximize. When an agent offers +15% coverage with zero new failing mutations, I treat that as a warning, not a win.

Real coverage for frontend is: can a user break the money path without a red test? If yes, the green build is lying.

Next time an agent hands you a shiny suite, break one real behavior on purpose before you merge. If CI stays green, you didn’t get tests — you got a costume.

title: RGH-GNN : Risk-Gated Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Financial Fraud Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Credit card fraud is a significant problem for financial institutions, resulting in substantial monetary loss each year. Fraud patterns and methods are continuously evolving, with fraudulent transactions often disguised to resemble legitimate activity. Real world transaction data for fraud detection is severely affected by class imbalance making it harder to detect these transactions. Fraudulent transactions are rarely isolated. Accounts, devices, and other common attributes are often shared across fraudulent activity, revealing relational patterns that individual transaction features alone cannot capture. Graph-based approaches model these relationships explicitly. However, standard graph neural networks aggregate neighbourhood information uniformly, which can dilute the already scarce signal carried by fraudulent transactions and limit detection of camouflaged fraud. This work presents RGH-GNN, a heterogeneous graph neural network that addresses this limitation by incorporating transaction-level risk scores, generated by a supervised LightGBM classifier as edge weights. It is used to guide message passing through a learnable risk-gated aggregation mechanism. It ensures that high-risk transactions contribute more strongly to learned representations rather than being diluted by uniform neighbourhood aggregation. RGH-GNN is evaluated on the IEEE-CIS fraud detection dataset against standard graph neural network models that are trained on the same heterogeneous graph. RGH-GNN outperforms all baselines across every evaluation metric, with an AUC-ROC score of 0.914. This demonstrates that incorporating engineered risk signals into graph-based message passing substantially improves fraud detection performance.

title: Node.js Healthcare Appointment Retrieval: Latency-Bounded Reranking and Failure Recovery
description:
Short answer: a healthcare appointment assistant retrieval architecture should bound retrieval and reranking with one response deadline, return evidence with a source URL or document ID, and use failure recovery only when the resulting answer remains truthful.

For a healthcare appointment assistant, failure recovery is not "try every retriever until one answers." The deciding constraint is the patient's wait time. A fresh clinic notice that arrives after the response deadline has zero practical value, while a fast old policy can be actively misleading. The architecture needs to optimize retrieval quality inside a latency budget, then make the evidence loss visible.

This is the useful before/after. Before: collect candidates, rerank everything, and discover the timeout at the UI. After: reserve time for each stage, cancel late work, and label the evidence class that survived. Tiny change. Big operational difference.

Put the latency budget ahead of the fallback order

Start at the user-visible deadline and work backward. Suppose the product owns a 2,000 ms response budget. That number is an example configuration, not a benchmark. Reserve part of it for answer generation and transport; retrieval and reranking get what remains. A timeout must be explicit at every boundary, because one slow source cannot be allowed to consume the complete interaction.

The order should follow the question. A request such as "What documents should I bring?" can use deliberately indexed clinic guidance. "Is the 3:30 appointment still available?" needs live, authoritative context. Vector search is the durable path; live retrieval is the freshness path. Combining them is useful when a reply needs both policy and a changing fact, but the combination is valid only if each claim keeps its own citation.

Do not hide this behind a single search_failed counter. Record the stage, elapsed budget, attempt, candidate count, accepted evidence count, and terminal decision. The diagram in words is short: intent -> parallel retrieval -> deadline gate -> rerank -> citation gate -> answer or handoff.

The deadline gate matters more than an optimistic retry count.

How should Node.js healthcare appointment retrieval balance quality, latency, and failure recovery?

Use a small state machine. Run only the retrieval paths required by the intent, cap their candidate counts, and rerank the evidence that arrives before the deadline. A retry is allowed only when enough budget remains for both the retry and the downstream reranker. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when it is present and apply exponential backoff. Don't tight-loop.

Here is a copyable orchestration core using Infrai's verified vector-query and web-search routes. Export request JSON that conforms to each route's public discovery schema into INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON and INFRAI_WEB_SEARCH_JSON; this keeps the sample runnable without guessing fields that can be checked mechanically. The code does not interpret either response shape. It sends both typed-at-the-boundary payloads, retains successful raw evidence, and makes the deadline decision explicit.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");
}

function readJson(name: string): unknown {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return JSON.parse(value) as unknown;
}

async function postWithRetry(
  path: "/v1/vector/query" | "/v1/web/search",
  body: unknown,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL(path, baseUrl), {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
      signal,
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
      const delayMs = Math.max(retryAfter * 1_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`retrieval rejected (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
  }
  throw new Error("retry budget exhausted");
}

async function retrieveWithinDeadline(timeoutMs = 1_200) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs);

  try {
    const [durable, live] = await Promise.allSettled([
      postWithRetry(
        "/v1/vector/query",
        readJson("INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON"),
        controller.signal,
      ),
      postWithRetry(
        "/v1/web/search",
        readJson("INFRAI_WEB_SEARCH_JSON"),
        controller.signal,
      ),
    ]);

    const evidence = [durable, live].flatMap((result) =>
      result.status === "fulfilled" ? [result.value] : [],
    );
    return { evidence, decision: evidence.length > 0 ? "review" : "handoff" };
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

const result = await retrieveWithinDeadline();
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`);

There is a deliberate hard edge here: raw responses go to a schema-aware citation and reranking step before any generated appointment claim. No citable evidence means a staff handoff or a request to confirm. That is a successful recovery outcome. It preserves trust and gives operations a clean signal instead of burying uncertainty inside fluent text.

One implementation detail deserves scrutiny. Promise.allSettled retains results from a failed sibling, which is useful for partial recovery, but the example's timer cancels only adapters that respect AbortSignal. Test that behavior. I'm not sure what timeout fits your scheduling system; your mileage may vary with geography, upstream rate limits, and the reranker. A trace-derived percentile, measured per intent, resolves that uncertainty better than a universal constant.

Make reranking loss observable

Reranking improves ordering only over the candidates it receives. Under pressure, candidate loss can happen before ranking: a live source times out, a durable query returns no match, or a citation gate removes a result. If the dashboard reports only reranker duration, a quality regression looks mysterious.

Emit one structured event per request with retrieval_deadline_ms, path_completed, path_timeout, candidates_before_gate, candidates_after_gate, rerank_input_count, rerank_output_count, and decision. Do not log raw patient questions or retrieved page bodies by default. Apply the organization's health-data handling rules to identifiers and free text.

Then alert on outcomes, not vibes. A rising handoff rate with stable reranker latency points upstream. A stable candidate count with fewer accepted citations points at metadata or source lifecycle. A growing timeout share after increasing top-k suggests that the quality knob consumed the latency budget.

That last case is easy to miss — and wonderfully testable. Replay fixed, non-sensitive queries against several candidate limits, then compare accepted evidence and deadline misses. The best top-k is the smallest value that delivers enough relevant, citable context within the budget; more candidates are not automatically better.

Recovery also starts during indexing

Runtime fallbacks cannot repair a collection that still serves deleted appointment guidance. Re-index changed content deliberately, preserve stable document identifiers, and remove records that disappeared from the source. Publish a new revision only after its current chunks are present and its deleted chunks are gone.

Consider a clinic page split into six records. Staff change Friday hours and delete the walk-in paragraph. An upsert of only the edited hours leaves the obsolete walk-in claim searchable. The correct unit of completion is the source revision, not the last successful chunk write: stage the current six-or-fewer records, delete records absent from that revision, mark the revision complete, and only then make it eligible. If ingestion stops early, keep the last complete revision available or require live evidence for affected intents. Every returned chunk must carry its source URL or document ID so a reviewer can trace the answer without recreating the retrieval run.

Keep it boring.

This lifecycle creates three metrics that runtime traces can actually use: active revision age, deletion lag, and rejected stale candidates. Together they distinguish "the reranker chose badly" from "the reranker never received current evidence."

Compare the operating model, not a feature checklist

The main choice is who owns the index, how live context enters the request, and how much latency control the team needs. These are different operating models, even when each product can return vectors.

Option Best fit in this assistant Latency and recovery trade-off Evidence handling
PostgreSQL + pgvector Appointment records already governed beside relational data Retrieval load can compete with transactional work; the team controls fallback logic Stable row IDs can anchor review and deletion
Elasticsearch Teams needing lexical and vector retrieval with detailed index control More tuning and cluster operations, with explicit control over query behavior Source metadata remains under team control
Pinecone Teams preferring a managed vector service A network dependency remains part of the request path Citation fields must be modeled as metadata
Live web retrieval Public clinic notices that change quickly Page availability and extraction add variable latency URLs are visible, but source trust still needs a policy

Infrai can fit a polyglot team that wants verified vector and web capabilities through a plain REST API: no SDK is required, so any service that sends HTTP can use the same integration style. Infrai uses one key for both sides of this fallback and puts the calls on one bill, removing a credential and reconciliation boundary from the recovery path. Its 295 routes across 20 modules use consistent interface conventions, so vendor routing does not require application code changes. The API is genuinely self-describing: its public discovery surface needs no key and returns the request and response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples for each capability. That gives CI a concrete contract to validate before a retrieval change ships. The platform does not choose freshness rules, citation policy, or the deadline budget for you.

The catch is real. Stick with PostgreSQL plus pgvector when data locality and relational transactions dominate. Choose Elasticsearch when custom index control and an existing operations model matter more than a smaller integration surface. Use Pinecone when managed vector search is the central requirement. Call an authoritative scheduling system directly when it is the only valid source for live availability; a general retrieval layer should not sit between a patient and the system of record without a concrete reason.

Test the degraded answer, not merely the happy path

Build deterministic fixtures for an empty durable result, a delayed live response, HTTP 429, a deleted document, and evidence without a citation. Assert the terminal decision and the evidence IDs, not model prose. For the 429 case, assert bounded exponential backoff and Retry-After handling; for the delayed source, assert that cancellation leaves enough time for reranking and response delivery.

The release decision is equally crisp. Ship a recovery change only when citation retention and accepted relevance improve without pushing deadline misses beyond the product's chosen threshold. If quality rises but latency breaches the patient-facing budget, narrow the candidate set, move volatile facts to the authoritative live source, or keep the existing path. Failure recovery is working when the assistant can say less, promptly, rather than invent more after waiting.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/get-started/overview
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429

title: DataPraxis: Scaling Analytics Tasks via Verified Workspace Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.26924v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose agents are increasingly expected to perform professional analytics work, which requires sustained reasoning, iterative investigation, and reliable evidence. Training these capabilities requires diverse and challenging tasks. However, generating tasks directly from raw data often overlooks deeper questions that emerge through analysis and provides limited evidence for verification. To address these limitations, we introduce DataPraxis, an analytics task synthesis framework based on verified workspace evolution. The framework progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings and artifacts, then inherits and combines these workspaces to uncover deeper questions. It constructs tasks from accumulated findings and their dependencies, verifying analytical results both during evolution and after task assembly. Using this framework, we construct DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified trajectories spanning diverse domains and output formats, to train DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves 55.11 on DABStep and 51.9 on JobBench, matching or surpassing frontier models such as GLM-5.2. DataPraxis-5K is available at huggingface.co/datasets/stargazerhust/DataPraxis-5k

title: Can reviewers understand added and deleted sprite changes without red and green?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Label added, removed, and changed sprite regions with text or distinct marks as well as color. A red-green overlay can be quick for some reviewers, but hue alone makes the review meaning fragile. Keep annotation meaning separate from the artwork's own palette.

Key Takeaways

  • Name each review state directly.
  • Make annotations distinguishable without their hue.
  • Preserve an unmarked source view for judging the art.

Review color is a second visual language

W3C's use-of-color guidance explains why information should not depend only on color. An art-review overlay is an interface conveying decisions, even when the underlying sprite is decorative content.

A red region might mean removed pixels in one tool and newly painted pixels in another. State the legend beside the comparison. Do not assume reviewers share a convention or can distinguish every overlay against the sprite.

Separate evidence from annotation

Retain the previous and candidate frames unchanged. Generate a distinct annotation layer that can be toggled off. This lets a reviewer inspect the actual silhouette without confusing a diagnostic tint with a proposed palette.

Use a readable label such as Added, Removed, or Changed, and consider distinct outline or hatch treatments. Review essential marks against adjacent colors using non-text contrast guidance. Decorative highlights and essential indicators have different responsibilities.

Keep selected-frame state visually separate from change type. A selection border should not make a removed region look approved or a changed region look like an error.

Example: red armor in a red deletion overlay

A character wears dark red shoulder armor. A review tool tints removed pixels red and added pixels green. The deletion region becomes hard to see against the armor, while a green weapon glow appears similar to the addition overlay.

A useful comparison offers an unmarked before/after view, a labeled change list, and annotation marks distinguishable by shape or pattern. The reviewer can identify a removed shoulder pixel without knowing whether its tint is red.

If the tool can only generate a color heatmap, accompany it with specific frame coordinates and a textual description. Do not claim that a grayscale screenshot alone establishes usability.

Review the task, not merely the legend

Ask a reviewer to locate a described removal, identify the candidate frame, and state whether the change is intentional. Record where the annotation causes confusion. This is a proposed task check, not a completed participant study.

Microsoft's additional-cue guidance provides broader context for redundant communication in game interfaces. Apply that principle to the review workflow without presenting it as certification of the exported game.

Accept the comparison when the intended states remain understandable, unmarked art is available, and comments identify the correct revision. Changing review annotations should not alter production pixels.

This procedure concerns an art-review interface. It does not redesign the game's item-rarity system or prove accessibility through a single simulated view. No review tool or participant test was executed here.

Related workflow

See game item rarity icons without color only for the adjacent decision. Keep the animation handoff checklist with the deliverable and preserve the art reference board for visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: When Does an Added Planning Capability Create Operational Value? An Observable Evidence Standard
description:
arXiv:2610.27305v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial artificial intelligence (AI) planning systems combine predictive models, optimization logic, controls, and governance rules, but improvement in the complete policy does not show whether one addition made an independent contribution or whether that contribution justifies its burden. We address this attribution problem with an observable evidence standard that separates opportunity to act, executed-plan change, operational consequence, equivalence, uncertainty, and operating scope. Using forecast-to-plan replay on Favorita, M5, and Walmart data, we apply the standard to heterogeneous planning additions. Three limits of single-indicator evaluation emerge. First, a composite policy can conceal negligible component contribution: one control changed only 15 of 681 executed plans. Second, changing execution does not guarantee stable benefit: the evaluated multi-period capability helped in several long-lead settings but was 7.6% more costly under tight capacity. Third, indirect evidence can prioritize review but cannot complete attribution. Independent runs produced different paths in 19 of 599 cases that a rule-based check predicted would be unchanged. Although a lower-cost diagnostic matched the full-evaluation winner in only 55.0% of cases, it selected an option within the $10^{-6}$ cost-equivalence tolerance in 79.5%; the remaining cases prevented the proxy from authorizing acceptance. These experiments establish capability-level contribution evidence; the organization completes the value decision by weighing it against implementation and sustaining burden. The resulting capability evidence record links the observations to validation, deployment scope, fallback, monitoring, redesign, and retirement decisions.

title: VPFlow: Value-Predictive Planning with Imperfect World Models for Offline Goal Reaching
description:
arXiv:2610.27280v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning enables skill acquisition by reaching any goal from any state without dense rewards. Model-based methods allow for planning by scaling test-time compute to solve complex tasks. Combining both holds appealing promise for pre-training on suboptimal demonstrations and zero-shot adaptation via goal specification and planning. Yet existing methods assume effective planning requires accurate next-state prediction in pixel or latent space. In this work, we show that value prediction is more useful for planning, whereas accurate state prediction is often unnecessary. Our key insight is that offline goal reaching naturally admits a closed-form Monte Carlo return, enabling value regression to replace temporal-difference bootstrapping. We use this return as the sole supervision for latent world models: imagined latents are trained to predict goal-reaching value rather than match future states, implicitly preventing representation collapse. These planning-oriented representations let imperfect world models imagine on the level sets of value field beyond dataset transitions. We then present VPFlow, a value-predictive planner that pairs the world models with a one-step flow policy and plans in its noise space via evolutionary search. It enables policy improvement with imagined generalized advantage and reduces out-of-distribution queries common in action-space planning. On 30 state and pixel OGBench datasets, VPFlow surpasses model-free baselines by at least 30.3 and 10.1 percentage points in success rate, respectively, and outperforms latent planners LeWorldModel, PLDM, and TD-MPC2. It achieves this despite a latent prediction error orders of magnitude larger than with state prediction, while minimizing this error lowers success rate. This demonstrates that value-predictive representations, not exact state prediction, are what offline planning requires.

title: WordPress Memory Exhausted Error: Fix It at the Right Layer
description:
If your WordPress site shows Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 268435456 bytes exhausted, a PHP process asked for more memory than the server allows. The fix is usually quick. The catch is that the common fix, one line in wp-config.php, fails on many sites because it changes the wrong layer.

Decode the number first

The limit is reported in bytes:

Bytes Limit
33554432 32 MB
67108864 64 MB
134217728 128 MB
268435456 256 MB
536870912 512 MB

The end of the message gives a file path. The folder after /wp-content/plugins/ or /wp-content/themes/ is your first suspect.

Three layers decide the limit

  1. Host or php.ini memory_limit is the real ceiling.
  2. WP_MEMORY_LIMIT in wp-config.php is only a request, capped by layer 1.
  3. Per-folder overrides such as .user.ini or .htaccess.

The smallest value wins. Ask WordPress for 256M on a 128M host and you still get 128M.

Fix 1: wp-config.php

Back up the file first, then add this above the "That's all, stop editing" line:

define( 'WP_MEMORY_LIMIT', '256M' );
define( 'WP_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT', '512M' );

Fix 2: php.ini, .user.ini or the hosting panel 

memory_limit = 256M

Most panels expose this as a PHP settings or INI editor page. On PHP-FPM hosts, a per-site .user.ini is usually the file that is read, and it can take a few minutes to apply.

Fix 3: .htaccess (Apache with mod_php only) 

php_value memory_limit 256M

On PHP-FPM or FastCGI this directive causes a 500 error. Remove it immediately if that happens.

If nothing changes

Open Tools → Site Health → Info → Server and read the PHP memory limit. If it still shows the old value, the change did not reach the right layer. Also check that you edited the right wp-config.php, that the line sits above the stop-editing comment, and that no cache is serving the old error.

Find the real culprit

Raising the limit hides the problem. To find it, log errors without showing them to visitors:

define( 'WP_DEBUG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_LOG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY', false );

Repeat the failing action, read wp-content/debug.log, and note the plugin path. Rename that plugin folder over SFTP to deactivate it and retest. A diagnostic plugin like Query Monitor, run on staging, shows memory per page and per plugin.

FAQ

Is it safe to raise the memory limit? Yes, going from 64M or 128M to 256M is routine. Avoid extreme values on shared hosting, and fix the cause if you keep needing more.

Why does the error only show in wp-admin? Image processing, updates and imports need more memory than front-end page views.

Will more memory speed up my site? No. Memory prevents crashes. Speed comes from caching, lighter plugins and good hosting.

The full guide, with a symptom-to-cause table and prevention checklist, is on my site: WordPress memory exhausted fix.

title: Looking Into The Past: The Impact of Context on Detecting Deceptive Statements
description:
arXiv:2610.27407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deception detection typically considers messages in isolation. Previous works in claim verification and role detection have displayed that additional information such as gameplay history is crucial to successful predictions. In this work, we demonstrate the value of preceding gameplay dialogue when applied to deceptive message detection within the hidden role game of Avalon. The findings show that LLMs can see improvement across a number of metrics, including accuracy by up to 31\% with the addition of gameplay context for the target message.

title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
description:
arXiv:2610.27296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
description:
arXiv:2610.27550v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth-order methods scale to high-dimensional tasks such as language model fine-tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We show that they cannot. We study finding $\varepsilon$-stationary points of $L$-smooth nonconvex functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ from exact function values, assuming that below the starting value the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix with trace at most $LE$; this is the effective rank condition used to explain zeroth-order fine-tuning. When $ET\le d$, the Gaussian two-point method that such fine-tuning uses needs only $O(ET)$ calls if it rejects steps that raise $f$, where $T=L\Delta/\varepsilon^2$ is the iteration count of gradient descent from initial gap $\Delta$, and we prove that every randomized method needs $\Omega(ET)$ calls, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In contrast, every deterministic method needs $\widetilde\Omega(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls, and adaptive subspace search attains $O(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$: a deterministic method pays about $d$ calls per discovered direction, and the trace budget allows about $\sqrt{ET}$ directions. Determinism thus multiplies the cost by a factor of order $d/(E+\sqrt{ET})$ up to logarithmic factors, which grows linearly with $d$ for fixed $E$ and $T$; once $E$ exceeds $T$ by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods need $\Omega(dT)$ calls, as without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for $C^\infty$ functions with the matrix bound on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, even when each call also returns gradient projections priced by rank.

title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.27046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

title: I Explored Respan Gateway: A Plugin-First, Open-Source LLM Gateway
description:
Every time I connect an application to a new LLM provider, I run into the same problem: how much provider-specific code do I have to add? One SDK expects one request format, another provider uses a different API, and switching models can mean changing far more than a model name. Then come retries, fallback logic, usage tracking, and debugging when a request fails.

Most gateways answer this with the same pitch: one endpoint, many providers. Respan Gateway is more interesting for how it’s built than for that pitch. It is an open-source Rust gateway with a very small core, where nearly everything, including the providers, is a plugin. I went through the documentation and the launch post to see what that design means for a developer and what I’d check before relying on it.

One caveat first: the project describes itself as pre-alpha, and its config and APIs may still change.

Why the Architecture Is the Interesting Part

Respan says it ran its hosted gateway on LiteLLM since 2024. As customers needed different API-key settings, routes, and limits, its wrapper code grew to more than 100,000 lines. Then, this January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors and forced a rollback. Respan says it never found the cause and now backports upstream fixes by hand. That is the company’s own account, and I haven’t tested LiteLLM myself. It does explain the design goal: add features without breaking existing ones.

The result is a small core inspired by Nginx, responsible only for dispatching events. Providers, protocols (chat, real-time voice, MCP), modalities (images, video), and gateway features like routing and fallbacks are all plugins. A provider is a short file. Respan cites Mistral’s at 22 lines, and provider quirks, such as Groq reporting token usage in its own field, are separate plugins with their own tests.

Here is how a request moves through it:

  1. A client adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it.
  2. That format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed events.
  3. Plugins run in registration order. They can choose a provider, filter either stream, make extra calls, return a response, or refuse the request.
  4. A provider format opens the upstream connection.

When client and provider speak the same API, and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and provider-specific fields pass through untouched. When the formats differ, requests translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage.

The trade-off: plugins are natively compiled Rust crates, not dynamically loaded or interpreted. Config-only template plugins cover common needs like adding a vendor or format without a rebuild. Custom logic means compiling it in. In the Hacker News launch thread, a commenter pointed out that this means a CI step instead of pulling a container image, and raised supply-chain concerns. Respan replied that compiled-in crates can at least be reviewed, and said it pulled its Docker image before launch because some APIs may still change. Official builds are prebuilt binaries on GitHub Releases.

Installing and Making a First Request

The quickstart documents two install paths: a binary from GitHub Releases, or cargo install --git. Linux x86_64 is shown here (macOS, arm64, and Windows builds are on the same page), using the version the docs name:

VERSION=v0.1.0
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway/releases/download/$VERSION/respan-gateway-$VERSION-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz" | tar xz
sudo mv "respan-gateway-$VERSION-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/respan-gateway" /usr/local/bin/

cargo install --git https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway respan-gateway

A source build has no web UI unless you build it first. Check the current release before copying the version number.

With no config file, every provider key in your environment becomes a provider:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export GEMINI_API_KEY="..."
respan-gateway

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export GEMINI_API_KEY="..."
respan-gateway

The gateway prints the providers it found, the endpoints it serves, and a request to try. The model name in each request decides where it goes, and a prefix like openai/gpt-5.5 forces a provider. The docs’ curl example sends a request in OpenAI format to Gemini:

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "gemini-3.6-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]}'

The same idea works from an SDK. Here, the OpenAI client talks to Claude:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8080/v1", api_key="unused")
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

With no client keys configured, the gateway answers only on your own machine.

The documentation describes the startup output and request log available at /ui/requests. I have not included a screenshot or claimed a local test result here.

One File: gateway.toml

Everything beyond relaying a request is configured in one gateway.toml. respan-gateway init writes a commented starter from the keys in your environment. This block is adapted from the configure docs:

client_keys = ["env:GATEWAY_KEY"]

[providers.openai]
vendor = "openai"
key = "env:OPENAI_API_KEY"

[providers.anthropic]
vendor = "anthropic"
key = "env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"

[providers.gemini]
vendor = "gemini"
key = "env:GEMINI_API_KEY"

[routes.cheap-and-good]
to = ["openai/gpt-5.5", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", "gemini/gemini-3.6-flash"]
pick = "cheapest"
needs = ["tools"]
tries = 2

[routes.fast]
to = ["anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", "openai/gpt-5.5"]
hedge = "800ms"

A client asks for cheap-and-good as if it were a model name. These are the documented behaviors that matter:

  • pick sets the order candidates are tried in: first, cheapest (input price plus three times output price), fastest, weighted, or random.
  • needs filters candidates to models that list capabilities like tools, reasoning, vision, or pdf.
  • Fallback is on by default, so a failed candidate falls through to the next.
  • tries allows 1 to 10 attempts per candidate. Backoff starts at 250ms, doubles each time, and caps at 10s.
  • hedge races the candidates instead. Each starts after the delay, and the first answer wins.

Fallback models may differ in context length, tool support, or quality. Retries can waste tokens and add latency. Hedging deliberately sends more than one upstream request, which can increase cost.

Run respan-gateway check before starting (--online also calls each provider and MCP server). You can reload without a restart by sending SIGHUP, starting with --watch, or using the web UI. An invalid file is refused while the old config keeps serving. To see where a model would go and why, open /ui/api/routes/explain?model=cheap-and-good.

Before deployment, run respan-gateway check and inspect /ui/api/routes/explain?model=cheap-and-good to confirm the configuration and routing behavior in your environment.

For a failure test, configure an invalid key or unreachable provider as the first candidate, send a request, and inspect the request log to verify the actual retry and fallback behavior.

What It Can Proxy

The documented scope is chat, images, speech (including transcription), video, and real-time voice. The docs give examples like the Anthropic SDK calling a GPT model, and an OpenAI Realtime client talking to Gemini Live. It handles tools, images, streaming, and reasoning parameters across formats. Embeddings aren’t on that list, so retrieval pipelines will still need a separate path.

Sixteen providers are built in, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, DeepSeek, Mistral, xAI, OpenRouter, and Ollama. Any other OpenAI-, Anthropic-, or Gemini-style endpoint works with a base_url. Translation has limits, and Respan itself says not every feature carries over between providers. Test the exact models and parameters you use.

MCP Tools Behind the Gateway

Each [mcp.NAME] block puts an MCP server behind the gateway, with its credentials staying on the gateway. The tool_loop plugin lets any chat model use those tools mid-request. The gateway runs the tool, feeds the result back, and returns only the final answer, so the client needs no MCP support.

This is powerful and worth treating carefully. By default, any client key can make the model call any tool you offer, using the server’s credentials. Use deny lists for destructive tools, and per-key tools globs to limit what each client can reach.

Request Logs and Tracing

The web UI shows each request’s provider, latency, tokens, and cost. By default, it keeps the last 1,000 requests in memory. The request_log plugin can also append each finished request to a JSONL file, without bodies or keys.

The optional respan plugin sends each request to Respan as a trace. Its content setting defaults to true, meaning messages and replies are sent if your prompts contain sensitive data; set content = false to send metadata only.

Where It Fits

  • LiteLLM is the established self-hosted option, and Respan’s own history is built on it. A newer pre-alpha project can’t match its track record, and Respan’s pitch is mainly about extensibility.
  • OpenRouter is a hosted router with one API and one bill. It isn’t a competitor in the self-hosted sense, since it’s one of the gateway’s built-in vendors and you can route to it from here.
  • Respan’s hosted platform runs the gateway for you, adds observability and evals, and bills centrally. That is how the company makes money. The open-source binary is the self-run version, and you can combine them by adding a Respan key as a provider.

I’ve kept these comparisons to differences I could support. Check each project’s current docs before relying on them.

Before Using It in Production

Because it’s pre-alpha, I’d treat this as a proof of concept rather than a critical dependency for now. My checklist:

  • Stability: Expect config and API changes. Pin versions and read release notes.
  • Provider compatibility: Test streaming, tool calls, structured output, images, and any provider-specific parameters your feature uses.
  • Failure behavior: Simulate rate limits, timeouts, and bad keys. Confirm what retries, what falls back, and what happens when every candidate fails.
  • Latency: Measure end-to-end with and without the gateway, including time to first token.
  • Deployment: There’s no official Docker image right now, and custom plugins mean a rebuild. Plan for how you’ll build and ship it.
  • Security: Set client_keys before exposing it beyond localhost (it refuses to start on a public address without them). Review the auth code you depend on. A commenter on the launch thread questioned the project’s MCP OAuth implementation, and Respan said it used Claude to generate code but reviewed every line.
  • State: Conversation state for translated Responses API clients lives in one gateway’s memory, so multi-instance setups need clients pinned to the right instance.
  • Privacy: Decide what the request log and the respan plugin may record.

Verdict

Respan Gateway is worth a look if you want a small, extensible gateway with swappable providers and features as plugins, and you’re comfortable with compiled Rust extensions. It’s less suited to teams that need a drop-in container and a stable API today. Run it against your own models, break it on purpose, and then decide.

To explore it yourself, start with the GitHub repository, then the open-source gateway introduction and quickstart. For how it relates to the hosted offering, see the Respan AI Gateway overview.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Respan Gateway?

An open-source Rust LLM gateway with a small core in which providers, protocols, and features are plugins. It translates between API formats and supports routing, retries, fallbacks, MCP tools, and a request log.

Is it open source?

Yes, under your choice of MIT or Apache-2.0. Confirm against the repository’s license files.

How do I install it?

Download a binary from GitHub Releases, or run cargo install --git https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway respan-gateway. There is no Python package.

What does it support?

Chat, images, speech, video, and real-time voice across OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and other providers, plus MCP tools. Embeddings aren’t supported.

Is it production-ready?

The project calls itself pre-alpha. Validate compatibility, failure handling, security, and deployment before relying on it.

For students, these skills can support financial education. For working professionals, they can improve familiarity with digital financial tools. Set aside time to examine financial records, account notices, and any changes to applicable platform requirements. Separate learning from financial activity. Use educational materials, demonstrations, or practice exercises where available before making decisions involving real money. Read instructions before beginning. Reviewing the requirements in advance can reduce confusion and help users prepare the information they need. Use official documentation. Platform help centers and published policies are useful references when questions arise about verification, account settings, or available features. Keep financial goals realistic. Learning about cryptocurrency does not require frequent trading or constant monitoring of market prices. A defined learning schedule can prevent digital finance from becoming an unnecessary distraction. Record important decisions. Brief notes about why a financial decision was made can help users review their reasoning later. A productive workflow should reduce unnecessary effort while improving understanding. It should not encourage people to bypass account requirements or treat account access as a substitute for financial knowledge. Section 6: Case Studies and Examples The following illustrative scenarios demonstrate how the principles of account verification, financial education, and organized digital workflows can apply in everyday situations. They are hypothetical examples rather than reports of independently verified individuals or specific outcomes. Example 1: A Student Learning About Cryptocurrency A university student is interested in blockchain technology and wants to understand how cryptocurrency exchanges operate. Initially, the student assumes that obtaining an account is the main step toward learning about the subject. After reviewing educational materials, the student realizes that account registration and identity verification are only parts of the broader process.
