The student also reviews the platform's official documentation to understand eligibility requirements and available educational resources. Where account access is appropriate, the student follows the authorized registration and verification procedures. Over time, the student develops a glossary of financial terms and keeps notes about the differences between exchanges, wallets, and blockchain networks. Learning point: Practical financial education begins with understanding concepts and requirements. Account access alone does not provide the knowledge needed to evaluate digital assets. Example 2: A Freelancer Organizing Financial Records A freelance designer receives payments through several digital services and wants to improve personal bookkeeping. The designer studies how transaction histories and downloadable statements can support financial organization. Instead of concentrating on account age or status, the designer creates a monthly recordkeeping routine. Relevant statements are stored by date, and income entries are categorized for later review. The designer also learns that different services may use different fee structures, transaction formats, and reporting methods. Keeping these differences documented makes it easier to compare records and prepare information for an accountant. When researching cryptocurrency exchanges, the designer examines the applicable account requirements and considers whether the platform's services meet the intended purpose. Learning point: Organized records and an understanding of transaction documentation can improve financial administration. These benefits do not depend on purchasing an established account. Example 3: A Small Business Owner Exploring Digital Finance A small business owner wants to understand whether cryptocurrency could become relevant to future business operations. Before considering any financial activity, the owner researches accounting requirements, applicable regulations, transaction documentation, and the availability of services in the business's jurisdiction. The owner creates a comparison sheet covering platform features, fees, reporting tools, and eligibility conditions. The business also consults an appropriate accounting professional about the implications of digital asset transactions. Rather than treating a verified account as evidence that a platform is suitable, the owner evaluates the business's objectives and documentation needs. The result is a more structured assessment process. Even if the business ultimately decides not to use cryptocurrency, the research provides useful knowledge about financial technology and recordkeeping. Learning point: Sound financial decisions depend on evaluating practical requirements, costs, and objectives instead of focusing on a single account feature. Example 4: An Adult Learner Improving Digital Literacy An adult learner wants to become more comfortable with online financial services. The learner starts by studying the account settings, verification terminology, transaction records, and customer support documentation commonly found on financial platforms. The learner practices recognizing official help resources and distinguishing platform requirements from general advice published elsewhere. When encountering unfamiliar instructions, the learner checks the relevant documentation rather than relying on assumptions. The learner also establishes a routine for reviewing financial records and writing down questions before contacting customer support. These habits gradually become useful across other digital services, including online banking and payment applications. Learning point: Understanding one financial platform can help develop transferable digital skills, including careful reading, documentation, independent research, and organized problem-solving. Taken together, these examples show that the main educational benefits come from knowledge, consistency, and informed decision-making. None requires the purchase of an account that was verified for someone else. Section 7: Step-by-Step Guide to Understanding Binance Account Verification The following six steps provide a practical framework for learning about account verification and applying that knowledge responsibly. Step 1: Define Your Learning Objective Begin by identifying what you want to understand. Your objective might be learning cryptocurrency terminology, reviewing digital financial records, studying exchange operations, or understanding identity verification. A clear objective helps you choose relevant educational resources and avoid spending time on features that do not support your goals. Write down two or three questions you want to answer. For example, you might want to understand what identity verification involves, how transaction histories work, or which services are available in your jurisdiction. Step 2: Review Official Platform Information Visit the official Binance website and locate the relevant help center or account documentation. Read the current information about registration, identity verification, eligibility, supported jurisdictions, and available account features. Requirements can change, so current documentation is more useful than relying entirely on older articles. If you consult general informational resources such as usasvcit, compare important statements with official documentation before treating them as authoritative. Step 3: Understand Identity Verification Requirements Learn what the platform requires from individuals seeking access to its services. Depending on the applicable rules, the process may include submitting identifying information, providing an accepted identity document, or completing additional verification steps. Make sure you understand the relationship between the account holder and the identity being verified. Verification should be completed through the platform's authorized process using the account holder's own accurate information. Do not assume that an account verified for another individual can be treated as your own verified account. Step 4: Prepare Accurate Information Before starting an authorized registration or verification process, read the instructions carefully and identify the information required. Ensure that your information is accurate and consistent with the platform's stated requirements. If a document is not accepted or a detail needs clarification, consult the official instructions or appropriate support channels. Preparing in advance can make the process easier to understand and reduce avoidable errors. Step 5: Learn the Account's Available Features After completing the applicable requirements and receiving access, familiarize yourself with the available account interface. Study profile settings, transaction histories, fee information, account statements, and educational resources. Feature availability may differ according to location, eligibility, and platform policies. Take notes about unfamiliar terms and look for official explanations before relying on your interpretation. Step 6: Establish a Regular Review Routine Create a simple schedule for reviewing account information and maintaining relevant financial records. For example, a monthly review might include checking transaction histories, organizing statements, reading important platform notices, and updating personal financial records. Use this process to reinforce your understanding of digital finance. The objective is to develop a sustainable habit of informed account management rather than simply completing a registration procedure. Following these steps creates a foundation for understanding cryptocurrency services, identity verification, and responsible digital financial administration. Section 8: Frequently Asked Questions
  6. What does a verified Binance account mean? A verified Binance account is an account for which the platform has completed the applicable identity verification requirements. The exact process and available services depend on current platform policies, jurisdiction, and eligibility. Verification does not guarantee investment success or access to every feature.
  7. Why is identity verification important on cryptocurrency platforms? Identity verification can help financial platforms meet applicable legal and regulatory obligations, establish account-holder information, and determine eligibility for particular services. Understanding these procedures helps users navigate digital financial systems more effectively.
  8. Is purchasing a previously verified Binance account the same as verifying my own account? No. A previously verified account may be associated with another individual's identity. Purchasing it does not establish that the buyer has completed the platform's verification requirements. The appropriate educational and practical approach is to understand the current rules and follow the authorized process for your own account.
  9. Can learning about Binance help with everyday financial management? Yes. Studying exchange interfaces, transaction histories, fees, and financial terminology can help develop recordkeeping, analytical thinking, and digital literacy. These skills may also be useful when working with online banking and other financial applications.
  10. What should beginners learn before using a cryptocurrency exchange? Beginners should understand basic cryptocurrency concepts, market volatility, transaction fees, account requirements, financial recordkeeping, and the services available in their jurisdiction. They should also review official documentation and avoid making financial decisions based on unfamiliar terminology or assumptions.
  11. Where can I find reliable information about Binance account verification? The official Binance website and help center are appropriate starting points for current account requirements and procedures. General educational resources, including usasvcit, may provide additional context, but important requirements should be checked against official documentation and applicable regulations. Conclusion Understanding the topic of buying verified Binance accounts provides an opportunity to explore a much broader subject: the role of identity, financial literacy, and responsible account management in the digital economy. A cryptocurrency exchange account is not simply a digital profile. It can connect an individual's identity, financial records, platform access, and interactions with digital asset markets. Understanding these connections helps users approach financial technology with greater clarity and confidence. The most valuable lessons concern accurate information, legitimate account ownership, identity verification, organized recordkeeping, and informed decision-making. These principles are useful not only for cryptocurrency exchanges but also for online banking, investment applications, and other digital financial services. Practical education should focus on understanding how account verification works, what requirements apply, and how financial information can be managed effectively. Purchasing an account verified under another person's identity does not replace the process of establishing one's own eligibility and completing the platform's required procedures. Beginners can make meaningful progress by studying official documentation, learning basic cryptocurrency terminology, reviewing transaction records, and developing consistent financial habits. Additional educational resources, including usasvcit, can serve as starting points for research when their information is evaluated alongside authoritative sources. Ultimately, digital financial competence is built through knowledge and practice. Understanding the systems behind an account is more valuable than focusing solely on its age or verification status. By applying the principles in this guide, readers can develop transferable skills, improve their understanding of digital finance, and make better-informed decisions about the financial technologies they encounter in everyday life. Call to Action Take the next step by strengthening your understanding of cryptocurrency and digital financial services. Start with the official Binance help center, review the identity verification requirements that apply to your location, and explore introductory educational materials about blockchain technology, transaction fees, and financial recordkeeping. Create a personal learning checklist, keep notes about unfamiliar concepts, and set aside time each week to review what you have learned. If you consult additional resources such as usasvcit, verify important procedural details against current official documentation. Focus on developing knowledge, maintaining accurate records, and understanding legitimate account procedures. These practical habits can support long-term digital literacy and help you approach financial technology with greater confidence.

title: Running OxiPNG, SVGO, rembg and FFmpeg in a browser tab: what actually worked
description:
A lot of the best file tools are command-line programs. OxiPNG shrinks PNGs losslessly, SVGO minifies SVGs, rembg removes image backgrounds, and FFmpeg does everything to video. They're excellent, but each one asks you to install Rust, Node, Python or a native binary first. That's fine on your own machine, and annoying on a locked-down work laptop, a Chromebook, or when you just need to do one file.

I build a small site of browser tools, and over the last few weeks I moved these engines into pages that run entirely in the tab. Here is what that involved, and where the browser version is honestly worse.

1. OxiPNG: the easy one

OxiPNG is written in Rust, and the jSquash project already publishes it compiled to WebAssembly (it's the same build Squoosh used). The .wasm file is only about 164 KB, so I self-host it instead of loading it from a CDN.

The whole pipeline is: read the file into an ArrayBuffer, call optimise(data, level), and compare sizes. Two things I learned:

  • Return the original when it doesn't get smaller. A lot of PNGs people upload were already optimised by some tool. Re-encoding them can produce a file that is the same size or larger, so the page keeps the input in that case.
  • Levels above 4 are not worth it in a tab. The CLI has -o 0 to -o 6 plus max. In single-threaded WASM even level 4 can take several seconds on a 5-megapixel image, and the higher levels only get slower, so I expose 1–4.

The rough CLI equivalent of what the page runs is oxipng -o 4 input.png --out output.png.

2. SVGO: use the browser build

SVGO 4 ships a svgo/browser entry point that avoids the Node-only config loader. I run it with preset-default and multipass: true, and let the user pick the number precision. That is close to npx svgo --multipass --precision 3 input.svg.

One SVGO 4 detail that bit me: removeViewBox is no longer in preset-default. Keeping the viewBox is usually what you want for responsive SVGs, so I made removing it an explicit opt-in with a warning.

Also worth saying: rendering the result as an <img> preview is not a sanitiser. The preview doesn't execute scripts, but the file you download is still the SVG you uploaded, minus whitespace.

3. rembg: same models, different runtime

rembg is a Python tool that runs the U²-Net family of segmentation models. You can't run rembg itself in a browser, but you can run the same ONNX models with ONNX Runtime Web. I use a small browser port of rembg's pre- and post-processing.

Practical choices:

  • Bundle the small model, fetch the big one on demand. U²-NetP is about 4.7 MB and ships with the site, so the first run works without a third-party request. The full U²-Net model is much larger, so it's only downloaded from Hugging Face if the user switches to it.
  • ONNX Runtime's WASM files are the real weight. They are around 13 MB, which is more than the model. I serve them from the site and load them only when someone opens the tool.
  • Not every model is available. rembg's newer models (isnet, BiRefNet, SAM) aren't on the page. The sensitivity slider is a cheap pixel pass on the mask, not rembg's alpha matting.

4. FFmpeg: it works, but it's slow

ffmpeg.wasm really does run FFmpeg commands in the tab. The trick that made the biggest difference was trying a stream copy first. To mute a video, the page runs:

ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c:v copy -an -movflags +faststart output.mp4

That doesn't re-encode anything, so it finishes almost instantly even in WASM. Only if the copy fails does it fall back to re-encoding with x264.

Everything else is limited by one fact: it's single-threaded. The multi-threaded FFmpeg core needs SharedArrayBuffer, which needs the page to be cross-origin isolated (COOP/COEP headers). Turning that on breaks a lot of ordinary third-party embeds, so for a general tool site I kept the single-threaded core. It's fine for a 30-second screen recording, and painful for a 10-minute 4K file. For big batches, native FFmpeg is the right tool, and the page says so.

5. Show the command, not just the button

The most useful change wasn't technical. Each tool page now shows the engine name, the exact version shipped, the licence, the equivalent command or code, and a short list of how it differs from the original. Developers trust a tool more when they can see that "PNG optimizer" means "OxiPNG level 4". It also helps people who will eventually move the job into a script.

What I'd tell someone doing the same

  1. Check whether a WASM build already exists (jSquash, ffmpeg.wasm, Tesseract.js, ONNX Runtime Web) before compiling anything yourself.
  2. Self-host the WASM if it's small, and lazy-load it only on the page that needs it.
  3. Always compare output size against input and keep the original if you didn't win.
  4. Be upfront about threads. Single-threaded WASM is noticeably slower than a native multithreaded CLI on CPU-heavy jobs, so say so instead of hiding it behind a spinner.
  5. Credit the projects properly. They did the hard part.

The pages are on onemilliontools.com, and there's an index of the engines at onemilliontools.com/open-source. They're free, and the files stay in your browser.

Disclosure: I build this site. I used AI assistance while drafting this post. The numbers above are from the site's own build (file sizes and the commands it runs), not benchmarks against other tools.

title: Every Test Passed. Then the UI Got Thrown Out.
description:
At 1:31 AM, the automated checklist reached its final item.

Eight checks: seven passed, one was marked "record current state," and not a single check was red. By every test report, the feature was done and ready to ship.

Then the user stopped everything.

The verdict was one short sentence that no test suite could argue with: the UI looks bad, redo all of it.

Most developers have been here. The pipeline is green, you feel the relief, and then a person looks at the thing and it feels wrong. The logic is sound. The product still isn't right.

The feature was a native screenshot tool for an open-source terminal app. Press a shortcut, freeze the screen, drag out a region, and draw on top of it. AI agents wrote most of the code; human developers set the direction and made the hard calls.

From the first line of code to the final UI took 10 hours 22 minutes and 27 commits.

Along the way, we ran into three nasty bugs on real hardware that the test suite never caught. Those bugs make up the first half of this story.

The second half is about what happened after that "redo all of it" order, and how we turned a vague complaint into hard numbers.

It all started with an architectural choice that seemed sensible at first, until we threw the whole thing away.

Why we threw away the macOS code to mirror Windows function by function

The tool had to ship on both Windows and macOS.

My first instinct was that each platform could do its own thing internally, as long as the visible features matched.

That idea didn't last long. Windows got the first build, and then macOS followed. A few hours later, the macOS code was thrown away. It was rewritten from scratch to mirror the Windows version function by function.

The spec said the two platforms had to behave the same, item by item. The only allowed difference was the modifier key: Command on macOS where Windows uses the Windows key. Both sides also had to run against the exact same test data and produce the exact same expected outputs.

The dev log puts the reason plainly (translated from Chinese): we want both platforms to produce the same exact value, not two values that are close.

Think of two cooks making the same dish. If each works from memory, you get two meals that taste "about the same." If both follow one recipe and weigh every ingredient on a scale, you get the exact same dish.

None of this had run on a physical machine yet. One of the early commit messages says so (again translated): "No human has pressed confirm on this version yet."

The first run on a real Windows machine broke the undo shortcut immediately.

The undo button on the screen worked fine, but the keyboard shortcut did nothing. The code checked the keyboard state at the exact moment the event got handled. When you tap a shortcut quickly, your fingers are already off the keys by the time the handler runs.

That was the easy one to fix. The next bug on Windows froze the whole app.

A thin white edge that froze the app in an endless loop

A screenshot tool needs text annotations. That means a floating text box sits next to a toolbar with pens, arrows, and other tools.

In some screen layouts, the text box ended up sitting right on top of the toolbar. To keep the toolbar buttons clickable, we cut a transparent hole in the text box where they overlapped.

Clicks worked again, but the cutout left a thin white edge behind. It was the text box's own white background bleeding through.

The obvious fix seemed to be a quick patch. Every time the text box moved, we forced the toolbar to repaint (redraw its pixels on screen) over the overlapping area to cover the white edge.

Instead, the app froze.

On a physical Windows machine, opening the text box sent CPU usage spiking. The program spun in place and locked up. Four tries, four hangs.

The cause was hidden deep inside how Windows draws native controls.

The native text box keeps an old behavior that lets a control paint outside its own bounds. That white edge was the control painting past its own border. Each forced repaint woke that out-of-bounds painting up again, which triggered another repaint request, spinning forever in an infinite loop.

The fix wasn't another patch. We swapped the native text box for one with that out-of-bounds painting turned off.

Once the control could no longer paint past its own edge, the white strip was gone for good.

Before you cover one patch with another, find the control that is drawing where it shouldn't be.

That was Windows. On macOS, a different bug was waiting in the same text box.

The macOS text box that typed "n你好" instead of "你好"

The next bug showed up on macOS.

In the screenshot text box, using the built-in Pinyin input method, you type n-i-h-a-o and press space to confirm. That should produce 你好 ("hello").

What actually showed up was "n你好". The first letter was stuck in front of the Chinese characters.

Here's some background if you have never worked with an IME (an Input Method Editor, the system tool used to type characters in languages like Chinese or Japanese). While you type Pinyin letters, they sit in a temporary composition buffer. macOS calls this active state marked text. Only when you confirm your selection does that buffer turn into real characters and commit to the field.

The bug came from an auto-grow feature. The text box starts one line tall and gets taller as you type.

The first time the box grew taller, the operating system switched the text layout engine underneath. That switch cleared the marked text state. Because the buffer was suddenly wiped out, the system treated the first letter, n, as already-committed text.

The dev log pinned it down (translated): "Didn't happen in earlier builds. Regression from the dynamic height change."

A regression is when previously working code breaks because of a new change.

The fix was to lock the text box to one layout engine from the moment it was created, and never let it switch. After that, we tested every font size on a real Mac, and 你好 came out clean.

The interesting part is that this bug never showed up in our automated tests. They run without real window management, and that's where the bug lives.

Anything that touches IME state, marked text, or window focus must be typed into on a physical machine.

Text input was fixed. The scrolling capture was next, and it had its own trap.

Why the scrolling screenshot refused to move past the first screen

The third problem was the scrolling screenshot, also called a long screenshot.

The concept is straightforward. The user scrolls down, the capture engine grabs frames quickly, compares each new frame to the last one to find where they overlap, and appends the newly revealed part to the bottom.

To find the overlap, we used a strict pixel diff (a row-by-row pixel comparison). If row X of the previous frame exactly matches row Y of the current one, the algorithm knows how far the page moved.

On a real machine, no matter how far you scrolled, the output image stayed stuck at one screen tall. Not a single new frame got merged.

The culprit was a column of pixels that never moved at all: the window border.

The page content scrolled, but the window border at the edge of the selected region stayed put. Every row in the comparison had a few border pixels that could never match. In a strict comparison, one mismatched pixel rejects the entire row. Every row got rejected, so the engine concluded there was no overlap anywhere.

The fix follows from that: before comparing frames, drop the pixel columns that stay completely still from top to bottom, so they don't count toward the match.

There's a trap in that rule. "Still" must mean the column is exactly identical all the way down, not just mostly identical. Take line numbers in a code editor. They look almost the same from row to row, but their small shifts are the best signal you have for tracking how far the page moved.

With the border handled, the scrollbar broke the algorithm next. The scrollbar thumb doesn't scroll with the page, and it doesn't stay still either. It moves a little, at its own separate ratio.

So the engine received a second rule. If a pixel column changes in at most two segments, and the changed part is less than half its height, it is treated as background noise and left out of the comparison.

We also added a safety rule for failure. If the user scrolls so fast that frames get dropped, the engine throws away the broken frame and displays a "slow down" message. It never forces a stitch.

Before you ask an algorithm to compare two things, cut out everything that shouldn't be part of the comparison.

That should have been the end of the night. It wasn't.

Turning "it looks bad" into hard pixel measurements

With those three bugs resolved, testing on real hardware went green. That brought us right back to 1:31 AM.

All 8 checks passed. Buttons responded, text input worked, and long screenshots stitched cleanly. QA had nothing left to mark as failed.

Then came the user review. The complaints were clear:

The icons didn't feel balanced in visual weight. The gray plate behind the selected tool looked cheap. The dots used to pick the font size didn't make sense. And the opaque text box covered what was underneath it.

Editing code against feedback like that is guesswork.

So we stopped writing code and started measuring pixels.

We used the app's own rendering code to draw each toolbar icon on its own, and we counted how many pixels it filled.

The hard numbers explained the imbalance immediately.

The lightest icon (undo) and the heaviest icon (mosaic) differed in filled area by 8.3x. Picture a shot put and a balloon sitting side by side in the same toolbar.

The shapes were misaligned as well. The long-screenshot icon was tall and thin like a pole, sticking up above the baseline. The arrow in the selection tool wasn't centered in its 16x16 grid; it leaned noticeably to the left.

The worst find was where the graphics came from. 5 icons were not drawn from vector paths at all. They were plain characters pulled from the host operating system's fonts. Windows and macOS ship different system fonts, so those 5 icons looked visibly different on the two platforms.

"It looks bad" was no longer a matter of opinion. It was now a table of pixel measurements. That table became the acceptance criteria for the UI rework.

When someone says something looks wrong and you can't argue with it, the first step is to find a way to measure it.

We had the data. But before we touched any code, we changed how we worked.

Locking in the mockup before writing a single line of native code

This time, no AI was allowed to touch the code.

We had already seen what happens otherwise. You build the UI in code, compile it, and show it to the user. If the visual direction is wrong, all the cross-platform work gets thrown out.

So we went mockup-first.

We built high-fidelity mockups using web technologies. A browser mockup isn't the native code that ships to users, but you can iterate on it more than ten times faster than on compiled code.

From the "redo all of it" order to the new UI spec being committed took 76 minutes. In that time, the mockup went through three major versions.

Each small request got settled directly inside the mockup: hover feedback, replacing the confusing font-size dots with a small and a large letter "T," and switching a solid border to a dashed one so it blocked less of the view.

Making those changes in native code would have meant editing and recompiling both platforms dozens of times. In the mockup, it was just dragging elements and changing values.

Any disagreement about looks that can be settled in a mockup should never make it into the code.

The visual design was locked in. Now we had to build it in native code without letting the two platforms drift apart by a single pixel.

One data file, two platforms, zero pixel difference

With the design settled, the engineering question was how to guarantee that the two platforms could never drift apart, even by a single pixel.

The lesson from the old version was clear. Each platform had its own separate implementation, and 5 icons ended up looking different on each.

This time, we established a single source of truth.

A single source of truth means one file that every platform reads from. Every UI parameter (color values, spacing, and Bézier control points) went into one standalone data file.

The Windows and macOS UI code was no longer written by the AI agents. Instead, a custom script reads that data file and generates the UI code for each platform automatically.

It works like casting parts from a single mold: parts from the same mold cannot drift past tolerance.

Rendering received the exact same treatment.

The native drawing APIs on Windows and macOS handle anti-aliasing slightly differently. Anti-aliasing is how graphics systems smooth the jagged edges of lines. Because the two systems drew lines differently, we stopped using the built-in line drawing and ran the same basic rendering code on both platforms.

To check our work, we pulled the outlines of all 60 icons as rendered on each platform and compared them pixel by pixel.

They matched exactly, with zero pixel difference.

The code was unified, and the icons were identical. Which brings us back to what that green test suite actually meant.

What a green test suite can and cannot promise

Boil those 10 hours 22 minutes down, and you get a clear lesson: automated tests are very good at catching logic bugs, but they are blind to how an app feels to use. A lot of what makes software feel well made sits outside the green checkmarks.

What automated tests can promise What a human still has to check
Pipeline is green, no errors Is a test case missing? Did a real problem quietly get downgraded to "record current state"?
Unit tests pass 100% Has it run on a physical machine? Has a person's hand gone through the interaction?
The visual glitch (white edge) is covered up in code Was the underlying cause removed, or just covered with another patch?
Frame comparison failed, logic stopped Did the algorithm drop the noise that never belonged in the comparison?
The feature works end to end Does it look and feel right? Was there a high-fidelity review before coding?
Both platforms are done Were both generated from the same data, or did each side settle on its own version?

Think back to 1:31 AM.

The all-green checklist didn't lie. It checked everything it was built to check. It just had no item for "does this look good."

Next time someone tells you all tests pass, ask one more question: beyond the code being correct, who decided how it should look and feel, and at what point?

The screenshot tool, new toolbar included, has shipped in Polter, a terminal for macOS and Windows built on Ghostty's rendering: https://github.com/Lugia123/polter

title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
description:
arXiv:2610.27290v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.

title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.27468v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.

title: A webmanifest cannot read a CSS variable, so our brand colour is spelled twice: once as OKLCH and once as hex
description:
Nakodo's stylesheet is 865 lines long and contains no hex colours at all: 98 of those lines declare an oklch() value. Every colour is an OKLCH ramp step, and everything else is a semantic alias pointing at one:

--color-paper-0: oklch(0.993 0.005 85);
--color-paper-50: oklch(0.972 0.012 85);
--color-paper-100: oklch(0.952 0.013 85);
...
--background: var(--color-paper-50);

There is a grep ban on raw palette classes and on hex values outside that file, written into the brand document. Then there is this, which is 20 lines of TypeScript and contains the same colour twice, written out by hand:

// Served at /manifest.webmanifest. Icons are in public/.
export default function manifest(): MetadataRoute.Manifest {
  return {
    name: BRAND.name,
    short_name: BRAND.name,
    description: BRAND.description,
    start_url: "/campaigns",
    display: "standalone",
    background_color: "#f9f5ed",
    theme_color: "#f9f5ed",
    icons: [
      { src: "/icon-192.png", sizes: "192x192", type: "image/png" },
      { src: "/icon-512.png", sizes: "512x512", type: "image/png" },
      { src: "/icon.svg", sizes: "any", type: "image/svg+xml" },
    ],
  };
}

A webmanifest is JSON read by the operating system. There is no cascade in it, no var(), no computed value, and nothing in it is ever resolved by a browser engine against a stylesheet. The same is true of the theme-color meta tag, our Open Graph image renderer and our email layout, so the full count of places that know this colour as a hex string is five:

$ grep -rn "f9f5ed" src/
src/app/layout.tsx:48:export const viewport: Viewport = { ..., themeColor: "#f9f5ed" };
src/app/manifest.ts:12:    background_color: "#f9f5ed",
src/app/manifest.ts:13:    theme_color: "#f9f5ed",
src/lib/seo/og.tsx:13:const PAPER = "#f9f5ed";
src/lib/email/layout.ts:15:  page: "#f9f5ed", // paper-50

Every one of those is a boundary where CSS stops: the OS, the OS again, the browser chrome, a PNG renderer, and a mail client. The comment on the last line is the only thing in the repository that says which ramp step the string is supposed to be.

The two spellings are the same colour, and nothing enforces it

#f9f5ed is not approximately --color-paper-50. It is exactly it. You can check that without trusting me, by converting the OKLCH value by hand:

import math
L, C, H = 0.972, 0.012, 85
a, b = C * math.cos(math.radians(H)), C * math.sin(math.radians(H))
l_, m_, s_ = L + 0.3963377774*a + 0.2158037573*b, L - 0.1055613458*a - 0.0638541728*b, L - 0.0894841775*a - 1.2914855480*b
l, m, s = l_**3, m_**3, s_**3
r  =  4.0767416621*l - 3.3077115913*m + 0.2309699292*s
g  = -1.2684380046*l + 2.6097574011*m - 0.3413193965*s
bl = -0.0041960863*l - 0.7034186147*m + 1.7076147010*s
f = lambda x: 12.92*x if x <= 0.0031308 else 1.055*x**(1/2.4) - 0.055
print("#%02X%02X%02X" % tuple(round(f(max(0, min(1, v))) * 255) for v in (r, g, bl)))
# #F9F5ED

So the real state of this codebase is: one colour, two notations, five copies of the second notation, and no test. Nudge the ramp step a thousandth of a lightness and the app's background moves while the Android splash screen, the browser's address bar tint, the social card and every email stay where they were. That drift would be invisible in the pull request and faintly visible in real life, as a seam where the browser chrome meets the page.

The fix is not to delete the hex, because nothing on those five boundaries can consume OKLCH. It is to have one of them: a single exported constant that the manifest, the viewport, the card renderer and the email layout all import, with one test asserting it matches the ramp step's conversion. That is maybe thirty lines including the conversion, and it is now on the list. Writing the post is what put it there, which is most of why I write them.

Two of the five already behave: name, short_name and description in the manifest come from the BRAND constant rather than being typed, so the string in an install prompt is the same string as the meta description on the home page.

Next links the manifest without being told to

Our root layout's metadata export has no manifest key in it. It sets a title template, a description, Open Graph defaults, Twitter card type and the icons, and that is all. The manifest link tag still ships on every page:

$ curl -s https://nakodo.app/ | grep -o '<link rel="manifest"[^>]*>'
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest"/>

That comes from the file convention: app/manifest.ts exists, so the route exists and the tag is injected. Which is convenient and worth knowing precisely, because it means deleting a manifest key from your metadata does not unlink the manifest, and the thing to delete is the file.

It also means the manifest is linked from every public page, including the marketing pages a stranger lands on, which leads to the next part.

The installed app opens a sign-in form 

start_url: "/campaigns",

/campaigns is the signed-in app. It is not public, and our proxy says so:

$ curl -sI https://nakodo.app/campaigns | grep -i '^http\|^location'
HTTP/2 307
location: /login?next=%2Fcampaigns

So: a visitor reads the pricing page, the browser offers to install Nakodo because the page links a manifest with icons over https, they install it, they open the icon, and they get a sign-in form.

I have thought about this one for a while and I am keeping it. For the case the installed app exists for, a customer who uses Nakodo weekly, start_url: "/campaigns" is exactly right: an installed window that opens on the marketing home page would be absurd, and a standalone window shares the browser profile's cookies, so a signed-in customer goes straight to their campaigns. For the stranger case, the redirect carries ?next=%2Fcampaigns, so signing in lands them where the icon said it would. The first run is one screen longer than it should be and it is not a dead end.

What I would not do is point start_url at /. That trades a correct destination for every real user against a tidier first launch for someone who installed an app they have no account for.

The one honest criticism left is that the install prompt is offered at all on a page where the product cannot be used. Chrome decides that, not us, from the manifest and the icons, and the manifest is link-tagged site wide by the convention above. Scoping the tag to the signed-in area would mean dropping the file convention and setting metadata.manifest per route group, which is a larger change than the problem.

Standalone, with no service worker, on purpose 

display: "standalone",

There is no service worker in this app. No sw.js, no caching layer, no offline page:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://nakodo.app/sw.js
307

That is the sign-in redirect answering for a file that does not exist, which is its own small joke.

standalone without a service worker is a legitimate combination and it is the one I want. It gives an installed window with no tab strip and no address bar, which is the whole benefit anybody gets from installing a dashboard. What it does not give is offline, and offline is meaningless here: every screen in Nakodo is a server render of live state, and the work it does happens on a cron while nobody is looking. An app shell cached on a phone would show a brand their campaign exactly as stale as the last time they opened it, which is worse than telling them the truth about the network.

If a service worker ever shows up in this repository it will be for web push, not for caching.

The icons, and the one the manifest does not own

Three entries, 192 and 512 PNGs plus the SVG at sizes: "any". The PNGs exist because Android's launcher and the install prompt want raster at known sizes, and 192 and 512 are the two the specification and Chrome's install criteria actually look for.

The apple touch icon is not in the manifest at all. It is in the page metadata:

icons: {
  icon: [
    { url: "/favicon.ico", sizes: "16x16 32x32 48x48" },
    { url: "/icon.svg", type: "image/svg+xml" },
  ],
  apple: "/apple-touch-icon.png",
},

iOS does not take home screen icons from a webmanifest's icons array, and it does not accept an SVG for apple-touch-icon either. So that one is a 180 by 180 PNG, sitting in public/, and if it were missing or an SVG, iOS would quietly use a screenshot of the page instead. That is the kind of bug nobody files, because the person affected assumes it is normal.

The .ico has explicit sizes for a smaller reason: without them, Chrome prefers the .ico over the SVG favicon, and the SVG is the one that follows the colour scheme.

What the file is worth

Twenty lines, of which four are decisions: where an installed window opens, what the splash screen looks like before the first paint, what display mode the window has, and which icons the OS gets. The colour duplication in it is not a mistake in the manifest, it is the shape of every boundary a design system has to cross, and the only real sin is that we cross it five times with five string literals instead of one.

The manifest is public if you want to read the whole of it, and the pricing page is where a browser will probably offer to install it.

title: One zone lost power in London, and the banks went dark with it
description:
Tuesday, just after 7am

Tuesday morning in London. People tapped their bank cards at the till and the payment was declined. Revolut transfers froze mid-send. Lloyds and HSBC customers could not get into their apps. In courts across England and Wales, video hearings stalled because the courts' video platform was down. Royal Mail tracking went quiet, and delivery networks wobbled.

None of these companies had a power cut. A Google Cloud data center zone did.

Just after 7am London time on Tuesday, October 20, a power event knocked out europe-west2-b, one of three availability zones inside Google Cloud's London region. Google's own status text put it plainly: "A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated."

What followed is the part worth studying. One zone, one of three, lost power. And banks, courts, and couriers across the country felt it.

Google has said it will publish a full analysis once its internal investigation is finished. Until then, nobody outside Google knows the complete chain of events. What follows is what the status page and the press record show, plus the mechanics of what a zone failure actually breaks. If you run anything in the cloud, this is your blast radius lesson for the week.

What Google said

The timeline, from Google's status page and press reports:

  • Just after 7am London time (06:08 UTC), Tuesday Oct 20. The power event hits zone europe-west2-b. Google: "Multiple services are experiencing issues in the europe-west2 region."
  • Through the morning. "Google Cloud services are unavailable in europe-west2-b zone; some services in europe-west2 region may experience elevated errors and intermittent network issues." The incident page listed dozens of affected products: Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, Memorystore, Persistent Disk, Cloud Load Balancing, Virtual Private Cloud, and more.
  • Around midday. Most services were back to normal by about 12:10pm London time, roughly six hours in. Full recovery of existing workloads was tentatively expected by early afternoon.
  • Late afternoon. The Ministry of Justice confirmed the courts' Cloud Video Platform had still not fully recovered. Some wounds take longer to close.

The customer list reads like a tour of British daily life: Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Halifax, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Nationwide, credit-reference firm Equifax, Royal Mail, DPD, property site Rightmove. The Telegraph reported cards declined at tills. The Guardian reported courts disrupted and millions unable to move money.

What a zone is, and what dies with it

A quick glossary, because the rest of this piece depends on it.

A region is a geographic area where a cloud provider operates, like London. Inside each region are availability zones: separate buildings, or clusters of buildings, each with its own power feed, its own cooling, and its own network connections. The London region, europe-west2, has three: a, b, and c. The idea is simple. If one building has a bad day, the other two keep going.

Your virtual machine lives in exactly one zone. Your disk lives in one zone too, with copies kept elsewhere for safety, but those copies are managed by the platform, not by you.

So when the power goes in zone b, everything physically in zone b stops at once. Virtual machines halt instantly, with no graceful shutdown. Disks stop being reachable. Anything that had its database primary in zone b stops answering. There is no orderly wind-down. The lights go out and the machines stop.

This is the part people nod along to and then get wrong in practice, because "we run in multiple zones" feels like a shield. It is a shield with holes. Here are the holes.

Why the surviving zones did not just absorb it

Failover takes time. Nothing in a distributed system switches over instantly. A database has to notice its primary is gone, hold an election, and promote a replica. A load balancer has to fail several health checks before it stops sending traffic to dead backends. DNS answers are cached, and each cached answer has a TTL, a countdown timer after which it expires. During every one of those windows, requests fail. Multi-zone does not mean zero-downtime. It means downtime measured in minutes instead of hours, if everything works as designed.

Your dependencies have zones too. Your app can run happily in zone a and still die, because it calls something that lived in zone b. A database primary. A NAT gateway. A load balancer component. A queue. Google's own status text admitted the mechanism: services across the region saw "elevated errors and intermittent network issues" because of shared infrastructure dependencies. A zone is not a sealed box. The region shares plumbing, and the plumbing runs through every zone.

You could not build replacements during the fire. Read this line from the status page again: "Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads." The system that creates virtual machines and clusters, the control plane, was itself degraded. Your running apps are the data plane. The API that manages them is the control plane. They are different systems, and this event hurt both. The usual escape plan, spin up fresh capacity in the surviving zones, was partially locked during the exact hours people needed it. The fire escape was bolted during the fire.

Two zones doing the work of three is not the same as three zones. Failover plans quietly assume spare capacity. When a third of a region's machines vanish, the survivors absorb their load on top of their own. Everything gets slower, queues grow, and some things fail that would have survived a smaller shock. One engineer's account in the press said the peer zones did not fully absorb the load. Capacity is the quiet part of every failover plan, and it is the part nobody load-tests.

The single-region trap

Here is the structural fact that made this outage national news instead of a footnote: europe-west2 is Google's only UK region. Customers who had built everything in London, sensibly, to keep data close to users, had no second UK location to fail over to.

Multi-zone protects you against one zone failing. Nothing inside a single region protects you against the region's shared systems failing, or against a zone failure cascading the way this one did through shared dependencies. Real protection is multi-region: running in London and somewhere else, with a tested plan to shift traffic. That roughly doubles your bill and your complexity, which is why most teams do not have it. The banks that went dark on Tuesday are a reminder of what that savings costs.

This happened before

The London region has been here before. On July 19, 2022, during the hottest day ever recorded in the UK, cooling failed in a building hosting europe-west2-a. Google's engineers could not get temperatures down, so they deliberately powered down part of the zone to save the hardware. That decision terminated about 35 percent of the virtual machines in that zone.

Different zone, different cause, same lesson. A zone is a unit of failure. It can go dark from heat, from power, from a bad config push, from a backhoe through a fiber bundle. The cause changes. The shape of the failure does not.

Audit your own blast radius

"We run multi-AZ" is a claim. Here is how to check whether it is true.

# Where do your VMs actually live? Not where you think. Where they are.
gcloud compute instances list --format="table(name,zone.basename())"

# Are your Kubernetes nodes spread across zones, or quietly all in one?
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone

Then ask the questions no dashboard answers for you:

  • Which zone holds your database primary right now? Your managed database console will tell you. Write it down.
  • If that zone went dark, how long until a replica gets promoted, and have you ever watched it happen? If the answer is "the docs say it is automatic," you have not tested it.
  • Which zone do your NAT gateways, load balancers, and file stores live in? These are the shared plumbing. They have zones too.
  • During the last incident, could you have created new capacity? If your control plane calls were failing, your runbook's step one was fiction.

The cheapest version of this audit is a game day: pick a zone, pretend it is gone, and walk through what breaks. The 2022 incident's official workaround was "relaunch your workloads in another region." That advice only helps if you know, before the bad day, that you can.

The question

Draw your blast radius on paper. Pick the single thing, a zone, a database primary, a region, whose failure at 7am would ruin your day. If you cannot name it, that is the audit, and it is overdue.

Do you know, right now, which zone your database primary lives in? When did you last check?

title: How Featured's users make 100K media pitches per month on Vercel
description:
Featured on Vercel

  • 3 engineers supporting 3 brands and 100,000+ users on Vercel

  • Migrated 374 Sanity sites from AWS Elastic Beanstalk to Vercel

  • AI SDK and AI Gateway power Featured's chat bot across 17 models

  • Workflow SDK replaced custom long-running job infrastructure

Featured is a co-pilot for public relations (PR) that subject matter experts and PR teams use to find media opportunities. Tell Featured's agents what you know, and it surfaces opportunities across journalist requests, podcasts, awards, and GEO, with no PR background required.

Founder Brett Farmiloe knows from experience how hard and time consuming getting press is. He spent 10 years running Markitors, a digital marketing agency with 500 small business clients. Every client, from an eyelash extension supplier to an equipment financing company, had real expertise to share, but no way to get it in front of journalists. PR, as Farmiloe puts it, "has always been about who has access to what." He founded Featured to change the question from who has access to who has knowledge.

Featured connects one of their users with a journalist or publisher every 6 seconds. Their agents deliver more than 100,000 media pitches per month, and have sent over 100 million Help A Reporter Out (HARO) emails in the past year.

Behind it all is an engineering team of just three people. With a team that lean, there's no time to manage servers or piece together custom integrations. Every hour spent on infrastructure is an hour taken away from building features what will help their customers land more media placements.

The cost of managing infrastructure by hand

Before Vercel, Featured’s infrastructure work pulled the team away from product development. Hosting lived on AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AI features depended on custom provider integrations, and long-running, multi-step jobs ran on separate orchestration infrastructure. Each layer worked, but each one added operational overhead for a three-person team supporting multiple brands.

One platform for compute, AI primitives, and model access

The migration to Vercel started with a forcing function: Featured needed to launch 374 Sanity sites at once, and every Elastic Beanstalk deploy had to be manually spun up, migrated, and then torn down.

When you multiply that process by almost four hundred, the math doesn't work, even when you divide it across a team of three. Vercel collapsed each site launch into to a single-click deploy.

Once the sites were live, the team evaluated Vercel for background jobs and AI tooling, eventually migrating their entire app and the agents that run in it.

Compute without the clusters

Deploys that once meant standing up a new EB instance, migrating the URL, and terminating the old one became a single click. On Vercel, all 374 sites shipped from one platform, and rollouts across all three brands now happen centrally, instead of one cluster at a time. "In hindsight, doing each one of those by hand was kind of crazy," Farmiloe admits.

AI SDK and AI Gateway: one abstraction for every model

AI SDK and AI Gateway handle all of Featured's model traffic through a single abstraction, so their team doesn't have to manage custom rate-limit or API integrations from multiple providers.

Featured routes across 17 models at any given time. Calling a model is one standardized function with a schema, and swapping providers is a configuration change instead of a rewrite. When a new model ships, the team can test it against Featured's use cases right away.

Workflow SDK for long-running backend jobs

After migrating their AI stack, Featured moved long-running jobs from a separate orchestration system onto Workflow SDK. These are the processes that can't live in a request cycle: monitoring the media around the clock, qualifying opportunities, and combining all of those signals to deliver more than 100,000 pitches a month.

Chat became the product

As users kept choosing conversation over navigation, the team made chat Featured's primary interface, and they deliver it through eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework.

eve's useEveAgent hook made the new interface easy to implement. Instead of wiring up an agent by hand, the team got durable sessions, streaming, tool calls, and approval prompts out of the box, with model calls routed through AI Gateway so they can pick the right model per task without managing provider keys.

What would have been a months-long rebuild was a week-long replace and refactor. Now, instead of a dashboard with dozens of buttons, users ask Featured questions, and the team adapts the product to their needs, not the other way around.

What's next

Featured is building toward being the AI layer for public relations, the same way dedicated agent platforms have emerged for legal and finance. The goal is to make it faster and easier for anyone with expertise to share their knowledge and get featured in the media.

The team's advice to other founders building in the agentic era:

  • Know that your data is your moat. For us, access to good information is what lets Featured connect people with the sources that want to publish them.

  • Lean on tested abstractions like Vercel instead of reinventing security and infrastructure by hand.

About Featured: Featured is a co-pilot for public relations that helps people find media opportunities, submit pitches, and get featured in the press. Featured also owns and operates Help A Reporter Out (HARO) and Connectively, journalist request platforms connecting sources with publishers.

title: I Built a Small LLM From Scratch — Here’s What I Finally Understood About Transformer
description:
I used to understand Large Language Models mostly from the outside.

I knew terms like:

  • Transformer
  • Attention
  • Embeddings
  • Tokens
  • Fine-tuning
  • GPT
  • LLM

But knowing the terminology is very different from understanding what actually happens inside a model.

So instead of only reading about LLMs, I decided to build a small language model from scratch using PyTorch.

The goal wasn't to build the next ChatGPT.

The goal was much more important for me as a learner:

What I Built

The model starts with Shakespeare text and learns to predict the next character.

The basic pipeline is:

Text
  ↓
Character Tokenization
  ↓
Token Embeddings
  ↓
Transformer Blocks
  ↓
RMSNorm
  ↓
Grouped Query Attention + RoPE
  ↓
SwiGLU Feed Forward Network
  ↓
Final Normalization
  ↓
Language Model Head
  ↓
Next-token prediction

The model configuration I worked with was:

Vocabulary size:       65
Embedding dimension:   256
Transformer blocks:     4
Query heads:            8
KV heads:               2
SwiGLU hidden size:     680
Context length:         256

The important thing is that these aren't just names in a diagram. I implemented the pieces and followed the tensors through the model.

1. First Problem: How Does Text Become Numbers?

Neural networks don't understand strings directly.

So the first step was tokenization.

For this project, I used a character-level tokenizer.

For example:

"Hello"

can become something like:

[20, 43, 50, 50, 53]

The tokenizer maintains two mappings:

char_to_idx = {
    character: integer
}

idx_to_char = {
    integer: character
}

Then:

def encode(s):
    return [char_to_idx[c] for c in s]

def decode(ids):
    return "".join([idx_to_char[i] for i in ids])

The important lesson for me was simple:

Before a model can learn language, language has to become numerical data.

The training examples are created by shifting the sequence by one position.

For example:

Input:  To be o
Target: o be or

So the model is continuously learning:

Given previous characters → predict the next character

This turns one sequence of length N into N next-token prediction examples.

2. RMSNorm — A Simpler Way to Normalize Activations

One component I learned about was RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Normalization).

Traditional LayerNorm performs operations involving the mean and standard deviation.

RMSNorm simplifies this.

Conceptually:

x
 ↓
calculate RMS
 ↓
normalize x
 ↓
learnable scale

The implementation is roughly:

rms = torch.sqrt(
    x.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + eps
)

output = (x / rms) * weight

The interesting part is that RMSNorm only needs a learnable scale vector.

My takeaway:

Normalization isn't just a mathematical trick. It helps keep the values flowing through a deep network under control.

The material compares RMSNorm with LayerNorm and notes its use in modern architectures such as LLaMA, Mistral, and Gemma.

3. RoPE — How Does a Transformer Know Where a Token Is?

This was one of the concepts I found most interesting.

A transformer needs positional information.

One approach is to add positional embeddings.

RoPE — Rotary Positional Embeddings — takes a different approach.

Instead of simply adding a position vector, RoPE rotates the Query and Key vectors.

The important intuition is:

Position 3 → Position 5
distance = 2

Position 7 → Position 9
distance = 2

RoPE allows the attention mechanism to capture this kind of relative positional relationship.

At a high level:

Query + position
Key + position
       ↓
rotations
       ↓
attention

The rotation is applied to pairs of dimensions:

(d0, d1)
(d2, d3)
(d4, d5)
...

and each pair gets its own rotation frequency.

The biggest lesson I took from this:

Position isn't just “where is this token?” — attention can benefit from understanding how far apart tokens are.

4. GQA — Reducing Attention Memory

Next came Grouped Query Attention (GQA).

This was especially useful because it showed me that modern LLM architecture isn't only about making models bigger.

It's also about making them more efficient.

Instead of giving every Query head its own Key and Value heads, GQA allows multiple Query heads to share KV heads.

In my model:

Query heads = 8
KV heads    = 2

So four Query heads share each KV head.

Conceptually:

Q0 ─┐
Q1 ─┤
Q2 ─┤──→ K0, V0
Q3 ─┘

Q4 ─┐
Q5 ─┤
Q6 ─┤──→ K1, V1
Q7 ─┘

This significantly reduces the size of the KV cache.

The implementation first projects Q, K and V, reshapes them into heads, applies RoPE to Q and K, and then expands the KV heads to match the Query heads.

This taught me an important engineering lesson:

AI engineering isn't only about model accuracy. Memory usage and inference efficiency matter too.

5. Causal Attention — Why Can't the Model See the Future?

During training, the model shouldn't be allowed to cheat.

Suppose we're predicting:

The cat sat

When predicting the next token after "The", the model shouldn't be able to look at "cat".

That's why causal masking is used.

Conceptually:

       T0 T1 T2 T3

T0     ✓  ✗  ✗  ✗
T1     ✓  ✓  ✗  ✗
T2     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✗
T3     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓

Each token can attend to itself and previous tokens, but not future tokens.

The attention computation looks roughly like:

scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * scale

scores = scores.masked_fill(
    mask,
    float("-inf")
)

weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)

out = weights @ v

This made the phrase “next-token prediction” much more concrete for me.

6. SwiGLU — The Feed-Forward Part Isn't Just ReLU

Another component I implemented was SwiGLU.

A traditional feed-forward network can look like:

Input
  ↓
Linear
  ↓
ReLU
  ↓
Linear
  ↓
Output

SwiGLU introduces a gating mechanism.

It has two paths:

             ┌──→ SiLU ──┐
Input ───────┤            × ──→ Linear ──→ Output
             └──→ Up ────┘

The core operation is:

gate = F.silu(self.w_gate(x))
up = self.w_up(x)

output = self.w_down(gate * up)

The gate learns which information should be emphasized or suppressed.

The training material describes this as a gated dual-path feed-forward network, with SiLU on the gate path and element-wise multiplication controlling information flow.

7. Putting Everything Together

A transformer block in my implementation follows this pattern:

Input
  │
  ├── RMSNorm
  │
  ├── GQA + RoPE
  │
  └── Residual Add
          ↓
        x'
          │
          ├── RMSNorm
          │
          ├── SwiGLU
          │
          └── Residual Add
                 ↓
               Output

In code:

x = x + self.attention(
    self.attn_norm(x),
    rope_cos,
    rope_sin
)

x = x + self.ffn(
    self.ffn_norm(x)
)

This is a pre-norm + residual architecture.

The residual connection means the block learns a change to the existing representation instead of having to completely rebuild it at every layer.

8. The Complete Mini LLM

The complete model then becomes:

Character IDs
     ↓
Token Embedding
     ↓
Transformer Block × 4
     │
     ├── RMSNorm
     ├── GQA
     │    └── RoPE
     ├── Residual
     ├── RMSNorm
     ├── SwiGLU
     └── Residual
     ↓
Final RMSNorm
     ↓
Language Model Head
     ↓
Logits
     ↓
Softmax
     ↓
Next Character

The model uses weight tying between the token embedding and language-model head.

The complete architecture in the project uses 4 transformer blocks, 8 Query heads, 2 KV heads, and a 256-dimensional representation.

9. Training the Model

Once the architecture was ready, the next question was:

How does it actually learn?

The training loop follows the familiar deep-learning pattern:

Get batch
   ↓
Forward pass
   ↓
Calculate loss
   ↓
Zero gradients
   ↓
Backward pass
   ↓
Gradient clipping
   ↓
Optimizer step

The project used:

Batch size:      64
Learning rate:   3e-4
Optimizer:       AdamW
Training steps:  3000

The training code follows:

xb, yb = get_batch(...)

logits, loss = model(xb, yb)

optimizer.zero_grad()

loss.backward()

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(
    model.parameters(),
    max_norm=1.0
)

optimizer.step()

Gradient clipping is used to reduce the risk of exploding gradients during training.

10. Training Loss vs Validation Loss

One thing I don't want to overlook when building ML models is evaluation.

A model getting better on training data doesn't automatically mean it's generalizing well.

So we can compare:

Training loss
      vs
Validation loss

A growing gap between them can be a signal of overfitting.

During evaluation, dropout is disabled and gradients aren't needed:

@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss():
    model.eval()
    ...
    model.train()

The training material uses the train/validation loss gap as an indicator for overfitting.

11. Finally: Generating Text

After training, the model can generate new text.

The process is autoregressive:

Prompt
  ↓
Model
  ↓
Predict next token
  ↓
Append token
  ↓
Model again
  ↓
Predict next token
  ↓
Repeat...

For example:

"ROMEO:"

gets encoded into token IDs.

The model predicts the next character, adds it to the sequence, and repeats the process.

The generation code takes the logits from the last position, converts them into probabilities using softmax, samples the next token, and appends it to the sequence.

12. Temperature Controls Randomness

Another concept that became much clearer after implementing generation was temperature.

Lower temperature:

More predictable
Less random

Higher temperature:

More diverse
More random

For example:

T = 0.3 → conservative
T = 0.8 → balanced
T = 1.5 → creative

So temperature doesn't make the model “smarter”.

It changes how we sample from its probability distribution.

What I Actually Learned From This Project

The biggest lesson wasn't memorizing what RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA and SwiGLU stand for.

It was understanding how the pieces connect.

Before this project, I could say:

“Transformers use attention.”

Now I can explain:

Text
 ↓
Tokens
 ↓
Embeddings
 ↓
Q / K / V
 ↓
RoPE
 ↓
Causal Attention
 ↓
GQA
 ↓
Residual Connection
 ↓
SwiGLU
 ↓
Repeated Transformer Blocks
 ↓
Logits
 ↓
Probability Distribution
 ↓
Next Token

That difference is important.

Knowing the vocabulary is not the same as understanding the system.

Why I Built This Instead of Only Using an LLM API

As someone preparing for an AI/ML engineering role, I think there is value in going one layer deeper.

Using:

response = client.chat(...)

is useful.

But understanding what happens underneath gives me a stronger foundation for:

  • debugging ML systems
  • reading research papers
  • understanding model architectures
  • optimizing inference
  • experimenting with transformers
  • explaining technical decisions during interviews

I don't expect a small Shakespeare model to qualify me for an LLM engineering role by itself.

But building it gave me something more valuable:

A mental model of how modern language models work.

My Biggest Takeaways

1. Build, don't just watch

Reading about transformers is useful.

Implementing one forces you to understand the tensor shapes and data flow.

2. Understand the “why”

Don't memorize:

RoPE
GQA
RMSNorm
SwiGLU

Ask:

Why is it there?
What problem does it solve?
What happens if I remove it?

3. Follow the tensors

One of the best ways I found to understand deep learning code is to constantly ask:

What is the shape here?

For example:

[b, seq, 256]
      ↓
[b, 8, seq, 32]
      ↓
attention
      ↓
[b, seq, 256]

4. AI engineering is more than model training

A good ML engineer needs to think about:

Data
↓
Architecture
↓
Training
↓
Evaluation
↓
Inference
↓
Efficiency

5. Projects become much more valuable when you can explain them

This is probably the biggest career lesson I took from this.

Don't just put:

“Built an LLM using PyTorch”

on a resume.

Be able to explain:

“I implemented character tokenization, causal next-token prediction, RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA with shared KV heads, SwiGLU, residual transformer blocks, AdamW training, validation loss evaluation, and autoregressive generation.”

That demonstrates actual understanding.

What's Next?

This project gave me a foundation.

My next step is to move from:

“I understand how the architecture works.”

to:

“I can build useful AI systems with it.”

That means exploring things like:

  • fine-tuning
  • embeddings
  • RAG
  • vector databases
  • evaluation
  • inference optimization
  • model deployment
  • AI agents
  • production ML pipelines

The goal isn't to learn every AI buzzword.

The goal is to build things, understand them, and document what I learn.

Final Thought

I'm learning that the fastest way to improve as an AI/ML engineer isn't to wait until I know everything.

It's to:

Learn → Build → Break → Debug → Explain → Share → Repeat.

This small LLM project was one step in that process.

And I'm going to keep documenting the journey.

Tech Stack: Python · PyTorch · Deep Learning · Transformers · LLMs

What would you recommend I build next — a RAG system, fine-tuned model, or an AI agent?
