title: When React Is Worth It, and When Simpler Is Better: A Practical Guide to Choosing Your Web Architecture
description:
When React Is Worth It — and When Simpler Is Better: A Practical Guide to Choosing Your Web Architecture

Choosing a web development stack is not simply about picking the most popular framework. It is about understanding what your product needs to do, how users interact with it, how its data changes, and what your team can maintain over time.

React is a powerful option for building interactive user interfaces, but not every website needs a client-side application. For some projects, static HTML or server-rendered pages provide a simpler and more maintainable solution.

The goal is not to avoid React. It is to use it when its capabilities solve a real problem.

In this guide, we will compare static sites, server-rendered applications, and React-based interfaces, then explore how to choose an architecture based on practical requirements rather than trends.

  1. Start with the user journey

Before choosing a framework, identify what users need to accomplish.

Consider three examples:

A company website: Visitors browse service pages, read articles, and submit enquiries.

A customer portal: Users sign in, view account information, download documents, and update details.

A reporting dashboard: Users filter datasets, change date ranges, compare results, and interact with charts.

All three require a web interface, but their technical requirements are different.

A company website may prioritise content delivery, accessibility, navigation, and search engine discoverability. A customer portal needs secure authentication, permissions, and reliable data handling. A reporting dashboard may require substantial client-side interaction and coordinated state across components.

Using the same architecture for all three might simplify some development workflows, but it does not automatically make it the best technical decision.

Start by asking:

How much interaction does each page require?

Does the content change frequently or depend on the current user?

Where should application state live?

What are the performance and accessibility requirements?

What infrastructure can the team operate and maintain?

These questions provide a better starting point than selecting a framework first.

  1. Static websites: when simplicity is an advantage

A static site serves pre-generated HTML pages alongside assets such as CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts. Developers can create pages directly or generate them from templates and content files.

This approach is often suitable for content-led websites where the majority of information is public and does not need to be generated separately for every request.

When should you choose a static architecture?

Consider static delivery when:

Most content changes relatively infrequently.

Pages follow predictable layouts.

Visitors mainly read content and navigate between pages.

Interactions are limited to features such as menus, forms, or simple widgets.

The team wants to minimise runtime infrastructure.

For example, a service page containing an introduction, a list of capabilities, and a contact link does not necessarily need a full client-side application.

A basic HTML page might look like this:
`<!doctype html>




Website Development Services
<meta
name="description"
content="Explore website development options for your business."

Website Development Services



Choose a website architecture that fits your content,
users and operational requirements.


Discuss your requirements


`

This is a minimal illustration rather than a complete production website. A real implementation would also require appropriate styling, accessible navigation, content maintenance, error handling, and any necessary privacy or analytics controls.

Static delivery does not mean a website must look basic. CSS and JavaScript can provide interactive features without turning every page into a React application.

There are trade-offs, however. Content updates need a suitable publishing process, and personalised or request-specific information requires additional services or runtime logic.

The principle: Choose static delivery when the content and interaction model are simple enough that a runtime application would add more complexity than value.

  1. Server-rendered applications: when the request matters

In a server-rendered architecture, the server generates HTML for a request and sends it to the browser. Depending on the framework, it may retrieve data, apply templates, enforce access rules, and construct the response before delivery.

This can be useful when a page depends on current data or server-side business logic.

When does server rendering make sense?

Consider server rendering when:

Pages need request-time data.

Content depends on account or user context.

Authentication and authorisation are central to the application.

You want meaningful HTML to arrive before client-side JavaScript runs.

Forms, links, and server-handled requests can support the user journey.

For example, an Express-style route might render a product listing using a template:
`app.get("/products", async (req, res, next) => {
try {
const products = await getPublishedProducts();

res.render("products", {
  title: "Products",
  products
});

} catch (error) {
next(error);
}
});`

This example assumes that Express, the template engine, and getPublishedProducts() have been configured elsewhere. It illustrates a pattern, not a complete production application.

The server retrieves the data and supplies it to the template. The browser receives rendered HTML rather than needing to construct the entire initial interface from an empty page.

What are the trade-offs?

Server rendering introduces operational responsibilities. The application must handle incoming requests, manage data access, return appropriate errors, and scale according to its workload.

It is not automatically faster. Slow database queries, inefficient external API calls, excessive server work, or poor caching can all affect response times.

Caching also requires care. Personalised responses must not accidentally be shared between users, and cached data needs an appropriate freshness policy.

Importantly, server rendering and React are not mutually exclusive. React can render HTML on the server, while modern frameworks can combine server rendering, static generation, and client-side interactivity.

The principle: Choose server rendering when request-time data and server-side processing justify the additional runtime responsibilities.

  1. React applications: when interaction becomes complex

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. Its value becomes more apparent when an interface contains reusable UI patterns and state that changes in response to user actions or incoming data.

Instead of treating the interface as one large block, developers can divide it into smaller components with defined responsibilities.

When is React worth using?

React may be a good fit when:

Users interact with multiple parts of the interface without navigating to a new page for every action.

Several components depend on shared application state.

The product contains complex forms, filters, tables, charts, or multi-step workflows.

Reusable interactive components are important.

The team can maintain the associated development, testing, and deployment processes.

Imagine a reporting dashboard where users change a date range, select a business unit, filter a table, and open a detail panel. Several components may need to respond to the same selections.

A component-based approach can help organise this behaviour.

Here is a small React example:
`import { useState } from "react";

export function QuantitySelector() {
const [quantity, setQuantity] = useState(1);

function decreaseQuantity() {
setQuantity(current => Math.max(1, current - 1));
}

function increaseQuantity() {
setQuantity(current => current + 1);
}

return (


type="button"
onClick={decreaseQuantity}
disabled={quantity <= 1}
aria-label="Decrease quantity"
>
−
  <output aria-live="polite">{quantity}</output>

  <button
    type="button"
    onClick={increaseQuantity}
    aria-label="Increase quantity"
  >
    +
  </button>
</section>

);
}`

The component manages its own quantity state and updates the displayed value when users interact with the buttons.

This is a deliberately small example, not a complete shopping-cart implementation. A real checkout flow would also need server-side validation, stock and price checks, error handling, and reliable transaction processing.

What does React add to the project?

React also introduces concepts and tools that developers need to understand. Depending on the application, these may include routing, data fetching, state management, build tooling, testing, and rendering strategy.

These costs are justified when they help manage genuine interface complexity. They are less compelling when a website mainly displays content and provides a few simple interactions.

React does not automatically make an application fast, accessible, secure, or search-engine friendly. Those outcomes depend on the implementation and surrounding architecture.

The principle: Choose React when structured components and stateful interaction provide enough value to justify the additional development and maintenance work.

  1. ## Comparing the Three Web Architecture Approaches

  • Mostly informational content

    • Static delivery: Often a strong fit.
    • Server-rendered application: Suitable.
    • React-based interface: Possible, but may be unnecessary.

  • Frequently changing server data

    • Static delivery: Requires an integration or regeneration strategy.
    • Server-rendered application: Often a strong fit.
    • React-based interface: Suitable with an appropriate data architecture.

  • Rich, coordinated UI state

    • Static delivery: Possible with JavaScript.
    • Server-rendered application: Possible with client-side enhancements.
    • React-based interface: Often a strong fit.

  • Personalised account pages

    • Static delivery: Requires additional services or runtime logic.
    • Server-rendered application: Often a strong fit.
    • React-based interface: Suitable alongside secure backend services.

  • Minimal runtime complexity

    • Static delivery: Often favourable.
    • Server-rendered application: Depends on the server setup.
    • React-based interface: Depends on the application and rendering model.

  • Interactive dashboards

    • Static delivery: Possible, but complexity can grow.
    • Server-rendered application: Possible with client-side enhancements.
    • React-based interface: Often a strong fit.

  • Search engine discoverability

    • Static delivery: Can work well with accessible HTML and sound technical SEO.
    • Server-rendered application: Can work well with server-generated HTML.
    • React-based interface: Depends on rendering, metadata, content access, and implementation.

Do not interpret the React column as meaning that every React page must render entirely in the browser. React supports different rendering strategies, and modern frameworks can generate HTML ahead of time or on the server before adding client-side behaviour.

Likewise, static websites can include interactive JavaScript, while server-rendered applications can progressively enhance their pages without becoming single-page applications.

The categories describe architectural tendencies rather than rigid boundaries.

  1. A practical framework for choosing your stack

Once you understand the options, use a structured decision process.

Step 1: Map the main user journeys

List the actions users need to complete.

For a company website, users might read service information, compare options, and send an enquiry. For an internal dashboard, they might filter records, update a status, and review changes.

If most journeys involve reading content and navigating between pages, a simpler architecture may be sufficient. If they involve many dependent controls and changing interface states, a component-driven approach deserves closer consideration.

Step 2: Identify where the data comes from

Ask whether a page can be generated ahead of time or requires current information at request time.

Public editorial content may suit static generation. Account information, permissions, or user-specific records need an appropriate server-side data and security model.

Adding React does not remove the need for a secure backend. Sensitive business rules and authorisation checks must not rely solely on client-side code.

Step 3: Decide where state belongs

Not all state needs a global store or complex client-side architecture.

A selected tab may only need local component state. Search filters may belong in the URL if users should be able to bookmark or share them. Persistent business records generally belong in a backend system.

Choosing the right location for each kind of state can prevent unnecessary complexity, regardless of framework.

Step 4: Assess the operational model

Consider who will deploy the application, monitor errors, update dependencies, manage content, and respond to incidents.

A technology choice that suits a team with established JavaScript tooling may be less suitable for a small team that wants to maintain a straightforward content-led website.

Include long-term maintenance in the decision, not just the initial build.

Step 5: Introduce complexity only when there is a reason

Before adopting a heavier architecture, identify the specific problem it solves.

That reason might be a complex interaction model, repeated UI patterns, request-time data requirements, or several distinct user journeys.

If the justification is simply that a framework is popular or familiar, revisit the requirements.

  1. Common architectural mistakes

Using React for every page by default

A single framework across a website can simplify some team workflows, but it is not automatically the simplest overall solution. A small content page may gain little from an application-level setup.

Evaluate the full cost, including development, build tooling, runtime behaviour, testing, deployment, and future maintenance.

Assuming static sites cannot be interactive

Static HTML can work alongside JavaScript, APIs, forms, and embedded interactive components. The important question is whether those additions remain easy to understand and maintain.

Treating server rendering as a performance guarantee

Generating HTML on the server can help deliver useful content early, but it does not eliminate slow data access, inefficient rendering, or poor caching. Evaluate the complete request path.

Building a hybrid architecture without clear boundaries

Combining static generation, server rendering, and client-side React can be effective. It can also create confusing data flows and multiple rendering paths if the team has no clear rules.

Define which pages are generated ahead of time, which need request-time data, and which interactions require client-side behaviour.

Ignoring accessibility and real-user performance

Framework selection does not replace semantic HTML, keyboard testing, sensible loading states, or performance measurement.

Review the experience on slower devices and networks. Test actual user journeys instead of assuming that a successful build means the interface is ready.

Conclusion: Choose the simplest architecture that fits

There is no single web architecture that is right for every product.

Static delivery can be an excellent choice for content-led websites. Server rendering can suit applications that need request-time data and server-side processing. React can provide structure and maintainability for interfaces with substantial interaction and shared state.

The strongest decision comes from matching the architecture to the user journey, data requirements, operational constraints, and the team's ability to maintain it.

Start with the simplest viable approach. Introduce more machinery when a clear requirement justifies it, and review the decision as the product evolves.

That is a more reliable basis for choosing a web development stack than adopting a framework simply because it is widely used.

title: The Vercel Bug Bounty Program is now publicly available
description:
In 2022, we launched a private bug bounty program through HackerOne. Over the last several years, we've worked with HackerOne's VIP program to refine our process, targets, and scope, onboarding thousands of their best researchers and hardening security across our platform.

We've translated those learnings into several public bounty programs:

  • The $1 million React2Shell hacker challenge

  • The $1 million Vercel Sandbox hacker challenge

  • Our OSS bug bounty program

Today, we are combining our private and OSS bounty programs into a single, public Vercel bug bounty program.

Why now

AI has fundamentally changed the nature of bug bounty programs, exponentially increasing the number of reports, both valid and invalid. Some companies are responding by moving to private programs.

At Vercel, we’ve found that public reports are still surfacing real, valuable findings. AI enables a much wider range of researchers to discover vulnerabilities, and we believe in evaluating reports on their own merit, so making our entire program public was the logical choice.

In preparation for the public launch, our security engineering team has streamlined our process and built tooling to filter out noise and expedite remediation. We have improved every step, from triaging reports to shipping and verifying fixes.

Our team and processes have been battle tested through our private program and several large public programs in the recent past. We are ready to open a comprehensive program to the public and have the best researchers out there responsibly explore every part of the platform.

What is covered

All products across the Vercel platform and our open-source projects are now part of our unified public program. Read the Scope page on HackerOne for full details on what is covered.

Consolidation makes sense for our processes, but we also received feedback from the research community that having multiple programs made disclosure confusing because there were multiple places to submit reports. A single program simplifies reporting across our platform and open-source projects.

New findings in our open-source projects should be reported to the main Vercel program, but if you already have submissions to the previous OSS program, you don't need to copy them over. We will still review every submission that was made through that program.

How to participate

If you’re a security researcher, visit our HackerOne program page for details, bounties, and guidelines.

To file a report, submit your findings through HackerOne with clear reproduction steps. Our security team reviews every submission and works with researchers via the disclosure process. We're committed to fast response times and transparent communication.

We appreciate the researchers who take the time to dig into our code and report issues responsibly. We would also like to thank all the researchers who have been working in our private program. You have helped build the foundation for this public program, and nothing will change for you. We look forward to your future submissions.

Learn more about security at Vercel.

Join our security team

If this kind of work excites you, we are hiring. Apply to join the Vercel security team.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

Read more

title: Debug HTTPS traffic with a free, open-source proxy (ProxyZip)
description:
Your app calls an API, something comes back wrong, and the only thing you can see is a spinner. The request is encrypted, the logs say nothing useful, and you end up guessing.

A debugging proxy fixes that: it sits between your app and the server, decrypts the HTTPS on your own machine and shows you every request and response. I built ProxyZip, a free, open-source HTTP and HTTPS debugging proxy, and this post walks through what it does using a small example.

TL;DR

  • Capture and inspect HTTPS traffic from any app on macOS, Windows and Linux
  • Pause a request, edit it and send it on
  • Mock an API that does not exist yet, or validate real traffic against an OpenAPI file
  • Turn captured requests into tests and run them in CI
  • MIT licensed, written in Rust, no account and no telemetry

What is ProxyZip?

ProxyZip is an HTTP and HTTPS debugging proxy with a desktop app and a command line. The engine is Rust (tokio, hyper, rustls); the app is Tauri and Svelte. The app and the proxyzip command run the same engine, so what you learn in one works in the other.

The example below uses a fictional shop API at api.shopwave.dev.

Install it 

# macOS
brew install --cask luispeixoto/proxyzip/proxyzip

# Windows
scoop bucket add proxyzip https://github.com/LuisPeixoto/scoop-proxyzip

Installers for macOS, Windows and Linux (.dmg, .msi, .exe, .AppImage, .deb, .rpm) are on the releases page. The command line alone installs with cargo install --git https://github.com/LuisPeixoto/ProxyZip proxyzip-cli.

Inspect HTTPS traffic

HTTPS needs one extra step. ProxyZip creates a local certificate authority on your machine; once you trust it, the proxy can show you what your apps send. The private key never leaves your disk, and you can exclude any host from decryption.

proxyzip ca install
eval "$(proxyzip env)"
proxyzip start --port 19191

proxyzip env points the current terminal at the proxy and makes curl, Node.js, Python, Go, Git, Cargo and others trust the certificate. Every finished request prints as it happens:

200 GET     https://api.shopwave.dev/v1/products 469B 1ms [mock]
200 GET     https://api.shopwave.dev/v1/products/sku_1042 142B 70ms [mock]

In the app you get the same requests as a list, with headers, cookies, timing, TLS details and the body as a JSON tree. Use jq filters on a body, or compare two requests side by side.

Binary protocols are covered too. gRPC, gRPC-Web and plain Protobuf messages are decoded even without the .proto files, which makes gRPC debugging a lot less painful.

Change traffic instead of only reading it

Right-click a request to set a breakpoint: the next matching request stops before it leaves, and you can edit the method, URL, headers or body. Map Local answers with a file from your disk, Map Remote sends the request to another host, and rewrite rules change headers, bodies and status codes. You can also throttle to a slow network or block a host to see how your app copes.

Mock an API that does not exist yet

When the backend is not ready, or has to fail in a specific way, a mock server answers for it: routes with status codes, headers, bodies and delays, plus a small template language. Right-click a captured response and choose Create a mock from this response, or import an OpenAPI 3 file.

proxyzip mock petstore.yaml --port 4010 --delay 200
proxyzip validate petstore.yaml capture.pzsession

proxyzip validate checks captured traffic against the specification and exits with 1 if anything does not conform, so it works as a CI step.

Turn requests into API tests

Select the requests of a flow, right-click and choose Add to a suite. A suite is a single .pzsuite file with checks on status and body, variables and environments, and values passed between steps with jq. It belongs in version control, and it runs headless:

proxyzip run checkout.pzsuite --env staging --junit report.xml

The command exits with 1 when a request fails and writes a JUnit report that CI systems can display. Postman collections run the same way.

Phones, emulators and AI assistants

To debug an iPhone or Android device, point its Wi-Fi proxy at your computer and open http://proxyzip.cert to install the certificate. The Devices window shows the address and a QR code, and has one-click setup for simulators and emulators. See the mobile debugging guide.

ProxyZip also has a built-in Model Context Protocol server, so assistants such as Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code can read your captured traffic. It is off by default, listens on localhost only, needs an access token and redacts secrets unless you ask otherwise. The MCP guide has the details.

Private and open

There is no account to create and nothing phones home; the only extra request is an optional, signed update check. The code is MIT licensed, so you can read it, fork it and ship it. Use it only on traffic you are allowed to inspect.

Try it

  • Website and docs: luispeixoto.github.io/ProxyZip
  • Source: github.com/LuisPeixoto/ProxyZip
  • Downloads: latest release

If it saves you an afternoon of guessing, a star on GitHub helps other developers find it, and issues and pull requests are welcome. What would you want from a debugging proxy that the tools you use today do not do?

title: LAMB: Latent Multi-Hypothesis Beliefs for Long-Horizon Large Language Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.26955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon language agents require compact memories that retain interaction evidence while preserving competing hypotheses about unobserved states. Although effective, many belief-state methods encode memory in discrete natural language, where repeated compression can omit evidence or prematurely discard plausible alternatives. We introduce LAMB, a recurrent framework for latent multi-hypothesis beliefs. A Common--Delta factorization combines a shared Common state for interaction evidence with weighted Delta components for competing hypotheses. Relative evidence from action-outcome predictions guides recurrent hypothesis updates without generating textual memory. A context-conditioned readout exposes hypotheses separately to the policy through a fixed-token belief prefix in the default configuration. The belief modules and policy are jointly trained using action imitation and auxiliary state, outcome, and observation-discrimination objectives. Across ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, LAMB matches or outperforms PABU, improving ALFWorld SR@30 and ScienceWorld success by 6.0 and 22.0 percentage points, respectively, and Crafter achievement progress by 26.37 points. On ALFWorld, it also reduces the redundant-action rate by 17.70 percentage points. These results support latent multi-hypothesis beliefs as compact memory for effective long-horizon decision making

  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud SDK

Breaking

590.0.0 (2026-10-20)

Breaking Changes

  • (Google Cloud CLI) Removed the gcloud-man-pages component. Use --help for full command documentation.
  • (App Engine) Removed the app-engine-grpc component from the Google Cloud CLI.
  • (Cloud Build) Removed the Cloud Build Local Builder component (cloud-build-local) from the Google Cloud CLI.

Google Cloud CLI

  • Updated bundled Python on Linux and Windows, and in the Alpine-based Docker images, to pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 and cryptography 50.0.1. 32-bit Windows uses pyOpenSSL 26.2.0 and cryptography 48.0.1, the newest releases that support it.

AI

  • Updated gcloud beta ai endpoints deploy-model to request automatic resources for Gemini deployments on GDC connected endpoints.
    • If no replica counts are specified, the minimum replica count defaults to 1 only for gemini-2.5-flash.
    • Specifying flags that apply only to dedicated resources, such as --machine-type or --accelerator, now prints a warning and deploys with dedicated resources.

Agent Identity

  • Added gcloud beta agent-identity auth-providers resolve-authorization command.

AlloyDB

  • Added --enable-public-dns flag to gcloud beta alloydb instances create|update.

Apigee

  • Fixed an issue where gcloud apigee commands would fail with an UnauthorizedRequestError for users who authenticate using Mutual TLS (mTLS).

App Engine

  • Updated gcloud beta app migrate-to-run to default to the App Engine application's region instead of us-central1 when neither --region nor the run/region property is set.

BigLake

  • Promoted --federated-catalog-identity-mode for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create to GA.
  • Promoted --federated-catalog-identity-mode for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs update to GA.
  • Promoted --metadata-service-directory-name for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create to GA.
  • Promoted --metadata-service-directory-name for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs update to GA.
  • federated value for --catalog-type flag of gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create is now supported.

Certificate Authority Service

  • Added --filter flag to gcloud privateca subordinates list. The flag is able to allow filtering results based on specified boolean expression.

Cloud Bigtable

  • Build with 1.26.4 to resolve CVE-2026-39820.

Cloud Bigtable Emulator

  • Rebuild cbt-emulator for CVE-2026-39820.

Cloud Dataflow

  • Promoted gcloud dataflow config-store-settings to GA.

Cloud Dataplex

  • Fixed gcloud dataplex dbt metadata-jobs create so that dbt resources whose names contain a dot, such as tests on a model with a decimal version, are no longer rejected by the import job.
  • Fixed gcloud dataplex dbt metadata-jobs create so that two dbt resources that map to the same Dataplex entry ID no longer fail the whole import job. The first is imported and a warning names the other.

Cloud IAM

  • Added --vendor-type flag to gcloud iam workforce-pools providers create-oidc, create-saml, update-oidc, and update-saml commands.

Cloud Resource Manager

  • Promoted gcloud resource-manager capability-configs to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud resource-manager boundary-configs to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud resource-manager boundaries to GA.

Cloud Run

  • Added --dry-run flag to gcloud beta run domain-mappings create to validate a domain mapping, including whether the domain is available, without creating it.

Cloud SQL

  • Added POSTGRES_19 to --database-version flag of gcloud sql instances create and gcloud sql instances patch.
  • Added --no-replication-lag-max-seconds-for-recreate flag to gcloud beta sql instances patch to disable recreating a lagging MySQL read replica.
  • Updated 'cloud-sql-proxy' packaged component to use 2.26.2 of the Cloud SQL Proxy.

Cloud Spanner

  • Improved error output when gcloud spanner cli runs an incompatible spanner-cli binary found on PATH instead of the spanner-cli component; users are now directed to install the component.

Cloud Workstations

  • Added enable-automatic-failover to --boost-config flag in gcloud beta workstations configs create and gcloud beta workstations configs update.

Compute Engine

  • Added compute instance-templates export command to all release tracks.
  • Removed WORKLOAD_IDENTITY choise in --identity-type flag.
  • Promoted --instance-flexibility-policy flag and min CPU platform and disk overrides to GA for gcloud compute instance-groups managed create and update.
  • Added compute instance-templates import command to all release tracks.

Database Migration

  • Added --failback flag to gcloud database-migration migration-jobs promote command to promote a migration job from destination back to source during the FAILBACK phase.

GKE Hub

  • Promoted --view, --memberships, --filter, and --sort-by flags on gcloud container fleet|hub config-management describe command to GA.

  • Updated gcloud container fleet|hub memberships register to allow skipping the Connect agent installation on non-GKE clusters via the --no-install-connect-agent flag.

Kubernetes Engine

  • Added the reservedSystemCpus kubelet config option to the gcloud container clusters create, gcloud container node-pools create, and gcloud container node-pools update commands. This option specifies the list of CPUs reserved for host system services.
  • Added ltsc2025 option to --windows-os-version flag of gcloud container node-pools create and gcloud container node-pools update to create or update Windows node pools using the Windows Server 2025 (LTSC2025) image.
  • Updated default kubectl to 1.35.9.
  • Additional kubectl versions:
    • 1.31.14
    • 1.32.13
    • 1.33.13
    • 1.34.12
    • 1.35.9
    • 1.36.5
    • 1.37.1
  • Allowed --num-nodes=0 for gcloud container clusters create to create a cluster without a default node pool on GKE versions that support it. Flags that only configure the default node pool, such as --machine-type and --enable-autoscaling, can't be used with --num-nodes=0.

Network Connectivity

  • Added --purpose flag to gcloud network-connectivity internal-ranges create to specify the purpose of the internal range.

Network Security

  • Promoted --wildfire-analysis-profile flag of gcloud network-security security-profile-groups create and gcloud network-security security-profile-groups update commands to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud network-security security-profiles wildfire-analysis command group and its create, delete, describe, list and update commands to GA.
  • Promoted add-submission-rule, delete-submission-rule, add-inline-cloud-analysis-rule and delete-inline-cloud-analysis-rule commands of gcloud network-security security-profiles wildfire-analysis to GA.

Service Extensions

  • Created a new set of commands for gcloud service-extensions extension-bindings (alpha and beta).
  • Added gcloud beta service-extensions cdn-edge-extensions command group to manage CdnEdgeExtension resources.

Subscribe to these release notes at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/google-cloud-sdk-announce.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Fixed

A security issue in GKE fleet management that could have allowed unauthorized configuration changes to clusters registered to a fleet has been resolved. The fixes are rolled out to all regions, and no action is required.

Fixed

This is an update to the release note regarding the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver issue published on October 2, 2026.

This issue has been resolved. You can upgrade your cluster control plane to the following versions to fix the issue for ubuntu_containerd and older cos_containerd node pools:

  • 1.36.5-gke.1032000 or later

  • 1.37.1-gke.1552000 or later

  • Specific 1.36.4 mitigation patches: 1.36.4-gke.1247001, 1.36.4-gke.1247002, 1.36.4-gke.1391001, 1.36.4-gke.1391003, 1.36.4-gke.1495001, 1.36.4-gke.1495003, 1.36.4-gke.2046001, 1.36.4-gke.2202002

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

For more information, see approximate aggregate functions (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL), HyperLogLog++ functions, and Sketches.

title: Google Cloud's Backup Generators Failed to Engage, and a Single London Zone Took Down UK Banks
description:
Google Cloud's backup generators failed to engage when mains power cut out at a London data center on October 20, 2026, and the resulting outage in a single availability zone reached far beyond that zone's own customers. Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and England and Wales's court video system all went down for hours, and the UK's financial regulators are now being asked in Parliament how much of the country's banking infrastructure sits behind one cloud region.

Jump to what we checked in our own redundancy claims if your own architecture assumes a zone failure stays contained to that zone.

What Happened in Google's London Region

The outage began at 06:08 UTC when the europe-west2-b zone, one of three availability zones in Google's only UK region, lost power at what Google later described as a third-party facility. According to an internal engineering update reported by Computer Weekly, mains power returned relatively quickly, but the site's backup generators failed to engage. That forced Google's engineers to keep a frontend and backend traffic drain on the zone while onsite technicians manually verified backup power was actually working.

Google's status page listed 38 distinct products affected, including Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud SQL, BigQuery, and Cloud Run. The company's own incident record shows the first public acknowledgment at 08:35 UTC with no workaround offered, a workaround added at 10:24 UTC advising customers to migrate workloads to another zone or region if they could, and the cause named around 12:12 UTC. Most customers were back by roughly 14:00 UTC, nearly eight hours after the power event began.

Why a Single Zone Outage Reached a Whole Region

Google's own architecture promises that regional services run across all three zones in a region specifically so that losing one zone costs capacity, not availability. That promise is why Compute Engine VMs and zonal disks pinned to europe-west2-b went down with no workaround, while regional services were supposed to keep running on the two healthy zones.

They mostly didn't. Google's status updates describe services across the broader europe-west2 region, not just the b zone, experiencing elevated errors and intermittent failures throughout the morning. Google has not yet explained why its two unaffected zones didn't fully absorb the load that the failed zone would normally have carried, and that gap is the detail its promised incident analysis will need to answer.

What We Checked in Our Own Redundancy Claims

We reviewed every place at Krova Cloud where we tell customers a service is "regionally redundant" and checked whether we had actually tested a full zone failure against it, rather than just designing for one. We found one internal monitoring service that was architecturally spread across zones but had never been through a real failover drill. We scheduled one for the following week, since a redundancy design nobody has tested is a hypothesis, not a guarantee.

What to Check in Your Own Cloud Architecture

  • If a vendor tells you a service is "regional" or "multi-zone," ask whether that claim has been tested against an actual single-zone failure, not just designed for one, since Google's own regional services didn't fully absorb this zone's load.
  • Identify every workload you run pinned to a single zone, since Google's own workaround for this incident, migrate to another zone or region, only works for architectures built to support it in advance.
  • Check whether your incident communications depend on the same cloud region you're reporting an outage about, a common and easy-to-miss single point of failure.
  • Ask your downstream vendors, banking apps, courts systems, and logistics platforms among them this time, which cloud region and zone each of their critical paths actually runs in, since the blast radius of this outage reached well past Google's own customer list.

The limitation worth stating plainly is that Google has not yet published the technical analysis it promised, so the exact reason regional services degraded alongside the failed zone is still unconfirmed.

The verdict doesn't need that analysis to land, though: a backup generator failing to engage at one facility was enough to disrupt banking, courts, and parcel delivery across an entire country, and the zone-isolation guarantee did not hold as cleanly as the architecture promises it should.

The Rule

A multi-zone design only protects you from a single-zone failure if the other zones can actually absorb that zone's load when it happens, not just in the architecture diagram. If you've never tested your own "regional" service against a real zone outage, you don't know whether you have that protection, you're just hoping the backup generator engages when the lights go out.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the Google Cloud outage on October 20, 2026?

A power event at a third-party facility hosting Google's europe-west2-b availability zone in London. Mains power returned, but backup generators failed to engage, requiring manual verification by onsite technicians before services could be restored.

Which services and companies were affected?

Google listed 38 affected products including Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud SQL, BigQuery, and Cloud Run. Downstream, Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, DPD, Rightmove, and England and Wales's court video hearing system all reported disruption.

How long did the outage last?

The incident began at 06:08 UTC and Google reported most services mitigated by roughly 14:00 UTC the same day, nearly eight hours later, though some customers reported longer recovery times.

Why did a single zone failure affect the whole region?

Google's regional services are designed to run across all three zones in europe-west2 so a single zone's loss doesn't cause a regional outage. Google has not yet explained why the two unaffected zones didn't fully absorb the failed zone's load during this incident.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: disposable VMs with redundancy claims we've actually drilled, not just diagrammed. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

title: Microsoft AI models are now available on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and Microsoft AI (MAI) have partnered to make MAI models available on AI Gateway. AI Gateway is one of a limited number of platforms offering access to MAI models.

MAI's focus on security and zero data retention (ZDR) align with Vercel's goal of giving AI Gateway users control over their data and transparency in how it is used for training.

MAI models on AI Gateway

MAI's latest audio models are now supported on AI Gateway. MAI-Voice-2.1 and MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash generate speech, while MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming returns transcript updates as audio arrives.

  • MAI-Voice-2.1 (microsoft/mai-voice-2.1) generates expressive speech in 23 languages and keeps a consistent speaker across longer passages. Use it for narration, audiobooks, podcasts, and lessons where delivery matters from start to finish.

  • MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash (microsoft/mai-voice-2.1-flash) brings the same multilingual speech generation to lower-latency interactions. It is suited to voice agents, assistants, and spoken replies that need to arrive quickly.

  • MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming (microsoft/mai-transcribe-2-streaming) returns partial transcripts while audio is still arriving. Applications can show live captions or follow a conversation as it happens, without waiting for the full recording.

AI Gateway bills these models at their listed rates, with no platform fee or markup on inference.

Get started

Use generateSpeech in AI SDK 7 with MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash to create a spoken response. The voice name selects Microsoft's Harper voice with the Flash model:

For longer audio such as narration, use microsoft/mai-voice-2.1.

Transcribe live audio

streamTranscribe takes a stream of audio chunks and returns transcript updates as the audio arrives. This example assumes microphoneStream is a ReadableStream of 16 kHz, 16-bit PCM audio:

Partial transcripts can change as more audio arrives, so replace the displayed text when a new partial arrives.

Additional resources

Explore MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash for speech generation and MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming for live transcription. See the MAI model page for the full family, or follow the speech quickstart to get started.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and viewing request traces. It also supports routing, retries, and failover across available providers.
